## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced in the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in which places in their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.*

*An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes—consistently similar throughout the entire work—and the low price; above all, this collection, unified, systematic, and chronological, brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.*

### Second Series

The Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the Greek-Latin price statement reads “octingentis et mille trecenta” [an OCR-corrupt or otherwise uncertain reading]. The purely Latin edition indeed embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## (Year 834.) Commentaries on the Four Books of Kings by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz

### Preface

[Column 0009A] To the most reverend lord, greatly venerated and esteemed among the members of Christ, Father Hilcuin, abbot and archchaplain of the sacred palace, Rabanus, the least servant of the servants of God: perpetual salvation in the eternal Lord.

Since we perceive your reverence to be everywhere distinguished, and have learned that it is beneficial to many, we earnestly and insistently ask in our continual prayers that divine mercy may permit this to continue for a long time and at last reward it with an eternal recompense. Moreover, because your holiness deigned, through a certain brother of ours whom we sent to the palace last year, to suggest to our lowliness that we should send you some volume useful to you, this suggestion made us not a little anxious [Column 0009B] about what we could suitably and worthily offer you—who are rich in every respect, in all knowledge and learning, and with whom there is a very great abundance of books. Since you did not specify by name any book that you wished me to send you, I considered composing a small work on the exposition of the Books of Kings, dedicating it to your name, and humbly sending it for your prudent approval.

I ask you to receive it in the spirit in which I have sent it to you. For I do not suppose that it is worthy of you, but, however it may be, it has nevertheless been produced from a devoted heart. I think that, if you are willing to read it again, it will not displease you in any respect, once you recognize that I wished to labor at this: to gather into one place, for the convenience of the reader, the sayings of the holy Fathers that are scattered through several copies and that explain the aforesaid book, so that the reader may find together what each of them understood at the various points of the history of the Kings, as well as in the order arranged by us.

There you will find what Father Augustine thought, and what the distinguished interpreter of the divine books, Jerome, thought; what Pope Gregory, blessed and most gracious teacher, thought; what Isidore, bishop of Seville, thought; what Bede, that noble teacher, and the other Fathers rightly understood, whose names it would take too long to enumerate [Column 0009D]. I have either set down the opinions of all these just as they were written by them, or explained their meaning by condensing it in my own words [Column 0010A].

I have noted in the margins of the pages the names of certain of them where their own words appear [Note: [Column 0009D] We have inserted these names in the text within parentheses. EDITOR.]; but where I expressed their meaning in my own words, or where, following the similarity of their interpretations, I composed something anew insofar as divine grace deigned to grant me ability, I took care to place beforehand the letter M, representing the name Maurus, which my teacher, blessed Albinus of revered memory, gave me. Thus the diligent reader may know what each person contributes from his own work and may determine what should be understood in each passage.

Moreover, I inserted in many places a tradition of the Hebrews from a certain Hebrew who is skilled in the knowledge of the Law in our own times [Praeterea ex capitulis Hebraei cujusdam, modernis temporibus in legis scientia periti, traditionem Hebraeorum non paucis locis, etc.], together with a note identifying his name [Column 0010B]. I did this not as though imposing his authority upon anyone, but simply because I found it written; I leave its verification to the reader’s judgment.

Above all, I ask you to pardon my presumption, that I, so inexperienced not only in speech but also in learning, have presumed to undertake so great a work. For I trusted not in my own power but in divine power, of which it is written: “Wisdom opens the mouth of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wisdom 10). He also made a human tongue resound from the mouth of a beast (Numbers 22). For I read that he said through the Prophet: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80). And elsewhere: “Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him and protect him, because he has known my name” (Psalm 91 [the text reads “XCX”]).

Nor do I doubt that there will be some who, wishing to display their own learning, will criticize our ineptitude. To them I shall respond not in my own words but in those of blessed Jerome: “Let those who wish read; but let those who do not wish cast it aside, sift the letters, and accuse the words of slander.” I shall be more strongly urged on to study by your affection than deterred by their disparagement and hatred.

For if this small work is received with favor by your graciousness, I shall try, with the Lord’s assistance, to labor over and present some further useful work to your holiness [Column 0010D]. May divine majesty deign perpetually to preserve your blessedness flourishing in happy success.

# The Commentaries on the Four Books of Kings Begin

## On the First Book

### Chapter One

[Column 0011A] Concerning Elkanah and his two wives, namely Hannah and Peninnah.

**(Chapter 1.)** “There was a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from Mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah,” and so forth.

Let us first speak historically about the prophet’s ancestry, so that afterward we may insert its allegorical meaning continuously. Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel, was of the tribe of Levi, but not of the priestly line of Aaron. For, as the Books of Chronicles relate, this same Elkanah was “the son of Jeroboam, son of Eliel, son of Thahu, son of Suph, son of Elkanah, son of Mahath, son of Amasai, son of Azoel, son of Hariah, son of Zephaniah, son of Thahath, son of Asir, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, son of Saar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, son of Israel.” (From a certain Hebrew writer [Column 0011B].)

His mother also is shown to have been from the tribe of Judah by the fact that he is called an Ephrathite. He was called an Ephrathite from Ephratha, the wife of Caleb, who is known to have been from the tribe of Judah. If anyone is troubled that he is called an Ephrathite from Ephraim rather than from Ephratha, let him observe in what follows that David is called the son of an Ephrathite man, although it is perfectly clear that the same Jesse was not from Ephraim but from the tribe of Judah; thus let him acknowledge that Elkanah was called an Ephrathite from Ephratha, not from Ephraim.

This man, being a strong man among the inhabitants of Ephraim, lived in the city of Ramathaim-zophim. (From Jerome.) That city is in the Thamnitic region near Diospolis; Joseph was from there, and in the Gospels he is said to have been from Arimathea (Matthew 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19 [Column 0011C]).

“And he had two wives; the name of one was Hannah, and the name of the second was Peninnah; Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.”

Hannah’s barrenness is therefore appropriately mentioned, since her childbearing was destined to be more celebrated, in the manner of the earlier Fathers, so that a greater joy after prolonged sorrow might be suggested by the parents’ acquired fertility. For just as Sarah, the legitimate wife of the patriarch Abraham, whom he married first, was initially barren while the Egyptian Hagar bore a son (Genesis 16), and just as Rachel herself was barren while her sister Leah bore children, when Jacob was serving his father-in-law for Rachel as his wife (Genesis 29), so also Elkanah’s better wife, who bore the prophet, was first barren and afterward, through the Lord’s grace, became fruitful [Column 0011D].

“And that man went up from his city on appointed days to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts in Shiloh,” and so forth. (From Jerome.) Shiloh is a city [Column 0012A] in the tribe of Ephraim. In that place the ark of the covenant and the tabernacle of the Lord remained from the time of Joshua son of Nun, after he had conquered the nations that possessed the Promised Land, until the time of Samuel.

For it is related in the Book of Joshua that the aforesaid leader, after casting lots before the Lord, distributed the promised land there among the individual tribes. Shiloh is ninety miles from Neapolis, in the region of Acrabatta. We also read that the patriarch Judah had a son named Shelah.

Elkanah therefore went up to this city with his household on the appointed days according to the Law, to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts. (From the Hebrew.) When it says “on the appointed days,” this means on the three festivals: Passover, Pentecost, and the feast of Tabernacles [Column 0012B]. Hence the Lord commanded in Exodus, saying: “Three times in each year you shall celebrate feasts for me” (Exodus 23). And again: “Three times a year,” he says, “every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God in the place which the Lord your God has chosen” (ibid.).

Since the ark of the Lord was at that time in Shiloh, Elkanah, who was himself a Levite, ate there after the sacrifices had been offered, together with his wives and sons and daughters.

“And he gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters; but to Hannah he gave one portion, sadly, because he loved Hannah. Now the Lord had closed her womb. Her rival also afflicted her and greatly distressed her, to such an extent that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb,” and so forth.

Notice that, just as the barren Sarah was despised when Hagar conceived (Genesis 16), so also Peninnah, fruitful in offspring, rivaled barren Hannah. For it is characteristic of the wicked to find consolation in attacking the good.

“But she wept and did not take food,” and so forth. Provoked by her rival, she did not joyfully take bodily food. But, according to the Prophet, her tears were bread to her day and night, and she mingled her drink with weeping (Psalm 42).

“Then Hannah arose after she had eaten in Shiloh and drunk, while Eli the priest was sitting on a seat before the doorposts of the temple of the Lord,” and so forth.

This Eli was the high priest, and after Samson he governed the people of Israel, as is found in the Hebrew book, for forty years [Column 0012D]; according to the Septuagint translators, for twenty years.

“When Hannah was bitter in soul, she prayed to the Lord, weeping profusely, and made a vow, saying: Lord [Column 0013A] of hosts, if you will look upon and see the affliction of your maidservant, and remember me and not forget your handmaid, and give your servant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life,” and so forth.

Perhaps she remembered the words of blessed Job, in which he said: “He who is mocked by his friend as I am will call upon the Lord, and he will hear him” (Job 12), because he considers labor and sorrow. Of him it is written: “To you, Lord, the poor man is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan, and the vows of the righteous are pleasing to you” (Psalm 10), and his eyes are upon their prayers (Proverbs 15).

“It came to pass, then, while she multiplied her prayers before the Lord, that Eli watched her mouth. Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice could not be heard at all. Eli therefore thought she was drunk and said to her: How long will you be drunk? Put away for a little while the wine with which you are soaked. Hannah answered him: Not so, my lord. For I am an exceedingly unhappy woman. I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can cause drunkenness. But I have poured out my soul in the sight of the Lord. Do not regard your handmaid as one of the daughters of Belial, for I have spoken until now out of the abundance of my sorrow,” and so forth.

Belial is interpreted as “without a yoke.” Notice that those who pursue drunkenness are called sons of Belial. Here is fulfilled what is written: “Man sees what is before his eyes, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Kings 16). Eli observed only the mouth of Hannah as she prayed, and because he could not hear her voice at all or perceive the movement of her lips, he thought she was drunk.

But because she lifted her heart upward and confessed to the Lord with her whole heart, the Lord looked upon her prayer and did not despise her petitions. An excellent manner of prayer has also been given to us by this example: we should not shape our prayers to the Lord with many words, but believe that we shall be heard through compunction of heart and an outpouring of tears, because “a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 51).

This is rightly accomplished if, after prayer has been completed, we remain in the same course of righteousness. Hence it also follows:

“And the woman went on her way and ate, and her countenance was no longer changed in different directions [Column 0013D]. And it came to pass after the cycle of days that Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord,” and so forth.

After the cycle of days—that is, after the return of the year—Hannah bore a son and called his name Samuel, which is interpreted as “petition of God,” or “his name is God,” because God was the author of his birth. He was entreated by a barren woman and granted her a son who would be considered worthy to stand in God’s temple for all his days in his service.

Mystically, however, Elkanah, the father of venerable Samuel, who was “God’s possession”—for Elkanah is translated as “possession of God”—is called a man because of the virtue of his mind. He is called not merely a man but “one man.” For he was not carried about as a wanderer in different directions, or as something changeable and unstable; rather, remaining firm and unshaken, he was one man.

Not only is that man called one, but all who possess one wisdom and confess one Christ Jesus and are filled with one Spirit of God are properly called one. Hence the Apostle says: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize” (1 Corinthians 9). Each foolish person is not one but many. Therefore Scripture says: “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus 27). Although the moon appears to be one in substance, through the changes of the days it is always other and different from itself. So also sinners, who are always changing in knowledge and desiring different things, are unstable in all their ways.

God is called one, not in the sense of number, but because he never becomes other than himself and therefore never changes, as in the saying: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 102).

“There was,” he says, “a certain man from Ramathaim-zophim, from Mount Ephraim.” (From Jerome.) Ramatha, or Armatha, as it appears in certain copies, is interpreted as “their height”; Zophim, as “watchtower” or “rock”; Ephraim, as “fruitfulness.”

He is said to have lived on Mount Ephraim and in Ramathaim-zophim—that is, in the height of contemplation of virtues—so that the sublimity or unity of his mind might not be cast down or divided by any thoughts of vices lying below or barking around him. For this reason he is said to be not from valleys, plains, or hills, but from Mount Ephraim, that is, from the fruitful mountain on which the nobility of all virtues is known to bear fruit [Column 0014C].

That man had two wives. Of these, as we said earlier, the first and nobler, Hannah, was barren, just as Sarah, Abraham’s first wife, was the nobler and was barren (Genesis 16). The second, Peninnah, was fruitful but less noble, like Abraham’s second wife, the Egyptian Hagar. Abraham therefore first became a father through the less noble marriage and afterward through the noble one.

So Elkanah, who is God’s possession, first becomes a father through his second wife, because the Lord had closed Hannah’s womb; just as he first opened Sarah’s womb, he opened Hannah’s womb after Peninnah had given birth.

Peninnah is interpreted as “conversion”; Hannah is interpreted as “grace.” Whoever wishes to become God’s possession should take these two wives and first join to himself the nobler one, namely grace. For grace is first joined to a person through faith, as the Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2).

Second, he should be joined to Peninnah, that is, to conversion, because after the grace of belief, the correction of conduct must follow. Peninnah first bears children for us, because through conversion we produce our first fruits. Unless we turn away from evil, we cannot become fathers through Hannah.

Peninnah has children, but they do not always attend the altar; nevertheless they are not fruitless, for they eat from the divine sacrifices. Therefore everyone who is converted from sin produces works of righteousness through conversion. Then Hannah, that is, the faithful soul, aroused by zeal, pours forth a good prayer to the Lord, so that she herself may bear children who attend upon God [Column 0015A], that is, children of grace.

The one who is free for God and always “meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1) is a son of grace. In the Gospel the pattern of this history is displayed. Thus “Martha is busy with much serving” (Luke 10); she completes works of righteousness and, through these, as it were, bears children of conversion. But Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet and hearing his word, is said to have chosen the better part, and she is understood to produce, as it were, offspring of grace, always saying: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 73).

Hannah bears a son, Samuel, of whom it is said: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Psalm 99). He is called “where God himself is”; for where the Spirit of grace is, there God is said to be. Hence Paul says: “And falling on his face, he will worship God, saying: Truly God is among you” (1 Corinthians 14).

Thus, unless works of conversion precede, we cannot produce the gifts of the divine Spirit.

“The woman therefore remained and nursed her son until she weaned him. And after she had weaned him, she brought him with her, with three calves, three measures of flour, and a jar of wine.”

In the Hebrew it does not read “three measures of flour,” but “one measure of flour.” This passage is known to have been corrupted among the Latins through the fault of copyists.

For if she offered three measures of flour together with three calves, she acted contrary to the commandment of the Law. The Law prescribes as follows:

“The first day of the seventh month shall be venerable and holy for you. You shall do no servile work; it is a day of trumpet blasts and trumpets. You shall offer as a burnt offering, for a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, one bull from the herd, one ram, and seven unblemished year-old lambs; and with their sacrifices, fine flour mixed with oil: three-tenths for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth for each lamb” (Numbers 29).

This tenth was the tenth part of an ephah. Hence it is understood that Elkanah did not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but nine-tenths, which according to the Hebrew measure make one ephah.

The fact that Hannah, after the child was born, did not wish to bring him to the house of God before he was weaned signifies that Mother Church should not advance any of her children to the priesthood until, educated beyond the milk of infancy and the smallness of understanding, she has made him capable of spiritual teaching. “For everyone,” says the Apostle, “who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness” (Hebrews 5).

She offers him with three calves and three measures of flour, or one measure of flour, and a jar of wine—that is, fully instructed in the sacrifice of devout confession, in the practice of good works, in the grace of sacred learning, and in faith in the Holy Trinity. He can say with the Prophet: “We will repay the Lord with the calves of our lips” (Hosea 14), and, remaining continually in the house of God, offer worthily the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

## Chapter Two

[Column 0016A] Hannah’s Song, which she sang after Samuel’s birth.

**(Chapter 2.)** “My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God,” and so forth.

In this song she is not found to pray except through only two statements: “I have rejoiced in your salvation,” and: “For there is no God besides you.” Yet the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5).

For those who are engaged in divine service regard all their actions and words as prayer, because the righteous person acts justly without ceasing. For this reason the righteous person will pray without ceasing.

And in the Psalms he says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141). That person lifts his hands who lifts up his actions. Alternatively: “When Moses lifted up his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he let them down, Amalek prevailed” (Exodus 17). For as long as God’s servant lifts his actions toward the Lord, the people of God prevail; but when he lets his actions fall, Amalek, the enemy of God, prevails.

“‘My heart has exulted,’ says Hannah, ‘in the Lord,’” and she necessarily added “in the Lord,” as Paul said: “Rejoice in the Lord always,” because someone can rejoice in carnal things. When people praise me, I do not rejoice in the Lord but in vanity. Let me therefore be pierced by the word of God when it says: “My heart has exulted in the Lord.”

Let the Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring, say what it recognizes as having been prophesied about itself long beforehand through the mouth of this devout mother:

“My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.”

Truly the heart has exulted because it has exulted in the Lord; and truly the horn has been exalted, because it has been exalted not from itself but in the Lord its God. Elsewhere he says: “The horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Psalm 75), because these horns are bestowed upon the righteous from the points of Christ’s cross. With them we shall fan away and destroy the opposing powers that lie in wait for our soul.

“My mouth has been enlarged against my enemies,” because even in the narrowness of tribulations the word of God is not bound, nor is it bound in those who proclaim it.

“For I have rejoiced in your salvation.” This Salvation is the Lord Jesus Christ, whom Simeon, as we read in the Gospel, embracing as a little child while recognizing him as great, said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2).

If I rejoice in the Lord’s salvation, then my mouth has been enlarged. Through meditation on the word of God we shall come to the elevation of the heart. Hence the Apostle says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Corinthians 6). For from the breadth of the heart wisdom is supplied to the mouth.

“There is none holy like the Lord.” He uses a distinction. He did not say, “There is none holy except the Lord,” but rather: “There is none like the Lord—holy and sanctifying, just and justifying.”

“For there is no other besides you, and there is none strong like our God.” “There is none holy,” he says, “besides you, Lord,” because no one becomes holy except through you. “And although there are those who are called many gods” (1 Corinthians 8), and many lords, nevertheless no one by nature is what God is, because he alone is the one who said to Moses his servant: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3).

For a shadow, in comparison with a body, is nothing; and smoke, in comparison with fire, is nothing.

“Do not multiply lofty words, boasting,” and so forth. Solomon also says: “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3). And elsewhere: “The Lord is in heaven, and you are upon earth; therefore let your words be few” (Ecclesiastes 5).

“Let old things depart from your mouth.” That is: let empty talk not come forth from your mouth. “Let no evil speech,” says the Apostle, “proceed from your mouth” (Ephesians 4).

“For God is the Lord of knowledge, and thoughts are prepared for him.” He knows you, and where no one knows. “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2). “Therefore whoever thinks he is something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Galatians 6).

These words are spoken to the adversaries of the city of God who belong to Babylon, who presume upon their own strength and glory in themselves rather than in the Lord. Among them are also the carnal Israelites of earthly Jerusalem, earthborn citizens, who, as the Apostle says, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness”—that is, the righteousness God gives to humanity, since he alone is just and justifying—“and wishing to establish their own”—that is, as though prepared for themselves by themselves, not bestowed upon them by him—“have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10), because they are proud and think that they can please God by their own power rather than by God’s.

But because God is the Lord of knowledge, he himself “sees the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 94). Why are they vain, except because they belong to human beings and do not come from the one from whom human beings themselves come?

“The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.”

The bow has been weakened—that is, the intention of those who seem so powerful to themselves that, through human sufficiency, without God’s gift and help, they can fulfill divine commandments.

“And the weak have been girded with strength.” These are those who trust only in God’s mercy and seek support from him, saying with the Prophet: “Have mercy on me, Lord, because I am weak” (Psalm 6).

The gentile people were weak when they had been alienated from God’s covenant. Now they have been girded with strength, when clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation, they trample underfoot the flaming darts of the ancient enemy with the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6) [Column 0017D].

“Those who were formerly filled have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have been filled,” and so forth.

Who are to be understood as “filled with bread” except those same people who seemed powerful, namely the Israelites, to whom the utterances of the Lord were entrusted? But among that people the children of the handmaid were diminished (Romans 3), when they withdrew and refused to believe in the Savior; and, with respect to those very loaves—that is, the divine utterances—which they alone among all the nations had then received, they understand only earthly things.

But the nations, to whom that Law had not been given, after they came to those utterances through the New Testament, traveled through the earth in great hunger, because in them they understood not earthly but heavenly things.

And as though the reason for this were being sought, she says: “Until the barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has become weak.” (From the Hebrew.)

In the Hebrew and in the Septuagint translation, the reading is not “many” but “seven.”

The Jews understand this passage as follows: when Samuel was born, Peninnah’s firstborn son died, and as each of Hannah’s sons was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died. But one must ask how this can stand, since Peninnah had seven children, whereas Hannah had no more than five. The Hebrews solve this question by counting two of Samuel’s sons together with Hannah’s children.

“For the barren woman,” he says, “has borne seven, and she who had many children has become weak.” (From Augustine.)

Here everything that was being prophesied shone forth for those who recognized the number seven. For this reason the Apostle John writes to seven churches (Revelation 1), thereby showing that he is writing to the fullness of one Church. Solomon also prefigured this earlier in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house and supported it with seven pillars” (Proverbs 9).

The city of God was barren among all the nations before this offspring, which we see, arose. We also see earthly Jerusalem, which had many children, now weakened, because whoever among the children of the free woman were in it constituted its strength. But now, because the letter is there and the Spirit is not, it has lost its strength and become weak.

“The Lord puts to death and gives life.”

He puts to death the one that had many children and gives life to this barren woman who bore seven, although it may more suitably be understood that he gives life to the same people whom he has put to death. For he seems to repeat this by adding:

“He leads down to the underworld and brings back.”

Those to whom the Apostle says, “If you have died with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3), are healthfully put to death by the Lord. He adds: “Think on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth” (ibid.), so that they may be those who traveled through the earth while hungry.

“For you have died,” he says (ibid.), because God healthfully puts them to death. Then it follows: “And your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Behold how God gives life to those same people.

But did he lead those same people down to the underworld and bring them back? Without controversy among the faithful, we see both accomplished rather in him, our head, with whom the Apostle said that our life is hidden in God. For “he who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8) put him to death in this manner; and because he raised him from the dead, he gave the same one life again.

And because his voice is recognized in the Prophet: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Psalm 16), he led the same one down to the underworld and brought him back. By this poverty of his we have been enriched.

“For the Lord makes poor and makes rich.” To understand what this means, let us hear what follows:

“He humbles and exalts.”

Certainly he humbles the proud and exalts the humble. For what is read elsewhere—“God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5)—is contained throughout the entire speech, whose name is interpreted as “his grace.”

Now there is added: “He raises up the poor from the earth.” I understand this of no one more fittingly than of him “who for our sake became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty we might be enriched” (2 Corinthians 8), as was said shortly before. He raised him from the earth so quickly that his flesh did not see corruption. Nor will I separate from him what was said:

“‘And from the dungheap he raises the needy.’ The needy is, of course, the same as the poor. By the dungheap from which he was raised, the Jewish persecutors are rightly understood. Among their number the Apostle said that he had persecuted the Church: ‘The things that were gains to me, he says, I counted as losses for Christ; indeed, I considered them not merely disadvantages but even dung, that I might gain Christ (Phil. III).’ He was therefore raised from the earth; he was exalted above all the rich as a poor man, and from that dungheap he was raised above all the wealthy as a needy man, so that he might sit with the mighty of the people, to whom he said: ‘You shall sit upon twelve thrones (Matt. XIX),’ granting them the inheritance of the throne of glory.

“‘For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and he set the world upon them.’ Because he himself ‘rules from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth (Ps. LXXII).’ ‘The pillars of the earth are the Lord’s,’ that is, the four regions of the world, in which he spread the world-wide extent of his Church, which praises his name from the rising of the sun to its setting. ‘He will guard the feet of his holy ones,’ that is, he will direct the works of his elect into the way of righteousness. ‘And the wicked shall be silent in darkness, because they will be sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. XXII);’ there they shall be silent, that is, they shall cease from the arrogance of their pride. ‘For a man shall not be strengthened by his own strength,’ that is, a man is powerful not through his own strength but through divine power—the man, that is, who is the people of believers.

“‘The Lord’s adversaries shall fear him, because the Lord will weaken his adversary.’ From the ambiguity of the Greek this may be understood as ‘and his own adversary.’ For when the Lord begins to possess us, the adversary who had been ours becomes his; and he will be overcome by us, not by our own strength, since a man is not powerful through his own strength. The Lord, therefore, will weaken his own adversary. The holy Lord is overcome by the saints whom the holy Lord of saints makes holy (?). And thus: ‘Let the mighty man not glory in his might; let the wise man not glory in his wisdom, nor the rich man in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows the Lord, and practices judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth (Jer. IX).’ He understands and knows the Lord in no small measure who also understands and knows that this very ability—to understand and know the Lord—is given to him by the Lord. But because a just recompense will come from the Lord upon the sons of Adam on the day of judgment, it follows:

“‘The Lord ascended,’ he says, ‘into the heavens and thundered; he himself will judge the ends of the earth, because he is just.’ This prophetess has maintained throughout the proper order of the believers’ confession. The Lord Christ ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. ‘For who ascended,’ as the Apostle says, ‘except the one who also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things (Eph. IV).’ He thundered, therefore, through his clouds, which he filled with the Holy Spirit when he had ascended. Concerning these clouds he threatened, through the prophet Isaiah, carnal Jerusalem—that is, the ungrateful vineyard—‘lest they should pour rain upon it (Isa. V).’

“‘The Lord will judge the ends of the earth’ was said as though it meant: The Lord will judge the extremities of man, since what is changed for better or worse during the intervening time will not be judged, but rather the condition in which the person being judged is found at the end. ‘And he will give power to his king,’ that is, to the Christian people; he gives them the power by which, like kings, they may rule the flesh and, in the one who poured out his blood for them, conquer the world. It follows: ‘And he will exalt the horn of his Christ.’ How will Christ exalt the horn of his Christ? We may rightly call all those anointed with his chrism “christs”; yet, with their head, they are all one Christ.

“These things Hannah prophesied, the mother of Samuel, that holy and greatly praised man. In him the change of the former priesthood was then prefigured, and now fulfilled, when she who had been abundant in children became weak, so that the barren woman who bore seven might have a new priesthood in Christ.

“In the meantime Samuel was ministering in the temple of the Lord, girded with a linen ephod—that is, a linen shoulder-piece—which differs from the ephod worn by the high priest. The former was only of linen and was permitted for use by those of lesser rank; the latter, which clothed the high priest, was woven from four colors—hyacinth, fine linen, scarlet, and purple—and from gold.

“‘And his mother made him a little tunic, which she brought to him at the appointed days, going up with her husband to offer the solemn sacrifice to the Lord.’ This little tunic, which Hannah his mother—that is, grace—fashioned and gave to the boy, signifies the simple teaching with which the inexperienced minds of believers are to be instructed. To such people Paul says: ‘I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able (I Cor. III).’ The food of the mature, however, is solid. The linen shoulder-piece likewise signifies chastity and continence together with good works. For whoever desires to perform divine ministry must first live chastely and continently, and then exercise himself in good works.

“Moreover, the sons of Eli sinned by profaning the divine rites before the Lord. Thus it is written: ‘The sons of Eli were sons of Belial, not knowing the Lord, nor the duty of priests toward the people.’ A little later it says: ‘The sin of the young men was therefore very great before the Lord, because they drew men away from the sacrifice of the Lord.’

“Josephus, the historian of the Jews, reports the following about these two sons:

“‘Eli the priest had two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, who were unjust toward men and impious toward the Divinity, sparing no iniquity. Some of the offerings they set aside for themselves on the pretext of honor, while others they carried off as though by robbery. They inflicted insults upon women who came for the sake of religion, using violence against some and persuading others with gifts; in no respect did their life differ from the worst tyranny. Therefore Eli the priest was condemned because of their iniquity, since he punished them for their sins with insufficient severity. He restrained them and rebuked them, but with the mildness and gentleness of a father, not with the severity and authority of a high priest.’

“From this sentence let priests learn how they are punished for the sins of their sons—that is, for the crimes of the people. Even though they may themselves be holy, the guilt of their subjects is nevertheless charged to them if they do not restrain them. A person who does not maintain discipline and does not correct his sons so that they live well and justly is estranged from God. Whoever does not rebuke his sons so that they may amend what they have done wrongly is impiously compassionate, because he indulges their vices and gives the wicked his consent to their own ruin.

“Hophni is interpreted as ‘madness of conversion.’ He is rightly so called, because he delays turning to what is better and is made far removed from true conversion to the Lord, which reforms a person from vices and sin. Phinehas is interpreted as ‘stopping the mouth,’ or ‘sparing the mouth.’ We read of two priests named Phinehas in Scripture (Exod. VI; Num. XXV): the righteous one, son of Eleazar, and the unrighteous one, son of Eli. There are also priests today who bear the type of each.

“Those priests, therefore, who guard their mouths and restrain themselves from evil and corrupt speech, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching that no evil word should proceed from their mouths (Eph. IV), are compared with Phinehas the son of Eleazar. Those, however, whose mouths are stopped—whether through ignorance, vice, or consciousness of sins—so that they do not properly offer the word of salvation to their neighbors, are compared with Phinehas the son of Eli.

“What follows in Eli’s words is:

“‘If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased. But if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?’

“Sin against a man is therefore not like sin against God. To sin against a man, whatever kind of sin it may be, is an offense committed against one’s neighbor, and its remission is easy. But to sin against God—that is, to depart from his worship—is the sin of impiety, and its remission is more difficult. Since, when someone sins against a man, he makes God favorable to himself by appeasing the man, but when someone sins against God, who will pray for him? In other words: through whom can he make the God against whom he has sinned favorable to himself?

“Nevertheless, this should not be understood to mean that those who have committed some offense in divine service have no hope of forgiveness, even if they undertake worthy repentance. Rather, forgiveness is more difficult, and greater repentance must be undertaken by those who have offended in matters consecrated to God than by one who has injured his neighbor in word or deed. For the greater the glory, the more serious the offense.

[Col. 0022A] “‘Then a man of God came to Eli and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Was I not plainly revealed to the house of your father when they were in Egypt, in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him from all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense to me, and to wear the ephod before me; and I gave to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the sons of Israel. Why do you kick away my victim and my offerings, which I commanded to be offered in the temple, and honor your sons more than me, so that you may eat the firstfruits of every sacrifice of my people Israel? Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: I plainly declared that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. For whoever glorifies me, I will glorify him; but those who despise me shall be held in dishonor. Behold, days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there shall be no old man in your house. And you shall see your rival in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel, and there shall be no old man in your house for all your days. Nevertheless, I will not wholly remove a man from you from my altar, but it will be so that your eyes may fail and your soul may waste away; and the greater part of your house shall die when it reaches manhood. This shall be a sign for you of what will happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: on one day both shall die,’ and so forth.

“‘Behold,’ he says, ‘days are coming, and I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house.’ By the arm he expresses the dignity and strength of the high priesthood. ‘So that there shall be no old man in your house’: by the old man he indicates the high priest. ‘And you shall see your rival in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel.’ The rival of the house of Eli was the priest Zadok, who, after Abiathar was deposed, received the priesthood from Solomon, as is read in Malachim [Kings] (III Kings II): ‘And Solomon expelled Abiathar, so that he would not be a priest of the Lord, in order that the word of the Lord might be fulfilled which he had spoken concerning the house of Eli.’

“‘Nevertheless, I will not wholly remove a man from you from my altar, so that your eyes may fail and your soul may waste away.’ For this reason the Lord says that he will not wholly remove from the house of Eli a man from his altar: so that there would always be someone from the house of Eli in the house of the Lord who would see another appointed to the dignity of the priesthood in his place; and, seeing himself deprived of that same dignity, his eyes would fail and his soul would waste away.

“(From Augustine.) Mystically, however, this prophecy concerning the change of the priesthood was not fulfilled in Samuel but was foreshadowed in the Lord Jesus Christ. After Samuel the priests continued to come from the line of Aaron, such as Zadok and Abiathar under David’s reign, and others thereafter, before the time came when what had long before been foretold concerning the change of the priesthood had to be brought about through Christ.

“For when he said: ‘I plainly declared that your house and the house of your father should minister in my sight forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me. Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify him; but those who despise me shall be held in dishonor. Behold, days are coming, says the Lord’—behold, these are the days that were foretold. For now there is no priest according to the order of Aaron.

“That he speaks of the house of his father not of a near and immediate father, but of Aaron, who was first appointed priest and from whose descendants the others would follow, is shown by what precedes, where he says: ‘I was revealed to the house of your father when they were in the land of Egypt, slaves in the house of Pharaoh; and I chose the house of your father from all the tribes of Israel to perform the priesthood for me.’ Which of his fathers was in that Egyptian slavery, from which, after they had been delivered, he was chosen for the priesthood, if not Aaron?

“Of his stock, therefore, he said in this passage that priests would no longer exist—a thing we now see fulfilled. There is no priest according to the order of Aaron. And whenever a man from his lineage sees the Christian sacrifice prevailing throughout the whole world, while that great honor has been taken away from him, his eyes fail and his soul wastes away from the excess of grief.

“More particularly, what follows concerns the house of this Eli to whom these words were spoken: ‘And everyone who remains in your house shall fall by the sword of men. And this shall be a sign for you: your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall both die on one day.’ This sign was therefore made concerning the change of the priesthood from this man’s house; by this sign it was signified that the priesthood of the house of Aaron would be changed. The death of the sons signified the death not of human beings but of the priesthood itself among the sons of Aaron.

“What follows, however, already concerns that priest whose figure Samuel bore by succeeding him. Accordingly, what follows is said of Jesus Christ, the priest of the New Testament:

“‘And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who shall do everything that is in my heart and in my soul, and I will build for him a faithful house.’ This is the eternal and heavenly Jerusalem. ‘And he shall pass,’ he says, ‘before my Christ all his days.’

“‘He shall pass’ means ‘he shall dwell,’ just as he had earlier said concerning the house of Aaron: ‘I said that your house and the house of your father would pass before me forever.’ When he says, ‘He shall pass with my Christ,’ this must certainly be understood of that house, not of the priest who is himself Christ, the Mediator and Savior. His house shall pass before him.

“‘He shall pass’ may also be understood as referring to the passage from death to life, throughout all the days during which this mortality continues until the end of the present age.

“When God says, ‘who shall do everything that is in my heart and in my soul,’ we should not suppose that God has a soul, since he is the creator of the soul. Rather, this is said figuratively, not literally, of God, just as are ‘hand,’ ‘foot,’ and the other bodily members.

“With regard to Samuel, it may rightly be understood that in all things he obeyed God’s will as a human being. With regard to the Lord and Savior, it means that, as the only-begotten Son, he is in all things conscious of the Father’s hidden purposes, in accordance with what he himself plainly testifies concerning himself: ‘I can do nothing of myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak; and he who sent me is with me; he has not left me alone, because I always do what is pleasing to him (John VIII).’

“The Father builds him a faithful house. ‘We are that house, if only we hold firmly to the confidence and glory of hope until the end (Heb. III).’ Otherwise, how can it be understood of Samuel that a faithful house was built for him which would proceed before Christ the Lord—that is, before Samuel himself—all his days, when we read later that his sons turned away from his ways, declined toward greed, and perverted judgment? Unless perhaps we understand his house here as the Israelite people, because throughout all the days of his priesthood it served the Lord. Of this it is written: ‘And all the house of Israel rested after the Lord (I Sam. VII);’ and shortly afterward: ‘Then the sons of Israel removed the Baals and the Astartes, and served the Lord alone (ibid.).’

“What follows is:

[Col. 0024B] “‘But it shall come to pass that whoever remains in your house shall come to be prayed for, and shall offer a silver coin and a piece of bread.’

“This is not said literally of the house of this Eli, but of that of Aaron, from whose lineage even to this day there are still some who come and are converted. Concerning them another prophet said: ‘The remnant shall be saved (Isa. XVI).’ Hence the Apostle says: ‘So therefore at this present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace (Rom. XI).’

“It is rightly understood of such remnants that it was said: ‘Whoever remains in your house shall come to be prayed for.’ Certainly, one who believes in Christ comes in this way, just as in the time of the Apostles very many came and believed from that same people. Even now there are some, though very few, who believe, so that what this man of God spoke may be fulfilled in them.

“What he immediately adds—‘He shall offer a silver coin and a piece of bread (Rom. X)’—what does the silver coin signify except confession with the mouth, which is made by believers unto salvation? Silver is customarily used to signify speech, as the Psalmist testifies where it is sung: ‘The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire (Ps. XI).’

“Let him also offer the bread of the altar sacrifice. Having cast aside the carnal sacrifices of the legal offerings, let him say:

[Col. 0024D] “‘Let me go, I beseech you, to one portion of the priesthood,’ that is, to that people made glorious by Christ the priest. To it Peter says: ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood (I Pet. II).’

“Since he adds, ‘that I may eat a morsel of bread,’ he has also elegantly expressed the very kind of sacrifice. Concerning it the Priest himself says: ‘The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world (John VI).’

“Because earlier he had said that he had given the house of Aaron food from the victims of the Old Testament, which had been the sacrifices of the Jews, he therefore says here that a morsel of bread is to be requested for eating. This is the sacrifice of Christians in the New Testament, as nourishment for faithful souls.

“It follows:

# CHAPTER III

On Samuel’s ministry in the temple and on the death of the sons of Eli the priest. How Eli was rebuked by the man of God for the crime of his sons, whom their father did not properly correct.

(CAP. III.) “‘Now the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious’”—that is, rare, as is made clear in what follows, when it says: ‘In those days there was no manifest vision.’

“Because of the sins of the people and of those who governed the people, the Lord no longer appeared openly to the people of Israel through visions or angelic responses, as he had done to their fathers. Therefore the historian says that the word of the Lord was precious at that time.

[Col. 0025B] “‘It came to pass, then, on a certain day, that Eli was lying in his place, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished,’ and so forth.

“Because of his extreme old age, Eli’s eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of the Lord while it was burning in the tabernacle before daylight, when that lamp was to be extinguished. For the Lord had commanded through Moses that the same lamp should shine until morning, as it says in the Book of Exodus: ‘Command,’ says the Lord, ‘the sons of Israel to bring you the purest oil from olive trees, crushed with the pestle, so that the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of the Lord; and Aaron and his sons shall set it in place, so that it may shine before the Lord until morning (Exod. XXVII).’

“Alternatively, this may signify that Eli remained in his blindness until he was utterly extinguished together with his offspring—that is, until he lost his bodily life.

“Mystically, however, Eli’s blindness signifies the blindness of the hearts of the Jews, who could not recognize the Savior when he was present, nor understand the brilliance of the miracles performed by him, nor grasp his teaching with attentive hearts, until the priesthood itself, together with the temple and the people, was utterly overthrown.

“In the meantime Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of the Lord was. Having been called three times by the Lord, he was finally instructed by the Lord’s voice that Eli would perish together with his sons because of their sins.

“By this third calling it may be prefigured that the boy himself would become a prophet, leader, and priest.

“When it is written, ‘Samuel did not yet know the Lord,’ he is said not to know the Lord because, through the mystery of prophecy, the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him.

“And what follows:

“‘The Lord said to Samuel: Behold, I am doing a deed in Israel, and whoever hears it, both his ears shall tingle,’ and so forth.

“Here the threat of God is against Eli and his house, because on account of the sin of Eli’s sons the ark of God would be captured, Israel would fall, his sons would perish, the house of Eli would be deprived of the priesthood of the house of the Lord, and, because of this event, the ears of those who heard it would tingle with overwhelming astonishment.

“‘Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of all his words fell to the ground.’

[Col. 0026A] “What is said about Samuel, after he reported to Eli in the morning the words of the divine oracle that he had received during the night—‘none of all his words fell to the ground’—signifies that nothing he said was ineffectual, but everything he foretold was fulfilled in events.

“For empty words fall to the ground: words that are to be regarded as worthless and trampled under the contempt of all, just as blessed Job said: ‘The light of my face did not fall to the ground (Job XXIX).’ He was accustomed to maintain such gravity in his expression that he was never relaxed by contemptible merriment; whenever he presented himself more cheerfully to those around him, he always did so for a definite and useful reason.

“‘And all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord,’ and so forth.

“(From Jerome.) By describing the boundaries of the land of Judea, he simultaneously encompasses the whole people.

“Dan is a village four miles from Paneas on the road to Tyre; it is still called by that name and forms the northern boundary of the province of Judea. The Jordan also bursts forth from that place and takes its name from it, for the Hebrews call a river or stream *or*. Dan is interpreted as ‘judgment’ or ‘judging.’

“Beersheba is still a large village in the tribe of Judah or Simeon, twenty miles from Hebron, extending toward the south; a garrison of Roman soldiers has also been stationed there. From that place the boundaries of the land of Judea begin and extend to Dan, which is seen near Paneas.

“Beersheba is interpreted as ‘well of satiety,’ or ‘well of the man,’ or ‘of the oath,’ because there Abraham and Isaac entered into a covenant with Abimelech by swearing (Gen. XXI and XXVI).

“No one should be troubled if he sometimes finds the same cities of Judea assigned to the tribe of Simeon or Benjamin. The tribe of Judah, strong in its most warlike men and frequently victorious over its adversaries, held primacy among all the tribes. Therefore the territories of other tribes are sometimes named within its boundary. Otherwise, Scripture very clearly teaches that Simeon lived in the midst of the tribe of Judah.

# CHAPTER IV

On the change of the priesthood of the old law. The battle of the Philistines against Israel, in which the ark of God was captured, the two sons of Eli were killed, the Israelite people were put to flight, and Eli died.

“After these things had been foretold by that prophet to Eli, who had offended the Lord of Israel, as a figure of the change of the Old Testament, the Philistines—that is, the Palestinians—drew up their battle line against them at Aphek. This place is near the village of Endor, in the city of Ezekiel, where Saul fought within the territory of Asher, in which the former inhabitants remained.

“Aphek is interpreted as ‘new fury’ or ‘one who seizes.’ This fittingly corresponds to what happened. Those who had deserved the Lord’s anger were seized by their enemies.

“The Israelites took the ark for their protection. The ark was captured by the enemies, and they were not merely defeated and put to flight; a great slaughter of the slain also took place.

[Col. 0027A] “This event nevertheless signifies something prophetic about the future. For that ark, captured by foreigners, indicated that the Testament of God would pass to the nations.

“When Eli the priest was told that the ark of God had been captured, he fell backward from his seat and died. And rightly so. For whoever turns backward from faith and truth must fall and immediately die.

“Mystically, when the ark of the Lord passed to the nations, the priesthood of the Jews perished and came to an end. The two sons of Eli also fell; one of their wives was widowed and soon died in childbirth because of the same upheaval.

“Josephus reports the following about this:

“‘When Eli also heard that the ark had been captured by the enemies, he was overcome with grief, because an immense burden had come upon him contrary to his expectation. Falling from his seat, he died when he had lived ninety-eight years, forty of which he had held the chief authority. On that same day the wife of Phinehas, his son, also died, unable to endure life after the death of her husband. When she was pregnant, the grief over her husband was announced to her; she gave birth to a seven-month child, whom for this reason they called Ichabod, a name signifying “inglorious,” because at that time such disgrace had come upon the army.’

“Eli was the first to hold the chief authority from the house of Ithamar, who was one of the sons of Aaron. At first the priests came from the house of Eleazar; from him the son received the honor, and Eleazar handed it down to his son Phinehas. After him his son Abiezer received this honor, and left it to his son Ozi. Ozi’s own son in turn succeeded him. After him Eli held the priesthood, and it is of him that we are now speaking. His lineage retained it until the time of Solomon. At that time they again received the priesthood from the house of Eleazar.

“(From Isidore.) Thus it was clearly prefigured that, after the priesthood of the Jews had been extinguished, the carnal Synagogue attached to it in a carnal manner would perish. When Eli was struck down from his seat, the high priests of the Jews had their seat left vacant, and the glory of the priesthood and kingdom was extinguished.

# CHAPTER V

On the Philistines’ placing the ark of God opposite the image of Dagon, because of which the Lord struck all the Philistines in their hindquarters as punishment for their insult.

[Col. 0027D] (CAP. V.) “‘The Philistines took the ark of God and carried it from the Stone of Help to Azotus,’ and so forth.

“(From Jerome.) The Stone of Help is the name of the place where Samuel set up one stone between Mizpah and Shen, as is shown in what follows.

“Azotus, also called Astro, is still a distinguished municipality of the province of Palestine and one of the five cities of the Allophylites. It was assigned by decree to the tribe of Judah, but was not retained by it, because it was entirely unable to drive out the former inhabitants.

“It is interpreted as ‘the fire of my father’ or ‘burning.’ Appropriately, that place where the idol of Dagon stood is called the fire of my father: for the arrival of the ark of God at Azotus was a conflagration for the devil, the father of all the wicked.

[Col. 0028A] “Dagon is interpreted as ‘fish of sorrow,’ signifying the ancient enemy who, placed in the sea of this world, devours fishermen. The Book of Job calls him Leviathan and Behemoth (Job III and XL).

“(From Isidore.) But what does it mean that, when the Philistines had placed the ark of the Lord in the temple of Dagon their god, they entered the temple and found Dagon prostrate, with his head shattered and both his hands cut off?

“As soon as the Testament of the Lord reached the nations, the idols that possessed the deceived world were immediately destroyed, and every error of images collapsed, unable to endure the presence of the Lord. For in the severed hands of Dagon the work of idolatry is cut off; and in his severed head the pride of the devil is signified, from whom sin had its beginning.

“That he was found on the threshold was also of certain and predetermined significance, so that idolatry might recognize its end. The threshold signifies the end of a journey.

“There is also a further important meaning in the fact that, amid the ruin and breaking of Dagon their god, only his back was found, all his other limbs having been broken. The back signifies flight. For all who flee give their backs to those pursuing them. Hence it is also written concerning the enemies: ‘For you will make them turn their backs (Ps. XX).’

“Where are the idols? They have perished; and if any remnants are hidden by some people, they are fleeing.

“As for the fact that those who captured the ark of God were struck in their hindquarters, this punishment appears to signify that if some receive the Testament of God but love what is behind them, they too will most justly be tormented. Like the Apostle (Phil. III), they ought to regard those same things as dung.

“For those who receive the divine Testament in such a way that, looking backward, they do not strip themselves of their former vanity, are like those enemies who placed the captured ark of the covenant beside their idols.

“And those old things fall even against their will, because ‘all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withered, and its flower fell (Isa. XL);’ but the ark of the Lord remains forever: namely, the hidden mystery of the kingdom of heaven, where the Word of God is.

# CHAPTER VI

That the Philistines, making a new cart drawn by milch cows, sent back the ark to Beth-shemesh; and on the mystical meaning of this event.

[Col. 0028D] (CAP. VI.) “‘Now the ark of the Lord was in the territory of the Philistines for seven months,’ and so forth.

“The seven months during which the ark of God was among the nations figuratively express the totality of time, which unfolds according to the number seven in its days; and they signify that the Testament of the Lord will remain among the nations until the consummation of the age.

“‘And the Philistines called together the priests and diviners, saying: What shall we do with the ark of God? Tell us how we shall send it back to its place. They replied: If you send back the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it back empty, but render to it what you owe for the sin; then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand does not withdraw from you. They said to them: What must we render to him for the offense? They answered them: According to the number of the provinces of the Philistines, you shall make five golden tumors and five golden mice, because the same plague was upon all of you and your rulers. You shall make likenesses of your tumors and likenesses of the mice that devastated the land, and you shall give glory to the God of Israel, if perhaps he will lift his hand from you, from your gods, and from your land,’ and so forth.

“The five golden tumors and the five golden mice, likewise made of gold, which the Philistines fashioned after the plague they had suffered and brought to the ark of the Lord, signify that certain carnal people, devoted to the five bodily senses and following the allurements of pleasures, when they have been chastised by the Lord, acknowledge their crimes and confess that they justly suffer those blows from the Lord; and, although compelled, they apply themselves to improving their lives.

“This is well signified by the five cities of the Philistines—Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon, Gath, and Ekron—which represent those who follow the actions of the outer man.

“(From Jerome.) Gaza is a city of the Evites, in which the Cappadocians lived after killing its former inhabitants. In ancient times it was the boundary of the Canaanites near Egypt. It fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, but that tribe could not retain it, because the Anakim—that is, the giants of the Allophylites—resisted with the greatest strength. It is still a notable city of Palestine.

“It is asked how a certain prophet says that Gaza will become an everlasting mound (Zeph. II). The matter is resolved in this way: the site of the ancient city scarcely offers traces even of its foundations; the city now seen was built in another place in its stead.

“Ascalon is a noble city of Palestine. It too was formerly one of the five satrapies of the Allophylites. It was separated and assigned by lot to the tribe of Judah, but was not retained by it, because it could not overcome its inhabitants.

“Gath, to which they transferred the ark of the covenant from Azotus, is now a large village called Geththam, between Antipatris and Jamnia. There is also another village called Gethim.

“Ekron belongs to the tribe of Dan, or, as I think, to the tribe of Judah, on the left of the Canaanites. It was one of the five former satrapies of Palestine and was assigned to the tribe of Judah, but was not retained by it, because it could not drive out its former inhabitants. Even today there is a large village of Jewish inhabitants called Ekron, lying between Azotus and Jamnia and facing east.

“Some think that Ekron is Strato’s Tower, later called Caesarea.

“Azotus, as we said above, is interpreted as ‘the fire of my father’ or ‘burning.’ Gaza is interpreted as ‘strength.’ Ascalon means ‘infamous fire’ or ‘ignoble fire.’ Gath means ‘winepress.’ Ekron is also interpreted as ‘instruction of sorrow’ or ‘barrenness.’

“For every infamous and ignoble desire, inflamed by the devil, urged on by opposing powers, and as though pressed out through the winepress of wickedness, pours forth the wine of bitterness in corrupt teaching and perverse action. Therefore it must necessarily tend toward death, where there is true sorrow and perpetual barrenness.”

[Col. 0030A] “Meanwhile, the Philistines made a new cart, placed the ark on it, and beside it a small chest containing golden tumors and mice, which they were paying as a guilt offering. They set the cart there, together with two cows that had calved, which had never worn a yoke, and shut up their calves at home,” in order to test from where the plague had come upon them, and so forth. (From Isidore.) Those cows of the foreigners, bearing the ark, prefigured the saints who renounce the world, who have drawn no yoke of sin. For just as those cows, out of affection for their young, did not at all turn aside from the straight road, so the saints who renounce the world ought not, under the pretext of family affection, to be hindered from their good purpose, as Moses says: “Those who say to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to their brothers, ‘I do not recognize you,’ and who did not know their own children: these have kept your covenant, O God, and observed your commandments: your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” (Deut. 33). For the one who desires to know God more intimately is the one who, out of love for holiness, desires not to know whatever they know carnally.

“And the cows,” he says, “went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh,” and so forth. (From Jerome.) Beth-shemesh is a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin, which is still shown to those traveling from Eleutheropolis toward Nicopolis, at the tenth milestone, facing east. There is another Beth-shemesh in the tribe of Naphtali, where the former inhabitants themselves also remained.

“And they proceeded by one road, going and lowing, and they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left,” and so forth. He rightly says that they proceeded by one road to Beth-shemesh, that is, walking along the royal road toward the house of the sun, namely, to the place of justice and truth. For Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun” and signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, where the Sun of justice always shines. “The cows went straight ahead, and they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left,” and so forth—that is, they were not lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity. Hence the Apostle says: “By the weapons of justice on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers and yet truthful,” and so forth (2 Cor. 6). (From Gregory.) If, therefore, we are heading toward the dwelling of the eternal Sun, it is surely fitting that we should not turn aside from God’s road for the sake of carnal affections. For it must be considered with all our strength that the cows placed beneath God’s cart proceed and groan; they give lowings from their inmost parts, and yet do not turn their steps back from the road. They feel love through compassion, but they do not bend their necks backward. Thus, certainly, God’s preachers, and all the faithful within holy Church, ought to be such that they both sympathize with their neighbors through charity and yet do not stray from God’s way through compassion. For the ark placed upon the cart proceeding to Beth-shemesh means drawing near, with heavenly knowledge, to the dwelling of inner light. But we truly head toward Beth-shemesh when, walking along the path of uprightness, we do not turn aside toward the neighboring paths of error out of affection for our children. Thus those who are placed beneath the yoke of sacred law and now carry the ark of the Lord through inward knowledge ought to walk, so that, grieving over the needs of their relatives, they do not turn aside from the road of uprightness on which they have begun. Their affection ought indeed to hold our mind, but ought not to turn it back, lest that same mind be either hard, if it is not touched by affection, or, if touched too deeply and bent, lax.

After the return of the ark from the land of the Philistines, Scripture continues:

[Col. 0031A] “These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned to the Lord as a guilt offering: one for Azotus, one for Gaza, one for Ascalon, one for Geth, one for Accaron,” and so forth. (From the Hebrew.) These five cities gave five tumors and five mice. The remaining cities of the provinces and the villages that were without a wall gave only mice. Therefore it is said: “from the walled city to the village that was without a wall.”

As for what follows: “And as far as Abel the Great, upon which they placed the ark of God.” Abel the Great is a city at the border of Israel. It is called Abel the Great, although it had previously been called Beth-shemesh, either because of the mourning that occurred there over the men of Beth-shemesh, or to distinguish it from the city of Abel-beth-maacah, concerning which a wise woman cried out to Joab, saying: “Let them ask in Abel” (2 Sam. 20). Thus it is to be understood that from the walled city to the village that was without a wall, and as far as Abel the Great, they gave mice. Upon it—that is, upon the mourning—they placed the ark of the Lord, which until that day had been in the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite. It therefore remained in his field until it was brought to Kiriath-jearim.

Regarding those who dared to look upon the ark of the Lord after it had returned from the land of the Philistines, although they were not of the Levitical lineage, it was said: “And he struck seventy men among the people, and fifty thousand of the populace.” “People” and “populace” are used indifferently for one and the same thing, for both are customarily translated from the one Greek word λαός (*laos*). But it seems to me that there is a distinction in the first clause of the verse, where “seventy men” has been added. “Men” signifies elders, so that the sense is that seventy of the people’s nobles were struck, while fifty thousand were struck from the common crowd. To prevent this from happening, in Exodus (chap. 20) the people stood at a distance and prayed, while Moses alone ascended to the Lord.

[Col. 0031D] “And the men of Beth-shemesh said: ‘Who can stand in the presence of this holy Lord God, and to whom shall he go up from us?’ And they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying: ‘The Philistines have brought back the ark of the Lord. Come down and take it to yourselves.’ (CHAP. 7.) So the men of Kiriath-jearim came, took the ark of the Lord, and brought it into the house of Abinadab on the hill. They consecrated Eleazar his son, so that he might guard the ark of the Lord,” and so forth.

What better meaning can be found in the fact that, after the men of Beth-shemesh were struck because they looked upon the ark of the Lord unworthily, they sent it to Kiriath-jearim, than the transfer of the Lord’s covenant from the Jewish people to the Gentiles? For when the Jews, straying from the path of their fathers, defiled the law with carnal observance and Pharisaic superstitions, they despised the sayings of the Savior and utterly refused to have the word of salvation preached to them by the ministers of the New Testament. Therefore, after the Lord’s resurrection, the apostles say to them: “It was necessary that the word of God should be preached to you first; but because you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). (From Jerome.) Kiriath-jearim, also called Cariathbaal, is the city of forests, one of the cities of the Gibeonites, belonging to the tribe of Judah, at the ninth milestone for those traveling toward Heliopolis. Uriah the prophet came from this city; Jehoiakim killed him in Jerusalem, as Jeremiah writes (Jer. 26). But in the book of Chronicles the son of Shobal is called Kiriath-jearim (1 Chron. 11). Kiriath-jearim itself is interpreted as “city” or “village of forests.”

Concerning this city it is mystically written in the psalm: “I will find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Behold, we heard of it in Ephratha; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. 131). The Lord’s place is the tabernacle of the Christian people’s heart and the courts of the Catholic Church, which, like heaven, he continually inhabits. The city of forests—that is, the assembly of the Gentiles—becomes a fitting place to receive the ark of the Lord into the house of Abinadab, whose name means “My father is willing,” and who could say with the Psalmist: “I will sacrifice to you freely, and I will confess your name, O Lord, because it is good” (Ps. 52).

Gibeah is interpreted as “hill” or “height.” There Eleazar, the son of Abinadab, is appointed priest to guard the ark of the Lord. Eleazar indeed means “help of God.” It is fitting that the one who guards the ark of the Lord is called “the help of God,” because holy men attribute whatever good they possess not to themselves but to God. Hence the Apostle says: “Such confidence we have through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit” (2 Cor. 3).

CHAPTER VII. Concerning Samuel’s exhortation to Israel to abandon Baalim and Astaroth and serve the Lord, and concerning the Israelites’ deliverance from the Philistines while he prayed, so that they no longer prevailed over them during Samuel’s lifetime.

[Col. 0032D] “And it came to pass that from the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied (for it was already the twentieth year), and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord,” and so forth. (From Bede.) The statement “that from the day when the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied (for it was already the twentieth year), and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord” should not be understood as though the twenty years during which the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim were to be counted all the way to the eighth year of David’s reign, when he brought it to Jerusalem amid a great gathering of the people. For it is found later that, in Saul’s time, it was carried out of that city and brought into the camp while he was fighting against the Philistines. For it is written: “And Saul said to Ahijah: ‘Bring near the ark of God.’ For the ark of God was there on that day with the children of Israel” (1 Sam. 14).
