Since it is certain that David brought it to Jerusalem after taking it from the house of Abinadab, into which it is now said to have been brought, it remains to be understood that in Saul’s days it was brought back from the camp and placed in the aforementioned city, from which, when David reigned, it would again be brought to Jerusalem.

The sense of the statement is therefore this: from the time when the ark remained in Kiriath-jearim, it was the twentieth year when the occasion arose for it to be transferred from there in Saul’s time on account of the war. Or certainly, it was the twentieth year while all the house of Israel still rested after the Lord, having rejected idols and serving him alone. No careful student of sacred history is unaware that they did this throughout Samuel’s entire period of leadership—which, according to Josephus, lasted fifteen years—and during the first period of Saul’s reign, which, according to the same historian, lasted twenty years. For afterward, when the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul and an evil spirit troubled him, especially to persecute David, innocent and just, it was necessary that some portion of his army or people should have become accomplices in his wickedness.

[Col. 0033B] “So the children of Israel removed Baalim and Astaroth, and served the Lord alone.” Astaroth is interpreted as “the work of explorers.” Baalim is interpreted as “those ascending” or “those above.” Therefore, whoever is a true Israelite—that is, a man who sees the Lord, or a mind that sees the Lord—removes from himself every work of evil spirits; he removes boastfulness and pride, and thus he will serve the Lord alone, because “there is no fellowship between light and darkness, nor any agreement between Christ and Belial” (2 Cor. 6).

“And Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpah,” and so forth. (From Jerome.) Mizpah is a city in the tribe of Judah, near which Jephthah lived, beside the city of Kiriath-jearim, of which we spoke above. Mizpah is interpreted as “watchtower,” “contemplation,” “attention,” or “place of judgment.” *Saphat* means “to judge.” This place therefore fittingly belongs to such a holy man, who judged the people entrusted to him in justice and truth and governed them with the greatest prudence.

[Col. 0033D] “Then Samuel took one suckling lamb and offered it as a burnt offering to the Lord. And Samuel cried to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him,” and so forth. “Samuel cried,” he says, “to the Lord for Israel,” and he heard him: “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers” (Ps. 33). And when he offered the suckling lamb as a burnt offering—that is, an innocent life—he slaughtered a saving sacrifice to the Lord through continence and consumed it entirely in the fire of charity as a pleasing fragrance.

[Col. 0034A] “When the foreigners advanced to battle against the Lord’s people, the Lord thundered over them, and they were thrown into confusion; they stumbled before Israel and were defeated, and they struck them as far as the place below Beth-car.” Beth-car is interpreted as “house of knowledge” or “house of the lamb.” When, through the preachers of the Gospel, the Lord thundered over his spiritual enemies, they were put to flight and fell before Israel—that is, before the people of God. And they pursued them as far as the house of knowledge, that is, until every error is overcome and God is truly known.

[Col. 0034B] “Then Samuel took one stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen (or, as another edition has it, between the new Mizpah and the old).” “And he called its name Ebenezer, which in Latin is ‘stone of help.’ And he said: ‘Thus far the Lord has helped us,’” and so forth. Mizpah, as we said above, is interpreted as “attention.” (From Isidore.) That stone of help is the mediator, the Savior, through whom one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new—that is, from the attention by which false, carnal blessedness was expected in a carnal kingdom, to the attention by which, through the New Testament, the truest spiritual blessedness is expected in the kingdom of heaven. Since nothing is better than this, God helps us thus far.

“And there was peace between Israel and the Amorite.” Amorite is interpreted as “bitter” or “speaking.” The Apostle says to the Ephesians: “You who once were far off have been brought near in the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one and, breaking down the middle wall of the barrier, abolishing in his flesh the enmity—the law of commandments expressed in decrees—in order to create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and to reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself. And coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near; for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.” Thus far the Apostle.

[Col. 0034C] “Samuel also judged Israel all the days of his life. And he went each year, making the circuit of Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and judged Israel in those places,” and so forth. Bethel is a city twelve miles from Jerusalem, on the right for those traveling toward Neapolis. It was formerly called Luz—that is, “almond tree”—and fell by lot to the tribe of Benjamin. As we have said, Bethel was formerly called Luz. For the place which some suppose to be another town called Beth-aven is not so; rather, from the time when golden calves were fashioned there by Jeroboam son of Nebat and worshiped by the ten tribes (1 Kings 12), it was called Beth-aven—that is, “house of the idol”—where previously it had been called the House of God.

[Col. 0034D] This Gilgal is the one we mentioned above, Gilgol, east of ancient Jericho, on this side of the Jordan, where Joshua circumcised the people a second time, celebrated Passover, and, when the manna ceased, Israel ate wheat bread (Josh. 5). At that very place they also set up the stones that they had taken from the bed of the Jordan, and there the tabernacle of testimony stood for a long time (Josh. 4). It fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, and to this day a deserted site is shown at the second milestone from Jericho, held in wondrous veneration by the inhabitants of that region. Some also suppose that another Gilgal existed near Bethel.

Gilgal is interpreted as “rolling” or “revelation.” It was therefore fitting that the prophet of God judged Israel at Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. Returning in this way to Ramah, where his house was, he judged Israel there and built an altar to the Lord. He thus gives us an example: when we are required to pass judgment in the house of God, we should judge our neighbors neither arrogantly nor rashly nor with a malicious mind, but according to what sacred Scripture reveals to us, with good intention and fraternal love. In this way let us return to our house at Ramah—that is, let us return to the inner chambers of our hearts, so that we may devote ourselves to contemplation of God and judge our life within ourselves, in order that on the altar of faith we may offer the Lord grateful sacrifices of good works and good will.

CHAPTER VIII. That Samuel appointed his two sons as judges over Israel, but they transgressed; wherefore the people asked for a king, and Saul himself, while seeking his father’s donkeys, came to the prophet, by whom he was anointed king.

[Col. 0035B] (CHAP. 8.) “And it came to pass, when Samuel had grown old, that he appointed his sons judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of the second was Abijah; they were judges in Beersheba. And his sons did not walk in his ways, but turned aside after greed,” and so forth.

Josephus reports the matter as follows: “At that time the prophet Samuel established the following arrangement between the Israelites and the other Canaanites: after the Canaanite people had been removed and the city restored to the Jews, he ordered them to assemble there and to practice various trades with one another. He himself, making the rounds of the cities twice each year, judged them, and for a long time carried out everything with equity. Then, weighed down by old age and prevented from performing his customary duties, he entrusted authority to his sons. The elder was called Joel and the younger Abijah. He appointed one in the city of Bethlehem, so that he might sit and judge there, and the other in Beersheba. But just as good and moderate men can be produced from the wicked, so wicked men can be produced from the good. For, forgetting their father’s devotion and walking in the opposite direction, they suppressed justice by gifts and shameful profits, and issued judgments not according to truth but according to rewards, turning to feasts and costly banquets. First, they did what was offensive to God; second, they became hostile to their father, who had acted with great zeal and foresight so that even the people might know how to preserve justice. Therefore the people, deeply distressed that the prophet’s sons had insulted his former way of life, returned again to their father, who was staying in the city of Ramah, and laid before him all the injustices of his sons. And because he was old and already weakened by age and could no longer govern affairs, they pleaded and begged him to choose one of them as king, who would both rule over the nation and afflict the Philistines, who owed them payment for their former injustice.”

[Col. 0035D] Joel is interpreted as “beginning” or “he was God.” Abijah is interpreted as “the Lord is father” or “the father was.” Thus those who did not persevere in the justice they had begun and neglected to preserve the fatherhood of the Lord are rightly called “he was God” or “the father was,” to signify that those who abandoned justice and fell into iniquity were unworthy of God’s fatherhood.

But because Samuel’s sons, as was said above, turned aside after greed, accepted gifts, and proved such unjust judges that the people could not tolerate them and requested a king for themselves in the likeness of the other nations, God, angered by these petitions, spoke as follows to the grieving prophet:

[Col. 0036A] “Hearken to the voice of the people in everything they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, so that I should not reign over them. According to all the works that they have done from the day when I brought them out of Egypt to this day, just as they abandoned me and served foreign gods, so they are also doing to you. Now therefore listen to their voice; nevertheless, testify against them and proclaim to them the right of the king who will reign over them,” and so forth.

Saul, therefore, who was appointed king over the Israelites after God had been offended, represents the Jewish people. For just as he was raised to royal prominence in keeping with the character of those who asked for a king to rule over them and despised the Lord’s gentleness, and became harsh, rigid, and proud, so that he oppressed them more with a slavish burden than he granted them freedom, so also the Jewish people, although they were anointed in their priests and kings, nevertheless, because they were the son of the slave woman who gives birth to slavery, could never attain perfect freedom through that anointing. This was especially so because they refused to receive the one who came to them, who was truly king and had come to them in gentleness; through his rule they could have become free, had they been willing.

CHAPTER IX. The following, as above.

[Col. 0036C] Saul is therefore interpreted as “request,” and he was of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Kish, “son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bechorath, son of Aphiah.” These names aptly express the type of the Jews. Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand.” Kish means “hard,” or “vomit of a man,” or “a man vomiting.” Abiel means “my father is God.” Zeror means “small” or “turbulent.” Bechorath is interpreted as “your firstborn.”

He therefore who was God’s firstborn, according to what is written in the prophet, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Jer. 31), and whose father was God, was a son of the right hand, because he often prevailed over his enemies after being strengthened by the Lord’s help. But because he was always ungrateful for God’s benefits and, stiff-necked, erupted into blasphemy, he became from great, small, and from peaceful, turbulent.

His anointing as king, however, bore the image of Christ. Hence blessed David, himself also called Christ, said to the man who falsely claimed to have killed Saul: “How were you not afraid to lift your hand against the Lord’s Christ?” (2 Sam. 1). Likewise, the fact that Saul stood taller than everyone else from the shoulders upward signifies that Christ our head is exalted above us; the Father caused him to sit with him in the heavenly places, exalted above every power, every principality, and every name that is named (Eph. 1).

Moreover, what is said of Saul—that he was chosen and good, and that among the children of Israel there was none better than he—belongs more to Christ than to Saul himself. Concerning him the prophet says in the person of the Lord: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen; I will place my Spirit upon him, and he will announce judgment to the nations” (Isa. 42). Jeremiah likewise says: “O king of the nations, yours is the glory among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms there is none like you” (Jer. 10). And in the psalm: “For who among the clouds is equal to the Lord, or who among the sons of God is like God?” (Ps. 88).

[Col. 0037A] The fact that Saul sought his father Kish’s lost donkeys and, on the road he took, came to the prophet, who anointed him king, signifies that the Jews, following the foolishness of carnal understanding, were seeking the luxury of this world along the byways of error. For the donkey is a brutish and lustful animal. When they came to the prophet—that is, to Moses—they heard from him that the donkeys had been found; that is, they learned that they would eat the good things of the land. From him they received the oil of anointing, and they were told in advance that the reins of the kingdom would be theirs, by which for a time he would rescue their brothers from the hands of their enemies.

The fact that Samuel leads Saul up to the high place and prepares refreshment there signifies that Moses and all the prophets, through their teachings, continually urged the Hebrew people toward higher things, so that, refreshed by spiritual knowledge, they might stand at the summit of the virtues and not fall back into the pit of vices. But the fact that Samuel appeared to Saul when Saul was seeking the Seer and spoke to him, saying:

[Col. 0037C] (CHAP. 9.) “I am the Seer. Go up before me to the high place, so that you may eat with me today; then I will let you go in the morning, and I will tell you everything that is in your heart. As for the donkeys that you lost the day before yesterday, do not be anxious, because they have been found,” and so forth. (From the Hebrew.)

As the Hebrews report, Saul had in his heart the knowledge that he would become king, because he had seen in a vision that he was placed at the top of a palm tree. That vision was a royal sign.

CHAPTER X. The following, as above.

[Col. 0037D] “When you depart from there and go farther, and come to the oak of Tabor, three men will meet you there going up to God at Bethel.” There these men were going to Bethel for the sake of prayer, where Jacob had erected a stone.

“After this you will come to the hill of God.” The hill of God was the place where the prophets lived.

“And the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them,” and so forth. The Jews say that he prophesied there concerning the future age, Gog and Magog, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishment of the wicked.

“When all these signs have come upon you, do whatever your hand finds to do, because God is with you,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: By these signs you will know that God has willed you to be king; therefore do everything that must be done by you in a royal manner, and God is with you.

[Col. 0038A] The fact that all the signs Samuel had foretold to Saul came to pass just as he had predicted, and that Saul himself, after passing the oak of Tabor—which is a mountain in the middle of Galilee, a lofty height in a remarkably rounded plain, and is interpreted as “coming light”—reached the hill of the Lord, the place so called because of some benefit bestowed by the Lord, and prophesied among the prophets who were standing there, signifies that everything the lawgiver and the prophets had foretold concerning the Jews came to pass for them, whether in prosperity or in adversity.

Yet the Jews themselves, holding the books of the law and the prophets, seem almost to have divined the future, since by reading and reciting them they are known to proclaim the future mysteries concerning Christ and the Church that were written in them. (From the Hebrew.)

[Col. 0038B] What is written about Saul himself—that when all who had known him yesterday and the day before saw that he was with the prophets and prophesying, they said to one another:

“What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” Another answered the other, saying: “And who is their father?” Therefore it became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” and so forth.

The question “Who is their father?” was uttered as though it meant: “Who is greater than he in dignity and wisdom?” For one who is so learned and wise can very well associate with the prophets and be called their father—that is, their teacher. In Scripture, “father” is sometimes used for “teacher,” as when Elisha calls Elijah “father,” that is, “teacher,” saying: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer” (2 Kings 2). And in the book of Job Elihu calls Job “father,” that is, “teacher,” in this way: “My father, let Job be tested to the end” (Job 34).

CHAPTER XI. The war of Nahash the Ammonite against Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul defeated while fighting with the Israelites.

[Col. 0038C] (CHAP. 11.) “After this Nahash the Ammonite came up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead,” and so forth.

What does this event signify—that Nahash the Ammonite wished to make a covenant with Jabesh-gilead on the condition that he would gouge out the right eyes of everyone, so that they might become a reproach throughout all Israel—if not the war of heretics against the Church? Nahash is interpreted as “serpent.” Ammon means “pressing,” “constricting,” or “people of sorrow.” Jabesh is interpreted as “dried up,” and Gilead as “heap of testimony.”

Thus Nahash, the ancient serpent and prince of the Ammonites—that is, of heretics, who are rightly called a people of sorrow because they do not possess the joy of the Holy Spirit—arranges a covenant with the people of the Church in order to gouge out everyone’s right eyes; that is, to take away the sight of sound and orthodox faith. For he wants them to be allied with him in such a way that, having only a left eye, they perceive only what is perverse.

But the mind of the faithful, dried up from all the stains of vices, gathers together a heap of testimony—that is, the statements of the holy Scriptures—in order that, fortified by their protection, it may be able to resist the most wicked enemy with courage. They send word throughout all the borders of Israel—that is, to the teachers of the Church who preside over the peoples—so that they may bring them aid and set the shield of faith against the enemies who oppose them.

[Col. 0039A] At once Saul, moved by the Spirit of the Lord, together with the prophet and priest Samuel, numbered the people, “and he found three hundred thousand warriors among the children of Israel, and thirty thousand men of Judah.”

“And he numbered them,” he says, “at Bezek.” (From Jerome.) Bezek is the city of King Adoni-bezek; even today there are two villages called Bezek, near one another, at the seventh milestone for those descending from Neapolis toward Scythopolis. Bezek is interpreted as “poverty,” and, if I am not mistaken, it can signify the small number of the elect. Hence Truth himself says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22).

Our king, Christ, who is priest and prophet, preparing to engage his enemies, chose from both peoples soldiers distinguished by faith in the Trinity and outstanding in the perfection of good works. He puts his enemies to flight and strikes them with the sword of the Spirit, from the morning when faith dawns until the light of knowledge and the warmth of charity spread throughout the entire city of the Church.

Therefore it is rightly written that those who remained after this slaughter were scattered, so that not even two of them were left together. For the gathering of the wicked is not joined by the bond of true love and the unity of faith; separated from one another by dissension, they become uncertain and unstable and, by the power of divine judgment, separated from one another in mind as well as in body, they will be scattered everywhere. Hence the Prophet said to the Lord: “Behold, your enemies, O Lord, will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered” (Ps. 91).

CHAPTER XII. The following, as above.

[Col. 0039C] In Samuel’s words to the people, reproving them for their wrongful choice of an earthly king when they had the Lord himself as king, the following was added:

(CHAP. 12.) “And the Lord sent Jerubbaal, and Bedan, and Barak, and Jephthah, and Samuel, and delivered you from the hand of your enemies all around, and you dwelt in security,” and so forth.

He names Jerubbaal, who in the book of Judges is called by another name, Gideon. Bedan is Samson himself, the strongest of men, concerning whom the aforementioned book relates that he defended Israel against the Philistines.

[Col. 0039D] “And Samuel cried to the Lord, and the Lord gave thunder and rains on that day,” and so forth. This Samuel, whom God heard when he invoked the Lord’s name, obtained rain in the time of harvest. (From Isidore.) For in the sacred Scriptures rain signifies the words of the Gospel or of the law, as Moses said: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32). Christ therefore gave this rain to the world in the time of harvest—that is, when the Gentiles had to be gathered—so that, just as grain is gathered into storehouses, the Gentiles might be gathered into the bosom of the Church.

CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Saul the king’s organization of his army; concerning Saul’s offense against the Lord when he offered the burnt offering; and concerning the Philistines’ prohibition against weapons being manufactured throughout the entire land of Israel.

(CAP. XIII.) “Saul was one year old when he began to reign. And he reigned over Israel for two years.” He spoke by anticipation about Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul. Concerning him it is likewise written later: “Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years.” Therefore, if all the time is reckoned together from the death of Eli through the period during which Samuel and afterward Saul ruled Israel, forty years are found, according to the testimony of Chronicles, up to Saul’s death. From this it is clear that when Saul began to reign—according to this computation—he had a son who was one year old, that is, in his first year. After Saul had closed his final day, this son held the kingdom of Israel for two years, until, after he was killed by brigands, the whole kingdom passed at once to David.

Some wish to understand the statement as referring to Saul himself, namely, that he had been one year old when he began to reign—that is, humble and gentle—according to what the Psalmist says: “If I was not humble-minded, like a child weaned at his mother’s breast” (Ps. CXXX). But that he reigned for two years means that he held the kingdom properly, which he is known to have done at the beginning of his reign. After, however, he had been abandoned by God because of his disobedience and God’s Spirit had departed from him, although he retained power, he seemed no longer to exercise rule but rather to lead a tyrannical life.

“And there were with Saul two thousand at Michmash, and at Mount Bethel a thousand with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin.” (From Jerome.) Michmash is still shown as a large village within the boundaries of Aelia, retaining its ancient name, eight miles distant from it, near the village of Ramah; its name is interpreted as “humility.” Gibeah, in the tribe of Benjamin, is the city of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, where Eleazar himself was buried. It is now a village called Gibeah, at the twelfth milestone from Eleutheropolis; there the tomb of the prophet Habakkuk is also shown. Gibeah is interpreted as “the hill of a cousin.”

It was fitting that three thousand Israelites should be chosen to fight against the Philistines, because only those who are suited for spiritual warfare, to fight against the enemies of the Church, possess the perfect faith of the Trinity, in which they can resist their enemies from a superior position.

(From the Hebrew.) In the passage where the historian, while recounting Saul’s battle against the Philistines, continues by saying, “When the men of Israel saw that they were placed in a narrow situation—for the people were distressed—they hid themselves in caves, in secret places, among rocks, in pits, and in cisterns. But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead,” a question of no little importance arises. If Israel hid itself in the places mentioned, what does the statement “But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan” mean?

The matter is resolved as follows. While certain Israelites were hiding—those who had deserted Saul and the people who were with him—some of them, namely those who are here called Hebrews, were terrified by fear, defected from Saul and from the men who were with him, and went down to the camp of the Philistines. The following passage makes this clearer and more evident, where it says: “But the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines yesterday and the day before, and had gone up with them into the camp, returned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.” Therefore all the Israelites who had hidden themselves on Mount Ephraim, when they heard what the Philistines had done, joined their own people in the battle.

“While Saul was still at Gilgal, all the people who followed him were terrified. He waited seven days according to Samuel’s appointed time, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal. And the people dispersed from him. Therefore Saul said: Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings; and he offered the burnt offering,” etc.

Some think that Saul offered the burnt offering without blame, since Samuel, whom he had expected according to the appointed seven-day period, had not come. But whoever carefully distinguishes this passage will find that Saul was rightly blamed and charged with disobedience.

Among the Hebrews, however, the passage is divided as follows: “And you shall go down before me to Gilgal; for I shall surely come down to you.” Then it continues: “For offering offerings and sacrificing peace offerings, you shall wait seven days, until I come to you and show you what you are to do.” Samuel therefore did not command Saul to await his arrival for seven days; rather, he wished Saul to wait for him during those same seven days in order to offer offerings and sacrifice peace offerings. Saul did not do this at all, and therefore he is rightly blamed and marked with the reproach of folly.

(From Augustine.) As for the words that Samuel is read to have spoken to Saul, who had transgressed the Lord’s command: “You have acted foolishly and have not kept the commandments of the Lord your God, which he commanded you. If you had not done this, the Lord would now have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But your kingdom shall not rise any further. The Lord has sought for himself a man according to his own heart, and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people, because you have not kept what the Lord commanded”—this should not be understood as though God had prepared Saul himself to reign forever and afterward had been unwilling to maintain that arrangement when Saul sinned. God was not ignorant that Saul would sin; rather, he had prepared his kingdom as a figure of the eternal kingdom.

Therefore he added: “And now your kingdom shall not stand for you.” What was signified in Saul did stand and shall stand. It shall not stand from Saul himself, because he was not destined to reign forever, nor was his offspring; nor, at least through descendants succeeding one another, would it appear that what was said “forever” had been fulfilled.

“And the Lord seeks for himself a man,” etc. Whether this signifies David or the Mediator of the New Testament himself, who was prefigured in the anointing with which David himself and his descendants were anointed, God does not seek a man as though he did not know where he was. Rather, through the figure of a man he speaks in human fashion, because by speaking in this way he also seeks us.

For we were already known not only to God the Father but also to his Only-Begotten Son, who came to seek what had perished, to such an extent that we were chosen in him before the foundation of the world. Therefore, when he said, “He will seek for himself,” he meant, “He will have his own.” Hence in Latin this verb takes a preposition and is rendered adquirit, “he acquires”; its meaning is sufficiently clear, although even without the added preposition quaerere, “to seek,” may be understood as “to acquire,” from which lucrum and quaestus—“profit” and “gain”—derive their names.

“Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had taken care lest the Hebrews make a sword or a spear,” etc.

The fact that the Philistines, so that they might more easily overcome the Hebrews, prevented there from being any blacksmith throughout the land of Israel, lest the Hebrews make a sword or spear, signifies that the devil strives—partly through pagans, partly through heretics, and partly through false Christians—to prevent teachers from existing in the Church who, by manufacturing spiritual weapons, might equip Christians engaged in battle.

For pagans, as we read in the histories, prevented Christians from being instructed in the liberal studies that the pagans considered of the highest importance. Likewise, we read that heretics persuaded the rulers of the nations to drive the defenders of the Catholic faith into exile, so that they could more easily turn a people deprived of its shepherd away from the truth. Even now, in the peace of the Church, that same ancient enemy strives in a similar manner to turn away from diligent instruction as many as he can of those who preside over peoples, lest they provide their subjects with the doctrine of truth, so that he may deceive the unwary more easily.

“For through the envy of the devil death entered the whole world” (Wis. II). Those who belong to his party imitate him. Thus the devil is bound by a twofold guilt: pride and envy—pride, by which he himself fell; envy, by which he strives to cast others down.

The Philistines are interpreted as “a double ruin,” and the Hebrews as “those who pass over.”

“For here we have no lasting dwelling, but we seek one that is eternal in the heavens” (Heb. XIII).

CHAPTER XIV. How Saul, about to fight against the Philistines, proclaimed a fast to the entire army; how Jonathan, unaware of it, broke the fast by tasting honey; and how for this reason he was scarcely freed from death by the prayers of the people.

Meanwhile Saul, as he proceeded to fight against the Philistines, proclaimed a fast for the whole army until they returned from battle. But his son Jonathan, seeing honey spread across the surface of the field, “extended the tip of his staff, dipped it into a honeycomb, tasted it, and his eyes were enlightened,” etc.

(From Isidore.) His eyes were not enlightened so that he could see, since he had seen before, but so that he might discern, because he had touched what was forbidden. For that fall, like Adam’s, made him attentive and rendered him ashamed.

By this event everyone who strives to serve God and, having become a participant in the Holy Spirit, enters the spiritual camp to fight, is warned that all the enticements of worldly pleasures must be despised. Jonathan’s name aptly expresses this. It is interpreted as “the gift of a dove,” or “the gift of the Lord.” He is rightly called the gift of a dove or of the Lord who, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, prepares himself to despise the enticements of the world.

For no one can attack the spiritual Allophyles—that is, the rulers of darkness—with manly courage if he still neglects to avoid the sweetness of this world: “For the lips of a prostitute drip honey” (Prov. V). That is, carnal pleasure introduces unlawful delight. According to mystical interpretations, Jonathan is thought to have tasted this honey and, being detected by lot, was scarcely freed through the prayers of the people.

Thus it is plainly evident that the person overcome by the pleasures and enticements of the world needs the intercession of the saints and the prayers of the brethren. For the greater the insolence with which he has resisted the unanimous counsel of ecclesiastical discipline, the greater is the help he requires from many, so that one who cannot be saved by his own merit may be reconciled through the devout prayers of others and freed from the danger threatening him.

(CAP. XIV.) “The people were exceedingly weary, and turning to the spoil, they took sheep, oxen, and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate with the blood. Saul was informed, and they told him that the people had sinned against the Lord by eating with the blood. He said: You have acted treacherously; roll a large stone over to me now. And Saul said: Scatter yourselves among the people and tell them that each man is to bring me his ox and his ram, slaughter it on this stone, and eat; then you will not sin against the Lord by eating with the blood. So all the people brought each his ox in his hand until night, and slaughtered them there,” etc.

They are said to have sinned against the Lord and to have eaten with the blood because, after slaughtering the victims, they did not offer the fat and the blood to the priests at the sanctuary according to the commandment of the law, even though they had the sanctuary with them.

When the sanctuary was far away, the blood of the victims that they prepared for their own food was commanded to be poured out upon the ground. But when the sanctuary was present, the blood of the sacrifices was commanded to be poured out upon the altar of the Lord, as it is written in the book of Deuteronomy: “You shall pour out the blood of your sacrifices upon the altar, but you yourself shall eat the flesh” (Deut. XII). The people mentioned above did not do this; therefore it is said that they sinned against the Lord and that they ate with the blood. The text continues.

“Saul built an altar to the Lord,” etc. At that time he first began to build an altar to the Lord. Therefore it must be asked: since he is earlier said to have built an altar when he was rebuked by Samuel, why is it said here, “At that time he first began to build an altar to the Lord”?

He is indeed said earlier to have built an altar, but because he built it disobediently, he is not understood to have built it to the Lord. Here, however, because he built it obediently and rightly, he is declared to have built it to the Lord.

CHAPTER XV. Concerning the war that Saul waged against Amalek at the Lord’s command, in which he offended the Lord through disobedience because, out of greed, he did not destroy all Amalek together with all its possessions; for this reason the Lord reproached him and rebuked him through the prophet.

(CAP. XV.) “And Samuel said to Saul: The Lord sent me to anoint you as king over Israel, his people. Now therefore hear the voice of the Lord. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, how he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt. Now therefore go and strike Amalek, and destroy all that belongs to him. Do not spare him, but kill man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.”

The Lord commanded that Amalek’s animals also be destroyed so that no remembrance of Amalek would remain even in his animals. For the Lord had said that he would blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Therefore Saul was commanded to destroy him utterly, from human being to animal. Since his memory—that is, the memory of Amalek—was not completely blotted out, Saul’s sin and disobedience were responsible.

Concerning Amalek, the book of Deuteronomy says: “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way when you were coming out of Egypt, how he met you and struck down the hindmost of your army, those who were exhausted and sitting down” (Deut. XXV).

Here the Hebrews understand “the exhausted” to mean those who, according to the law, were unclean and remained outside the camp. The Amalekites are said to have struck them down because, as they themselves report, they cut off their circumcision and, in mockery of God, threw it toward heaven.

“Saul said to the Kenite: Go away, withdraw, and depart from him, lest I involve you with him. For you showed mercy to all the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt,” etc.

The Kenite is Jethro, Moses’ relative. The Kenites were descended from him; they had gone down to Amalek and lived with him, since he was their kinsman and they possessed an inheritance in his land. The Kenite is said to have shown mercy to the children of Israel either because he sheltered Moses in the land of Midian or because he gave Moses advice about how to govern the multitude of the people.

At the Lord’s command Saul entered into battle against Amalek. After all the enemies had been killed, he spared Agag the king and was unwilling to destroy everything according to the Lord’s command. For this the Lord became angry with him. Afterward Samuel came to Saul and rebuked him for this deed, saying:

“When you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head over the tribes of Israel? And the Lord anointed you king over Israel?” etc.

What is cast down by the rebuke of the Lord’s word except the pride of the exalted king? Anyone who has been placed in authority can profitably apply this to his own correction.

When Saul considered himself little in his own eyes, he was made head over the tribes of Israel. But, supported by temporal power, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself to the rest because he had greater power than all, he considered himself great above everyone. In a remarkable manner, when he appeared little to himself, he was great before the Lord; but when he appeared great to himself, he was little before the Lord.

Often, when the mind is inflated by the abundance of its subjects, it is corrupted into the luxury of pride, with the very height of power acting as its seducer. The person who knows both how to hold power and how to oppose it governs that power well. He governs it well who knows through it to rise above faults, and knows within it to live in equality with others.

For the human mind is often lifted up even when it is supported by no power. How much more does it raise itself on high when power is also joined to it? Yet the person who knows carefully to take from power what helps him, to conquer what tempts him, to regard himself as equal to others, and nevertheless to place himself above sinners in the zeal of retribution, surely administers that power well.

For it is written: “They have made you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Eccli. XXXII).

And when Saul excused himself by saying that he had preserved everything according to what had been commanded him, he said:

“I heard the voice of the Lord, and I walked in the way by which the Lord sent me. I brought back Agag, king of Amalek, and I destroyed Amalek. But the people took from the spoil sheep and oxen, the firstfruits of what had been slaughtered, to sacrifice to the Lord their God at Gilgal.”

Samuel said: “Does the Lord desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, and not rather that the voice of the Lord be obeyed? For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams. For resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry.”

(From Augustine.) Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slaughtered, whereas through obedience one’s own will is slaughtered. Therefore each person placates God more quickly when, having restrained the pride of his own will before God’s eyes, he offers himself with the sword of the commandment.

Disobedience is compared with the sin of divination so that the great virtue of obedience may be demonstrated. What should be thought about obedience’s praise is therefore shown more clearly by contrast. If resistance is like the sin of divination, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith, or is that by which anyone is convicted of unbelief, even if he appears faithful.

Hence Solomon says in praise of obedience: “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XXI). An obedient man speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we conquer ourselves in our hearts.

For this reason Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

For what would happen if he did his own will? Would he cast out those who came to him? Who does not know that the Son’s will does not differ from the Father’s will? But because the first man, who wished to do his own will, departed from the joy of paradise, the Second, coming for the redemption of humanity and showing that he did the Father’s will and not his own, taught us to remain within.

Therefore, when he does not his own will but the Father’s, he does not cast out those who come to him, because by subjecting us to obedience through his example, he closes the path by which we might depart.

Again he says: “I can do nothing from myself; but as I hear, I judge” (John V). We are commanded to preserve obedience even unto death. But if he judges as he hears, then he will also obey when he comes as judge. Therefore, lest obedience seem burdensome to us until the end of the present life, our Redeemer judges while preserving obedience even when he comes as judge.

What wonder, then, if sinful humanity submits itself to obedience during the shortness of the present life, when the Mediator of God and humanity does not abandon obedience even while he rewards the obedient?

It must be understood, however, that evil is never done through obedience. Sometimes, however, a good deed that is being performed ought to be interrupted through obedience.

The tree in paradise that God forbade humanity to touch was not evil. Rather, so that the well-created human being might grow through the better merit of obedience, it was fitting that God should also forbid him something good, so that the virtue of his action might be more genuine, inasmuch as, abstaining from a good thing, he showed humility by submitting himself to his Creator.

But note what is said there: “Eat from every tree of paradise, but do not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II). When someone forbids subjects some good thing, he must grant many others, lest the obedient mind perish completely if it is entirely deprived of good things.

The Lord permitted his creature to eat from all the trees of paradise while forbidding one, so that he might restrain the creature whom he did not wish to destroy but to advance more easily from one tree, the more widely he released him to all the others.

But since we are sometimes commanded to receive the prosperous things of this world and sometimes its adversities, we must understand most carefully that obedience is sometimes nothing if it contains something of one’s own will, and sometimes is very small if it contains nothing of one’s own will.

When worldly success is commanded, when a position of authority is ordered, the person who obeys in order to obtain these things empties obedience of its virtue if he also longs for them from his own desire. For he does not place himself under obedience who serves the desire of his own ambition in order to obtain the prosperous things of this life.

Again, when contempt of the world is commanded, when disgrace and humiliation are ordered, unless the mind itself desires these things, the person who unwillingly and reluctantly descends to what is despised in this life diminishes the merit of his obedience. Obedience is brought to harm when the mind’s own wishes do not in any measure accompany it in accepting the reproaches of this world.

Obedience must therefore possess something of its own in adversity, while in prosperity it must in every way possess nothing of its own, so that in adversity it may be more glorious insofar as it is joined even by desire to the divine ordering, and in prosperity it may be more genuine insofar as it is entirely separated, for the time being, from the present glory that it receives from God.

“Saul said to Samuel: I have sinned, because I transgressed the word of the Lord and your words, fearing the people and obeying their voice. But now, I beg you, bear my sin and return with me, that I may worship the Lord.

Samuel said to Saul: I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord; and the Lord has rejected you, so that you may not be king over Israel.”

The prophet rebukes the king for the disobedience by which he did not take care to fulfill the Lord’s command, and he predicts that Saul will lose the kingdom because he was unwilling to follow the certainty of God’s commands.

And rightly is the person cast down from the height of power who does not know how to hold the kingdom properly. He holds authority properly who subjects himself in humility to his superior in order to obey, and places himself before his inferior with authority in order to teach. If Saul had obeyed God’s commands, he would have ruled the people properly.

“Samuel turned to leave, but Saul seized the edge of his cloak, and it was torn. Samuel said to him: The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor, who is better than you.”

Consider the mystery: just as the high priest tore his garment during the Lord’s Passion (Matt. XXVI), so King Saul is now described as tearing the prophet’s garment. In both cases, through both powers—the royal and the priestly—the tearing of garments occurred, to show that the stability of kingdom or priesthood could not be established among the Jewish people, who refused to receive the true king and priest who came to them, namely the Lord Christ.

“Moreover, the Victor in Israel will not spare and will not be turned by repentance. For he is not a man, that he should repent,” etc.

The Victor in Israel is the Lord, to whom every victory is rightly attributed, because he is not changeable but judges all things according to justice and truth.

It should be noted, however, that another edition has:

“Samuel said: I will not return with you, because you have rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord rejects you, so that you may not be king over Israel. And Samuel turned his face to leave, and Saul seized the edge of the double garment, and tore it. Samuel said to him: The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today, and he will give it to your neighbor who is good over you. And Israel will be divided in two, and he will not turn back, nor will he repent, because he is not like a man who repents; he threatens, and does not remain.”

(From Augustine.) The one to whom it is said, “The Lord rejects you, so that you may not be king over Israel, and the Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today,” reigned over Israel for forty years—the same span of time as David—and heard this at the beginning of his reign.

We should therefore understand it to have been said because no one from Saul’s lineage was destined to reign. We should turn our attention to David’s lineage, from which, according to the flesh, arose “the Mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II).

The wording found in many Latin manuscripts is not, “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand,” but, as we found it written in the Greek manuscripts, “The Lord has torn the kingdom from Israel, from your hand.” The phrase “from your hand” is therefore to be understood together with “from Israel.”

This man also figuratively represented the person of the people of Israel, which people was destined to lose the kingdom, while Christ Jesus our Lord would reign through the New Testament not carnally but spiritually.

When it is said, “And he will give it to your neighbor,” this refers to kinship according to the flesh. For Christ is from Israel according to the flesh, as Saul also was.

As for the addition, “who is good over you,” it may indeed be understood as “better than you,” and some have interpreted it in this way. But it is better understood as “good over you,” meaning that because he is good, he is therefore over you, according to that other prophetic statement: “Until I place all your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. CIX). Israel is among these enemies, for Christ took the kingdom away from his persecutor, although there was also there “an Israelite in whom there was no deceit” (John I), a kind of grain among that straw.

For the apostles came from there, as did so many martyrs, the first of whom was Stephen (Acts VII); and from there came so many churches that the apostle Paul mentions, glorifying the Lord in their conversion.

Concerning this matter, I have no doubt that what follows should be understood: “And Israel will be divided in two.” That is, Israel hostile to Christ and Israel adhering to Christ; Israel belonging to the slave woman and Israel belonging to the free woman.

These two groups were initially together, just as Abraham was still attached to the slave woman, until the barren woman, made fruitful through the grace of Christ, cried out: “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Gen. XXI).

Because of Solomon’s sin, when his son Rehoboam was reigning, we know that Israel was divided in two and continued in that state, with each part having its own kings, until the whole nation was overthrown and deported by the Chaldeans in a great devastation.

But what does this have to do with Saul, when, if such a threat were intended, it would more properly have been threatened to David, whose son Solomon was? Finally, the Hebrew people are not now divided among themselves, but are scattered throughout the lands indiscriminately in fellowship with the same error.

The division, however, that God threatened under the person of Saul, who represented that kingdom and people, signifies a division of the kingdom and people that is eternal and unchangeable.

This is indicated by the addition: “And he will not turn back, nor will he repent, because he is not like a man who repents; he threatens, and remains.” That is, a man threatens and does not remain; God, however, does not change as a human being does.

Where Scripture says that God repents, a change in circumstances is signified, while divine foreknowledge remains unchangeable. Therefore, where it says that he does not repent, it is understood that he does not change.

Through these words we clearly see that a divinely pronounced judgment concerning this division of the people of Israel was declared to be wholly unalterable and perpetual.

For all who have passed over to Christ, or are passing over, or will pass over, were not of that hostile group from the standpoint of God’s foreknowledge, though they belong to the same nature of the human race. All Israelites who adhere to Christ and persevere in him will never be joined with those Israelites who persist in being his enemies to the end of this life. Rather, they will remain forever in the division that was here foretold.

“Samuel said: Bring Agag, king of Amalek, to me. And Agag was brought to him, exceedingly fat. Agag said: Does bitter death separate us in this way? Samuel said: Just as your sword made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women. And Samuel cut Agag into pieces before the Lord at Gilgal,” etc.

When some people read in Scripture that the saints spared none of their enemies, they become cruel; thirsting for human blood, they say: “The righteous also struck down their enemies in such a way that none was left alive by them.” They do not understand that mysteries are shadowed forth in these words and that we are thereby more especially shown that, when fighting against vices, we must leave none of them behind but destroy them all.

For if we spare them, we must know that this is counted as guilt against us, just as it was counted against Saul, who preserved the king of Amalek alive. How can anyone remain righteous if he continues to preserve some sin within himself, as Saul did?

But the saints, represented by Samuel, rage against their enemies—that is, against the vices of sinners—in such a way that they do not allow any sin to remain unpunished.

CHAPTER XVI. How, after Saul had been rejected, David was chosen by Samuel as king, and how David himself played the lyre before the raging Saul.

(CAP. XVI.) “The Lord said to Samuel: How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and come; I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided a king for myself among his sons,” etc.

Therefore, after Saul had been rejected because of his disobedience, God sent Samuel to Jesse; and, taking a horn of oil, Samuel anointed David as king.

But let us see how this same David prophetically signified Christ. David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” And what is stronger than that Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev. V), who conquered the world (John XVI)? And what is more desirable than the one of whom it is said: “The one desired by all the nations has come” (Hag. II)?

This David is anointed as a future king, announcing Christ through that anointing. For Christ is named from chrism, that is, from anointing.

After Jesse’s seven older sons had been rejected, the youngest in age was chosen for the kingdom. For, with the Jewish priesthood and kingdom—that is, those of the former people, who observed the Sabbath according to the law—rejected, Christ our Lord, the head of the lesser people, exercised an everlasting priesthood and was anointed as king. His kingdom has no end, and all nations, languages, and tribes will serve him.

David was transferred from the pastoral duty of tending animals to the kingship of human beings. Our David, however, Jesus himself, was taken away from the oxen of the Jewish people and transferred to reign over the nations. For Christ is no longer in Judea; he was taken away from there and now feeds the flocks of the nations.

Therefore, when the Lord had departed from Saul because of his disobedience, Saul was seized by an evil spirit, “and the evil spirit from the Lord tormented him.”

“Then Saul’s servants said to him: ‘Behold, an evil spirit from the Lord is agitating you,’” and so forth. In this book the question is often raised concerning the spirit that agitated Saul: if it was from the Lord, why was it evil; if it was evil, why is it called the Lord’s? This statement, contained in two words, embraces both God’s just authority and the devil’s unjust power. For the same spirit is evil through its most wicked will, and the Lord’s through the most just authority it has received. Why, then, is the devil called the Lord’s spirit? Because of his ministry: God makes good use even of all evil spirits, whether for the condemnation of some, for correction, or for testing. And although wickedness is not from God, authority nevertheless comes from no one but God. (From Gregory.)

Thus the ancient enemy of the human race, although he always desires to afflict the righteous, cannot prevail in the matter of temptation unless he receives power from our Creator. Hence every will of the devil is unjust; yet, with God’s permission, all his power is just. Of himself he unjustly desires to tempt anyone at all, but God justly permits those who are to be tempted to be tempted, and to be tempted in the manner in which they are to be tempted.

Thus it is rightly said here: “An evil spirit from the Lord is agitating you.” Behold, one and the same spirit is called both the Lord’s and evil: the Lord’s, namely, by the permission of just authority; but evil, by the desire of an unjust will.

(From Isidore.) The same is also said elsewhere (I Kings 26): “A sleep from the Lord,” which had seized Saul’s soldiers when David took the spear and cup from beside the head of the sleeping man—not because that sleep was then from the Lord so that he might sleep, but because the sleep that had then overtaken the men had been infused by God’s will, so that David, his servant, would not be perceived as present in that place.

The spirit of God is therefore called evil—that is, God’s minister for doing in Saul what the most powerful Judge of all judged that he should suffer—for that spirit was not God’s in the will by which it was evil; but in the creature by which it had been created, and in the power which it had received not from itself but from the Lord of all, by his equity, it was God’s. It therefore ought not to be feared, because it can do nothing unless permitted.

(From Gregory.) In the Gospel also, when the Lord was driving Legion out of a man, it said: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Matthew 8). The only power, then, that should be feared is that which, after permitting the enemy to rage, makes even his unjust will serve the use of a just judgment.

(From Isidore.) Now David was skilled in musical songs. For the rational and measured harmony of diverse sounds, joined together in concordant variety, represents to the Church in an orderly way the unity that daily resounds in many forms and is modulated with mystical sweetness. While still a boy, David, singing sweetly—or rather, powerfully—on the lyre, restrained the evil spirit that was at work in Saul. This was not because such power belonged to the lyre itself, but because the figure of Christ’s cross, mystically represented by wood and the stretching of strings, and the passion itself that was being sung, already then crushed demonic spirits.

Allegorically, by this deed we are instructed by David to show compassion toward our neighbor. A proud rich man is often to be soothed by the charm of exhortation, because hard wounds are often softened by gentle fomentations, and the fury of the insane is frequently restored to health when a physician speaks soothingly. When one condescends to them with sweetness, the sickness of madness is alleviated.

Nor should it be observed negligently that, when an opposing spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his insanity. For whom does Saul signify, if not the exaltation of the powerful? And whom does David indicate, if not the humble life of the saints? When, therefore, Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated as David sings; for when the minds of the powerful are turned into fury through pride, it is fitting that they should be recalled to mental health by the tranquility of our speech, as though by the sweetness of a lyre.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning David’s battle against Goliath the Philistine, whom he himself killed by a cast stone

[Column 0051B] (CHAPTER XVII.) “After this, the Philistines led their armies out for battle at Socoh of Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah, in the territory of Dammim.”

(From Jerome.) Socoh is a town in the tribe of Judah. Even today there are two villages for travelers going to Aelia from Eleutheropolis, at the new milestone of the public road: one situated on a mountain and the other in the plain; they are called Socoh. It is interpreted as “branch” or “humility.”

Azekah is a city of the Canaanites in the territory of the tribe of Judah, as far as which Joshua pursued the five kings (Joshua 10). Even today a village called Azekah lies between Eleutheropolis and Aelia. Azekah is interpreted as “strength” or “snare.”

Duma, or Dammim, in the tribe of Judah, is a large village in the Daroma—that is, in the southern region—within the territory of Eleutheropolis, seventeen miles distant from it. Duma is interpreted as “silence” or “joy.”

“Saul and the men of Israel, moreover, gathered in the Valley of the Terebinth.” The terebinth is at Shechem, beneath which Jacob hid the idols (Genesis 35), near Neapolis.

“And they drew up their battle line to fight against the Philistines,” and so forth. Here Josephus says:

“After not much time had passed, the Palestinians gathered again and, assembling an army greater than all the Israelites, encamped between Socoh and Azekah. Against them Saul again led out his army. He set up camp on a certain mountain and forced the Palestinians to abandon their former camp and come to the opposite side of the mountain that Saul had occupied. A mountain lying between them divided their armies.”

“And a bastard went out from the camp of the Philistines, named Goliath, from Gath, six cubits and a span tall. He had a bronze helmet on his head and wore a coat of mail. The weight of his coat of mail was five thousand bronze shekels. He had bronze greaves on his legs, and a bronze shield covered his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam. The iron of his spear itself weighed six hundred iron shekels, and his shield-bearer went before him. Standing, he shouted against all the ranks of Israel and said to them: ‘Why have you come prepared for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose one man from among yourselves and let him come down to single combat. If he can fight with me and strike me, we shall be your servants. But if I prevail and strike him, you shall serve us and be our servants.’ And the Philistine said: ‘Today I have reproached the armies of Israel. Give me a man who will enter single combat with me,’” and so forth.

(From the Hebrew.) He is called a bastard because he was born of a giant as father and a woman of Gath as mother.

“David, however, was the son of an Ephrathite man from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse, who had eight sons.” It is asked why he is said here to have had eight sons, when in Chronicles (I, 2) no more than seven are read of. The matter is resolved as follows. Nathan the prophet, the son of his son Shemaah, had been brought up and nourished in the place of a son. For seven of his sons are recorded as having been brought before Samuel, while the eighth was in the pasture. It is clear that Nathan was among those brought forward; he is also called Jonathan. Concerning him it is said in the final part of Samuel: “Jonathan, son of Shimea, the brother of David, struck him” (II Samuel 21). It should be noted that wherever he is called a prophet, he is written as Nathan, not Jonathan.

“The battle of the Philistines against Israel” may not inappropriately be understood as the battle of evil spirits against the Church of God. From the camp of the Philistines, therefore, there comes forth a bastard named Goliath, of immense stature, who can rightly signify the devil’s pride. Our David engaged him in single combat, struck him down, and delivered God’s people from fear of him. David had killed both a lion and a bear: the bear, namely, the devil; the lion, Antichrist—the one now secretly lying in wait for human beings, the other raging openly in the future.

(From Isidore.) This David overcame the giant in battle when foreigners were fighting against the people of God. Pride challenged humility; the devil challenged Christ. Holy David took up weapons of war in order to advance against Goliath. Because of his age and the small stature of his body, he could not carry those weapons; he cast off what burdened him, took five stones from the stream, and placed them in a shepherd’s pouch. Armed with these, he advanced and conquered.

This was what that David did. But if we search out the mysteries, Christ is understood in David. Foreseeing the time of the revelation and commendation of the grace of the New Testament, he laid down the weapons and took five stones. He laid down the bodily sacraments of the Law, which were not imposed upon the nations. He laid down what we do not observe. For in the Old Law we both read and do not observe these things, yet we understand that some signification was set forth and established beforehand.

Finally, he laid down these weapons as the burdens of the sacraments of the Old Law, and took up the Law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. He therefore took those five stones from the stream—that is, from the world. For the mortal world flows and passes away, and whatever comes into the world flows past. They had been in the stream like stones among that people. At first they were useless there and lay idle; they profited nothing, while the river flowed over them.

But what did David do so that the Law itself might become useful? He received grace. For the Law cannot be fulfilled without grace. “The fullness of the Law is love” (Romans 13). Since grace causes the Law to be fulfilled, grace is signified by milk. For milk is something freely given in the flesh: the mother does not seek to receive but strives to give; she gives this freely and is saddened if there is no one to receive it.

How, then, did David show that the Law cannot operate without grace? He wished to join those five stones—by which the Law was signified in the five books—to grace, and so placed them in the shepherd’s pouch, with which milk was accustomed to be drawn. Armed with these, he advanced against proud Goliath, who boasted and presumed upon himself.

He took one stone and cast down the devil. He struck him on the forehead, and he fell in that part of the body where he did not bear the sign of Christ. You may also attend to this: he placed five stones but sent one. Five books were chosen, but unity conquered. “The fullness of the Law is love,” as the Apostle says: “bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4).

Then, having struck and thrown him down, he took his sword and cut off his head. Our David did this also: he cast down the devil from his own people when those who belonged to him believed, those whom he held in his hand and through whom he slaughtered the other souls. They turn their tongues against the devil, and thus Goliath’s head is cut off with his own sword.

(From Gregory.) Likewise, a man full of a faith that is customarily reckoned to the saints as righteousness gathers the very testimonies of sacred Scripture that a heretic produces and uses them to convict the obstinacy of his error. For when they bring against us testimonies of the sacred Law, they bring with them the means by which they are to be conquered.

Thus David, who signifies the Lord and is interpreted as “strong of hand,” and Goliath, who means “revealed” or “transmigrating” and signifies the pride of heretics, spoke through these events what we express in words. Goliath came to battle with a sword, but David with a shepherd’s pouch. David overcame that same Goliath and killed him with his own sword. We too do this, for we have been granted to become David’s promised members through his condescension: we conquer proud heretics who bring forward sentences of sacred Scripture by the very words and sentences that they themselves produce.

“David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he placed his armor in his own tent.”

(From the Hebrew.) The statement that David brought the Philistine’s head to Jerusalem is an anticipation of what he did later. As for his armor—that is, the Philistine’s armor—it should not be understood that he placed it in his own tent, but in the Lord’s tabernacle; from that tabernacle he later received these things from the priest Abimelech.

At the time when Saul saw David going out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army: “From what lineage does this young man descend, Abner?” Abner said: “As your life lives, O king, I do not know.”

This follows the manner of speech used in the statement: “Naboth blessed God and the king” (I Kings 21). It is as though he had said: “May your soul not live, O king, if I know”—or: “May I see your death, if I know.” Alternatively, since the conjunction *si* (“if”) is sometimes placed in the sense of the adverb “not,” as in the Psalmist’s statement, “If they shall enter into my rest” (Psalm 94), meaning “They shall not enter into my rest,” *si novi* (“if I know”) may be understood as meaning “I do not know.” He uses an oath by the king’s life and asserts that he does not know David’s origin.

The patriarch Joseph also used this manner of speech in Genesis against his brothers when he said: “By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave this place until your youngest brother comes” (Genesis 42).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Jonathan’s covenant with David and the betrothal of Michal, Saul’s daughter

After the victory in which David killed the giant, Scripture says that “Jonathan’s soul was joined to David’s soul,” and that Jonathan loved him “as his own soul,” and so forth.

Jonathan most fittingly represents those who believed in Christ from among the Jews. Having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, they abandoned, for love of Christ, everything they could possess in the world and followed the Redeemer himself. Hence the Apostle Peter said to Jesus concerning himself and his companions: “Lord, behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 19). And it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “All who were owners of fields came, sold them, and brought the prices of what they had sold before the apostles’ feet. It was distributed to each according to his need” (Acts 4).

Thus Jonathan gave his clothing, from his tunic to his belt, just as each of the believers strove to contribute everything he could possess in this world to the profit of Christ.

“When David returned, having struck down the Philistine, the women came out from all the cities of Israel, singing and leading dances to meet King Saul, with tambourines of joy and sistrums; and the women sang as they played, saying: ‘Saul has struck down a thousand, and David ten thousand.’”

The king’s spirit took this badly. From this arose Saul’s envy and the seeds of hatred against David.

(From Isidore.) So also the Jews, hearing Christ preached in the churches—Christ whom they themselves had handed over to death—and seeing believers rejoice in his praises because of his victory, by which he triumphed over the ancient enemy, were deeply offended.

For Saul, a cunning pretender, wishing to expose David to danger without appearing to do so through his own ambushes, sought to bind him to the marriage of his daughter Michal, provided that David brought him one hundred foreskins of the Philistines as a victor. David gave him two hundred in place of the hundred; and from the very thing by which he was believed likely to perish because of the royal demand, he gained a more glorious trophy.

So also the Jews, while striving against God’s will to kill Christ, brought about the salvation of the nations through the very means by which they believed they were extinguishing him. But the fact that David first brought the foreskins of foreigners and only then became joined to Saul’s daughter in marriage signifies that Christ did not first promise himself in marriage to the Synagogue until he had already become glorious among the nations. First, among the nations, he cut away the pollution of the flesh; afterward he was joined to the Synagogue.

For it is written: “After the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” He offered twice as many—that is, two hundred—foreskins either on account of the Jews and the nations acquired, or because the number acquired from the nations is greater than that of believing Jews.

Saul then increased his hatred against David to such an extent that, for the healing of his spirit, he tried to pin David to the wall with a spear while David was playing the psaltery in the customary manner.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Saul wished to pin David, while he was playing the lyre, with a spear; and how Saul was deceived by the statue placed in the bed and the hairy goatskin when he sought to kill David

But what does it mean that, when an opposing spirit invaded Saul, David took up the lyre and calmed his madness? Saul signifies the exaltation of the Jews, while David signifies Christ’s humility. When Saul is therefore seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated as David sings; for when the minds of the Jews are turned into fury through blasphemy, it is fitting that they should be recalled to salvation by the tranquility of evangelical speech, as though by the sweetness of a lyre.

Saul attempted to pin David, while he was playing, to the wall with a spear, but David withdrew from Saul’s presence. The spear passed into the wall, striking nothing. Thus also, while Christ was preaching the Gospel, the Jews plotted to inflict death upon him. But while he withdrew from them alive for the salvation of the nations, their malice wounded only the hardness of their own minds.

[Column 0055C] CHAPTER XIX. “So Saul sent his guards to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning. But David departed by night, fled, and was saved. When Saul’s messengers came, they found a statue placed in the bed and a hairy goatskin at its head,” and so forth.

Let us therefore hear what this means: Saul sent to guard David’s house so that he might be killed. This pertains not to the Lord’s cross, but nevertheless to his passion. Christ was crucified, died, and was buried. That burial was therefore like a house, to guard which the kingdom of the Jews sent guards when guards were appointed over Christ’s tomb.

How, then, was the house guarded so that David represented Christ and Christ might be killed, when Christ was killed not in the burial but on the cross? This refers to the body of Christ, because to kill Christ was to remove the name of Christ. For no one would have believed in Christ if the lie of the guards who had been bribed had prevailed—namely, that “while we were sleeping, his disciples came and stole him” (Matthew 28).

To wish to kill Christ, then, was to extinguish the name of his resurrection, so that the lie might be preferred to the Gospel. But just as Saul was unable to kill David, so the kingdom of the Jews could not erase the memory of Christ. Those who, relying upon Saul’s power—that is, upon the kingdom of the Jews—sought to presume against Christ stumbled upon the stone of stumbling as upon a statue; and the kid appeared to them to be a lamb. For they persecuted as a sinner the one in whom they found no sin.

“It was reported to Saul by those who said: ‘Behold, David is in Naioth at Ramah,’” and so forth.

(From Jerome.) Naioth is a place in Ramah, where David sat. Ramah, in the tribe of Benjamin, is Saul’s city, six miles from Aelia, toward the north, opposite Bethel. Jeremiah also mentions it. There is another Ramah in the tribe of Asher. Naioth is interpreted as “beauty,” and Ramah as “exalted.” These names of the places therefore fit well with the events accomplished in them, because the sayings of the prophets possess both elevation of knowledge and beauty of expression.

(CHAPTER XX.) “So Saul sent executioners to seize David. When they saw the company of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them, the Spirit of the Lord also came upon them, and they too began to prophesy,” and so forth.

(From Isidore.) David, therefore, avoiding the blow of the royal hand and escaping Saul’s persecutions, fled and came to Samuel. Saul sent messengers to seize David. When they saw Samuel among the prophets and the company of prophets who were prophesying at that time, the messengers who had been sent received the same spirit and prophesied. The same thing happened when others were sent, and likewise with a third group. Finally, when Saul himself came, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him; he walked as he entered and prophesied.

(From the Hebrew.) A major question arises here. Earlier it is read: “Samuel did not see Saul until the day of his death.” How, then, is Saul said here to have prophesied before Samuel?

The Hebrews resolve this question in two ways. Either Samuel did not see him because, when Saul joined the company of prophets, Samuel hid himself so that Saul would not see him; or Samuel did not see him wearing the royal garments in which he had been clothed when it was said, “He did not see him until the day of his death”—with “wearing the royal garments” understood. His stripping himself is therefore to be understood not as removing all his clothing, but as removing the royal garments.

(From Isidore.) It is also asked how those messengers who had been sent to seize a man and lead him to death deserved to become participants in such a spirit. Saul himself, who had sent them, came seeking to shed innocent blood, yet deserved to receive that spirit and prophesy.

As far as the literal sense is concerned, it is not surprising that a reprobate man prophesied briefly and temporarily, since many like him are also recorded as having possessed the gift of prophecy—such as that reprobate Balaam, whom Scripture does not fail to declare condemned by divine judgment (Numbers 22, 23, and 24). Yet they possessed prophecy.

Nor do those words written in the Gospel give little testimony to this view: many will say on that day, “Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank, [we prophesied and cast out demons,] and in your name we performed many miracles” (Matthew 7). Yet he will say to them: “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity” (ibid.).

Mystically, however, the example of this Saul and his messengers in this passage represents certain heretics who possess something good from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, such as the Scriptures of the Law and the Gospel and the sacraments of baptism. When they come to the Catholic Church, what they possess must in no way be violated or handed over as though they did not possess it. Yet they must not therefore trust in salvation because we do not reject what we believe they have received. They must recognize unity and fellowship in the bond of peace. Without this, whatever they may have possessed—however holy and venerable—makes them all the more unworthy of the reward of eternal life, because they did not make good use of the gifts they received in this transitory life.

Likewise, the example and image of this Saul and his messengers here appropriately represents the Jews.
