While they desire to oppose Christ, they have the sacraments of the Law and the Prophets in their mouths as testimony to Christ; and they dispute the Scriptures with the Church, as though with the prophets, just as those men prophesied with the prophets.

## CHAPTER XX. How Saul sent messengers to seek David, who, when they came to the company of prophets, themselves also prophesied; and how Saul afterward came there and prophesied naked all day; concerning Jonathan’s words to David and the sign of the arrow that he gave him

When Jonathan said to David, whom he grieved to see wearied by his father’s unjust persecutions: “If I live, you will show me the mercy of the Lord. But if I die, you will not withdraw your mercy from my house forever, when the Lord has eradicated David’s enemies, each one from the earth.”

When Scripture added, “Jonathan therefore made a covenant with the house of David,” it immediately continued: “And the Lord required it from the hands of David’s enemies,” and so forth.

He did this by anticipation, inserting into the history beforehand something that happened much later—when, after Saul’s death, the kingdom was transferred to David’s house, and those who had unjustly persecuted him were punished by divine vengeance. When the Lord required from the hands of David’s enemies an account of why they had afflicted the holy man, they were then compelled to answer for the hatred with which they had raged against him for so long. The same may equally be understood of Absalom, Sheba son of Bochri, and David’s other enemies.

Alternatively, if you wish to know what the Lord required from the hands of David’s enemies, it can, unless I am mistaken, be understood from the preceding statement in which it was said that Jonathan had made a covenant with the house of David. The later phrase may be understood to mean that the Lord required this from the hands of David’s enemies: namely, why they themselves had not wished to enter into a covenant of peace with him, when they saw that the Lord was with him.

Scripture appears to insert this sentence here by anticipation in order to confirm the truth of Jonathan’s testimony, in which he had said: “When the Lord has eradicated David’s enemies, each one from the earth.” For David’s enemies were indeed eradicated from the earth—not because David himself took vengeance on his adversaries, but because the Lord judged on his behalf.

He rightly adds: “Jonathan made David swear again, because he loved him; for he loved him as his own soul.” Thus the man who embraced David with such perfect love according to God’s Law was shown to be exempt from the destruction of his enemies. Although he was soon taken away by death and could not, as he had hoped, possess an earthly kingdom jointly with David, he nevertheless received without any contradiction a share in the heavenly kingdom with the one whom he loved for the glory of his virtues for so long, since he too was a man of virtue.

“Jonathan came into the field according to David’s arrangement, and a little boy was with him. He said to his boy: ‘Go and bring me the arrows that I shoot,’” and so forth.

What does it mean that Jonathan, wishing to preserve David, while David was hiding in the field beside the stone, shot two arrows as a signal, which the little boy, ignorant of what had happened, gathered and brought back into the city? It signifies that God the Father had hidden his only-begotten Son, whom he had determined to send for the salvation of the human race, in the letter of the Law, unknown to the Jews.

David was therefore hidden in the field—that is, Christ was set forth in the world. Concerning him the Evangelist John says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1).

He sat beside the stone because he was written upon the tablets of the Law, as in the statement: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6), and: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exodus 20).

Saul, hating David, sat at the meal and judged him to be a man of death. In the same way, Jewish unbelief, feasting at the Passover meal, plotted Christ’s death.

When morning had dawned, Jonathan came into the field according to David’s arrangement, and the little boy was with him. He shot one arrow, and then another. At the dawning of the morning of faith, God the Father first brought forth the testimony of the Law concerning Christ. Then he sent the prophets to testify concerning his coming.

Hence it is written: “Your arrows go forth in the light, in the brightness of the lightning of your weapons” (Zechariah 9).

Jonathan’s boy gathered the arrows and brought them to his master, knowing nothing at all of what was being done. So also the Jewish people, carrying the books of the Law and the Prophets as though they had been written by God, honored them, but did not recognize the one whom Moses and the Prophets had signified, although he was present among them.

## CHAPTER XXI. How David fled to the priest Abimelech, by whom he was fed, and because of this the priest and a company of priests with him were killed by Saul; and concerning David’s flight to Achish, king of Gath

(CHAPTER XXI.) “David therefore arose again and fled that day from Saul’s presence. He came to the priest Abimelech, from whom he also took Goliath’s sword and received the bread of the Presence.” This event “brought death upon the priest and punishment upon the religious city.”

First, it must be considered what David meant when he replied to the priest’s question and said: “Indeed, if women are concerned, we have abstained from them since yesterday and the day before yesterday, when we went out, and the vessels of the boys were holy.”

(From the Hebrew.) This too can be understood as follows. Abimelech asks whether David and his young men, whom he had said he was taking to such-and-such a place, were clean. David replied enigmatically in the plural about himself, saying: “The vessels of the boys were holy”—that is, from marital intercourse.

When he says: “Moreover, this way is polluted,” the Hebrew reads: “Moreover, this way is common.” It is to be understood thus: “This way is common”—as though he were saying: The Law commands that an outsider should not eat from them, and you ask whether the boys are clean, although even if they were clean they ought by no means to eat them. This way is common because you are asking in a common, ordinary manner.

When it follows: “But it will be sanctified today in the vessels,” he says that it itself—that is, in the vessels—will be sanctified in the mind, because he would not have eaten from them unless bodily necessity and the danger to his life compelled him.

(From Isidore.) This, then, is the historical truth of the events. But as far as the prophetic mystery is concerned, it was fulfilled in Christ our Lord. Placed in the flesh, while avoiding Jewish persecution, he passed over to the apostles, with whom he also took the food he desired: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” (Luke 22).

From those who received him he took Goliath’s weapons—that is, the devil’s weapons—for he himself plundered the strong man’s spoils (Luke 11). Against those, therefore, by whom Christ was received, the devil brought tribulations and death. “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ,” as the Apostle says, “will suffer persecution” (II Timothy 3). And the Lord says: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15).

“There was there on that day a certain man among Saul’s servants, inside the tabernacle, whose name was Doeg the Edomite.”

(From the Hebrew.) The Hebrew has: “detained before the Lord.” Doeg the Edomite had been detained by a vow, by which he had bound himself to remain for several days in the Lord’s tabernacle and devote himself to prayer.

This Doeg the Edomite—who was keeper of camels, that is, of an unfruitful and crooked flock, and whose name is interpreted as “moved” or “anxious,” and who also struck down Abimelech the high priest—for Abimelech is interpreted as “my brother is king”—represents Judas the betrayer. Through Judas, the devil worked by deceit against our Redeemer, who is truly king, so that after his betrayal the Church would also suffer persecution, very many of Christ’s disciples and priests would be killed, and they would endure the gravest persecutions for his name.

But in the house of Abimelech only Abiathar, the chief of the priests, remained unharmed by Saul the persecutor, because no one can harm Christ, the chief of the priests, who ascended victorious into heaven.

Meanwhile, as David was fleeing from Saul, he wished to hide with a certain king of Gath named Achish. But when his glory had been so celebrated that the king to whom he had fled might, through envy, devise some evil against him, he feigned insanity. As though seized by madness, he “changed his expression; saliva ran down his beard, he collapsed in their hands, and fell at the entrance of the gate.”

“And Achish said: ‘Why have you brought this man to me? Were madmen lacking among us?’ And so he dismissed him.”

(From Isidore.) Achish is interpreted as “How is it?” This signifies ignorance and the word of one who wonders and recognizes—a situation fulfilled among the Jewish people. When they saw Christ, they did not recognize him; before them he changed his expression and departed.

There were then the carnal precepts of the Law, there was sacrifice according to Aaron; afterward he himself established a sacrifice from his body and blood according to the order of Melchizedek. He changed his expression in the priesthood; he changed it in the commandments, giving another Testament after emptying out the carnal observance. He collapsed in their hands when they seized and crucified him.

And he fell at the entrance of the gate—that is, he humbled himself. For this is to fall as far as the entrance of our faith. The entrance of the gate is the beginning of faith. From there the Church begins and reaches as far as vision. When it believes what it does not see, it will deserve to enjoy those things when it begins to see him face to face.

As for the saliva that in the guise of a madman flowed down over his beard, the Apostle explains this by saying: “Jews demand signs, and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to the nations foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God; for what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings” (I Corinthians 1).

Saliva signifies weakness. But because what is foolish of God is stronger than human beings, note that the saliva is displayed, yet attend to the fact that it runs down over the beard. As weakness is shown in the saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. He therefore concealed his power beneath the body of his weakness; because outwardly he was weakened, it appeared as saliva, while inwardly divine power was concealed like a beard.

## CHAPTER XXII. How David fled into the cave of Adullam, where his brothers and all his father’s household visited him, and many others gathered to him
## (CHAPTER XXII)

“David fled into the cave of Adullam, where his brothers and all his father’s household visited him; and all those who were in distress, oppressed by debt, and embittered in spirit gathered to him, and he became their leader,” etc.

What does it mean that, while David remained in the cave, his brothers and all his father’s household came to him? It means that those from the Synagogue who believed in him came to him. And all those who were in distress and oppressed by debt gathered to him. This is what he himself said when he invited them to come to him: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI).

For all who recognize that they are situated in the straits of vices, possessing no breadth of charity, and are oppressed by debt—that is, by the assessment of sins which they were paying to the devil when they presented their members to serve wickedness unto wickedness (Rom. VI)—must be embittered in spirit; that is, they must fittingly perform penance for their former offenses and come to David, namely, to our Beloved, so that he may become their leader. For he is the one who “has been appointed by God judge of the living and the dead, the mighty God, the Father of the age to come, the Prince of Peace, whose kingdom shall have no end. And he shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. His power is eternal, and his kingdom shall not be given to another.”

“And the prophet Gad said to David: ‘Do not remain in the stronghold; depart and go into the land of Judah,’” etc. In a remarkable manner Gad the prophet is introduced here, although in what precedes no mention was made of him. He is introduced in the same way as the prophet Elijah in the passage where it says: “And Elijah the Tishbite, one of the inhabitants of Gilead, said” (III Kings XVII).

Thus, from the mouth of the Lord, the prophet Gad told David not to remain among the nations and in a polluted land, but to return to the land of Judah and there, according to the Lord’s will, endure the persecution of his enemies.

## CHAPTER XXIII

That David hid in the wilderness of Ziph, in the forest, and the Ziphites betrayed him to Saul.

(CHAPTER XXIII.) At the time when Abiathar son of Ahimelech had fled to David, he had come down on that day bringing the ephod with him. This was the ephod that Moses had made at the Lord’s command (Exod. XXXIX), as he had also made the breastpiece, in which were instruction and truth; and in it David also consulted the Lord.

And David said to the Lord: “If the men of Keilah will hand me over into Saul’s hands, and if he will come down, as your servant has heard? Lord God of Israel, make it known to your servant.” And the Lord said: “He will come down,” etc.

It is as though he were saying: If you remain here, Saul will come down, and the men of Keilah will hand you over to him. He was making known to him their intention. And rightly do the men of Keilah—who had proved ungrateful for David’s benefits, since he himself had rescued them from the hands of the Philistines—signify the faithlessness or fickleness of the Jews. They, always ungrateful for the mercy of our Redeemer, plotted against him among the powers of this world and deliberated how to ambush him.

Keilah is interpreted as “cast toward a sling,” or “exalting itself.” And it is written in the psalm: “The wicked walk about on every side” (Ps. XI); and elsewhere: “The fool changes like the moon” (Exod. XXVII).

(CHAPTER XXIV.) “David was in the wilderness of Ziph, in the forest,” etc.

(From Jerome.) Ziph means “a barren” or “dark,” or “misty” mountain, near Ziph, where David sat close to Carmel, which in Scripture is called Carmel. For this is the name by which a village of the Jews is still called, from which Nabal the Carmelite came. One of Caleb’s descendants was also called Ziph. Read the book of Chronicles (I, II).

What, then, does it mean that the Ziphites betrayed David, who was hiding among them, to Saul, and plotted his death with him, except that the Jews—whom the Ziphites rightly signify, and whose name is interpreted as “germinating”—while they desired to germinate in an earthly kingdom, were deliberating with their rulers about the death of the Savior: how they might seize him after he had been betrayed by his disciple and hand him over to the authorities to be killed?

## CHAPTER XXIV

That David, hiding in a cave in the wilderness of Engaddi, secretly cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak when Saul entered the same cave to relieve himself.

(CHAPTER XXIV.) “David went up from there and dwelt in the safest places, in Engaddi,” etc.

(From Isidore.) In the wilderness of Engaddi, when Saul was eager to pursue David, David entered a cave and hid there. But the king, unexpectedly caught in an ambush, fell into what he had devised against the innocent. For it is written: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it” (Ecclus. XXVII).

David, repaying good for evil, did not kill his enemy, but, as evidence of what had happened, he cut off and carried away the edge of the royal cloak. It would certainly have been easier to destroy an adversary caught in an ambush than merely to outwit him.

What, then, does it mean that this man, fleeing from Saul’s presence, hid in a cave? Why did he hide except so that he might be concealed and not found? What does it mean to be covered by a cave except to be covered by earth? Whoever flees into a cave is covered by earth so that he may not be seen.

Jesus bore earth—flesh, which he had received from the earth—and concealed himself in it, so that God might not be found by the Jews. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II).

Why, then, did they not find the Lord of glory? Because he had covered himself with a cave: that is, he presented the weakness of the flesh to their eyes and concealed the majesty of his divinity beneath the covering of his body, as in the recess of a cave. Not recognizing God, they persecuted a man. He could not die except in man, nor could he be seized except in man. Thus he placed earth before those who sought him for evil, while he preserved life for those who sought him rightly.

According to the flesh, therefore, he fled from Saul’s presence into a cave, because he suffered, concealing himself before the Jews to such an extent that he died. But why did he wish to remain patient even unto death, so that he might flee from Saul’s presence into a cave, which may be understood as the lower part of the earth?

It is certainly manifest and known to all that he was placed in a tomb which had been hewn out in rock (Matt. XXVII). This tomb, then, was the cave. Into it our David fled from Saul’s presence. For the Jews pursued him until he was placed in the cave.

But what does it mean that Saul the persecutor entered the cave to relieve himself, except that the Jews discharged the malice conceived in their minds against Christ like a foul odor, and revealed by their worse deeds the harmful things they had devised among themselves when they killed Christ?

Yet David did not wish to kill Saul. Although he had him in his power while hidden in the secret recess of the cave, he preferred to preserve him rather than kill him. So Christ, while he was in the cave of the flesh, had the persecuting people in his power and did not kill them. For it had been written about them through the prophet: “Do not kill them” (Jer. XLI).

Finally, David silently cut off only the upper edge of Saul’s cloak, to show prophetically that Christ did not kill the Jews but merely took away from them the glory of the kingdom, leaving them empty of authority or dominion because of their persecution. For the cutting off of the cloak signifies the amputation of the kingdom.

Saul also demonstrated this elsewhere when he sinned through disobedience. When he begged forgiveness and asked Samuel to return with him to appease God, and Samuel refused and turned his face away to depart, Saul seized the corner of his garment and tore it. Samuel then said to him: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand today and will give it to your neighbor, and Israel will be divided into two peoples” (I Kings XV).

Therefore this king figuratively represented the person of the Jews, signifying that they would lose the kingdom while persecuting Christ.

If anyone seeks the moral meaning of this event, it may be understood in this way: Saul represents wicked rulers.

(From Gregory.) Saul’s relieving his bowels means that wicked superiors extend the malice conceived in their hearts even to works of miserable odor, and reveal what they have devised by carrying out harmful thoughts in outward deeds. Yet David feared to strike him, because the devout minds of subjects, abstaining from every plague of detraction, do not strike the lives of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they criticize their imperfections.

If at times, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves and speak humbly of certain extreme and outward faults of their superiors, they cut the edge of the cloak silently, as it were. For when they detract, at least harmlessly and secretly, from the dignity of those set over them, they stain the garment of the king placed above them.

Yet they return to themselves and reproach themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of a word. Hence it is rightly written there: “After this David struck his heart, because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.”

The deeds of superiors are not to be struck down by the sword of the mouth, even when they are certainly judged worthy of reproach. If the tongue ever slips against them, even in the smallest matter, it must be restrained by the distress of repentance, so that the person may return to himself whenever he has sinned against the authority placed over him and may dread the judgment against himself of the one who has been set above him.

For when we sin against our superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them over us. Thus Moses too, when he learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord” (Exod. XVI).

## CHAPTER XXV

On the death of Samuel and the story of Nabal and Abigail his wife, and how they dealt with David.

After this Scripture proceeds to narrate the death of Samuel and David’s flight, saying:

(CHAPTER XXV.) “Samuel died, and all Israel assembled, mourned for him, and buried him in his house at Ramah. David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran,” etc.

(From Jerome.) Paran is now a town beyond Arabia, joined to the Saracens who wander about in the wilderness. The children of Israel traveled through this region when they moved their camp from Mount Sinai. It is, as we have said, beyond Arabia, opposite the southern region, and lies three days’ journey east of Aila.

Scripture also records that Ishmael lived in the wilderness of Paran (Gen. XXI). Hence the Ishmaelites, who are now called Saracens. We read that King Chedorlaomer struck those who were in the wilderness of Paran.

“There was a certain man in the wilderness of Maon, and his possessions were in Carmel,” etc.

The history that recounts Nabal and Abigail his wife seeks a mystical interpretation. Nabal, of whom it is said that he was a hard, wicked, and malicious man, represents the Jewish people. Some of them, intoxicated by the grape of gall and the cluster of bitterness, stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, always resisted the Holy Spirit. Following a carnal understanding of the Law, they became fools.

The name Nabal expresses this well. It is interpreted as “foolish” or “mad.” Hence, when Christ came and through the apostles sought from them the refreshment of faith and good works, they rejected him, saying: “We do not know where this man is from. We are disciples of Moses” (John IX).

Abigail, of whom Scripture reports that she was a very prudent and beautiful woman, represents that portion of the people who, having been converted from the Jews to the faith, deserved to please the Lord. The name Abigail expresses this well. It is interpreted as “the joy of my father.”

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV). She, often pleading through the prophets and the apostles for the salvation of the Jewish people, offered our David an acceptable offering of good works and devout dedication. After the death of her husband, who perished madly in his folly, David took her in marriage and presented her to himself as a bride without spot or wrinkle (Eph. V).

(From Bede.) Abigail, interceding for herself and her household, said this to David, whom her husband, overcome by folly and drunkenness, had offended:

“If a man should ever rise up in pursuit of you and seek your life, the life of my lord will be kept as though in the bundle of the living with the Lord your God. But the lives of your enemies will be whirled about as in the force and circle of a sling,” etc.

By a most beautiful comparison she distinguishes the condition of the righteous from the lot of the reprobate. She calls the souls of the righteous living, so that, conversely, she may indicate that the souls of the others have been overtaken by spiritual death, according to the prophet’s saying: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII).

She compares the righteous to a bundle and the others to a stone in a sling. A bundle is tied together so that it may remain whole and be preserved. A stone is placed freely in a sling so that it may be cast away.

Thus, indeed, in this world the elect are compressed by the pressures of tribulations, so that, warned by them, they may bind themselves more closely to one another in mutual charity and, joined together by the hand of their Redeemer, may be preserved forever. But the more widely the reprobate are allowed in this life to pursue their own pleasures, as though free, the farther they will be cast away in the future from the glory of the divine vision, so that it may rightly be said of them: “Indeed, they have been expelled from your hand” (John X).

She wonderfully describes the providence of the Almighty, saying that the soul of the holy man is kept with the Lord as though in a bundle of the living. Just as it is very easy for anyone to preserve a bundle of grass or hay held in his hand, so the power of our Lord and Savior protects all the elect throughout the world, from the beginning to the end of the age, without difficulty, so that none of them may perish in any way.

This accords with what he himself says about them in the Gospel under the figure of sheep: “They will follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand.”

As a single bundle is tied together with any sort of cords, so the whole company of the saints is bound together by one and the same faith, hope, and charity, and surrounded by the one protection of God.

In the literal sense, the meaning is clear: although enemies pursued him, David’s soul was always preserved in the lot of the living. But his enemies, as adversities pressed upon them, were disturbed by unstable movement like a stone whirled in a sling, and so were to be driven from their territories or even removed from human affairs.

“Early in the morning, when Nabal had digested the wine, his wife told him these words,” etc.

(From Gregory.) What does Abigail suggest to us by the arrangement of her report, except that we correct angry people more effectively if we withdraw from them while they are in the very agitation of their anger? When disturbed, they do not know what they are hearing. But when they return to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed that they were borne with so calmly.

To a mind drunk with rage, everything certain appears, as it is said, perverse. Thus Abigail rightly kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk and rightly disclosed it after he had digested the wine. For he could recognize the evil he had done precisely because he had not heard of it while drunk.

“Saul gave Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Phalti son of Laish, who was from Gallim,” etc.

(From Bede.) According to the Hebrews, that Phalti did not have relations with her. For if he had, David would never afterward have taken her back, since such intercourse is wholly prohibited by the Law.

This same Phalti was from Gallim, that is, from “inundation.” This inundation is understood as the Law. For he was a teacher of the Law, from Bahurim, that is, “from the chosen.”

When Michal was given to him by Saul, Phalti—meaning “escaping”—is the interpretation. When the same Michal was taken away from him, Phaltiel—meaning “escaping from God”—is the interpretation. He is called “escaping from God” because God protected him so that he would not touch her and become a transgressor of the Law.

“Her husband followed her, weeping as far as Bahurim” (II Kings XXXI). He is said to have wept out of joy, because the Lord had protected him from touching her.

## CHAPTER XXVI

That David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, found him sleeping but did not kill him; instead, he took only the spear and the cup of water.

(CHAPTER XXVI.) “The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying: ‘Behold, David is hidden on the hill of Hachilah, which is opposite the wilderness.’ Saul arose and went down into the wilderness of Ziph,” etc.

Again David, fleeing from Saul’s presence, came to the king’s camp. When he found him sleeping, he neither struck nor killed him, but took only the spear that was beside his head and the water flask.

“When all were sleeping, he went out from the camp and crossed to the summit of the mountain.”

(From Isidore.) What is this, then, except that the Jews persecuted Christ? But they slept while persecuting him, because they were not vigilant in heart. Hardness of heart is a kind of sleep. They slept in the old life; they did not keep watch in the new.

Christ came. He did not kill them, but took from them the cup of water—that is, the grace of the Law. He also took away the royal scepter, namely, the power of the kingdom, which they regarded as something great, by which they protected themselves temporally, and which through unbelief they wielded against the Lord.

Then our victorious David returned from their camp and ascended to the height of the heavenly mountains.

## CHAPTER XXVII

The account continues with David’s deeds.

(CHAPTER XXVII.) “David and his men went up, and they made raids upon the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. For these villages had been inhabited in the land from ancient times.”

These villages were not under the authority of Achish. They are said to have been inhabited in the land from ancient times because they had been settled peacefully and securely and had suffered the depredations of no enemy.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Again concerning the death of Samuel.

(CHAPTER XXVIII.) “Samuel died, and all Israel mourned for him, and they buried him in Ramah, his city,” etc.

Above, it is said that he was buried in his house at Ramah. “In his house” means in his family and kinship.

A question arises: since he has already been read of above as dead, why is his death repeated here? According to the Hebrews, his death is repeated here because of his resurrection, and so that the condemnation of Saul might be shown to be just. Saul was dead in his sins and, having abandoned God, consulted the python contrary to the Law.

## CHAPTER XXIX

Concerning the woman who summoned the dead, who at Saul’s request raised Samuel, who revealed to him his approaching death.

“After Samuel’s death, the Philistines gathered against Israel, and Saul consulted the Lord; but he did not answer him, neither by dreams nor by priests,” etc.

(From a certain Hebrew source.) The Hebrew has: “Neither by instruction nor by prophets.”

The Lord answered through dreams, as the same Hebrews assert, because by fasting and praying they sought that a divine oracle be given to them, and the Lord revealed through dreams what was to happen. Saul is read as having done no such thing in this passage.

“By instruction” means through the ephod, which the priest wore upon his breast. “Nor by prophets,” because the Lord gave no answer when they consulted them. These prophets are said to have been Samuel’s disciples; when they were prophesying, Saul joined himself to them and prophesied.

Saul then sought a woman who summoned the dead, so that she might raise Samuel for him. Immediately after he had been raised, he said to him:

“Why have you disturbed me, so that I should be raised?” etc.

According to the historical sense, the question arises whether the woman who summoned the dead actually called the prophet himself from the underworld, or whether she produced some other imaginary illusion through the deceit of demons.

On this question the blessed Bishop Augustine, of revered memory, wrote as follows to Simplicianus, Bishop of Milan:

“You ask, then, whether an evil spirit could raise the soul of a righteous person and summon it, as it were, from the hidden barriers of the dead, so that it might appear and speak with Saul. Is it not rather more astonishing that Satan himself took up the Lord and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple? (Matt. V.)

“Whatever the manner in which he did this, the manner in which the thing concerning Samuel occurred, so that Samuel was raised, is likewise hidden—unless perhaps someone should say that the devil was more easily permitted to take the living Lord wherever he wished and set him wherever he wished than to raise the spirit of the dead Samuel from its dwelling.

“If the Gospel does not disturb us in that matter because the Lord willed and permitted it to happen without any diminution of his power or divinity—just as he allowed himself to be seized, bound, mocked, crucified, and killed by the Jews themselves, although they were perverse and unclean, doing the works of the devil—then it is not absurd to believe that, by some dispensation of the divine will, it was permitted that the spirit of the holy prophet should appear before the king’s eyes, not unwillingly or under the domination of magical power, but willingly and in obedience to the hidden dispensation of God, which remained unknown to the woman and to Saul, so that it might strike him with the divine sentence.

“Nevertheless, another and easier interpretation may be possible: that we should not believe that Samuel’s spirit was truly raised from its rest, but rather that some phantom or imaginary illusion was produced by the devil’s contrivances. Scripture therefore calls it by the name of Samuel because images are accustomed to be called by the names of the things whose images they are.

“Thus everything that is painted or fashioned is called by the name of the thing whose image it is. When a picture of a man is painted, each proper name is used without hesitation, and it is said: ‘That is Cicero; that is Sallust; that is Achilles; that is Hector; this is the river Simois; that is Rome,’ although these are nothing other than painted images.

“Likewise, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, the figures made of metal by God’s command over the ark of the covenant, for the purpose of signifying a great reality, were also called cherubim (Exod. XXV).

“Again, when someone sees a dream, he does not say, ‘I saw an image of Augustine,’ but, ‘I saw Augustine,’ although at the time when someone saw such a thing Augustine might have known nothing of it. It is therefore entirely clear that it is not the men themselves but their images that are seen.

“Pharaoh likewise said that he had seen ears of grain and cattle in his dreams, not images of ears of grain or cattle (Gen. XLI).

“If, then, it is clearly established that images are called by the names of the things whose images they are, it is not surprising that Scripture says that Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the fabricated devices of him who transforms himself into an angel of light and equips his ministers as ministers of righteousness (I Cor. XI).

“Now, if it troubles anyone that the evil spirit foretold the truth to Saul, it may also seem strange how the demons recognized Christ, whom the Jews did not recognize (Luke VIII; Acts XIX).

“When God wishes someone to recognize truth through even the lowest spirits—truth concerning temporal matters alone, belonging to this mortal life—it is easy and not incongruous for the Almighty and Just One, for the punishment of those to whom these things are foretold, so that they may suffer in advance by foreknowing the evil that threatens them, to grant, by the hidden arrangement of his mysteries, even to such spirits some power of divination. Thus they may foretell to human beings what they hear from the angels.

“They hear only as much as the Lord and governor of all either commands or permits. Hence the spirit of the python in the Acts of the Apostles also bears witness to the Apostle Paul and attempts to act as an evangelist (Acts XVI).

“Yet these spirits mix in deceptions, and what they have been able to know as true they foretell not so much to teach as to deceive. Perhaps this is the reason that, when that image of Samuel foretold to Saul that he would die, it also said that he would be with him. This is certainly false.

“For in the Gospel we read that the good and the evil are separated by a great interval after death, when it testifies that a great abyss lay between the proud rich man, who was already suffering torments in the underworld, and the man covered with sores who had lain at his gate and was already placed in rest (Luke XVI).

“Or, if Samuel said to him, ‘You will be with me,’ so that this referred not to equality of happiness but to a common condition of death—since both were human beings and both could die, and the dead man foretold death to the living—then, under either interpretation, it is clear that this passage can have an ending that is not contrary to the faith.

“Unless, perhaps, through a deeper inquiry it should be discovered with certainty whether or not the soul, after it has departed from this life, can be summoned by magical incantations and appear to the eyes of the living, still bearing the features of the body, so that it can not only be seen but recognized.

“And if this is possible, whether the soul of a righteous person too, not indeed compelled by magical rites but willing to appear through more hidden mysteries [or, according to another reading, commands], in obedience to the supreme Law—if this should become clear to be impossible, then both interpretations should not be admitted in the exposition of this Scripture. Rather, with the one excluded, the likeness of Samuel, produced by a diabolical rite, should be understood as an illusion.

“But since, whether this can happen or cannot happen, Satan’s deceit and his skillful activity in fabricating images are nevertheless constantly alert to deceive human senses in many ways, we should proceed cautiously. We should not prejudge more careful investigations, but should rather suppose that something of this kind was done by an evil spirit through the ministry of that woman who summoned the dead, so long as we are not granted the ability to devise and explain anything more.”

These are the things that the most blessed Augustine then wrote concerning the woman who summoned the dead and Samuel.

## CHAPTER XXX

That David defeated the Amalekites and recovered at Ziklag the spoil they had taken.

(CHAPTER XXX.) Meanwhile, while David was proceeding with Achish, king of the Philistines, into battle against Israel, the Amalekites rose up, attacked Ziklag, and burned it, taking captive everything belonging to David and his men.

David returned to pursue the Amalekites and found an Egyptian servant exhausted, whom the Amalekites had abandoned on the road because he was ill. David restored him with food and made him the guide of his journey. In this way he pursued the Amalekites, found them feasting, and utterly destroyed them.

(From Augustine.) We must therefore consider what it means that, while David was absent, the Amalekites invaded Ziklag and took the spoil. Amalekites are called “a people who licks.” What is signified by a “licking people” except the minds of worldly people, who, while delighting only in temporal things, as it were lick all earthly possessions by circling around them?

A licking people, as it were, makes spoil when those who love earthly things increase their profits through the losses of others. They do this while David is absent because they neglect to keep the Redeemer before the eyes of their hearts.

What does it mean that the Egyptian servant of the Amalekites grows weary on the road except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left weak and despised by that same world, unable to run along with it and becoming numb, broken by adversity?

But David finds him because our Redeemer, truly mighty of hand, sometimes converts to his love those whom he finds despised by the glory of the world. He feeds him with food because he refreshes him with knowledge of the word. He chooses him as a guide for the journey because he also makes him his preacher.

And because he had been unable to follow the Amalekite, he becomes David’s guide. For the one whom the world abandons as unworthy not only receives the Lord into his converted mind but also, by preaching, brings him into the hearts of others.

David, with this man as his guide, finds the Amalekites feasting and destroys them. This is because those who were despised by the world as companions, when they preach Christ, destroy the world’s joy. Often, therefore, those who previously could not run with worldly people in this world overcome the minds of worldly people by preaching.

## CHAPTER XXXI

The battle of the Philistines against Jerusalem, and the death of Saul and his sons.

(CHAPTER XXXI.) “When the battle began, the Philistines struck Israel with a great slaughter, and Saul and Jonathan fell in the battle. Saul seized his sword and fell upon it. When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell upon his sword and died with him,” etc.

(From a certain Hebrew source.) The Hebrews say that this armor-bearer was Doeg the Idumean, who, seeing Saul dead, killed himself out of fear of David.

“Saul died, therefore, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer and all his men,” etc.

These “men” are to be understood as his household servants. Saul’s three sons who were killed with him were Jonathan, Abinadab—also called Jesui—and Melchishua. Ishbosheth, however, was at home. He is said to have been born in the year in which Saul was made king, and is also read to have been forty years old when he began to reign. From this it is inferred that Saul reigned forty years.

One may ask why he is called Jesui in one place and Abinadab in another. Jesui is interpreted as “equal.” He is called “equal” because the son is said to have been equal to his father in merit.

Abinadab is interpreted as “my father is willing.” By his own will, Saul his father acquired, through evil deeds, the fate by which he was killed together with his sons.

Finally, the prophet first figuratively laments Saul and Jonathan. Although they were powerful and had always prevailed over their enemies, they were immediately wounded and fell in the midst of battle.

“How,” he says, “have the mighty fallen in the midst of battle?”

In the same way, the devout community of Christians now mourns those who, while resisting demons, slip in the world—which is slippery, for Gelboe is interpreted as “slippery mountains”—and, abandoning hope of restoration, kill themselves with their own sword, namely, through the destructive despair of escaping the ancient enemy, just as Saul died by falling upon his sword.

The Philistines—that is, the evil spirits—strip the slain of their virtues and attribute the victory to their own strength, although it occurs in such cases by God’s just permission.

But our David, in his members—that is, in elect and holy men—mourns the fall of those who have fallen. He does not rejoice in the destruction of the dying, but protests so that such a report may not be proclaimed in the cities of the foreigners. That is, he commands the faithful to guard themselves carefully on every side and to fortify themselves with the shield of faith, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, wearing the helmet of salvation, and wielding the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, against their adversaries, lest they should ever again be disgracefully overcome and bring joy to their enemies.

# BOOK II

## CHAPTER I

That David ordered the Amalekite who reported the crime to be struck down before him because of Saul’s death; David’s mourning for Saul and Jonathan, and his command that the sons of Judah be taught the bow.

(CHAPTER I.) “After Saul had died, David returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and remained two days at Ziklag. On the third day, a man appeared, coming from Saul’s camp, with his clothes torn and dust upon his head. When he came to David, he fell upon his face and bowed down. David said to him: ‘Where do you come from?’ He answered him: ‘I have escaped from the camp of Israel.’ David said to him: ‘What has happened? Tell me.’ He replied: ‘The people fled from the battle, and many of the people fell and died. Saul also and his son Jonathan have perished,’” etc.

(From a certain Hebrew source.) The Hebrews say that this Amalekite was the son of Doeg. For the Amalekite and the Idumean are one people: Esau’s firstborn son was Eliphaz, and Eliphaz’s son was Amalek.

The Hebrews also assert that the diadem and bracelet which the man brought to David had been entrusted to him by his father Doeg.

What, then, does it mean that the Amalekite who falsely claimed before David that he had killed King Saul received from the heavenly Judge the punishment of just vengeance? It accords with what is written: “Everyone who digs a pit will fall into it” (Ecclus. XVII); and: “Those who strike with the sword will perish” (Matt. XX); and again: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I).

He received punishment because everyone who plots evil against his neighbor or rejoices in his destruction receives the penalty of just retribution.

“David seized his garments and tore them, and all the men who were with him did likewise. They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, for Jonathan his son, for the people of the Lord, and for the house of Israel,” etc.

(From the same source.) By “the people of the Lord” he means the priests, and by “the house of Israel” he means the whole people of Israel in general.

“David sang this lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son, and he commanded that they teach the sons of Judah the bow, as it is written in the Book of Jashar,” and so forth.

That which is written about David, when he mourned Saul and Jonathan who had been slain—namely, that he commanded the sons of Judah to be taught the bow—he did this because, since he already knew that the Philistines abounded in archers, and since Saul had perished especially from their arrows, his own soldiers too might learn the same art of warfare in order to defeat them.

Alternatively (from the Hebrew): David commanded that the sons of Judah be taught the bow—that is, that the kings of Judah be taught courage, namely, that they should be strong and attentive in the fear of the Lord and in the commandments of God, lest through disobedience they depart from strength and the fear of the Lord like Saul, and perish in the same way in which he perished.

But concerning what follows, “as it is written in the Book of Jashar,” and so forth: they assert that this very book can nowhere today be found, not even among the Hebrews themselves. The same is true of the Book of the Wars of the Lord, which is mentioned in the Book of Numbers (Num. XXI), and of the songs of Solomon, and of his exceedingly wise discussions concerning the nature of trees and of all herbs, as well as of beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. Likewise, the Book of the Words of the Days says:

“The rest of the deeds of Solomon, both the earlier and the later, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat” (2 Chron. IX).

There are many volumes of this kind, which Scripture proves to have been written, but which are plainly no longer extant today. For when Judaea was devastated by the Chaldaeans, the library gathered in ancient times was consumed by hostile fire along with the other wealth of the province. From it, the few books that are now contained in Holy Scripture were later restored through the diligence of Ezra, the priest, prophet, and scribe. Hence it is written of him:

“Ezra went up from Babylon, and he was a swift scribe in the law of Moses” (1 Esdras I).

“Swift,” that is, because he devised more readily formed letter-shapes than the Hebrews had possessed up to that time. And in the letter of the king of the Persians it is written:

“Artaxerxes, king of kings, sends greetings to Ezra, the priest and most learned scribe of the law of the Lord of heaven” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, some say that this Book of Jashar should be understood as the very Book of Kings, in which the righteous prophets are contained—namely Samuel, Gad, and Nathan. In their book it is written how Saul, having departed from the fear of the Lord, perished through his disobedience.

“Your renowned ones, O Israel, have been slain upon your mountains,” and so forth (from the Hebrew). In the Hebrew it reads, “upon your heights.” The sense is: “O Saul, the glorious ones of Israel have been slain upon your heights,” because they perished together with you in the sins of your disobedience. For your disobedience concerning idols was reckoned as “the heights,” just as it is written in the Book of Samuel:

“For obedience is better than sacrifice, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams; for rebellion is like the sin of divination, and stubbornness is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. XV).

“How the mighty have fallen! Do not announce it in Gath, nor proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult,” and so forth.

The prophet, astonished, laments the sudden fall of the leaders of his people and forbids anyone to rejoice at such a calamity or to spread news of it through the cities of the enemies. For Gath and Ashkelon are cities of the Allophyli.

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits; for there the shield of Saul was cast away, as though he had not been anointed with oil,” and so forth.

Because of the fall of the mighty and the ruin of his people, he speaks as though indignant to the very place of the slaughter, abhorring the deed that had been done there; yet not without a great mystery, as is shown shortly afterward.

“The arrow of Jonathan never turned back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty,” and so forth.

He wishes to indicate by this that Jonathan and Saul, in their own times, were exceedingly warlike and powerful in battle.

“Saul and Jonathan, beloved and comely in life, were not divided even in death. Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions,” and so forth.

He praises the beauty of their appearance and the steadfastness of their spirit, adding, through the rhetorical figure of hyperbole, a comparison with the eagle and the lion.

“Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet amid delights, who provided golden ornaments for your apparel,” and so forth (from the Hebrew).

He clothed them in scarlet and provided golden ornaments for their apparel from the spoils of the enemies whom he conquered.

“How the mighty have fallen in battle”—the implied phrase is, “because of your sin”—“Jonathan was slain upon your heights.”

The Hebrew does not contain “was.” The sense is: “O Saul, Jonathan, upon your heights—that is, in the sin of your disobedience—slain,” with “was” understood.

Behold King and prophet David, who did not return evil to those who repaid him with evil. When Saul and Jonathan fell in battle, he cursed Mount Gilboa in his lament, saying:

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits; for there the shield of Saul was cast away, as though he had not been anointed with oil,” and so forth.

What, then, had the mountains of Gilboa done wrong when Saul died, so that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them and the word of the sentence should dry them of every shoot of verdure? But because Gilboa is interpreted as “a flowing down,” and through Saul, the anointed and dead man, the death of our Mediator is represented, the mountains of Gilboa appropriately signify the proud hearts of the Jews. While these flow downward into the desires of this world, they became involved in the death of Christ, that is, of the Anointed One. And because the Anointed King dies bodily among them, they themselves are dried up from every dew of grace.

Of them it is rightly said:

“So that they could not be fields of firstfruits” (Isa. X).

For the proud minds of the Hebrews were not firstfruits. Remaining for the most part in unbelief at the coming of the Redeemer, they did not wish to follow the beginnings of faith. For Holy Church, fruitful in her firstfruits through the multitude of the nations, scarcely receives at the end of the world the Jews whom she will find; gathering what is last, she places them like remnants of the harvest. Concerning these remnants Isaiah says:

“Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.”

The mountains of Gilboa may nevertheless have been cursed from the prophet’s mouth for this reason: when fruit does not arise because the earth has dried up, the owners of the land may be struck by the harm of barrenness, so that they themselves might receive the sentence of the curse, because, on account of their iniquity, they had deserved to “receive among themselves the death of the King.”

## CHAPTER II

How David, anointed king over the house of Judah, sent messengers to return thanks to the men of Jabesh-gilead for the burial of Saul and his sons. Concerning Abner, son of Ner, who appointed Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, king over Israel, while David reigned in Hebron over the tribe of Judah alone. Concerning the battle between Abner and the men of Ish-bosheth and Joab and David’s men at Gibeon, and the killing of Asahel, the brother of Abner.

(CHAPTER II.) “David therefore went up, together with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. David also brought with him each of the men who were with him, together with his household, and they dwelt in the towns of Hebron.”

David’s ascent with his two wives to Hebron signifies the gathering of two peoples into the Catholic Church. For Hebron is interpreted as “marriage.” And rightly is the holy Church alone called marriage: she alone is the good bride, namely, the bride of the heavenly King. Concerning her it is said in the Song of Songs:

“There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens without number. One is my dove, my perfect one; one is she to her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” (Song of Songs VI).

There David brought each of the men, together with his household, to that place, because every believer is called into that fellowship through the preaching of the Gospel.

“There is neither Jew nor Greek, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; but Christ is all and in all” (Rom. X; Gal. III).

“And the men of Judah came and anointed David there, that he might reign over the house of Judah.”

The men of Judah anoint David king so that he may reign over the house of Judah, because the elect, through the good reputation of sacred preaching and the pursuit of virtue, rightly confess Christ to be king over his entire people, despite the proud and contemptuous who spurn the grace of God. They confess him to be the one to whom “all authority has been given by the Father in heaven and on earth, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

“And it was reported to David that the men of Jabesh-gilead had buried Saul,” and so forth.

This is narrated more fully in the Book of Chronicles, where it explains how it happened:

“When the men of Jabesh-gilead had heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, each of the brave men joined together, and they took the bodies of Saul and his sons, brought them to Jabesh, and buried their bones beneath the oak that was in Jabesh; and they fasted for seven days. Thus Saul died because of his iniquities, because he had transgressed the commandment of the Lord that he had commanded, and had not kept it. Moreover, he had consulted a woman who practiced divination and had not hoped in the Lord; therefore he killed him and transferred his kingdom to David the son of Jesse” (1 Chron. X).

What does it mean that David gives thanks to the men of Jabesh-gilead because they buried the bones of Saul and his sons, except that it greatly pleases our Redeemer when someone consigns to oblivion the wicked deeds of those who died in their sins, and does not imitate by his conduct the things he knows displeased the Lord, but instead chooses to do what he remembers the Lord commanded?

“But Abner, son of Ner, commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, and led him through the camps, and appointed him king over Gilead, over Geshur, over Jezreel, over Ephraim, over Benjamin, and over all Israel,” and so forth.

(From the Hebrew.) In the Hebrew it reads: “He brought him across to Mahanaim,” which is interpreted as “camps.” “He brought him across” is to be understood as meaning beyond the Jordan, and that he appointed him king at Mahanaim over Gilead and over Geshur. The Hebrew has “Ašturi,” that is, “over the tribe of Asher.”

“But the house of Judah followed David alone.”

What does it mean that Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul—whose name is interpreted as “man of confusion”—reigned over all Israel with the aid of Abner, whose name is interpreted as “lamp of the father,” while the house of Judah alone followed David? It means that, among the former people, only believers and those who truly confess the Lord follow David, our Lord and Savior, whereas among the rest the error of confusion still reigns, instigated by the devil, who often disguises himself as an angel of light.

“And the number of days that David dwelt reigning in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months,” and so forth.

It is appropriate that David reigned in Hebron for seven years and six months. Hebron, as we said above, is interpreted as “marriage,” or “eternal vision,” because our Savior reigns in the Catholic Church, which is also his bride, throughout the entire period of this life, which runs according to the number of the seven days, in accordance with the saying:

“Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

And after the completion of the number six—that is, the perfection of good work—he will lead all his elect to the true Sabbath, that is, to eternal rest, where they will also enjoy the perpetual vision of God (Isa. LXVI).

(From Jerome.) Hebron is a city in the tribe of Judah, formerly called Arbe, although it is incorrectly called Arbor in the Greek codices. Thus Arbor is corruptly written in our codices, whereas in the Hebrew it is read as Arbe, that is, “four,” because three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were buried there, as well as Adam the great, as it is written in the Book of Joshua, although some suppose that he was buried at the place of Calvary.

This same Hebron was formerly the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling place of giants; afterward it became David’s kingdom in the tribe of Judah, a priestly and refuge city. It lies to the south of Aesia [possibly an uncertain place-name] at a distance of approximately twenty-two miles. There the oak of Abraham, also called Mamre, was displayed down to the reign of King Constantius, and his mausoleum is still visible at the present time. Although a church has now been built there by our people, the place around it, with its terebinths, is still venerated in superstition by all the nations; beneath one of them Abraham once received angels as guests.

Thus this place was first called Arbe, and afterward received the name Hebron from one of the sons of Caleb. Read the Book of Chronicles (1 Chron. II). It was founded seven years before the city of Egypt was founded.

“And Abner, son of Ner, went out, together with the men of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, from the camp to Gibeon. Joab, son of Zeruiah, and David’s men also went out and met them beside the pool of Gibeon. When they had come together, they sat facing one another, these on one side of the pool and those on the other. Abner said to Joab, ‘Let the young men arise and play before us.’ Joab answered, ‘Let them arise.’ So twelve men from Benjamin, on the side of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, arose and crossed over, along with twelve of David’s men. Each man seized the head of his counterpart, drove his sword into the side of his opponent, and they fell together,” and so forth.

Josephus explains this passage as follows:

“Abner advanced a very select army to engage the tribe of Judah, for he was angry with those by whom David had been appointed king. Joab, son of David’s sister Zeruiah, whose father was Sar, was sent by David to meet him. He had been appointed commander of the army against Abner. His brothers Abishai and Asahel were also with him, together with all David’s armed men.

“Thus, when he came to a certain spring in the city of Sabaa, he drew up his line for battle. When Abner said that he wished to determine which of them had the stronger army, the two sides agreed to send twelve men to fight. Those who advanced between the lines began the contest as if in play; then David’s men abandoned their swords, seized the heads of their opponents, and pierced their loins and sides with their swords, until all had been killed as though by a single design.

“When these men had fallen, the rest of the army was also plundered. As the fierce battle continued, Abner’s people were defeated, and Joab did not cease pursuing them as they fled, ordering the armed men to hasten after their tracks and not to stop killing them.

“His brothers also fought most vigorously, among whom the younger Asahel was especially distinguished. He possessed such glory for the speed of his feet that, in a race, he could surpass not only men but even horses. He pursued the commander Abner, advancing straight on without turning to either side.

“When Abner looked back, saw the force of his pursuer, and told him to stop pursuing him and take the arms of one of the soldiers, Asahel still would not entirely desist from his effort. Abner again warned him to withdraw, lest he be compelled to strike him, and told him that thereafter he would have no confidence even before his brother. When Asahel despised his words and continued to flee behind him, Abner, forced to do so, cast his spear and suddenly pierced him with a mortal wound.”

“Then Abner spoke to Asahel, saying, ‘Withdraw; do not follow me, lest I be forced to strike you to the ground.’ But he despised him and would not turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him with the back of his spear in the groin, pierced him through, and he died,” and so forth.

Whom did Asahel prefigure except those whom furious anger seizes and drives headlong? The more insanely they are carried away, the more cautiously they must be made to turn aside. Thus Abner, whose name in our language means “lamp of the father,” fled, because the tongue of teachers—which judges the light of God from above, when it sees someone’s mind being violently carried away by an outburst of rage—does not wish to strike the pursuer when, out of piety, it refrains from returning verbal javelins against the angry.

But when the angry do not moderate themselves by any consideration, and, like Asahel, do not cease pursuing and raging, those who attempt to restrain the furious must by no means rise up in fury themselves. They must display whatever tranquility they possess and bring forward certain things subtly, by which they may cleanse the mind of the enraged person indirectly.

Thus, when Abner stood against his pursuer, he did not pierce him with the point but with the back of the spear. To strike with the point is to confront someone with the force of open rebuke. To strike the pursuer with the back of the spear is to touch the angry person calmly in certain respects and, as if by sparing him, overcome him.

Asahel immediately fell, because agitated minds, when they perceive that they are being spared and yet are inwardly touched under the guise of tranquility by the reasoning of the replies, immediately fall from the position they had assumed. Those who recoil from the force of their own passion under the blow of gentleness die, as it were, without iron.

## CHAPTER III

The long conflict between the house of David and Saul, and the names of David’s six sons who were born to him in Hebron. How Abner exhorted the people to leave Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, and transfer their allegiance to David; how Joab deceitfully killed Abner, and how David struck him with a sentence of curse through prophecy on account of this.

(CHAPTER III.) “There was therefore a long conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David. David grew stronger, continually becoming more powerful. But the house of Saul diminished day by day.”

What, then, is the house of David except the city of God, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, which is partly still a pilgrim on earth and partly already reigns with the Lord in heaven? And what is the house of Saul, the proud and impious king, except Babylon, that city full of confusion, which seduces all the nations and makes them commit fornication in its prostitution? (Rev. XVII–XVIII.)

There is therefore a long conflict between the house of Saul and the house of David, because the one that is according to the flesh persecutes the one that is according to the spirit (Gal. IV). But the house of David will rejoice all the more in the growth of its sons as the house of Saul rages against it through persecutions. The latter, daily declining in its iniquity, will waste away and at last, according to its deserts, sink with its head into the depths of the abyss.

“And sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, from Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; after him came Chileab, from Abigail, the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. The third was Absalom, the son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur. The fourth was Adonijah, the son of Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, the son of Abital; and the sixth was Ithream, from Eglah, David’s wife,” and so forth.

(From the Hebrew.) Since David’s other wives have been noted above and are not called David’s wives, why is Eglah alone called David’s wife here? Eglah herself is Michal. She alone is called his wife here because, in his youth, he first took her as his wife, and she is also said to have died in childbirth. Hence it is written later:

“Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no son until the day of her death, because she died in that very childbirth.”

What do the six sons born to him in Hebron signify except the perfection of the saints in faith, word, and deed, which the Church, their mother, daily bears to her bridegroom, namely, our Savior? From this spiritual marriage, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, sons of light are daily born into eternal life.

“Abner also addressed the elders of Israel, saying: ‘Yesterday and the day before, you were seeking David, that he might reign over you. Now, therefore, act, for the Lord spoke to David, saying: By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from all his enemies,’” and so forth.

What does it mean that Abner exhorts all the people of Israel to leave Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, and come to David with a ready and devoted heart, except that the holy teachers, who are called “the lamp of the father,” full of the light of faith and knowledge, proclaim the name of the Lord among all nations and exhort them, so that, rejecting the worship of idols and abandoning the error of confusion together with its author, the devil, they may hasten without delay to come to our David, who is truly strong-handed and desirable, whom the prophet describes as “the desire of all nations” (Hag. II), and strive to remain perpetually under his rule?

For Joab, whom Abner killed by speaking deceitfully and striking him in the groin, signifies none other than the ancient enemy, who daily strives to overthrow the faithful through deceptive persuasions and attempts to kill them through the contagion of harmful lust. Joab is interpreted as “enemy,” or “the same father.” For the devil is the head of all the wicked. Hence the Savior says to such people in the Gospel:

“You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John VIII).

Our David is therefore immune from this blow, because “God tempts no one” (Jas. I). He himself is the one who does not tempt with evil, and he wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II). “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the whole world” (Wis. II). Those who belong to his side imitate him.

The name and person of Joab may also appropriately be transferred by allegory to the Jewish people, who were always enemies of the preachers of the Gospel and persecuted the faith of Christ wherever they could. Concerning them Paul writes to the Thessalonians:

“For you became imitators, brothers, of the churches of God that are in Judaea in Christ Jesus. For you suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, persecuted us, do not please God, and are hostile to all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thereby always filling up their sins. For the wrath of God has come upon them to the end” (1 Thess. II).

But when David, excusing himself concerning the murder of the innocent, said:

“I and my kingdom are guiltless before God for ever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner. Let it come upon the head of Joab and upon all the house of his father; and let there not fail from the house of Joab one suffering a discharge of semen, one holding a spindle who is leprous, one falling by the sword, and one lacking bread”—

he denoted the unbelief and misery of the Jews.

Upon the head of Joab—that is, upon the rulers and priests of that people—and upon all the house of his father, namely, the synagogue of Satan and the assembly of the wicked, will come the iniquity of the impious,

“so that all the righteous blood shed upon the earth may be required of them, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah” (Matt. XXIII).

And let there not fail from this house of Joab one suffering a discharge of semen—that is, flowing away in various desires—because such people place all their hope in the pleasures of this life. There too are lepers holding a spindle, that is, stained by various errors and following the instability of heresy and worldly luxury:

“They will heap up teachers for themselves according to the desires of their hearts, having itching ears, and they will turn their hearing away from the truth.”

There too there will not fail one falling by the sword and lacking bread, because, while they continually lack that bread which descended from heaven and do not deserve to be nourished by it, they will not escape the sword of future vengeance.

## CHAPTER IV

How Rechab and Baanah killed Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul.

“The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came and entered the house of Ish-bosheth on a hot day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon. They entered the house. The female doorkeeper of the house, while cleaning wheat, fell asleep. Taking ears of wheat, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin,” and the rest.

(From the Hebrew.) These two men were commanders over the expeditions of Ish-bosheth. After Abner’s death, as the Hebrews relate, they plotted with Mephibosheth to kill Ish-bosheth together and establish Mephibosheth as king; and Mephibosheth himself became the informer concerning this plot. For this reason the same Mephibosheth is introduced here in the following manner.

(CHAPTER IV.) “Now Jonathan, the son of Saul, had a son who was disabled in his feet. He was five years old when the messenger came from Saul and Jonathan from Jezreel,” and so forth.

When Baanah and Rechab saw that their plot had been betrayed by Mephibosheth, they fled in terror to Gittaim, and remained there as resident aliens until that time. “That time” is to be understood as the time when they returned from there and entered the house of Ish-bosheth on a hot day, taking ears of wheat and striking him in the groin. They took ears of wheat as though for the sake of firstfruits, so that they might appear to be paying honor to the king and their deceit might not be detected.

(From Gregory.) Mystically, the doorkeeper cleans wheat when the guardianship of the mind separates virtues from vices by discernment. If she falls asleep, she admits assassins to the death of her own master, because when the vigilance of discernment ceases, it opens a path for evil spirits to kill the soul.

They enter and take away the ears because they immediately remove the shoots of good thoughts; and they strike in the groin because they kill the strength of the heart through the pleasure of the flesh. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with the pleasure of the flesh.

This Ish-bosheth would by no means have succumbed to an unexpected death if he had not appointed a woman—that is, a weak guard—to the entrance of the house, that is, to the entrance of the mind. A strong and watchful sense ought to be placed at the doors of the heart, one that is not overwhelmed by the sleep of negligence or deceived by the error of ignorance.

Hence he was rightly called Ish-bosheth, who, with a woman as guardian, was stripped by hostile swords. For Ish-bosheth means “man of confusion.” He is a man of confusion who is not fortified by the strong guardianship of the mind, because while he imagines that he is practicing virtues, the vices that creep in secretly kill him unawares. The entrance of the mind must be fortified with every virtue, lest at some time the lurking enemies penetrate it through an opening left by neglected thoughts.

## CHAPTER V

How all the tribes of Israel and the elders of Israel came to David at Hebron; how he began to reign at the age of thirty and completed forty years of reign. Concerning David’s battle against the Jebusite and his capture of the citadel of the city, which he called the City of David. Concerning David’s wives and concubines, whom he had in Jerusalem, and his sons and daughters. Concerning David’s battle against the Philistines.

(CHAPTER V.) “All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, saying: ‘Behold, we are your bone and your flesh,’” and so forth.

What does this gathering of the tribes of Israel to David signify except the gathering of all the nations to Christ? They say to him, as though flattering him, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh,” because they love and venerate in him the incarnation that he assumed from our nature in the Virgin’s womb, and desire to submit themselves to his rule and to serve him at all times.

Hence the Psalmist says:

“All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule the nations” (Ps. XXI).

“The elders of Israel also came to the king at Hebron,” when prophets and apostles, in one faith and with equal devotion, hasten together to our Mediator. Concerning them it is written:

“The princes of the peoples gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Ps. XLVI).

And elsewhere:

“He will be glorified in the presence of his elders” (Ps. CVI).

“David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months; and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah,” and so forth.

(From the Hebrew.) It is asked why the total is not reckoned as forty years and six months. The Hebrews resolve this in two ways. They say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months; therefore those same six months were rightly excluded from the total of his reign. They also say, alternatively, that David suffered from a bodily illness for six months in Hebron, and therefore those same six months were not counted in his reign.

They say that he began to reign in Hebron from the time when, after defeating the Amalekites, he sent gifts from their spoils to the elders of Judah—to those who were in Hebron, to those who were in Bethel, and to the others who were in the places where David himself and his men had dwelt.

Mystically, the fact that David began to reign at the age of thirty prefigured that our Lord came to baptism at the age of thirty and began to preach the Gospel of the kingdom. His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his power will not be given to another. The number forty, which consists of four times ten, signifies the fullness of times and the perfection of things.

“And the king and all the men who were with him went to Jerusalem against the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land. They said to David, ‘You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame,’ saying, ‘David shall not enter here.’ But David captured the stronghold of Zion. This is the City of David. For David had promised a reward on that day to whoever struck the Jebusite, touched the conduits of the housetops, and removed the lame and the blind who hated David’s life. Therefore it is said as a proverb: ‘The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple.’ David dwelt in the stronghold and called it the City of David. He built around it, from the Millo inward. And he advanced, becoming stronger and greater, and the Lord God of hosts was with him,” and so forth.

Josephus narrates the matter as follows:

“David rose up and came with everyone to Jerusalem, where the Jebusites lived. They were descended from the Canaanites. They closed the gates against him and placed the blind, the lame, and all the lepers upon the wall as objects of mockery for the king, saying that the blind prevented him from entering the city. They did this while despising him because of the city’s nearby fortifications.

“The king became angry and began to besiege Jerusalem, striving with great zeal and labor to capture it, so that at the very beginning of his rule he might demonstrate his strength. He threatened both them and anyone else who might attempt to resist him, and with great courage captured the lower city.

“Since he was still unable to take the citadel, the king, being eager for military action, began to promise honors and gifts, urging the soldiers on, so that whoever climbed up the hills below to the citadel and captured it might possess command of the army of the entire people.

“While everyone hastened to climb and no one delayed because of the promised reward, Joab, the son of Zeruiah, outstripped them all. Climbing to the summit, he shouted to the king and demanded command of the army.

“The king expelled the Jebusites from the upper citadel, rebuilt the city, called it Jerusalem, and dwelt there throughout his reign.”

Mystically, David’s expulsion of the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land, from Jerusalem signifies our Redeemer’s expulsion of hostile powers from the hearts of the faithful and his establishment of his dwelling there. For Jebusite is interpreted as “trampled,” and Jerusalem as “vision of peace.”
