Our Lord not only acquired for himself, through the mystery of the cross, a trophy of glory by destroying every principality of the devil; he also granted his faithful power over every strength of the devil. Hence he says to his disciples in the Gospel:

“Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over every power of the enemy” (Luke X).

It was therefore rightly said that David, after expelling the blind and the lame who hated David’s life, captured the citadel of Zion and called it his city, because when our Savior has expelled evil spirits, together with the multitude of vices, from any soul and has claimed it for himself through the illumination of wisdom, then it will rightly be called the citadel of Zion—that is, of contemplation—and the vision of peace. Then the following words of the Psalmist will rightly be said of it:

“God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. His place has become peaceful, and his dwelling is in Zion. There he broke the horns of bows, the shield, the sword, and the battle.”

“David knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that he had exalted his kingdom over his people Israel. David took still more concubines and wives from Jerusalem after he had come from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David,” and so forth.

But perhaps someone may say: If David bore the image of Christ, how is he said to have had many wives and concubines, when Christ the King both abhors and condemns these things?

I answer: This took place figuratively. David’s many wives indicated the image of the many peoples and nations who are joined to the fellowship of Christ through faith. His concubines signify the churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of Christ’s name; but because they follow Christ for the sake of carnal profit, they are called not wives but concubines.

Finally, if kings today have several wives or concubines, it is a crime, because the figures have now passed away for which permission was granted concerning wives or concubines. But now, since the figures have passed away, no permission is given.

[Col. 0082D] “Now the Philistines heard that they had anointed David king over Israel, and they all went up to seek David. When David heard this, he went up to the stronghold. The Philistines, meanwhile, came and spread themselves out in the valley of Rephaim. And David consulted the Lord, saying: ‘Shall I go up against the Philistines, and will you deliver them into my hand?’ And the Lord said to David: ‘Go up, for I will certainly deliver the Philistines into your hand.’ So David came to Baal-perazim and struck them there. And he said: ‘The Lord has divided my enemies before me, as waters are divided.’ Therefore the name of that place was called Baal-perazim. And they left their images there, which David and his men carried away.” (From the Hebrew.)

[Col. 0083A] David carried them away and ordered them burned with fire, as the Book of Chronicles makes clear, saying: “And they left their gods there, which David ordered to be burned” (I Chron. XIV).

“David again consulted the Lord. He answered him: ‘Do not go up, but circle around behind them and come upon them opposite the weeping ones.’” (From the Hebrew.) In Hebrew it reads not “opposite the pear trees,” but “opposite the weeping ones.” Thus he commands him to come opposite the weeping ones—that is, opposite their idols, where their idols were, in which they trusted. These idols are called “weeping ones” because they are worthy of weeping and lead those who worship them to weep over their miseries. Thus, because of their blasphemy, the divine word here calls their idols “weeping ones,” just as elsewhere the idol of Moab is called “the pollution of Moab.”

[Col. 0083B] “And when you hear the sound of one walking in the tops of the weeping ones, etc.” That is, when you hear from the angelic powers that their idols—in which all their strength lies—are being crushed and trampled down. Then you shall enter into battle, because then the Lord will go out before your face to strike the camp of the Philistines. For the Lord executed judgments against their idols, just as he did against the gods of the Egyptians.

## CHAPTER VI

Concerning David’s bringing up of the ark and, because of the contrary event—that is, the striking down of Uzzah the Levite—turning it aside to the house of Obed-edom, and from there transferring it to his own house. And when he had completed offering holocausts and peace offerings, he distributed food to the whole multitude of Israel. Also, concerning David’s being mocked by Michal, the daughter of Saul, as he danced before the ark of the Lord.

[Col. 0083C] (CHAP. VI.) “David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, to bring up the ark of God, placing it upon a new cart. When they came to the threshing floor of Nachon, Uzzah stretched out his hand toward the ark of God and grasped it, because the oxen were kicking and had made it swerve. And the Lord was angry with indignation against Uzzah, and struck him because of his rashness. He died there beside the ark of God,” etc. (From Bede.)

In the history of the blessed king and prophet David, who is said to have brought up the ark of God, humility is commended, pride condemned, and rashness punished. For David himself, who was not ashamed humbly to dance before the ark of the Lord, soon deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God who was to be born from his lineage; but his wife, who despised that same humility and was not deemed worthy to be made fruitful by his seed, paid the penalty of perpetual barrenness. The priest, too, who touched the ark with inconsiderate rashness, expiated the guilt of his presumption by a premature death. Here it is necessary to consider how greatly one sins who approaches the body of the Lord as a guilty person, if that devout priest was punished with death because he seized the ark—which represented the Lord’s body—with less reverence than he ought.

Yet, according to the allegory, David signifies Christ, and the ark the Church. David sought to bring the ark into his own city; but, when a contrary circumstance intervened, he turned it aside elsewhere for a time, and thereafter completed what had greatly delighted him. For when the Lord appeared in the flesh, he preached the Gospel [Col. 0084A] to the children of Israel, that is, to his own people; “but a partial blindness has happened in Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI).

But so that these matters may become clearer, let us examine them one by one. David gathered all the chosen people from Israel, thirty thousand, because the Lord established the primitive Church in Israel—not indeed the whole of Israel, but joining to himself those who were chosen. “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed” (Rom. IX). They are said to have numbered thirty thousand, that is, to have been perfected in the firmness of faith, works, and hope. Three pertains to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; ten pertains to works because of the Decalogue of the Law; a thousand pertains to hope because of its perfection in eternal life, above which there is nothing, just as no number is greater than a thousandfold perfection. For even if you say “thousands,” whether thirty thousand or even a thousand thousand, you do not pass beyond the number one thousand by counting it itself, but multiply it either by itself or by repeatedly applying smaller numbers to it.

Therefore multiply three by ten, lest faith without works be dead. Likewise multiply thirty by a thousand, so that faith, which works through love, may hope for its reward nowhere but in heaven. Thus the chosen from Israel signify peoples rightly believing, working, and hoping.

The men of Judah who were with David signify the apostles and teachers, who clung more familiarly to Christ’s side, as it were. Surrounded by this twofold army, the Lord rejoices to bring up the ark—that is, to enlarge the Church—and to implant it in the hearts of those who did not believe.

The ark is placed upon a new cart so that the grace of the New Testament may be poured into minds renewed in baptism, and the new wine may be entrusted to new wineskins for preservation.

Previously the ark had been in the house of Abinadab, who was in Gibeah, because the same faith of the Church that is now preached flourished even before the time of the Lord’s incarnation in those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs and prophets. For Abinadab, whose name is interpreted as “my spontaneous father,” signifies both Abraham, the father of faith, and Moses, the lawgiver. Each of them guards the ark in Gibeah, because he fortifies the breasts of believers with lofty examples of virtue. Hence Gibeah is interpreted as “hill”; it is a place in the city of Kiriath-jearim.

When the ark had been brought outside, David and all Israel danced before the Lord [Col. 0084D] with various kinds of musical instruments, because, as soon as the proclamation of the new grace began, the Lord invited everyone to offer praises to God the Father in humility, saying: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John XII); “to one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, to another the grace of healings,” etc. (I Cor. XII).

As the ark proceeded—that is, as the primitive Church grew—they came to the threshing floor of Nachon, that is, the prepared threshing floor, namely, the Church of the Gentiles, which was to be consecrated in the truth of faith. Concerning it John says: “For he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. III).

There the priest who touched the ark incautiously, as though to steady it, was immediately struck down by the Lord and died. For when the Jewish people envy the Gentiles, they deprive themselves of the gift of salvation; when they wish to mix the Law with the Gospel, they deprive themselves of the grace of both.

“And he grasped it,” it says, “because the oxen were kicking.” For the oxen’s kicking signifies that the preachers of the Gospel were acting more freely with regard to the faith and were not proceeding according to the custom of the Law, but were interpreting the Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and sacrifices spiritually. Those who came down from Judea to teach the brethren attempted to correct them as though they were wandering, saying: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts XV). Of these James said to Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts XXI).

Because of the priest’s death, David did not wish to turn the ark of the Lord aside to himself in the city of David, but turned it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. This signifies that, when the Jews rejected the word, lest preaching that was heard but not received should harm them further, the apostles were taken from them and sent to instruct the Gentiles.

Therefore the place of the threshing floor of Nachon—which demonstrates the faith of the Gentiles, the house of grace, as prepared—is called “the striking of Uzzah,” namely, because “through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Rom. XI).

Obed-edom, whose name is interpreted as “serving man,” is the man concerning whom the Lord says to the Father: “You will appoint me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know has served me” (Ps. XVII). There, promising the rejection of the Jews, as though the death of Uzzah, he says: “You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people” (ibid.).

The name of the city also fits. For Gath is interpreted as “winepress,” signifying the cross, on which “the true vine” (John XV) was willing to be trodden and pressed. From this, the whole people of the Gentiles may rightly be called Gittites when it says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI).

The three months during which the ark remains there signify faith, hope, and charity. Just as a month is completed by its days, so each virtue reaches perfection by its own successive stages. These months continue to pass until the fullness of the Gentiles enters.

At last David, returning, will bring the ark into the city of David, because, when Enoch and Elijah preach, the Lord will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children (Luke I).

[Col. 0085D] “Sacrificing oxen and rams.” This means that he crowns with the blood of martyrdom those who thresh the Lord’s threshing floor and lead his sheep, while also openly manifesting the example of his own incarnation and passion—an example not previously believed by the Jews. This is signified by the fact that David himself was girded with a linen ephod. For linen, produced from the earth and brought to the whiteness of a garment through much labor, displays the truth of human flesh triumphing amid the scourges.

But while everyone rejoiced and resounded with hymns as they entered the heavenly citadel, Michal alone, the daughter of Saul, was absent from those bringing the ark. Indeed, from the window she despised David as he humbled himself, because among the Jews who will believe at the end of the world there will be some who will follow Christ only in profession but the Antichrist in their works.

To these it rightly applies that Michal herself—who, to signify the instability of carnal people, is interpreted as “all water”—is called not David’s wife but Saul’s daughter. For they serve Christ only in faith, and they will not be crowned in his kingdom, but will be condemned by the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitated.

Let the wicked rage and despise the humility of the Church: nevertheless, the ark of the Lord enters its appointed place.

“It is placed in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it.” That is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is implanted in the hearts of all whom the Lord had predestined for eternal life (Acts XIII).

David offers holocausts and peace offerings before the Lord; that is, Christ commends the faith and devotion of the Church to the Father—he “who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us”—and, in David’s example, blesses the humble and faithful, feeding them with the nourishment of the saving mystery.

“He distributed to each person one cake of bread,” namely, of him who descended from heaven and gives life to this world.

“And one portion of roast beef,” namely, of the fattened calf that was slaughtered for the younger son returning to his father and roasted in the fire of passion, saying: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI).

“And a piece of fried bread mixed with oil”: namely, the flesh utterly cleansed from the stain of sin, but, for the sake of human salvation, roasted in the frying pan of the cross, abundant in the delights [Alternative: “in the abundant love of the cross for human salvation,” etc.] [Col. 0086C]

And rightly one cake of bread and one portion of meat are given, because “there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. IV).

In another sense, the faithful receive these gifts when “we, though many, are one bread and one body” (I Cor. X) in Christ, and when each person chastises the wantonness of his flesh, subjects it to servitude, and cooks it in the fire of the Holy Spirit; likewise, they make the exceedingly rich fruits of good works boil with compassion for their neighbor.

But, by contrast, Saul’s daughter enters the king’s chamber in vain and produces no fruit from the seed conceived, because those who receive the word of God only with the ear, without the offspring of good works, await the day of everlasting death.

(From Gregory.) Often, because they cannot be understood, either the deeds or the words of better people displease those who are worse. Yet they should be all the less rashly criticized by them, since they can in no way be truly grasped. Often something is done by the great in a discretionary manner that is considered an error by the lesser. Often many things are said by the strong which the weak judge precisely because they do not understand them.

This is well signified by that ark of the covenant, which was tilted when the oxen kicked. Because the Levite believed that it was about to fall, he wished to raise it up, and immediately received the sentence of death.

For what is the mind of the righteous except the ark of the covenant, carried by oxen that kick and therefore made to incline? Sometimes even one who rules well, when shaken by the confession of subject peoples, is moved by the very delight of condescending to accommodate them. But in what is done through such accommodation, the inclination itself is considered a fall of strength by the inexperienced.

[Col. 0087A] Hence some subjects extend against this hand the hand of criticism, but by that very rashness immediately fall away from life. The Levite, therefore, as though helping, stretched out his hand, but, by his offense, lost his life: for whenever the weak criticize the deeds of the strong, they themselves are rejected from the company of the living.

Sometimes holy men, condescending to the least, say certain things, while they utter other things as they contemplate the highest realities. When fools do not understand the force either of condescension or of elevation, they criticize these things audaciously.

And what is it to wish to correct the righteous in his condescension except to raise up the inclined ark with the proud hand of criticism? What is it to criticize an unfamiliar expression except to regard the movement of his strength as a fall into error?

But the person who presumptuously raises up the ark of God loses his life, because no one would dare to correct the saints in what is right unless he had first thought better of himself than of them. Hence that Levite is rightly called Uzzah, which is interpreted as “strong” or “robust in the Lord.” For presumptuous people would never judge the deeds or words of their betters as weak unless they believed themselves, with an audacious mind, strong in the Lord.

“Michal, the daughter of Saul, came out to meet David and said: ‘How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants,’” etc.

When David brought back the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem by dancing, he was mocked by Michal, the daughter of Saul and his wife. It is worthwhile to consider how many gifts of virtue David himself had received, [Col. 0087C] and how firmly he preserved himself in humility amid them all.

Who would not have been puffed up by having broken the jaws of lions, shattered the arms of bears, been chosen over many brothers, been anointed to govern the kingdom after the rejected king, struck down Goliath—feared by all—with a single stone, brought back numerous foreskins after killing the Philistines at the king’s command, finally received the promised kingdom, and possessed the entire Israelite people without any opposition?

And yet, when he brings the ark of God back to Jerusalem, as though forgetting that he had been placed above everyone, he dances before the ark in the presence of the assembled people. And because dancing before the ark was, as is believed, the custom of the common people, the king whirls about in dance in divine service.

Behold, the one whom the Lord had singularly preferred to all others despises himself beneath the Lord, making himself equal to the least and displaying himself as lowly. He does not recall the power of the kingdom; he does not fear to become lowly in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; he does not recognize himself as distinguished by honor above the others before the ark of the one who had given him honor. Before God he performed weak and humble acts in order, through humility, to strengthen what he had done bravely before men.

What others think of his deeds I do not know. I am more astonished by David dancing than by David fighting. By fighting he subdued the enemy; by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself.

When Michal, the daughter of Saul, still insane with the swelling pride of royal descent, despised his humility and said: “How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and stripping himself naked as one of the buffoons is stripped naked,” she immediately heard him reply: “I will play before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.” And shortly afterward: “I will play, and I will become even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes.”

As though he openly said: “I seek to become contemptible before men, because through humility I desire to preserve my nobility before the Lord.”

There are some who think humbly of themselves, who, placed in positions of honor, understand that they are nothing but dust and ashes, yet refuse to appear contemptible before men. Contrary to what they think inwardly about themselves, they cover themselves outwardly with a rigid dignity.

There are others who desire to appear contemptible to men and, by displaying themselves as abject, despise everything they are; yet inwardly they swell with pride before themselves, as though because of the very merit of the usefulness they have displayed. Thus they are all the more exalted in heart the more they suppress pride in outward appearance.

David detected both these battles of a single pride with great discernment and overcame them with remarkable strength. Because, while thinking humbly of himself inwardly, he does not seek outward honor, he declares: “I will play, and I will become more contemptible.” And because, by displaying himself as contemptible outwardly, he does not swell inwardly, he adds: “And I will be humble in my own eyes.”

As though he openly said: “I consider myself inwardly to be as I display myself outwardly when I despise myself.”

What, then, will those do whom learning exalts, if David—who knew that the Redeemer was to come from his own flesh and announced his joys prophetically—nevertheless pressed down the neck of his heart with the strong heel of contempt for himself, saying: “And I will be humble in my own eyes”?

## CHAPTER VII

That David, wishing to build a house for God, was forbidden by the prophet Nathan in the word of the Lord, because his son was to complete it, by the disposition of divine providence.

(CHAP. VII.) “Now it came to pass, when the king was sitting in his house and the Lord had given him rest on every side from all his enemies, that he said to Nathan the prophet: ‘Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is placed in the midst of skins?’ And Nathan said to the king: ‘Go, do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you.’ But it came to pass that night, and behold, the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: ‘Go and speak to my servant David. Thus says the Lord: Will you build me a house in which to dwell? For I have not dwelt in a house from the day when I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt to this day, but I have walked in a tabernacle and in a tent through all the places that I passed through with all the children of Israel,’” etc.

When the prophet, questioned by the king, replied, “Do all that is in your heart,” and afterward, instructed by the Lord, forbade the same things that he had previously permitted, it is plainly evident that the spirit of prophecy does not always illumine the minds of the prophets, because, as it is written of the Holy Spirit: “He breathes where he wills” (John III).

For this reason, when Elisha saw a weeping woman but did not know the cause, he said to the servant who tried to restrain her: “Leave her, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not revealed it to me” (IV Kings IV).

Almighty God arranges this through a great dispensation of mercy. For when he sometimes grants and sometimes withdraws the spirit of prophecy, he both raises the minds of the prophets to lofty heights and preserves them in humility, so that those who receive the spirit may discover that they are from God, while those who do not possess the spirit of prophecy may recognize what they are from themselves.

That David was forbidden to build the house of God because he was a man of blood suggests morally that the person who undertakes to correct the faults of others ought to be clean in himself: he should not think about earthly things or succumb to low desires, so that he may see more clearly what others must avoid, the more truly he himself avoids these things in knowledge and life.

An eye burdened by dust does not clearly examine a speck in another member. Nor can hands wipe away dirt that has been thrown upon something while they themselves are holding mud.

With regard to the sequence of the ancient translation, the divine voice aptly indicates by its reference to David, who was occupied with external wars, when it says: “You shall not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood.”

The person who devotes himself to correcting the minds of his neighbors by good instruction builds the temple of God. For we are the temple of God, because we are built for true life through his indwelling, as Paul testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (I Cor. III).

But a man of blood is forbidden to build the temple of God, because one who is still immersed in carnal actions ought to be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbors spiritually.

“Through all the places,” he says, “that I passed through with all the children of Israel.” These places through which the Lord says he passed are to be understood as Shiloh, Gilgal, Nob, and the other places where the tabernacle and the ark of the Lord were located.

“Have I ever spoken to any of the judges of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying: ‘Why have you not built me a house of cedar?’”

He did not command any of the judges to build him a house of cedar because all of them fought against enemies, and all were shedders of blood. Yet your son, against whom the wars of enemies will not rise and who will not be a man of blood, will build me a house.

“And now you shall say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I took you from the pastures, following the flocks.” And a little later: “And I made your name great, like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.”

“The Lord made your name great,” he says—that is, as he made the names of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of Moses and Joshua, whose names are very famous on earth.

“And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant it, and it will dwell under it.” Here the divine word describes the time of Solomon, when the children of Israel would have peace all around and would not be afflicted and oppressed as they had been oppressed and afflicted in the time of the judges.

“If he does anything wicked, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men,” and so forth.

By “the rod of men” he means the sword of enemies. The “blows of the sons of men” are the afflictions of human bodies, by which people are deservedly scourged by the Lord for their sins. These statements can be understood in this way according to the historical sense. But what they signify according to the allegory must be examined more deeply.

(From Augustine.) When many prosperous things had happened to King David, he considered making a house for the Lord—that famous temple of exceptional renown, which was afterward built by his son King Solomon. While he was considering this, the word of the Lord came to the prophet Nathan, who was to carry it to the king. There God said that a house would not be built for him by David, nor had he for so long a time commanded anyone among his people to make him a house of cedar:

[Col. 0090B] “And now,” he says, “you shall say this to my servant David: Thus says the Lord Almighty: I took you from the sheepfold, to be ruler over my people Israel; and I was with you in all the things in which you walked; and I destroyed all your enemies from before your face, and I made you renowned according to the name of the great ones who are upon the earth.

“And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant it, and it will dwell apart; and it will no longer be disturbed, nor will the son of iniquity continue to humble it as at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies, and the Lord will announce to you that you will build a house for him.

“And it will be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that I will raise up your seed after you, who will come from your body, and I will prepare his kingdom. He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be his father, and he will be my son.

“And when his iniquity comes, I will rebuke him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men. But I will not remove my mercy from him, as I removed it from some whom I removed from before my face. And his house will be faithful, and his kingdom forever before me; and his throne will be established forever.”

Whoever thinks that this great promise was fulfilled in Solomon is greatly mistaken. He notices what was said: “He will build me a house,” because Solomon built that famous temple; but he does not notice what is said: “His house and his kingdom will be faithful forever before me.”

Let him therefore consider and observe Solomon’s house, full of foreign women worshiping false gods, and Solomon himself—once a wise king—seduced and cast down by them into that same idolatry. Let him not dare to suppose either that God made this promise deceitfully or that God could not have foreseen that Solomon’s house would be such.

[Col. 0091A] We ought no longer to doubt this, since we have already seen these things fulfilled in Christ our Lord, “who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I), lest we vainly and foolishly seek some other person here, as the foolish Jews do.

Indeed, they themselves understand so clearly that the son whom they read as promised to King David in this passage was not Solomon that, although the one who was promised has already been revealed with such clarity, they still claim in their wondrous blindness that they await another.

A certain image of the future reality was indeed present in Solomon, in that he built the temple and had peace according to his name. For Solomon means “peaceful” in Latin. At the beginning of his reign he was also remarkably praiseworthy.

But even in his own person he announced beforehand, under the shadow of the future, what was to come; he himself did not present Christ the Lord. Hence certain things are written about him as though they had been foretold of him, although Holy Scripture, by prophesying through deeds also, in a certain way outlines in him the figure of future things.

For, besides the books of the divine history, where he is reported to have reigned, the seventieth Psalm is the first to be inscribed with his name in its title. In it many things are said that cannot at all suit him but fit the Lord Christ with perfect clarity, so that it is evident that in the one there was some kind of shadowy representation, while in the other the reality itself was presented.

It is known within what boundaries Solomon’s kingdom had been confined; yet in that psalm we read, to say nothing of other matters: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” [Col. 0091C] (Ps. LXXI). We see this fulfilled in Christ.

For he began his rule from the river, where, after he had been baptized by John and identified by John, he began to be recognized by the disciples, who called him not only Teacher but also Lord.

Nor did Solomon begin to reign while his father David was still alive—a thing that happened to none of those kings—for any other reason than that this too might sufficiently make clear that he is not the one whom this prophecy foreshadows. The prophecy speaks to his father, saying: “And it will be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that I will raise up your seed after you, who will come from your body, and I will prepare his kingdom.”

How, then, because of what follows—“He will build me a house”—will Solomon be thought to be the one prophesied, and not rather, because of what precedes—“When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you”—understood as the promise of another peaceful one, who was foretold as arising not before David’s death, as Solomon did, but after it?

However long a time might intervene before Christ Jesus came, undoubtedly he who was promised to King David had to come after the king’s death, the one who would build a house for God—not of wood and stones, but of human beings, such as we rejoice that he builds.

To this house the Apostle says, that is, to Christ’s faithful: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are” (I Cor. III).

The Lord’s blessing in the seed of David is not to be hoped for only for a time, as it appeared in the days of Solomon, but forever. In this most certain hope it is said: “Let it be, let it be,” as it is written at the end of Psalm LXXXVIII: “Blessed be the Lord forever. Let it be, let it be.” The repetition of this word confirms that hope.

Understanding this, David says in the Second Book of Kings: “And you have spoken concerning the house of your servant for a long time.” Therefore, shortly afterward, he says: “Now begin, and bless the house of your servant forever,” etc.

For he was then going to beget a son from whom his lineage would be carried onward to Christ, through whom his house—and that same house of God—was to be eternal.

The house of David is so called because of David’s lineage; but the house of God is the same house because it is the temple of God, made not of stones but of human beings, where the people will dwell forever with God and in God, and God with the people and in his people, so that God may be the one filling his people and the people be full of their God: “And God will be all in all” (II Cor. XV).

He is himself the reward in peace, who is the strength in battle.

Therefore, although according to the Septuagint Nathan’s words say: “And the Lord will announce to you that you will build a house for him,” David’s words afterward say: “For you, Lord Almighty, God of Israel, have revealed this to your servant, saying: ‘I will build you a house.’”

For we too will build this house by living well and by God’s assistance, so that we may live well, because “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

When the final dedication of this house comes, then what God spoke here through Nathan will take place, saying:

[Col. 0092C] “And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant them, and they will dwell apart; and they will no longer be disturbed, and the son of iniquity will not continue to humble them, as at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Whoever hopes for so great a good in this world and on this earth is foolishly wise. Beforehand, someone might think that this was fulfilled in Solomon’s peace. For Scripture commends that peace in the shadow of the future through an exalted prophecy.

But this suspicion has been carefully forestalled, since, after it says, “And the son of iniquity will not continue to humble him,” it immediately adds: “As at the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Judges had been appointed over that people before kings began to exist among them, from the time when they received the promised land. And certainly the son of iniquity—that is, the foreign enemy—humbled them at intervals, during which periods of peace are recorded as alternating with wars. Indeed, periods of peace are found there that lasted longer than Solomon’s, who reigned forty years. Under the judge called Ehud, there were eighty years of peace (Judg. III).

Far be it, then, that Solomon’s times should be believed to have been promised in this promise; still less should the time of any other king. None of them reigned in such great peace as Solomon, nor did that nation ever hold the kingdom in such a way that it was free from anxiety about being subjected to enemies, because, amid such changeability of affairs, no people has ever been granted such security that it would not fear hostile incursions against this life.

The place, therefore, that is promised as a dwelling of such peace and security is eternal and belongs to the eternal, in the mother Jerusalem that is free, where the people of Israel will truly be. For this name is interpreted as “seeing God.” In desire for this reward, the life of faith must be lived during this sorrowful pilgrimage.

[Col. 0093A] “Then King David went in and sat before the Lord, and said: ‘Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far? Yet even this seemed a small thing in your sight, Lord God, unless you also spoke concerning the house of your servant for a long time. This is the law of Adam, Lord God.’” (From the Hebrew.)

“This is the law of Adam, Lord God,” that is, “It is the law of man, Lord God, that he should serve you in simplicity of heart and purity, while you deal with him according to your mercy, as you have deigned to deal with me, your servant.”

It continues:

“What more can David add to speak to you? For you know your servant, Lord God. Because of your word, and according to your heart, you have done all these great things.”

“Because of your word”—the word that you promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—you have done all these things for me, your servant. What he says, “according to your heart,” is understood as “according to your mercy.”

“For there is none like you, nor is there any God besides you, in all that we have heard with our ears.”

“There is no God,” he says, “like you, who has done the great things that we have heard with our ears.”

“Before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its god.”

The Hebrew has: “From the nations and their gods.” The sense is: “Before your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt”—that is, from the hand of the Egyptians, whom you killed in the Red Sea—and from their gods, against whom you executed judgments.

“For you, Lord of hosts, God of Israel, have revealed the ear of your servant, saying: ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found his heart, to pray to you with this prayer,” etc.

The Lord had revealed to him through the prophet that he would build a house for him; therefore David says that he had found his heart—that is, he had found courage in his heart—to pray to him with this prayer.

# CHAPTER VIII. David’s battle against the Philistines, and how, when he struck down the Moabites, he measured them with a cord, making them equal with the ground; also how he struck the Syrians in the Valley of Salt, and concerning David’s sons as priests

## (CHAP. VIII)

“After this it happened that David struck the Philistines and humbled them; and David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines,” and so forth.

The “bridle of tribute” consisted of the five cities of the Philistines, which frequently made Israel tributary to themselves. David took these cities from them, humbled them, and made them tributary to himself. Hence it is also read in Chronicles: “David struck the Philistines and humbled them; and he took Gath and its villages from their hand” (1 Chronicles XVIII).

“And he struck Moab, and measured them with a cord, making them equal with the ground. He measured two cords: one for killing and one for bringing to life. And Moab became subject to David, paying tribute,” and so forth.

What is written about David—“He struck Moab, and measured them with a cord, making them equal with the ground”—must be understood hyperbolically. It could not happen that human beings living upon the earth should be humbled to such an extent that, with a cord stretched over them to prove it, they appeared equal to the very surface of the earth. Rather, Scripture wished by this expression to intensify the immense humiliation of the captured and subjugated nation, saying that they had been made equal with the earth: as though they had been so unmanned and despised that they could no longer be worth more than the earth itself, which contained no human beings.

You have many examples of this kind of expression in the Scriptures, such as the Gospel passage: “There are also many other things that Jesus did, which, if they were written down one by one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written” (John XXI). How could the world contain books that could have been written in the world? Scripture used such an expression to convey the greatness and multitude of the Lord’s works. Likewise, in David’s lament: “Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions” (2 Samuel I). A very similar expression is found in secular literature:

> They who surpassed the snows in whiteness and the winds in speed.  
> [Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.]

When he says that he measured them with a cord, he uses “cord” allegorically for a lot, since the extent of fields is customarily measured with a cord. Hence it is written: “And by lot he divided the land for them with the cord of distribution” (Psalm LXXVII). This signifies that David divided the regions of the Moabites among whatever heirs he wished, with as free a disposition as any owner might divide his own fields at will by drawing a cord here and there.

“He measured two cords: one for killing and one for bringing to life.” This too is said allegorically, signifying that David had it entirely in his power, with no one resisting, which of them he would give over to death as rebellious and which he would spare as submissive.

As for David’s subjugating Moab—which is interpreted as “from the father”—and Damascus Syria and the other regions to his authority, making them tributary, this mystically signifies that Christ, holding all nations under his dominion, makes them render the burden of servitude, while each nation, united in confession of his name, devoutly pays him the substance of good works.

Damascus is a famous city of Phoenicia, bearing the same name by which Abraham’s servant’s son, Masec, was also called. Damascus is interpreted as “cup of blood”; Syria is interpreted as “exalted” or “moist.” And rightly so: she who was formerly moistened by lust, proud in spirit, and inexplicably thirsty for human blood now, cleansed by the baptism of Christ, exalted through progress in the virtues, desires to receive the cup of his blood.

What else does it signify that David sanctified to the Lord the golden, silver, and bronze vessels that he had taken from all the nations, except that Christ signifies by this all those whom he summons to his faith from every nation: some as gold, that is, splendid in spiritual understanding; others as silver, that is, shining with the brilliance of eloquence; and others as bronze, that is, resounding with divine preaching? Serving faithfully in the tabernacle, they may fittingly perform the Lord’s ministry forever.

“He also made a name for himself when he returned, having struck down eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt after Syria had been captured,” and so forth.

*(From the Hebrew.)* He is said to have made a name for himself because, after eighteen thousand had been struck down in the Valley of Salt, he erected a triumphal arch for himself. He also made a name for himself because, after Damascus Syria and Zobah Syria had been defeated, he is said to have erected another triumphal arch.

If anyone is troubled that in many Latin manuscripts David is found to have struck down not eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt but twelve thousand, let him know that this was introduced into those manuscripts through the error of scribes. In truth, David struck down eighteen thousand in that same Valley of Salt, whereas Joab struck down twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm Fifty-Eight.

What is signified by the multitude struck down by David in the Valley of Salt except that our Redeemer, through the strictness of his judgment, extinguishes the folly of immoderate slumber in those who think wrongly about him? Hence it is said by a certain wise man: “A hard heart will fare badly at the end, and whoever loves danger will perish in it” (Ecclesiasticus III).

“And David’s sons were priests.”

# CHAPTER IX. How much kindness David showed to Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son

## (CHAP. IX)

“And David said: ‘Is there perhaps anyone remaining from the house of Saul, that I may show him mercy for Jonathan’s sake?’ Now there was a servant from the house of Saul named Ziba. When the king summoned him, he said to him: ‘Are you Ziba?’ And he answered: ‘I am your servant.’ And the king said: ‘Is anyone still remaining from the house of Saul, that I may show him the mercy of God?’ And Ziba said to the king: ‘There remains a son of Jonathan, disabled in his feet.’”

Behold, David did not forget his oath and covenant, which he had formerly made with Jonathan (1 Samuel XX); rather, he fulfilled toward the son the mercy that he had promised to the father. This deed both demonstrated his fidelity according to the historical sense and displayed the mysteries of the allegory in the event.

It has often been said that David represents the person of Christ; and it was also mentioned above that Jonathan—which is interpreted as “gift of the dove” or “gift of the Lord”—bears the type of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Jonathan therefore had a little son named Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, as Scripture testifies. David ordered him to be summoned to him, when God’s predestination and foreknowledge chose for divine service the one whom it saw to be weak in speech and action for carrying out the affairs and worldly business of the age. For the one whom the world despises because of the arrogance of exaltation, God acquires because of the devotion of humility.

Mephibosheth is interpreted as “from the mouth of shame.” Therefore the one whose speech and presence the world’s pride despises will, by God’s gift, appear useful for spiritual ministry in the Church.

What does it mean, then, that David, seeking from Ziba, Saul’s servant, someone from Saul’s lineage, discovered Mephibosheth through Ziba’s disclosure, except that our Redeemer, examining the number of the elect among those who have despised the world, causes them to come to him? For Ziba is interpreted as “one who comes forth.”

When Ziba was questioned by the king, he answered that Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son, was in the house of Machir son of Ammiel, in Lodabar. This circumstance fits the present interpretation well. Machir is interpreted as “selling” or “from infirmity”; Ammiel as “his people is God”; Lodabar as “he himself is the word.”

Thus our David, choosing the despised things of this world and the things that are not, so that he might destroy the things that are (1 Corinthians I), found them saleable to the world and established in infirmity, judged them worthy for his people, and attached them to himself through the word of preaching. He granted them royal honor among his sons. Hence, giving Saul’s fields and servants to Mephibosheth, David also ordered Mephibosheth himself to be his table-companion at his table together with his sons.

For the grace of our Mediator, which, according to Mary’s words, “has brought down the powerful from their thrones and exalted the humble” (Luke I), and, according to Hannah’s prophecy, “raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap, to seat him with princes and hold the throne of glory” (1 Samuel II), takes despised persons from the world, makes them possessors of virtues, and daily refreshes them with himself at the table of the Holy Scriptures through spiritual knowledge.

Thus it happens that such people produce offspring whose name is interpreted as Micha. For *Micha* sounds in Latin as “Who is this?” Such people frequently become objects of the people’s wonder: recently removed from the world’s contempt, they will appear glorious in the Church by God’s gift.

# CHAPTER X. David’s battle against Ammon, king and son of Ammon, because he had dishonored David’s messengers sent to him

## (CHAP. X)

“After this it happened that the king of Ammon died, and Ammon his son reigned in his place. And David said: ‘I will show kindness to Ammon son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me,’” and so forth.

When David fled from the presence of Achish, king of Gath, he came to Nahash, king of Ammon, who showed him great kindness and bestowed gifts upon him (1 Samuel XXII). From Nahash, therefore, he came to the cave of Adullam, where his father, his mother, and his entire household came to him. From there he went to Moab and left his father, mother, and whole household with him.

As for what Achish, king of Gath, said: “Will this man enter my house?” (1 Samuel XXI), David departed from there and fled to the cave of Adullam, and so forth. “He departed from there” should be understood as “from the house of Nahash,” and from there he fled to the cave of Adullam.

If it is asked why David returned to him—that is, to Achish—before whose presence he had fled, this Achish must be understood to have been the son of that Achish from whom David fled. Hence, later on, Achish, with whom David went into battle against Saul, is said to have been the son of Maoch. He did not receive this patronymic name from his father, but from his mother, who was called Maacah. Thus he did not take this name from his father, because David had rejected him.

Accordingly, Ammon, king of the Ammonites, treated David’s messengers badly: “He shaved off half of their beards, cut their garments in half as far as their buttocks, and sent them away.” When this was reported to David, he sent to meet them. For they were men shamefully humiliated, and David commanded them, saying: “Remain at Jericho until your beards grow, and then return,” and so forth.

What else does this signify except the devil’s war against the Church? Ammon, which is interpreted as “their sorrow,” who can better be understood as the devil? For he appears to be the ruler of the spiritual Ammonites, that is, of the evil spirits—the people of sorrow, always confined in distress—who desire to oppress and constrain human beings.

Ammon therefore shaves half the beard of David’s messengers when the ancient enemy corrupts and dishonors the speech or conduct of certain preachers of the word of God. He cuts their tunics as far as the groin when he reveals before human eyes the shameful deeds that he himself has persuaded them to commit.

Yet such people, whom the devil so confounds, must necessarily sit in Jericho until their beards grow—that is, they must remain a reproach and disgrace to the better sort and become an anathema to all until, through diligent good works, the appearance of a beard, namely the growth of virtues, arises in them and they are judged worthy of the presence of their king.

Nor should we believe that our David permits his soldiers to be many without overcoming his enemies with an assembled army and avenging the injuries done to his own—not only now confounding his adversaries through the victory of his saints, but also, at the final judgment, handing them over to be tormented by a just sentence in everlasting fires.

## (CHAP. XI)

“Now it happened, as the year turned, at the time when kings usually go out to war, that David sent Joab and his servants with him,” and so forth.

*(From the Hebrew.)* In the Hebrew it is read as follows: “At the time when kings had gone out to war, David sent Joab,” and so forth.

By “these kings” he meant those who had gone out to fight against David, namely the king of Rehob, Istob, Zobah, and Maacah, who were certainly kings of Syria and wished to fight. They had been hired by the king of Moab against David, by whom they are recorded to have been defeated.

# CHAPTER XI. David’s offense, which he committed with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite

“When these things were taking place, it happened that David rose from his bed after midday and walked on the roof of the royal house. He saw a woman washing herself opposite, on her roof. The woman was exceedingly beautiful. Therefore the king sent and inquired who the woman was. And it was reported to him that she was Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. David sent messengers and took her. When she had entered to him, he slept with her. Immediately she was cleansed from her uncleanness, and she returned to her house, having conceived a child,” and so forth.

*(From Isidore.)* I shall now touch upon David’s sin and what it signified prophetically, as briefly as I can. The meanings of the names themselves sufficiently show what this deed prefigured.

As we have said, David is interpreted as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” Bathsheba is interpreted as “well of satiety” or “seventh well.” Whichever of these interpretations of her name we adopt for what we intend to say, it agrees sufficiently.

For in the Song of Songs the bride, who is the Church, is called a well of living water (Song of Songs IV). The name of the number seven is joined to this well in the symbolism of the Holy Spirit, because of the meaning of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit came, sent from heaven (Acts II). To forty-nine, which is seven times seven, one is added, by which unity is commended.

In this connection the apostolic saying lives: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians IV).

Thus, through a spiritual gift—that is, through the number seven—the Church became a well of satiety, because in her there was made “a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life; whoever has it will never thirst” (John IV).

But whoever her husband was, what else does the interpretation of his name signify except the devil? All those whom God’s grace liberates had been bound to him in a most evil marriage, so that the Church might be joined first to the Savior, “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians V).

Uriah is interpreted as “my light is God”; Hittite means “cut off,” either because he “did not stand in the truth” (John II) but, through the merit of pride, was cut off from his heavenly light, which he had from God; or because, falling and having lost his true strength, he “transforms himself into an angel of light” (1 Corinthians XI), daring to say to God: “My light is God.”

This David, then, sinned gravely and wickedly. God rebuked his crime through the prophet, and David himself washed it away through repentance.

Nevertheless, he who is “desirable to all nations” (Haggai II), walking as though upon a roof because he “set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm XVIII), loved the Church washing herself upon the roof—that is, cleansing herself from the filth of the world, surpassing and trampling upon the earthly house through spiritual contemplation. Having begun an initial acquaintance with her [the source reading is uncertain], he afterward killed the devil, who had been completely separated from her, and joined her to himself in everlasting marriage.

Let us therefore hate the sin, but let us not extinguish the prophecy. Let us love that David as much as he ought to be loved—the one who in mercy freed us from the devil. Let us also love this repentant David, who healed so grievous a wound of iniquity in himself through a humble confession.

*(From Gregory.)* The sins of such men in Sacred Scripture, namely David and Peter, were recorded so that the fall of the great might serve as a warning to the lesser. Their repentance and forgiveness are likewise made known there so that the recovery of the lost might become a hope for those who are perishing.

Therefore, when David fell from his state, let no one grow proud; and when David rose again after his fall, let no one despair.

Behold how wonderfully Sacred Scripture raises the humble by the same word. It reported one deed, and in different ways recalled the proud to fear and humility, but the humble to confidence in hope.

O immeasurable medicine of a new kind, which, set forth in one and the same order, both dries up swollen things by pressing them down and fills parched things by lifting them up! It terrified us by the fall of the great, but strengthened us by their restoration.

Thus, always thus, the mercy of divine providence both restrains us when we grow proud and cherishes us lest we fall into despair.

But because the occasion required that David be brought forward and we have recalled the memory of so great a crime, perhaps the reader’s mind will be troubled by the question why almighty God does not preserve from bodily vices those whom he has chosen eternally and whom he raises even to the summit of spiritual gifts.

Since we believe that this question can be answered readily enough, let us reply briefly. Some people, through the virtues they have received and the grace bestowed in good works, fall into the vice of pride, yet do not recognize the place to which they have fallen. Therefore the ancient enemy, who already rules inwardly, is permitted to enter outwardly as well, so that those who are exalted in thought may be cast down through the lust of the flesh.

We know that at times it is a lesser matter to fall into bodily corruption than to sin through silent thought and deliberate pride. But when pride is believed to be less shameful, it is avoided less carefully. People are more ashamed of lust because everyone recognizes it as shameful.

Thus it often happens that some, after falling from pride into lust, become ashamed of the hidden evil of their fault through their manifest fall, and then correct greater faults as well, when, prostrate in lesser matters, they are more grievously confounded. They see themselves guilty in lesser things, though they had believed themselves free in more serious ones.

Therefore, by the merciful dispensation of the Lord, the evil spirit is sometimes released to drag a person from one fault into another. And while he strikes more severely, he loses the one whom he had seized; by the very means through which he appears to have conquered, he is overcome.

It is pleasing to consider how greatly God holds us within the fortified shelter of grace through the favor of his mercy. Behold: the one who exalts himself because of virtue returns to humility through vice. The one who is lifted up by the virtues he has received is wounded not by a sword but, so to speak, by a medicine.

For what is virtue except a medicine? And what is vice except a wound? Because we turn the medicine into a wound, he turns the wound into a medicine, so that we who are struck by virtue may be healed through vice.

We turn the gifts of virtues toward the use of vices; he takes up the allurements of vices and strikes at the stronghold of virtues and the state of salvation in order to preserve it, so that we who flee from the humility of the physician may at least cling to him when we are falling.

Yet amid these things it must be understood that many people, because they fall in many ways, become more tightly bound. When the ancient enemy strikes them with one vice so that they collapse, he also binds them with another so that they cannot rise.

Let a person therefore consider against what adversary he is waging war. If he realizes that he has already sinned in some matter, let him at least fear being led from one fault into another, so that he may diligently avoid the wounds by which he is often killed. For it is exceedingly rare that our enemy serves the salvation of the elect even through wounds.

As we have said, the Lord often subjects his elect to the tempter for their instruction. Thus, after the gates of paradise and after the secrets of the third heaven, so that Paul might not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, an angel of Satan was given to him (2 Corinthians XII).

But, as we stated earlier, this very temptation is arranged so that those who could have perished through exaltation may be saved from destruction through humility.

Therefore, by a hidden order of providence, where the devil’s iniquity is permitted to rage, there the goodness of God is mercifully brought to completion. Our adversary obeys the commands of heavenly grace precisely where he exercises the anger of his most wicked will.

This same event may also be understood in another way according to mystical meanings, if anyone wishes to examine it with a pure understanding.

Whom does David, walking on the roof, represent except the one of whom it is written: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Psalm XVIII)?

And what is it to bring Bathsheba to himself except to join the law of the letter, united to a carnal people, to himself through spiritual understanding?

Bathsheba is called the seventh well because, through knowledge of the law and the infusion of spiritual grace, perfect wisdom is supplied to us.

What else does Uriah signify except the Jewish people? His name is interpreted as “my light is God.” The Jewish people, because they are exalted by the knowledge of the law they have received, glory as though in the light of God.

But David took his wife away from him and joined her to himself. For the strong of hand, which is what David means, appeared in the flesh as the Redeemer. By making known that the law speaks spiritually about him, he showed that, insofar as it was held according to the letter, it was foreign to the Jewish people, and he joined it to himself because he declared that he preached himself through it.

David nevertheless urged Uriah to go to his house and wash his feet. This signifies that the incarnate Lord, coming into the world, commands the Jewish people to return to its conscience and wipe away the filth of its works with tears, so that it may understand the commandments of the law spiritually. After so much hardness in the commandments, when it finds the fountain of baptism, it should return to the water after its labor.

But Uriah, who remembered that the ark of the Lord was beneath coverings, replied that he could not enter his house. The Jewish people might say: “I see the commandments of God in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to my conscience through spiritual understanding.”

For he says, as it were, that the ark is beneath coverings because he understands the commandments of God only by applying the ministry of carnal sacrifice.

Yet David calls this Uriah, who is unwilling to return home, to his table. Although the Jewish people despises returning to its conscience, the Redeemer nevertheless comes and preaches the spiritual commandments, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John V).

The Jewish people therefore holds the law, which speaks of his divinity, while the same people scorns believing in him. Hence Uriah is sent to Joab with letters by which he is to be killed, because that same Jewish people carries the law by which it is convicted and must die. While it retains the commandments of the law and strives to fulfill them, it itself carries the judgment by which it will be condemned.

What, then, can be called more wicked than David in this deed, or purer than Uriah? Yet again, in the mystery, what is more sacred than David? What is found more faithless than Uriah? The former, through the fault of his life, signifies innocence in prophecy; the latter, through the innocence of his life, expresses guilt in prophecy.

For the power of sacred eloquence narrates past events in such a way that it expresses future ones; it approves a matter in the deed while contradicting it in its ministerial function; it condemns events as they happened while urging that they be enacted mystically.

# CHAPTER XII. The counsel of Joab the commander, saying to David: “Be present at the victory of the battle, lest afterward the victory be attributed to me rather than to you.” David fulfilled this counsel, crushing the Ammonites and driving iron chariots over them

After the prophet Nathan had rebuked the king for the evil he had done:

## (CHAP. XII)

“David said to Nathan: ‘I have sinned against the Lord.’ Nathan said to David: ‘The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die,’” and so forth.

*(From Gregory.)* If the Lord took away David’s sin, which was so detestable, what does it mean that he afterward endured everything that the Lord had said to him through the prophet concerning that same sin?

Without doubt, the Lord does not leave wrongdoing without punishment. Either the person himself punishes it in himself through repentance, or God strikes while taking vengeance together with the person. Sin is therefore not simply spared, because it is never released without punishment.

If David deserved to hear after his confession, “The Lord has taken away your sin,” yet was afterward afflicted by many torments and, in fleeing, paid the penalty for the guilt he had committed, so we are absolved from the guilt of our first parent by the water of salvation, yet, while washing away the guilt of that same fault, we who have been absolved still die bodily. For the Lord cuts away our sins either through us or through himself, even when he releases them.

Among his elect he strives to cleanse away the stains of iniquities through temporal affliction, which he does not wish to be seen in them eternally.

“And David consoled his wife Bathsheba. He entered her and slept with her. She gave birth to a son and called his name Solomon, and the Lord loved him. And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he called his name ‘Beloved of the Lord,’ because the Lord loved him,” and so forth.

“And he called his name,” it says, “Beloved of the Lord, because the Lord loved him.”

*(From the Hebrew.)* In the Hebrew it is read as follows: “And he called his name Ididam, that is, beloved of the Lord, for the Lord’s sake.” He is called “beloved of the Lord for the Lord’s sake” because of God’s gratuitous mercy, by which he deigns to love him, although he was unworthy of that love and mercy, since it was evident that he was illegitimate.

“Joab therefore fought against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and was attacking the royal city. And Joab sent messengers to David, saying: ‘I have fought against Rabbah, and the City of Waters must be taken,’” and so forth.

It should be noted that in Hebrew, when Rabbah is written with the addition of a name, as in “Rabbah of the sons of Ammon,” it is written *Rabbath*; when it is written without the addition of a name, it is not *Rabbath* but *Rabba*.

“Now therefore gather the remaining part of the people, besiege the city, and capture it, lest, when the city has been destroyed by me, the victory be attributed to my name.”

Josephus says the following:

> “Joab was vigorously afflicting the Ammonites through the siege, cutting off their water and the abundance of their other resources, and forcing them to suffer greatly from lack of food and drink. For everyone drank from a small well. Although they had a possible means of assistance, they did not use it more freely, lest they perish. Having done this, Joab wrote to David and reported the matter, asking him to come to the city so that the victory might be attributed to his name. David therefore gathered the whole people and set out against Rabbah. When he had fought and captured it, he took the diadem of their king from his head. It weighed a talent of gold and contained extremely precious gems, and it was placed upon David’s head,” and so forth.

In Chronicles it is likewise written: “David took the crown of Melchom from his head; and he found in it a talent’s weight of gold and very precious gems, and he made a diadem for himself from it” (1 Chronicles XX).

*(From the Hebrew.)* Melchom is not the king’s proper name; rather, *Mechom* is interpreted as “their king.” He is called “their king,” as the Hebrews maintain, because it was their idol that is called Milcom here. David is said, according to the law, to have melted and purified the gold and gems of this diadem and made a diadem for himself from them; here it is said to have been placed upon his head.

“But he also carried away a very great quantity of the city’s spoil. And bringing out its people, he sawed them and drove iron chariots over them; he divided them with knives and passed them through a brick mold. Thus he did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon,” and so forth.

Hence the Books of Chronicles narrate:

> “He also took very much spoil from the city. He brought out the people who were in it and made threshing-sledges, drags, and iron chariots pass over them, so that they were cut apart and crushed. Thus David did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon; and he returned with all the people to Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles XX).

He sawed them with iron chariots and divided them with knives, as bricks are divided, since bricks are made from straw and mud.

What does this victory of David over the Ammonites signify, since his commander began the battle but the king himself completed it, except the victory of our king among all nations?

The commander David wages war against the enemies when the order of holy preachers raises the shield of faith against the powerful of the world. But the conclusion of the contest and the triumph of the battle are attributed solely to the king Christ, because all power and authority of the kingdom are ascribed to him: “It is God,” according to the Apostle, “who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians II); and “he always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians II).

David therefore took the hostile people’s king’s crown from his head and fashioned a diadem for himself from it, when our Redeemer, taking the kingdom away from the opposing power, prepared for himself a glorious emblem.

What crown of the true David can be better understood than the assembly of the Catholic people, which nobly surrounds our head, namely Christ the king, with believing hearts, and, living worthily, fittingly crowns him?

For all the labor, contest, and victory of the saints is referred to the honor of the heavenly king, because he is the one “to whom every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is bent, so that every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II).

Rabbah, therefore, is a city of the kingdom of Ammon, which is now called Philadelphia; the prophet Jeremiah also mentions it (Jeremiah XLIX). Rabbah is interpreted as “many.” The Savior says in the Gospel: “Many will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VIII).

# CHAPTER XIII. The incest Ammon committed with his sister Tamar, for which his brother Absalom killed him

## (CHAP. XIII)

“After this it happened that Amnon, David’s son, loved Absalom’s exceedingly beautiful sister Tamar by name, and became desperately enamored of her,” and so forth.

The incest that Amnon, David’s elder son, committed with his sister Tamar, and the parricide that Absalom perpetrated against his brother Amnon—what they might signify spiritually I do not know, unless perhaps the deed warns us morally always to act cautiously and prudently, lest vices gain dominion over us and the prince of sin, who promises a false peace to those in danger, find us unprepared and slaughter us unexpectedly.

Absalom is therefore interpreted as “Father of peace” or “the peace of the Father”; Amnon as “giving”; and Tamar is rendered in Latin as “bitterness.”

Whoever gives his members over to lust and hands himself over to serve iniquity unto iniquity falls into the bitterness of sin, even if the enemy displays himself as though he were a father of peace and falsely promises that prosperity will result from such deeds.

We must return quickly to repentance after committing a crime, lest the devil, if we continue to serve drunkenness and become slack in the luxury of this age, conspire against our destruction through the evil spirits who obey him and deliver us to everlasting death.

“Absalom, fleeing, went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur,” and so forth.

*(From the Hebrew.)* Talmai was the father of Maacah, Absalom’s mother. The Hebrews say that David captured her in battle and, after cutting her hair and trimming her nails according to the law, took her as his wife (Deuteronomy XXI), and that he fathered Tamar and Absalom by her.

“King David ceased pursuing Absalom.”

In the Hebrew it is read: “The king ceased going out after Absalom.” David is said to have wished to go out in order to bring Absalom back; but, considering in his heart that every time he saw him he would recall to his memory the grief of Amnon’s death, he is therefore said to have ceased going out after Absalom—that is, in order to summon him back to his own place.

As for the statement “because he had been consoled over Amnon’s death,” it should be understood in this way: after he had wished to go out after Absalom in order to bring him back and see him, he began to be consoled over Amnon’s death. For as long as Absalom was thought likely to be brought back so that David might see him, the death of his son Amnon continually came before his mind.

Alternatively, he is said to have been consoled over Amnon’s death because he knew that Amnon was wicked and deserving of death and had perished deservedly.

# CHAPTER XIV. How Joab sought through the woman of Tekoa to reconcile the king with Absalom

## (CHAP. XIV)

“Now Joab son of Zeruiah, understanding that the king’s heart had turned toward Absalom,” and so forth.

Joab is said to have seen that the king’s heart had turned toward Absalom because he saw David sighing for Absalom; from this he understood that his heart had turned toward him.

“He sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman.”

Tekoa is a city from which the prophet Amos came. The Hebrews believe that this woman was the grandmother of that same prophet Amos.

“She answered: ‘Alas! I am a widowed woman. My husband is dead, and your handmaid had two sons who quarreled with each other in the field. There was no one who could restrain them, and one struck the other and killed him. And behold, the whole family has risen against your handmaid, saying: Hand over the one who struck his brother,’” and so forth.

In truth, as the Hebrews relate, this widow had two sons who quarreled in the field over their father’s inheritance, and one was killed by the other. Nevertheless, the widow placed herself in the role of David and her two sons in the roles of Amnon and Absalom. The family that rose against her son she placed in the role of David’s remaining sons.

“Then the woman of Tekoa said to the king: ‘Upon me, my lord the king, be the iniquity, but the king and his throne be innocent,’ etc.” As though she were saying: Since one of my sons rose up against the other, let the iniquity be upon me, if there must be any at all; but upon you, O King David, let there be no iniquity, because you are without guilt in the matter of those two brothers’ conflict. And just as I am without guilt because my two sons rose up against each other and one was killed by the other, so you too are without guilt because Absalom killed Ammon, who deserved death.

“Then the woman said: ‘May the king remember the Lord his God, so that the avengers of blood may not multiply, and may they by no means kill my son.’” Here “remembrance” is used in place of an oath. It is as though she were saying: May the king remember his promise—or rather, the oath by which he promised me, invoking the Lord his God, that the avengers of blood should not multiply.

“Then the woman said: ‘Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God? And in speaking this word, has the king not sinned by failing to bring back his banished one?’” etc. From this passage what was said a little earlier is demonstrated: “King David ceased to go after Absalom”—that is, he ceased so that no one would go out and bring Absalom back. Hence the woman says: “And in speaking this word, has the king not sinned by failing to bring back his banished one?” But when she says, “Why have you devised such a thing against the people of God?”, she calls Absalom himself—or those who had gone away with him—the people of God. They were like captives and exiles because they were not being restored to God’s inheritance, lest perhaps, compelled by circumstances, they should serve foreign gods in a foreign land. Nor does God wish a soul to perish, but he turns back, considering how it may not perish completely because it has been cast away. It is as though she were saying: God calls sinners, who are held captive by the devil, so that they may turn back to him. And you, who ought to imitate him, why do you not act in the same way?

## CHAPTER XV  
### Concerning Absalom’s conspiracy against David

(CHAP. XV.) “After forty years Absalom said to the king: ‘I will go and pay my vows which I vowed to the Lord in Hebron,’ etc.” The fortieth year was being reckoned from the time when Saul, because of David, killed the city of Nob together with eighty-five priests (I Sam. XXII). Therefore this same fortieth year is placed here to show that divine vengeance was being stirred up against David, because he had deceived Abimelech the priest and, on his account, the slaughter of so many priests had taken place.

Reader, beware of the numerous faulty manuscripts in which one finds written “after four years,” not “after forty years.” In the more reliable manuscripts, and in the Hebrew text, it is written not four but forty years. If someone contentious should wish to maintain that the four years are correct, he will plainly discover, if he examines the matter carefully, that he is mistaken when he reckons them from the time Absalom killed his brother Ammon until the time when he said to his father, “I will go and pay my vows which I vowed to the Lord in Hebron.” For after killing Ammon, Absalom spent three years in Geshur with King Talmai; and after being recalled from there, he spent two years in Jerusalem without seeing his father; and in the sixth year he saw his father and prepared rebellion against him.

For he falsely claimed that he had made a vow—that is, that he would pray in the place where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rest. “Then Zadok came, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God; and they set down the ark of God. And Abiathar went up until all the people who had gone out from the city had finished passing by.” They are said to have set down the ark of God so that the Lord might be consulted through Abiathar the priest concerning where David should go. Abiathar is said to have “gone up,” that is, to have prayed. Since no divine oracle was given to him, David therefore said in what follows that the ark of God should be returned to the city.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### The account of Absalom’s conspiracy continues
