(CHAP. XVI.) “And the king said: ‘What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse,’”—but let him only curse. Abishai alone had said, “I will go and cut off his head”; and David answered Abishai and Joab, saying, “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah?” As though he were saying: Do you wish to kill this man, just as you killed Abner?

“For the Lord commanded him to curse David. And who is there who would say, ‘Why has he done this?’” The understood meaning is: “Why has he done this?”—not the Lord, but Shimei.

Shimei, who cursed David, is, as the Hebrews say, Nabaath, the father of Jeroboam, who is called the son of Gemini; in his zeal for the house of Saul he cursed David. His grandfather’s name, however, was Gemini, and Shimei himself belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph. Hence that same Shimei said to David: “I am the first today of all the tribe of Joseph” (II Sam. XIX).

“When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, had come to Absalom, he said to him: ‘Hail, king; hail, king.’ Absalom answered him: ‘Is this,’ he said, ‘your kindness toward your friend?’” In Hebrew it reads: “Is this,” he said, “your mercy toward your friend?” It should be pronounced not as an affirmation but as a question of denial. The sense is: Is it an act of mercy—or should it be called mercy—that you have abandoned David, your friend, and have not gone with him?

## CHAPTER XVII  
### The account continues as above

(CHAP. XVII.) “Ahithophel said to Absalom: ‘I will choose twelve thousand men for myself, and I will rise and pursue David this night. I will fall upon him while he is weary and his feet are weakened, and I will strike him. When all the people who are with him have fled, I will strike the king when he is left alone, and I will bring back all the people, just as everyone ordinarily returns.’” That is, just as those ordinarily return who, having lost their king in battle, return; so the whole people of Israel will return to you.

“And when any one has fallen at the beginning, whoever hears it will say: ‘A slaughter has taken place among the people who followed Absalom’; and every brave man, whose courage is like that of a lion, will melt with fear.” In Hebrew it is written: “And the brave man himself, whose heart is like a lion’s, will melt with fear.” This too should be pronounced not as an affirmation but as a denial. This brave man is to be understood as David, as the following passage also makes clear:

“For all Israel knows that your father is strong, and that all who are with him are valiant. Jonathan and Ahimaaz were standing beside the spring of Rogel. A maidservant went and reported it to them, and they departed.” This maidservant had gone to the spring of Rogel with cloths, supposedly for washing, so that the matter would not be detected at all. The boy who reported the affair to Absalom is said to have been the young son of that same maidservant.

David came to the camp called Mahanaim in Hebrew. In that place the angels of God met Jacob, as it is written in Genesis: “And Jacob called the name of the place Mahanaim,” that is, “camps” (Gen. XXXII). These observations, according to the Hebrews’ understanding, are sufficient as a historical account.

But according to the allegorical sense, we must consider what it signifies that Absalom, the parricidal son, pursues his father. At first his father, turning aside, flees before him, confident of victory because he knew that the impious man would perish. Yet he mourned him with great grief and lamented the death of the parricide. For it is written that David fled from the face of his son, who was waging war against him. Elsewhere it is written of the people of Jerusalem, with the Lord saying: “I have nourished and exalted sons; but they have despised me” (Isa. I).

His impious son may therefore be understood figuratively as the Jewish people, which handed him over. Absalom, as has already been said, is understood as “the father’s peace.” This seems strange in the historical account: how can he be understood as the father’s peace when he pursued his father in war? But those who attend carefully to the allegory observe that Absalom is Jerusalem, which is itself also interpreted as “peace.” Christ fled from its face when, by suffering and abandoning it, he withdrew among the Gentiles through faith.

Others understand Absalom as Judas the betrayer, whom Christ endured with such great and astonishing patience, as though he did not know his thoughts, even admitting him to the banquet at which he commended and handed on to the disciples the figure of his body and blood. Finally, at the very moment of his betrayal, he also accepted a kiss. It is rightly understood that Christ offered peace to his betrayer, although the betrayer was inwardly ravaged by such a wicked design. Thus Absalom is called “the father’s peace” because the father possessed the peace which he did not possess.

Ahithophel, therefore, who departed from David and transferred himself to Absalom, signifies heretics, who depart from the path of truth, join themselves to the ancient enemy, and follow error. Ahithophel is interpreted as “my brother falling”; the Gilonite means “he has migrated.” Against such people the Prophet rebukingly says: “In the Lord I trust; how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. X), etc.

And deservedly such people end their own lives by the noose of their deceit and malice, since they tried to corrupt another’s life by wicked persuasion. Thus Ahithophel perished by hanging in his own house, though he had plotted against David’s life in another man’s house. Hence it is written: “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Ecclus. XXVII); and: “The wicked will be caught in their own snares.”

Hushai the Archite, David’s ancient friend, signifies believers from the Gentiles. Although they were at times seen to be with Absalom, they did not share in his wicked deeds, nor did they ever consent to Ahithophel’s unjust counsels; rather, they remained faithfully with David.

Hushai is interpreted as “Ethiopian”; Archite as “my length.” Hence it is also written in the Prophet: “The Ethiopian will change his skin” (Jer. XIII); and in the Psalm: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII). For after the Gentile people stripped themselves of the blackness of sins, they never withdrew from the Lord’s following.

The fact that David’s concubines, whom he had left to guard the house, were violated by fornication signifies that the apostate angel deceives certain people who appear to rule and guard God’s people by seducing them through heretical perversity. David does not again enter into them, but he provides sustenance for them while they remain under guard. They too live shut away in widowhood until the day of their death.

For when heretics, straying from the way of truth, refuse to return to it, they are not worthy of dwelling with Christ. Rather, shut away—that is, separated—they will be alienated from his fellowship. Yet he “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V) does not refuse to provide such people with food through his benefits in this world, so that through the benefits bestowed he may give them an opportunity to convert.

Whoever among the faithful, pierced by the illumination of divine grace, endures being borne from the depths to the heights on the wing of heavenly contemplation through holy desire should place before the eyes of his mind the deeds of the holy fathers who preceded him, exercise himself in their imitation, and advance. Whatever presently pricks him through vice, he should restrain either by recalling past evils, or extinguish by the consolation of former gifts, or—as has been said—be stirred toward better things by imitating the fathers who came before.

As we proposed, this must be confirmed by clearer examples. To speak of one among many, so that the diligent reader may understand many things through one example: whoever is oppressed by insults and cannot preserve the virtue of patience should recall what David did. When Shimei pressed him with so many reproaches and armed nobles sought to avenge him, David said: “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse. For the Lord commanded him to curse David. And who is there who would dare say, ‘Why has he done this?’”

A little later he said: “Let him curse, according to the Lord’s command. Perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction and repay me good for this day’s cursing.” By these words he plainly indicates that, because of the crime committed against Bathsheba, he recalled to mind the evil he had perpetrated while fleeing from the son who had risen against him. He endured calmly what he heard and regarded the insulting words not so much as reproaches as aids, by which he might be cleansed and might judge that mercy could be shown him.

We tolerate insults well when, in the secrecy of our minds, we return to the evil deeds we have committed. What strikes us as an injury will seem slight when we see in our own conduct that what we deserve is worse. Thus it comes about that insults deserve gratitude rather than anger, since, through their intervention, we trust that a more severe punishment may be averted before God the judge.

Jonathan, whose name is interpreted as “gift of a dove,” and Ahimaaz, whose name is interpreted as “who is my brother,” had been appointed to investigate what had happened between Absalom and David and to report it. Fleeing from Absalom, they turned aside into the house of a certain man in Bahurim, who had a well in his vestibule, and descended into it. “The woman took a covering and spread it over the mouth of the well, as though drying parched grain, and so the matter remained hidden.” This should not be thought to be without a mystery.

What do these two young men, Jonathan and Ahimaaz, signify except those who, reborn through the grace of the Holy Spirit and enrolled among the number of the brethren, flee from Absalom when they seek to escape malignant spirits? They stood beside the spring of Rogel, which is interpreted as “sad” or “downward,” when, for the sake of their desire for the heavenly kingdom, they seek to bear mourning and contempt in this world.

“They therefore quickly turn aside, fleeing into the house of a certain man in Bahurim”—a place interpreted as “chosen” or “young”—when they recall the times of youth. They descend into the well that was in the vestibule when they humbly submit themselves to repentance, which is necessary for everyone in this present age, before the end of this life.

“The woman spread a covering over the mouth of the well” when the Church strives, through continual prayer, to conceal the sins of youth and the ignorance of her children. “As though drying parched grain” when she restrains the wantonness of the flesh through the severity of self-control. “And so the matter remained hidden”—namely, the transgression of human life—for through continual prayer in the compunction of tears and through chastisement of the body, all sins are concealed, and human beings are protected and freed from the persecution of the ancient enemy.

“When David came to the camp at Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim brought him beds, carpets, earthen vessels, wheat and barley, flour and parched grain, beans and lentils, roasted chickpeas, honey and butter, sheep and fattened calves. They gave these to David and to the people who were with him to eat, for they supposed that the people were weary with hunger and thirst in the wilderness,” etc.

This Shobi was the son of Nahash the king, against whom Saul fought. Nahash himself had also shown kindness to David when he was fleeing from Saul. After Nahash died, David said: “I will show kindness to Ammon as his father showed kindness to me” (II Sam. X). But after Ammon was killed by David—he had insulted David by shaving his servants—this Shobi was appointed by the same David in his brother’s place. For he is recorded as having come to David with the others and offered him beds, carpets, earthen vessels, and the other things that follow.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Concerning the battle of David’s servants against Israel and the death of Absalom, whom David mourned

(CHAP. XVIII.) “Therefore the people went out into the field against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim. There the people of Israel were struck down by David’s army, and a great slaughter took place on that day, twenty thousand men. The battle there was spread over the face of all the land, and the forest consumed far more of the people than the sword devoured in battle,” etc.

The Hebrews maintain that this forest, which is said to have consumed more than the sword devoured, contained exceedingly savage beasts. More were consumed by these beasts than were devoured by the sword.

“It happened that Absalom encountered David’s servants while he was riding a mule. When the mule went beneath a thick and large oak, his head caught in the oak, and, suspended between heaven and earth, the mule on which he had been riding passed on,” etc.

What does it signify that Absalom, fleeing on a mule, was suspended in an oak by the hair of his head, except that the Jews, devoted to the folly of carnal understanding and corrupting the law through Pharisaic superstition, found through the very law they had received for the correction of life an occasion of death?

Hence the Savior also said to them in the Gospel: “Do not suppose that I will accuse you before my Father. Moses, in whom you trust, is the one who accuses you” (John V).

Joab thrusts three spears into Absalom’s heart when the ancient enemy instilled pride, avarice, and envy—or faithlessness—into the heart of the Jewish people; these were especially the causes of their destruction.

They were proud because, in contempt of God, they fashioned idols. They were greedy because they preferred passing possessions to the delights of virtue. They were faithless and envious because they not only opposed the words of the Law and the Prophets, but also scorned the presence of the Savior himself and showed themselves ungrateful for his benefits.

Hence, during his Passion, they said to Pilate with blasphemous voice: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX); and: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (ibid.).

After his death Absalom was cast into a great pit, when every wicked person after the death of the flesh sinks into the lake of hell. A heap of stones is piled over him when the hardness of his mind is thereby approved.

David therefore wept for Absalom after he had been killed, when the Lord mourned the destruction of the Jewish people, as it is read in the Gospel: “Seeing the city of Jerusalem, he wept over it” (Luke XIX). He had such compassion for its misery that he continued even to the death of the cross in its instruction and care for its salvation.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### Concerning Mephibosheth’s coming to meet the king, the return of all Israel to David, and the conspiracy of Sheba son of Bichri against David

(CHAP. XIX.) “Then all the people came before the king; but Israel fled to their tents,” etc. The whole people who are said to have come before the king are those who had remained with David. But by “Israel fled to their tents” are understood those who had rebelled in conspiracy with Absalom.

“Mephibosheth also, the son of Jonathan, came down to meet the king with unwashed feet.” It should be noted that in Hebrew it reads not “with unwashed” but “with bent feet.” For, as the Hebrews report, Mephibosheth had made himself wooden feet, which he used almost as natural feet, as lame people commonly do; and he was lame.

The king said to Mephibosheth: “Why do you continue to speak? What I have said stands. You and Ziba shall divide the possessions,” etc. In Hebrew it reads: “I have said, You and Ziba shall divide the field.”

Because David was forgetful in this matter of the friendship and covenant—or rather, the oath—which he had with Jonathan, and nevertheless gave a cruel judgment, saying, “You and Ziba shall divide the field,” for this reason Rehoboam and Jeroboam divided his kingdom.

In the Book of Samuel, Mephibosheth is recorded under that name, which is interpreted as “shameful mouth.” In Chronicles (I Chron. VIII), however, the same Mephibosheth is called Meribaal, interpreted as “contending with the Most High.” He is said to have contended with the Most High, that is, with God, because David had brought him back in peace.

When that same Mephibosheth said to the king, “Let him also take everything, since my lord the king has returned peacefully to his house,” it is not thought that he said this with a grateful spirit but in mockery, as one murmuring against God, because the Lord David had brought him back in peace.

Barzillai said to the king: “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? But your servant is Chamaam,” etc. In Hebrew: “Behold, your servant Chamaam; let him go with you, my lord the king.”

Chamaam is interpreted as “sighing.” As long as he remained with his father, he was called “sighing.” But after he passed into the instruction of King David, he was called not Chamaam but Chanaon, which is interpreted as “faithful.”

The saying is found in an old proverb: “Let those who ask inquire at Abel, and so they will prosper” (II Sam. XX). In Hebrew, however, it is not called a proverb.

This saying is a saying of the Law, in which the Lord commanded through Moses (Deut. XX) that, when the Israelites were about to enter the land of Canaan and destroy the nations, they should first offer peace. If peace were accepted by them, those who accepted it would become their tributaries. If they did not accept peace, then they would be destroyed by the children of Israel.

For this reason the wise woman of the city is said to have cried out: “Am I not the one who answers truthfully in Israel, and you seek to destroy the city?” Why do you rush to destroy the Lord’s inheritance? It is as though she were saying: Why do you wish to destroy this city before offering peace by inquiry, as the Law commands? Why do you also fail to observe among us Israelites the same law that was once observed in dealing with foreigners?

The return of the Israelite people to David after the killing of Absalom therefore signifies nothing other than the return of the former people to Christ after the destruction of wicked teachers.

Sheba son of Bichri, who by leading the people astray turned them away from David, is best understood as signifying error, which long held dominion in the synagogue of the Jews and subverted the people from hearing the truth. Sheba is interpreted as “sect,” from *secare*, “to cut,” not from *sectari*, “to follow.” Bichri is interpreted as “my firstborn.”

Israel, of whom it is written, “Israel is my firstborn son, whom I brought out of Egypt” (Exod. XX), followed Sheba—that is, error—and separated itself from the house of David, that is, from the Church, when it despised and rejected her assembly.

After, through the suggestion of the wise woman—that is, through the instruction of spiritual teaching—he had cut off Sheba’s head, meaning that he had cast the devil from his heart, he immediately returned to David, when he worshiped Christ the Son of God with a believing heart.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Concerning Joab’s treacherous killing of Amasa

(CHAP. XX.) “Then Joab said to Amasa: ‘Hail, my brother,’ and he took Amasa’s chin in his right hand as though he were kissing him. But Amasa did not notice the sword which Joab had. He struck him in the side and poured out his entrails on the ground; and he died, and Joab did not inflict a second wound,” etc.

What does it mean that Joab held Amasa’s chin with his right hand but secretly moved his left hand toward the sword and spilled out his entrails, except what is plainly understood? To hold the chin with the right hand is to flatter someone as though with kindness. But he moves his left hand toward the sword who strikes secretly out of malice.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Concerning the three-year famine that occurred in Israel because of the killing of the Gibeonites, whom Saul killed as though out of zeal, and in reparation for which his offspring was destroyed; and concerning David’s four battles against the Philistines, in which men of extraordinary height were found, one of whom had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot

(CHAP. XXI.) “There was also a famine in the days of David for three successive years. David consulted the oracle of the Lord. The Lord said: ‘It is because of Saul and his bloodstained house, because he killed the Gibeonites,’” etc.

The sons of Saul who, while still boys, killed the priests and the Gibeonites at Nob together with Doeg the Edomite are these: Armoni and Mephibosheth, whom Rizpah daughter of Aiah bore to him, and the five sons of Michal, Saul’s daughter, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai, who was from Meholah.

It is asked why they are called the sons of Michal, since not Michal but her sister Merab was the wife of Adriel son of Barzillai. The matter is resolved as follows: Merab naturally gave birth to them, but Michal, David’s wife, who is also called Aeglah, raised them in the place of sons and adopted them as her own children. For this reason they are called her sons.

“For the children of Israel had sworn to them, and Saul wished to strike them in his zeal, as though on behalf of the children of Israel and Judah,” saying that Joshua had gratuitously allowed those same Gibeonites to live and had unjustly taken their spoil from the children of Israel and Judah (Josh. IX). Therefore he ordered them to be killed, as though out of zeal for Israel and Judah.

The priest Ahimelech was the cause of this vengeance against the Gibeonites.

This history, which figuratively recounts the famine that came upon Israel because the Gibeonites had been killed, signifies the barrenness of good works among peoples because of the negligence of teachers. They do not take care to provide their subjects with the nourishment of the word of the Lord, since they devote themselves to earthly desires.

Hence, according to the Prophet, “They suffer neither hunger nor thirst for water, but hunger and thirst to hear the word of the Lord” (Amos VIII).

The Gibeonites are killed when the pursuit of a disciplined way of life and the restoration of repentance after a fall are taken away from the unwary by heretics or by evil spirits. Gibeon is interpreted as “hill of sorrow.”

And rightly are the Gibeonites said to have been killed when the indolent, after committing crimes, are deceived by the devil through a vain hope of security. They say: “Let us do evil, so that good may come”—whose condemnation is just (Rom. III).

“But Rizpah,” whose name is interpreted as “neostraton” or “course,” “the daughter of Aiah,” whose name is interpreted as “his brother,” “taking sackcloth, spread it beneath her upon the rock until water dripped down upon them from heaven. She did not allow the birds to tear them by day or the beasts by night.”

This occurs when the devout concern of the saints, coming to the aid of such people, applies itself to the rigor of fasting and the earnestness of prayer until it obtains God’s mercy from heaven for them, restraining wicked human beings and evil spirits from further corrupting their lives through their wicked suggestions.

“Now there was again a battle between the Philistines and Israel. David went down with his servants, and they fought. When David was exhausted, Ishbibenob, who was of the race of Rapha, whose spear weighed three hundred ounces and who was girded with a new sword, attempted to strike David. But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to his aid and struck the Philistine and killed him. Then David’s men swore, saying: ‘You shall not go out with us to battle, lest you extinguish the lamp of Israel.’

“There was also a second battle at Gob against the Philistines. Then Sobochai of Husath struck Saph, who was of the stock of Arapha. There was also a third battle at Gob against the Philistines. In it Adeodatus, son of the forest, a worker in many threads (*Polymitarius*), a Bethlehemite, struck Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver’s beam,” etc.

The Hebrew explains Adeodatus in this way: Gob is interpreted as “a pit.” It is called a pit because, just as someone is cast into a pit of lions, so David sent himself against Goliath.

Adeodatus himself is David. He is called Adeodatus because he was chosen by God for the kingdom. “Son of the forest” means that he was brought out from the forest where he had pastured sheep. “The cloth-worker” means that his mother was of the family of Bezalel. “The Bethlehemite” means that Naomi and Ruth returned to Bethlehem in a time of abundance (Ruth I). And because Ruth became known through Boaz on account of bread (Ruth II), that place was called “house of bread.”

That Adeodatus himself is David is shown by what follows: “These four were born to Rapha in Gath; and they fell by the hand of David and his servants.”

The Jews also believe that this Rapha, the mother of the giants, was Orpah, Naomi’s daughter-in-law.

It should be noted that Josephus, the Jewish historian, when he mentions this passage in the seventh book of the *Antiquities*, agrees with the Book of Kings concerning two battles fought against the Philistines. Concerning the third battle he says:

“After this defeat the Philistines again made war. When David sent an army against them, a brave man named Ephan, his kinsman, appeared. Fighting alone against the strongest of the Philistines, he killed some and put others to flight; many of them also fell in the battle.”

Whether he called this same Adeodatus “Ephan,” or designated someone else by this name, is uncertain.

“The fourth battle took place at Gath. There was a tall man who had six fingers on his hands and six toes on his feet—that is, twenty-four in all—and he was of the race of Rapha. He blasphemed Israel. Jonathan son of Samaa, David’s brother, struck him. These four were born to Rapha in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and his servants,” etc.

What do these four battles of David and his servants against the Philistines signify except the battle of Christ, which throughout the whole time of this life he continually wages in his members against all the faithless of this age and against spiritual wickedness?

Although worldly arrogance or the insolence of evil spirits may rise up against the Church of Christ, every power of the adversaries yields before the true David—that is, when Christ the King commands and arranges the battles of his servants—and all the adversaries are defeated, overthrown, and reduced to nothing.

Hence the Psalmist confidently says in the person of the Church: “Human salvation is vain. In God we shall act with strength, and he himself will bring those who afflict us to nothing” (Ps. LIX).

## CHAPTER XXII  
### David’s song, which he sang to the Lord on the day when he delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul

(CHAP. XXII.) “David spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said: ‘The Lord is my rock, my strength, and my savior. God, the Lord, is my strong one; I will hope in him,’” etc.

It is asked why only the seventeenth psalm is found written in the Books of Kings. The psalm is not found there without reason as the sole one, for it signifies that kingdom in which we have no adversary.

Its title is: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.” For whom is David a figure except the one who came according to the flesh from the seed of David? In his body, which is the Church, he still suffers enemies. Hence he thundered from heaven at the persecutor whom he slew with his voice and, transferring him into his own body, in a certain sense consumed: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX).

When is this body of his delivered from the hand of all its enemies, except when “the last enemy, death, is destroyed” (I Cor. XV), so that we may attain the kingdom of God?

“The Lord,” he says, “is my rock and my strength.” This psalm cannot apply to one person alone, but will be subject to four divisions.

First, the Prophet speaks, giving thanks that divine mercy has deigned to deliver him from grave dangers: “The pangs of death surrounded me.”

Second, the Church speaks. Before the Lord’s coming she endured innumerable calamities; afterward, when he had mercy on her, he granted her the remedy of holy incarnation and, through the gift of baptism, gathered a Christian people from the whole world: “God who girded me with strength.”

Third, in the dew of mercy the voice of Christ the Savior descends, where his power and might are described through beautiful allusions: “The Lord lives, and blessed is my God.”

Fourth, the words of the Catholic Church are again set forth, and with great exultation the gifts granted by the divinity are praised.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### The catalogue of David’s mighty men and their distinguished deeds

(CHAP. XXIII.) “These are the last words which David son of Jesse spoke,” etc. Why “last words,” unless because they signify the final confession of praise which, after conquering the enemy and accomplishing victory over death, the saints will sing to God forever?

“The man to whom the Christ of the God of Jacob was appointed, the outstanding psalmist of Israel.” He was the noble Psalmist who, as a prophet, most clearly prophesied about Christ the Son of God, his incarnation, and the redemption of the human race.

“The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was upon my tongue. The God of Israel spoke to me; the Strong One of Israel, the ruler of men, the just one,” etc. The Spirit of the Lord, who is the Holy Spirit, and the word of the Lord, who is the Son of God, granted the Prophet to utter truthfully, by his grace, the things he had foretold.

“A ruler in the fear of God, like the light of dawn when the sun rises, shining in the morning without clouds, and like rain causing grass to spring from the earth.”

Whoever exercises rule over his subjects in the fear of God brings forth works of light, illuminated by the sun of justice. Nothing obscure will remain in them; watered by the rain of heavenly grace, he produces shoots of virtue while living in the flesh.

“My house is not so great with God that he would make an everlasting covenant with me, firm in all things and secure. For all my salvation and every desire are in it, and there is nothing from it that does not sprout.”

Hence the same Prophet says in the Psalms that “the blessed man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night is like a tree planted beside streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season; its leaf does not fall, and everything he does prospers” (Ps. I).

[Col. 0115D] “But the transgressors shall all be torn out like thorns, which are not removed by hand; and if anyone wishes to touch them, he shall arm himself with iron and a spear-shaft, and, set on fire, they shall be utterly consumed, etc.” Hence it is written in the Gospel: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, VII). And again: “The Son of Man,” he says, “will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all stumbling-blocks and those who commit iniquity, and they will throw them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII). That man, then, like one touching thorns, “shall arm himself with iron and a spear-shaft”: because, sharing in the sins of others, he is weighed down by the burden of iniquities on account of the hardness of his heart, [Col. 0116A] pierced by the darts of his own sins, and his works, deserving the eternal fires of Gehenna, will be reduced to nothing.

Next is woven the catalogue of mighty men, in the figure of the saints, who, although they attain the sublimity of the virtues, nevertheless do not reach the excellence of the divine Trinity. Hence it is written there: “He did not attain the first three.” For “who will be made equal to the Lord, or who will be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Accordingly, what is said of the chief of the mighty men, David—whose name is indeed omitted in the Book of Kings but who is called Jesbaam in the Book of Chronicles (I Chron. XI), and is said to have been the son of Achamoni—namely, “He is the tenderest worm of the wood,” designates both the man’s military strength and his modest civility. For just as a woodworm appears tender and fragile throughout its body, and also very small, yet consumes the strongest substance of the wood, making it cavernous [Al.: or worm-eaten], and from gnawing wood receives the name *teredon*; so he appeared agreeable to everyone at home, quiet, and humble, yet in public combat he displayed himself as vigorous and intolerable to his enemies.

But this chief of the mighty men, the Hebrew supposes, was David himself. Of him it is written as follows: “Sitting in the chair, the wisest chief among the three, he is like the tenderest worm of the wood, who killed eight hundred at one assault.”

I have said that these words express David’s wisdom, humility, and strength: wisdom in “the wisest,” humility in the example of the worm, and his greatest strength in the killing of the eight hundred.

“After him was Eleazar, the son of his paternal uncle, the Ahothite, among the three mighty men who were with David when they taunted the Philistines and gathered there for battle. When the men of Israel had gone up, he stood and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stiffened with the sword, etc. And after him was Shammah, son of Age the Hararite, and the Philistines gathered at the outpost. Now there was a field full of lentils. When the people had fled from the face of the Philistines, he stood in the middle of the field, struck the Philistines, and the Lord accomplished a great deliverance, etc.”

Concerning these mighty men Josephus relates the following here: “The first of all was Eusebius, son of Achineas, who, frequently breaking into the enemy’s battle line, never ceased fighting until he had killed nine hundred of them. After him was Eleazar, son of Dodi, who had been with the king at Sarpha. Once, when the Israelites feared the army of the Palestinians and therefore fled, he alone stood firm, rushing upon the enemy; he killed many of them, so that the sword clung to his right hand because of the blood of the slain. When the Israelites saw that the Palestinians had been put to flight, they descended from the mountains and pursued them. A marvelous and most famous victory then followed, when Eleazar had killed so many enemies, the Israelites were pursuing them, and they were taking the spoils of the slain.

“The third was the son of Heli, named Semeias. [Col. 0117A] He too, during the battles with the Palestinians, when they had drawn up their line at the place called Maxilla, and the Hebrews again fled in fear of their army, alone bore the brunt of their battle line and army. Some of them he struck down; others, unable to withstand his force and courage, he pursued as they turned to flee.”

“Moreover, three men who were leaders among the thirty had previously gone down and come to David at the cave of Odollam during the harvest. The camp of the Philistines had been set up in the Valley of the Giants, while David was in the stronghold.”

Hence Josephus says: “These three men demonstrated the works of your hands and of your battles. At that time, when the king was in Jerusalem, an army of Palestinians came to wage war. Then David [Col. 0117B] went up into the city’s citadel, as we have said, to consult the Lord about the war. The enemy’s camp was fixed in the valley, extending as far as the city of Bethlehem, which is twenty *stadia* distant from Jerusalem.

“David therefore said to his companions: ‘We have good water in my country,’ and he especially praised the water that was beside the well at the gate. He wondered whether anyone would provide him with a cup from it, which he would desire more than if someone brought him a large sum of money for a time.

“When these three men heard this, they immediately ran out, making their way through the midst of the enemy, and came to Bethlehem. Having drawn the water, they returned again to the king through their camp, so that the Palestinians, astonished at their confidence and greatness of spirit—for so few had despised them—ceased their advance.”

By these three, namely, who brought water from Bethlehem, he wished to understand the three mentioned above: Jesbaam son of Achamoni, whom Josephus calls Eusebius son of Achima; Eleazar son of Achai, whom he says was the son of Dodi; and Semmaa son of Age, whom he calls Semegem son of Heli.

But the Hebrew whose interpretation of this book’s meaning I have explained in many places believed these three to have been Abishai son of Zeruiah, Sibbecai the Hushathite, and Jonathan son of Shammah, David’s brother. These men are mentioned above in the battles with the Philistines. Scripture seems to me to favor his interpretation, for it concludes the account of the three men who brought water to David as follows:

“Abishai also, the brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah, was chief among these three. He raised his spear against three hundred, whom he killed, and was renowned among the three; he was more distinguished among the three and was their chief, but he did not attain the first three.”

Here it is evident that Abishai was a chief and was counted among the following three. But he did not reach the first three mentioned above—namely, Jesbaam, Eleazar, and Shammah—whose exceedingly valorous deeds he related above.

But in refusing to drink the water offered to him, and instead pouring it out as a libation to the Lord, David gave his soldiers an example of courage and steadfastness. He conquered nature, so that, although thirsty, he did not drink; by his example the whole army would learn to endure thirst.

If you wish to look more deeply and perceive the mystery, David thirsted not for the water that is Bethlehem, but in the spirit foresaw Christ, born in that same Bethlehem from the Virgin. Therefore David wished to drink not the water of a stream, but the washing flowing from Christ’s side. That is, David thirsted not for the element of water, but for Christ’s blood.

Thus he did not drink the water offered to him, but poured it out to the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for Christ’s sacrifice, not for a natural stream; for that sacrifice in which there is forgiveness of sins; for that eternal fountain which is not sought through the dangers of others but erases the dangers of others.

It must be considered with the greatest care that one who remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this means he may make satisfaction to his Creator. One who has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, so that he may reproach himself in small matters, since he remembers that he transgressed in great ones.

The Law of the Old Testament rightly forbids coveting another man’s wife, but it does not punishably forbid a king to command his soldiers to perform brave deeds or to desire water. We all know that David, pierced by the sword of desire, both coveted and took another man’s wife. Worthy punishments followed his guilt, and through the mourning of repentance he corrected the evil he had committed.

Later, when he was sitting opposite the enemy’s ranks, he desired to drink water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers, breaking through the midst of the opposing crowds, brought him unharmed the water he had desired. But the man instructed by scourges immediately reproached himself for having desired water at the risk of his soldiers, and, pouring it out to the Lord, offered it as a libation, just as it is written there: “He poured it out to the Lord.”

For the water poured out was changed into a sacrifice to the Lord, because through repentance he put to death the guilt of his desire and self-reproach. Thus the man who once had not feared to covet another’s wife later recoiled from having coveted water. Because he remembered committing unlawful acts, he was now strict with himself and abstained even from lawful things.

“And Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a very valiant man, great in deeds, from Kabzeel.”

It should be noted that, according to the aforementioned Hebrew, the Hebrew text does not have “great in deeds,” but “master of deeds.” Kabzeel is interpreted as “assembly of God.” He was therefore master of the assembly of God, that is, of the Cherethites and Pelethites, whose names are interpreted as “those who kill” and “those who give life.”

“He struck down the two lions of Moab.” Chronicles calls them “the two Ariels of Moab” (I Chron. XI). These, then, were very valiant men in the kingdom of Moab; hence they are called Ariel, or lions. For *Ariel* is interpreted as “battles of God.” Benaiah, when challenged by them, overcame and killed them.

But concerning Benaiah it is said: “He also went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern on a snowy day.” Josephus explains more clearly how this happened. The cistern was exceedingly deep; in winter, when everything was covered with snow, it too had been leveled by a great accumulation of snow. When a lion, unaware of the danger, fell into it and, trapped there, cried out with a great roar, people ran to see what had happened.

When Benaiah came with the others to witness the spectacle, he immediately leapt into the cistern, attacked the lion in the midst of the snow, and killed it.

Snow can therefore be understood now as the brightness of innocence and grace, and now as winter and the coldness of charity. When we read in the Books of Kings that a certain Benaiah of the mighty men of Israel descended into a cistern and struck a lion in snowy weather, I think that snow is used there without distinction. For both Christ’s grace, which shone forth in this world, and the coldness of the love of God, by which human beings grew cold, could be signified by the name of snow in sacred Scripture.

Figuratively, however, we understand Benaiah as the Savior, who, according to the force of his name, is interpreted as “the Lord is builder.” Concerning him the Prophet had foretold that the Church would be built through him, saying: “The Lord builds Jerusalem” (Ps. CXLVII). Likewise: “The Lord built Zion” (Ps. CI).

Scripture used this same word with its proper meaning in the making of Eve, who bore the type of the Church, saying: “And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman” (Gen. II). And Paul, seeing her being built, says: “You are God’s building” (I Cor. III).

Nor should we pass over the fact that the Hebrew believes this lion whom Benaiah killed ought to be understood as Joab, who was killed in the middle of the cistern—that is, in the house of the Lord, where he held the horns of the altar (III Kings II).

Therefore the altar is called a cistern, because just as the water of a cistern brings cleansing, so too this cistern—the sanctuary of the Lord—nevertheless expiated sins. “On a snowy day”: because through death he expiated sin, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You will wash me,” which was fulfilled “in the middle of the cistern,” “and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. L); this was fulfilled in what he says, “on snowy days.”

Concerning what is subsequently related—“He also killed an Egyptian, a man worthy of spectacle”—he believes that this man was Shimei, son of Gera, who cursed David.

It should be known that this same Shimei was from Bavicim, that is, “from the elect.” He was therefore called an Egyptian because he imitated the deeds of that Egyptian who blasphemed God and whom Moses killed in the wilderness at the Lord’s command. That man blasphemed God, while this one cursed the prophet and king.

“Worthy of spectacle”: he was also being watched so that, if he returned to Jerusalem, he would be killed. “Having a spear in his hand,” that is, the law of God; had he meditated upon it by remaining in Jerusalem, he would not have been killed.

Because he made the king’s command void by going outside Jerusalem, Benaiah therefore went down against him with a rod—that is, with the uprightness of justice—and the spear, which he no longer held uprightly, was forcibly taken from him.

“These things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did, and he was also named among the three mighty men who were among the thirty more distinguished; nevertheless, he did not reach the three.”

This is understood to mean that he deserved to be named among the three mighty men—that is, Abishai, Sibbecai, and Jonathan—since he could be equal to them in strength. These three also stood above the thirty.

And lest anyone be troubled by the fact that in the total not thirty but thirty-seven are read, the thirty-seven are as follows. These seven are the stronger: David, who is called Adeodatus; Abishai; Sibbecai; Jonathan; Eleazar; Shammah son of Age the Hararite; and Benaiah. There are seven.

The thirty are: Asael; Eleanam; Semma; Sarath; Elichaeles; Ira; Abiezer; Mobonnai; Selmon; Maarai; Eled; Itai; Banaian; Eufronites; Abdas; Abialbon; Azmavet; Eliaba; Semma of Arari; Aiam; Elipheleth; Eliam; Esrai; Farai; Giga; Albani; Seleth; Naarai; Ira; Iareb; Uriah the Hittite.

Uriah the Hittite is therefore placed last because of what follows.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0120B] Concerning David’s offense, by which he offended the Lord in numbering Israel, and concerning the plague directed against Israel on account of it.—How David appeased the Lord by offering burnt offerings on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

**(CHAP. XXIV).** “And the anger of the Lord continued to burn against Israel.” Retribution had already been carried out against David and his household; but in the battle, where he had not resisted David when Uriah was killed, divine retribution had not yet been exacted. He is therefore placed last, so that the retribution for his death might be displayed in the battle.

“And he moved David against them, saying: ‘Go, number Israel and Judah.’ And the king said to Joab, the commander of his army: ‘Go through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and number the people, [Col. 0120C] so that I may know their number,’ etc.”

The deeds of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that often, because of the wickedness of the flock, even the life of a good shepherd may fall into sin. David—the man praised by God’s testimony, the prophet conscious of heavenly mysteries—sinned by numbering the people when he was suddenly inflated by the swelling of pride. Yet, while David sinned, the people received the punishment.

Why was this? Because the hearts of rulers are disposed according to the merit of their peoples. The just Judge corrected the sinners by chastising them, although the king had sinned on their account. But because he himself, growing proud by his own will, was not free from guilt, he too suffered the punishment of his sin. For the raging anger that struck the people bodily also struck down their ruler through the innermost sorrow of his heart.

Certainly it is true that the merits of rulers and peoples are so interconnected that often the life of the people becomes worse through the guilt of shepherds, and often the life of shepherds is changed through the merit of the people. But because rulers have a more certain Judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of those who govern them.

For the Lord did not without reason himself “pour out the money-changers’ coins and overturn the seats of those selling doves” (John II), clearly signifying that although through teachers he judges the life of the people, through himself he examines the deeds of teachers. The faults of subjects, too, which are either overlooked by teachers or cannot be judged by them, are undoubtedly reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, while the matter is conducted in sound faith, it is a mark of virtue to tolerate whatever belongs to one’s predecessor. Nevertheless, what displeases should be humbly suggested, if perhaps it may be possible to correct it. But one must take the greatest care lest defenses of disordered justice pass into pride: while uprightness is loved carelessly, humility—the teacher of uprightness itself—is lost, and lest anyone despise having as his superior one whom it may happen that he criticizes in some action.

Against this swelling of pride in subjects, the mind is subdued to the keeping of humility if one constantly considers one’s own weakness. We neglect to examine our powers truthfully, and because we believe ourselves capable of greater things, we judge those who have been placed over us severely. The less we know ourselves, the more we see those whom we strive to criticize.

These are evil signs, which are often committed by subjects against superiors and by superiors against subjects. Those who rule consider all their subjects less wise than they themselves are; and, conversely, those who are subordinate judge the actions of their rulers. If they themselves happened to hold authority, they think they could act better.

Thus it often happens that rulers see less wisely what ought to be done, because the very cloud of pride darkens their eyes; and sometimes a person who is subordinate, once he has become a superior, does what he formerly criticized as a subordinate, and, because he perpetrates what he had judged, is ashamed—at least because he had judged it.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care lest the higher position exalt their hearts through an estimation of singular wisdom, so subjects must take care lest they despise the deeds of their rulers. If the life of teachers is rightly criticized, their subjects ought nevertheless, even when displeased, to honor the teacher. But this must be observed carefully: do not cease to venerate someone whom you see being changed.

For a subtle path of uprightness and humility must be followed, so that the reprehensible deeds of teachers may displease in such a way that the minds of subjects do not depart from preserving reverence for the teaching office.

“Joab therefore gave the king the number of the census of the people. And there were found in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who could draw the sword, and in Judah five hundred thousand fighting men.”

It should be noted, however, that in Chronicles it is read: “A thousand thousand and one hundred thousand from Israel, and from Judah four hundred and seventy thousand” (I Chron. XXI). This should be understood as meaning that Joab counted them, but did not wish to disclose their total to David except to the extent that it is written in the Book of Samuel.

“David’s heart struck him after the people had been numbered, and David said to the Lord: ‘I have sinned greatly in this deed, but I beg you, Lord, to take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly,’ etc.”

In the Book of Exodus it is likewise written: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘When you take the census of the sons of Israel according to their number, each shall give the Lord a price for his life, and there shall be no plague among them when they are counted. Everyone who passes into the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the measure of the sanctuary. A shekel contains twenty obols; half a shekel shall be offered to the Lord. Everyone who is counted, from twenty years of age and above, shall give the price. The rich shall not add to the half-shekel, and the poor shall not subtract from it. You shall receive the money that has been contributed by the sons of Israel and give it for the uses of the tabernacle of testimony, so that it may be a memorial for them before the Lord and may make atonement for their lives’” (Exod. XXX).

“David forgot to do this; for that reason he offended God, and on that account a plague came upon Israel.”

Referring to this passage, Josephus reports as follows: “When the prophets had declared to David that God was angry with him, he began to plead and to ask that he might be shown favor and receive forgiveness for his sin. Then the Lord sent the prophet Gad to him, bringing three conditions of punishment, so that he might choose whichever one he preferred: whether he wished famine to arise in the land for seven years, or to be defeated by his enemies in battle for three months, or whether disease and sickness should come upon the Hebrews for three days.

“But he, falling into anxiety over this choice among all evils, was distressed and seemed greatly confused in mind. When the prophet said that this was altogether imminent and demanded an answer quickly, so that he might report to God the condition he had chosen, the king considered that, if he chose famine, he would seem to act against others, since he himself, possessing much grain, would not suffer want while the others would be in distress.

“Likewise, if he chose victory by the enemies for three months, he himself, having very brave men and guards around him, would fear nothing, while the army would be exposed to destruction. Among these alternatives, however, he chose the common suffering of kings and subjects, in which fear is equal for all, saying: ‘It is much better to fall into the hands of God than into the hands of enemies.’

“When the prophet heard this, he reported it to the Lord, who sent disease and death upon the army of the Hebrews. They died in different ways, and the sickness could not easily be recognized as having one cause. Death indeed affected all, but many perished through various causes of illness that could not easily be identified.

“One person died after another, and the evil, secretly impending, brought death swiftly. Some perished amid severe pains, surrendering their lives with bitter groaning. Others wasted away under the very afflictions, so that they could not even care for their bodies but collapsed from exhaustion. Others, when sudden darkness seized their efforts, were suffocated and immediately expired. Others died upon the dead whom they were burying, leaving their burials unfinished.

“When the deadly sickness began to kill them from the morning hour until the hour of the midday meal, seventy thousand had perished. The angel of the Lord was beside the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”

In Chronicles it is likewise written: “The angel of the Lord was standing beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the Lord standing between earth and heaven, with a drawn sword in his hand turned against Jerusalem; and both he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell prone upon the ground” (I Chron. XXI).

“When David saw the angel striking the people, he said to the Lord: ‘I am the one who sinned; I acted wickedly. These people, who are sheep, what have they done? Let your hand, I beg you, be turned against me and against my father’s house.’ Then Gad came to David on that day and said to him: ‘Go up and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite,’ etc.”

Finally, *Areuna* is interpreted as “threshing floor,” and *Ornan* in Latin sounds like “light for us.” It was therefore fitting that, when David wished to appease the Lord for the offense he had committed, he was commanded to build an altar on the threshing floor of Areuna or Ornan, so that everyone might infer from this that Divinity cannot otherwise be appeased by a human being unless, on the threshing floor of the heart, one establishes for him an altar of devoted humility through the light of certain faith and true love, on which one offers God the acceptable sacrifice of pious confession and praise.

This is clearly revealed by the same prophet in the Psalms, where it is said in the person of the Lord: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. XLIX). And again: “The sacrifice for God is a troubled spirit; God does not despise a broken and humbled heart” (Ps. L).

The threshing floor of Areuna, or the threshing floor of Ornan, is Jerusalem itself. David therefore bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty silver shekels. In Chronicles it is read as follows: “David therefore gave Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold of the most exact weight” (I Chron. XXI). It must be understood that he bought the oxen for fifty silver shekels, but the threshing floor for six hundred gold pieces.

“David built an altar there to the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings; and the Lord was reconciled to the land, and the plague was restrained from Israel.”

The Book of Chronicles likewise relates: “The tabernacle of the Lord, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering were at that time on the high place at Gibeon. David was unable to go to the altar to entreat God there, for he had been struck with exceedingly great fear when he saw the sword of the angel of the Lord.

“David said: ‘This is the house of the Lord God, and this is the altar for the burnt offering of Israel.’ And he commanded that all the resident foreigners in the land of Israel should be gathered, and he appointed them as stonecutters to quarry and polish stones, so that the house of God might be built” (ibid.).

According to the Hebrews, it had once happened in that place that Abraham offered his son Isaac. When he was already prepared to kill his son and present him as a burnt offering, a ram suddenly appeared and stood beside the altar; Abraham sacrificed it instead of his son, as we have related.

# BOOK III

[Col. 0123]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0123C] Concerning David’s old age and coldness, and Abishag the Shunammite, who warmed him.

**(CHAP. I).** “King David had grown old and had many days of life. Although they covered him with garments, he was not warm. Therefore his servants said to him: ‘Let us seek for our lord the king a young virgin; let her stand before the king, warm him, sleep in his bosom, and warm our lord the king.’ So they sought a beautiful young woman throughout all Israel. They found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king. The girl was exceedingly beautiful; she slept with the king and ministered to him. But the king did not know her, etc.”

David, seventy years old, once a warlike man, could not be warmed as old age grew cold in him. A girl is therefore sought from throughout Israel—Abishag the Shunammite—to sleep with the king and warm his aged body.

Does this not seem to you, if you follow the dead letter, either a piece of mime or a comic trick of the wool-workers’ art? An old man, cold, is wrapped in garments and does not grow warm except in the embrace of a young woman. Bathsheba was still alive; Abigail and the other wives and concubines whom Scripture mentions remained. All are rejected as though they were cold, and the aged man grows warm in the embraces of one alone.

Abraham was much older than David, yet while Sarah lived he did not seek another wife. Isaac had twice David’s years, and while Rebecca was already an old woman he never grew cold. I say nothing of the men before the Flood, who, after nine hundred years, did not seek the embraces of girls—not merely with their aged limbs, but with limbs almost already decayed.

Certainly Moses, leader of the Israelite people, was one hundred and twenty years old and did not replace Zipporah. What, then, is this Shunammite wife and virgin, so ardent that she warmed the cold man, yet so holy that she did not provoke the warm man to lust?

Let the wisest Solomon explain his father’s pleasures and tell of the embraces of the peaceful warrior:

“Acquire wisdom, acquire understanding; do not forget, and do not turn away from the words of my mouth. Do not abandon her, and she will seize you; love her, and she will guard you. The beginning of wisdom: acquire wisdom, and in all your possessions acquire understanding. Surround her, and she will exalt you. Honor her, and she will embrace you, so that she may give your head a crown of graces, and a crown of delights will protect you” (Prov. IV).

Almost all the virtues of the body are altered in old people, and as wisdom alone increases, the other things diminish. Fasts, sleeping on the ground, journeys here and there, receiving travelers, defending the poor, devotion to prayer and perseverance, visiting the sick, and the labor of the hands by which alms may be provided—and, not to extend the discussion further, everything performed through the body—become lesser when the body is broken.

I do not say that wisdom—which in many old people withers through age—grows cold in young people and in those still of more vigorous age, especially those who have attained knowledge through toil and the most ardent study, through a holy life and frequent prayer to the Lord. Rather, I say that youth endures many battles of the body and, amid the incitements of vices and the pricklings of the flesh, is stifled like a fire among green branches, so that it cannot complete its full radiance.

But the old age of those who trained their youth in honorable deeds and meditated on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I) becomes more learned with age, more refined through experience, and wiser with the passage of time; it will reap the sweetest fruits of its former studies.

The sacramental meaning of Abishag’s very name also indicates the greater wisdom of the elderly. It is interpreted as “my father is abundant” or “the roar of my father.” The word “abundant” is ambiguous, but in the present passage it signifies virtue: that in the elderly wisdom is greater, overflowing, and abundant. In another passage, however, “abundant,” in the sense of “unnecessary,” is used.

Abishag, that is, “roar,” is properly so called because it is the sound of the sea’s waves, and, so to speak, a rumbling coming from the deep is heard. This shows that in the elderly there dwells an exceedingly abundant thunder of divine speech, beyond the human voice.

Moreover, *Shunammite* is said in our language to mean “scarlet,” signifying that wisdom is hot and fervent through divine reading. Although this indicates the mystery of the Lord’s blood, it also displays the fervor of wisdom.

Hence the midwife in Genesis (Gen. XXXVIII) ties a scarlet thread on the hand of Perez, who received the name “Divider,” that is, Perez, because he had divided the wall separating two peoples. Rahab the prostitute, as a type of the Church, also hung out a cord containing the mystery of blood, so that her house might be saved when Jericho perished (Josh. II).

For this reason Scripture also mentions the holy men elsewhere: “These are they who came from the heat of the house of Rechab” (I Chron. II). And our Lord says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke XII). Having been kindled in the hearts of the disciples, he compelled them to say: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV).

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0125D] Concerning Adonijah, who desired to reign in place of his father David and also sought to have Abishag the Shunammite as his wife; and concerning what David commanded Solomon about his adversaries.

**(CHAP. II).** “Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying: ‘I shall reign.’ He made for himself a chariot and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him, etc.”

That Adonijah, David’s older son, wished to succeed his father in the kingdom through the pride of arrogance and not through the virtue of discipline signifies nothing other than the Jewish people. The Jewish people appears like the elder son because it received the law first; despising the Gentile people, which was called later through God’s grace, it believed that the Lord would reign with itself alone.

Hence the name Adonijah—interpreted as “the Lord is ruler”—aptly expressed the type of the one who believed that he alone would rule with the Lord. But the people of the Church is appointed to the kingdom by divine ordinance together with the true Solomon, that is, our Peaceful One (Eph. I), whose body it is. On account of its faithlessness, the elder son—that is, the earlier people—was deservedly cast down from it.

This Adonijah, then, when Bathsheba intervened—her name interpreted as “daughter of fullness”—desired to corrupt Abishag the Shunammite. The Jewish people, through observance of the ceremonies of the law, by which it was full and completely satisfied, wished to violate the true wisdom of spiritual understanding, which is joined to our David; but it did not deserve the companionship of the one whose immaculate bed it sought to violate.

What David commanded his son Solomon concerning the just retribution of those who had been his support or had unjustly harmed him, although he himself had tolerated them most patiently while reigning, signifies nothing better than the future retribution of the coming judgment. In that judgment the wicked will receive everlasting punishment as their reward, while the righteous will receive eternal blessedness.

Even in the present time God’s patience often permits the good to be troubled and oppressed, while conversely it allows the reprobate to enjoy temporal pleasures and earthly prosperity. Yet in the future, through the Judge of the living and the dead, he will restore certain rewards to both, when “he will say to those who are at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.’ But to those who are at his left hand he will say: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.’ And these will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXIV).

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0125D] Solomon’s judgment concerning the women who disputed about the infants.

## Chapter III.

“Then two prostitute women came to the king and stood before him. One of them said: ‘I beg you, my lord: I and this woman lived in one house, and I gave birth beside her in the room. On the third day after I had given birth, this woman also gave birth, and we were together; there was no one else in the house with us except the two of us. Now this woman’s son died during the night, for while sleeping she had lain upon him. Rising at dead of night, she silently took my son from beside me, your handmaid, while I was sleeping, and placed him in her bosom. But her own son, who was dead, she placed in my bosom. When I rose in the morning to give milk to my son, he appeared to be dead. Examining him more carefully in the clear light, I discovered that he was not my son, whom I had borne.’ The other woman replied: ‘It is not so; your son is dead, but mine is alive.’ To the contrary, the first said: ‘You are lying; my son is alive, and your son is dead.’ And in this manner they contended before the king,” and so forth. (From Gregory.)

It should be noted that after the Lord has illuminated the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, he immediately tests us by visiting us with the sting of temptation. For by approaching he raises our hearts toward virtue, and by withdrawing he permits them to be shaken by temptation. If, after receiving the gifts of virtue, the soul is shaken by no temptation, it then boasts that it possesses these things from itself. Therefore, so that it may possess those gifts of firmness and humbly acknowledge its own weakness, it is lifted to the heights through the approach of grace, and through grace’s withdrawal it is shown what proceeds from itself.

This is aptly suggested to us by the history of sacred reading, in which Solomon is remembered as having received wisdom divinely and yet, immediately after that same wisdom, as having been assailed by the question of prostitutes. For as soon as he received the grace of so great a revelation, he endured the contest of shameful women. Indeed, often, when the regard of inner generosity illuminates our mind with the virtues granted to us, slippery thoughts immediately disturb it also, so that the mind, exalted by an immense gift and then struck by temptation, may discover what it is.

Thus Elijah, visited from above by the word, opened the heavens (III Kings XVIII), and yet, suddenly tested in his weakness, fleeing through the wilderness, he became afraid of a single woman (III Kings XIX). Thus Paul is taken up to the third heaven (II Corinthians XII) and, penetrating the secrets of paradise, beholds them; yet, returning to himself, he struggles against the battle of the flesh. He bears another law in his members (Romans VII), and the Spirit grieves to be wearied by the rebellion of that law.

Therefore God tests a person after granting a gift because, by bestowing the gift, he raises the person up, and, withdrawing it for a little while, shows the person to himself. Without doubt, we endure this until we are wholly reformed from the stain of sin of the earth into the substance of the incorruption that has been promised.

As far as the simple historical sense is concerned, it is clear that a boy of twelve years, contrary to the measure of his age, judged from the deepest perception of human nature. Hence all Israel admired and feared him: plainly, things that were evident did not escape him, since he had so prudently detected what was hidden.

As regards the typological meanings, since the Apostle says, “All these things happened to them figuratively, but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Corinthians X), some of the Greeks maintain that the passage should be understood of the Synagogue and the Church, and that the remaining details should be referred to the time when, after the cross and the resurrection, the true Solomon—that is, the Pacific One—began to reign both among Israel and among the people of the Gentiles.

There is no doubt that in Scripture the Synagogue and the Church are called adulterous women and prostitutes. At first sight this seems blasphemous. But if we turn to the prophets—to Hosea, who took a prostituted wife and begot children of prostitution, and afterward an adulterous woman (Hosea I); and to Ezekiel, who reproves Jerusalem as a prostitute because she followed her lovers, spread her legs to every passerby, and built a brothel in a prominent place (Ezekiel XVI)—we should recognize that Christ came for this very purpose: to give prostitutes in marriage and to make one sheepfold out of two flocks, destroying the dividing wall and gathering into the same folds the sheep that had previously been diseased.

These are the two rods joined together in Ezekiel, concerning which the Lord speaks through Zechariah (Zechariah II): “And I took for myself two rods; I called one Beauty, and I called the other Cord, and I pastured the flock.” That prostitute in the Gospel also, who “washed Jesus’ feet with her tears, dried them with her hair, and whose sins were all forgiven” (Luke VII), plainly signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles.

I have recalled this at the outset so that no one may think it incongruous for the women to be called prostitutes, when one of them is granted possession of the son by Solomon’s judgment. A prudent reader may ask how a prostitute can signify the Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle (Ephesians V). We do not say that the Church remained a prostitute, but that she had been one. The Savior is likewise recorded to have entered a meal in the house of Simon the leper (Matthew XXVI), not because he was a leper at the time when he had the Savior as his guest, but because he had previously been a leper. Matthew too is called a tax collector in the catalogue of the apostles (Matthew X), not because he remained a tax collector after attaining apostolic dignity, but because he had previously been a tax collector, so that where sin had abounded, grace might abound all the more (Romans V).

At the same time, consider what the Church says against the slanderous Synagogue: “I and this woman lived in one house.” After the resurrection of the Lord and Savior, one people was gathered from both peoples. And how elegantly the Church says, “I gave birth beside her in the room”! For the Church from the Gentiles, which previously did not possess the Law and the Prophets, gave birth in the house of the Synagogue. She did not leave the room but entered it. Hence she says in the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song of Songs II). And again, taking me in without disdain: “I will bring you into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who conceived me” (Song of Songs VIII).

“On the third day after I had given birth, this woman also gave birth.” If you consider Pilate washing his hands and saying, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matthew XXVII); if you consider the centurion confessing before the gallows, “Truly this was the Son of God” (ibid.); and if you consider those who, before the Passion, desired to see the Lord through Philip (John XII), you will have no doubt that the Church gave birth first, and that afterward the Jewish people were born—the people for whom the Lord prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

Three thousand believed on one day, and another five thousand (Acts II). “We were together” (Acts IV). “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (ibid.).

“There was no one else in the house with us except the two of us.” No blaspheming Jews, no Gentiles serving idols.

“Now this woman’s son died during the night.” While she follows observance of the Law and joins the grace of the Gospel to the yoke of Mosaic teaching, she is covered by the error of darkness.

“His mother, sleeping, lay upon him.” She could not say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs V).

“Rising at dead of night, she took the son from beside” the sleeping Church.

“And placed him in her own bosom.” Read again the whole of the Apostle’s Epistle to the Galatians, and you will observe how eagerly the Synagogue hastens to make the children of the Church her own. The Apostle says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians IV).

She took one, not in order to possess him but to kill him; for she did this not out of love for the child but out of hatred for her rival. And through the ceremonies of the Law she placed her own dead son in the bosom of the Church. It would take too long, if I wished to go through each point, to explain how, through the Apostle Paul and ecclesiastical men, the Church has understood that the son held under the Law was not her own, and how in the light she recognized the one whom she had not seen in the darkness.

Hence the quarrel arose in the presence of the king, one saying, “Your son is dead, but mine is alive,” and the other replying, “You are lying; my son is alive, and your son is dead.” “And in this manner they contended before the king.”

Then King Solomon—who is plainly understood as the Savior, according to the seventy-first psalm, which is inscribed to Solomon, where there is no doubt that the remaining things said apply not to the dead Solomon but to the majesty of Christ—pretends ignorance and, in accordance with the dispensation of the flesh, feigns human emotions, as in another place: “Where have you laid Lazarus?” (John II); and to the woman suffering from an issue of blood: “Who touched me?” (Mark V).

He calls for the sword, concerning which he had said: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matthew X).

The Lord tempers nature according to nature and wishes, according to the will of both women, to divide the living son between the Law and grace—not because he approves this, but because, in order to expose the Synagogue’s slander, he says that he wishes it. The woman who did not want the Church’s son to live in grace or to be freed through baptism is glad for the child to be divided, not so that she may possess him but so that she may kill him. The Church, knowing that he is hers, willingly yields him to her rival, provided that he may at least live with the adversary, lest, divided between the Law and grace, he be struck by the Savior’s sword. Hence the Apostle says: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you observe the Law, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians V).

Another interpretation. (From Gregory.)

What is signified here, under the names of nursing mothers, if not the order of teachers? And what is signified by their sons, if not the persons of disciples? For teachers are awake in knowledge but asleep in life. While they nourish their hearers, whom they feed through the vigils of preaching, they neglect to do what they say; through the sleep of torpor they kill and crush those whom they appeared to nourish with the milk of words.

Hence, when they themselves live reprehensibly and are unable to have disciples of praiseworthy life, they often attempt to draw others’ disciples to themselves, so that, while they show that they possess good followers, they may excuse before human judgments the evil things they do, and may conceal, as it were, their deadly negligence beneath the life of their subjects. Thus the woman who destroyed her own son sought another’s.

Yet Solomon’s sword found the true mother, because the final examination of the strict Judge reveals whose fruit lives and whose perishes. There too one must carefully observe that the living son is first ordered to be divided so that afterward he may be returned to his mother alone. For in this life the disciple’s life is permitted, as it were, to be divided, since he is sometimes allowed to have merit before God and at other times praise before human beings.

But the false mother does not fear to have the one whom she did not beget killed, because arrogant teachers, ignorant of charity, if they cannot attain the fullest reputation of praise through another’s disciples, cruelly persecute their lives. Set ablaze by the torches of envy, they do not want others to live in possession of what they see themselves unable to possess.

Therefore the perverse woman cries out:

“Let him be neither mine nor hers.”

For, as we have said, those whom they do not see serving them for the sake of temporal glory, they begrudge others their life in truth. But the true mother strives that her son may at least be with the stranger and live, because genuine teachers allow others to receive from their disciples the praise of teaching, while those disciples do not lose the integrity of their lives.

This same mother is wholly recognized by the compassion of her heart, because teaching is approved in the examination of charity.
