She alone deserved to receive the whole child, who seemed to yield the whole of him, because faithful superiors, in that they not only do not begrudge others the praise arising from their good disciples but also entreat their disciples’ benefit and progress for others, receive their sons whole and living when, in the supreme examination, they obtain the joys of the reward due to their perfected lives.

## Chapter IV. Concerning Solomon’s Power, by Which He Ruled over All; His Wisdom, Wealth, and Luxuries; and the Peace He Possessed in His Kingdom

That Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs and that his songs numbered five thousand; and that he discoursed about beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish.

Concerning the building of the house of God, and how the construction of the tabernacle signifies one and the same Church of Christ.

Enumerating the princes of Solomon who had been assigned various offices in his kingdom or presided over different provinces, Scripture continues as follows:

“But Solomon had under his dominion all the kingdoms of the land of the Philistines, from the river to the boundary of Egypt, offering him tribute and serving him all the days of his life.”

And whom does this signify better than our Pacific One, whom that same Solomon prefigured? For he holds under his dominion all the kingdoms of the earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting, as Scripture testifies: “From sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth, all peoples, languages, and tribes will serve him, offering him gifts” (Psalm LXXI)—namely, gifts of right faith and good works.

“Kings of Tarshish,” it says, “and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents, and all the kings of the earth will adore him; all nations will serve him.”

What follows—“all the days of his life”—means “for ever and ever,” because he will remain forever: “His power is an everlasting power; his years will not fail, and there will be no end of his kingdom” (Daniel VII; Psalm CI; Luke I).

“Now Solomon’s provision for each day was thirty measures of fine flour and sixty measures of meal, ten fattened oxen and twenty oxen from the pasture, and one hundred rams, apart from deer, gazelles, and buffaloes, and fattened birds.”

What does this food of Solomon signify, then, except the nourishment of our King Jesus Christ, who is well fed by the right faith and good works offered to him daily by the Catholic Church?

The “thirty measures of fine flour” can express faith in the Holy Trinity, according to what is contained in the Law of the Lord; and the “sixty measures of meal,” the perfection of good works. The “ten fattened oxen” signify teachers of the Decalogue; and the “twenty oxen from the pasture,” preachers of the New Testament, who possess within themselves, as it were, a doubled Decalogue when they preach the New and Old Testaments equally, full of love of God and neighbor.

The “one hundred rams”—whom do they signify better than those who rule well in the Lord’s flock and hasten, together with those subject to them, to attain the glory of eternal blessedness?

The hunting of various animals may also appropriately be understood as the acquisition of human beings, who are caught daily from various nations in the nets of the Gospel by “spiritual hunters” (Jeremiah XVI) and are brought into the pasture of our Savior.

“Solomon also had peace on every side all around. Judah and Israel dwelt without any fear, each one under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon,” and so forth.

Isaiah likewise says this about the Redeemer: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isaiah IX). Under his protection, the true Judah and the true Israel dwell without any fear, with their hearts raised toward God. They despise earthly things and do not fear the threats of enemies, but persevere continually in the praises of God, delighting in God’s grace and in the sweetness of charity, which they unceasingly possess toward God and neighbor.

“Solomon had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen. The officials of the aforementioned king provided them with food.”

What is signified by the number forty except the times of the ancient Law? Moses fasted for forty days in order to receive it (Exodus XXXIV), and the Israelite people, instructed through it, remained in the wilderness for forty years.

The number twelve signifies the present time, in which the apostolic teaching of the New Testament nourishes the people. The stalls of Solomon’s horses are also aptly counted by the number forty or twelve, because in both peoples—the legal people and the evangelical people—those who are understanding are invited to the stalls of the Holy Scriptures, so that they may receive there the nourishment of sacred teaching and become fit for the cavalry of the supreme King.

“And the aforementioned officials of the king provided them with food,” since each of the teachers strives, through the word of right faith and the example of good works, to supply them with healthy nourishment.

Hence the following Scripture says of them:

“They also supplied the provisions for King Solomon’s table with great care at the proper time, and barley and straw for the horses and beasts.”

For, so that nothing may be lacking to those who remain in the king’s house, the entire order of holy preachers labors—by writing and speaking—so that the Lord’s table may abound in a wealth of books, and so that each of the faithful may receive suitable nourishment from them.

“God also gave Solomon wisdom and very great prudence and breadth of heart, like the sand that is on the seashore. And Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the East and of Egypt; and he was wiser than all human beings,” and so forth.

God certainly gave our Solomon wisdom and prudence beyond all human beings and every rational creature. Concerning him John says: “He whom God sent speaks the words of God. For God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John III).

And elsewhere Truth itself says: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John V).

Hence Paul says of the Lord Christ: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers: all things were created through him and in him. And he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Colossians I).

“And he is the head of the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place in everything; because in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily. And in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians II).

The wisdom of the true Solomon therefore surpasses that of all, because there is a great difference between those who are wise by participation in wisdom and the one who is the source of wisdom and origin of virtues.

Hence what follows: “And he was renowned among all the nations around,” because his name is preached throughout the whole world. “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

“Solomon also spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered five thousand,” and so forth. (From Isidore.)

What is signified by the three thousand proverbs except the fullness of faith handed down in the Law, in the Gospels, and in Christ? For when the whole of it is expounded in many ways through allegorical meanings under the mystery of the Trinity, it is called, as it were, three thousand proverbs.

His five thousand songs are understood through the five bodily senses. Whoever governs these well by various virtues is blessed, and through them sings, as it were, five thousand songs to the Lord.

“Solomon discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop.”

By the name cedar, the height of glory in the elect is understood. Hence the prophet testifies: “The righteous will flourish like the palm tree and multiply like the cedar that is in Lebanon” (Psalm XCI).

Hyssop, however, is a lowly herb clinging to a rock, by which the humility of Christ is signified. Our Redeemer therefore discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop, because, descending from the lofty excellence of heavenly glory, he reached the humility of the flesh.

The name cedar can also signify the proud exaltation of the wicked, as David says: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” (Psalm XXVIII). Christ therefore discourses from the cedar to the hyssop, because he himself judges both proud hearts and humble ones.

He discoursed about wood when he hung upon the cross. Then the arrogance of the world bent down like a cedar, and he brought it down even to the humility of hyssop—that is, to the foolishness of the cross and the contemptible word of faith. Hence Paul says: “For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God. For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.’”

And shortly afterward: “Because, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.”

“And Solomon discoursed about beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish.”

Our Solomon discourses about each species of animals, because “all things are naked and open to his eyes, and no creature is invisible in his sight” (Hebrews IV). He knows all human thoughts; he numbers the multitude of the stars (Psalm CXLVI); the abyss lies open to him, and hell is not hidden before him (Psalm CXXXVIII).

It is as though he were discoursing when he sets before us the account of each thing and reveals in his Scriptures the mysteries that had been hidden from ages and generations, so that we may consider the blessedness of angels, the usefulness of human beings, and the cunning of evil spirits; and thus, rejecting what is evil, choose what is good, and always follow him toward one another and toward all.

“And people came from all nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and from all the regions of the earth; and they heard his wisdom.”

Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “It shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord will be prepared at the summit of the mountains, and it will be exalted above the hills; all nations will flow toward it, and many peoples will go and say: ‘Come, let us ascend to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways, and we will walk in his paths; for the Law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’” (Isaiah II).

(From Bede.)

The house of God that King Solomon built in Jerusalem was made as a figure of the holy universal Church. From the first elect person to the last, who will pass away at the end of the world, it is built daily through the grace of the peaceful King, namely its Redeemer. Part of it still journeys away from him on earth; part of it, having escaped the hardships of pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven, where, after the final judgment has been completed, the whole Church will reign with him.

The elect angels also belong to this house, whose likeness is promised to us in the life to come, as the Lord says: “Those who are considered worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage. For they can no longer die, because they are equal to the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection” (Luke XX).

The mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, also belongs to this house, as he himself testifies when he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). Explaining this, the Evangelist added: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

The Apostle said concerning us: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

If, then, he became the temple of God through the humanity he assumed, it is certainly evident that the material temple held the figure of all of us—of the Lord himself and of his members, which we are. It signified the Lord himself as the uniquely chosen and precious cornerstone founded in the foundation, and us as living stones built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets—that is, upon the Lord himself.

The same spiritual house of God is also signified by the tabernacle once made in the wilderness through Moses. But that house was on the journey by which the people were coming to the promised land, whereas this one was built in the promised land itself and in the city of Jerusalem. The former was carried frequently from place to place through the ministry of the Levites, so that at last it might be brought into the land of the promised inheritance; the latter was constructed immediately in the homeland itself and the royal city, so that it might stand forever upon an inviolable foundation until it fulfilled the heavenly function of the figures entrusted to it.

In the former, therefore, the labor and exile of the present Church may be figured; in the latter, her future rest and blessedness. Or, since the former was made solely by the children of Israel, while the latter was made also by proselytes and Gentiles, the fathers of the Old Testament and that ancient people of God may principally be expressed figuratively in the former, and the Church gathered from the Gentiles in the latter.

Although the structure of both houses has been examined more fully in the spiritual sense, so that through many figures it may be shown and suggested that the daily labors of the present Church, the everlasting rewards and joys of the heavenly kingdom in the future, the first election of the Church from Israel, and the salvation of all nations in Christ are represented.

## Chapter V. How Hiram, King of Tyre, Assisted Solomon in the Work of the Temple; How Many Laborers Solomon Had for the Work of the Temple; and What Kind of Stone the Temple Was Made Of

The history of Kings relates (Chapter V) that Solomon, intending to build a house for the Lord, sought assistance from Hiram, king of Tyre, who had always been David’s friend and who also maintained peace with Solomon after Solomon had obtained the kingdom. Hiram immediately showed himself ready to assist him in everything, so that he gave him craftsmen, wood, and gold, according to the needs of the work. In return for this kindness, Solomon gave him every year many measures of wheat and oil as food for his household.

No one doubts that Solomon, whose name is interpreted “peaceful,” signifies both by his name and by the most serene condition of his kingdom the one of whom Isaiah said: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isaiah IX).

Hiram, whose name in Latin is said to mean “living on high,” figuratively expresses believers from the Gentiles who are glorious both in life and in faith. Nor does anything prevent us from understanding Hiram, because he was a king and assisted Solomon in the construction of the house of the Lord by royal power, as typologically declaring the rulers of those things who have been converted to the faith. Through their aid the Church has often been assisted and nobly increased, and against heretics, schismatics, and pagans she has been strengthened by official decrees.

Solomon therefore asked Hiram for assistance in the work of the temple because, when the Lord came in the flesh and resolved to build for himself a beloved house, namely the Church, he chose helpers for the work not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. For he appointed ministers of the word from both peoples.

Hiram sent Solomon cedar and fir wood cut from Lebanon, to be placed in the house of the Lord. This signifies that the converted Gentile world sent to the Lord men who had once been distinguished in the world but had already been cast down and humbled by the axe of the Lord’s rebuke from the mountain of their pride; instructed according to the norm of evangelical truth, they were to be placed in the building of the Church, each according to his merit or his time.

“He also sent craftsmen.”

For the Gentile world offered to the Lord philosophers converted to true wisdom, who, by the grace of their learning, were rightly appointed to govern peoples also. Such was Dionysius the Areopagite in the time of the apostles, and afterward the most gentle teacher and powerful martyr Cyprian, along with many others.

“He also sent gold.”

This is understood in almost the same sense, since it indicates men distinguished by wisdom and intellect. For all these offerings, the Gentile world expects from the Lord the gifts of heavenly grace: namely, the wheat of the word of God and the oil of charity, anointing, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

It also aptly accords with the realities of the Church that Solomon, requesting assistance for the holy work, says to Hiram: “Therefore command your servants to cut cedars for me from Lebanon, and let my servants be with your servants.”

For Hiram’s servants, who cut cedars from Lebanon for Solomon, are teachers chosen from the Gentiles. Their duty is to correct and lay low those who rejoiced in the possessions and glory of this world, freeing them from the arrogance of pride, and to transfer their desires to the service of their Redeemer.

These servants were with Solomon’s servants and labored together at the work in question because the first teachers from the Gentiles necessarily had to be instructed in the word of faith by the apostles themselves, who had learned from the Lord, lest, if they began to teach without masters, they should become teachers of error.

For this reason Solomon wished Hiram’s servants to cut the wood from Lebanon for him: they were more skilled than his own servants at cutting it. But he also wished his own servants to be present at the same time, so that they might show the cutters what dimensions the wood ought to have.

The meaning of this figure is evident. The apostles knew more reliably the word of the Gospel that they had heard from the Lord. But Gentiles converted from error and transformed into the truth of the Gospel knew the errors of the Gentiles better, and the more certainly they knew them, the more skillfully they learned how to overcome and abolish them.

“Solomon selected laborers from all Israel. The levy was thirty thousand men, and he sent them to Lebanon, ten thousand each month in rotation, so that they would spend two months at home,” and so forth.

Here it should first be noted that Solomon did not choose laborers from all Israel without reason, nor was there any portion of the people from which men worthy of so great a work were not taken. For priests are not to be chosen from one lineage of Aaron alone; rather, those who are capable of building the house of the Lord either by their example or by their teaching must be sought from the whole Church. Wherever they are found, they should immediately be promoted to the office of teachers without respect of persons.

When such men are appointed to instruct unbelievers and call them into the fellowship of the Church, they are sent, as it were, as vigorous and chosen men to cut the materials for the temple in Lebanon.

The number of thirty thousand, by which these cutters of wood were counted, may appropriately be referred to the figure of those who are perfected in faith in the Holy Trinity, which is especially fitting for teachers.

But since the thirty thousand were arranged so that ten thousand applied themselves to the holy work during each month, we should weigh more carefully the mystery of the number ten. Ten thousand men from Israel are sent to cut wood for the work of the house of the Lord because all who are to be appointed teachers and instructors of the foolish must themselves observe in every respect the ten commandments of the Law and show their hearers that they must observe them.

They must also hope for the future rewards in heaven, which are customarily signified by the number ten, and must continually declare to their hearers that they too should hope for them.

The three months, whose intervals were assigned to each of the woodcutters, typologically declare the perfection of the three evangelical virtues: almsgiving, prayer, and fasting.

By almsgiving are understood all the things that we benevolently do for our brothers in order to fulfill love of neighbor. By prayer are understood all the things by which, through inward compunction, we are joined to our Creator. By fasting are understood all the things by which we guard ourselves from the contagion of vices and the allurements of the world, so that with a free mind and chaste body we may always cling to the love of our Creator and our neighbor.

These, then, are the three months of the temple’s laborers. Since a month is completed by the fullness of the days of the lunar cycle, it rightly manifests through itself the fullness of every spiritual virtue, in which the minds of the faithful are regarded by the Lord’s daily illumination, like the moon by the sun.

“And Adoniram was over this levy,” and so forth.

Adoniram, whose name in Latin is said to mean “my exalted Lord,” whom does he better indicate than the one whose name he imitates—namely, the Lord and Savior?

Adoniram is placed over the temple laborers so that, through his provision, he might properly arrange in which months each should go out to work and in which months they should return again to care for their own house. This occurs when our Lord and Savior, through his more intimate illumination, instructs the minds of the holy preachers to discern when it is appropriate to undertake the work of building the Church by preaching or by performing other acts of piety, and when it is fitting to return again to examine their own conscience, as though returning to inspect their own house, and to make it worthy of the heavenly Inspector and Visitor through prayers and fasts.

“Accordingly, Solomon had seventy thousand of those who carried burdens, and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain, besides the overseers who directed each kind of work, numbering three thousand three hundred, who commanded the people and those who performed the work, and so forth.”

By “stonecutters” he means cutters of stones. These same stonecutters, figuratively, signify what the cutters of wood also signify: namely, preachers who exercise the minds of the foolish with the chisel of the word of God, striving to transform them from the strength and deformity in which they were born, and carefully rendering them, once regularly formed, suitable for the unity of the faithful—that is, for the building of the house of God.

The fact that both wood and stones are cut in the mountain, and that both materials, cut and prepared, are transferred to the mountain of the Lord’s house, plainly conveys the meaning that we were all born on the mountain of pride. For we derive the origin of our flesh from the transgression of the first man, which pride caused. But whoever among us has been foreordained by God’s grace to life is cut away through catechetical instruction and reception of the sacraments of faith from the mountain of pride and transferred to the Lord’s mountain, because, rescued from the power of darkness, we reach the stronghold of virtues, which exists in the unity of the holy Church.

It should be noted, however, that those workers were so distributed that some cut stones in the mountain, while others carried burdens. For the gifts of the Spirit are diverse: some possess steadfastness for speaking and reproving the insolent; some are gentler, suited to consoling the fainthearted and supporting the weak; and some, endowed with both virtues, come together for the work of the Lord’s house. Such people the Apostle wished those to become to whom he says: “Reprove the disorderly, console the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (I Thess. V).

The overseers who directed each kind of work are the very authors of sacred Scripture, whose teaching instructs us in all things: how it is fitting to teach the gentler and reprove the contemptuous, and how we ought to bear one another’s burdens so that we may fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

The aforesaid workers are rightly said to have numbered seventy thousand and eighty thousand. Seventy, on account of the sabbatism of souls—for the seventh day was consecrated as the Sabbath, that is, as rest. Eighty, on account of the hope of the resurrection, which proceeded in the Lord on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath, and which we too expect to occur on the eighth day and in the eighth age.

The overseers numbered three thousand three hundred, clearly on account of faith in the holy Trinity, which the sacred writings preach to us. But the fact that, in place of the three thousand three hundred overseers, three thousand six hundred are recorded in the book of Chronicles refers entirely to the same perfection of those exalted men (II Chron. II). Since the number six completed the adornment of the world, perfect works of goodness are rightly represented by it. And because Holy Scripture teaches that works of righteousness must be possessed together with faith in the truth, the overseers of the temple’s works are rightly said to have numbered three thousand six hundred.

Nor should it be passed over that these seventy and eighty thousand burden-bearers and stonecutters, together with their overseers, were not Israelites but proselytes—that is, foreigners who lived among them. For it is written in the book of Chronicles: “Solomon therefore counted all the proselyte men who were in the land of Israel, after the census which David his father had taken, and they were found to number one hundred fifty thousand and three thousand six hundred. From them he made seventy thousand carry burdens on their shoulders, and so forth” (ibid.).

The term “proselytes” was used in Greek for those born among other nations who, after receiving circumcision, passed over into the faith and fellowship of the people of God.

Thus the workers of the Lord’s house came from the children of Israel, from proselytes, and from the nations. From the children of Israel were the thirty thousand sent to cut cedars from Lebanon. These of whom we have now spoken, the stonecutters, were from the proselytes. From the nations came Hiram himself and his servants, who cut wood from Lebanon together with Solomon’s servants. Therefore every kind of human being through whom the Church was to be built was represented beforehand in the building of the temple. For Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles converted to the truth of the Gospel build the one and same Church of Christ, whether by living rightly or by teaching.

“The king commanded them to quarry great stones, precious stones, for the foundation of the temple, and to square them, and so forth.”

Mystically understood, the foundation of the temple is none other than that which the Apostle indicates when he says: “For no one can lay another foundation except that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III). He can rightly be called the foundation of the Lord’s house because, as Peter says: “There is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved” (Acts IV).

Great and precious stones are brought to this foundation when men outstanding in deeds and holiness cling to their Creator with the familiar holiness of their minds, so that, the more firmly they place their hope in him, the more strongly they may be able to direct the lives of others—which is to bear the breadth of the wall.

The stones that were placed in the foundation of the temple to support the whole building are properly the prophets and apostles, who received the word and sacraments of the truth from the Wisdom of God itself, whether visibly or invisibly. They are rightly ordered first to be squared and then placed in the foundation. For everything square customarily remains fixed, whichever way it is turned. To this figure the hearts of the elect are compared: they have learned to stand so firmly in the stability of faith that no adversity arising from circumstances, not even death itself, can incline them away from the uprightness of their state.

“Whom Solomon’s masons and Hiram’s masons hewed.”

Precious stones are hewn when each of the elect, through the instruction and diligence of the saints who preceded them, abandons whatever harmful and empty thing they possess within themselves and displays before the sight of their Creator the rule of the righteousness implanted in them, like the stable form of a square.

These stones were hewn not only by Solomon’s masons but also by Hiram’s masons, because teachers of the holy Church arose from both peoples.

“Moreover, the Giblites prepared wood and stones for building the house.”

Giblos is a city of Phoenicia, which Ezekiel mentions when he says: “Your wise men, Tyre, became your pilots, the elders of Giblites and its wise men” (Ezek. XXVII). In Hebrew the name is written Gobal or Gebal, which is interpreted as “defining” or “delimiting.” This name suitably applies to those who prepare human hearts for the spiritual building constructed from the virtues of the soul. For they can teach their hearers faith and works of righteousness only when they themselves, first instructed in the sacred pages, have carefully learned with certain definition of the truth what faith must be held and by what path of virtues one must walk.

For the person who usurps the office of teacher while ignorant of the discernment of the catholic faith takes that office upon himself in vain. Those who attempt to teach others a rule they themselves have not learned build not a sanctuary for the Lord but a ruin for themselves.

In building the house of God, therefore, wood and stones must first be cut from the mountain, because those whom we seek to establish in the faith of the truth must first be taught to renounce the devil and to be rescued through rebirth from the lot of the first transgression in which they were born.

Next, precious and great stones must be sought and placed in the foundation of the temple, so that, once their former way of life has been rejected, we may remember to examine their life and conduct in all things and propose for imitation to our hearers those whom we know to cling especially to the Lord through the virtue of humility.

The wall of good works must be raised upward, and, as though walking upon courses of stones placed one above another, we must advance “from virtue to virtue” (Ps. LXXXIII).

Or certainly, the great, precious, and squared foundation stones are, as we said above, the teachers of the Churches, who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself. The courses of stones or of wood placed above them are the priests and teachers who follow, each in his own time. Through their preaching and ministry the structure of the Church either grows or is adorned with virtues.

What color the stones were with which the temple was made is clearly stated in the book of Chronicles, when David, showing Solomon the expenses for the temple that he had prepared, says: “I have prepared in great abundance every precious stone and Parian marble” (I Chron. XXIX).

By “Parian marble” he means white marble, such as that island customarily produces. It is one of the Cyclades. Josephus also indicates that the temple was made of this stone, saying: “He therefore raised the temple up to the vaulted roof, and constructed it of white stone.” Its height was sixty cubits.

The mystical meaning is not hidden. It is evident to everyone that the white marble from which the Lord’s house was constructed signifies the clean conduct and conscience of the elect, chastened from every blemish of corruption—such as that wise architect wished those precious stones to be whom he placed upon the foundation of Christ, redeemed with gold and silver. “Beloved,” he says, “let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.”

## CHAPTER VI. When and where the temple was built; what its measurements were; and how many years were spent building it

(CHAP. VI.) “It came to pass, therefore, in the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month Zio, which is the second month of Solomon’s reign over Israel, that he began to build the house for the Lord, and so forth.”

In the statement, “in the fourth year, in the month Zio, which is the second month of Solomon’s reign over Israel,” the order of the meaning is: in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Zio, which is the second month. He calls the second month May. For April, in which Passover is celebrated, was the beginning of the months among the Hebrews, the first of the months of the year.

It is therefore plainly evident that, immediately after Passover had been completed, he began to build the house of the Lord, and that the people, consecrated by the mystical solemnity, applied their hands to the mystical work.

The departure from Egypt is mentioned when the tabernacle began to be built so that the reader might be reminded how many years passed between the building of the two houses and might recognize that a spiritual sacrament is contained in this total of time.

Four hundreds and eighty make four hundred and eighty. Four appropriately corresponds to evangelical perfection, on account of the number of Evangelists. One hundred corresponds to the teaching of the Law, on account of the equal number of years of the lawgiver. In this number also the primitive Church openly received the grace of the Holy Spirit, showing that those who use the Law lawfully—that is, those who recognize and embrace the grace of Christ in it—are rightly filled with the grace of his Spirit, by which they burn more intensely in his love.

We have said that the tabernacle which Moses and the children of Israel made in the wilderness signifies the synagogue, while the temple which Solomon and the children of Israel built with the assistance of proselytes and Gentiles can signify the Church of the Gentiles.

The worship and religion of the tabernacle continued for four hundred and eighty years, and then the temple began to be built. The fact that the Lord’s house began to be built in the fourth year of King Solomon can be mystically referred to the following: after the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation had been completed—the dispensation written in the four books of the Gospel—and the Holy Spirit had been sent from heaven, the structure of the Church began.

That it began in the second month can be referred to the election of the Gentiles, who, after Israel, received into themselves the building of their Creator in the second place. Hence a second month was permitted in the Law for celebrating Passover by those who, being “unclean because of a dead person, or being far away on a journey” (Num. IX), could not come to celebrate Passover in the first month.

Here we are most plainly represented: unclean because of the death of our soul and still far away from the people of God, we could not celebrate the first Passover, which took place in the flesh and blood of the lamb. But today we celebrate the second Passover, which has taken place in the body and blood of our Redeemer, by whom we were sought and cleansed.

Where the temple was built is more clearly shown in the book of Chronicles, where it is written: “Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father, in the place which David had prepared on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite” (II Chron. III).

The Lord’s house is therefore built in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—because the Church, spread throughout the whole world, stands in one and the same faith and fellowship of catholic truth. For God is not in the division of minds, but “his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV).

It is built on a mountain, namely, on the Lord and Savior himself, of whom Isaiah says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Ps. II). And he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V).

For he is the mountain of mountains, who arose from the earth according to the origin of the flesh he assumed, but by the singular height of his dignity surpasses the power and holiness of all earthly beings.

On this mountain the city or house of the Lord has been built, because, unless our hope and faith fix their root in him, they are nothing. He is rightly called Mount Moria—that is, “of vision”—because he deigns to see and help his elect, whom he preserves for the eternal vision of his glory, while they labor meanwhile in this present life.

“Which had been shown to David his father.”

The Lord had been shown to David, as also to the other prophets, as the one who was to come in the flesh. It is fitting that he was spoken of as being on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite, because the Church is also customarily designated by the term “threshing-floor,” as John says of the Lord: “His winnowing-fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing-floor” (Matt. III).

Ornan, whose name is interpreted as “illuminated,” was by nationality a Jebusite. By nationality he signifies the Gentiles; by his name he shows that the same people would be enlightened by the Lord and changed into sons of the Church. To them the Apostle rightly says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

Jebus is the same city as Jerusalem. Jebus is interpreted as “trampled,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” As long as Ornan the Gentile ruled there, it was called Jebus; but when David bought there the place for the holocaust, and Solomon built the temple for the Lord there, it was no longer called Jebus but Jerusalem.

For as long as the Gentiles remained ignorant of divine worship, they were trampled upon and mocked by unclean spirits, following mute idols wherever they were led. But when the grace of their Creator looked upon them, they immediately found within themselves both a place and a name of peace.

“The house which King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits in length, twenty cubits in width, and thirty cubits in height, and so forth.”

The length of the house signifies the long-suffering of the holy Church, by which, in the exile of this pilgrimage, she patiently endures every adversity until she reaches the homeland for which she waits.

The width signifies charity, by which, with the bosom of the mind enlarged, she rejoices to love not only friends in God but also enemies for God’s sake, until the time comes when, whether her enemies have been converted to her peace or have been utterly destroyed, she may rejoice with her friends alone in God.

The height proclaims the hope of future recompense. In view of it, she willingly despises all things below, whether those that soothe or those that oppose, until, having passed beyond both, she may deserve only to “see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI).

Here it should be noted that the thirty cubits of height did not extend to the roof of the temple but to the lower upper chamber. For it is plainly written in the book of Chronicles that the height was one hundred and twenty cubits (II Chron. III); we shall speak of this afterward.

“There was a portico before the temple, twenty cubits in length, corresponding to the breadth of the temple; and it had a breadth of ten cubits before the front of the temple.”

The temple faced east, as did the tabernacle, and the entrance of the portico was on the east, opposite the entrance of the temple. The Jewish historian Josephus teaches this most explicitly, so that, when the equinoctial sun rose, it could pour its rays in straight lines through the entrances of the portico, the temple, and the sanctuary upon the ark of the covenant.

Because the temple signifies the holy Church, what could be clearer than that the portico which stood before the temple and was accustomed to receive the light of the sun more closely should symbolically proclaim that part of the Church which preceded the times of the Lord’s incarnation?

In it are the patriarchs and prophets, who first received for this world the rising “sun of righteousness” (Mal. IV) and bore witness to the Lord born in the flesh—by living, by preaching, and even by dying.

The door of the temple, therefore, is the Lord, because no one comes to the Father except through him (John XIV), and as he says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

The door of the portico is prophetic speech, which led those entering, as by a straight path, to the door of the temple, because it openly proclaimed the grace of the temple of the Lord and Savior, by which he was to redeem the world.

The whole structure of the portico therefore signifies the faithful of that time; the door in the portico represents the teachers, who opened to the others the light of life and the gate of entry to the Lord. There is rightly one door, because all the saints agree in faith and love of the truth.

This portico was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the temple, because the ancient righteous, through the long-suffering of devoted minds, desired to come to the Church’s expansion in the charity of God, which is in Christ our Lord.

“He made in the temple windows with sloping sides.”

The windows of the temple are the holy teachers and all the spiritual people in the Church. To those who, in ecstasy of mind, behold God, it is granted to see more particularly than others the secrets of heavenly mysteries.

When they publicly disclose to the faithful what they see in secret, they are like windows that, having received the sun’s light, fill all the inner chambers of the temple.

Hence the same windows are rightly said to be sloping—that is, wider inside—because whoever has received even for a moment the radiance of heavenly contemplation must immediately enlarge the bosom of the heart by more rigorous discipline and prepare himself through diligent practice to undertake greater things.

“And he built floors around the wall of the temple, around the walls of the house, surrounding the temple and the sanctuary, and he made side-chambers all around. The upper floor was five cubits wide; the middle floor was six cubits wide; and the third floor had seven cubits of width.”

In the Gospel, where the Lord is tempted by the devil, these floors are called the pinnacles of the temple (Matt. IV). We also read that James, the brother of the Lord and an apostle, was raised onto the pinnacle of the temple, from which he might preach to the people.

Whether it was customary for teachers to sit in these floors and address the crowd standing below, we nowhere find written. The sacramental meaning, however, is clear: these three floors signify three grades of the faithful—married people, the continent, and virgins. They are distinguished by the height of their profession, yet all belong, through the fellowship of the same faith and truth, to the house of the Lord and cling to it with steadfast mind.

It is beautifully said that the upper floor had a width of five cubits, the middle six, and the third seven. The upper floor was therefore narrower than the others, the middle wider than the upper, but it was made narrower than the lowest, because the higher profession of virtue ought to follow a narrower way of life.

Each floor had side-rails around it, that is, balustrades, so that anyone standing or sitting on those floors could not easily fall to the lower levels. We read that this happened to King Ahaziah in Samaria (IV Kings I).

These side-rails aptly signify the daily protections of divine protection toward us. Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The Lord will send an angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Ps. XXXIII).

King Ahaziah of Samaria, who had separated himself from the house of David, climbed into the upper chamber, but he fell through the lattice. Thus heretics and schismatics may seem to climb some height of good action, but because they do not possess the framework of ecclesiastical unity, they continually fall back to the lowest depths of vice, as though the protections of their side-rails were open and unsubstantial. Deprived of divine help, they perish through the arrogance of their own obstinacy.

By what method the aforesaid floors were attached to the walls of the temple is explained when it is added:

“But he placed beams around the house on the outside, so that they would not be attached to the walls of the temple, and so forth.”

The beams that strengthened and adorned the house within were of such length that their ends projected outside. In the lowest course they were seven cubits, in the middle six, and in the uppermost five; and the floors were constructed upon these projecting ends. They were not fixed into the walls of the temple but were placed beside the walls, upon beams that extended from them.

What, then, are typologically signified by the beams of the house that carried the floors, if not the holy preachers? While they themselves occupy an exalted and honorable place in the Church of God, through their preaching they lift up the weaker and more fragile from the desire for lowly things and suspend them toward the desire and hope of heavenly things. Through their intercessions also they help them to persevere in what they have begun.

We read in Chronicles (II Chron. III) that the beams of the temple, like its other interior parts, were covered with gold. This was undoubtedly done so that those portions of the beams which were inside the temple would be covered with sheets of gold, while those visible outside would not be gilded but would display to all the appearance and form of cedar, while still carrying the floors placed upon them.

What projected from the beams on the outside signifies the life of the saints insofar as it could become known to us on earth. What shone within the temple, gilded, symbolically proclaims the glory in which they rejoice in the heavenly homeland in the sight of their Creator.

“When the house was being built, it was built of hewn and finished stones. No hammer, axe, or any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.”

These words properly concern that part of the Church which, after the labors and struggles of this age, has deserved to be admitted to eternal rewards. For only the perfect and unstained enter there, chastened from every blemish of iniquity.

“For nothing defiled will enter that city, nor anyone who commits abomination and falsehood, as John wrote in the Apocalypse” (Rev. XXI).

There no hammer, axe, or any iron tool is heard, because here we are beaten by adversities and exercised by the discipline of truth, so that there we may be arranged in places appropriate to our merits. When chastisement has ceased, we shall be joined to one another only by the bond of love and, filled with one Spirit, shall be pervaded by it.

“The door of the middle side-chamber was on the side of the right-hand part of the house, and by a spiral staircase they went up to the middle upper chamber, and from the middle one to the third, and so forth.”

Some, misunderstanding this passage, think that the temple door was on the south, not noticing that, if Scripture had wished to signify this, it would not have said, “The door of the middle side-chamber was on the side of the right-hand part of the house,” but would rather have said simply, “The house had a door toward the south.”

Now, however, it signifies something quite different. It calls the southern side of the temple the right-hand part of the house; in its eastern portion there was a door made at the very corner near the ground. Those who entered it immediately ascended step by step to higher places, having a route of ascent through the inner parts of the wall, until by this path they reached the middle upper chamber and from the middle chamber the third.

Nor should it be doubted—although Scripture does not say so—that those ascending in this way had frequent windows on the south, by whose light they could certainly make their entire journey without danger or stumbling.

This passage properly refers to the Lord’s body, which he took from the Virgin. The door of the middle side-chamber was on the side of the right-hand part of the house because, when the Lord had died on the cross, “one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance” (John XIX).

And it is fitting that it says, “on the side of the right-hand part of the house,” because the holy Church believes that his right side was opened by the soldier.

The Evangelist also used an apt word when he did not say, “He struck his side,” or “He wounded it,” but “He opened it,” as though it were “the door of the middle side-chamber,” through which a path to heavenly things was opened for us.

Finally, he added: “And immediately blood and water came out” (ibid.). Water, by which we are washed in baptism, and blood, by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice.

Through this door we ascend to the middle upper chamber and from the middle to the third, because through faith and the mysteries of our Redeemer we ascend from the present way of life in the Church to the rest of souls after death. Again, from the rest of souls, when the day of judgment arrives, we shall advance to the immortality of bodies, as to the third upper chamber, entering it through a higher progress, so that thereafter we may live forever in the great blessedness of both body and soul.

This journey took place invisibly, so that only those who had entered knew it, although those standing outside could see the door itself. For the actions of the faithful in this age and the celebrations of the sacraments can also be observed by the reprobate. But the mysteries of faith and the inner grace of love are recognized by no one except the person who, guided by the Lord, ascends through them to heavenly things.

“For whoever says that he knows God but does not keep his commandments is a liar” (I John II).

It should certainly be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned above reached to the middle upper chamber. Then another thirty cubits were added up to the third upper chamber, until the covered porticoes that surrounded the temple on the south, north, and west were reached, as we learn from Josephus’s account.

From there another sixty cubits were counted up to the highest roof of the temple, and thus the entire height of the house, according to the book of Chronicles, was completed at one hundred and twenty cubits (II Chron. III).

The portico that stood before the front of the temple toward the east also had the same total height in cubits, according to the testimony of the aforesaid book. That book calls the porticoes around the temple which we mentioned earlier storerooms and chambers.

“David gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico, the temple, the storerooms, the upper chamber, and the chambers within the inner sanctuary, and of the house of atonement” (I Chron. XXVIII).

There he also mentions the outer buildings that stood outside the priests’ court, surrounding the temple, when he immediately adds: “And likewise of all that he had conceived: the courts, the chambers around the treasury of the house of the Lord, and the treasuries of the holy things.”

The fact that the entire height of the temple was one hundred and twenty cubits refers to the same sacramental meaning as the fact that the primitive Church in Jerusalem, after the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men (Acts I, II).

Fifteen, which is composed of seven and eight, is sometimes customarily referred to the meaning of the future life, which is now lived in the sabbatism of the souls of the faithful but will be perfected at the end of the age in the resurrection of immortal bodies.

When that fifteen is multiplied into a triangle—that is, when all its parts are added together—it makes one hundred and thirty. Therefore the great blessedness of the elect in the future life is suitably signified by the number one hundred and twenty, and the third upper chamber of the Lord’s house is suitably completed by it, because after the present labors of the faithful and after the rest of souls received in the future, the full happiness of the entire Church will be completed in the glory of the resurrection.

“He built the house and completed it. He also covered the house with ceilings of cedar, and so forth.”

The ceilings are floors that, arranged and adorned with great beauty, are fastened from below to the beams. Because the house of the Lord was made with threefold height, it likewise had three ceilings.

What could the ceilings more clearly signify than the more exalted righteous in the holy Church? Their work and teaching are set before all as an example, standing out, as it were, higher and farther above. Through their intercessions and exhortations they protect the minds of the weak, so that they do not fail in temptations.

These ceilings are rightly described as cedar. Cedar is a tree of entirely incorruptible nature, pleasant in scent, bright in appearance, driving away and destroying serpents when kindled by its fragrance.

All these qualities suit the perfect, whose patience is unconquerable, whose reputation for virtue is outstanding, whose presence is most pleasing to all good people, and whose authority in refuting and confounding those who resist the truth is utterly steadfast. In this life and in the future they shine with singular excellence above others.

“And he built a floor over the entire house, five cubits in height.”

This signifies the balustrades that were made around the highest roof of the house, lest anyone who reached higher places should suddenly fall to the lowest. Moses commanded that this be done in every house anyone built: “When you build a new house,” he says, “you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you be guilty if someone falls from it and plunges headlong” (Deut. XXII).

These floors, or parapets, are above called side-rails, where, after it had been said, “He built floors around the wall of the temple, around the walls of the house, surrounding the temple and the sanctuary,” it immediately adds: “And he made side-rails all around.”

In these side-rails we understood divine protections to be signified. While we still labor in this age and strive according to our capacity toward higher things, they help us daily so that we do not fail.

It is rightly remembered that this highest floor, on the roof of the Lord’s house, was five cubits high, because in that homeland the presence of the divine glory so fills us that our sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch find nothing sweet except to love the Lord our God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and to love our neighbor as ourselves (Deut. VI).

“And he covered the house with cedar wood.”

Here he means the very highest roof of the house—that is, the floor placed upon the highest beams. For the temple did not have a roof rising to a peak above, any more than the tabernacle did; rather, it was flat, as is customary among all who build houses in Palestine and Egypt.

This same floor with which the house was covered signifies the ceilings: that is, the most distinguished men in the glory of the resurrection, who by singular holiness attain the very summit of virtue.

Of one of them it is said: “Among those born of women there has not arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI). If you wish to know the greatness of this man in comparison, hear what the angel says to his father: “He will go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke I).

“And he built the walls of the house on the inside with cedar panelling, from the floor of the house up to the tops of the walls, and he covered the interior up to the ceiling with wood, etc.” The house was clothed with cedar on the inside. On the outside, however, the stone of which it had been made shone with such brilliance that it seemed to be covered with white marble.

In the mystical sense, the walls of the temple are the peoples of the faithful, from whom the holy universal Church is composed. Their breadth signifies the extension of the walls throughout the world; their height, however, signifies every hope and intention raised toward heavenly things. Or certainly, the height of the wall, which consists of courses of stones placed one upon another, signifies the present state of the Church. Here the elect, all built upon the foundation of Christ, succeed one another in order through the cycles of time; bearing one another, they fulfil the law of Christ, which is love (Galatians VI).

For those who are now instructed by teachers who came before them themselves in turn instruct others. Thus, like courses of stones placed one upon another in the house of God, each generation of holy men is supported by the firm stability of those before it, so that it too may be strong enough to support others, even to the last righteous people who will be born at the end of the world. These, placed as though at the highest summit of the house of God, are indeed taught and supported by others, but they themselves have no one whom they may teach or whose weakness they must endure.

The walls are clothed inside with cedar panelling when the hearts of the faithful overflow with love of the virtues. For just as the nature of cedar typically proclaims perfect men—as the Lord said above—so, in appropriate passages, it not inappropriately signifies the loftiness of the virtues by which one reaches that same perfection. Everything is covered with wood from the floor of the house to the tops of the walls, up to the ceiling, when the elect, from the first rudiments of faith to the perfection of good action and to the entrance into the heavenly homeland, do not cease to labour at good works; and when, from the first righteous people to the last at the consummation of the age, all devote themselves to the virtues, by whose merit they may rightly declare: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” in every place (II Corinthians II).

“And he covered the floor with fir boards.” How this was done is explained more fully in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written: “He also laid the floor with the most precious marble, with great splendour” (II Chronicles III). Hence it is clear that he did not place the fir boards with which he had covered the floor directly upon the ground. Rather, he first covered it with marble, then placed the boards upon the marble, and added a third covering of gold over these two, as is read below.

Just as the height of the wall, rising upward and reaching to the ceiling, signifies the progress of the virtues by which the elect reach the heavenly kingdom—or certainly the choirs of the elect themselves, succeeding one another through the changing ages—so the levelness of the floor fittingly demonstrates their harmonious humility, by which, while they are still placed in temporal life, they live together in mutual love.

That floor was laid with the most precious marble and was immediately covered with fir boards, because the life of the saints must first be fortified in the heart by the firmness of faith and then adorned in action by the breadth of spiritual virtues. Otherwise, what benefit would there have been in the splendour of the most precious marble being covered by wooden boards, if it did not secretly signify some mystical meaning and teach that the abundance of good works must be supported by the strength of undefiled faith?

The fir, because of its height and its enduring strength, appropriately represents the mind of the elect, which rejects every low desire, is always intent upon contemplation of heavenly things, and is distinguished above all by the virtue of patience. The sheets of gold placed over the marble and the fir boards signify the breadth of “love,” and its beauty is “from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Timothy I). Just as gold is more precious than other metals, so love shines in the temple of God with a light superior to the other virtues.

“He also built, at the rear of the temple, a structure twenty cubits long, with cedar panelling from the floor to the upper parts; and he made the inner house, the oracle, in the Holy of Holies, etc.” By the rear part of the temple he means the west. The temple had its entrance toward the rising of the sun, while toward the setting was the inner house, that is, the Holy of Holies.

When the panelling separating the inner house from the outer one is said to have been built from the floor to the upper parts, this does not mean up to the ceiling, which was suspended thirty cubits above the floor, as stated above. It means only up to a height of twenty cubits, as is made clear below. Above this panelling there remained an open and empty space up to the ceiling, ten cubits high and twenty cubits long, corresponding to the breadth of the house. Through this opening the smoke of the incense from the altar of incense was accustomed to rise into the Holy of Holies and penetrate to cover the ark of the Lord.

In this arrangement of the house of the Lord, the figure of the mystery is clearer than daylight, with the Apostle explaining it: the former house, into which the priests continually entered to complete the services of the sacrifices, is the present Church, where, devoting ourselves daily to pious works, we offer sacrifices of praise to the Lord.

The inner house, which was made at the rear of the temple, is the life promised to us in heaven. It is “inner” in relation to the conduct of our exile, because there, in the presence of the supreme King, an everlasting solemnity of the blessed—both angels and human beings—is celebrated. Hence it is rightly said to the faithful servant: “Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew XXV). Yet it is “rear” in time, because after the labours of this age we are brought into it.

The panelling that divides the two houses from one another is the enclosure of heaven, whose opening we daily long for; and, as far as the Lord grants us, we continually knock with devout persistence until it is opened and we are permitted to enter. Although we are not yet permitted to enter before the dissolution of our bodies, we nevertheless have an open door of divine mercy, through which we may send ahead the incense of our prayers, almsgiving, fasting, and other good works.

For this reason the cedar wall of the inner house had an opening above along its entire length, where the smoke of the incense could enter, because “the eyes of the Lord are upon his house night and day, and his ears attend to the prayers of his servants” (Psalm XXXIII); and this is true throughout the whole breadth of the Church spread across the world.

The altar of incense, which stood in the outer house but near the entrance of the inner house, was a type of the perfect, who, although still held in the flesh in this world, are suspended toward heavenly things by their every desire. Like burning incense, they send upward smoke into the Holy of Holies, because, aflame with heavenly love, they strike the ears of their Creator with the frequent voices of their prayers.

The smoke of the incense found a widely open entrance above, because the purer people are on earth and the nearer they dwell, as it were, to the heavenly homeland, the more quickly they receive from the Lord everything they ask.

The inner house was rightly made twenty cubits long, because of the mystery of the twofold love, of which we also spoke above. In the present life this love illuminates the minds of the elect in large part; but in that homeland, when the works of the other virtues have ceased, it alone reigns forever (I Corinthians XIII).

“Now the temple itself before the entrance of the oracle was forty cubits.” We said that the temple itself before the entrance of the oracle bore the type of the present Church. Hence it was rightly forty cubits long. This number is often used to signify the present labour of the faithful, just as fifty signifies future rest and peace.

The commandments are contained in the number ten, and by their observance one reaches life. The same number ten also signifies the eternal life that we desire and for which we labour. The world in which we struggle to attain that same life is four-square. Hence the Psalmist, foreseeing that the Church would be gathered from the nations, said: “He will gather them from the regions, from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm CVI).

“And the whole house was clothed inside with cedar, having its mouldings and skilfully fashioned joints, and projecting carvings, etc.” We have said that cedar signifies the unsurpassable beauty of the virtues, with which all the wood of the house of the Lord is clothed inside when the hearts of the righteous shine only with the love of good works.

The house has its mouldings and skilfully fashioned joints in the cedar boards when the same elect are joined to one another by the most beautiful bond of love, so that, although the multitude of the faithful is innumerable, they may rightly be said to have one heart and one soul, through the fellowship of a common faith and love (Acts IV). The mouldings that were applied to the joints of the boards so that one panelling might be formed from them all are the works of love by which holy brotherhood is joined together and throughout the whole world is built into one house of Christ.

That house also has projecting carvings when the saints do not conceal the works of the virtues, but display outwardly, in manifest expression before all, what they are and what they do, offering themselves as an example of how to live.

“Everything was clothed with cedar boards, and no stone at all could be seen in the wall. And the stones of the wall, or of the floor, and the boards and the gold, etc.” All these signify the life of the saints in the Church, with this distinction when they are set together: the saints are living stones, cemented together by the strength of faith into one and the same rule.

The cedar or fir boards are the saints, joined to one another in one and the same faith through the breadth of various virtues according to the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The sheets of gold are the saints who possess love surpassing knowledge and rejoice with one another in its most pleasing radiance.

The blessed Apostle gathered these three into one statement when he said: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” The stone represented unconquerable faith, the cedar fragrant action, and the gold love transcending all things.

The stone wall is clothed with cedar boards when the profession of faith is adorned with good works, lest it be judged idle or dead. Yet because the Law was written on stone, while the teaching of the Gospel was confirmed through the wood of the Lord’s Passion—hence that people was circumcised in the foreskin with stone, whereas we are consecrated on the forehead by the sign of the cross—the stone walls of the temple, or the floor laid with the most precious marble, may appropriately represent those who lived faithfully and perfectly under the Law.

The cedar or fir boards, however, may signify the righteous of the New Testament, who, desiring to come after the Lord, deny themselves and, taking up their cross, follow him daily (Matthew XVI). And since the righteous of both periods await the common glory of heavenly recompense, a third kind, sheets of gold, is added to the stones and precious woods.

Nor should it appear contradictory that we said above that the portico before the temple represented the faithful of ancient times, while the temple itself represented those who came into the world after the time of the Lord’s Incarnation, and that the inner house represented the joys of the heavenly kingdom granted to the righteous of both periods. For now we say that the stone walls signify the ancient people of God, the cedar panelling the new people, and the golden sheets the rewards of both in heaven, since the same walls of the temple were found in the portico, in the temple itself, and in the Holy of Holies in the same manner.

“Joined together from stones and wood and gold.” The repetition of the same figures in different things is manifold. But this too must be said: both under the Law and before the written Law there were many who served the Lord according to the Law—who did not kill, commit fornication, steal, or bear false witness against their neighbour; who honoured father and mother and loved their neighbours as themselves. These belonged to the stone walls and porticoes.

There were others of greater perfection who, abandoning the affairs of the world and taking up their cross, followed the Lord. As the Apostle writes, they “experienced mockeries and blows, and moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, they were cut in two, they were tempted, they died by the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, oppressed—of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebrews XI).

These, who lived an evangelical life before the manifest times of the Gospel, what else were they but cedar panelling shining in the portico before the entrance of the temple? And since the same heavenly kingdom received both groups together, although in distinct dwellings, the portico of the temple, after the stone and cedar, was covered inside with gold.

In the present time there are very many who, content with the legal precepts we mentioned above, believe that these are sufficient for them, provided only that they may deserve to attain life. There are others who strive toward perfection: they sell all that they possess and follow the Lord, mindful of the promise in which he foretold that such people would receive at the resurrection not only life but also a special honour:

“Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX).

The former belong figuratively to the walls of the temple made of white stone; the latter to the cedar boards. Both await from the Lord the rewards of perpetual light, like sheets of gold with which they may be adorned.

Among them there are precious stones; there are boards of aromatic wood, both covered with gold, because those who walked blamelessly in the law of the Lord and those who perfectly received the grace of the Gospel alike enjoy eternal life.

“But he had made the oracle in the middle of the house, in the inner part, in order to place there the ark of the covenant of the Lord.” This was explained earlier by anticipation. The inner house signifies the hidden homeland of heaven; the ark of the covenant signifies the Lord and Saviour, in whom alone we have a covenant of peace with the Father. After his resurrection, ascending into heaven, he placed at the right hand of the Father the flesh that he had taken from the Virgin.

“Now the oracle was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, etc.” When he says that it was twenty cubits high, he signifies the cedar wall that separated the oracle—that is, the Holy of Holies—from the outer building, as we also said above.

The oracle, where the ark was, measured twenty cubits in length, breadth, and height—that is, it was square—because in that heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints behold Christ the King in his beauty, only the grace of divine and fraternal love shines everywhere.

This is also established by the words that follow:

“And he covered it and clothed it with the purest gold.” This plainly means that the walls of the heavenly city were filled with the grace of love.

“But he also clothed the altar with cedar.” This refers to the altar of incense, which stood before the oracle, concerning which it is added shortly afterward: “But he covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.” Hence it may be understood that the same altar was made of stone, clothed with cedar, and then covered with gold.

Figuratively, it signifies the life of the perfect righteous, who are placed, as it were, near the oracle, because, having abandoned lowly pleasures, they devote all their care to entering the heavenly kingdom. Hence it was rightly not the flesh of victims but only incense that was burned on this altar: such people no longer need to slaughter within themselves the sins of the flesh and the enticements of thought, but offer before their Creator only the fragrances of spiritual prayers and heavenly desires through the fire of inward love.

“He also covered the house before the oracle with the purest gold and fastened sheets with golden nails.” We have said that the house before the oracle represents the present Church, where we burn with love for our Redeemer, yet are still unable to see him face to face. Hence this house was appropriately covered with the purest gold, but was separated from the oracle by an intervening wall.

The oracle is so called when either a divine address to human beings or an angelic utterance is granted together with the revelation of hidden things. Hence the oracle was rightly made in the inner sanctuary, that is, in the inner house, because in the heavenly homeland both the vision and speech of the angels toward us, and the very presence of God, will be revealed.

The house before the oracle is therefore covered with gold because the perfect righteous in this life—where they cannot yet hear openly from the Father, that is, cannot yet see the Father openly—adorn faith and the work of righteousness with divine love, through which they may deserve to reach the full knowledge of God.

The sheets of gold with which the house is covered are the manifold works of piety that pure love displays in service either to its Creator or to the needs of the brethren. The golden nails with which the sheets were fastened are the commandments of love, or the promises of eternal glory, by which, through the grace of Christ, we are held firm so that we do not fail in the exercise and pursuit of the virtues.

Hence it is rightly written of these same nails in the Book of Chronicles: “He also made golden nails, so that each nail weighed fifty shekels” (II Chronicles III). In Scripture the number fifty commonly represents the remission of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal rest.

“And each nail weighed fifty shekels, by which the sheets of gold were fastened to the walls of the house of the Lord.” For the heavenly words by which we advance and are preserved in the love of good works promise us forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal Sabbath-rest in the future (Isaiah LX). These are the nails of love.

There are also other nails, those of fear, by which beginners and those who have not yet reached perfection mortify the enticements of vices and carnal pleasures. These are the sayings of truth by whose instruction we are taught to crucify our flesh with its vices and desires. The Prophet desired to possess them when he said: “Nail my flesh with the nails of your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Psalm CXVIII).

Then, reaching more perfect things, he says of the nails of love: “But it is good for me to adhere to God” (Psalm LXXII).

“And there was nothing in the temple that was not covered with gold, but he covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.” The portico before the temple was gilded because the fathers of the Old Testament pleased God through love. The temple itself was gilded because that same “love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans V).

The inner house was gilded because in the heavenly homeland love alone reigns; there it reigns all the more truly and securely because God himself, who is love, is seen (I Corinthians XIII). There it is all the more certainly established because the mediator of God and human beings himself, who alone is acquainted with the Father’s secrets, is always seen like the ark of the covenant (I John IV).

The fact that the upper chambers too were covered with gold refers to the same meaning. For just as the inner house of the Holy of Holies, where the ark was, signifies the inner life of the saints in the presence of their Creator and Redeemer, according to the Psalmist’s words, “You will hide them in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Psalm XXX), so the upper chambers signify that same life as existing on high, that is, in heaven and not in this world, as the Apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are on earth” (Colossians III).

“And he made in the oracle two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high, etc.” Cherubim—as the prophet Ezekiel plainly declares (Ezekiel X)—is the name of an angelic rank; in the singular it is cherub, in the plural cherubim.

Hence, appropriately, the cherubim made in the oracle may be understood as the angelic ministries that always stand before their Creator in heaven. They are rightly said to have been made of olive wood, because the angelic powers have been anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, lest they ever wither in the love of God.

They are ten cubits high because they enjoy the tenfold measure of eternal life, possessing within themselves the inviolate image of their Creator and perpetually preserving the holiness, righteousness, and truth that they received at their first creation. The denarius consists of ten obols and is accustomed to contain within itself the name and image of the King. Therefore it most fittingly corresponds to the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the holy angels always retain the image of their Creator, according to which they were made, and the elect receive again his image, which they had lost through sin.

“Five cubits was the wing of one cherub, and five cubits the wing of the other cherub—that is, ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other wing.” When wings are used in the figure of holy human beings, they signify their virtues, by which they continually fly toward heavenly things and delight to have their way of life there.

When wings are used to signify angels, what could they more aptly represent than the grace of their perpetual and unwavering blessedness? They always remain in the heavens in the service of their Creator. Or they signify that they are endowed with the lightness of spiritual nature, so that wherever they wish, they arrive immediately, as though flying.
