They are represented with wings here, and they have also been shown with wings to the prophets.

It is rightly said that one wing of the cherub was five cubits and the other wing five cubits, because the angelic powers guard the law of God, written in five books, with tireless devotion: loving the Lord their God with all their strength and loving their neighbours as themselves. “For love is the fullness of the law.”

Their neighbours are the angelic spirits themselves, one to another, and the elect human beings, their fellow citizens. Hence both wings of the cherub are said to have been of the same measure, because with the same devotion by which they love one another in God, they also desire our fellowship as we ascend to them. Thus the wings together complete ten cubits, when, in the twofold expression of love, the angels rejoice in the presence of their Creator.

“The second cherub was also ten cubits, of equal measure; and there was one work in the two cherubim, etc.” Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of the same love of which we are speaking, because love cannot exist with fewer than two. Hence the Saviour also took care to send his disciples to preach in pairs, tacitly teaching that those who preach the word of faith must hold the virtue of love above all else.

The two cherubim were of one measure and one workmanship because in the heavenly homeland there is no disparity of wills or thoughts, where all are illumined by one and the same vision and glory of God who is present.

“And he placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner temple. The cherubim stretched out their wings, and one wing touched one wall, while the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall. Their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple.” What was said above makes clear why the cherubim were placed in the middle of the inner temple, since their dwelling is always in heaven.

The cherubim stretched out their wings as though to fly, because the angelic spirits always have their minds prepared to obey the divine will. The fact that one wing touched one wall and the wing of the second cherub touched the other pertains to the administration of love that the angels provide for us. The fact that their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple expresses the grace of love with which they embrace one another.

It is rightly added:

“And he covered the cherubim with gold.” The Creator exalted their nature with immortal splendour and filled their minds with the light of true love and humility.

It should certainly be noted that when Moses made the tabernacle, he also made two golden cherubim, which he placed upon the mercy-seat over the ark. Solomon, however, added two others, much larger, to place in the temple; beneath their wings he placed the ark in the middle, together with the mercy-seat and the earlier cherubim (Exodus XXXVII).

Thus there were two cherubim in the tabernacle but four in the temple; both groups, however, belong to one and the same meaning. The work was repeated and made more august through Solomon, so that it might be shown figuratively that, after the Lord’s Incarnation, the Church having multiplied, the sublimity of the citizens of heaven would be revealed more widely to the nations.

They praise the Creator for the gift of blessedness bestowed upon them in such a way that they also rejoice in our deliverance and introduction into that same blessedness. They stretch their wings toward one another over the ark when they refer every good they have received to the praise of the Lord and Saviour. They stretch their other wings toward the walls of the oracle when they rejoice to see holy human beings with them and touch, as it were, with the tips of their wings those whom they celebrate as having been companions and imitators of their purity in this life.

They touch the two opposite walls with their wings because they have with them as possessors of the heavenly hall the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. This does not mean that there is a local distinction between the two peoples in that homeland, but that the inward festivity of blessedness becomes greater through the fellowship of a brotherhood united in God.

The cherubim therefore stretch their wings toward both walls of the oracle, because, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland, they stir the righteous of both peoples by the vision of their glory to praise their Creator. The heavenly hosts rejoice not only in the happiness of the righteous human beings whom they have with them inside; they also diligently care for us, who are still placed outside and cry to the Lord from the depths.

Hence it is rightly written of these same cherubim in the Book of Chronicles: “They stood with their feet upright, and their faces were turned toward the outer house” (I Chronicles III). For they desire that we should be raised from the misery of this pilgrimage and come to their fellowship.

Thus they stand with their feet upright, and thus they stretch their wings toward the walls of the oracle covered with gold, while their faces are turned toward the outer house: the angels preserve their innocence perpetually, and rejoice in the blessedness of holy souls in heaven, yet they do not cease to bring help to the elect whom they see still wandering on earth, until they introduce them also into the heavenly homeland. “For they are all ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews I).

The two cherubim may also signify the two Testaments. These cherubim were made in the oracle because, in the counsel of divine providence— inaccessible and incomprehensible to us—it was determined before the ages when, how, and through which authors sacred Scripture would be composed.

They were made of olive wood because they give us the light of knowledge, with the flame of the love of God assisting, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. They are ten cubits high because they proclaim that God must be served through observance of the Decalogue, and because they show that those who faithfully serve God will be rewarded with the tenfold measure of the everlasting kingdom.

They have two wings because they declare that the authors of their Testament always strove and reached toward heavenly things with tireless purpose, through hardships no less than through prosperity, and they show that their hearers must do the same. One wing of the cherub was five cubits and the other five cubits because, amid every changing variety of fleeting things, the saints extend all the senses of their body in the service of their Creator.

“And there was one work in the two cherubim,” because the writers of both Testaments serve God with one and the same purity of conduct and devotion of love; with one harmonious voice and faith they proclaim God.

The inner wings of the cherubim therefore touched one another over the ark because the Testaments agree in their equal testimony concerning the Lord. Likewise, with their outer wings one touched one wall and the other the other, because the Old Testament was written especially for the ancient people of God, while the New was written for us, who came to faith after the Lord’s Incarnation. We are rightly compared with the second wall, that is, the northern one, since after the cold and darkness of idolatry we were granted knowledge of the light of truth.

The cherubim have their faces turned toward the outer house because the divine books were composed for our sake—those of us who still stand outside and have been saved not in reality but “in hope” (Romans VIII). Their writers, already reigning with the Lord and praising him in heaven, care for our salvation and intercede with his mercy on behalf of our errors.

“And he carved all the walls of the temple all around with varied carvings and with the turning tool, etc.” All the walls of the temple all around are all the peoples of the holy Church. Established upon the foundation of Christ, they have filled the whole circuit of the world, and the building of faith, once begun, does not cease daily to increase through the new offspring of its members, like the addition of precious stones.

These walls are carved with varied carvings when “to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues” (I Corinthians XII).

And, to come to the other virtues—which may all be possessed—“love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians V), and the other fruits of the Spirit: what are these but the carvings of the walls of the temple, since they are the adornment of the minds of God’s people?

The same walls are carved with the turning tool when the faithful are strong in their readiness to do everything the Lord commands and to endure everything he permits, saying sincerely in every circumstance that arises: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Psalm XXXIII), and: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody to the Lord” (Psalm LVI).

They are carved with the turning tool when they devote themselves so thoroughly to the virtues that no opposition from surrounding circumstances and no blandishments can turn them from the path of those virtues. Because turning with the lathe surpasses the other crafts in speed and preserves for itself the rule by which the work may be completed without error, it aptly signifies the devout life of the saints, which is always prepared to obey the divine will and, trained by long practice in the virtues, has learned to fulfil it without straying into error.

“And he made in them cherubim and palms and varied pictures, as though projecting from the wall and emerging from it.” Solomon makes cherubim on the walls of the temple when the Lord grants his elect to direct their lives according to the rule of the holy Scriptures, in which there is a multitude of knowledge.

He makes cherubim when he teaches them, according to their capacity, to imitate in this world the chastity of angelic conduct—a way of life practised especially through vigils and divine praises, and through sincere love of the Creator and of one’s neighbour.

He makes palms when he fixes the memory of eternal recompense in their minds, so that they may be less able to fall from the citadel of righteousness because they always keep the reward of righteousness before the eyes of their hearts.

He makes varied pictures, as though projecting and emerging from the wall, when he grants the faithful manifold works of the virtues—for example, compassion, kindness, humility, patience, and gentleness.

“He covered the floor of the house with gold, inside and outside, etc.” “Inside and outside” refers to the oracle and to the temple itself. Solomon therefore covered the floor of the house with gold inside and outside because our peaceful King completely and fully separated the angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven from the baseness of the other mortals by the gift of love.

[Col. 0158B] “At the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olive wood, and five-sided doorposts at the corners, and two doors of olive wood.” What he had first said—“he made doors of olive wood”—he seems to have wished to explain more clearly when he added, “and two doors of olive wood.” For there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary, but that same entrance was closed by two doors and opened again when they were unfastened. Likewise, the temple and the portico before the temple had no more than one entrance, certainly for a reason grounded in mystery, because “there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God” (Ephesians 4). One entrance into the present Church through baptism, and one entrance into the heavenly kingdom through works of faith, are to be hoped for.

That there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary is testified by what is written below concerning the ark: “And when the poles projected, and their ends were visible outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary, they did not appear farther out” [1 Kings 8]. Here, if I am not mistaken, it is plainly shown that there was one entrance to the inner sanctuary, and that it was directly opposite the ark, which stood in the middle of that same inner sanctuary. Its doors can be understood symbolically in many ways. For they most appropriately signify the angelic spirits, through whose ministry we are brought into the dwelling of our heavenly homeland; and they likewise represent the apostles and apostolic men, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given (Luke 16). Having received from the Lord the authority to bind and loose, they admit the worthy within the gate of the kingdom, while by excommunication [Col. 0158D] or anathema they expel the obstinate, impure, and proud from the entrance to eternal life.

The works of righteousness also, by whose merit one reaches the heavenly kingdom, can rightly be represented typologically by the doors through which one entered the Holy of Holies, in accordance with what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “The keeping of the laws is the consummation of incorruption; and incorruption makes one near to God. Therefore the desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom” (Wisdom 6).

All these interpretations aptly correspond to the fact that the same doors were made of olive wood, since angels and perfected human beings alike display themselves gloriously in God’s house through the fruit of mercy and works of light. Indeed, all the elect open for themselves an entrance to their heavenly homeland through the weapons of light and piety. There are two doors, either because holy angels and human beings love God and their neighbors, and no one can enter the gate of life except through this twofold love; or because the same gate of life is opened to the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

“The doorposts have five sides,” because the court of heaven receives not only the souls of the elect but also opens its gates at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory.

“And he carved upon them representations of cherubim, and figures of palm trees, and very prominent reliefs, and overlaid them with gold, and so forth.” *Anaglypha* in Greek are what are called in Latin *caelaturae*, “engraved work.” For the works of virtue exercised throughout the whole world by the Church in her holy and perfected members—and especially by those entrusted with the care of the faithful and given the keys of the kingdom of heaven—must be pursued with every diligence, so that, insofar as they surpass others in rank, they may equally excel them in the merit of good action.

They have carved representations of cherubim upon them when, as far as is possible for mortals, they imitate the angelic life on earth both in mind and in action. They have figures of palm trees when they constantly contemplate, with fixed attention, the gifts of heavenly reward. For the palm is the adornment of the victor’s hand. They have very prominent reliefs when they display to all who look upon them the most certain evidence of good works—works that no one can in any way interpret in a sinister sense. And all these things are covered with sheets of gold [Col. 0159C] when—as has often been said and must always be said—the radiance of love surpasses the other flowers of virtue in the great members of the Church.

The Books of Chronicles report that a veil was also added to these doors: “He also made a veil,” it says, “of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and embroidered cherubim upon it” (1 Chronicles 3). This was done for the sake of beauty, so that even among the gilded walls the pure silk might shine. Yet it was hung before the ark and the entrance to the inner sanctuary with a fitting symbolic meaning belonging to the same mystery as the doors, so that, just as the doors were opened at the appropriate times, the veil might also be drawn aside whenever those arrived who were to enter the Holy of Holies.

The diligent unveiling of this veil, according to the Law, signifies the opening of the heavenly kingdom, which was granted to us through the incarnation of our Lord and Savior. Hence also, “when he had been baptized, the heavens were opened” (Matthew 3), to show that through baptism—which he himself consecrated for us—we were to enter the gate of our heavenly homeland. And when he died upon the cross, the same “veil was torn in two from top to bottom” (Matthew 27), so that it might be clearly taught that the legal figures had then reached their end, and that the truth of the Gospel, the heavenly mysteries, and the entrance itself into heaven were no longer to be foretold and signified figuratively, but were now about to be opened immediately to all who, from the beginning of the world until that time, had passed from the world in faith in the truth.

Appropriately, the same veil, beneath which one entered the inner sanctuary, is remembered as having been made of violet [Col. 0160A], purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with cherubim also woven into it. Violet, which imitates the color of heaven, is suitably compared with desires for heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and itself presents a bloodlike appearance, not improperly signifies the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, into which we must be initiated by carrying our cross. Scarlet, which burns with a red color, fittingly expresses the virtue of love. Concerning this, the disciples who had walked with the Lord said in wonder: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24.)

Fine linen, which grows from the earth through green vegetation and, through the long labor of craftsmen, loses its natural greenness and is brought to a gleaming white appearance [Col. 0160B], fittingly signifies the chastisement of our flesh. The Apostle commands its innate moisture, so to speak, to be dried up when he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3). He shows elsewhere to what degree of whiteness he wishes this to be brought, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service” (Romans 12).

Cherubim are woven into these materials, which are made from four distinguished colors, when in everything we piously do we are protected, by the Lord’s gift, from the poisoned arrows of demons through angelic protection. Cherubim are woven into the veil when, in the good things we do, we continually make use of a multitude of knowledge, always looking to the divine utterances; and, lest we stray from the path of virtue, we continually direct our footsteps by keeping our eyes upon them.

“And at the entrance of the temple he made four-sided doorposts of olive wood; and two doors of fir wood on either side; and each door was double, and opened by folding back upon itself,” and so forth. Just as the entrance to the inner sanctuary, by which one reached the ark of the Lord and the cherubim, signifies the entrance into the heavenly kingdom, where we hope and desire to be introduced to the vision of our Creator and of the citizens of heaven, so the entrance into the temple typologically represents the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter the present Church [Col. 0160D]. The former signifies our entrance into sight; the latter, our entrance into faith.

Hence the doorposts of this entrance were plainly made four-sided, either on account of the four books of the Gospel, by whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of truth; or on account of the four principal virtues—“prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice”—upon whose firmest foundation the whole structure of good actions rests.

Prudence is that by which we learn what we ought to do and how we ought to live. Fortitude is that by which we carry out what we have learned ought to be done. The Prophet briefly gathers these virtues into a single verse when he says: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation” (Psalm 26). Illumination, namely, so that he may teach us what we ought to do; salvation, so that he may strengthen us to accomplish it.

Temperance is that by which we discern lest we be found to devote more or less attention than is right to prudence or fortitude. And because whoever uses prudence and fortitude temperately will, without any contradiction, be proved just, justice follows as the fourth virtue after prudence, fortitude, and temperance.

The two doors made for this entrance are the love of God and of one’s neighbor. They are rightly said to have been made “on either side,” because they face one another so closely that neither can exist without the other. “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God; and everyone who loves him who begot him also loves him who has been begotten by him” (1 John 5). And again, as he says: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4.)

Accordingly, the outer door is rightly understood as brotherly love, and the inner door as divine love. The former comes first in time, while the latter is higher in divinity; and through the former one enters into the latter, because through love of one’s neighbor one learns how the Creator ought to be loved.

It should also be noted that, in the entrance to the inner sanctuary, two doors are said to have existed, but they are not said to have been double. In the entrance to the temple—that is, to the earlier house—there were likewise two doors, but each was double. For in the present life we necessarily enter and pursue a life in which we preserve love of God and neighbor through faith and action, through patience and kindness. In the future life, however, where we shall see God and our neighbors in the inner light of blessedness, we shall enjoy this same twofold love without any labor at all, indeed amid a great abundance of divine sweetness.

Hence the inner entrance of the house appropriately had two doors, but they were simple. Faith is not necessary there, where everything that we now believe and hope will be seen in manifest light. The labor of works is not necessary there, where we shall be given the eternal reward of the things for which we labor here. Patience is not necessary there, where no one inflicts anything adverse. The generosity of kindness is not needed there, where no one is in need.

We have discussed the figure of the doors according to our limited ability, following in the footsteps of the Fathers. Yet, according to the actual form of the building, provision was made for the sake of beauty that there should be two doors in one and the same entrance to the temple. For the walls of the house, which were one hundred and twenty cubits high, necessarily also had a certain thickness. The doors were attached at the outer edge of this thickness, so that each door was flush with the wall, and whoever stood either inside or outside the temple and looked at the door would see what appeared in every respect to be a single wall.

Likewise, since the cedar wall was twenty cubits in length and height, it too must have had considerable thickness. Therefore two doors were also made at its entrance, so that a door flush with the wall would be visible from either side, both inside and outside. And since the door had the same carvings as the wall, the wall appeared truly to be one continuous expanse, presenting one aspect for the sake of beauty and prefiguring another through the dispensation of mystery.

After the temple doors have been described, the text continues:

“And he carved cherubim, palm trees, and very lofty reliefs, and covered everything with sheets of gold, worked square according to the rule.” For the same mysteries of faith, hope, and love that the most exalted and perfect grasp in an exalted manner, and that all the elect will fully know in the divine vision, are also delivered to beginners being catechized, to be learned and confessed according to each person’s capacity, so that those initiated into the sacred mysteries may eventually attain even to grasping what they have piously believed.

[Col. 0162B] “And King Solomon built the inner court with three rows of hewn stones and one row of cedar wood, and so forth.” He speaks briefly of the inner court and appears to be entirely silent about the outer one. Yet the Books of Chronicles mention both, where it is written: “He also made the court of the priests, and the great basilica, and doors for the basilica, which he covered with bronze” (2 Chronicles 4).

The inner court, which is called the court of the priests because priests and Levites ministered there, was surrounded by the temple on every side. But on the eastern side, where the temple entrance was, it was set much farther from the temple than on the other three sides. For in that area, that is, in front of the temple, the sacred ministries were performed: there stood the bronze altar for offering sacrifices to the Lord, and there were ten basins for washing those sacrifices [Col. 0162C]. There also stood the bronze sea for washing the hands and feet of the priests when they entered to minister.

According to Josephus, this court was three cubits high, so that it might prevent the others from entering the temple and signify that this was permitted only to priests. It had a gate on the eastern side, to which the people brought their sacrifices; the priests received them there and carried them to the altar.

Concerning the outer court, which the Books of Chronicles call the great basilica, Josephus writes as follows:

“Outside this temple he built another court, made in the form of a quadrangle, raising very large and broad porticoes, and establishing lofty and spacious gates in its four sides, one toward each of the four winds, at the four corners. There he placed golden doors.”

A little later he says:

“Into this sanctuary, then, all the people who possessed the lawful purification entered.”

Cassiodorus the senator distinguishes these porticoes in three rows in the picture of the temple that he placed in his *Pandect*—as he himself recalls in his exposition of the Psalms. He places the first row outside the court of the priests, running squarely around it on every side; the second, in the same manner, outside the innermost porticoes, surrounding them on every side; and the third, likewise, encircling the preceding porticoes on every side.

Thus the temple was fortified on every side by a threefold protection of buildings. The pavement beneath the open sky between the several buildings was made of marble; the inner walls of the surrounding structures—that is, those facing the temple—were formed with columns, while the outer walls were solid. In this way the entire structure of the temple was rationally distinguished according to the variety of its levels.

The high priest entered the Holy of Holies. Purified and unpurified priests, together with Levites and singers, entered the temple itself. Into the innermost court of the great basilica came purified Jewish men, standing and praying in the open air when the weather was clear, but taking refuge in the nearest porticoes when there was a storm. Purified Jewish women entered the outer court. The outermost court was for Gentiles and for Jews who had recently come from among the Gentiles, until the sixth day of purification.

We have found these distinctions represented in Cassiodorus’s picture and have thought it worthwhile to record them briefly, judging that he learned them from the ancient Jews and that so learned a man would not have wished to propose as a reading model something he had not first recognized as true.

These are the places mentioned by the highest of the Psalms of Ascents, which begins:

“Behold, now bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 133).

In these porticoes Jeremiah and the other prophets preached the word to the people; in these the Lord and the apostles preached. In one of them the Lord sat teaching (John 8), when the Pharisees who were testing him brought him an adulterous woman to be judged. In these he found those selling and buying sheep, oxen, and doves, and expelled them from the temple together with their merchandise (John 2). In these Peter and John found and healed a lame man and led him with them inside to pray (Acts 3). In these the whole multitude of the people was praying when the angel appeared to Zechariah at the altar of incense while he was offering incense, and taught him about the birth of the Lord’s forerunner (Luke 1).

These courts and their porticoes could not, however, conceal the view of the temple from those looking toward it from a distance, because the place where the temple stood was much higher than the place where the porticoes were founded. For, as Josephus writes, although the outermost structures of the courts were erected only to a height of four hundred cubits, they reached as far as the summit of the mountain on which the temple had been built.

We have thought these details concerning the structure of the temple worth communicating to the diligent reader. But in whatever matters the sacred Scripture has chosen usefully to report, let us seek figures of the mysteries; in the remaining matters, let us use the account simply for historical knowledge.

The temple building within the court of the priests expresses figuratively the life of perfected and exalted men in the holy Church—those, namely, who both draw near to the Lord through the excellence of their virtues and customarily show others the way of salvation by word and deed.

The word “priest” (*sacerdos*) received its Latin name from the fact that he ought to provide sacred guidance to those who are lesser. In Scripture this name is understood mystically to include not only ministers of the altar—bishops and priests—but also all who excel in the height of right conduct and saving doctrine. They do not minister only to themselves but also to many others, since, by presenting their bodies “as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans 12), they spiritually perform a priestly ministry.

The apostle Peter was not speaking only to bishops and priests, but to the whole Church of God, when he said: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (1 Peter 2). The ancient people of God were also marked with this honor of dignity, when God said to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the children of Israel.” And shortly afterward: “You shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation” (Exodus 19).

The great basilica, which stood outside the court of the priests and into which the whole multitude of the people ordinarily gathered to worship or to hear the word, figuratively signifies the life and conduct of the carnal in the holy Church. To such people the Apostle says: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

They are rightly represented by the great basilica, because there is without doubt a much greater number of such people in the holy Church than of the perfect. But insofar as they surpass the perfect in number, they fall short of them in merit. Hence this basilica is appropriately called great: although it contains many, it does not admit them into the inner parts of the gilded temple for the service of the altar, nor even into the court of the priests.

For although all who are carnal and still weak in the Church, through the merit of a chaste faith and piety, devoutly belong to the company of the elect, they are still far from equaling those who confidently declare: “I dare not speak of anything except what Christ accomplishes through me for the obedience of the Gentiles by word and deed” (Romans 15). And again: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4).

The common people did indeed come as far as the court of the priests. They brought their sacrifices to its gate, where the priests received them, and they followed with their eyes the sacrifices offered upon the altar. When the temple was opened, they also directed their gaze toward it from a distance, but they did not have the ability to enter the court of the priests. Yet from below they cried out to the Lord.

For the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer him the vows of piety of which they are capable. They direct their eyes from afar toward the temple of God when they eagerly rejoice to learn and admire the life of the exalted, and when they embrace with pious reverence those whom they cannot follow by imitating their virtue.

They see the sacrifices of the priests consumed upon the altar by the sacred fire because they recognize that the works of the great are graciously accepted by the Lord through the Holy Spirit. They also bring their own sacrifices to the court of the priests to be offered to the Lord through them when, by doing the good things of which they are capable, they are both strengthened by the exhortation of their elders and teachers and commended to the Lord through their intercession.

They also offer their sacrifices to the priests to be commended through them to the Lord when, with a view to the highest reward, they give to the holy who are in need the necessities of this world that they themselves possess, in obedience to the Lord’s admonition: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

It is rightly remembered that the court of the priests was built with three rows of hewn stones and one row of cedar wood. The three rows of hewn stones are faith, hope, and love. They are rightly called “hewn,” because each person must necessarily learn with careful diligence how to believe, what to hope for, and what to love.

The one row of cedar wood is good action itself, displayed without the corruption of pretense. Without its addition, faith, hope, and love cannot be genuine. It has often been said that cedar wood, on account of the pleasantness of its fragrance and the imperishable strength of its nature, signifies perseverance and the reputation of a pious action [Col. 0165B].

All the elect who desire to please God by faith, hope, love, and action ascend as far as this court. The perfect rise above it through the great grace of their merits when they advance to such a height of virtue that they can say to their hearers: “Be imitators of us, as we also are of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11), and can glory and say: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” (1 Corinthians 6.)

“ In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the month of Ziv; and in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul”—that is, the eighth month—“the house was completed in all its work and in all its furnishings. And he built it in seven years.”

The meaning of the allegory is clear: why was the house of the Lord built in seven years? Because the holy Church is built from elect souls throughout the whole period of this present age, which is carried out in six ages by the cycle of seven days; and at the end of the age it brings its own growth to completion.

Or, rightly, it is built in seven years because of the signification of spiritual grace, through which alone the Church receives what makes it the Church. Isaiah enumerates the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11), without which no one can become faithful, preserve the faith, or attain the crown of righteousness by the merit of faith.

But the fact that in the eighth year, and in its eighth month, the house was completed in all its work and furnishings pertains to the future age and the day of judgment. Then the holy Church will have reached such perfection that nothing further can be found that could be added to it. For it will then possess what that pious man who desired God humbly asked from the Lord, saying: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14).

Yet a question arises that must not be dismissed: how is the house of the Lord said to have been completed in the eighth month in all its work and furnishings, when it is later read that its dedication was completed in the seventh month? It is not credible that Solomon, building the temple for seven years, completed it in the eighth month of the eighth year but postponed the dedication of the completed building until the seventh month of the ninth year.

It therefore seems more plausible that the house was built in seven years and seven months, so that the solemnity of its dedication was celebrated in that same seventh month, and that on the twenty-third day of that month, as the Books of Chronicles report (2 Chronicles 7), Solomon dismissed the people to their tents. Thus, after one week had passed and the eighth month had arrived, the house of the Lord was found complete, both in all its works and in the dedication that had already been completed.

Unless, perhaps, it should be thought that after the temple had been dedicated, some further furnishings were added for its ministry up to the beginning of the eighth month, the king hastening matters so that the temple might be dedicated entirely in the seventh month, which was wholly solemn. In this way both statements would prove true: the temple was completed in all its works and furnishings in the eighth month, and it was dedicated in the seventh month.

CHAPTER VII. On the bronze columns, and so forth; on the vessels of the house of the Lord made in the region of the Jordan; on the hinges of the doors in the completion of the work of the house of the Lord.

(CHAPTER 7.) “King Solomon also sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre, the son of a widow woman from the tribe of Naphtali, whose father was a Tyrian, a worker in bronze, full of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, to perform every work in bronze. When he came to King Solomon, he performed all his work,” and so forth.

This too was done for the sake of mystery. The Tyrian craftsman whom Solomon took as an assistant in his work signifies the ministers of the word chosen from among the Gentiles. He is fittingly said to have been “the son of a widow woman from Israel,” in whose person the Church of the present age is sometimes represented. Her husband—namely, Christ—having tasted death, rose again and ascended into heaven, leaving her meanwhile as a pilgrim upon earth.

There is no need to labor over the explanation of how the sons of this widow are holy preachers, since all the elect individually confess themselves to be sons of the Church. The Prophet also makes a special promise concerning these same preachers of the New Testament, saying: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44).

Hiram performed all Solomon’s work because holy teachers, while faithfully devoting themselves to the ministry of the word, perform the work of God. By speaking outwardly, they open the way of truth for those whom God himself has ordained to eternal life by enlightening them inwardly. “I planted,” he says, “Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

He performed this work in bronze because the diligent teacher seeks to entrust the word to those who desire to receive it piously and guard it perseveringly, and who also strive, by preaching to others, to spread more widely what they themselves have rightly learned. Bronze is known to be a very durable metal and highly resonant.

“And he cast two bronze columns, seventeen cubits high, each column.”

These are the columns of which Paul says: “James, Cephas, and John, who were reputed to be columns, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision” (Galatians 2). [Col. 0167A] In these words he seems to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they signified and why two were made.

They signify the apostles and all spiritual teachers, strong in faith and action and raised upright toward heavenly things. They are two so that by preaching they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcised into the Church.

They stood in the portico before the doors of the temple and wonderfully adorned its entrance on both sides with their beauty and splendor. The Lord is the door of the temple, because no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14). And as he says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10).

The columns stand on either side before this door when ministers of the word show the entrance to the heavenly kingdom to both peoples, so that whether someone comes to the faith of the Gospel from the light of legal knowledge or from the harshness of paganism, he may have those ready who demonstrate the way of salvation to him both by word and by example.

Or, certainly, because the Books of Chronicles say of these same columns: “He placed the columns in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left” (2 Chronicles 3), two columns were made and arranged in such a way as to teach us that, in prosperity and in adversity alike, we must keep the entrance to our heavenly homeland before the eyes of our mind.

It should be carefully noted in the sentence from the Books of Chronicles that I have cited that the portico of the temple was also called the threshold of the temple. And when we read in the prophets that the priests prayed between the vestibule and the altar, this should be understood as between the portico and the altar.

It is rightly remembered that each column was eighteen cubits high, for three times six makes eighteen. That three pertains to faith because of the Holy Trinity, and six to action, because the world was made in that number of days, is clearer than light. And three is multiplied by six when “the righteous lives by faith” (Habakkuk 7), and increases the knowledge of pious belief through the execution of good action.

The column before the doors of the temple is eighteen cubits high when every outstanding preacher publicly teaches everyone that we can attain the joys of the life above only through faith and works of righteousness.

“And a line twelve cubits long encircled each column,” when every teacher sent to preach either to Jews or to Gentiles takes care to do and teach only what the Church has received and learned through the apostles.

For if anyone wishes to live or preach otherwise, and either despises the apostolic decrees or chooses to establish any novelties according to his own desire, he is not a column suited to the temple of God. By refusing to follow the apostolic statutes, he is like a line of twelve cubits that does not fit either because of the thinness of his inertia or because of the bulk of his swollen pride.

“He also made two capitals, to be set upon the tops of the columns, cast in bronze, one capital five cubits high and the other capital five cubits high,” and so forth.

The heads of the columns—that is, their uppermost part—are the inmost thoughts of faithful teachers. By their thoughts devoted to God, all their works and words are directed, just as the limbs are directed by the head.

The two capitals placed upon these heads are the two Testaments, to whose meditation and observance holy teachers submit themselves wholly in mind and body. Hence each capital rightly had a height of five cubits, because the Scripture of the Mosaic Law is contained in five books. The entire sequence of the Old Testament also encompasses five ages of the world.

The New Testament proclaims nothing else to us except what Moses had predicted would be proclaimed through it and what the prophets had proclaimed.

“And, in the manner of a net and chains woven together with marvelous workmanship, each cast capital of the columns was made.” The Books of Chronicles express it this way: “And also chainlets in the inner sanctuary, and he placed them upon the heads of the columns” (2 Chronicles 3).

The appearance of chains and the likeness of a net in the capitals signify the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints, concerning which the Psalm says: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44)—that is, in a garment of radiant love, surrounded by a variety of spiritual gifts.

Or certainly, the many interweavings of chains and the spreading of the net signify the many different persons among the elect. When they cling to the words of holy preachers by faithfully listening and obeying, the nets and chainlets set upon the capitals of the columns offer to all who look upon them the marvel of their unity.

[Col. 0168C] “Seven rows of netting on one capital, and seven rows of netting on the other capital.” The number seven ordinarily signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as John bears witness in the Apocalypse. When he said that he had seen a Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes, he immediately added by way of explanation: “These are the seven spirits of God, sent into all the earth” (Revelation 5).

The prophet Isaiah explains this more clearly when, speaking of the Lord who was to be born in the flesh, he says: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11).

Thus there were seven rows of netting on each capital, because the fathers of both Testaments received the grace of the one and the same sevenfold Spirit so that they might become elect.

“Then he made the columns and two rows around each of the latticeworks, so that they might cover the capitals.”

There were indeed two rows of latticework around the capital, but each row proceeded in a sequence of seven strands until, having circled the capital, it returned again into itself, as though forming a circle. Nor is the symbolic meaning of why there were two rows of latticework hidden, since it is clear that the virtue of love has a twofold distinction: namely, when we are commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves. But each of those rows has latticework of seven strands, because neither God nor our neighbor can be loved without the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0169A]

These latticeworks were made so that they might cover the capitals—that is, surround them on every side in a circle—because every page of Holy Scripture, when rightly understood, proclaims throughout the grace of love and peace. For the capitals signify the volumes of the divine utterances, while the latticeworks signify the bonds of mutual love; and the capitals are covered with latticework when the sacred utterances are, so to speak, shown to be clothed on every side with the gift of charity. For even in those things that we do not understand in the Scriptures, charity lies hidden; and in those things that we understand, charity lies widely revealed. Appropriately, then, it is added concerning these same latticeworks, or capitals:

“Which were above the top of the pomegranates.”

[Col. 0169B]

For pomegranates—whose nature is to enclose many seeds within a single outer rind—are aptly placed as a figure of the holy Church, which habitually includes innumerable hosts of the elect within the catholic protection of one faith. They may also signify the life and conduct of each individual righteous person, who, enclosing many emblems of spiritual thoughts and virtues like numerous seeds within a single rind, takes care to protect them with the firm guardianship of faith and humility, lest they be scattered.

And by a wholly fitting mystery the heads of the columns were surrounded in a circle by pomegranates, because holy teachers must recall the life of the faithful who came before them and must always fortify their own deeds and words on every side by their examples. Otherwise, if they should live or teach in a manner different from the rule of those earlier faithful, they would go astray.

[Col. 0169C]

When it has been said that the latticeworks covered the capitals, which were above the top of the pomegranates, it appears, according to the order of the work itself, that the pomegranates had been made around the capitals on the lower side, and that from those same pomegranates the latticeworks arose, by which the capitals were partly covered. The symbolic meaning is also clear: why the latticeworks were attached above the top of the pomegranates, since both pertain almost to one meaning, whether of spiritual persons or of spiritual virtues. For we know that virtues are born from virtues, and that the saints walk “from virtue to virtue, until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Ps. LXXXIII),” a virtue beyond which none greater can be approached. Hence the Apostle also says: “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope (Rom. V).”

“But the capitals that were above the heads of the columns were fashioned like the work of a lily, in a portico of four cubits.”

For what is signified by lilies except the brightness of the heavenly homeland and the beauty of paradise, fragrant with the flowers of immortality? And what by four cubits except the evangelical message, which promises us entrance into that eternal blessedness and shows us the path by which it is reached? Therefore, when the holy teachers show us the promised thresholds of the heavenly kingdom in the four books of the holy Gospel, they display, as the heads of the columns, a work of a lily four cubits in extent.

Here it should be noted, according to the literal sense, that when the work of a lily in the capitals is said to be four cubits, and it is not added whether this refers to breadth or height, it is left to the reader’s judgment whether it should be understood in height or in breadth. [Col. 0170A] It is entirely certain, however, that the column encircled by a cord of twelve cubits had a thickness of four cubits. For every circle has three times as much circumference as the space across its diameter. Thus the bronze sea, because it had a diameter of ten cubits, as is read below, consequently had a circumference of thirty cubits.

Yet because it is said that the work of the lily was four cubits, whether it indicates breadth or height, the meaning of the figure is nonetheless clear: for it was only through the Gospel that the world heard that most desired voice: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near (Matt. IV).” What follows is:

[Col. 0170B]

“And again there were other capitals at the top of the columns above, corresponding in measure to the latticeworks,”

that is, of such breadth as the column itself, although the text nowhere tells us what its height was. These capitals, whatever their nature and whatever their size—for Scripture does not explicitly specify their measurements—appear to have been added in the manner of lilies. If one takes pleasure in seeking some mystical meaning in their construction, they may not inappropriately signify the sublimity of the everlasting kingdom, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him (Isa. LXIV; 1 Cor. II).”

But because the same fellowship of the citizens above is granted to the faithful of both peoples, it is rightly added:

[Col. 0170C]

“And there were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the circuit of the second capital.”

We have said that pomegranates represent either the whole holy Church or each of the faithful. The number one hundred, which is the first number reached on the right hand, is sometimes customarily placed as a figure of eternal blessedness. This number of pomegranates is doubled around the circuit of the second capital, to mystically indicate that the people of both Testaments are to be united in Christ and brought to the crown of eternal life.

“And he set up two columns in the portico of the temple. When he had set up the right-hand column, he called it by the name Jachin, ‘firmness.’ Likewise he raised the second column and called its name Boaz, ‘in strength,’ etc.”

[Col. 0170D]

The right-hand column, as we said above, expresses the figure of those teachers who established the primitive Church in Jerusalem; the second, of those who were sent to preach to the Gentiles. Or certainly the right-hand column signifies those who foretold by prophecy that the Lord would come in the flesh; the second, those who bear witness that he has already come and redeemed the world by his blood.

The two columns were appropriately designated by similar names, since one was called “firmness” and the other “in strength,” so that it might be shown that one strength of faith and works was present in all teachers. At the same time, the inertia of our own age was silently reproved: some teachers, priests, and columns of the house of God want to be seen and called such, although they have within themselves no firm faith with which to despise the splendors of the world and desire invisible goods, no strength with which to correct errors, and not even the diligence required to understand the errors of those placed under their authority. [Col. 0171A]

“He also made the molten sea, ten cubits from brim to brim, round all around, etc.”

This molten sea was made as a figure of the Savior’s font, by which we are cleansed for the remission of sins. For the priests washed in it, as the Books of Chronicles plainly testify (2 Chron. IV). In Scripture, all the elect are figuratively called priests, because they are members of the High Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ.

And Scripture rightly gave this vessel the name “sea,” specifically in memory of the Red Sea, in which a figure of baptism had first gone before through the destruction of the Egyptians and the liberation of God’s people. [Col. 0171B] The Apostle explains this when he says: “For all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. X).”

The sacrament of baptism both seeks for us purity of life in this world and promises us the glory of eternal life in the world to come. Both of these are signified in a single statement by this bronze sea, when it is said to be ten cubits from brim to brim. For by the ten commandments the Lord expressed in the Law everything that we ought to do; and by the denarius he likewise signified the reward of good works, when he foretold that it would be given to those laboring in the vineyard (Matt. XX).

“Therefore the sea was ten cubits from brim to brim.”

For from the first person baptized in the name of Jesus Christ to the last, who will believe and be baptized at the end of the age, the entire company of the faithful must enter upon one and the same way of truth and hope from the Lord for a common crown of righteousness. [Col. 0171C]

It was round all around, so that the whole world might be signified as being cleansed in the circle of the laver of life from the defilement of sins. Concerning this it is rightly added:

“Its height was five cubits.”

For whatever we sin by sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch—all of this the grace of God releases for us through the washing of the life-giving font. But the remission of past sins is not sufficient if each person does not thereafter strive to persist in good works. Otherwise the devil, who had gone out from a person, sees that the person is idle in good deeds, returns in greater force, and makes “the last state of that person worse than the first (Matt. XII).” [Col. 0171D] Hence it is appropriately added:

“And a cord of thirty cubits encircled it all around, etc.”

For the cord may aptly signify the discipline of the heavenly commandments, by which we are bound back from our own wills, as Scripture says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken (Eccl. IV).” For observance of God’s commandments, established in the hearts of the elect by faith, hope, and love of the heavenly reward, cannot be dissolved by any obstacle of temporal things.

“And sculpture ran beneath the brim, encircling it and encompassing the sea for ten cubits. Two rows of historiated sculptural figures were cast.”

Since it was stated above that a cord of thirty cubits encircled the sea, and it is now added that this sculpture, placed beneath the brim, encompassed it for ten cubits, it is clear from both statements that the vessel was spread out and flared like a bowl: from the circumference of thirty cubits that it had at the brim, it narrowed down to ten cubits. [Col. 0172A]

Sculpture is called “historiated” when it imitates certain stories or events. Therefore the historiated sculptures by which the sea was surrounded rightly designate examples from earlier times. We must carefully contemplate these, so that we may see by what works the saints pleased God from the beginning, with what obstinacy the wicked persisted in their crimes, and with what misery the reprobate perished because of their crimes.

“And it stood upon twelve oxen, of which three looked toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east.”

[Col. 0172B]

The twelve oxen, then, are the twelve apostles and all who have undertaken, in their place, to govern the holy Church in Christ. These oxen carry the sea placed upon them when the apostles and the successors of the apostles strive to fulfill with willing devotion the duty of evangelizing entrusted to them.

They look three toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east when they preach the faith of the Holy Trinity in every region of the fourfold world.

“Whose hindquarters were all hidden within.”

[Col. 0172C]

All the hindquarters of the oxen are hidden within, because the reward with which holy preachers will be endowed forever has already been determined in the judgment of the inner assessor, but remains entirely concealed from us, who are still outside. Yet they cannot be ignorant of this: everyone who receives the laver of baptism for salvation and life must possess faith, hope, and charity; and without these three virtues no one can now perform anything or enter into life. Hence it rightly follows:

“The thickness of the laver was three handbreadths.”

The thickness of the laver in the sea is the firmness of virtue in baptism. Its thickness is three handbreadths when the commandment of baptism is fortified by the strength of faith, hope, and love. It is shown to be of no benefit to those who receive it unless the firm certainty of these virtues confirms both their minds and their works. [Col. 0172D]

“Its brim was like the brim of a cup, and like the leaf of a spreading lily.”

By the brim of the cup, the taste of the Lord’s passion is expressed; by the leaf of the spreading lily, the revealed glory of his resurrection.

“It held two thousand baths, etc.”

The number one thousand is customarily used in Scripture as a sign of perfection, because it makes the number ten solidly square. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred, which is already a square figure but is not yet complete. To make it rise in height and become solid, multiply one hundred by ten, and the result is one thousand. By this perfected number the stable, unconquerable, and, as it were, squared conscience of the righteous is signified: however one turns a square, it remains standing. So the mind of the elect, confronted by no assault of temptations, knows how to be bent from the steadfastness of its certainty. [Col. 0173A]

A bath is a Hebrew measure, which they call *bath*, containing three modii. It is the same as the *ephah*, which they call *epha*. But the *ephah* pertains to the measure of various crops—wheat, barley, and legumes—whereas the bath is used for liquid substances, wine, oil, and water.

Therefore, because the bath is the standard of a fixed measure, it designates works of equity and justice, in which those who are baptized for the remission of sins must be instructed. The sea held one thousand baths when the water of baptism washed the Jewish people and conveyed them to the kingdom of heaven. It received another thousand when it also made the multitudes of the nations, reborn in the same font and confirmed in works of righteousness, participants in that same everlasting kingdom. [Col. 0173B]

“And he made ten bases, each base four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high, etc.”

The same mysteries of our salvation are prefigured in many ways and by many means. The same apostles and apostolic men who are signified by the oxen carrying the sea are also signified by the bases prepared for carrying the lavers; and the lavers themselves bore the same symbolic meaning as the sea.

For, as the Books of Chronicles relate (2 Chron. IV), they washed in them everything that they were going to offer as a burnt offering. The burnt offering of the Lord may generally be understood as the whole multitude of the elect, [Col. 0173C] which, according to the voice of the forerunner John the Baptist, was baptized by him in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matt. III).

Thus, just as the priests who washed in the sea express the form of those who through baptism become sharers in the supreme priesthood that is in the Lord Jesus Christ, so also the burnt offerings most appropriately represent the same people, since after the washing of baptism they are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. The victim is washed in the laver when one of the faithful is drenched with the water of baptism. It is offered as a burnt offering when, through the laying on of the bishop’s hand, it receives the gift of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0173D]

The fact that ten bases were made for carrying the lavers could be interpreted mystically in this way: the ministers of the life-giving font call those whom they instruct to the eternal joys of blessedness, which are customarily represented by the number ten. But because it is written distinctly below concerning these same lavers that five of them were placed on the right side of the temple and five on the left, the mysteries of the number five should rather be considered in them.

The bases of the lavers were placed on both sides of the temple so that it might be signified that the grace of the sacred font was to be opened to both peoples of God. There were five on either side—as we already said in the exposition of the sea, which was five cubits high—in order to demonstrate figuratively that everything in which the faithful had sinned through the five bodily senses was forgiven through the washing of baptism.

Thus, just as the single sea placed upon twelve oxen expresses the unity of baptism that was to be preached throughout the whole world by the apostles, so also the two rows of lavers mystically show that the Gentiles, together with the Jews, were to be gathered into one fellowship of faith through the water of baptism.

[Col. 0174A]

The fact that each base was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high is easy to understand. Length pertains to the patience of long-suffering; breadth to the expansion of love; height to hope of heavenly reward.

There are four principal virtues, upon which the remaining structure of the virtues rests: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Therefore the bases had a length and breadth of four cubits, because holy preachers—whether they endure outwardly the adversities of the world and the length of present exertions and labors, or inwardly expand their hearts in joyful love of their Creator and their neighbors—always take care to practice the virtues: discerning prudently between good and evil, enduring adversity courageously, restraining the heart from the desire for pleasures, and maintaining justice in their actions.

The bases were three cubits high when, through the practice of the virtues—which they exercise with patience amid evils and love of good things—they strive with constant attention to attain the vision of the Holy Trinity.

“And the work of the bases was engraved with recessed work, and sculptures were between the joints.”

He appears to call “joints” those places where the boards of the lavers themselves were joined to one another, so that one base was made from four or five boards. [Col. 0174C] What sort of sculptures the bases had between these joints—that is, on their own sides, front and back, right and left, and also above—is made clear by what follows:

“Between the little crowns and the interlacings were lions, oxen, and cherubim, and likewise joints above.”

Thus no part of the surface of the bases was flat. Rather, it was everywhere engraved with mystical figures, because the minds of the saints—or rather, their entire manner of life—display the grace of virtues in all things. No hour passes them by empty and vacant in which they cease to devote themselves to pious works, words, or at least thoughts.

They have little crowns engraved upon them when they pant with tireless desire for entry into eternal life. They have interlacings when, amid their desires for the heavenly life above, they never [Col. 0174D] dissolve the bonds of fraternal fellowship that is near at hand.

They have lions between the little crowns and the interlacings when they raise their minds toward the hope of heavenly things and expand them toward love of their neighbors in such a way that they do not delay exercising the fervor of stern rebuke against those who sin and have been entrusted to them.

They have oxen together with the lions when they offer that same rebuke with a spirit of gentleness; when, in the fervor of correction, they never cease to have a cloven hoof of discerning action and speech; and when they never cease to turn the words of divine reading over in their mouths, as though chewing the cud:

“And above the lions and oxen were cords hanging down, as though made of bronze.”

The cords hang above the lions and oxen when holy teachers, both in the severity of strictness with which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of leniency with which they forgive penitents, hold fast to the judgment of their author, lest by binding or releasing anyone unjustly they should deserve to be justly bound by him whose judgment cannot err. [Col. 0175A]

“And four wheels for each base, and bronze axles. And on the four sides were cast shoulder-pieces beneath the laver, facing one another.”

The four wheels are the four books of the Gospels. They are most aptly compared to wheels, because just as the revolving wheel runs with very swift motion wherever it is directed, so the evangelical message, at the Lord’s command, quickly filled all the regions of the world through the apostles.

Just as a wheel raises the cart placed upon it from the ground and, once raised, carries it wherever the driver directs, so [Col. 0175B] evangelical preaching lifts the minds of the elect from earthly desires to heavenly longings and, once lifted, leads them—whether toward progress in good action or toward the ministry of preaching—wherever the assisting grace of the Spirit wills.

For it is said below:

“For such were the wheels as are customarily made for a chariot.”

We read concerning the saints: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice (Ps. LXVII).” If, then, the bases of the lavers are holy teachers who minister to us the laver of life, and the four wheels of the bases are the four books of the Gospels, what are the axles of the wheels, which carry the bases, except the hearts of those same teachers? By diligently attending to the evangelical commands, these lift the teachers above the desires of the weak, just as inserted axles raise the base higher from the ground.

[Col. 0175C]

The shoulder-pieces, placed before the wheels to prevent them from slipping from the axles, signify the proclamations of the prophets, by which evangelical and apostolic Scripture is confirmed, lest it perhaps fall into doubt for any reader.

It is rightly said that the shoulder-pieces placed beneath the lavers on the four sides faced one another, because all prophetic Scripture agrees with itself, having been composed by one Spirit of God. There were four shoulder-pieces for each base, corresponding to the number of wheels—not because there are only four prophetic books, but because in everything the prophets and Moses said, they supplied testimony to the words of the four evangelists, so that, through the agreement of both Testaments, one faith and love of Christ might strengthen the hearts of us all. [Col. 0175D]

“The opening of the laver was within, at the top of the head, while what appeared outside was one cubit, entirely round; and likewise it had one and a half cubits.”

The opening of the laver was one cubit because of the unity of confession and faith by which we are all baptized in the confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (Eph. IV).”

The opening itself was at the top of the head to teach that through baptism a way has been opened for us to the heavenly kingdom. The laver itself was one and a half cubits in breadth, [Col. 0176A] signifying the perfection of works together with the beginning of contemplation. For the complete cubit in the laver signifies the perfection of good action, which, without any doubt, was possessed by the man concerning whom the Lord said to the ancient tempter: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil (Job I)?”

The other half-cubit is the vision of God, which is customarily granted in part even in this present life to the faithful who remain here, as Job, after overcoming his adversary, says while speaking with the Lord: “With the hearing of the ear I heard you, but now my eye sees you (Job XLII).”

For it is written below: “One wheel had a height of one cubit and a half.” And shortly afterward:

[Col. 0176B]

“At the top of the base there was a rounded projection of one and a half cubits, fashioned in such a way that the laver could be placed upon it from above.”

The lavers, then, had a measure of one and a half cubits, because we are washed in the font of life by that faith through which we deserve to enter life by works of righteousness. Nevertheless, while we live here, we cannot be without sin; nor can we fully see the sweetness of heavenly life, although in part we can taste it and love it during the present life.

The wheels too were measured at one and a half cubits, because Scripture in the evangelical reading shows how those who wish to be perfect ought to live and demonstrates in the present the hope of eternal reward, while promising that the nature of that reward will be revealed and granted to us in the future.

[Col. 0176C]

The bases themselves also had a breadth of one and a half cubits at their tops, where they received the lavers, because those supreme teachers and ministers of the saving font shone as perfect in their works during this life, but enjoyed the light of contemplation only in part. Hence they also say: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished (1 Cor. XIII).”

“In this manner he made ten bases, with one casting, one measure, and a similar engraving; he also made ten bronze lavers.”

Why ten bases were made, with an equal number of lavers placed upon them, has already been stated above. But the fact that all the bases or lavers had one casting, one measure, and similar engraving was not intended to signify that the merits of all teachers could be equal. Rather, it signified that the faith of the Gospel by which they are instructed is one; the sacrament of baptism by which they are washed is one; and the Spirit by which all the elect are consecrated is one and the same, although they possess different gifts in that Spirit, who “divides to each one as he wills (1 Cor. XII).” [Col. 0176D]

“One laver held forty baths.”

The number forty is customarily a figure of great perfection, because four times ten makes forty. [Col. 0177A] Ten are the commandments by which all our activity is prescribed in the divine Law; four are the books of the Gospels, in which, through the dispensation of the Lord’s Incarnation, the entrance into the heavenly homeland has been opened to us.

And because all who belong to the mystery of holy baptism must, together with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, display the fruit of right action, it is fitting that each laver in which the burnt offerings were washed held forty baths.

As for what follows, “It was four cubits,” whether in height or breadth, the meaning of the mystery is readily apparent. One laver was four cubits either because of the four books of the holy Gospel, in which the form of baptism has been prescribed for us; or because of the four cardinal virtues, in which every faithful person, if faithful not in vain, ought to be instructed; or rightly because of the four regions of the world, in which the laver of salvation is administered, [Col. 0177B] as the Psalmist says: “Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, from the lands he gathered them: from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea (Ps. CVI).”

When he said above, “Likewise it had one cubit and a half,” and did not add whether this referred to height or breadth, it appears that he intended the bottom of the laver itself to be understood as having this breadth. This is very easily inferred, if I am not mistaken, from the measure of the base on which each laver was placed, which is described as follows:

“At the top of the base there was a rounded projection of one and a half cubits, fashioned in such a way that the laver could be placed upon it from above.”

The breadth of the bottom of the lavers, then, was one and a half cubits. The capacity of the lavers themselves was four cubits, but whether this refers to height, breadth, or both, let the one who knows say.

[Col. 0177C]

“And he placed ten bases, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.”

The right and left sides of the temple are said not to be inside the temple itself, but before the temple—namely, toward the eastern region, in the inner court, which was properly called the court of the priests.

He placed five on the right side of the temple because of the Jews, who had anciently been accustomed to use the Sun of righteousness through the teaching of the Law; and five on the left because of us, who had long remained attached in blind heart to the servitude of the one who said: “I will place my seat in the north (Isa. XIV).” This is plainly to say: “I desire to rest in those hearts which I perceive to be alienated from the light of truth and the breath of divine love.” [Col. 0177D]

“But he placed the sea on the right side of the temple, facing eastward toward the south.”

This too was placed in the same court, toward the east. When he says “on the right side of the temple,” he repeats the same thing by saying “toward the south.” For those entering the court from the east had first to turn toward the south, where the sea stood in the very corner, prepared for the priests’ washing. Then, as they proceeded inward, the lavers placed on both sides, for washing the victims, met them.

Within these stood a bronze base, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, [Col. 0178A] upon which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple. Then, as they advanced farther, the altar of burnt offering stood before them near the middle of the court. After that came the portico, or vestibule, of the temple, in which bronze columns stood around the entrance of the temple.

Therefore, the fact that he placed the sea on the right side of the temple signifies that through the washing of baptism we ought to reach the heavenly kingdom, which is figuratively represented by the right side in the proper sense: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (Mark XVI).”

For whenever the right and left are both understood in a good sense, they signify either the Jews and the Gentiles, as we said above in the exposition of the bases; or the present life of the Church and the future life; or the joys and sorrows of the world; or something of that kind. But when the right side is understood absolutely in a good sense, it more often signifies eternal joys.

The fact that he placed the sea facing east refers to the same meaning: through the washing of the sacred font, the splendor of inner brightness is revealed to us. Its placement on the southern side of the court signifies that through receiving the Holy Spirit the faithful are accustomed to be kindled with the fervor of true love. For in Scripture the heat of the southern sun customarily signifies both the ardor of love and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through whom that same love is poured into the hearts of the elect. [Col. 0178B]

“All the vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of yellow bronze. The king cast them in the region of the Jordan, in clayey ground, etc.”

The vessels of the house of the Lord were aptly cast in the region of the Jordan, in the river in which our Lord deigned to be baptized and, [Col. 0178C] having been immersed in its waters, transformed the element of water for us into the washing away of sins. And because every baptism of the faithful, by which they are consecrated to the Lord, is celebrated as an imitation of that baptism by which he himself sanctified the waters, the vessels of the house of the Lord were rightly made in the region of the Jordan.

For we cannot otherwise become vessels of election and mercy unless, looking to his baptism, which he underwent in that river, we too strive to be washed in the life-giving river.

It should also be noted that he says these same vessels were made not only in the region of the Jordan but also in its plain, signifying the multiplication of the faithful, which was to occur not only in Judea but also across the breadth of all the nations, fulfilling the prophecy: “The plains will rejoice, and everything that is in them (Ps. XCV).”

[Col. 0178D]

But the clayey ground from which the molds for casting the vessels of the Lord were made—what can it better be understood as than Holy Scripture, from which we receive the rule for living well? Just as clay hardened by fire displays the form of the Lord’s vessel, showing how great and of what kind it ought to be, so Scripture shows us the rule of righteousness that we are to follow. It also sets before us the examples of the saints, who persevered invincibly in the fire of tribulations, to be followed in all things if we desire to be chosen and precious vessels in the house of the Lord.
