And bronze melted by fire enters the clay molds so that the vessel may become suitable for heavenly ministries, when we, having been salutarily humbled and softened by the flame of our divine love—or even by human adversity—enter the way of the fathers by doing good works, so that by running well we may attain the rewards of the fathers. [Col. 0179A]

“Solomon made all the vessels, the golden altar, and the table on which the bread of the Presence was to be placed, golden, etc.”

The golden altar signifies the hearts of the perfect righteous, gleaming with the light of inward charity and chastity; and the position of that altar is also appropriate for signifying their exalted state. For it stood before the entrance of the Holy of Holies, as we read plainly in the account of the tabernacle’s construction. On this altar, indeed, neither the blood of sacrifices nor libations was burned, but only incense. Its smoke, rising upward, covered the ark and filled the oracle with the fragrance of sweetness. In this was represented the figure of the saints who, neglecting desires for temporal things and seeking heavenly realities with undivided purpose, are placed, as it were, within and near the oracle. They are not far removed from the veil by which the temple and the Holy of Holies are separated, because in body alone do they dwell on earth; in all else, according to the inward person, their whole way of life is in heaven.

From such an altar the smoke of the incense ascends into the Holy of Holies, where the ark is hidden, when the prayers of the saints, kindled by the flame of charity, reach all the way to heaven, “where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. III). For on this altar the blood of sacrifices is not burned, but only incense, because such men do not possess works of flesh and blood with which they might sacrifice and slay offerings to the Lord upon the altar of their hearts; rather, they offer him only the vows of tears and prayer, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom.

He also made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high. Moses did indeed make an altar of incense in the wilderness, having one cubit in length, another in width, and two cubits in height (Exod. XXXVII). Scripture does not say how large Solomon made that altar, but only says that he made a golden altar. It is clear, however, that he could not have made it as large as the altar of burnt offering; for if it had been twenty cubits in length and width, it would have filled the entire width of the temple. Therefore, in proportion to how much farther outside the altar of burnt offering was placed than the altar of incense, and how much inferior it was in the kind of offering and the usefulness of its metal, so much did it surpass the latter in the magnitude of its dimensions and the frequency of its sacrifices. For there are plainly far more people to whom it is said, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX), than there are those who take delight in hearing, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor” (ibid.).

Yet the dimensions of this altar are not without mystical meaning and numerical significance. It had twenty cubits in length, the same in width, and ten cubits in height. We spoke above, in the exposition of the temple and its vestibule, about this number; but now we must say briefly that if the altar of burnt offering represents in the Church those who seek to consecrate their body and soul to God through the fire of his love, then their perseverance in good works is figured by the altar’s length, their breadth in the love of God and neighbor by its width, and their hope in awaiting the vision of God by its height.

The fact that the altar’s length and width were each twenty cubits certainly signifies the great perfection of that tireless perseverance and sincere love which is granted to us through observance of both Testaments. For four times five completes the number twenty. The five books of the Mosaic Law correspond to the four books of evangelical freedom. When, enlightened by the grace of the Gospel, we attain spiritual understanding of the Law and keep it, we truly complete the number twenty.

Let the same number be found in the altar’s length and width, when the hearts of the elect, instructed by both Testaments and assisted by the one author of both Testaments, preserve perseverance in good works even amid persecutions and display the joyfulness of love even toward those who persecute them. The number ten ordinarily signifies hope for heavenly rewards, as the Lord affirms when he declares that those who labor in the vineyard of the great householder will be rewarded with a denarius (Matt. XX). The same altar, made as a figure of the elect in order to signify their perpetual life, was ten cubits high.

When it was said that Solomon made a golden altar, the following was immediately added:

“And the table on which the bread of the Presence was to be placed, golden, etc.”

The golden table is sacred Scripture, fruitful in the clarity of spiritual understanding. Concerning it the Psalmist says to the Lord: “You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me” (Ps. XXIV). Lest our troubling adversaries bend us toward error, our Creator has prepared for us the table of heavenly knowledge, through which we may be strengthened in the faith of the truth.

The bread of the Presence signifies the holy teachers. Whoever seeks rightly will always find in the divine books either their works or their saving words set before us as an example of life. Hence, appropriately, the same bread was commanded to be made twelve loaves in Exodus: namely, on account of the twelve apostles, through whose ministry the Scripture of the New Testament was composed for us, and the mysteries of the Old Instrument—namely, the Old Testament—were revealed by the Lord’s gift. By this number not only those apostles but all who, by preaching the word, minister the nourishment of life to the faithful are signified, because all follow the very form of teaching that the apostles received from the Lord.

But when we read in Chronicles that “Solomon made ten tables, and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left; and also a hundred golden bowls” (II Chron. IV), it is credible that these were made not so much for the bread of the Presence as for carrying the vessels of the Lord—namely, the bowls, which Scripture reports as having been made along with them, as well as the incense vessels, censers, mortars, and the other objects mentioned below.

For when the same book of Chronicles shortly afterward adds, “Solomon made all the vessels of the house of God, and the bronze altar and the tables, and upon them the bread of the Presence” (II Chron. IV), either it uses the plural number for the singular, in a manner very common in Scripture, as in Joshua: “But the children of Israel transgressed the commandment, and took of the accursed thing” (Josh. IV), although Achan alone, and not several of the children of Israel, did this; or certainly, because the bread of the Presence used to be baked before the Sabbath so that it could immediately be placed upon the table of the Presence on the Sabbath, it could have happened that newly made, freshly baked loaves were placed upon those tables at once and kept covered there during that night, until early morning, when the old loaves had been offered and the hot ones were placed upon the table of the Presence.

These ten tables, however, do not conflict with the figure of the one table of the Presence. Just as one table laden with twelve loaves signifies the unanimous harmony of all Scripture, fortified by apostolic authority, so not without reason do ten golden tables announce in figure the prophetic utterances of the divine Law. These either offer us refreshment from the word of God, like the bread of the Presence, or set before us the examples of the faithful, like the splendor and wonders of the vessels of the Lord placed upon them.

The tables are rightly five doubled, not only because the Lawgiver wrote five books, but also because the entire sequence of the Testament embraces five ages of the world. The number of the tables is doubled: five are placed on the right and five on the left, when, after the Lord’s Incarnation, the same Scripture is entrusted either to both peoples of God, namely, Jew and Gentile, or is shown to be full of evangelical figures—whereas it had formerly been thought that the ancient people of God should understand it only according to the letter.

“And five golden lampstands on the right, and five on the left, opposite the oracle, of the finest gold, with something like lily blossoms and golden lamps above.”

Just as tables are rightly placed as a type of sacred Scripture, since they both supply the bread of God’s word to those who hunger for righteousness and bear vessels of heavenly service—that is, they set the deeds of these men before us as an example—so the same divine utterances are most fittingly represented by lampstands, because they bring the light of wisdom to those who wander.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (Ps. CXVIII). Solomon likewise says: “For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is light” (Prov. VI).

Why five lampstands were placed on the right and five on the left is readily apparent from what we have discussed concerning the tables. When he had said, “five on the right and five on the left,” he appropriately added, “opposite the oracle.” The oracle, where the ark was, as has often been said, signifies access to the heavenly homeland, “where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. III), conscious, as it were, of the Father’s mysteries.

The golden lampstands of the temple are placed opposite the oracle because the divine utterances always look toward the dwelling of the heavenly city, so that they may infuse our hearts with knowledge and desire for it, and kindle those who have their bodily origin from earth to seek and merit in heaven the seat of an everlasting dwelling.

If you ask what typological distinction there is between the lampstands and their lamps, we may rightly understand the lamps to be holy men who, filled with the oil of the Holy Spirit, themselves burn with the fire of love in their hearts and bring the light of knowledge to their neighbors through their speech. The lampstands, however, which raise these lamps on high so that they may be seen far and wide in the Church, are sacred Scripture, which by its reading displays to us the virtues and teaching of the saints.

The Lord’s saying concerning John supports this interpretation: “He was a burning lamp” (John V). We may also say, most fittingly, that the lamps are the divine utterances, according to the Psalmist’s statement, which we cited above: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (Ps. CXVIII).

The lampstands of these lamps, however, are all the saints who, bearing both their hearts and bodies, continually subject them with humble purpose to the Lord’s commandments. Whoever cares to follow his own will in nothing, but attends in all things to what sacred Scripture says, and, submitting himself to its commandments, strives to listen to its promises, bears the golden lamps of Scripture like a golden lampstand in the house of God. For he strives to subject the chaste members of his body and the chaste thoughts of his mind to doing what God commands; and this with as firm a purpose as the lampstand must have when, standing upright and firmly directed toward the heights, it keeps the lamps placed upon it not only from falling but also from any movement that would disturb its position.

When he had said, “And five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, opposite the oracle, of the finest gold,” he added, “and something like lily blossoms, and golden lamps above.” Literally, it appears that the upper part of the lampstands was fashioned in the form of an expanded lily, just as we read that the lampstand of the tabernacle was made. Its central shaft and the branches proceeding from it, with their cups and spheres, are described as having had very many lilies.

The blossoms of the lily, as has often been said, signify the beauty of the ever-green land of the living, concerning which blessed Peter says that we have been regenerated by the Lord “into a living hope, into an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance, kept unfading in the heavens.” And golden lily blossoms were fittingly made on the lampstand of the house of God, because divine Scripture, rejecting temporal joys, habitually urges us to desire the good things of the heavenly homeland.

Just as the lampstand, erected on high, has golden lily blossoms and lamps at its summit, so all the elect who are contained in that sacred Scripture are shown, with their minds raised toward the heights, to have sought and received heavenly goods from the Lord.

“And the hinges of the doors of the inner house of the temple, the Holy of Holies, and of the doors of the house of the temple, were of gold, etc.”

If the doors of the inner house of the Holy of Holies are the angelic ministries that open for us, when we depart from the body, the entrance to heavenly life, and if the doors of the house of the temple are the holy teachers and priests who, by instructing, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, first open for us the thresholds of the present Church, what are the hinges of both sets of doors except the minds and hearts of those same angels and holy men? By these they adhere immovably to the contemplation and love of their Creator, so that they may rightly fulfill the ministry divinely entrusted to them, precisely because they never turn their eyes from the will of the one whom they serve.

The doors are opened and closed at the appropriate time, but at no time do they leave their hinges, because angels and holy men, whether in this life receiving the faithful through faith or in the other life receiving the elect through hope, always keep their minds fixed at the root of inward love. Hence it is rightly said that those same hinges were made of gold, whether on account of the splendor of their own merit or on account of the love that they possess for him.

“And Solomon completed all the work that he was doing in the house of the Lord.”

Solomon completes the work that he was doing in the house of the Lord when our peaceful King glorifies all the elect with the immortality of the resurrection on the last day. Otherwise, as long as the present condition of this world continues, Solomon does indeed carry out the work of the house of the Lord, but he does not yet complete it, because the Lord inspires and assists the hearts of the elect so that they may do good, yet grants no one who remains in this life to be without sin. That gift is reserved for the blessedness of the future life.

He completes every work of his temple and makes it suitable for dedication when he brings his elect, transferred from this life, into the eternal kingdom. This is also well signified by the fact that the temple was built in seven years but completed and dedicated in the eighth. For the whole of this time revolves through seven days; the eighth is the day of the future judgment and resurrection, concerning which the sixth and eleventh psalms received their titles. To this time the following appropriately pertains:

“And he brought in the things that David his father had sanctified, silver and gold and vessels, and placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord.”

Silver pertains to the brilliance of eloquence, gold to the splendor of wisdom, and vessels in general to rational creatures. David, Solomon’s father, sanctifies silver when God strengthens the eloquent, by the grace of his Spirit, to speak the word of the Gospel. He sanctifies gold when, filling those endowed with natural intelligence with his Spirit, he enlightens them to contemplate the wonders in his Law. He sanctifies vessels when, having generally bestowed the grace of the same Spirit on all the children of the Church, he inflames them to love and desire the gifts of everlasting salvation.

Solomon brings this silver, this gold, and these sanctified vessels into the temple when our Lord, after the universal judgment has been completed, introduces all the elect—the assembly of teachers as well as of the rest of the faithful—into the joy of the heavenly kingdom. He places vessels of various kinds, whether silver or gold, in the treasuries of the house of the Lord when he “hides” those who have deserved to enjoy the abundance of his sweetness “in the secret place of his face, away from the disturbance of men” (Ps. XXX).

There are appropriately many treasuries in which the vessels of election are stored, but there is one house of the Lord in which those treasuries have been made, because there is one Church in which all the elect are contained, however much they differ in merits; and there is one, not a different, heavenly homeland promised to all the elect, although “as star differs from star in brightness, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV). The Lord himself, who is the judge of both and the distributor of rewards, demonstrated this in one sentence when he said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

## CHAPTER VIII

That when the ark of the Lord was brought into the oracle of the temple, into the Holy of Holies, its poles no longer appeared outwardly as they had formerly been accustomed to appear.—Concerning the fact that the cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud; and concerning the dedication of the temple by Solomon and the people of Israel.

(CHAP. VIII.) “And the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place, into the oracle of the temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above. And when the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the oracle, they no longer appeared outwardly; and they have remained there to the present day. In the ark there was nothing except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel as they came out of the land of Egypt, etc.”

The statement that the ark was brought into the Holy of Holies and that, although the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary, they no longer appeared outwardly, is written more clearly in the book of Chronicles: “The poles,” it says, “by which they carried the ark, because they were somewhat longer, had their ends visible before the oracle. But if anyone had been a little farther outside, he could not see them.”

Here it should be noted that, although the ends of the poles were visible before the oracle to those who came nearer and looked more carefully, it could not happen that the ends themselves projected before the oracle. For plainly, when the oracle was closed and the veil was hung before its doors, the poles also, together with the ark and the cherubim, necessarily had to be hidden inside. This could not have happened if the projecting poles had occupied the space needed for closing the doors.

Scripture took care to explain the position of these poles so carefully not without reason, but with regard to a great sacramental mystery. For it is clear that the outer house of the temple signifies the Church journeying on earth, while the Holy of Holies signifies the inward happiness of the heavenly homeland.

The ark brought into the Holy of Holies typologically announces the humanity of Christ, assumed and brought within the veil of the royal heaven. The poles by which that ark was carried signify the preachers of the word, through whom he himself became known to the world.

In the ark there was a golden urn containing manna, because “in Christ the man dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. II). There was Aaron’s rod, which, though cut off, had blossomed again (Num. XVII), because all power of judging belongs to him whose judgment seemed to have been taken away in the humility of his passion. There were also the tablets of the covenant, because “in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II).

The poles by which it was carried adhered to it, because the teachers who once labored in the word of Christ now rejoice together in the glory of Christ through his present vision. For one of them said of himself, “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I), and thereby left this to be understood of all his fellow laborers.

The ends of the poles appeared outside before the oracle not always, but when it happened that the doors of that oracle were opened; nor did they appear to everyone, but only to those who approached first and strove to look more attentively at what was inside. Only those who had entered the oracle were permitted to see what the ark itself was like and how it had been placed, because no saint who is still situated in this life, even if he raises himself greatly in the height of his mind, fully beholds the glory of his Redeemer there; only the citizens of that homeland do so.

The poles have also been hidden with the ark in the oracle, because even now all the perfect elect who went before us from the world are hidden “in the secret place of God’s face, away from the disturbance of men” (Ps. XXX). Yet the ends of those poles are sometimes seen by those who approach when the oracle is opened, whenever divine grace grants those who are more perfect and who purify the eye of their hearts with undivided purpose to contemplate something of the joy of the heavenly citizens. This contemplation is not granted to those who have withdrawn a little farther away, because the more they remain outside with wandering minds, the less they see what the inward joys are.

“And it came to pass, when the priests had gone out from the sanctuary, that the cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord, etc.” (From Gregory.)

The fact that the cloud filled the house of the Lord and the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud signifies the proud pontiffs and teachers of the Jews. While they disdain to investigate the mysteries of Christ’s birth, they lost the ministry owed by their faith through the cloud of error. The darkness of unbelief filled their minds so completely that, as their own merits demanded, they did not recognize the worship of faith.

The cloud, therefore, filled the Synagogue, that is, the house of the Lord. And the priests could not minister because of the cloud, because, while they disdainfully neglected to investigate the mystical meanings in the Old Testament, hidden beneath the veil of the letter amid the obscurities of allegories, they lost the ministry owed by their faith because of the cloud.

It was then in the cloud of his teaching that the Lord uttered his voice to them, when he spoke openly even about himself. For what is clearer than, “I and the Father are one” (John X)? But because the minds of his hearers had been filled with the darkness of unbelief, the intervening cloud hid it like a sunbeam that had been sent forth.

“And King Solomon and the children of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord.”

The temple of the Lord is the holy Church, as was shown above. Christ the King dedicated it when he cleansed it with his blood, sanctified it by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and multiplied it with diverse gifts of virtue.

The children of Israel also dedicate it with him when each of the faithful, according to the gift bestowed upon him by God, strives through the word of preaching and works of virtue to turn his neighbors, as many as he can, toward better and more perfect things. “The temple of God,” says the Apostle, “is holy, which you are” (I Cor. III).

But the King and the people, the head and the members, do not bring this sanctification to completion equally, because John says of Christ: “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John I). Hence Paul says: “So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III).

But how much human dedication is worth, the same Apostle explains afterward when he says: “He who plants and he who waters are one; and each will receive his own reward according to his labor. For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (ibid.), etc.

Therefore, he himself sanctifies his temple by inhabiting it as God and Lord, while we do so by living in a manner worthy of his dwelling. It follows:

“On that day he sanctified the middle of the court that was before the house of the Lord. For he made there a burnt offering and a sacrifice and the fat of peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the Lord was too small and could not contain the burnt offering and the sacrifice and the fat of the peace offerings.”

What, then, does it mean that Solomon sanctified the middle of the court, offering there a burnt offering and a sacrifice because the bronze altar, which according to the ordinance of the Law had been placed before the doors of the temple, could not contain everything, except that Christ now fully accomplishes in the Catholic Church those things which, because of its weakness, could not be completed in the Law?

For it—the Catholic Church—is the court of the house of the Lord, because through it entrance is opened into the temple of the Lord, namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. Since, therefore, all the burnt offerings and sacrifices could not be offered upon the typological altar of the Old Testament, because everything there was done figuratively, our King and Priest raised up a new altar of faith in the Catholic Church, upon which rich burnt offerings and acceptable sacrifices are offered spiritually to God every day.

Hence the Lord, rejecting the old sacrifice, says through the prophet: “I did not desire burnt offerings and the blood of victims” (Isa. I). And again, approving the sacrifice of the New Testament, he spoke through the Prophet in the Psalms: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX).

“Therefore Solomon held a solemn festival at that time, and all Israel with him, a very great multitude, from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, before the Lord our God, etc.” (From Bede.)

The statement that Solomon held a solemn festival, and all Israel with him—a very great multitude from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt—before the Lord, signifies by the entrance of Hamath the northern region of the Promised Land, and by the brook or torrent of Egypt, as Chronicles calls it (II Chron. VII), the southern region.

I think it will please the reader if I set down at greater length some material from the words of Saint Jerome.

(From Jerome.) It is written in the book of Numbers, where the whole Promised Land is divided in brief speech according to its four regions:

“The southern region shall begin from the wilderness of Zin, which is beside Edom, and shall have its boundaries opposite the east, at the Salt Sea. They shall go around the southern region by the ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass through Senna and reach the south as far as Kadesh-barnea. From there the boundaries shall go out to a village named Addar, and extend as far as Azmon; and the boundary shall turn from Azmon to the torrent of Egypt and end at the shore of the Great Sea” (Num. XXXIV).

In the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel this is expressed as follows:

“The southern region, toward the south, shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Meriboth—that is, of contradiction—and Kadesh also, and the torrent as far as the Great Sea” (Ezek. XLVII).

This signifies that the boundary circles the exceedingly great wilderness of Zin, which is beside Edom, and the Red Sea; then, by the ascent of the Scorpion, through Senna and Kadesh-barnea, and the court or village of Addar and Azmon, it reaches the torrent that flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura.

This southern boundary begins at Tamar, a city in the wilderness, which Solomon also built with marvelous works and which is today called Palmyra. In Hebrew too it is called Tamar, which in our language means “palm.” It extends as far as the waters of contradiction, Kadesh, which is undoubtedly in the wilderness, and the torrent entering the Great Sea, the sea that stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine.

The book of Numbers continues:

“The western region shall begin at the Great Sea, and shall be closed by the same boundary” (Num. XXXIV).

That is, from sea to sea: from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, to the place where Hamath is, a city of Syria. Ezekiel also names it in this region:

“The boundary,” he says, “from the sea to the Great Sea shall be directly from the border, until you come to Hamath” (Ezek. XLVII).

It is now called Epiphany—or Epiphania—the name having been changed after Antiochus, the cruelest of tyrants; for he had the surname Epiphanes.

The book of Numbers continues:

“On the northern side,” it says, “the boundaries shall begin from the Great Sea, proceeding as far as the highest mountain; from there you shall come to Hamath, as far as the boundaries of Sedad. The boundaries shall go on to Sephrona and the village of Enan. These shall be the boundaries on the northern side” (Num. XXXIV).

The Hebrews say that the northern region begins at the Great Sea, which extends along the shores of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria—which is called Coele—Cilicia, and through Egypt reaches Libya.

When it says, “proceeding as far as the highest mountain,” those same Hebrews believe that it signifies either Mount Amanus or Taurus, which seems more likely to us. “The boundaries,” it says, “shall go on to Sephrona.” For this reason they now call a town of Cilicia Zephium.

As for what follows, “and the village of Enan,” in place of which Aserenan is written in Hebrew—meaning “the court of the fountain”—this is the boundary of Damascus. Hence Ezekiel says:

“And the boundary shall be from the sea to the court of Enon, or Aserenan, the boundary of Damascus” (Ezek. XLVII).

Thus the northern region extends from north to north.

“From there,” he says, “they shall measure the boundaries toward the eastern region, from the village of Enan as far as Sephania; and from Sephania the boundaries shall descend to Rebla, opposite the fountain. From there they shall reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth, and extend as far as the Jordan, and finally end at the most salty sea” (Num. XXXIV).

From the end of the northern region, namely, the court of Enan, the boundaries extend as far as Sephania, which the Hebrews call Aphamia. From Aphamia the boundaries descend to Rebla, which is now called Antioch in Syria.

And so that you may know that this Rebla signifies the city now most famous in Coele-Syria, the text continues: “opposite the fountain.” This plainly signifies Daphne, whose fountain supplies the aforesaid city with an abundance of water.

“From there,” it says, “the boundaries shall reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth,” that is, the lake of Tiberias. It is called a sea, although it has fresh water, according to the idiom of Scripture, which calls gatherings of waters “seas.”

“And they shall extend,” it says, “as far as the Jordan, and finally end at the sea,” either the Dead Sea or, as others think, the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Ahila is situated.

The book of Kings next relates that the aforesaid festival was celebrated by Solomon and the children of Israel for seven days and seven days—that is, fourteen days—and that the people were dismissed on the eighth day. We must consider how the same matter is written in Chronicles:

“Therefore Solomon held a solemnity at that time for seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of Egypt. And he made an assembly on the eighth day, because he had dedicated the altar for seven days and celebrated the solemnity for seven days. Therefore, on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, he dismissed the people to their tents” (II Chron. VII).

But I think that nothing else is intended here except that, when the seven days of the temple’s dedication had been completed, the days of the Feast of Booths followed. According to the Law, this feast began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (Lev. XXIII) and ended on the twenty-second day. When both festivals had therefore been properly completed, and the eighth day of the Feast of Booths had ended, King Solomon dismissed the people to their dwellings, rejoicing and exulting over the good that the Lord had done for David, Solomon, and his people Israel.

(From Josephus.) Josephus appears to support this understanding, saying:

“Solomon therefore dismissed the assembly after he had celebrated sacrifices for himself and for all the Hebrews—namely, twenty-two thousand calves and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. For it was then that sacrifices were first celebrated in the temple, and all the Hebrews feasted together with their wives and children. In addition, the king, celebrating before the temple the festival called the Feast of Booths, feasted with all his people together, with great splendor and magnificence, for fourteen days.

“When these things had been sufficiently provided and nothing was lacking in the worship of divine piety, each person, dismissed by the king, returned to his own home, giving thanks to the king for the providence he had shown and for the works he had accomplished, and praying to God that he might grant them Solomon as king for a long time. As they returned, they went forth in great joy and delight, singing aloud, so that they reached their homes in that happiness without weariness.”

Mystically, the fact that Solomon, after completing the work of the temple, celebrated a festival, and all Israel with him—a very great multitude from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt—before the Lord God signifies the inward joy that the saints perpetually possess with their king Christ, the true Peacemaker. Nor do the very places by which the boundaries of the land of Israel are described, namely Hamath and the Brook of Egypt, contradict this interpretation. For Hamath is interpreted as “the Lord’s truth.” And what better can we understand by the brook or torrent of Egypt than temporal death? Since no one dwelling in Egypt—that is, in the darkness of this world—can escape it, as the Prophet testifies, saying: “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” (Psalm XVIII). Hence it is written in the Psalm concerning that very Mediator of God and human beings: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Psalm CIX). The torrent was the turbulent persecution of the Jews, from which the Lord Christ drank on the way—that is, in this life—while he endured it in the body. But when it says “on the way,” this is shown in the Latin expression, and a very swift passage is indicated, by which travelers customarily journey to another dwelling.

“For Christ,” because of the merit of his glorious Passion, “was given the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians II). Therefore all Israel, from the Brook of Egypt to Hamath, celebrates a festival with Solomon when, after the end of the present life, the saints truly enjoy eternal joys with the Lord Christ.

The fact that they celebrated the same festival for seven and seven days may signify that the elect, enlightened by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, rejoice now in hope during this life, which proceeds according to the number seven of its days; and that then, in the true Sabbath—that is, in the future rest of souls—they will rejoice in the perception of truth. The fact that what follows says that on the eighth day Solomon dismissed the people, who departed blessing the king, each to his own tent, rejoicing with an eager heart over all the good things that the Lord had done for David his servant and for his people Israel, signifies that after the end of this life, and after the Sabbath-rest of the holy souls who now rest before the day of judgment, in the eighth age—that is, on the day of the resurrection—the saints will receive immortal bodies and will be placed in heavenly dwellings according to the qualities of the blessed. There they will always rejoice with an eager heart, [Col. 0190A] exulting and praising God for all the good things that almighty Father has bestowed upon the Christian people in the Lord Christ.

## CHAPTER IX. How, after building the temple and the royal palace, Solomon built many cities and fortified with walls the villages belonging to them; and how three times each year he offered burnt offerings; and how he established a fleet to bring gold from Ophir

**(CHAPTER IX.)** “King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee. Hiram went out from Tyre to see the towns that Solomon had given him; but they did not please him, and he said: ‘Are these the cities that you have given me, brother?’ And he called them the land of Chabul to this day, etc.” (From Josephus.)

Josephus relates the matter as follows: “The king of Tyre contributed much gold and silver toward the building, as well as cedar and cypress timber; Solomon in turn repaid him with great compensations, sending him each year wheat, wine, and oil, commodities that he especially needed because, as we have said, he lived on an island. In addition, he gave him twenty cities in the region of Galilee, situated not far from Tyre. After he had gone around them and examined them, and the gift had displeased him, he sent to Solomon and said that he had no need of the cities. From that time they were called the land of Gabalon; for in the Phoenician language the name signifies ‘to displease.’”

Yet in the book of Hebrew names we find *Chabul* interpreted as “a shoot” or “sprout.” We do not find how this name can mean “to displease,” unless perhaps it was said ironically: “a shoot,” since it did not produce the fullness of fruits.

“Therefore Solomon built Gezer, and Lower Beth-horon, and Baalath, and Tamar in the land of the wilderness, and all the villages belonging to them; and he fortified whatever was without a wall, etc.”

The cities that Solomon is said to have built—namely, Millo and the wall of Jerusalem, Ezer, Megiddo, Gezer, Beth-horon, Baalath, and Tamar—signify the beauty of the holy Church, which the true Solomon prepared for himself, in the joy of his kingdom, for praise and everlasting gladness. Millo is interpreted as “fulfillment”; Ezer as “separated” or “sanctified”; Megiddo as “his upper room”; Gezer as “cutting off” or “division”; Beth-horon as “house of the mountains”; and Baalath as “ascending.”

The holy Church, therefore, is itself “the city of the living God” (Hebrews XII), where the will of God is fulfilled every day. It has been separated from every error of unbelievers and sanctified in faith and good works. In it there is refreshment in the virtues; it distinguishes the clean from the unclean and virtues from vices; and it is the house of the mountains—that is, the dwelling place of the saints. Like a palm tree, flowering with the fruit of righteousness, it “goes from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Psalm LXXXIII). Solomon fortified all the villages belonging to these cities and everything that was without a wall, because Christ has so fortified the assembly of his faithful by the protection of his grace that they might always remain unconquerable by spiritual enemies.

“Solomon made tributaries to this day all the people who remained of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not of the children of Israel; that is, their descendants who remained in the land, whom the children of Israel could not exterminate. But Solomon did not appoint any of the children of Israel to serve; they were warriors, his ministers, princes, and commanders.”

Our Peacemaker made tributaries of all the people who were not of the children of Israel, since he keeps under his power those who are not numbered among the children but are placed in a servile condition, and employs each of them for his own service. Whether Jews, Gentiles, or heretics, they remain under his dominion, because he is the ruler of all and uses them according to his will. All things are placed within his will, and no one can resist it. Although such people oppose him in many ways, they often serve the needs of the Church, since in the present time they provide necessities and offer assistance from their own resources (Acts XV).

But concerning the children of Israel—that is, those who are not children of the slave woman but are free, whom the Son of God himself liberated by his blood (Galatians IV)—our Solomon did not appoint anyone to serve, because he compels no one to live according to a pagan rite, nor does he compel anyone to observe the ceremonies of the old law in the time of the New Testament. Rather, he makes them warriors, fighting against spiritual wickedness with the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians VI); and makes them his ministers, offering him spiritual service in good works (Romans VI, VII, VIII); and princes and judges, so that they may rule themselves well and subdue the wantonness of the flesh (Galatians V), or so that they may govern their subjects well and lead them along the path of righteousness.

What follows—“There were five hundred and fifty appointed as overseers over all Solomon’s works; they had the people under them and commanded them in their assigned tasks”—signifies, does it not, those who by the grace of the Holy Spirit are worthy to possess knowledge of the Lord’s law and are able to govern both themselves and others well? On the fiftieth day after Passover, therefore, the law was given in the Old Testament on Sinai (Exodus XX), and in the New Testament the Paraclete Spirit came upon the apostles and those who were with them (Acts II).

“The king Solomon also offered burnt offerings and peace offerings three times each year upon the altar that he had built for the Lord, and he burned incense before the Lord, etc.”

Our Peacemaker likewise offers burnt offerings to the Lord three times each year, when in his members he presents to God “an acceptable sacrifice” through faith in the Holy Trinity (Romans XII). Each believer offers a burnt offering to the Lord when, by disciplining the body, he mortifies it and hastens to consume all the desires of the flesh in the fire of the Holy Spirit. He offers peace offerings when he presents the gift of good works. He offers sacrifices when he expends the vows of his lips in the praise of the Lord.

He must offer all these things upon the altar that he built for the Lord, because whatever he undertakes in abstinence, in good works, and in thanksgiving should be offered wholly to God with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit upon the altar of the heart, where the divine fire ought always to burn—that is, where the flame of charity ought always to blaze. Thus he will burn incense before the Lord when he prepares pure prayer for God in the secrecy of his heart and asks for what is worthy and pleasing to God. But one who asks for transitory things and for what belongs to worldly luxury is not said to burn incense before the Lord, because he is not shown to pray with a pure conscience.

“Solomon also made a fleet at Ezion-geber, which is beside Elath on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. Hiram sent his servants in the fleet, sailors and men experienced in the sea, together with Solomon’s servants. When they had come to Ophir, they brought from there four hundred and twenty talents of gold to King Solomon.” (From Jerome.)

Ezion-geber is said to have been an island not far from Elath on the Red Sea, where the fleet of Jehoshaphat of that period was wrecked. Ophir is the name of a province, named after Ophir, one of the descendants of Eber. Those who came from his line are said to have lived from the river Rosna as far as the region of Judea called Hieria, as Josephus relates.

I therefore think that the fleet Solomon made at Ezion-geber—which is interpreted as “hastening,” “strong,” or “manfully”—is none other than the Church of the faithful. Set upon the sea of this world, it devotes itself to acquiring the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and the riches of the virtues. There are Hiram’s servants there, sailors and men experienced in the sea, together with Solomon’s servants, while Gentiles educated in secular wisdom are joined in the unity of faith with those who are learned in the law of Moses.

Our Solomon sends these people to Ophir—which is interpreted as “weakening”—so that they may bring back to him the gold acquired there, when he commands them to seek a precious meaning within the lowliness of the letter. Thus they bring to the king the total of four hundred and twenty talents of gold when, in the two Testaments, they discover the precious meaning of history, allegory, tropology, and anagoge, and attribute and offer it to wisdom and divine counsel.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the queen of Sheba, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom; how Solomon made supports for the house of the Lord from thyine wood, etc.; and how he was magnified above all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom

**[Col. 0192D] (CHAPTER X.)** “The queen of Sheba also, having heard of Solomon’s fame, came in the name of the Lord to test him with riddles. She entered Jerusalem with a very great retinue and riches, with camels carrying spices, an exceedingly great quantity of gold, and precious stones. She came to Solomon and spoke to him about everything that was in her heart, etc.”

The queen of the South, who, coming from the remotest regions, was stirred up to desire to hear Solomon’s wisdom, already prefigured the Church that was to come from the Gentiles, desiring Christ. She was the one who, according to the Prophet, “is clothed in embroidered garments, in a robe of gold,” and who “has forgotten her own people and her father’s house” (Psalm XLIV); she ran with a barbarian people, though not with a barbarian mind. In outward appearance she was a foreigner, but inwardly she desired to become a citizen of the saints.

Therefore she is considered worthy not only of the heavenly reward of resurrection, but also, by apostolic authority, of judging adulterous Jews at the very word of the Judge, because, admiring Christ in Solomon, she had fulfilled in a mystical image the disposition of the true heavenly queen, the Church. Hence Queen Sheba herself, astonished at Solomon and his glory, said because of his wisdom:

“True is the report that I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came myself and saw with my own eyes and proved that scarcely half had been told me. Your wisdom and your works are greater than the report that I heard, etc.”

This aptly applies to the holy Church, which, having heard of Christ’s miracles, was moved to seek him. But after it came to him through baptism and faith, and, considering the testimonies of Holy Scripture, recognized the power of his divinity, everything previously told to it about him seemed small in comparison with what it had perceived. Therefore, in wonder, it breaks forth into his praise, saying:

“Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants, who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God, who was pleased with you and set you upon the throne of Israel, because the Lord loved Israel forever and appointed you king, so that you might administer judgment and righteousness.”

The Psalmist likewise brought forth similar words, burning with desire for the heavenly kingdom and speaking in the person of the saints:

“How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God.” And shortly afterward: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm LXXXIII).

Those, therefore, are blessed and truly blessed whose king is Christ, and who are worthy to enjoy his eternal vision, to behold his glory, which he possesses with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and to receive perpetually the wisdom by which he deigns to reveal himself to the pure in heart (Matthew V). Thus they will prove true what is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah LXIV; I Corinthians II).

“King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything that she desired and asked of him, apart from what he had freely offered her as a royal gift.”

Our Peacemaker will give everything she asks to the true queen, namely his Church, concerning whom it is written: “You have granted him the desire of his soul and have not withheld from him the request of his lips” (Psalm XX). And in the Gospel he himself says: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XV). He freely bestows not only what we ask, but also what human frailty either does not know how to ask for or presumes to request.

“The king made supports for the house of the Lord and for the royal palace from thyine wood, and citherns and lyres for the singers. Such thyine wood had not been brought or seen to the present day, etc.” (From Josephus.)

Josephus relates the matter as follows: “At the same time, precious stones and pine-like wood were brought to the king from the land called the Golden Land. They seemed suitable for strengthening the temple and the royal palace and for making musical instruments. From them he made citherns and nablas, so that the Levites might sing a hymn to God. Of all the things ever brought to the king, none surpassed them in size and beauty. Let no one suppose that they were like the pine wood that is now called by that name because of the price at which merchants sell it. Those pieces were indeed round in appearance, like pine wood, but much whiter and exceedingly lustrous. I have said this so that no one might be ignorant of the nature of the true pine.”

It is rightly said that King Solomon made supports for the house of the Lord and the royal palace, and citherns and lyres for the singers, from precious wood, because our Creator places precious trees—that is, holy teachers whose faith never withers and whose leaves of words never fall, but who produce the fruit of good works in their season (Psalm I)—as a protection for the house of God and the royal palace, that is, for the strengthening of his Church. Surrounded on every side by their teachings and examples, the Church does not suffer the collapse caused by errors and sins.

Such men are rightly said to have been fashioned like citherns and lyres for praising the Lord, because “everything they do prospers” (ibid.), and they do not cease to proclaim the Lord’s praise in adversity and prosperity, in heart, mouth, and action. According to the Apostle (Colossians III), whatever they do in word or deed, they do everything for the glory of God. Concerning them it is said through the Prophet in the person of the Lord: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they will never be silent, praising the name of the Lord” (Isaiah LXII).

“The king Solomon also made two hundred shields of pure gold; six hundred shekels of gold were assigned to the plates of one shield; and three hundred shields of tested gold, for three hundred minas of gold covered one shield. The king placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon, etc.”

In the Books of Chronicles it is likewise written: “King Solomon made two hundred golden spears, six hundred gold pieces being expended on each spear, and also three hundred golden shields, three hundred gold pieces covering each shield. The king placed them in the armory that was built in the woodland” (II Chronicles IX).

The golden shields and spears, which were used—as is shown below—by the commanders who kept watch before the entrance of the royal palace, signify nothing other than the spiritual armor possessed by holy preachers. They guard the house of God and keep watch at its entrance so that they may block access to cunning plotters and prevent them from deceiving the innocent. Concerning them it is written in the Song of Songs: “Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed, chosen from the mighty men of Israel; all hold swords and are most skilled in war” (Song of Songs III). (From Bede.)

Holy preachers defend the present rest and peace of the Church against the attacks of heretics, while the more perfect among them watch with fixed attention over the inward rest of the heavenly homeland. It is rightly added by repetition: “chosen from the mighty men of Israel.” For Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” All who strive toward the joys of divine vision are rightly designated by the name Israel. But among them those are most mighty who are exalted either by the gift of heavenly contemplation or who properly undertake the ministry of preaching.

They are also fittingly designated by the number sixty, because such people await the tenfold reward of eternal recompense for the perfection of good works. “All holding swords and most skilled in war”—holding those swords of which the Apostle says: “Take also the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI). They are most skilled in those wars about which the same Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (ibid.), etc.

They are rightly called most skilled, because those who, enclosed in flesh and set upon the earth, fight against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places need great skill in warfare. Indeed, they need great skill and great grace from God, since the frailty of the flesh fights against an archangel who has been trained in warfare for so many thousands of years.

Thus it is rightly said that two hundred spears were made from a total of six hundred shekels, because the fathers of both Testaments are known to be perfect in teaching and conduct, since whatever they taught in speech they proved by good examples. The three hundred shields, each covered with three hundred gold pieces, signify their perfect faith, which they held in the confession of the Holy Trinity.

It is therefore fitting that the guardians of God’s house carry golden spears and shields, because holy preachers, who are guardians of the holy Church, shine with the brightness of heavenly wisdom; they pierce enemies with the javelins of their words and extinguish the fiery darts of the wicked one by repelling them with the shield of sacred faith.

The statement that “the king placed them in the house of the forest of Lebanon” aptly agrees with this mystery. For what does the forest of Lebanon signify except the Church of the Gentiles, which, cut down from the growth of pride, is suitably fitted into the structure of the house of God? Hence the Psalmist says: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm CXXXI), etc.

“The king Solomon also made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with very pure gold. It had six steps. The top of the throne was rounded at the back, and there were two hands on either side holding the seat; two lions stood beside each hand, and twelve young lions stood upon the six steps, on either side, etc.”

The throne that King Solomon made is therefore rightly understood as the holy Church, in which our Peacemaker is recognized as reigning and administering his judgments. For the soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. It is fittingly remembered that the throne was made of ivory—not merely because this refers to riches, but because the elephant, whose bones these are, is said to possess extraordinary chastity. Among four-footed animals it has great intelligence; it mates temperately with its female and does not take a second wife. This is suitably applied to chaste souls, for those are known to have been ivory who followed the commandments of Christ the Lord through chastity.

“He overlaid it with very pure gold.”

He caused the splendor of his glory to shine within it when, through signs and miracles, he displayed the power of his majesty.

“This throne had six steps.”

What is signified by the number six except the perfection of good works? “For six days God completed the adornment of the world, and on the seventh he rested from his works” (Genesis II). Moreover, six is the first number recognized as perfect through its parts. It has one-half, three; one-third, two; and one-sixth, one; and one, two, and three make six.

Since the world also consists of six ages, in which it is permitted to work, let anyone who desires to reach the heavenly homeland hasten to ascend by good works, because unless one ascends by good deeds, one cannot reach it. It follows:

“And the top of the throne was rounded at the back.”

For what does the rounded shape of the throne at the back signify except eternal rest, which will be future for the saints after this life? There everyone who labors well in this life is rewarded with the recompense of his work and enjoys everlasting rest.

Hence, in the Song of Songs, this same throne is mentioned under another example, where it is said: “King Solomon made for himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver, its back-rest of gold, and its purple ascent; its interior he paved with love” (Song of Songs III). (From Bede.)

It is called a litter because it either carries the bodies of those sitting or reclining at a banquet, or because it is customarily carried from place to place as circumstances require. The holy Church is rightly compared with it, since by the ministry of its preachers it carries believers to the refreshment of eternal life.

The litter of our king is therefore the holy Church, constructed from the strong fathers, as from incorruptible cedar woods, in the minds of believers. It is rightly called a litter because each day it carries souls to the eternal banquet of its Creator. The litter has pillars made of silver, because holy preachers shine with the light of eloquence.

Upon the silver pillars there is a golden back-rest, because through what the holy preachers proclaim clearly, the minds of their hearers discover the radiance of inward glory in which they may rest. Again, he made a back-rest in the litter when he promised the faithful hope of perpetual rest: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI).

He made this back-rest of gold because he prepared for us eternal rest, radiant with the glory of his divine vision. And no ascent to this litter is found except a purple one, because no one enters the Church unless imbued with the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion. Hence he himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John VI).

“He paved its interior with love, because of the daughters of Jerusalem.”

That is, with the very love by which he suffered for us. “Greater love than this no one has, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). This is what he added: “because of the daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, because of souls burning with desire for heavenly things. The greater the love that God commended to us by suffering for us, the more people he inflamed to love him in return and to suffer for him.

“And there were two hands, on either side, holding the seat.”

What do the two hands holding Solomon’s seat signify except the consolations of divine grace, which raise the holy Church to the heavenly kingdom? These are aptly described by the number two, because this is preached and especially commended in both Testaments. For no good can be accomplished except through divine assistance (I Corinthians III; Philippians II). Hence Truth itself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

“And two lions stood beside each hand.”

What are signified by the lions except the fathers of both Testaments, who learned to rule both themselves and others well through strength of spirit? “Two lions therefore stood beside the hands,” because in the Law and in the Gospel the holy fathers attributed whatever good they did not to themselves but to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, because of your mercy and your truth” (Psalm CXLIV). And the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (II Corinthians XV). Again: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (Jeremiah IX; I Corinthians I).

It follows: “And twelve young lions stood upon the six steps, on either side.”

What are signified by the twelve young lions except the order of preachers who follow apostolic teaching? They stand above the six steps on either side because they strive to strengthen the steps of good works on every side by their teachings and examples, so that the devout labor of those beginning well in their work may not falter, but may firmly preserve uprightness in the progress of the virtues.

What follows—“No work like this was made in all the kingdoms”—aptly applies to the holy Church, concerning which it is written: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day. Her sons rose up and called her most blessed, and her husband praised her. Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Proverbs XXXI).

It follows:

“But all the vessels from which King Solomon drank were of gold, and all the furnishings of the house of the forest of Lebanon were of purest gold. Silver was not valued, nor was it considered of any worth in the days of Solomon, etc.”

All the vessels that serve the ministry of our Peacemaker are made of gold, because all the souls of the saints, which are God’s vessels, shine with the splendor of wisdom and love as they serve the divine will; they contain the water of life, and “it will become in them a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV).

Silver was not valued in the days of Solomon, because, according to the Apostle, “the kingdom of God is not in word but in power” (I Corinthians IV). The preaching of the Gospel does not consist “in persuasive words of human wisdom,” but “in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest in human wisdom but in the power of God” (I Corinthians II).

Hence Truth itself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VII). And again: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew V).

“King Solomon was magnified above all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. And the whole earth desired to see Solomon’s face, to hear his wisdom, which God had given into his heart. Each person brought him gifts, vessels of silver and gold, clothing, and weapons of war.”

It is rightly said that King Solomon was magnified above the kings of the earth, because our Peacemaker is exalted above all the heights of the saints, who are truly called kings, and no one can be compared with him. “For who among the clouds can be equal to the Lord, or who can be like God among the sons of God? God, who is glorified in the council of the saints, is great and fearsome above all who surround him” (Psalm LXXXVIII). And again: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm CXL).

Hence John also says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

“And the whole earth desires to see the face of our king.”

For the whole Church of the saints desires only this: to reach the sight of his glory. Thus it is said through the Prophet: “My heart has said to you, ‘I have sought your face’; your face, Lord, I will seek” (Psalm XXVI). And elsewhere: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm XLI).

“And each person brings him gifts.”

Each person strives to offer God service in word or deed, according to the strength available to him.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the foreign women whom Solomon loved

**(CHAPTER XI.)** “King Solomon loved many foreign women: the daughter of Pharaoh, Moabite women, Ammonite women, Edomite women, Sidonian women, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning whom the Lord had said to the children of Israel: ‘You shall not enter in to them, nor shall they enter in to yours, etc.’” (From Isidore.)

What more shall I say about the rest of Solomon’s deeds? Holy Scripture severely rebukes and condemns him, and makes no mention at all of his repentance or of God’s indulgence toward him; nor does it at all become clear what good he might signify, at least in allegory. This is a lamentable downfall—unless someone should perhaps say that the foreign women, whose love inflamed him, signify the Churches chosen from the Gentiles.

This might perhaps be understood without absurdity if they had abandoned their gods because of Solomon and worshiped his God. But when he offended his own God because of them and worshiped their gods, no good can be inferred from the matter. Nevertheless, I do not think that it signifies nothing; rather, it signifies evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters.

In Solomon’s person there appears an extraordinary excellence and an extraordinary downfall. Therefore what existed in him at different times—first good and afterward evil—is displayed in the Church in this present age at the same time. For I think that his good deeds signify the good people of the Church, while his evil deeds signify the evil people of the Church, as within the unity of one threshing floor, in that one man: the good as grain and the evil as chaff (Matthew III); or within the unity of one field, the good as wheat and the evil as weeds (Matthew XIII).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the division of the ten tribes from the house of David because of Solomon’s sin, and how Rehoboam, abandoning the counsel of the elders, obeyed the persuasion of the young

“It happened at that time that Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, and the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road, covered with a new cloak. They were only two in the field. Ahijah seized the new cloak with which he was covered, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to Jeroboam: ‘Take for yourself ten pieces. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and give you ten tribes. One tribe, however, shall remain for him because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem, the city that I chose from all the tribes of Israel, etc.’”

The fact that after Solomon’s death ten tribes were separated from the house of David while two remained sufficiently indicates what the Apostle says concerning that entire people: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans XI).

Jeroboam, who separated the ten tribes from the house of David and from the temple of God and led them into idolatry, signifies heretics, who love dissension, divide the unity of the Catholic faith by heresies, and thus hand over to the worship of evil spirits those who obey them. Jeroboam is interpreted as “judging the people.” Heretics too seem to judge the people when they make them followers of their error.

The words of the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite, who was sent to Jeroboam, aptly correspond to this matter. He spoke as follows:

“Take for yourself ten pieces. For thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom of Solomon away, and I will give you ten tribes. Yet one tribe shall remain his, for the sake of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city that I chose from all the tribes of Israel.”

Jeroboam received the ten pieces when, by violating the precepts of the Law, he corrupted them. And one tribe remained with David’s offspring, when the lot of the Elect remained, in accordance with apostolic teaching, within the rule of the Catholic faith, because “there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV).

Finally, Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, who abandoned the useful counsel of the elders and followed the advice of young men—although he belonged to the house of David, nevertheless did not walk in his way—for, as Scripture testifies: “Judah did evil in the sight of the Lord in his days, and provoked him beyond all that their fathers had done in their sins, which they had committed. They also built for themselves altars, statues, and sacred groves on every high hill and under every leafy tree. [Col. 0200B] There were also effeminate persons in the land. And they committed all the abominations of the nations, which the Lord had destroyed before the face of the children of Israel” (III Kings XIV).

He therefore signifies wicked rulers in the Church, who, devoted to earthly desires, neglect to care for their subjects and delight in the multitude of those who obey them, yet do not show fitting concern for those entrusted to them. Rehoboam is interpreted as “the breadth of the people,” and those may rightly be called “the breadth of the people” who, walking along the broad and spacious way by which many go to death, refuse to enter the narrow way, which belongs to the few and leads to eternal life (Matt. VII). Abandoning the counsel of the holy Fathers, whose words and examples strive toward the height of perfection, they choose to obey the commands of young men—that is, of those who, enslaved to youthful desires, burden them with wicked praise and flattery.

And what is said through the prophet comes to pass in them: “As is the people, so also is the priest. For all, from the least to the greatest, are intent on greed” (Isa. XXIV; Jer. VI), “and the blind, leading the blind, fall together into the pit of destruction” (Matt. XV). The Wisdom of God threatens such men, saying: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccles. X). Conversely, concerning the holy people and their king, Christ, it continues in praise, saying: “Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes are born at their proper time, because whatever they do shall prosper.”

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the prophet who rebuked Jeroboam for idolatry, but, deceived by a false prophet, ate contrary to the Lord’s command and was therefore killed by a lion on the road

“Behold, a man of God came from Judah by the word of the Lord to Bethel, while Jeroboam was standing beside the altar and offering incense. He cried out against the altar by the word of the Lord and said: ‘Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who now burn incense upon you, and he shall burn human bones upon you,’ etc.”

Therefore, what does the prophet who had been sent by God to Bethel to rebuke Jeroboam for the idolatry he had practiced signify, when he was deceived by a false prophet, ate and drank there contrary to the Lord’s command, and for that reason was killed by a lion on the road, except that when someone is lifted up in heart by prosperity so that he despises the Lord’s commandments, he is torn by the tooth of evil persuasion by the lion “who prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (I Peter V), and is killed through consent to sin?

For this reason it is always necessary to seek the help of almighty God and his protection, and to hope with one’s whole heart in his mercy. (From Gregory.) For what is a human being, whatever his merit may be, if he is abandoned by the protection of his Creator? That protection is thought less necessary when it is always possessed. Yet it is often beneficially withdrawn, so that a person may be shown how utterly he is nothing without it. Thus the hand of God sometimes makes us recognize ourselves through adversity, while, without our knowing it, it carries us through prosperity. For when deprived of support we begin to fall, yet are held up by assistance; and what made us tremble in our fall becomes instruction, while what keeps us standing becomes guardianship.

Let no one, therefore, consider himself possessed of any virtue, even when he is able to act bravely, because if divine protection abandons him, he is suddenly weakened and overwhelmed precisely where he boasts that he is standing firmly. For what are we to make of the fact that the man of God, sent to prophesy against the altar of Samaria, exercised the authority of free speech in the presence of the king, and miraculously stiffened the king’s outstretched arm so that it became rigid, yet soon mercifully restored it to health; and that, when invited into the king’s house, he refused to eat because he had observed the Lord’s command forbidding him to eat on the road—[Col. 0201C] yet on that same road he was both deceived into eating and, after being fed, perished?

What do we gather from this on careful consideration—what, so to speak, do we suspect must be feared—except that perhaps he silently gloried within himself that he had despised the king for the sake of the Lord’s commands? Then, shaken from his inner firmness, he was soon overcome, and from the very place where glory had arisen in his heart, guilt stole upon him in his actions. Thus, deceived by the false prophet’s words, he learned that his resistance to the king’s command had not been due to his own strength.

He rightly received the sentence of death from the mouth of the one whose deception had led him astray from the commands of life, so that he might truly receive punishment from the same source through which he had carelessly incurred guilt.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Shishak, king of Egypt, and how, because of Rehoboam’s sins, he plundered Jerusalem, carrying away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king, as well as the golden shields that Solomon had made, in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers; and concerning the continual war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and between Asa, king of Judah, and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout all their days

“In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak, king of Egypt, came up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures, and carried off everything. He also took the golden shields that Solomon had made. In their place King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers and to those who kept watch before the entrance of the king’s house. Whenever the king entered the house of the Lord, those who held the office of going before him carried them; afterward they returned them to the armory of the shield-bearers, etc.”

The account of this king is related more fully in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written as follows:

“In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak, king of Egypt, came up against Jerusalem, because they had sinned against the Lord, with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. The common people who came with him from Egypt were without number: Libyans, Troglodytes, and Ethiopians. He captured the fortified cities in Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.

“Then Shemaiah the prophet entered to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem while fleeing from Shishak, and said to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: You have abandoned me, and I abandon you into the hand of Shishak.’ The princes of Israel and the king, terrified, said: ‘The Lord is righteous.’

“When the Lord saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying: ‘Because they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them. I will give them a little help, and my wrath shall not drip upon Jerusalem through the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless, they shall serve him, so that they may know the difference between serving me and serving the kingdoms of the earth.’

“Then Shishak, king of Egypt, withdrew from Jerusalem, taking away the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house; he carried everything away with him, including the golden shields that Solomon had made. In their place the king made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers who guarded the vestibule of the palace” (II Chron. XII).

What, then, does it signify figuratively that, because of Rehoboam’s sin, Shishak, king of Egypt, carried away the treasures from the house of the Lord and the royal treasures, except that wicked rulers, because of their negligence, provoke the king of Egypt—that is, the prince of darkness—against Jerusalem in a symbolic sense, namely, against the Church entrusted to them, where he seems for a time to exercise dominion?

He carries away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures when he takes from the careless and negligent both knowledge of the holy Scriptures and the practice of virtues. Shishak is therefore interpreted as “linen of sackcloth,” or “the joy of sackcloth.” Since linen signifies refinement, while sackcloth, which is made from goats’ hair, signifies sins, what can be understood more aptly by “linen of sackcloth” than the cunning of the devil’s deceit in persuading people to sin?

Shishak carries off Jerusalem’s riches when the devil, who deceives craftily and rejoices in the multitude of sins, plunders ecclesiastical persons of spiritual knowledge and virtuous works, and drags those who seemed to be ornaments of the Church, stripped of their riches, down with him into the abyss of his destruction.

The same meaning is also suggested by the fact that this king took away the golden shields Solomon had made, in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers. Solomon made golden shields and gave them to the guardians of his house when our Redeemer entrusted spiritual knowledge, through the two Testaments, to the teachers of the Church for the protection of his people.

The ancient enemy removes this knowledge through the negligence of rulers. For when they are intent on earthly matters and never care for heavenly things, he leaves them stripped of knowledge in their former office, as though they had been robbed of their possessions in their own house.
