Finally, when such men see themselves deprived of spiritual understanding, they seek an abundance of words through eloquence, so that by the sound of their speech, like the strength of bronze shields, they may offer protection against enemies on behalf of those subject to them.

But just as bronze is inferior to gold in value, so empty eloquence is inferior to the fruit of true wisdom. Hence a certain wise man says of eloquence: “Where there are many words, there is often poverty” (Prov. XII). And in the Psalter it is written: “The man of many words shall not be established upon the earth” (Ps. CXXXIX).

For it is written of wisdom: “Wisdom is more precious than all riches, and nothing that is desired can compare with her. Length of days is in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. III).

Whoever wishes to offer the Church suitable defense against heretics and against all enemies must accomplish this by the aid of wisdom. Eloquence without wisdom contributes nothing to this purpose; indeed, it does great harm.

As for what follows, namely, that there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and between Asa, king of Judah, and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout all their days, I think it signifies nothing other than that the holy Church, which persists in the unity of the faith, is always at war with heretics and schismatics and with all who strive to violate the Catholic faith.

“For all who wish to live piously in Christ,” as the Apostle says, “suffer persecution” (II Tim. III). For the ancient dragon persecutes the woman, lying in wait for her heel, and she shall crush his head (Gen. III).

Asa is interpreted as “taking up” or “lifting up,” and Baasha as “confusion” or “dryness.” The people of the Church are rightly called “taking up” or “lifting up,” because they suspend their minds upon heavenly desires, despise the confusion of earthly passions together with their instigator, the devil, and regard them as though they were dry and useless things.

## CHAPTER XV. How the word of the Lord came to Jehu, son of Hanani, against Baasha, king of Israel, foretelling the punishments that would come upon him because he had caused Israel to sin; and concerning Omri, king of Israel, and how he bought the mountain of Samaria; concerning the times of Ahab, and how Hiel of Bethel built Jericho, laying its foundations in Abiram, his firstborn, and setting up its gates in Segub, his youngest son

[Col. 0203D] **(CHAP. XVI.)** “The word of the Lord came to Jehu, son of Hanani, against Baasha, saying: ‘Because I raised you from the dust and appointed you leader over my people Israel, yet you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and caused my people Israel to sin, provoking me with their sins, behold, I will cut off the posterity of Baasha and the posterity of his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam, son of Nebat. Whoever of Baasha dies in the city, the dogs shall eat; and whoever of his people dies in the countryside, the birds of the sky shall eat,’ etc.”

These words are directed against all sinners, and especially against heretics and pagans, since they continually add new sins to their former sins and, corrupted by examples of evil, surpass their predecessors in crimes.

“‘I will cut off,’ he says, ‘the posterity of Baasha and the posterity of his house, and I will make his house like the house of Jeroboam, son of Nebat.’”

The Lord cuts off Baasha’s posterity when he avenges the sins of the wicked after the end of their life. He also cuts off the posterity of his house when he condemns their fellow citizens to eternal torments. He will make Baasha’s house like the house of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, when he hands sinners who persist in their iniquity over to the torments of hell together with the devil and his angels.

Baasha, as we have said, is interpreted as “confusion” or “dryness”; Jeroboam as “dividing the people”; and Nebat as “spontaneous” or “voluntary.” Whoever, therefore, follows the confusion of errors and sins and, neglecting to have the wife of spiritual grace, persists in the dryness of sins until the end of life, will have his posterity cut off like that of the devil. The devil generated death for himself through his own will to be proud, yet he seems to divide the people of the lost when he is recognized as exercising among them not the judgment of equity but the judgment of condemnation.

Then the posterity of sinners and of all the wicked will be cut off, together with their head, the devil, when the Judge of the living and the dead, at the end of the world, will say to those standing at his left: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels. And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV).

“‘Whoever,’ he says, ‘of Baasha dies in the city, the dogs shall eat; and whoever of his people dies in the countryside, the birds of the sky shall eat.’”

What does it mean to die in the city except for someone to remain in the Church as one of the faithful yet become liable to capital crimes? He dies in the city who practices wicked works within the Church of God. He is torn by the mouths of dogs when he is rebuked, convicted, and condemned by the judgments of the holy teachers.

Of these dogs it is written in the Psalm: “They shall go around the city like dogs” (Ps. LVIII). Dogs are so called from *cavere*, “to beware,” because it is the habit of dogs to defend those places where they know that food is to be found.

The city that these dogs surround is Jerusalem, spread universally throughout the world. That Paul went around it, the Letters that resounded throughout all the nations like sacred divine utterances testify, for the salvation of the human race.

O blessed dog, who pursues unbelieving peoples, drives away thieves, and guards the holy sheepfolds, whose barking resounded throughout the entire world like a mighty trumpet!

“‘Whoever,’ he says, ‘of Baasha dies in the countryside, the birds of the sky shall eat.’”

Those from Baasha—that is, from the body of the devil, full of confusion—die in the countryside who, separated outside the Church, serve idolatry or heresies with mouth and detestable works. The birds of the sky eat them, namely those birds of which the Gospel says, in the parable of the sower, that the seed scattered beside the road was eaten by birds (Matt. XIII; Luke VIII). These birds will eat them when, laden with sins, they carry them away with themselves into eternal destruction.

“In the thirty-first year of Asa, king of Judah, Omri reigned over Israel for twelve years; he reigned in Tirzah for six years. He bought the mountain of Samaria from Shemer for two shekels of silver, built upon it, and called the name of the city that he had built by the name of Shemer, the lord of the mountain of Samaria.”

How this happened is made clear by Josephus’s words, in which it is written:

“In the thirtieth year of King Asaph, Omri assumed the kingdom and held it for twelve years. For six of these years he ruled in Tirzah; the remaining years he spent in the city called Maraon, or, in Greek, Samaria. He named it Somareon after a certain Somaros, who had sold him the mountain on which he established the city. In no respect did he differ from the earlier kings, except that he was worse.”

“And Ahab continued in his deeds, provoking the Lord, the God of Israel, beyond all the kings of Israel who had been before him. In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho, etc.” (From Bede.)

What is written concerning the time of Ahab’s reign—“In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. In Abiram, his firstborn, he laid its foundations; and in Segub, his youngest, he set up its gates”—has this clear meaning: when the aforementioned builder of the city began to lay its foundations, his firstborn son, named Abiram, died. And when, after the city had been built, he attempted to fortify its gates, he lost the youngest of his sons, named Segub.

Joshua had foretold that this would happen when, after destroying the city, he consigned it to the ban with a curse: “Cursed before the Lord be the man who rises up and builds this city, Jericho. In his firstborn let him lay its foundations, and in his youngest child let him set up its gates” (Josh. VI).

Since Hiel is interpreted as “uniting with God,” and Bethel as “the house of God,” Hiel of Bethel restores the walls of Jericho, which Joshua had destroyed and placed under a ban, whenever one of those who in the Church had assumed the religious habit returns to the commission of crimes that the Lord Jesus had forgiven him on the day of baptism, and luxuriously resumes the pomp of the devil, which he himself had anathematized.

He also restores Jericho’s ruins when he prefers the doctrines of errors or the fables of the pagans to the ecclesiastical truth with which he had been instructed, as though, going out from Bethel, he were raising Jericho from its ruins. Such a person is deservedly cursed before the Lord, and loses his firstborn in the laying of the foundations of the wicked city and his youngest in the setting up of its gates, because he loses the foundations of faith, from which good buildings ought to begin, and the barriers of good action by which they ought to be completed.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Elijah the Tishbite; how, while hidden by the brook Cherith, ravens fed him, bringing him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening

**(CHAP. XVII.)** “And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Ahab: ‘As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain during these years except according to the word of my mouth,’ etc.” [Col. 0206A]

(From Jerome.) Tishbe, from which Elijah is called the Tishbite, is a city of the region of Gilead.

(From Gregory.) Concerning the statement, “As the Lord God lives, in whose sight I stand,” it should be understood that we come into the sight of the Lord in two ways. First, when here we carefully examine our sins, place ourselves in his sight, and judge ourselves with tears. Second, we come into the sight of the Lord when, at the final judgment, we stand before his tribunal. For whenever we bring the power of our Creator back into our awareness, we stand in his sight.

Thus it is rightly said now through Elijah, the man of God: “As the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, in whose sight I stand.” Here the righteous man stands in God’s sight so that he may live faithfully; there, so that he may truly receive the crown of life.

“And the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Depart from here and go toward the east, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan; and there you shall drink from the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.’ He went, therefore, and acted according to the word of the Lord. When he had gone, he sat beside the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. The ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning, and likewise bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook. After some days the brook dried up, for it had not rained upon the earth, etc.”

What, then, does Elijah signify? His name is interpreted as “the Lord God,” or “my God,” or “the strong God.” Does he signify anyone other than Christ our Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII)?

Our Elijah was hidden at the brook Cherith, which is interpreted as “bald,” and there he drank from the brook, when at the place of Calvary, where the power of his glory was hidden, he tasted from the stream of our mortality.

The ravens fed Elijah, bringing him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening, when the Gentile people, coming from the blackness of sins to Christ the Lord, offer to Christ, who thirsts for our salvation, the bread of faith and the hope of resurrection, having been illumined by his grace. They offer these in the morning, that is, at the beginning of evangelical preaching; and likewise they bring bread and meat in the evening when, preserving the same faith undefiled to the end of the world, they present it to the coming Judge together with the resurrection of the flesh.

After some days the brook dried up, because, when the course of the present age has been completed, “it is swallowed up and perishes; there is neither mourning nor crying, because the former things have passed away” (I Cor. XV; Rev. XXI).

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the widow of Zarephath, who fed the prophet, and whose flour and oil the Lord therefore blessed; and concerning the son of the woman, the head of the household, whom Elijah raised

“And the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Arise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and remain there. For I have commanded a widow there to feed you,’ etc.” (From Bede.)

Elijah is sent to be fed by a foreign widow. This widow signifies the Church of the nations, which, having long been abandoned by its Creator, nourished a people ignorant of true faith and righteousness like a poor son with scanty resources—that is, it instructed a people lacking the fruit of the word—until the prophetic word arrived.

Israel’s fleece having been dried out, as though the door of heaven had been closed (Judg. VI), and Judea suffering from hunger, the prophetic word was there both fed and fed others: it was received by believers and itself refreshed believers.

Thus this same widow is rightly said to have dwelt in Zarephath of Sidon. Sidon is interpreted as “useless hunting,” while Zarephath means “furnace” or “the narrowness of bread.” For “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V). Where the pursuit of acquiring useless things was exercised like the hunting of birds, where the burning of dreadful thirst and the prior scarcity of spiritual bread prevailed, there oil and flour were blessed by the prophetic mouth.

“She intended to gather two pieces of wood before she died.” Here not only the name of the wood but also the number of the pieces expresses the sign of the cross, by which the bread of eternal life has been prepared for us.

Her flour and oil are blessed—that is, the grace of the Lord’s body and the anointing of chrism, or the fruit and joy of charity. When these are expended, they are said not to fail. “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

This widow, whom the Lord fed not with grain but with the bread of the word, is the same one of whom it is said in the Psalm: “Blessing I will bless his widow” (Ps. CXXXI), and so forth—namely, the one of whom the Apostle says: “When her husband is dead, she is free to marry whom she wishes” (I Cor. VII).

When the Law ceased, “whose end is Christ” (Rom. X), the Church, making its passage into the freedom of grace, was joined to Christ as though it were the widow of the Law.

Now the oil of grace and the flour of blessing do not cease in her vessels, while hunger remains in nearly all the nations. The hunger of their life and the famine of their faith in the Trinity were fittingly prefigured by that former three-year famine.

“After these things the son of the woman, the head of the household, became ill, and his illness was so severe that no breath remained in him. Therefore she said to Elijah: ‘What have I to do with you, man of God? Have you come to me so that my iniquities may be remembered and you may kill my son?’ And he said to her: ‘Give me your son.’ He took him from her bosom, carried him up to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him on his bed, etc.”

This act of Elijah in raising the dead son of the widow with whom he was staying, whose flour and oil he had blessed, aptly expresses the act of our Redeemer in raising the people who had been converted to faith.

For what widow can be better understood here than the synagogue of the Jews, widowed by the death of Moses, which was nourishing a little son—that is, the carnal people of the Jews?

At the coming of Elijah, that is, of our Savior, this son became weak, because, by not believing in him but despising him, he suffered from the violent fever of unbelief.

Accordingly, the mother herself, lamenting the child’s sickness before the prophet, says: “What have I to do with you, man of God? Have you come to me so that my iniquities may be remembered and you may kill my son?” So the synagogue of the Jews complained about the Savior’s coming, as though he himself were the cause of the destruction of the Jewish people.

Hence Caiaphas, conspiring with the crowd over Christ’s death, said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI).

But just as the prophet, not provoked by the widow’s words but moved by compassion, said to her, “Give me your son,” and took him from her bosom, carried him up to the upper room where he was staying, laid him on his bed, stretched himself out, and measured himself over the child three times, cried out to the Lord, and said, “My Lord God, let the soul of this child, I pray, return into his body”—so also our Redeemer, not provoked by the malice of the Jews but moved by compassion for the believing people, took him from his mother’s bosom when he removed him from the carnal observance of the Law, and placed him on his bed, that is, showed him that he would have life through his death.

He stretched himself out three times and measured himself over the child when, by preaching and performing healings, he taught him the faith of the Trinity. And crying out to the Father, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XIII). And again: “Father,” he said, “glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you. Just as you gave him authority over all flesh, so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII).

[Col. 0208C] Elijah was heard, “and the child’s soul returned into him, and he revived. He took him and restored him to his mother,” when our Lord, saving the believing people, displayed signs and miracles to unbelievers so that they might truly know that the one who believes in his name lives.

And so it will happen that, overcome by the truth, the Jewish people will proclaim to Christ the words of the woman marveling at the child’s resurrection and say: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning Elijah’s disputation against Ahab’s prophets, and how, by offering sacrifice, he showed that the true God is the God of Israel, while the idols worshiped by Ahab are false gods; and concerning the rain that Elijah obtained

[Col. 0208D] **(CHAP. XVIII.)** “After many days the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying: ‘Go, show yourself to Ahab, so that I may give rain upon the face of the earth.’ Elijah therefore went to show himself to Ahab, etc.”

When Elijah gathered all Israel and disputed against the prophets of Baal, and they strove in vain, he repaired the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed. He took twelve stones, corresponding to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, and built an altar of stones in the name of the Lord. He made a water channel, as though by two furrows around the altar, arranged the wood, divided the ox into its parts, and placed it upon the wood. Then he said: “Fill four jars with water and pour it upon the burnt offering and upon the wood.” Again he said: “Do this a second time.” When they had done so a second time, he said: “Do the same thing a third time.” They did so a third time, “and the water ran around the altar, and the trench was filled with water.”

What could this more fittingly signify than that our Redeemer, contending against and overcoming the prince of this world and his servants, repairs the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed—that is, purifying the hearts of his faithful from every stain of iniquity—and dedicates an altar to God. It is said to have been constructed from twelve stones because a most pleasing altar to God is built from those who follow the prophetic and apostolic faith or teaching. Upon it “a sacrifice of praise in the odor of sweetness” is offered daily (Heb. XIII; Eph. V).

“He made a water channel, as though by two furrows around the altar,” producing streams from a contrite heart and a humbled spirit: tears arising from fear of Gehenna and desire for eternal life.

“There he also arranged the wood,” because he established the sayings and deeds of the saints as examples for believers.

“He divided the ox into its parts and placed it upon the wood,” when he taught the faithful to shape all their actions according to the example of the holy Fathers.

“He commanded water to be poured upon the burnt offering and upon the wood once, twice, and three times,” because at all times it is necessary for us to cleanse our words, thoughts, and deeds through pure prayer and the compunction of tears, and not to cease before the water channels are filled—that is, until the future joy that succeeds present sorrow is perfectly completed.

And so it will be according to what follows:

“Fire fell from heaven at Elijah’s invocation and devoured the burnt offering, the wood, and the stones; it also licked up the dust and the water that was in the channel,” when the scrutiny of the heavenly Judge, perfectly examining our words and deeds and our whole life, tests us as silver is tested by fire and places us, immortal and blessed, in an everlasting dwelling, so that, like the men of Israel, we may sing forever in gladness: “The Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves. We are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIX).

After the altar of the Lord had been cleansed and the burnt offerings consumed, Elijah, the prophet of God, said to the people:

“Seize all the prophets of Baal, and let not one of them escape.” When they had seized them, Elijah led them to the brook Kishon—which is interpreted as “their hardness”—and killed them there.

So also our Redeemer, when the day of judgment arrives, “will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and those who practice iniquity, and they will cast them into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets are, and where the devil who deceived them has also been cast. There they will be tormented according to the hardness and impenitent character of their hearts, day and night, forever and ever” (Matt. XIII; Rev. XX; Rom. II).

“After these things Elijah went up to the summit of Carmel, bowed down to the ground, and placed his face between his knees. He said to his servant: ‘Go up and look toward the sea.’ When he had gone up and looked, he said: ‘There is nothing.’ Again he said to him: ‘Return seven times.’ On the seventh occasion, behold, a small cloud, like a man’s footprint, etc.”

What is signified by this except that, when Christ the Son of God was born among human beings and assumed the tenderness of our flesh, after he had tasted death and ascended victoriously from the world to heaven, he sent from above to the earth the rain of divine grace through the sevenfold Spirit, so that it might cleanse us from sin and make us produce spiritual fruits?

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Elijah’s flight from Jezebel, and how, sitting in the shade of a juniper tree, he asked that his soul might die, while the angel of the Lord fed him there with bread baked under ashes and water; and how Elijah, hiding in a cave on Mount Horeb, was consoled there by the Lord through various forms of speech, and the Lord commissioned him to anoint kings and Elisha as prophet in his place, and gave them power to strike with the sword
## CHAPTER XIX

Elijah was afraid, “and arose and went wherever his will led him. He came to Beersheba of Judah and left his servant there, and went on into the wilderness, a day’s journey. When he had come and sat beneath a juniper tree, he asked that his soul might die, and said: ‘It is enough for me, Lord; take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.’ And he cast himself down and fell asleep beneath the shade of the juniper,” etc.

*(From Gregory.)* Holy men, who, when lifted up by the Spirit, are carried away to the heights, are restrained by certain temptations for as long as they remain in this life, lest they become proud through some kind of elation, so that they may never be able to advance as far as they wish. And lest they be lifted up by pride, a certain measure of their virtues is also imposed upon them. Hence it is that, although Elijah had advanced to great heights through so many virtues, he was held back by a certain measure when he later fled from Jezebel—although she was a queen, she was nevertheless only a woman.

For I consider this man of extraordinary virtue: drawing fire from heaven (III Kings XVIII), on a second occasion consuming fifty men with all their attendants at a sudden request (IV Kings I), opening the heavens by his word to bring rain (III Kings XVII, XVIII), raising the dead, and foreseeing all that was to come—and yet again there comes to mind with what fear he fled before a single woman. I contemplate a man struck by fear, asking death from the hand of God, yet avoiding death from the hand of a woman by fleeing. For he was seeking death while he fled, saying: “It is enough for me; take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.”

How, then, was he so powerful that he could perform all those virtues? And how was he so weak that he feared a woman, unless the dispensations of the heavenly will are weighed according to the measure of a hidden balance, so that holy men themselves are both greatly empowered through the power of God and, in turn, restrained by a certain measure through their own weakness? In those virtues Elijah recognized what he had received from God; in these weaknesses he recognized what he could do of himself. That power was the virtue; this weakness was the guardian of virtue. In those virtues he showed what he had received; in these weaknesses he preserved what he had received. Through miracles Elijah was revealed; through weaknesses he was preserved.

“Then, behold, an angel touched him and said to him: ‘Arise and eat.’ He looked, and behold, at his head was a cake baked under the ashes and a vessel of water. So he ate and drank, and again fell asleep. And the angel of the Lord returned a second time, touched him, and said to him: ‘Arise, eat, for a great journey remains before you.’ When he had risen, he ate and drank, and walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God,” etc.

What, then, does Elijah’s being fed twice by the angel signify, if not the weakness of our nature, for which a single meal is not sufficient, but a double one is required, so that we may be able to ascend to the things above? For just as the body cannot continue without bodily nourishment, so the soul cannot live without the word of God. For the angel who fed Elijah—whom could he more suitably signify than the angel of the supreme counsel, by whose aid we subsist both in bodily and spiritual nature?

After Elijah had risen from sleep, eaten, and drunk, he walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God. So also, when we shake off from ourselves the sleep of sluggishness, we must, strengthened by divine consolation, hasten with the utmost diligence by the steps of good works throughout the whole period of this present life to ascend the mountain of God and to his holy place, so that there we may find eternal rest.

“When he had come there, he remained in a cave. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him and said to him: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ He replied: ‘I have been very zealous for the Lord, the God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant. They have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it away.’ And he said: ‘Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord.’ And behold, the Lord will pass by, and a great and powerful wind will overturn the mountains and shatter the rocks before the Lord. The Lord is not in the wind. And after the wind, a disturbance of fire. The Lord is not in the fire. And after the fire, the sound of a gentle breeze. When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak, went out, and stood at the entrance of the cave,” etc.

*(From Gregory.)* The spirit before the Lord overturns mountains and shatters rocks, because the terror that rushes upon us at his coming and casts down the height of our heart melts it. But the Lord is said not to be in the spirit of upheaval or in the fire; yet his presence in the sound of a gentle breeze is not denied. For surely, when the mind is suspended in the sublimity of contemplation, whatever it is able to perceive perfectly is not God. But when it perceives something subtle, this is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. We perceive, as it were, the sound of a gentle breeze when, in sudden contemplation, we subtly taste the flavor of uncircumscribed truth. What we know of God is then true, when we recognize that we cannot fully know anything concerning him. Hence it is rightly added there:

“When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak and, entering, stood at the entrance of the cave.”

After the sound of the gentle breeze, the prophet covered his face with his cloak, because in that most subtle contemplation of truth he recognizes how deeply human beings are covered by ignorance. To draw a cloak over the face is to veil the mind by consideration of its own weakness, lest it dare to seek higher things, and lest it rashly open the eyes of its understanding beyond itself; rather, it reverently closes them to that which it cannot grasp. The one who does this is described as having stood at the entrance of the cave.

For what is our cave except this dwelling of corruption, in which we are still held by our old condition? But when we begin to perceive something of the knowledge of divinity, we stand, as it were, at the entrance of our cave. For although we cannot advance perfectly, yet, yearning for knowledge of the truth, we already catch something of the breeze of freedom. To stand at the entrance of the cave, therefore, is to begin to emerge toward knowledge of the truth after restraining the obstacle of our corruption.

Hence also the Israelites are remembered as standing at the entrances of their tents while they gazed from afar upon the cloud descending in the tabernacle (Exodus XXXIII), because those who behold the coming of divinity in either way are, as it were, already proceeding out of the dwelling of the flesh.

“Behold, a voice came to Elijah, saying: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ And he replied: ‘I have been very zealous for the Lord, the God of hosts, because the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant. They have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; I alone have been left, and they seek my life in order to take it away.’”

*(From Gregory.)* It is certain that the one who, while doing what is right, neglects the merits of better people extinguishes the eye of his heart through the darkness of elation. Conversely, the one who carefully considers the good deeds of others illuminates himself with a great ray of humility, because, when he sees the things he himself has done being done openly and observed by others, he suppresses the swelling of pride that seeks to break forth from within him on account of his uniqueness.

Hence God truly says to Elijah, who thought himself alone: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal.” Thus, when he recognized that he was not the only one remaining, the glory of elation that arose in him from his sense of uniqueness was bent down.

He was a prophet and had often known heavenly mysteries. What, then, was difficult about recognizing that faithful servants of God still remained in this world? But here we must carefully observe how wickedly elation closes the eye of the heart, since the man who, when humble, knew the hidden things of God did not know the obvious things when he had become proud.

“And the Lord said to Elijah: ‘Go and return on your way through the wilderness toward Damascus. When you have arrived there, you shall anoint Hazael as king over Syria, and Jehu son of Nimshi you shall anoint as king over Israel; but Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint as prophet in your place. And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill.’”

This should not be understood to mean that Elisha, the prophet of God, would become a murderer and a tyrant. Rather, it should be understood spiritually: divine justice, which repays each person according to his works, sometimes punishes human sins by manifest vengeance and sometimes by hidden judgment. It takes vengeance through kings and rulers; it takes vengeance through prophets and priests, when it causes some guilty people to be punished by the sword and pierces others with the sword of the tongue.

Thus David, Solomon, and the other kings exacted punishment from the guilty when they ordered them to be slain. Likewise, it is written elsewhere concerning the punishment of the proud and disobedient: “I hewed them down through the prophets, he says, and killed them by the words of my mouth” (Hosea VI).

“Then Elijah departed from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing.”

Thus Elijah departed and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing with twelve yoke of oxen. This occurred when our Redeemer, descending from heaven, acquired by divine judgment a people still intent upon earthly works; in this people he brought about salvation when he converted them to the faith.

For Elijah is interpreted, as we have also said, as “the Lord God”; Shaphat as “judging”; and Elisha as “the salvation of my God.” Admirably, the prophet cast his cloak over him when the Lord clothed him with the Catholic faith. “All,” says the Apostle, “who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians III).

“But he immediately left the oxen, ran after Elijah, and said: ‘Let me kiss, I beg you, my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.’”

This occurred because, as soon as the chorus of the elect heard the Lord speaking through the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV), it immediately ceased yearning after earthly profits and serving worldly desires. It devoted itself entirely to the service of Christ, yet did not cease preaching the word of life to others.

This is what it means to kiss father and mother: to desire to correct by speech as many as one can, whether from the Jews or from the nations.

[Col. 0213D] “So Elisha took a yoke of oxen and slaughtered it. He cooked the flesh on the plow of the oxen, gave it to the people, and they ate.”

This signifies the Christian people, slaughtering carnal desires and turning all their exertion toward the work of evangelization, so that they may provide sufficient nourishment for their hearers. He himself follows our Elijah and ministers to him: that is, by following his footsteps, faithfully observing his commands, he strives to render him a fitting ministry of good works.

## CHAPTER XX

[Col. 0214A] The war of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, against Ahab, king of Israel, when a prophet appeared to strengthen him and victory was given to him through the young men of the provincial governors. How Ben-hadad, king of Syria, once defeated, renews the battle against Israel, but is similarly overcome by him; and how, when he sought refuge in the mercy of the king of Israel, the latter made a treaty with him without the Lord’s command, for which reason he is rebuked by a prophet sent by the Lord.

*(Chapter XX.)* “Now Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his entire army, together with thirty-two kings, and horses and chariots; and he went up and fought against Samaria and besieged it,” etc.

*(From Bede.)* When Ben-hadad, king of Syria, besieging Samaria and beginning to attack it again, said: “May the gods do this to me and add this also, if the dust of Samaria will suffice to fill the handfuls of all the people who follow me,” this is the meaning.

In accordance with the custom of cities, Samaria had earth inside the walls almost level with the walls themselves, so that, without the support of the adjacent earth, the battering ram’s blows might not repeatedly bring them down when pressed by the hand of the enemy. Outside, however, the height of the walls rose far above the surface of the ground, especially since, as Scripture reports, the city itself had been situated on the summit of a mountain.

The arrogant king, therefore, terrifying the besieged city, declared that he had such a great multitude of soldiers with him that, even if each of his soldiers brought only a single stone, clod of earth, or piece of wood for constructing a ramp against the city, a ramp would rise that would appear equal to the level of the city itself, which lay within the walls, so that the attackers could cast weapons or torches against the city from equal height.

Curbing the rashness of his arrogance with a restrained saying, the king of Israel replied: “Tell him: Let not the one who girds himself boast as the one who ungirds himself.”

But one thing is “girded,” another “ungirded,” and another “not girded.” A person is girded when he goes about surrounded by a belt. He is ungirded when he has recently removed his belt—for example, when he is about to enter a bath, climb into bed, or perhaps put on another tunic. He is not girded when he has recently put on a tunic but has not yet secured himself by wrapping a belt around it.

Thus, in a military expedition, the one who has been assigned to it is rightly called girded, that is, clothed in armor. The one who has completed the battle and returned home victorious is properly called ungirded, because, having laid aside his weapons, he enjoys the leisure of the desired peace. But the one who has not yet begun to fight or to prepare himself for battle is rightly said to be not girded.

Therefore the king of Israel said to the king of Syria, who was boasting as though he had already captured Samaria, which he had only begun to besiege: “Let not the one who girds himself boast as the one who ungirds himself.” As though he were openly saying: “Do not boast as if you were victorious in the hazards of war when, still stationed in the battle line, you do not know whom victory will follow.”

He was certainly speaking the truth. For as soon as the battle began, Ben-hadad returned home—not triumphing over defeated enemies, but fleeing after his own army had been slaughtered.

Mystically, Ben-hadad, the enemy of Israel, signifies the devil, the enemy of all good things, who gathers various armies of evil spirits to overthrow the people of God. But he is defeated through the young men of the leaders of Israel, when the ancient enemy is put to flight through good hearers of holy teachers—those who strive to fulfill by their deeds what they hear with their ears—and his entire army is driven back by the soldiers of Christ.

They are rightly said to number two hundred and thirty-two, because those who perfectly possess knowledge of both Testaments and preserve faith in the Trinity together with the twofold love of God and neighbor are shown to be fully equipped for every kind of service in the army of the supreme King.

“Ben-hadad, king of Syria, also fled on horseback with his horsemen. Then the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and struck Syria with a great slaughter,” etc.

What does it mean that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, is described as fleeing on horseback with his horsemen, except that the devil, the prince of all the wicked—whose eyes are lifted up (for Syria is interpreted as ‘lofty’)—trusting in the horse of his pride, together with his horsemen, namely all the proud, is overcome and put to flight by the army of Christ, that is, by the humble and God-fearing?

For “he is the head over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI). And the king of Israel will strike the horses and chariots, because it is written of the King of kings himself that “he drowned Pharaoh’s chariots and his army, his horse and his rider, in the Red Sea” (Exodus XV), when he submerged the spiritual wickednesses, together with the true Pharaoh—the ancient enemy—in the water of baptism, wiping away the sins of the human race.

[Col. 0215C] “Then the prophet approached the king of Israel and said to him: ‘Go, strengthen yourself, and know and see what you are to do; for next year the king of Syria will go up against you,’” etc.

The fact that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, once defeated, renews the battle against Israel signifies that the devil never ceases from the intention of his malice. Although he is often defeated by holy men, he nevertheless renews the battle against them; and while he is defeated in one way, he immediately attempts to conquer in another.

Hence the servants of the king of Syria said to him: “Their gods are gods of the mountains; therefore they overcame us. But it is better that we fight against them in the plains, and we shall overcome them.” This means that evil spirits, always devising their schemes deceitfully, strive, if they are defeated in spiritual matters, to prepare war in bodily matters.

This is what the devil and his entire army especially strive for: to cast human souls down from the heights to the depths, so that they may more easily overcome them. If they see people desiring heavenly things, they bring earthly and perishable things before them to love. If they see them giving thanks to God for granted prosperity, they strive to break them through adversity.

But just as the words of the king of Syria and his servants did not agree with their deeds—for where they trusted that they could overcome, they were themselves overcome—so also the prince of death is often defeated, together with his army, precisely where he thought he could prevail: “For God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are” (I Corinthians I).

The ancient enemy therefore tested blessed Job. When he asked the Lord that Job’s possessions and children be handed over to him so that by this means he might overthrow his mind, and yet did not prevail in this, he finally asked that power be given to him over Job himself (Job I). When this was granted, as though he would immediately become the victor, he wounded Job’s flesh with a grievous ulcer (Job II). But the more violently he pursued him, cast down from prosperity into suffering, the more powerfully he was overthrown by Job’s patience.

And the Apostle Paul was given “a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet him” (II Corinthians XII), so that strength might be perfected in weakness.

“Then a certain man from the sons of the prophets said to his companion by the word of the Lord: ‘Strike me.’ But he refused to strike him. He said to him: ‘Because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord, behold, when you depart from me, a lion will strike you.’ And when he had withdrawn a little from him, a lion found him and struck him. Then, meeting another man, he said to him: ‘Strike me.’ He struck him and wounded him.”

*(From Josephus.)* Josephus gives the following account of this same matter:

“Meanwhile, a certain prophet named Micaiah approached one of the Israelites and asked him to strike him on the head according to the will of God. When the man refused, he foretold that, because he had disobeyed his God and his command, he would be killed when a lion encountered him. When this had happened to that man, the prophet again approached another and ordered him to do the same. When the man struck him and bloodied his head, he bound it up and approached the king, saying that, while he had been stationed in the army, he had received a prisoner from a certain tribune to guard, and that the tribune had told him that, if the prisoner escaped, he himself would die. When the prisoner escaped, the man who had handed him over threatened to put him to death.

“Then, when Ahab replied that his death was entirely just, the prophet loosened the bandage from his head, and Micaiah was recognized. He had used this parable because of the words he was about to speak to the king. For he said that, since God had granted Ahab permission to escape punishment from the enemy, Ahab himself had spared his enemy Ben-hadad, even though Ben-hadad had blasphemed God. Therefore God had decreed that Ahab himself should be killed by that enemy, while the people should be destroyed by an invasion of his army.

“Ahab, enraged, ordered that the prophet be kept in confinement. But, confounded by Micaiah’s words, he returned to his own house.”

According to the laws of allegorical interpretation, servants of God must especially take care not to flatter themselves with destructive security, following the example of Ahab, king of Israel, as long as the enemy remains alive. Otherwise, while they regard themselves as perpetual victors, they may be swiftly struck down through the devil’s deceit, which offers peace in advance.

For just as the prophet then foretold to the king that, because of his thoughtless clemency, a just vengeance would soon come, so prophetic speech now foretells that, if we make a pact with the devil, eternal punishment will thereby threaten us.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0217A] How Ahab, king of Israel, desired the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite and, after Naboth was killed through Jezebel’s plot, seized it for himself; and how, for this reason, he was rebuked by the prophet Elijah.

*(Chapter XXI.)* “After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab, king of Samaria. Ahab therefore spoke to Naboth, saying: ‘Give me your vineyard, so that I may make it into a vegetable garden, because it is nearby and close to my house,’” etc.

Scripture relates that Ahab, king of Israel, desired the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which was in Jezreel beside the king’s palace, so that he might make a vegetable garden there. When Naboth refused to give it to him, the same Naboth, through the counsel of his most wicked wife, namely Queen Jezebel, was stoned and killed after false witnesses had been introduced; and his vineyard was seized and possessed by the king.

Let us therefore consider who this Naboth the Jezreelite was and what his vineyard signified. Naboth is interpreted as “conspicuous” or “a sitting”; Jezreel as “the honor of God” or “the seed of God.” And whom can we more suitably call the honor or seed of God than the Son of God, “who is the splendor of his glory and the figure of his substance, whom God appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” (Hebrews I)?

To him the Psalmist, praying, says: “You who sit upon the cherubim, appear before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh; stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Psalm LXXIX).

This Naboth had a vineyard concerning which Isaiah speaks at length in his song, concluding: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah V). And in the Psalm: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it” (Psalm LXXIX).

“He surrounded it with a hedge,” as we read in the Gospel (Matthew XXI)—that is, either with the wall of the city or with the assistance of angels. “And he dug a winepress in it” (ibid.)—either an altar, or those winepresses whose titles are prefixed to three Psalms, namely the eighth, the eightieth, and the eighty-sixth. “And he built a tower” (ibid.), unquestionably the temple, of which Micah says: “And you, tower of the mist, daughter of Zion” (Micah IV). “And he leased it to tenants” (Matthew XXI), whom elsewhere he called the workers or cultivators of the vineyard.

Ahab, whose name is interpreted as “brother of the father,” desired this vineyard. He signifies the Jewish people, from whom Christ deigned to assume flesh, “in order to make a vegetable garden in it”—that is, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to have germinated, to transplant every fragile doctrine through Pharisaic superstition.

But when Naboth refused to give this vineyard—that is, when Christ did not consent to the superstitions of the Pharisees—his wicked wife Jezebel, that is, the synagogue of the Jews, plotted his death. Jezebel is interpreted as “a cohabitant” or “a vain flowing,” which aptly suits the synagogue: it seemed to dwell in the house of the Lord, but flowed away through various desires of vanity.

Jezebel therefore sent letters to the elders and nobles who were in the city, so that, after false witnesses had been introduced, they might give false testimony against Naboth, claiming that he had cursed God and the king; and thus they might lead him outside the city and stone him to death. This occurred when the synagogue, through the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees, plotted the death of Christ.

It is likewise written in the Gospel: “The chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, in order to put him to death, and they did not find any, although many false witnesses came forward. Finally two false witnesses came and said: ‘This man said: I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days’” (Matthew XXVI).

The two false witnesses therefore gave false testimony against Naboth, saying that he had cursed God and the king. And the Jews, through two false witnesses, charged Christ with attributing to himself divine power and nature. Hence, when Pilate said to the Jews: “Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no case against him,” the Jews answered him: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX).

Naboth was therefore stoned outside the city at Jezebel’s instigation, so that, after he had died, Ahab might possess his vineyard. So also our Savior suffered outside the gate, being crucified at the place of the skull, while the synagogue, stirred up by zeal, incited the people to demand Christ’s death, so that they might live more securely after he had been killed.

Hence, as though offering counsel, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII). And: “If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him” (John XI).

The inheritance of Christ is therefore the Church, given to him from all the nations. The Father did not leave it to him as he died; rather, Christ wonderfully acquired it through his own death and possessed it by rising again.

After he had been killed, the wicked tenants sought to seize it (Matthew XXI), when the Jews who crucified him attempted to extinguish the faith that comes through him, to advance instead their own righteousness, which comes from the law, and to implant it among the nations for their instruction (Romans X).

The heir of the vineyard is killed outside the vineyard (Matthew XXI), “because Jesus, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews XIII).

It is fitting for this mystery that, in the place where the dogs licked Naboth’s blood, according to the prophet’s saying, they also licked Ahab’s blood, and that in the field of Jezreel they ate Jezebel’s flesh. For when those dogs of whom it is written, “Many dogs have surrounded me” (Psalm XXI), sought the blood of our Redeemer with poisonous tongues, they themselves were also slaughtered by those dogs of whom Scripture likewise says: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matthew XV). Thus the most wicked plunderers and criminal possessors of the Lord’s vineyard were slaughtered in the same place where the Lord suffered, and their flesh was given to beasts and birds to eat.

And so that wicked people, who during the Lord’s Passion cried out with profane voices, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXV), deserved to have their foul blood poured out in that same place where they demanded that their Savior be killed.

Josephus reports that on the solemn day of Passover people from all Judea gathered in Jerusalem, as though compelled by some deadly force. He says that there were three million men, evidently because divine justice had chosen this time for vengeance, so that the entire multitude, which on the days of Passover had violated its Savior and the Christ, the Salvation of the Lord, with bloodstained hands and sacrilegious voices, might, during those same days, be shut up together as in a single prison and suffer the destruction of the savage punishment it deserved.

## CHAPTER XXII

The vision of the prophet Micaiah, who foretold the death of Ahab, king of Israel.

*(Chapter XXII.)* “Then the king of Israel called a certain eunuch and said to him: ‘Hurry and bring Micah son of Remla.’ Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, sat each on his throne, clothed in royal apparel,” etc.

When Micaiah was summoned to the king of Israel and likewise to the king of Judah, he prophesied against the king of Israel, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and the army of heaven standing at his right hand and at his left. And it was said: ‘By what means shall I deceive Ahab, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ One said one thing, and another something else. Then one spirit came forward and said: ‘I will deceive him.’ And it was said: ‘By what means will you deceive him?’ He replied: ‘I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’”

*(From Gregory.)* What should we understand by the throne of the Lord except the angelic powers, over whose minds God presides from above and disposes all things below? And what is meant by the army of heaven except the multitude of ministering angels?

What, then, does it mean that the army of heaven is said to stand at his right hand and at his left? God, who is within all things in such a way that he is also outside all things, is confined neither by right nor by left. Rather, the right hand of God signifies the elect portion of the angels, while the left hand of God signifies the reprobate portion of the angels.

For not only the good serve God, to assist, but also the evil, to burden those unwilling to return. Nor does the designation “army of heaven” prevent the reprobate portion of the angels from being understood as included within it. We call the birds that we know to hang in the air “the birds of heaven” (Matthew VI, 8). And concerning these same spirits Paul said: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI). Naming their head, he said: “According to the prince of the power of this air” (Ephesians II).

The army of angels therefore stands at the right and at the left, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the mind of the reprobate, serving its own wickedness, obeys the judgment of God’s strictness.

Hence a deceitful spirit is immediately described as coming forward into the midst, through whom King Ahab, in accordance with his merits, was to be deceived. For it is not permissible to believe that a good Spirit wished to serve deceit by saying: “I will go out and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.”

But King Ahab was worthy, because of his preceding sins, to be condemned by such deception, so that he who had often fallen willingly into guilt might at some point be captured unwillingly for punishment. By hidden justice, permission is given to evil spirits so that those whom they willingly strangle in the snare of sin they may also unwillingly drag into the punishment of sin.

Indeed, the one who does not change his wicked life and does not turn his mind away from committing sins, when he consults a prophet, hears—by God’s arrangement—those things which he deserves to hear as one destined for condemnation.

For behold, to mention one or two examples among many: the house of Israel had withdrawn from the worship of almighty God into the slavery of idols, yet it often came to the prophets, by whom it was accustomed to be deceived, seeking prosperity. When, while acting perversely, it deserved to hear promises of prosperity from the mouths of the prophets, what else were the heavenly judgments accomplishing except that the sinful people were being caught in their own heart? Thus, because they had sinned by following unbelief, they were deceived by the flattering words of their prophets, so that they no longer feared that they had sinned and afterward would be dragged more harshly to punishment, because they now lived more securely in guilt.

But behold, by the gift of almighty God, a very large part of the human race has now been removed from the worship of idols, openly professes the true faith, and refuses to submit in worship to wood, stone, or any creature. Anyone, therefore, who is established in the faith may now safely consult a prophet, because he will hear what it is fitting for a faithful person to hear.

I would say confidently that, if he had withdrawn from other impurities and wicked deeds, he would be secure. For when Paul, the outstanding preacher, cries out, “Greed, which is the worship of idols” (Colossians III), whoever remains subject to greed is not free from the worship of idols.

Thus the one who pants under the heat of greed appears indeed to stand in the faith, but he desires to acquire what belongs to others, longs to seize worldly honors, and covets temporal glory. If he consults a prophet about this same glory, it is entirely just that, in accordance with the merit of his guilt, he should hear prosperity from the prophet’s mouth, so that he who refused to hear the words of God in holy Scripture telling him to despise earthly things and seek heavenly things may, by God’s judgment, hear from the mouth of his prophet that by which he will fall into greater bondage. Delighted and nourished by hope of earthly glory, he will always be led downward.

Nor was that Spirit good who desired to be a liar in the mouth of the prophets. Hence it was stated beforehand that “the army of heaven stood at his right hand and at his left.” God, who is uncircumscribed truth, has no left hand in that eternal blessedness called his right hand, because nothing displeasing can exist there.

But because he sees all things together and observes everything at once, he is described as having the army of heaven at his right and left—in the same power, I mean, by which he sees good and evil spirits—so that by the right hand we understand the elect angels and by the left the reprobate spirits.

Nor should it disturb us that the rejected angels are also called the army of heaven. Although they have been expelled from the ethereal heaven, they still dwell in the aerial heaven, as Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI).

But since the Third Book of Kings closes its account not long after the death of Ahab, let us likewise bring the third book of this exposition to an end at this point, so that, together with the history, we may take a fresh beginning concerning the events that follow.

## INTO THE FOURTH BOOK

[Col. 0221]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0221A] Concerning Ahaziah, the king who fell through the lattice of his house and, because of this illness, sent to consult the idol of Ekron; whereupon the angered Lord gave him an appropriate answer through the prophet.

## Chapter I

“Now Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab had died. And Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper chamber which he had in Samaria, and became ill; and he sent messengers, saying to them: ‘Go, consult Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, whether I may recover from this illness of mine.’ But the angel of the Lord spoke to Elijah the Tishbite, saying: ‘Rise and go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and say to them: Is there no God in Israel, that you are going to consult Baalzebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore thus says the Lord: From the bed on which you have climbed, you shall not descend, but you shall surely die,’ etc.”

After the most wicked king Ahab had died, a wicked heir succeeded him, namely his son Ahaziah. Scripture relates of him that he did evil in the sight of the Lord, and walked in the way of his father and his mother, and in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin. He also served Baal, worshiped him, and provoked the Lord God of Israel, according to all that his father had done.

But he did not prosper for long, because he fell through the lattice of his upper chamber, which he had in Samaria, and became ill. He sent messengers to Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, to consult him about whether he might recover from this illness. When Elijah, meeting his messengers, had announced to him his approaching death, he sent a commander of fifty with the soldiers under his authority to bring him to him. But after these had been consumed by heavenly fire, he sent another commander of fifty, who likewise was burned with his men. He also sent a third, who was spared.

Thus this king signifies the Jewish people, and especially its rulers, who, devoted to sins and vices, rejected—indeed persecuted—the truth. Hence we read in the Gospel that “the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest Jesus” (John 7). And again: “So they sought to arrest him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come; and he went away to the mountain alone to pray” (ibid.). And again: “They plotted,” he says, “to kill him. Therefore Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim” (John 11).

The house of Ahaziah, therefore, is the Synagogue of the Jews, which was surrounded on every side by the precepts of the Law, as by the lattice of an upper chamber. But just as Ahaziah, falling through the lattice by which he ought to have been protected, suffered a grave illness, so the Jewish people, departing from the observance of the Law, fell into the hopeless sickness of sins. Because it had abandoned divine protection, it did not deserve to find remedies for salvation. For, as the impious king had done, it fled to the protection of false gods, by whom it was injured rather than helped.

Therefore it is rebuked by the prophetic mouth, and its approaching death is foretold to it. Hence Isaiah says:

“And when they say to you: ‘Seek the mediums and the diviners who chirp in their incantations,’ surely a people should not seek a vision from its God on behalf of the living from the dead? To the Law rather and to the testimony. And if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them. And it will pass through it, it will fall and hunger. And when it has become hungry, it will grow angry and curse its king and its God. And it will look upward and gaze upon the earth. And behold, distress and darkness, dissolution and anguish, and oppressive gloom; and it will not be able to escape from its distress” (Isaiah 8). (From Isidore.)

The king sends two impious commanders of fifty, with the soldiers under them, to bring Elijah before him; they are consumed by divine fire. But the third commander of fifty, who is sent, is saved.

The number fifty signifies confession of penitence, by which the remission of sins is declared. Therefore the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge Christ as perfect God and as the author of penitence, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John 8). These will be extinguished in the future conflagration of divine fire. But the third commander of fifty, because he turned to faith in the Trinity and recognized the mysteries of penitence, merited pardon.

## Chapter II

Concerning Elijah’s being carried into heaven by a whirlwind, and Elisha’s request that a double spirit of Elijah be made to dwell in him. Elisha’s miracle at Jericho, where he invoked the Lord and changed the waters into sweetness; and concerning the boys who mocked Elisha and were therefore torn apart by two bears.

“Now it happened that, when the Lord was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah and Elisha were going from Gilgal. And Elijah said to Elisha: ‘Stay here, because the Lord has sent me as far as Bethel.’ To him Elisha said: ‘As the Lord lives and as your soul lives, I will not abandon you,’ etc.” (From Gregory.)

What does it mean that Elijah is said to have been taken up into heaven? Do we believe that, while he was still placed in this corruptible flesh, he was brought before the resurrection and ascension of the Lord into the bosom of that supreme rest? But the aerial heaven is one thing, and the ethereal heaven another. The aerial heaven is close to the earth, and therefore we speak of the birds of heaven (Matthew 6, 8), because we see them flying through the air.

Elijah, therefore, was raised into the aerial heaven, so that he might suddenly be led into some hidden region of the earth, where he would live already in great rest of body and spirit until he returns at the end of the world and pays the debt of death. For Elijah, being raised up, signified the Lord’s Ascension. He postponed death; he did not escape it. But our Redeemer, because he did not postpone death, conquered it, consumed it by rising again, and manifested the glory of his resurrection by ascending.

It should also be noted that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might plainly be shown that a mere human being needed help from another. For those aids were provided and displayed by angels, since he could not ascend even into the aerial heaven by his own power, being weighed down by the weakness of his nature.

But our Redeemer is not read to have been raised by a chariot or by angels, because he who had made all things was carried above all things by his own power. He was returning there where he was, and returning from there where he remained, because when he ascended into heaven through his humanity, through his divinity he continued to contain both earth and heaven.

Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers (Genesis 37), prefigured the selling of our Redeemer, so Enoch, translated (Genesis 5), and Elijah, raised into the aerial heaven, signified the Lord’s Ascension. The Lord had one herald and witness of his Ascension before the Law, and another under the Law, so that he himself might eventually come, the one who could truly penetrate the heavens.

Therefore the order in their two raisings is distinguished by certain stages of progression. For Enoch is said to have been translated, whereas Elijah was carried up into heaven, so that afterward there might come one who, neither translated nor carried up, would by his own power penetrate the ethereal heaven, and who would bestow upon us who believe in him the purity also of the flesh, so that under him the virtue of chastity might increase through the progress of time.

In their very translation—those who, as servants, signified the Lord’s Ascension—and in the person of the Lord himself, who ascended into heaven, this distinction is likewise shown. Enoch, who was translated, was begotten through intercourse and begot through intercourse. Elijah, who was carried up, was begotten through intercourse, but did not himself beget through intercourse. The Lord, however, was taken up neither begetting through intercourse nor begotten through intercourse.

But it is asked how Elisha, when his teacher Elijah offered him an opportunity to make a request, asked for a double spirit of Elijah, when the Lord says in the Gospel: “A disciple is not above his teacher; but everyone, when perfected, will be like his teacher” (Luke 6). If the mystery of this request is considered, it is judged to have been not an excessive but a necessary petition.

“Elijah therefore said to Elisha: ‘Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you.’ And Elisha said: ‘I ask that a double portion of your spirit be made to dwell in me.’ He replied: ‘You have asked for a difficult thing. Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken away from you, it shall be yours; but if you do not see me, it shall not be.’”

Whom does Elijah signify in this passage, if not our Head, namely the Lord Redeemer? And whom does Elisha signify, if not his body, which is the Church? Our Elijah gives an opportunity to ask when he says in the Gospel: “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7). And again: “Ask,” he says, “and you will receive, so that your joy may be full” (John 16).

Having received this confidence, Elisha—that is, the Christian people—asks the Lord that the Spirit of Christ may be made double in them; that is, that there may be a double grace of the Holy Spirit, namely in the remission of sins and in the bestowal of virtues.

Our Redeemer, therefore, “who had no sin, neither committed sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (John 8), did not need the remission of sins. But he performed works of virtue in the Holy Spirit, as he himself says in the Gospel to the Jews: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11).

The works of the holy Trinity—namely of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are therefore inseparable, as the Truth bears witness, saying: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5). And the Apostle says: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12).

The Church rightly asks to receive a double Spirit of Christ, because it needs both the remission of sins, which Christ did not need, and the gift of virtues, which Christ bestows from his fullness through the Holy Spirit. “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4)—namely, to those who place their hope firmly in him.

Hence Elijah says to Elisha:

“If you see me when I am taken away from you, it shall be yours; but if you do not see me, it shall not be.”

For unless someone fixes the eyes of right faith upon him, so as faithfully to believe in his passion, resurrection, and ascension to the Father, he will not obtain the fruit of his petition. The subsequent account makes this clear.

For Elijah, with Elisha accompanying him, came to the waters of the Jordan, “took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the waters, which were divided in both directions, and both crossed over on dry ground.” When Elijah had been carried away, Elisha picked up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen to him. “And he returned and stood on the bank of the Jordan; and with Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen to him, he struck the waters, and they were not divided. And he said: ‘Where is the God of Elijah, even now?’ And he struck the waters, and they were divided this way and that, and Elisha crossed over,” etc.

What does Elijah’s cloak signify, if not the Lord’s Incarnation, through which our Redeemer broke open the river of death and prepared for us a passage to life? Elisha retained this cloak after Elijah’s crossing, because after Christ’s ascension into heaven the Church preserved faith in Christ’s Incarnation, through which it strives to cross the waves of the present life.

But just as Elisha, striking the river with the cloak, did not divide the waters until he had said, “Where is the God of Elijah, even now?” and then struck the waters, which were divided, so the Church cannot perform any works of power without invoking the Lord’s name, because, as he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

For human effort is nothing unless divine help is present. Hence the Apostle also said: “It is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). And the Prophet says to the Lord: “In you we shall scatter our enemies, and in your name we shall trample those who rise against us,” etc. (Psalm 43.)

“The men of the city said to Elisha: ‘Behold, the dwelling-place of this city is very good, as you yourself, lord, perceive; but the waters are bad, and the land is barren.’ But he said: ‘Bring me a new vessel, and put salt into it.’”

Elisha asked the people to heal the barren and harmful waters of Jericho. He received a new earthen vessel, threw salt into it, and lowered it into the river; immediately the waters in the river were healed. By this deed the prophet foretold that “the Word would become flesh and dwell among us” (John 1).

Therefore, in the likeness of the Word, he placed salt—that is, wisdom—in an earthen vessel, namely in the human body, and, putting it into the water, submerged it. This signified that all peoples, who under the figure of waters were barren throughout the whole world, would receive fruitfulness and blessing through Christ’s Incarnation.

“Elisha went up from there to Bethel. And as he was going up by the way, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: ‘Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!’ When he had looked back and seen them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord. And two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys apart,” etc.

The prophet Elisha, as we have often said, also bore the figure of Christ. Indeed, this name is interpreted as “the salvation of the Lord.” And who is the salvation of God other than his Son, who everywhere is also called the Savior?

Those little ones mocking the salvation of God—that is, Elisha—represented the Jews, who jeered at the Lord the Savior at the cross and said: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead,” because Christ was about to ascend the cross at the place of Calvary.

But when Elisha turned and cursed them, and two bears came out of the forest and killed forty-two blaspheming boys, so Christ, after his passion and resurrection from the dead, after he ascended into heaven, just as Elisha ascended to Bethel—that is, to the house of God—turned and cursed the Jews. In the forty-second year of his Ascension, he sent two bears from the forests of the nations, namely Vespasian and Titus, who struck them down in a cruel massacre.

## Chapter III

Concerning the war of the three kings—namely, the kings of Judah and Israel and Edom—against the king of Moab, and concerning the victory granted to them by the Lord.

“Now Mesha, king of Moab, raised many sheep, and paid the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams with their wool. But when Ahab had died, he broke the covenant that he had with the king of Israel,” etc.

After these events, war was waged by three kings—namely the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom—against Moab. When the prophet Elisha was consulted by them, after other matters he added these words:

“Make a channel for this torrent, ditches and ditches. For thus says the Lord: You shall not see wind or rain, yet this channel shall be filled with water, and you shall drink, you and your families and your cattle. And this is a small thing in the sight of the Lord; moreover, he will also deliver Moab into your hands. And you shall strike every fortified city and every choice city, and you shall cut down every fruitful tree, stop up all the springs of water, and cover every excellent field with stones,” etc.

What, then, do these three kings waging war against Moab signify, if not the rulers of the faithful, who, through faith in the holy Trinity, fight against the prince of this world and against his people—that is, philosophers, heretics, schismatics, and all the wicked—“with the shield of faith and spiritual weapons” (Ephesians 6)?

Moab, therefore, who is born of incest and is interpreted as “from the father,” aptly applies to those to whom the Lord said: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8).

These people oppose the Church, partly with threats, partly with persecutions, and partly with deceit and false fabrications. But through the power of Christ, who is the head of the Christian people, they are overcome and driven away. To them the Lord’s prophet says:

“Make a channel for this torrent, ditches and ditches. You shall not see wind or rain, yet this channel shall be filled with water, and you shall drink, you and your families.”

Behold, the Lord’s prophet gives counsel to the people wearied by thirst through a miracle performed by the Lord. Likewise, prophetic words offer the faithful counsel concerning how they may quench their thirst with spiritual teaching and refresh their minds.

He therefore commands that ditches be made in the channel of the torrent, and thus foretells an abundance of water without wind or rain. What is it to make ditches in the channel of the torrent, if not to seek the deep mysteries in the sacred Scriptures with good zeal? They are filled without rain or wind, because divine power often bestows wisdom upon those who seek it without human assistance. Hence the Apostle John says: “You have no need that anyone should teach you, but as his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2).

Therefore human beings and animals drink—that is, both the intellectually gifted and the simple receive teaching. For as suitable as the soul of the recipient is, so much instruction for its salvation will it find there. It continues:

“And this is a small thing in the sight of the Lord; moreover, he will also deliver Moab into your hands.”

It is not enough for the servants of God to know hidden mysteries; they must also proclaim them to others and “refute those who contradict them” (Titus 1). A sure victory over the enemy has been promised to them, “so that they may strike every fortified city and every choice city.”

By fortified cities and all choice cities we may understand worldly prudence, in which philosophers and heretics place their greatest confidence. These, therefore, will be overthrown by the preachers of the holy Gospel. Hence the Apostle says:

“The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive in obedience to Christ, and being ready to punish every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10).

“All the fruitful trees shall be cut down.”

Not those trees that produce good fruit, but those that generate deadly nourishment: cut down at the roots by divine judgment, they will become fuel for eternal fire.

“All the springs of water shall be stopped up,” when the heresiarchs, together with their followers, are condemned by Catholic teachers.

“And every excellent field shall be covered with stones,” when the beauty of heretical and philosophical speech is overwhelmed by the weight of anathema. Nothing will remain in the land of Moab except only clay walls—that is, the false reasonings of fragile teachings—which, surrounded by slingers, namely the holy preachers of the Church, are refuted for the most part and reduced to nothing.

But when the Moabites, after the sun had risen, saw the waters opposite them red like blood, they thought that the three kings who had come against one another for battle had killed one another, and thus they were deceived.
