So philosophers, thinking the word of Christ’s cross foolishness, mock Christ’s passion and regard the Church’s martyrdom as madness.

But, according to the Apostle, “what is foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and what is weakness of God is stronger than human beings, because the prudence of the flesh is death, but the prudence of the spirit is life and peace” (1 Corinthians 1; Romans 8). (From Jerome.)

To demonstrate that in this passage Moab is understood as the pride of philosophers—concerning whom it is said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (Isaiah 29; 1 Corinthians 1)—a few examples from the prophets must be explained.

Amos says:

“Thus says the Lord: For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not revoke his punishment, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes” (Amos 2).

Indeed, whatever in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever pertains to earthly wisdom, is thought to be strong—this is overturned by dialectic and, like a conflagration, dissolved into ashes and embers, so that nothing may be proved to be what had been thought most powerful.

Isaiah also rebukes Moab’s pride, saying:

“We have heard of Moab’s insult; he is exceedingly insulting. I have taken away his pride” (Isaiah 16).

Jeremiah too, prophesying against all the nations, speaks specifically to Moab:

“Because you trusted in your fortifications” (Jeremiah 48).

And shortly afterward: “You have confidence in your glory.” And again: “Because you say, ‘We are strong branches.’” Then: “The day of Moab is near, when it will come, and its wickedness is exceedingly great.” And more plainly he says: “How the glorious staff, the rod of magnificence, has been broken!” And again: “The horn of Moab has been broken.”

These things are said under the name of Moab, so that the wickedness of the world, which is foolish and always carries itself up to heaven, may be crushed.

## Chapter IV

Concerning how Elisha delivered a woman from her creditor through the blessing of oil; also concerning the Shunammite woman whose son Elisha raised; concerning the bitter stew which Elisha sweetened by adding flour; and concerning the offering of the man who came to Elisha.

“A certain woman, one of the wives of the prophets, cried out to Elisha, saying: ‘Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant was one who feared the Lord. And behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons to serve him.’ Elisha said to her: ‘What do you want me to do for you? Tell me, what do you have in your house?’ She replied: ‘Your handmaid has nothing in her house except a little oil with which I anoint myself.’ He said to her: ‘Go, ask from all your neighbors for empty vessels—not a few—and enter and shut your door when you and your sons are inside, and pour into all these vessels; and when they are full, take them away,’ etc.” (From Gregory.)

What is signified by this woman, if not the holy Church, the mother of two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile, as of two sons? Previously, through an evil deed, by consenting to the persuasion of the crafty spirit, she had received from her creditor, as it were, a coin of sin, and she feared losing the two sons whom she had begotten in faith.

But obeying the words of the prophet—that is, the commands of sacred Scripture—she pours out the little oil she possesses into empty vessels. For while many empty minds drink from the small measure of divine love that comes from the mouth of one teacher, they are filled to the brim, through overflowing grace, with the ointment of divine love.

Even now, many hearts that had previously been empty little vessels are full of the ointment of the Spirit, although they seemed to have been filled only from a small quantity of oil. When this is given to one person after another, and faith is received by the hearers, the woman—namely the holy Church—having been delivered, is no longer held under the debt of her creditor.

“Now it happened one day that Elisha was passing through Shunem. There was a prominent woman there, and she detained him so that he might eat bread. And whenever he passed that way, he turned aside to her to eat bread.”

This woman, who received the prophet as a guest, can aptly indicate the origin of the Israelite people, which existed in the patriarchs. Therefore, just as this woman deserved to receive Elisha the prophet as a guest, so that people deserved to receive the Lord of the prophets as a guest. For Abraham and Sarah deserved to receive and feed three men beside the valley of Mamre (Genesis 18).

To this woman, who had no son, the prophet promised, saying:

“At this time and at this same hour, if life accompanies you, you shall have a son in your womb.”

She replied: “No, I beg you, my lord, man of God; do not lie to your handmaid.” And the woman conceived and bore a son at the time and at the same hour that Elisha had said.

The Lord likewise spoke similar words to Abraham, saying: “Returning, I will come to you at this time, life accompanying you, and Sarah your wife shall have a son” (Genesis 18). When Sarah heard this, she laughed behind the door of the tent, secretly saying: “After I have grown old, and my lord is aged, shall I give myself to pleasure?” But the Lord visited Sarah, as he had promised her, and fulfilled what he had spoken. And she conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time which he had foretold, saying:

“After the boy had grown, he was struck with a pain in the head and died at midday during the harvest.”

When the Israelite people had increased in Egypt and had been led out by Moses into the wilderness, and had heard the Lord’s voice in fire and darkness, at the very time when it ought to have been enlightened by the light of knowledge, it immediately returned in its mind to idolatry and died (Exodus 19–20).

“And Elisha said to Gehazi, his servant: ‘Gird your loins, take my staff in your hand, and go. If a man meets you, do not greet him. And if anyone greets you, do not answer him, and place my staff upon the boy’s face.’” (From Gregory.)

What does it signify that the boy sent by Elisha with the staff does not raise the dead man by himself, but Elisha comes, stretches himself over the dead man, draws himself together over his limbs, walks back and forth, and breathes seven times into the dead man’s mouth, immediately restoring him to living light through the ministry of compassion? It signifies that God, the author of the human race, grieved over the human race as over a dead boy, when in compassion he looked upon us extinguished by the sting of iniquity.

And because through Moses he brought forth the terror of the Law, he sent the staff, as it were, through a boy. For through the Law God held the rod when he said:

“If anyone does this or that, let him die.”

Therefore fear was unable to raise us from the death of sin; but the grace of gentleness, breathed upon us, lifted us back to the condition of life. The boy with the staff was unable to raise the dead, “because,” as Paul bears witness, “the Law brought nothing to perfection.”

But he himself, coming by his own power and humbly stretching himself over the corpse, drawing himself together over the dead man’s limbs so that they might be made equal to his own, did so because “although he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being.”

“He walked back and forth,” because he calls both Judaea nearby and the nations situated far away.

“He breathed seven times upon the dead man,” because, through the opening of the divine gift, he breathes the grace of the sevenfold Spirit upon those lying in the death of sin.

“And immediately the living man rises,” because the one whom the rod of terror could not raise is restored to life by the spirit of love.

“Now there was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets were dwelling before him. And he said to one of his servants: ‘Set on the large pot and cook stew for the sons of the prophets,’ etc.”

“There was,” he says, “a famine in the land”—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord (Amos 8). And the sons of the prophets dwelt before Elisha, when the sons of holy preachers, “who walk in the law of the Lord and search out his testimonies, seeking him with their whole heart” (Psalm 118), always live in the presence of the Lord Savior.

“The boy went out into the field to gather wild herbs so that he might cook stew from them. And he found something like a wild vine and gathered from it wild gourds of the field. Cutting them up, he made stew in the pot.”

This happens when someone devoted to the letter of the Law, or a student of philosophical disciplines, seeking nourishment from the word, finds the bitterness of the legal letter or something deadly in the books of philosophers, mixes it with evangelical truth, and, cooking such a stew in the pot of his heart, prepares such teaching as food for his hearers.

For the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (1 Corinthians 3). And again: “The prudence of the flesh,” he says, “is death, but the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8).

When the faithful people perceive this, they cry out that there is death in the pot, detesting such teaching as a deception of souls and raising their voices against it. But at Elisha’s command, flour is put into the pot, when spiritual knowledge is introduced into such a mixture, so that, with all the bitterness of perversity removed, healthy nourishment may be prepared from it for the faithful.

“A certain man came from Baal-shalisha, bringing to the man of God the firstfruits of bread, twenty barley loaves, and new grain in his sack,” etc.

The man from Baal-shalisha is described as coming and bringing to the man of God the firstfruits of bread, twenty barley loaves, and new grain in his sack. Whom can we more suitably understand by this man than the assembly of the holy Fathers, who excel in strength of spirit and good works?

He is rightly said to have come from Baal-shalisha. For Baal-shalisha is interpreted as “having the third.” Therefore the one who preserves the number three in belief and confession of the holy Trinity is rightly from Baal-shalisha.

This man offers the man of God the firstfruits of bread when, inspired by his grace, he offers to our Redeemer books composed concerning the origin of creatures. He offers twenty barley loaves—that is, the Decalogue of the Law contained in the writings of Moses and the prophets. He offers new grain in his sack when he presents the New Testament after the advent of our Mediator in the writings of the holy Gospel and the apostles.

Our Elisha therefore commands his servants, namely the holy preachers, to distribute this offering to the faithful people; that is, according to the Gospel saying, “as a learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, to bring forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matthew 13), so that they may be refreshed by the nourishment of the divine word.

We read of this mystery repeated in the Gospel, when “five thousand people” are said to have been satisfied at the breaking of “five loaves” (Matthew 14), and likewise “four thousand people” at the breaking of “seven loaves,” and when, after the crowds had been satisfied, “twelve baskets or seven hampers of fragments” were gathered (Matthew 15). For no one can grasp all the mysteries of divine Scripture without something remaining for him after he has been satisfied, according to the Lord’s word.

## Chapter V

Concerning Naaman the Syrian, whose leprosy Elisha cured in the name of the Lord.

“Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a great man with his lord and held in honor. For through him the Lord had given deliverance to Syria. He was a strong and wealthy man, but a leper,” etc.

This Naaman, who is described as commander of the army of the king of Syria, whom can he better signify than the Gentile people, who throughout the three-part world exercised supremacy through the power of warfare and enjoyed the splendor of worldly possessions? This is expressed in the interpretation of his name. Naaman is interpreted as “beauty,” or “their commotion.”

But although this man was strong and wealthy, he is nevertheless remembered as a leper, because, although he seemed to rule through the power of his kingdom and the abundance of his possessions, he appeared foul through the wickedness of error and the leprosy of idolatry.

“Now raiders had gone out from Syria and had taken captive from the land of Israel a little girl, who was in the service of Naaman’s wife. She said to her mistress: ‘Would that my lord had gone to the prophet who is in Samaria! Surely he would have cured him of the leprosy he has,’ etc.”

Raiding bands went out from Syria, which is interpreted as “loftiness,” when the Gentiles, led by desire and entangled in various businesses, wandering throughout the whole earth, placed their hope in the uncertainty of riches.

Coming from there into the land, they took captive a little woman. While placed in captivity, she testified concerning the prophet in Israel, because fame about Israel, carried by the merchants of the nations, disclosed throughout the whole world to the curiosity of human beings—which is signified by Naaman’s wife—that the true prophet and Savior of all remained in Judaea.

“Naaman therefore entered in to his lord and reported to him, saying: ‘Thus and thus the girl from the land of Israel spoke.’”

This occurs when those to whom knowledge of the word of God has come suggest to those set over them the greatness of spiritual knowledge.

“The king of Syria sends a letter to the king of Israel for the healing of his servant.”

This occurs when the leaders of the nations, hearing that God is in Israel—for “God is known in Judaea; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75)—and looking ahead to the salvation of their own people, send an embassy to Judaea in order to receive the faith of the Savior through apostolic teaching.

Hence Cornelius the centurion sent from Caesarea to Joppa to Peter (Acts 10), and in a vision a Macedonian man appeared to Paul, exhorting him to come and help those who were in Macedonia, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 16).

“When the king of Israel had read the letter, he tore his garments and said: ‘Am I God, that I can kill and make alive?’”

What does this king of Israel signify? Having heard the embassy of Syria seeking healing from the prophet of Israel, he was terrified. He signifies the priests, scribes, and Pharisees, the rulers of the Jews, who, observing that crowds were gathering from everywhere to our Redeemer for the sake of their salvation, regarded it as blasphemy and tore their garments, just as we read in the Gospel that the chief priest did after hearing Christ’s preaching (Matthew 26).

But although the king of Israel was frightened by such a message, the prophet of God, recognizing that those people had migrated to him, persuaded them to come to him, saying:

“Let him come to me, so that he may know that there is a prophet in Israel,” because our Lord “those whom he foreknew, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Romans 8).

“Then Naaman came with horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha’s house. Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying: ‘Go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will regain its health and you will be cleansed.’ Naaman became angry and went away, saying: [Col. 0232B] ‘I thought that he would come out to me, stand and invoke the name of the Lord his God, touch the place of the leprosy with his hand, and cure me.’”

When the Gentile people come to the house of our Elisha—that is, the holy Church—they receive from the messenger sent by him the instruction to wash themselves seven times in the Jordan, and thus regain their health and be cleansed, because through angelic preachers the Lord says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3). And again: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16).

The waters of the Jordan therefore signify holy baptism, because in them our Savior consecrated baptism for us. But the fact that Naaman, indignant at such an answer, [Col. 0232C] despised the washing of the Jordan’s water signifies the simplicity of the inexperienced, who were unable to understand its spiritual efficacy, because “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2).

“Then, when he had turned away and was departing in anger, his servants approached him and spoke to him: ‘Father, if the prophet had told you to do something great, surely you ought to have done it; how much more, since he has now said to you, “Wash, and you will be cleansed”?’ So he went down and washed seven times in the Jordan according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was cleansed.”

The servants of Naaman therefore rightly persuaded him, with better counsel, to fulfill the prophetic command, because the Lord often reveals what is better through a younger person; and, according to Peter’s words, “God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10). [Col. 0232D] He went away and washed seven times according to the word of the man of God, and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, because everyone cleansed in the waters of baptism through the invocation of the sevenfold Spirit will regain health and be brought back to the infancy of an innocent life, so that he may be deemed worthy to attain entry into eternal life. Hence Truth himself says to his disciples: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18).

Finally, “Naaman returned to the man of God with all his company, came and stood before him, and said: ‘Truly I know that there is no God in all the [Col. 0233A] earth except in Israel.’” This is the catholic confession: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matthew 22), since “all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (Psalm 95). And so that you might recognize that all the sacraments of baptism have been prefigured here—in baptism we are commanded to renounce Satan and confess faith in God—Naaman denies that he will henceforth sacrifice to foreign gods and declares that he will serve the Lord alone in all things. He also rejoices to take some of the holy land with him, because those who have been baptized ought also to be strengthened through participation in the Lord’s body.

“Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, said: ‘My master has spared this Syrian Naaman, by not accepting from him what he brought. As the Lord lives, I will run after him [Col. 0233B] and take something from him.’”

After this Scripture relates that Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, coveted the money that the aforementioned Syrian had offered to the man of God; but, when his master refused to accept anything from it, Gehazi shamefully acquired it through a lie—what his master had, out of faith, refused to accept.

Gehazi, whose name means “seeing a precipice,” or “vision of a valley,” signifies the Jewish people, who were once called the Child of God, as the prophet Hosea says: “Israel was a child, and I loved him” (Hosea 11). But after rejecting the Gospel and crucifying the Son of God, they cast themselves from such dignity into the pit of avarice and, pursuing earthly desire—which the sons of God, reborn through baptism, rejected—brought upon themselves, by the sentence of the just Judge, the leprosy of error that believers had laid aside. [Col. 0233C] Likewise, all who, after baptism and a more reformed life, return to their former vices become entangled once more in the filth from which they had hoped to be freed. Hence it is written: “The dog returns to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire; so too the fool repeats his folly” (2 Peter 2; Proverbs 26).

## CHAPTER VI. On the sons of the prophets complaining about the narrowness of their dwelling, and on the iron being brought back from the water through Elisha

(CHAPTER 6.) “The sons of the prophets said to Elisha: ‘Behold, the place where we live before you is too narrow for us. Let us go as far as the Jordan, and let each of us take from the forest a piece of timber, so that we may build [Col. 0233D] a place there for ourselves to dwell.’ He said: ‘Go.’ One of them said: ‘Come, then, you also, with your servants.’ He answered: ‘I will come.’ And he went with them. When they had come to the Jordan, they were cutting wood. It happened that, while one was cutting a piece of timber, the iron of the axe fell into the water. He cried out and said: ‘Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing.’ The man of God said: ‘Where did it fall?’ He showed him the place. Then Elisha cut a piece of wood and threw it there, and the iron floated. He said: ‘Take it.’ The man stretched out his hand and took it,” and so on.

This action aptly applies, by its symbolic meaning, to our Redeemer. (From Isidore.) When wood was being cut with axes, the iron sprang from the wood, sank into the depth of the river, and returned to the piece of wood that Elisha threw down upon it from above. So too, when Christ’s presence, working through the body, cut down the impious Jews as fruitless trees—for John had said of them, “Behold, the axe is laid to the roots of the trees” (Matthew 3)—during the intervening Passion, the body itself departed and descended into the depths. Laid in the tomb, it rose again when the spirit returned to it, as though to its handle. [Col. 0234A]

Alternatively, the iron in the handle signifies the gift of understanding in the heart. (From Gregory.) To cut wood by this means is to rebuke those who act wrongly. Sometimes, when one acts carelessly and fails to avoid the fall of vainglory in the knowledge he has received, the iron is lost in the water, because through disordered conduct understanding becomes foolish. We know that this understanding is given precisely so that it may be restored before the eyes of the Giver through good action. [Col. 0234B]

Hence the man who had lost the iron rightly cried out: “Alas, alas, alas, my lord! And I had borrowed this very thing.” The elect have this characteristic: whenever the fault of vainglory furtively intrudes upon their knowledge, they quickly return to their heart and pursue with tears whatever they find within themselves to be condemnable before the eyes of the strict Judge. In their weeping they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed, but also the good things that, having received the gift, they ought in good faith to have returned. For they feel themselves all the more sinful when, because of the good works they could have performed but neglected, they are held liable as debtors.

Therefore the one who loses the iron rightly cries: “Alas, alas, alas! And I had borrowed this very thing,” as though he were saying: “Through the dissolution of negligence I lost what I had received from the creditor’s grace in order to return it through good works.” [Col. 0234C] Yet God never abandons the mind that truly acknowledges itself in sin. Hence Elisha immediately comes, throws down a piece of wood, and brings the iron to the surface, because our Redeemer, looking upon us mercifully, humbles the sinner’s heart and reforms the understanding that he had lost.

“The wood sinks, and the iron is brought to the surface,” because our Redeemer both humbles the heart that is exalted in its thoughts and restores knowledge. Hence another translation says that he broke the wood, threw it in, and thus raised the iron. To break the wood is to crush the heart’s pride. To throw the wood down to the depths is to humble the exalted heart, as we have said, through knowledge of its own weakness. [Col. 0234D] The iron returns to the surface because understanding returns to its former use in practice.

Since, therefore, the gift of understanding that one receives is scarcely guarded amid so many difficulties, great care must be taken lest it grow sluggish through idleness, and care must be taken lest it vanish through the vice of pride in the stimulation of activity. Holy men do not exult merely when they recognize what they are doing. Rather, when they do what they have understood—even if, in understanding, they rejoice more abundantly in the gift of the Giver—they nevertheless consider with sorrow the obligation of action, so that through action they may repay what has been granted to them in understanding.

For a debtor is foolish if he gladly receives borrowed money but pays no attention to the time when he must return it; [Col. 0235A] the joy of receiving is properly restrained when, with diligent foresight, the appointed time for repayment is also kept in mind. [Col. 0235A]

## CHAPTER VII. On the king of Syria lying in wait for Elisha

“But the king of Syria was waging war against Israel, and took counsel with his servants, saying: ‘Let us set an ambush in this place and that place.’ The man of God sent word to the king of Israel, saying: ‘Beware of passing through that place, because the Syrians are lying in ambush there.’ So the king of Israel sent men to the place that the man of God had told him about, and he anticipated the Syrians and kept watch there,” and so on.

Whom does this king of Syria more fittingly signify here than earthly power, which, often thinking arrogantly, persecutes the people of God—that is, the sons of light? [Col. 0235B] Through Elisha, namely through the teaching of our Lord, they are taught to guard against the ambushes of enemies, as in the saying: “Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10). And again: “Beware of men” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “Beware of false prophets” (Matthew 7). Recognizing this, worldly power plans to kill the prophet himself, when it hastens to extinguish Christ in the hearts of the elect.

“Therefore the king of Syria sent horses and chariots and the strength of his army there. When they had come by night, they surrounded the city.” Thus everyone who, trusting in the weapons of wickedness, prepares ambushes for Christ’s servants wages war against the Church, blinded by the night of treachery.

[Col. 0235C] “Rising early, the servant of the true God went out, saw the army surrounding the city, and reported to him, saying: ‘Alas, alas, my lord, what shall we do?’” and so on.

This statement denotes those who, because of faintness of heart, fear bodily punishments. The prophet answered him: “Do not be afraid, for there are more with us than with them.” And the Savior says to his disciples: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, because I have overcome the world” (John 16). And again: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more that they can do to you; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10). And during his Passion the Lord said to Peter: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26). [Col. 0235D]

“When Elisha had prayed, he said: ‘Lord, open his eyes, that he may see.’ And the Lord opened the eyes of the servant, and he saw. And behold, the mountain was full of fiery horses and chariots surrounding Elisha.”

It is very necessary, therefore, that our Elisha open the eyes of our heart, so that we may consider and understand “that all who trust in him will not be put to shame” (Psalm 124).

“Elisha prayed to the Lord, saying: ‘Strike, I beg you, this people with blindness.’ And the Lord struck them so that they could not see, according to the word of Elisha.”

It is good, therefore, for those whose eye causes them to stumble that it be plucked out and cast away from them (Matthew 5), [Col. 0236A] so that the gaze of pride and wickedness may be closed and the eye of sound faith and simplicity may be opened. Hence the Apostle says: “If anyone among you seems to be wise, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3).

“The king of Israel said to Elisha, when he had seen them: ‘Shall I strike them, my father?’ He answered: ‘You shall not strike them. For you did not capture them with your sword or your bow, so that you might strike them. Set bread and water before them, so that they may eat and drink and go to their lord.’”

After Elisha had brought the enemies into Samaria, he did not permit them to be killed, but prepared a great provision of food for them and sent them away in peace. Likewise, the Lord first blinded Saul, who had long been kicking against the goad; then he filled him magnificently with spiritual knowledge [Col. 0236B] and sent him to preach his Gospel among the nations (Acts 9). He also commanded us, saying: “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the famine that occurred in Samaria because of the siege by Ben-hadad, king of Syria, and on the Israelites’ miraculous deliverance through the Lord’s grace

“After these events, Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered his entire army, went up, and besieged Samaria. And a great famine occurred in Samaria,” and so on.

Scripture relates that Ben-hadad, king of Syria, besieged Samaria. When famine arose, the people were greatly afflicted; but, as the Lord had mercy, [Col. 0236C] the word of the Lord was revealed to Elisha, and he foretold future consolation for the people, saying:

(CHAPTER 7.) “Thus says the Lord: ‘At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will be sold for one stater, and two measures of barley for one stater, at the gate of Samaria.’ When one of the commanders, upon whose hand the king leaned, did not believe this, he said to the man of God: ‘Even if the Lord were to make floodgates in heaven, could what you say possibly happen?’ He answered: ‘You will see it with your eyes, but you will not eat of it.’”

In this passage Ben-hadad with his army may mystically be understood as the devil, who, through envy, incites the hearts of the wicked to wage war against the Church. Under this king are now the false Jews of whom it is written in the Apocalypse: “They say that they are Jews, and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan” (Revelation 2). [Col. 0236D] Under this king are the pagans, and also the heretics.

When persecution is inflicted by the ancient enemy through such people, the people of God—who are placed in Samaria, that is, in the keeping of divine law—are afflicted. A severe famine arises when teachers are not permitted to preach the word of God freely. But when Elisha reveals it—that is, when our Redeemer judges through the Gospel—salvation, which “is far from sinners” (Psalm 119), is recognized as near to those who fear God.

Our Lord says to his servants: “At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will be sold for one stater, and two measures of barley for one stater, at the gate of Samaria.” What, then, is the measure of fine flour except the perfect measure of divine wisdom contained in the New Testament? And what do the two [Col. 0237A] measures of barley signify except knowledge of the Law and the Prophets? They are compared with one stater, that is, catholic faith. “At the gate of Samaria” means in apostolic preaching, through which one enters the Church.

“‘At this time,’ he says, ‘tomorrow a measure of fine flour will be sold for one shekel.’” It is as though he had said: When the storm of persecution that is occurring today has ceased, tomorrow—that is, in the future—the Lord will grant rest and tranquility, so that the preaching of the Gospel may be brought to completion among believers.

At the time of the Lord’s Passion there was, as it were, a famine of the word of the Lord, when the apostles abandoned him and all fled (Matthew 26), and shut themselves indoors out of fear of the Jews. Again it is written: “No one dared to speak openly about him” (John [Col. 0237B] 7). But when the day of the resurrection shone forth, the time had arrived when Christ’s companions, seeing him alive and later seeing him ascend into heaven, freely preached the word of God to both Jews and Gentiles after receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit (John 20). Thus Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled: “The waters have burst forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert; what was dry land has become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water” (Isaiah 35).

Hence the Lord, speaking through that same prophet, says: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money, hasten, buy and eat. Come, buy without money and without any exchange, wine and milk. Why do you weigh out money for what is not bread, and your labor for what does not satisfy? Listen, listening to me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in abundance. Incline your ear and come to me; listen, and your soul will live.” [Col. 0237C]

After the enemies were thrown into confusion and put to flight, Scripture adds that four leprous men went to the Syrian camp. Finding no one there, they ate and drank, carried away gold, silver, and clothing, and hid them. Afterwards, moved by remorse, they announced this in the city and provided signs of the deliverance.

Who, then, are these lepers except those who, devoted to various vices or entangled in different errors, bring the filth of an inward disease outward and display it on their skin? The Lord often converts such people to the faith, cleanses them from error and vices, and makes them messengers of true salvation.

“Therefore the lepers entered the Syrian camp, ate and drank, and carried away gold and silver from it,” when, though despised in this world, they devote themselves to philosophical study and acquire subtlety of understanding and elegance of expression, by which they may serve the needs of the Church, properly equipped. [Col. 0237D] Thus the Lord frequently grants such people both sharpness of intellect and the gift of true wisdom.

They are rightly said to be four, so that, imbued with the learning of the four Gospels, they may preach the truth to the four parts of the world. For we read in the Gospel that the Lord ate with tax collectors and sinners, and that a woman who was a sinner in the city watered his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment (Luke 7). He made Matthew an apostle [Col. 0238A] and evangelist from a tax collector (Matthew 9). “After his resurrection he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and announced it to those who had been with him, while they were mourning and weeping” (Mark 16).

As for that commander upon whose hand the king had leaned, who had distrusted the prophet’s words and had been stationed at the gate, “the crowd trampled him at the entrance, and he died according to what the man of God had said.” This commander represents the scribes and Pharisees, who, possessing the key of knowledge, did not themselves enter the catholic Church through faith and hindered those who wished to enter. [Col. 0238B] Truth himself says to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before men. You yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit those who are entering to enter” (Matthew 23).

The one whom the crowd trampled at the gate stood uselessly before the door of faith and obstructed the steps of those entering. Therefore, rightly trampled—that is, condemned by the judgment of the just Judge—he will be sent into everlasting darkness. The Lord also says in the Gospel: “If salt has lost its savor, it is good for nothing any longer except to be thrown outside and trampled by men” (Matthew 5).

## CHAPTER IX. On the anointing of Jehu as king

(CHAPTER 9.) “Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him: ‘Gird your loins, take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead. When you arrive there, [Col. 0238C] you will see Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. Enter, raise him up from among his brothers, and bring him into an inner chamber. Taking the flask of oil, pour it over his head and say: “Thus says the Lord: I have anointed you king over Israel,”’” and so on.

The history of the Books of Kings then relates how the Lord appointed Jehu to eradicate the house of Ahab and kill the priests of Baal. He struck Joram, king of Israel, and Ahaziah, king of Judah, and caused Jezebel, the most wicked queen, to be thrown from the palace at Jezreel.

Jehu may typologically signify the rule of the nations, which our Lord and Redeemer appointed to exercise judgment in the sacrilegious city that killed the prophets and the God of the prophets and persecuted his apostles; to destroy it through a righteous zeal; to overthrow the empty priesthood [Col. 0238D] that it had meaninglessly retained after Christ’s coming; to overturn the temple; and also to cast down from the height of royal power the impious Synagogue, which had always thirsted for the blood of the saints, and to kill its rulers.

## CHAPTER X. On the tyranny of Athaliah, mother of King Ahaziah

(CHAPTER 11.) “Athaliah, mother of Ahaziah, seeing that her son was dead, rose up and killed all the royal offspring.”

The history that follows recounts the tyranny of Athaliah, mother of King Ahaziah. When she saw that her son was dead, she rose up and killed all the royal offspring.

“But Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were being killed, together with his nurse from the bedchamber; [Col. 0239A] she hid him from Athaliah so that he would not be killed. He remained secretly with her in the house of the Lord for six years,” because Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the high priest.

This Athaliah, therefore, who attempted to extinguish David’s offspring and destroy the royal line, aptly expresses the impiety of the Synagogue, which through wickedness of mind was lying in wait for the seed of David—that is, Christ—and always harbored hatred against him. She once appeared to reign when she was observing the ceremonies of the Law temporarily.

Athaliah is interpreted as “the temporal one of the Lord.” But the vigor of Jehosheba is interpreted as “the abundance of the Lord,” that is, the Church, in which true delights are found. [Col. 0239B] Joash, whose name is interpreted as “the memory of the Lord,” namely Christ, in whom the memory of the Lord’s name resides, is preserved so that he may not be killed in the hearts of the elect by the cruelty of the serving enemy. Rather, he is nourished in the house of Jehoiada the high priest, whose name means “beloved of the Lord,” concerning whom the Father’s voice says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3, 17). His house is the holy Church, where he remains in the faith of the elect and daily brings about the growth of his body (1 Timothy 3), until, at the time of judgment, he raises the scepter of his kingdom and his power against those who were planning to suppress him, and consigns the murderess of the saints to eternal punishments (Revelation 19).

## CHAPTER XI. On Jehoiada the high priest, and how he established Joash, son of Ahaziah, as king

[Col. 0239C]

(ibid.) “In the seventh year Jehoiada sent for the centurions and soldiers, took them with him, and brought them into the temple of the Lord. He made a covenant with them and adjured them in the house of the Lord; then he showed them the king’s son and commanded them, saying: ‘This is what you must do. One third of you who come in on the Sabbath shall keep watch over the royal palace; another third shall be at the gate of Sur; and another third shall be at the gate behind the dwelling of the shield-bearers. You shall guard the watch of the house of Messa. The two parts of you, all who go out on the Sabbath, shall guard the watch of the house of the Lord around the king, and you shall surround him, with weapons in your hands. If anyone enters the temple precincts, let him be killed. [Col. 0239D] You shall be with the king when he enters and when he goes out.’”

The centurions did everything that Jehoiada the priest had commanded them. Each took his men, those who entered on the Sabbath together with those who went out after the Sabbath, and they came to Jehoiada the priest. He gave them the spears and weapons of King David, which were in the house of the Lord. Each man stood with his weapon in his hand, from the right side of the temple to the left side of the altar and the building, around the king,” and so on.

Anyone who carefully recalls what was said above about the courts of the house of the Lord can understand how these things were done and in what places. But, so as not to weary the reader, let us omit what has already been explained and turn to what was said about the division of the crowd, the arrangement of which is as follows. [Col. 0240A]

(From Bede.) There were twenty-four courses of priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, which succeeded one another in order through as many weeks. On the Sabbath a new group entered upon its service, while after the Sabbath the group that had ministered during the preceding week returned home. But on this occasion, because it was necessary to enlarge the army around the new king, the high priest retained both those whose week of service was beginning and those who had already completed their week, preventing them from departing.

He had also summoned from all the cities of Judah other Levites and the heads of the families of Israel to Jerusalem through the centurions sent for this purpose, as the Books of Chronicles relate (2 Chronicles 23): [Col. 0240B] he divided them, so that they might bring out the king’s son, in this manner: all who had completed their Sabbath duty and were about to depart were divided into two groups and stood around the king, armed, in the inner parts of the court. The remaining multitude—that is, those who were not of the tribe of Levi—guarded the outer gates of the courts against the queen’s fury, in case she attempted any hostile action.

Those who had recently come for the Sabbath—the priests, Levites, and doorkeepers—were divided into three groups. They watched over the king’s house, that is, the palace, lest the queen, having gathered an army, defend it against the king; and they guarded the gate of the dwelling of the shield-bearers, through which one descended from the temple to the palace, as is said below.

“They brought the king out from the house of the Lord and came by way of the gate of the shield-bearers into the palace, [Col. 0240C] and he sat upon the royal throne.” The gate of Seireff and the house of Messa, which are mentioned together with the gate of the shield-bearers, seem to have been located there.

The book of Chronicles calls the shield-bearers the king’s guardians. After relating that Rehoboam made bronze shields in place of gold ones, it adds: “He delivered them into the hands of the commanders of the shield-bearers, who guarded the entrance of the palace” (2 Chronicles 12).

That same book recounts all these matters more distinctly: “One third of you who come on the Sabbath, of the priests, Levites, and doorkeepers, shall be at the gates. Another third shall be at the king’s house, and another third at the gate called the Foundation Gate. Let all the rest of the people remain in the courts of the house of the Lord; no one else shall enter the house of the Lord except the priests and those Levites who minister. They alone shall enter, because they are consecrated; and all the rest of the people shall keep the watches of the Lord. [Col. 0240D] Let the Levites surround the king, each with his weapons” (2 Chronicles 23).

What follows concerning the same matter is: “He brought out the king’s son and placed upon him the diadem and the testimony.” By the diadem he signifies the royal insignia of the head; by the testimony he signifies the decrees of God’s Law, by which the king is instructed what he ought to do and how he ought to live.

Finally, the Books of Chronicles say more explicitly: “They placed the diadem upon him and gave him the Law to hold in his hand” (2 Chronicles 23). This was certainly a matter of great and salutary prudence: after the death of the tyrannical and impious queen, when the son of the legitimate king succeeded to the throne, the discipline of observing God’s Law was entrusted to him together with the royal garb, so that, seeing himself set over the people for their governance, he might remember that he himself ought to be governed by submission to the divine laws. [Col. 0241A]

## CHAPTER XII. On the zeal of Jehoiada the high priest in restoring the temple

(CHAPTER 12.) “Joash said to the priests: ‘Let the priests receive all the money of the holy things that is brought into the temple of the Lord by those who pass by, the money offered for the price [Col. 0241B] of a person, and whatever they freely and voluntarily bring into the temple of the Lord according to the inclination of their heart; and let them use it, according to their order, to repair whatever damage they see to be in need of restoration in the house,’” and so on.

Our King commands his teachers to receive all the money that passersby offer in the temple of the Lord as the price of a person and as the vow of their heart. Whatever is contributed to the Lord’s treasury by righteous passersby—whether spiritual knowledge or good examples—should be applied through the work of the priests, that is, preachers, to the restoration of the spiritual temple, so that they may repair whatever they find damaged there through error or vice, lest through the negligence of teachers the multitude of hearers perish.

But what follows—“Until the twenty-third year of King Joash the priests did not repair the damage to the temple”—signifies that, before the Savior’s coming, although the teaching of the Law existed among the Jewish people, it was corrupted in many respects through the negligence of teachers, until the one who gave the Law himself came and taught that, through faith in the holy Trinity, the Decalogue of the Law was to be observed spiritually in the writings of Moses [Col. 0241C] and the Prophets.

“King Joash called Jehoiada the high priest and the priests and said to them: ‘Why have you not repaired the damage to the temple? Therefore, do not receive any more money according to your order, but return it for the restoration of the temple,’” and so on.

Likewise our Lord, commanding the teachers of the Gospel, says: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for harvest. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (John 4). And again: “Go,” he says, “preach the Gospel to every creature. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers. You have received without payment; give without payment” (Mark 16; Matthew 10).

“And Jehoiada the high priest took a treasury chest, opened an opening in its top, and placed it beside the altar, on the right of those entering the house of the Lord. The priests who guarded the doors put into it all the money that was brought into the temple of the Lord.” [Col. 0241D]

Thus our high priest, who offered himself as an unblemished sacrifice to God, placed one treasury chest—that is, he established one catholic Church. He made an opening in its top because he prepared from it a passage to heaven. He placed it beside the altar, on the right of those entering the house of the Lord. The altar is the body of the Lord, beside which the treasury chest was placed because the Church is joined to it; and it is on the right of those entering the house of the Lord because the purpose of the elect, who enter the Church through faith, is to reach eternal blessedness, which is signified by the right hand. [Col. 0242A]

The priests who guard the door of the temple put into it all the money brought to the temple of the Lord, when the holy preachers who guard the entrance of faith offer the vows of the faithful to God in words and deeds and commend them properly to him in the Church through prayers.

“The king’s [Col. 0242B] scribe and the high priest went up, poured out, and counted the money that was found in the house of the Lord. They gave it, by number and measure, into the hands of those who were in charge of the builders of the house of the Lord, who spent it on the carpenters and masons who worked on the house of the Lord.”

He calls the king’s scribe and the high priest the highest teachers, who distributed the money contributed by number and measure to those in charge of the carpenters and masons—that is, to the stewards of the divine word. These stewards distributed the measure of the evangelical grain to their fellow servants who work in the house of the Lord and construct works of virtue in the divine building.

What else did the apostles do, whom divine election established as leaders in the Church, when through the disciples subject to them they scattered the seeds of the divine word throughout the whole world, so that they might perfect among their hearers workers suited to the will of God? Some built with timber, when they strove to prepare themselves and those who obeyed them as fruitful trees in the house of the Lord. Others repaired the roofs when they vigorously rebuked those things brought about through heresy and unbelievers [the printed Latin is syntactically uncertain]. “So the restoration of the house of the Lord was completed in all that required expenditure, for strengthening the house of the Lord.” [Col. 0242C]

This accords with the Apostle’s saying: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4). And shortly afterward: “He himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (ibid.). But what follows—[the supplied source ends here incomplete].

“Nevertheless, jugs for the temple of the Lord, forks, censers, trumpets, and every golden and silver vessel were not made from the same money that was brought into the temple of the Lord.” This signifies that one method must be used for fashioning vessels for the service of the Lord, and another for preparing the timbers and stones for the building of the house; for one kind of instruction is required by which beginners are imbued with faith, and another by which those already mature are instructed toward the fullness of knowledge.

The vessels of the house of the Lord may rightly be understood as those who are already capable of receiving divine gifts and become suitable for God’s service. The jugs, then, may signify those who contain within themselves the water of divine wisdom. The forks, too, may signify spiritual teachers, whose duty is to distribute the body and blood of the Lord to believers, to deny them to unbelievers, and likewise to apportion spiritual nourishment from the word to each person as is appropriate. For there are certain things in the words of God which he has deigned to reveal to our lowliness and grant for the nourishment of our refreshment. There are also other things of such profound depth that they are disclosed only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, while they utterly exceed the measure of our capacity.

The censers, however, clearly signify those who offer pure prayer to God from a clean conscience and sincere faith, and who can say with the Prophet: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 104). But what else are the trumpets than holy preachers, who throughout the whole world send forth the voice of evangelical preaching? Concerning their persons it is said through the prophet: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Psalm 58). And the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18). It follows:

“And no account was required from those men who received the money in order to distribute it to the craftsmen, but they handled it in good faith,” and so forth. (From Bede.) He demonstrates the devotion of those about whom the passage speaks: they had shown such zeal in religion that no one doubted that they handled the Lord’s money without suspicion of any fraud and faithfully offered it, after taking it from the treasury, to the craftsmen for strengthening the house, according to what was needed in each case.

Therefore those who received the spiritual money of the word of God for distribution to their fellow servants—that is, to the divine workers—must consider how much faith and discretion are required of those who must give an account of this same money, so that they may strive to be found no less faithful in spiritual matters than those others were found to be in material matters.

“But they did not bring into the temple of the Lord the money for the offense or the money for sins, because it belonged to the priests.” This knowledge shows that no one ought easily to entrust himself to his own judgment, but should know that confession of sins and penance must be undertaken according to the judgment of the priests. They possess the knowledge to distinguish between clean and unclean, to judge the mark of leprosy, and either to condemn or to declare clean (Leviticus 10).

## CHAPTER XIII

On the illness of Elisha, during which, at the Lord’s command, he foretold to King Joash that the Syrian nation would be struck. The death of Elisha, the man of God, at whose burial a dead man touched his body and immediately came back to life.

### (Chapter XIII)

“Now Elisha was ill with the illness from which he also died. And Joash, king of Israel, went down to him and wept before him, saying: ‘My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer.’ And Elisha said: ‘Bring a bow and arrows.’ When he had brought the bow and arrows to him, he said to the king of Israel: ‘Place your hand on the bow.’ When he had placed his hand there, Elisha placed his hands over the king’s hands and said: ‘Open the eastern window.’ When he had opened it, Elisha said: ‘Shoot an arrow.’ And he shot. And Elisha said: ‘The arrow of the Lord’s salvation, and the arrow of salvation against Syria. You shall strike Syria at Aphek until you destroy it,’” and so forth.

Why does the prophet command the king of Israel to bring a bow and an arrow, unless it is because our Redeemer commands the rulers of the Church to clothe themselves with spiritual weapons and fight against the ancient enemy? For in sacred discourse the bow is sometimes used for sacred discourse itself, since it consists of both Testaments, as though of a horn and a string. Through the Old Testament the horn is represented because of its hardness; through the New, which was made when the Lord became incarnate, the string is signified. When the string is drawn, the horn is bent, because when the New Testament is examined, the Old is drawn away from the hardness of the letter and bent toward spiritual understanding, since the rigid force of its hardness is not retained.

The arrows are the very words which teachers utter. Hence it is also rightly said through the prophet concerning holy teachers entering among the Gentiles: “They will enter there with arrows and a bow” (Isaiah 7). When, therefore, we weigh the statements of sacred Scripture, we draw the bow. When we give words of instruction, we shoot arrows.

“Elisha placed his hands over the king’s hands,” when the Lord directs and strengthens the actions of teachers in his temples. He commands him to open the eastern window and shoot the arrow, because he urges his people first to be illumined by the light of knowledge and true teaching, and then to send forth the darts of their words.

“And Elisha said: ‘The arrow of the Lord’s salvation, and the arrow of salvation against Syria. You shall strike Syria at Aphek until you destroy it.’” The arrow of the Lord’s salvation, then, is holy preaching when it is presented appropriately, and it is the sure destruction of spiritual enemies when it is carried out perseveringly.

It is not lawful for the steward of the word of God ever to grow sluggish through inactivity, since he has been commanded to care for the Lord’s flock. For inertia among teachers greatly harms devoted hearers. The prophet says: “Cry out, do not cease” (Isaiah 58). And the Apostle says to Timothy: “I testify before God and Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; insist whether the time is favorable or unfavorable; rebuke, entreat, reprove, with all patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4).

Therefore a teacher ought not, because of greed, neglect the care of souls, but should rather strive through devotion toward eternal rest. This is signified by *Apher*, which is interpreted as “he will contain” or “he will seize.” Hence the same Apostle, after listing the vices that accompany greed, addressed the disciple mentioned above, saying: “But you, man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, devotion, faith, love, patience, gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith; seize eternal life, to which you were called” (1 Timothy 6).

“And Elisha said to the king: ‘Take the arrows.’ When he had taken them, he said to him again: ‘Strike the ground with the arrow.’ When he had struck it three times and then stopped, the man of God became angry with him and said: ‘If you had struck it five or six or seven times, you would have struck Syria until its destruction. But now, striking it three times,’” and so forth.

Behold, the prophet commands the king to strike the ground with the arrow. When he strikes it three times and stops, the prophet becomes angry with him because he did not strike the ground more often. So also teachers are commanded to strike the ground—that is, carnal people—with the arrow of preaching. Those who do this with insufficient zeal are rightly reproved by divine rebuke.

For what is it to strike the ground with the arrow three times except to impress the faith of the Trinity upon carnal people through teaching? But when a teacher has done this sufficiently and has led people to faith, it is necessary that he continue in the word until he teaches them to govern the five bodily senses and to devote themselves to good works, which are expressed through the number six. He must also urge them to meditate on spiritual knowledge, which the grace of the sixfold Spirit establishes in the sacred Scriptures and adds to the human race through the twofold Testament.

Those who believe that faith alone, without good works and meditation on God’s law, is sufficient for salvation are rightly reproved by the prophet, because, according to the judgment of the apostle James (James 2), “as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.” And elsewhere it is written: “The one who does not know shall not be known” (1 Corinthians 14).

“Therefore Elisha died, and they buried him. Now raiding bands from Moab came into the land that same year. As some men were burying a man, they saw the raiders and threw the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When it touched the bones of Elisha, the man came back to life and stood on his feet,” and so forth.

What does this raising of a dead corpse to life through contact with Elisha’s bones signify except the life of the faithful, which truly rests upon the death of Christ? Whoever, therefore, touches Christ’s death with firm faith and truly places his hope in him will undoubtedly share in his resurrection. For Truth itself says: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live. And everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11). And elsewhere: “As Moses,” he says, “lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XIV

On Amaziah, king of Judah, who struck Edom in the Valley of Salt.

Concerning Amaziah, king of Judah. (Chapter XIV.) “He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, ten thousand men; and he seized Sela in battle, and called its name Jezethel, to the present day,” and so forth.

The Valley of Salt was the place where salt was made, either from haylike salt-bearing vegetation, as in many places, which was cut, dried, and burned, or by heating salty well waters and boiling them until they reached the firmness of salt, or by some other process by which salt is customarily made. In this place Joab is also read to have struck twelve thousand Idumeans.

It should not be passed over that, in place of “the Valley of Salt,” the old edition seems to have put *Gemela* as the name of the region. Sela, however, is a famous city of Arabia in that same land of Edom; it is mentioned in the Book of Numbers and is still called by this name by the Syrians. *Jezethel*, the name which the victorious Amaziah imposed upon it, is interpreted as “assembly of God” or “help of God.” He acted faithfully so that it might be committed to perpetual memory that he had captured it either through the assembly of the people of God or with God’s help.

## CHAPTER XV

On Azariah, king of Judah, who is also called by another name, Uzziah, and likewise on Jeroboam, king of Israel.

### (Chapter XV)

“In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah, king of Judah, became king. He was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem,” and so forth.

Azariah is Uzziah, who, because he despised the Lord, was struck with leprosy by the Lord beside the altar when he wished to offer sacrifice contrary to the law of Moses and strove to present burnt offerings (2 Chronicles 26).

Uzziah, the leprous king, can signify the devil, whose leprosy of iniquity is incurable. When he refused to recognize his own measure and attempted to seek greater things, he was made conspicuous by the foulness of a most terrible leprosy, expelled from the house of God, and remained leprous to the end, separated from the people of God.

While this king was reigning and, insofar as he could, destroying the priesthood, the prophet Isaiah could not see that magnificent vision in which he saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty throne (Isaiah 6). As long as he held the kingdom in Judah, the prophet did not lift his eyes to heaven; the heavenly things were not opened to him; the Lord Sabaoth did not appear; nor was the holy name heard faithfully in the service.

But when that man died, all the things that the subsequent passage displayed revealed themselves in open light. Something similar is also written in Exodus: while Pharaoh lived, the people of Israel did not sigh toward the Lord from their labor in clay, bricks, and straw. While he reigned, no one sought the God of the father Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But when he died, “the children of Israel sighed,” as Scripture says, “and their cry rose up to the Lord” (Exodus 2), although, according to the historical sense, they ought rather to have rejoiced at that time and to have sighed earlier, when they were conquering.

While Ezekiel was prophesying, Pheltias son of Benaiah also died, and after the death of that wicked leader: “I fell,” he says, “on my face and cried out with a loud voice, saying, and I said: ‘Alas, alas, Adonai God, are you bringing the remnant of Israel to an end?’” (Ezekiel 9).

If, therefore, in Uzziah, Pharaoh, Pheltias, and others of this kind you understand opposing powers, you will see how, while they live, none of our people sees, sighs, or falls into repentance.

“Let not sin reign,” says the Apostle, “in your mortal body” (Romans 6). When sin reigns, we build cities for the Egyptians, we wallow in ash and filth; instead of grain we pursue straw, and instead of solid rock we pursue works of clay. (From Bede.)

Concerning Jeroboam, king of Israel: “He restored the borders of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah” (2 Kings 14).

Hamath, now called Epiphaneia, was the northern boundary of Israel. The Sea of the Arabah, which is called *Araba* in Hebrew, designates the Dead Sea. In length it extends for 580 stadia as far as Zoara of Arabia, and in breadth for 150 as far as the vicinity of Sodom. Josephus mentions this place as follows:

“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Amaziah, the eleventh [king], Jeroboam son of Joash, reigned in Israel at Samaria for forty years. This king was exceedingly impious and unjust toward God, worshiping idols and committing many inappropriate and alien practices. Yet he became the occasion of many benefits for the people of Israel.

To him Jonah prophesied that he would defeat the Syrians in battle and enlarge his own kingdom: in the north as far as the city of Emath, and in the south as far as Ispaltitis. For these had formerly been the boundaries of the Canaanites, as Jesus the prince determined those regions.

Accordingly, Jeroboam encamped against the Syrians and devastated their entire province, just as Jonah had prophesied.”

## CHAPTER XVI

On Ahaz, king of Judah, because of whose sins Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight.

### (Chapter XVI)

“In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah, became king. Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord his God, as David his father had done, but walked in the way of the kings of Israel. Moreover, he consecrated his son, making him pass through fire, according to the idols of the nations whom the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel,” and so forth.

Josephus narrates the matter in this way:

“Jotham changed this life when he had lived forty-one years, of which he had reigned twelve; he was buried in the royal tombs. The kingdom then came to his son Ahaz, who, being impious toward God and a transgressor of his father’s law, imitated the kings of the Israelites, established altars of idols in Jerusalem, and sacrificed upon them. On them he also offered his own son as a burnt offering, according to the custom of the Canaanites, and committed many other crimes besides.

He also transformed the *musach of the Sabbath*, which he had built in the temple, and the king’s outer entrance into the temple of the Lord, on account of the king of the Assyrians,” and so forth.

I have read in a certain book that the *musach of the Sabbath* was explained as a certain place or building situated in the vestibule of the temple of the Lord, where kings, when they went to the temple on the Sabbath for prayer, deposited money for alms. Thus the *musach of the Sabbath* was the treasury of the kings, just as the *corbona* was that of the priests.

It appears that Ahaz did not transform that building and the king’s outer entrance into the temple of the Lord because divine worship was to be performed there, but so that it might be profaned together with the temple, since he was eager to please the Assyrian king more than the God of his fathers and the Lord.

The Book of Chronicles seems to support this interpretation, where it is written:

“Accordingly, after Ahaz had stripped the house of the Lord and the house of the kings and the princes, he gave gifts to the king of the Assyrians; yet this did not benefit him. Indeed, in the time of his distress he increased his contempt for the Lord. King Ahaz himself sacrificed victims to the gods of Damascus, which had struck him, and said: ‘The gods of the kings of Syria help them; I will appease them with sacrifices, and they will help me.’ But they became his ruin and the ruin of all Israel” (2 Chronicles 28).

“Then, after stripping all the vessels of the house of God and breaking them, Ahaz closed the doors of the temple of the Lord and made altars for himself in every corner of Jerusalem. In all the cities of Judah he also built altars for burning incense and provoked the Lord, the God of his fathers, to anger.”

Since we have found these things written in this place, we have judged that they should be set down here, prepared to listen to the opinion of anyone who may explain them more accurately.

“Then Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight. When they besieged Ahaz, they were unable to overcome him.”

The impious king, who had abandoned the Lord, the God of his fathers, and followed the idols of the nations, was rightly abandoned by the Lord’s help. Rezin, king of Syria—that is, Aram—and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel in Samaria, rose up against him and came to Jerusalem to attack it.

We read in the Book of Chronicles (2 Chronicles 28) that Rezin, king of Damascus, after defeating Ahaz, transferred many people from Judea to Damascus; and that Pekah son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes called Israel, which reigned in Samaria, struck 120,000 armed men of Judea in a single day and led away captive to Samaria 200,000 women, boys, and girls, together with immense booty.

Again they came into Judea and wished to conquer Jerusalem, but they could not, because the Lord helped Ahaz. In this way, under the pretext of the mercy by which he was rescuing the besieged people, the Lord announced that his Son would be born from a Virgin, as the Book of the prophet Isaiah records.

To show that this was not due to Ahaz’s own merit but to the Lord’s grace, Isaiah is finally commanded to go out to meet him at the end of the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road of the fuller’s field, and to say to him:

“See that you remain quiet; do not fear, and do not let your heart be afraid because of these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the anger of the fury of Rezin, king of Syria, and the son of Remaliah. They say: ‘Let us go up against Judah, rouse it, tear it away to ourselves, and set the son of Tabeel as king in its midst.’

Thus says the Lord God: ‘It shall not stand, and this shall not happen. For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin. And yet, within sixty-five years, Ephraim shall cease to be a people’” (Isaiah 7).

The two tails of smoking firebrands—that is, of smoking torches—are Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Samaria. The reason is that in them the kingdom of Syria, that is, Damascus, and the kingdom of Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, which were also called Ephraim, came to an end.

The sixty-five years, however, are counted not from the time of Ahaz but from Uzziah. Thus the Hebrews explain the passage as follows: Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, at the time when Isaiah also began his prophetic ministry, first prophesied against Israel, saying: “Israel shall surely be led away captive from its land” (Amos 7). The heading of his prophecy is also directed against Samaria, and he began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah, king of Judah, two years before the earthquake.

They wish this earthquake to have occurred at the time when Uzziah entered the temple of God and claimed the priesthood for himself; the earth was struck, the ashes of the altar were scattered, and the king himself was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26).

They maintain that this happened in the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah, when twenty-seven years of his reign remained. For he reigned fifty-two years in all. After him his son Jotham reigned for sixteen years, and his son Ahaz for another sixteen. After him Hezekiah reigned, and in the sixth year of his reign Samaria was captured. Thus the total is sixty-five years.

For it is written that, under King Ahaz, Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, went up against Damascus, devastated it, transferred its inhabitants to Cyrene, and killed Rezin; and that he laid an ambush for Pekah son of Remaliah, and Hoshea son of Elah struck and killed him and reigned in his place over Israel for nine years.

Then Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, came and besieged Samaria, which is now called Sebaste, for three years; in the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign he captured it, defeated Hoshea, put him in prison, transferred Israel to Assyria, and settled them in Ailah and in Thabor, beside the river Gozan, in cities—or, as the Septuagint translated it, in the mountains of the Medes.

According to the allegorical sense, the interpretation is straightforward. When Ahaz, the impious king, was reigning, the king of Aram, whose name is interpreted as “lofty” and “exalted,” signifying the arrogance of worldly wisdom, and Pekah son of Remaliah—which, according to the prophet Hosea, is also associated with the tribe of Ephraim, from which Jeroboam son of Nebat established the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, separated God’s people from the house of David, and is therefore related to heretics—agree among themselves to attack the Church.

When the house of David hears this—that house which we read in Ezekiel has received the good shepherd—and its people, believing simply in the Lord, are afraid, they are afraid for this reason: they are compared not to fruitful trees but to a fruitless forest.

It is beyond doubt that these same heretics and Gentiles fight against the house of David with the swords of arguments and dialectical skill, so that although they disagree among themselves, they agree in attacking the Church, according to the saying that Herod and Pilate, though they were at odds with each other, were united in friendship during the Lord’s passion (Luke 23).

Isaiah is commanded to go out to meet the impious king, leaving his own place—not at the beginning of the aqueduct, but at the farthest limits of the upper pool, which was in the fuller’s field, where filth and stains were cleansed (Isaiah 7). Although Ahaz was reigning over Judah, because he was impious he remained at the farthest limits of the upper pool.

Therefore God has compassion not so much on the king, whom he considered unworthy of salvation, as on his people. The two tails of smoking torches, as we said earlier, represent worldly wisdom and heretical speech, whose end is burning.

They had formed their plan in vain: they intended to go up against Judah, seize it as though it were negligent and asleep, unite it to their errors, and set over it as king the son of Tabeel—that is, the good God. Each adversary considers truth to be with himself and his own teaching to be the best.

Finally, the heretic Marcion thinks that the good Son of God—that is, Christ—belongs to another god and not to the just God, whose prophets they are; he calls that God bloodthirsty, cruel, and a judge.

While they say these things, the Lord threatens them that their plan shall not stand. Yet this present world never stands for long, and the things of the world rule within their own boundaries and cities. When the time of consummation arrives—and this is sixty-two years, when the affairs of the world that were made in six years, and all things belonging to the five senses, have reached their end—then everything must be dissolved: the things which Gentiles and heretics do not believe will come, and which, because of their unbelief, they do not understand when they are spoken.

## CHAPTER XVII

On the transfer of the ten tribes that ruled in Samaria to the Assyrians by Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians; and on the fact that in their places this same king brought in other settlers, who worshiped there the gods they had worshiped in their own land, and nevertheless also worshiped the God of Israel.

### (Chapter XVII)

“The Lord was exceedingly angry with Israel, and removed them from his sight, and none remained except the tribe of Judah alone. But Judah itself did not keep the commandments of the Lord its God. Nevertheless, it walked in the errors of Israel, which Israel had committed. The Lord rejected all the descendants of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, until he cast them away from his presence,” and so forth.

What does the overthrow of the Israelites, perpetrated by the kings of Assyria, signify except the astonishing and deeply lamentable ruin of the ecclesiastical people? The Assyrian king—that is, the devil—brings this about daily with his army, devastating and besieging them. Because of their committed sins, he tears them from their own dwelling places and carries them into a foreign land, where they take greater pleasure in mourning than in uttering songs of joy.

Hence the Psalmist also recalls this same thing in mystical language, saying:

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments. For there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who carried us away said: ‘Sing us one of the songs of Zion.’ How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136).

Concerning the nations brought into Samaria by the king of the Assyrians, it is said:

“And each nation made its own god. They placed them in the shrines on the high places that the Samaritan people had made, each nation in its own cities in which they lived. For the men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; the men of Cuth made Nergal; and the men of Hamath made Ashima. The Hivites, moreover, made Nibhaz and Tartak,” and so forth.

In the Book of Places it is indeed read that Benoth and Nergal were cities which the Samaritans who had crossed over from Babylonia built in the region of Judea. Ashima was also a town built by those who had come there from Hamath; Nibhaz and Tartak were cities which the Hivites founded in that same land of Judea.

It appears, however, from the sequence of the words and the idols that these nations had formerly worshiped in their own land, that the names may be understood here in this sense. For when it had been said, “Each nation made its own god,” the statement “For the men of Babylon made Succoth and Benoth” seems to have been added to complete the thought—that is, “the tents of Benoth.”

If I am not mistaken, the translator would have done better to render *Socoth* by the Latin *tabernacula* (“tents”) and to set down the name of the idol, *Benoth*, by itself, just as the text plainly says in what follows:

“But those who were from Sepharvaim burned their sons with fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.”

Here it is shown that Adrammelech and Anammelech were idols of the city of Sepharvaim. Consequently, it seems to follow that Nergal was the idol of the Cuthaeans, Ashima that of the Hamathites, and Nibhaz and Tartak those of the Hivites.

After this Scripture reports concerning the Samaritans themselves that, while they worshiped the Lord, they also served their gods, according to the customs of the nations from which they had been transferred to Samaria. Not long afterward it continues:

“So these nations feared the Lord, but nevertheless served their idols. Their children and their grandchildren also act as their fathers did, down to the present day.”
