Since heretics are understood in the person of the Samaritans, their wickedness is appropriately expressed in the foregoing statement. Heretics possess certain sacraments in common with the holy Church, and rightly understand certain statements of the sacred Scriptures; nevertheless, they do not cease to serve the idols of their errors.

They seem to themselves to preserve the fear of God correctly when, according to their own understanding, they believe that they favor the truth. But those who disdain to possess the unity of the catholic faith truly reveal that they obey the will of malignant spirits.

It is not only the first inventors of the errors, signified by the fathers of the Samaritans, who do this. Their followers also act in the same way; these are rightly understood to be represented by the names of their children and grandchildren.

## CHAPTER XVIII

On Hezekiah, during whose reign Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, sent messengers to Jerusalem with a strong force to blaspheme the living God.

### (Chapter XVIII)

“In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, became king. He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah. He did what was good before the Lord, according to all that David his father had done. He destroyed the high places, shattered the statues, cut down the sacred groves, and broke the bronze serpent which Moses had made. For until that time the children of Israel had burned incense to it, and he called it *Nehushtan*. He placed his hope in the Lord, the God of Israel,” and so forth.

Hezekiah rightly called the serpent to which the children of Israel burned incense, and which he himself broke, *Nehushtan*, because he placed his hope in the Lord, the God of Israel, not in the bronze serpent. For *Nehushtan* is interpreted as “their bronze,” so that those who worshiped it as a divine power might recognize that it was metal, not God.

Because Hezekiah, in destroying the high places, shattering the statues, cutting down the sacred groves, and likewise crushing all the images, bears the type of the Savior—for Hezekiah is interpreted as “one who lays hold of the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord”—he appropriately bears the figure of our Redeemer in the very fact that he crushed the bronze serpent made by Moses.

For not only did our Lord and Redeemer, of whom the Prophet says, “The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle” (Psalm 24), crush the idols of the nations and destroy all their images, so that they might possess knowledge of the one almighty God and be rightly devoted to his worship; he also crushed the very letter of the Mosaic law, which the legal people continually recited in their reading and held in high esteem, and taught them to understand its spiritual meaning.

“In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. Then Hezekiah, king of Judah, sent messengers to the king of the Assyrians at Lachish, saying: ‘I have offended; withdraw from me, and I will bear whatever you impose upon me.’ The king of the Assyrians then imposed upon Hezekiah, king of Judah, three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold. Hezekiah gave all the silver that was found in the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king,” and so forth.

The historical account is clear. It is described in the Books of Kings, in Chronicles, and likewise in the prophecy of Isaiah in essentially the same way.

“Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign. He reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, rebelled against the king of the Assyrians, and did not serve him. Then Sennacherib entered Judea and besieged its fortified cities. While he was besieging Lachish, Hezekiah sent him three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, after breaking the doors of the temple and removing the plates which he himself had fastened there.

Then the king of the Assyrians sent Tartan and the Rabshakeh with a strong force to Jerusalem. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the overseer of the palace, went out to them, together with Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder,” and so forth.

This is the Eliakim of whom Isaiah said in his vision of the Valley of Zion: “I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah,” and so forth (Isaiah 22). He was high priest after Shebna, the overseer of the temple. The Hebrews report that Shebna, terrified by the Rabshakeh’s threats, handed himself over to the Assyrians and betrayed Jerusalem, and that, except for the fortress of Zion and the temple, the Assyrians captured the whole city.

Some also think that Shebna went out with Eliakim to the Rabshakeh. They assert that the Rabshakeh, who spoke in Hebrew, was the son of the prophet Isaiah and that he too had been a traitor; they say that Isaiah’s other son, who had been left behind, was called Jashub, a name which in Latin means “the remnant.”

Others, however, think that he was a Samaritan and therefore knew the Hebrew language, and that he blasphemed the Lord so audaciously and impiously. With a kind of contrary power and arrogance of his own, he imitated the prophets who said, “Thus says the Lord.” He said instead: “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians.”

First, when he said, “You trust in Egypt,” this was false. No historical account says that Hezekiah sought Pharaoh’s aid. What he adds—“If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’”—is true. But he again joins falsehood to truth, claiming that Hezekiah had removed the Lord’s high places and altars. He had done these things not against God but for God, so that, after destroying idolatry and the ancient error, he might command that God be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his temple was.

To display the small number of the besieged, he promises two thousand horses whose riders Hezekiah would not possess. This did not arise from the weakness of the people, as though they were ignorant of horsemanship, but from their observance of God’s commandments, for God commanded Moses that the king of Israel should not multiply horses or wives for himself (Deuteronomy 17).

“If,” he says, “you are unable to withstand even the least of the servants of King Sennacherib, how will you withstand his full power?”

But in response to his statement, “If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God,’” he cleverly replied that he had come not by his own will but at the Lord’s command.

“‘The Lord said to me: Go up against this land and destroy it.’” And the meaning is: Certainly I could not have come here without the Lord’s will. But since I have come, and have captured many cities, while part of Jerusalem remains untouched, it is clear that I have come by his will.

“Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, said to Rabshakeh: We beg you to speak to us, your servants, in Aramaic, for we understand this language; and do not speak to us in Judean, in the hearing of the people who are on the wall.” Rabshakeh answered them: “Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak these words, and not rather to the men who sit on his wall, so that they may eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you?” etc.

Rabshakeh’s accusation is a testimony to Hezekiah: after the cities of Judah had been captured, he had trusted in the Lord and encouraged the people to hope in the Lord. Therefore Rabshakeh wishes to destroy what he had built, and says to the people:

“Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, and do not let him give you confidence in the Lord God.” But the fact that Eliakim [Col. 0254A] and Shebna and Joah humbly beg Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic has this meaning: Why is it necessary to disturb the people with false terrors and boast of empty power? Speak the language that the people do not know, for we ourselves understand your language. To this he arrogantly replied:

“‘Has my lord,’ he said, ‘sent me to your lord and to you?’” etc., through: “And drink their urine with you.” By this he shows that they are to be overcome by hunger and thirst. At the same time he joins enticement to fear, so that those whom he cannot conquer by terror he may deceive by persuasion. And he says in the person of the king:

“Make a blessing with me”—that is, do what will result in your blessing. Bless the king of Assyria and acknowledge him as lord, so that you may receive rewards [Col. 0254B] until I return from Egypt, or, after Shebna has been captured, return. Live in your own city, enjoy your possessions, and afterward I shall lead you to a land like your land. Yet he did not name it, because he could not find one like it, but he does not state the comparison; for each person desires the land in which he was born. (From Bede.) Others think that the land of Media was promised to them, since it resembles the land of Judah both in location and in produce.

When Rabshakeh says, among his other blasphemies against God, shouting against Jerusalem:

“Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim, Ana, and Ava? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” he shows that the Samaritans had served the gods of all these cities or peoples. Since they were not gods but idols, it was fitting that the worshipers of vanity should deservedly be overthrown.

Hamath is a city of Coelesyria, now called Epiphania, near Emesa, as we noted above. Arpad is a city of Damascus, which Jeremiah also records as having been conquered by the king of Assyria (Jer. XLVII). Sepharvaim—which, in the plural, means “books” or “letters”—is the name of the places from which the Assyrian migrants settled in Samaria, as we find in the books concerning those places. Yet in Isaiah this word also appears to be the name of a city, where it is plainly said: “Where is the god of the city of Sepharvaim?” (Isa. XXXVI), although it is expressed in the plural, like Thebes and Athens.

For Ana and Ava, the old edition, as though they were the name of a single city, gives Anengava. Indeed, in Hebrew it is written this way. But since the fifth syllable, placed in the middle of the name, signifies “and” among them, it can also be divided so that one reads Ane and Gave, as Aquila translated it; or Ana and Ava, as our translator rendered it.

“If, then,” he says, “with so many gods present we easily defeated ten tribes, how much more shall we defeat Jerusalem alone, with one God as its protector?” Truly just Hezekiah, acting in all things with prudence, forbade him to be answered, lest he provoke him to still greater blasphemies.

“Then Eliakim, son of Hilkiah, the governor of the palace, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah, son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with torn garments and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh.”

## CHAPTER XIX

Hezekiah’s prayer in the temple of the Lord against the words of the king of Assyria. Concerning the angel of the Lord striking one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians, and concerning the death of Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians.

**(CHAP. XIX.)** “When Hezekiah heard this, he tore his garments and was covered with sackcloth. He entered the house of the Lord and sent Eliakim, the governor of the palace, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amos. They said to him: ‘Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation and blasphemy. The children have come to the point of birth, but the woman in labor has no strength,’ etc.” (From Jerome.)

They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming; the king also tore his garment, because he believed that it was on account of the sins of the people and of himself that Rabshakeh had come as far as the gate of Jerusalem and spoken such things against the Lord. Wonderful was the king’s humility and prudence. Laying aside royal attire, he went from the palace to the temple wrapped in sackcloth. He sent the chief priests to Isaiah, not in robes but in haircloth, covered with sackcloth, and said: “This day is the day of our tribulation, of God’s rebuke, and of the enemies’ blasphemy.” He gives the likeness of a woman in labor who has reached the moment of delivery but cannot give birth.

“Perhaps the Lord your God will hear.” For we do not dare to call the Lord of us all “our Lord,” since, while he is angry, we suffer such things; instead, we call him your Lord. And we have this hope of vengeance: that the living God is being blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols. Raise, therefore, a prayer for the remnant of the people that is under siege.

Isaiah anticipated them, because by the same Spirit by which he knew future events he had also heard the absent king:

“‘Thus you shall say to your lord,’ he said, ‘what the Lord says: Do not fear the words with which not you but I have been blasphemed.’” I do not mention everything that I shall do to the king of Assyria, lest I seem to boast of my power. But an impulse—not from God, but from the adversary—will be given him, and when he hears the message and returns to his own land, he will fall by the sword. Thus Hezekiah would hear at once the two things he desired: that he would be delivered from the siege, and that his enemy would die in his own land.

[Col. 0255D] “So Rabshakeh returned and found the king of Assyria attacking Libnah. For he had heard that he had withdrawn from Lachish. When he heard concerning Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, that they were saying, ‘Behold, he has gone out to fight against you,’ and he was marching against him, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying: ‘Thus you shall say to Hezekiah, king of Judah: Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, nor say: Jerusalem shall not be delivered into the hand of the king of Assyria,’” etc.

In accordance with God’s will, Rabshakeh abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and went to his lord, whom he found attacking Libnah after either capturing or abandoning Lachish. Sennacherib, however, went to meet the king of Ethiopia and sent messengers and letters to Hezekiah, so that he might terrify by words those whom he had not conquered by force. Herodotus relates that Sennacherib fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium; when the city was already about to be captured after the embankments had been constructed, Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, came to their aid.

[Col. 0256A] “When Hezekiah had received the letter from the hands of the messengers and read it, he went up to the house of the Lord, spread it out before the Lord, and prayed in his presence, saying: ‘Lord God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes, Lord, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, who sent to reproach the living God,’” etc. (From Jerome.)

Earlier, terrified by fear of the Lord, Hezekiah had not dared to open his mouth in the temple or pour out free [Col. 0256B] prayers. But now, because he hears Isaiah saying:

“Do not fear the face of the words that you have heard,” etc., he boldly entreats the Lord:

“Then Isaiah, son of Amos, sent to Hezekiah, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have heard what you prayed to me concerning Sennacherib, king of Assyria. This is the word that the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and mocked you; behind you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached, and whom have you blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel,’” etc.

Finally, Hezekiah boldly entreats the Lord. He did not send to Isaiah as he had done before; nor does the prophet himself go to him, but he sends messengers to bring him God’s answer. [Col. 0256C] “The virgin of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem” is called virgin and daughter because, while all the nations worship images of the dead, she alone preserves the chastity of the worship of God and the devotion owed to one divinity. She did not answer him while he was present, lest she provoke him to greater blasphemy, but after he had departed she shook her head, confident of vengeance and secure in punishment.

“By the hand of your servants”—that is, you blasphemed the Lord not through yourself but through your servants, so that your arrogance might be greater.

“The height of the mountains and the summits of Lebanon, the tall cedars and the choice fir trees.” This should be understood metaphorically either of all the nations and their rulers, or of Jerusalem, which is Lebanon. The cedars and fir trees are all the powerful and nobles; the height of the summit and the wooded heights of Carmel are the temple.

When he adds: “I dug and drank water, and with the sole of my foot I dried up all the streams of the embankments,” he said this either because, on account of the multitude of his army, he dried up every watercourse and was compelled to dig wells for himself, or because he devastated with his army all the peoples signified by the waters.

“Have you not heard what I did long ago? From ancient days I formed it, and now I have brought it about; and it came to pass for the uprooting of the hills of combat and of fortified cities. Their inhabitants, with their power shortened, trembled and were confounded. They became like the grass of the field, the green pasture, and the grass upon the roofs, which dries up before it matures. I know your dwelling, your going out and your coming in, and your madness against me when you raged against me. Your arrogance has risen into my ears. Therefore I shall put a ring in your nostrils and a bridle on your lips, and I shall lead you back by the way you came,” etc.

These words are to be understood as spoken by God against the words of the Assyrian: the Lord thus answered his blasphemy. Do you not know that you did these things by my will, and that I foretold these future events and commanded them to be done through you? Therefore what I decreed long ago has been fulfilled in its time: the hills—that is, the rulers who had previously fought among themselves—and the most strongly fortified cities were uprooted because I withdrew my hand and did not provide my customary aid. They trembled, perished, and were compared not to olive trees, [Col. 0257B] vineyards, and fruitful trees, but to hay, grass, and the plants of rooftops, which hinder crops and wither before reaching maturity.

Thus I knew beforehand your sitting, your going out, and your coming in, and I spoke through the prophets of the madness with which you were to rage against me. Through them I knew that you would one day say:

“I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I shall place my throne; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

Therefore your fury and arrogance have reached my ears, and I shall no longer bear with you, so that you may understand that whatever you were able to do, you were not able to do by your own strength but by my decision. For the impious nations and the fruitful trees deserved to be cut down and fall through you, as through my ax and saw.

“Therefore I shall put a ring—or a hook—in your nostrils,” so that I may restrain your blaspheming mouth and you may no longer dare to speak such things. “I shall also put a bridle on your lips,” one that will tame your fierceness, and I shall lead you back to Assyria.

“But for you, Hezekiah, this shall be the sign: Eat this year what you find; in the second year, what grows of its own accord. In the third year sow and reap,” etc.

It should be noted that in the Book of Isaiah, where the words of the prophet himself to King Hezekiah are recorded, they are related in this way:

“Eat this year what grows of its own accord, and in the second year eat fruit. But in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And what has been saved of the house of Judah, and what remains, shall again put down roots below and produce fruit above, because a remnant shall go out from Jerusalem, and salvation from Mount Zion; the zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this” (Isa. XXXVII).

Now he speaks to Hezekiah himself. “This,” he says, “shall be the sign of the things I foretell as future: this year you shall eat what grows of its own accord”—or, according to the Septuagint, “what you previously sowed.” In the second year, according to Symmachus, “eat fruit,” or, according to the same translators, what sprouts from past crops and seed fallen upon the ground. In the third year, once the Assyrian has been driven away and the siege relaxed, sow and reap.

For the remnant of this small city, now surrounded by the enemy’s army and not believing that it will escape, will receive such abundance and prosperity in all things [Col. 0258A] that it will be filled with the thickest fruits like a tree firmly established with a deep root. From Jerusalem and Mount Zion the remnant shall go out and fill the land of Judah—not by its own merit, but by God’s mercy, indeed by the zeal with which he was zealous on behalf of his people against the impious.

“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow there. He shall not seize it with a shield, nor cast up an embankment around it. By the way he came, by that way he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord. I shall protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

By the hope of future events he drives away present fear. He says that they will be preserved not through their own merit but through God’s mercy—indeed through the memory of their father David, in whom they are reminded both of their own negligence and of his faith and righteousness, since God loves righteousness so greatly that he protects descendants through the virtue of their ancestors.

“It happened, then, that on that night the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. When he arose at dawn, he found all the bodies of the dead, and he departed.”

One hundred and eighty-five thousand very powerful men were slain by one angel in a single night. Without wounds being visible, savage death passed through them, separating their souls from their bodies by the Lord’s will. Concerning this, it is written in Chronicles:

“The Lord sent his angel, who struck every mighty man, warrior, and commander of the army of the king of Assyria; and he returned with shame to his own land” (II Chron. XXXII).

He was spared for this reason: so that he might learn God’s power, restrain his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness to the majesty of the one whom shortly before he had despised.

“And Sennacherib, king of Assyria, returned and remained in Nineveh. While he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword and fled to the land of Armenia; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.”

Pharaoh too was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he might perish last; and this man likewise was destined to suffer. When he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch his god, as though he had returned victorious from his enemies, and was triumphantly and joyfully moving about the shrine of his idol, the despiser of the true God was slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity. He did not perish by an angel’s sword, which he shared with many others, but by the parricide of his sons.

When they fled to the land of Ararat, which is understood as Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded his father. Scripture testifies that he sent the inhabitants of Samaria there so that the land would not remain uncultivated. Ararat is a level region in Armenia through which the Araxes flows, of extraordinary fertility at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that region.

Therefore the ark in which Noah and his children were delivered, when the Flood had ceased, was not carried generally to the mountains of Armenia called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararat (Gen. VIII).

## CHAPTER XX

Concerning Hezekiah’s illness and the word of the Lord delivered to him through Isaiah the prophet.—Concerning the sign requested by Hezekiah in the return of the sun’s course.—Concerning the messengers sent by Berodach, king of Babylon, to Hezekiah, and the word of the Lord that Isaiah reported to Hezekiah concerning those messengers.

**(CHAP. XX.)** “In those days Hezekiah fell ill unto death, and Isaiah, son of Amos, the prophet, came to him and said: ‘Thus says the Lord God: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,’” etc.

So that Hezekiah might not become proud after his unbelievable triumphs and victory in the midst of captivity, he was visited with bodily weakness and heard that he would die, so that, turning to the Lord, he might bend his sentence. We read the same thing in the prophet Jonah (Jon. III), [Col. 0259B] and in the threats against David, which are said to be future but did not occur (II Sam. XII). It is not that God changes his decision, but that, calling the human race to knowledge of himself, the Lord is said to repent of evils.

Nothing that happens to human beings in this world occurs without the hidden counsel of almighty God. For God, foreknowing everything that would follow, decreed before the ages how all things would be ordered through the ages. It was already determined for human beings how much worldly prosperity would follow them and how much the ferocity of adversity would strike them, lest excessive prosperity raise up his elect or excessive adversity weigh them down. It was also determined how long each person would live temporarily in this mortal life.

For although almighty God added fifteen years to the life of King Hezekiah, when he allowed him to die he already knew that he would die. Here a question arises: How can the prophet say to him, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,” when, after the sentence of death had been pronounced, life was immediately added to him because of his tears? The Lord, through the prophet, stated the time at which he deserved to die; yet the divine decrees were not overturned, because it had also been fixed before the ages that the years of his life would be increased through God’s generosity. The additional period of life, unexpectedly added outwardly, had been established inwardly without any alteration in divine foreknowledge.

“He turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying:” Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall because he could not go to the temple, etc. He turned toward the wall of the temple, according to the place where Solomon had built the palace; or simply toward the wall, lest he appear to display his tears to those sitting nearby. Or, rightly, according to Jeremiah, toward his heart, which he calls the surrounding wall, so that he might pray to the Lord with his whole mind.

“I beg you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is pleasing before you,” etc.

Happy is the conscience that, in a time of affliction, remembers good works. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). And elsewhere it is written: “Who will boast that he has a pure heart?” (Prov. XX).

This is resolved as follows: perfection of heart is spoken of here in the sense that he had destroyed the idols, opened the doors of the temple, crushed the bronze serpent, and done the other things that Scripture records. (From Gregory.)

Often righteous people, afflicted by certain necessities, are compelled to confess their own works. But when the wicked hear their words, they think that these have been spoken through pride rather than truth. They weigh the words of the righteous according to their own hearts and do not believe that genuine good can be spoken humbly. Just as it is a serious fault for a person to claim for himself what he is not, so it is often no fault at all if he humbly speaks of the good that he truly possesses.

Thus it often happens that the righteous and the wicked say things that sound alike, while their hearts are entirely different. In the same words by which the Lord is offended by the wicked, he is also pleased by the righteous. For the Pharisee entered the temple saying:

“I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I possess.” Yet the tax collector departed more justified than he (Luke XVIII).

King Hezekiah likewise, when afflicted by bodily distress and brought to the point of death, said in compunction during his prayer: “I beg you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart.” Yet the Lord neither despised nor rejected this confession of his perfection; rather, he immediately heard him in his prayers. Behold, the Pharisee justified himself in deed. Hezekiah asserted that he was righteous even in thought. The one offended the Lord by the very thing through which the other pleased him.

Why is this, then, except that almighty God weighs the words and thoughts of each person? In his ears, those things are not proud which are spoken from a humble heart?

[Col. 0260C] “Hezekiah wept with great weeping, and before Isaiah had gone out halfway through the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Return and say to Hezekiah, leader of my people: Thus says the Lord God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears; and behold, I have healed you. On the third day you shall go up to the temple of the Lord, and I shall add fifteen years to your days. Moreover, I shall deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I shall protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.’” (From Jerome.)

He wept with great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his own death. At that time Hezekiah had no children. For after his death Manasseh began to reign in Judah when he was twelve years old. From this it is clear that Manasseh was born after the third year of the life granted to Hezekiah. Therefore the whole reason for his weeping was that he despaired that Christ would be born from his offspring.

Others maintain that all holy men are frightened by death because of the uncertainty of judgment and ignorance of God’s sentence, not knowing what dwelling place they will have. At the same time, the question concerning the event itself is resolved, as are the bonds of necessity and causation: the day of death is not fixed for each person in such a way that it cannot be changed, but by God’s will and through causes unknown to mortals a person either lives or dies.

Especially since the necessity of death once decreed may now be postponed, and since we read that many were raised after death. The prophet returns to the king at the Lord’s command, so that the one who had struck him might himself heal him. Hezekiah is called the leader of the Lord’s people and the son of David, whose works he followed. He had acted rightly in all things, like David his father; his prayer is heard, and his tears are seen, because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, had wept with great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his eyes.

Fifteen years are added to his life, although he had not asked for them; in addition, security for the kingdom is promised while he is still alive. But if, as some think, being alive in the body is a condemnation, according to the words: “Return, my soul, to your rest,” and elsewhere: “Bring my soul out of prison,” then death should be desired so that we may be freed from prison. How, then, does the Lord now grant as a benefit that the one who was to be freed should remain in prison for another fifteen years?

“Isaiah said: Bring a cake of figs.” When they brought it and placed it upon his ulcer, he was healed.

The Hebrews say that the word *sim*, which the Septuagint omitted, means an ulcer, not a wound. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion likewise translated it as *helkos* (“ulcer”), by which they wish a royal disease to be understood. For sweet things are considered contrary, whether taken as food or applied to the body. Therefore, to demonstrate God’s power, health was restored through things that were harmful and contrary.

Others suspect that *sim* means not an ulcer but an abscess, when the swollen body is filled with cooked and putrefying pus. According to medical practice, all such matter is drawn to the surface of the skin by means of dried and crushed figs. Therefore medicine should not be despised when it is established by use and experience, since God also made this remedy.

“Hezekiah had said to Isaiah: ‘What shall be the sign that the Lord will heal me, and that I shall go up to the temple of the Lord on the third day?’ Isaiah said to him: ‘This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will perform the word he has spoken. Do you want the shadow to advance ten lines, or to return ten steps?’” etc.

A sign was given that the sun should return ten steps, which, according to Symmachus, we render as lines and a sundial. He understands the steps as lines in order to make the meaning clearer for readers. Or the steps may have been constructed by mechanical art in such a way that, as the shadow descended over each one, it marked the intervals of the hours. (From Bede.)

It was the tenth hour of the day when the prophet spoke these words to the king: “Do you want,” he said, “the shadow to advance ten lines,” as the sun proceeded over the earth through the northern regions toward the east, where, beneath the earth, it would daily complete the customary course of its movement; “or do you want the shadow to return the same number of steps,” with the face of the sun turned backward and the sun itself returning eastward by the southern region?

“But the king said: ‘It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines. I do not want this to happen, but for it to return backward ten steps,’” etc.

He saw that it could be a greater miracle if the sun followed a course contrary to its customary movement than if, proceeding according to its usual course, though much higher—that is, raised above the earth toward the east—it should fly onward like the morning of a second day, without any intervening night.

For those who live on the island of Thule, which lies beyond Britain, or in the farthest regions of the Scythians, see this happen for several days every summer: while the sun is at sunset and beneath the earth for the rest of the world, it nevertheless appears above the earth for them throughout the entire day. They clearly see it return low from west to east until, at the proper time, it is restored to the whole world by the common rising, as both the histories of the ancients and people of our own age who come from those regions abundantly report.

But those who inhabit the inner regions of the south have never seen the sun return from west to east through the southern regions. (From Jerome.)

This sign was also a type of the present and future, so that, just as the sun returned to the beginning of its course, so Hezekiah’s life returned to the years that had been unwoven; and, as we live in the weeks and the eighth day, the span of our life might be extended through the resurrection of Christ.

Those who show holy places in this province customarily point out, within the temple enclosure, the steps of the house of Hezekiah—or of Ahaz—by which the sun descended. But I shall never believe that the house not merely of Ahaz, who was an impious king, but of any righteous king, stood within the temple of God. Solomon is said to have offended God among other things because he built the *Millo* on high, from which he was accustomed, while walking in the temple court, to look down from the tower of the palace.

Some people transfer the ten steps of the lines to the mystery of Christ and interpret the shadows of the figures as Christ’s descent, by which the Sun of righteousness, Christ, again ascended after the resurrection. (From Isidore.)

The first step of descent from God was into the angel, because he was the messenger of the great counsel. Thus Jacob is addressed by the angel in these words: “The angel of God,” he says, “said: ‘I am the God to whom you anointed a pillar and made a vow.’” This shows both the angel and God.

The second step of descent was from the angel into the patriarchs, because, as the Apostle says, “he himself worked in all things” (I Cor. XII).

The third was in the giving of the Law, because he himself also spoke in the Law (Exod. XX).

The fourth step was in Joshua son of Nun, so that he might lead the people into the promised land (Josh. I).

The fifth was in the judges, because through them he himself ruled the same people.

The sixth was in the kings of Judah, because he reigned in them.

The seventh was in the prophets, because he was announced through them.

The eighth was in the high priests, because he himself is the supreme priest (Heb. V).

The ninth was in the human being.

The tenth was in the Passion.

Through these ten steps, as through the shadow of the ancient Law, Christ descended. Again, after his resurrection, Christ, the Sun of righteousness, ascended through the same steps into heaven and illuminated all that shadow of the Law with the rays of truth (John I), revealing what was obscure, opening what was closed, and uncovering everything that was hidden.

“At that time Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah. For he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill. Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival [Col. 0263A] and showed them the house of spices, the gold and silver, the various spices, the ointments, the house of his vessels, and everything that he had in his treasuries. There was nothing that Hezekiah did not show them in his house and throughout his dominion” (Isa. XXXIX).

Above we read (IV Kings XVIII) that in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, came against all the fortified cities of Judah, captured them, and afterward besieged Lachish, passed on to Libnah, and sent part of his army to Jerusalem. After one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army had been slain by the angel, he fled to Nineveh and was killed by his sons; Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place. Hezekiah fell ill and, at the prophet’s announcement, recovered his health. An unbelievable sign occurred: the sun returned by ten hours’ intervals to its rising, and the day became almost double (IV Kings XIX).

Now we read that “at that time”—that is, in the same year in which all these things took place—Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah. Esarhaddon had succeeded his father Sennacherib among the Assyrians, but Scripture is silent concerning either his death or his life. From this it is clear that at that time there was one kingdom of the Assyrians and another of the Babylonians.

Indeed, the Assyrians captured Samaria—that is, the ten tribes. But later we read that Judah and Jerusalem were captured by the Chaldeans, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar. Since the Babylonians practiced the observation of the stars and knew the courses of the heavenly bodies through long use and study—as was also demonstrated at the Lord’s birth—they understood that the sun had returned and that the day had been doubled, and they took this as service to the one whom they thought to be the only god, namely, the sun.

When they investigated the cause and explanation of this miracle, they learned, as the report spread through all nations, that the course of the most conspicuous sign had been changed because of the illness of the king of Judah. That this is not my own conjecture but the testimony of Holy Scripture is confirmed by the Words of the Chronicles, which say after other matters:

“He is the Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon and diverted them below, toward the west of the city of David. In all his works he prospered in whatever he undertook. Nevertheless, in the embassy of the princes of Babylon who had been sent to him and had questioned him about the portent that had occurred in the land, God abandoned him in order that he might be tested and that everything in his heart might become known” (II Chron. XXXII).

He was left to temptation for this reason: after such a great victory, the sun’s return, and the congratulations of the most powerful kingdom, his heart had been lifted up. Accordingly, the same book records:

“Many brought sacrifices and offerings to the Lord in Jerusalem and gifts to Hezekiah, king of Judah; and he was exalted before all the nations. In those days he fell ill unto death, and he prayed to the Lord, and he heard him and gave him a sign” (IV Kings XX). “But he did not repay according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was exalted; and wrath came against him and against Judah and Jerusalem” (II Chron. XXXII).

Again, Holy Scripture says that the pride of his heart was moderated by repentance, adding:

“And afterward he humbled himself because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah” (ibid.).

Hezekiah therefore rejoiced at the arrival of the envoys of Merodach, whom the Hebrews believe to have been the father of Nebuchadnezzar, and at the presentation of gifts and the congratulations on his recovery.

“He showed them” (according to the Septuagint) “the house of Nechotha,” for which Symmachus translated, “his house of spices, the treasuries of silver and gold, perfumes, and the finest ointment”—in Hebrew, “good oil”—“and all the treasuries of vessels of Gaza,” or, as it is read there, “of his vessels.”

*Gaza* means “wealth” in the language of the Persians; it is not a Hebrew word but a foreign one.

“There was not,” he says, “a word”—which, according to Hebrew usage, is frequently used for “a thing”—“that he did not show them in his house and throughout his dominion.”

Hence God’s anger was entirely justified: Hezekiah had shown not only his own treasures and the treasures of the palace, but also those of the temple. Certainly the temple had been within his authority, since he had already removed the gold plates from its doors.

“Then the prophet Isaiah entered King Hezekiah and said to him: ‘What did these men say, and from where did they come to you?’ And Hezekiah said: ‘They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon.’ And he said: ‘What did they see in your house?’ And Hezekiah said: ‘They saw everything that is in my house; there was nothing, whether word or thing, that I did not show them among my treasures.’ And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: ‘Hear the word of the Lord of hosts. Behold, days are coming when everything that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up to this day, will be carried away to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the Lord. And some of your sons who will go out from you, whom you will beget, will be taken away; and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.’ And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: ‘Good is the word of the Lord that he has spoken.’ And he said: ‘Let there only be peace and truth in my days,’ etc.

The Hebrews relate that Hezekiah fell ill for this reason: after the Jews’ unprecedented victory and the death of the Assyrian king, he did not sing praises to the Lord as Moses had sung when Pharaoh was drowned (Exodus 15), Deborah when Sisera was killed (Judges 5), and Hannah when Samuel was born (1 Samuel 2). Thus he was reminded of his frailty. Again, after the restoration of his bodily health and the greatness of the sign, another occasion for pride was offered him—an occasion which, as a prudent worshiper of God, he ought to have avoided. He should not have displayed to foreigners the riches which he possessed through God’s granting.

From this, according to the laws of moral interpretation, we also learn that ‘pearls should not be cast before swine, nor what is holy given to dogs’ (Matthew 7). Whoever is faithful hides his affairs in the spirit. But whoever acts otherwise has all his virtue weakened, his posterity perishes, and, having lost his masculine strength, he is reduced to feminine softness.

Isaiah therefore enters the king and, as though ignorant, asks:

‘What did these men say, and from where did they come?’ He asks two questions: ‘What did they say?’ and ‘From where did they come?’ He answered one and passed over the other; this must be read with emphasis and marked pride: ‘They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon.’ The more distant the land from which they came, the more glorious he appears, since they came on his account. And he says, ‘They came to me,’ when he ought to have said: ‘They came to glorify God on account of the greatness of the sign.’ He adds, ‘from Babylon,’ a city most powerful throughout the whole world.

Again Isaiah asks: ‘What did they see in your house?’ He answered partly truthfully: they had seen everything in his house, and there was nothing that he had not shown them among his treasures. But he kept silent about the other matter, from which he feared offense: that he had shown them everything under his authority—without doubt, even the temple vessels. Therefore Isaiah, speaking the judgment of God, declares: ‘Hear the word of the Lord of hosts: The time will come when all these things that are in your house—and that were acquired not by your labor but by the labor of your fathers—will be carried away to Babylon, and some of your offspring will become eunuchs in the royal court.’

From this the Hebrews wish Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah—who were of royal descent—to have been made eunuchs; there is no doubt that they were in the service of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 1).

‘And Hezekiah said: “Good is the word of the Lord that he has spoken.”’ In this he is reproached by the Hebrews for not imitating the goodness of Moses, who said to the Lord: ‘Either forgive them this guilt, or, if you will not, erase me from your book that you have written’ (Exodus 32). Hence the apostle Paul also wishes himself to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers, who are Israelites (Romans 9).

*(From Gregory.)* This prophetic judgment pronounced against Hezekiah can therefore be understood mystically as directed against hypocrites. After they have grown great through mighty virtues, they neglect to beware of the snares of evil spirits and refuse to conceal their good deeds within those virtues. By displaying them, they make themselves targets for their enemies, and by betraying them they suddenly lose whatever they have labored to accomplish over a long period.

Hence the Psalmist says: ‘He delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy’ (Psalm 77). The strength and beauty of the proud are delivered into the enemy’s hands because every good that is displayed through a desire for praise is secretly surrendered to the adversary’s power.

Those who expose their riches to the knowledge of their enemies invite them to plunder. For as long as we are separated from the security of our heavenly homeland, we walk along the road of lurking thieves. Whoever therefore fears being robbed on the journey must hide the good things he carries.

O wretched people! In their desire for human praise, they scatter within themselves the fruits of their labors. When they long to display themselves to foreign eyes, they condemn what they do. Evil spirits provoke them to boastfulness and, by capturing their works—as we have said—strip them bare.

This is why Truth said through the Gospel: ‘Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you’ (Matthew 6). This is why the Psalmist says of the Church of the elect: ‘All the glory of the king’s daughter is within’ (Psalm 44). Paul says: ‘This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience’ (2 Corinthians 1).

The Church, the king’s daughter, generated through the preaching of spiritual rulers in the work of goodness, has her glory within because what she does contains no boastfulness for display. Paul calls the testimony of his conscience his glory because he does not seek the favor of another’s lips and does not know how to place the joys of his life outside himself.

What we do must therefore be concealed, lest, carrying these things carelessly along the road of this life, we lose them through the assault of thieving spirits.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, who practiced repentance after his sin and thereby deserved to be released from prison.

*(Chapter 21.)* ‘Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place. Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem,’ etc.

After Hezekiah’s death, Scripture also relates that his son Manasseh reigned in Jerusalem. When he turned to the worship of idols and the practice of abominations, abandoning the God of his fathers and the good examples that he had observed in his father Hezekiah, the Lord spoke to him and to his people, but they were unwilling to pay attention.

‘Therefore he brought against them the commanders of the army of the king of the Assyrians. They captured Manasseh, bound him with chains and fetters, and led him to Babylon. After he had been brought into distress, he prayed to the Lord his God and practiced profound repentance before the God of his fathers. He entreated him, and he heard his prayer; he brought him back to Jerusalem, to his kingdom, and Manasseh knew that the Lord alone is God’ (2 Chronicles 33).

This repentance of Manasseh is an example: after committing crimes, no one should despair of God’s mercy, but should rather, through suitable repentance, maintain hope of forgiveness, provided that he completes it properly.

## CHAPTER XXII. On King Josiah, who cleansed the whole land of Judah from the pollution of idols.

After him his son Ammon, an idolater, reigned. After Ammon, his son Josiah, a most righteous king, reigned. He cleansed away all the pollution of idols that his fathers had fashioned and devoted himself vigorously to the worship of God. And rightly so, since long before this the prophet had foretold it concerning him.

The name Josiah is interpreted as ‘whose sacrifice belongs to the Lord,’ or ‘the salvation of the Lord,’ or ‘the strength of the Lord.’ *(From Bede.)*

Concerning this same king it is then related that, when he heard the book of the Lord’s law, which Hilkiah the priest had found in the house of the Lord, he tore his garments and sent Hilkiah the priest and the others who are subsequently enumerated to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum, ‘who lived in Jerusalem in the Second Quarter,’ etc.

What is meant by the phrase ‘in the Second Quarter’ is explained in the Book of Chronicles, where it is written concerning the aforementioned King Hezekiah: ‘He also worked diligently and rebuilt the entire wall that had been destroyed, and constructed towers above it and another wall outside it’ (2 Chronicles 32).

Zephaniah also remembers this place, saying: ‘A voice of crying from the Fish Gate, and wailing from the Second Quarter’ (Zephaniah 1). For this, the old edition translated the place as a proper name, *Maseva*. *Maseva* is interpreted as ‘second.’ Therefore, when the prophetess is said to have lived ‘in the Second Quarter,’ understand this as meaning in the section of the second wall.

Concerning King Josiah it is said: ‘He also defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through fire to Molech’ (2 Kings 23). These places are frequently mentioned in Scripture, especially in the Book of Kings and by the prophet Jeremiah.

The valley of Hinnom, or of the son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall of Jerusalem, toward the east; in it is a most beautiful grove watered by the springs of Siloam. Tapheth, or Topheth—for both forms are written—was a place in the same valley near the Fuller’s Pool, which Scripture mentions, and near the field of Haceldama, which is still shown on the southern side of Mount Zion.

At Tapheth, because it was a very pleasant place and still offers the delights of gardens, they used to sacrifice to demons at an altar and consecrate their children to them by an accursed fire, or offer them as burnt offerings. Thus it is written in the Book of Chronicles concerning King Ahaz: ‘He himself burned incense in the valley of Ben-Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire’ (2 Chronicles 28).

*Ben-Hinnom* means ‘son of Hinnom.’ The valley of Hinnom is called in Hebrew *Gehinnom*. From its name, the punishment of hell in the New Testament is called *Gehenna*: just as those who served idols in the valley of Hinnom perished there, as the prophets testify, so sinners who have sinned are punished by eternal condemnation.

Jeremiah, after relating that the Lord commanded him and said, ‘Go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate’ (Jeremiah 19), says shortly afterward: ‘This place shall no longer be called Topheth, or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. And I will destroy the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword.’

Isaiah also most plainly calls Topheth hell. When he was describing the everlasting destruction of the devil under the name Assyria, saying, ‘At the voice of the Lord Assyria will be terrified; he will be struck with the rod, and there will be a passage of the rod firmly established, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him’ (Isaiah 30), he immediately added how he would perish there, saying: ‘For Topheth has long been prepared; it has been prepared for the king, deep and wide.’ Beautifully he says ‘wide,’ because *Topheth* means ‘breadth.’

‘Its fuel,’ he says, ‘is fire and abundant wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulfur, sets it ablaze.’

## CHAPTER XXIII. That Josiah defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom; removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the Sun at the entrance of the temple of the Lord; polluted the high places; and, digging up the tombs of the dead, burned them. —On the most celebrated Passover that Josiah made for the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign. —On Josiah’s death and the substitution of his son Ahaz in the kingdom of Judah, after whom Jehoiakim reigned in place of his captive brother. —On King Jehoiakim, who is also called Jeconiah by another name.

*(Chapter 23.)* Josiah defiled Topheth—whether by placing there the bones of the dead, as he is subsequently said to have done with other sites of idols, or by scattering various unclean things there—so that the place might appear to all who saw it suited more to abomination than to pleasure.

Concerning the same King Josiah it follows: ‘He also removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the Sun at the entrance of the temple of the Lord.’ Shortly afterward: ‘He burned the chariots of the Sun with fire.’

This shows clearly that at that time the Jews were enslaved to the superstition of all idolatrous nations. They believed the sun to be a god in the manner of the Gentiles and had submitted to its image, which they had made, the chariots and horses that they placed in its service—and this in the courts of the temple of the Lord.

For the Gentiles commonly paint or fashion the image of the sun by placing a beardless boy in a chariot and harnessing horses to him, as though they were seeking heaven in their course. They make him a boy because the sun, as though born each day in a new rising, never falls into old age throughout the ages.

As for their assigning chariots and horses to him, John, bishop of Constantinople, thinks this was taken from the miracle of the prophet Elijah, because Elijah was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses. Since the sun is called *helios* in Greek, as Sedulius also showed when he sang of Elijah’s ascent, saying:

> How well the path of heaven shines before the lightning,  
>  
> It suits Elijah, radiant both in merit and in name.  
>  
> He was worthy of this power; for if in the language of the Greeks  
>  
> One letter is changed by an accent, he is the sun.

The Greeks, hearing from the Israelites—who were reputed to possess divine writings—that Elijah had been transported to the heavens in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses, or perhaps seeing this very event depicted among other things on a wall, believed, deceived by the closeness of the name of the sun—which is called *helios* in Greek, as stated above—that this represented the sun’s passage through the heavens. They turned a miracle accomplished by divine power into an argument for an error invented by human foolishness. The Jews themselves tried to imitate them, lest they appear in any respect less foolish than the most foolish of the Gentiles.

Concerning the same king it is said shortly afterward:

‘The high places also that were in Jerusalem, on the right side of the Mount of Offense, which Solomon king of Israel had built for the idol Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites—the king polluted them and broke their statues.’

It is clearer than daylight that Scripture commonly calls high places sites situated on leafy hills, where people either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the pleasantness of the locations, offered victims to the Lord in opposition to the prohibition, having abandoned the altar that was in the temple. Hence, in this book, it is often said concerning kings who were not perfectly righteous: ‘Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places.’

It calls the Mount of Offense the mountain of the idol because it is customary in Scripture to call idols offenses: either God is offended by them, or they offer offense and ruin to their worshipers. This is made clear in the very statement that follows: ‘which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth, the idol of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the offense of Moab, and Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites.’

Here too, unless I am mistaken, something is openly revealed that would better not have been revealed: namely, that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry into which he had fallen. For if he had produced worthy fruits of repentance, he would have worked above all to remove from the holy city the idols that he had built. He would not have left, as a stumbling block to fools, the things that he himself, though exceedingly wise, had made in error, as though they had been made wisely and rightly.

Scripture mentioned this place above as well, saying: ‘Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain that is opposite Jerusalem, and for Molech, the idol of the sons of Ammon’ (1 Kings 11). It should not appear contradictory that the mountain on which these idols were made is there said to be opposite Jerusalem, while here it is asserted to have been situated in Jerusalem. It was, in fact, placed so near the city that it seemed to belong to the city itself and to contaminate it with the filth accumulated there.

‘Josiah turned and saw there the tombs that were on the mountain. He sent and took the bones from the tombs, burned them upon the altar, and defiled it.’

Why did Josiah order the bones of the dead to be burned upon the altar, unless to show that their sacrifices had been profane? They not only offered the sacrifices of animals to demons; through the error of idolatry they also handed themselves over to the power of demons. By the just judgment of God, they were destined to be destroyed together with the altar that they had built for idols.

Mystically, this signifies that all who have been enslaved to the service of the devil and have ended their sacrilegious lives in time will be consumed by eternal torments, as God repays them according to the proper merits of their deeds.

‘Josiah returned to Jerusalem and commanded all the people, saying: “Keep the Passover to the Lord your God, according to what is written in the book of this covenant,”’ etc.

The fact that the aforementioned king, after removing idols from the land and taking away the mediums, diviners, and every impurity and abomination, is said to have celebrated a most renowned Passover for the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign teaches us morally to cleanse first the land of our heart from all vices and purify our actions from every contamination of sins and from dead works, so that we may serve the living God.

Thus we celebrate a Passover pleasing to the Lord, ‘not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth’ (1 Corinthians 5).

According to allegory, this Josiah represents the Lord and Savior, who is rightly called the salvation and strength of the Lord. He is the one of whom Scripture says: ‘The Lord is strong; the Lord is mighty in battle’ (Psalm 23). And elsewhere: ‘He himself will save his people from their sins’ (Matthew 1).

He, in his zeal for God, cleanses the land of Judah and Jerusalem from all impurities and abominations. Through the prophet he said: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me’ (Psalm 68). John says of him: ‘His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor’ (Matthew 3).

Malachi also says of him: ‘Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts; and who can consider the day of his coming, and who will stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ herb. He will sit refining and cleansing silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi. He will refine them like gold and silver, and they will belong to the Lord, offering sacrifices in righteousness. Then the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God, as in the days of old and as in former years. And I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers; against those who defraud the hired worker of his wages, oppress widows and orphans, and thrust aside the foreigner, and do not fear me, says the Lord of hosts’ (Malachi 3).

Our Josiah therefore celebrates the true Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign, when, in the eighth age, after the universal resurrection has taken place, he will lead his saints, perfected in good works, to receive the denarius of eternal blessedness, after all scandals have first been cast out of his kingdom (Matthew 20; Matthew 13).

Concerning this the aforementioned prophet says: ‘For behold, the day is coming, burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who practice wickedness will be stubble; and the coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, leaving them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name, the Sun of Justice will rise, and healing will be in his wings. You will go out and leap like calves from the herd, and you will trample the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet’ (Malachi 4).

It is rightly said that no Passover like this had been celebrated since the days of the Judges who judged Israel, nor throughout all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah, as in the eighteenth year of King Josiah in Jerusalem. For when the figures have been removed, the saints will truly pass on the day of judgment from death to life and from corruption to glory.

Thus they will rejoice forever in the sight of their Creator in the heavenly Jerusalem, because ‘the God of gods will be seen in Zion’ (Psalm 83). ‘That city needs neither sun nor moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb. The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it. Its gates will not be shut by day, for night will not be there. They will bring the glory and honor of the nations into it, and nothing unclean will enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life’ (Revelation 21). ‘And the name of the city from that day will be: The Lord is there’ (Ezekiel 35). ‘Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy wondrous in the city of the surrounding region’ (Psalm 30).

‘After King Josiah was killed at Megiddo, the people of the land took Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in his father’s place. Pharaoh Neco bound him at Riblah, brought him to Egypt, and imposed a tribute upon the land of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. He made Eliakim, the son of Josiah, king in place of Josiah his father, and changed his name to Jehoiakim,’ etc.

What else does the killing of Josiah signify—he who was slain by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo—except the persecution of the ancient enemy against holy preachers, whom he strives through envy to deliver to death and remove from the land of the Church, so that he may more easily scatter and attack the whole people?

Pharaoh is interpreted as ‘one who scatters,’ Neco as ‘striking,’ and Megiddo as ‘from temptation.’ When the devil is permitted to rise against the saints, this alone is what he does, and for this he struggles with all his strength: by tempting and striking the Lord’s flock, to scatter it, and first to remove those whose support should have enabled the rest to fight against the enemy.

‘The people of the land took Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, and made him king in place of his father.’ Jehoahaz, whose name is interpreted as ‘held back,’ signifies evil teachers whom the earthly people—that is, people devoted to earthly desire and consenting to their vices according to their own ways—choose according to their own character.

Pharaoh bound them at Riblah and led them to Egypt when the devil, weakening the hearts of rulers through a multitude of flatterers, deceives them. *Riblah* is interpreted as ‘multitude.’ Thus he plunges them, bound with the chains of sins, into the dark abyss of spiritual Egypt.

‘In place of Jehoahaz, Neco appointed Jehoiakim king and imposed upon the land a tribute of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.’

When the evil spirit demands the measure of his service from the people of the lost, he requires that they be wholly ready to obey him in both understanding and speech. Therefore Jehoiakim, at Pharaoh’s command, exacted from each person according to his strength that he should give both silver and gold, so that he might return it to Pharaoh. For the devil, through men devoted to him, demands that each person pay the tax of sin according to his strength; and thus, through wicked rulers, he daily prepares destruction for their subjects.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That Nebuchadnezzar carried King Jehoiakim to Babylon with his mother, wives, eunuchs, and the rest of the people, together with part of the vessels of God. —On King Zedekiah, who, because of the greatness of his crimes, was handed over with his sons and all the people.

*(Chapter 24.)* ‘In his days Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years; then he rebelled against him again,’ etc.

Once someone has surrendered himself to any vice, he will be subject not to one master but to many. Thus Jehoiakim, whom Pharaoh had previously compelled to pay tribute to him, is now forced by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to serve him for three years.

But whom else should we understand Nebuchadnezzar to be than the one whom we said was Pharaoh: namely, the prince of confusion and the ruler of the darkness of this world (Ephesians 6)? When the ancient enemy persuades someone to pay him the tax of sin, he immediately urges him to bring the whole person under his dominion and render complete service.

What else, then, is it to be a servant of the king of Babylon for three years except to be subjected to the ancient enemy through persuasion, pleasure, and consent, and to be wholly devoted to vices, as though freely possessed by him?

But it often happens that such people, admonished by God’s mercy, begin to contemplate rebelling against the evil spirit. Hence it is added: ‘He rebelled against him again.’ Yet rebellion is not enough if one does not persevere in the struggle. Whoever desires to cast off the power of the ancient enemy must fight against him courageously and implore aid from the highest power through continual prayers, so that, helped by divine grace, he may overcome the strongest enemy and escape the harshest yoke.

‘After Jehoiakim, Jehoiakim his son reigned in his place, and he did evil before the Lord according to all that his father had done. At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up against Jerusalem, and the city was surrounded with fortifications. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against the city with his servants to besiege it.

Jehoiakim, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon, he and his mother, his servants, his princes, and his eunuchs. The king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign. He brought out from there all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house, and broke into pieces all the golden vessels that Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord.

He carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty army—ten thousand—into captivity, as well as every craftsman and smith; nothing was left except the poor of the people of the land. He also carried Jehoiakim to Babylon, together with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, and his eunuchs, and led the judges of the land into captivity from Jerusalem to Babylon. The king of Babylon also led to Babylon all the men of valor, seven thousand, and the craftsmen and smiths, one thousand—all the strong and fighting men,’ etc.

*(From Bede.)* In reporting that Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty army—ten thousand—into captivity, Scripture adds: ‘And every craftsman and smith.’ This is related to what is narrated above concerning the Philistines who ruled over the people of Israel, when it says: ‘Now no smith was found throughout all the land of Israel. For the Philistines had said, “Otherwise the Hebrews will make swords or spears”’ (1 Samuel 13).

Just as at that time they took care that the Hebrews, having smiths, should not make weapons with which to resist, so now the Chaldeans, after destroying Jerusalem and laying waste the whole land of promise, strive to ensure that no craftsman and no smith remains there who could repair the defiled walls of the city or mend what had been destroyed. Rather, whatever skill they had found among the exterminated people, they carried it all away to Babylon, so that it might either be useless thereafter or serve the needs of that city.

Because this lamentable history corresponds so closely to the negligence of our own time, I do not think its allegory should be left unspoken.

It is clear that Jerusalem and the land of Israel signify the city of Christ, that is, the holy Church; while Babylon and the Chaldeans or Philistines signify the city of the devil, that is, the entire multitude of evil human beings or angels.

Israel serves the Philistines or Chaldeans when the faithful, remaining in the Church in name only, are deceived by unclean spirits or people and submit the necks of their minds either to greed, lust, or any other sin.

Nebuchadnezzar carries Jerusalem and all the princes, the mighty army—ten thousand—into captivity when teachers of peoples, and those who seemed to serve the Lord with unconquerable spirit and preserve the law’s Decalogue faithfully in love of God and neighbor, are suddenly overcome either by the allurements of the world or by adversities. They either defile themselves with greater crimes or, turning toward heresy, openly incur the mark of apostasy.

What other weapons are there by which, resisting the devil, we defend the freedom given to us by God, except the words of Scripture? In them, through the examples of the Lord himself and of his saints, we learn with the greatest clarity the order by which the battles against vices are to be overcome.

The Philistines deprive the children of Israel of weaponsmiths when evil spirits delay the minds of the faithful from meditation on sacred reading by inserting worldly business into their lives, lest they themselves gain confidence to resist through its practice, or perhaps kindle others who cannot read by exhorting or correcting them to resist vices.

They remove the weaponsmiths when they overwhelm those who know the sacred words with such crimes that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they had learned.

They transfer every craftsman and smith from Jerusalem to Babylon when they turn away from their purpose those who were accustomed, through the manifold working of virtues, to benefit many and fortify the city of God against attacks of temptation, and compel them to devote the ability that they ought to have applied to the defense of the holy Church instead to the will of the king of vices.

If in this passage we wish to understand a *smith* not as a maker of doors or walls but rather as a worker in gold and gems, the meaning plainly reaches the same spiritual conclusion. It has been said concerning wisdom that it is gold and an abundance of gems. Therefore we can understand its craftsmen more appropriately as teachers, who, so long as they live and teach rightly, devote the skill of their art to the adornment of the holy city.

But if they should happen to go astray, what else happens except that they are carried away captive to Babylon by the king of the Chaldeans?

To understand the migration of the craftsman and smith from Jerusalem to Babylon as the burial of the talent of the heavenly word in the earth—that is, the conversion of spiritual knowledge to the works of sinners—and the carrying away into captivity of all the strong and fighting men, that is, those who seemed to be strong men and fighters but were deceived by the cunning of evil spirits and held captive in the prison of spiritual Babylon: it is necessary for us to work diligently so that we may escape the power of the most savage king.

Let us be watchful and sober; let us always place the fear of God before our eyes and flee entirely from forgetfulness of his commandments. Let us build for ourselves a tower of good works and climb into it through progress in life, ‘clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, having the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God’ (Ephesians 6).

Let us guard the gates of our senses, lest death enter through our windows (Jeremiah 9). With every care let us guard our heart, because from it life proceeds. Above all, let us place our hope in the goodness of the heavenly King, asking that by his grace we may be delivered from every evil.

Thus we shall always remain free from spiritual enemies, because ‘the Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvation of his Christ; he saves all who hope in him’ (Psalm 27; Psalm 17).

‘After Jehoiakim had been taken captive, Nebuchadnezzar appointed Mattaniah, his uncle, in his place and gave him the name Zedekiah. Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil before the Lord according to all that Jehoiakim had done,’ etc.

What else can we understand in Zedekiah except what we previously said concerning Jehoiakim: namely, evil rulers in the Church who misuse a divine office and gift and falsely usurp for themselves the name of righteousness?

*Mattaniah* is interpreted as ‘gift’ or ‘present’; *Zedekiah* as ‘the righteous one of the Lord.’ He is said to have reigned eleven years, which signifies that he was a transgressor of the law. For the number eleven, which exceeds ten, signifies exceeding the Decalogue. Nor can someone rightly be called a king who refuses to rule himself and those subject to him according to the Lord’s commandments.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Nabuzardan, commander of the army of the king of Babylon, who devastated the land of the Jews, destroyed the cities, burned the temple, consumed the royal houses with fire, and carried all the spoil with him to Babylon.

*(Chapter 25.)* ‘It happened in the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came, he and his whole army, against Jerusalem. They surrounded it and constructed fortifications around it. The city was shut up and besieged until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the month. Famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land,’ etc.

The number nine, which is one less than ten, signifies the imperfection of the law, just as eleven signifies transgression.

It is rightly said that Nebuchadnezzar besieged the city in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, in the tenth month and on the tenth day of the month. For when evil shepherds neglect to perfect in deed and teaching the commandments of the Decalogue that they possess in knowledge, the ancient enemy with his army necessarily surrounds the people entrusted to them with a siege. Having built a fortification of error and vices, he closes the city and hems it in, so that famine prevails in the city: namely, famine of the word of God, when the bread of teaching is not freely distributed to the people of the land.

‘The city was breached, and all the men of war fled by night.’

The people’s defense is breached by the various temptations of evil spirits. Those who ought to have defended the city with weapons, surrounded by the night of ignorance and the darkness of sins, flee, because, according to the voice of truth: ‘The hired servant, and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep’ (John 10).

And the Apostle says: ‘Those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night’ (1 Thessalonians 5).

But what follows—that they “fled by the way of the gate that lies between the double wall toward the king’s garden”—secretly reproves the negligence of teachers who, standing between the double wall of the two Testaments, seek not to fight but to escape; and who prefer to luxuriate in pleasures, signified by the garden, rather than to resist the enemy with the shield of faith.

“Moreover, the Chaldeans were besieging the city all around. So Zedekiah fled by the way that leads to the plains of the wilderness; and the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook him in the plain of Jericho, and all the warriors who were with him were scattered and abandoned him,” etc. When evil spirits surround the people, the ruler flees—not to the mountains, of which it is written, “The mountains are around him, and the Lord is around his people” (Ps. 124), but to the plains of the wilderness, that is, to the expanse of luxury. Hence it is written: “Narrow and confined is the way that leads to life, and broad and spacious the way that leads to death” (Matt. 7).
