“And they overtook him in the plain of Jericho, and all the warriors who were with him were scattered and abandoned him.” Rightly, therefore, when the virtues that ought to have defended a person desert him, he is captured in the plain of Jericho—that is, in the defection of the carnal sense. For Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” and signifies the waning of the flesh. Hence that man who was descending from Jerusalem to Jericho is described as having fallen among robbers (Luke 10).

“So they seized the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, who pronounced judgment against him.” That is, he exercised just judgment upon him.

“But the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, put out his eyes, bound him with chains, and brought him to Babylon.” (From Gregory.) The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons at Riblah before his eyes and also tore out his eyes. While Holy Scripture recounts Zedekiah’s captivity, it announces the order of inward captivity. For the king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, [Col. 0276A] the possessor of inward confusion: he first slaughters the sons before the eyes of the one who is watching, because he often destroys good works in such a way that the mind itself, now captive and grieving, sees that it has lost them. For the mind often gives birth to good works, yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, it loses through love what it has produced. It considers the losses it suffers, yet does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. But while it is struck by the sight of wickedness being committed, it is eventually brought, through the practice of sin, to the point where it is deprived even of the light of reason. Hence the king of Babylon, after first destroying the sons, puts out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the evil spirit, first removing good works, afterward takes away the light of understanding. Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah. For Riblah is interpreted as “punishment.” Indeed, the light of reason is eventually closed to the one who is weighed down by evil practice and the multitude of his iniquity.

“In the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month—that is, the nineteenth year of the king of Babylon—Nabuzardan, commander of the army and servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and burned the house of the Lord, the king’s house, and the houses of Jerusalem. He burned every house with fire. The entire army of the Chaldeans that was with the commander of the soldiers destroyed the walls of Jerusalem all around. The rest of the people who remained in the city, the deserters who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the common people, Nabuzardan, the commander of the army, led away,” etc. The order of the time therefore corresponds to the rationale of the punishment. In the fifth month the city is read to have been laid waste, because it scorned to keep the Pentateuch of the Law. And on the seventh day of the month, because it did not observe the Sabbath rest and acted in every way contrary to the divine commandments, falsely flattering itself about its security because of its dwelling in holy places. Hence the Lord says through Jeremiah:

“Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.’ For if you thoroughly amend your ways and your practices, if you execute justice between a man and his neighbor, if you do not oppress the resident alien, the widow, and the orphan, and do not shed innocent blood in this place, and if you do not go after foreign gods to your own harm, then I will dwell with you in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers, from age to age forever. Behold, you trust in lying words that will not profit you: stealing, killing, committing adultery, swearing falsely, offering sacrifices to the Baals, and going after foreign gods whom you do not know. Then you come and stand before me in this house upon which my name has been invoked, and you say, ‘We have been delivered,’ because we have committed all these abominations. And now, because you have done all these works, says the Lord—and I spoke to you, rising early and speaking, but you did not listen—I will treat this house upon which my name has been invoked, in which you trust, and the place that I gave to you and your fathers, as I treated Shiloh; and I will cast you from my presence, as I cast out all your brothers, the whole offspring of Ephraim” (Jer. 7).

Nabuzardan came; his name is interpreted as “winnowing fan” [Col. 0277A] or “the prophecy of another’s judgment,” acting according to God’s just judgment against sinners. The commander of the army of the king of Babylon set fire to the intelligible house of the Lord, Jerusalem, when the ancient enemy—who is both the king of confusion and the prince of all the wicked, whether evil spirits or impious human beings—invades the faithful people and overturns the house of the king and the houses of Jerusalem, that is, the rulers and those who seemed to remain in the vision of peace, inflaming them with desire.

“And he burned every house with fire,” when he disturbed each person’s conscience through the flame of unlawful love.

“And he destroyed the walls of Jerusalem all around,” when he dissolves, among those who despair, the intention of prayer and the pursuits of virtue, which he knows are effective against him, so that they may not run through hope of pardon to divine assistance and grasp the defenses of a reformed life.

“And leading the people into captivity, he left the vine-dressers and farmers from the poor of the land,” because he takes captive through vices those who could have been useful in word and example, and entrusts agriculture to the dull-minded, so that not the wine of spiritual grace and the grain of sound doctrine may bear fruit in the vineyards and fields of the peoples, but rather the thorns and briars of vices may grow up.

“But the bronze columns that were in the temple of the Lord, the stands, and the bronze Sea that was in the house of the Lord, the Chaldeans broke apart and carried all the bronze to Babylon.” We may understand the bronze columns and stands as teachers, who ought to support others through the sonority of preaching and the firmness of faith. [Col. 0277C] The bronze Sea signifies the bath of baptism, or the compunction of tears. Indeed, the spiritual Chaldeans strive, through the negligence of teachers, to remove and break all these things from the house of the Lord, so that not even a shard remains by which a little ember might be carried away from the conflagration.

“They also took the bronze pots, the shovels, the forks, the bowls, the mortars, and all the bronze vessels in which they ministered.” For, removing the various offices in the ecclesiastical orders from the service of God, they turned them to their own most wicked use.

“And the censers and bowls.” When, by obstructing them, they overturn prayer by which the divinity could be appeased, and the cup of the word by which the weary ought to have been refreshed.

“Whatever was gold, gold; whatever was silver, silver—the commander of the army took away.” For the wicked enemy strives to remove from the house of the Lord both precious understanding and the beauty of eloquence, and to lead them with him into confusion.

“The commander of the army also took Seraiah, the chief priest, and Zephaniah, the second priest, and three doorkeepers; and from the city he took one eunuch who was overseer of the warriors, and five men of those who had stood before the king, whom he found in the city; and Shophar, the commander of the army, who examined the recruits from the people of the land; and six men from the common people who were found in the city. Nabuzardan, the commander of the soldiers, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah. The king of Babylon struck them down and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and Judah was carried away from his land.” For the devil seeks to deceive and take captive through sins not only ordinary people but also the strong and the leaders in the Church. Hence it is written of him in Job: “His food is choice” (Tob. 41).

He also took Seraiah, whose name is interpreted as “bound,” the chief priest, when he binds the first order of the Church, which is found in bishops, in the chain of vices through love of earthly pleasure.

“He likewise took Zephaniah,” whose name is interpreted as “hidden,” the second priest, when he subjects to his own lord those of the second order—that is, the presbyters—who had buried the talent of God’s word in the earth and hidden it.

“And three doorkeepers”: namely, those doorkeepers who ought to have opened the door of faith and, holding the key of knowledge, neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter (Luke 11).

“And from the city he took one eunuch who was overseer of the warriors.” This eunuch signifies those whom Holy Scripture elsewhere calls foolish virgins (Matt. 25). They held vessels empty of oil in their hands, practicing abstinence from bodily intercourse but unwilling to have the oil of grace and mercy in their hearts. They are appointed over warriors in vain, since they do not take care to avoid arrogance.

“He also took five men of those who had stood before the king,” namely, those who, serving pleasure through the five bodily senses, always attended upon the king of vices.

“And Shophar, the commander of the army, who examined the recruits from the people of the land.” Shophar is interpreted as “one who scatters” [Col. 0278C] or “one who divides,” signifying those who, instead of nurturing in the Church the inexperienced whom they ought to have trained for the service of Christ, scatter them through evil examples and separate them from the company of the faithful through error.

“And six men from the common people” who had been found in the city—that is, foolish workers, rightly called by the name of the common people because they had neglected to learn the usefulness of divine counsels and to fulfill them in their deeds. Taking all these, Nabuzardan, the commander of the soldiers, brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.

“And the king of Babylon struck them down and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath,” because when the ancient enemy tears such prey from the Church through his wickedness and carries it away, this is what he desires, this is what he pursues with all his effort: to bring those whom the king of confusion strikes at Riblah—that is, in the multitude of crimes and love of pleasures—to the slaughter of everlasting death. Hence Scripture says: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many are those who enter by it” (Matt. 7).

“And Judah was carried away from his land,” when those who seemed to possess in the Church the confession of God’s name are removed from the land of virtues through many crimes and sins and led away into the kingdom of confusion and error. Whoever continues to serve wickedly under that dominion will not deserve, through the leadership of Jesus, to return to the land of Judah and rebuild the temple of the Lord there. After the misery of the present life, such people will be handed over to the prison of everlasting death, where “their worm will never die, and the fire will not be quenched” (Isa. 66). In them the judgment of the blessed apostle Peter will be fulfilled, when he says: “For it would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Pet. 2). For, as the Truth also testifies: “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten severely; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten lightly” (Luke 12).

[Col. 0279B]

(ANNO 834.) COMMENTARIES OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE TWO BOOKS OF CHRONICLES.

RABANUS’S PROLOGUE ON THE BOOK OF CHRONICLES TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS.

[Col. 0279]

[Col. 0279B] To the most serene, most glorious, most noble, and most excellent in true religion, LOUIS, king, Rabanus, the most insignificant servant of the servants of God, with bended knees wishes eternal salvation in Christ.

Since I had often heard from others, for some time past, that you were most devoted and energetic as a servant of God in the cultivation of piety, and afterward saw and confirmed in person that what I had previously learned only by hearsay was true, I considered how I might offer you some service, as is fitting for a most beloved lord. Through our labor, your noble intellect might thereby exercise itself fruitfully in the divine laws and, by investigating the testimonies of the sacred books, be instructed to hold the government of the kingdom legitimately according to the examples of the Fathers who preceded us.

Therefore I resolved to offer to your affection my little exposition of the book of Chronicles, which the Hebrews call *Dibre hayyamim*, that is, “Words of the Days.” Although it is not worthy of so great an excellence, I hope it will not be unwelcome to your benevolence, so that you might possess a service from our smallness most suitable to your rank.

For it was fitting that the history of the kings of Judah—that is, of those who confess—should be offered to a most Christian king, most devoted to the divine commandments, with its spiritual meaning explained to some extent. Since your noble prudence governs the ecclesiastical people, redeemed by the precious blood of the Son of God (Acts 20), and thoroughly accustomed to confessing the name of God, it is therefore fitting for a most pious prince—that is, for the ruler of the members of the true King, Christ, the only-begotten Son of God—to possess and practice the manner of government according to divine Scripture, especially since Wisdom, which shines forth most clearly in those writings, admonishes and says: “Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just” (Prov. 8). And again: “The desire for wisdom,” it says, “will lead to an everlasting kingdom” (Wis. 6).

“If you delight in thrones and scepters, kings of the peoples, love wisdom, so that you may reign forever.” Receive, therefore, the history of the former kings, and above all love in it the spiritual meaning pertaining to the grace of Christ. For the law of God is spiritual (Rom. 7), and revelation is needed in order that it may be understood and that, with unveiled face, we may contemplate the glory of God (2 Cor. 3). Hence in the Apocalypse the book sealed with seven seals is shown (Rev. 5), and no one opens it unless the one who holds the key of David unseals it—he who opens and no one closes, who closes and no one opens (Rev. 3).

Therefore it should be known that among the Scriptures of the Old Testament the present history of Chronicles holds no insignificant place. Concerning it the blessed Jerome, that most skillful interpreter of the divine books, says:

“Thus the book of Chronicles, an epitome of the same Testament, is so great and so important that if anyone should claim for himself knowledge of the Scriptures without it, he mocks himself. For throughout, by individual names and connections of words, histories omitted in the books of Kings are touched upon, and innumerable questions of the Gospel are explained.”

I have recalled these things so that the reader may know how useful this book is for investigation and understanding. For what could I, as though a learned teacher, have searched out or explained all its mysteries? Following the footsteps of the Fathers, I arranged in order what I found explained by them and what, by God’s grace, I was able to investigate myself according to the likeness of their meaning, and I took care to gather it into a single little work.

I did not resolve to write long and flourishing discourses, in which showy eloquence plays to applause, but commentaries on the divine histories, whose task is to pass over what is evident and discuss what is obscure. Some years ago, at the request of Abbot Hildonius, I published four books of commentaries on the books of Kings according to the understanding of the catholic Fathers. I also personally presented them in our monastery to your most sacred father, the Emperor Louis. In them, as in the present work, I inserted in many places the narrative of Josephus, the historian of the Jews, as well as the opinions of a certain Hebrew who in our own times flourished in knowledge of the Law. I did not do so in such a way as to drag an unwilling reader into assent to their traditions, but rather left those matters to his own judgment and examination.

Moreover, if these things offend some people, the fault is not ours but perhaps lies in their perverse judgment—people who prefer to criticize the little works of others rather than compose their own, who, out of hatred for our name, consider not the matters themselves but the persons, and approve the silence of others more than our diligence. We have simply set down what we found. It is our task to cite witnesses; it is theirs to judge the credibility of the witnesses.

But you, most noble king, defend us against the bites of the envious, and protect us with the shield of faith and the sword of divine zeal, because, whatever we may be, we are your devoted servants and helpers by the grace of God. May divine power and the eternal majesty of Christ graciously preserve you, reigning happily here and everywhere, now and forever.

THE EXPOSITION ON CHRONICLES BEGINS. BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0281]

CHAPTER ONE. [Col. 0281B] Catalogue of the generations from Adam to Abraham. Also, from Abraham to Israel.

(I Chron. 1.) Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Noah was the tenth from Adam, as is clearly shown in the book of Genesis and likewise stands out in the first chapter of Chronicles. He also had three sons, namely Shem, Ham, and Japheth, through whom, after the flood, the renewed human race spread abroad.

Noah is appropriately said to be tenth in the catalogue of the fathers, because he was perfect. For it is first written of him: “Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generations. He walked with God, and begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth” (Gen. 6).

[Col. 0281C] The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai and Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. Japheth, Noah’s son, had seven sons, who possessed the land of Asia from the Amanus and Taurus mountains of Coelesyria and Cilicia as far as the river Tanais; in Europe they extended as far as Gadeira, leaving their names to places and peoples. Many of these names were later changed, while the others remain as they were.

Gomer means the Galatians; Magog, the Scythians; Madai, the Medes; Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks, whence the Ionian Sea; Tubal, the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom Celtiberia derives its name, although some suppose them to be Italians; Meshech, the Cappadocians, whence a city among them is still called Marecha. The Seventy Interpreters, however, consider the Capturini to be Cappadocians. Tiras means the Thracians, whose name has not been greatly altered. These seven peoples, then, whom I have said were descended from Japheth, inhabit the northern region.

The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The Greeks call Ashkenaz Rhegmos; Riphath means the Paphlagonians; Togarmah, the Phrygians.

The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to his language, his clans, and his nation” (Gen. 10). From the Ionians, that is, the Greeks, came the Elishans, who are called Aeolians. Hence the fifth Greek language is called Aeolic; they call it [an uncertain or corrupt Greek term in the source]. Josephus considers Tarshish to mean the Cilicians, saying that the letter of aspiration was corrupted by later generations into *t* [or “tay”]. Hence their metropolis is called Tarsus, a city renowned through the apostle Paul (Acts 21).

Kittim means Cyprus, from which the Cypriots are still named in the cities. Dodanim means the Rhodians, for so the Seventy Interpreters translated it. Let us read the books of Varro on antiquities, those of Capito of Smyrna, the Greek Phlegon, and the other most learned writers: nearly all the islands, the shores of the whole world, and the lands near the sea were occupied by Greek settlers. As we said above, from the Amanus and Taurus mountains they possessed all the coastal regions as far as the British Ocean.

[Col. 0282C] The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan (Gen. 10). Cush is still called Ethiopia by the Hebrews. Mizraim is Egypt. Put is Libya, from whom the river of Mauretania is still called the Phur, and the whole region around it is the land of Put. Many writers, both Greek and Latin, bear witness to this. Why the ancient name of Libya remained in only one part of the climatic region while the rest of the land was called Africa is not relevant to this place or time. Canaan, however, obtained the land that the Jews afterward possessed after expelling the Canaanites.

The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca (Gen. 10). Seba gave his name to the Sabaeans, concerning whom Virgil writes:

“... the rod of fragrant incense belongs to the Sabaeans.”

And elsewhere:

“... and a hundred altars of the Sabaeans  
are warm with incense.”

Havilah means the Gaetuli, who dwell adjacent to the wilderness in the more remote part of Africa. Sabtah gave its name to the Sabathaeans, who are now called the Astarobi. Raamah and Sabteca gradually lost their ancient names, and what names they now bear in place of the old ones is unknown.

The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan (Gen. 10). This Sheba is written with the letter *sin*; the Sheba mentioned above is written with *samekh*, from whom we said the Sabaeans were named. This Sheba, then, is interpreted as Arabia. For in the seventy-first Psalm, where we have, “The kings of Arabia and Sheba will offer gifts” (Ps. 71), the Hebrew reads, “The kings of Sheba and Sheba”: the first name is written with *sin*, the second with *samekh*. Dedan is a people of Ethiopia in the western region.

Cush begot Nimrod: “he began to be mighty on the earth” (Gen. 10). Nimrod is called mighty because he was the first among the peoples to seize an unprecedented tyranny. [Col. 0283B] Of him it is written in Genesis that he was “a mighty hunter before the Lord” (Gen. 10), because he turned people away from the worship of God.

Josephus accordingly relates the following about him:

“Nimrod, son of Ham, son of Noah, made them arrogant toward the injury and contempt of God. Since he was bold and exceedingly strong in hand, he persuaded them not to attribute to God the happiness that came to human beings through him, but to say that it was provided to them by their own strength. He drew his kinsmen into the cause of tyranny, himself presuming to turn people away from the fear of God and to place their hope in their own strength. They considered it madness to believe in God, who had threatened the earth with an almost limitless flood. For this reason they urged that a tower be built higher than the floodwaters could reach. The multitude was inclined to obey Nimrod’s commands, considering service to God a burdensome duty; they built the tower, abandoning none of their efforts.”

Nimrod reigned in Babylon and in Marech—that is, in Edessa and Machad, which is now called Nisibis—and in Chalamie, which later, after its name was changed, was called Seleucia by King Seleucus, or certainly the place now called Ctesiphon.

Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, and Naphtuhim, as well as Pathrusim and Casluhim. “From these came the Philistines and the Caphtorim” (Gen. 18). Apart from the Lehabim, from whom the Libyans were later named—for previously they were called Putites—and the Casluhim, who afterward were called Philistines, whom we incorrectly call Palestinians, the other six peoples are unknown to us. Overthrown in the Ethiopian war, they passed into oblivion together with their former names. They possessed the land of Gaza as far as the remotest borders of Egypt.

Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and the Hittite, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite, the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite (Gen. 10). Sidon was the firstborn of Canaan; from him the city in Phoenicia is called Sidon. Then came the Arkite, who founded Arka, a town situated opposite Tripoli at the foot of Lebanon. Not far from it there was another city named Sivy, which, later destroyed by wars through various misfortunes, preserved only the ancient name of the place.

The Arvadites are those who possessed the island of Arvad, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait. Samaria is a distinguished city of Coelesyria. Hamath, too, is still called by both Syrians and Hebrews by the name it had among the ancients. The Macedonians who ruled in the East after Alexander called it Epiphany. Some think that Antioch received this name. Others, although not correctly, confirm their opinion with a seemingly plausible name: they suppose that Emmaus, the first stopping place from Antioch for travelers going to Edessa, is called by this name and is the same place that the ancients called Hamath.

The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram (Gen. 10). They occupy the part of Asia from the Euphrates River [Col. 0284B] as far as the Indian Ocean. Elam is the ancestor of the Elamites, the rulers of Persia. It has already been said of Asshur that he founded the city of Nineveh. Arphaxad is the ancestor of the Chaldeans; Lud, of Lydia; Aram, of the Syrians, whose metropolis is Damascus.

The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash (Gen. 10). Uz, founder of Trachonitis and Damascus, held the principality between Palestine and Coelesyria. Hence the Seventy Interpreters, in the book of Job, where the Hebrew reads “the land of Uz,” translated the region as Ausitis, or, as it were, Usitis. Hul is the ancestor of the Armenians. Gether is the ancestor of the Acarnanians or Carians. In place of Mash, the Seventy Interpreters said Meshech, who are now called the Maeonians.

[Col. 0284C] Arphaxad begot Shelah, who himself begot Eber. Eber had two sons: the name of one was Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided; the name of his brother was Joktan (Gen. 10). Eber, from whom the Hebrews were called, gave his son Peleg a name through prophecy. Peleg is interpreted as “division,” because in his days the languages were divided at Babylon.

Philo relates in his book of Questions on Genesis that, while Noah was still alive, nine hundred fourteen thousand one hundred men were born from the three sons of Noah, apart from women and children. Leaders were appointed over them: Joktan was leader of the sons of Shem, Nimrod of the sons of Ham, and the sons of Japheth were placed under the leadership of Phenech. After Noah’s death, all these leaders gathered from every direction with their assembled forces in the plain of Shinar; there they attempted to build a tower (Gen. 11).

When they had begun to build the tower, God divided their languages and changed their appearances, and each person no longer recognized his brother, nor did they understand one another’s language. Thus, when the builders ordered their servants to bring stones, the servants brought water; and when they requested water, the servants brought straw. Their understanding having thus been disrupted, they ceased building the city, and the Lord scattered them over the face of the whole earth.

Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan (Gen. 10). I have been unable to discover the later names of these peoples; but because they are far from us, they may still be called by these names. They possessed the entire region of India from the river Cophene, a region called Hieria.

Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abram: this is Abraham. Wise reader, observe that just as at the beginning he placed ten generations from Adam to Noah, so he preserved the sum of ten generations from Shem to Abraham—not without the most sacred mystery of that number itself.

The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael; and these are their generations. The firstborn of Ishmael was Nebaioth, followed by Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael. Ishmael had twelve sons, of whom Nebaioth was the firstborn. From him the whole region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is still called Nabataea, and it is part of Arabia. Their families, towns, villages, small fortresses, and tribes are also celebrated under these names. From one of them come Kedar in the desert, Dumah as another region, Teman to the south, and Kedemah to the east.

The sons of Abraham’s concubine Keturah, whom she bore, were Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan were Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.

Keturah is interpreted in Hebrew as “joined” or “bound.” For this reason the Hebrews suppose that, with her name changed, she was the same as Hagar, who after Sarah’s death passed from being a concubine to being a wife. This seems to provide an excuse for Abraham’s age, so that, as an old man after the death of his elderly wife, he might not be accused of indulging in new marriages.

Leaving aside what is uncertain, we say this: according to the historians of the Hebrews, the sons born to Abraham by Keturah occupied [lacuna] and Arabia, which now [lacuna] as far as the borders of the Red Sea. It is said that one of Abraham’s descendants, named Epher, led an army against Libya and settled there after defeating the enemy; his descendants, from the name of their ancestor, called the region Africa.

Alexander, who is called [lacuna], and [a corrupt phrase in the source] surnamed Machus, bears witness to this matter as he recounts barbarian history in Greek. As for the statement, “The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim,” some think that Asshurim should be translated as “merchants,” Letushim as “workers in bronze,” and Leummim as *phylarchs*, that is, leaders of many tribes and peoples. Others contend that the Syrians were called Asshurim and that many regions of India were occupied by the sons of Abraham and Keturah.

Abraham begot Isaac, whose sons were Esau and Israel. Although Abraham had several sons, Sarah had only Isaac, according to the promise; Isaac’s sons were the twins Esau and Israel, born from a single union with Rebecca, Isaac’s wife (Gen. 25).

The sons of Esau were Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, Korah. It is narrated in the book of Genesis (Gen. 26, 27, 36) that Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite; and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth. Adah bore Eliphaz. Basemath bore Reuel. Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.

The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, and Timna. Scripture recalls him in the book of Job (Job 2, 22). But a question arises: since Timna is read in Genesis (Gen. 36) to have been Eliphaz’s concubine, from the race of the Horites who lived among the Idumaeans [Col. 0286B] in the land of Seir, and since she bore him Amalek, how is she here counted among the sons—especially when it is read below that Timna was the sister of Lotan?

The sons of Esau, who is also Edom. Seir means “hairy” in Hebrew, because he was entirely hairy, like a pelt. Edom means “red” or “ruddy” in Hebrew. Because he sold his birthright for red food (Gen. 25), he acquired the name Ruddy, that is, Edom. The Hebrews solve this question by saying that Timna was Esau’s concubine and bore him a son, Amalek, but that he was nevertheless raised as a son among the other sons.

The sons of Shobal were Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. Alian, who was of the race of the Horites, is written in Genesis (Gen. 36) as Alvan, that is, “exalted.” In Chronicles, however, he is Alian, that is, “cast out,” signifying that the Horites were exalted before Edom took that land, but were cast out after they lost their homeland to Edom when he triumphed over them.

Shephi, the son of Shobal, is read in Chronicles as “one-footed”; in Genesis he is also called Sepho (ibid.), that is, “two-footed.” Both forms, however, are written with the letter *sin*. He is called “two-footed” because, in the course of time, he was more effective through the multitude of his descendants than in the first ancestor.

The sons of Zibeon were Aiah and Anah. Concerning Anah it is written in Genesis: “This is Anah who found hot springs in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys of Zibeon his father” (ibid.). Another edition has: “This is Anah who found *iamim* in the wilderness while he was pasturing the donkeys of Zibeon his father.”

Many and varied discussions of this passage occur among the Hebrews. Among the Greeks and our own writers, however, there is silence about it. Some think that *iamim* means “seas”; for the word is written with the same letters as the word that is now written here. They therefore suppose that, while he was pasturing his father’s donkeys in the wilderness, he discovered gatherings of water which, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, are called “seas”—that is, that he found a pool, whose discovery in the desert would be difficult.

Some think that “hot springs” is signified by a word borrowed from the neighboring Punic language, which is closely related to Hebrew. Others suppose that he allowed male wild asses to mate with female asses and discovered such a union, from which very swift female asses called *iamim* were born. Most think that he was the first to cause herds of mares to be mounted by asses in the wilderness, so that new animals contrary to nature—mules—might be born from them.

Anah’s son was Dishon. The sons of Dishon were Amaran [Hamram], Eshban, Jithran, and Cheran. Amaran, son of Dishon, son of Anah, is Hamaran in Chronicles (“stained with filth” or “drunken”); in Genesis he is Amadan, “desirous.” Amaran and Amadan, however, are names of one and the same man.

The sons of Ezer: Balaan, Zavan, Jachan, and so forth. Jachan, the son of Ezer, of the race of the Horrites, is called Achan in Genesis, that is, “one who troubles.” In Chronicles, however, he is Jachan, that is, “troubled.” For the names of the ancients were changed through various events, to signify a mystery in the alteration of names. If a prudent reader applies diligent investigation to this difficulty, he will easily be able to discover a sober understanding.

These are the kings who ruled in the land of Edom before there was a king over the children of Israel: Bale, son of Beor, and the name of his city was Denaba. Denaba was the city of Balac, son of the king of Edom. After him Jobab reigned, although to me the matter appears very different. To this day there is a village called Denaia, eight miles from Arsopolis on the road toward the Arnon; and another Dannaba lies upon Mount Fogor, at the seventh milestone from Jebus.

Balac died, and Jobab, son of Zare, from Bosra, reigned in his place, and so forth. From this some suspect that he was Job, as is added at the end of his book. The Hebrews, however, assert that he was descended from the stock of Nachor. Philo, in the aforementioned book of his Questions on Genesis, relates that Job lived in those times and married Dinah, daughter of Jacob, whom Shechem, son of Hamor, had previously violated (Gen. XXXIV). Before Job’s suffering, when Satan sought him out to test him (Job I), he says that Job fathered seven sons and three daughters by her, and that they perished in that very trial. But after the Lord had healed Job’s affliction and restored everything to him twofold, his aforementioned wife again bore him seven other sons and three daughters, whose names were the same as those of the former children: Eliphaz, Ermol, Diasat, Philaas, Diphaz, Cellud, and Thedom; and the names of his daughters were Meruli, Iaz, and Zeli.

Bosra, or Bosor, is a city in the desert beyond the Jordan, which fell to the tribe of Reuben, on the eastern side of Jericho; it is a priestly city and a city of refuge. This is the Bosra that is the metropolis of Arabia. There is also another Bosor, the city of Esau, in the mountains of Idumea, which Isaiah recalls when he says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, his garments ruddy from Bosra?” (Isa. LXIII).

When Jobab had died, Husam from the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Theman is the region of the princes of Edom, in the land of Gebal, taking its name from Theman, son of Eliphaz, son of Esau. To this day there is also a village called Theman, five miles distant from the city of Petra. A garrison of Roman soldiers was stationed there; Eliphaz, king of the Temanites, came from that place. One of the sons of Ishmael was also called Theman. It should be known, moreover, that every southern region is called Theman in Hebrew.

Husam also died, and Adad, son of Badad, reigned in his place. He struck Midian in the land of Moab, and the name of his city was Avith. Midian is a city named after one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah. It lies beyond Arabia Felix, in the desert of the Saracens, toward the east of the Red Sea; hence the people are called Midianites and the region Midian. We also read that the daughters of Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, are called daughters of Midian. But this is another city bearing the same name, near the Arnon and Arcopolis, of which only ruins are now visible. As for what follows—“The name of his city was Avith”—it indicates a village in the land of Bashan, near Mount Gilead, which fell to the lot of the tribe of Manasseh.

When Adad too had died, Samla of Masreca reigned in his place. Masreca is a city of the kingdom of Edom, around Gabelene.

Samla also died, and Saul of Rehoboth, which lies beside a river, reigned in his place. Rehoboth is a city beside a river, where the king of Edom was located; to this day there is a fortress in the region of Gebalene, as well as a large village called by this name.

When Saul had died, Balanan, son of Achobor, reigned in his place. He too died, and Adad reigned in his place. The name of his city was Phau. His wife was called Meetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezaab. His name is interpreted as “chief”; he founded the city of Phau in the region of Gebal. His wife was called Meetabel, which is interpreted as “the kindness of the Lord.” She was the daughter of Matred, that is, “of the administrator,” daughter of Mezaab, which is interpreted as “of the goldsmith.” Thus two mothers are counted here, to signify a mystery through the different interpretations of their names: namely, that a goldsmith begot an administrator, and an administrator begot the kindness of God. For from the depth of understanding arises eloquent speech, which produces faith in the hearts of its hearers, and through faith the grace of God is won.

After Adad had died, chiefs began to rule in Edom in place of kings: the chief of Thamna, the chief of Alva, the chief of Jetheth, the chief of Oolibama, and the rest. It should be noted that he first spoke of kings of Edom and afterward of chiefs, although the chiefs came first and the kings later. Here he names some of the mothers of these chiefs, the wives of Esau: for example, Oolibama, Esau’s wife, and Thamna, the concubine of Eliphaz. In Genesis (chap. XXXVI), however, Alva is read, whose interpretation is “elevation.” In Chronicles, likewise, Alicha is read, meaning “above her.”

## CHAPTER II. On the generation of the twelve patriarchs from their father Israel, and on the genealogy of the patriarch Judah continued through his various sons

(I Chron. II.) The sons of Israel were: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. There were twelve sons of Israel, but eight were born of free women and four of slave women. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun were born of Leah, Jacob’s wife; Joseph and Benjamin were born of Rachel; Dan and Naphtali of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant; and Gad and Asher of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant (Gen. XXXV). From these twelve sons of Israel the entire people was propagated, and, with the Lord’s gift, the promised land was possessed.

Now let us consider what the four wives of Jacob signified. Two of them were free women and two were slave women. We have seen the Apostle (Gal. IV) understand the free woman and the slave woman whom Abraham had as the two Testaments. But there, since there is one of each, what he says appears more easily; here, however, there are two and two. Furthermore, there the son of the slave woman was disinherited, whereas here the sons of the slave women receive the promised land together with the sons of the free women. Therefore something is undoubtedly signified here.

Although Jacob’s two free wives are thought to pertain to the New Testament, into whose freedom we have been called, they are not two without reason, except because two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ: one temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which we contemplate the love of God. Leah is interpreted as “laboring,” while Rachel is “the beginning of laughter” or “the word.” The activity of this life, in which we live by faith, is therefore laborious in its works, and uncertain as to the outcome by which it may reach the benefit of those whom we wish to assist. This is Leah, Jacob’s first wife; for this reason she is also said to have had weak eyes (Gen. XXIX). “The thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our plans are uncertain” (Wis. IX).

The hope of eternal contemplation of God, possessing a sure understanding of truth, is Rachel. Hence she is also said to have been beautiful in face and appearance (Gen. XXIX). Every devout student loves her, and for her sake serves the grace of God, through which our sins, even if they have been like scarlet, will be made white as snow (Isa. I). Laban is interpreted as “whitening,” and Jacob served him for Rachel. No one turns under the grace of the remission of sins to serve righteousness except in order to live peacefully in the Word, from whom is seen the Beginning who is God.

The sons of Judah were Her, Onan, and Shelah. These three were born to him from the daughter of Shua, the Canaanite. Her, Judah’s firstborn, was evil before the Lord, and He killed him. The sons of Judah are described more fully in the book of Genesis (chap. XXXVIII), where it is related that the two elder sons were killed by the Lord—namely, Her and Onan—and the reason is shown. It says:

“Judah gave his firstborn Her a wife, and he was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and He killed him. Then Judah said to Onan his son: ‘Go in to your brother’s wife and join yourself to her, so that you may raise up offspring for your brother.’ But he knew that children would not be born to him. When he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his seed on the ground, so that children might not be born in his brother’s name. Therefore the Lord struck him, because he did a detestable thing.”

Now Tamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah. Thus all Judah’s sons were five. In Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, the Jewish people are understood, from whose tribe kings were chosen as husbands. Her name is rightly interpreted as “bitterness.” For she gave the Lord a cup of gall.

The two kinds of rulers who do not act rightly among the people—one consisting of those who do harm, the other of those who benefit no one—are signified by Judah’s two sons. One was wicked, although guilty before the Lord; the other spilled his seed on the ground, so that he would not give seed for the fertilization of Tamar. There are no more than two kinds of people useless to the human race: those who do harm, and those unwilling to provide benefit, who, if they possess any good, lose it in this earthly life, as though spilling it upon the ground.

Because the one who harms is worse than the one who does no good, the first is called “wicked,” while the second, who spilled his seed upon the ground, is called “detestable.” The name of the elder, Her, is interpreted as “leathern” or “of skin,” like the tunics with which the first human beings were clothed when, in punishment for their condemnation, they were sent out of paradise. The name of the second, Onan, is interpreted as “their sorrow.” Whose sorrow? Surely that of those who benefit no one, although they possess the means by which they could benefit, and who lose that means upon the earth.

The removal of life, signified by “skin,” is a greater evil than the [negation] of life, signified by “their sorrow.” Yet God is said to have killed both, signifying that He removed the kingdom from such people.

The third son of Judah, who was not joined to that woman, signifies the time from which kings ceased to arise for the Jewish people from the tribe of Judah. He was indeed Judah’s son, but Tamar did not take him as her husband, because no one from the tribe of Judah reigned among the Jewish people. Hence his name, Shelah, is interpreted as “his dismissal.”

Holy and just men do not belong to this interpretation. Although they lived in that period, they belong nevertheless to the New Testament; through prophecy they were knowingly useful, as David was at the time when Judea had already begun to have no kings. Herod the Great must not be counted among its kings as Tamar’s husband. He was a foreigner and was not joined to her by that covenant of justice, that is, by the bond of anointing as by a marriage contract. Rather, as an outsider, he ruled her, having received that power from the Romans and Caesar.

The same is true of his sons, the tetrarchs, one of whom was called Herod after his father and agreed with Pilate in the Lord’s Passion (Luke XXIII). These foreigners were so far from being counted among the kings of the Jews in the mystical sense that the Jews themselves publicly cried out, gnashing their teeth against Christ: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

This statement was not true except in that universal condemnation. Caesar was indeed king of the Romans, but not properly of the Jews. Yet, in order to deny Christ and continue to worship Caesar, they cried out in this way. At the time when kingship had already departed from the tribe of Judah, Christ, the true Savior and our Lord, had to come—one who would not harm but would benefit greatly. For this had been prophesied:

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

This one too, joined to Tamar—that is, to the Jewish people in a special sense—received two sons from her. The first, called Zerah, while both were twins in their mother’s womb, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it. Then, when he withdrew his hand, the other, called Perez, came forth first in birth (Gen. XXXVIII). This figuratively indicated that Israel would extend its hand into the works of the Law, but would withdraw it stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself; afterward the people of the nations would burst forth, so that those who were last would become first, and those who were first would become last (Matt. XX).

The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Zerah were Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all. The sons of Carmi were Achar, who troubled Israel and sinned by stealing what had been devoted to destruction. This Achar, who is called Achan in the book of Joshua son of Nun (Josh. VII), was the son of Carmi, who was the son of Zabdai or Zimri, who was the son of Zerah from the tribe of Judah.

Achan is interpreted as “a serpent lying in wait”; Achar as “troubled.” The truth of these names demonstrates that the one who, through avarice, lay in wait to steal something devoted to destruction, was caught in his crime and troubled in the punishment of his crime. Mystically, this suggests that the person who, after putting on the garment of faith, introduces the habits of worldly conduct is like one who takes a cloak from what has been devoted to destruction.

The person who defrauds Jericho of what has been devoted to destruction is likewise one who brings heretical doctrines or the superstitious studies of secular literature into the Church. This is the golden rule, expressed in splendid language. Arius, Marcion, and Basilides defrauded it: they stole golden rules from Jericho and attempted to introduce an erroneous philosophical sect into the Church, thereby defiling the whole Church of the Lord, so that many were destroyed through them. Therefore, cast out as accursed, like a heap of stones, they were crushed and destroyed beneath the multitude of their sins.

The sons of Hezron who were born to him were Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelub. Chelub is Caleb, one of the twelve scouts whom Moses sent from the desert into the land of Canaan to inspect the promised land (Num. XIII). Together with Joshua son of Nun, he alone of all the men who had come out of Egypt entered the promised land and received the suburbs of Hebron as his possession.

Chelub, as it is read in Chronicles, is interpreted as “my dog.” The name Caleb, which is found as *ineptatio* [“ineptitude”; the reading is uncertain], is plainly said to mean “dog.” It should also be stated here that Hezron and Jephunneh are names of one and the same man. Thus Caleb is sometimes read as the son of Hezron and sometimes as the son of Jephunneh.

Ram begot Amminadab. Amminadab begot Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah. Nahshon also begot Salma, from whom Boaz arose. It should be noted that in Chronicles Salma is written *par*, whereas in Ruth he is called Salmon (Ruth IV), “peaceful.”

Boaz begot Obed, who himself begot Jesse. Jesse begot Eliab, his firstborn; Aminadab, the second; Shimea, the third; Nathanael, the fourth; Raddai, the fifth; Asom, the sixth; and David, the seventh. Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail.

The question arises why the book of Kings says that Jesse had eight sons, while Chronicles records no more than seven. For it is written there: “David was the son of an Ephrathite from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse, and he had eight sons” (I Kings XVII).

This question is solved among the Hebrews as follows: they say that the prophet Nathan, the son of Shimea, had been raised and nourished in the place of his own son, and was therefore counted among the sons there. For seven of Jesse’s sons are said to have been brought before Samuel (I Kings XVI), while the eighth was in the pastures. It is evident that Nathan was added among them; he is called Jonathan, and at the end of Samuel, when the killing of the giant is recounted, it is said of him: “Jonathan struck him, the son of Shimea, the brother of David” (II Kings XXI). It should be noted that wherever he is called the prophet, he is written Nathan, not Jonathan.

The sons of Zeruiah were Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three. Abigail begot Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite. In Chronicles Amasa is said to be the son of Jether the Ishmaelite, while in Kings he is called Jethra the Israelite (II Kings XVII). This difference of names arose from the quality of their merits. Jethra is interpreted as “remainder,” while Jether means “a small remainder”; the remainder is joined to the Israelites, and the small remainder to the Ishmaelites.

Caleb, son of Hezron, took a wife named Azubah, by whom he begot Jerioth. Her sons were Jazer, Shobab, and Ardon. When Azubah had died, Caleb took Ephrath as his wife, and she bore him Hur, and the rest.

Ephrath is Mary, the sister of Moses. After Azubah’s death she married Caleb, and she bore him Hur, the father of Uri and grandfather of Bezalel, who was master of the craftsmen in the construction of the tabernacle in the desert, as is written in Exodus (Exod. XXXI, XXXV, XXXVI, and XXXVII).

Hur is the man of whom Scripture relates that, when Joshua son of Nun was fighting with the children of Israel against Amalek, Aaron and Hur supported Moses’ hands while he sat upon a stone. Thus his hands did not grow weary until sunset (Exod. XVII).

After this Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir, father of Gilead, and took her when he was sixty years old; she bore him Segub. Segub also begot Jair, who possessed twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead, and the rest.

When he says “after this,” he means after Hezron had received sons from Azubah and Ephrath, Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir, father of Gilead. Machir was the son of Manasseh, son of Joseph, who received his inheritance beyond the Jordan, Moses assigning him the land of Gilead. Hence it is written in the book of Numbers:

“Moses gave Gilead to Machir son of Manasseh, and he dwelt in it. Jair son of Manasseh went and captured its villages, which he called Havvoth-jair [the villages of Jair]” (Num. XXXII).

Thus the possession of the sons received its name from the names of their ancestors. It should also be noted that this Jair was judge after Tola and judged Israel for twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode upon thirty young donkeys and were chiefs of thirty cities, which were named after him, as is read in the book of Judges (Judg. X).

When Hezron had died, Caleb went in to Ephrath. Hezron also had a wife named Abiah, who bore him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa. After his father’s death, Caleb took Ephrath as his wife; but whether this occurred in Egypt or in the desert is not clear.

Hezron had a fourth wife, Abiah, who bore him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa (II Kings XIV). But whether she was taken before or after the other wives is not clearly shown. Tekoa is the city from which Joab took the wise woman who sought to reconcile Absalom with King David through the likeness of her own son, as is recorded in the book of Kings.

The sons of Jerahmeel, Hezron’s firstborn, were born: Ram, his firstborn, then Bunan, Aran, Asum, and Achia. Up to this point, the historian has woven together the genealogy of Hezron’s two younger sons, Ram and Caleb. He narrated them first because he wished in some way to make known the royal and priestly dignity. Now he returns to express the genealogy of the firstborn, Jerahmeel, which he had previously passed over.

Jerahmeel also took another wife, named Atarah, who was the mother of Onam. Onam, the son of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron, received his name from Onan, Judah’s son, who died. They differ in this respect: Judah’s son is written in Hebrew with a *nun*, whereas Jerahmeel’s son is written with an *ayin*.

Onam had sons, Shemei and Jada. The sons of Shemei were Nadab and Abishur. Abishur’s wife was named Abigail, and she bore him Ahobban and Molid. The sons of Nadab were Seled and Apphaim. Seled died without children. The son of Apphaim was Ishi, and Ishi begot Sheshan. Sheshan begot Oholai, and the rest.

The Hebrews say that this Oholai, son of Esau Sheshan—who was the son of Ishi, son of Apphaim, son of Nadab, son of Shemei, son of Onam, son of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah—was Elimelech, Naomi’s husband and the father of Mahlon and Chilion. For this reason it is written below that Sheshan had no son but sons: the two sons mentioned above died without children.

The sons of Caleb, Jerahmeel’s brother, were: Mesha, his firstborn—he was the father of Ziph—and the sons of Mareshah and the father of Hebron, and the rest. Ziph is the name of the place from which the Ziphites came to Saul (I Kings XXIII). Hebron likewise is the place where David reigned for seven years before he reigned in Jerusalem (II Kings V).

When he says of Mesha, Caleb’s firstborn, “He was the father of Ziph and the sons of Mareshah, the father of Hebron,” he signifies that these places later received their names from Caleb’s descendants. For, as is read in Joshua (Josh. XIV), Caleb received Hebron and its suburbs by lot and drove out from there the son of Anak.

Ephah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Haran, Mosa, and Gezez. Haran begot Gezez, and so forth. Gezez is interpreted as “barber.” Therefore the Jews think that he was Nabal the Carmelite, who, when he was shearing his sheep, received David’s messengers with ingratitude (I Kings XXV).

These were Caleb’s sons. He now recapitulates Caleb’s descendants from Ephrath, which he had previously passed over when he related that Hur was born from Ephrath—that is, from Mary, Moses’ sister.

The sons of Hur, Ephrath’s firstborn, were: Shobal, father of Kiriath-jearim; Salma, father of Bethlehem; and Ariph, father of Beth-gader. Kiriath-jearim, Bethlehem, and Beth-gader are names of places and cities, called after their founders and possessors.

Kiriath-jearim, also called Kiriath-baal—that is, “city of forests”—is one of the cities of the Gibeonites, belonging to the tribe of Judah, nine miles from Diospolis on the road from Aelia. Bethlehem likewise is the city of David, in the territory of the tribe of Judah, where our Lord and Savior was born (Matt. II). It lies six miles from Aelia toward the southern region, beside the road leading to Hebron. There the tomb of Jesse and David is shown, and about a thousand paces away stands the tower of Eder, interpreted as “tower of the flock,” which once prophetically signified beforehand the shepherds who would know of the Lord’s birth.

The sons of Shobal, father of Kiriath-jearim, who saw half of the resting places, were from the clan of Kiriath-jearim: the Jethrites, the Aphuteites, the Shematites, and the Maserites. From these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.

I have read a twofold interpretation of this passage. Some say that Shobal, father of Kiriath-jearim, “saw half of the resting places,” that is, received the middle portion beside the tombs of the patriarchs, which were in Kiriath-arba. His sons were the Jethrites, Aphuteites, Shematites, and Maserites; from them came the Zorathites and Eshtaolites, who received the names of places—namely, Zorah and Eshtaol, where Samson was buried. They wished “resting place” to be understood as “tomb.”

Others assert that “half of the resting places” should be understood as half of a period: the half of the time during which the children of Israel began to possess the promised land. This means from the time when Moses gave the land of Gilead beyond the Jordan to Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh (Num. XXXII), until the time when the other tribes received their portions, Joshua dividing them by lot. They say that Shobal died in the middle of this period and thus saw half of the resting places—that is, reached the midpoint of that period.

Mystically, however, this Shobal, whose name is interpreted as “vain old age” or “garments for carrying,” signifies the Jews. In ancient times they were called the people, and they were the first to receive the Law, written by God himself on tablets of stone. They also carried the books of the Law and the prophets written in scrolls, but they were in no way able to understand the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, which resounded within them.

Therefore they saw half of the resting places, because they read only the history and did not deserve to recognize its mystery. One sees half of the resting places who observes the Sabbath of the Law in a carnal manner. But the one rejoices that he possesses the fullness of the resting places who, after the labor of good works, will receive the reward of eternal blessedness in the heavenly kingdom.

Thus the Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews about that ancient rest and introducing a verse from the Psalmist—“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV)—distinguishes this spiritual rest, which we believe you will receive in Christ, saying: “For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward have spoken of another day. Therefore a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. For whoever has entered his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his” (Heb. IV).

In another sense, one sees half of the resting places who, after the labor of the present life, feels rest only in the soul. But one contemplates the perfection of the resting places when, together with the soul’s immortality, he enjoys eternal life in the incorruption of the body. For now, before the day of judgment, according to the knowledge of the Apostle John (Rev. VI), the souls of the saints each receive a single robe. Then all God’s elect will be honored with two robes, and, perfected in both soul and body, they will deserve to rejoice without end in the eternal contemplation of God.

The sons of Salma were Bethlehem and the Netophathites, the crown of the house of Joab, and half of the resting place of Zorah. Thus the sons of Salma, son of Hur, also included the Netophathites. Concerning them, in the book of Kings, where it lists the mighty men who helped David reign over Israel, it is written:

“Asahel, brother of Joab, was among the Thirty, and Elhanan, son of his uncle, from Bethlehem.” A little later: “Heled, son of Baana the Netophathite” (II Kings XXIII).

They are written as the crown of the house of Joab because of the fellowship by which they used one another’s assistance in battle. What follows concerning Bethlehem and Netophah—that they were half of the resting place of Zorah—signifies that they possessed lands in the place called the tomb of Zorah. This place was mentioned above, because the Zorathites and Eshtaolites received the names of those places.

The clans of the scribes who dwelt at Jabez, singing and resounding, and living in tents. These are the Kenites, who came from the heat of the house of Rechab’s father. The Hebrews report that Jabez, son of Zobeda, of whom Scripture speaks later, was a teacher highly skilled in the Law of God. The sons of the Kenites, who is also called Hobab and was Moses’ kinsman, sat before him.

Thus they are called scribes in the book, and for this reason they are said to sing and resound, because they were constantly occupied with the Law of God and the reading of the prophets. The history of Kings also relates that they lived in tents. They are said to have come from the heat of the house of Rechab’s father because they were born from the stock of Rechab; the prophet Jeremiah also speaks of them in his book.

Mystically, however, whom could this Jabez, the teacher of scribes and singers, signify better than our Redeemer, who is the true teacher of holy teachers and of those who rightly sing praises to God? Jabez is interpreted as “drying up.” And who could better be called the one who dries up than that same Mediator between God and human beings, who through his Gospel and the grace of the Holy Spirit dried up and extinguished the flow of carnal desires in his faithful?

Through his aid the prophets were inspired, the apostles instructed, the evangelists educated, and all who rightly think and healthfully speak about God are called his pupils.

The Kenites—that is, “possession” or “those possessing”—signify all the elect who are in the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world. Concerning this Church the Lord himself says through the prophet Isaiah: “Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. XIX). Another prophet, speaking in the person of the Church, says to him: “The Lord is my portion, said my soul” (Lam. III). And the Psalmist says: “I said, Lord, you are my portion; I will keep your law” (Ps. CXVIII).

He possesses the Church because she is his bride and inheritance; he is possessed by her because her future reward in heaven will be the perpetual recompense of the saints.

These people are also said to have come from the heat of the house of Rechab’s father. Rechab is interpreted as “chariot” or “those who ascend,” because, inflamed and enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit from the Father of lights, they strive to ascend into heaven by the chariot of virtues, so that there they may be joined to their head, whose blood they acknowledge themselves to have been redeemed by.

Hence Truth himself says: “No one comes to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him” (John VI). And the Apostle says: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII).

The statement that the Kenites were remembered as living in tents signifies that all the faithful remain in the pilgrimage of the present life as though in tents. But when the present life has ended, they will rejoice that they have fully received in the heavenly homeland what they remembered seeking in their earthly pilgrimage.

## CHAPTER III. On David the king and his descendants through the succession of kings, up to and beyond the Babylonian captivity

(I Chron. III.) David had these sons, who were born to him in Hebron: Amnon, his firstborn by Ahinoam the Jezreelitess, and the rest.

He now returns to explain the genealogy that he previously left aside when he enumerated the offspring of Ram, son of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah. He reached Jesse and his seven sons, the youngest of whom was David. David had Amnon, his firstborn, by Ahinoam the Jezreelitess.

Jezreel is the place where Naboth lived, whom the impious Jezebel, wife of Ahab king of Israel, ordered killed (III Kings XXI).

The second was Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite, who had been the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. In the book of Kings, Daniel is called Chileab (II Kings III), which is interpreted as “judging the father.” The Hebrews think that he was given this name because, when disputing with Mephibosheth about questions of the Law, he appeared victorious and seemed in him to avenge his father, lest a warrior should be mocked in debate by a weak man.

David’s third son was Absalom, whom he had by Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital; and the sixth was Ithream, whom his wife Eglah bore to him (II Kings III).

The question arises: since David’s other wives have been mentioned above and are not called David’s wives, why is Eglah alone called David’s wife here? Eglah is Michal. She alone is called his wife here because he first obtained her as a wife in his youth, and she is also said to have died in childbirth.

Eglah is therefore interpreted as “heifer.” If anyone wishes to know the mystery of this name, let him recognize that the name “heifer” properly suits the synagogue of the Jews because of the yoke of the Law, which it had undertaken to bear but had corrupted through wantonness. Concerning it Hosea says: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I passed over the beauty of her neck” (Hos. X).

She married our David when he joined her to himself by giving her a covenant. But she died in childbirth, because when the incarnation of the Word of God appeared and the Gospel was preached in the world—when she ought to have borne offspring of good works through right faith—she was scandalized by his Passion and incurred the death of eternal condemnation.

Thus six sons were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months. He reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem. The following passage, where the whole period of David’s reign over Israel is enumerated, is written:

“David, son of Jesse, reigned over all Israel. The days during which he reigned over Israel were forty years. He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem” (I Chron. XXIX).

Hence a question arises: why, in the total of forty years of his reign, are the six months omitted? The Hebrews solve this in two ways. They say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months; therefore those same six months were rightly excluded from the total of his reign. They also give another explanation: that David suffered from an illness for six months while in Hebron, and for this reason those same six months were not counted in his reign.

They reckon him to have begun reigning in Hebron from the time when, after defeating the Amalekites, he sent gifts from their spoils to the elders of Judah—to those who were in Hebron, to those who were in Bethel, and to the others who were in the places where David himself and his men had sojourned (I Kings XXX).

[Col. 0297D] Moreover, in Jerusalem sons were born to him: Simmaa, Sobab, Nathan, and Solomon, four from Bathsheba, daughter of Ammiel; also Jebaar, Elisama, Eliphalet, Noge, Nepheg, and Japhia; and likewise Elisama, Eliada, and Eliphaleth, nine in all. These sons of David, except for two, are similarly enumerated in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 5). Noge and Eliphaleth, however, are not found numbered there.

But the fact that what was said above about David’s kingdom is distinguished and recounted in separate places should not be thought pointless. Rather, Holy Scripture, by counting the time of David’s reign, gathers separately the years during which he reigned in Hebron and separately those during which he ruled in Jerusalem over all Israel; it thereby suggests a venerable mystery.

Thus six sons of David [Col. 0298A] were born in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months. What, then, is signified by David’s reign in Hebron except Christ’s reign in the saints who existed from the beginning of the world until his coming in the flesh? It is plainly evident to all that David, whose name is interpreted as “strong-handed” or “desirable,” signifies Christ, because in his Passion he conquered the ruler of the world and appeared desirable to his disciples in the glory of his Resurrection.

Hebron, however, is interpreted as “marriage,” or, as others wish, “participation in sorrow,” or “fortitude.” The fathers of the Old Testament may rightly be designated by the name of marriage: some were deemed worthy to be joined to him through circumcision, some through the commandment, and some through the offering of sacrifices. To them, although in type and figure, he granted knowledge of their faith insofar as it seemed appropriate to them. Yet although they had been strong in belief, they could in no way be free from participation in sorrow, since they did not doubt that after death they would descend to the underworld.

Therefore, while our David reigned there for seven years and six months, on account of the Sabbath and the work of the six days—observances that in those times were held in especially high regard both in reading and in practice—six sons were born to him. These are those who strove with all their strength to lead a perfect life through good works and the keeping of God’s commandments.

Did he not belong to the company of the one who said, “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 72)? And again: “My soul clung after you; your right hand upheld me” (Psalm 62). Likewise another prophet says to the Lord himself: “Behold, this is our God. We waited for him, and he will save us; this is the Lord, we endured for him; we shall exult and rejoice in his salvation” (Isaiah 25). “Lord, we endured for you; your name and your memorial are the desire of the soul. My soul desired you in the night, and with my spirit within me, etc.” (Isaiah 26).

Hence, through Jeremiah, the Lord himself says to Judah: “I remembered you, taking pity on your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown. Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his harvest. All who devour him will be guilty; evils will come upon them, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 2).

[Col. 0298D] Moreover, David’s reign in Jerusalem, where he reigned over all Israel, signifies the time after the Lord’s Incarnation, Passion, and Ascension into heaven, when the Church of the Gentiles was to come to faith in Christ. Of this he himself says in the Gospel: “And I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

At that time he who is our peace made both one, and brought those who were far near in his blood. He destroyed the dividing wall of the enclosure, abolishing enmity in his flesh and annulling the law of commandments by decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new person, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the Cross, killing enmity in himself (Ephesians 2).

The number of years of David’s reign in Jerusalem was therefore thirty-three years. What is signified by the number thirty together with three except faith in the Holy Trinity with the fulfillment of the commandments? These, then, rightly belong to the kingdom of our David: those in whom faith is found not feigned but true, namely, the faith that works through love (Galatians 5).

And rightly are they said to dwell in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—because those abide in the vision of peace who do everything they understand, say, and do for the glory of God (Philippians 1) and for the attainment of eternal blessedness. Hence the Psalmist says: “Great peace have those who love your law, O Lord, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm 118).

The total number of David’s sons who were born to him in Jerusalem is therefore thirteen; in this, the mystery of faith and the commandments previously mentioned may be understood.

But what does it mean that these same sons are divided into four and nine? For it is written:

“Moreover, in Jerusalem sons were born to him: Simmaa, Sobab, Nathan, and Solomon, four from Bathsheba, daughter of Ammiel; also Jebaar, Elisama, Eliphaleth, Noge, Napheg, and Japhia; and likewise Elisama, Eliada, and Elipheleth, nine.”

Thus he first enumerates four born from Bathsheba and then the others in succession. What is signified by the number four in evangelical teaching except the four principal virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance?

These are said to have been born from Bathsheba, who was the daughter of Ammiel, because they are known to have arisen in the people of believers from the special grace of God. Bathsheba is interpreted as “daughter of seven,” or “daughter of fellowship,” or also “daughter of the oath”; Ammiel means “my people of God.”

According to the oath that the Lord swore to our fathers, he raised up from David a seed full of every virtue, “in whom all the nations of the earth would be blessed” (Genesis 22). Those nine sons who are subsequently enumerated belong to the same mystery, because in the number nine the number three is multiplied by itself.

And all who wish to become children of God, preserving in this present life the confession of the Holy Trinity in faith, hope, and love, strive to reach eternal vision and the fellowship of the holy angels through the perfection of good works.

According to the rule of moral interpretation, this distinction of the places and times of David’s reign can also be transferred to human mortality, so that here too the same mystery may be understood which the tradition of the holy fathers expressed in Jacob’s two wives, Leah and Rachel, and in Lazarus’s two sisters, Martha and Mary, who served while the Lord was dining in their house (John 12).

For what is expressed by Hebron except the labor of the active life, where the beginning of the kingdom is prepared but is completed only amid great weariness from cares? There, six sons of David are born during seven years, because the perfection of good works is offered to God through the activity of the faithful in the course of the present life.

And rightly this is called “participation in sorrow,” because the service that we extend through compassion to our needy neighbors cannot be fully accomplished without an admixture of pain. Hence the Lord answered Martha, who was occupied with frequent service, saying: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. Yet one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10).

[Col. 0300A] Moreover, David’s dwelling and kingdom in Jerusalem can very suitably, in the mystery, be applied to the beauty of the contemplative life. There he reigns over all Israel, and the greatest harmony among peoples is described, because, once all contradictions of unlawful pleasures have been subdued, the pure mind dwells with all the affections of the heart in divine contemplation.

In that vision of peace the soul rejoices, because it delightfully makes peace in the eternal sweetness of the joy to come. There thirteen sons of David are begotten, because the keeping of all the commandments, through faith in the Holy Trinity and in the sole love of the Creator, is brought forth by souls from the grace of Christ in a most salutary birth of fruitfulness.

All these were sons of David, apart from the sons of the concubines, and they had a sister, Tamar. All these sons of our David, who were born to him through the childbirth of the holy catholic Church, have a sister Tamar, whose name is interpreted as “palm,” because they await eternal recompense.

But the sons of the concubines are excluded. They were not worthy to be numbered among the other sons, because Jews, heretics, and schismatics could in no way possess a share in this fellowship, where the grace of the heavenly kingdom awaits only the noble sons of David, born from a noble marriage. For, as Scripture testifies, “the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Galatians 4). They are wild men remaining in the wilderness and wandering perpetually in uncertain settlements: “Their hand shall be against all, and the hand of all against them.”

The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, whose son Abijah begot Asa. From him was born Jehoshaphat, the father of Jehoram, and so forth. He counts David’s descendants through the succession of kings up to the Babylonian captivity, as the same order is attested in the Book of Kings.

The sons of Josiah were: Johanan, the firstborn; Joachim, the second; Zedekiah, the third; and Shallum, the fourth. From Joachim were born Jeconiah and Zedekiah.

Here Josiah is said to have had four sons. Yet at the end of this book (2 Chronicles 36), and likewise in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 23–24), where the succession of kings after Josiah is enumerated, no more than three are found: first Joahaz; second Eliakim, whom Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, called Joachim after changing his name; and third Zedekiah.

Johanan and Shallum are not recorded there. Hence the opinion of the Hebrews is that Johanan, the firstborn of Josiah’s sons, had two other names, namely Joahaz and Shallum. Thus we also find written in Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord concerning Shallum, son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father: He who went out from this place shall not return here again, but in the place to which I have transported him, there he shall die, and he shall not see this land again” (Jeremiah 22). For the name Shallum is interpreted as “transported.”

As for the statement that Jeconiah and Zedekiah were born from Joachim, Jeconiah is the same person who is called Joachim. After his father Joachim, he reigned in Jerusalem for three months and ten days (2 Chronicles 36).
