[Col. 0301A] But Joachim, his father, who was also called Eliakim, was bound in chains and taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldeans, together with part of the vessels of the Lord (Daniel 1). The prophet Ezekiel was also transported in that captivity while still a boy, as Josephus testifies, and likewise Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, as the beginning of the Book of the Prophet Daniel shows (Daniel 1).

Although some teachers assert that Ezekiel and Daniel and the three young men were transported together with Jeconiah, son of King Joachim, because the aforesaid King Nebuchadnezzar likewise transported this Jeconiah to Babylon with the other vessels of the house of God, the treasures of the royal house, the king’s mother, his eunuchs, the judges of the land, and all the mighty men of the army, ten thousand in number (2 Chronicles 36). In his place Mattaniah was appointed, namely Zedekiah, his uncle, the son of King Josiah, who was likewise later transported to the Chaldeans.

The sons of Jeconiah were: Asir, Shealtiel, Melchiram, Pedaiah, Senneser, and Jecamiah, Shema, and Nadabiah. From Pedaiah were born Zerubbabel and Shimei, and so forth.

Asir and Shealtiel are the names of one man, according to the Hebrews; and he himself is Pedaiah, the father of Zerubbabel and Shimei. Hence, in the Book of Ezra (1 Esdras 3) and in the Gospel of Matthew (Matthew 1), Zerubbabel is described as the son of Shealtiel.

Pedaiah is interpreted as “redeemed by the Lord,” Asir as “imprisoned,” and Shealtiel as “shoot of the Lord.” These names aptly suit the holy teachers, through whose study and ministry the ecclesiastical people are generated. Chastised by adverse afflictions, yet redeemed by the Lord’s grace, they strive healthfully to produce shoots of virtue both in themselves and in those subject to them.

Senneser, then, the son of Jeconiah, is the one who is called Sheshbazzar in Ezra; Cyrus entrusted the vessels of the house of the Lord to him (1 Esdras 1, 5). Senneser is interpreted as “formed,” while Sheshbazzar means “afflicted.”

These names also mystically suit the guardians of God’s vessels—that is, of holy souls—since our Lord, whom King Cyrus signified by his name and by the release of the captives, who is the heir of all things, rescues from Satan’s power those whom he predestined for eternal salvation and offers them to the priests of the Church to be reconciled through repentance.

And rightly Scripture says there that the vessels of Judah were counted under the authority of a chief, because “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2), and none of his sheep perishes (John 10) when they confess his great and terrible name (Psalm 110). For Judah is interpreted as “confession.”

The son of Shecaniah was Shemaiah, whose sons were Hattush, Jegaal, Bariah, Naariah, and Shaphat, six in number, and so forth.

How can he say that there were six sons when only five are found written, from Hattush to Shaphat? The Hebrews solve this question as follows. Shecaniah had one son, Shemaiah, who had five sons: Hattush, Jegaal, Bariah, Naariah, and Shaphat. These five, together with their father Shemaiah, who was his father’s only son, completed the number six.

[Col. 0302A] Hence Shecaniah is said to have had six sons, because the son and the grandsons are counted together.

## CHAPTER IV

The enumeration of the sons of Judah and those born from his sons; and concerning Jabez, who was illustrious among his brothers. Concerning Caleb and his sons Machir and the men of Rechah. Concerning the sons of Kenaz and those born from him. Concerning Shelah, son of Judah, and the family of the household of those who worked in fine linen; and concerning the potters who dwelt in plantations and settlements belonging to the king. Concerning the sons of Simeon and what was done through them; and concerning the sons of Gad.

**1 Chronicles 4.** The sons of Judah were Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.

How, then, are Perez, Hezron, and the other three who follow said to be sons of Judah, when elsewhere we read that Perez and Zerah were sons of Judah, while Hezron was the son of Perez?

The Hebrews assert that, with the names changed, the same sons of Judah whom Scripture mentions elsewhere under other names are expressed here. They say that Perez, whose name is interpreted as “division,” bears his proper name here. Hezron, however, is the same as Zerah, but Hezron is interpreted as “court,” while Zerah means “rising.” Carmi likewise is Hez, for Carmi is interpreted as “my only one,” while Hez means “watchful.”

They say that Hur is the same person who is called Onan in Genesis (Genesis 38). Hur is interpreted as “left,” while Onan means “murmuring.” Shobal likewise is the same as Shelah, the last of the three sons whom Judah’s wife, whose name was Shua, bore. Shobal is interpreted as “ear of grain” or “empty old age,” while Shelah means “sent” or “his shadow.”

Thus the prudent reader, who knows how to distinguish between the shadow of the Law and the truth of the Gospel, and what should be referred to the present Church and what to the future one, can easily understand what mystery lies hidden in this diversity of names.

Raiah, son of Shobal, begot Jahath, from whom Ahumai and Laad were born. These are the families of Sarath. This also is the clan of Etham: Jezreel, Ishmah, and Idbash, and so forth.

Shobal begot Raiah; Raiah begot Jahath; Jahath begot Ahumai and Laad; Laad begot Etham; Etham begot Jezreel, from whom the city took its name, in which Naboth dwelt (1 Kings 21).

As for what follows—“The name of their sister was Ashelphuni”—some suspect that she was the mother of Samson, born from the tribe of Judah. Her husband was Manoah from the tribe of Dan, and he is also said in the Book of Judges to have been from Saraba (Judges 13), just as it is written a little above here: “These are the families of Sarath.”

Phanuel, father of Gedor, and Ezer, father of Hushah: these were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, father of Bethlehem.

Phanuel and Ezer were brothers and sons of Hur, son of Caleb, the firstborn of Miriam, the sister of Moses and Aaron, whom Scripture calls Ephrathah under another name. Laad and Hushah, however, are names of places possessed by the sons of Hur mentioned above.

But it is surprising that Hur is here called the father of Bethlehem, when above Salma is written as having been its father—unless perhaps he calls the ancestor “father,” because Hur was the father of Salma, who was the father of Bethlehem.

Ashhur, father of Tekoa, had two wives: Helaah and Naarah.

[Col. 0303A] This Ashhur was the son of Hezron, born from another mother, as was shown above, and the brother of Caleb.

Naarah also bore Ozem, Hepher, Teman, and Haahashtari; these were the sons of Naarah. The sons of Helaah were Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan.

Koz begot Anub and Zobebah, and the family of Aharhel, son of Harum. Jabez was illustrious among his brothers.

The order of Scripture here seems confused. For after the sons of Helaah and Naarah have been enumerated, it suddenly introduces the family of Aharhel, son of Harum, and then proceeds to speak of Jabez.

The Hebrews explain this passage as follows: Ashhur begot Ethnan by his wife Helaah; Ethnan begot Koz; Koz begot Zobebah; and Zobebah begot Jabez, who was a teacher of scribes, as was shown above.

The reason that the family of Aharhel, son of Harum, is introduced between Koz and Jabez is that Aharhel himself is Obab, son of Aram—that is, Jethro, the kinsman of Moses. Since Jabez taught those who lived in tents, as was already said above, they are therefore introduced into his genealogy, as though they had been begotten by his ancestors.

The statement that Jabez was illustrious among his brothers mystically shows our Redeemer exalted above all the height of the saints by the power of his virtue. Of him the Prophet says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Psalm 44). And again: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

His mother called his name Jabez, saying, “Because I bore him in pain.”

Here we must not understand the mother to be the Virgin Mary, who, incorrupt and undefiled, bore the Lord our Savior for us without the pain of childbirth. Rather, we should understand the synagogue of the Jews, from which he deigned to receive flesh. She bore him in pain because, on account of unbelief, his coming brought her the greatest grief and anguish.

Thus, moved by jealousy of his good works, they plotted to kill him, saying, “The place and the nation” (John 11).

Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying: “If you will indeed bless me, enlarge my boundaries, your hand be with me, make me free from evil so that it does not oppress me,” and so forth.

This prayer aptly suits the spiritual Jabez, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world (John 10), who came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12), so that he might burn up and consume the sins of the human race. John pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

God therefore blessed this Jabez by multiplying his sons, whom the holy Church bears to him through the water of baptism. He enlarged his boundaries because he gave him the inheritance of all the nations (Psalm 2) and extended his possession to the ends of the earth.

The hand of the Lord was with him, because the power of the Godhead worked virtues and miracles through him. According to Paul, he is the power and wisdom of God, through whom all things in heaven and on earth were created (1 Corinthians 1; Colossians 1).

The malice of the envious could not harm him, nor did the devil have any dominion over him, because he found no sin in him. Hence he himself says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

These things therefore took place first in the Head. Through his gift, however, his members and body—which is the holy Church—will be blessed, for God has enlarged its boundaries to the ends of the earth.

Through Isaiah it is said to her: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your dwellings; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations and inhabit deserted cities” (Isaiah 54).

The hand of the Lord is with her, because the Son of God works in her; he is the arm and right hand of the Almighty. The malice of persecutors and heretics will not be able to oppress her, because the Truth himself foretold to his faithful servant, the apostle Peter, that the gates of hell would not prevail against her (Matthew 16).

Nor will the devil rule over her, because power was given her by the Lord to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Luke 10).

God therefore granted our Jabez everything for which he prayed, because he gave him all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28), so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2).

Caleb, brother of Shua, begot Mahir, who was the father of Eshton. Eshton begot Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, father of the city of Nahash.

Above we read that Caleb was the son of Hezron, whose brothers were Ram and Jerahmeel. The Hebrews therefore say that Ram, Caleb’s brother, is here called Sicha. Ram is interpreted as “exalted,” while Sicha means “humble.”

This can aptly express, by allegory, the type of the Jewish people. Once exalted in the worship of the one God and in royal power, because it refused to receive Christ when he came to it, it became humble and despised, in accordance with that Gospel parable which says that the first will be last and the last first (Matthew 20).

The Jews, who formerly were first under the Old Testament, are now last in the grace of the New Testament; while the peoples of the Gentiles, who were then last, are now first. Thus “the head has become the tail, and the tail the head” (Deuteronomy 28).

Caleb begot Mahir; Mahir begot Eshton; and Eshton begot Tehinnah. As for the statement that Tehinnah was the father of the city of Nahash, it may be understood either as Bethlehem or as the mother of Jesse, because Jesse is called Nahash, “serpent,” in another passage.

As for what follows—“These are the men of Rechah”—some understand David to be designated by the name Rechah. Rechah is interpreted as “tender.” Hence David says of himself: “I am tender and anointed king” (2 Samuel 23). In another passage he is described as tender, like a little worm of wood.

They are therefore called the men of Rechah because they were recorded here in order to express David’s genealogy.

The sons of Kenaz were Othniel and Seraiah. The sons of Othniel were Hathath and Meonothai. Meonothai begot Ophrah; Seraiah begot Joab, father of the Valley of Craftsmen, for there were craftsmen there, and so forth.

The sons of Kenaz were therefore Othniel and Seraiah. But Joab is said to have proceeded from Seraiah, and, according to the interpretation of his name, he is called the father of the Valley of Craftsmen because craftsmen for the building of the house of the Lord came from his sons.

According to allegory, the craftsmen who lived in the valleys can signify teachers of the Law—those whom knowledge does not puff up but love builds up (1 Corinthians 8). They especially devote themselves to humility and rightly preserve the rules of moderation. Such was Gamaliel, an honorable teacher of the Law, and his disciple, the apostle Paul (Acts 5 and 22), as well as others like them, whose words and examples are edifices of virtue.

The sons of Ezra were Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon.

Because this passage seems difficult, let us state what the Hebrews think of it, insofar as we have learned from their writings. They say that this Ezra, whose name is interpreted as “help,” is Amram himself, the father of Moses and Aaron.

Jether, interpreted as “remainder,” is Aaron; Mered, interpreted as “rebelling,” is Moses. Epher or Efer, whose name means “dust,” was Eldat. Jalon was Medat.

These two belonged to the number of the seventy elders whom Moses received from the Lord to assist in governing Israel itself (Exodus 24). They are also said to have prophesied in the camp when Moses, together with the others, had gone to the tabernacle before the Lord, as is read in the Book of Numbers (chapter 11).

For they relate that, after receiving the Law in the wilderness, Moses instructed his father to send away his mother because she was his aunt. She was the daughter of Levi. After separating from her, Amram took another wife, from whom he had these two sons, Eldat and Medat.

What follows is: “And he begot Miriam, and Shammai, and Jesbah, father of Eshtemoa. His wife also, the Jewess, bore Jared, father of Gedor, and Heber, father of Soco, and Jekuthiel, father of Zanoah.”

They wish Shammai to be understood as Moses, whose name is interpreted as “heavenly”; Jesbah as Aaron, whose name is interpreted as “praise”; and “father of Eshtemoa”—that is, “of abiding fire”—because the sons of Aaron used fire in their continual sacrifices.

They wish all the names that follow in succession to be understood as names of Moses, on account of his various deeds.

First is Jared, “descending,” because he descended from the mountain with the tablets of the Law. He is called father of Gedor, “hedge,” because he surrounded the people, as it were, with a hedge through the Law.

Heber, “binder,” is applied to him because he joined the people to the service of God. He is called father of Soco, “prophecy,” because he himself was often a teacher of prophets.

Jekuthiel means “hoping in the Lord,” and he is so named because he had hope of delivering the people from Egypt. He is called father of Zanoah, interpreted as “governor,” because he exercised great governance over the people in the wilderness—or because through his teaching he daily governs those who follow him.

After these names Scripture continues: “These were the sons of Bethiah, daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took.”

For this reason it calls Pharaoh’s daughter the mother of Moses in this passage. According to the proper meaning of her name, she is also called “daughter of the Lord,” namely because of the good will she had shown in raising the child. Mered is therefore said to have taken her after Moses because, having abandoned the worship of idols, she turned to the worship of the one God.

As for the earlier statement, “His wife, the Jewess, bore Jared,” they say that the Jewess was Jochebed, the mother of Moses and Aaron.

The sons of Shelah, son of Judah, were Er, father of Lecah, Laadah, father of Mareshah, and the families of the household of those who worked in fine linen [Col. 0306B] in the House of the Oath.

Also listed are the one who made the sun stand still, and the men of Falsehood, and Secure and Burning, who were chiefs in Moab, and those who returned to Lahem.

The name Er is placed here to preserve the memory of his former name, which belonged to the man whom the Lord killed on account of his wickedness (Genesis 38).

The families of the household of those who worked in fine linen in the House of the Oath are those who dwelt with Bezalel to complete the work of the tabernacle (Exodus 36). It is called the House of the Oath, as is the tabernacle of the covenant, because in it God made a covenant with humanity and confirmed the oath that he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

What follows—“the one who made the sun stand still”—returns to the offspring of Perez, from whom David arose. He judged it appropriate to bring the genealogy of Judah, from which the royal tribe arose, to its conclusion in David.

For they relate that this man was Elimelech, the husband of Naomi (Ruth 1), the father of Mahlon and Chilion. In his time the sun stood still because of transgressions of the Law, so that, when they saw so great a miracle, they might be converted to the Lord their God.

Because they refused to do this, famine consequently prevailed. He who had seemed foremost in the tribe of Judah was driven from his homeland by the want of famine, together with his wife and sons, and died with his sons in that same foreign land.

They say that the “men of Falsehood” were Mahlon and Chilion, who here are called Secure and Burning. They are said to have been chiefs in Moab because they took Moabite wives. In Hebrew this is expressed more precisely, as we have learned from scholars of that language: they are called not chiefs but husbands.

What follows—“those who returned to Lahem”—indicates Naomi and Ruth, who returned to Bethlehem, to bread, after the famine, when they heard of the abundance of bread in Bethlehem. And because this story is written in the Book of Ruth, it follows here. These, however, are the ancient words.

These were the potters who dwelt in plantations and enclosures near the king, engaged in his works; and they remained there.

He says that the descendants who came from Ruth dwelt individually in plantations and enclosures, because this planting reached royal dignity and the fortification of the people. “They remained there,” that is, in Bethlehem, near the king, engaged in his works, because King David arose from them, whose works are proclaimed with the highest praises.

Mystically, however, by these potters who labor in plantations and enclosures we understand none other than the holy teachers, who form and fashion the vessels of the Lord—for we call “forming” what we call “fashioning,” and therefore we call those who fashion clay potters.

These potters labor in plantations and enclosures because they cultivate the Lord’s vineyard by the word of faith, plant it through their teachings, and fortify it on every side through their exhortations and prayers. They remain near the king in his works because, abiding in the faith of Christ, everything they say and do they do for the glory of God.

The sons of Simeon were Jamuel and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul, and so forth.

The sons of Simeon are recorded as six in Genesis (Genesis 46), but here Sober is omitted because no descendants proceeded from him.

Some names are changed for particular reasons. In Genesis we read Jemuel, interpreted as “sea of God”; in Chronicles, however, it is Jamuel, “speaking with God.”

Another is called Ohad in Genesis, but Jarib in Chronicles. Ohad is interpreted as “praise,” while Jarib means “quarreling,” because from his descendants came Zimri, who sinned with a Midianite prostitute and was killed by Phinehas the priest.

In Genesis Lachim is written (ibid.), and it is interpreted as “preparation”; in Chronicles the same person is called Zerah, interpreted as “rising.”

Shaul is mentioned under the same name in both books, but here the text omits that he was the son of a Canaanite woman and, because of the closeness of his brother’s name, derives him from Zerah, whose name is interpreted as “beautiful rising.”

Their brothers did not have many sons, and the whole family could not equal the number of the sons of Judah.

It is clear that Simeon did not possess as much fertility of offspring as Judah. Hence in the Book of Joshua son of Nun (chapter 19) it is said that Simeon received an inheritance according to its families within the possession of the sons of Judah.

They dwelt in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, and so forth.

These cities belonged for the most part to the possession of the tribe of Judah. What follows, however, says:

“These were their cities until the reign of King David.”

This shows that Ziklag and Beersheba, which belonged to the tribe of Judah and had been seized by the tribe of Simeon, were restored by David to Judah’s former inheritance.

“And all their villages around these cities as far as Baal,” and so forth.

Baal is the very place that elsewhere is called Kiriath-baal, of which it was said above. What follows, however, says:

These are the named chiefs of their clans, and they were greatly increased in the houses of their alliances. They set out to enter Gador, toward the east of the valley, in order to seek pasture for their flocks. They found rich and very good pastures, and a broad, peaceful, and fertile land, in which people of the stock of Ham had formerly lived. These, whom we have described above by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and struck down their tents, [Col. 0308A] as well as the inhabitants who were found there, and destroyed them to the present day; and they dwelt in their place, because they found exceedingly rich pastures there.

After listing those whom they counted from the stock of Simeon and setting forth their deeds, the text signifies, according to the mystery, that the holy teachers, who are the leaders of the Church and who foresee pastures for Christ’s flocks, set out toward Gador, to the east of the valley, in order to seek suitable pasture there. And what is expressed by Gedor, which is interpreted as “his hedge,” except the holy Church, which is the protection and defense of faithful souls? There, therefore, are pastures toward the east of the valley—that is, up to the incarnation of the Word of God, of whom Paul says: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II). Whoever seeks pasture there will find it exceedingly rich, because the Truth itself says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out, and will find pasture” (John X). Everyone, therefore, who seeks the pastures of virtues will find them rich and very good there; and there the land is broad, peaceful, and fertile, because there the spiritual grace of God’s gift abounds most copiously.

But when it says, “in which people of the stock of Ham had formerly lived,” it signifies that a multitude of the nations had gathered there from the worship of idols, so that they might become worshipers of the one true God, since previously they had been servants of various vices. These came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah—that is, at the time of Christ’s coming. For he is the power of God the Father (I Cor. I), whom Hezekiah designates by his name; for Hezekiah is interpreted as “the strength of the Lord.” They struck down their tents and the inhabitants who were found there, and destroyed them to the present day. Each believer strikes down the tents of the impious and their inhabitants when, renouncing impiety and worldly desires (Tit. II), he is cleansed through Christ’s baptism from all the filth of sins, and thereafter strives by his grace to live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us in order to redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works (ibid.). Thus, therefore, what is written will come to pass: “And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God.”

From the sons of Simeon, five hundred men also went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Phaltias, Naaria, Raphaia, and Oziel, the sons of Jesi. They struck down the survivors of the Amalekites who had been able to escape, and dwelt there in their place to this day. What are the five hundred men meant to signify except the fathers of the New Testament? These went to Mount Seir and struck down the survivors of the Amalekites, because, trampling underfoot the pride of this world and crushing the deformity of vices, they suppress the remnants of evil spirits through the gift of the Holy Spirit. They are said to have been supported by four leaders, because, truly instructed in evangelical doctrine, they can fittingly wage spiritual warfare [Col. 0309A] against evil spirits. And it is appropriately said that they dwelt there after striking down the survivors of the Amalekites, because, once the wicked inhabitants had been expelled, they substituted an ordered succession of virtues in the place of vices; possession of these virtues makes a person blessed.

It is fittingly added, “to this day,” since this can be said for as long as the end of the world has not arrived. For the holy Church remains until the consummation of the age; in it spiritual warfare is waged daily against enemies, and victory over them is won daily.

## CHAPTER V. On the sons of Reuben and their deeds

**(I Par. V.)** The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: for he himself was his firstborn; but when he violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, the sons of Israel, and he was not reckoned as the firstborn.

The historical meaning is clear: Reuben’s birthright was taken away because he slept with Bilhah, the concubine of his father Jacob, and violated her (Gen. XXXVI). Hence the honor of the firstborn was transferred to Joseph, the younger son, whose descendants multiplied greatly and surpassed the other tribes in royal power among the ten tribes that were in Samaria.

Mystically, however, this demonstrates the fall of the former people, whose it was—according to what was owed to the firstborn—to receive the priesthood and the kingdom. But because he ascended the bed of God his Father and defiled his couch, when he seized and suspended on the cross the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested (Col. II), and stained it with iron, [Col. 0309C] for this reason the dignity of the firstborn was transferred to the spiritual Joseph, that is, to Christ and the people of the Church. To him the Father’s voice says in the psalm: “Before the morning star I begot you; you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Moreover, Judah, who was the strongest among his brothers, from his stock chiefs arose, and so forth.

Through the patriarch Judah, therefore, our Redeemer is represented, namely, the head of the Catholic Church. Hence it is written concerning him: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). He was the strongest among his brothers because God the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above all his companions (Ps. XLIV). From his stock chiefs arose—that is, the apostles and teachers of the New Testament. Concerning them the Prophet speaks to Christ himself in the psalm, saying: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them as princes over the whole earth” (ibid.).

In the same way, therefore, both the dignity of the firstborn and the principate of the kingdom belong to the mediator between God and human beings, because he is “the firstborn from the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth,” who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood (I Cor. XV; Col. I; Apoc. I).

The sons of Joel: Samaiah his son, Gog his son, Semei his son, Micha his son, Reia his son, Baal his son, Beera his son, whom Thelgathphalnasar, commander and king of the Assyrians, led captive. He was [Col. 0310A] chief in the tribe of Reuben, and so forth. Beera, the son of Baal, from the stock of Reuben, is said to have been the chief of the prophet Hosea, whom the king of the Assyrians led into captivity together with the ten tribes that were in Samaria.

In the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites and killed them. They dwelt in their tents throughout the whole region facing the east of Gilead. It should be noted that Hagar, from whom the Hagrites arose, was Keturah, whom Abraham married after Sarah’s death (Gen. XXV). For when the following passage says that the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh fought against the Hagrites, it goes on to say that the Itureans, the Naphishites, and Nodab provided them assistance; these were certainly sons of Ishmael. It should also be known that Nodab in Chronicles is called Kedmah in Genesis. Kedmah is interpreted as “of the ancient ones,” and Nodab as “womb.”

The Hagrites and all who had been with them were delivered into their hands, because they called upon the Lord while they were fighting; and he heard them, because they had trusted in him. As long as the children of Israel devoted themselves to divine worship according to the precepts of the Law, they had the Lord favorable to them, as helper and defender against their enemies. But when they abandoned him and established the worship of idols according to the custom of the nations, they immediately experienced him as an avenger, although previously they had possessed him as their protector. For when it says, “It was the Lord’s war,” it signifies that the battle was brought to an end with the destruction of the enemies by the Lord’s assistance.

[Col. 0310C] They dwelt in their place until the deportation. That is, until they were handed over to the Assyrians because of their sins.

And God stirred up the spirit of Pul, king of the Assyrians, and the spirit of Thelgathphalnasar, king of Assyria, and he deported Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. He led them to Lahela, Abor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.

It should be noted that in the book of Kings it is reported that Pul, king of the Assyrians, received a thousand talents of silver from Menahem, son of Gadi, king of Israel, so that he might assist him and strengthen his kingdom (IV Kings XV), but not that he deported him to Assyria. Likewise, in the same book it is read that Thelgathphalnasar, king of Assyria, in the days of Pekah, king of Israel, took Aion, Abel-beth-Maachah, Janoah, [Col. 0310D] Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and all Galilee, the whole land of Naphtali, and deported them to Assyria. Finally, it relates that Salmanasar, king of the Assyrians, besieged Samaria for three years, captured Hoshea, son of Elah, king of Israel, and deported Israel to Assyria; he placed them in Lahela and in Habor beside the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes (IV Kings XVII).

Hence the question arises: how is it written in Chronicles that Pul and Thelgathphalnasar, kings of the Assyrians, deported Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh and led them to Lahela, Habor, Ara, and the river Gozan, when Kings reports that King Salmanasar completed this action—that he deported Israel to Assyria and placed them in the aforementioned places? [Col. 0311A]

This question can be resolved as follows: the earlier kings of the Assyrians are said to have carried out this deportation because they themselves first began among the Assyrian people what that same people later sought to complete under subsequent kings. Chronicles, however, does not mention Aram, and Kings omits it. The Hebrews believe that this is the city of the Medes where Gabelus lived, from whom Tobias sought to recover the ten talents of silver entrusted to him (Tob. I, IV, IX).

## CHAPTER VI. On the sons of Levi and the singers whom David appointed to sing before the Lord’s ark; on Aaron and his sons

**(I Par. VI.)** Johanan begot Azariah; he is the one who exercised the priesthood in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem.

It is asked, since the sons of Levi were listed above through Aaron and his sons according to the succession of the priesthood, how, on reaching Azariah the son of Johanan, Scripture can say that he was the one who exercised the priesthood in the house that Solomon built in Jerusalem, when other priests likewise served in that house, concerning whom no such statement is made. He alone is therefore praised with this distinction because he resisted King Uzziah when he wished to offer sacrifice in the temple of God (II Par. XXVI), and because of his steadfastness of spirit and zeal for the Law he is plainly said to have fulfilled the priestly office.

Azariah begot Amariah, Amariah begot Ahitub, Ahitub begot Zadok, Zadok begot Shallum, Shallum begot Hilkiah, and Hilkiah begot [Col. 0311C] Azariah. Azariah begot Seraiah, and Seraiah begot Jehozadak. Jehozadak went forth when the Lord deported Judah and Jerusalem, and so forth.

Some say that Jehozadak was Ezra the priest, who, returning from Babylon together with Zerubbabel and the sons of Judah, restored the temple of the Lord and the city of Jerusalem. This seems to be demonstrated by the book of that same Ezra, where it says: “After these events, in the reign of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, Ezra son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub, son of Zerahiah, son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth, son of Zechariah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest from the beginning” (I Esd. VII), and so forth.

They also report that this same Ezra was the prophet Malachi, who is the last among the Twelve Prophets, because many things contained in his book are also recalled by this prophet, who says: “The priest’s lips shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

Others, however, assert that Jehozadak was the father of Jesus the high priest, whom the prophet Zechariah mentions in his book (Zech. III). They say that Ezra was a just priest, a man who enjoyed great glory among the multitude of the people in Babylon, and who returned from there with a very large crowd to Jerusalem in the time of King Artaxerxes.

The sons of Samuel: his firstborn was Vashni and Abiah. It should be noted that in the book of Kings Joel is named among Samuel’s sons (I Kings VIII), while the same person is written as Vashni in Chronicles. Since, therefore, Abiah, the son of Samuel, was appointed judge and was a receiver of gifts—as the Hebrews report—and this Joel, who is also Vashni, was the elder son, but, knowing this, did not rebuke him for it, both are said to have committed the sin.

For it is written: “And it came to pass, when Samuel grew old, that he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of the second was Abiah; they judged in Beersheba. But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside after avarice, accepted gifts, and perverted judgment. Therefore all the elders of Israel gathered together, came to Samuel at Ramah, and said to him: ‘Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint a king for us, to judge us as all the nations have’” (ibid.).

[Col. 0312B] These are the men whom David appointed as singers of the house of the Lord, from the time when the ark was placed there; they ministered before the tabernacle of the testimony, singing until Solomon built the house of the Lord in Jerusalem. They stood at their appointed place in the ministry.

These, then, are the men who served together with their sons. “From the sons of Kohath,” and so forth. Here, by anticipation, while recounting their genealogy, he gave a preliminary account of the duties of David’s singers, who sang praises with musical instruments; in its proper order it is shown how they performed those duties.

But when Heman the singer is said to be the son of Joel, the son of Samuel, and after his genealogy has been completed Asaph is said to be his brother, this does not refer to birth but to kinship. He is called a brother not because he was the son of the same father or mother, but in the manner in which we customarily call relatives brothers.

Ethan, son of Kishi, son of Abdi, son of Malluch, son of Hashabiah, son of Amaziah, son of Hilkiah, son of Amazai, son of Bani, son of Shemer, son of Mahli, son of Mushi, son of Merari, son of Levi.

This Ethan was one of the three singers who clashed bronze cymbals before David in praise of God. It should be noted that, just as Levi had three sons—Kohath, Gershon, and Merari—so these three singers traced their origin to the individual sons: Heman from Kohath, Asaph from Gershon, and Ethan from Merari, as the present history testifies.

Mystically, these three singers who sounded on bronze cymbals signify the holy teachers who, imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity, according to the arrangement of the true David, send forth throughout the whole world the mighty sound of evangelical preaching. Of them the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). And appropriately it adds:

Their brothers also, the Levites, who were appointed for the entire ministry of the tabernacle of the house of the Lord.

For the entire ecclesiastical order, according to the tradition of the apostles, who hold primacy among the holy teachers, performs the whole ministry of the tabernacle of the true God, which is the holy Church—the house, certainly, of the living God, built of living stones. Hence the teacher of the nations, instructing his disciple, says: “I write these things to you, hoping to come to you shortly. But if I delay, so that you may know how it is necessary for you to conduct yourself in the house of God, [Col. 0313A] which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth” (I Tim. III).

Aaron and his sons burned incense on the altar of burnt offering and on the altar of incense, carrying out every work of the holy of holies and praying for Israel, according to all that Moses, the servant of God, had commanded. These are the sons of Aaron: Eleazar his son, Phinehas his son, Abishua his son, Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son, Meraioth his son, Amariah his son, Ahitub his son, Zadok his son, Ahimaaz his son, and so forth.

I think that Aaron and his sons signify nothing more suitably than our Redeemer and the people of the Church, to whom Peter says in his Epistle: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition” [Col. 0313B] (I Pet. II). The supreme Pontiff himself, who, taking flesh from the seed of David, became a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX), instructed them to offer to God upon the altar of faith the burnt offering of good works and the incense of sacred prayer, and to pray for Israel—that is, for the state of the holy Church—according to all that Moses, the servant of God, commanded: namely, according to the precepts of the Law that was given through Moses.

The fact that Aaron’s genealogy is repeated and extends as far as Ahimaaz is thought to have been done for the praise and remembrance of Ahimaaz, because he acted faithfully toward David in all things.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Benjamites

**(I Par. VII.)** The sons of Uzzi: Izrahiah, from whom were born Michael, Obadiah, Joel, and Jesiah, five chiefs in all.

How does he say that Izrahiah had five sons, when only four are found? Unless perhaps Izrahiah himself, their father, is counted with them; he was the only son of his father Uzzi, according to the rule that we set forth above in another place.

The sons of Becher: Zamirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abiah, Anathoth, and Alemeth. Wherever it is written in the Law, “All these were the sons of” someone, this is done either because of excellence in merit or because of an ancient usage of speech, so that they are called the sons of the one whose imitators they were.

The sons of Balah: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, and Chenaanah. From the offspring of this Ehud, therefore, is said to have come the judge Ehud, who is read of in the book of Judges (Jud. III). This Chenaanah is the one from whom came the Benjamites who committed the outrage against the Levite’s wife, as it is written in Judges (Jud. XIX).

The sons of Naphtali: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shallum, the sons of Bilhah. This Bilhah was Jacob’s concubine (Gen. XXX) and Rachel’s maidservant. The sons of Naphtali are therefore called Bilhah’s, because Naphtali, from whom these men were descended, was Bilhah’s son.

Moreover, the son of Manasseh was Asriel; and his concubine Sirah bore Machir, the father of Gilead. The Hebrews assert that this Sirah was the daughter of a son of Balah. During a famine, her father had led her into Egypt to sell her; Manasseh, who was in charge of the storehouses, received her compassionately, gave food to her father, and then took her in marriage.

Machir took wives for his sons Huppim and Shuppim, and had a sister named Maacah. The name of the second was Zelophehad. And the daughters of Zelophehad were born, and so forth.

The order of the wording here appears confused, since it first gives the two names Huppim and Shuppim as sons of Machir, and then says, “The name of the second was Zelophehad,” who had daughters about whom we read in the book of Numbers (Num. XXVII) that they asked Moses for an inheritance among their brothers.

But the Hebrews explain this passage as follows: Huppim and Shuppim were the names of one man, namely, the first son of Machir; Zelophehad was his second son, and their sister was Maacah. Heron took her as his wife when he was sixty years old; she also bore him a son named Segub, as was shown above.

After enumerating the sons of Manasseh through Machir, the text adds:

These are the sons of Gilead and Machir, the son of Manasseh; his sister Regina bore a handsome man, and so forth.

Some report that this Regina, who was the sister of Ulam, the son of Perez, the son of Machir, as the history above shows, was the mother of Jesus the son of Nun, whom they call a handsome man because of his outstanding virtue and leadership. Others say that this same Regina was Deborah, the wife of Lapidoth, the prophetess (Jud. IV). But let whoever can discover certainty regarding this opinion speak.

The sons of Ephraim: Shuthelah, Bared his son, Tahath his son, Eladah his son, Tahath his son, and the son of Zabad, and his son Shuthelah, and his son Ezer and Elad. The men of Gath, natives of the land, killed them because they had gone down to seize their possessions. Ephraim their father mourned for many days, and his brothers came to console him, and so forth.

Concerning this chapter, the Hebrews devise the following story: they say that Ephraim’s sons Ezer and Elad, having gathered a multitude from Israel while their father was still alive, attempted to return to the promised land, but were killed by the men of Gath, a Philistine city. Hence the other tribes were later led through the wilderness, so that they would not see the bones of their brothers. Thus it is said in the psalm: “The sons of Ephraim turned back in the day of battle” (Ps. LXXVII).

The brothers who came to console Ephraim may either be understood as those who remained from the patriarchs, or as the kinship that we have often called by the fraternal name. After this, once the sons of Benjamin have been enumerated, the text adds:

## CHAPTER VIII. Again on the Benjamites; on the descendants of King Saul, who arose from that tribe

**(I Par. VIII.)** These are the sons of Ehud, chiefs of the clans dwelling in Geba, who were transferred to Manahath. Manahath is interpreted as “sepulcher.” They were therefore transferred to Manahath when they fell by the sword because of the crime committed against the Levite’s wife, and were nearly reduced to the last remnant, since no more than two hundred men remained from the whole tribe (Jud. XX).

But what follows—“Naaman, Ahiah, and Gera; he transferred them”—indicates that the first two, Naaman and Ahiah, were chiefs but nevertheless submitted to Gera. Hence they are described in the singular: “He transferred them.” From this Gera came the descendants of Gera, who was the father of Shimei.

Beraiah and Shema were chiefs of the clans dwelling in Aijalon; they drove out the inhabitants of Gath. Beraiah and Shema are said to have driven out the inhabitants of Gath because they avenged their brothers Ephraim, whom the men of Gath had struck down with the sword.

The sons of Ulam were mighty men, drawing the bow with great strength, and they had many sons and grandsons, up to one hundred and fifty. Here the number one hundred and fifty refers to the sons of Ulam, so that the meaning is: “The sons of Ulam were one hundred and fifty,” by the figure called hyperbaton.

## CHAPTER IX. Which of the children of Israel first lived in Jerusalem, and the offices of the priests and Levites; the genealogies of Saul and his sons are also repeated

**(I Par. IX.)** Thus all Israel was counted, and their number was written in the book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. They were transferred to Babylon because of their offense.

The children of Israel were therefore counted either under David, as Scripture reports, or under Solomon, or under some other king; nevertheless, because of their offense, they were transferred to Chaldea—partly by Thelgathphalnasar, partly by Salmanasar, and partly by Nebuchadnezzar—where many of them also perished [Note: [Col. 0315D] II Kings XXIV; I Par. XXI; IV Kings XV, XVII, XXV.]. But when it says:

The first to dwell in their possessions and in their cities were Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the Nathinim, and so forth.

It should be known that Nathinim is interpreted as “lords,” or “those who serve in humility.” They are the Gibeonites, whom Joshua spared in regard to their lives but assigned to the service of the temple, so that they might bring its water and wood (Josh. IX).

Azariah also, son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the high priest of the house of God, and so forth.

This is Hilkiah the high priest, who found the book of the Law—that is, Deuteronomy—in the temple of the Lord in the days of Josiah. He is said to have been the father of the prophet Jeremiah (IV Kings XXII).

Bacbakkar the carpenter, too, and Galal, and Mattaniah son of Micah, son of Zichri, son of Asaph; and Obadiah son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun; and Berechiah son of [Col. 0315D] Asa, son of Elkanah, who dwelt in the courts of Netophah, and so forth.

Bacbakkar is described as a carpenter because he practiced his craft in the house of the Lord; he was of the tribe of Levi. Berechiah was the son of Asaph, the son of Elkanah, who dwelt in the courts of Netophah. Netophah is the name of a place and is interpreted as “renowned.” Heled son of Baana lived there; concerning him it was said above: “Those who were the crowns of the house of Joab” (I Par. II).

Obadiah was the son of Shemaiah, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun, Jeduthun the singer of David.

They kept watch at the king’s gate toward the east, from the sons of Levi according to their divisions. They were singers who came together with David in their turns to sing the psalms, [Col. 0316A] because before the temple was built, the ark of the covenant was in the palace, and they served there.

Shallum, son of Korah, son of Abiasaph, son of Korah, together with his brothers and his father’s household (Num. XVI).

The first Korah is written with aleph and sounds like *Cora*. The second is written with he and sounds like *Core*. *Cora* is interpreted as “calling out,” and *Core* as “nail.” This is the one who is written of in Numbers as having rebelled against Moses.

But when it says:

These are the Korahites, assigned to the work of the ministry, guardians of the vestibules of the tabernacle,

it signifies that these men guarded the outer entrance of the tabernacle. Their fathers, however, who are written below and who have titles in the Psalter, guarded the inner entrance of the Lord’s tabernacle and were singers.

What follows also—

And their family heads, according to the divisions of the camp of the Lord, guarding the entrance—

refers by “camp” to the dwelling of the sons of Levi around the Lord’s tabernacle, as well as to the arrangement of the camps of the other children of Israel, just as it is most clearly described in Numbers (Num. II).

Phinehas, son of Eleazar, was their leader before the Lord, and so forth.

This shows that Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson—as the Hebrews report—was still living at that time and arranging the divisions of those who ministered in the tabernacle. These are the twenty-four divisions that are described below as having been organized by David for the service of the tabernacle. They are mentioned in the Gospel when Zechariah is said to have gone out by lot from the division of Abijah to offer incense in the temple of the Lord (Luke I).

[Col. 0316C] There were doorkeepers for the four winds—that is, toward the east, the west, the north, and the south. Their brothers lived in the villages and came on their Sabbaths from time to time. The entire number of gatekeepers was entrusted to these four watches. They were also over the chambers and treasuries of the house of the Lord. They lived around the temple of the Lord at their posts, so that, when the time came, they themselves might open the doors in the morning.

In the following passage, where the entire arrangement of the ministry of the Lord’s tabernacle established by David is recalled, it is shown that these four Levites were entrusted with the whole number of gatekeepers. It is written there as follows:

“Of Hosa, that is, of the sons of Merari, Semri was chief. [Col. 0316D] Because he had not had a firstborn, his father appointed him chief. Hilkiah was second, Tabeliah third, and Zechariah fourth. All these—the sons and brothers of Hosa—were thirteen. They were divided among the gatekeepers so that, as leaders of the watches, they might always minister in the house of the Lord, like their brothers. Lots were cast equally for small and great, by their families, for each of the gates. The eastern lot fell to Shelemiah. For Zechariah his son, a very prudent and learned man, the northern region fell by lot. Obed-edom and his sons received the south, where the council of the elders was located. Sephim and Hosa received the west, by the gate that leads to the road of ascent, watch corresponding to watch” (I Par. XXVI).

According to spiritual understanding, who are the four leaders of the gatekeepers except the holy teachers? Through the four Gospels they keep open the door of faith for believers and close it against blasphemers. With Peter, Christ entrusted them with the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XVI, XVIII; John XX). They guard the doors toward the four winds because, through the four regions of the world, they call every people to the faith of the Lord from all directions and preserve the holy Church with vigilant protection.

But what follows—

From their group were also those who were over the vessels of the ministry; for according to the number, vessels were both brought in and carried out by them, and those who had charge of the utensils of the sanctuary, and those who were over the fine flour, wine, oil, incense, and [Col. 0317B] spices—

refers, according to the historical sense, to the fact that from the assembly of the Levites men were appointed over the vessels of the ministry and the utensils of the sanctuary, to supervise the fine flour, wine, and oil that belonged to the sacrifices, as well as the incense and spices from which ointments and perfumes were prepared. This is described distinctly and separately in the book of Numbers (Num. III, IV): what the Kohathites, the Gershonites, and the Merarites had for their ministry, and what Aaron and his sons had under their particular care above the others.

Hence it adds:

The sons of the priests prepared ointments from the spices.

Mystically, from the assembly of holy preachers are appointed those who maintain vigilant custody over the vessels of the divine ministry—that is, over the souls of the faithful, in whom God’s will is administered daily. Under their care are also the fine flour, wine, and oil, in which the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood are prepared and the grace of the Holy Spirit is given through a special anointing. They also fittingly prepare the incense of sacred prayers and the spices of virtues in the Church of God, making them fragrant and rendering acceptable wine before God.

Mattathias the Levite, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was in charge of what was fried in the pan.

Who is signified by Mattathias, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, except our Redeemer, who is the firstborn of the dead and the prince of the kings of the earth (I Cor. XV; Col. I; Apoc. I)? The Father sanctified and sent him into the world (John X), so that through the suffering of the cross he might redeem the human race.

The meanings of the names themselves express this well. For Mattathias is interpreted as “house of God,” Shallum as “tearing away” or “release,” and Korah as “dissipating” or “destroying.” For almighty God, intending to dissipate and tear away the dominion of the devil, did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, so that, grinding his flesh in the millstone of suffering and frying it with the oil of mercy in the pan of the cross, he might free the guilty world from Satan’s power and from the bonds of sins.

Mattathias was in charge of what was fried in the pan because Christ is the author of the heavenly sacraments, in which bread and wine are offered daily in remembrance of his passion. He is also the head of all the saints, [Col. 0318A] who, instructed by his example, have learned to crucify their flesh and to surrender themselves to sufferings for his name (Gal. V).

Moreover, some of the sons of Kohath, their brothers, were in charge of the bread of the Presence, so that they might prepare fresh loaves every Sabbath, and so forth. For twelve loaves of the bread of the Presence were prepared, at the Lord’s command to Moses (Lev. 24), to be placed upon the table of the Lord, which stood in the tabernacle according to the ordinance of the law; there also stood the altar of incense and the lampstand of light. The loaves were baked, as Josephus writes, two by two before the Sabbath, and on Sabbath morning, after being offered, were placed upon the sacred table, six set opposite the other six, with two golden dishes full of incense placed upon them. They remained there until the following Sabbath, when other loaves were brought in their place. Those removed were presented to the priests, and after the incense had been burned in the sacred fire in which all the burnt offerings were made, other incense was added over the loaves.

Mystically, the twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle are the twelve apostles and all their followers in doctrine within the Church. When they continue, until the consummation of the age, to refresh the people of God with the nourishment of the word, the twenty loaves of the Presence never depart from the Lord’s table. And rightly these same loaves were made not from ordinary flour but from fine flour, because plainly whoever ministers the word of life to others must first apply himself to the fruits of virtue, so that what he urges by preaching he may commend by his conduct, being conformed to the example of the one who said of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone” (John 12).

And rightly the same loaves were commanded to be set upon the table six on each side, on account, namely, of the harmony of charity and fellowship. For the Lord is also said to have sent his disciples out two by two to preach (Mark 6; Luke 10), figurally indicating that holy teachers never differ from one another either in their assertion of the truth or in the affection of love.

But the incense placed over the loaves, exceedingly bright and pure, signifies the power of prayer, because those same teachers commend to the Lord both the ministry of their preaching and the devotion of their works. For that incense signifies prayer the Psalmist testifies when he says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” [Col. 0318D] (Ps. 140). The brightest incense is placed over the loaves as a memorial of the Lord’s offering, when pure prayer is added to the devout action and teaching of the saints, so that, through the proper joining of both, the memory of the sacred offering may always appear before the supreme Judge.

Rightly, moreover, the loaves are commanded to be changed before the Lord on every Sabbath. For the loaves that had been placed on the Lord’s table for the six days of labor are changed for new ones on the Sabbath, when each of the teachers of the holy Church, having completed the period of his holy labor, is rewarded in heaven and leaves others after him to labor at the same work of the word, under the same hope of reward. Thus it happens that the Lord’s table never remains without bread; rather, as soon as one loaf is removed, another is substituted in its place, while, through the ministers of the word succeeding one another in order, the apostolic Church never lacks those who display either the faith of devotion or purity of conduct in both word and deed.

And rightly it is said that members of the sons of Kohath were appointed over the bread of the Presence, because the patience of our Redeemer taught the apostles and preachers of the Gospel to make themselves and their people an acceptable offering through steadfast patience and the virtue of discernment. The Truth himself says to them in the Gospel: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21). For no teacher can properly carry out his office unless he has striven to adorn himself with the ornament of patience and discernment, so that he may be discerning in speech as well as in conduct, and strong when adversity arrives, if it must be endured.

Appropriately, it follows that the leaders of the singers, by the families of the Levites who dwelt in the chambers, served continually in their ministry day and night, and that the heads of the Levites remained leaders by families in Jerusalem, because it is most fitting that, the more someone is placed over others, the more devoted he should become in divine services. For the one preserves the primacy of his ministry who is intent on remaining in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—so that, by fleeing worldly turmoil and subduing the rebellious movement of his flesh, he may be able to keep a tranquil mind in contemplation of God, and thus properly sing with the Psalmist: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord. Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” [Col. 0319B] (Ps. 121). “Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem” [Col. 0319C] (Ps. 134).

In Gibeon dwelt the father of Gibeon, Jehiel, and the name of his wife was Maacah. His firstborn son was Abdon, and then Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, and Nadab. Jehiel is the same person who in the Book of Kings is called Abiel (1 Kings 9), the father of Kish, the father of Saul. Abiel is interpreted “my father is God,” whereas Jehiel means “deserted by God,” perhaps because of the difference in the merits indicated by their names. It should be noted that among the sons of Jehiel, Kish and Ner are called brothers, as they indeed are, and this is also found in the Book of Kings. Later, however, it is said that Ner begot Kish—not in the sense that he fathered him, but in the sense that he raised him; he is therefore said to have begotten him.

These dwelt opposite their brothers, in Jerusalem, with their brothers. The text reads “Loci” (sic): they are said to have dwelt in Jerusalem [Col. 0319D].

Ner begot Kish, and Kish begot Saul; and Saul begot Jonathan, Melchishua, Abinadab, and Ishbaal. The son of Jonathan was Meribbaal, and Meribbaal begot Micah. Abinadab, the son of Saul, is called Aminadab in the Book of Kings, where he is also said to have been killed with his father (1 Kings 31). Abinadab is interpreted “my father is a vow,” whereas Aminadab means “my people is a vow.” Ishbaal, likewise the son of Saul, is the same as Ishbosheth; and Meribbaal is the same as Mephibosheth. Meribbaal is interpreted “contending against the husband,” whereas Mephibosheth means “disgrace from the mouth.”

## CHAPTER X. The battle of the Philistines against Israel, and the death of King Saul and his sons

**(1 Chron. 10.)** The Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled from the Philistines, and the wounded fell on Mount Gilboa (1 Kings 31). When the Philistines had drawn near, pursuing Saul and his sons, they struck Jonathan, Abinadab, and Melchishua, the sons of Saul. The battle became heavy against Saul, and the archers found him and wounded him with arrows. Saul said to his armor-bearer: “Draw your sword and kill me, lest these uncircumcised men come and mock me.” But his armor-bearer, overcome with fear, refused to do this. Therefore Saul seized his sword and fell upon it. When his armor-bearer saw this—namely, that Saul was dead—he too fell upon his sword and died. Thus Saul and his three sons died, and his entire house fell together, and so forth.

Passing over the many things that the history in the Book of Samuel recounts concerning Samuel and Saul’s rule and deeds, the author of this book mentioned only Saul’s death and that of his sons, as well as the fall of his house, in order to signify secretly through mystery that it had not been necessary to describe the life of one whose sinful conduct did not deserve to receive an honorable end. It also signified figuratively the end of the Jewish kingdom and the ancient priesthood. Rather, by recalling the fall of the aforesaid king, the author turned entirely to David, in order to narrate his good deeds and his most noble administration of the kingdom. David bears the type of the true David, namely Christ the King, who was born from his offspring according to the flesh and possesses the kingdom of heaven and earth.

Accordingly, when it says that, as the time of David’s kingdom approached, the Philistines fought against Israel, as they had always been accustomed to do, and that the Israelites fled, it signifies that, as the time of the new grace drew near, the Gentiles, as they had formerly been accustomed to do, attacked the chastity of Israel’s faith through examples of depravity: at one time displaying perverse practices destined for destruction, at another the worship of idols, following the example of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to fornicate (Num. 25).

The children of Israel fled from the Philistines, and the wounded fell on Mount Gilboa [Col. 0320D]. Those who appeared strong in contemplating the will of God—which is what the name “Israel” signifies—were deceived when they followed too carelessly the works and teaching of the Gentiles. They perished, corrupted by the luxurious pride signified by the name of Mount Gilboa, that is, “slippery.” But secular wisdom also greatly aided the destruction of heretics. Hence one of our writers aptly said: “Philosophers, the patriarchs of heretics, stained the purity of the Church with perverse teaching.”

When the Philistines had drawn near, pursuing Saul and his sons, they struck Jonathan, Abinadab, and Melchishua, the sons of Saul. The surrounding Gentiles attacked with all their determination to destroy the kingdom of Judea and remove its sons from their midst [Col. 0321A]. Through their corruption they perverted the priests, scribes, and Pharisees, the sons—that is, the leaders—of that kingdom. They also hindered the heretics from preaching or worshiping the grace of the Holy Spirit with a simple heart. This is to strike Jonathan, that is, “the gift of a dove”: they prevented them from praising the Father, who made us his children not by nature but by adoption, with a worthy confession. This is signified by the slain Abinadab, that is, “of my willing father”: they opposed belief that salvation would come to the world in Christ’s kingdom. This is indicated by the slain Melchishua, whose name is said to mean “my king is salvation.”

I believe that the one who seduced Arius the philosopher killed Melchishua, as it were; the one who seduced Macedonius killed Jonathan; and the one who seduced Mani killed Abinadab, since the teacher of corruption instructed the first to deny the omnipotence of the true King Christ, the second to disparage the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the third to blaspheme the goodness of the supreme Father.

The battle became heavy against Saul, and the archers found him and wounded him with arrows. The Gentiles acted with all their strength to remove the kingdom of Judea. Men thoroughly trained in the deception of idols drew near to it, and the leaders of that kingdom were seduced and corrupted by those who, having seized the simplicity of truth from their hearts, inflicted upon them a many-sided wound of fraud and cunning. For just as an enemy sword indicates open persuasion toward idolatry and more serious crimes, so an arrow represents the arguments of subtler deceptions.

Saul did not perish by the sword of the Philistines but by their arrows, because the leaders of the Jewish kingdom did not perish with the kingdom through open crimes, which no one would doubt to be deadly, but rather through those that, under the appearance of piety, introduced the most impious poison of death. For example, when God said, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20), they instructed their hearers to say to their parents: “Whatever gift from me may benefit you” (Matt. 15), and thus to cease entirely from honoring them. Likewise they said: “Whoever swears by the temple is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound by his oath” (Matt. 23), and other things of this kind, which the Lord brings forth against them in the Gospel with manifold reproach—above all, the fact that they killed the Lord of the law and the Gospel himself as though he were a transgressor of the law.

When all these arguments of crime are produced with the admiration of Gentile cunning, as an intellect trained in philosophical studies is bent toward wicked arts, they fall, struck by the arrows of the Philistine archers. Nor is there any obstacle to understanding the archers as unclean spirits, through whose deceits those imbued with them perished.

Saul said to his armor-bearer: “Draw your sword and kill me, lest these uncircumcised men come and mock me.” Saul’s armor-bearer signifies the teachers of the law. For just as the weapons and arrows of the Philistines signify the deceptions of the wicked, so mystically the Israelites’ weapons are to be understood as nothing other than the spiritual words of teaching, by which the people of God ought to have been protected from every danger.

But Saul, wounded by the archers until evening, preferred to perish by the sword of his armor-bearer rather than by that of the uncircumcised, because the leaders of the Jewish kingdom, having once adopted the resolve to die in their sins, preferred to be destroyed by their teachers, who dissolved the commandments of the law and instructed them accordingly, rather than to perish through the fellowship of the Gentiles, whom they called common and unclean. Indeed, they feared to enter the praetorium of the Gentile, lest they be defiled, so that they might eat the Passover (John 18); yet they did not fear to defile that same Passover, turned to their own destruction, with innocent blood.

His armor-bearer refused to do this, overcome with fear. Therefore Saul seized his sword and fell upon it. When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell upon his sword and died [Col. 0322B]. The Hebrews say that his armor-bearer was Doeg the Edomite. Seeing Saul dead, Doeg killed himself out of fear of David. They also say that the young man who carried Saul’s diadem and bracelets to David was the son of that same Doeg the Edomite, and they report that Doeg himself had been Saul’s servant, accompanying him when he went to seek his father’s she-asses (1 Kings 6).

There is no doubt that among the reprobate teachers of the law there were some who would not willingly pervert the sharpness of the word through a sinister interpretation in order to kill their hearers. Nevertheless, those same hearers, whether by despising what they had received rightly from their teachers or—what is worse—by blaspheming it, turned it to their own destruction. When the teachers saw their spiritual death—that is, their persistence in sinning—the ministers of the word themselves, having deteriorated over time, made the testimonies of the law, which they had feared to interpret wrongly, an occasion of ruin for themselves by wrongly despising them.

Would that we did not know that these things also happen among us today! Heretics, too, wounded by the arrows of their sins and changing the words of the divine utterances into arguments for their own error, turn the weapons of their enemies against their own breasts as they hasten toward death. And any brother who remains within Catholic unity, when he has learned some skill for the common advantage of the Church and of those among whom he lives, but pollutes it with the contagion of pride, vainglory, love of money, or any other vice, pierces himself with his own sword. For what he ought to have used to defend against the enemy instead aids the enemy.

Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his whole house fell together [Col. 0322D]. He says that his house fell together, not in the sense that no one remained from it—for Mordecai was descended from it—but in the sense that it no longer reigned. Figuratively, he demonstrates that the Jewish people not only lost the kingdom but also the place of their possession: they do not merely fail to possess in the land of Canaan the land promised to them, but have been scattered among the nations of the whole world.

When the men of Israel who lived in the plains saw this, they fled. And when Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and scattered here and there. The Philistines came and dwelt in them. The unlearned, who had no knowledge of the true remedies of humility or of the bath of saving baptism, saw the learned and teachers of Judea defeated in spiritual combat, with sin triumphant. They also saw a considerable part of the common people, whose hearing had been small and limited, driven from the seat of their former steadfastness by the pursuing adversary. Shaken at once by the ruin of their elders, they too lost all the works of virtue and defenses of spiritual knowledge that they had possessed. Then the sins of the Gentiles came and, by their perverse occupation, corrupted all the pursuits of virtue among the unbelieving Jews. Unclean spirits came and occupied hearts that had abandoned the steadfastness of faith.

Or certainly, the Gentiles came and, by believing, made their own the excellent pursuits that had once belonged to the Jews. For they also caused the divine utterances—which the Jews had already begun, to a considerable extent, to abandon—to be interpreted for themselves; and when the Jews had rejected them, they received the faith of Christ together with those divine utterances of Holy Scripture, and, as though by inhabiting them, possessed them [Col. 0323B].

On the following day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his sons lying on Mount Gilboa. After stripping him and cutting off his head and removing his armor, they sent him throughout their land to be carried about and displayed in the temples of their idols and before the people. They consecrated his armor in the shrine of their god and fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.

Here a question arises, because it is written in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 31) that they hung Saul’s body on the wall of Bethshan, not that they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon. For they had already sent the head throughout the land of the Philistines, so that it might be announced in the temple of their idols and among the people. It could, however, have happened that the Philistines first fastened Saul’s head to Dagon, and afterward, carrying it away, sent it to be borne through various places of their land as a means of displaying their triumph.

The Hebrews also offer another explanation: they say that Bethshan was itself called the house of Dagon, interpreted “house of the sleeper,” and that Saul’s head or body was suspended there. For there is another Bethshan in Judges and Joshua, interpreted “house of security” (Josh. 17; Judg. 1).

Therefore, what else does it signify spiritually that they fastened the head of slain Saul in the temple of Dagon than that evil spirits plunge into the abyss of hell the soul that has fallen into pride and the death of sins, in punishment for its guilt? Dagon is interpreted “fish of sorrow” [Col. 0323D]; and rightly is he called the fish of sorrow who, plunged into the abyss of hell, experiences the pain of eternal torment.

The destroyers, whether human beings or demons, persecuted Judea with the weapons of impiety until they utterly removed the very foundation of the true kingdom and tore away the defenses of the sacred law by which it had prevailed against every adversity. As soon as they had cast it down, as a sign of their own triumph, they hastened to spread its downfall as a cause of joy among their accomplices far and wide, as rumor proclaimed it. To increase their crime, they attempted to introduce into the infernal shrines—that is, to equate with the doctrines of demons—the armor of God which the blessed apostle Paul commands us to put on as we wage war against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 6), and which he himself first put on, fighting the good fight, finishing the course, and keeping the faith, so as to receive from God the crown of righteousness (2 Tim. 4).

This, I say, the armor of the heavenly soldier, taken away from the Jews, the impious—both deceived and deceiving—attempted to bring into infernal dwellings, that is, to equate the divine utterances with the teachings of demons. It is clear that they did and do this in two ways: either, by interpreting spiritual sayings carnally, they understand them perversely, and, treating the same Scriptures as common writings unsupported by any heavenly authority, toss them about as they please; or else they openly set up the Jewish people themselves, deprived of the citadel of their kingdom, as though reduced to nothing and handed over to the power of their enemies, for their own mockery and as a public proverb.

Figuratively, this is the mutilated body of Saul, hung on the wall of Bethshan—that is, the house of the enemy—to be displayed by impious hands [Col. 0324B]. Heretics, too, when they deprive those who are laid low by the arrows of their previous sins of the protection of charity, which is the citadel of all virtues, cut off their heads like the unclean spirits cut off Saul’s head, persuading them to follow their own sense rather than that of Scripture. They strip away their armor when they turn the divine utterances toward their own—that is, demonic—meaning.

They place Saul’s armor in the temple of Astarte. For Astarte is not only an idol; since her name is interpreted as “creation of spies,” she also signifies the teaching of evil spirits, who prowl around the folds of the faithful, continually investigating whether they can devour anything from them. When they terribly convert the very works by which people had served God to the service of their own wickedness, they suspend the members of light, deprived of life, on the wall of the enemy’s house [Col. 0324C].

When the men of Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men rose up individually, took the corpses of Saul and his sons, brought them to Jabesh, and buried their bones beneath the oak that was in Jabesh.

Jabesh, interpreted “dried up,” signifies the Church, which the fervor of righteousness—the Sun, that is, the inspiration of divine love—restrains from every flow of carnal desire and every defilement of flesh and spirit. Hence such a Church is rightly described as set upon a mountain (Matt. 5). Gilead itself is also called “a heap of witness,” signifying that the most exalted life of the saints is fortified by suitable testimonies of Scripture so that it cannot be bent toward error.

This is the city that, at the beginning of his reign, when he was still serving the Lord with humble devotion, Saul liberated from the siege of enemies. When, therefore, the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard all that the Philistines had done to Saul, all the strongest men rose up, and so forth.

When the inhabitants of the city of Christ, set upon a mountain, heard this—namely, that Judea, from which they remembered that heralds and ministers of salvation had come to them in the patriarchs and apostles, had been despised by the Gentiles and made an object of mockery—they all rose up courageously for the work of the word. Walking themselves in the path of virtue amid the darkness of those who had gone astray, they prevented public rejoicing over the fall of those whose offense had brought salvation to the Gentiles, as though they belonged to the house of the devil.

“If the first portion is holy,” they say, “so is the whole lump. And if the root is holy, so are the branches. But if some of the branches have been broken off, while you, though a wild olive, have been grafted in among them and have become a sharer in the root and fatness of the olive, do not boast against the branches,” and so forth—the things that the Apostle set forth for the Romans in marvelous and manifold discourse (Rom. 11).
