The corpses, whether understood as fleshly people or as fleshly things, signify the stronger among them and the works of virtue. They buried the bones in the grove of Jabesh when, if they found anything of virtue or weakness among the weak, they preferred not to despise it as worthless but to join it to the fruitful works of the saints. If they recognized anyone among the carnal and fragile who was striving after the virtues of the soul, they took care to number him among the fellowship of the saints.

The fruit of good works is appropriately expressed by a grove. Anyone who reads in Genesis what kind of grove Abraham planted at Beersheba (Gen. 21) knows how to understand this rightly [Col. 0325B].

Moreover, because it is read in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 31) that the men of Jabesh burned the corpses of Saul and his sons, this demonstrates that holy men leave the weakness of the Jews’ fall to the judgment above, so that they may recognize that God acted or permitted these things according to the incomprehensible counsel of his will, in keeping with the height of the riches of his wisdom and knowledge (Rom. 11). In this passage we should understand the burning according to the command given concerning the reception and investigation of the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, under the figure of eating the lamb: “If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. 12).

They fasted for seven days. Literally, it is rightly customary to fast for the dead for seven days, so that they may reach rest, because after the six ages of this world, in which we labor in the flesh, the seventh is that second age of rest for souls divested of the flesh. In it, that glorious time is awaited in blessedness, when we may deserve to rise again. The seventh day under the law (Exod. 20), and the seventh or fiftieth year (Lev. 25), in which rest from works was granted, figuratively foreshadowed this pattern of rest and resurrection.

The Lord himself displayed the example of our hope and faith through his dispensation: crucified on the sixth day of the Sabbath, resting bodily in the tomb on the seventh, and on the eighth—which is also the first day of the week—rising again. Thus the faithful who are fellow citizens and kinsmen of those who still observe the fleshly manner rightly retain sadness and continual grief in their hearts, fasting, as it were, for seven days, because, while their brothers and relatives remain established in error, they cannot possess complete joy. But when those others too have perfectly understood the mystery of the eighth day—that is, of the Lord’s Resurrection and their own—both groups, with the grace of Christ’s help, will rejoice together in perpetual festivity.

Finally, the burial of Saul and his sons by the men of Jabesh-gilead can also be understood in another way according to the moral sense. The fact that the men of Jabesh-gilead buried the corpses of Saul and his sons signifies tropologically that holy men detest the death of the wicked and consign their examples to the burial of oblivion. They do not wish to set them before themselves for imitation. They fast for seven days because they spend the whole period of this life—which proceeds through the number seven, according to the days of the week—in continence and abstain from every evil work, lest they perhaps be killed by a similar death.

Thus Saul died because of his iniquities, because he transgressed the Lord’s commandment, which the Lord had given, and did not keep it (1 Kings 15); moreover, he consulted a woman with a pythonic spirit (1 Kings 28) and did not hope in the Lord. Therefore God killed him and transferred his kingdom to David, the son of Jesse.

Saul’s death aptly expresses the destruction of the Jewish kingdom, as was said above. Because they repeatedly transgressed God’s commandments, and because of the idolatry that they worshiped after abandoning God, they lost both life and kingdom at once. The kingdom was transferred to David, the son of Jesse—that is, to Christ and the Christian people [Col. 0326B].

## CHAPTER XI. The conquest of the Jebusites by David, who dwell in Jebus, that is, Jerusalem

**(2 Chron. 11.)** All Israel gathered to David at Hebron, saying: “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh; yesterday and the day before, when Saul was still king, you were the one who led Israel out and brought it in. For the Lord your God said to you: ‘You shall feed my people Israel, and you shall be their prince.’”

All the elders of Israel therefore came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them before the Lord; and they anointed him king over Israel according to the word of the Lord, which he spoke through Samuel (1 Kings 16).

What does this gathering of the tribes of Israel to David signify except the gathering of all the Gentiles to Christ? They say to him, as though flattering him: “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh,” when they love and venerate the incarnation that he assumed from our nature in the Virgin’s womb, desire to submit themselves to his authority, and long to serve him at all times. Hence the Psalmist says: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his sight, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule the nations” (Ps. 21).

The elders of Israel also came to the king at Hebron when the prophets and apostles gathered to our Mediator in one faith and with equal devotion. Of them it is written: “The princes of the people gathered together with the God of Abraham” [Col. 0326D] (Ps. 46). And elsewhere: “In the sight of his servants he will be glorified” (Ps. 106).

It is fittingly said that David made a covenant with the Israelites before the Lord, and that they anointed him king over Israel. This signifies that, once the Gospel had been established, Christ entered mystically into a covenant with the faithful, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning the observance of God’s commandments and the reward to come.

They anointed him King over all Israel because all believers share one confession, one religion, and one certain conviction: under the rule of Jesus Christ they carry on spiritual warfare at all times, awaiting his future coming on the day of judgment, when he will come in the clouds with great power and majesty to judge the living and the dead (Luke 21), and to render to each according to his works (Matt. 16).

David and all Israel also went to Jerusalem—which is Jebus, where the Jebusites, inhabitants of the land, were dwelling—and those who lived in Jebus said to David: “You shall not enter here.” But David captured the fortress of Zion, which is the city of David, and said: “Whoever strikes the Jebusite first shall be prince and commander.” Joab, the son of Zeruiah, went up first and became commander. David dwelt in the fortress; therefore it was called the city of David, and so forth.

Josephus, in the seventh book of his Antiquities, reports this as follows:

“David rose up and came with everyone to Jerusalem. The Jebusites inhabited the city; they were of the race of the Canaanites. They closed their gates against him and set upon the wall, for the king’s mockery, the blind, the lame, and all the lepers, saying that the blind would prevent him from entering the city. They did these things because they despised him, trusting greatly in the strength of their walls.

“The king became angry and began to besiege Jerusalem, striving with great zeal and labor to capture it, so that at the very beginning of his rule he might demonstrate his strength. He therefore threatened both them and any others who might perhaps have the desire to resist him, and with great force captured the lower city.

“Since he was still unable to take the citadel, the king began, by promising honors and gifts, to urge soldiers through them to undertake the military task, so that whoever climbed the intervening hills into the citadel and captured it would possess command over the entire people’s army. Since everyone hastened to climb and no one delayed out of concern for the promised reward, Joab, the son of Zeruiah, outstripped them all. Having climbed to the summit, he shouted to the king and demanded command of the army.

“The king then expelled the Jebusites from the upper citadel, rebuilt the city, and called it Jerusalem. He dwelt there throughout the entire period of his reign.”

Mystically, David’s expulsion from Jerusalem of the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land, signifies that our Redeemer expels hostile powers from the hearts of the faithful and thus establishes his dwelling there. For Jebusite is interpreted “trodden underfoot,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.”

Our Lord not only acquired a trophy for himself through the mystery of the cross by destroying every principality of the devil; he also granted his faithful power over every force of that ancient enemy. Hence he says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

Therefore it is rightly written in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 5) that David, after expelling the blind and the lame who hated David’s soul, captured the fortress of Zion and called it his city. For when our Savior has expelled evil spirits together with the host of vices from any soul and has claimed it for himself through the illumination of wisdom, it will rightly be called the fortress of Zion—that is, of contemplation and the vision of peace. Then the Psalmist rightly says of it: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel. His place has become established in peace, and his dwelling is in Zion; there he broke the horns, the shield, the sword, and the battle” [Col. 0328A] (Ps. 75).

The statement that he built the city of David all around, from Millo to the surrounding circuit, while Joab demolished the rest of the city, demonstrates that David fortified the city of Jerusalem with walls both through his own industry and through the skill of his devoted soldier.

I have read in someone’s book that Joab did not build the rest of the city but “drew it out,” meaning that, when the Jebusites were perishing by the sword, any Israelites who had been found among them were saved by Joab. Josephus, however, relates that David fortified the upper city, joined the citadel to it, made one continuous body on every side, and surrounded the whole with a wall. He appointed Joab over the work of the walls, and David expelled the Jebusites and called the city Jerusalem.

For under the patriarch Abraham it was called Solyma. Some say that Homer later also called it Jerusalem. For *Hieron* in the Hebrew language means “fortification.”

Mystically, the fact that David built the city all around signifies that Christ first preached the Gospel in Judea and strengthened his Church by surrounding it on every side with the fortification of his faith. The fact that Joab rebuilt the rest of the city signifies that, after the Lord’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven, the apostles and preachers of the Gospel converted many of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ through their teaching, so that they might be fellow workers with the truth and, according to their measure, build God’s spiritual edifice with devoted mind and strenuous action of devotion.

Hence Paul, writing to certain believers, says: “We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s cultivated field; you are God’s building,” and so forth (1 Cor. 3).

These are the chiefs of David’s mighty men who helped him become king over all Israel, according to the word of the Lord spoken to Israel. And this is the number of David’s warriors: Jesbaam son of Achamoni, chief among the Thirty; he lifted his spear against three hundred slain at one time. Josephus calls this Jesbaam “Eusebius” and says that he was the son of Achimaas, who, repeatedly breaking into the enemy line, never ceased fighting until he had killed nine hundred of them.

But the Hebrew whose statements I have included in some places in the exposition of Kings, and have inserted not a few times in the present work, wants this Jesbaam to be understood as David himself. He interprets the name Jesbaam as “sitting among the people,” and Achamoni as “most wise.” He maintains that this is demonstrated in the Book of Kings, where it is written: “Sitting in the seat, most wise” (II Kings XXIII). But he says that he was compared to the worm of a tree because his wisdom was diminished on account of the sin he committed against Uriah (II Kings XI). Similarly, he reports that this signifies what is narrated in the Book of Kings (II Kings XXIII): that he killed eight hundred at a single assault, whereas here in Chronicles it says that he killed three hundred—his reputation being reduced because of the aforementioned sin of adultery and murder.

[Col. 0329A] After him came Eleazar, son of his paternal uncle, Aboites, who was among the mighty. For Aboi, as the Hebrews relate, was the brother of Eleazar, who was the most powerful among the Three. Josephus says that these were Eusebius son of Achimaas, Eleazar son of Doli, and Semeias son of Eli.

Now three of the chiefs among the Thirty came down to the rock where David was, at the cave of Odollam, when the Philistines had encamped in the Valley of Rephaim. David was then in the stronghold, while the Philistines’ garrison was at Bethlehem. David therefore desired water and said: “Oh, if someone would give me water from the cistern of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!” So these three went through the middle of the Philistine camp, drew water from the cistern of Bethlehem that was by the gate, and [Col. 0329B] brought it to David for him to drink. But he refused, and instead poured it out as a libation to the Lord, saying: “Far be it from me, in the presence of my God, to do this and drink the blood of these men, for they brought it at the risk of their lives.” For this reason he refused to drink it, and so forth.

The Hebrews assert that David did this not so much because he thirsted for water, but also to test whether such brave men could be found among his followers who would dare this deed. But when water had been brought to him by them at such great danger to human life, he was unwilling to drink it; rather, he chose to sacrifice it to God, giving him thanks for having granted Israel such courageous men.

Mystically, however, David thirsted not for the water that is in Bethlehem, but foresaw in the spirit Christ, who was to arise from the Virgin in that same Bethlehem. [Col. 0329C] Therefore he wanted to drink not the water of a stream, but the bath flowing from Christ’s side. That is, David did not thirst for the element of water, but for the blood of Christ. Hence he did not drink the water offered to him, but poured it out to the Lord, signifying that he thirsted for Christ’s sacrifice, not for a natural stream: that sacrifice in which there is forgiveness of sins; that eternal fountain for which no one seeks through the dangers of others, but which would erase the dangers of others.

According to the tropological sense, we must consider with the greatest care that anyone who remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this he may make satisfaction to his Creator. One who has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted, censuring himself in small matters because he remembers having sinned in great ones.

The Law of the Old Testament certainly forbids coveting another man’s wife, but it does not punishably forbid a king to command brave deeds of his soldiers or to desire water. And we all know that, pierced through by the sword of covetousness, David both desired and took another man’s wife; worthy blows followed upon his guilt, and through the lamentation of repentance he corrected the evil he had committed (II Kings XI). Later, when he was sitting far behind the enemy lines, he desired to drink water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers broke through the middle of the hostile ranks and brought him, unharmed, the water he had desired. But the man educated by scourges immediately reproached himself for having desired the water at the risk of his soldiers, and, pouring it out to the Lord, offered it as a libation, as it is written there: “He poured it out as a libation to the Lord” [Col. 0330A] (II Kings XXIII). For the water poured out was transformed into a sacrifice to the Lord, because through the repentance of his self-reproach he slaughtered the guilt of covetousness. Thus the man who once had no fear of coveting another’s wife afterward abstained even from what was lawful, namely, from water.

Abisai, the brother of Joab, was himself chief of the Three. He too lifted his spear against three hundred slain. He was the most renowned of the Three, the second distinguished among the Three, and their chief. Nevertheless, he did not attain to the first three. From this it appears that Abisai was the most renowned chief among the three wise men. But he did not reach the first three mentioned above, namely Jesbaam, Eleazar, and Sennua, whose most courageous deeds he narrated earlier.

Allegorically, [Col. 0330B] this statement shows that no saint, although he may excel among his own people through the excellence of his virtues, nevertheless reaches equality with the power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “For who among the clouds shall be made equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God? God, who is glorified in the council of the saints, great and terrible above all who surround him,” and so forth (Psalm LXXXVIII).

Banaiah, son of Joiada, a very powerful man, had performed many deeds at Cabseel. He struck down two “Ariels” of Moab, and he went down and killed a lion in the middle of a cistern during a time of snow. He also struck an Egyptian man whose height was five cubits and who had a spear like a weaver’s beam. He went down [Col. 0330C] against him with a staff, snatched away the spear that he held in his hand, and killed him with his own spear, and so forth.

The fact that the Book of Kings says of Banaiah (II Kings XXIII) that he struck two lions of Moab, while Chronicles calls them two Ariels of Moab, has one and the same meaning. These very powerful men were therefore in the kingdom of Moab; hence they are called “Ariels of Moab,” for Ariel means “lion of God.” Banaiah killed them after they had challenged him and he had overcome them.

As for what is said of Banaiah—“He went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern in the days of snow”—Josephus explains more fully how it happened. The cistern was evidently exceedingly deep. In winter, when everything was filled with snow, it too had been leveled by a great accumulation of snow. When a lion, unaware of the danger, came upon it and fell in, trapped there, it cried out with a great roar. People ran to see what had happened. When Banaiah came with the others to witness the spectacle, he leapt down into the cistern, immediately attacked the lion amid the snow, struck it, and killed it.

Snow, therefore, may figuratively signify now the warmth of innocence and grace, now winter and the coldness of charity. What we read here, and likewise in the Books of Kings—that a certain Banaiah from among the strong men of Israel went down into a cistern and struck a lion in a time of snow—I think the snow is placed in those passages without distinction, because both the grace of Christ, which shone forth in this world, and the coldness of the love of God, by which human beings have grown cold, may be signified under the name of snow.

We understand Banaiah figuratively as the Savior, who, according to the force of his name, means “the Lord is the builder.” Of him the Prophet had prophesied that the Church would be built through him, saying: “The Lord builds Jerusalem” (Psalm CXLVI). Likewise: “The Lord has built Zion” (Psalm CI). Scripture used this word with its proper meaning in the creation of Eve, who bore the type of the Church, saying: “And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman” (Genesis II). And Paul, seeing that it was being built, says: “You are God’s building” (I Corinthians III).

And it is rightly said that Banaiah performed many deeds, because our Banaiah continues to work even now. He is the creator of all things with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and in the Gospel he says of himself: “My Father is working until now, and I am working. Whatever he does, the Son likewise does” (John V).

He is said to be from Cabseel, that is, from the “assembly of God,” because the whole congregation of the saints belongs to him, and he is the head of the body, the Church (Colossians I). He went down and killed the lion in the middle of the cistern in a time of snow because, descending from heaven to earth and becoming human, he killed the lion, the devil, who possessed the world lying numb in the cold of unbelief, and by his death thrust him down into the depths of hell.

He struck the Egyptian man whose height was five cubits, going down against him with a staff, snatching away the spear he held in his hand, and killing him with his own spear. For, by the staff of his cross, he overcame Antichrist, most hideous through the blackness of sins, who abuses the bodily senses to commit crimes, and he condemned the guilty one to perpetual punishment by his own wickedness. [Col. 0331C]

Nor should we pass over the fact that the Hebrew mentioned above thinks that this lion whom Banaiah killed should be understood as Joab, because he was killed in the middle of a cistern—that is, in the house of the Lord, where he was holding the horns of the altar (III Kings II). Therefore the altar is called a cistern, because just as a cistern supplies water, so also the Lord’s sanctuary expiated sins. It was “in the days of snow” because through death he expiated sin, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Psalm L).

Furthermore, concerning what is subsequently narrated—“He also killed the Egyptian man,” whom the Book of Kings calls “a man worthy of spectacle” (II Kings XXIII)—he thinks that this Egyptian man was Semei son of Gera, who cursed David (II Kings XVI). It should be known, however, that this same Semei was from Baurim, that is, from “the chosen,” and that he was therefore called an Egyptian because he imitated the deeds of that Egyptian who blasphemed the Lord and whom Moses, at the Lord’s command, killed in the wilderness (Leviticus XXIV). That man blasphemed the Lord, while this one cursed the prophet and king.

And he is rightly called “worthy of spectacle.” He was being watched so that, if he went out from Jerusalem, he would be killed. He had a spear in his hand, that is, the law of God; if he had meditated upon it by remaining in Jerusalem, he would not have been killed. Because he made the king’s command void by leaving Jerusalem, Banaiah therefore descended against him with a staff—that is, with the uprightness of justice—and the spear, which he was no longer holding correctly, was forcibly taken from him.

“These things,” it says, “Banaiah son of Joiada did. He was the most renowned among the three mighty men and first among the Thirty. Nevertheless, he did not reach the Three.” This is understood to mean that he deserved to be named among the three mighty men—Jabisai, Subachai, and Jonathan—since he could equal them in strength. According to the Hebrews, these three also stood above the Thirty.

What follows is this:

“David placed him in his own ear,” showing that through intimacy and trust he wanted him to be privy to his secrets.

Having enumerated through these passages David’s stronger men who helped him reign over Israel, Scripture adds, saying:

## CHAPTER XII

Concerning the coming of the children of Israel to David at Hebron, to establish him as king over Israel. A catalogue of David’s mighty men who helped him become king over all Israel. Concerning the coming of the children of Gad, Benjamin, and Judah to David. Concerning those who defected to him from Manasseh while David was at Ziklag; concerning Joiada, chief of the stock of Aaron; and concerning the children of Issachar, who offered assistance to David.

*(I Chronicles XII.)* These also came to David at Ziklag while he was still fleeing from Saul son of Kish. They were very powerful and distinguished warriors, drawing the bow, throwing stones with slings with either hand, aiming arrows, and so forth.

Historically, this demonstrates that they were agile and energetic for every military action. Allegorically, however, it signifies that the spiritual soldiers of Christ must not be sluggish but zealous, and that they ought to become strong and prudent in both prosperous and adverse circumstances. Thus, according to the Apostle, walking along the royal road, they should fight in sincere love, in the word of truth, and in the power of God, with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, as deceivers yet truthful, and so forth (II Corinthians VI).

Men from Gad also defected to David while he was hiding in the wilderness: very powerful men and excellent warriors, holding shield and spear. Their faces were like the faces of lions, and they were swift like gazelles on the mountains, and so forth.

“From Gad,” he says—that is, from the tribe of Gad—very powerful men fled to David at the time when he was hiding in the wilderness while fleeing from Saul. He compares them to lions because of their courage of mind, and to gazelles because of the clarity of their perception or the agility of their bodies.

Mystically, he teaches us who have professed the warfare of Christ not to be children, wavering in our thoughts, but stable and immovable, abounding in the work of the Lord, providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings, seeing how carefully we should walk—not as foolish but as wise—so that, whether we eat or drink or do anything else, we may do all things for the glory of God (I Corinthians XIV; I Corinthians XV; II Corinthians VIII; Ephesians V; I Corinthians X).

These were chiefs of the army from the children of Gad. The least was in command of one hundred soldiers, and the greatest of one thousand. These are the men who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it is accustomed to overflow its banks; and they put to flight all who lived in the valleys, toward the eastern and western regions, and so forth.

After describing the chiefs who defected from the tribe of Gad to David, the writer of the history immediately added: “The least was in command of one hundred soldiers, and the greatest of one thousand.”

This, unless I am mistaken, can be transferred to the mystery, because the chief of the Lord’s army—that is, any Catholic teacher—although he might be called “least” because of his practice of humility, nevertheless is rightly placed over one hundred soldiers who, in the camp of the Church, perform the service of Christ with humble devotion, because he strives for perfection in the virtues.

“And the greatest of one thousand.” The one may be called greatest who, supported by the protection of knowledge, diligently undertakes the labor of preaching with good examples, confirming in action what he teaches in words. For this reason he will appear worthy of eternal blessedness, which is signified by the number one thousand.

For the angel, speaking to the Prophet in Daniel’s vision, seems to distinguish these matters in this way, saying among other things: “Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament; and those who instruct many in righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Daniel X).

Blessed Jerome explains this statement in his commentary on Daniel as follows:

> “Teachers will have the likeness of the heavens; and those who instruct others will be compared with the radiance of the stars. For it is not enough to know wisdom unless you also instruct others; and one who does not build up another by the silent speech of teaching cannot receive a reward while idle.”

Theodotion likewise rendered this passage as follows:

> “And those who understand shall shine like the splendor of the firmament; and, having overcome many, like those who are forever and beyond.”

Some people are accustomed to ask whether a learned saint and a simple saint receive the same reward and have one dwelling in heaven (John XVIII). Hence, according to Theodotion, it now says that the learned possess the likeness of the heavens, while men without learning are compared with the radiance of the stars. The difference between learned holiness and holy simplicity is therefore as great as the distance between heaven and the stars.

For this reason the Apostle Paul, writing to his disciple, says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine” (I Timothy V). And to the Thessalonians he says: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize them and to be at peace with them” (I Thessalonians V).

“These are the men,” he says, “who crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it is accustomed to overflow its banks.” What is signified by the river Jordan, in which the Lord was baptized, if not the water of baptism? The holy teachers therefore crossed the Jordan in the first month, when it is accustomed to overflow its banks, because when the Son of God appeared in the flesh and consecrated that year which the prophet Isaiah had foretold would be acceptable to the Lord (Isaiah LXI), immediately after he consecrated the sacrament of baptism by his own baptism, they spread the gift of that sacrament throughout the whole world by preaching and baptizing most abundantly.

“And they put to flight all who lived in the valleys toward the eastern and western regions.” This means that all who were found—whether from the Jews, whom the eastern region signifies because of the rising of legal knowledge, or from the Gentiles, whom the western climate expresses because of the setting of natural prudence, which they had betrayed by worshiping idols—taking pleasure in worldly matters and secular desires, and unwilling to ascend to the stronghold of virtue and the summit of wisdom, fled before the preaching of the Gospel, because they could in no way resist the divine Majesty. Hence the Prophet says to the Lord in the person of the Savior: “You have given me the back of my enemies, and you have destroyed those who hate me” (Psalm XVII). And Jeremiah says: “He who troubles the sea, and its waves roar—the Lord of hosts is his name” (Jeremiah XXXI).

Men also came from Benjamin and Judah to the stronghold where David was. David went out to meet them and said: “If you have come to me in peace, to help me, let my heart be joined to you. But if you are lying in wait for me on behalf of my adversaries, although I have no iniquity in my hands, may the God of our fathers see and judge.”

Then the Spirit of the Lord clothed Abisai, chief among the Thirty, and he said: “We are yours, O David, and with you, son of Jesse. Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers. For your God helps you.”

So David received them and appointed them chiefs of companies.

What is signified by the soldiers who came to David from the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, whom he himself, after testing their faith, appointed chiefs over the companies, if not teachers of the Jews and the Gentiles?

Paul, who arose from the tribe of Benjamin, testifies concerning them in his Epistle, saying: “Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should preach the word of God among the Gentiles, and they among the circumcised” (Galatians II).

These men, therefore, coming to our Redeemer, were tested by knowledge of all who worshiped him, in accordance with the strength of their faith. Hence there is the passage in which the Lord, questioning his disciples in the Gospel about whom people said that he was, and having heard from them the various opinions of men concerning him, finally asked for their own faith, saying: “But who do you say that I am?”

Our Abisai, namely the Apostle Peter, answered for them all, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Jesus answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI).

In this way, therefore, for the praise of their faith, not only Peter but also the other apostles and the remaining holy teachers were rewarded, because, according to the statement of the man David, they were appointed chiefs over all the earth and have authority to bind and loose as the cause of justice dictates to them.

In another place the Truth itself, arranging its preachers, says to them in the Gospel: “Amen I say to you: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVIII).

And after the resurrection he appeared and breathed upon them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX).

Blessed, therefore, is the person who preserves unharmed until the end of life the gift he has received through God’s grace, guarding it with humility, so that when the heavenly master comes according to his promise, and finds him acting in this way, he may set him over all his goods (Matthew XXIV).

When he had therefore returned to Ziklag, the following men defected to him from Manasseh: Ednas, Josabaad, Jedihel, Michael, Josabad, Eliu, and Salathi, chiefs of the soldiers in Manasseh. These men provided David assistance against the raiders, and so forth.

These men who came from Manasseh to David began to come at the time when David had decided, as the history shows, to go into battle with the Philistines against Saul (I Kings XXIX). But when he was sent back by the Philistines and returned to Ziklag, he found that his wives had been carried away captive by the Amalekites and that the city had been burned, as the Book of Kings relates (I Kings XXX). Then these men came and provided David assistance against the raiders who had plundered the wives of David and of those who were with him, as well as their sons and daughters.

Mystically, these seven chiefs who came from Manasseh signify the first teachers of the Church from Judea. Enlightened by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, they provided assistance to our David against the raiders—that is, against the Hebrews, heretics, and also evil spirits, who always strive to seize by deceit whoever they can and hand them over to the captivity of error and vices.

One of these chosen men was also the one who, writing to the disciples, said: “We are God’s helpers. You are God’s agriculture. You are God’s building” (I Corinthians III). “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place” (II Corinthians II).

And there is also what follows: “For every day they came to David to assist him, until a great number was formed, like the army of God.”

Although the Hebrews say, according to the historical sense, that the number of those who came to David’s aid increased until it reached the number of armed men who came out of Egypt—that is, six hundred thousand, whom Moses led through the Red Sea into the wilderness (Exodus XIV)—nevertheless, in a higher understanding, this signifies that the number of the faithful grows daily in the army of our David, until the full number of God’s elect, who have been predestined to eternal life, is completed: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans VIII).

Furthermore, what follows—

“This also is the number of the chiefs of the army who came to David when he was in Hebron, to transfer the kingdom of Saul to him, according to the word of the Lord”—

is appropriately applied to this mystery, because holy teachers, that is, faithful disciples, chiefly desire and strive with all their strength that the historical worship of the ancient Law be transferred into the spiritual understanding of the Gospel, so that the old things may pass away and all things become new (II Corinthians V).

Joiada also, chief from the stock of Aaron, and with him three thousand seven hundred. Sadoc too, a young man of excellent character, and his father’s household, twenty-two chiefs.

The Hebrews relate that this Joiada, chief from the stock of Aaron, was Phinehas son of Eleazar. He is called a young man in comparison with him because he was so in age and merit. When it says that chiefs came with him, this signifies that the number of priests who had been appointed in the house of Sadoc—that is, in the house of Levi—according to the precepts of the Law, was present.

From the sons of Issachar came two hundred chiefs, learned men who knew the individual times and what Israel ought to do. All the remaining tribes followed their counsel.

They relate that the teachers of the Law were from the tribe of Issachar. They were learned men who knew how to distinguish the individual times according to the Law. They were the teachers of the Law, the calculators of times, and the masters who determined the appropriate celebration of festivals and observed the other ceremonies of the Law.

Hence it was said in the blessings with which Jacob blessed each of his sons: “Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant to tribute” (Genesis XLIX).

Mystically, Issachar, whose name means “reward,” refers to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is written as a strong donkey because formerly the people of the Gentiles were like a brutish and lustful animal, existing without any reason. Now, however, it is strong: it subjects the hidden things of the mind to our Savior and, bowing its neck to the dominion of the Redeemer, bears the yoke of evangelical discipline.

This one lies down between the boundaries. For to lie down is to await rest at the end of the world, seeking nothing of the things now present in the midst of time, but desiring the final things. And the strong donkey saw rest and an excellent land, because the simple Gentile people raise themselves to the strength of good works for this reason: that they are journeying toward the homeland of eternal life.

Therefore it also places its shoulder beneath the burden, because, desiring to reach the promised rest, it willingly bears all the burdens of the commandments. Hence it became a servant to tribute—that is, by offering to its king and Christ the gifts of faith and good works.

Or it serves tribute when it presents the ministry of the word to devoted hearers, to whom it owes the Lord’s talent, which it must hand over for multiplication through the increase of good works. Hence Paul says of his preaching: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans I).

And elsewhere: “For if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory to me, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That, preaching the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel without charge, so that I may not abuse my authority in the Gospel. For although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might gain the more. To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to those under the Law, as though I were under the Law—although I myself was not under the Law—that I might gain those under the Law; to those without the Law, as though I were without the Law—although I was not without the law of God but under the law of Christ—that I might gain those without the Law. I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak. I became all things to all, that I might save all. And I do everything for the sake of the Gospel, that I may become a participant in it” (I Corinthians IX).

Behold, this spiritual merchant shows that he pays tribute not to one person but to many, because by preaching the word of faith to Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of Christ, and by good examples, he adapted himself to all in such a way that he pleased all, benefited all, and induced each person, in the character of a servant, to offer obedience to him eagerly.

Hence it follows:

“All the rest of the tribes followed their counsel.”

For it is just that all the faithful should not refuse to obey the holy teachers in the Gospel of Christ. Hence also, after those who came to David from each tribe have been enumerated, it is added:

“All these men were warriors and ready for battle; they came to Hebron with a perfect heart to make David king over all Israel. And all the rest of Israel were of one heart, that David should become king.”

The apostles and apostolic men come together to our David and are joined to him in a special marriage. All the rest—both from the Jews and from the Gentile people—desire with one heart and equal devotion, and strive with all their strength, that David may become king, so that they themselves may become the kingdom of Christ, to whom the Truth itself says: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

They were there with David for three days, eating and drinking what their brothers from Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali had prepared for them, and so forth.

For at all times those who hold the faith of the Holy Trinity remain in the same devotion, so that they may joyfully receive as nourishment what the first teachers—that is, the apostles—provided them from divine doctrines, and may continually give thanks with rejoicing to the giver of all for the good things they have received.

## CHAPTER XIII

Concerning the fact that David consulted with the tribunes, centurions, and all the chiefs, so that, after gathering a multitude of priests and Levites, they might bring the ark of the Lord back to him from the house of Abinadab. Concerning Uzzah the Levite, who was driving the cart and stretched out his hand to support the ark lest it fall, and was struck by the Lord because he touched it presumptuously. When David saw this, he was astonished and turned the ark aside into the house of Obededom [Col. 0337D] the Gittite, where it remained for three months.

*(I Chronicles XIII.)* David consulted with the tribunes, centurions, and all the chiefs, and said to the whole assembly of Israel: “If it pleases you and if the word I speak comes forth from the Lord our God, let us send to our remaining brothers in all the regions of Israel, and to the priests and Levites who live in the suburbs of the cities, that they may gather to us and that we may bring back to ourselves the ark of our God. For we did not seek it in the days of Saul.”

The whole multitude agreed that it should be done, for the word pleased all the people.

What does it mean that David consulted with the tribunes, centurions, and all the chiefs of Israel in order that, after gathering the multitude, he might transfer the ark of God from the hill of Cariathiarim to himself, if not that our Redeemer, together with the apostles, prophets, and evangelists, arranged how the faith of his incarnation should be transferred from the former people to the salvation of the Gentiles through the words of the Law and the Prophets, with the teachers of the Gospel ministering?

This is what it means to transfer the ark of God from the hill of Cariathiarim, which is “envy” and is interpreted as “city of forests,” to himself: namely, to bring the faith of the Lord from the eminence of the Scriptures placed among the Jews, where the abundant shadow of many figures is found, to the understanding of the Gentile people, where the Church of Christ is founded.

And it is rightly written that David said they had not sought it in the days of Saul. For, while the condition of the Synagogue continued during the times of the Old Testament, they did not seek the ark of the Lord, so to speak, because the spiritual sense hidden in the letter could not be brought forth openly for the people by the Synagogue, as it was revealed under the grace of the New Testament to those who believed in Christ.

Hence the Apostle Paul glories in his Epistle: “According to the revelation, the mystery was made known to me in the mystery of Christ, which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are coheirs, members of the same body, and participants in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the eternal purpose which he made in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Ephesians III).

When this plan pleased everyone, David gathered all Israel from Shihor of Egypt as far as one enters Hamath, in order to bring the ark of God from Cariathiarim. [Col. 0338C]

Shihor of Egypt is a river, as they say, that has been diverted. Concerning it, it is written in Jeremiah: “What have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Shihor?” (Jeremiah II). For this reason the interpreters have rendered it “turbid water,” because Shihor is interpreted as “new firmament” or “turbid” (Amos VI).

Hamath is a city of Damascus, which the king of the Assyrians conquered. In Amos it is also written as “Hamath-rabbah,” which in our language sounds like “great Hamath.” It is now also called Epiphany.

Finally, through these two names, Shihor and Hamath, the whole Promised Land is encompassed, from which all Israel was gathered to David. Through Shihor—that is, the stream or torrent of Egypt—the southern part of the land is designated; and through Hamath, the northern part.

David and all the men of Israel went up to the hill of Kiriath-jearim [Col. 0338D], which is in Judah, to bring from there the ark of the Lord God, who sits above the cherubim, where his name had been invoked. They placed the ark on a new cart from the house of Abinadab. Uzzah and his brothers were driving the cart. David and all Israel, meanwhile, were celebrating before the Lord with all their strength, with songs, lyres, psalteries, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets.

He says, “David and all the men of Israel went up to the hill of Kiriath-jearim, which is in Judah, to bring from there the ark of the Lord.” Here I do not think that the Writer means by “all the men of Israel” every male who had reached manhood, but rather that he intends the more distinguished and noble men. The number of the men who gathered for this purpose appears to be given in the Book of Kings [Col. 0339A], where it is written: “David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand,” and so forth (2 Kings 6).

Kiriath-jearim, therefore, which elsewhere is called Kiriath-arba, “city of forests,” is one of the cities of the Gibeonites, belonging to the tribe of Judah, for travelers going from Aelia to Diospolis in the ninth mile. Uriah the prophet was from this place; Jehoiakim killed him in Jerusalem, as Jeremiah writes (Jer. 26). The son of Shobal was also called Kiriath-jearim, as was shown earlier in the present book.

When they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah stretched out his hand to support the ark. For an unruly ox had tilted it slightly. So the Lord became angry against Uzzah and struck him because he had touched the ark, and he died there before the Lord. David was grieved because the Lord had divided Uzzah, and he called that place “the division of Uzzah,” down to the present day.

It should be noted that in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 6), where this place is mentioned, it is called not the threshing floor of Chidon but the threshing floor of Nacon. Aquila interprets *Nacon* as “prepared threshing floor.” *Chidon*, however, means “shield.” It is reported that this was the place where Joshua stood when he was told: “Raise the shield against the city of Ai” (Josh. 8).

As for what is written about Uzzah—that the Lord struck him because he touched the ark, and that David was grieved because the Lord had struck Uzzah—the Hebrews report that Abinadab the priest ordered his two sons, Uzzah and Ahio, to carry the ark of the Lord on their shoulders, according to the command of the Law. But because they neither carried it themselves nor gave it to the people of Kiriath to carry, Uzzah was punished by death. There was sin in the transgression of the commandment, but the punishment for the sin had already appeared when they supported the ark after placing it on a cart. Therefore he was struck.

“The striking of Uzzah” is said to consist in this: his arm and shoulder, where the ark of the Lord ought to have been carried, became withered; and a certain distinction was made at that place—that is, a division between obedience and disobedience.

Then David feared the Lord at that time, saying: “How can I bring the ark of the Lord to myself?” For this reason he did not bring it to himself—that is, into the city of David—but turned it aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. The ark of God remained in the house of Obed-edom for three [Col. 0339D] months. And the Lord blessed his household and everything that he possessed.

David therefore turned the ark of the Lord into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite because Obed-edom himself was a Levite, and because David did not yet know why God’s indignation had come upon Uzzah. But after he learned the reason for which Uzzah had been struck, he ordered that the ark be carried on the shoulders of the Levites, as is shown below.

Thus, in the history of the blessed king and prophet David, in which he is said to have brought the ark, humility is approved, pride condemned, and rashness punished. David himself, who was not ashamed to dance humbly before the Lord (2 Kings 6), soon became worthy to receive the promise of the Son of God who was to be born from his line (2 Kings 7); but his wife, who despised that same humility in him, was not found worthy to bear children from his seed and suffered the punishment of perpetual barrenness.

The priest, too, who touched the ark with thoughtless rashness, purged the guilt of his presumption by an untimely death. Here it is necessary to consider how great is the offense of one who approaches the body of the Lord while guilty, if that devout priest was punished by death who seized the ark—that is, the figure of the Lord’s body (1 Cor. 11)—with less reverence than he ought to have shown.

In allegorical terms, however, David signifies Christ, and the ark signifies the Church. David sought to bring the ark into his own city; but when an opposing circumstance intervened, he turned it aside elsewhere for a time, and thereafter completed what had greatly pleased him. For the Lord, appearing in the flesh, preached the Gospel to the children of Israel, that is, to his own people. But a partial blindness came upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles entered, and thus all Israel would be saved (Rom. 11).

To make these matters clearer, let us examine them one by one. David therefore gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, as it is written in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 6), because the Lord established the primitive Church from Israel—not all Israel, but associating with himself those who were especially chosen. “For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel,” but the children of the promise are counted as descendants (Rom. 9).

They are reported to have numbered thirty thousand, that is, to have been perfected in the steadfastness of faith, works, and hope. Three belongs to faith because of the confession of the Holy Trinity; ten belongs to works because of the Decalogue of the Law; and one thousand belongs to hope because of its perfection in eternal life, above which there is nothing, just as no number is greater than a thousand [Col. 0340C].

For even if you say ten thousand, thirty thousand, or even a thousand thousand, you do not go beyond the number one thousand itself by counting; rather, you multiply it, either by itself or by repeatedly multiplying through smaller numbers. Therefore multiply three by ten, so that faith may not be dead without works. Likewise multiply thirty by one thousand, so that faith, which works through love (Gal. 5), may hope for its reward nowhere but in heaven.

The chosen people from Israel therefore signify those who rightly believe, work, and hope. The men of Judah who were with David signify the apostles and teachers, who clung more intimately to Christ’s side as his companions. Supported by this twofold army, the Lord rejoices to bring the ark—that is, to enlarge the Church—and to implant it in the hearts of those who did not believe [Col. 0340D].

The ark is placed on a new cart so that the grace of the New Testament may be poured into minds renewed in baptism, and so that new wine may be entrusted to be preserved in new wineskins (Matt. 9).

Previously the ark had been in the house of Abinadab, which was in Gibeah, because the faith of the Church that is now preached also flourished before the time of the Lord’s incarnation among those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs and prophets. Abinadab, whose name is interpreted as “My father is willing,” signifies either Abraham, the father of faith, or Moses, the lawgiver. Each of them guards the ark in Gibeah, because by the lofty example of his virtue he fortifies the breasts of believers.

Hence Gibeah is interpreted as “hill”; it is the place in the city of Kiriath-jearim. Once the ark had been brought outside, David and all Israel celebrated before the Lord [Col. 0341A] with various kinds of musical instruments. For as soon as the proclamation of the new grace began, the Lord invited all people to offer praises to God the Father in humility, saying: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12). To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, to another gifts of healing, and so forth (1 Cor. 12).

As the ark advanced—that is, as the primitive Church grew—the historical account in the Book of Kings (2 Kings 6) says that they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, that is, to the prepared threshing floor, namely, the Church of the Gentiles, to be consecrated by the truth of faith. John says of it: “He will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor.” Or they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, that is, “protection of the shield,” according to what is contained in the present history, because within that same Church there is certain protection for the faithful through God’s help [Col. 0341B].

Hence they say with the prophet: “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5). There the priest who touched the ark too carelessly, as though correcting it, was immediately struck down by the Lord. This signifies that the Jewish people, while envying the Gentiles, deprive themselves of the gift of salvation; while seeking to mix the Law with the Gospel, they remove from themselves the grace of both.

“And he held it,” it says, “because the oxen were kicking” (2 Kings 6). For the oxen’s kicking signifies that the preachers of the Gospel were acting more freely with regard to faith, not entering according to the custom of the Law, but interpreting the Sabbaths, new moons, circumcision, and sacrifices spiritually.

Those who came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15), tried to correct them as though they were straying. James says of these people to Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts 21).

Because of the priest’s death, therefore, David did not wish to turn the ark of the Lord to himself in the city of David, but turned it into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. This signifies that, when the Jews rejected the word so that the preaching they had heard and received might no longer do them harm, the apostles were taken away from them and sent to instruct the Gentiles (Acts 13).

Hence the place of the threshing floor of Nacon, which signifies the faith of the Gentiles prepared for the grace of the Lord, is called “the threshing floor of the struck Uzzah,” because through the fault of those people salvation was bestowed upon the Gentiles (Rom. 11).

Obed-edom, whose name means “serving man,” is surely the one of whom the Lord says to the Father: “You will appoint me as head of the nations; a people I did not know has served me” (Ps. 17). There, after anticipating the rejection of the Jews, like the death of Uzzah, he says: “You will rescue me from the disputes of the people” (ibid.).

The name of the city of Gath also suits him. *Gath* means “winepress,” signifying the cross, on which the true Vine graciously consented to be trodden and pressed. The entire people of the Gentiles may rightly be called Gittites when it says: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The three months during which the ark remained there signify faith, hope, and love. Just as a month is completed by its days, so each virtue reaches perfection through its own stages. These months continue to run until the fullness of the Gentiles enters (Gal. 6).

## CHAPTER XIV

On the fact that, after the kingdom had been established over Israel, David took other wives in Jerusalem, who bore sons and daughters; and on the fact that David struck the Philistines at Baal-perazim, and in another victory struck them at Gibeon as far as Gezer.

(1 Chron. 14.) David knew that the Lord had established him as king over Israel and that his kingdom had been exalted over his people Israel. David also took other wives in Jerusalem, and they bore sons and daughters, and so forth.

But perhaps someone may say: If David bore the image of Christ, how is he said to have had many wives and concubines, when Christ the King both abhors and condemns such things? This happened figuratively. David’s many wives signified the image of the many peoples and nations who are joined to the faith of Christ in fellowship with him.

His concubines, however, signify the churches of heretics, who boast that they sow under the title of Christ’s name. But because they follow Christ for the sake of carnal profits, they are called not wives but concubines.

Finally, if kings today have several wives and concubines, it is a crime, because the figures for which permission was granted concerning wives or concubines have now passed away. But now that the figures have passed away, no permission is granted.

When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over all Israel, they all went up to seek him. When David heard this, he went out to meet them. The Philistines came and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.

David consulted the Lord, saying: “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hand?” God said to him: “Go up, and I will deliver them into your hand.” When they had gone up to Baal-perazim, David struck them there and said: “God has burst through my enemies by my hand as waters burst through; therefore the name of that place was called Baal-perazim,” and so forth.

What does it mean that, when they heard of David’s anointing as king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek him, except that, when the grace of the Gospel and the rule of Christ had been proclaimed throughout the world, the nations of all peoples first rose up everywhere to oppose the Gospel of peace?

They came to seek him not in order to receive him with the devotion of faith, but to resist him through the deceit of wickedness. Therefore, seeking in such a manner, they were not worthy to find him, as Truth itself says to the Jews: “I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come” (John 8).

Why could they not come, except because they were unwilling to believe? For without faith no one can be saved.

David therefore goes out to meet his enemies when he openly displays to them the gifts of his benevolence. But whoever proves ungrateful for God’s gifts acquires death for himself by his own judgment.

Our David strikes them at Baal-perazim when he joins the multitudes of the faithful to himself by the election of grace, and, driving away the impious and blasphemous through the discernment of righteous judgment, thrusts them down into Tartarus in condemnation [Col. 0343A].

Another time the Philistines attacked and spread out in the valley. David again consulted the Lord, and God said to him: “You shall not go up after them. Withdraw from them, and come against them opposite the pear trees. When you hear the sound of someone walking on the tops of the pear trees, then go out to battle; for God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines,” and so forth.

What does it mean that the Lord gives, as a sign of his coming in judgment against his enemies, the sound of someone walking on the tops of the pear trees, except that the invisible God, who surpasses all things in majesty, displays the greatness of his power through visible works?

This accords with Paul’s statement: “His invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divinity, have been understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1).

Mystically, the Lord instructs his faithful to seek the help of his assistance in all things and to trust that they can make progress in the conflict of their struggles to the extent that they perceive the divine coming to be present with them.

The tops of the pear trees can therefore signify, by their meaning, the height of the perfection of the saints. The Lord accordingly gives a sign to the teachers sent to preach throughout the world, so that they may know when and where it is necessary to exercise the ministry of preaching. That is, they are to follow, through the service of their devotion, wherever the Holy Spirit, who presides over the pure hearts of the elect, directs them by his prompting and admonition.

Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles that Paul and Silas, apostles of Christ, passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia but were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word of God in Asia. When they came to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. After passing through Mysia, they went down to Troas. During the night a vision appeared to Paul: a certain Macedonian man was standing and pleading with him, saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us.” When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to depart for Macedonia, having become convinced that God had called us to evangelize them (Acts 16).

It should be noted, however, that where our edition reads “on the tops of the pear trees,” they say that in Hebrew it is not “pear trees” but “those who flow.” This may be understood as follows: he commands them to come opposite “those who flow”—that is, opposite their idols, where their idols were, in which they placed their trust.

Those idols are called “those who flow” because they are worthy of tears and lead those who worship them to the tears of misery. Thus, by “their flowing ones,” this divine statement calls their idols, because of their blasphemy, “the idol of Moab” and “the defilement of Moab.”

“And when you hear,” he says, “the sound of one walking upon them, on the tops of those who flow”—that is, when you hear from the angelic powers that the pagan idols, in which all their strength lies, are being broken and trampled down—then you shall enter battle. For then the Lord will go out before your face to strike the camp of the Philistines. In their idols the Lord carried out his judgments, just as he did against the gods of the Egyptians.

David did as God had commanded him, and struck the camp of the Philistines from Gibeon to Gezer [Col. 0344A].

Our David did as God the Father had commanded him and struck the camp of the Philistines when he crushed the attack of the evil spirits and also overthrew the power of the world, rescuing us from the power of darkness and transferring us into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. 1).

He fittingly shows us, through the names of the places, the works of his power. From Gibeon to Gezer he struck the camp of the Philistines. *Gibeon* means “hill” or “height,” while *Gezer* means “its hedge” or “division.”

Our King therefore struck his enemies, who persisted on the hill of pride; he crushed the hedge of their hardness, divided and cast down the conspiracy of their obstinacy, so that he alone might rule throughout the whole world [Col. 0344B].

Then it follows:

“And the name of David became famous in all the regions, and the Lord placed the fear of him upon all the nations,” and so forth.

For, as the Apostle says, Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2).

There is also the statement that follows.

## CHAPTER XV

On the fact that David appointed singers who sang with musical instruments before the ark of the Lord—namely, Heman, Asaph, Ethan, and the others who were with them [Col. 0344C].

(1 Chron. 15.) David made houses for himself in the city of David, built a place for the ark of God, and pitched a tabernacle for it.

This mystically signifies that, within the one Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, he established many assemblies under his name, bearing the name of peoples, so that in one house there might be different dwellings. Hence John also writes in his Apocalypse to seven churches (Rev. 1).

The fact that he built a place for the ark of God and pitched a tabernacle for it signifies that in the present Church he commended the mystery of his Incarnation and taught that the sacrament of his Passion was to be observed.

Then David said: “It is unlawful for the ark of God to be carried by anyone except the Levites, whom the Lord chose to carry it and minister to him forever” (Num. 4) [Col. 0344D].

This statement demonstrates that our Redeemer does not wish unworthy and idle persons to perform ecclesiastical office, but those who are learned in knowledge and approved for upright conduct. They are to carry the ark of God—that is, the holy Church—on the shoulders of devoted labor, through the word of right faith and the example of good works, and in this way minister to him forever.

Hence Paul instructs his disciple, saying: “You, however, be vigilant in all things, work hard, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry, be sober” (2 Tim. 4). “Take care to present yourself as an approved worker to God, an unashamed one who handles the word of truth rightly” (2 Tim. 2). And again: “Be strengthened,” he says, “my son, in the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who will be capable of teaching others” [Col. 0345A].

David gathered all Israel in Jerusalem so that the ark of God might be brought to its place, which he had prepared for it, as well as the sons of Aaron and the Levites, and so forth.

David gathers all Israel in Jerusalem when Christ calls his chosen ones and all who belong to God’s portion into his Church, so that there they may venerate the mysteries of his Incarnation. He gathers not only subjects but also prelates, whom the sons of Aaron and the Levites prefigure, for this principal celebration and greatest solemnity, because there it is fitting for all to assemble: the small and the great, young men [Col. 0345B] and virgins, and elders with the young, to praise the name of the Lord.

It is rightly said that the ark was to be brought to its own place, which David had prepared for it, because not only David but all the prophets, by their words and deeds, prophetically made room in the Church for the future Incarnation of Christ, so that they might receive him more swiftly when he came because they knew beforehand that he had been foretold.

The priests and Levites were consecrated to carry the ark of the Lord God of Israel. The sons of Levi carried the ark of the God of Israel on their shoulders, on the poles, as Moses had commanded, according to the word of the Lord (Num. 4).

According to the rule of allegorical interpretation, the consecration of the priests and Levites teaches that ministers of the New Testament must possess pure doctrine and a clean life. Elsewhere they are told: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 11).

It is therefore fitting for the bearers of the Lord’s ark to be consecrated according to the commandment of the Lord’s Law, because they must commend to their hearers, through words of right faith and examples of good works, the Incarnation of the Son of God, the Redemption of the human race, eternal life, and Christ’s future judgment.

David also told the leaders of the Levites to appoint from among their brothers singers with musical instruments—namely, nablia, lyres, and cymbals—so that they might make sounds of joy resound on high, and so forth (1 Chron. 23).

It is therefore related elsewhere in the present history that, when the prophet David had grown old in devoted age, he selected four thousand young men from the Israelite people. They were to make the psalms that he himself had produced under the inspiration of the Lord resound with instruments—lyres, nablia, cymbals, trumpets—and with their own voices, in great joy arising from heavenly grace [Col. 0345D].

This harmonious combination was divided into three parts. The rational part belonged to the human voice; the irrational part to musical instruments; and the common part was adapted from both, so that the human voice might be produced in definite melodies and the music of the instruments might join with it in harmonious proximity.

Thus that sweet and joyful music prophetically proclaimed the Catholic Church, which, through diverse languages and varied harmony, was destined by the Lord’s provision to grow together into one concord of faith.

We frequently find names taken from this number in the titles, such as Jeduthun, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and similar names. They were not, as some wish, the authors of the psalms. Rather, because they were overseers who proved suitable administrators for the craftsmen and for those responsibilities, they received honor through such remembrance, since they served in the holy office with devoted minds.

Moreover, these names are known to indicate appropriate meanings concerning the matters themselves. The men mentioned above were not chosen to compose psalms; we read only that they were gathered to sing. No history testifies that they were psalm-writers, and it is presumptuous to say what cannot be confirmed by any authority.

Let us now present, from the statements of our predecessors, what the musical instruments mentioned in the present passage were.

The *nablas* is the same as the psaltery. In Hebrew it is called *nablum*; in Greek, *psalterion*; in Latin, *laudatorium*, “instrument of praise.” Concerning it, the fifty-sixth and one-hundred-seventh psalms say: “Awake, psaltery and lyre” (Ps. 56; 108). It is not shaped like a lyre, but like a square shield, with ten strings, as it is written: “On the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you” (Ps. 144).

The psaltery therefore has a broad belly at the upper part, where the strings are fastened. Struck skillfully with a plectrum, they are said to produce the sweetest song. Its arrangement appears contrary to that of the lyre, since what the one contains at the bottom, the other, in reverse position, carries at the top.

The psaltery with ten strings is the Church with the ten words of the Law, understood as square against every heresy through the four Gospels [Col. 0346C].

Next comes the lyre, concerning which the forty-second psalm says: “I will confess to you on the lyre, O God, my God.” This is a customary instrument among the Hebrews. Experts say that it is constructed with twenty-four strings, in the form of the Greek letter delta, and that through the fingers of Pindar it is stirred into various modes by diverse, ringing, and flute-like sounds.

The lyre of which we are speaking spiritually represents the Church. Since it has the teaching of the twenty-four elders and a threefold form like the letter delta, it doubtless signifies the faith of the Holy Trinity. Through the hands of the apostle Peter and the other apostles and teachers of the Gospel, who are its preachers, it is stirred into various modes of the Old and New Testament, in one way according to the letter and in another according to the figurative meaning [Col. 0346D].

The lyre is called *lyra* from Greek ἀπὸ τὸ *lyrim*, that is, “from the variety of sounds,” because it produces different tones. It too can signify the Church, which expresses a sweet sound through the diversity of its various teachings—through history, allegory, moral interpretation, and anagogy—yet does not depart from the simplicity of harmony.

Cymbals are certain bowls or basins which, when struck against one another, make a sound. Concerning them the psalm says: “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals” (Ps. 150).

We should understand well-sounding cymbals as our lips. They are rightly placed among musical instruments, because there is a certain likeness to cymbals in them, and because human voices are shown through them to produce the sweetest harmony. Harmony is the joining together of different things brought into one agreement. This also occurs in the human voice, when the times and syllables themselves are brought into one concord of sound.

Our cymbals, therefore, are lips struck and precisely attuned to the sound of the voice. They sound beneficially when they are moved with the greatest devotion to the praises of the Lord.

Cymbals are also properly made of mixed metals, formed as very small bowls, with bellies on their sides. When struck together with artistic modulation, they produce a very sharp sound with pleasing consonance.

Hence it follows:

The singers Heman, Asaph, and Ethan clashed bronze cymbals. Zechariah, Uzziel, Semiramoth, Jehiel, Ani, Eliab, Maaseiah, and Benaiah sang hidden things on nablia [Col. 0347B].

“Hidden things” are called *arcana*. When they took the instruments into their hands, they sang future mysteries through the coming of the Holy Spirit, proclaiming, by singing the Psalms to the accompaniment of the psaltery, the coming of the Lord and Savior, which he had arranged in the wondrous secrecy of his divinity for the salvation of human beings. This word is mentioned in the title of the forty-fifth psalm.

Mattithiah, Eliphalu, Macenias, Obed-edom, Jehiel, and Ozaziu sang on lyres “for the octave.” “For the octave,” as some wish to understand it, signifies the coming of the Lord on the day of judgment, when, after the week of the world has ended, he will come to judge the world.

Hence the sixth psalm, which is sung throughout in trembling at the divine judgment, is marked with such a title [Col. 0347C]. The number eight itself is also recognized in the divine Scriptures as containing the mysteries of great things.

Eight souls entered Noah’s ark and were saved while the world was perishing (Gen. 7). David was the eighth son of Jesse, and it is established that he was chosen by the Lord (1 Sam. 16). On the eighth day circumcision also purified the Hebrews (Gen. 17). Likewise, on the eighth day, Sunday, the Lord rose from the dead (Matt. 28), on which the hope of the human race was raised from the hell of the ungodly to the summit of heaven.

This is the number that mathematicians call the first *quadrantal* number in operation; Philolaus the Pythagorean calls it geometrical harmony, because all harmonic proportions seem to converge in it.

Chenaniah, leader of the Levites, presided over prophecy and led the melody, for he was very wise, and so forth [Col. 0347D].

Chenaniah is said to preside over prophecy in order to lead the melody because, instructed by the spirit of prophecy, he recalled the melody and words to the singers’ memory.

Prophecy is divine inspiration, which announces the outcomes of events, either through the deeds or through the words of certain people, with unchanging truth. Concerning it someone rightly said: “Prophecy is sweet speech, the honeycomb of heavenly teaching, composing the sweet honey of divine utterance.”

Hence David himself says in the one-hundred-eighteenth Psalm: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 119)!

The gifts of this grace were bestowed in many ways. To encompass a few of the many, it operated through human actions, as with Noah’s ark (Gen. 7; 1 Pet. 5), Abraham’s sacrifice (Gen. 15), and the crossing of the Red Sea (Exod. 14).

It also operated through the births of the twins Esau and Jacob, who bore the mysteries of future events (Gen. 25); through angels, as when they spoke to Abraham, Lot, Zechariah, and Mary (Gen. 18–19; Luke 1); through visions, as with Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the other saints (Isa. 1; 7; Ezek. 1; 10); through dreams, as with Solomon and Daniel (1 Kings 3; Dan. 7); and through a cloud and a voice from heaven, as with Moses.

It is therefore clear that holy David was filled not through human actions, nor through the birth of twins, nor through angels, visions, dreams, a cloud and a voice from heaven [Col. 0348B], nor through any other mode, but through heavenly inspiration.

As we read of him in the First Book of Kings: “The Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day onward” (1 Sam. 16). The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “If David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matt. 22).

By this statement we clearly recognize that the psalms were prophesied through the Holy Spirit.

It should certainly be known that all prophecy either speaks or acts concerning past, present, or future time. Prophecy is a very exalted and truthful mode of speech.

Prophecy was not at some time bestowed by human will; rather, holy men of God spoke while inspired by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet. 1). The apostle Paul also says: “The one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding, encouragement, and consolation” (1 Cor. 14).

A little later he says: “The one who prophesies builds up the Church of God”—clearly, when through the gift of speech he makes unknown and exceedingly necessary matters fully known.
