Those who have been given the ability to understand well or to interpret the divine Scriptures do not appear to be excluded from the gift of prophecy, as the Apostle says in his First Epistle to the Corinthians: “The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets” (1 Cor. 14).

Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Nathanael, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah, and Eliezer, the priests, sounded trumpets before the ark of the Lord [Col. 0348D].

What else are these seven priests who sounded trumpets before God than holy preachers filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit? They sound like trumpets when they preach God’s Gospel in the Church of Christ and disclose to the faithful, with authoritative testimony, the sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation.

A trumpet is made in various shapes and forms. One kind is made for assembling the people, another for victory, another for pursuing enemies, another for besieging cities, and so forth.

Among experts in these matters, the customary trumpet is described as being made in this way: air is blown into three bronze pipes at a narrow opening, and through four bronze channels for the voice, which produce fourfold sounds through a bronze base, they emit an exceedingly loud and powerful roar [Col. 0349A].

Figuratively, this signifies that the Gospel, inspired divinely at the narrow opening in the birth of Christ, through the threefold confession of the three persons of the Holy Trinity, emits throughout the whole world a voice with immense force, like the sound of a trumpet for assembling the people, through the four bronze channels of the voice—that is, through the four evangelists—by the stability of a bronze foundation, namely, faith and works.

[Col. 0350A] We have carried the first book of the commentaries on Chronicles from the beginning of the volume up to the passage where the musical instruments are described, which David, king and prophet together, arranged for praising the Lord. Here we bring that book to an end, and with a different introduction we shall begin what follows concerning David’s deeds and his mystical distributions.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0349]

[Col. 0349A] (Ibid.) David, all the elders of Israel, and the tribunes went to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord [Col. 0349B] from the house of Obed-edom with great joy. When the Lord had helped the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, seven bulls and seven rams were sacrificed.

David was clothed in a linen robe, as were all the Levites who carried the ark, the singers, and Chenaniah, the leader of prophecy among the singers. David was also wearing a linen ephod.

All Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord with rejoicing and the sound of the horn, while trumpets, cymbals, nablia, and lyres resounded.

When the ark of the covenant of the Lord had reached the city of David, Michal, the daughter of Saul, looked through the window and saw King David dancing and playing, and she despised him in her heart (2 Kings 6).

# CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0349C] Concerning the fact that, when David had brought the ark of the Lord with rejoicing into the tabernacle that he had pitched for it, the priests offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord; and David blessed the people in the name of the Lord and distributed to everyone individually, from man to woman, a round loaf of bread, a portion of roasted buffalo meat, and a cake of fine flour fried in oil. Concerning the Levites whom David appointed to minister before the ark of the Lord, and concerning Asaph and his brothers. Concerning the song that David composed for praising the Lord. Concerning the fact that David returned to bless his household.

(I PAR. XVI.) Therefore they brought the ark of God and set it in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it; and they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord. When David had finished offering the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord and distributed to everyone individually, from man to woman, a round loaf [Col. 0349D] of bread, a portion of roasted buffalo meat, and a cake of fine flour fried in oil (II REG. VI).

After the ark of the Lord had remained for three months in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, David assembled the elders of Israel, together with the tribes and the Levites who were to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and brought it into his own house. For after the fullness of the nations has entered into the faith of Christ (ROM. XI), at last the ark of God will return to the city of David—that is, to the Jewish people—when, through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, it is converted by the grace of Christ. There our king, sacrificing oxen and rams—that is, crowning with the blood of martyrdom those who thresh the ark of the Lord and exercise leadership over his sheep—also openly manifests the example of his own incarnation and Passion, insofar as it was not believed by the Jews. For this is signified [Col. 0350A] by the fact that David himself was girded with a linen ephod. Linen, produced from the earth and brought to the whiteness of clothing through manifold labor [Col. 0350B], reveals the truth of human flesh triumphing amid scourges.

Yet while all were rejoicing and hymns were resounding at the entrance of the heavenly ark, Michal alone, the daughter of Saul, was absent from those leading the ark; indeed, looking out from the window, she despised David in his humiliation. This is because, at the end of the world, among the Jews who believe, there will be some who follow Christ only in profession, but in practice follow the Antichrist. To these it fittingly applies that the same Michal, who—signifying the instability of carnal people—is interpreted as “every kind of water,” is called not David’s wife but Saul’s daughter. For they serve Christ only in respect of faith; they will not be crowned in his kingdom, but will be condemned by the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitated.

But let the wicked rage and condemn the humility of the Church: nevertheless [Col. 0350C] the ark of its Lord enters its place, is set in the midst of the tabernacle that David had pitched for it—that is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is implanted in the hearts of all whom the Lord had predestined to eternal life.

David offers burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord; Christ, who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us (ROM. VIII), commends to the Father the faith and devotion of the Church. Following the example of David, he blesses the faithful and humble, feeding them with the nourishment of the mystery of salvation. He distributes to each one a single *collyris* of bread, namely, that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to this world (JOHN VI); one portion of roasted buffalo meat, namely, that fattened calf which was slaughtered for the younger son returning to his father (LUKE XV) and roasted in the fire of the Passion, saying: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” [Col. 0350D] (PS. XXI); and fine flour fried in oil, that is, flesh utterly cleansed from the stain of sin, yet, for the sake of human salvation, richly tormented in the frying-pan of the delights of the cross.

And rightly one round loaf of bread and one portion of meat are given, because there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all (EPH. IV). The faithful receive these gifts in another sense when “we, though many, are one bread and one body in Christ” (I COR. X): each person disciplines the wantonness of the flesh and subjects it to servitude, cooking it in the fire of the Holy Spirit; likewise, they make the fruits of good works, rich with the oil of mercy, boil with compassion for their neighbor.

On the other hand, the daughter of Saul, having entered the king’s chamber in vain, bears no fruit from the seed she has conceived, because those who receive the word of God only with the ear, without the offspring of good works, await the day of perpetual death.

When David brought back the ark of the Lord into Jerusalem by dancing, and Michal, the daughter of Saul and his wife, mocked him, it is pleasing to contemplate the moral meaning: how many gifts of virtue David himself had received, and how strong a humility he preserved amid them all. Who would not have been lifted up by having broken the jaws of lions, torn apart the arms of bears, been chosen over his despised shepherd brothers, been anointed to govern the kingdom after the rejected king, struck down the dreaded Goliath with one stone, and, after the Philistines had been slain at the king’s command, brought back numerous foreskins; by finally receiving the promised kingdom and possessing the whole Israelite people without any opposition [Note: [Col. 0351D] I SAM. XVII; I SAM. XVI; I SAM. XVII; I SAM. XVIII; II SAM. II, III]? Yet when he brought back the ark of God to Jerusalem, as though he had forgotten that he had been set above everyone else, he danced among the people before the ark; and because dancing before the ark was, as is believed, the custom of the common people, the king whirled about in the service of God through his dancing.

Behold the one whom the Lord had singularly preferred to all others: under the Lord, he humbled himself, making himself equal to the least and displaying himself as despised. He did not recall the power of his kingdom; he did not fear becoming lowly in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; he did not recognize himself as superior to the others in honor before the ark of the one who had granted him honor. Before God he performed what was weak and lowly, so that through that humility he might strengthen what he had performed valiantly before human beings.

I do not know what others think of his deeds; for my part, I marvel more at David dancing than fighting. By fighting, indeed, he subdued an enemy; but by dancing before the Lord, he conquered himself.

Michal, the daughter of Saul, still insane with the swelling pride of royal descent, despised him in his humiliation and said: “How glorious was the king of Israel today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and naked, as though one of the buffoons were naked” (II SAM. VI). At once she heard: “I will dance before the Lord, who chose me rather than your father.” A little later he said: “I will dance, and I will make myself even more contemptible than I have been, and I will be humble in my own eyes.”

It is as though he openly said: “I seek to become contemptible before human beings, because through humility I seek to preserve the kingdom for myself before God.”

There are therefore some who think humbly of themselves: placed in positions of honor, they reckon themselves to be nothing but dust and ashes; nevertheless, they shrink from appearing lowly before human beings, and, contrary to what they think inwardly about themselves, they conceal themselves outwardly beneath a kind of rigid dignity [Col. 0351D].

There are also some who desire to appear contemptible to human beings and, by displaying themselves as cast down in everything they are, despise themselves; nevertheless, inwardly they swell up within themselves, as though because of the very merit of the contempt they have displayed. The more they suppress pride in outward appearance, the more exalted they are in their hearts.

David detected both these great battles of a single pride with profound watchfulness and overcame them with remarkable virtue. Because, while inwardly thinking humbly of himself, he does not seek outward honor, he declares this by saying: “I will dance, and I will make myself even more contemptible.” And because, by displaying himself outwardly as contemptible, he did not swell inwardly at all, he adds: “And I will be humble in my own eyes.” It is as though he openly said: [Col. 0352A] “As I display myself outwardly, despising myself, so I regard myself inwardly.”

What, then, will those do whom learning elevates, if David knew the Redeemer who was to come from his own flesh and announced his joys prophetically, and yet pressed down the neck of his heart within himself with the strong heel of discernment, saying: “And I will be humble in my own eyes”?

David appointed before the ark of God some of the Levites to minister, to remember his works, and to glorify and praise the Lord, and so forth. Pay attention, reader, to the order and office of the Levites as David appointed them: “to minister,” he says, “to remember his works, and to glorify and praise the Lord.” Here you will be able to consider the ordering of our whole life within the Christian religion.

He ministers to God who presents to the Lord a pure heart together with chaste conduct. He remembers his works who diligently practices meditation on the law of God according to the rule of the Catholic faith. He glorifies and praises the Lord who praises him not only in the speech of preaching and the voice of rejoicing, but also through the accomplishment of good works.

Thus the office of that minister is worthily fulfilled, of whom the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my minister be” (JOHN XII). For whoever rightly serves the Lord in heart, mouth, and deed will possess with him the joys of eternal blessedness.

On that day David appointed Asaph and his brothers as leaders for giving thanks to the Lord, and so forth. What does it mean that David appointed Asaph as leader for giving thanks to the Lord, except that our Redeemer established the order of the holy teachers, who are devoted to the apostolic office, at the summit of ecclesiastical dignity?

The meaning of his name itself seems fittingly to foreshadow this. For *Asaph* means “gathering.” And he is rightly called “gathering” who endeavors, through upright speech and good example, to convert many to the faith of Christ and to the worship of piety.

Thus Asaph and his brothers are appointed leaders for praising the Lord when holy apostolic men are ordained by the Lord himself to call together and unite the number of the faithful in the faith. Concerning them the Psalmist, in admiration, says to the Lord: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored; their principality has been exceedingly strengthened” (PS. CXXXVIII). And again: “You will appoint them,” he says, “as leaders over the whole earth; they will remember your name, Lord, throughout every generation and lineage” (PS. XLIV).

After this, the historian inserted the form of praise that David himself composed, saying: “Give thanks to the Lord and invoke his name.” The title of this psalm is “Alleluia.” And rightly so, because it unfolds entirely in praises of God.

This ornament of speech first began with the present psalm; it is not found previously to have been set down by anyone, although many writers of the ancient Hebrews existed. We must know, however, that *Alleluia* has a neuter ending, as Saint Jerome also clearly indicates in his exposition of this same psalm. We believe that he found this in the Hebrew sources; therefore, wherever the occasion arises, we shall follow the rule established by that most learned man, since the word ought to remain one and undivided, not altered by the presumption of any language.

For among them *Alleluia* is said to mean “praise the Lord”: *allelu* means “praise,” while *al* signifies the invisible Lord. Jerome is said to have transmitted in his letter to Marcella an explanation that this is one of the ten names of God. He said:

The first name of God is *el*, that is, “strong.” Next is *eloim*, from *eloe*, both of which mean “God.” Hence we frequently find it doubled, as in: “God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (PS. XXI), and: “God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the light” (PS. LXII), and similar passages.

The fourth is *Sabbaoth*, which means “of hosts.” The fifth is *elon*, which we call “the Most High.” The sixth is *Asserheiae,” which is read in Exodus: “He who is has sent me” (EXOD. III). The seventh is *Adonai*, which we generally call “Lord.” The eighth is *Ia*, which is applied only to God and sounds as the final syllable in *Alleluia*. The ninth is the tetragrammaton, which is called ineffable. The tenth is *Adona*, that is, “strong and sufficient to accomplish all things,” and so forth.

It is plainly a new title, distinguished by the brevity of the expression itself. It is a cherished formula for churches and fittingly suited to holy feasts. From it the tongue of singers is adorned. The joyful court of the Lord responds to it, and this insatiable good is continually renewed through ever-changing figures.

“Give thanks,” he says, “to the Lord, and invoke his name; make known among the peoples his inventions.”

In this verse the order of the statements consists of three parts. First he says: “Give thanks to the Lord,” that is, praise him, and acquire for yourselves the grace of divinity through good deeds. This itself is to praise the Lord: to offer him honor with the mouth and to carry out his commands through works. The confession meant here is that which never ceases to celebrate the Lord’s praises, since what follows also declares such a vow and action.

Next he urges that the Lord be invoked, so that we may gratefully hear the sacred mystery of praise. Something good must first be offered, so that the judge may hear us with favor.

Third he says: “Make known among the peoples his inventions.” This can aptly apply to glorious evangelists, most holy apostles, and now holy priests, who are known to announce his mighty works throughout the nations.

[Col. 0353D] Sing and play psalms to him, and recount all his wonders.

He explains what he said above: “Give thanks to the Lord.” Singing pertains to the hymns that are to be offered; playing psalms pertains to setting forth pious works. He said that the wonders were to be recounted only after these two things had been placed first.

“Everything” signifies the matters he is about to mention. It is not within human powers to recount everything that the power of Divinity accomplishes, as it is written in Psalm 105: “Who will speak of the powers of the Lord? Who will make all his praises heard?” (PS. CV). But this figure is called “the whole from a part,” something you will frequently find in the Scriptures.

Nor can this saying of the Gospel otherwise be correctly understood: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (JOHN I), as though he had not also assumed a soul, which he graciously chose especially to save.

[Col. 0354A] Praise his holy name.

That person rightly praises the name of the Lord who correctly preaches sound faith and, by living well, commends it worthily to others through good works. In Psalm 104 it is likewise written: “Praise yourselves in his holy name” (PS. CIV).

Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.

Lest anyone perhaps attribute his good action to his own powers, the careful teacher warns the weak, saying that one must glory not in one’s own judgment but in the Lord, so that they may avoid false boasting when they recognize that these things have been granted by divinity. Thus it is also read in another psalm: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (PS. XXXIII).

He does not therefore forbid us to be praised, since this cannot be denied to good actions; but let us be praised in the Lord [Col. 0354B], who provides the things we accomplish well. And so that they might derive consolation from this, he says: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.” Let it rejoice, that is, if the Lord is praised, but not if someone is praised for his own ability. It ought to be especially good and glorious for us when the name of the one who generously bestows beneficial gifts upon us is exalted.

Hence it was extremely shameless for certain people to say anything against this, despite such frequent testimonies—indeed, almost the whole law—having been brought forward against them.

Seek the Lord and his power; seek his face always.

He exhorts those who have chosen to seek him to strengthen themselves for future rewards. But this desire and this seeking must not be brought to an end here after only a little while, because he added: “Always.” Especially since it is written: “Whoever asks receives; whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (MATT. VII).

When he says: “Seek his face always,” he signifies the presence that only the humble and devoted seek. No one can desire the judge unless he trusts in his kindness; and when he desires the judge’s presence, he restrains himself from wicked action.

The Apostle sought the judge’s face when he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give me on that day” (II TIM. IV). Such a person rightly sought the face of the judge, since he anticipated that he would be crowned by the Lord’s mercy.

Remember his wonders that he performed, his signs [Col. 0354D], and the judgments of his mouth.

A little later he recounts the names and benefits of the patriarchs, so that the devout people may perceive that no one served the Lord with empty devotion. The wonders therefore refer to the division of the Red Sea, the prodigies, and the plagues that he sent upon Egypt. “The judgments of his mouth” refers to the fact that he fulfilled everything he is known to have promised to Moses his servant.

Thus, in a single verse, he briefly stated beforehand, as a proposition, what he was afterward going to discuss at greater length. Yet he wants all this to be understood concerning the Lord Christ.

The offspring of Abraham, his servants; the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.

What he said above—“Remember”—is to be supplied. It must be examined, however, with what great discrimination the prophet calls Abraham’s seed “servants,” while recalling Jacob’s sons as the Lord’s chosen ones.

For the Jews, the obstinate people whom he prefers to have understood here, were the seed of Abraham according to the flesh. He rightly calls them servants, because, through unbelief, they refused to be sons. The Lord himself says to them: “If you were Abraham’s sons, you would do the works of Abraham.”

By the sons of Jacob he signifies the most faithful Christians, who are known to be heirs of the Lord.

He himself is the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all the earth.

The seed of Abraham and the seed of Jacob are mentioned so that they may believe our Savior to be not the Lord of one nation but the Lord of the whole world. For just as the Church has been spread everywhere, so his judgments have undoubtedly been propagated throughout the world.

By saying “he himself is the Lord,” he reminds us that the one whom the Jewish people determined should be crucified is to be understood. [Col. 0355B] But those who do not heed this utterance themselves declare that they are especially alienated from the patriarchs.

Remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations.

He commands them to remember—that is, not to hand it over to any forgetfulness—and he adds “forever,” because whatever the Lord has promised will remain with everlasting firmness.

By his covenant, or testament, he signifies the preaching of the prophets, who foretold the incarnation of the Word. Then follows: “Which he commanded.” To command is to speak something through another person; this happened when the prophets of the age were given to prophesy future things.

“For a thousand generations”: a finite number is used for an infinite one, though this is enclosed within the end of this age, where one human generation succeeds another in the following age.

Which he made with Abraham, and his oath with Isaac, and established it with Jacob as a commandment, and with Israel as an everlasting covenant.

This responds to what he said above, “his covenant.” For the things that were promised or sworn to the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac in the Old Testament, he established—that is, confirmed—for Jacob and Israel in the New Testament, which is eternal.

It has often already been said that Jacob and Israel frequently signify the Christian age. His New Testament is properly called eternal because no other will ever succeed it; in it is the complete fulfillment of all the promises.

Saying: “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the cord of your inheritance.”

Canaan is interpreted as “humble.” Therefore he appropriately signifies that Christians will receive the land of the humble [Col. 0355D]—that is, what he said above, the everlasting covenant. For this land of humility and lowliness is received by the faithful in such a way that it is preserved as an eternal gift.

The cord of inheritance signifies the twisted straits of the world, which the Lord dissolved through his Passion for the salvation of all. For through his assumption of flesh our inheritance is confirmed; in it we receive the eternal patrimonies of heavenly life, if we are worthy to believe in it firmly and wholly.

This comparison was handed down by those among whom fields and possessions were divided by a stretched cord.

When they were few in number, and few, its sojourners, and they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people.

He has come to the third part, in which he next enumerates how great a benefit divine power granted to the patriarchs. Accordingly, what follows proceeds from that:

He did not permit anyone to oppress them, but rebuked kings on their behalf: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

Here he signifies the time when the king of the Egyptians was divinely warned not to presume upon Abraham’s wife (GEN. XII). The same is known to have occurred in the case of Isaac (GEN. XXVI). Therefore it is clearly shown that they were protected by divine defense.

Hence it must be examined why he chose to call the patriarchs mentioned above “anointed ones,” since anointing had not yet been instituted. For this matter began with Saul (I SAM.).

But since they were Christians in spirit and are proved to have been devoted to his faith, as the Lord says concerning Abraham: “He desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced,” they were rightly called by the sacred name, because they are proved already to have loved the faith of Christ.

For these are also the Lord’s own words: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (JOHN VIII).

Sing to the Lord, all the earth.

By saying “all the earth,” he signifies the Catholic Church, which is known to be spread throughout the whole world. In a brief summary he both refuted Judaism, because he admitted the nations, and destroyed the claim of the people of God, because he did not deny grace to the universality of confession.

For, if he wanted human beings to be understood, he said “sing,” since human beings can truly sound forth praises to the Lord. Moreover, he applied the plural number to “earth,” which certainly would not fit if he had intended the terrestrial globe itself.

Announce his salvation from day to day.

“Day from day” plainly signifies two days. We judge this to pertain to the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, both of which correspond to the brightness of the eternal sun. Hence the Lord Savior is rightly announced by those through whom he was shown both to be coming and to have come. The prophets promised his advent; the evangelists declared that he had come. Thus the two heavenly days are proved to have announced his glory.

Tell his glory among the nations and his wonders among all the peoples.

After saying above, “Announce his salvation,” here he says: “Tell his wonders and his glory.” This is most suitably placed. The Lord Savior was to be announced; his glory, however, was to be recounted among the nations.

Let the Jew hear how many wonders they preached, and understand that he was rejected because of the wickedness of his obstinacy: for he does not say, “Tell it to the Hebrews,” but “to the nations.” And lest you understand this otherwise, he also added: “Among all the peoples,” by which statement he comprehensively included every nation.

Then follows: “His wonders.” This is the mystery of the Incarnation: although he is most high, he became most lowly for our liberation. We also understand how greatly the building of the holy house advanced, since it is known to have embraced the entire earth.

For the Lord is great, and exceedingly praiseworthy, and terrible above all gods.

Here he says why his wonders and glory ought to be proclaimed: because “the Lord is great.” This figure is called *aetiologia*, the giving of a reason.

“Great” pertains to power, which is mightier than all things. “Praiseworthy” pertains to mercy, because, while we were captives, he redeemed us with precious blood. “Exceedingly” applies to both, because it could not be expressed how great or how praiseworthy he is. But since the judgment of the one considering him failed, he fittingly added “exceedingly.”

Thus, without explaining what he intended, he signifies it most abundantly; he made clear what he wished without comprehending it. Then follows: “He is terrible above all gods.”

Here we must understand the gods whom impious paganism fashioned for itself through presumptuous invention. For he reveals who they are in the following verse. Although they may seem worthy of worship and fear to foolish minds, the Lord is far more terrible, since neither the multitude of his wonders can be comprehended nor the fullness of his majesty recognized.

For all the gods of the nations are idols, but the Lord made the heavens.

In the Psalter, however, it is read: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens” (PS. XCV).

Marvelously, through the fifth species of definition, which in Greek is called *cata ante lexin* and in Latin is called an adverb, it has been comprehended what the gods of the nations are: demons.

For demons are beings who benefit no one; rather, they always deceive and always mock those who believe in them. Although demons are called *scientes* in Latin, as though they were “knowing beings,” this is nevertheless an insult in human speech when we speak as though they were judged worthy by their creation—not without reason, since they possess no knowledge who do not follow the will of their Creator.

We likewise call philosophers wise; but the Apostle’s definitive judgment follows concerning them, saying: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (I COR. III). Hence it is necessary that here “knowing” be understood as “not understanding.”

A demon is therefore a substance created by God, just as is the excellent substance of the good angels, superior to human beings. But through the exercise of its own pride it reached such a point that, having laid aside its natural dignity, it continually persists in evil works.

These are the demons who destroy others and deceive themselves. These are indeed the gods of the nations, who hasten, through fruitless prophecies and vain foretellings of the future, to deceive the souls of those who enclose themselves in them.

Then follows: “But the Lord made the heavens.” Behold, truly a praise worthy of the Lord. For when he says, “He made the heavens,” he sufficiently shows that all created things were made by him.

Thus we include lesser things within greater ones when we say “the city was built” or “the house was enclosed”; for the remaining parts are included wherever a general name is used.

Consider also where the statement “the Lord made the heavens” tends. Those gods were discovered through the false imagination of human beings; but the Lord made the heavens, which they deserve neither to approach nor to inhabit.

Or “the heavens” signifies the apostles and holy men, who, by the Lord’s gift, are accustomed to command demons. Thus the demonstrative manner of speaking is completed briefly.

Above he condemned the gods of the nations, and afterward added praises of the Lord, because the brightness of day is more welcome when dark night has preceded it.

Praise and magnificence are before him; strength and joy are in his place.

By presenting a general statement, he shows the usefulness of the Catholic religion, since he has undertaken to admonish. He says how those who have deserved to attain forgiveness of sins are made magnificent.

Magnificence rightly follows confession, because no one can be magnificent except one who has been cleansed by the Lord’s mercy. Therefore confession and magnificence are before the Lord: just as the magnificence attributed to the Lord is true, so the confession that has deserved it must be pure.

“Strength and joy are in his place.” The Lord’s place may be understood as his presence, which the saints enjoy in their life. Therefore strength and joy are there, because there are immortality and perpetual blessedness.

Bring to the Lord, families of the peoples, bring to the Lord glory and dominion; give to the Lord glory for his name; lift up the sacrifice, and come into his presence, and worship the Lord in holy beauty.

After proclaiming the Lord’s mighty works and the gifts of the blessed, in the second part he moves the nations more earnestly to bring the Lord glory and dominion, laying aside all hesitation.

The families of the peoples are the nations of different races. They bring the Lord glory and dominion when they believe, confess, and proclaim him to be the true and omnipotent Lord and ruler of all. Such a sacrifice pleases in God’s presence.

Worshipers of this kind worship the Lord in holy beauty because, with believing hearts, they confess him to be the author of eternal splendor.

In Psalm 95 it is written: “Bring to the Lord, countries of the nations, bring glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name. Take up sacrifices and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy place” (PS. XCV).

When he says “countries of the nations,” he signifies more than if he had said only “nations.” A nation can contain some foreigners; when a people is called a *natio*, however, it does not include newcomers but indicates only a people of one blood.

Here, however, “countries of the nations” is said so that no native, no guest, and no foreigner might be excluded. For *patria* is so called as though from “the father’s courts.”

Then follows: “Bring to the Lord glory and honor.” He also urges the whole human race to bring glory and honor to the Lord.

The Lord’s glory is present when someone conducts himself in a praiseworthy manner. The Lord is glorified in such people when he is praised through the conduct of the faithful, as he says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (MATT. V).

The Lord’s honor, however, is present when we give him thanks for his gifts and confess that whatever good we have received was bestowed by him. Thus it is read in the Gospel: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this Samaritan?” (LUKE XVII).

Just as above in the psalm he said “sing” three times by repetition, so here the word “bring” is composed three times, so that you may always recognize the mysteries of the Holy Trinity as present in Christian doctrine.

They bring glory to his name who are changed for the better through devoted zeal and confess the Trinity, consubstantial in itself and omnipotent in all things, distinguished only by persons and not by a difference of nature.

When he says: “Take up sacrifices and enter his courts,” he does not mean sacrifices of cattle but the pure offerings of conscience, from which not blood flows but devout tears pour forth. These are the sacrifices of which he said in Psalm 50: “A contrite and humbled heart he will not despise” (PS. L).

But consider that he first placed “take up,” and only then “enter,” because those who do not carry such sacrifices are judged not to enter the courts of the Lord.

Nor should it be received casually that he used the plural number, “courts.” The courts of the Lord are the apostles or prophets, through whom the faithful people enter to the Lord.

“Worship,” he says, “the Lord in his holy hall,” or, as it is found in another edition [Col. 0359B], “in his holy court.” For these two names are used interchangeably in Scripture, since in Greek also *aulen* means “court.”

The Lord is truly worshiped when the sacrifices he mentioned above have been brought, so that the supplication of the one who confesses may deserve to reach the ears of the Creator.

Nor is it without significance that in the preceding verse he used the plural “courts,” while here he says “court” in the singular. For from those courts—the patriarchs, apostles, and prophets—one comes into this court, namely, the Catholic Church, where the power of his majesty is worshiped.

Then follows:

Let the whole earth be moved from his presence.

Having told the faithful, “Take up good works and enter,” he now says that lovers of the world are to be removed from his presence. For he did not say: “Let the whole earth be moved before his face” [Col. 0359C]—an expression we use even today of those whom we have made strangers to our sight.

They are rightly called “earth,” because they do not abandon earthly vices. Although others have said that this should be understood in a favorable sense, so that the earth is shaken when, by the Lord’s mercy, a sinner is led to repentance.

Thus the incomprehensible depth of the divine Scriptures is understood in different ways, so that it is shown to remain one through variety.

He founded the world immovable by himself.

Here we must understand the world as the holy Church, which is spread throughout the whole earth. Therefore it is said that this world is not to be shaken at all, because it perseveres in the solidity of faith, in which the Lord founded it immovable—not like the one of which he said above: “Let the whole earth be shaken before his face.”

Let that earth be shaken, so that it may be converted from evil works; but let this one not be shaken, since it stands firm in the solidity of true faith.

Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult.

As has often been said, “the heavens” signify the apostles and prophets, or the remaining faithful, upon whom divine majesty is known to sit as upon heaven. “The earth,” however, indicates sinners who, through the benefit of repentance, have deserved to return to God’s grace.

That earth itself can exult at the coming of its judge, since it understands that it has been absolved from sins.

Say among the nations: The Lord has reigned.

In the Psalter, however, it is added: “The Lord has reigned from the wood.” He commands those whom he instructed to worship the Lord in the holy court to proclaim the revered mysteries to the nations, so that among the nations they should say that the Lord will reign from the wood of the cross.

Not from that wood of paradise from which the devil appeared to hold the human race captive, but from this wood, from which freedom lifted its head and rose into life. On that wood the death of transgression hung; on this one the faith of confession shone forth. That wood led to the underworld; this one sends to the heavens.

“Has reigned” should be understood as “has been made known,” when the Lord Savior appeared to the world. For when did he not reign, since he has always persevered with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the power of his omnipotence?

Some translators do not have “from the wood,” but for us it is enough that the phrase has been confirmed by the authority of the Seventy translators. For the cross of the Lord corrected the crooked and distorted world [Col. 0360B] of the earth.

The sea roars, and its fullness; let the fields rejoice, and everything that is in them. Here “the sea” stands for the peoples, because, established upon the salt waters of this age, they are tossed about by various temptations. These are moved to joy when they have received the gifts of conversion. For, so that you might understand the totality of the nations, he added, “its fullness.” Here likewise we ought to understand “fields” in a good sense, because we call those things fields which are stretched out in most beautiful evenness. Thus by “fields” he means men distinguished by the praise of righteousness, not timid through pride, nor harsh through anger, but completely filled with gentle meekness. It follows:

Then the trees of the forest will praise before the Lord, because he has come to judge the earth. “Then,” he says, referring to the second coming, when he will judge the world. Trees of the forests by themselves produce bitter and barren fruits; but when they have been grafted, they grow rich with the sweetest abundance. Thus the nations, which had previously been like trees of the forests, when brought forth for fruitful cultivation, will rejoice with great gladness before the face of the Lord. But when he says, “all the trees,” he wishes that part to be understood which could be mingled with good works and transformed. Those whom he had said would rejoice as believers, he does not say will rejoice in corners or in secret places, but before the face of the Judge, when joy is immeasurable and abundant, when rewards are bestowed and security without end is granted.

And lest you think that this refers to the Lord’s first coming in the incarnation, he says in the psalm, “For he has come to judge the earth.” For if he had ended the sentence in that first clause, it might perhaps have suggested the coming which has already taken place; but when he added, “For he has come to judge the earth,” he wished us to understand only the coming which we still know to be future. The prophet Ezekiel also bears witness to this:

> Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I will bring spirit into you, and you shall live; and I will put sinews upon you, and bring flesh upon you, and stretch skin over you, and give my spirit into you, and you shall live; and you shall know that I am the Lord (Ezek. 37).

Daniel likewise says:

> And many of those sleeping in the earth’s fissures will rise: some to eternal life, and some to reproach and confusion (Dan. 12).

Here “the earth” signifies the entire people of the world, so that he may establish eternal rewards for the good and eternal punishments for the wicked.

[Col. 0361A] Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Just as the psalm above declared in its first verse that this confession ought to be directed toward the praises of the Lord, so here too it indicates that this confession is to be applied as a remedy of repentance. Yet there is no doubt that it also pertains to the Lord’s praises, since it is a greater glory of mercy to spare one who confesses than to grant pardon to one who merely intimates confession.

The congregation appears to speak as the repentant people of the Hebrews, and the prophet, by divine inspiration, addresses the remaining people, so that, having condemned the perversity of their ancient error, they may return to divine clemency. And lest anyone be terrified by the multitude of his sins, he added, “for he is good.” For who would hesitate to return to one whom he knows can come to his aid most swiftly? The Lord is rightly called good: he feeds the offender, waits for the one who has gone astray, makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5). This is also declared by the voice of Truth himself: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10).

He added, “For his mercy endures forever.” The Lord’s mercy endures forever for those who hope in his clemency and who, fearing his justice, submit themselves through obedience to his will, according to the psalmist’s words: “The Lord is well pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. 146). Hence the blessed virgin Mary also says in the Gospel canticle: “His mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him” (Luke 1).

It should also be noted that, according to another edition, where one reads, “For his mercy is unto the age,” this implies that, once the Lord’s goodness has been heard, human negligence should not withdraw anyone from diligent and earnest supplication. He therefore states the ground of the remedy, so that, by the Lord’s gift, one ought to hasten to prompt confession. “Unto the age” signifies the course of this present life, in which all who sin are miserable, and in which it is permitted for our hearts to be converted and mercy to be sought. For there is condemnation in confessing sin where judgment is already known to be present.

And say: Save us, God our Savior, and gather us from the nations, and rescue us from the peoples, so that we may give thanks to your holy name and rejoice in your praises. The earlier people, whose person was represented by the preceding words, after filling themselves with an abundance of the Lord’s praise, entreats the Father and Lord to perfect his Church from the gathering of the nations, adding this as well: “And let us rejoice in your praises”—that is, not in human boasting, but in you, where true glory and joy without end are firmly established.

Observe that here the Father is said to save. The Son is also read to save, as in the saying: “The Son of Man came to save what had perished” (Luke 19). The Holy Spirit is also proclaimed to save, as in the passage addressed to Titus: “He saved us through the bath of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3). Thus the equality and unity of the indivisible Trinity are indicated both by similar words and by similar powers. Amen.

Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age and forever; and let all the people say, “Amen,” and sing hymns to the Lord. This is the praise which, in the preceding verse, he wished the assembled peoples to utter. The holy Church also now sings this, consoling herself with so great a present good. But he says that this should be done from this age to the age that is everlasting, so that continuous praise may never become wearisome.

Yet when the devout people of the Jews sing the hymns mentioned above, who is the one who says in another manner, “Amen, Amen”? As it seems to me, it is the people of the uncircumcision, who at that time were not yet in the faith when this was sung. Nevertheless, through the power of prophecy, this people was destined to be introduced, so that, out of love for universality, it might say, “Amen, Amen”—that is, “Let it be, let it be” (Matt. 18). Thus even today, when priests are praying in the churches, the response “Amen” is given, so that the pious intention of the priests and the sound devotion of the people may agree together in prayer, and so that the sought-for unity of the faithful may more easily obtain what is asked, according to the Gospel saying in which the Savior tells his disciples:

> Amen, I say to you, that if two of you agree on earth concerning anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.

Accordingly, he left Asaph and his brothers there before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, so that they might minister continually before the ark, each day and in their appointed turns. Observe, reader, that the ministers of the Lord ought to remain continually in his ministry and minister to him each day before the ark. You will see that those who administer the divine word are not permitted to devote themselves to earthly business, but ought rather to devote themselves daily and without ceasing to evangelical preaching in the Church of God. Yet they do not do so uniformly, but distinctly, according to the character of their hearers. Hence, through different ministers, different melodies of song and different priestly offices are carried out in the tabernacle of the Lord.

Moreover, he appointed Obed-edom and his sixty-eight brothers, together with Obed-edom son of Jeduthun and Uzza, as doorkeepers; but Zadok the priest and his brothers, the priests, before the tabernacle of the Lord on the high place that was in Gibeon, to offer burnt offerings to the Lord upon the altar of burnt offering continually, morning and evening, and so forth. Accordingly, what is said here—that Zadok the priest and his brothers were appointed to the tabernacle of the Lord, which was on the high place of Gibeon, to offer burnt offerings to the Lord upon the altar of burnt offering continually, morning and evening—is understood in different ways.

Some say that, after the children of Israel entered the land of Canaan, the tabernacle of God was first at Shiloh, then at Obe, afterward at Gibeon, and finally at Zion; that only the ark of the covenant was captured for a time by the Philistines, and afterward brought back. Others assert that there was a place in Jerusalem called Gibeon, and that David placed there the tabernacle of the covenant and the ark of the covenant of the Lord. “Gibeon” is interpreted as “hill”; and they think that “high place” was spoken on account of the exalted nature of divine worship.

Furthermore, we find it written in the Book of Places that Gibeon was the metropolis and royal city of the Aeneans, and that it fell by lot to the tribe of Benjamin. Even now a village of that name is shown in the fourth mile from Bethel, toward the west, near Ramah and Rimmon, where Solomon, offering sacrifices, received a divine oracle. It too had been set apart for the Levites.

All the people returned to their homes, and David returned to bless his household as well. Here David is said to bless his household—that is, to engage in conjugal relations, so that he might increase the number of his children. Others think that “blessing” is used here by antiphrasis, while “the household” means Michal, the daughter of Saul, whom David rebuked because she was indignant when she saw him leaping before the ark of the covenant of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XVII

Concerning the words that David spoke to Nathan the prophet [Col. 0363B] about the building of the temple, and the Lord’s response through the same prophet to David; and concerning the confession with which David praised the Lord for all the benefits bestowed upon him.

**(I Chron. 17.)** When David was living in his house, he said to Nathan the prophet: Behold, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of the covenant of the Lord is under skins. And Nathan said to David: Do everything that is in your heart, for God is with you.

That night the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: Go and speak to David my servant: Thus says the Lord: You shall not build me a house in which to dwell. For I have not dwelt in a house from the time when I brought Israel out, even to this day; rather, I have always moved from place to place with the tabernacle, dwelling in a tent with all Israel.

When the king had questioned him, the prophet had answered: “Whatever is in your heart, go and do it.” But afterward, instructed by the Lord, he prohibited the very things that he had previously permitted. It is therefore plainly evident that the spirit of prophecy does not always illuminate the minds of the prophets, because, as it is written concerning the Holy Spirit, “He blows where he wills” (John 3).

Thus it happened that Elisha saw a woman weeping but did not know the reason; and when the servant wished to restrain the boy, he said: “Leave him, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not revealed it to me” (2 Kings 4). Almighty God arranges this through a great dispensation of mercy. For when he sometimes gives and sometimes withdraws the spirit of prophecy, he both raises the minds of the prophets to the heights and preserves them in humility, so that, when they receive the Spirit, they may discover what they are from God, and, again, when they do not possess the spirit of prophecy, they may recognize what they are from themselves.

But that David was forbidden to build a house for God because he was a man of blood suggests morally that the one who takes care to correct the faults of others ought to be clean within himself: he must not think about earthly things or succumb to base desires, so that he may see what others ought to avoid all the more perceptively because he himself shuns these things more truly in knowledge and conduct. An eye burdened by dust can by no means clearly see a blemish on a limb. Nor can hands holding mud wipe away dirt that has fallen upon them.

According to the sequence of the translation, the divine voice signifies this to David, who was engaged in external wars, when it says: “You shall not build me a temple, because you are a man of blood.” He builds the temple of God who devotes himself to correcting the minds of his neighbors through instruction. For we are the temple of God, because through his indwelling we are established for true life, as Paul bears witness when he says: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3). But a man of blood is forbidden to build the temple of God, because one who still lies engrossed in carnal actions ought to be ashamed to form the minds of his neighbors spiritually.

Did I ever speak even to one of the judges of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people, saying: “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?” Now therefore you shall speak to my servant David: Thus says the Lord of hosts: I took you when you were following the flock in the pastures, so that you might be leader of my people Israel. I was with you wherever you went, and I destroyed all your enemies before you, and I made you a name like the name of one of the great men who are celebrated on the earth.

Therefore he did not command a house of cedar to be built for him by any of the judges, because all of them had fought against enemies and all had been shedders of blood. “And the Lord made you a name,” it says, “like the name of one of the great men who are celebrated on the earth.” Thus he made Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, and Joshua, whose names are most famous throughout the earth.

And I gave a place to my people Israel. It will be planted and dwell there, and it will no longer be disturbed; nor will the children of iniquity wear them down as at the beginning, from the days when I gave judges to my people Israel. And I humbled all your enemies. Therefore I announce to you that the Lord will build a house for you. And when you have completed your days, so that you may go to your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build me a house, and I will make his throne firm forever. I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me; and I will not remove my mercy from him as I removed it from the one who was before you. I will establish him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne will be most firmly established forever.

Anyone who thinks that so great a promise was fulfilled in Solomon has gone far astray. He noticed the statement, “He will build me a house,” because Solomon built that famous temple, but he did not notice what is said: “His house and his kingdom will be faithful forever before me” (1 Kings 11). Let him therefore look upon Solomon’s house, full of foreign women worshiping false gods, and upon Solomon himself, the wise king, led astray and cast down by them into the same idolatry. Let him not dare to think that God either falsely promised this or was unable to foresee what kind of house Solomon’s would become.

We ought not to hesitate here, since we have already seen these things fulfilled in Christ our Lord, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1), lest we foolishly and vainly seek some other person here, like the carnal Jews. Indeed, they themselves understand so fully that the son whom they read was promised in this passage to King David was not Solomon that, although the one who was promised has already been revealed with such clarity, they still say, with marvelous blindness, that they hope for another.

A certain image of the future reality was indeed present in Solomon: he built the temple, had peace in accordance with his name—for “Solomon” means “peaceful” in Latin—and was remarkably praiseworthy at the beginning of his reign. Yet, by the shadow of what was to come, he also prophetically represented Christ the Lord himself. Hence certain things are written about him as though they had been foretold of Christ, while Holy Scripture, prophesying even through accomplished events, in a certain way sketches the figure of future things in him.

For apart from the books of divine history, where is Solomon said to have reigned? The seventy-first psalm is also inscribed with his name in its title, and in it many things are said which cannot at all apply to him but apply with the greatest clarity to Christ the Lord, so that it is evident that in Solomon some sort of figure was shadowed, whereas in Christ the reality itself was presented.

It is known within what limits Solomon’s kingdom had been confined, and yet in that psalm we read, to say nothing of other matters: “He will rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth.” We see this fulfilled in Christ. For he began his rule from the river where he was baptized by John. With John pointing him out, he began to be recognized by the disciples, who called him not only Master but also Lord.

Nor did Solomon begin to reign while his brother David was still alive—for this happened to none of those kings—for any other reason than that this too might make sufficiently clear that he is not the one prefigured by the prophecy that speaks to his father, saying: “And it shall be, when your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, that I will raise up your offspring after you, who will come from your body, and I will prepare his kingdom.”

How, then, because of what follows—“He will build me a house”—will Solomon be thought to have been the one prophesied, and not rather, because of what precedes—“When your days are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you”—will another peaceful one be understood to have been promised, one who, unlike Solomon, was foretold to arise not before but after David’s death?

However long a time might intervene before Christ Jesus came, undoubtedly he had to come after the death of King David, to whom he was promised in this way: he was the one who would build a house for God, not from wood and stones, but from human beings, such as the house whose construction fills us with joy. To this house the Apostle says, that is, to the faithful of Christ: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3).

The Lord’s blessing in the seed of David is not to be hoped for merely for a certain period, as it appeared in Solomon’s days, but forever. In this most certain hope it is said, “Let it be, let it be,” as it is written at the end of Psalm 87: “Blessed,” it says, “is the Lord forever. Let it be, let it be.” This is either the confirmation of that hope or its repetition.

Understanding this, David says in the Second Book of Kingdoms: “And he spoke concerning the house of your servant forever,” and so forth (2 Sam. 7), because a son had then been born from whom the lineage would proceed to Christ, through whom his eternal house—the same as the house of God—was to come into being. The house of David is so called because of David’s lineage; the house of God is the same house because it is God’s temple, made of human beings rather than stones, where he will dwell forever: the people with God and in their God, and God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15). He himself is the reward in peace, who is the strength in war.

Therefore, although according to the Septuagint Nathan’s words say, “And the Lord will announce to you that you will build his house,” afterward David’s words say: “For you, Lord almighty, God of Israel, have revealed to your servant’s ear, saying: I will build you a house.” We too will build this house by living well, and God will build it by assisting us so that we may live well: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126).

When the final dedication of this house comes, then what God said here through Nathan will take place: “And I will establish a place for my people Israel, and I will plant them, and they will dwell apart, and they will no longer be anxious, and the son of iniquity will no longer humble them, as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Whoever hopes for this great good in this age and on this earth is foolishly wise. Would anyone think that it was fulfilled in Solomon’s peace? Scripture commends that peace, as a shadow of the future, with excellent proclamation. But this suspicion has been carefully forestalled, since after the words “the son of iniquity will no longer humble him,” it immediately adds, “as from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel.”

Judges had been appointed over that people before kings began to exist among them, from the time when it received the promised land. And indeed the son of iniquity—that is, a hostile foreigner—humbled it at intervals, during which periods of peace are recorded as alternating with wars. There are found there periods of peace longer than the peace Solomon had, for he reigned forty years. Under the judge called Ehud there were eighty years of peace (Judg. 3).

Far be it, then, that Solomon’s times should be thought to have been promised in this prophecy—still less the times of any other king. None of them reigned in as great a peace as Solomon, nor did that nation ever possess the kingdom in such a way that it was free from anxiety about being subjected to enemies. For amid such great mutability in human affairs, such security was never granted to the people that it would not fear hostile incursions against this life.

Therefore the place promised for such peaceful and secure habitation is not earthly but eternal; and eternal habitation is owed in the mother Jerusalem above, where the people of Israel will truly be. For this name is interpreted as “seeing the Lord.” In desire for this reward, the life of faith must be conducted throughout this sorrowful pilgrimage.

In accordance with all these words and with the entire vision, Nathan spoke thus to David. When King David had come and sat before the Lord, he said: Who am I, Lord God, and what is my house, that you should grant me such things? Yet even this seemed too little in your sight; therefore you also spoke concerning the house of your servant for the future, and you made me distinguished above all human beings, Lord my God.

What does David mean when he says that the Lord made him distinguished above all human beings? Unless this is taken as hyperbole, it cannot stand at all according to the historical sense. According to the allegorical sense, however, the one designated there is he who was born from the seed of David according to the flesh—namely, our Redeemer. The Father raised him from the dead, exalted him, and established him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He subjected all things beneath his feet and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all (Eph. 1).

He also gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee might bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2).

Lord, there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, among all those whom we have heard with our ears. And what other nation is there like your people Israel? One nation on earth to which God went, to redeem it and make it a people for himself, driving out nations before it by his greatness and terrors, before the people whom he redeemed from Egypt? And you established your people Israel as your people forever.

Although this passage may seem to commemorate the earlier people’s departure from Egypt and settlement in the promised land, it most certainly signifies, with greater dignity, the liberation of the faithful people from spiritual Egypt and their transplantation into the lands of the holy Church, for the praise and honor of the Lord’s name. That people is the people of God and the true Israel, perpetually devoted to divine worship.

But ancient Israel, now deprived of honor and religion, has also been deprived of the dignity of its name and of possession of the place, especially since, scattered throughout the entire world, it wanders uncertainly without law, priesthood, or the renowned worship of God’s temple.

For you, Lord my God, have revealed your servant’s ear so that you might build him a house. And therefore your servant has found confidence to pray before you, and so forth. “You have revealed,” he says, “your servant’s ear”—that is, you have instructed his heart with an eternal hearing that you would build him a house, namely, by multiplying his descendants and enlarging his seed. From this you gave him confidence to speak about you and to proclaim your glory and praise before everyone.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Concerning David’s defeat of the Philistines and his humbling of them, of the Moabites, of Hadadezer king of Zobah, and of the Aramean of Damascus; concerning the golden, silver, and bronze vessels taken from them, which King David consecrated to the Lord; concerning Abishai’s defeat of Edom in the Valley of Salt and his establishment of a garrison in Edom, so that Idumea might serve David; and concerning David’s reign over Israel and the officials whom he appointed over the people.

**(I Chron. 18.)** After these events David defeated the Philistines, humbled them, and took Gath and its villages from the hand of the Philistines. He also defeated Moab, and the Moabites became servants of David, bringing him tribute.

By “the villages of Gath” he means the smaller cities that belonged to the metropolis. For there were five notable cities of the Philistines: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Since they were in the land of promise, they had been assigned by lot to the children of Israel, but they were not possessed by them until David’s time. Rather, they themselves often made Israel tributary to them. David humbled them, however, and, reversing the former arrangement—by which they had demanded tribute—made them tributary to himself.

Mystically, these five cities can be understood as the five bodily senses placed in the land of our flesh. As long as our old self reigned within us, they bound us with various obligations of unjust tribute. But when the true David received the kingdom within us, the exactors of tribute suddenly became tributaries; and whatever there was in our rebellious flesh was subjected to the rule of the spirit.

What he says about Moab—that the Moabites became servants of David, bringing him gifts—signifies mystically that Christ, holding all nations under his dominion, makes them render the due service owed to him, while each nation, united in confession of his name, devoutly pays him the tribute of good works.

At the same time David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, in the region of Hamath, when he went out to extend his rule as far as the Euphrates, and so forth. They say that Zobah was a city belonging to Syria of Hamath, a metropolis also called Epiphany.

Josephus shows how David devastated Syria, saying:

> When Addus, king of Damascus in Syria, heard that David had defeated Adadezer, he came with a very large army, as a friend bringing assistance, intending—as he hoped—to free him from oppression. Having engaged David again near the Euphrates, he was defeated in battle. For, when the Hebrews struck them, nearly twenty thousand of Addus’s army fell; the rest turned and fled.

The present history subsequently records this event.

Mystically, Hadadezer, whose name is interpreted as “beautiful help,” and the king of Zobah, which is interpreted as “burning” or “turning,” signify the natural fervor of paganism in its savagery. Our David fought against this and conquered it in battle, because by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 5), he overcame its errors and made it, once converted to the faith through the preaching of the Gospel, into beautiful help.

He hamstrung all the horses of the chariots, except for one hundred chariots, which he kept for himself. This means that he cut away everything rebellious against him through pride of mind and the loftiness of human wisdom that he found in them, reserving only what he judged useful and fit for the work of evangelical preaching from their studies.

The Aramean of Damascus also came to aid Hadadezer, king of Zobah. David defeated twenty-two thousand of his men and placed soldiers in Damascus, so that Syria too might serve and offer tribute. Damascus, a noble city of Phoenicia, is called by the same name as Masech, the son of Abraham’s handmaid. Damascus is interpreted as “exalted” or “moist.” And rightly so: what previously, moistened by lust and set above the spirit, thirsted insatiably for human blood, now, cleansed by the baptism of Christ and exalted by progress in the virtues, longs to receive the cup of his blood.

David also took the golden quivers that Hadadezer’s servants had possessed and brought them to Jerusalem. Golden quivers, unless I am mistaken, can signify the doctrines of the pagans, in which testimonies of human philosophy and the liberal disciplines were contained. The mystical David took these away from Hadadezer—that is, from paganism—and brought them to Jerusalem when he converted such disciplines, through holy teachers, to the service of the Catholic Church.

For the disciplines of the liberal arts are by no means useless there for conquering error and confirming the truth, provided that they are treated with piety and sound faith. It follows:

Likewise, he took a great quantity of bronze from the cities of Hadadezer, Tebah and Chun, from which Solomon made the bronze sea, the columns, and the bronze vessels. It is therefore rightly written that Solomon made the bronze sea, the columns, and the bronze vessels from the bronze that David had taken from Tebah and Chun, cities of Hadadezer. For our peaceful king converted to the use of his Church the beauty of eloquent speech, drawn from paganism converted through humility, for commending the grace of baptism and strengthening the faith, and he converted the preaching of sound doctrine to this purpose.

“Tebah” is interpreted as “the little one has come,” and “Chun” as “beauty.” Thus rightly does the person who acknowledges himself little through humility become beautiful and splendid in the adornment of virtues.

King David also consecrated to the Lord all the golden, silver, and bronze vessels, together with the silver and gold that he had taken from all the nations—from Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon, as well as from the Philistines and Amalek.

What does it signify that David sanctified to the Lord the golden, silver, and bronze vessels that he had taken from all the nations, except that Christ sanctifies to the Lord all whom he calls from every nation to his faith: some in the place of gold—that is, distinguished by spiritual understanding; others as silver—that is, shining with the brilliance of eloquence; and others resonant with divine preaching, so that, faithfully discerning in his tabernacle, they may most worthily perform his ministry forever?

Abishai, son of Zeruiah, defeated Edom in the Valley of Salt—eighteen thousand men—and established a garrison in Edom, so that Idumea might serve David, and so forth. In the Book of Kingdoms it is written as follows:

> David also made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt, after he had captured Syria (2 Sam. 8).

He is said to have made a name for himself because, after eighteen thousand had been struck down in the Valley of Salt, he erected a triumphal arch for himself. He also made a name for himself when, after conquering Syria of Damascus and Syria of Zobah, he is understood to have erected another triumphal arch.

And if anyone is troubled by the fact that in many Latin manuscripts David is found to have struck down not eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt but twelve thousand, let him know that this has arisen through a scribal error that has become established in those manuscripts. In truth, David struck down eighteen thousand in the same Valley of Salt, while Joab struck down twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm 58. Here, however, eighteen thousand are reported to have been killed by Abishai; and this is understood to have been done by him as commander of the bravest soldiers, but the victory is attributed to David because of the dignity of the royal name.

For what else is signified by the multitude struck down by David in the Valley of Salt, except that our Redeemer, through the discriminating division of his judgment among those who think wrongly about him, [lacuna]

> Extinguish the folly of immoderate taste. Hence it is said by a certain Wise Man:

> The one who is perverse of heart does not find good, and the one who twists his tongue falls into evil (Prov. 17).

Thus David reigned over all Israel and administered judgment and justice to all his people. What does it mean that David is read to have administered judgment and justice to all his people, except that our Savior continually bestows judgment and equity upon the entire people of the Church?

The historical David did not preserve justice everywhere, for transgression of the law shows him to be blameworthy (2 Sam. 11). But the true David, who committed no sin and came to take away the sins of the world (1 Pet. 2), assigns judgments to his entire people, concerning whom it is written: “The righteous Lord loves righteousness; his face beholds equity” (Ps. 10). “There is no partiality with God, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10). “He loves mercy and truth; he will give grace and glory” (Ps. 8). “Blessed is the Lord forever, from age to age, and let all the people say: Let it be, let it be” (Ps. 81).

Moreover, Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder. The recorders—that is, the remembrancers—were those who, having noted events and causes, brought them to the king’s memory.

Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests. In Chronicles Abiathar’s son is written as Abimelech, but in Kingdoms as Ahimelech. “Abimelech” is interpreted as “my father is king,” while “Ahimelech” means “my brother is king”; the difference between the names arose from the events themselves (1 Sam. 21).

Morally, this instructs the priests of the Church that those who, because of the dignity of their office, occupy the place of fathers should, through humility, gentleness, and equality of fellowship, be regarded by the name of brothers. Thus they may know what the chief of the apostles warned the shepherds of the Church in his Epistle, saying: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 3).

And Susa the scribe, while Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the forces of the Cherethites and Pelethites. Susa is written in Paralipomenon, whereas in Kings he is called Saraiah (IV Kings 25); Susa is interpreted as “joy,” and Saraiah as “prince of the Lord.” Cherethites, moreover, is interpreted as “destroyers,” and Pelethites as “admirable ones” and “life-givers.” Some say that these were the seventy judges appointed in their place whom Moses, at the Lord’s command, had selected in the wilderness (Exodus 24). Others say that the Cherethites were assigned to exact punishment from the guilty, while the Pelethites were appointed to defend the innocent from their oppressors.

Now the sons of David were first at the king’s hand. Hence it is written in Kings that the sons of David were priests (II Kings 8); but both passages agree in meaning, since the present text calls those among them “first” as priests on account of their nobility and precedence. These were the men born in Hebron. Mystically, however, the true sons of David are the five faithful ones whom the holy Church gives birth to through water and the word. These become priests because they are members of the supreme Priest, who, having become high priest according to the order of Melchizedek, possesses an everlasting priesthood (Psalm 109; Hebrews 7). Thus the apostle Peter, writing to believers, says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of possession” (I Peter 2). And again: “They themselves, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses, into a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (ibid.). They are rightly said to be first at the king’s hand, because through good works they deserve to draw near to the heavenly King; in them he himself produces an admirable effect of the virtues as an example to others. For the more one advances in faith, which works through love, the more he rejoices that he possesses proximity to the supreme King.

## CHAPTER XIX

On Hanun son of Nahash, king of the Ammonites, who insulted David’s messengers sent to him, and on the war waged against him for this reason.

**(I Chronicles 19.)** It happened that Nahash, king of the sons of Ammon, died, and his son reigned in his place. David said: “I will show kindness to Hanun, son of Nahash, for his father showed me favor.” Nahash was king of Ammon, who is mentioned in Kings as the man against whom Saul first fought in defense of Jabesh-gilead and whom he defeated (II Kings 10). Since he was therefore an enemy of Saul, he showed favor to David whenever the latter came to him (I Kings 11).

David sent messengers to console him over the death of his father. When they had arrived in the land of the sons of Ammon to console Hanun, the princes of the sons of Ammon said to Hanun: “Perhaps you think that David has sent men to you to honor your father and console you; but you do not realize that his servants have come to you in order to spy out, investigate, and search your land.” Hanun therefore shaved the heads of David’s young men, shaved them, cut their garments in half as far as the groin, and sent them away. In Kings it is written that he shaved off half of their beards and cut their garments in half as far as the buttocks. But in Paralipomenon it is read that Hanun himself shaved the heads of David’s young men, shaved them, and cut their garments in half as far as the groin (II Kings 10). There is no contradiction in what is found, since what is lacking in one account is contained in the other. Hence it is inferred that they were shaven-headed, had their beards shaved, and had their garments cut in front and behind.

When they had gone away and reported this to David, he sent to meet them, for they had suffered a great insult. He ordered them to remain at Jericho until their beards grew, and then to return, and so forth. What else does this signify than the wickedness of the devil against the Church?
