For Hanun, whose name is interpreted as “their sorrow,” whom could he better signify than the devil, who appears to be the ruler of the spiritual Ammonites—that is, of the evil spirits—the people of sorrow, who are always placed in distress, by which he desires to oppress and constrain human beings?

Hanun therefore shaves half of the beard of David’s messengers when the ancient enemy stains and dishonors the speech or conduct of certain preachers of the word of God by corrupting it. He cuts their garments as far as the groin when he reveals to human eyes the shameful deeds that he himself had persuaded them to commit. But it is necessary that those whom the devil thus confounds should sit in Jericho until their beards grow—that is, until they become a reproach and disgrace to the better sort and become anathema to all—until, through good effort, the appearance of a beard, that is, an increase of virtues, arises in them and they are judged worthy of the presence of their king.

Certainly one must not believe that our David will allow his soldiers to remain unavenged. He will overcome his enemies when he gathers his army and will avenge the injury done to his own—not only now confounding his adversaries through the victory of his saints, but also, at the final judgment, handing them over to be tortured in everlasting fire by a just sentence.

## CHAPTER XX

On the fact that Joab struck Rabbah and destroyed it, whose triumph he attributed to David’s name; and on the various wars that David completed against the Philistines, in which he also killed certain giants.

**(I Chronicles 20.)** It happened, after the year had come full circle, at the time when kings customarily go forth to war, that Joab gathered the army and the strength of the forces and devastated the land of the sons of Ammon. In Hebrew it is read as follows: “At the time when kings had gone forth to war.” By “these kings” he means those who went forth to fight against David—namely, the king of Rehob, the king of Istob, the king of Zobah, and the king of Maacah. These were certainly kings of Syria who, having been hired for pay by the king of Moab, wished to fight against David; they are said to have been defeated by him.

He went on and besieged Rabbah. David, however, remained in Jerusalem while Joab struck Rabbah and destroyed it. David took the crown of Milcom from its head and found in it a talent’s weight of gold and very precious gems; from these he made himself a diadem, and so forth. Milcom is not, in fact, the proper name of the king; rather, Milcom is interpreted as “their king.” According to the Hebrews, “their king” is the name of their idol, which is here called Milcom. David is said to have melted and purified the gold and gems of this diadem according to the law and to have made himself a diadem from them.

The Hebrews further relate that it was unlawful for a Jewish man to desire any gold or silver from idols because of the precepts of the law, which forbid idolatry. Therefore Ithai the Ethusite, who had come to David from the Philistine nation, tore the diadem from Milcom’s head, so that it would be permissible for the Hebrew king to take from a man’s hand what he was not permitted to take from the head of an idol.

What does this victory of David over the Ammonites signify—the victory which his commander began by fighting, but which the king himself completed—except the victory of our King among all nations? David’s commander wages war against the enemies when the order of the holy preachers raises the shield of faith against the mighty of the world; but the end of the struggle and the triumph of the war are attributed solely to Christ the King, because all royal power and authority are ascribed to him. For, according to the Apostle, “it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). And “he always leads us in triumph in Christ” (II Corinthians 2).

David therefore took the crown of the hostile people’s king from his head and fashioned a diadem for himself from it, when our Redeemer, taking the kingdom from the opposing power, prepared for himself a noble and beautiful insignia. What crown of David can better be understood than the assembly of the Catholic people, which nobly surrounds our head, namely Christ the King, with a believing heart and, living worthily, fittingly crowns him? For every labor, struggle, and victory of the saints is referred to the honor of the heavenly King, because he is the one before whom “every knee bows, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth,” and every tongue confesses “that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2).

Rabbath is therefore a city of the kingdom of Ammon, which is now called Philadelphia and which the prophet Jeremiah also mentions (Jeremiah 49). Rabbath is interpreted as “many.” The Savior says in the Gospel: “Many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8).

After this, a war began at Gezer against the Philistines. In it Sobachai the Hushathite struck Saphai of the race of the Rephaim and humbled them. Josephus relates this war in the seventh book of his histories as follows:

> “When the Palestinians had gathered at the city of Gezer, the king, hearing of this, sent an army against them. Among them there was at that time an excellent champion, and Sabba the Chetean fought with the greatest distinction. He was one of David’s strongest men. He famously killed many of the enemy and overcame, by the great daring of his strength and courage, the offspring of the giants who exulted in their might. Among the Hebrews he was the author of this victory.”

When the text says, “In it Sobachai the Hushathite struck Ziphaim of the race of the Rephaim,” Kings has “of the stock of Arapha,” because they were the sons of Orpah, Naomi’s daughter-in-law, from the land of Moab (II Kings 21). What is written as Gezer in Paralipomenon is written as Gob in Kings (ibid.). Gob is interpreted as “a pool” or “a locust.” Gezer is interpreted as “arrangement,” signifying that just as locusts destroy grass, so the sons of Arapha destroyed Israel.

Another war was fought against the Philistines. In it “the God-given son of the Forest, the Bethlehemite,” struck the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear-shaft was like a weaver’s beam. Where the present text reads “the God-given son of the Forest,” the Hebrews say that the text reads: [lacuna] “Elhanan son of Jare,” which is interpreted as “forest.”

In Kings this war is likewise described as follows: “There was a third war at Gob against the Philistines, in which Adeodatus, son of the Forest, the Polymitarius, a Bethlehemite, struck Goliath the Gittite, whose spear-shaft was like a weaver’s beam” (ibid.).

A Hebrew interpreter therefore explains Adeodatus in this way: Gob is interpreted as “a pool.” It is called a pool because, just as a person is thrown into a pit of lions, so David himself cast himself against Goliath. Adeodatus is David himself; he is called Adeodatus, “God-given,” because he was chosen by God for the kingdom. “Son of the Forest” means that he was brought forth from the forest where he pastured sheep. “Polymitarius,” “the many-threaded one,” is used because his mother was of the race of Beseled. “Bethlehemite” is used because Naomi and Ruth returned to Bethlehem in a time of abundance, and because Ruth became known to Boaz on account of bread; for this reason the same place was called “the house of bread.”

That Adeodatus himself is David is made clear by what follows, where it says: “These were born of Arapha in Gath, and they fell into the hands of David and his servants.” The Jews also consider this Arapha, the mother of the giants, to be Orpah, Naomi’s daughter-in-law, as we showed above.

Another war also occurred at Gath. In it there was a very tall man who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—that is, twenty-four in all—and he too had been born from the stock of Rapha. He blasphemed Israel, and Jonathan son of Shimea, David’s brother, struck him.

Josephus writes of this war as follows:

> “After the Palestinians had rested for a short time, they again encamped around a city that was not far from the borders of the Hebrews. Among them was a man who, in his boldness, was six cubits tall; he also had on each foot and on each hand one finger more than nature normally grants, that is, six. Against him, Jonathan son of Sames fought from David’s army beside the wall; after defeating him, he attained the summit of the greatest glory as the author of the entire victory. For that Palestinian also boasted that he was descended from the offspring of giants. After this battle they no longer engaged in combat against the Israelites.”

It should be noted that in Paralipomenon Scripture counts three principal wars of David against the Philistines, whereas in Kings it counts four. The fourth war there is the one also placed first (II Kings 28), in which Jesbi of Nob, who was of the race of Arapha, tried to strike David while David was fighting against the Philistines. His spear weighed three hundred ounces, and he was girded with a new sword. Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David’s aid and killed the Philistine after striking him.

Both numbers, however—three and four—can be fitted to one meaning. There are three divisions of time: past, present, and future. Likewise, four changes divide the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. What do these four wars of David and his servants against the Palestinians signify except the war of Christ, which throughout the whole time of this life is ceaselessly waged in his members against all the faithless of this age and against spiritual wickedness? Although worldly arrogance or the insolence of the wicked may rise up against the Church of God in Christ, nevertheless every power of the adversaries yields to the true David, that is, to Christ the King, when he commands and directs the battles of his servants; all adversaries are conquered, overthrown, and reduced to nothing.

Hence the Psalmist confidently says in the person of the Church: “Vain is the salvation of man. In God we shall do valiantly, and he himself will bring those who afflict us to nothing” (Psalm 59).

## CHAPTER XXI

On the fact that David ordered the Israelites to be counted and thereby offended the Lord, because of which a most grievous plague of mortality was sent upon Israel; and on the fact that, after seeing the angel of the Lord who had struck down the people, David made an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings there, and called upon the Lord, who heard him.

**(I Chronicles 21.)** Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to count Israel. David said to Joab and to the rulers of the people: “Go and count Israel from Beersheba to Dan, and bring me the number, so that I may know it.” Joab answered: “May God increase his people a hundredfold beyond what they are. Why does my lord the king seek this, so that it may be reckoned as a sin against Israel?” But the king’s word prevailed. Joab went out, traveled throughout all Israel, and returned to Jerusalem.

How can the text say that the taking of the census ordered by the king was reckoned as a sin against Israel, when the transgression appears to have been the king’s rather than the people’s? But he calls “sin” the death that first entered the world as the consequence of sin (Romans 5). This death therefore spread among the people alone. Nevertheless, one must understand that the acts of rulers are arranged according to the qualities of their subjects, so that, because of the evil of the flock, even the life of a good shepherd may fall into wrongdoing.

That man who was praised by God’s testimony (I Kings 13), that David the prophet who was conscious of heavenly mysteries, was suddenly inflated with the swelling of pride when he counted the people and thereby sinned; yet, while David sinned, the people received the punishment. Why was this? Because the hearts of rulers are disposed according to the merit of the peoples. The just Judge corrected the fault of the sinner by their punishment, since he had sinned on their account. But because he himself—growing proud by his own will—was not free from guilt, he also received the punishment of his own fault. For the wrath that struck the people bodily also overthrew their ruler through inward anguish of heart.

It is certainly true that the merits of rulers and peoples are so mutually connected that often, through the guilt of shepherds, the life of the people becomes worse, and often, through the merit of the people, the life of the shepherds is changed. But because rulers have their own Judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of those who rule. For the Lord did not cast down the money-changers’ tables and overturn the seats of those selling doves through no purpose of his own (Matthew 21): he clearly signified that, through teachers, he judges the life of the people, but that he examines teachers through himself.

Even the faults of subjects—which teachers either neglect to judge or are unable to judge—are, without doubt, reserved for his judgment. Therefore, provided that faith is preserved, it is indeed a virtue if whatever concerns a superior is endured. Nevertheless, what displeases should be humbly suggested, if it may perhaps be possible to correct it. But one must take the greatest care that an unregulated defense of justice does not pass into pride, lest, while righteousness is loved carelessly, humility—the very teacher of righteousness—be lost; lest anyone despise having as his superior one whom he happens to find blameworthy in some action.

Against this swelling of pride, the mind of subjects is subdued for the preservation of humility when its own weakness is constantly considered. We neglect to examine our own strength truthfully; and because we believe ourselves stronger than we are, we judge those who have been placed over us with severity. The less we know ourselves, the more we see those whom we strive to rebuke. These are individual evils often committed by subjects against superiors and often by superiors against subjects: those who rule consider all their subjects less wise than they themselves are, while those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers and think that, if they themselves happened to hold authority, they could act better.

As a result, rulers often see less prudently what ought to be done, because the very cloud of exaltation darkens their eyes; and sometimes one who is subject does, after becoming a superior, what he formerly condemned when subject. Because he commits what he had judged, he is at least ashamed that he judged it. Therefore, just as superiors must take care lest the higher position exalt their hearts through the opinion that they alone possess wisdom, so subjects must ensure that the actions of their rulers do not become displeasing to them.

If the life of teachers is rightly criticized, their subjects ought nevertheless to revere the teacher even when displeased. One must also carefully observe that, if you scorn imitating someone, you do not therefore scorn venerating him. A subtle balance of righteousness and humility must be maintained, so that the blameworthy actions of teachers displease the minds of their subjects without causing those minds to depart from preserving reverence for the teaching office.

David gave him the number of those whom they had surveyed, and the total number of Israel was found to be one million one hundred thousand men who drew the sword. From Judah there were four hundred seventy thousand warriors. He did not count Levi and Benjamin, because he carried out the king’s command unwillingly.

In Kings, however, it is written as follows: “Joab gave the king the number of the census of the people, and there were found in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men who drew the sword, and in Judah five hundred thousand fighting men” (II Kings 24).

The Hebrews assert that the number recorded in Paralipomenon—namely, one million one hundred thousand men who drew the sword from Israel and four hundred seventy thousand warriors from Judah—was found by Joab, but that the writer did not wish to disclose the total except insofar as it is written in the book of Samuel, where only those who survived the angelic slaughter are included.

As for the statement that Levi and Benjamin were not counted: Levi was not counted because of the dignity of the priesthood, since it held precedence; Benjamin was not counted because, in recent times, it had nearly fallen into destruction by the fraternal sword.

What had been commanded displeased the Lord, and he struck Israel. David said to the Lord: “I have sinned greatly in doing this. I beg you, Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted foolishly.” And the Lord spoke to Gad, David’s seer, saying: “Go and speak to David, and say to him: Thus says the Lord. I give you three choices; choose one that you wish me to do for you.”

When Gad had come to David, he said to him: “Thus says the Lord: Choose what you wish: either three years of pestilence, or three months of fleeing before your enemies, unable to escape their sword, or three days of the sword of the Lord and death ranging through the land, with the angel of the Lord killing throughout all the borders of Israel. Now therefore consider what answer I shall give to the one who sent me.”

David said to Gad: “I am pressed by anguish on every side, but it is better for me to fall into the hands of the Lord, for his mercies are many, than into the hands of men.” The Lord therefore sent a pestilence upon Israel, and seventy thousand men fell in Israel, and so forth.

In the book of Kings it is written as follows: “David’s heart struck him after the people had been counted. David said to the Lord: I have sinned greatly in this deed. But I beg you, Lord, transfer the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted exceedingly foolishly,” and the rest.

Here one must note that David is said to have offended the Lord by counting the people because he did not observe the precepts of the law in this matter. For in the book of Numbers the Lord is read to have commanded Moses as follows: “Take the census of the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, by their clans and their houses, recording the names of each one, every male from twenty years old and upward, all the strong men of Israel; and you shall count them by their companies, you and Aaron” (Numbers 1).

Since David ordered everyone to be counted generally, both those under twenty years of age and those over twenty, he therefore experienced God’s indignation.

The book of Exodus likewise says: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: When you take the census of the sons of Israel according to their number, each shall give a price for his life to the Lord, and there shall be no plague among them when they have been counted. Everyone who is registered shall give half a shekel according to the measure of the sanctuary. A shekel contains twenty obols. Half a shekel shall be offered to the Lord. Whoever is counted, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the price. The rich shall not add to the half-shekel, and the poor shall not subtract from it. You shall take the money received, which has been contributed by the sons of Israel, and give it for the uses of the tabernacle of testimony, so that it may be a memorial for them before the Lord and he may show mercy to their lives” (Exodus 30).

David forgot to do this, and for that reason he offended the Lord; because of this, the plague came upon Israel.

Nor should we pass over the fact that Josephus, mentioning this passage, reports the following:

> “When the prophets declared to David that God was angry with him, he began to entreat him and to ask that he be gracious and grant pardon for his sin. Then God sent the prophet Gad to him, carrying three conditions of punishment, so that he might choose whichever of them he approved: whether he wished famine to arise in the province for three years, or to be defeated by his enemies in battle for three months, or whether disease and sickness should occur for days among the Hebrews. He, however, falling into the anxiety of this choice among all the worst possibilities, was troubled and appeared greatly confused in mind. When the prophet said that one of these things was certainly imminent and demanded an answer quickly, so that he could report the condition chosen by David, the king reflected that, if he chose famine, he would seem to impose it upon others while he himself, possessing abundant grain, would not suffer want whereas the others would be in distress. Likewise, if he chose three months of victory for the enemy, he himself, having very brave men and guards around him, would fear nothing, nor would his army be subjected to it. In these circumstances, therefore, he chose a common suffering of kings and subjects, in which fear would be equal for all, saying that it was better to fall into the hands of God than into those of enemies. Hearing this, the prophet reported it to God, who sent disease and death into the army of the Hebrews. They were dying in different ways, so that the sickness could not easily be recognized. Some died from the causes of many illnesses, which could not readily be identified. One died after another, and the secretly approaching evil brought death swiftly. Some perished amid severe pains and gave up their spirit with cries and groans. Others were inflamed by the very sufferings, so that they could not care for their bodies but collapsed from exhaustion. Others, when sudden darkness snatched away their efforts, were immediately suffocated and expired. Others died upon the very dead whom they were burying, leaving their burials unfinished. When the pestilential illness began killing them from the morning hour until the completion of the hour of the midday meal, seventy thousand were finished.”

When the text says that seventy thousand men were killed from Israel, only the heads of the people and the elders are counted here. The Hebrews assert that, from the entire people, as many thousands were killed as the number recorded in Paralipomenon exceeds the number contained in Kings. They say that in Paralipomenon both those who remained and those who were killed were counted together, whereas in Kings they are designated only as “VI” [the reading is uncertain], as was shown above.

He also sent an angel to Jerusalem to strike it. When it was being struck, the Lord saw and had compassion because of the magnitude of the evil, and he commanded the angel who was striking: “Enough; now let your hand cease.”

As for the statement that the Lord saw and had compassion, the Hebrews say that the priest Zadok, clothed in priestly vestments, entreated the Lord, imitating his father Aaron, and that the Lord saw his prayers and devotion and had compassion.

The angel of the Lord was standing beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of God standing between earth and heaven, with a drawn sword in his hand turned against Jerusalem. Then he and the elders of Israel, clothed in sackcloth, fell facedown upon the ground.

David said to the Lord: “Am I not the one who ordered the people to be counted? I am the one who sinned; I am the one who did evil. What has this flock deserved? Lord my God, let your hand, I beg you, turn against me and against my father’s house, but let your people not be struck.” The angel of the Lord commanded Gad to tell David to go up and build an altar to the Lord God on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, and so forth.

In Kings it is likewise written: “The angel of the Lord was beside the threshing floor of the Jebusite,” and so forth (II Kings 24).

Finally, Areuna is interpreted as “ark,” and Ornan in Latin sounds as “light for us.” It was therefore fitting that, when David wished to appease the Lord for the offense that he had committed, he was commanded to build an altar at the threshing floor of Areuna or Ornan. From this everyone may infer that the divine power cannot otherwise be appeased by a human being unless, in the threshing floor of his heart, by the light of right faith and true love, he devoutly establishes an altar for God, on which he offers to God the acceptable sacrifice of pious confession and praise.

The same prophet rightly makes this clear in the Psalms, where he speaks in the person of the Lord: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Psalm 49). And again: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50).

The threshing floor of Areuna, or the threshing floor of Ornan, is Jerusalem itself.

David therefore gave Ornan six hundred shekels of gold of the fairest weight for the site, built an altar there to the Lord, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. In Kings, however, it is written: “David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver” (II Kings 24).

Hence the Hebrews maintain that, in this difference of numbers, the oxen should be understood to have been bought for fifty shekels of silver, while the threshing floor was bought for six hundred shekels of gold.

Others say that this difference in the purchase means that what is recorded in the book of Kings—that the threshing floor was bought for only fifty shekels—expresses only the site of the altar where he offered the burnt offering. What Paralipomenon relates, however, namely that the threshing floor was purchased for six hundred shekels of gold, signifies the site of the entire temple, where Solomon later built the temple and its courts.

He called upon the Lord, and the Lord answered him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering. Under Moses, and under David, Solomon, and Elijah alone, fire descended from heaven upon an altar (III Kings 18). Under Manoah, however, an angel burst forth from the rock in flame (Judges 13).

The Lord then commanded the angel, and he returned his sword to its sheath. Immediately, when David saw that the Lord had answered him on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed victims there.

The tabernacle of the Lord that Moses had made in the desert and the altar of burnt offerings were at that time on the high place at Gibeon. David was unable to go to the altar to entreat the Lord there, for he had been terrified by the sight of the sword of the angel of the Lord. David ought, according to what was commanded in the law, to have sacrificed offerings on the Lord’s altar before the tabernacle of the covenant; but because of the sudden crisis he had no time to go there, or perhaps the matter did not occur to him.

He therefore calls the sword of the angel of the Lord the plague of death that the Lord sent upon human beings through angelic ministry. Thus in Exodus the Lord is read to have descended into Egypt and killed the firstborn of the Egyptians (Exodus 12); but this too, like the present event, is believed to have been accomplished through angelic ministry, because the divine nature is not moved locally. Rather, remaining eternally the same in itself, it disposes, governs, and directs all things by its eternal power.

## CHAPTER XXII

On the fact that David determined to build a temple to the Lord in that place, which was accomplished by his son Solomon, to whom he gave very abundant funds and resources; and on the fact that David instructed Solomon concerning the construction of the Lord’s temple and assigned to him various implements of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, as well as wood and stones, which he himself had gathered for this purpose, together with many craftsmen and masons for the work of the temple.

**(I Chronicles 22.)** David said: “This is the house of God, and this is the altar for the burnt offering of Israel.” He ordered proselytes from the land of Israel to be gathered and appointed masons to cut and polish stones for the building of the house of the Lord.

According to the Hebrews, it had once happened at that place that Abraham offered his son Isaac, when, having already been prepared to kill his son and present him as a burnt offering, a ram suddenly appeared and stood entangled in the thicket; Abraham sacrificed it in place of his son, as we have said (Genesis 22).

David gathered proselytes from the land of Israel and appointed masons to split and polish stones because our Redeemer chose from the land of the Church craftsmen for the house of God. With the axe of the Scriptures they would cut down the unformed ways of human beings, and with the adze of the word of God they would polish them, so that they might fit together appropriately in the spiritual building through the various joints of faith and love, in accordance with what is said through Hosea: “I hewed them by the prophets, and I killed them by the words of my mouth; and my judgments shall go forth as the light. For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than a burnt offering” (Hosea 6).

David also prepared a great quantity of iron for the nails of the doors and for the joinings and connections, and an immeasurable weight of bronze. The cedar wood that the Sidonians and Tyrians brought to David could not be reckoned.

What did David’s preparing these things for his son Solomon for the building of the house of God signify except that the Fathers of the Old Testament, from whom Christ according to the flesh derived his origin (Romans 9), prepared through teaching and action the instruments appropriate for the building of the spiritual edifice, so that, when our King came—truly the peaceful one—he might confirm the faith of the Gospel through their contributions, that is, through their testimonies, and adorn his Church with the various ornaments of the Scriptures?

He also prepared a great quantity of iron for the nails of the doors and for the joinings and connections when he ordered the firmness of faith through sacred teachings, so that those entering the Church might be fastened by the goads of the fear of God and might be bound to one another through the covenant of love and fellowship in that same faith.

Hence the same Psalmist entreats the Lord, saying: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I am afraid of your judgments” (Psalm 118). Elsewhere he speaks of that particular Jerusalem, saying: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is joined together in unity” (Psalm 121). And shortly afterward: “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers.”

He also prepared bronze when melodious readings and spiritual songs were composed by those same holy Fathers for the instruction of the holy Church.

He also prepared cedar wood when he preserved in those same Scriptures men renowned for their virtues as examples for the faithful: Abel, Enosh, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, and the other patriarchs, who walked with the Lord and were taken from the world, whose righteousness was not forgotten; Moses and the prophets, who foretold the coming of the righteous one (Acts 7) and proclaimed through pious teachings the mysteries that the holy Church now holds for salvation; and the other righteous men who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained the promise (Hebrews 11).

The Sidonians and Tyrians therefore brought these woods to Jerusalem, because not only through the apostles preaching and through the first dispensers of the Gospel from Judea, but also through those teachers who were chosen from among the nations for the work of the word, such men came to the knowledge of the Church that, through their teachings and examples, the house of God was built daily from living stones.

David said: “Solomon my son is a little child, and tender; but the house which I intend to build for the Lord ought to be such that it is named in all regions. Therefore I shall prepare everything necessary.” For this reason, before his death he prepared all the expenses. He called Solomon his son and commanded him to build a house for the Lord God of Israel.

When David says that Solomon his little son was a child and tender, while the house he had decided to build would be great, this signifies that in the times of the Old Testament the knowledge of Christ’s incarnation was obscure in comparison with the truth of the Gospel, in which all those things were openly declared that had been indicated figuratively in the law. Or it signifies that at that time there was a small number of believers, who are the members of Christ, in comparison with the faithful who were to exist under the New Testament. For then was fulfilled what is written: “God is known in Judah [only], and his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV); and now what the same prophet foretold in another psalm, saying: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and they shall glorify your name; for you are great and do wondrous things. You alone are God” (Ps. LXXXV).

For this reason, before his death he prepared all the expenses, since the law and the prophets alike showed by their prophecies how holy men, distinguished by virtues and the splendor of wisdom, belonged to the spiritual building of the house of God. Did Moses not prepare the expenses of God’s house, when he spoke to the children of Israel in Deuteronomy, saying:

“O Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances?” (Deut. X).

“Be children of the Lord your true God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make baldness over the dead, because you are a holy people to the Lord your God” (Deut. XIV).

Thus also Isaiah—did he not prepare the resources for building the house of God? By the spirit of prophecy, speaking in the person of the Lord to the future people of believers, he says:

“Hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen. Thus says the Lord, who made and formed you from the womb, your helper: Do not fear, Jacob my servant and upright one whom I have chosen; for I shall pour water upon the thirsty and streams upon the dry land. I shall pour out my Spirit upon your seed and my blessing upon your stock” (Isa. XLIV).

And again:

“Your walls,” he says, “are always before my eyes. Your builders have come; those who destroyed and devastated you shall go out from you. Lift your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered and come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament and surround yourself with them like a bride” (Isa. XLIX).

And elsewhere:

“I shall dwell in them and walk among them; they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Lev. XXVI).

Hence Jeremiah also says:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—a covenant which they made void, and I ruled over them, says the Lord. But this shall be the covenant that I shall make with the house of Israel: after those days, says the Lord, I shall place my law within them and write it upon their heart; I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. No longer shall a man teach his neighbor, or a man his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord, because I shall forgive their iniquities and shall remember their sin no more” (Jer. XXXI).

By all these testimonies, therefore, it is shown that the house of the heavenly building had been foretold long beforehand, but was truly completed at the coming of Christ our Lord. For when he came, he himself bestowed the blessing which he had formerly given through his servant under the law; and through the preaching of the Gospel, with the grace of the Holy Spirit illuminating it, he bestowed knowledge of himself upon all without respect of persons—now in faith, but afterward in the contemplation of truth itself.

David said to Solomon:

“My son, it was my desire to build a house for the name of the Lord my God; but the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘You have shed much blood and fought many wars; you shall not build a house for my name, because you have shed so much blood before me’” (1 Chron. XXII).

What does it mean that David says the Lord forbade him to build God’s house because of the shedding of much blood, except that it shows that the Jews, because of their carnal observance of the law, their bloody works, and the physical slaughter of victims, could not restore to the Lord the temple of the spiritual building? For while they eagerly pursued earthly things, they were less concerned to seek heavenly things.

Or it signifies those Jews whose hands were stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Lord himself. Because of the ferocity of their hearts, they could not recognize the mercy of Christ, who came into this world to save sinners (1 Tim. I), cleansing those who believe in him from every stain of sin and making them a people acceptable to himself, zealous for good works (Tit. II).

Therefore Truth himself reproaches that same people under the name of Jerusalem in the Gospel, saying:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house is left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

This dignity, therefore, of building the true temple was reserved for our peaceful one. Concerning him the Lord himself said to David:

“The son who shall be born to you shall be a man of greatest quiet; for I shall cause him to rest from all his enemies round about, and for this reason he shall be called peaceful. I shall give peace and rest to Israel throughout all his days. He shall build a house for my name; he shall be my son, and I shall be his father. I shall establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.”

In the seventy-first psalm, whose title is “A Psalm concerning Solomon,” the prophet David foretells, through manifest mysteries, the coming of our peaceful one—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ. Among other things he says:

“Justice shall arise in his days, and abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted.”

And likewise: “He shall arise in the day, at the time of the holy incarnation, when he was to be born from the Virgin.” For Justice is the Word of the Father, who made every creature and all temporal things. Of him it is written: “Truth has arisen from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven.” He added: “And abundance of peace, until the moon is exalted” (Ps. LXXXIV). Here also “he shall arise” must be understood.

The abundance of peace, therefore, exists while the religion of the Christians is spread throughout the whole world. “Until the moon is exalted,” he said—that is, as long as the Church extends and increases, or until the appointed number of the predestined is complete. A little earlier in the same psalm he says: “Let the mountains receive peace for your people” (ibid.). By the mountains are signified the apostles and prophets, who, firmly raised toward heavenly things, draw near to heavenly grace. Such men receive peace—that is, Christ—to preach him to the faithful people. For that people is the Lord’s, which has believed in him and conducted itself in a spiritual manner.

Concerning this peaceful one Isaiah writes:

“For a child is born to us, and a Son is given to us; and the government is upon his shoulder. His name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His government shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isa. IX).

He is our peace, according to Paul’s testimony, who made both one (Eph. II), and who says to his disciples in the Gospel:

“My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

When he came into the world, he preached peace to those who were near and peace to those who were far away, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father (Eph. II).

“He,” he says, “shall build a house for my name.” This house, as the Apostle testifies, is us, if we retain firm faith to the end (Heb. III). Hence the Apostle of the Gentiles, writing to the Gentiles themselves, says:

“Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone. In him the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you also are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit” (Eph. II).

“And he,” he says, “shall be my son, and I shall be his father; and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.”

The eighty-eighth psalm agrees with this statement, where it is written in the person of the Lord:

“He shall call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation’; and I shall make him my firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth. Forever I shall keep my mercy for him, and my faithful covenant with him. I shall establish his seed forever and his throne as the days of heaven.”

This is said according to the form of a servant. In these four verses the wickedness of the Jews and heretics is utterly overthrown. For what could be clearer or more explicit than that he is to be believed the Son who calls upon the Father, and again is to be believed the Father who calls him Son? Although these two names are relative to one another, and one would be sufficient for the power of both to be understood, nevertheless, in order to exclude every doubt of ambiguity, he used both and confirmed both. Yet the mad perversity of the Jews does not cease to go astray, even though the cause of their error has been removed.

What follows—“And I shall make him my firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth”—must also be examined. Why did he say “firstborn,” as though the Father had begotten the Son substantially in such a way that another son would follow? This manner of expression is plainly characteristic of divine Scripture. So also in the Gospel, concerning Joseph and Mary, it says: “And he did not know her until she had borne her firstborn son” (Matt. I). Will it therefore follow that the Virgin Mary is to be believed to have borne another son after the Lord Christ? Yet he is rightly called firstborn, although he alone is shown to have been begotten from the substance of the Father.

For he himself says: “I am Alpha and Omega, the last and the first, the beginning and the end, the prince and origin of David.” Thus this expression ought not to occasion a question, since he is plainly both the beginning and the end.

“I shall place him, I shall establish him”—as he says in the second psalm: “But I have been established as king by him”—“exalted above the kings of the earth,” as it is said in the seventy-first psalm: “And all the kings of the earth shall worship him.”

“Forever,” he says, “I shall keep my mercy for him, and my faithful covenant with him.” This too is said according to the form of a servant, because he received the Father’s mercy in eternal honor, and perpetual authority was given to him in heaven and on earth (Matt. XXVIII). The faithful covenant belongs to him because whatever the prophets foretold about him was fulfilled with complete truth.

“And I shall establish his seed forever, and his throne as the days of heaven.” “Forever and ever” signifies eternity. The seed of David is Christ the Lord, who is established in eternal glory and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. His throne is the power of the future judgment, which will be carried out with such truth that it will shine with heavenly brightness before all the saints.

It should certainly be understood that these days are different from one another: those days succeed one another in alternating cycles, whereas the future day is perpetual, with continuous light. Concerning it the eighty-third psalm says: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands.” Or it is rightly called “the day of heaven,” since, because the earth interposes itself, it cannot have nocturnal darkness.

“Behold, in my poverty I have prepared the expenses for the house of the Lord: one hundred thousand talents of gold, and one million talents of silver; but of bronze and iron there is no weighing, for the quantity is beyond number. I have prepared wood and stones for all the expenses” (1 Chron. XXII).

When David says that in his poverty he prepared the expenses for the house of the Lord, although these words indicate his humility, they signify figuratively the insufficiency of the letter of the law, which serves the manifold knowledge of the New Testament. Because of its weakness and uselessness, it brought nothing to perfection, as the Apostle testifies:

“For the law is a representation of the true and heavenly things, having a shadow of the things to come, not the very image of the realities” (Heb. VII; X; Gal. IV).

Elsewhere he also called it “an element of this world” (Col. II). For every earthly thing, when compared with heavenly things, and temporal things when set beside eternal things, appear to be small. Nevertheless, a structure that seeks to rise upward must necessarily place its foundations below, and thus be raised toward higher things.

David prepared the expenses for the house of the Lord—one hundred thousand talents of gold and one million talents of silver—because the fathers of the Old Testament abundantly inserted in their writings both profundity of meaning and beauty of expression. Their perfection is also indicated by perfect numbers. No one doubts that the numbers one hundred and one thousand are perfect. Likewise, the perfection of the same object is shown by the word “talent,” which surpasses the other weights in magnitude.

When he says that there is no weight of bronze and iron, this signifies that the firmness of the divine testimonies cannot be valued, because it is unchangeable. Hence the Savior says to his disciples in the Gospel:

“Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill. Amen, I say to you: not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things come to pass” (Matt. V).

And elsewhere:

“Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Mark XIII).

Moreover, David prepared wood and stones for all the expenses of the buildings, because the law and the prophets, cutting down and polishing various human persons—whom the names of wood and stones designate, wood because of loftiness of mind and stones because of hardness of heart—with the axe of the word, prepared them most suitably for the construction of God’s house.

“You also have many craftsmen, masons and builders, craftsmen in every kind of wood, most skilled in making work in gold and silver, bronze and iron” (1 Chron. XXII).

The craftsmen of God’s house are the holy preachers. They are sometimes called masons, sometimes builders, sometimes carpenters, and sometimes workers in gold, silver, and the other metals, on account of their various activities, because the speech of preachers must be formed according to the character of their hearers. The wise must be taught in one way, the foolish in another; the proud in one way, the humble in another; the strong in one way, and the weak in another.

David also commanded all the princes of Israel to help Solomon his son:

“You see,” he said, “that the Lord your God is with you, that he has given you rest on every side, delivered all your enemies into your hands, and subjected the land before the Lord and before his people. Therefore give your hearts and souls to seeking the Lord your God; arise and build the sanctuary of the Lord God.”

David’s command to all the princes of Israel to help his son Solomon in the work of the temple shows that the law and the prophets taught with firm authority that all who rightly exercised leadership over Israel—that is, those who excelled in knowledge and virtues in the Church—should help the true Solomon in building the spiritual house, by teaching rightly and living well.

Hence Moses says to the children of Israel:

“The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him. And whoever will not listen to that prophet shall be exterminated from among his people” (Deut. XVIII).

Likewise David himself, appointing the mystical workers and ministers of the Lord’s temple, says in the Psalms:

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams. Bring to the Lord the fatherlands of the nations [Latin *patriae gentium*, reading uncertain]; bring to the Lord glory and honor. Bring to the Lord glory for his name. Take up sacrifices and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy court” (Ps. XXVIII).

To this one he also says through Isaiah:

“I have brought my righteousness near; it shall not be far away, and my salvation shall not delay. I shall give salvation in Zion and my glory to Israel. Behold, I have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and his way has been made straight. Draw near to him and hear. With a voice of rejoicing proclaim it; make this heard and carry it to the ends of the earth. Say: ‘The Lord shall redeem his servant Jacob’” (Isa. XLVI; XLVIII).

Hence it is said through Jeremiah:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely. This is the name by which they shall call him: ‘The Lord our righteous one.’

“Hear the word of the Lord, house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue the oppressed from the hand of the slanderer, lest my indignation go forth like fire and be kindled, with no one to extinguish it.

“Behold, I shall restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob and have mercy on his dwellings; the city shall be built upon its height, and the temple shall be founded according to its order. From them shall go forth praise and the voice of those who praise; I shall multiply them, and they shall not decrease; I shall glorify them, and they shall not grow weak. Their children shall be as at the beginning, and their assembly shall remain before me. I shall punish all who afflict them. Their leader shall arise from among them, and their ruler shall come forth from their midst. I shall draw him near, and he shall approach me. For who is this who applies his heart and draws near to me? says the Lord. You shall be my people, and I shall be your God” (Jer. XXIII, XXI, XXX).

In the same way, the other prophets proclaimed this in their words and urged it by their examples: each person was to prepare a dwelling for the coming Savior in his heart and build the Lord’s sanctuary in his mind by right faith and good will, so that the ark of the Lord’s covenant might be brought into them—that is, faith in Christ’s incarnation—and vessels consecrated to the Lord, namely, the example and wondrous deeds of holy men.

For the vessels of God are the souls of the saints, in which divine wisdom dwells and various gifts of the Holy Spirit are contained. Hence a certain Wise Man says: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” And again: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. I).

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### David made his son Solomon king over Israel and gathered all the princes of Israel, the priests, and the Levites, whose duties he arranged according to each ministry.

**(1 Chron. XXIII.)** Then David, old and full of days, made his son Solomon king over Israel and gathered all the princes of Israel, the priests, and the Levites.

What does it mean that David, old and full of days, made Solomon king, except that, after the completion of the Old Testament, the incarnation of the Savior foretold beforehand succeeded it, bringing to the human race the rule of right faith, understanding, and holy conduct by which eternal blessedness might be attained? This accords with the saying of the Apostle Paul, who writes to the Galatians:

“When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. IV; the source cites Col. IV).

All the princes of Israel, the priests, and the Levites were therefore gathered there, when the individual orders of various ministries were assembled for the service of Christ, so that they might carry out his ministry worthily.

The Levites were counted from thirty years old and above, and 38,000 men were found. Of these, 24,000 were chosen and assigned to the ministry of the house of the Lord; 6,000 were officers and judges; 4,000 were gatekeepers, and an equal number were singers praising the Lord with instruments, which David had made for singing.

What is signified by the Levites being thirty years old and above, except that all who serve in the ministry of the Lord must preserve faith in the Holy Trinity together with fulfillment of the commandments? Hence 38,000 men were found among those counted, because whoever serves God in holy faith and good works to the end will belong to the grace of the resurrection and to eternal blessedness, which are signified by the number eight.

That 24,000 of those chosen were assigned to the ministry of the house of the Lord signifies that the true ministers of Christ must devote themselves to works of light and not turn aside from the way of righteousness. For [probably “twenty-four”] hours illuminate the whole circuit of the world and drive away the shadow of darkness. Hence the Savior sent seventy-two disciples to preach (Luke X), because he wished to show that faith in the Holy Trinity together with works of light is sufficient for each person’s righteousness: three times twenty-four, or four times three, makes seventy-two. By this number the diversity of languages and the series of the books of the Old and New Testaments are also comprehended.

The officers and judges are described as numbering 6,000. And what is indicated by this except that no one ought to seek the dignity of this order who does not strive to possess perfection of doctrine and virtues? For the world was created in the number six, and humanity was made on the sixth day (Gen. I), on which our Redeemer is also understood to have been born. It is therefore fitting that one who remembers having been created perfect by a perfect Creator and redeemed should strive, according to the measure of his ability, to possess that perfection.

David appointed 4,000 gatekeepers and an equal number of singers praising the Lord with instruments, so that it might be shown that whoever wishes worthily to perform the office of gatekeeper or singer must preserve evangelical doctrine and the commandments. For whoever does not follow its path will never attain the summit of that office.

David distributed them according to the divisions of the sons of Levi—Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, and so forth. David’s distribution of the Levites according to the number of the three sons of Levi signifies that the text of the divine law and the reading of the prophets teach the ministers of the Lord—those acquired through God’s grace and added to the number of the faithful—to preserve faith in the Holy Trinity together with the practice of virtues.

The names of those fathers demonstrate this. Levi means “added” or “taken up”; Gershon, “a sojourner there” or “their expulsion”; Kohath, “molars” or “patiently”; Merari, “bitter” or “of bitterness.”

Everyone who has been taken up into the house of the Lord, added to the assembly of the saints, and instructed in the ecclesiastical mysteries must first cast out from his mind every impurity and filth of vices and renounce the pleasures of the world, so that he may become on earth, with the prophet, a sojourner and pilgrim (Ps. XXXV), and, with the Apostle, crucified to the world (Gal. VI).

Then he should strive to maintain discernment concerning mortality in his conduct, guide his life honorably by the four-horse chariot of the virtues, and strive to advance toward heavenly things—that is, by prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. He should patiently endure every adversity, knowing that if he prevails and perseveres in this, he will receive a sure reward for it in the future.

Finally, with fervent spirit he should learn to desire heavenly things, and consider all present things worthless and bitter. In this way the worthy minister of the Lord will appear in the true temple of God, which is the Church, and will be useful.

Aaron was set apart to minister in the holy of holies, and his sons forever, to burn incense to the Lord according to its rite and bless his name perpetually.

What can be better understood by Aaron and his sons than Christ and his members, whose priesthood is eternal (Ps. CIX)? He was set apart to minister in the holy of holies because, alone found without the stain of sin, he entered the mysteries of heavenly secrets. According to Paul’s testimony:

“Others indeed became priests without an oath, but he with an oath, through him who said to him: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever.’ To that extent Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant. The others became priests in greater numbers because death prevented them from remaining; but he, because he remains forever, possesses an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is able to save forever those who approach God through him, always living to intercede for us” (Heb. VII).

Therefore the incense of his prayer is always pleasing to God.

What follows is:

“Moses also, the man of God, had sons counted among the tribe of Levi,” and so forth.

This signifies that not a few from the former people belong to the ecclesiastical priesthood, as is clearly demonstrated in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the primitive Church in Jerusalem, where it is written:

“The word of the Lord increased, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem. A great multitude of priests obeyed the faith” (Acts VI).

After this, when the princes from the sons of Levi have been enumerated, Scripture continues:

“These are the sons of Levi according to their kindreds and families, princes according to their divisions and the number of the heads of each, who performed the work of the ministry of the house of the Lord from twenty years old and above.”

What does it mean that the ministers of the house of the Lord are counted from twenty years old and above, except that it shows that all who wish to serve in the Lord’s ministry must observe the Decalogue in the two commandments of love and perform ecclesiastical ministry according to their requirements? For upon these two commandments—that is, love of God and of neighbor—the whole law and the prophets depend (Matt. XXII). The fullness of the law, according to Paul’s judgment, is love (Rom. XIII).

Hence the chief of the apostles teaches how God must be served in this love, saying:

“Applying all diligence, minister virtue in your faith, knowledge in virtue, self-control in knowledge, patience in self-control, godliness in patience, brotherly affection in godliness, and love in brotherly affection. For if these things are present and abound among you, they will not leave you idle or fruitless in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these things is blind and groping, having forgotten the cleansing of his former sins. Therefore, brothers, strive all the more to make your calling sure through good works. For if you do these things, you will never fall; for in this way an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you” (2 Pet. I).

David said:

“The Lord God of Israel has given rest to his people and a dwelling in Jerusalem forever; and it will no longer be the duty of the Levites to carry the tabernacle and all its vessels for service.”

As long as the children of Israel were in the wilderness, and when they began to possess the land of Canaan by warfare, the Lord’s tabernacle was carried through various places. After the temple had been built, however, this change of locations was no longer necessary; but in the Lord’s temple the Lord’s sanctification was established. Mystically, this signifies that the worship and observance of the Old Testament, imitable through various figures, was always diverse within itself. When it came to the Gospel, it found there the stability of its movement, because “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I).

According to David’s commands, the number of the sons of Levi was also counted from twenty years old and above. They were to be under the authority of the sons of Aaron for the worship of the house of the Lord—in the vestibules, the chambers, the place of purification, the sanctuary, and all the works of the ministry of the Lord’s temple.

When David distributed the Levites from twenty years old and above, according to the command of the law, under the authority of the sons of Aaron—that is, the priests—they were appointed for the worship of the house of the Lord, so that the younger might learn to obey the elders, and the elders, assisted by the younger, might be able to fulfill their duty in the ministry of the house of the Lord more worthily.

So also in the present Church the lesser ranks must always be subject to the greater through humility, and the greater must rightly preside over the lesser through love, so that all the members may be at peace.

When he says:

“In the vestibules and chambers”—

a vestibule is a place before the doors, called the porch or entrance of a private house, or an open space. It is called this because the doors of temples or any buildings are clothed with it. Chambers are rooms or bedrooms that had been prepared for the dwelling of the Levites and priests. In these, therefore, the serving Levites kept watch, so that they might teach the ministers of the true temple of the Lord to guard its entrance diligently, admit those who were worthy, and cast out and repel those who were unworthy. For the heavenly key-bearer must always be vigilant and cautious in all things.

“The priests were over the loaves of the presentation, the offering of fine flour, the flat cakes and unleavened bread, the frying pan, the roasting, and every weight and measure.”

Some manuscripts read, “over the boiling fine flour,” and others, “over the roasting only.” This is an error. In the Hebrew, “fine flour,” which was mentioned a little earlier, is not found here; instead, “over the roasting only” is written, with ears of grain understood. For when the firstfruits of the ears of grain were brought, they were roasted and the *grava* were eaten—a kind of food commonly called *graveas*. Nor is the reading found in some manuscripts—“over every weight and measure”—present in the Hebrew. It does not say “weight,” but only “measure.” They think this signifies both what is measured with the hands beneath the arms or with ropes and what is measured in vessels.

It was the priests’ responsibility to ensure that everything assigned to the temple ministries was done suitably and rationally, according to order and measure.

The Levites were to stand in the morning to give thanks and sing to the Lord, and likewise in the evening, both at the offering of the Lord’s burnt offering and on Sabbaths, new moons, and the remaining solemnities, continually before the Lord, according to the number and rites appropriate to each matter.

When the priests had performed the duties written above, David appointed the Levites to come forward for singing and for the other offices entrusted to them. Thus it is written in what follows:

“Then David and the officers of the army separated for the ministry the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who were to prophesy with lyres, harps, and cymbals, serving according to their number in the office assigned to them.”

When it says that they stood morning and evening to give thanks to the Lord, this means at the hours when the continual sacrifice was offered according to the precepts of the law, and on festivals—that is, Sabbaths, new moons, and the remaining solemnities—in each of which offerings were specially appointed to be offered to the Lord, according to the rite of the law delivered to the children of Israel through Moses.

Mystically, however, the Levites and singers of the Lord’s house signify the holy Church, which praises the Lord not only in private places and at appointed times, but in every place and at every time, always and everywhere. Hence, dancing in the psalter with the prophet, it says:

“I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXIII).

To it also the Apostle speaks, saying:

“Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. V).

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Concerning the twenty-four valiant men by whom David distinguished the sons of Eleazar and the sons of Ithamar for serving God in the Lord’s temple according to their divisions.

*(1 Chronicles 24.)* Now the divisions of the sons of Aaron were as follows. The sons of Aaron were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Nadab and Abihu died before their father without children; and Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests. David—that is, Zadok from the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech from the sons of Ithamar—divided them according to their divisions and ministry. More sons of Eleazar were found among the principal men than sons of Ithamar. He divided them—namely, the sons of Eleazar—into sixteen heads of families, and the sons of Ithamar into eight according to their families and households. Moreover, he divided both families among themselves by lot. For there were leaders of the sanctuary and leaders of God, both from the sons of Eleazar and from the sons of Ithamar.

What else is signified by David’s arranging the priestly line, ordering both households—namely, Eleazar and Ithamar—and the ministry of the priesthood and the dignity of the high priesthood, except that our Redeemer chose not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles those who would worthily serve in the ecclesiastical priesthood?

In Eleazar, the elder son of Aaron—whose name is interpreted “my God is a helper” or “help of God,” and who, as the first in the succession of his sons, ruled the Levitical stock while holding the high priesthood—the figure of the ecclesiastical priesthood and spiritual sacrifice can properly be understood. For the sacrifice of bread and wine is first read to have been offered through Melchizedek (which plainly foreshadowed the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood), before sacrifices of cattle and offerings of animals were instituted through Aaron and the Levitical tribe (Genesis 14). Hence, according to Paul’s judgment, “the one who received tithes was himself tithed”: for Levi was still in the loins of his father Abraham when Melchizedek met him (Hebrews 7).

Likewise Ithamar, whose name is interpreted “bitter,” and who through David rose to the summit of Levitical honor, is a type of those who, through our Redeemer, were transferred from the Jewish people and the figurative observance of the Law and its ceremonies to the worship of the truth of the Gospel and the New Testament. Properly, therefore, the Jewish people are called “bitter,” since, although they were chosen by the Lord in the place of the firstborn and had been well nourished by the service of angels and heavenly food, they never completely abandoned the bitterness of their rebelliousness. Hence the Lord himself says to them through the prophet:

“I planted you as my chosen vine, wholly true seed. How have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jeremiah 2)

And again: “I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isaiah 5).

For this reason, more sons of Eleazar than of Ithamar were chosen for the priesthood: “because she who was desolate has more children than she who has a husband” (Psalm 54). And she who had been barren “bore seven,” while “she who had many children was weakened” (1 Samuel 2).

By the number seven, therefore, the perfection of the universal Church is signified because of the sevenfold Spirit. For this reason the apostle John also writes to seven churches, while now showing himself to write toward the fullness of one Church (Revelation 1). Solomon likewise prefigured this earlier in Proverbs: “Wisdom built her house and supported it with seven pillars” (Proverbs 9).

Furthermore, the fact that sixteen heads of families were appointed among the sons of Eleazar, but only eight among the sons of Ithamar, refers to the same meaning: namely, that the Church has a double grace for the work of the synagogue. Sixteen consists of two eights. Under the Law, circumcision of the flesh had been instituted on the eighth day. In the Gospel, the special circumcision of hearts and the future resurrection of bodies are expressed by the same number, when those who have rightly kept in this life the forms of the eight evangelical beatitudes will ascend to the reward of eternal recompense in the heavenly kingdom.

What follows—“For there were leaders of the sanctuary and leaders of God, both from the sons of Eleazar and from the sons of Ithamar”—shows that no one properly reaches the ministry of the sanctuary or the leadership of the priesthood except through God’s choice and appointment. Thus every display of pride and every desire for earthly gain is excluded, as is the avarice of the simoniacal plague. Nor is anyone permitted to seek with money what divine generosity is accustomed to bestow freely upon the humble.

Nor is it without mystery that David is said to have divided both families among themselves by lots. This lot is mentioned so often in the divine Scriptures that it seems to bear some great, hidden secret of divine judgment. For it is written in Leviticus that one lot is to be given to the Lord and one to the “transmitter” [or “one who sends away”]. Moses likewise divided the land beyond the Jordan among certain tribes by lot. Jesus son of Nun also distributed the promised land among the sons of Israel by lot. The lot exposed Jonah when he was hiding (Jonah 1). In Solomon we read: “The lot restrains disputes, and decides between the mighty” (Proverbs 18). In the New Testament, that is, in the Acts of the Apostles, the lot designated Matthias as an apostle (Acts 1). The apostle Paul also says, writing to the Ephesians, that he was called by lot according to the purpose of the one who works all things according to the counsel of his will (Ephesians 1). Thus, writing to the Colossians, he says: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the lot of the saints in light” (Colossians 1).

Although many things are read to have been divided by lot in both the Old and the New Testament, no one has dared deny that by this means it was shown by God what a devout mind had asked for in humble prayer. Yet lots must not be trusted rashly or indiscriminately, since, as Jerome says, the privileges of individuals cannot become a common law. Nor should divinity in any way be tested by human curiosity, according to what is written: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6). Nevertheless, if some people, compelled by necessity, think that the Lord should be consulted by lot, following the example of the apostles, they should observe that the apostles did this only after gathering an assembly of the brethren and pouring out prayers to God.

Shemiah, son of Nethanel, the Levitical scribe, recorded them before the king and the leaders, Zadok the priest, and Abimelech son of Abiathar, together with the heads of the priestly and Levitical families: one household, which presided with the others, being that of Eleazar; and the other household, which had the rest under it, being that of Ithamar.

The fact that Shemiah, son of Nethanel, the Levitical scribe, is said to have recorded the lots themselves before the king and the priestly leaders signifies that a teacher should handle in pure and sincere speech, before God and human beings, all the mysteries contained in the Law according to the order of right faith, and bring them to the knowledge of his hearers. The names themselves aptly demonstrate this through their interpretations. For Shemiah means “hearing the Lord”; Nethanel, “the gift of God”; Zadok, “just”; Abimelech, “my brother is king”; and Abiathar, “superfluous father.”

Whoever properly hears the Lord by rightly learning his Law and obeying his commandments is himself a son of God’s gift, because he possesses this grace only as a divine gift. Thus the learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, the minister of the true temple, describes the priestly order before the king—namely, Christ—or before the Christian people (Matthew 13). He may rightly be called a king because he is the body of Christ and rightly governs his life, ruling well over himself (Revelation 1, 3). Although he is born from a superfluous father—that is, from a Gentile people—he nevertheless possesses priestly as well as royal dignity and is deservedly reckoned under the name “Just.”

The first lot came out for Jehoiarib, the second for Jedaiah, the third for Harim, the fourth for Seorim, the fifth for Malchijah, the sixth for Mijamin, the seventh for Hakkoz, the eighth for Abijah, the ninth for Jeshua, the tenth for Shecaniah, the eleventh for Eliashib, the twelfth for Jakim, the thirteenth for Huppah, the fourteenth for Jeshebeab, the fifteenth for Bilgah, the sixteenth for Immer, the seventeenth for Hezir, the eighteenth for Aphses, the nineteenth for Pethahiah, the twentieth for Jehezkel, the twenty-first for Jachin, the twenty-second for Gamul, the twenty-third for Delaiah, and the twenty-fourth for Maaziah.

These were their divisions according to their ministries, so that they might enter the house of the Lord according to their appointed order and ritual, under the authority of Aaron their father, as the Lord God of Israel had commanded.

What else is signified by the Levitical tribe and priestly order being distributed into twenty-four lots except that it shows the Catholic Church to possess fully a priestly and royal dignity, and to preserve perfectly the teaching of the Law and the Gospel (1 Peter 2)? The apostle and evangelist John saw this Church in his Apocalypse under the same number—twenty-four—seated around the throne of God in the figure of elders, upon twenty-four thrones (Revelation 1), thereby showing that the whole Church of God, generated from the patriarchs and apostles through the two Testaments, reigns perpetually with Christ.

He sees it seated because of its judicial dignity in Christ. For all its members will sit and judge, in one head and through one head. Otherwise, how could the saints sit in judgment while standing at the right hand of the judge?

The twenty-four elders may also be understood as those who complete the perfection of works, which is commended by the number six, through the clear preaching of the Gospel. For four times six makes twenty-four. Moreover, the same apostle records that these elders were clothed in white garments and had golden crowns on their heads, to show that those clothed in good works will seek the joys above through the perpetual memory of the mind. For the head often signifies the mind.

When he says that these divisions were according to their ministries and according to their order, under the authority of Aaron their father, the name Aaron signifies the high priest, who, although chosen by the final lot, presided over the others in the order of his division, at the lesser ranks, and arranged what had to be done in the house of God. For, as was said above, there were leaders of the sanctuary and leaders of God, both from the sons of Eleazar and from the sons of Ithamar.

Josephus also recounts these lots as follows:

“He divided them according to their generations, and, separating the priests from the tribe, found twenty-four generations among them. From the household of Eleazar there were thirteen, and from Ithamar eight. He commanded each generation to minister to God for eight days, from Sabbath to Sabbath. Thus all the generations received their lot, in the presence of David, Zadok, Abiathar, and all the leaders. The first generation that came up was written first, the second likewise, then the third, and so on until the twenty-fourth. This division remained until the present day.

“He also made twenty-four divisions from the tribe of the Levites and caused them to come up by lot in the same manner. He established that they too should minister for eight days, according to the priestly order. But those who were descended from Moses he honored more highly: he appointed them keepers of the treasures of God and of the vessels which kings might happen to dedicate to God. He commanded all from the tribe of Levi together with the priests to serve God day and night, as Moses had commanded him.”

## CHAPTER XXV  
### On the fact that David and the commanders of the army set apart for the ministry of the Lord the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who were to sing with harps, psalteries, and cymbals before the ark of the Lord

*(1 Chronicles 25.)* Thus David and the commanders of the army set apart for the ministry the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who were to prophesy with harps, psalteries, and cymbals, serving according to their appointed office, each according to his number, and so forth.

David chose and set apart, together with the elders of the people, three leaders of the singers—namely Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun—so that they and their sons might prophesy with harps, psalteries, and cymbals according to the office assigned to them. This prefigured that the true David, our King and Lord, wills every order of ecclesiastical ministry to perform its office in administering faith in the holy Trinity. No one can worthily sing his praises except the one who praises him in faith, hope, and charity, confessing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The names of these three leaders aptly demonstrate this by their interpretations. Asaph means “gathering”; Heman, “their heart”; and Jeduthun, “leaping over.” Whoever gathers the meanings of the divine books with an attentive mind, and, leaping over every desire for earthly things, examines and handles them according to the rule of charity—such a person will surely sing worthy praises to the divine majesty.

What the instruments themselves signify—namely, the harp, the psaltery, and the cymbals—has been explained above.
