Their number, together with their brothers who were trained in the song of the Lord, all of them teachers, was 288.

The teachers of the song of the Lord are aptly said to have numbered 288, to show that those who expound the canon of the divine books with evangelical understanding may rightly be called teachers of divine praise. For four times seventy-two makes 288; and it is known to all that the books of the Old and New Testaments number seventy-two. Therefore, whoever wishes to perform divine service properly must devote himself to the four principal virtues, give the greatest attention to meditation on evangelical teaching, and take care to shape according to its rule whatever he has learned or whatever he teaches.

They cast lots for their divisions equally, the older and the younger alike, the learned and the unlearned alike, and so forth.

In every order a careful choice is necessary, lest anyone, through his own presumption, dare to confer or accept a rank in the ecclesiastical order. Hence the statement that the older and the younger alike, the learned and the unlearned alike, were subject to the lots teaches this. Paul likewise writes to Timothy: “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5). And again: “You therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. What you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be competent to teach others” (2 Timothy 2).

Thus, by the several orders, he teaches how each person should reach a rank and how he ought to conduct himself in it, since it is dangerous to undertake any burden that one knows oneself entirely unable to bear.

Having enumerated the gatekeepers and their origin, Scripture continues:

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### On the gatekeepers and the leaders of the Lord’s guards, all of whom, being divided into divisions, fulfilled their ministries and provided for the treasures of the house of the Lord

*(1 Chronicles 26.)* These were divided among the gatekeepers, so that they might always serve in the house of the Lord as leaders of the guards, together with their brothers. Lots were cast equally, for the small and the great alike, according to their families, for each gate.

The eastern lot fell to Shelemiah. For Zechariah his son, a most prudent and learned man, the northern sector fell by lot. Obed-Edom and his sons were assigned to the south, where the council of the elders of the house was located. Shuppim and Hosah were assigned to the west, beside the gate leading to the road of ascent, guard opposite guard.

To the east there were six Levites; to the north, four by day; and likewise to the south, four by day; and where the council was, two and two. In the chambers of the gatekeepers on the west there were four on the road and two in each chamber. These were the divisions of the gatekeepers, the sons of Korah and Merari.

The gatekeepers and leaders of the guards of the house of God are holy teachers who watch over the entrance of the Church and examine the faith and devotion of individuals who approach the baptism of Christ and the true religion. These are chosen by lot equally, the small and the great alike, because they are promoted to the honor of rank not according to respect for persons but according to understanding of wisdom and integrity of life.

Hence the chief of the apostles replied to the Jews disputing among themselves about the admission of the Gentiles to the faith: “In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10).

The eastern lot therefore fell to Shelemiah. What else is signified by Shelemiah, whose name means “the Lord repays,” except the office of the apostles and the first teachers of the Gospel, to whom the eastern gate—that is, the primitive Church among the Jews—is entrusted? They are rightly called “the Lord repays,” because just as the Lord promised to the ancient fathers, so he fulfilled it in their children.

Hence Isaiah says of them:

“Behold, I create Jerusalem as rejoicing and her people as joy. I will rejoice in Jerusalem and exult in my people; they shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not plant and another eat. For as the days of a tree shall be the days of my people, and the works of their hands shall grow old among my chosen. They shall not labor in vain, nor bear children for confusion, because they are the offspring of the blessed of the Lord, and their descendants are with them.”

For Zechariah his son, a most prudent and learned man, the northern sector fell by lot.

By Zechariah, whose name means “mindful of the Lord,” and who was the son of Shelemiah, the teachers of the Gentiles are signified—those who were appointed by the apostles themselves and by the first preachers of the Gospel to preach to the Gentiles. Such were Barnabas and Saul, of whom, while the disciples were praying and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13).

By the northern sector, which sends forth a cold wind, the coldness of the Gentiles’ unbelief is represented. Yet many of them come to the faith; hence the northern gate and its gatekeepers are assigned to them.

Of these Jeremiah says:

“There will be a day when the guards will cry out on Mount Ephraim: ‘Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the Lord our God.’ For thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I will bring them from the land of the north, and I will gather them from the ends of the earth. Among them will be the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and the woman in labor together. A great assembly of those returning will come here in weeping, and in prayers I will lead them by streams of water along a straight path, and they will not stumble on it’” (Jeremiah 31).

Obed-Edom and his sons were assigned the guard of the gates toward the south. What else is signified by Obed-Edom except those teachers who were appointed to preach to the Jews? Of them Paul writes to the Galatians:

“When they recognized the grace that had been given to me, Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision” (Galatians 2).

Luke also recounts of them in the Acts of the Apostles:

“Those who had been scattered because of the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews alone” (Acts 11).

The Jewish people are rightly represented by the south, because, instructed by the sayings of the Law and the Prophets, they were near to receiving the warmth of faith and the light of divine wisdom. Obed-Edom and his sons are therefore rightly assigned to open the gates of the house of God, so that the names of the ministers might correspond to the persons receiving those ministries.

For Obed means “serving,” and Edom means “red.” Those who were sons of the slave woman, begotten into servitude at Mount Sinai and stained red by the blood of Christ, openly bore their guilt. It was therefore fitting that through the humility and condescension of teachers they should be brought back to the rank of dignity from which they had fallen.

Paul expressed their piety and gentleness in his own person in his Epistle, saying:

“Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, that I might win more. To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win the Jews. To those who are under the Law I became as one under the Law, although I myself was not under the Law, that I might win those under the Law. I became all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 9).

And shortly afterward:

“I became weak to the weak, that I might win the weak.”

What follows—“where the council of the elders of the house was located”—shows that the apostles and prophets came from this same people and were rightly called elders because of the maturity of their wisdom. Of them Moses says in the song of Deuteronomy: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will speak to you” (Deuteronomy 32). And in Proverbs it is written: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Proverbs 13). Whoever hears the counsel of these elders will surely find a true remedy for his soul.

Furthermore, what follows:

“Shuppim and Hosah to the west, beside the gate leading to the road of ascent”—

the western sector, where the sun sets, signifies the final period of this age near the end of the world, when the most severe persecution under Antichrist will occur and, according to the Lord’s judgment, many will be scandalized (Matthew 24). According to Paul’s judgment, lawlessness will abound and the charity of many will grow cold.

The gatekeepers of this gate are the teachers of that time, who will raise up the Church, trampled down by persecutions, through their doctrines and strengthen it through their exhortations. Their names aptly express this. Shuppim means “humble” or “of the plain,” and Hosah means “divining.”

At that time the Church will be humbled by the persecutions of its enemies, although it will be strengthened by the doctrines of the saints. It becomes “of the plain” through movements of wantonness, but it will be raised up by the deeds of the imperfect. Both matters are demonstrated by the divine utterances.

It is written in the prophet Daniel’s final vision that the angel said to the prophet:

“Go, Daniel, because the words are closed and sealed until the appointed time, until many are chosen, purified, and tested as by fire; and all the wicked will act wickedly. But the learned will understand” (Daniel 12).

Paul writes similarly to Timothy:

“Know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, uncontrolled, savage, without kindness, betrayers, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God, having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3).

It is rightly said that this gate was beside the road of ascent, because the age of that time will be near the day of judgment. Then, receiving immortal bodies in the resurrection, people will be invited by the presence of just judgment to possess the kingdom of the heavenly Father.

The statement that the guard was opposite the guard signifies the harmony of the divine Testaments. What the holy Fathers before the Lord’s incarnation prefigured in type concerning the future mysteries of the Church, the teachers of the Gospel now demonstrate in the clearest action after the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. The rest of the faithful, from Jews and Gentiles alike, likewise confirm this through one faith, one baptism, and the worship of one God celebrated throughout the world.

“To the east,” he says, “six Levites; to the north, four by day; and likewise to the south, four by day; and where the council was, two and two. In the chambers of the gatekeepers on the west, four on the road and two in each chamber. These were the divisions of the gatekeepers, the sons of Korah and Merari.”

When he says that there were six Levites in the east and four appointed in the other sectors, the number six first signifies the good work of divine ministers. The number four expresses evangelical teaching together with the fullness of the four principal virtues.

Whoever wishes to become a gatekeeper of the divine temple—that is, a teacher of the holy Church—must strive to possess evangelical teaching together with the perfection of good works, so that those who approach the door of the spiritual building may properly enter through the teachers’ instruction and example and may worthily sing praises to the Lord there.

The Psalmist invites them to praise the Lord:

“Enter his gates with confession, his courts with hymns of praise. Praise his name, for the Lord is gracious; his mercy is forever, and his truth endures from age to age” (Psalm 99).

Nor is it without mystery that he says these gatekeepers were two by two in the chambers and on the road. This signifies that the custodians of the Lord’s house, whether they are in the chambers—that is, caring inwardly for themselves—or on the road—that is, preaching the word of God outwardly to others—must always observe the two commandments of charity according to the rule of the divine Testaments.

Moreover, Ahijah was over the treasures of the house of the Lord and the sacred vessels. Who is the one placed over the treasures of the house of the Lord except our Redeemer, in whose power are all the gifts of virtue and wisdom possessed by the holy Church? For Ahijah is interpreted “my brother.”

Of him Paul says:

“Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light; who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. For in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. All things were created through him and in him. He is before all things, and all things hold together in him. He is the head of the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in all things. For in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily, and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 1).

The sons of Laadan, the sons of Gershon. From Laadan: heads of families. Laadan and Gershon, Jehieli. The sons of Jehieli were Zetham and Joel, his brothers, over the treasures of the house of the Lord. The Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites. But Shebuel, son of Gershon, son of Moses, was in charge of the treasures.

Finally, the sons of Moses, who, as Josephus testifies, were honored more highly by David and placed over the treasures of the house of the Lord, signify that teachers from the Jewish people were appointed over the house of God, to whom the ornaments of the holy Church—that is, the beauty of souls—were entrusted. For the apostles and the first teachers of the Gospel came from that people, and they are rightly called keepers of the treasures because they were stewards of the heavenly mysteries.

His brother was also Eliezer, whose son was Rehabiah, whose son was Isaiah, whose son was Joram, whose son was Zichri; and his son was Shelomith. Shelomith himself and his brothers were over the treasures of the holy things that King David, the heads of families, the commanders, the centurions, and the army leaders had sanctified from the spoils and booty of battles, which they had consecrated for the restoration and furnishing of the temple of the Lord.

Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, Joab son of Zeruiah, and others sanctified all these things. This statement shows that the gifts of the leaders are the treasures of the holy ones. Whatever the aforementioned kings or commanders took from the spoils of the enemies, they converted into furnishings for the temple of the Lord. Mystically, this signifies that whoever, laboring well, acquires some virtue through good works must ascribe it to God’s grace rather than to his own merits, and must transfer everything to God’s praise, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113).

Over the Izharites were Chenaniah and his sons, for the external work over Israel, to teach and judge them.

Who are those workers who perform Israel’s external works except those who in the holy Church, with simplicity of mind, devote themselves to the humility of obedience, striving with devoted mind and diligent action to accomplish whatever their teachers command them? Although they may not be competent to teach others with their speech, they nevertheless show their neighbors the doctrine of virtues through their works.

The patriarch Jacob prefigured these people; it is written of him that “the simple man dwelt in tents” (Genesis 25). Nathanael also prefigured this in the Gospel, to whom the Savior himself bore witness, saying: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1).

Chenaniah was placed over such workers. His name is interpreted “my bronze-worker,” or “my nest,” or “possession.” For the one who especially pursues humility and gentleness, becoming an imitator of the Lord and offering good examples outwardly, becomes inwardly in his soul a nest and possession of God.

Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66). The Truth himself likewise says to the disciples in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11).

Hashabiah and his brothers, 1,700 very able men, were in charge of Israel beyond the Jordan toward the west, in all the works of the Lord and in the service of the king.

The Israelites who received their possession beyond the Jordan can here signify those who, content with their mediocrity, do not wish, because of the disturbances of this age, to pass beyond their present understanding and aspire to the highest progress in knowledge and virtue. Nevertheless, they do not neglect to practice through good works the commandments they know to be good.

They are represented by the scribe who asked the Lord in the Gospel:

“Good Teacher, what good must I do to have eternal life?”

He said to him: “Why do you ask me about the good? One is good: God. But if you wish to enter life, keep the commandments.”

He said to him: “Which ones?”

Jesus said: “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; and love your neighbor as yourself.”

The young man said to him: “I have kept all these things; what do I still lack?”

Jesus said to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.”

When the young man heard this word, he went away sad, for he had many possessions (Matthew 19).

It is one thing to keep the external commandments through action, and another to set aside external things and turn one’s whole self inward toward divine contemplation. But since no one can perform even these external good works except by God’s gift, Hashabiah is said to have been placed over them. For Hashabiah is interpreted “the Lord acting.”

These people can rightly say to the Lord with the Prophet: “You have accomplished all our works for us” (Isaiah 26). Hence the Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

The leader of the Hebronites was Jeriah, according to their families and kindreds.

Hebron, the city where David received the beginning of his kingdom, can signify those who begin the beginning of their way of life and prepare a kingdom for the Lord in their conduct. Jeriah, the leader of the Hebronites, is interpreted “fearing the Lord,” because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Eccl. I).

Whoever restrains himself from evil actions through fear and strives to do whatever good he can, cleaving to the fear of the Lord, is governed by him. Hebron also expresses this appropriately through its interpretation, for it means “marriage.” If such a person perseveres in the fear of the Lord and continually strives to progress by making himself better, he will surely pass from fear to love—namely, the love that “casts out fear” (1 John 4)—and will no longer be called a servant but a son.

What follows:

“In the fortieth year of David’s reign they were counted, and very able men were found at Jazer of Gilead, with 2,700 of their brothers of mature age, heads of families, and so forth”—

shows that this census was made in the final year of David’s reign, when, before his death, he arranged everything, assigned each person according to his duties, and, by designating and showing his son Solomon everything that had to be done, rationally explained how the administration of the kingdom was to be maintained.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On the various leaders who were over the Israelites according to David’s arrangement; on those who were over David’s property—that is, in the cities, villages, fields, vineyards, olive groves, and over the flocks; and on David’s counselors and those who were with the king’s sons
The Israelites, according to their number, their family heads, tribune-commanders, centurions, and prefects who served the king according to their divisions, entering and departing month by month throughout the year—24,000 in each division—were in command, and so forth. Josephus relates this as follows:

> “After this he divided the army into twelve cohorts, with their commanders, centurions, and tribunes. Each cohort had 24,000 men, whom he ordered to attend upon King Solomon for thirty days, from the first hour until the last, with their chiliarchs and centurions. He appointed for each cohort the day which he judged suitable and just, as well as other men to oversee the treasuries, villages, fields, and pack animals.”

The twelvefold number, therefore, most fittingly designates the apostolic order. Christ, the true Light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), compared them in the Gospel to the twelve hours of the day (John 11); and, calling them the light of this world (Matthew 5), he commanded them to spread the light of faith throughout the whole world, saying: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 21). Thus those months arrange that year which the Lord—as it is written in the Gospel, when he read the words of the prophet Isaiah in the synagogue (Luke 4)—declared to be acceptable to the Lord; and by arranging it, he distributed the people of the Church for the service of the true Solomon. Therefore, in each month 24,000 were assigned to royal service. What mystery this number contains has already been stated above: namely, that the whole perfection of the Law and the Gospel is figuratively manifested in it.

David did not wish to count those younger than twenty years, because the Lord had said that Israel would be multiplied like the stars of heaven. Joab son of Zeruiah began the census but did not complete it, because wrath had fallen upon Israel on account of it; and for this reason the number of those who had been counted was not entered in the royal annals by David. It was customary, whenever a census was taken, to count from the age of twenty upward those who could go out to war or perform some other service. But because David first commanded Joab to count everyone generally, both those under twenty and those over twenty, he consequently experienced God’s indignation, and they were not entered in the records of King David.

The *fasti*, therefore, are annal-books in which the deeds of kings and consuls are recorded; they are so called from the fasces. The census of the people conducted by Joab was not inserted into the deeds of King David because, when God’s indignation intervened, that entire number was thrown into confusion, and they were not distributed according to it among the ministries or assigned to any offices.

Over the king’s treasuries was Azmoth son of Adiel. The treasury of our King is spiritual knowledge and the riches of virtues. In these our peacemaker delights, and from these he honors those devoted and faithfully obedient to him. Azmoth is suitably placed over them, for his name is interpreted as “strong through death,” because the knowledge and teaching of those who possess steadfastness of mind and shine with the virtue of patience are proven sound. Hence a certain Wise Man says: “A man’s instruction is discerned through patience” (Proverbs 19). And again: “A patient man,” he says, “is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit is better than one who captures a city” (Proverbs 16). Azmoth is also appropriately called the son of Adiel, which is interpreted “God is my Father,” because the saints clearly know that whatever they possess of the power of the virtues is theirs by God’s gift.

Jonathan son of Ozias presided over those treasuries that were in the cities, villages, and towers. In this passage “treasuries” signifies not only money but all possessions. Figuratively, the office of the true Solomon is rightly entrusted in cities, villages, and towers to one who preserves the dignity of the name Jonathan and the faith and works of his father Ozias. Jonathan is interpreted as “gift of God,” and Ozias as “strength of the Lord.” Whoever, therefore, receives the light of knowledge by God’s gift and vigorously preserves the rectitude of faith through good works, not inappropriately receives the care and guardianship of the Churches of God.

Ezri son of Chelub was in charge of agricultural work and of the farmers who cultivated the land; Shemaiah the Ramathite was over the cultivators of the vineyards; and Zabdi the Aphonite was over the wine-cellars. Who could better represent the person of a farmer and cultivator of vineyards than one who exercises the office of preacher and teacher in the Church? The pages of the divine books prove this by clear indications. Thus, in an evangelical parable, the Lord testifies that, after removing the wicked farmers, he entrusted his vineyard to other farmers who would return its fruit to him in its seasons (Matthew 21). In another parable, the master of a household hired laborers for his vineyard at different hours (Matthew 20). The Lord’s vineyard, as Isaiah testifies, is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are its beloved plant (Isaiah 5).

The wine-cellars can have the same significance as the storehouses in the Gospel where wheat is gathered: there the fruit of our labor is collected and kept for the future, and each cultivator will receive the fitting reward of his labor. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The one who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life” (John 4). Nor does the interpretation of the names of the overseers contradict this sense. Ezri is interpreted as “helped by the Lord,” Shemaiah as “hearing the Lord,” and Zabdi as “a mighty or abundant flow.” For whoever hears the Lord by attending to his commands, and whom he himself helps by his mercy so that he may accomplish in action what he understands, gathers an abundant fruit of good works unto eternal life.

Balanan the Gederite was over the olive groves and fig orchards in the plains, and Joash was over the oil storehouses. The olive groves and fig orchards, where olives and figs grow, signify gatherings of the saints, who have in their breast the oil of mercy and charity, and in their conduct the sweetness of gentleness and humility. These virtues are found in the plains because they are open and readily available to all, and seek not partiality toward persons but the rectitude of good will. The oil storehouses can likewise signify the places where the fruits of the individual virtues are gathered, for which their workers will be worthily rewarded in the future. Thus Balanan, whose name is interpreted as “having grace,” is set over the olive groves and fig orchards, because no one has an abundance of good deeds except by God’s gift. Joash, moreover, whose name is interpreted as “hoping” or “the strength of the Lord,” guards the oil storehouses, because no one will attain the reward unless, with steadfast hope, he directs the strength of his mind toward the heavenly kingdom.

Setrai the Sharonite was placed over the herds that grazed in Sharon. By the name “herds,” the Jewish peoples of the synagogue may be signified: they bore the yoke of the Law and supplied their hearers with the milk of simple teaching. Setrai is placed over them; his name is interpreted as “my hearer” or “my hiding place.” He signifies the choir of the prophets, who, instructed by inward hearing through the grace of the Holy Spirit, brought forth in figurative speech the mysteries hidden from the ages, to be revealed through the Gospel.

[Col. 0404D] “And over the cattle in the valleys, Saphat son of Adil.” By the name “cattle,” the persons of teachers may be understood. Through their teachings they cultivate the hearts of the humble, and by the evangelical plow they till the soil of the Church, causing the fruits of virtues to sprout. Their master and leader is called Saphat, which is interpreted as “he judged”; he is the son of Adil, that is, “of the father of grace,” signifying the apostolic order, which by the Lord’s own election is placed over the other teachers. To them the author of all good has also granted judicial authority, saying to them in the Gospel:

> “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

[Col. 0405A] “Over the camels, Ubil the Ishmaelite; and over the asses, Jadaiah the Meronathite.” Through camels and asses, animals that are deformed and unclean, the Gentiles may be represented. Once corrupted by the strength of their sins, they practiced the uncleanness of lust; but when they came into the possession and kingdom of our David, they received as their teachers Ubil and Jadaiah. These teachers despised human philosophy and the world’s empty deception and chose the simplicity of Christ’s Gospel, not wishing to be considered great but humble and despised (Colossians 2). Their names plainly demonstrate this. Ubil is interpreted as “foolish” or “without understanding,” while Jadaiah means “was half.”

Thus the Teacher of the Gentiles, writing to the Corinthians who thought highly of themselves, says:

> “Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the strong; and God chose the base and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh might boast in his presence” (1 Corinthians 1).

And again:

> “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘I will seize the wise in their craftiness’” (1 Corinthians 3). “And again: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile’” (ibid.).

Over the sheep also was Jaziz the Hagrite. By the name “sheep,” the simple and gentle may be understood. Whoever follows the Lord’s command in his actions—the command that the Lord Jesus gave to his disciples in the Gospel, saying, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11)—is rightly called a sheep of the Lord.

Aziz the Hagrite is appointed shepherd over these sheep, because the one who turns to the Lord’s service with his whole mind and all his strength, who longs for the future life with complete devotion and recognizes himself as a stranger and pilgrim in this world, will, rightly assisted by the Lord, worthily fulfill the guardianship of the Lord’s flock.

Jonathan, David’s uncle, a counselor, a prudent and learned man, together with Jahiel son of Achamoni, was with the king’s sons. What is signified by Jonathan—whose name is interpreted as “gift of the Lord” or “a dove has given”—if not the apostles and prophets, who descended from the former people and the stock of the patriarchs? Fully instructed not only in the letter of the Law but also in spiritual prudence through the gift of the Holy Spirit, they were deemed worthy to know the secrets of the true David. Hence Truth himself says to these same apostles in the Gospel:

> “I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

Jahiel son of Achamoni was associated with him in the fellowship of counsel; that is, he represents those preachers of the Gospel who had come to the faith from the Gentiles. The names themselves express this well, for Jahiel is interpreted as “the rest of God,” and Achamoni as “of thorns.” Those who had been exceedingly harsh through the error of paganism and the thorns of vices were made, through the rectitude of conversion, the rest of God. Hence the Lord says through the prophet:

> “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

What follows—“They were with the sons of the king”—shows that the holy teachers are guardians of the faithful, who, regenerated through sacred baptism, were deemed worthy through the grace of the Holy Spirit to belong to God.

Achitophel was also the king’s counselor. What is signified by Achitophel, who had once been David’s counselor but later, corrupted by desire, plotted with Absalom against David’s life, if not Judas Iscariot, who fell from the summit of the apostolate into the pit of betrayal? The name Achitophel expresses this well: it is interpreted as “my falling brother,” or “my rushing brother,” or “my plotting brother.” He had held a place of intimacy with the Savior himself among the other apostles; but later, seduced by avarice among the Jews and meditating the Lord’s death, he brought upon himself the ruin of perpetual death.

Accordingly, Achitophel—as the Book of Kings relates (2 Samuel 17)—when he saw that his counsel had been foolishly rejected, chose to end his life by hanging himself in his own house. Likewise Judas, as the Gospel bears witness, when he saw that Jesus had been condemned to death, moved by remorse, returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood.” But they said: “What is that to us? You see to it.” After throwing the silver into the temple, he withdrew and went away and hanged himself (Matthew 27).

The Jews themselves may also appropriately be understood through Achitophel. Once exceedingly dear because of the prerogative of their fathers (Romans 9) and renowned through their converse with God, they were scandalized by the incarnation and Passion and became exceedingly savage enemies. Accordingly, receiving punishment proportionate to their merits, they were killed by the Roman authorities in their own house—that is, in Jerusalem.

“And Chushai the Archite, the king’s friend.” Chushai, whose name is interpreted as “Ethiopian,” remained faithful to David in everything. He signifies the people of the Gentiles, who, after coming to the faith, persevered in faithfulness to the end. Thus, distinguishing between the two peoples, the Lord says through the Psalmist:

> “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped from their paths” (Psalm 17).

After Achitophel, Joiada son of Benaiah and Abiathar was counselor. The substitution of Joiada in Achitophel’s place signifies that, when Judas transgressed and fell from the apostolate, the twelfth place did not remain vacant. Instead, by the arrangement of Peter and the other apostles, Matthias—who knew the grace of God, humble and faithful—succeeded to the place of the transgressor. He humbly preserved the grace that he had received as God’s gift.

The interpretations of the names Joiada and Benaiah themselves show this well. Joiada is interpreted as “knowing” or “recognizing,” and Benaiah as “builder of the Lord.” The one whom God’s grace had chosen beforehand for the apostolate was strengthened and preserved in that dignity by the recognition of sound faith.

What follows—“and Abiathar”—historically shows that Abiathar son of Abimelech the priest was for a time among David’s counselors. But because he deviated in the election of Adonijah, whom he wished to make king together with Joab instead of Solomon, he signifies those who in the Church do not preserve, because of earthly desire, either their office or the grace they received by divine gift. According to the judgment of the true Solomon, if they refuse to remain in the prison of repentance according to the example of Achitophel, they will be punished with everlasting punishment.

The commander of the king’s army was Joab. Joab, a most warlike man and exceedingly vigorous in military action, can here signify those who, devoting themselves to the perfection of the virtues, pursue every form of wickedness with all their strength. His name is interpreted as “enemy” or “the same father.” In their person the same prophet says to the Lord in the Psalter:

> “I directed myself toward all his commandments; I hated every path of iniquity” (Psalm 117).

The apostles of Christ are believed to have fully possessed this position of dignity, for they deserved to hear from the Lord himself in the Gospel: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5). And again: “Behold,” he says, “I give you power over serpents and scorpions and over all the strength of the enemy” (Luke 10). Those who are most perfect in the exercise of the virtues rightly appear most glorious, surpassing the other faithful in dignity.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. David’s Last Words, in Which He Exhorted His Son Solomon and All Israel Concerning the Building of the Temple and the Worship of God

[Col. 0407C] David therefore gathered all the leaders of Israel, the commanders of the tribes, and the chiefs of the divisions who served the king; also the tribunes and centurions who were over the king’s property and possessions; and the sons, together with the eunuchs, and every powerful and exceptionally robust man in the army of Jerusalem, and so forth.

It may be asked how eunuchs are said to have been summoned to so great an assembly, when the authority of the Law forbids Israelites to be castrated or marked by any mutilation, and foreigners could scarcely be admitted to such a private and honorable council. Hence the Hebrews say that those are called eunuchs here who, alienated from all worldly activity, devoted themselves solely to prayer and reading, and who had wives not for the sake of lust but for the purpose of having children. Josephus, their historian, calls them Essenes, according to the name of their sect.

David gave his son Solomon the plan of the vestibule, the temple, the storerooms, the chambers in the inner recesses, and the house of propitiation, as well as of all the courts and side chambers around it; the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of the sacred things; the divisions of the priests and Levites; everything pertaining to the work of the house of the Lord; and all the vessels used in the ministry of the Lord’s temple. He specified the weight of gold for the ministry vessels and the weight of silver according to the different kinds of vessels and works, and so forth.

What does it mean that David gave his son Solomon the plan of the entire house of God, which Solomon himself was to build, and supplied all the expenses for it, except that the psalms of David, together with the mystical words and deeds of himself and of the other fathers who lived under the Old Testament, prefigured through figures and enigmas everything that our incarnate Peacemaker was going to construct spiritually in his Church?

There it was foretold how all the nations of the earth would receive access to enter the Church through faith and the sacrament of baptism; what the Church’s most venerable condition would be in the present life; what the perfection of the saints and their reward would be in the heavenly kingdom; how the various ministries and the progress of individuals would be ordered; and what reward would be given in the future to each according to his merits. These things were prefigured through the various chambers and side rooms, because there are many dwelling places in the kingdom of God (John 14), and also through the various vessels of different weights.

There the splendor of wisdom was prefigured in gold, and the brightness of preaching in silver—gifts that the Holy Spirit bestows on each of the faithful, distributing to each as he wills (1 Corinthians 12). If anyone wishes to know more fully how all these things were ordered and established in the holy Church, let him read the various expositions written by the holy teachers concerning the construction of the tabernacle, the temple, and its vessels; there he will find everything clearly explained.

What follows after this is:

[Col. 0408B] “He also gave gold for the tables of the showbread, according to the different tables; likewise silver for the other silver tables; also for the forks, bowls, and censers of purest gold; and golden lions, distributing weight according to the size of each lion. Likewise, he set aside different weights of silver for the silver lions. For the altar on which incense was burned he gave the purest gold, so that from it there might be made the likeness of a chariot of cherubim extending their wings and covering the ark of the Lord’s covenant.”

Nowhere, however, are lions or small lions said to have been made either in Exodus, in the construction of the tabernacle, or in Kings, in the building of the temple, except for the carved work that is said to have been made in certain temple furnishings—such as the ten bases and their panels, where lions, oxen, cherubim, and palms are mentioned as sculpted and engraved. Nor is it reported that cherubim were formed in the likeness of a chariot; only that two cherubim were made to cover the ark with their wings.

Since, therefore, mention is now made here of small lions, likewise of lions, and also of a chariot of cherubim, we must ask what mystery this indicates. For it is written in the prophet Ezekiel that in the first vision he saw beside the river Chebar a likeness of four living creatures, and this was their appearance:

> “The likeness of a human being was upon them; each had four faces and each had four wings; their feet were straight, and the sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot.”

And a little later:

> “The likeness of their faces was the face of a human being; the face of a lion on the right side of all four; the face of an ox on the left side of all four; and the face of an eagle above all four,” and so forth (Ezekiel 1).

Likewise, in another vision later on, the same prophet says:

> “Each had four faces: the first face was the face of a cherub, the second face the face of a human being, the third the face of a lion, and the fourth the face of an eagle. And the cherubim were lifted up. This was the living creature that I had seen beside the river Chebar. When the cherubim moved, the wheels moved alongside them; and when the cherubim lifted their wings to rise from the earth, the wheels did not remain behind but stayed beside them. When they stood, the wheels stood; and when they were lifted up, the wheels were lifted up with them, for the spirit of life was in them. The glory of the Lord departed from the threshold of the temple and stood over the cherubim; and the cherubim lifted their wings and rose from the earth before me. As they went out, the wheels also followed them. And it stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, and the glory of the God of Israel was over it. This was the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar, and I understood that they were cherubim. Each had four faces and each had four wings, with the likeness of human hands beneath their wings; and the likeness of their faces was the same faces that I had seen beside the river Chebar” (Ezekiel 10).

Since, therefore, a passage has been found where the chariot of cherubim over which the glory of God presided is described, let us explain its special significance according to the statements of the Fathers.

Of the four living creatures, whose appearance was like that of a human being, except that each had four faces and four wings, straight feet, and the sole of a foot resembling the imprint of a calf’s foot, some think that the four Gospels are signified by the names of these creatures.

Matthew is signified by the human being, because he described Christ as a human being: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1).

The lion is referred to Mark: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in the prophet Isaiah: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God’” (Mark 1).

The calf refers to Luke’s Gospel, because it begins with the priesthood of Zechariah.

The eagle refers to the beginning of John, who, flying aloft, began in this way: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

Others, following the foolish wisdom of the philosophers, suspect that the two hemispheres are represented in the two cherubim of the temple: ourselves and the antipodes, as though they were human beings lying on their backs and falling.

Most people, following Plato, refer the rational, irascible, and concupiscible parts of the soul to the human being, the lion, and the calf. They place reason, knowledge, understanding, counsel, virtue, and wisdom in the citadel of the human cherub; savageness, anger, and violence in the lion, which reside in the gall; and lust, luxury, and the desire for every pleasure in the liver—that is, in the calf, which clings to earthly works.

They further posit a fourth faculty, above and beyond these, which the Greeks call *synteresis* (the “spark of conscience”). It is not extinguished even in Cain’s breast after he was expelled from paradise; though overcome by pleasures or fury, and sometimes deceived by the very appearance of reason, we still perceive that we are sinning.

They properly assign this to the eagle, which does not mingle with the other three but corrects them when they go astray. In Scripture it is sometimes called the Spirit, who intercedes for us with ineffable groanings. “No one knows the things that belong to a human being except the spirit that is in him” (Romans 8; 1 Corinthians 2). Paul also prays, when writing to the Thessalonians, that this spirit be preserved whole together with soul and body (1 Thessalonians 5).

Yet we see that this conscience too is sometimes cast down, according to what is written in Proverbs: “When the wicked comes to the depths of sins, he despises” (Proverbs 18). Some even abandon their proper place and have no shame or modesty in their offenses; they deserve to hear: “You have the face of a prostitute; you do not know how to blush” (Jeremiah 3).

God therefore governs this chariot as a charioteer, restraining it when it runs with disordered steps, making it teachable, and compelling it to obey his command. We too shall address this discussion of the parts of the soul—that is, of the human being, whom these philosophers call the lesser world.

There are those who simply believe that, according to the view of Hippocrates, the four living creatures signify the four elements from which everything is composed: fire, air, water, and earth.

They therefore think that the four wheels, rising from earthly things to heavenly ones, are bound to the individual fourfold creatures and to the mixture of those same elements. They also understand them as signifying the circle of the seasons, which is completed in three-month periods, and the revolving year, which received its name from always turning and returning upon itself. Of these things it has beautifully been said in a single verse:

> “Spring, summer, autumn, winter, and month and year.”

They think that the statement “it was in the wheel” signifies year after year. Another poet says:

> “And the year rolls back upon itself along its own tracks.”

They wish the heaven that we see to be understood through the likeness of the firmament, which is compared with crystal. Beneath it, they say, the four living creatures revolve and pass; and the throne of sapphire color, together with the human figure seated above it in human likeness, describes the rule of almighty God, who governs all things and has everything beneath his feet. Finally, they believe that this is called the vision of the likeness of the Lord’s glory, through which, as through a kind of painting and image, Providence is displayed.

The fact that the feet of the living creatures are said to be straight, and the sole of the foot like that of a calf—round and earthly—indicates that they fly upward to heavenly things and, with all angles removed, follow roundness, which is the most beautiful of all figures. The flashing sparks with which everything is filled indicate light; and the human hand beneath the wings of the human being, the lion, the calf, and the eagle signifies that reason sustains everything and raises it from earthly humility to heavenly things.

These interpretations can be applied to the Gospels and to everything we have set forth above. According to the anagogical sense, just as the four living creatures signify the four Gospels and the four evangelists, so under their form they may also signify perfect persons.

[Col. 0411A] Every chosen person who is perfect in the way of the Lord is at once human being, calf, lion, and eagle. The human being is a rational animal; the calf is customarily slaughtered in sacrifice; the lion is the strongest of beasts and fears no encounter; and the eagle flies to the heights and fixes its eyes upon the reflected rays of the sun.

Everyone who is perfect in reason is therefore a human being; when he mortifies himself with respect to pleasures of this kind, he is a calf. Because, through this voluntary mortification, he possesses the strength of security against every adversity, he is a lion. Hence it is written: “The righteous is confident like a lion, without terror” (Proverbs 28).

Because he contemplates sublimely the things that are heavenly and eternal, he is an eagle. Since every righteous person becomes a human being through reason, a calf through the sacrificial mortification of himself, a lion through the strength of security, and an eagle through contemplation, each perfect person may rightly be signified through these and the other living creatures. We say this in order to show that what has been said about the four living creatures also pertains to each of the perfect.

The statement that the glory or majesty of the Lord, which had stood at the threshold of the temple, stood over the cherubim, and that the cherubim, lifting their wings, rose up—as the prophet saw—with the wheels following alongside, and stood at the entrance of the eastern gate of the house of the Lord, shows that God’s protection gradually departs from Israel.

At first it was in the temple; then it stood in the court of the temple, or at the threshold. When it departed from the temple, cloud and darkness filled the inner chambers of the temple. Again the glory itself sat upon the cherubim; and while they stood, flew away, and went toward the exterior, the wheels followed, and the glory stood at the eastern gate of the house of the Lord.

When the prophet saw this, he said: “This is the living creature that I saw beneath the God of Israel beside the river Chebar, and I understood that they were cherubim.”

What new thing had he seen that made him understand that they were cherubim, when previously he had not understood this? In our language, “cherubim” means “a multitude of knowledge”: the knowledge of God’s mysteries, his throne, and his resting place. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself” (Psalm 79).

The glory of the Lord always sits in a multitude of knowledge, and it is manifested when it is shown that all things are governed by providence. No one should say that anything happens by chance: “The Lord has abandoned the earth, and the Lord does not see” (Ezekiel 8–9). Hence the cherubim’s vision and their aspiration signify forgetting what is past and stretching themselves toward the future.

Behold, according to what we promised, we have shown from the opinions of the holy Fathers how the cherubim are the chariot of God. If anyone is not pleased with this explanation, let him seek another, if perhaps he finds one somewhere that is better and more fitting.

[Col. 0411D] “All these things,” he says, “came to me in writing from the hand of the Lord, so that I might understand all the works of the pattern.” The Hebrews relate that the model of the temple and its vessels, shown by Moses on the mountain, passed to Joshua, then to the judges, to Eli, to Samuel, to David, and finally to Solomon. Hence he now says that it came to him from the hand of the Lord.

Alternatively, the hand of the Lord is the Son of God himself, through whose gift David himself and all the others received whatever they were able rationally to recognize and set forth rightly concerning the structure of the holy Church.

## CHAPTER XXIX. David’s Blessing, by Which He Blessed the Lord with All Israel, Sacrificing Victims to the Lord and Offering Burnt Offerings; Where They Anointed Solomon, Son of David, a Second Time as Prince for the Lord, and Zadok as High Priest. Concerning Solomon’s Sitting upon David’s Throne and All Israel’s Obedience to Him, and How God Gave Him the Glory of the Kingdom, Such as No King in Israel Had Possessed before Him

[Col. 0412B] The leaders of the families and the nobles of the tribes of Israel, together with the tribunes, centurions, and officials over the king’s possessions, promised contributions and gave for the work of the house of the Lord five thousand talents of gold and ten thousand solidi; ten thousand talents of silver; eighteen thousand talents of bronze; and one hundred thousand talents of iron. Whoever possessed precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the Lord through the hand of Jahiel the Gershonite, and so forth.

What does it mean that, when David offered exceedingly abundant expenses for the building of the house of God, the family leaders, nobles, tribunes, and the other dignitaries also spent various gifts from their own resources on the same work, except that each person who has learned to govern himself and those who are with him well and properly, with God’s grace going before him, ought, insofar as he is able, to labor through good zeal and devoted humility to win his neighbors and accomplish the work of God?

He should strive with all his strength to build the holy Church—the gift of God—in the splendor of wisdom, the brilliance of words, the resonance of preaching, the firmness of faith, and the jewels of various virtues. For, according to Paul’s statement, each person will receive his reward from the Lord according to his labor. If anyone builds upon God’s foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones, he will receive a reward, and his work will endure. But whoever constructs fragile works—that is, wood, hay, and straw—will suffer loss when the fire of the future judgment burns them (1 Corinthians 3).

After Scripture reports David’s prayer, it adds the following:

David then instructed the whole Church, saying: “Bless the Lord our God.” And the whole Church blessed the Lord, the God of their fathers, and they bowed down and worshiped the Lord, and afterward the king. They sacrificed victims to the Lord and offered holocausts on the following day: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, with their libations, and with every rite, in the greatest abundance, throughout all Israel. They ate and drank before the Lord on that day with great joy, and they anointed Solomon the son of David a second time; they anointed him to the Lord as ruler, and Zadok as high priest.

While David was blessing the Lord, the whole Church, instructed by him, blessed and worshiped the Lord, sacrificing victims to him and offering holocausts, because the congregation of the faithful, admonished by the writings of the prophets and likewise stirred by the words and examples of the holy Fathers, celebrates praises and hymns to God by sacrificing to him the offerings of devout confession and of holy conduct bearing the fruit of good works. It offers holocausts—that is, bulls of pious labor, rams of righteous governance, and lambs of true simplicity and innocence—with libations, namely, of sacred prayers. That the measure of the aforesaid animals is described by the number one thousand signifies that the faithful of Christ bring offerings to God with the intention that, through his grace, they may deserve to attain the perfect blessedness of eternal life. This is their joy; this is the whole intention of their heart and soul: that by this hope each person may strengthen himself and, because of the need arising from future hunger, strive to fill himself with works of virtue.

But when it is added that he anointed Solomon the son of David a second time to the Lord as ruler, and Zadok as high priest, it signifies that all the faithful, in sound faith and devout confession, alike honor and venerate the Lord Savior in both royal and priestly dignity. Since Solomon is interpreted as “peaceful,” and Zadok as “just,” these names befit no one better than our Redeemer, who is our King and priest. For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. II); he is just and loves righteousness, and is judge of the living and the dead. Every faithful person first anointed this true Peaceful One as king and priest when, in receiving holy baptism, he confessed with believing heart that he was truly king and priest, the mediator between God and human beings. He anoints him a second time when he proclaims and praises him before others through devout teaching and good practice. Hence the bride says to the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song I), because the company of the faithful, through a strong reputation for good works and preaching, carries his name far and wide to the knowledge of many. Concerning him Paul says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place” (II Cor. II).

Solomon sat upon the throne of the Lord as king in place of David his father, and he pleased everyone, and all Israel obeyed him. All the princes and powerful men, and all the sons of King David, also gave their hands and became subject to King Solomon. The power of the true Solomon pleases everyone, since all who are of sound mind delight in being subject to his rule—namely, all the princes and powerful men and all the sons of King David. For no power and no dignity of this present world can rightly disdain the dominion of this king, for whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, who has led many sons into glory, the author of our salvation (Hebr. II). Therefore they all surrender their hands to him and will be subject, serving him and doing his will. It follows:

The Lord therefore magnified Solomon over all Israel and gave him the glory of a kingdom such as no king of Israel had possessed before him. For our Peaceful One is great, and greatly to be praised, and a great King above all gods; no king in the whole world can be compared with him, because all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him (Col. I). He ascended above all the heavens in order to fulfill all things (Eph. IV); his kingdom is the kingdom of all ages, and his dominion extends through every generation and lineage.

David, son of Jesse, therefore reigned over all Israel, and the days during which he reigned over Israel were forty years: he reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. He died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and glory. I believe enough has already been said above concerning the time during which David reigned. But the statement that he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and glory, signifies that he ended his present life with an abundance of virtues and works of light, worthy of future rest and the heavenly kingdom.

For I do not remember having read anywhere of anyone who died in a good old age after leading a vicious and sinful life. Abraham died at the age of one hundred and seventy-two in a good old age, at an advanced age, and full of days (Gen. XXV). Isaac died, consumed by age, and was gathered to his people, old and full of days (Gen. XXXV). Jacob died at the age of one hundred and forty-four and was gathered to his people (Gen. L). Joseph died after completing one hundred and ten years of his life, and he was embalmed with spices (ibid.). Moses died at the age of one hundred and twenty; his eye was not dim, nor were his teeth weakened (Deut. XXXIV), but, perfected in life and conduct, he looked with the other Fathers toward eternal rest. On the contrary, “men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. LIV). But those are wretched, and their hope is among the dead (Wis. XIII), who, although—as it seemed to them—they lived out their days in prosperity (Job. XXI), nevertheless descend in a moment to the underworld, where “their worm shall not die, nor their fire be quenched” (Isa. LXVI).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0413]

## CHAPTER ONE

On the beginning of Solomon’s reign: how he offered a thousand victims at the high place of Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the Lord’s covenant then stood. On how he gathered chariots, horsemen, and teams of horses from various provinces.

**(II Chron. I.)** Solomon, son of David, was strengthened in his kingdom, and the Lord his God was with him, and he exalted him greatly. What does it mean that Solomon the son of David is said to have been strengthened in his kingdom, except that it shows our Savior—of whom Solomon, in his name and in the construction of God’s house, prefigured a type—to possess an exceedingly firm dominion? Although, according to his divinity, he possesses an everlasting kingdom with the Father and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, according to the dispensation of the humanity he assumed, he is then said to have been consecrated in his kingdom when, through the passion of the cross, he triumphed over the author of death and acquired for himself the heavenly and earthly kingdom (Col. II). Hence, rising from the dead and appearing to his disciples, he said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” and so forth (Matt. XXVIII). And “the Lord,” he says, “was with him” (Acts X), because the Father is always with the Son. Hence Truth itself says: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John VIII). For this reason Peter also said to the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles: “Men, brothers, you know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.” God the Father magnified him (Acts X), that is, exalted him on high, and gave him “the name that is above every name” (Phil. II).

Solomon commanded all Israel, the tribunes, centurions, commanders, and judges of all Israel, the heads of families, and he went with the whole multitude to the high place of Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the Lord’s covenant stood, which Moses, the servant of God, had made in the wilderness. David had brought the ark of God from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it and where he had set it up, namely, in Jerusalem. He had also placed before the Lord’s tabernacle the bronze altar which Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, had made, and Solomon offered a thousand victims upon it (Exod. XXXVI, XXXVII, XXXVIII, XXXIX).

Gibeon, from which the Gibeonites came suppliantly to Joshua (Josh. IX), was formerly the capital and royal city of the Hivites, and it fell by lot to the tribe of Benjamin. It too was set apart for the Levites (Josh. XVIII), as was shown above. I therefore wonder why Josephus wrote that Solomon, coming to Hebron, sacrificed to God on the bronze altar which Moses had made, unless perhaps he wished Hebron itself to be understood as the high place of Gibeon, because David first began to reign there (Exod. XXXVIII). Gibeon is interpreted as “height” or “the hill of a paternal kinsman.”

And behold, that same night God appeared to him, saying: “Ask what you wish me to give you.” Solomon said to God: “You showed great mercy to David my father and made me king in his place. Now therefore, Lord God, let your word be fulfilled which you promised to David my father. For you have made me king over your numerous people, who are as innumerable as the dust of the earth. Give me wisdom and understanding, so that I may go in and out before your people. For who can worthily judge this great people of yours?” and so forth.

Here we should consider morally that, if Solomon, made king in the earthly Jerusalem, did not ask God for gold, riches, possessions, or worldly glory, how much more necessary is it for the rulers of God’s holy Church, to whom the care and governance of souls have been entrusted, not to seek earthly possessions or the riches of the world, but to desire wisdom, knowledge of God’s law, and the riches of virtues, so that they may worthily judge God’s people and rightly and reasonably teach them to understand their entrance into the faith and their departure into the vision of eternal blessedness.

Solomon therefore came from the high place of Gibeon to Jerusalem, before the tabernacle of the covenant. The statement “before the tabernacle of the covenant” signifies the Lord’s ark, in which the tablets of the Lord’s testimony and covenant, which he made with Israel, had been placed—especially since it is written above: “The tabernacle of the Lord, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of holocausts, were at that time on the high place of Gibeon, and David was not able to go to the altar to entreat the Lord there, for he had been terrified with exceedingly great fear when he saw the sword of the Lord’s angel” (I Chron. XXI). After David brought the Lord’s ark into his own house, it remained there until the temple was built; then Solomon transferred it to the Lord’s temple.

He reigned over Israel and gathered chariots and horsemen for himself. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, and he stationed them in the cities of the chariots and with the king in Jerusalem. By “cities of the chariots” he means towns, buildings, and places that had been built in the land of Judah or in Jerusalem for the stationing of chariots, as the following words show, where it says: “and with the king in Jerusalem.”

Mystically, however, the chariots and horsemen of spiritual David signify the ministries of angels and human beings, who daily serve the Creator and obey his will in all things. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of rejoicing; the Lord is among them” (Ps. LXVII). It is customary for divine Scripture to speak allegorically, so that when it says one thing through David, it wishes another to be understood. Thus, here the chariot signifies the bound-together union of human beings, because charity binds the saints together just as animals are joined by reins and yokes. Hence the Lord also says: “For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI).

The unanimity of the saints is therefore the Lord’s chariot, because he sits upon it like a charioteer and guides it by the law of salvation for the service of his will. But to show that this course was not devoted to horses but attributed to human thoughts, he says: “Ten thousandfold.” This is rightly understood to refer to innumerable peoples, not to horses. He added: “Thousands of rejoicing,” which must certainly be understood of the faithful. And to show the fullness of joy, he said: “The Lord is among them,” who is the culmination of great exultation and the sweetness of every good.

But since Scripture says that Solomon had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, what is signified by the number four hundred, in which forty tens are counted, except the times of the ancient Law? Moses fasted for forty days when he was about to receive it, and the Israelite people, who were instructed by it, remained forty years in the wilderness (Exod. XXIV). And what is signified by the number twelve except the time of Christ’s grace, in which apostolic teaching nourishes the people of the New Testament by instructing them? It is fitting that Solomon’s chariots and horsemen are counted by the numbers forty and twelve, because through both Testaments holy men, instructed in the sacred writings, are made fit for God’s seat; and, presiding over them, he leads and governs us according to his will.

Horses were also brought to him from Egypt and from Kue by the king’s merchants, who went and bought a chariot of horses for six hundred silver pieces and a horse for one hundred and fifty. A similar trade was carried on throughout all the kingdoms of Syria. Some say that Kue was an island of the Cyclades; the Hebrews, however, say that this name signifies “assembly.”

Horses were brought to Solomon from Egypt and from Kue by the king’s merchants when, through spiritual merchants—that is, holy teachers from the nations—rational human beings, vigorous in understanding and action, are converted to the faith of Christ and, by living worthily, are made fit for the divine seat. Hence Scripture says that a chariot of horses was bought for six hundred silver pieces, and a horse likewise for one hundred and fifty, because, through the most beautiful language of the divine Testaments, and through the labor of holy preachers to make known the truth of the faith, human beings are brought into the service of the heavenly King.

The number six hundred, in which sixty tens are counted, signifies the perfection of evangelical teaching, in which the perfection of the whole Law truly consists—especially since our Redeemer suffered on the sixth day for the salvation of the human race and completed everything written concerning him in the Law and the Prophets. Hence, hanging on the cross, when vinegar placed upon a sponge with hyssop was offered to him, after he had received the drink he said: “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit (John XIX).

One hundred and fifty, in which three fifties are contained, clearly signifies the sanction of the Old Testament, on account of Pentecost and the jubilee, and on account of that threefold division of the Scripture of the Old Testament which the Savior made in the Gospel when he said: “It is necessary that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

Thus, from the various nations, spiritual chariots and horses are brought to the true Solomon, because his Church is gathered from every nation under heaven. Hence, according to the voice of the Psalmist: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. LXXI).

## CHAPTER II

On how Solomon chose workmen for God’s house and sent to Hiram, king of Tyre, asking his assistance, which Hiram willingly granted. On the number of proselytes assigned to the work of God’s house.

Solomon resolved to build a house for the name of the Lord and a palace for himself. He counted seventy thousand men who carried burdens on their shoulders, and seventy thousand who cut stones in the mountains, with three thousand six hundred appointed over them.

The house of God which King Solomon built in Jerusalem was made as a figure of the holy universal Church. From the first elect person to the last who is to be born at the end of the world, it is built daily by the grace of the peaceful King, namely, its Redeemer. Part of it still makes its pilgrimage away from him on earth; part of it, having escaped the hardships of pilgrimage, already reigns with him in heaven; and, when the final judgment has been completed, the whole will reign with him (I Cor. XV).

The elect angels belong to this house, whose likeness is promised to us in the future life, as the Lord says: “Those who are deemed worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they can no longer die. They are equal to the angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection” (Luke XX).

The Mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, also belongs to it, as he himself testifies when he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). Explaining this, the Evangelist added: “He was speaking about the temple of his body” (I Cor. III). The Apostle also says of us: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

If he became God’s temple through the humanity he assumed, and we become God’s temple through his Spirit dwelling in us, it is clear that that material temple represented all of us—namely, the Lord himself and his members, which we are. Yet it represented him uniquely, as the singularly chosen and precious cornerstone, founded in the foundation; and us as living stones built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, that is, upon the Lord himself (Eph. II; I Pet. II).

The same spiritual house of God is also represented by the tabernacle once made in the wilderness through Moses. But that house was on the journey by which the people came to the promised land, whereas this one was built in the promised land itself and in the city of Jerusalem. The former was frequently carried from place to place by the ministry of the Levites until it was brought into the land of the promised inheritance; the latter was constructed at once in the homeland itself and the city, so that it might always stand upon an inviolable foundation until it fulfilled the function of the heavenly figures entrusted to it (Exod. XXXVI, XXXVII, XXXVIII, XXXIX).

In the former, therefore, the toil and exile of the present Church may be figured; in the latter, future rest and blessedness. Or, certainly, because the former was made by the sons of Israel alone, while the latter was made also by proselytes and Gentiles, the fathers of the Old Testament and that ancient people of God may principally be expressed figuratively in the former, while in the latter the Church gathered from the Gentiles may be represented. Nevertheless, when the construction of both houses is examined more precisely in a spiritual sense, it is shown through many figures to suggest both the daily labors of the present Church and the enduring rewards of the future, the joys of the heavenly kingdom, the election of the first Church from Israel, and the salvation of all nations in Christ.

That Solomon is said to have resolved to build a house for the name of the Lord and a palace for himself pertains to the same meaning, because the holy Church of God is God’s house, which he perpetually inhabits, and the palace of the heavenly King, where he displays the greatness of his glory to all nations.

The true workmen of Solomon are all the elect, who either make themselves suitable for God’s building by believing rightly and doing good, or prepare others, by teaching them, for the future glory of God’s temple. What the numbers seventy, eighty, six hundred, and three signify, we shall explain below.

He also sent to Hiram, king of Tyre, saying: “As you acted toward David my father and sent him cedar wood so that he might build himself a house in which he lived, so act toward me, that I may build a house for the Lord my God, to consecrate it for burning incense before him, for fumigating spices, for the perpetual presentation of bread, and for holocausts morning and evening, also on Sabbaths, New Moons, and festivals of the Lord our God, forever, as was commanded to Israel,” and so forth.

The history of Kings relates (III Kings V) that, when Solomon was about to build a house for the Lord, he sought assistance from Hiram, king of Tyre, who had been David’s friend at all times. After Solomon had obtained the kingdom, Hiram also began to maintain peace with him, and he soon showed himself ready to assist him in everything, giving him craftsmen, wood, and gold according to his needs. In return for this kindness, Solomon gave him every year many *chori* of wheat and oil as food for his household.

There is no doubt that Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” signifies both by his name and by the serene condition of his reign the one of whom Isaiah said: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace” (Isa. IX). Hiram, whose name in Latin is said to mean “living on high,” figuratively represents believers from the Gentiles who are glorious in life as well as in faith.

Nor is there anything to prevent Hiram, because he was a king and helped Solomon in the building of the Lord’s house with royal steadfastness, from typologically signifying those converted rulers of earthly affairs through whose aid the Church is often nobly enlarged for life and raised up against heretics, schismatics, and pagans by the decrees of rulers.

Solomon therefore asked Hiram for assistance in the work of the temple because, when the Lord came in the flesh and planned to build the house he loved, namely, the Church, he chose helpers for the work not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. From both peoples he took ministers of the word.

Hiram sent Solomon cedar and fir wood cut from Lebanon, to be placed in the Lord’s house, because the converted Gentiles sent to the Lord men who had once been distinguished in the world, but who, cut down and humbled by the Lord’s preparation from the mountain of their pride, were to be placed in the Church’s building, each according to his merit or time, after being formed according to the rule of evangelical truth.

He also sent craftsmen, because the Gentiles offered to the Lord philosophers converted to true wisdom, who, by virtue of their learning, could rightly be appointed to govern peoples as well. Such was Dionysius the Areopagite in the time of the apostles, and later the most gentle teacher and courageous martyr Cyprian, along with very many others.

He also sent gold, which is understood in almost the same sense, because it represents men distinguished by wisdom and intelligence. In return for all these offerings, the Gentiles await gifts of heavenly grace from the Lord: wheat, namely, the word of God, and oil, namely, charity and the anointing and illumination of the Holy Spirit.

The matter is aptly suited to the affairs of the Church when Solomon, seeking assistance for the holy work, says to Hiram:
