“Send me therefore a learned man who knows how to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, in purple, crimson, and violet, and who knows how to carve engravings with the craftsmen whom I have with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father prepared. Send me also cedar, juniper, and pine wood from Lebanon. For I know that your servants know how to cut timber from Lebanon. My servants shall be with your servants, so that abundant timber may be prepared for me. For the house which I desire to build is exceedingly great and renowned.

“Moreover, I shall give as provisions to your servants who are to cut the timber twenty thousand kors of wheat, an equal number of kors of barley, twenty thousand measures of oil, and so forth.”

The servants of Hiram who cut cedars from Lebanon for Solomon are chosen teachers from the Gentiles. Their duty is to lay low, by correcting the pride of those who rejoice in the possessions and glory of this world, and to transfer their desires to the service of their Redeemer. Solomon’s servants were with these servants and applied themselves together to the work mentioned, because the first teachers from the Gentiles necessarily had to be instructed in the word of faith by the teaching of the apostles themselves, who had learned from the Lord. Otherwise, if they began to teach without teachers, they would become teachers of error.

For this reason Solomon wished Hiram’s servants to cut timber for him from Lebanon: they were more skilled than his servants at cutting. But for this reason also he wished his own servants to be present with them, so that they might show those who were cutting what dimensions the timber ought to have. The meaning of this figure is readily apparent: the apostles knew more certainly the word of the Gospel which they had heard from the Lord. But Gentiles converted from error and transformed into the truth of the Gospel knew the errors of the Gentiles better; and the better they knew them, the more skillfully they learned to defeat and abolish them.

King Hiram of Tyre said in the letter he sent to Solomon: “Because the Lord loved his people, therefore he made you king over them.” He added: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth, who gave David the king a wise, learned, intelligent, and prudent son, so that he might build a house for the Lord and a palace for himself.

“I have therefore sent you a prudent and highly skilled craftsman, Hiram [Hebrew: Abif], my father, the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, whose father was a Tyrian. He knows how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, marble, and wood, also in purple, violet, fine linen, and crimson; he knows how to engrave every kind of carving and to devise prudently whatever may be necessary for the work, with your craftsmen and with the craftsmen of my lord David your father,” and so forth.

When Hiram says in his letter to Solomon, “I have sent you a prudent and highly skilled craftsman, my father Hiram, the son of a woman from the daughters of Dan, whose father was a Tyrian,” he shows that Hiram was descended from Salomith of the tribe of Dan, concerning whom we read in the book of Numbers (Num. XXXIV). The Hebrews, however, relate that his father was a Hebrew descended from Oholiab of the tribe of Dan, who worked with Bezalel in the wilderness (Exod. XXXVI).

As for the fact that Hiram calls him a Tyrian, the Hebrews say that this was done by translation. For in their language *Zochri* is understood as “molding.” Tyre, which they call *Ozor*, can in some places be understood as “narrowness,” and in others as “formed.” Hiram calls him his father because he had come from the land of Israel to dwell abroad, taught him the fear of the Lord, and led him to the knowledge of God.

Mystically, Hiram signifies the teachers from the Gentiles whom the Gentiles sent to the Church. These know how to work in gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and marble, and also in purple, violet, fine linen, and crimson. Gold signifies the brightness of wisdom; silver, the splendor of eloquence; bronze, the sonority of preaching; iron, the firmness of faith; marble, the beauty of virtues; wood, the greenness of good works; purple, the shedding of blood in martyrdom; violet, heavenly conduct; fine linen, bodily chastity; crimson, the fullness of charity.

The spiritual Hiram knows how to work in all these materials, because in the Church of God he knows how to be energetic and useful in each of these forms, so that every virtue of God’s house may shine with fitting splendor before human eyes for their instruction and may become acceptable before the divine gaze through the fragrance of good will.

When Hiram says to Solomon, “We shall cut timber from Lebanon for you, whatever you require, and we shall bring it by rafts over the sea to Joppa; it will be your task to transport it to Jerusalem,” this signifies that the Gentiles, having heard the fame of the Gospel, send various kinds of people with faith to receive baptism. Yet it belongs to the true Peaceful One alone, namely, our Redeemer, to cleanse their sins through the heavenly sacraments and insert them into the unity of the holy Church.

Hence John says in the Gospel: “He who sent me to baptize with water said to me: Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I).

King Solomon therefore counted all the proselytes who were in the land of Israel, after the census which David his father had taken, and they were found to number one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred. From them he made seventy thousand carry burdens on their shoulders, eighty thousand cut stones in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred supervise the work of the people.

Proselytes were called in Greek those who, born from other nations, passed over into the faith and fellowship of God’s people after receiving circumcision. The workmen of the Lord’s house therefore came from the children of Israel, from proselytes, and from the Gentiles.

From the children of Israel came the thirty thousand who were sent to cut cedars from Lebanon, as the book of Kings relates (III Kings V). From the Gentiles came Hiram and his servants, who cut timber from Lebanon together with Solomon’s servants. Thus every kind of human being through whom the Church was to be built preceded the construction of the temple.

For Jews, proselytes, and Gentiles converted to the truth of the Gospel build the one and same Church of Christ, whether by living rightly or by teaching. Solomon therefore had seventy thousand men who carried burdens and eighty thousand stonecutters on the mountain, apart from the supervisors who presided over the individual tasks, numbering three thousand three hundred, as it is written in Kings (ibid.), commanding the people and those who performed the work.

He calls them stonecutters. The stonecutters and the woodcutters figuratively signify the same thing: holy preachers who work upon the minds of the ignorant with the axe of God’s word, striving to transform them from the crookedness and deformity in which they were born and, once they have been instructed according to the rule, to make them suitable for the unity of the faithful, namely, the building of God’s house.

The fact that both timber and stones are cut on the mountain, and that both materials, once cut and prepared, are brought to the mountain of the Lord’s house, makes the meaning clear: we were all born on the mountain of pride, because we drew the origin of our flesh from the transgression of the first human being, which pride caused. But all who, by God’s grace, have been predestined to life are cut away through catechesis and the reception of the sacraments of faith from the mountain of pride and transferred to the mountain of the Lord’s house. For, rescued from the power of darkness, we reach the citadel of virtues, which exists in the unity of the holy Church.

It should be noted that these workmen were distributed in such a way that some cut stones on the mountain, while others carried burdens. The gifts of the Spirit are diverse. Some possess greater steadfastness in speaking and rebuking the obstinate; some are appointed to console the fainthearted and strengthen the weak; some, endowed with both virtues, are suited to the work of the Lord’s house. Such are those whom the Apostle wished to be formed when he says: “Rebuke the unruly, console the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (I Thess. V).

The supervisors who presided over the individual tasks are the authors of sacred Scripture, by whose teaching we are instructed in every matter: how it is fitting to teach the ignorant and rebuke the contemptuous, and how we ought to bear one another’s burdens so that we may fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

The aforesaid workmen are rightly said to number seventy thousand and eighty thousand: seventy because of the Sabbath-rest of souls—for the seventh day was consecrated as the Sabbath, that is, as rest; eighty because of the hope of the resurrection, which first appeared in the Lord on the eighth day, that is, after the Sabbath, and which is also hoped for in us on the eighth day and in the eighth age.

The supervisors numbered three thousand three hundred, clearly on account of faith in the Holy Trinity, which the sacred writings preach to us. But in the history of the present book, namely, Chronicles, three thousand six hundred supervisors are written instead of the three thousand three hundred supervisors counted in the history of Kings (III Kings V). This pertains entirely to the same perfection of exalted men.

Since the Lord completed the adornment of the world in the number six, good works are rightly often represented as perfected by it. And since Holy Scripture teaches that works of righteousness are to be possessed together with faith in the truth, it is rightly stated that the supervisors of the temple’s work numbered three thousand six hundred.

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0423B]

On the construction of God’s house, and its length, breadth, and height. On how he covered the larger house with wooden panels, adorned it above with sheets of gold, and carved it with various designs. On the floor of God’s house, which he paved with the most precious marble. On the Holy of Holies and the making of the cherubim therein. On the veil that was spread before the Lord’s ark and separated the Holy of Holies from the sanctuary. On the two columns among those which Solomon cast and set in the vestibule of the temple.

Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, which had been shown to David his father at the place that David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite (2 Sam. 24; 1 Chron. 21). Thus the house of the Lord was being built in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—because the Church, enlarged throughout the whole world, rests upon one and the same faith and communion in catholic truth. For God is not in the division of minds, but “His place has been made in peace, and His dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75).

It is built on a mountain, namely, on the Lord and Savior himself, of whom Isaiah says: “And it shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2). And he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5). For he is the mountain of mountains, who indeed arose from the earth through the origin of the flesh he assumed, but by the unique summit of his dignity surpasses the power and holiness of all earthly beings. On this mountain, assuredly, the city or house of the Lord has been built, because if our hope and faith do not take root in him, they are nothing. [Col. 0423D]

And rightly it is called Mount Moriah, that is, of vision, because he deigns to see and assist his chosen ones, whom he preserves for the eternal vision of his glory, while they labor meanwhile in this life. “Which had been shown to David his father.” For the Lord who was to come in the flesh had been shown to David, just as to the other prophets.

The same place was rightly the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, because the Church too is customarily designated by the word “threshing floor,” as John says of the Lord: “Whose winnowing fan is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. 3). Ornan, whose name is interpreted as “illuminated,” was by nation a Jebusite. By nation he signifies the Gentiles; by his name he shows that they were to be illumined by the Lord and changed into sons of the Church. To them the Apostle rightly says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Jebus is the same city as Jerusalem, as was shown above. Jebus is interpreted as “trampled down,” whereas Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” As long as Ornan of the Gentiles ruled in it, it was called Jebus; but when David bought the place of the holocaust in it, and Solomon built the temple of the Lord there, it was no longer called Jebus but Jerusalem. For as long as the Gentiles remained ignorant of divine worship, they were trampled down and mocked by unclean spirits, following mute idols wherever they were led; but when the grace of their Creator looked upon them, they immediately found within themselves both the place and the name of peace.

He began to build in the second month, in the fourth year [Col. 0424B] of his reign. In the Book of Kings this is written as follows: “And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv—which is the second month—of Solomon’s reign over Israel” (1 Kings 6). The order and meaning are: In the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month. By the second month he means May. For among the Hebrews, the month in which Passover is celebrated was the beginning of the months of the year. From this it is plainly evident that, immediately after Passover had been completed, he began to build the house of the Lord; and the people are consecrated by a mystical solemnity, because he applied his hand to the mystical work.

In Kings there is also mention of the departure from Egypt, when the tabernacle began to be built [Col. 0424C] (ibid.), so that the reader may be reminded how many years passed between the building of the two houses and may recognize that this total span of time too contains a particular sacramental meaning. The worship and observance of the tabernacle continued for four hundred and eighty years, and then the temple began to be built.

That the house of the Lord began to be built in the fourth year of King Solomon may be understood mystically as signifying that, after the dispensation of the Lord’s Incarnation had been completed—which is written in the four books of the Gospel—the structure of the Church began when the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven (Acts 2). That it began in the second month may be referred to the election of the Gentiles, who, after Israel, received the building of their Creator in themselves in the second place.

Hence a second month was also permitted in the Law for celebrating Passover by those who, being unclean in soul or situated far away on a journey, were unable to come to celebrate Passover in the first month (Num. 9). Here we are most clearly represented: unclean because of the death of our soul and still situated far from the people of God, we could not celebrate the first Passover, which was accomplished in the flesh and blood of our Redeemer, by whom we were sought out and cleansed.

These are the foundations that Solomon laid in order to build the house of the Lord: sixty cubits in length, according to the first measure, and twenty cubits in width. The portico before the front, which extended lengthwise according to the measure of the width, was twenty cubits; its height, moreover, was one hundred and twenty cubits.

Finally, in the Book of Kings the dimensions [Col. 0425A] of this house are written as follows: “The house that Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high” (1 Kings 6).

The length of the house signifies the long-suffering of the holy Church, which she endures and tolerates in the exile of this pilgrimage until she reaches the homeland for which she waits. The width signifies charity, by which, with the heart enlarged, she rejoices to love not only friends in God but also enemies for God’s sake (Matt. 5), until the time comes when, whether her enemies have been converted to her peace or utterly destroyed, she may rejoice with her friends alone in God.

The height proclaims the hope of future recompense. In view of it, she willingly despises all things below, whether they delight or oppose her, [Col. 0425B] until, having passed beyond both, she deserves to see only the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Ps. 26).

Here it should be noted that the thirty cubits of height did not reach to the roof of the temple but only to the lower upper chamber. For in the present book of Chronicles it is plainly written that the height was one hundred and twenty cubits (1 Kings 6). It should carefully be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned in Kings reached to the middle upper chamber. Then another thirty cubits were added up to the third upper chamber, where the doors around the temple, on the south, north, and west, reached the roof, as we learn from Josephus’s account. Then another sixty cubits were counted up to the highest roof of the temple, and thus the entire height of the house, according to the Book of Chronicles, was completed at one hundred and twenty cubits.

The portico that stood before the front of the temple toward the east, according to the testimony of the aforementioned book, likewise had the same total height of cubits. That book calls the porticoes around the temple which we mentioned storage rooms and chambers. Hence it is written in the earlier book: “David gave Solomon his son the plan of the portico of the temple, and of the storage rooms, the upper chamber, and the chambers in the inner sanctuary, and of the house of propitiation” (1 Chron. 28).

There he also mentioned the exterior buildings that stood outside the priests’ court around the temple, when he immediately added: “And also of all that he had conceived concerning the courts and the chambers around the treasuries of the house of the Lord and the treasuries of the holy things.”

That the entire height of the temple was one hundred and twenty cubits refers to the same mystery: the primitive Church in Jerusalem, after the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this number of men. Fifteen, which consists of seven and eight, is sometimes understood to signify the life to come, which is now carried on in the sabbath-rest of faithful souls but will be completed at the end of the world through the resurrection of immortal bodies. Fifteen, taken as a triangular number—that is, counted together with all its parts—makes one hundred and twenty. Therefore the great blessedness of the elect in the life to come is aptly signified by the number one hundred and twenty.

Appropriately, the third upper chamber of the house of the Lord is completed here, because after the present labors of the faithful and after the rest received by souls in the future, the full happiness of the entire Church will be completed in the glory of the resurrection. [Col. 0426A]

He also covered the larger house with boards of cypress wood and fastened sheets of refined gold over the whole of it. By “the larger house” he means the temple itself, which stood before the inner sanctuary. For the structure was divided into three parts: the portico before the temple; the temple itself, in which stood the altar of incense, the table of the bread of the Presence, and the lampstand of light; and the inner sanctuary, that is, the Holy of Holies, where the ark of the covenant and the cherubim were placed behind the veil.

All these may be distinguished according to their spiritual meaning, so that we may say that the portico [Col. 0426B] before the temple represents the figure of the faithful of ancient times; the temple itself represents those who came into the world after the time of the Lord’s Incarnation; and the inner house represents the joys of the heavenly kingdom, which are given to the righteous of both groups.

It should therefore be noted that the walls of this house were made of precious stones, covered with cypress or cedar wood, and further clothed with sheets of gold. Hence it is written in Kings: “And the whole house was clothed with cedar, having its carved moldings, its carefully fashioned joints, and its projecting carvings” (1 Kings 6).

The stones of the wall or pavement, the boards, and the gold all signify the life of the saints in the Church, but with this distinction when they are placed together: the living stones are the saints, joined to one another by the strength of faith according to one and the same rule; the cedar or cypress boards are the saints, connected with one another in one and the same faith through the breadth of various virtues according to the gift of the Holy Spirit; the sheets of gold are the saints who possess the surpassing charity of knowledge and rejoice together with one another in this most pleasing radiance.

The blessed Apostle gathered these three into one understanding when he said: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5). The stone held the figure of unconquered faith; the cedar or cypress, of fragrant action; gold, of love that transcends all things.

He carved palms and what resembled chains embracing one another into it. The carving of palms is a depiction [Col. 0426D] of the virtues through which true victory is attained and the future reward of heaven is earned. The chains embracing one another are the services of charity, by which holy brotherhood is joined together and throughout the whole world is formed into one house of Christ.

This house also, according to what is written in Kings (1 Kings 6), has projecting carvings, since the works of the virtues of the saints do not conceal themselves in secret but openly reveal to everyone, in clear expression, what kind of people they are and what they do as an example of life.

He also paved the floor of the temple with very precious marble, with much adornment. In Kings the floor of the house of God is described as follows: “He covered the floor with boards of fir” (1 Kings 6). From this it is clear that he did not place the fir boards with which he was to cover the floor directly on the ground, but first covered it with marble, then placed the boards over the marble, and added a third covering of gold over these two, as is read below.

Just as the breadth of the wall, rising upward and reaching to the ceilings, signifies the progress of the virtues by which the elect reach the heavenly kingdom—or, certainly, the choirs of the elect themselves succeeding one another through changing ages—so the evenness of the floor appropriately demonstrates their harmonious humility, by which, placed together in this temporal life, they conduct themselves toward one another socially, at the prompting of charity.

That this floor was laid with very precious marble and much adornment, and that this marble was immediately covered with fir boards, signifies that the life of the righteous must first be fortified in the heart by the firmness of faith and then adorned in action by the breadth of spiritual virtues. Otherwise, what benefit would there have been in the beauty of the most precious marble, covered with wooden boards, if it did not silently signify something mystical and teach that the fullness of good works must be supported by the strength of undefiled faith?

The fir, because of its height and its long-lasting strength, appropriately signifies the mind of the elect, which scorns even the lowest desires, is always intent upon contemplation of heavenly things, and is especially excellent in the virtue of patience.

The sheets of gold placed over the marble or fir boards signify the breadth of charity proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1). For just as gold is more precious than other metals, so charity shines with a unique brightness, surpassing the other virtues, in the temple of God. Concerning this it is subsequently added:

The gold was of the purest kind; from its sheets he covered the house, its beams, doorposts, walls, and doors. Solomon covered the walls of the temple with gold when the Redeemer illumined the blind son with the light of wisdom and charity; and he covered the beams when he especially exalted the holy teachers with that same light of wisdom and with the honor of contemplation and love.

He covered the doorposts and doors when, with the Lord himself opening it, he showed to all who entered the Church the inner sanctuary of faith in the truth by which it shines. Therefore the Lord is the door of the temple, because no one comes to the Father except through him (John 14). And as he says elsewhere: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out and find pasture” (John 10).

He also carved cherubim on the walls. That is, he formed an angelic way of life in human conduct, so that just as God is laudably served by angels in heaven, so he might also be devoutly served by human beings on earth.

He also made the Holy of Holies, twenty cubits long, according to the width of the house, and likewise twenty cubits wide, and covered it with sheets of gold, as if with six hundred talents. Hence Kings also says: “The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high” (1 Kings 6).

The inner sanctuary is called the “oracle,” because it is the house that is also called the Holy of Holies, since either divine speech to human beings or evangelical discourse is granted together with the mystery of the revelation of hidden things. Hence the oracle was rightly made in the inner sanctuary, that is, in the interior house, because in the heavenly homeland the vision and speech of angels will be revealed to us, together with the very presence of God.

When it says that it was twenty cubits high, it signifies the cedar wall that separated the oracle, that is, the Holy of Holies, from the outer building. The oracle itself, where the ark was, had twenty cubits in length, width, and height—that is, it was square—because in that heavenly homeland, where the eyes of the saints see Christ the King in his beauty, only the vision of divine and fraternal charity shines everywhere.

This is further established by the following words [Col. 0428B]: “And he covered it with sheets of gold.” This is plainly to say that he fulfilled the duties of heavenly charity. What follows, “as if with six hundred talents,” signifies, through the name of the talent by which perfection of weight is indicated, the perfection of charity—as it does also in the number six hundred, in which the number one hundred is multiplied by six.

He also made golden nails, so that each nail weighed fifty shekels; and he covered the upper chambers with gold. In Scripture the number fifty commonly signifies the remission of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and eternal rest. Each nail weighed fifty shekels, and by these the sheets of gold were fastened to the walls of the house of the Lord, because the heavenly words by which we advance and are preserved in the love of good works promise us forgiveness of sins through the grace of the Holy Spirit and promise an eternal sabbath-rest in the future (Isa. 66).

These are the nails of love. There are also other nails of fear, by which beginners and those who have not yet reached perfection mortify the allurements of vices and bodily pleasures, being pierced by those words of truth through whose instruction we are taught to crucify our flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5). The Prophet desired to possess these when he said: “Pierce my flesh with the fear of you, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118). But when he had again reached more perfect things, he spoke of the nail of love: “But it is good for me to adhere to God” (Ps. 72).

That the upper chambers too were covered with gold refers to the same meaning. Just as the inner house, the Holy of Holies where the ark was, signifies the inner life of the saints in the sight of their Creator and Redeemer, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You will hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of men” (Ps. 30), so the upper chambers signify that this same life is on high, that is, in heaven, and not in this world, as the Apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Col. 3).

He also made in the Holy of Holies two cherubim in sculpted work and covered them with gold. The wings of the cherubim extended twenty cubits, so that one wing was five cubits and touched the wall of the house, while the other wing [Col. 0429A] extended five cubits and touched the wing of the other cherub. Likewise, one wing of the other cherub was five cubits and touched the wall, while its other wing, five cubits long, touched the wing of the other cherub.

Thus the wings of both cherubim were spread out and extended for twenty cubits. They themselves stood with their feet upright, and their faces were turned toward the outer house.

This is also more fully related in the Book of Kings, where it is written: “He made in the inner sanctuary two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high. One wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits—that is, ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other wing. The second cherub was also ten cubits, of equal measurement, and there was one workmanship in the two cherubim [Col. 0429B]—that is, one cherub was ten cubits high, and likewise the second cherub. And he placed the cherubim in the midst of the inner temple. The cherubim extended their wings, and one wing touched one wall, while the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall; and their other wings touched one another in the middle of the temple. He also covered the cherubim with gold” (1 Kings 6).

“Cherubim,” as Ezekiel clearly declares (Ezek. 10), is the name of an angelic dignity. In the singular it is “cherub,” and in the plural “cherubim.” Accordingly, in the figures of the cherubim made in the oracle, the angelic ministries that always stand before their Creator in heaven may aptly be understood.

They are rightly said to have been made of olive wood, because the angelic powers have been anointed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that they may never wither away from the love of God. They are ten cubits high because they enjoy the life of eternity through the number ten, possessing within themselves the inviolate image of their Creator, preserving perpetually the holiness, justice, and truth that they received at their first creation.

The number ten consists of ten units and customarily contains within itself the name and image of a king. Therefore it most aptly corresponds to the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the holy angels always remain in the image of their Creator, according to which they were made, and where human beings who have been chosen receive again his image, which they had lost through sin.

“One wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits,” that is, together they had ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other. When wings are used as a figure of holy human beings, they signify their virtues, by which they always fly toward heavenly things and are placed among the company of angels. What could this signify more clearly than the grace of their perpetual and unfailing blessedness, since they always remain in heavenly places in the service of their Creator?

Or, certainly, because they are endowed with the lightness of spiritual nature, so that wherever they wish they immediately arrive, as if flying—and they are represented with wings here and shown with wings in the prophets. It is rightly said that one wing of the cherub was five cubits and the other five cubits, because the angelic powers guard the law of God, which is written in five books, with tireless devotion, loving the Lord their God with all their strength [Col. 0430A] and loving their neighbors as themselves. “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13).

Their neighbor consists of the angelic spirits themselves, one to another, and of the elect human beings, who are likewise their fellow citizens. Hence each wing of the cherub is said to be of the same measure (Heb. 12), because in the very devotion by which they love one another in God, they also desire our fellowship as we ascend to them.

Thus the wings together complete ten cubits when, in the twofold expression of charity, the angels rejoice in the presence of their Creator. The second cherub also had wings of ten cubits, of equal measure, and there was one workmanship in the two cherubim.

Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of the same charity of which we are speaking, because charity cannot exist with fewer than two. Hence the Savior took care to send his disciples two by two to preach (Mark 6; Luke 10), silently teaching that those who preach the word of faith must hold the virtue of love above all things.

The two cherubim were of one measure and workmanship, because there is no difference of wills or thoughts in the heavenly homeland, where all are illumined by one and the same vision and glory of the God who is present.

“And he placed the cherubim in the midst of the inner temple. The cherubim extended their wings, and one wing touched one wall, while the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall. Their other wings touched one another in the middle wall of the temple.”

It is clear from what has been said above why the cherubim were placed in the midst of the inner temple, whose dwelling is always in heaven. The cherubim extended their wings as if to fly, because angelic spirits always have their minds prepared to serve the divine will.

That one wing touched one wall and the wing of the second cherub the other wall refers to the administration of charity that the angels provide for us. That the other wings touched one another in the middle expresses the grace of love by which they embrace one another.

It rightly follows: “He also covered the cherubim with gold,” because the Creator both exalted their nature with immortal charity and filled their minds with the light of true love and humility.

It should be noted that when Moses made the tabernacle, he also made two golden cherubim, which he placed on the mercy seat above the ark (Exod. 37). Solomon added two others, much larger, to place in the temple; beneath their wings he placed the ark in the middle, together with the mercy seat and the earlier cherubim. Thus there were two cherubim in the tabernacle but four in the temple. Both sets, however, pertain to one and the same meaning.

The work was repeated and made more magnificent by Solomon so that it might be taught figuratively that, after the Lord’s Incarnation, the Church having been multiplied, the sublimity of the citizens of heaven was to be disclosed more broadly to the nations. They praise the Creator for the gift of blessedness bestowed upon them in such a way that they rejoice together also over our deliverance and introduction into the same blessedness.

For they extend their wings toward one another over the ark when they refer the benefit of the life they have received to the praise of the Lord and Savior. They extend their other wings toward the walls of the oracle when they rejoice to see holy human beings with them, touching them, as it were, with the tips of their wings—those whom they rejoice to have been their companions and imitators of their purity in this life.

They touch two walls equally with their wings because the faithful of both peoples, Jews and Gentiles, possess with them the heavenly palace—not because there is a spatial distinction between the two peoples in that homeland, but because the inner festival of blessedness becomes greater through the fellowship of a brotherhood united in God.

Therefore the cherubim extend their wings toward both walls of the oracle, because the heavenly hosts, rejoicing in the heavenly homeland over the righteous of both peoples, also stir them by the vision of their glory to praise their Creator. The heavenly ranks rejoice not only over the happiness of the righteous whom they have with them within, but also care diligently for us, who are still placed here and cry to the Lord from the depths.

Hence it is rightly written of these same cherubim in the history of the present book: “They stood with their feet upright, and their faces were turned toward the outer house.” For they desire that we, upright from the misery of this pilgrimage, should come to their fellowship.

Thus they stand with upright feet, and thus they extend their wings, covered with gold, toward the walls of the oracle, while their faces are turned toward the outer house. The angels preserve their innocence perpetually in this way, and in this way they rejoice together over the blessedness of holy souls in heaven, while they do not cease to bring aid to the elect whom they see still journeying on earth, until they introduce them also into the heavenly homeland.

“For all are ministering spirits sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1).

The two cherubim may also represent the two Testaments. These cherubim were made in the oracle because, in the counsel of divine providence—which is inaccessible and incomprehensible to us—it was ordained before the ages when, how, and through which authors sacred Scripture would be composed.

They were made of olive wood because they grant us the light of knowledge with the flame of the love of God assisting them, the love that is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5). They are ten cubits high because they proclaim that God must be served through observance of the Decalogue. Hence they show that those who faithfully serve God will be rewarded with the denarius of the eternal kingdom (Matt. 20).

They have two wings because, mindful of the covenant of their Creator, they declare that they have always pressed on and arrived at heavenly things with tireless purpose through adversity as well as prosperity; and they show their hearers that the same must be done here.

“One wing of the cherub was five cubits, and the other wing of the cherub was five cubits,” because amid every variation of passing things the saints extend all the senses of their body in service of their Creator.

“There was one workmanship in the two cherubim,” because the writers of both Testaments serve God with the same purity of conduct and devotion of charity. They proclaim the Lord with one harmonious voice and faith.

Thus the inner wings of the cherubim touched one another over the ark because the Testaments agree in their equal testimony concerning the Lord. Likewise, with their outer wings one touched one wall and the other the other wall, because the Old Testament was written specifically for the ancient people of God, while the New was written for us, who came to faith after the Lord’s Incarnation.

We are rightly compared to the second wall, that is, the northern one, because after the cold and darkness of idolatry we were granted knowledge of the light of truth. The cherubim have their faces turned toward the outer house because the divine books were composed for our sake—we who still stand outside and have been saved not in reality but in hope (Rom. 8). Their authors, already reigning with the Lord and praising him in heaven, care for our salvation and intercede before his mercy for our errors.

He also made a veil of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and linen, and wove cherubim into it. What he relates here about the veil before the oracle is omitted in Kings; but there it is related which is not found here: that at the entrance of the oracle he made little doors of olive wood, five-sided doorposts, and two doors of olive wood (1 Kings 6).

This veil was made for the sake of beauty, so that even among the gilded walls it might gleam because of its silk; but it was hung before the ark and the entrance of the oracle with a fitting signification of the same mystery as the little doors. Just as the little doors were opened at appropriate times, so the veil was to be revealed whenever those arrived who were to enter the Holy of Holies.

The continual unveiling of this veil signifies, according to the Law, the opening of the heavenly kingdom, which was given to us through the Incarnation of our Lord and Savior. Hence, when he was baptized, the heavens were opened, to show that through baptism, which he himself consecrated for us, we were to enter the gate of the heavenly homeland (Matt. 3).

And when he was dying on the cross, the same veil was torn in two from top to bottom (Matt. 27), to teach plainly that the legal figures had then reached their end, and that the truth of the Gospel, the heavenly mysteries, and the very entrance into heaven were no longer to be foretold and signified figuratively but were now at last to be opened immediately to all who, from the beginning of the world up to that time, had passed from the world in faith in the truth.

It is fitting that this same veil, beneath which one entered the oracle, is remembered as having been made of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and linen, with cherubim woven into it. Hyacinth, which imitates the color of heaven, is aptly compared with the desires for heavenly things.

Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and itself bears a blood-red appearance, not inappropriately signifies the mystery of the Lord’s passion, which we must imitate by carrying our cross.

Scarlet, which glows with a red color like flame, appropriately impresses upon us the virtue of love. Those disciples who had walked with the Lord said in wonder: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24).

Linen, which grows from the earth in a green shoot and, through the long practice of artisans, strips off its natural greenness and is brought to a white appearance, aptly signifies the chastisement of our flesh. The Apostle commands its innate moisture, as it were, to be dried up when he says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the worship of idols” (Col. 3).

He shows elsewhere to what degree of whiteness this linen should be brought, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service” (Rom. 12).

The cherubim are woven into it and are made with these same four distinguished colors when, with the Lord granting it, we protect everything we do piously from the poisoned arrows of demons through the assistance of angels.

The cherubim are woven into it when, in the good works we perform, we make continual use of an abundance of wisdom, always looking to the divine words and constantly directing our footsteps by their guidance, lest we stray from the hill of the virtues.

He also made two columns in front of the doors of the temple, thirty-five cubits high. Their capitals were five cubits [high]; he also made something like chains in the inner sanctuary and placed them upon the capitals of the columns. He also made one hundred pomegranates, which he set between the chains. He placed the columns themselves in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left. He called the one on the right Jachin, that is, “firmness”; and the one on the left Booz, that is, “in strength.”

In the Book of Kings, however, where the arrival of Hiram the craftsman to Solomon is recounted, it is written of these columns as follows:

> When he had come to King Solomon, he completed all his work. He cast two bronze columns, one column eighteen cubits high, and a line of twelve cubits encircled each column. He also made two capitals, to be placed upon the tops of the columns, cast in bronze: one capital five cubits high, and the other capital five cubits high, fashioned as though in the form of a net and chains interwoven with one another by marvelous workmanship. Both capitals of the columns were cast. There were seven lattices of network on one capital, and seven lattices on the other. He completed the columns and two rows around each of the lattices, to cover the capitals that were above the top of the pomegranates. He made the same for the second capital. The capitals that were above the tops of the columns had been fashioned like lily-work in the portico, four cubits; and again there were other capitals at the summit of the columns above, alongside the measurement of the column, opposite the lattices. There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital, and so forth. (III Kings VII)

These are the columns of which Paul says:

> James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision. (Galatians II)

By these words he seems, as it were, to explain the mystery of the material columns: what they symbolized, and why two were made. For they signify all the apostles and spiritual teachers—strong, assuredly, in faith and works, and raised upward through contemplation toward heavenly things. They are two so that, by preaching, they may bring both the Gentiles and the circumcision into the Church.

They stood in the portico before the doors of the temple, and on either side they wonderfully adorned its entrance with their dignity and beauty. The door of the temple is the Lord, because “no one comes to the Father except through him” (John XIV). And as he says elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X). The columns placed on either side surround this door when the ministers of the word show both peoples the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, so that whether someone comes to the faith of the Gospel from the light of legal knowledge or from the harshness of paganism, he may find them ready to point out the way of salvation both by word and by example.

Or certainly, according to what is written about these same columns in the present historical account—that is, in Chronicles:

> He placed the columns themselves in the vestibule of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left.

For this reason two columns were made and positioned in such a way as to teach us that, both in prosperity and in adversity, we must keep the entrance to our heavenly homeland before the eyes of our mind.

It should certainly be noted in this passage of Chronicles that the portico of the temple was also called the vestibule of the temple; and where we read in the Prophets that the priests prayed “between the vestibule and the altar,” this should be understood as meaning “between the portico and the altar.”

It is rightly recalled that each column was eighteen cubits high. For three times six makes eighteen. That three pertains to faith because of the Holy Trinity, and six to activity, because the world was made in that number of days, is perfectly clear (Genesis II). Three is multiplied by six when “the righteous lives by faith” (Habakkuk II) and increases the kinship of pious belief by carrying out good works.

The column before the doors of the temple is eighteen cubits high when every outstanding preacher openly teaches all that we cannot attain to the joys above except through faith and works of righteousness.

But when Chronicles says that the columns were thirty-five cubits [high], it likewise indicates, through allegorical meaning, the perfection of teachers. Thus, if the number seven is multiplied by five, or five by seven, they complete the number thirty-five. Five, because of the five books of the law of Moses, seems to express the Old Law; seven, because of the sevenfold Spirit remaining in the flower of the root, seems to express the Gospel.

Hence the Lord is described in the Gospel as feeding five thousand men with five loaves (Matthew XIV), and elsewhere four thousand men with seven loaves (Matthew XV). The aforesaid columns therefore had thirty-five cubits, to signify that the apostles of Christ and the teachers of the Gospel possess perfect knowledge of the two Testaments.

To them the Lord says in the Gospel:

> To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables. (Mark IV)

And after his resurrection he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV), giving them the Holy Spirit, who made everything known to them, just as he himself had promised them:

> But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything and bring to your remembrance everything that I have said to you. (John XIV)

He also made two capitals, to be placed upon the tops of the columns, cast in bronze: one capital five cubits high and the other capital five cubits high.

The tops of the columns—that is, their highest part—are the inmost hearts of faithful teachers. Just as the members are directed by the head, so all their works and words are directed by thoughts devoted to God.

The two capitals placed upon these tops are the two Testaments, to whose meditation and observance holy teachers submit themselves wholly in mind and body. Thus each capital rightly had a height of five cubits, because Mosaic-law Scripture is contained in five books, and the series of the Old Covenant encompasses five ages of the world.

The New Testament therefore proclaims nothing other than what Moses had foretold would be proclaimed through it, together with the prophets.

Both capitals of the columns were cast as though in the form of a net and chains interwoven with one another by marvelous workmanship. Hence it was written earlier in the historical account that Hiram had made something like chains in the inner sanctuary and placed them upon the tops of the columns.

The appearance of chains and the likeness of a net in the capitals signify the variety of spiritual virtues in the saints, of which it is sung to the Lord in the Psalms:

> The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded by the variety of diverse gifts. (Psalm XLIV)

Or certainly, the many-stranded interweaving of chains and the spreading of the net indicate the manifold persons of the elect. When they faithfully listen and obey, clinging to the words of holy preachers, they resemble the nets and chains attached to the tops of the columns, displaying to all who look upon them the marvel of their connection.

There were seven lattices of network on one capital, and seven lattices on the other. The number seven commonly signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, as John attests in the Apocalypse. After saying that he had seen a Lamb having seven horns and seven eyes, he immediately added by way of explanation:

> These are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth. (Revelation V)

The prophet Isaiah explains this more openly when, speaking of the Lord who was to be born in the flesh, he says:

> And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him. (Isaiah XI)

There were therefore seven lattices of network on each capital because the fathers of both Testaments received, through the grace of the one and the same sevenfold Spirit, the gift of being elect.

He completed the columns and two rows around each of the lattices, so that they might cover the capitals. There were two rows of lattices around the circumference of the capital, so that, forming a kind of circle, each returned into itself.

The figure of the mystery is not hidden: it is clear why there were two rows of lattices, since the virtue of love is known to have a twofold distinction. We are commanded to love the Lord with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves (Deuteronomy VI).

Each of those two rows, however, has seven lattices of network, because neither God nor our neighbor can be loved without the grace of the Holy Spirit.

These lattices were made to cover the capitals—that is, to surround them on every side in a circle—because every page of Holy Scripture, when rightly understood, speaks throughout of the grace of love and peace.

The capitals are the volumes of the divine utterances; the lattices are the bonds of mutual love. The capitals are covered by the lattices when the sacred utterances, so to speak, are shown to be clothed on every side with the gift of charity. For even in those things that we do not understand in the Scriptures, charity lies hidden; and in those things that we do understand, charity lies broadly revealed.

It is rightly added concerning these same lattices or capitals:

> Which were above the top of the pomegranates.

Pomegranates, whose nature is to surround many seeds within a single outer rind, aptly represent the figure of the holy Church, which habitually encloses innumerable hosts of the elect within the catholic protection of one faith.

They may also signify the life and conduct of each individual person, who, like many seeds enclosed by a single rind, embraces within himself the evils of thoughts and the emblems of spiritual virtues, and takes care to surround them with the firm guardianship of faith and humility, lest they fall away.

And with a wholly appropriate mystery the capitals were encircled by pomegranates, because holy teachers must recall the life of the faithful who came before them and always fortify their own actions and words on every side by their examples, lest they err by living or teaching otherwise than their rule requires.

When it is said that the lattices covered the capitals that were above the top of the pomegranates, the order of the work itself seems to indicate that the pomegranates were made around the lower part of the capitals, and that from those same pomegranates the lattices arose, by which the capitals were covered to some extent.

The figure of the mystery is evident: the lattices were attached above the top of the pomegranates because both refer almost to one meaning, whether of spiritual persons or of virtues. For we know that virtues arise from virtues, and that the saints walk “from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion” (Psalm LXXXIII)—a virtue beyond which none greater can be approached.

Hence the Apostle also says:

> Knowing that tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces testing, and testing produces hope. (Romans V)

The capitals that were above the tops of the columns had been fashioned like lily-work in the portico, four cubits high.

What is signified by lilies except the homeland of heavenly brightness and the loveliness of paradise, fragrant with the flowers of immortality? What is signified by four cubits except the evangelical word, which promises us entrance into that eternal blessedness and shows us the way by which it is reached?

When holy teachers show us the promised lights of the heavenly kingdom in the four books of the Gospel, they display, as it were, upon the tops of the columns a work of lily-work four cubits high.

Here it should be noted, according to the literal sense, that when the work of lily-work in the capitals is said to be four cubits, without specifying whether this refers to width or height, it is left to the judgment of the reader to decide whether it should be understood in height or in width.

It is established, however, without any doubt, that the column which a twelve-cubit cord encircled had a thickness of four cubits. For every circle has three times as much circumference as it has space across its diameter. Thus the bronze sea, because it had a diameter of ten cubits, consequently had thirty cubits in circumference, as will be read below.

But whether the statement that the lily-work was four cubits refers to width or height, the meaning remains perfectly clear, because only through the Gospel did that most desired voice resound:

> Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. (Matthew III)

What follows—“And again there were other capitals at the summit of the columns above, alongside the measurement of the column, opposite the lattices”—says “alongside the measurement of the column” to mean that they had as much breadth as the column itself. How great their height was is not reported at all.

I think that this same present account later names them epistyles, when it enumerates the construction of the temple according to its individual features. But whatever kind and whatever size these capitals may have been—for Scripture does not clearly specify their dimensions—they seem to have been added in the manner of lilies.

If one delights in seeking something mystical in their construction, they may appropriately signify the sublimity of the everlasting kingdom, concerning which it is written:

> Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him. (I Corinthians II)

But because the same fellowship of the citizens above is granted to the faithful of both peoples, it is rightly added:

> There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.

For we have said that the pomegranates represent either the whole holy Church or each of the faithful individually. The number one hundred, which reaches the right hand, is sometimes customarily placed as a figure of eternal blessedness.

This number is doubled around the second capital to indicate the mystery that the people of both Testaments, to be united in Christ, are to be brought into the crown of eternal life.

What is later said in this history—that among the other things Hiram the craftsman made for King Solomon in the construction of the temple, he made four hundred pomegranates and two lattices, so that two rows of pomegranates were joined to each lattice, which covered the epistyles and capitals of the columns—contradicts neither the historical narrative nor the allegorical meaning in any way.

According to the historical account, just as there were two columns, two capitals, and two epistyles, so there were also two lattices: one for each column, with two rows of pomegranates attached to each lattice—that is, two hundred pomegranates attached to each. Twice two hundred makes four hundred.

Mystically, just as we said that the number one hundred signifies eternal blessedness, and two hundred the peoples of both Testaments who are to be united there in Christ, so now we affirm that through the number four hundred the four Gospels promise that same blessedness to all who rightly believe in God and faithfully preserve this faith through good works to the end of life; it is to be granted by the giver of every good thing in the heavenly kingdom.

> And he set up two columns in the portico of the temple. When he had set up the column on the right, he called it by the name Jachin, that is, “firmness.” Likewise he raised the second column and called its name Booz, that is, “in strength.”

As we said above, the right-hand column represents those teachers who established the first Church in Jerusalem; the second represents those who were sent to preach to the Gentiles.

Or certainly, the right-hand column signifies those who foretold by prophecy that the Lord would come in the flesh; the second signifies those who testify that he has already come and redeemed the world by his blood.

The two columns were appropriately designated by similar names: one was called “firmness,” the other “in strength,” so that one strength of faith and works might be shown to exist in all teachers, while the sluggishness of our own time might be silently reproved. For some teachers, priests, and those who wish to be seen and called pillars of the house of God show themselves as such, although they possess absolutely no firm faith for despising the pomp of the world and desiring invisible goods, no strength for correcting the errors of those placed under their authority, and not even enough diligence to understand them.

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the altar of burnt offering; the bronze sea and the oxen upon which it was placed; the ten basins in which the sacrifices were to be washed; the ten golden lampstands and ten tables; the courts of the house of the Lord and their distinctions; the various vessels that Hiram made for Solomon in the region of the Jordan, casting them in clay soil. Concerning the golden altar—that is, the altar of incense—and the table of the Presence, together with the lampstand and its lamps, and the other ministerial vessels. Concerning the inner and outer sacrifices of the temple.

He also made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high.

It is written later that Solomon made all the vessels of the house of God, together with the golden altar, the tables, and upon them the loaves of the Presence, and so forth (Exodus XXXVII).

Moses indeed made the altar of incense in the wilderness, one cubit long, one cubit wide, and two cubits high. But how large Solomon made this altar, the Book of Kings or Chronicles does not say; it only says that he made it of gold.

It is clear, however, that he could not make it as large as the altar of burnt offering. For if it had been made ten cubits long and ten cubits wide, it would have filled the entire width of the temple.

Therefore, to the degree that the altar of burnt offering was placed farther outside than the altar of incense, and to the degree that it was inferior in the kind of offering and in the baseness of its metal, it surpassed the other in the size of its dimensions and in the frequency of sacrifices.

For there are many more to whom it is said, “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments,” than there are those who delight to hear, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have, and give to the poor” (Matthew XIX).

Yet the measurement of this altar is not without mystical meaning or significance in its number. It was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high. We spoke above, in the exposition of the temple and its vestibule, about this number.

But it should also be said briefly now that, if the altar of burnt offering represents in the Church those who seek to consecrate their body and soul to God through the fire of his love, their perseverance in good works is signified by the length of the altar, their breadth in love of God and neighbor by its width, and their hope in awaiting divine visitation by its height.

That the length and width of the altar were each twenty cubits clearly signifies the great perfection of that unwearied endurance and sincere love which is granted to us through observance of both Testaments.

For four times five completes the number twenty. There are five books of the Mosaic Law, while there are four books of evangelical freedom. When, enlightened by the grace of the Gospel, we attain to the spiritual understanding and observance of the Law, we complete the number twenty.

The same number is found in the length and width of the altar when the hearts of the elect, taught by both Testaments and assisted by the one author of both Testaments, preserve perseverance in good works even amid persecutions and show the cheerfulness of love even toward those who persecute them.

The number ten commonly signifies hope in heavenly rewards, as the Lord affirms when he testifies that those who labor in the vineyard of the great householder will be rewarded with a denarius (Matthew XX). The same altar, made as a figure of the elect, is therefore said to be ten cubits high, to signify their perpetual life.

The cast bronze sea was ten cubits from lip to lip, round all around; it was five cubits high, and a cord of thirty cubits encircled it. There was also a likeness of oxen beneath it, and exteriorly, carvings extending for ten cubits, as though in two rows, surrounded the belly of the sea.

The oxen were cast, and the sea itself was placed upon twelve oxen. Three of these faced north, three west, three south, and the remaining three east, with the sea set above them. The hindquarters of the oxen were inside, beneath the sea.

Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its lip was like the lip of a cup or like the rim of an open lily. It held three thousand measures.

These same details are contained in the Book of Kings, although they are reported there in a mixed order. Therefore, it is pleasing to reproduce here, for the most part, what was said there in the exposition of the same passage.

This cast sea was made as a figure of the saving bath in which we are cleansed for the remission of sins. For the priests washed in it, as the Book of Chronicles will testify below.

It is clear that in Scripture all the priests are figuratively called the elect, because they are members of the supreme Priest, our Lord Jesus Christ.

Scripture rightly gave this vessel the name “sea,” as a reminder of the Red Sea, in which the form of baptism first preceded through the destruction of the Egyptians and the liberation of God’s people (Exodus XIV), as the Apostle explains when he says:

> Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. (I Corinthians X)

The sacrament of baptism seeks purity of life for us in this world and promises us the glory of eternal life in the future.

Both of these are signified in one statement by this bronze sea when it is said to be ten cubits from lip to lip. For in the ten commandments the Lord expressed everything that we ought to do (Exodus XX). Likewise, he signified the reward of good works by the denarius when he declared that it should be given to those laboring in the vineyard (Matthew XX).

The sea was therefore ten cubits from lip to lip because, from the first person baptized in the name of Jesus Christ to the last person who will believe and be baptized at the end of the world, the whole chorus of the faithful must enter by one and the same way of truth and hope for a common crown of righteousness from the Lord.

It was round all around so that the whole world might be signified as being cleansed from the filth of sins by the bath of life.

It is appropriately added:

> Its height was five cubits.

For whatever we have sinned by sight, by hearing, by smell, by taste, or by touch, all this the grace of God forgives us through the washing of the life-giving font.

But the remission of past sins is not enough if thereafter a person does not strive to persist in good works. Otherwise, when the devil who has gone out from a person sees that the person is idle from good works, he returns with greater force and makes that person’s final condition worse than the first (Luke XI).

Hence it is appropriately added:

> And a cord of thirty cubits encircled its circumference.

The cord clearly signifies the discipline of the heavenly commandments, by which we are bound back from our own wills, as Scripture says:

> A threefold cord is not easily broken. (Ecclesiastes IV)

For the observance of God’s commandments, established in the hearts of the elect by faith, hope, and love of the reward above, cannot be undone by any obstacle of temporal things.

And carved work surrounded it beneath the lip, extending for ten cubits around the sea. There were two rows of cast carved work depicting scenes.

Since it was said above that a cord of thirty cubits went around the sea, and it is now added that this carved work, placed beneath the lip, extended for ten cubits, it is clear from both accounts that the vessel was shaped like an open and spreading bowl, narrowing from the thirty cubits of circumference that it had at the lip to ten cubits.

Carved work depicting scenes is that which imitates certain histories or events. Therefore, the scenes carved around the sea rightly signify examples from earlier times, which we must observe attentively so that we may see by what works the saints pleased God from the beginning, with what obstinacy the wicked persisted in crimes, and with what misery the reprobate perished because of their crimes.

And it stood upon twelve oxen, three of which faced north, three west, three south, and three east.

The twelve oxen are the twelve apostles and all those who, in their place, have accepted the governance of the holy Church in Christ.

These oxen carry the sea placed upon them when the apostles and the successors of the apostles strive to fulfill with ready devotion the duty of preaching the Gospel entrusted to them.

They face three toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east when they preach the faith of the Holy Trinity in all the regions of the four-cornered world.

All their hindquarters were concealed inside. The hindquarters of the oxen are hidden inside because the reward with which holy preachers will be endowed forever has already been determined by the judgment of the inner Judge; but it remains altogether hidden from us, who are still outside.

Yet this cannot at all be hidden from us: everyone who receives the bath of baptism for salvation and life must possess faith, hope, and charity. Without these three virtues, no one can either accomplish anything worthwhile or enter into life.

Hence the Book of Kings rightly adds:

> The thickness of the basin was three inches. (II Kings VII)

The thickness of the basin in the sea is the firmness of virtue in baptism. Its thickness is three inches when the reception of baptism is fortified by the strength of faith, hope, and love.

Nor is baptism shown to be beneficial to those who receive it in any other way unless the firm certainty of these virtues strengthens both the mind and the works of those who receive it.

Whereas the Book of Kings says that the thickness of the basin was three inches, here in Chronicles the breadth of its thickness is said to be a palm. Josephus likewise agrees, saying that its thickness was four fingers and clearly demonstrating the size of that palm.

All these details can nevertheless be referred allegorically to the same meaning: whoever performs works of righteousness according to the teaching of the four Gospels, with faith, hope, and charity, will receive the reward of eternal life in the heavenly kingdom.

> Its lip was like the lip of a cup and like the rim of an open lily.

By the lip of the cup is expressed the taste of the Lord’s Passion; by the leaf of the open lily, the revealed glory of the Resurrection.

It held three thousand measures, or, according to the Books of Kings, two thousand baths.

The number one thousand is commonly used in Scripture to signify perfection, because it makes the number ten into a solid square. Ten multiplied by ten makes one hundred. That figure is already square, but still flat. To make it rise in height and become solid, multiply one hundred by ten, and the result is one thousand.

This number accordingly signifies the stable, unconquerable, and, as it were, squared conscience of the righteous. However one turns a square, it stands; so the mind of the elect cannot be bent from the uprightness of its position by any assault of temptations.

The sea held three thousand measures when the sacrament of baptism, given in the faith of the Holy Trinity, was shown to confer the remission of all sins upon those washed in it.

Elsewhere it says that the sea held two thousand baths. A bath is a Hebrew measure, which they call *bath*, containing three modii. It is also the *ephah*, which they call *epha*. But the *ephah* belongs to the measurement of various grains—wheat, barley, and legumes—whereas the *bath* is used for liquid substances, wine, oil, and water.

Thus the bath, because it is a fixed standard of measurement, signifies works of equity and righteousness, in which those who are baptized for the remission of sins must be instructed.

The sea held one thousand baths when the water of baptism washed the Jewish people and conveyed them into the heavenly kingdom. It received another thousand when it also made the multitudes of the nations, reborn in the same font and strengthened by works of righteousness, participants in that same everlasting kingdom.

He also made ten basins and placed five on the right and five on the left, so that in them they might wash everything that they were about to offer as a burnt offering. In the Sea, however, the priests washed themselves.

How these basins were made is narrated more fully in the Book of Kings, where it is written:

> He made ten bronze stands, four cubits long for each stand, four cubits wide, and three cubits high. The construction of the stands themselves was openwork, and there were carvings between the joints. Between the wreaths and festoons were lions, oxen, and cherubim; and similarly above, at the joints. Above the lions and oxen were bronze strips hanging down like reins. There were four wheels for each stand, with bronze axles, and at the four corners were cast supports beneath the basin, facing one another. The mouth of the basin was within, at the top of the stand; and what appeared externally was entirely round, one cubit in diameter, and likewise it had a circumference of one and a half cubits. At the corners of the columns were various engravings, while the spaces between the columns were square, not round. The four wheels, which were at the four corners of the stand, were joined beneath the stand. Thus a wheel was one and a half cubits high. Such were the wheels as are usually made for a chariot. Their axles, spokes, rims, and hubs were all cast. The four supports at the four corners of each stand were cast from the stand itself and joined to it. At the top of the stand there was a rounded structure one and a half cubits in diameter, fashioned so that the basin could be placed upon it, with its own engravings and various carvings. On those panels, which were bronze, and at the corners, he carved cherubim, lions, and palms, as though in the likeness of a standing man, so that they appeared to be added around the circumference rather than engraved. In this manner he made ten stands, all cast in one piece and alike in measurement and carving. He also made ten bronze basins. Each basin held forty baths and was four cubits in measure. He placed one basin on each of the ten stands, and so forth. (III Kings VII [1 Kings 7]; [Col. 0443A].)

The mysteries of our salvation are prefigured in many different ways, though they are one and the same. For the same apostles and apostolic men who are signified by the oxen bearing the Sea are also signified by the stands prepared to carry the basins, just as the basins themselves represent the same spiritual washing typified by the Sea. For, as the Book of Chronicles relates, they washed in them everything that was offered as a burnt offering.

The Lord’s burnt offering may generally be understood as the whole multitude of the elect, who, in accordance with the voice of the Forerunner, was baptized by him in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3). Thus the priests who washed in the Sea express the figure of those who through baptism are made participants in the highest priesthood, which is in the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0443B]. In the same way, their burnt offerings most fittingly foreshadow those who, after the washing of baptism, are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

The victim is washed in the basin when one of the faithful is drenched with the water of baptism. It is offered as a burnt offering when, through the laying on of the bishop’s hand, he receives the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The fact that ten stands were made to carry the basins may be interpreted mystically in this way: the ministers of the life-giving washing call those whom they instruct toward the joys of eternal blessedness, which are customarily signified by the number ten. Yet because it is subsequently written specifically of these same basins that five were placed on the right side of the temple and five on the left, the mysteries of the number five should rather be discerned in them [Col. 0443C].

The stands bearing the basins were placed on both sides of the temple, so that the grace of the sacred font might be shown to be offered to both peoples of God. There were five on each side so that, by the interposition of the Sea—which, as we have already said, was five cubits high—it might be typologically demonstrated that everything in which the faithful had sinned through the five bodily senses is remitted through the washing of baptism.

Thus, in the one Sea set upon twelve oxen, the unity of baptism is expressed, the baptism that was to be preached throughout the whole world by the apostles. Likewise, through the two rows of letters it is mystically shown that the Gentiles together with the Jews were to be gathered into one fellowship of faith through the water of baptism.

The fact that each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high is easily understood. Length pertains to the patience of long-suffering; width to the expansion of love; height to the hope of heavenly recompense. There are four principal virtues, upon which the rest of the structure of the virtues rests: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Therefore the length and height of the stands were measured by four cubits, because holy preachers—whether they endure the adversities of the world and the length of exile and present labors outwardly, or expand their hearts through the inner joy of love for their Creator and their neighbors—always strive to devote themselves to the virtues: prudently distinguishing between good and evil, bravely enduring adversity [Col. 0444A], restraining the heart from the desire for pleasures, and maintaining justice in their conduct.

The stands are three cubits high when, through the practice of the virtues—which they exercise with patience amid evils and love of good things—they strive with continual devotion to attain the vision of the Holy Trinity.

“The construction of the stands themselves was engraved with openwork, and there were carvings between the joints.” By “joints” he seems to mean those places where the panels of the basins themselves were joined together, so that one stand was formed from four or five panels. That the stands had equal carvings between these joints—that is, with their impressed sides facing front and back, right and left, and also above—is explained by what follows: “Between the wreaths and festoons were lions, oxen, and cherubim, and similarly above, at the joints” [Col. 0444B].
