No part of the surface of the stands was flat; rather, they were carved throughout with mystical figures, because the minds of the saints—indeed, their whole manner of life—display the grace of the virtues in every respect. No hour passes them by empty or vacant in which they cease to devote themselves to pious works, words, or thoughts.

They have wreaths carved upon them when, in their desire for the heavenly life that is above, they never dissolve the bonds of fraternal fellowship that is near at hand. They have lions between the wreaths and festoons when they so raise their minds toward heavenly hopes and so enlarge them toward love of their neighbors that they do not delay in exercising the fervor of severe scrutiny against those sinners entrusted to them.

They have oxen together with lions when they temper the very attack of correction with a spirit of gentleness; when, in the fervor of reproving, they never cease to possess the cloven hoof of discerning action and speech, nor to turn the words of divine reading over in their mouths as though ruminating.

“And above the lions and oxen were strips hanging down like reins, made of bronze.” Reins hang above the lions and oxen when holy teachers, both in the severity of discipline by which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of leniency by which they forgive the penitent, fear the judgment of their Creator, lest by binding or releasing anyone unjustly they should themselves deserve to be justly bound by him whose judgment cannot err.

“And there were four wheels for each stand, with bronze axles, and at the four sides were cast supports beneath the basin, facing one another” [Col. 0444D].

The four wheels are the four books of the Gospels. They are most appropriately compared to wheels, because just as a wheel, rolling swiftly, runs wherever it is driven, so the evangelical word, at the Lord’s command, quickly filled every region of the world through the apostles. Just as a wheel lifts the cart placed upon it from the earth and carries it, once lifted, wherever the driver directs it, so evangelical preaching raises minds from earthly desires to heavenly longings and, once raised, leads them—whether toward progress in good works or toward the ministry of preaching—wherever the assisting grace of the Spirit wills.

For it is said subsequently that these were wheels such as are usually made for a chariot. We read of the saints:

> The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands of those who rejoice. (Isaiah 67 [68])

If, then, the stands of the basins are holy teachers who minister to us the washing of life, and the four wheels of the stands are the four books of the Gospels, what are the axles of the wheels, which support the stands, except the hearts of those same teachers? While these hearts earnestly attend to the evangelical commandments, they raise them above the desires of the weak, just as axles inserted into wheels lift the stand higher from the ground.

The supports placed before the wheels, preventing them from slipping away from the axles, are the proclamations of the prophets. Through them the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures are confirmed, so that none of their readers might perhaps fall into doubt. It is rightly said that the supports placed beneath the basin at the four sides faced one another [Col. 0445B], because the whole prophetic Scripture agrees with itself, having been composed by the one Spirit of God.

There were four supports for each stand, corresponding to the number of wheels—not because there are only four prophetic books, but because in all that the prophets and Moses spoke, they furnished testimony to the words of the four Evangelists, so that from the agreement of both Testaments one faith and love of Christ might strengthen the hearts of us all.

“The mouth of the basin was within, at the top of the stand, and what appeared externally was entirely round, one cubit in diameter, and likewise it had one and a half cubits.”

The mouth of the basin was one cubit because of the unity of confession and faith by which all are baptized in the confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28), as the Apostle says:

> One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. (Ephesians 4)

The mouth was at the top of the stand to teach that through baptism a way has been opened for us to the heavenly kingdom.

The basin itself had a diameter of one and a half cubits, signifying the perfection of works and the beginning of contemplation. The whole cubit in the basin signifies the perfection of good action. Without any doubt, this was possessed by the one of whom the Lord said to the ancient tempter:

> Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil? (Job 1)

The other half-cubit is the vision of God, which is customarily granted in part even in the present life to those who are newly faithful. Thus Job, after conquering his adversary, says while speaking with the Lord:

> I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you. (Job 42)

It is written subsequently:

> One wheel was one and a half cubits high.

And shortly afterward:

> At the top of the stand there was a rounded structure one and a half cubits in diameter, fashioned so that the basin could be placed upon it.

The basins were one and a half cubits in measurement because we are washed in the font of life with the faith that we may deserve to enter life through works of justice, although, as long as we live here, we cannot be without sin. We are able here, meanwhile, to taste and love the sweetness of heavenly life in part, but we cannot fully see it by any means [Col. 0446A].

The wheels too were measured as one and a half cubits, because the evangelical Scripture shows how those who wish to be perfect ought to live, and demonstrates to us in the present the hope of eternal recompense; yet it promises that the nature of that recompense will be revealed and granted to us in the future.

The stands themselves also had a diameter of one and a half cubits at their top, where they received the basins, because those supreme teachers and ministers of the saving washing shone forth as perfect in their works in this life, but enjoyed the light of contemplation only in part. Hence they say:

> For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be brought to an end. (1 Corinthians 13)

“In this manner he made ten stands, all cast in one piece and alike in measurement and carving. He also made ten bronze basins” [Col. 0446B].

Why ten stands were made, with an equal number of basins placed upon them, has already been explained. But the fact that all the stands and basins had one casting, one measurement, and similar carving was not intended to signify that the merits of teachers can be equal. Rather, it signified that there is one faith of the Gospel by which they are instructed, one sacrament of baptism by which they are washed, and one and the same Spirit by whom all the elect are consecrated, although they possess different gifts in that same Spirit, who distributes to each one as he wills (1 Corinthians 12).

“Each basin held forty baths.” The number forty commonly represents the type of great perfection, since four times ten makes forty [Col. 0446C]. There are ten commandments, by which all our activity is prescribed in the divine law; and there are four books of the Gospels, in which, through the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, the entrance into our heavenly homeland has been opened to us. Since all who belong to the ministry of holy baptism ought, with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, to display the fruit of righteous action, it is fitting that each basin in which the burnt offerings were washed should hold forty baths.

What follows—“It was four cubits”—whether it refers to height or width, is readily understood as a mystery. One basin was four cubits, either because of the four holy books of the Gospels, in which the form of baptism has been prescribed for us; or because of the four cardinal virtues, in which every faithful person, if faithful not in vain, ought to be instructed; or certainly because of the four regions of the world in which the washing of salvation is administered, as the Psalmist says:

> Those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, from the regions he gathered them, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea. (Psalm 105 [106])

When he previously said, “It likewise had one cubit and a half,” and did not add whether he meant height or width, it seems that he wished us to understand that the bottom of the basin had this width. This is very easily inferred, if I am not mistaken, from the measurement of the stand on which each basin was placed, which is described as follows:

> At the top of the stand there was a rounded structure one and a half cubits in diameter, fashioned so that the basin could be placed upon it. [Col. 0447A]

The width of the bottom of the basins was therefore one and a half cubits, while the capacity of the basins was four cubits. But whether he speaks of height, width, or both, let the one who knows say.

“And he set up ten stands, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.”

By the right and left sides of the temple he does not mean inside the temple itself, but before the temple, on the eastern side, namely in the inner court, which was properly called the priests’ court.

He placed five on the right side of the temple for the Jews, who had anciently been accustomed to use the sun of righteousness through the teaching of the Law; and five on the left for us, who had long clung in our blindness to the servitude of him who said:

> I will set my throne in the north. (Isaiah 14)

This means plainly: “I desire to rest in the hearts of those whom I regard as alienated from the way of truth and from the flame of divine charity” [Col. 0447B].

He placed the Sea on the right side of the temple, facing east toward the south; it too was set in the same court toward the east. What he says, “on the right side of the temple,” he repeats by saying “toward the south.” For those entering the court from the east first had to turn toward the south, where the Sea stood in the very corner, prepared for the washing of the priests. Then, as they proceeded inward, they encountered the basins for washing the sacrifices, placed on both sides.

Within these stood a bronze platform five cubits long, three cubits wide, and three cubits high, on which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple. Proceeding farther, they encountered the altar of burnt offering opposite the middle of the court. Beyond that came the portico, or vestibule, of the temple, in which bronze columns stood around the entrance to the temple.

That he placed the Sea on the right side signifies that through the washing of baptism we ought to reach the heavenly kingdom, which is rightly signified by the name “right”: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16).

When right and left are both taken in a good sense, they signify either Judaism and the Gentiles—as we said above in the exposition of the stands—or the present life of the Church and the future life, or the joys and sorrows of the world, or something of this kind. But where “right” is placed absolutely, it more often signifies eternal joys.

That he placed the Sea facing east refers to nearly the same meaning: namely, that through the washing of the sacred font the splendor of eternal brightness is opened to us [Col. 0447D]. That he placed it on the southern side of the court signifies that through receiving the Holy Spirit we are accustomed to be kindled with the fervor of true love. For in Scripture the heat of the midday sun commonly signifies the ardor of love and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through whom that same love is poured into the hearts of the elect (Romans 5).

He also made ten golden lampstands according to the form in which they had been commanded to be made, and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left. He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, and so forth.

Of this it is written in the Book of Kings:

> Five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left, before the inner sanctuary, of refined gold, with flowers like lilies and golden lamps above. (III Kings VII [1 Kings 7]; [Col. 0448A])

Just as tables are rightly placed typologically for the sacred Scripture, because they both supply the bread of God’s word to those who hunger for righteousness and bear the vessels of heavenly ministry—that is, they set before us the deeds of the righteous as an example—so too the same divine words are most fittingly represented by the lampstands, since they bring the light of wisdom before those who are wandering.

Hence the Psalmist says:

> Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths. (Psalm 118 [119])

Hence Solomon says that the commandment is a lamp and the law is light (Proverbs 6).

It is rightly said that there are twice five lampstands, not only because the Lawgiver wrote five books, but also because the entire sequence of the Old Testament embraces five ages [Col. 0448B]. The number five is doubled, and five are placed on the right and five on the left, when after the Lord’s incarnation the same Scripture is entrusted either to both peoples of God, namely Jews and Gentiles, or is shown to be full of evangelical figures, which once had been thought to be understood by the ancient people of God only according to the letter.

When he had said, “five on the right and five on the left,” he appropriately added, “before the inner sanctuary.” The inner sanctuary, where the ark was—as has often been said—signifies the shrine of the heavenly homeland, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3), conscious, as it were, of the Father’s mysteries.

The golden lampstands of the temple are placed before the inner sanctuary because the divine words always look toward the dwelling of the heavenly city, so that they may infuse our hearts with knowledge and desire for it, and kindle those who have an eternal origin in the flesh to seek and merit a dwelling-place of perpetual residence in heaven [Col. 0448C].

If you ask what typological distinction there is between the lampstands and their lamps, we may rightly understand the lamps to be holy men who, filled with the oil of the Holy Spirit, themselves burn with the fire of love in their hearts and bring the light of knowledge before their neighbors through their speech. The lampstands that raise these lamps on high, so that they may be seen far and wide in the Church, are the sacred Scripture, which demonstrates the virtues and teaching of the saints to us through its reading.

The Lord’s saying about John supports this interpretation:

> He was a burning and shining lamp. (John 5)

Or, in the reverse order, we may also most appropriately say that the lamps are the divine words, in accordance with what we quoted above from the Psalmist:

> Your word, Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths. (Psalm 118 [119])

The lampstands of these lamps, however, are all the saints, who constantly submit both their hearts and bodies, in humble devotion, to carrying out the Lord’s commandments.

For whoever does not seek to follow his own will in anything, but attends in all things to what holy Scripture says, striving to submit himself to its commandments and to listen to its promises, carries its golden lamps like a golden lampstand of the house of God. He strives to submit the chaste members of his body and the pure thoughts of his mind to doing what God commands [Col. 0449A]. He does so with an intention as steadfast as the lampstand must be, firmly raised toward the heights, so that it may preserve the lamps placed upon it not only without falling but also without any movement from its position.

When he had said, “Five golden lampstands on the right and five on the left before the inner sanctuary, of refined gold,” he added, “with flowers like lilies and golden lamps above.” Literally, this seems to indicate that the upper part of the lampstands was fashioned in the form of an open lily, just as we read that it was made in the lampstand of the tabernacle. Its central shaft and the branches proceeding from it are said to have had many cups and spheres in the form of lilies (Exodus 37).

The flowers of the lily—as has often been said—signify the pleasant youth of the ever-green land, of which blessed Peter says:

> The Lord regenerated us into a living hope, into an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, preserved in heaven. (1 Peter 1)

It is fitting that golden lily flowers were made on the lampstand of the house of God, because divine Scripture, having rejected temporal joys, is accustomed to summon us to seek the good things of our heavenly homeland [Col. 0449B]. And just as the lampstand, standing upright on high, has golden lily flowers and lamps at its summit, so all the elect who are contained in the same sacred Scripture are shown to have sought and received heavenly goods from the Lord with their minds raised toward the heights.

After the account of the lampstands, the text in the Book of Chronicles adds a plural number concerning the tables, saying: “He also made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, and one hundred golden bowls.” In Kings, however, the singular number is found, where, after the golden altar made by Solomon has been mentioned, it immediately adds:

> And the golden table upon which the bread of the presence was to be placed. (III Kings VII [1 Kings 7]; [Col. 0449C])

The golden table is sacred Scripture, rich in the brightness of spiritual knowledge. Of it the Psalmist says to the Lord:

> You have prepared a table before me in the presence of those who trouble me. (Psalm 32 [23])

Our Creator has prepared for us a table of heavenly knowledge, by which we may be strengthened in the faith of truth, lest our adversaries, by troubling us, bend us toward error.

The loaves of the presence are the holy teachers, whose salutary works and words are set before us as an example of life in the divine pages, and whom anyone who seeks rightly finds there. Hence, in Exodus, twelve loaves are expressly commanded to be made (Exodus 25), on account of the twelve apostles, through whose ministry the Scripture of the New Testament was composed for us and, by the Lord’s gift, the mysteries of the Old Testament were revealed.

By their number not only those same apostles are signified, but all who, by preaching the word, minister the nourishment of life to the faithful, because all follow the same form of teaching that the apostles received from the Lord.

What we read above in the Book of Chronicles—that Solomon made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left, as well as one hundred golden bowls—makes it credible that these tables were made not so much for the bread of the presence as for carrying the vessels of the Lord: namely, the bowls, which Scripture likewise reports to have been made, together with the censers, incense vessels, mortars, and other objects that are read of in what follows [Col. 0450A].

For when the same book of Chronicles shortly afterward adds:

> Solomon made all the vessels of the house of the Lord, the bronze altar, the tables, and upon them the bread of the presence,

it either uses the plural number for the singular, in the very common manner of the Scriptures—as in Joshua: “But the children of Israel transgressed the commandment and took from the devoted things” (Joshua 7), although Achan alone, and not several Israelites, had done this—or else, because the bread of the presence was customarily baked before the Sabbath so that it could immediately be placed on the table of the presence on the Sabbath, it may have happened that newly baked loaves were placed on those tables and kept there uncovered during that night, until early morning, when the old loaves were removed and the hot ones were placed on the table of the presence [Col. 0450B].

These ten tables do not differ from the figure of the one table of the presence. Just as the one table, laden with twelve loaves, signifies the unanimous harmony of the whole of Scripture, fortified by apostolic authority, so not inappropriately the ten golden tables figuratively proclaim the words of the divine Law and the Prophets. These either offer us refreshment from the word of God, like the loaves of the presence, or present to us examples of the faithful, like the splendor and miracles of the vessels of the Lord placed upon them.

Why the tables were placed five on the right and five on the left is readily apparent from what we discussed above concerning the lampstands.

He also made the court of the priests, the great basilica, and the doors of the basilica, which he overlaid with bronze. Concerning this, it is written in the [Book of] Kings: “And King Solomon built the inner court with three rows of dressed stones and one row of cedar timbers” (1 Kings 6). He speaks briefly of the inner court, and seems altogether to pass over the outer court in silence. In the Books of Chronicles, however, both are mentioned.

The inner court, therefore, which is called the court of the priests because the priests and Levites ministered there, was surrounded on every side by the Temple. On the eastern side, where the entrance was, it was set much farther away from the Temple than on the other three sides, because, naturally, the ministries of the holy things took place on that side, that is, in front of the Temple. There was the bronze altar for offering sacrifices to the Lord; there were the ten basins for washing those same sacrifices; and there stood the bronze Sea for washing the hands and feet of the priests when they entered to minister. This court, as Josephus relates, was three cubits high, so that it might both prevent the others from entering the Temple and signify that this was permitted to the priests alone. It had a gate on the eastern side, to which the people brought their sacrifices and offerings; from there the priests received them and carried them to the altar.

Concerning the outer court, which the Books of Chronicles call the great basilica, Josephus writes as follows:

> “Outside this Temple he built another court, made in the form of a quadrangle, raising very large and broad porticoes, and setting up in it lofty and spacious gates on the four sides of the world. Each of these was oriented at its four corners toward one of the four winds, where he placed golden doors.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Into this sanctuary all the people entered who had undergone purification and the observance of the lawful rites.”

Cassiodorus the senator, in his depiction of the Temple, which he placed in his *Pandect* (as he himself mentions in his commentary on the Psalms), divided these porticoes into three orders: the first order he placed outside the court of the priests, extending in a square on every side; the second, likewise, outside the innermost porticoes, running all around in a circle; and the outermost, similarly, surrounding the preceding porticoes on every side. Thus the Temple was fortified on all sides by a threefold protection of buildings. A pavement of marble was laid in the open air between the individual buildings, while the inner walls of the structures—that is, those facing the Temple—were made of columns, and the exterior walls were solid. In this way the entire structure of the Temple was rationally distinguished according to the variety of its levels.

The high priest entered the Holy of Holies; both purified and unpurified priests entered the Temple itself, together with the Levites and singers. Purified Jewish men stood and prayed in the open air in the innermost court of the larger basilica when the weather was clear; in bad weather they withdrew into the nearest porticoes. Purified widows entered the inner court; Gentiles and Jews who had recently come from the Gentiles, up to the sixth day of purification, entered the outermost court.

Since we found these things distinctly represented in Cassiodorus’s picture, we have briefly noted them here, judging that he had learned them day by day from ancient sources and that so learned a man would not have wished to present to his readers as an example anything that he had not first recognized as true.

These are the places mentioned by the Psalm of the highest degrees, which begins:

> “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 133).

In these porticoes Jeremiah and the other prophets preached the word to the people; in these the Lord and the apostles did likewise. In one of them the Lord was seated teaching when, while the Pharisees were testing him, an adulterous woman was brought before him for judgment (John 8). In them he found those selling and buying sheep, oxen, and doves, and expelled them from the Temple together with their merchandise (Luke 19). In them Peter and John found and healed a lame man, and led him inside with them to pray (Acts 3). In them the whole multitude of the people was praying when the angel appeared to Zechariah, who was offering incense, at the altar of incense, and fully instructed him concerning the birth of the Lord’s forerunner (Luke 1).

These courts and porticoes could not, however, conceal the view of the Temple from those looking at it from a distance, because the place where the Temple stood was much higher than the place on which the porticoes had been founded. For, as Josephus writes, although the outermost structures of the courts were raised to a height of four hundred cubits, they nevertheless did not reach the summit of the mountain on which the Temple had been built.

We believe that these details concerning the structure of the Temple ought to be communicated to the diligent reader. In whatever matters Holy Scripture has considered it useful to speak, let us seek the figure of the mysteries; in the rest, let us proceed simply for the sake of historical knowledge.

The Temple building within the court of the priests represents the life of perfect and exalted men in the holy Church—those, namely, who ought to draw near to the Lord through the excellence of their virtues and to show the lesser a guide to salvation by word and deed. The priest, in fact, received his name in Latin from the fact that he ought to provide sacred leadership to the lesser. In Scripture this name is mystically applied not only to ministers of the altar, namely bishops and presbyters, but also to all who stand out through the elevation of upright conduct and saving doctrine and who benefit not themselves alone but many others. When they present their bodies as “a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Romans 12), they clearly exercise a priestly ministry spiritually.

The apostle Peter was not speaking only to bishops and presbyters, but to the whole Church of God, when he said:

> “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Peter 2).

The ancient people of God were also marked with this dignity of honor, when he himself said to Moses:

> “Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and declare to the children of Israel…”

And shortly afterward:

> “And you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation” (Exodus 19).

The great basilica, however, which stood outside the court of the priests and into which the entire multitude of the people was accustomed to gather either to worship or to hear the word, figuratively signifies the life and conduct of the carnal in the holy Church. To such people the Apostle says:

> “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

They are aptly represented by the great basilica, because without any doubt the number of such people in the holy Church is much greater than that of the perfect. But to the extent that they surpass them in number, they fall short in merit. Hence this basilica, although it accommodates many, does not admit them into the interior of the gilded Temple, or to the service of the altar, or even into that same court of the priests. For although all who are still carnal and weak in the Church belong, through the merit of their chaste faith and their devotion to the Lord’s mercy, to the company of the elect, they are nevertheless far from equaling those who are proved able to say confidently:

> “For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me for the obedience of the Gentiles by word and deed” (Romans 15).

And again:

> “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Timothy 4).

The common people did indeed approach as far as the court of the priests. They carried their sacrifices to its gate and watched with their eyes as the priests received them and offered them on the altar. When the Temple was opened, they also directed their gaze toward it from afar, but they had no ability to enter the court of the priests. Nevertheless, from below they cried out to the Lord, because the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer him the vows of devotion that they are able to offer.

They direct their eyes from afar toward the Temple of God when they earnestly rejoice in learning and admiring the life of the exalted. Those whom they cannot follow in imitation of virtue, they embrace with the affection of devout veneration. They see the sacrifices of the priests consumed on the altar by the sacred fire, because they recognize that the great works of great men are graciously accepted by the Lord through the Holy Spirit. They also bring their own sacrifices to the court of the priests to be offered to the Lord through them, when, while doing the good works of which they are capable, they are both strengthened by the exhortation of their elders and teachers and commended to the Lord through their intercession.

They likewise offer their sacrifices through the priests to be commended to the Lord when, out of regard for the highest reward, they give the necessities of this world—which they themselves possess abundantly—to the holy poor in need, as the Lord admonishes and says:

> “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

The court of the priests was suitably built with three rows of dressed stones—faith, hope, and charity—and rightly with dressed stones, because it is certainly necessary that each person possess the diligence to learn how he ought to speak, what he ought to hope for, and what he ought to love. The one row of cedar timbers is good action itself, displayed without the corruption of pretense; without its addition, faith, hope, and charity cannot be genuine. It has often been said that cedar wood, on account of its fragrance and the incorruptible strength of its nature, signifies the perseverance and good reputation of devout action.

All the elect who have desired to please God by faith, hope, love, and action have ascended as far as this court. The perfect transcend it through the exalted grace of their merits when they advance to such a summit of virtues that they can say to their hearers:

> “Be imitators of us, as we also are of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11).

And they glory and say:

> “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more matters of this life?” (1 Corinthians 6).

The statement that the doors of the basilica were overlaid with bronze signifies that the entrance of faith must be prepared by the clear proclamation of preaching, so that all who come may learn how, through faith in Christ and the sacraments that bring salvation, they ought to enter the Church of Christ; and, after they have entered, how religiously they ought to conduct themselves within it.

Hiram also made the kettles, the flesh-hooks, and the bowls, and completed all the king’s work in the house of the Lord. The kettles were made, as the Book of Exodus records, to receive the ashes of the altar of burnt offering (Exodus 27). The *creagae*, that is, the forks, were kept for the service of the altar so that the flesh of the victims, cooked in the cauldrons, might be taken out with them and brought for the eating of those who were to be refreshed by it. The bowls were for offering libations.

The kettles receive the sacred ashes when the faithful either piously recall in their minds, for their own preservation, the examples and mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, or carefully contemplate the death of the righteous who went before them. Having labored through great struggles for the Lord, they now, having finished their course, rejoice without end in the prize they have received. Thus, by considering the virtues of their predecessors, they too may become great, according to the Apostle’s command:

> “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13).

The flesh-hooks likewise correspond appropriately to figures of the holy preachers, whose ministry it is to refresh the souls of the faithful with the word of faith and, according to the rule of apostolic discretion, to provide still inexperienced disciples with the rational and guileless milk of simple doctrine (1 Peter 2), but to minister solid food of more exalted doctrine to the mature (Hebrews 5).

For whoever knows how to understand the mysteries of Christ in summary and receive them for imitation is satisfied as though refreshed by the flesh of a saving sacrifice. And because it belongs to spiritual teachers to discern most carefully which mysteries ought to be entrusted to which persons for hearing, the priests are rightly commanded through Moses to make forks, with which they may arrange the flesh of the sacrifices as appropriate: bringing some portions for people—but for clean people to eat—while leaving others to be consumed by the fires of the altar.

There are some other matters contained in the words that he has deigned to reveal to our lowliness and grant for the nourishment of our refreshment. There are also other matters of such great depth that they are open only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and altogether exceed the measure of our capacity. The bowls signify the broader and more open discourse of sacred doctrine, which beneficially supplies a draught of wisdom to those who thirst devoutly and grants suitable refreshment through the ministries of preachers to those who labor devoutly, so that, aided by this consolation, they may reach the fountain of eternal life. Whoever drinks from it, as the Truth itself testifies, will not thirst forever (John 6).

It should also be noted that where the Books of Chronicles read that Hiram made kettles, flesh-hooks, and bowls, the Book of Kings has “kettles, basins, and jars” (1 Kings 7). The basins, therefore, are said to be bronze vessels having equal breadth at the bottom and at the mouth, so that, when covered from above, they could keep warm whatever one wished. A jar is a certain kind of vessel for libations, used to offer wine.

Finally, in Exodus we read of bowls, dishes, and cups being made, in which libations were to be offered in the tabernacle of the Lord (Exodus 37). And what are the various vessels made for offering libations except the various distinctions of divine speech according to the differing capacities of those who hear? The same doctrine cannot suit everyone. The wise must be taught in one way, the foolish in another; the rich in one way, the poor in another; the healthy in one way, the sick in another; the old in one way, the young in another; men in one way, women in another; the celibate in one way, the married in another; those set over others in one way, and their subjects in another.

Yet all these vessels belong to the table of the tabernacle, and all to the offering of libations, because whatever a prudent teacher says differently according to the differences among his hearers is found in its entirety within the rule of sacred Scripture and rouses the hearts of those who hear it to offer vows of good works to the Lord.

This diversity of works in holy preaching was signified by the mouth of the Lord himself when he said:

> “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matthew 24).

The faithful and prudent steward gives his fellow servants their measure of wheat at the proper time when the discerning minister of the word observes not only the appropriate time for speaking but also carefully investigates the quality and understanding of his hearers and adjusts the manner of his speech according to their differences.

All the vessels Hiram his father made for Solomon in the house of the Lord were of the purest bronze. The king cast them in the region of the Jordan, in clayey ground between Succoth and Zeredathah. There was an immeasurable number of vessels, so great that the weight of the bronze could not be determined. Concerning this, it is written in the Book of Kings:

> “All the vessels that Hiram made for King Solomon in the house of the Lord were of burnished bronze,” and so forth (1 Kings 7).

The vessels of the house of the Lord were suitably cast in the region of the Jordan, in that river in which our Lord deigned to be baptized (Matthew 3). By being immersed in its waters, he transformed the element of water for us into the washing away of sins. And because every baptism of the faithful, by which they are consecrated to the Lord, is celebrated as an imitation of that baptism by which he himself sanctified the waters, the vessels of the house of the Lord were rightly made in the region of the Jordan.

For we cannot otherwise become vessels of election and mercy unless, looking toward the baptism that he underwent in that river, we too strive to be washed in such a river. It should be noted, however, that he says the same vessels were made not only in the region of the Jordan but also in its plain, signifying the multiplication of the faithful that was to occur not only in Judea but throughout the expanse of all nations. The prophecy was fulfilled which says:

> “The plains shall rejoice, and everything that is in them” (Psalm 95).

Something similar is found where the same psalmist, speaking of the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation in the person of those who came to faith when the secrets of the Incarnation were fulfilled, says:

> “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm 132).

“We heard of it in Ephrathah,” because we read that the mysteries of the Lord were promised to the patriarch David, who was from that same city:

> “From the fruit of your womb I will set his Christ to come in the flesh” (ibid.).

“We found it in the fields of the forest,” because, once these things had been revealed in the height of the nations, we came to know them throughout the world, we saw them, and we became participants in them.

Thus the king cast the vessels of the house of the Lord in the plain of the Jordan, because by the baptism of salvation through which he would make vessels of mercy, the Lord filled the whole breadth of the world.

But what can the clayey earth from which the molds for casting the Lord’s vessels were made be understood as better than sacred Scripture, from which we receive the rule of right living? Clay hardened by fire presents the form of the Lord’s vessel—how great and of what kind it ought to be—when Scripture shows us the rule of righteousness that we must follow. It sets before us for imitation the examples of the saints who remained unconquered in the fire of tribulations, if we desire to be recognized as chosen and precious vessels in the house of the Lord.

The bronze, melted by its fire, enters the molds of clay through which the vessel can be made suitable for heavenly ministries when we, having been beneficially humbled and softened by the flame of divine love or even by human adversity, enter the way of the fathers by doing good, so that by running well we may reach the rewards of the fathers. We do not always need to be constrained by the rules of good action; once the good work has been completed, the palm and blessed reward are to be hoped for. For the vessels were not always held enclosed in shapeless clay. Rather, when they had reached their perfection, they were brought into the light after the barriers of the molds had been broken and were placed in the Temple of the Lord according to their respective locations.

We say this not because the works of the saints will ever perish, but because, once they have received the crown of righteousness that they merited by doing good, all the duties of laborious activity will cease. Who in that life would suffer martyrdom for the faith of Christ, when the adversaries have been expelled and all the elect rejoice in the presence of Christ? Who would bury the dead there, where the earth belongs only to the living? Who would console the grieving there, where God wipes away every tear from the eyes of the saints (Revelation 7; 21)? Who would open his house to a traveler and guest there, where all the elect together possess a dwelling from God, “a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5)? Who would bring me bread when I am hungry or drink when I am thirsty there, where “the Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Psalm 23)?

When the molds, once necessary for the vessels, have therefore been broken apart, the vessels themselves now gleam splendidly in the house of God. For at the end of the world not only will the persecutions cease which the elect suffer for the sake of righteousness, but also the laborious works of righteousness by which, of their own accord, they toil for eternal blessedness. They will rejoice solely in the radiance of the immortality received through the vision of their Creator.

Solomon made all the vessels of the house of God, together with the golden altar, the tables, and the loaves of the bread of the Presence upon them; also the lampstands with their lamps, to shine before the inner sanctuary according to the ordinance, all of purest gold. Why did he earlier say that Hiram made all the vessels for Solomon in the house of the Lord, and now say that Solomon himself made all the vessels of the house of the Lord, unless to show historically that Solomon himself made the Temple’s work by giving the instructions, while Hiram made it by carrying them out?

Allegorically, however, this signifies that our Redeemer, through the holy preachers and all his faithful, prepares the adornment of the Church and brings about works of virtue, because everything that they rightly understand, rightly desire, and faithfully do belongs entirely to his gift. In the Gospel he says to his disciples:

> “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

The Apostle James says of him:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (James 1).

The golden altar signifies the hearts of the perfect righteous, shining with the light of inward charity and purity. The location of that altar also suitably signifies their exaltation. It stood before the door of the Holy of Holies, as we plainly read in the account of the making of the tabernacle (Exodus 37). On this altar neither the blood of sacrifices nor libations was burned, but incense alone. Its smoke, rising upward, covered the ark and filled the inner sanctuary with the fragrance of sweetness.

In this was expressed a figure of the saints, who, neglecting desires for temporal things and seeking heavenly things with their whole attention, are placed as though within, near the inner sanctuary, and are not far removed from the veil that separates the Temple and the Holy of Holies. In body they inhabit the earth alone; in their inner person, however, they have their entire way of life in heaven.

The smoke of incense rises from such an altar into the Holy of Holies, where the ark is kept hidden, when the prayers of the saints, kindled by the flame of charity, reach heaven itself, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3). For not the blood of sacrifices but incense alone is burned on this altar (Exodus 37), because such men do not possess works of flesh and blood that they sacrifice and slay to the Lord on the altar of their heart. They offer him only the vows of tears and prayer, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom.

Solomon also made a bronze altar for burnt offerings and sacrifices; its construction and mysteries have already been explained above, as have the meanings of its measurements.

When he had spoken of the lampstand made with its lamps and placed before the inner sanctuary, he added:

> “And certain flower-work for the lamps, and golden tongs: all were made of pure gold.”

By “certain flower-work” he means forms of lilies made on the lampstand, upon which the lamps were placed. The golden tongs he calls *emunctoria*, the snuffers with which the wicks of the lampstand were trimmed so that, renewed, they might shine more brightly. The other tongs, which were commanded to be made for the use of the altar, were bronze.

But what do these tongs, with which the lamps were trimmed, signify except the interpretation of the spiritual sense through the offices of teachers? They transfer the words of sacred discourse from history to allegory and from shadow to truth. Placed, as it were, upon the mystical lampstand as the light of knowledge in the Church of God, they multiply and renew that light by preaching. They are therefore said to have been made of purest gold, because they are exceedingly bright with the light of true wisdom.

He also made incense vessels, censers, bowls, and mortars of purest gold. The incense vessels and censers, and so forth—the vessels in which incense was made fragrant—can aptly represent the hearts of the elect, in which pure and sweetly fragrant prayer is offered to the Lord. Concerning this the psalmist says:

> “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 141).

Hence, in the Apocalypse, John saw the saints holding golden bowls full of fragrances; and immediately, by way of explanation, he added:

> “Which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5).

These prayers, prepared from the spices of virtues in the mortar of a pure conscience, offer the Lord the sweetest fragrance.

He carved the golden doors of the inner Temple—that is, of the Holy of Holies—and the golden exterior doors of the Temple. Concerning this, it is written in the Book of Kings:

> “The hinges of the doors of the inner house of the Temple, the Holy of Holies, and of the doors of the house of the Temple were of gold” (1 Kings 7).

If the doors of the inner house, the Holy of Holies, are the angelic ministries that open for us, when we depart from the body, the entrance to heavenly life (Luke 16), and if the doors of the house of the Temple are the holy teachers and priests who, by instructing, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood, first open for us the thresholds of the present Church, what are the hinges of both sets of doors except the understanding and hearts of those same angels or holy men? By these they adhere immovably to the contemplation and love of their Creator, so that they may rightly fulfill the ministry divinely entrusted to them, since they never turn their eyes away from the will of the one whom they serve.

The doors are opened and closed at the proper time, but they never at any time leave their hinges, because the holy angels and human beings—whether they receive the faithful and elect into this life of faith or into that life of hope—always keep their minds fixed at the root of eternal love. Hence these hinges are rightly said to have been made of gold, whether on account of the splendor of their own merit or of the love that they possess toward God.

The statement that the doors of both the inner and the outer house were carved signifies that not only the angelic powers but also the teachers of the holy Church of God are honorable through the adornment of various virtues and beneficial for us to imitate. Whoever strives, in the present life, to draw near to their beauty in righteousness, holiness, and truth through faith, hope, and charity will undoubtedly rejoice in the future life that he is a participant in their glory.

## Chapter 5

Concerning the fact that Solomon brought into the Temple of the Lord everything that his father David had vowed—gold and silver, and all the vessels together with the ark of the Lord and the equipment of the tabernacle—and concerning the fact that, when the priests placed the ark in the Holy of Holies, the Levites sang praises to God with cymbals, psalteries, and lyres, when a cloud filled the house of the Lord.

Thus all the work that Solomon had done in the house of the Lord was completed. Solomon completes what he was doing in the house of the Lord when our peaceful King, on the last day, glorifies all the elect with the immortality of the resurrection. Otherwise, as long as the present state of the world continues, Solomon does indeed carry out the work of the house of the Lord, but does not yet complete it, because the Lord inspires and assists the hearts of the elect so that they may do good, yet grants no one who dwells in this life alone the condition of being without sin. He reserves that gift for the blessedness of the life to come.

He completes every work of his Temple and makes it fit for dedication when he brings his elect, transferred from this life, into the eternal kingdom. This is aptly signified by the fact that the Temple was built in seven years but completed and dedicated in the eighth. For all this time revolves through seven days, while the eighth is the day of judgment and the future resurrection, to which the sixth and eleventh psalms are titled. The following passage plainly belongs to that time:

Solomon therefore brought in, at the dedication, everything that his father David had vowed. He placed the silver, the gold, and all the vessels in the treasuries of the house of God, and so forth.

David, Solomon’s father, vowed silver for the splendor of eloquence, gold for the brilliance of wisdom, and vessels generally for rational creation—or, as it is written in the Book of Kings, he sanctified the silver (2 Kings 8). The Father sanctifies the silver when God strengthens eloquent people through the grace of his Spirit to speak the word of the Gospel. He sanctifies the gold when, filling those endowed with natural intelligence with his Spirit, he enlightens them to consider the wonders of his law. He also sanctifies the vessels when he grants the grace of the same Spirit generally to all the children of the Church, kindling their love for them and their desire for the gifts of perpetual salvation.

Solomon brings this silver, this gold, and these sanctified vessels into the Temple. Hence it is written next:

The Levites carried the ark and brought it in, together with all the equipment of the tabernacle. The priests, together with the Levites, carried the vessels of the sanctuary that had been in the tabernacle, and so forth.

When our Lord, after the universal judgment has been completed, brings all the elect—both the company of teachers and that of the other faithful—into the joy of the heavenly kingdom, he places vessels of various kinds, silver and gold, in the treasuries of the house of the Lord. He does this when he hides those who have been worthy to enjoy the abundance of his sweetness in the secrecy of his presence, away from the disturbance of human beings (Psalm 31).

There are fittingly many treasuries in which the vessels of election are stored, but there is one house of the Lord in which these same treasuries have been made. For there is one Church in which all the elect are contained, however much they differ in merits; and there is one, not diverse, heavenly homeland promised to all the elect, although “as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15).

The Judge himself and distributor of rewards demonstrated both things in one declaration when he said:

> “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14).

Solomon therefore made one house of the Lord, with many treasuries in it for receiving vessels of different kinds; yet he prepared them sanctified by one blessing, because there is one house of the Father, “not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5), but many dwelling places in it (John 14) for receiving all whom the Lord blesses because they fear and love him, the small together with the great.

The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord to its place, that is, to the inner sanctuary of the Temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim, so that the cherubim spread their wings over the place where the ark had been placed and covered both the ark and its poles. Because the poles by which the ark was carried were somewhat longer, their ends appeared before the inner sanctuary. If someone had been standing a little farther outside, however, he could not have seen them. Thus the ark remained there until the present day.

There was nothing else in the ark except the two tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb, when the Lord gave the law to the children of Israel as they came out of Egypt.

Concerning this, it is likewise written in the Book of Kings:

> “The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the Temple, into the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above. And since the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the inner sanctuary, they did not appear farther outside. They remained there until the present day. In the ark there was nothing except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel as they came out of the land of Egypt” (2 Kings 8).

When it is said that the ark was brought into the Holy of Holies and that, because the poles projected, they appeared farther outside, it should be noted, in accordance with what is written in the Books of Chronicles, that although the ends of the poles were visible before the inner sanctuary to those who approached more closely and looked more carefully, it could not have happened that the ends themselves projected before the inner sanctuary. For it was necessary that, once the inner sanctuary had been closed and the veil hung before its doors, the poles, the ark, and the cherubim also be concealed inside. This could not have happened if the poles, projecting too far, had not left room for the doors to be brought forward and closed.

Their position, therefore, Scripture took care to explain—not without reason, but with close attention to the great mystery involved. For it is clear that the outer temple building signified the Church journeying on earth, while the Holy of Holies signified the inner blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Likewise, the ark brought into the Holy of Holies signified Christ’s humanity assumed and brought within the veil of the heavenly kingdom; the poles by which the ark was carried typologically signify the preachers of the word, through whom he himself was made known to the world.

But when it is said that there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb, when the Lord gave the law to the children of Israel as they came out of Egypt, this shows generally [Col. 0460C] that there was nothing in the ark contrary to the commandments of the Lord contained in the two tablets. Only those things were stored there which, in accordance with the commands of that same law, had been enacted in a figurative pattern for the worship of the one God and for the commendation of our faith, so that the figure and shadow of future things might in every respect bear witness, by word and deed, to the truth that was to come; and so, when that truth appeared in the world, the figure might receive at the fitting time firm confirmation through the fulfillment of its history.

Yet there was in the ark, as the apostle Paul attests in his Epistle to the Hebrews, a golden urn containing manna: “For in Christ’s humanity the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Heb. IX). There was Aaron’s staff, which, after being cut off, had flowered again, because all power of judgment belongs to him whose judgment seemed to have been taken away in the humility of his passion [Col. 0460D]. There were also the tablets of the Covenant, because in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II). The poles by which it was carried were attached to it, because the teachers who once labored in the word of Christ now rejoice in Christ’s glory through the vision of his presence. For what one of them said about himself—“I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. I)—he plainly left to be understood of all his fellow workers.

The ends of the poles appeared outside, before the inner sanctuary, not always, but whenever it happened that the doors of that sanctuary were opened; and even then they were visible not to everyone, but only to those who drew nearer and carefully endeavored to see what was inside. The ark itself—what it was like and how it had been placed—could be seen only by those who had entered the inner sanctuary [Col. 0461A], because no saint still living in this present life, however greatly he may raise himself in the height of his mind, fully beholds the glory of his Redeemer there; only the citizens of that homeland behold it completely.

The poles, too, were stored with the ark in the inner sanctuary, because those who are now perfected and chosen, who have gone before us from the world, are hidden in the secret place of God’s face, away from the disturbance of men (Ps. XXX). Yet the ends of their poles are sometimes seen, when the inner sanctuary is opened, by those who draw near, whenever divine grace grants the more perfect and those who cleanse the eye of their heart with complete devotion the contemplation of something at least of the joy of the heavenly citizens. Such contemplation is not granted to those who have withdrawn somewhat farther away, because the more they remain outside with wandering minds, the less they rejoice in the inward joys [Col. 0461B].

For all the priests who could be found there had been consecrated, and at that time the divisions of the courses and ministries among them had not yet been made—both the Levites and the singers, that is, those under Asaph, those under Heman, and those under Jeduthun. When these fourteen companies cast lots to determine who should minister first, second, or third, all the consecrated men served together.

Their sons and brothers, clothed in fine linen, made music with cymbals, psalteries, and lyres, standing on the eastern side of the altar; and with them were one hundred and twenty priests, sounding trumpets. Let us see how Josephus relates the account of the priestly garments made by Solomon:

“He made priestly robes for the high priests, with the garments that hung down to the feet, the shoulder pieces, and the breastpieces, and with a thousand precious stones. The crown on which Moses had inscribed ‘the Lord’ was one; it remained to this day. For the priests he also made ten thousand robes woven of fine linen and purple belts for each, and two hundred thousand trumpets according to the command of Moses. Likewise, for the Levites who sang hymns, two hundred thousand linen robes, and forty thousand musical instruments invented for leading the hymns, called nabla and cinara, made from selected material.”

Solomon constructed all these things abundantly and magnificently for the honor of God, showing no thrift, but using exceptional generosity for the adornment of the temple, which he also stored in the treasuries of God [Col. 0461D]. Mystically, what is signified by the linen robes except bodily chastity, shining with the beauty of purity? All who are to attend the divine service should therefore put this on and resound with his praise in mouth, conduct, and action. The cymbals signify confession by the mouth; the psalteries, mortality; and the lyres, the mortification of the flesh and the diligence of good works, furnished with twenty-four spiritual strings—that is, with prophetic and apostolic teachings.

And it is rightly said that they stood on the eastern side of the altar, because beside the altar of faith they awaited the rising of the eternal light. With them stood the one hundred and twenty priests, because the holy teachers are represented by the number one hundred and twenty: the lawgiver completed the course of his years according to this number, and in the upper room of Zion, on the day of Pentecost, believers received the grace of the Spirit, the Paraclete, in this same number. Through strong preaching they made known to crowds of the faithful the splendor of the sun of righteousness, so that both groups—those teaching and those hearing—might be adorned with the light of true wisdom (Acts II) [Col. 0462A].

Thus, when all together were singing with trumpets, voice, cymbals, instruments, and music of various kinds, and raising their voices on high, the sound was heard from a great distance. When they began to praise the Lord and say, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever,” the house of God was filled with a cloud, and the priests could not stand and minister [Col. 0462B] because of the darkness. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God.

What does it mean that the priests and Levites, while singing God’s praise in the temple with instruments and music of various kinds, could not stand and minister because of the darkness—or, as it is written in the Book of Kings, because of the cloud (III Kings VIII)—except that, when the Savior and his apostles were preaching the Gospel, the proud chief priests of the Jews, as their deserts required, were unable to minister in the house of the Lord because of the cloud, while they heard the divine mysteries through parables (Matt. XIII)?

Because in the Old Testament they disdain to investigate the mystical meanings covered by the veil of the letter amid the dark obscurities of allegories, they lost, because of the cloud, the ministry owed by their faith. At that time the Lord also uttered his voice to them in the cloud of their teaching, when he spoke openly even about himself. For what is clearer than, “I and the Father are one” (John X)? What is clearer than, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII)? But because a cloud of unbelief had filled the minds of the hearers, the intervening cloud concealed the ray of sunlight that had been sent forth.

Therefore, as we have already said, the cloud intelligently signifies darkness. Because, when the Lord appeared in the flesh, the priests’ understanding suffered darkness concerning him, the cloud filled the synagogue—that is, the house of the Lord. The priests could not minister because of the cloud, because, having been darkened by the plague of their faithlessness concerning the meaning of God’s incarnation, they lost the ministry of the true priesthood.

For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God [Col. 0462D], because the mysteries that had previously lain hidden in the law beneath shadow and veil had, through the coming of the mediator between God and humanity, all emerged into the light in the Gospel for those who rightly believed and worthily received them. But for the others, who were unwilling to approach the faith, the former obscurity remained—indeed, blindness remained even more deeply. Hence the Truth himself said in the Gospel to the disciples who asked him about certain of his parables: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and those who see may become blind” (Luke VIII).

## CHAPTER VI

**On the bronze platform on which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple of the Lord; and on the solemn dedication of the temple in the festive month and the very great celebration of that festival.**

Then Solomon said: “The Lord promised that he would dwell in darkness; but I have built a house for his name, so that he might dwell there forever.” And he turned his face, blessed the whole assembly of Israel, and so forth.

This accords with the saying of blessed Job: “He makes the clouds his hiding place” (Job XXII); and with the Psalmist’s words: “Darkness is beneath his feet” (Ps. XVII). The hiding place of the Lord, therefore, is Sacred Scripture, which conveys heavenly mysteries through many parables and figures. But what is covered and concealed from unbelievers and the proud opens the entrance to its secret meaning to the humble and to those who rightly seek God through the catholic faith, according to what the Savior, rejoicing in the Spirit, said to the Father in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to infants; yes, Father, because such was your good pleasure before you” (Matt. XI).

Solomon had made a bronze platform and placed it in the middle of the court. It was five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high; he stood upon it, and so forth.

What is signified by the bronze platform that Solomon made except the solidity of true humility? Our Savior taught this above all by his word and demonstrated it by his example. Its length is measured according to the number five, because, in accordance with the tradition of God’s law, he commends to us the long-suffering of patience and the breadth of love [Col. 0463C]. Its height is three cubits because he teaches us to hold firmly to the confession of the Holy Trinity in faith, hope, and love, and to persist in it at all times by good works.

## CHAPTER VII

**That after twenty years he first built the house of the Lord, his own house, and many cities; subdued foreigners; and made them tributaries.**

And the king and all the people dedicated the house of God. The priests stood at their duties, and the Levites with the instruments of the songs of the Lord, which David the king had made for praising the Lord: “For his mercy endures forever.”

The house of the Lord is the holy Church, as was shown above [Col. 0463D]. Christ the King dedicated it when he cleansed it with his blood, sanctified it by the grace of his Spirit, and increased it with various gifts of virtue. The children of Israel also dedicate it with him whenever each of the faithful, according to the gift bestowed on him by God, strives through the word of preaching and works of virtue to turn as many of his neighbors as he can toward better and more perfect things. “The temple of God,” says the Apostle, “is holy, and that is what you are” (I Cor. III).

But the king and the people, the head and the members, do not accomplish this sanctification equally, because of Christ Jesus it is said: “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace” (John I). Hence Paul says: “So neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III) [Col. 0464A]. Yet the same Apostle subsequently explains how much human preaching accomplishes, saying: “He who plants and he who waters are one. Each will receive his own reward according to his labor. For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (ibid.).

Thus he himself sanctified his temple by inhabiting it as God and Lord, while we sanctify it by conducting ourselves worthily of his dwelling. The text continues:

Solomon also sanctified the middle of the court before the temple of the Lord. For he had offered there burnt offerings and the fat of peace offerings, because the bronze altar that he had made could not hold the burnt offerings, sacrifices, and fat.

What, then, does it mean that Solomon sanctified the middle of the court by offering a burnt offering and sacrifice there? It means that the bronze altar, which according to the institution of the law had been placed before the doors of the temple, could not contain everything, except insofar as Christ now accomplishes fully in the catholic Church those things that could not be perfected in the law because of its weakness.

For the court itself is the house of the Lord, because through it entry is opened into the temple of the Lord, the heavenly Jerusalem. Since all the burnt offerings and sacrifices could not be offered on the typical altar of the Old Testament because everything there was done figuratively, our King and Priest raised a new altar of faith in the catholic Church. On it rich burnt offerings and acceptable sacrifices are offered spiritually to God every day.

Hence the Lord, rejecting the former sacrifice through the prophet, says: “I did not desire burnt offerings and the blood of victims” (Isa. I); and again in the Psalms: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX). Therefore it was written above that King Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel, and all who had gathered, sacrificed before the ark rams and oxen without number, because whatever God’s elect, who are members of the King, do in good works and appropriate governance of themselves and their dependents is known to be an acceptable sacrifice to God.

Solomon therefore held a solemn festival at that time for seven days, and all Israel with him—a very great assembly, from the entrance of Hamath to the Wadi of Egypt, and so forth.

When it is said that Solomon held a celebrated festival and all Israel with him, a very great multitude, from the entrance of Hamath to the stream of Egypt before the Lord, the entrance of Hamath signifies the northern region of the promised land, while the stream or torrent of Egypt, which the Books of Chronicles mention, signifies the southern region.

I think it will be agreeable to the reader if I set down here some passages in Latin drawn from the words of Saint Jerome. It is written in the Book of Numbers, where the whole promised land is divided in a brief account according to its four regions:

“The southern region will begin at the wilderness of Zin, which is beside Edom, and its boundaries will face eastward toward the Salt Sea. They will surround the southern region by the ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass into Zin and reach from the south as far as Kadesh-barnea. From there the boundary will go out to the village called Adar and extend as far as Azmon. The boundary will turn in a circuit from Azmon to the Wadi of Egypt and will end at the shore of the Great Sea” (Num. XXXIV).

For this reason, in the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel, it is said: “The southern region is from Tamar as far as the waters of Meribah at Kadesh, and the torrent as far as the Great Sea” (Ezek. XLVII). This signifies the very broad wilderness of Zin, which is beside Edom, and the boundary’s circuit around the Red Sea; then it passes by the ascent of the Scorpion, through Zin and Kadesh-barnea, and reaches the court or village of Adar and Azmon, as far as the Wadi of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocolura.

This southern boundary begins at Tamar, a city in the wilderness, which Solomon also built with marvelous works and which is now called Palmyra. In Hebrew, Thamar means what in our language is “palm,” and the boundary extends to the waters of Meribah at Kadesh, which certainly lies in the wilderness, and to the torrent entering the Great Sea that stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine.

The Book of Numbers continues:

“The western region will begin at the Great Sea, and its boundary will close there; that is, from sea to sea—from the torrent of Rhinocolura, which flows into the sea, to the place where Hamath, a city of Syria, is situated.” Ezekiel also names this region: “The sea region, the Great Sea, from the boundary directly until you come to Hamath,” which is now called Epiphany—its name having been changed by Antiochus, the most cruel of tyrants, who bore the title Epiphanes.

“Now,” it says, “for the northern region, the boundaries will begin at the Great Sea and reach as far as the highest mountain; from there they will come to Hamath, as far as the boundaries of Zedad. The boundaries will go to Ziphron and the village of Hazar-enan. These will be the boundaries on the northern side” (Num. XXXIV).

The Hebrews say that the northern region begins at the Great Sea, which extends along the shores of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria called Coele, and Cilicia, and runs through Egypt toward Libya. As for the statement that the boundaries will reach the highest mountain, the Hebrews think that this means either Mount Amanus or the Taurus, the latter of which seems more likely to us.

“The boundaries,” it says, “will go as far as Ziphron.” For this reason, today they call a town in Cilicia Zephium. As for what follows, “the village of Hazar-enan,” the Hebrew has Haserenan, which is interpreted as “the court of the fountain”; it is the boundary of Damascus.

Hence Ezekiel says: “The boundary will be from the sea to the court of Enon [or Asez], the boundary of Damascus, and from the north to the north, the boundary of Hamath—the northern region” (Ezek. XLVII).

“From there,” it says, “they will mark out the boundaries toward the eastern region, from the village of Hazar-enan to Shepham; from Shepham the boundaries will descend to Riblah, opposite the fountain of Daphnis. From there they will reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth, extend to the Jordan, and finally close at the very salty sea” (Num. XXXIV).

Thus, from the end of the northern region—that is, from the court of Enan—the boundaries extend to Shepham, which the Hebrews call Apamea. From Apamea the boundaries descend to Riblah, which is now called Antioch of Syria. To show that this Riblah signifies the city that is now the most distinguished in Coele-Syria, the text continues, “opposite the fountain,” which plainly refers to Daphne, from whose spring the city mentioned above receives an abundance of water.

“From there,” it says, “the boundaries will reach eastward to the Sea of Chinnereth,” that is, the Lake of Tiberias.

It is called a sea, although it has fresh water, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, which call gatherings of waters “seas.” “They will extend,” it says, “to the Jordan and finally close at the sea,” either the Dead Sea or, as some think, the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Aila is situated.

When it is said that Solomon held a festival at that time for seven days, together with all Israel—a very great assembly—from the entrance of Hamath to the Wadi of Egypt, and that he held an assembly on the eighth day because he had dedicated the altar for seven days and celebrated the festival for seven days, and thus dismissed the people to their tents on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, I do not think anything else is intended here except that, when the seven days of the temple’s dedication had been completed, the Feast of Booths followed. According to the law, it began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and ended on the twenty-second.

Therefore, when both festivals had been properly completed and the eighth day of the Feast of Booths had ended, King Solomon dismissed the people to their homes, rejoicing and glad over the good that the Lord had done for David, Solomon, and his people Israel.

Josephus seems to support this interpretation when he says:

“Solomon therefore dismissed the assembly after celebrating sacrifices for himself and for all the Hebrews—namely, twenty-two thousand calves and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. At that time sacrifices were first celebrated in the temple, and all the Hebrews feasted there with their wives and children. In addition, the king celebrated before the temple, with all his people, the festival called the Feast of Booths, in great splendor and magnificence, feasting together for fourteen days. When these provisions had been supplied in abundance and nothing was lacking for the worship of divine piety, each person, dismissed by the king, returned home, giving thanks to the king for the care he had shown and for the works he had accomplished. They prayed the Lord to grant them Solomon as king for a long time. They departed and returned with great joy and delight, singing hymns, so that they came home without weariness because of their happiness.”

Mystically, the fact that Solomon, after completing the work of the temple, held a celebrated festival, and that all Israel with him—a great multitude—from the entrance of Hamath to the stream of Egypt, celebrated before the Lord God, signifies the eternal joy that the saints possess forever with their true King, the Peacemaker.

Nor do the very places by which the boundaries of the land of Israel are described—namely, Hamath and the stream of Egypt—contradict this meaning. Hamath is interpreted as “the Lord’s truth”; and what can we better understand the stream or torrent of Egypt to signify than temporal death? For no one living in Egypt—that is, in the darkness of this world—can escape it. As the prophet testifies: “Who is the one who lives and will not see death?” (Ps. XLVIII) [Col. 0467A]. Hence it is written in the psalm concerning the mediator between God and humanity himself: “He will drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head” (Ps. CIX).

The torrent was the turbulent persecution of the Jews. The Lord Christ drank from it on the way—that is, in this life, while he endured it in the body. The phrase “on the way” shows the violence inflicted and indicates its very swift passage, by which travelers are accustomed to journey to another dwelling. Because of the glorious merit of his passion, Christ was given the name that is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II).

Thus all Israel holds a celebrated festival from the stream of Egypt to Hamath with Solomon whenever, after the end of the present life, the saints truly enjoy eternal joys with the Lord Christ [Col. 0467B]. Their celebrating the same festival for seven and seven days may signify that the elect, illuminated by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, rejoice now in this life, whose course is marked by the number seven, in hope; and then, in the true Sabbath—that is, in the future rest of souls—they will rejoice in the perception of truth itself.

Thus, on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, he dismissed the people to their tents, rejoicing and glad over the good that the Lord had done for David, Solomon, and his people Israel.
