The Lord had done good to David because, after forgiving the sin he had committed against Uriah the Hittite, he granted him the kingdom forever. He also did good to Solomon, because he not only permitted him to enter the Church—the law having forbidden one born from a foreign woman to enter it—but also exalted him to the kingdom. He did good to his people Israel as well, because, after the enormous number of transgressions by which they had often violated the Lord’s commands through contempt, he allowed them to possess a most magnificent temple for his worship and granted them rest from their enemies on every side for a considerable time, until, adding new sins to their former ones, they justly received the deserved punishment.

When it is said that on the twenty-third day of the seventh month—that is, on the eighth day of the Feast of Booths, as the Book of Kings says—Solomon dismissed the people to go to their tents, this signifies that after the end of this life and after the Sabbath-rest of the holy souls who now rest before the day of judgment, in the eighth age—that is, on the day of the Resurrection—the saints will receive immortal bodies and be placed in heavenly dwellings according to the quality of their merits [Col. 0467D]. There they will always rejoice with eager hearts, glad and praising the Lord for all the good things that the almighty Father has bestowed upon the Christian people in the Lord Christ.

## CHAPTER VIII

**On the commanders of Solomon’s army and the Levites and priests whom he appointed for the service of the Lord; where Solomon sent ships to Ophir so that they might bring him gold from there; and concerning the queen of Sheba; and how Hiram’s servants, together with Solomon’s servants, brought gold from Ophir, as well as thyme-wood and very precious stones.**

After twenty years had passed, during which Solomon had built the house of the Lord and his own house, he built the cities that Hiram had given to Solomon and settled the children of Israel there [Col. 0468A].

What does it mean that Hiram is said to have given Solomon cities that Solomon then built and in which he settled the children of Israel, when the Book of Kings reports rather that it was not Hiram who gave cities to Solomon, but Solomon who gave Hiram twenty towns in the land of Galilee? Hiram therefore went out from Tyre to see the towns that Solomon had given him. They did not please him, and he said: “Are these the towns that you have given me, my brother?” And he called them the land of Cabul to this day (III Kings IX).

The Hebrews resolve this question by saying that the twenty cities Solomon had given to King Hiram were not accepted by him but rather rejected. Therefore, because Hiram did not wish to have them, Solomon assigned them to his own uses [Col. 0468B].

Solomon also built Palmyra in the wilderness and built other very strongly fortified cities in Hamath. Josephus relates the matter as follows:

“When King Solomon saw that the walls needed towers for defense and other protection—for, according to the importance of the city, its fortifications in walls also had to be extensive—he accomplished these things and surrounded the city with especially notable towers.”

And shortly afterward:

“Proceeding into the wilderness of upper Syria and conquering it, he established there a very large city, two days’ journey distant from upper Syria, one day’s journey from the Euphrates, and six stages from great Babylon. The reason this city stood so far removed from the inhabited regions of Syria was that water was found nowhere in the lower land, whereas in that place alone springs and wells abounded exceedingly. Building this city and enclosing it with very high walls, he called it Thadamor. It was so called by the Syrians to this day, while the Greeks call it Palmyra.”

He also built Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon, walled cities with gates, bars, and bolts, as well as Baalath and all the very strongly fortified cities that belonged to Solomon.

Beth-horon is the city as far as which Joshua pursued the enemy kings. It fell by lot to the sons of Joseph, that is, to Ephraim. There are two villages approximately twelve miles from Aelia on the road to Nicopolis. Because of their location, one is called Upper Beth-horon, which Solomon built, and the other Lower Beth-horon, which was given to the Levites as a possession [Col. 0468D].

Baalath is a city in the tribe of Judah. In addition, the Book of Kings says that other cities were built by Solomon in the same way—namely, Ezer, Megiddo, and Gezer, as well as Millo. Through the mystery of their names, all these display the beauty of the holy Church, which the true Solomon prepared for himself in the joy of his kingdom, for praise and everlasting gladness.

Millo is interpreted as “fulfillment”; Ezer as “separated” or “sanctified”; Megiddo as “his upper room”; Gezer as “cutting off” or “division.” Beth-horon is interpreted as “house of the mountains,” and Baalath as “ascending.”

The holy Church, therefore, is the city of the living God, where God’s will is fulfilled daily. It has been separated from every error of unbelievers and sanctified in faith and good works. There is the refreshment of virtues. It distinguishes the clean from the unclean and virtues from vices. It is also the house of the mountains—that is, the dwelling place of the saints—and, flowering like a palm through the fruit of righteousness, it ascends from virtue to virtue so that it may see the God of gods in Zion.

Solomon fortified all the villages belonging to him that were without a wall, because Christ so fortified the assembly of his faithful by the protection of his grace that they might always remain unconquerable by spiritual enemies.

Everything that Solomon wished and planned, he built in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the entire land under his authority.

What is meant here by Lebanon? It may signify the temple, which was clothed in the beauty of cedars and at the same time fastened with plates of gold, according to what is written in Zechariah: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zech. XI). Or it may signify the other royal buildings that were likewise constructed with cedar wood brought from Lebanon, such as the armory of the house of the forest of Lebanon and several others.

Josephus seems to agree with this interpretation when he reports the following about Solomon’s buildings:

“It is difficult to enumerate the size and variety of the houses and royal halls: how great the largest were, how great those below them, and how great those beneath the earth, which could not be seen; and likewise the beauty of the upper rooms and gardens, which were delightfully made for viewing, so that bodies exhausted by heat might escape the burning force of the sun. In short, he furnished the entire royal house with white stone, cedar, gold, and silver, in the greatest splendor and wealth. He covered the chambers and walls with gold and made them shine as did the temple of God” [Col. 0469C].

Mystically, our Solomon built everything he wished and planned in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout the entire land under his authority, because he orders and dispenses all things in heaven and on earth according to the inclination of his own will. Concerning him it is written in the psalm: “All that the Lord has willed, he has done in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. CXXXIV). No one can resist his will, because he himself is Lord of all; at his name every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II).

“He will reign forever and ever, and his kingdom will have no end” [Col. 0469D].

Solomon subdued all the people who had been left from the Hittites and Amorites, and so forth—those who were not of the stock of Israel: the descendants and posterity whom the children of Israel had not killed—and made them tributaries to this day.

But from the children of Israel he did not appoint anyone to serve in the king’s works, for they were warriors, chief commanders, and commanders of his chariots and cavalry.

Our peaceful King makes tributaries of every people who are not among the children of Israel, since he keeps under his power those who are not numbered among the children but are placed in a servile condition, and uses each for his own service. Whether Jews, gentiles, or heretics, they remain under his dominion, because he is the ruler of all and uses them according to his will, in whose will all things have been established.

Although such people often oppose him in many ways, they nevertheless frequently serve the needs of the Church, since in the present age they provide what is necessary and offer assistance from their possessions.

But from the children of Israel—that is, those who are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, whom the Son of God liberated by his blood—our Solomon did not appoint anyone to serve as a slave. He does not compel anyone to live according to gentile custom, nor does he compel anyone to observe the ceremonies of the old law in the times of the New Testament. Rather, he makes them warriors who fight against spiritual wickedness with the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit; he makes them his ministers, that is, those who offer him special service through good works; and he makes them commanders and leaders, so that they may rule themselves well and restrain the wantonness of the flesh, or so that they may govern their subjects well and lead them into the path of righteousness [Col. 0470B].

All the commanders of King Solomon’s army were two hundred and fifty, and they instructed the people.

It is therefore established that the number one hundred, which in counting on the fingers is transferred from the left hand to the right, sometimes represents heavenly life in Scripture. Just as the right hand is preferred to the left, so by merit the life to come is preferred to the present life. The mystery of this number is frequently found in the divine writings.

Noah completed the building of the ark in his hundredth year, because the Lord will perfect in the future life the holy Church that he is meanwhile building in this present life. When Abraham was one hundred years old, the son of promise, Isaac, was born, because the blessing of the inheritance promised through his seed to all the families of the earth will be given in the future heavenly homeland [Col. 0470C]. He himself dwelt as a sojourner for one hundred years in the promised land, because those who become Abraham’s children through faith must lead a pilgrim life in the present Church, in hope of the heavenly inheritance.

Isaac sowed in Gerar, which is interpreted as “sojourning,” and in that same year found a hundredfold return, because whatever the children of promise accomplish as good while sojourning in this life, they will receive their reward in the heavenly life as soon as they depart from the body.

In this figure, too, the seed of the evangelical word that fell on good soil produced fruit a hundredfold, because whoever leaves temporal goods for Christ and for the Gospel receives a hundredfold in the present age, and in the age to come eternal life—that is [Col. 0470D], now, in hope of heavenly life, the joy of fraternal fellowship, and then, in reality, life itself in the kingdom of heaven. The number fifty, therefore, signifies the remission of sins, eternal rest, and the grace of the Holy Spirit: for in the psalm bearing that number repentance, confession, and remission of sins are described; through the Jubilee the future rest is fulfilled; and through Pentecost, at the coming of the Spirit the Paraclete, the sevenfold grace is expressed. Accordingly, our Solomon appointed two hundred and fifty commanders over his entire army, because from both peoples he chose pastors and rulers of the Church, who, enlightened and fully instructed by the grace of the Holy Spirit, daily taught their people profitably to seek the remission of sins, the life of eternal [Col. 0471A] rest, and everlasting blessedness, and labored with all their strength so that they might attain these through progress in good works and in right faith.

Then Solomon offered holocausts to the Lord upon the altar of the Lord that he had built before the portico, so that offerings might be made upon it each day according to the commandment of Moses: on Sabbaths, at new moons, and on feast days, three times a year—that is, at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles. And according to the arrangement of David his father, he established the priests’ duties in their ministries and the Levites in their order, so that they might praise and minister before the priests according to the rite of each day.

Our Peacemaker offers through his members, on the altar of Catholic faith [Col. 0471B] that he built in his Church before the entrance to the heavenly homeland, holocausts of good works to the Lord each day—that is, throughout the whole period of the present life, until the consummation of the age. He offers also on Sabbaths, at new moons, and on feast days, three times a year, when, for eternal rest, the newness of the future life, and the reception of heavenly joy, he presents with pious intention and supreme devotion whatever they judge acceptable and pleasing in the divine sight, in faith in the Holy Trinity. A holocaust, therefore, is said to be wholly burned: for the holocaust is consumed upon the altar when, in the heart of any elect person who has vowed himself entirely to God, in both flesh and heart, a good work is performed in the fervent fire of charity.

Moreover, our king orders the duties of the priests [Col. 0471C] and the ministries of the Levites according to the arrangement of David his father, since, in accordance with what is written about him in the Law and the Prophets, he arranges and distributes everything in his Church according to the rite of each day—that is, according to the appropriateness and suitability of each period—in such a way that each order, fulfilling its office, performs divine service and ministry properly and in due order. But how divine service is worthily fulfilled, at the appropriate time and by suitable persons, only he knows in whose hand all times rest, together with those who serve the time. He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light: the holy God, the Trinity, reigning throughout every age.

For through apostolic teachers and [Col. 0471D] suitable ministers of the New Testament—who have been taught not by the letter alone but by the Spirit of the living God—he ordains, according to the ineffable manner of his arrangement, when and how resistance should be made to the raging persecutors of the Christian religion through the steadfastness of faith and the courage of preachers; how and when, through the prudence of Catholic teachers, the wickedness of their error should be condemned and opposed to raging heretics; and also how, at the opportune time, moral instruction and understanding of spiritual knowledge should be profitably supplied to devoted hearers, for the correction of life and the education of the mind, through the diligence and skill of spiritual teachers. Thus he does everything according to his will, [Col. 0472A] counsel, and wisdom, so that the rationale of his dispensation may be manifested and the salvation of the elect people mercifully completed.

Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Elath, on the shore of the Red Sea, which is in the land of Edom. Hiram sent him ships and sailors skilled in navigation through his servants, and they went with Solomon’s servants to Ophir. From there they brought four hundred and fifty talents of gold and delivered them to King Solomon.

Ezion-geber is said to have been an island not far from Elath in the Red Sea, where Jehoshaphat’s fleet was battered by the violence of a storm. Ophir, however, is the name of a province, named after Ophir, one of the descendants of Eber; those descended from his stock are reported to have lived from the river Cophne as far as the region of Judea called Hieria, as Josephus relates. [Col. 0472B]

The fleet, therefore, that Solomon made at Ezion-geber—which is interpreted as “hastening,” “strong,” or “manfully”—I believe to be none other than the Church of the faithful. Set upon the sea of this world, she applies herself to acquiring the treasures of wisdom and knowledge and the riches of virtues. There are Solomon’s servants, since Gentiles trained in secular wisdom are joined in the unity of faith with those who are learned in the Law of Moses. Our Solomon sends these people to Ophir, which is interpreted as “weakening,” so that they may bring back gold from there, when he commands them to seek a precious meaning within the lowliness of the letter. Thus they deliver to the king the total of four hundred and fifty talents of gold when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, they discover in the divine books the precious meaning of history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy, and, attributing it to divine wisdom and counsel, offer it to him. [Col. 0472C]

## CHAPTER IX

On the two hundred spears and three hundred golden shields, and the ivory throne that Solomon magnificently made; on Solomon’s magnificence, wealth, power, and end.

When the queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame, she came to Jerusalem to test him with riddles, bringing great wealth, camels bearing spices, a great quantity of gold, and precious gems. Sheba is a royal city of Ethiopia, which Josephus reports was called Meroe by Cambyses, after the name of his sister.

The queen of the South, who, summoned from the earth’s farthest boundaries, came desiring to hear Solomon’s wisdom, prefigured the Church that was later to come from the Gentiles, longing for Christ. According to the prophecy, she ran clothed in a garment embroidered with gold, having forgotten both her people and her father’s house. Though barbarian by nation, she was not barbarian in mind; openly a stranger, she desired in secret to become a citizen of the saints. Hence she is considered worthy not only of the heavenly reward of resurrection, but also, through apostolic authority, of judging adulterous Jews by the very mouth of the judge, because, marveling at Christ in Solomon with a true desire for the heavenly kingdom, she fulfilled the mystical image of the provident Church. [Col. 0472D]

The fact that this woman is said to be the queen of Sheba expresses the power of her conversion through the significance of the name itself. For Sheba is interpreted as “conversion” or “captivity,” since, truly converted to the faith of Christ, she deserved to belong to the lot of his captives. Of him it is written: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4). [Col. 0473A]

She brought spices, gold, and precious gems to the true Solomon on camels, when she brought to the faith of Christ Gentiles deformed by the power of their sins, yet flourishing in intelligence and zeal and made capable, by divine gift, of receiving from holy preachers who dispense to them the radiance of wisdom, the spices of a good reputation, and the precious gems of manifold virtues. With all these gifts she honored our Solomon with solemn devotion—or rather, honored by him and receiving from him the greater grace of spiritual gifts, since he himself bestowed them.

Hence, shortly afterward, it is written: “King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and requested, far more than she had brought to him,” because in the present life he granted her the grace of the Holy Spirit together with the gift of wisdom and virtues, and in the future he will bestow eternal life upon her in the sight of his glory. [Col. 0473B]

When she had come to Solomon, she spoke to him about everything that was in her heart, and Solomon explained to her everything she had proposed; there was nothing that he did not make clear to her.

The Church inquires of King Christ, wishing to learn everything that she considered in her heart to be salutary and necessary—that is, seeking from him the truth of faith, the rectitude of holy religion, and the blessedness of the future life, and asking how she might serve his worship faithfully in every way in this world [Col. 0473C] and eternally enjoy his contemplation in the heavenly kingdom. He made everything she desired to know clear to her through knowledge of his Law and the grace of the Holy Spirit. There is nothing that he has not made clear to her, insofar as he permits her to know certain things partially, to see some things in an enigma, and to receive a foretaste of the blessings of heavenly joy. In that place, however, he will grant perfect knowledge, when she will see face to face and know as she is known.

Concerning the perfection of this knowledge, Truth itself, speaking to the Father in the Gospel on behalf of the disciples, says: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you; and these have known that you sent me. And I have made your name known to them, and I will make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17).

[Col. 0473D] After she had seen Solomon’s wisdom and the house he had built, as well as the food of his table, the dwellings of his servants, the offices of his ministers, their garments, and the victims they sacrificed in the house of the Lord, she had no spirit left in her because of her astonishment. And she said to the king:

“The report was true that I heard in my land concerning your achievements and wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came myself, saw with my own eyes, and tested it. I had scarcely been told half of your wisdom. You have surpassed the report by your achievements. Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants who stand before you continually and hear your wisdom. Blessed be the Lord your God, who desired to set you upon his throne as king for the Lord your God.”

These words indeed aptly apply to the holy Church, which, provoked by hearing of Christ’s miracles, was moved to seek him. But after she reached him through baptism and faith, and, considering the testimonies of Holy Scripture, recognized the power of his divinity, everything previously reported to her about him seemed small in comparison with the grace she had received. Therefore, in admiration, she breaks into his praise, saying: “Blessed are your men, and blessed are your servants who stand before you always and hear your wisdom,” and so forth. [Col. 0474A]

The Psalmist, too, burning with desire for the heavenly kingdom, uttered similar words from the person of the saints: “How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh rejoice in the living God.” And shortly afterward: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Psalm 83). [Col. 0474B]

Those, therefore, are blessed—and truly blessed—whose king is Christ, who are worthy to enjoy his eternal vision, and who rejoice to receive perpetually both his glory, which they behold with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the wisdom by which he himself deigns to reveal himself to the pure in heart. Thus they will prove true what is written: “What God has prepared for those who love him, eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart.”

Moreover, Hiram’s servants, together with Solomon’s servants, brought gold from Ophir, thyine wood, and very precious gems. From the thyine wood the king made steps in the house of the Lord and in the royal palace, as well as harps and psalteries for the singers. Such wood had never been seen in the land of Judah. [Col. 0474C]

This is written in the Book of Kings: “King Solomon made supports for the house of the Lord and for the royal house from thyine wood, and harps and lyres for the singers. Such thyine wood has not been brought or seen to the present day” (III Kings X).

Josephus relates the matter as follows:

“At that same time, precious stones and pine wood were brought to the king from the land called Golden Land. He used them for strengthening the Temple and the royal houses, and for musical instruments. From them he made harps and nablas (stringed instruments), so that the Levites might sing a hymn to God. Of all the things ever brought to the king, those transported on that day surpassed the others in size and beauty. Let no one suppose that the pine wood now called by that name because of its price among sellers resembles it. That wood was rounded in appearance like pine, but much whiter and exceedingly brilliant. I have said this so that no one might be ignorant of the nature of the true pine.” [Col. 0474D]

It is rightly said that King Solomon made supports or steps for the Lord’s house and the royal house, as well as harps and lyres for the singers, from exceedingly precious wood. For our Creator places precious wood—that is, holy teachers, whose faith never withers and whose leaves of words never fall, but who produce the fruit of good works in their seasons—for the defense of the house of the Lord and of the royal house, that is, for the strengthening of his Church. Surrounded on every side by their teachings and examples, she does not experience the collapse caused by errors and crimes. [Col. 0475A]

Such men are rightly said to have been fashioned like harps and lyres for praising the Lord, because whatever they do prospers, and they do not cease to proclaim the Lord’s praise amid adversity and prosperity alike, in heart, mouth, and deed. According to the Apostle, whatever they do in their work, they do everything for the glory of God. Concerning them the Lord says through the prophet: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they will never be silent, praising the name of the Lord” (Isaiah 62).

The weight of gold brought to Solomon each year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, apart from the amount brought by envoys of various nations and by merchants. All the kings of Arabia and the satraps of the lands brought [Col. 0475B] gold and silver to Solomon.

What, then, does the weight of gold brought to Solomon, increased according to the quality of the number six, signify, except the perfection of the gifts that we must bring to our king? In sixty, the denary is multiplied by six; in six hundred, likewise, the hundred is shown multiplied by six. The denary signifies the perfection of the commandments, and the hundredfold the reward of eternal blessedness. For our king greatly desires our perfection, so that he may have those whom he may reward with a perfect recompense.

Hence Truth itself says to his followers in the Gospel: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5). And to the scribe who asked about attaining eternal life he replied: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” And shortly afterward: “If you wish,” he said, “to be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” [Col. 0475C]

To the apostles he said: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left brothers or sisters, or father or mother, or wife or children, or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19).

Various nations and merchants, all the kings of Arabia and the satraps of the lands, offer gold and silver to Solomon, because every nation and every person strives according to his strength to bring our Peacemaker the gift of right faith, purity of understanding, fullness of holy confession, and a clear conscience, while seeking at all times to devote himself to his service in harmony with good works. [Col. 0475D]

Hence it is written of him in the Psalter: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba will bring presents; and all the kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Psalm 71).

King Solomon therefore made two hundred golden spears from the total of six hundred gold pieces expended on each spear. He also made three hundred golden shields, each covered with three hundred gold pieces, and the king placed them in the armory that was planted with trees.

Concerning this, it is written in the Book of Kings: “King Solomon also made two hundred shields of the purest gold; he gave six hundred shekels of gold for the plates of one shield, and three hundred shields of tested gold. Three hundred minas of gold covered one shield. And the king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon” (III Kings X). [Col. 0476A]

The golden shields and spears, therefore, which, as what follows shows, were used by the commanders who kept watch before the entrance of the house—what do they signify except the spiritual armor possessed by all preachers who guard the house of God and keep watch at its door, so that they may block the entrance to cunning plotters and prevent them from deceiving the innocent?

Concerning them it is written in the Song of Songs: “Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s couch, among the strongest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled in battle” (Song of Songs 3). For the holy preachers defend the peace and tranquility of the present Church against the attacks of heretics, while the more perfect among them, with fixed intention, contemplate the inner rest of the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0476B]

It is rightly added by repetition that they are “among the strongest of Israel.” Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God.” All who strive toward the joys of the divine vision are rightly called Israel; but “the strongest,” he says, are those among them who are elevated either by the gift of heavenly contemplation or by undertaking the ministry of preaching properly. They are fittingly designated by the number sixty, because such people await the denary of eternal recompense in return for the perfection of good works.

“All holding swords”: concerning these the Apostle says, “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” “Most skilled in battle”: concerning these he likewise admonishes, saying, “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and powers,” and so forth. [Col. 0476C]

They are rightly called highly skilled, because those who, enclosed in the flesh and placed on earth, fight against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly realms require great skill in battle. They need great skill—or rather, great grace from God—when the frailty of the flesh fights against an archangel trained for battle through so many thousands of years.

The two hundred spears, therefore, made from a total of six hundred gold pieces or shekels, as the Book of Kings records, rightly signify the fathers of the Old Testament, who are known to have been perfected in teaching and conduct, since whatever they taught in word they demonstrated through good examples.

The three hundred shields, each covered with three hundred gold pieces, signify their perfect faith, which they possessed in the confession of the Holy Trinity. The guardians of God’s house therefore rightly carry spears and golden shields, because the holy preachers who guard the holy Church, shining with the brightness of heavenly wisdom, pierce their enemies with the javelins of words and deeds, and extinguish the fiery darts of the wicked one by repelling them with the shield of holy faith. [Col. 0476D]

The statement that the king placed them in the armory planted with trees also aptly accords with this mystery. The armory in which spiritual weapons are stored is therefore the holy Church, in which various forms of virtues and teachings are preserved. By these the faithful are well fortified and protected, and all their enemies are bravely defeated. This armory is said to have been planted with trees because diverse human persons, drawn from the nations of various peoples, have been gathered there and planted in the Catholic faith, both for the adornment of the Church herself and for manifesting the delights of the heavenly king. [Col. 0477A]

The king also made a great ivory throne and covered it with the purest gold, with six steps by which one ascended to the throne, a golden footstool, two armrests on either side, and two lions standing beside the armrests. There were also twelve other young lions standing upon the six steps, six on each side. No such throne existed in any kingdom.

The throne that King Solomon made is rightly understood as the holy Church, in which our Peacemaker, reigning, is known to carry out his judgments, because the soul of the just person is the seat of wisdom. [Col. 0477B]

It is rightly remembered that it was made of ivory. This should not be understood merely as an embellishment appropriate to wealth, but also because the elephant, whose bones these are, is said to possess extraordinary holiness. Among quadrupeds it is especially intelligent, and among beasts it mates with only one female and does not take a second mate. This is fittingly applied to chaste souls, who are known to have been ivory-like because they followed the commandments of Christ the Lord through chastity.

He covered the throne with exceptionally bright gold because he caused the radiance of his glory to shine in the Church when, through signs and miracles, he displayed the power of his majesty.

This throne had six steps. What is signified by the number six except the perfection of good works? In six days God completed the adornment of the world, and on the seventh he rested from his works. The number six is also the first number recognized as perfect through its parts: it has one-half, three; one-third, two; and one-sixth, one. One, two, and three together make six. [Col. 0477C]

Since, therefore, the world consists of six ages in which it is permitted to work, whoever desires to reach the heavenly homeland should hasten to ascend through good works, because without good deeds no one will reach it.

The throne is said to have a golden footstool. By the golden footstool we may understand holy and religious people, shining with the splendor of virtues, in whose hearts the divine majesty deigns to dwell. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” [Col. 0477D] Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.”

Alternatively, those who are weak in the body of Christ—that is, penitents—may be designated by the name of footstool. By truly repenting of their sins, they strive through pious labor to recover the grace that they had lost by sinning.

Or those who are converted to Christ at the end of the world may be called a footstool. They are nevertheless golden because, tested by the fire of the persecutions and tribulations that the fury of Antichrist will intensify at that time, they are found thoroughly proven through patience.

“And two armrests on either side.” In the Book of Kings it is likewise written: “And two hands, one on either side, holding the seat.” What, then, do the two armrests, or two hands, holding Solomon’s seat signify except the consolations of divine grace, which raise the holy Church to the heavenly kingdom? They are appropriately described by the number two because this is preached and especially commended in both Testaments: nothing good can be brought to completion except through divine assistance. [Col. 0478A]

Hence Truth himself says: “Without me you can do nothing.”

“And two lions stood beside the armrests.” What are signified by the lions except the fathers of both Testaments, who through strength of spirit learned to rule well both themselves and others? The two lions therefore stood beside the hands because, in the Law and in the Gospel, the holy Fathers attributed whatever good they did not to themselves but to God.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, because of your mercy and your truth.” And the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” Again: “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord.” [Col. 0478B]

“And twelve young lions stood upon the six steps, on either side.” What are signified by the twelve young lions except the order of preachers who follow apostolic teaching? They stand above the six steps, on either side, because they strive to fortify the steps of good works on every side through their teachings and examples, so that the pious labor of those beginning well in their work may not falter, but may firmly preserve uprightness as it progresses in virtue.

The statement that no such throne was made in all the kingdoms aptly applies to the holy Church, concerning which it is written: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will see the last day. Her sons rose up and preached well; her husband—and they will praise her. Many daughters gathered riches; you surpassed them all.” [Col. 0478C]

The account continues:

All the vessels of the king’s banquet were gold, and the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of purest gold. Silver was considered worthless in those days.

Thus it is written in the Book of Kings: “All the vessels from which King Solomon drank were gold, and all the furnishings of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of purest gold. There was no silver, nor was it considered to have any value in Solomon’s days.”

All the vessels that serve our Peacemaker’s ministry are made gold, because all the souls of the saints, which are vessels of God created to serve the divine will, shine with the splendor of wisdom and the radiance of love. They contain the drink of living water, and in them it will become a spring of water welling up to eternal life. [Col. 0478D]

Silver was not considered to have any value in Solomon’s days because, according to the Apostle, “the kingdom of God is not in word but in power,” and the preaching of the Gospel does not consist in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest in human wisdom but in the power of God.

Hence Truth himself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven.” Again: “Whoever breaks one of these commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.” [Col. 0479A]

The king’s ships went to Tarshish with Hiram’s servants once every three years, and brought back gold, silver, ivory, monkeys, and peacocks.

What does it mean that Solomon’s servants went with Hiram’s servants to Tarshish once every three years and brought back gold, silver, and ivory, except that our Redeemer sends the apostles and teachers of the Gospel from the Jewish people, together with those preachers whom he chose from the Gentile peoples, into the world with a threefold confession but one faith, so that they may bring him, in the persons of believers, the gold of wisdom, the silver of eloquence, and the ivory of chastity? [Col. 0479B]

Let them bring monkeys and peacocks as well. The monkey is an ingenious animal and imitates certain human actions. It may appropriately signify, figuratively, the persons of philosophers, who at times imitate the rational insights of true wisdom and display the practices of moral life in their disciplines. When these are converted to the faith of Christ through the diligence of preachers, they will be an acceptable gift to our Peacemaker.

Likewise, peacocks, because of the variety of colors they display in their feathers, may signify those who display outwardly the appearance of various virtues for the sake of human praise. But when, through the labor of teachers, they are inwardly reformed by faith and learn to practice these virtues solely for the love of God, they are then wholly suited to the delights of the eternal king.

Solomon was therefore magnified above all the kings of the earth in wealth and glory. All the kings of the lands desired to see Solomon’s face, to hear the wisdom that God had given in his heart, and they brought him gifts, and so forth. [Col. 0479C]

It is rightly said that the king was magnified above all the kings of the earth, because our Peacemaker is exalted above the entire height of the saints, who are truly called kings, and no one can be compared with him. For “who among the clouds is like the Lord, or who is like the Lord among the sons of God?” He is the God who is glorified in the counsels of his majesty and feared above all that surround him. Again: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number.”

Hence John says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” [Col. 0479D]

The whole earth desires to see the face of our king, because the entire Church of the saints desires only to reach the sight of his glory. To him the prophet says: “My heart has said to you, ‘Your face I have sought’; your face, Lord, I will seek.” And elsewhere: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

Each person brings him gifts when, according to the strength granted to him, he strives to offer God service in word or deed.

Solomon also had forty thousand horses in his stables, and twelve thousand chariots and horsemen. He placed them in the chariot cities and wherever the king was in Jerusalem.

What does the number forty signify except the times of the ancient Law? [Col. 0480A] Moses fasted for forty days when he was about to receive it, and the Israelite people, who were instructed through it, remained in the wilderness for forty years.

The horses of Solomon are rightly counted by the number forty and placed in stables, because the insolence of the former people had been bound and restrained by the harshness of the old Law.

The number twelve signifies the present time, in which apostolic authority, presiding over the peoples of the Gentiles, nourishes them through the teaching of the New Testament. These horses were placed in the chariot cities—that is, under the guardianship of disciplines—and wherever the king was in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace.

The differences between the places show distinctions in spiritual progress. Those placed in the chariot cities signify people who, subjected to the Church’s various disciplines, are instructed by spiritual teachers in the observance of true religion. Those who have already been instructed in every teaching of virtue and are capable of serving the heavenly king deserve to have the presence and nearness of the true Peacemaker. Concerning them it is written: “The chariot of God is multiplied ten thousandfold, thousands rejoicing; the Lord is among them.” And elsewhere: “For you will ascend, ascending upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.” [Col. 0480B]

The figure of this riding was also shown literally in the Lord, when, as he was going toward Jerusalem, he sat upon a donkey while the crowds that went before, followed, and came to meet him sang: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

In that riding salvation resounded, because it signified the spiritual journey of those who, with the Lord as their guide, are led through the apostles to the realms of that Jerusalem which is above, which is the mother of us all. [Col. 0480C]

He also exercised authority over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and to the borders of Egypt. It is written in the Psalms concerning the kingdom and dominion of the true Solomon—that is, of our Peacemaker: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71). This, however, cannot in any way apply to Solomon son of David, who is known to have been king only among the Jewish people. By “sea” we must understand the Ocean, which, as some say, surrounds and encloses the whole area of the earth with its encircling rim. For if you wish to understand this as referring to our seas, you will not be able to comprehend the circumference of the entire world, which this true king signifies.

It follows: “And from the river to the ends of the earth.” This is a beautiful brevity, but it pours forth immense mysteries for us. “From the river”—he means from the Jordan, from which throughout the whole world the saving rule of sacred baptism flows forth. Our king therefore rules over all kings—that is, over all who rightly exercise the power of governance—from the river Euphrates, which is interpreted as “fruitful” or “increasing,” to the land of the Philistines, that is, of those “falling doubly.” For *Philistim* is interpreted as “double ruin.” His grace and power overflow from the beginning of baptism in the Jordan, through the forgetfulness of sins, to the conversion of all nations to the faith, so that where there had been a falling away into carnal desires, there the seed of good works may be established; and where there had been the double ruin of peoples through both idolatry and wicked conduct, there, through confession of the true faith and the worship of genuine piety, the life of the faithful may rise toward the heavenly kingdom.

His power also extends to the borders of Egypt—that is, to the darkened minds of unbelievers, whom he turns away from error and fills with the light of his faith. Hence the prophet immediately attaches the following words to the verse mentioned above: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth.” We must understand the Ethiopians as sinful peoples. For just as they are clothed in extremely dark skin, so the souls of sinners are darkened by the obscurity of their crimes. These Ethiopians, who are sinners, fall before him when they humbly prostrate themselves in repentance.

He adds: “And his enemies shall lick the earth.” Those whom the Lord’s mercy must spare, he said, would fall before him; but these are called the obstinate enemies—the Jews—who will remain in their stubbornness. What, then, is their punishment? “They shall lick the earth,” that is, they shall taste the earth; for each person tastes what he licks, and for them the ground is punitive food, as it was for the serpent. We rightly refer this to their humiliation, since those who refused to believe in Christ the Lord have been condemned to such retribution.

And he provided such an abundance of silver in Jerusalem that it was like stones, and such a multitude of cedars that it was like the sycamores growing in the lowlands. What is expressed by stones except the hardness and insensibility of the nations? And what is signified by silver except the brilliance of eloquence and the delightfulness of ecclesiastical teaching? What by cedars except sublimity and the fragrance of virtues?

The true Solomon therefore provided in the mystical Jerusalem an abundance of silver like stones when he converted to meditation on God’s law and to the preaching of the Gospel the hearts of the Gentiles, which had been insensible to the understanding of almighty God and had worshiped stones as deities. Nor were the nations signified without reason by the name of stones, since they worshiped stones; for it is written: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.” Concerning these stones John the Baptist says in the Gospel: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Children of Abraham were raised from stones because, when the hard hearts of the Gentiles believed in the seed of Abraham, they became children of the one to whose seed they were joined. Hence the distinguished preacher says to those same Gentiles: “But if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.”

Similarly, our Peacemaker provided in Jerusalem such a multitude of cedars, like sycamores, by bringing the Gentiles from barrenness to fruitfulness, because he raised to the fruitfulness of good works and the height of virtues those who, desiring earthly things, were unable to lift themselves upward. We said above, and now repeat the same point by way of reminder, that the cedar is a tree of incorruptible nature, pleasant fragrance, and shining appearance; when kindled by its scent, it drives away and destroys serpents. All these qualities correspond to the perfect: their patience is unconquerable, their reputation for virtue outstanding, their presence most pleasing to all good people, and their authority utterly steadfast in defeating and refuting those who resist the truth. In this life and in the future they shine with unique eminence above the other saints.

The rest of Solomon’s deeds, both earlier and later, are written in the words of Nathan the prophet, in the books of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the vision of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat. Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years. He slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David.

When Scripture speaks of Solomon’s earlier deeds, it means the deeds he performed before he transgressed: the building of the Temple, the variety of offerings, and so forth—his actions that possess a mystical significance, as we have shown above. The later deeds it mentions are those he performed after he violated God’s law by marrying foreign women, who led him all the way into idolatry.

What, then, shall I say about these deeds of Solomon, which sacred Scripture severely reproves and condemns, while making absolutely no mention of his repentance or of any divine mercy toward him? Although the Hebrews assert that he wrote the book of Ecclesiastes in his repentance, no good meaning at all presents itself, even allegorically, in this lamentable sinking, unless someone should say that the foreign women with whom he had fallen passionately in love signify the churches chosen from among the Gentiles. This interpretation might perhaps be understood without absurdity if they had abandoned their gods for Solomon’s sake and worshiped his God. But when he offended his Lord for their sake and worshiped their gods, no good meaning can be conjectured from it. Nevertheless, I do not think that it signifies nothing; rather, it signifies evil, as we said concerning Lot’s wife and daughters.

In the person of Solomon, a remarkable excellence and a remarkable sinking are evident. What therefore appeared in him at different times—first good and afterward evil—is displayed in the Church, in this present age, simultaneously and at one time. For I think that his good deeds signify the good members of the Church, while his evil deeds signify its wicked members: just as, within the unity of that ark, we understand the good as the grain and the wicked as the chaff; or, within the unity of a single field of grain, the good as wheat and the wicked as weeds.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0483]

## CHAPTER X  
[Note: [Col. 0483D] Let the reader not be surprised if, in what follows, the numerical order of the chapters is sometimes interrupted. In the archetype according to which this work was arranged, and which we follow in all respects, we found matters arranged in this way.]

[Col. 0483A] On the reign of Rehoboam and Jeroboam.

(II Chron. 10.) Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered there to make him king. When Jeroboam son of Nebat, who was in Egypt—he had fled there before Solomon—heard this, he immediately returned. They summoned him, and he came with all Israel. They spoke to Rehoboam, saying: “Your father imposed a very harsh yoke upon us. You must command us more leniently than your father, who laid a heavy servitude upon us, and lighten the burden somewhat, so that we may serve you.” He said to them: “Return to me after three days.”

When the people had departed, he took counsel with the elders who had stood before his father Solomon while he was still alive, saying: “What counsel do you give me, so that I may answer this people?” They said to him: “If you please this people and soothe them with gracious words, they will serve you always.” But he abandoned the counsel of the elders and began to consult the young men who had been brought up with him and were in his retinue, and so forth.

The Hebrews believe that those elders who had stood before Solomon, Rehoboam’s father, were Benaiah son of Jehoiada and Jahiel son of Achmoni, who was also called Chila by another name. After abandoning their counsel, Rehoboam began to consult the young men—that is, Aduram, who is later described as being stoned, and others like him, whose folly is exposed by the advice they gave.

Scripture does not always call someone “young” according to age, but according to instability of mind. Rehoboam was not young in age at that time, since he began to reign in the forty-first year of his life; but in understanding he was brutish and childish.

Mystically, Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, who abandoned the useful counsel of the elders and followed the counsel of the young men, although he belonged to the house of David, did not walk in David’s way. For Scripture, bearing witness in the books of Kings, says: “Judah did evil in the sight of the Lord in those days, and they provoked him beyond all that their fathers had done in their sins, because they sinned. They also built for themselves statues, altars, and sacred groves on every high hill and under every leafy tree. There were also male prostitutes in the land. And they committed all the abominations of the nations that the Lord had destroyed before the face of the children of Israel.”

He therefore signifies wicked rulers in the Church, who, devoted to earthly desires, neglect to care for their subjects. They take pleasure and rejoice in the multitude of those who obey them, yet they do not show fitting concern for those entrusted to them.

Rehoboam is interpreted as “breadth of the people.” Those may rightly be called the breadth of the people who, walking along the broad and spacious road by which many go to death, refuse to enter the narrow way, which belongs to the few and leads to eternal life. They abandon the counsel of the holy Fathers, whose words and examples strive toward the height of perfection, and choose to obey the commands of the young—that is, of those enslaved to youthful desires, who burden them with unjust praise and flattery. Thus what the prophet says comes to pass among them: “As is the people, so is the priest.”

For all, from the least to the greatest, pursue greed; and the blind, leading the blind, fall together into the pit of destruction. The wisdom of God threatens them, saying: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10). Conversely, concerning the holy people and the praiseworthy King Christ, it continues: “Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at the proper time” (ibid.), because “whatever they do shall prosper” (Ps. 1).

## CHAPTER XII  
How Shishak, king of Egypt, came to Jerusalem and oppressed Rehoboam, taking away the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the royal house.

(II Chron. 12.) In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem—because they had sinned against the Lord—with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. The common people who came with him from Egypt were without number: Libyans, Troglodytes, and Ethiopians. He captured the fortified cities in Judah and came as far as Jerusalem.

The prophet Shemaiah entered before Rehoboam and the princes of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem while fleeing from Shishak, and said to them: “Thus says the Lord: You have abandoned me, and I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak.” The princes of Israel and the king were dismayed and said: “The Lord is righteous.”

When the Lord saw that they had humbled themselves, the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah, saying: “Because they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them. I will give them a little help, and my wrath will not be poured out upon Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak. Nevertheless, they shall serve him, so that they may know the difference between serving me and serving the kingdoms of the earth.”

Shishak king of Egypt therefore withdrew from Jerusalem after taking away the treasures of the house of God and of the royal house. He carried everything away with him, including the golden shields that Solomon had made. In their place King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers who guarded the entrance of the palace.

What, then, is figuratively indicated here? Because of Rehoboam’s sin, Shishak king of Egypt took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures. This signifies that wicked rulers, because of their negligence, provoke the king of Egypt—that is, the prince of darkness—against the symbolic Jerusalem, namely, the Church entrusted to them, where they themselves seem to rule for a time. He takes away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures when he strips the unchaste and sluggish of knowledge of the holy Scriptures and of works of virtue.

Shishak is therefore interpreted as “fine linen and sackcloth,” or “joy of sackcloth.” Since fine linen signifies subtlety, while sackcloth, made from goats’ hair, signifies sins, what could “fine linen and sackcloth” better signify than the devil’s cunning deceit in persuading people to sin? Shishak takes away the wealth of Jerusalem when the devil, who deceives craftily and rejoices in the multitude of sinners, plunders ecclesiastical people of spiritual knowledge and virtuous works, and plunges those who seemed to be ornaments of the Church, stripped of their possessions, with himself into the abyss of his destruction.

Nor does the fact that the same king took away the golden shields that King Solomon had made, in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers, fail to bear upon the same meaning. Solomon, making golden shields, gave them to the guardians of his house when our Redeemer entrusted spiritual knowledge, through the two Testaments, to the teachers of the Church for the protection of his people.

The ancient enemy removes this knowledge through the negligence of rulers. When they are absorbed in earthly matters and care less about heavenly things, he leaves them stripped of their former office and knowledge, as though they had been robbed of their possessions in their own house.

Finally, when such men see that they have been deprived of spiritual understanding, they seek an abundance of words through eloquence, so that by the resonance of their speech, like the strength of bronze shields, they may provide protection for those subject to them against their enemies. But just as bronze is inferior to gold, so empty eloquence is inferior to the fruit of true wisdom.

Hence a certain wise man says concerning eloquence: “Where there are many words, there is often poverty.” And it is written in the Psalms: “The man of many words shall not be established on the earth” (Ps. 139). Concerning wisdom it is written: “Wisdom is more precious than all works, and nothing that is desired can be compared with it. Length of days is in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3).

Whoever wishes to provide the Church with timely defense against heretics and against all enemies ought to accomplish this by the aid of wisdom. Eloquence without wisdom contributes nothing to this purpose; indeed, it does great harm.

The first and later deeds of Rehoboam are written in the books of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, and are carefully explained. Shemaiah is the same prophet who above reproved Rehoboam and the sons of Judah for their transgression and sins. Iddo, or Jaddo, is the prophet who was sent by the Lord to Samaria to reprove Jeroboam concerning the altar he had made. He was also killed by a lion because, having been deceived by a false prophet contrary to the Lord’s command, he ate there.

Rehoboam and Jeroboam fought against each other throughout all their days. Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and his son Abijah reigned in his place.

## CHAPTER XIII  
[Col. 0486A] On the reign of Abijah son of Rehoboam.

(II Chron. 13.) In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah reigned over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Micaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.

What is read both in the book of Chronicles and in the books of Kings—that there was war between the kings of Judah and the kings of Israel throughout all their days—I do not think signifies anything other than that the holy Church, which persists in the unity of faith, is always at war with heretics and schismatics and with all who strive to violate the catholic faith. For, as the Apostle says, “all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution,” because the ancient dragon persecutes the woman, lying in wait for her heel.

Abijah therefore stood on Mount Semeron, which was in Ephraim, and said: “Hear, Jeroboam and all Israel. Do you not know that the Lord God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, to him and to his sons?” And so forth.

Semeron was a city captured by Joshua after its king had been killed. Josephus says that it is now called Sebaste, a town in Palestine where the relics of Saint John the Baptist are buried. We read in the books of Kings that Omri, king of Israel, purchased Mount Semeron from a man named Shemer and built a city on its summit, which he called Semeron after the name of its former owner.

Abijah pursued the fleeing Jeroboam and captured his cities: Bethel and its dependent settlements, Jeshanah with its dependent settlements, and Ephron with its dependent settlements.

Bethel was a city twelve miles from Jerusalem, on the right for those traveling toward Neapolis. It was formerly called Luz—that is, Almond-tree—and fell to the tribe of Benjamin, near Bethan and Hai, which Joshua conquered after killing its king.

Those who, following the error of the Greeks, think that it was anciently called Ulamluzah are seriously mistaken. They have confused the Hebrew word with the name of the little city itself, since *Ulam* means “formerly,” that is, *proteron*. Formerly it was called Luz, Bethel, and also Bethaum, which some think was another town. The Hebrews believe it to be the same as Bethel. But from the time when golden calves were made there by Jeroboam son of Nebat and worshiped by the ten tribes, it was called Bethaum—that is, “house of an idol”—whereas it had previously been called the house of God.

Jeshanah is a city in the tribe of Judah, and Ephron likewise lies in the tribe of Judah. Hence, toward the north, a very large village called Ephrea is still known, twenty miles from Jerusalem.

Jeroboam was no longer able to resist in the days of Abijah. The Lord struck him, and he died. God did not strike Jeroboam, as most people think, since, according to the book of Kings, in the twentieth year of his reign Asa son of Abijah had ruled over Judah and Jerusalem; rather, he struck Abijah, because, as the Hebrews assert, after capturing Bethel he preserved the idols as a stumbling-block for Israel.

## CHAPTER XIV  
[Col. 0487A] On Asa, king of Jerusalem.

(II Chron. 14.) Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. His son Asa reigned in his place. In his days the land rested for ten years.

Asa did what was good and pleasing in the sight of his God. He overturned the altars of foreign worship and the high places; he broke the statues and cut down the sacred groves. He commanded Judah to seek the Lord, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and all the commandments. He removed from all the cities of Judah the altars and shrines, and he reigned in peace, and so forth.

This is Asa who, at the beginning of his reign, restored divine worship and did what was good and pleasing in God’s sight. He overturned the altars of the idols and broke the images. Thus he earned the Lord’s favor, so that, fighting against the Ethiopians, he won a victory and slaughtered them to the point of annihilation. Because the Lord fought for him and aided his army, they were crushed.

But afterward, falling into a worse state, he sought the help of the Assyrians against Baasha, king of Israel, and imprisoned the prophet Hanani, who had been sent to him by the Lord to rebuke him for this. In doing so he gravely offended the Lord. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, he fell into a very serious illness and suffered the most severe pain in his feet, from which he died. Even in his illness he did not seek the Lord, but, trusting instead in the art of physicians, was deceived.

He therefore typologically signifies those who begin with a good beginning but end with an evil conclusion. After renouncing idolatry and rejecting service to the devil, after receiving the grace of baptism and the anointing of sacred chrism, they immediately undertake works of piety at the beginning of their life. But in more mature age, and near the end of the present life, when they ought to have devoted themselves to virtue, they fall back into vices and delight in wicked acts.

Although, while they were devoted to divine worship, they may have overcome and driven away the spiritual Ethiopians and the rulers of this darkness, nevertheless, after they have given themselves over to the pleasures of the present life and sought as helpers the Assyrians who hold the kingdom of confusion, they are justly abandoned to such an extent that, seized by various illnesses of error, they are deprived of fruitful actions. No longer able to advance by the steps of good works, they bring their wicked life to an end in eternal death, without repentance or amendment of conduct.

## CHAPTER XVI  
On Asa, continued.

(II Chron. 16.) Asa slept with his fathers and died in the forty-first year of his reign. They buried him in his tomb, which he had prepared for himself in the city of David. They placed him on his bed, which was filled with spices and “ointments of harlots,” prepared by the art of perfumers, and they burned them over him with excessive ostentation.

Historically, “spices and ointments of harlots” refers to the perfumes that the luxurious customarily use for the sake of lust. It should be noted, however, that among kings, as the Hebrews report, the burning of precious garments together with spices was performed as a mark of honor. Hence it is written elsewhere: “They will make a burning for you like the burnings of the great,” because among the ancients it was customary for the precious royal ornaments they possessed to be burned on the funeral pyre after their death, though without the bodies.

Figuratively, the spices and harlot’s ointments that were burned on Asa’s bed in his honor signify the vain ostentation of reputation. Philosophers or poets, after the death of their kings, and false Christians likewise after the death of their teachers, lavish such honors upon them. They heap excessive praise upon those whose entire conduct was full of shame, and they cast these things into the fire, showing that everything they produced here without usefulness or the edification of their brothers is subject to the fires of Gehenna.

Hence it is written in Job concerning wicked men: “Their pride has been cut down, and fire has devoured their remnant” (Job 22). And in the Psalm: “Their graves are their houses forever; their dwellings are from generation to generation. They have called their names upon their lands” (Ps. 48).

It is the custom of fools to follow the rites of the pagans, which they are accustomed to perform at funeral commemorations, when, in foolish superstition, they celebrate the praises of the dead in their lands—that is, at their graves—and believe that these acts benefit the dead because they appear to be paying tribute to their memory.

## CHAPTER XVII  
On Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, his good works, and the provision made for his kingdom.

[Col. 0488C] (II Chron. 17.) Jehoshaphat, his son, reigned in his place and grew strong against Israel. He established contingents of soldiers in all the walled cities of Judah and stationed garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had captured.

The Lord was with Jehoshaphat, who walked in the earliest ways of his father David. He did not trust in the Baals, but in the God of his father. He followed his commandments and did not imitate the sins of Israel.

When it says of Jehoshaphat that he walked in the earliest ways of his father David, it shows that he was a most careful executor of the divine testimonies, as David his father had been at the beginning of his reign, before he sinned concerning Uriah’s wife. Although the shame of that sin may seem to obscure his reputation, the praiseworthy satisfaction of his repentance prepared eternal remembrance for him.

The Lord established the kingdom in his hand, and all Judah brought gifts to Jehoshaphat. He acquired immeasurable wealth and great glory. When his heart had taken courage because of the ways of the Lord, he removed the high places and sacred groves from Judah, and so forth.

Finally, King Jehoshaphat prefigures the people of believers from the Gentiles. Abandoning the error of their ancestors, they come to our Redeemer, washed in sacred baptism and anointed with holy chrism. From Christ they receive the Christian name and royal dignity. To them the apostle Peter says in his Epistle: “But you are a chosen race by the Lord, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2).

The interpretation of his name confirms this well. Jehoshaphat is interpreted as “the Lord’s dowry,” or “one who has been given.” The Church of the Gentiles, purchased at the price of Christ’s blood and endowed with the pledge of the Spirit, earned participation in the heavenly Bridegroom and fellowship in the kingdom. She acquired immeasurable riches, whether in the gathering of various nations into the faith or in the acquisition of diverse virtues, and great glory consisting in a special wisdom, concerning which it is written in Proverbs: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. 31).

All Judah offered her gifts, because every believer rejoices in presenting to the true King, within her unity, the gifts of sound doctrine and good works. He removed the high places and sacred groves from the land of Judah because he strives to remove every stumbling-block from the gatherings of believers.

This king sends his princes and priests into the cities of Judah to teach the people the commandments of the Lord’s law, when he sends holy teachers to various peoples to preach the Gospel of Christ to them. Thus what is written concerning Jehoshaphat will be fulfilled:

The fear of the Lord therefore came upon all the kingdoms of the lands surrounding Judah, and they did not dare to wage war against Jehoshaphat. The Philistines also brought gifts and a tribute of silver to Jehoshaphat, while the Arabians brought seven thousand seven hundred rams and just as many male goats.

Because of the glorious name and the virtues performed in the Church, the boldness of the pagans is restrained, and the hearts of the nations are stirred so that they may bring to the true King Christ, who is the head of the Church, gifts of right belief, pay the tribute of good works and devout confession, and bring him the sheep of their simplicity.

This means seven thousand seven hundred rams and just as many male goats: enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, they offer men capable of teaching because of their knowledge and integrity in good works, and through confession and repentance they subject a multitude of sinners to his service. Rams are leaders of the flock, and under the law they were sacrificed in peace offerings. Male goats, however, were offered for sin.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
On Jehoshaphat, continued.

(II Chron. 18.) Jehoshaphat was therefore very rich and renowned, and he was joined to Ahab by marriage alliance. After some years he went down to him in Samaria. At his arrival Ahab slaughtered many rams and oxen for him and for the people who had come with him, and persuaded him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.

King Ahab of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah: “Come with me to Ramoth-gilead.” He answered him: “I am as you are, and my people are as your people; we shall be with you in the war.”

As we said above, Jehoshaphat signifies the Christian people, who hold the catholic faith and preserve the Christian religion. But the impious Ahab, who reigned in Samaria, represents the leaders of heresy, who lead a crowd of the lost along the byways of error and drag them into the precipice of eternal death.

The fact that Jehoshaphat, joined to Ahab by marriage alliance, went down to him in Samaria and offered him aid against his enemies figuratively demonstrates those who, from among the Catholics, incline themselves toward friendship with heretics. Although they do not depart from the path of the true faith, they nevertheless do not completely avoid the association and communion of those who err. This can in no way occur without guilt, especially since the apostle Paul teaches that a heretical person must be avoided after one and a second admonition, and John says in his Epistle: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him” (2 John). For whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works.

Hence Wisdom also says: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever associates with the proud will put on pride” (Eccl. 13). For this reason Jehoshaphat himself was reproved by Jehu the seer, son of Hanani—namely, the prophet who had rebuked Asa—for having offered assistance to an impious man and joined himself in friendship to those who hated the Lord.

The company of heretics must therefore be avoided, because light has no fellowship with darkness, nor can Christ in any way have agreement with Belial. Nor can we drink together from the Lord’s cup, in which there is a health-giving draught of wisdom, and from the cup of demons, in which the deadly poison of wickedness is served.

The king of Israel therefore summoned one of the eunuchs and said to him: “Call Micaiah son of Imlah quickly.” The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were each sitting on his throne, dressed in royal attire. They were sitting in the open space beside the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them, and so forth.

Finally, the prophet Micaiah was summoned before the king of Israel and the king of Judah together, and he prophesied against the king of Israel, saying:

I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and the whole army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left. And the Lord said: “Who will deceive Ahab, king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” When one said one thing and another something else, a spirit came forth, stood before the Lord, and said, “I will deceive him.” The Lord said to him, “By what means, then, will you deceive him?” He replied, “I will go forth and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord said, “You will deceive him and prevail; go forth and do so.”

What else should we understand by the Lord’s throne except the angelic powers, over whose minds God presides from above and disposes all things below? [Col. 0490D] And what else is signified by the army of heaven except the multitude of ministering angels? What, then, does it mean that the army of heaven is said to stand at his right and at his left? God, who is so within all things that he is also beyond all things, is enclosed neither by a right nor by a left. Rather, the right side of God designates the chosen part of the angels, while the left side of God designates the reprobate part of the angels. For it is not only the good who minister to God and render assistance, but also those who, unwilling to return, impose burdens. Nor is it forbidden to understand the reprobate part of the angels by the expression “the army of heaven”; for those whom we know to have been suspended in the air we call “the birds of heaven.”

And concerning these same spirits Paul said: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). Declaring their head, he said: “According to the prince of [Col. 0491A] the power of this air” (Eph. II). Thus the army of angels stands at the right and at the left, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine mercy, while the mind of the reprobate, serving wickedness, obeys the judgment of God’s severity.

Hence immediately afterward a deceitful spirit is described as springing forth, through whom King Ahab was to be deceived in accordance with his deserved punishment. For it is not right to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deceit, saying, “I will go forth and become a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” But because King Ahab, by his preceding sins, was worthy to be condemned by such a deception, so that the one who had often fallen willingly into guilt might at some point be dragged unwillingly into punishment, hidden justice grants permission to wicked spirits: those whom they strangle willingly in the snare of sin, they also drag unwillingly into the punishment of sin. [Col. 0491B]

Accordingly, when one who does not change his reprobate life and does not turn his mind away from committing sins asks a prophet for some answer, by God’s ordering he hears from the prophet’s mouth what he deserves to hear as one destined for condemnation. For, to speak of one or two examples among many, the house of Israel had withdrawn from the worship of almighty God into slavery to idols. Yet it often came to the prophets, whom it was accustomed to deceive, seeking favorable answers. When, because of its perverse conduct, it deserved to hear favorable things from the mouth of the prophets, what else were the heavenly judgments doing except trapping the sinful people in their own heart? The people had sinned by following faithlessness, and so they were deceived by the flattering words of their prophets in such a way that they no longer feared that they had sinned; and the more securely they now lived in guilt, the more harshly they would later be dragged to punishment. [Col. 0491C]

But now, by the generosity of almighty God, a very large part of the human race has been removed from the worship of idols and publicly professes the true faith; it refuses to submit to wood, stones, or any other creature. Therefore anyone who has been established in the faith may now consult a prophet with confidence, since he will hear what it is fitting for a faithful person to hear. I shall speak boldly: if he had withdrawn from impurities and wicked actions, he would be secure.
