For when Paul, that outstanding preacher, cries out that greed is the worship of idols, whoever is still subject to greed is not free from the worship of idols.

If, then, someone who pants with the fever of greed seems indeed to be established in the faith, but covets the possessions of others, desires to seize the honors of the world, and longs to possess temporal glory, and if he consults a prophet about that same glory, it is entirely just that, according to the merit of his guilt, he should not hear favorable things from the prophet’s mouth. He refused to hear the words of God in the sacred writings, so that he might despise earthly things and aspire to heavenly ones; therefore, by divine judgment, he hears from the prophet’s mouth that by which he falls more tightly bound. While he is delighted and nourished by hope of earthly glory, he is continually led downward by his own desires. [Col. 0491D]

Nor was that spirit good who desired to be a liar in the mouth of the prophets. Hence it was stated above that the army of heaven stood at his right and at his left. God, who is uncircumscribed truth, has no left side in that eternal blessedness which is called his right, because there can be nothing displeasing to him. But because he sees all things together and beholds everything at once in that power by which he saw both good and evil spirits, the army of heaven is described as being at his right and at his left. As we said above, by the right we understand the elect angels, and by the left the reprobate spirits.

Nor should it be troubling that even the rejected angels are called the army of heaven. Although they have been expelled from the ethereal heaven, they still dwell in the aerial heaven, as Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

## CHAPTER XX

### Concerning Jehoshaphat

After these things the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon, and with them some of the Ammonites, gathered against Jehoshaphat in order to fight him. By adding “the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon and the Ammonites,” the text shows that the Edomites were joined with the Moabites and Ammonites to fight against Israel. Accordingly, it is related later that the sons of Ammon and Moab rose up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir in order to kill and destroy them. But the writer of the history, out of reverence for the name of their brotherhood, preferred to note secretly what had been done by the allies under an associated name rather than to proclaim publicly, in an explicit statement, the impiety of shameless men. This is especially so since the Book of Numbers relates that, when the sons of Israel were coming out of the wilderness, they were not permitted to inflict any harm upon the Edomites, because the Lord forbade it. [Col. 0492B]

It should be noted, however, that Josephus thinks those who had gone into battle with the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon were Arabs. [Col. 0492C]

Messengers came and reported to Jehoshaphat, saying: “A great multitude is coming against you from the regions beyond the sea, from Syria; and behold, they are stationed at Hazazon-tamar, which is Engedi.”

By saying “beyond the sea,” he indicates not places beyond the Tyrrhenian Sea, but those situated beyond the Salt Sea, which is also called the Asphalt Lake or the Dead Sea, where the Jordan flows into it. When he says that the hostile army was stationed at Hazazon-tamar, which is Engedi, he means that Engedi is in the tribe of Judah, where David hid in the wilderness that lies in the Aulon of Jericho—that is, in the plain region. Even to this day it is called Engadda, a very large village of the Jews, beside the Dead Sea. From there opobalsamum is also brought, and there are vineyards which Solomon calls Engedi. [Col. 0492D]

Josephus likewise reports this, saying that they pitched their camp near the city of Gaddi, which lies around the Asphalt Lake, three hundred stadia from Jerusalem. The finest palm and opobalsamum grow there; for Thamar means “palm.”

Jehoshaphat, terrified by fear, devoted himself entirely to entreating the Lord and proclaimed a fast throughout Judah. Judah assembled to implore the Lord, and people also came from all their cities to beseech him. Jehoshaphat stood in the midst of the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of the Lord before the new court, and said: “Lord, God of our fathers, you are God in heaven and you rule over all the kingdoms of the nations. In your hand are strength and power, and no one can resist you,” and so forth. [Col. 0493A]

The new court is the temple of the Lord. It is called a court because King Jehoshaphat cleansed it of all the impurities with which the kings who practiced idolatry had polluted it. Thus the court which the sons of Israel had previously made old by sinning, they then restored to its former newness by repentance.

When the prophet Jahaziel, sent to Jehoshaphat, says: “Do not fear or be dismayed by this multitude, for the battle is not yours but God’s. Tomorrow you will go down against them. They will ascend by the slope called Sis, and you will find them at the top of the ravine that is opposite the wilderness of Israel. You will not be the ones who fight; only stand confidently and you will see the Lord’s help for you,” and so forth, the Hebrews believe that this place was the slope of Sis, as though it were the wilderness of Jeruel. They say that it was called Sis—that is, “cauldron” or “pot”—because a very great multitude of enemies was cut to pieces there. Jeruel, therefore, is interpreted as “the fear of God,” because, as a result of the manifest help of God which he bestowed upon those who hoped in him, fear grew on every side among the foreigners living around Judea. [Col. 0493B]

[Col. 0493C] In the mystical sense, the three divisions of the enemy—that is, of the Moabites, Ammonites, and Edomites—signify a threefold host of enemies and persecutors of the holy Church: namely, pagans, Jews, and heretics. They gratuitously stir up war against the faithful and strive to take away the name of Christ together with the Christian religion. But the mystical Jehoshaphat, that is, the people of the Church, prepares to fight against them not with bodily weapons but with spiritual ones.

For he persists in prayers and seeks heavenly assistance with the inward desire of his heart, so that the one of whom it is written—“The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle; the Lord, whose name is the Destroyer of wars”—and elsewhere, “He besieges the gates of the enemies and himself overthrows the camps of the hostile; he humbles the proud, crushes the insolent, and protects from every danger those who trust in him”—may act on his behalf.

For what else does the ecclesiastical order and the whole assembly of the faithful do each day except, like Jehoshaphat, instructed by prophetic speech, invoke the Lord with complete devotion of soul, praise him with the pious voice of confession, sing psalms through good works, and patiently await heavenly judgment and divine assistance? [Col. 0493D] Therefore the pious Judge, hearing those who cry out to him, delivers them and turns the plots of their enemies back upon their own heads, so that by the very rivalry with which they conspired to kill the innocent, they tear one another apart and, finally, are handed over to the torments of Gehenna and everlasting death.

Jehoshaphat therefore came, and all the people with him, to strip the dead of their spoils. They found among the corpses various kinds of equipment, clothing, and very precious vessels, and they plundered them so thoroughly that they could not carry everything away; indeed, for three days they were unable to remove the spoils because of the abundance of the booty.

On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Blessing. Since they had blessed the Lord there, they called that place the Valley of Blessing [Col. 0494A] down to the present day. Then every man of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and Jehoshaphat at their head returned to Jerusalem with great joy, because the Lord had given them joy over their enemies.

What else does it mean that Jehoshaphat and the sons of Israel came to gather the spoils of those who had been killed, and gathered them for three days, except that the holy teachers, together with the rest of the faithful, gather from the spoils of the enemies mentioned above whatever they have usefully produced in physics, ethics, and logic by reading, writing, and teaching, and, through faith in the holy Trinity, convert it beneficially to the use of the whole Church? What unjust possessors held without any remedy for their salvation because of the faithlessness of their hearts, those who devoutly believe in the Lord and faithfully hold the holy religion possess thereafter for the perpetual healing of their souls. [Col. 0494B]

Accordingly, it is fittingly said that on the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Blessing to bless the Lord, and thus entered Jerusalem with great joy. For the Valley of Blessing is the humility of the holy Church, where praises are fittingly sung to God each day. Concerning it, it is written in the Psalm: “The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys will abound in grain; they will cry out and indeed sing a hymn” (Ps. LXIV, 14). Whoever, instructed through faith and baptism in the holy doctrine of the four Gospels, reaches the unity of the holy Church will there rightly praise God and worthily conduct himself before him. Together with that mother of all the faithful, in the vision of perpetual peace, he will deserve to enter with everlasting praise and joy.

[Col. 0494C] After this, Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, entered into an alliance with Ochozias, king of Israel, whose deeds were exceedingly wicked. He became his partner in making ships that would sail to Tarshish, and they built a fleet at Ezion-geber. But Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying: “Because you made an alliance with Ochozias, the Lord has struck your works, and the ships have been destroyed; they have not been able to go to Tarshish.”

We said above that the association and friendship of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, with the kings of Samaria represented those who, from the number of Catholics, joined themselves by some alliance to the fellowship of heretics—a pact of friendship which is wholly displeasing to God. Accordingly, it is also related that the ships which the king of Judah and the king of Samaria sent together to Tarshish were destroyed at Ezion-geber, because the Lord struck their works. [Col. 0494D] This signifies that whatever is undertaken jointly in the voyage of the present life with the counsel or faction of heretics will be shown, in the final vengeance, to have been displeasing in the sight of God. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

## CHAPTER XXI

### Concerning Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, and the exceedingly evil end of his life

Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of David. His son Joram reigned in his place. He had brothers, sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jahiel, and Zechariah, and Azariah and [Col. 0495A] Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and so forth.

When Scripture, therefore, enumerates Joram’s six brothers, namely the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and then adds, “All these were sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah,” it signifies that they imitated the perfection of the works of Jehoshaphat, their king, while their brother Joram was continually declining into worse things. For this reason we read that Joram killed them together with the princes of Israel.

[Col. 0495B] For he had abandoned the Lord, the God of his fathers. Moreover, he built high places in the cities of Judah and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, and Judah to transgress. Letters were brought to him from the prophet Elijah, in which it was written:

“Thus says the Lord, the God of David your father: Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father and in the ways of Asa, king of Judah, but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel and have caused Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, imitating the fornication of the house of Ahab; moreover, you have killed your brothers, the house of your father, who were better than you: behold, the Lord will strike you with a great plague, together with your people, your sons, your wives, and all your possessions.”

This vengeance, therefore, which had been foretold through the prophet against King Joram, was fulfilled in him according to his merits through the agency of the Philistines and Arabs, when they devastated his land, plundered all his possessions, and carried away his sons and wives as well.

In the allegorical sense also, Joram—whose name is interpreted as “Who is exalted?”—was born of the religious man Jehoshaphat but turned aside to faithlessness and caused the sons of Judah to commit fornication, imitating the fornication of the house of Ahab. He can signify those who, instructed in the Catholic faith and reborn through Christian baptism, were taught the mysteries of the Church, but, abandoning the truth of the faith, follow the errors of heretics. They not only themselves depart from the path of sound doctrine but also strive to lead others with them along the byways of error.

[Col. 0495C] Therefore Elijah—that is, prophetic speech—rebukes them, since every sanction of the divine books reproves such people and, deservedly, censures them with the gravest denunciations because of their perversity.

For this reason, recalling his benefits through Ezekiel and reproaching the perversity of the people, the Lord says to Judah:

[Col. 0495D] “I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God, and you became mine. I washed you in water and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. I clothed you in garments of varied colors, put shoes of violet leather on you, girded you with fine linen, and dressed you in delicate cloth. I adorned you with ornaments, placed bracelets on your hands and a necklace around your neck, gave you an earring for your mouth and rings for your ears, and set a crown of beauty upon your head. You were adorned with gold and silver, and clothed in fine linen, embroidered work, and garments of many colors. You ate fine flour, honey, and oil. You became exceedingly beautiful and advanced to royal dignity. Your name went out among the nations because of your beauty, for you were perfect in my beauty which I had placed upon you, says the Lord your God.

“But, trusting in your beauty, you committed fornication and prostituted your name to every passerby, so that you became his. Taking some of your garments, you made for yourself high places sewn together here and there, [Col. 0496A] and committed fornication upon them as had never been done and never would be. You took the vessels of your adornment, and from my gold and silver which I had given you, you made male images for yourself and committed fornication with them. You took your garments of many colors, covered them with them, and placed my oil and my incense before them. You placed before them my bread which I had given you—the fine flour, oil, and honey with which I had nourished you—as a sweet fragrance.”

And a little later:

[Col. 0496B] “Therefore, prostitute, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Because your bronze was poured out and your disgrace was exposed in your fornications with your lovers and with all your abominable idols, in the blood of your sons whom you gave to them, behold, I will gather all your lovers with whom you have been joined, and all those whom you loved, together with all those whom you hated. I will gather them against you from every side, expose your disgrace before them, and they will see all your shame. I will judge you with the judgments of adulteresses and of those who shed blood. I will give you over to the blood of wrath and jealousy. I will deliver you into their hands, and they will destroy your brothel and demolish your place of prostitution. They will strip you of your garments, take away the vessels of your adornment, and leave you naked and full of disgrace,” and so forth.

“But you will suffer from the worst disease of the womb until your vital organs gradually emerge, day by day,” and so forth.

Thus the wombs—that is, the minds of heretics—are afflicted with the worst disease of faithlessness until their vital organs gradually emerge day by day; that is, until the whole vigor of their understanding, growing senseless through folly, utterly loses the living knowledge of true wisdom. [Col. 0496C]

The spiritual Philistines and Ethiopians will devastate them, plundering all the substance of their labor that is found in the house of their way of life. Moreover, they will carry away their sons and wives—that is, their carnal concern and the fruits of their wicked works—with all their possessions into places of darkness and into the depths of hell’s Tartarus. They will die from the worst disease of their punishment. No people will perform the customary solemn funeral rites for them; rather, they will be erased from the book of the living and will not deserve to be enrolled with the righteous in the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0496D] But the righteous will possess the land of the living and inhabit it forever and ever. The enemies of the Lord, however, as soon as they have been honored and exalted, will fail; like smoke they will fail. Their memory will perish with a sound, and their name will no longer be remembered in the assembly of the saints (Ps. XXXVI). Hence what follows:

He died of a very grievous illness, and the people did not perform funeral rites for him according to the custom of burning, as they had done for his ancestors. He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for eight years in Jerusalem. He walked in an evil way. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

## CHAPTER XXII

### Concerning Ochozias, son of Joram, and his wicked deeds; concerning Joas, king of Judah and Jerusalem, whom the high priest Joiada preserved; concerning the killing carried out by Athalia, who established herself as queen over the two tribes

[Col. 0497A] **(II Chronicles XXII.)** The inhabitants of Jerusalem appointed Ochozias, his youngest son, king in his place; for all the older sons who had been before him had been killed by the bands of Arabs who had attacked the camp. Ochozias, son of Joram, king of Judah, reigned. Ochozias was forty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for one year in Jerusalem.

A very perplexing question arises here, where it is said that Joram reigned for eight years and lived to be forty, while his son Ochozias was forty-two years old when he began to reign. The situation would therefore be that he begot a son two years before his own father had been born. Unless it is understood in another way, even a simple reader recognizes how absurd this is.

[Col. 0497B] The Hebrews therefore solve the question in this way: Joram himself, who is here described as having lived forty years and reigned eight years, lived forty years and reigned twenty-eight. The eight years attributed to him in his reign are those during which he ruled before he killed his brothers, while he was still living innocently. The remaining twenty years during which he ruled afterward are removed from the reckoning because he spent them in illness and tribulation. For this reason the same years are attributed to his son, who is said, according to what is written in the Book of Kings, to have begun to reign when he was no more than twenty-two years old, so that the years remaining from the total would not produce an error in the investigation of the chronology. Ochozias lived twenty-three years, of which he reigned only one. Comparison with the reading of the Book of Kings provides considerable assistance in resolving this question.

[Col. 0497C] Accordingly, Azariah, son of Joram, king of Judah, went down to visit Joram, son of Ahab, who was ill at Jezreel. Here Azariah was called Ochozias a little earlier. For Ochozias is interpreted as “grasping the Lord,” while Azariah means “the Lord’s help.” For this reason the Hebrews think that his name was changed to a better one in this passage, because he had gone down, in accordance with the Lord’s command, to visit a sick man.

[Col. 0497D] It was indeed God’s will concerning Ochozias that he should come to Joram and, when he had come, go out with him against Jehu, son of Nimshi, whom the Lord anointed to destroy the house of Ahab. When Jehu overthrew the house of Ahab, he found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ochozias’s brothers, who were ministering to him, and killed them. Seeking Ochozias himself, he caught him hiding in Samaria, brought him to himself, and killed him.

[Col. 0498A] The history of the Book of Kings relates how, through the prophet Elisha, the Lord appointed Jehu to eradicate the house of Ahab and kill the priests of Baal. Jehu struck Joram, king of Israel, and Ochozias, king of Judah, and caused Jezebel, the most impious queen, to be thrown from the palace at Jezreel. Typologically, Jehu can signify the rule of the nations, which the Lord and our Redeemer appointed to exercise judgment in the sacrilegious city that killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets and persecuted his apostles. He appointed it to destroy that city through just vengeance, overthrow the empty priesthood which it pointlessly maintained after Christ’s coming, and subvert the temple. He also appointed it to cast down from the height of royal power the impious Synagogue, which had always thirsted for the blood of the saints, and to kill its rulers.

There was no hope that anyone from the offspring of Ochozias would reign. When his mother Athalia saw that her son was dead, she arose and killed the entire royal line of the house of Joram. But Jehosheba, the king’s daughter, took Joas, the son of Ochozias, stole him away from among the king’s sons while they were being killed, and hid him with his nurse in a bedroom.

[Col. 0498B] Jehosheba, who had hidden him, was the daughter of King Joram, the wife of the high priest Joiada, and the sister of Ochozias. For this reason Athalia did not kill him. He was therefore hidden with them in the house of God for six years, during which Athalia reigned over the land.

[Col. 0498C] Athalia, who attempted to extinguish the seed of David and destroy the royal line, aptly expresses the wickedness of the Synagogue, which through the evil disposition of its mind lay in ambush for the seed of David—that is, Christ—and always harbored hatred against him. It once seemed to reign when it observed the ceremonies of the law for a time. Athalia is interpreted as “the Lord’s temporal one.”

But through the courage of Jehosheba—which is interpreted as “the Lord’s fullness,” that is, the Church, in which true delights are found—Joas, whose name means “the memory of the Lord,” namely Christ, is preserved. In him the memory of the Lord’s name remains, so that through the cruelty of the raging enemy he may not be killed in the hearts of the elect, but may be nourished more fully in the house of the high priest Joiada, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord’s beloved.” Of him the Father’s voice says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII).

His house is the holy Church. There, dwelling in the faith of the elect, he daily brings about the growth of his body, until at the time of judgment he raises the scepter and power of the kingdom against those who were plotting to suppress him, and assigns the murderess of the saints to eternal punishments.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### The continuation of the preceding subject

**(II Chronicles XXIII.)** In the seventh year, Joiada took courage and summoned the centurions: namely, Azariah son of [Col. 0498D] Jeroham, Ishmael son of Johanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elizaphat son of Zichri, and he entered into a covenant with them. They went throughout Judah, gathered the Levites from all the regions of Judah, and the heads of the families of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem. The whole multitude entered into a covenant in the house of the Lord with the king, and so forth.

The same matter is also related in the Fourth Book of Kings; in its exposition we have inserted what we found explained from the statements of the Fathers. But now we think it appropriate to include how Josephus, the Jewish historian, reports this, so that the diligent reader, after hearing the accounts of different writers, may more easily recognize the truth of the matter.

He reports it in this way:

“Ochozias had, by the same father, a sister named [Col. 0499A] Jehosheba, to whom the high priest Joiada was married. She entered the royal house, where the sons of the kings had been killed, and found a one-year-old infant named Joas hidden with his nurse. Carrying him into a bedroom, she shut him in and secretly nourished him there, while she and her husband Joiada kept him in the temple for seven years, during which Athalia reigned in Jerusalem over the two tribes.

“In the seventh year, Joiada disclosed this plan to five centurions and urged them to stand with him against the things Athalia had done and to hand the kingdom over to the child. After receiving from them an oath that security would be prepared for those who undertook such actions, he revealed to them what had to be done and completed.

“Then the men to whom the priest Joiada had entrusted his plan went throughout the whole province, gathered the priests and Levites from it, and together with all the tribal leaders brought them to Jerusalem to the high priest. He immediately required an oath from them that they would keep secret what they learned from him until his undertaking could be fulfilled. When they had sworn, he was confident and brought out the one whom he had raised from the line of David.

“‘This,’ he said, ‘will be your king from that house which you know the Lord foretold would reign over us forever. I advise you to arrange that one-third of you guard him in the temple, station four groups at all the temple gates, and let another part hold the gate that leads to the royal chambers. Let another unarmed multitude remain in the temple, and permit no armed man to enter, except the priests alone.

“He ordered them also to have part of the priests and Levites stand around the king himself, surrounding him with drawn swords, so that if anyone armed dared to enter the temple, he would be killed immediately. They were to guard the king so firmly that they would fear nothing.

“The men obeyed the high priest’s plan and demonstrated their willingness through their deeds. Meanwhile Joiada opened the armory which David had established in the temple. He distributed among the centurions, priests, and Levites whatever weapons he found there—spears, quivers, and every other kind of weapon he came upon—and stationed the armed men around the temple, so that they seemed to fill the whole entrance with their own force and to make an effort to form something like a wall.

“They brought Joas out into the midst of the boys, placed the royal diadem upon him, and Joiada anointed him and solemnly appointed him king. The people, rejoicing, cried out: ‘Long live the king!’

“But when Athalia suddenly learned of the tumult and the unexpected praises, she was greatly disturbed. She rushed out of the royal residence with her army. When she came to the temple, some priests immediately confronted her, while they prevented the armed men who followed her from entering. They had been appointed by the high priest, as has been said, to guard the entrances of the temple.

“Then Athalia, seeing the boy standing upon the royal platform with the royal diadem placed upon him, tore her clothing, cried out loudly, and ordered the death of the one who had plotted against her and attempted to take away [Col. 0500A] the sovereignty.

“Joiada, however, summoned the centurions and ordered them to lead Athalia out into the Kidron Valley and kill her there, lest they pollute the temple by killing the sorceress there. He gave one further command: if anyone wished to bring her assistance, he too was to be killed by the same sentence.

“Then a certain man to whom her execution had been assigned took Athalia and led her to the king’s Mule Gate, where he killed her.”

This is what Josephus says.

As for the statement in the history that the high priest Joiada and his sons anointed Joas king and cried out, “Long live the king,” the sons of Joiada are used synecdocheically for Zechariah alone. He was a prophet, and Joas later killed him, so that the killing of the man who had anointed him king might add greatly to his condemnation.

[Col. 0500B] When Athalia heard the voice of those running and praising the king, she entered among the people in the temple of the Lord. When she saw the king standing upon the platform at the entrance, with the princes and troops around him, she tore her clothing and said: “Treason! Treason!” and so forth.

By “the platform” he means that column or base which Solomon prepared in the temple. Concerning it, it was written above that Solomon made a bronze base and placed it in the middle of the temple. It was five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. He stood upon it and afterward, with his knees bent before the whole assembly of Israel and his palms raised toward heaven, prayed.

[Col. 0500C] Joiada made a covenant between himself, the whole people, and the king, so that the people might belong to the Lord. What else does it mean that Joiada is said to have made a covenant between himself, the whole people, and the king, except that he placed himself in the position of the law and of God, whose minister he was? This is shown in the Book of Kings, where it is written:

“Joiada therefore made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people, so that they would be the Lord’s people.”

Hence his name is interpreted as “knowing the Lord” or “loving the Lord,” because he taught the sons of Israel to know the Lord.

Joiada therefore made a covenant between the Lord, the people, and the king, so that both—the king and the people—would obey God and his law. He made a covenant between the king and the people—that is, so that the people would act faithfully toward the king and the king would rule the people with justice, under the authority of the priests and Levites, whose duty it was to explain to them the Lord’s commandments and his lawful ordinances. [Col. 0500D]

## CHAPTER XXIV

### Concerning Joas’s command that the priests restore the damaged parts of the house of the Lord, and his renewal of the worship of the temple; concerning the end of the high priest Joiada and the killing of his son Zechariah, whom King Joas ordered to be killed between the temple and the altar; concerning the death of Joas
(II Chronicles 24.) After this Joash decided to restore the house of the Lord. He gathered the priests and Levites and said to them: “Go out to the cities of Judah and collect from all Israel money for the repairs of the temple of your God each year, and do this promptly.” But the Levites acted negligently. The king summoned Joiada the chief priest and said to him: “Why have you not taken care to compel the Levites to bring from Judah and Jerusalem the money established by Moses, the servant of the Lord, so that the whole multitude of Israel might bring it into the tent of testimony?”

The money established by Moses to be brought into the tent is that which the Lord commanded Moses in Exodus, saying: “When you take the census of the Israelites according to their number, each shall give the Lord a payment for his life, and no plague shall be among them when they are counted. Everyone who is enrolled shall give half a shekel according to the measure of the sanctuary. A shekel contains twenty obols. Half a shekel shall be offered to the Lord. Everyone who is counted, from twenty years of age and upward, shall give the payment. The rich shall not add to the half-shekel, and the poor shall not subtract from it. The money received from the Israelites for the service of the tent of testimony shall be a memorial for them before the Lord, and he shall be propitious toward their lives” (Exod. III).

In the spiritual sense, “the census of the Israelites” designates the census of all the elect, whose names are written in heaven. Each gives a payment for his life to the Lord when he offers him, through good works, the service of diligent obedience. Otherwise there will be a plague among them when they are counted, since perpetual vengeance awaits those who, though nominally joined to the number of the faithful, refuse to offer the Lord the perfect works of faith. Of such people it is said: “They shall give no reconciliation to God, nor the price of the redemption of their soul” (Ps. XLVIII).

For “the redemption of a man’s soul is his riches,” as Solomon says (Prov. XIII)—whether temporal riches, when he distributes them and gives them to the poor, so that his righteousness may endure forever and ever, or spiritual riches, that is, righteousness itself, which he has practiced either by showing mercy to the poor or by doing other good works.

“Everyone who passes to the name” [the reading *navem* is uncertain] shall give half a shekel, that is, twenty obols. Nothing else can more suitably be understood by this than observance of the Decalogue. Whoever knows how to understand the law correctly recognizes that it contains the whole fullness of faith and works, together with the promise of future recompense. In the first three commandments the love of God is contained; in the following seven, the love of one’s neighbor. As the Apostle testifies, “the fullness of the law is love.”

Nor should another mystery contained in the same number, ten, be passed over. The name *Jesus* begins among the Hebrews with *iod* and among the Greeks with *iota*; each of these letters in its own language is the sign of the number ten. They offer ten obols as the price of their soul who, believing in Jesus Christ, display upon their forehead and in their profession the sign of his name, which begins with the number ten. Perhaps for the sake of this mystery the Lord testifies in the Gospel that not one *iota* can pass away from the law, because the power of the Decalogue contained there, and the faith in his name mystically signified there, can never be corrupted by any disturbance caused by unbelievers.

The money received from the Israelites is brought in as a memorial for them before the Lord when everything good that we do is preserved in eternal remembrance with our Creator and Judge, so that from the fruits of good works that we have offered him he may deign to be gracious toward us. The same money is preserved for service when the conduct and actions of subsequent believers in Christ are strengthened by good works, and their juniors strive to become such as they recognize those to have been whom they know to reign with the Lord.

The narrative continues:

“For the most wicked Athaliah and her sons had destroyed the house of God, and from all the things that had been consecrated for the temple of the Lord they had adorned the shrine of the Baals.”

He does not say that Athaliah’s sons destroyed the house of God with her because she had sons living at that time—for earlier it is recorded that, when Ahaziah had died, because he had no son she attempted to kill the entire royal offspring—but he calls the priests of the idols her sons. They stripped the temple of its ornaments and adorned their idols with them. In sacred speech, people are very often called sons not by birth but by imitation.

Therefore the king commanded, and they made a chest and placed it outside beside the gate of the Lord. It was proclaimed throughout Judah and Jerusalem that each person should bring to the Lord the payment that Moses, the servant of the Lord, had imposed upon all Israel in the wilderness. All the princes and all the people rejoiced, entered, and put their contributions into the chest of the Lord, so that it was filled, and so forth.

What else is meant by the fact that King Joash rebuked the priests for being sluggish and insufficiently zealous in restoring the temple of the Lord, and that the money contributed by the people at the king’s command was handed over through the ministers to masons and craftsmen so that they might repair the cracks in the walls and rebuild the damaged roofs, except that our Redeemer—whom Joash prefigured by this action and also by his name, for it is interpreted “the strength of the Lord”—commands his teachers to receive all the money offered by those who pass into the temple of the Lord as the price of their souls and as the vow of their hearts? Whatever spiritual knowledge or examples of good works these passers-by contribute to the treasury of the Lord is, through the offices of the priests—that is, the preachers—applied to the restoration of the spiritual temple, so that wherever they find something cracked by error or damaged by vices, they may restore it, lest through the negligence of teachers the multitude of hearers perish.

The king and Joiada gave the money to those in charge of the work on the house of the Lord. They hired from it stonecutters and craftsmen for the various works, to restore the house of the Lord; also workers in iron and bronze, so that what had begun to collapse might be supported, and so forth.

When our king and priest together, who offered himself to the Father for us, entrusted the money of the divine word to worthy stewards, so that they might distribute the measure of evangelical grain to their fellow servants who work in the house of the Lord and construct works of virtue in the divine building, what, then, did the apostles do, whom divine election established as leaders in the Church, when through the disciples subject to them they scattered the seeds of the divine word throughout the whole world? They did this so that they might perfect among their hearers workers capable of doing God’s will.

Some worked with wood, when they rebuilt themselves and those who obeyed them after the things broken by heresy and schisms. Others cut stones, when they sternly rebuked those who were hard-hearted and unbelieving. Others worked with iron and bronze, when they properly sought from each person the firm strength of right belief and the clear confession of catholic truth. Thus the restoration of the house of the Lord was completed in all the things that required expenditure for fortifying the house of the Lord, according to the Apostle’s saying: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV). And shortly afterward: “He himself,” he says, “gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.”

When they had completed all the work, they brought before the king and Joiada the remaining money from which vessels for the service of the temple and for the burnt offerings had been made, as well as bowls and other vessels of gold and silver, and so forth.

To some who consider the harmony of Scripture insufficiently, this statement seems contrary to the one written in the Book of Kings, where it says: “Nevertheless, basins for the temple of the Lord, forks, censers, trumpets, and every vessel of gold and silver were not made from the money that was brought into the temple of the Lord” (IV Kings XII).

For it is not stated here that the sacred vessels for the service of the temple and for the burnt offerings were made from the same money that the people offered in the temple of the Lord for the restoration of the house of God, but from the remaining money, that is, money contributed from other donations. It could have happened that money offered at different times supplied the material for different works.

Mystically, this signifies that one principle must govern the formation of spiritual vessels for the service of the Lord and another the preparation of wood and stones for the building of the house. One doctrine is required to instruct beginners in the faith, and another to teach those already mature toward the fullness of knowledge.

The vessels of the house of the Lord can aptly be understood as those who are already fit to receive divine gifts and become capable of God’s service. In Chronicles, only bowls are specifically named, together with the other vessels that are not individually described. These bowls can express breadth of intellect or expansiveness of heart through love. Such vessels are especially well suited to the service of God.

Nor is it without mystery that Kings records the making of basins, forks, censers, and trumpets. The basins can signify those who contain within themselves the water of divine wisdom. The forks can signify particular teachers, whose office is to distribute the body and blood of the Lord to believers and to deny them to unbelievers, as well as to distribute to each person the appropriate nourishment of the word. For there are certain things in the words of God that Christ has deigned to reveal to our humility and grant for the refreshment of our feasts. There are also things of such great depth that they are open only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and entirely exceed the measure of our capacity.

The censers figuratively represent those who offer pure prayer to God from a clean conscience and sincere faith, and who can say with the Prophet: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL).

The trumpets signify nothing other than the holy preachers who throughout the whole world send forth the voice of evangelical preaching. Of their persons it is said through the prophet: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. LVIII). And the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII).

Joiada grew old, full of days, and died when he was one hundred and thirty years old. They buried him in the city of David with the kings, because he had done good for Israel and for his house.

What does it mean that Joiada is said to have done good for Israel and for his house, except that throughout all the days of his priesthood he rightly governed the Israelite people, which is often called the house of Jacob or the house of Israel in Scripture, and diligently instructed them in the worship of God? Once God had been appeased toward them, blessings of prosperity and peace could come to them.

Josephus says that he was buried in Jerusalem in the royal tombs because he had restored the rule of David’s dynasty. The number of years of Joiada’s life itself can aptly signify the perfection of his life, for which he deserved to attain eternal blessedness. It also figuratively indicates to us that, if we strive to complete the time of the present life in faith in the Holy Trinity and in the profession of good works, then, with his grace assisting us, we shall reach eternal blessedness, which is at the right hand of God, and shall enjoy eternal rest with his saints, who are the true kings, forever.

After Joiada died, the princes of Judah entered and paid homage to the king. He, won over by their attentions, consented to them. They abandoned the temple of the Lord, the God of their fathers, and served the sacred groves and carved images. Because of this sin, wrath came against Judah and Jerusalem.

The Hebrews report that the princes of Judah paid homage to King Joash as though he were God, and that he gladly accepted honors beyond what was human from his subjects. Thus he greatly offended the Lord, whose wrath he soon experienced. No madness can be greater than for a corruptible creature to usurp for himself the honor of eternal deity and, through the arrogance of pride, refuse to recognize his own measure.

For this reason Herod is also recorded in the Acts of the Apostles as having been struck by an angel, because he did not give honor to the Lord. Therefore we must flee every form of pride and arrogance completely, because God resists the proud, and every arrogance is an abomination before God. To the humble, however, the divinity of God grants grace, and the Spirit of God rests upon the humble and quiet. “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

The Spirit of the Lord therefore clothed Zachariah, the priest and son of Joiada. He stood before the people and said to them: “Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord, which will not benefit you? You have abandoned the Lord, so that he may abandon you.”

They gathered against him, stoned him at the king’s command in the court of the house of the Lord, and King Joash did not remember the mercy that Joiada, his father, had shown him, but killed his son. As he was dying, Zachariah said: “May the Lord see and avenge.”

Here a question arises: Why, when the Lord recalls in the Gospel that Zachariah was killed between the temple and the altar, does he say that he was the son of Barachiah, when the present history clearly identifies him as the son of Joiada? For this reason some offer various opinions concerning the passage.

Some say that he was Zachariah the son of Barachiah, the eleventh of the Twelve Prophets, and that his father’s name agrees with this identification. But Scripture does not say where he was killed, especially since in his time scarcely even the ruins of the temple remained.

Others wish Zachariah, the father of John, to be understood, relying on certain apocryphal books that claim the prophet was killed because he had proclaimed the Savior’s coming. Since this has no authority from Scripture, it is rejected as readily as it is asserted.

Others hold that this is the Zachariah who was killed by Joash, king of Judah, between the temple and the altar, as the history in Kings relates. But it must be observed that this Zachariah was not the son of Barachiah but the son of Joiada the priest. Hence the account says: “Joash did not remember the good things that his father Joiada had done for him.”

Since we retain the identity of Zachariah and the place of his death agrees, let us ask why he is called the son of Barachiah rather than of Joiada. *Barachiah* in our language means “blessed of the Lord,” while the Hebrew name *Joiada* signifies the righteousness of the priest. In the Gospel used by the Nazarenes, we likewise find “son of Joiada” written in place of “son of Barachiah.”

More simple-minded brothers, pointing to the ruins of the temple and altar, or to the exits of the gates leading toward Siloam, think that the red rocks were stained with Zachariah’s blood. We do not condemn an error that arose from hatred of the Jews and devotion to the faith.

When the year had passed, the army of Syria came against him. It entered Judah and Jerusalem, killed all the princes of the people, and sent all the spoil to the king in Damascus. Although the number of Syrians who had come was very small, the Lord delivered an immense multitude into their hands because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers. They also carried out shameful judgments against Joash and, when they departed, left him in great sickness.

Josephus likewise relates that Hazael, king of the Assyrians, sent an army into the province of the Jews, which devastated it and depopulated Gath. When he was about to come to Jerusalem, Joash, fearing a siege, emptied all the treasures of God, the royal treasures, and the treasures of the temple service, and sent them to the king of Syria. He did this to redeem the city, lest it suffer oppression or face the danger of losing everything. When the Syrian king had been satisfied with a great amount of money, he did not encamp against Jerusalem.

The same king of Syria also devastated Samaria, because at that time Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, held the kingdom. By acting wickedly, as the earlier kings of Israel had done, he seemed to have despised God. Hazael humbled him. He took away many large cities from him and slaughtered his soldiers. Thus the people of Israel suffered these things according to the prophecy of Elisha, when Hazael killed his master, because Elisha had foretold that Hazael would reign over the Syrians and the inhabitants of Damascus.

His servants rose against him in vengeance for the blood of Joiada the priest’s son. They killed him in his bed, and he died. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the tombs of the kings. Those who plotted against him were Zabad, son of Shimeath the Ammonite woman, and Jehozabad, son of Shimrith the Moabite woman.

Finally, the Hebrews assert that the Ammonites and Moabites plotted against King Joash for this reason: detesting Zachariah’s unjust killing, they wished by avenging the priest of God to make the wickedness of the Israelites more glaring. They did this although they were sons of foreigners.

## CHAPTER XXV

On the reign of Amaziah, son of Joash, in Jerusalem.

Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan, from Jerusalem. He did what was good in the sight of the Lord, though not with a perfect heart.

It may be asked how Scripture can say that Amaziah did good in the sight of God but not with a perfect heart, since no work can in any way be good in the sight of God if it is not done with a good intention—especially since, as Scripture testifies, the Divinity looks upon the heart and fittingly rewards the will according to its effect.

He is said to have done good in the sight of God because he displayed before human beings a certain appearance of good works, which it is clear pleases God. They considered these works good because they saw only their outward appearance and praised them according to that appearance. But before God they were not acceptable, because they had been done with a corrupt intention. Therefore Amaziah, continually falling into worse things, finally collapsed into idolatry and perished through it, because he did not possess a sound root in his heart that could earn God’s grace through the worship of piety.

Amaziah therefore gathered Judah and organized them by families, with tribunes and centurions, throughout Judah and Benjamin. He counted those twenty years old and upward and found thirty thousand young men who could go out to battle and carry spear and shield. He also hired from Israel one hundred thousand strong men for one hundred talents of silver.

But a man of God came to him and said: “O king, do not let the army of Israel go with you, for the Lord is not with Israel, nor with all the sons of Ephraim. If you think that wars depend upon the strength of the army, God will make you be defeated by your enemies. For it belongs to God both to help and to turn men to flight,” and so forth.

It is asked why it was said that the Lord was not with Israel and with all the sons of Ephraim. Why is Israel named first, a term that includes all ten tribes, and afterward the sons of Ephraim specifically? This was to make clear that all—both subjects and rulers who reigned in Samaria after Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim—were guilty and polluted by idolatry. The Lord rejected their fellowship in war with the tribe of Judah because they carried idols with them, whose worship was especially displeasing to God.

Amaziah, however, confidently led out his people and went to the Valley of Salt. He struck ten thousand of the sons of Seir, while another ten thousand men were captured by the sons of Judah. They brought them to the edge of a certain cliff and threw them headlong from its summit. They all burst apart.

In Kings the following is written about the same Amaziah: “He struck Edom in the Valley of Salt—ten thousand—and captured Sela in battle, and called its name Joktheel to the present day” (IV Kings XIV).

The Valley of Salt was a place where salt was produced—either from salt grass, which was cut, dried, and burned in many places, or from certain salt wells, whose waters were heated and boiled until they reached the hardness of salt, or by whatever other process is customarily used to make salt. It is also recorded that Joab struck twelve thousand Idumeans in this place.

Nor should it be passed over that, in place of “the Valley of Salt,” the old edition gives *Gemela*, as though it were the name of a region.

Sela is a famous city of Arabia in the same land of Edom; in the Book of Numbers it is called Rekem, and it is still so called by the Assyrians. *Joktheel*, the name Amaziah gave it after his victory, is interpreted “assembly of God” or “help of God,” since God acted so that a memorial might remain that he captured it either through an assembly of the people of God or with God’s help.

Josephus, however, does not call Sela any particular city at this place where Amaziah defeated the Idumeans. He says only that, after killing ten thousand, Amaziah captured an equal number alive, led them to a great rock situated in Arabia, and threw them down from it.

After the slaughter of the Idumeans and the bringing back of the gods of the sons of Seir, Amaziah set them up as gods for himself, worshiped them, and burned incense to them. Therefore the Lord became angry with Amaziah and sent him a prophet, who said to him: “Why have you worshiped gods that did not deliver their own people from your hand?”

While the prophet was saying this, Amaziah answered him: “Are you the king’s counselor? Be quiet, lest I kill you.”

The Jews relate that King Amaziah set up the gods of the sons of Edom as gods for himself after their death because, when the ten thousand who had been thrown down from Sela in Arabia were falling, they gave such responses to their worshipers: that they had been killed because they had been negligent in their worship. When Amaziah saw them giving responses of this kind and saw their altars being taken away, he was deceived by this error and worshiped them.

They say that this prophet, who was sent to rebuke the king for the idolatry he foolishly practiced, was Eleazar, son of Dodai—that is, of his uncle.

The prophet ceased speaking and said: “I know that the Lord has determined to kill you, because you have done this evil and, in addition, have not listened to my counsel.”

What does it mean that the prophet says that the Lord had determined to kill Amaziah, when he himself says through another prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII)? And the Apostle says of the Lord himself: “Who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II).

How can he be said here to desire to kill, when he desires that no one perish, except that he desires the sinner to turn from his sins and live, but condemns by a just judgment the one who persists in sins? Thus Amaziah perished because, warned by the prophet to help himself through the counsel of repentance, he did not obey; instead, he persisted in the crime he had begun until the end of his life.

Amaziah, king of Judah, therefore formed a wicked plan and sent to Joash, son of Jehoahaz, son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying: “Come, let us look at one another.”

But he sent messengers back, saying: “The thornbush that is in Lebanon sent to the cedar in Lebanon, saying: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ And behold, the beasts that were in the forest of Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush. You said: ‘I have defeated Edom,’ and therefore your heart is lifted up in pride. Remain at home. Why provoke disaster against yourself, so that you and Judah with you may fall?”

What did the king of Israel indicate to King Amaziah by this comparison except that, although Amaziah had been born of noble parents—that is, from the royal stock of David—he had become degenerate and base because of the foulness of idolatry and had failed to consider his proper measure? In his pride he sought things greater than was fitting and lost the modest position that he could have held comfortably if he had wished.

Hence Aesop’s fable tells of the jackdaw that tried to appropriate peacock feathers as an ornament by theft and, through the tearing of the other birds, was stripped of its own beauty. It is not good to neglect one’s own proper goods and to pursue those belonging to another through fraud and greed.

King Joash of Israel therefore went up, and they confronted one another. King Amaziah of Judah was at Beth-shemesh of Judah. Judah fell before Israel, and each man fled to his tent.

Joash, king of Israel, captured Amaziah, king of Judah, son of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh and brought him to Jerusalem. He demolished its wall from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate, four hundred cubits long. He also took all the gold and silver and all the vessels he found in the house of the Lord and with Obed-edom, as well as in the treasuries of the royal palace, and so forth.

Beth-shemesh is a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin. It is still shown today from Eleutheropolis through Gennicopolis, at the tenth milestone toward the east, where Amaziah and Joash also fought one another. There is another Beth-shemesh in the tribe of Naphtali, belonging to the kingdom of the ten tribes in Samaria.

When Kings says that Beth-shemesh was a town of Judah, this signifies that it belonged to the kingdom of Judah—that is, to the two tribes over which the house of David ruled. According to the geographical location, however, it belonged to the allotment of Benjamin.

The fact that Scripture says Joash took the treasures he found in the house of God and with Obed-edom shows that he took not only the vessels he found in the house of God but also those kept with the doorkeepers and guardians of the temple. In the earlier book it is related that David selected sixty-two men from the sons of Obed-edom to minister in the house of God and to guard the temple.

The rest of the deeds of Amaziah, earlier and later, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. After he turned away from the Lord, they conspired against him in Jerusalem. When he had fled to Lachish, they sent men there and killed him. They carried him back on horses and buried him with his fathers in the city of David, and so forth.

It is rightly said that from the time Amaziah turned away from the Lord, a conspiracy arose against him in Jerusalem. From the time he refused to listen to the prophet’s counsel and was unwilling to turn to the Lord, the conspiracy was prepared, though it was delayed until it reached its completion.

“They carried him back on horses and buried him.” Scripture does not say without reason that he was carried on horses, because he had worshiped the gods of Edom, which were carried on horses. For this reason he was not carried on human shoulders, since he had neglected to serve the God of Israel, whose sacred objects were commanded to be carried on the shoulders of the Kohathites (Num. IV).

## CHAPTER XXVI

On King Uzziah and his presumption, by which he wished to offer sacrifice in the temple, and how leprosy was sent upon him as punishment.

(II Chronicles 26.) Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah, from Jerusalem. He did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, according to everything that Amaziah his father had done. He sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, who understood and saw God.

This Uzziah had two names, because the one called Uzziah in Chronicles is called Azariah in Kings (IV Kings XV). *Uzziah* is interpreted “strength of the Lord,” and *Azariah* “help of the Lord.” He is rightly called the strength or help of the Lord because, as long as he acted rightly, aided by divine assistance, he successfully waged many wars and triumphed everywhere over his enemies. But after he attempted unlawful things through pride, he was struck with leprosy and darkened the dignity both of his name and of his honor. Once he became a leper and was excluded from the people, he lived apart in a separate house until the day of his death.

As for the statement that Uzziah sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, who understood and saw the Lord, the Hebrews relate that this Zechariah was the son of Zechariah, son of Joiada. He was born after his father’s death and was therefore posthumous; for this reason he inherited his father’s name. He was called “understanding” because of the priesthood and “seeing” because of prophecy.

When he sought the Lord, he directed him in everything. Thus he went out and fought against the Philistines. He demolished the wall of Gath, the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod. He built towns in Ashdod and in Philistia, and God helped him against the Philistines and against the Arabs who lived in Gurbaal.

They say that Gurbaal is the place called Gerar in Genesis, where Abimelech was king and where Abraham sojourned with his wife Sarah, as Genesis records.

Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem over the Corner Gate and over the Valley Gate, as well as others on the same side of the wall, and he strengthened them, and so forth.

The Gate of Ephraim, previously said to have been destroyed by Joash king of Israel, is now called the Valley Gate. The writer of the history did not wish to use in the account of its construction the name he had used in describing its destruction. Nor was this without reason, because Ephraim was sacrificing to idols at that time and had shared with its king Joash in the destruction of Jerusalem’s gate. In the rebuilding, Ephraim did not deserve to be named by its proper name; instead, the gate was called the Valley Gate because of the humiliation and baseness of its originator.

Ezra also mentions this gate in the restoration of the city after the return from Babylonian captivity, where he says: “Hanun and the inhabitants of Zanoah built the Valley Gate” (II Esd. III).

We know that the Valley of Jehoshaphat, also called Gehenna—that is, the Valley of Hinnom—is on the eastern side of the city of Jerusalem. Through it the Kidron stream, mentioned in the Gospel, flows from the north toward the south whenever it receives excessive waters from the rains.

But on the western side of the city we also read of the Valley of Gihon. The Book of Chronicles says of King Manasseh of Judah: “After this he built a wall outside the city of David, westward, in the valley” (II Chron. XXXIII).

Gihon is the name of the spring where Solomon was anointed king outside the city. Whether, therefore, Ezra signifies this valley, or that one, or any other valley of the same place, the mystery is clear: the Valley Gate is built in Jerusalem when either those recently imbued with knowledge of divine faith and truth, or those restored in the chastity of faith who had strayed from teachers of the truth, are instructed to observe among other virtues the virtue of humility. Through it they may deserve to be exalted by the greater grace of God, as holy Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV).

Uzziah also prepared for them—that is, for the entire army—shields, spears, breastplates, bows, and slings for throwing stones. He made in Jerusalem machines of various kinds, which he placed on the towers and at the corners of the walls, so that they could shoot arrows and hurl great stones. His name spread far and wide because the Lord helped him and strengthened him.

But when he had grown strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. He neglected the Lord his God, entered the temple of the Lord, and wished to burn incense upon the altar of incense, and so forth.

At first Uzziah was therefore a righteous man and did what was right in the sight of the Lord: he built the temple, constructed a water conduit, offered vessels, and for this merit overcame his adversaries, which is the greatest indication of piety. He had many prophets under his rule.

As long as the priest Zechariah, surnamed “the Understanding,” lived, Uzziah pleased God and entered his sanctuary with every reverence. But after Zechariah died, wishing to offer the gifts himself, he invaded the priestly order—not so much piously as audaciously. When the Levites and the other priests protested, “Are you not Uzziah the king, and not a priest?” he refused to listen. Immediately leprosy covered his forehead, according to the prophet’s word: “Fill their faces, O Lord, with disgrace” (Ps. LXXXII).

The forehead was the part of the body that the priest protected with a golden plate. In Ezekiel the Lord commands it to be marked with the impression of the letter *tau*. David rejoiced concerning it, saying: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV). In that same place the insolent Philistine was killed when struck by the stone from the sling.

Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years. During this period Aemilius ruled among the Latins and Agamnestor among the Athenians. After his death the prophet Isaiah saw the prophetic vision, as he himself testifies—that is, in the year in which Romulus, the founder of the Roman empire, was born, as can be made clear to those who wish to read the book of times.

The rest of the deeds of Uzziah, both the earlier and the later, was written by Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet. Isaiah records in his book of prophecy what he had foretold while Uzziah was alive, as well as what he saw after Uzziah’s death, including this passage: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and exalted” (Isa. 6). The understanding of this spiritual vision intimates a venerable mystery. While the leprous king was alive and, so far as lay in him, was destroying the priesthood, Isaiah could not see the vision. As long as that man held the kingdom in Judah, the prophet did not raise his eyes to heaven; the heavenly things were not opened to him; the Lord of Hosts did not appear; nor was the holy name faithfully heard in the ministry. But when he died, everything that the following passage revealed displayed itself in open light.

Something similar is written in Exodus: while Pharaoh lived, the people of Israel, occupied with work in clay, bricks, and straw, did not sigh toward the Lord. While he reigned, no one sought the God of their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But when he died, the sons sighed, as Scripture says, and their cry rose up to the Lord, although, according to the historical account, they ought rather to have rejoiced then and sighed earlier, while he was alive. When Ezekiel too was prophesying, Pheltias son of Benaiah died, and after the death of the most wicked leader he says: “I fell upon my face, and cried out with a loud voice, and said: Alas, alas, Lord Adonai, you are bringing the remnant of Israel to an end” (Ezek. 11).

If, therefore, you understand Uzziah, Pharaoh, Pheltias, and the others of this kind as hostile powers, you will see how, while they are alive, none of our people sees, sighs, or falls into repentance. “Let sin not reign,” says the Apostle, “in your mortal body” (Rom. 6). While sin reigns, we build the cities of Egypt, lie in ashes and filth, and pursue works of clay, using straw for a fortress and imitating solid stone.

Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the field of the royal tombs because he was leprous; and his son Jotham reigned in his place.

What is signified for us by the burial of Uzziah—who, we are told, was buried not in the city of David, nor in the royal tombs, but in the field of the royal tombs because he was leprous—if not that all heretics and schismatics are unworthy of ecclesiastical fellowship and communion, and that their memory does not deserve to be kept among Catholics? For through the stains of errors and vices they separated themselves from their number and fellowship.

It does not seem unworthy to insert here, for the sake of knowledge of the facts, how Josephus relates the story of this same king. It is reported as follows:

“He therefore fell through an event in his prosperous fortune and descended to his ancestral sins, which also overtook him after he had abandoned the splendor of his good qualities and the greatness of his possessions. When a solemn day and general festival were approaching, he put on the priestly robe and entered the temple to offer incense to God upon the golden altar. But Azariah the high priest, together with eighty other priests, prevented him from doing this, since such duties belonged only to those who were descended from Aaron. As they shouted that he should leave and not act against the laws of God, he became angry and threatened them with death unless they were silent.

“Meanwhile a great earthquake occurred. As the people stood amazed, the brilliance of the sun shone with extraordinary intensity, fell upon the king’s face, and immediately leprosy appeared upon him. Before the city, at a place called Eroge, half of the mountain was split toward the west and, rolling forward for four stadia, came to rest against the eastern mountain, so that it both blocked the roads and crushed the royal cities.

“When the king’s priests saw that leprosy had seized his face, they disclosed his misfortune to him and urged him to leave the city as one polluted. Confounded by this event, and since he now had no confidence at all, he did what they commanded. Although he had been raised above the minds of ordinary men and, because of this, had acted impiously toward God, he nevertheless endured this pitiable and disgraceful affliction. After spending some time outside the city, living on, though his son had assumed the kingdom, he eventually died, sorrowful because of what he had done.

“He lived sixty-nine years, of which he reigned fifty-two; but he was buried alone in the gardens.”

This earthquake, therefore, which occurred in the time of Uzziah, although the histories of Kings and Chronicles do not mention it, is nevertheless remembered by the prophet Amos. At the beginning of his book we read: “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake” (Amos 1).

Similarly, the prophet Zechariah speaks of this same event among other matters, saying:

“The Lord will go out and fight against those nations, as he fought on the day of battle. His feet will stand on that day upon the Mount of Olives, which is opposite Jerusalem on the east. The Mount of Olives will be split in two from its middle toward the east and toward the west, with a very great cleft; half of the mountain will separate toward the north and half toward the south. You will flee to the valley of my mountains, because the valley of the mountains will reach as far as the nearest place. You will flee just as you fled from the face of the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah” (Zech. 14).

The Hebrews, however, maintain that this happened in the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah, leaving twenty-seven of his years still remaining. For he reigned fifty-two years in all.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On King Jotham and His Good Deeds

Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. Why does Scripture enumerate Jotham’s years at the beginning of his reign in the same manner as at its end, unless it signifies that he persevered in the justice he had begun until the end of his life? Whoever begins to live well and brings a religious life to a good conclusion is rightly praised, since the periods of his life deserve commendation. It is also rightly said that he reigned in Jerusalem, because, governing well the kingdom entrusted to him, both in himself and in his subjects, he earned the attainment of the vision of eternal peace.

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord, and constructed much upon the wall of Ophel. He also built cities in the mountains of Judah, and fortresses and towers in the forests.

The high gate of the house of the Lord, the Hebrews say, is the one called “Beautiful” in the Acts of the Apostles. It is still called by the Hebrews the Gate of Jotham, because he built it. Ophel, however, was a tower not far from the temple, of extraordinary height. Hence it received the name Ophel, that is, “of darkness” or “cloudy,” because it raised its head as far as the clouds.

Accordingly, where it is written in Micah, “And you, cloudy tower of the daughter of Zion” (Mic. 4), the Hebrew has, instead of “cloudy tower,” “tower of Ophel.”

The present book of Chronicles also mentions this tower and indicates in what part of the city it stood when, speaking of King Manasseh—as we have cited above—it reports that he built a wall outside the city of David, west of Gihon in the valley, from the entrance of the Fish Gate all around as far as Ophel.

In the mystical sense, whom does this King Jotham, whose life and deeds are praised, signify better than our Redeemer? Of him the psalmist says: “For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, and terrible above all gods” (Ps. 95). His perfection is expressed by the name Jotham itself. For it is interpreted as “completed” or “perfect.” Concerning the Lord the Savior, Paul writes to the Hebrews: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from what he suffered; and, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 5).

He built the high gate of the house of the Lord because, through the wonderful power of his incarnation, he accomplished the mystery by which he joined to himself the Church, which is the true house of God. That he is rightly called a gate, the Truth himself shows in the Gospel when he says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). This gate is rightly called high, because of it the psalmist says: “The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens” (Ps. 113).

Holy teachers are also called gates, because through their preaching we learn the entrance to life. Heretics, on the other hand, are called the gates of hell, since, according to the Lord’s testimony, they cannot prevail against the Church built upon the rock.

The tower of Ophel can aptly signify the loftiness of the holy Scriptures. Although it lays its foundations in history, it nevertheless raises the summit of spiritual meaning to a height and places it amid the clouds, concealing the greatness of divine knowledge from human eyes. Hence it is written: “Darkness is beneath his feet, and he made darkness his hiding place.” Darkness is beneath his feet because he is not seen by those below with the clarity with which he rules above. “He mounted upon the cherubim and flew.” Cherubim means “fullness of knowledge.” Therefore he is said to have mounted above the fullness of knowledge and to have flown, because no knowledge comprehends the height of his majesty. He flew because he carried himself far above our understanding. He flew upon wings because he transcended the knowledge of angels. “He made darkness his hiding place,” because, while we are obscured by the darkness of our weakness, God is hidden from us through our ignorance, so that for now he may not be seen by us in eternal and innermost brightness.

Hence in the Song of Songs the bride says to him: “Rise, my beloved” (Song 8). Again, the Lord mounted upon the cherubim and flew because he withdrew the mystery of his incarnation from human understanding, above the fullness of knowledge that could exist in human beings. However brightly the knowledge of the incarnation may shine in spiritual beings, it cannot grasp how it happened that he who always exists was conceived, that the author of humankind before the ages was born human at the end of the ages, that the Word became flesh, and that God became an infant.

Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David; and his son Ahaz reigned in his place.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On King Ahaz and His Abominable Deeds

Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the sight of the Lord, like David his father, but walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. Moreover, he cast images for the Baals.

He was the one who burned incense in the valley of Ben-Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire, according to the rites of the nations whom the Lord destroyed at the coming of the children of Israel. It is written in the book of Kings concerning King Josiah that he defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through the fire to Molech. Scripture frequently mentions these places, especially in the book of Kings and in the prophet Jeremiah.

The valley of Ben-Hinnom, or of the son of Hinnom, lies beside the wall at Jerusalem toward the east. It contains a very beautiful grove watered by the springs of Siloam. Tapheth or Topheth—for both forms are written—was a place in the same valley near the Pool of the Washer, which Scripture mentions, and near the field of Akeldama, still shown today on the southern side of Mount Zion.

At Topheth, because the place was extremely pleasant and still provides the delights of gardens, they used to set up an altar, sacrifice to demons, and consecrate their children through the abominable fire, or offer them as a burnt offering. Hence the historical account now says of Ahaz: “He was the one who burned incense in the valley of Ben-Hinnom and passed his sons through the fire.”

Ben-Hinnom indeed means “son of Hinnom,” while the valley of Hinnom is called in Hebrew Gehinnom. From its name the punishment of hell is called gehenna in the New Testament, because, just as those who served idols perished in the valley of Hinnom, as the prophets testify, so sinners are punished with eternal damnation because of the things they have committed.

Accordingly, when Jeremiah reported that the Lord had commanded him and said, “Go out to the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate,” he shortly afterward added: “This place shall no longer be called Topheth or the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. I will destroy the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword” (Jer. 13).

Isaiah too most clearly calls Topheth hell. When he described the perpetual destruction of the devil under the name Assyria, saying, “At the voice of the Lord Assyria will be terrified, struck with the rod; and the passage of the rod will be founded, which the Lord will cause to rest upon him,” he immediately added how and where he would perish: “For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king, deep and broad” (Isa. 30). He aptly says “broad,” because Topheth means “breadth.” “Its fuel is fire and abundant wood; the breath of the Lord, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.”
