Josephus shows how Ahaz passed his offspring through the fire, saying:

“Moreover, Jotham changed his life after having lived forty-one years, of which he reigned sixteen, and was buried in the royal monuments; and the kingdom came to his son Ahaz. Since he was impious toward the Lord and transgressed his ancestral laws, imitating the kings of Israel, he set up altars of idols in Jerusalem and sacrificed upon them. On these he also offered his own son as a burnt offering, in the manner of the Canaanites, and perpetrated many other crimes besides.”

Thus Ahaz, who was born of a righteous father but fell into faithlessness and the crime of idolatry, signifies heretics. They are instructed in the sacrament of faith by Catholic fathers, but, turning toward apostasy, they do not fear to offer divine worship to the images of their errors. They sacrifice the fruit of their womb—that is, the inclination of their wicked deliberation—to the demon in the fire of zeal, like all adulterers whose mind, according to the judgment of Hosea, is “like an oven heated by the baker” (Hos. 7). “Their heart is divided, and he will crush their images and despoil their altars” (Hos. 10).

Just as Ahaz, after stripping the house of the Lord and the houses of kings and princes, gave gifts to the king of Assyria, yet gained nothing from him, so these people melt the gold of their keen intellect and the silver of their learning into the worship of idols, so that they may perish. They invoke Egypt and go to the Assyrians when they seek protection from the powers of this world; but they are captured and slain in their passage, because “cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord.”

Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of Jerusalem; for they did not receive him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. It is not fitting that heretics should share fellowship with Catholics in the future rest, since here they were always divided from them in faith and conduct.

Hence, under the person of their head, the prophet says in the psalm: “You loved wickedness rather than goodness, and iniquity more than speaking righteousness. You loved all words of destruction and a deceitful tongue; therefore the Lord will destroy you forever, he will tear you away, and he will remove you from your tabernacle and your root from the land of the living” (Ps. 52). For this reason it is said in Ecclesiasticus: “God has destroyed the memory of the proud and left the memory of the humble in understanding” (Sir. 10).

Therefore Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abijah, daughter of Zechariah. The Hebrews assert that this Zechariah, whose daughter Abijah is remembered as Hezekiah’s mother, was a posthumous son of Zechariah the prophet and priest whom King Joash had killed.

He did what was pleasing in the sight of the Lord, according to everything that David his father had done. In the very first year and month of his reign he opened the doors of the house of the Lord and restored them.

Note, reader, that it says Hezekiah opened the doors of the house of the Lord and restored them in the very first year and month of his reign. How could he otherwise have been in every respect an imitator of David his father, who, devoted to God from childhood, fully established the worship of God among the people of Israel at the beginning of his reign, unless he immediately began to restore the rite of the law and its ceremonies, which had been abolished by his father Ahaz?

Morally, the very energy and maturity of Hezekiah in the worship of the house of God admonish the rulers of the Church not to be sluggish or dull in the office entrusted to them, but to do everything diligently and devoutly. Hence Paul writes to Timothy: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his coming and his kingdom: preach the word, be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke with all patience and doctrine.” And again: “But you, be watchful in all things, labor, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry, be sober” (2 Tim. 4).

In the mystical sense, Hezekiah, who carried out the work of God not so much through himself and his own people as by urging others through messengers to similar zeal, represents the Lord and Savior. The interpretation of his name also testifies to this. For Hezekiah is interpreted as “one who lays hold of the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord.” Hence Paul says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Elsewhere he says of him: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily, and he is the head of every principality and power” (Col. 2); he is “the strong and mighty Lord, the mighty Lord in battle” (Ps. 24). “He disarmed the powers and principalities and openly triumphed over them in himself, erasing the record of debt that stood against us with its decrees, which was hostile to us; he took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross” (Col. 2:15).

He therefore washed away with his blood the transgressions of the fathers and all the violations that occurred under the law, and fully restored the worship of piety in the Church. He sent his messengers to summon the nations to faith: first the prophets, then the apostles. For through the preaching of his Gospel he brought many not only from Judea but also from other nations to the Catholic faith and true religion.

He ordained that the Passover should be celebrated in the second month, because, with the shadow of the former law having ceased, he taught the observance of a new celebration of the true Passover. Of this Paul says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). In the times of the law the Passover could not be perfectly celebrated, since at that time only the Jewish nation observed it figuratively. The nations had not yet been sanctified, though through the Gospel of Christ they were to be summoned to celebrate the true Passover. Hence the history of Hezekiah says:

## CHAPTER XXX  
### On Hezekiah King of Judah and the Good Works by Which He Most Gloriously Displayed Divine Worship

After the king, the princes, and the whole assembly of Jerusalem had taken counsel, they decreed that they should celebrate the Passover in the second month. They had not been able to celebrate it at the proper time because the priests who could suffice had not been sanctified, and the people had not yet assembled in Jerusalem.

This was therefore already prefigured in that command of the law by which the Lord ordered through Moses that those who were unclean in soul or were far away on a journey should celebrate the Passover in the second month. This is understood to have been proclaimed as a type of the calling of the nations, who, having fornicated with all the demons, seemed unclean in soul but, cleansed by a saving confession, were commanded to pass over to a second birth, as it were in the second month.

Hence, after the sanctification of the priests and the ministries of the Levites, and after the rejoicing of the Jewish people, the text continues:

“There was also a great celebration of the proselytes from the land of Israel and of those dwelling in Judah, such as had not occurred in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.”

This agrees with what follows shortly afterward.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### Hezekiah Continued

All Israel who had been found in the cities of Judah went out, and they broke the images, cut down the sacred groves, demolished the high places, and destroyed the altars—not only throughout all Judah and Benjamin, but also in Ephraim and Manasseh—until they had utterly destroyed them. Then all the children of Israel returned to their possessions and cities.

After the coming of our Redeemer into the world, idolatry was destroyed not only in Jerusalem and Judea but among all the nations throughout the whole world; the images of error were shattered, and the pride of the devil fell everywhere. As the number of the faithful increases daily, the worship of demons also decreases and diminishes, until at the end of the world death itself, the last enemy, will be overwhelmed. Then what is written will be fulfilled: “The Lord alone will reign on that day.” The idols will be utterly crushed when, after the universal judgment has been completed, the saints enter the heavenly kingdom with Christ, while sinners sink with the devil into the depths of hell.

## CHAPTER VXXII  
### On Sennacherib King of Assyria and the Threats He Made against Jerusalem and the Temple of the Lord, against Whom Vengeance Was Inflicted by the Lord; on Hezekiah’s Illness and Recovery; on the Embassy of the Assyrians to Hezekiah Concerning the Sign That Had Occurred; and on the Death of Hezekiah

After these and similar events, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians came, entered Judah, and besieged the fortified cities, wishing to capture them. When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and that the entire force of the war was directed against Jerusalem, he took counsel with the princes and the mightiest men to block the springs that flowed outside the city. With everyone’s decision in agreement, he gathered a very large multitude, and they blocked all the springs and the stream that flowed through the middle of the land, saying that the kings of Assyria should not come and find an abundance of water.

That Hezekiah, while the Assyrians were attacking the land of the Jews and fighting against Jerusalem, ordered the springs and the stream flowing through the middle of the land to be blocked, so that the approaching kings of Assyria would not find an abundance of water, signifies that diligence and caution must be used against pagans and heretics who resist and blaspheme. The mysteries of divine sacraments must be concealed from them, and the word of God must not be thrust shamelessly upon blasphemers who do not know how to honor holy doctrine through devout conduct but rather strive to tear it apart with poisoned mouths.

Hence the Lord commands his disciples in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart” (Matt. 7). Hence Paul writes to Titus: “Avoid a heretical person after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Tit. 3). Hence the psalmist says: “I set a guard over my mouth while the sinner stood against me; I was silent and humbled, and I refrained from good things” (Ps. 39). Solomon likewise commands in Proverbs: “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well; keep them for yourself alone, so that strangers may not share them with you” (Prov. 5). Everything should be entrusted to trustworthy ears and concealed from the faithless.

He also diligently repaired the whole wall that had been destroyed, built towers upon it, and constructed another wall outside. He restored the Millo in the city of David, made armor and shields of every kind, and appointed commanders of the warriors in the army, and so forth.

This concerns the holy city, of which it is written: “The city of our strength is the Savior” (Isa. 26), because, being situated upon a mountain, it cannot be hidden. Of it it is also written elsewhere: “The river’s rushing waters gladden the city of God” (Ps. 46); and again: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 87).

He is the one who founds and fortifies it, of whom the Father speaks: “This man built my city.” He restores every wall of sound faith and true religion that had been damaged in some places by the wickedness of pagans or heretics, and he builds towers of virtues. He also places another wall outside, that is, an outer defense, which builders of fortifications usually call a breastwork, when he teaches the practice of good works. For it is not enough to possess the wall of faith unless faith itself is confirmed by good works.

This wall and outer defense are built from living stones, which, according to the prophet, are rolled upon the earth. The same king made armor and shields of every kind when he gathers the various testimonies of the holy Scriptures and composes evangelical doctrine as a defense for his Church. He appoints teachers to be commanders of particular companies of warriors and to lead the entire army rightly and rationally, defending the camp of the Church appropriately against every enemy.

After these things had been done, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians sent his servants to Jerusalem. He himself was besieging Lachish with his entire army. He sent them to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the people who were in the city, saying:

“Thus says Sennacherib king of the Assyrians: In what are you trusting as you sit besieged in Jerusalem? Now Hezekiah is deceiving you, to deliver you to death through hunger and thirst, claiming that the Lord your God will rescue you from the hand of the king of Assyria.

“Was it not Hezekiah who destroyed his high places and altars and commanded Judah and Jerusalem, saying: ‘You shall worship before one altar, and on it you shall burn incense’? Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of the lands? Have the gods of the nations been able to rescue their lands from my hand? Who among all the gods of the nations whom my fathers devastated was able to rescue his people from my hand, so that your God could rescue you from this hand?

“Therefore do not let Hezekiah deceive you, and do not let him mislead you with empty persuasion; do not believe him. For if no god of all the nations and kingdoms was able to rescue his people from my hand and from the hand of my fathers, then certainly your god will not be able to rescue you from my hand.”

His servants also spoke many other things against the Lord God and against Hezekiah his servant. He wrote letters full of blasphemy against the Lord God of Israel and spoke against him: “Just as the gods of the other nations could not rescue their people from my hand, so the God of Hezekiah will not be able to rescue his people from this hand.”

Moreover, with a great shout, they called out in the Jewish language to the people who were sitting on the walls of Jerusalem, to terrify and disturb them and capture the city. They spoke against the Lord of Jerusalem as against the gods of the peoples of the earth, the work of human hands.

All these matters are related more fully in the history of Kings and in the volume of the prophet Isaiah. In Kings it is written that in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign:

“He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He did what was good in the sight of the Lord, according to everything that David his father had done.” A little later it says: “He trusted in the Lord God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him. He clung to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps; he kept his commandments, which the Lord had commanded Moses. Therefore the Lord was with him, and in everything he undertook he acted wisely. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and did not serve him.”

In the sixth year of his reign, Salmanasar king of Assyria captured Samaria and the ten tribes called Israel, and transported them to Assyria, settling them in Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes.

Seven years later, that is, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria entered Judea and besieged its fortified cities, wishing to capture them. While he was besieging Lachish, Hezekiah sent messengers to him, saying: “I have sinned; withdraw from me, and whatever you impose upon me I will bear.”

After he had paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold at the king’s command, and after the doors of the temple of the Lord had been broken and the plates that Hezekiah himself had attached had been removed, the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaces from Lachish to King Hezekiah with a large force to Jerusalem.

When they had gone up, they came to Jerusalem and stood beside the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the road to the field of the Washer. They called for the king. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the steward of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah the recorder went out to them. Rabsaces said to them: “Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria,” and so forth, as the same history relates at length (2 Kings 18).

Afterward Sennacherib himself heard that Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, was bringing war against him. He went out to meet him, but nevertheless sent messengers and letters to Hezekiah, intending to terrify by words those whom he had not yet conquered by force. Just as he had said to the people, “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you,” so he spoke the same blasphemy to the king: “Do not let your God deceive you.”

He cited examples from earlier times, saying that just as the gods of other lands had been unable to rescue them from his hands, so Jerusalem would not be rescued. Herodotus relates that Sennacherib king of Assyria fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium; when the city was already about to be captured after the embankments had been built, Tirhakah king of Ethiopia came to its aid, and in a single night, near Jerusalem, 185,000 Assyrian soldiers fell to pestilence. Berossus, the Chaldaean writer of history, relates the matter most fully. Their reliability must be sought in their own books.

Hezekiah took the letters from the hands of the messengers and read them. He went up to the house of the Lord, spread them out before the Lord, and prayed:

“Lord of Hosts, God of Israel, who sit above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes, Lord, and see; hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to blaspheme the living Lord.

“Truly, Lord, the kings of Assyria have laid waste lands and their territories and have given their gods to the fire. For they were not gods, but the works of human hands, made of wood and stone; and they destroyed them.

“And now, Lord our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord God.”

Against the blasphemies of King Sennacherib, Hezekiah took up such weapons as these. The prophet Isaiah also prayed, as the history of the present book shows, saying:

Hezekiah the king and Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet prayed against this blasphemy and cried out to heaven. The Lord sent an angel who struck every strong man, warrior, and commander in the army of the king of Assyria. He returned with disgrace to his own land. When he had entered the house of his god, the sons who had come forth from his own body killed him with the sword, and so forth.

The angel of the Lord went out and struck 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians. When they rose in the morning, behold, all were corpses. Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned, and lived in Nineveh. When he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch his lord, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons struck him with the sword and fled to the land of Armenia. Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place (2 Kings 19).

One hundred eighty-five thousand exceptionally strong living men were slain by one angel in a single night. Without wounds, a savage death passed through them, separating their souls from their bodies by the Lord’s will. The king alone was spared at that time so that he might learn the power of God, that his blaspheming mouth might be silenced, and that he might become a witness to the majesty he had shortly before despised.

So Pharaoh was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he might perish at the end. The same fate awaited this man. When he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and worshiped in the temple of Nesroch his lord as though he had carried off a victory over his enemies, and when he advanced in triumph and rejoicing into the shrine of his idol, the despiser of the true God was slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity—not by the sword of an angel, which had brought death to many, but by the murder committed by his own sons.

When they fled to the land of Ararat, which is understood as Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded his father. Scripture testifies that he sent inhabitants to Samaria, so that the land would not remain uncultivated.

The region of Ararat in Armenia is a plain of extraordinary fertility, through which the Araxes flows at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that place. Therefore the ark in which Noah and his children were saved when the flood had ceased was not carried generally to the mountains of Armenia that are called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararat.

In those days Hezekiah fell ill to the point of death, [Col. 0522B] and he prayed to the Lord, and He heard him and gave him a sign. But he did not repay him according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was lifted up; and wrath came against him and against Judah and Jerusalem, and so forth. All these matters are found more fully written in the Book of Kings, where we read that Hezekiah fell ill to the point of death, and that Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet came in to him and said: “Thus says the Lord God: Give orders to your household, for you shall die and not live.” He turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is pleasing before you.” And Hezekiah wept with a great weeping (IV Kings XX). “For whom the Lord loves he chastises, and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

[Col. 0522C] So that Hezekiah’s heart might not be lifted up after his unbelievable triumphs and victory from the midst of captivity, he is visited with bodily illness and hears that he is to die, so that, turning back to the Lord, he might bend his sentence. We read the same thing in the prophet Jonah and in the threats against David—things said to be future that did not happen—not because God changed his sentence, but because he summoned the human race to knowledge of himself. For “the Lord is repentant concerning evils.” Hearing that he was to die, he does not ask for life and many years, but leaves it to God’s judgment to grant what he wills. He knew that Solomon had pleased God precisely because he had not asked for additional years of life; but, turning to the Lord, he recounts his deeds, how he had walked before him in truth and with a [Col. 0522D] perfect heart. Happy is the conscience that, in a time of affliction, remembers good works. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V); and as it is written elsewhere: “Who will boast that he has a pure heart?” This is resolved as follows: the perfection of the heart is here said to consist in the fact that he destroyed the idols of the temple, opened the doors, crushed the bronze serpent, and did the other things that Scripture records. But he wept with a great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his own death. At that time Hezekiah had no sons. For after his death Manasseh, being twelve years old, began to reign in Judah. Therefore all his weeping was because he despaired that Christ would be born from his seed.

Others maintain that all holy men are terrified by death because of the uncertainty of judgment and ignorance of God’s sentence—what dwelling-place they will have. At the same time, the question of fate is resolved, as are the bonds of necessity and causation: the day of death is by no means fixed in advance for each individual, but by God’s will and by causes unknown to mortals a person may either live or die, especially since the necessity of death that has now been decreed is sometimes deferred, and we read that many were raised after death.

Before Isaiah had gone out through the middle of the court, the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “Return, and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tear. Behold, I have healed you.” And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: “What will be the sign that the Lord has healed me?” The prophet answered him: “This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will accomplish the word he has spoken. Do you wish the shadow to advance ten lines, or to return ten steps?” Hezekiah said to him: “It is easy for the shadow to grow ten lines; I do not want that to happen, but for it to turn backward ten steps.” And when, at Isaiah’s invocation, the sign had been accomplished by the power of the Lord, Isaiah ordered that a mass of fresh figs be brought. When they had brought it and placed it upon his wound, he was healed (IV Kings XX).

Isaiah, the Lord’s prophet, then returns to the king by the Lord’s command, so that he himself might heal the one whom he had struck. He is called “Hezekiah, the leader of my people,” and the son of David, whose works he followed. For he had done what was right according to all that David his father had done, whose works he followed. His prayer is heard and his tears are seen, because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, and had wept with a great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his sight. Fifteen years are added to his life, although he had not asked for them; moreover, while he is still alive, security for the kingdom is promised.

But if, as some think, living in the body is a condemnation, and according to the words, “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Psalm CXV), and elsewhere, “Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm CXLI), death is to be desired so that we may be freed from prison, how does the Lord now grant as a benefit that the one who was to be freed should remain fifteen years longer in prison?

A sign is given: the sun is to return ten steps. We, following Symmachus, have rendered these as lines and a sundial; he understood the steps as lines in order to make the meaning clearer to readers. Alternatively, the steps may have been constructed by mathematical art in such a way that, as the shadow descended over each one, it marked the intervals of the hours. This sign was an indication of the present age and a type of the future: just as the sun returned to its beginning, so Hezekiah’s life would return to additional years; and for us, living in the hebdomad and the ogdoad, the span of life is extended through Christ’s Resurrection.

The guides of the holy places in this province customarily show, within the temple enclosure, the steps of the house of Hezekiah or Ahaz, by which the sun descended. But I will never believe that the house of Ahaz—I do not say of Ahaz, who was an impious king, but of any righteous king—was in the temple of God, since Solomon is said to have offended the Lord for this among other reasons: he built the Millo on high, from which, while walking in the temple court, he was accustomed to look down from the tower of the palace.

[Col. 0524A] This is the Hezekiah who stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon and diverted them westward to the city of David. In all his works he prospered in whatever he undertook. Nevertheless, when the princes of Babylon had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had occurred over the land, the Lord abandoned him so that he might be tested and so that everything that was in his heart might become known.

The portent that is said to have occurred over the land signifies the sun’s return by ten lines, of which we have spoken above. The Babylonian envoys came to Hezekiah to investigate this mystery. But the Lord abandoned him so that he might be tested. He did not restrain him through the prophet from showing the foreigners his treasures and the treasures of the Lord’s house, thereby making known everything that was in his heart—that is, the undisguised pride of his mind, by which he sinned before God, was brought to human knowledge through the result of his first act.

Therefore the punishment brought against him and those who served him is rightly displayed. Hezekiah’s deed clearly demonstrates how harmful the vice of vainglory (*cenodoxia*) is to human souls. He is approved in everything by the testimony of consummate righteousness and of the Holy Scriptures, yet after innumerable praises of virtue he was cast down by a single weapon: pride. Such righteousness and such virtues, such faith and devotion—qualities that deserved to change nature itself and the laws of the whole world—perish through a single act of boasting.

Thus, as though all his virtues had never existed and had been handed over to oblivion, he would immediately have incurred the Lord’s anger, had he not appeased it by recovering humility. He had fallen from so lofty a summit of merits because pride had filled him; therefore he could ascend again to the height he had attained only by the same steps of humility.

All vices that have been overcome wither; defeated day by day, they become weaker and are diminished and cooled either by place or by time, or else, weakened by opposing virtues, they are more easily guarded against or avoided. But this vice, once cast down, rises more fiercely to the struggle; and when it is thought extinguished, it grows stronger through its own death. Other kinds of vice ordinarily attack only those whom they have overcome in combat. This one, however, pursues its own conquerors more fiercely. The more powerfully it has been struck down, the more violently it engages them through the pride of that very victory. This is the subtle strategy of the enemy: he makes the soldier of Christ succumb to his weapons, when he was unable to defeat him by armed enemies.

Other vices, as we have said, sometimes become quiet through the benefit of place; when the material, opportunity, and occasion for sin have been removed, they tend to grow sluggish and diminish. But this vice, when it enters the desert with the one who flees to it, is not excluded by a new place, nor does it wither when external material is removed. It draws strength only from the successes of the virtues of the one whom it attacks.

Some vices, as we have stated above, are also softened and disappear with the passage of time. But for this one, unless longevity is grounded in diligent and prudent discernment, length of time not only does no harm, but even knows how to heap up fuel for vanity. Finally, other disturbances, weakened by the virtues opposed to them and fighting as though in the open against an experienced opponent, are more easily overcome and guarded against. But this one, inserted among the virtues and mingled with the battle-line, like one fighting in blind night, deceives the unsuspecting and unwary with greater ferocity.

Hezekiah slept with his fathers, and they buried him above the tombs of the sons of David; and all Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem celebrated his funeral rites. The statement that Hezekiah was buried above the tombs of the sons of David shows that his tomb was built higher than those of the other sons of David—a distinction granted for his merit and his devotion to the Lord.

[Col. 0525B] And Manasseh his son reigned in his place.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### On Manasseh, his son, and Ammon, his descendant

Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. He did evil before the Lord, according to the abominations of the nations whom the Lord had overthrown before the children of Israel. He turned back and rebuilt the high places that Hezekiah his father had demolished; he constructed altars to the Baals, made sacred groves, worshiped the whole host of heaven, and served it.

He also built altars in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said: “In Jerusalem my name shall be forever.” He built them for the whole army of heaven in the two courts of the house of the Lord, and made his sons pass through the fire in the valley of Ben-hinnom. He observed dreams, followed omens, devoted himself to magical arts, and kept magicians and enchanters with him. He did much evil before the Lord, provoking him, and so forth.

Josephus narrates similar things about Manasseh the king, adding that, when he turned to cruelty, he killed all the righteous among the Hebrews and spared neither the prophets, of whom he killed one each day. Hence the Hebrews relate that the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two with a wooden saw by Manasseh himself and by the princes of Judah. They turned this into a charge against him because he had called them princes of Sodom and Gomorrah and had said: “I saw the Lord seated upon a lofty throne” (Isaiah VI).

Yet the Lord himself says through Moses: “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exodus XXXIII). They also held against Isaiah what he had said to Hezekiah by the word of the Lord: “I will add fifteen years to your days” (IV Kings XX), although it is found written through Moses: “You shall fulfill the number of your days” (Exodus XXIII). Likewise, they objected to his saying: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah LV), although elsewhere it is written: “Who is so near as the Lord our God whenever we call upon him?”

Josephus further adds that the king of Babylon and the Chaldaeans sent an army that devastated their region of Judaea, and that Manasseh the king was captured by deceit, brought to him, and subjected to whatever tortures he wished. Then Manasseh understood what evils he was in and recognized himself as the author of them all. He begged God to make his enemy merciful and compassionate toward him. God heard his prayer and granted that, released by the king of Babylon, he should return to his kingdom. Thereafter he lived more correctly and restored divine worship; through repentance he wiped away the guilt of his former offenses, as the present history plainly demonstrates.

Manasseh’s repentance is an example showing that, after committing crimes, no one ought to despair of God’s mercy. Rather, through suitable repentance, one should hope for pardon, provided that one completes that repentance properly.

After Manasseh, his son Ammon reigned. With the same madness by which his father had first worshiped idols as gods, he sinned even more grievously than his father. His servants rose against him and killed him in his own house, God rendering him a just recompense according to his own merits.

After Ammon, his son Josiah, a most righteous king, reigned. He corrected all the filth of the idols that his fathers had fashioned and diligently devoted himself to the worship of God—and rightly so, since long before this it had been said of him through the prophet. Josiah is interpreted as “whose sacrifice belongs to the Lord,” or “the salvation of the Lord,” or “the strength of the Lord.”

In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still a boy, he began to seek the God of his father David. In the eleventh year after he had begun to reign, he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the sacred groves, the images, and the carved idols. They destroyed the altars of the Baals before him, and demolished the images that had been placed upon them. He also cut down and crushed the sacred groves and scattered their fragments over the graves of those who had been accustomed to sacrifice to them.

Moreover, he burned the bones of the priests upon the altars of the idols and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem. In the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, he likewise overturned everything.

Why did Josiah order the bones of the dead to be burned upon the altar, unless to show that their sacrifices had been deadly, and that they not only offered animal victims to demons but also, through the error of idolatry, handed themselves over to the power of demons? By God’s just judgment, they were to be destroyed together with the altar they had built for the idols.

In the mystical sense, this signifies that all those who have surrendered their lives to the service of the devil and ended them in sacrilege will be consumed by eternal torments, God repaying them according to the merits of their deeds.

Then the account continues concerning the same king: when he heard the book of the law of the Lord, which Hilkiah the priest had found in the temple of the Lord, he tore his garments and sent Hilkiah the priest and the others listed afterward to pray for him, and for the remnant of Israel and Judah, concerning all the words of the book that had been found in the house of God. They went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum. The Hebrews assert that Shallum was the maternal uncle of Hananeel, the father of Jeremiah. She lived in “the Second” in Jerusalem.

What is meant by the statement that she lived in “the Second” is explained above in the history of the present book, where it was written concerning the aforementioned King Hezekiah: “He acted industriously and repaired the entire wall that had been destroyed, and built towers and another wall outside” (II Chronicles XXXII). Zephaniah also mentions this place, saying: “A cry from the Fish Gate and a wailing from the Second” (Zephaniah I). The old edition translated this as though it were the proper name of a place, *in Masena*. For *Masena* is interpreted as “the Second.” Therefore, when it is said that the prophetess lived in “the Second,” understand it as the section of the second wall.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### On King Josiah and his good deeds, whom Necho, king of Egypt, killed in battle

Josiah celebrated the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem; it was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month. He appointed the priests to their offices and urged them to minister in the house of the Lord. He also spoke to the Levites, through whose instruction all Israel was sanctified by the Lord, saying:

“Place the ark in the sanctuary of the temple that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built; for you shall no longer carry it,” and so forth.

The Hebrews relate that the ark of the Lord, which Josiah now ordered to be brought back into the temple, had been removed from the temple in the time of Ahaz, when the images were brought by him into the temple. It was taken to the house of Shallum, the husband of Huldah and the maternal uncle of Jeremiah, where it remained until the time of Josiah. For the ark of God could not be in a place where images had been introduced and the most impious customs and rites of the Gentiles were observed.

The fact that the aforementioned king, after removing the idols from the land, together with the soothsayers, diviners, and every impurity and abomination, is said to have celebrated a most solemn Passover to the Lord in the eighth year of his reign teaches us morally first to cleanse the land of our heart from every vice, to purify our actions from every stain of sin and from dead works, so that we may serve the living God, and thus celebrate a Passover pleasing to the Lord: “Not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Corinthians V).

According to allegory, this Josiah represents the Lord Savior, who is rightly called “the salvation and strength of the Lord,” because he is the one of whom Scripture says: “The Lord is strong, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm XXIII). And elsewhere: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matthew I).

He cleanses the land of Judah and Jerusalem by the zeal of God from every impurity and abomination. Of him the Prophet says: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm LXVIII). John also speaks of him: “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor” (Matthew and Luke III). Malachi says of him:

“Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts. Who can consider the day of his coming, and who will stand to behold him? For he is like a refining fire and like fuller’s soap. He will sit refining and purifying silver; he will cleanse the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver. And they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness, and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall be pleasing to God, as in the days of old and as in former years. And I will draw near to you for judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers; against those who defraud the hired worker of his wages, oppress widows and orphans, and crush the sojourner, and do not fear me, says the Lord of hosts” (Malachi III).

Therefore our Josiah celebrates the true Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign, when, in the eighth age, after the general resurrection has been accomplished, he leads his saints, perfected in good works, to receive the denarius of eternal blessedness. First all scandals have been expelled from his kingdom, concerning which the aforementioned prophet says:

“For behold, the day is coming, burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who practice wickedness shall be straw; the coming day shall set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, and shall leave them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings. You shall go out and leap like calves from the herd, and you shall trample the wicked when they are ashes beneath the soles of your feet” (Malachi IV).

It is rightly said that no Passover like this had been celebrated from the days of the judges who judged Israel, nor throughout all the days of Israel and the kings of Judah, as in the eighteenth year of King Josiah in Jerusalem. For, once the figures have been removed, the saints will truly pass on the day of judgment from death to life and from corruption to glory. Thus, in the presence of their Creator, they will rejoice forever in the heavenly Jerusalem: “For the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Psalm LXXXIII). That city needs neither sun nor moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb. The nations shall walk by its light, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it. Nothing unclean, nor anyone who practices abomination or falsehood, shall enter it, except those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation XXI). And the name of the city from that day onward shall be “The Lord is there”: “Blessed be the Lord, for he has made his mercy marvelous” (Psalm XXX).

Necho, king of Egypt, went up to fight at Carchemish beside the Euphrates, and Josiah came out to meet him. But Necho sent messengers to him and said: “What have I to do with you, king of Judah? I am not coming against you today, but I am fighting against another house—that is, against the house of the king at Remmon, son of Jabrimon, who ruled at Carchemish; [the intervening clause is textually unclear: ‘which, at that time when Necho also killed King Josiah’]. God has commanded me to go there quickly. Stop acting against God, who is with me, lest he kill you.”

The king of Egypt says that the Lord commanded him to go quickly because, from the words of the prophets—that is, Jeremiah and the others—he could have known the Lord’s will to execute vengeance upon a sinful people. Hence the Rabshakeh also says to Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians: “The Lord commanded me to go up against this land,” because the prophets of Israel had already prophesied that he would go up against it; for this was by no means hidden from him.

Josiah did not wish to turn back. He prepared for battle against him and did not heed the words of Necho, which came from the mouth of God. Instead, he went on to fight in the plain of Megiddo. There he was wounded by archers and said to his servants: “Take me out of the battle, for I am severely wounded.” They transferred him from his chariot to another chariot that followed him in royal fashion and carried him to Jerusalem.

He died and was buried in the mausoleum of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned him, especially Jeremiah, whose male and female singers continue to repeat laments over Josiah down to the present day, and so forth.

Josephus reports the following about this battle. While Josiah surpassed everyone in peace, wealth, and glory, Necho, king of the Egyptians, encamped beside the Euphrates River to fight against the Medes and Babylonians, who had overthrown the rule of the Assyrians. He desired to reign in Asia. When he came to the city of Mende, which belonged to Josiah’s kingdom, King Josiah prevented him from passing through his province on the way to the Medes.

Necho then sent ambassadors to him and explained that he was not leading an army against him but was hurrying to the Euphrates River. He added that Josiah ought not to provoke him by obstructing his campaign, lest he go to a foreign war instead of the battles toward which he was headed. Josiah did not heed Necho’s words but insisted that he would not allow him to pass through his territory. I think that he was pressing him so that what was imminent might occur.

While Josiah was arranging the battle line of his army and, riding in a chariot, was passing from one chariot to another, a certain Egyptian shot him and checked him in his haste for battle. Immediately, being severely wounded, he ordered the army to withdraw and returned to Jerusalem because he had been wounded. He was buried magnificently in the tombs of his fathers.

He lived thirty-nine years and reigned for thirty-one of them. All the people mourned him for many days with great grief and lamentation. The prophet Jeremiah composed a song for his death in mournful melody, which is known to have survived to this day.

This same prophet also foretold the future destruction of the city. In writing, he left both the captivity now experienced by us and the various Babylonian migrations. Nor did he alone foretell that these things would come upon the people: the prophet Ezekiel too, being the first to write two books about them, left them for the people.

Both were priests. Jeremiah, however, remained in Jerusalem from the fourteenth year of King Josiah until the city and the temple were laid waste.

According to allegory, what does the killing of Josiah signify—he who was slain by Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo—if not the persecution of the ancient enemy against holy preachers, whom he tries through envy to deliver to death and remove from the land of the Church, so that he may more easily scatter and attack the whole people?

Pharaoh is interpreted as “one who scatters,” Necho as “striking,” and Megiddo as “from temptation.” For the devil is permitted to rise up against the saints, and this is all that he does and strives for with all his strength: by striking the flock of God through temptation, to scatter it, and first to remove those whose support ought to have enabled the others to fight against the enemy.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Col. 0530A] On Joahaz and Jehoiakim, the sons of Josiah, and their deaths; on the fact that King Jehoiachin was led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, together with his mother and servants; and on King Zedekiah and the destruction of the city of Jerusalem.

The people of the land therefore took Joahaz, son of Josiah, and made him king in place of his father in Jerusalem, and so forth.

Joahaz, whose name is interpreted as “held back,” signifies wicked rulers whom the people of the land—that is, carnal people devoted to earthly desire and consenting, according to their own habits, to their vices—choose for themselves. Pharaoh bound them at Riblah and led them into Egypt, when the devil, weakening the multitude of flatterers, deceives the hearts of rulers. For *Reblath* is interpreted as “multitude,” and thus spiritual Egypt plunges those bound by chains of sins into a dark abyss.

In place of Joahaz, Necho appointed Jehoiakim king and imposed a heavy levy upon the land: one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. This means that the evil spirit demands from the people of the lost the burden of his service, so that in every respect they may be ready to obey him both in understanding and in speech. Accordingly, Jehoiakim, following Pharaoh’s command, required each person according to his means to give both silver and gold, so that he might repay it to Pharaoh. For the devil, through men devoted to him, demands from each person, according to his ability, the payment of a tax of sin, and thus daily prepares destruction for those under wicked rulers.

Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. [Col. 0530C] He did evil before the Lord his God. Against him came Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Chaldaeans, and led him bound with chains into Babylon. He also carried the vessels of the Lord there and placed them in his own temple.

It should be noted that concerning this same Jehoiakim, son of King Josiah, it is written in the Book of Kings: “Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place” (IV Kings XXIV). Josephus, however, seems to assert that Jehoiakim himself, the father, was killed in Jerusalem by the king of Babylon, although he was taken captive to Babylon. In the fourteenth book of his *Antiquities* he reports as follows:

“When the king of Babylon entered the city, he kept faith in no respect, but killed the strongest and most beautiful young men of Jerusalem together with King Jehoiakim. He also ordered Jehoiakim to be thrown outside the walls unburied, and appointed his son Jehoiachin king over the whole province. He took captive to Babylon three thousand men who held offices, among whom was the prophet Ezekiel, while he was still a boy.”

Such, then, was the end of King Jehoiakim, who lived thirty-six years and reigned eleven. His successor in the kingdom was King Joachin, [‘onos’—reading uncertain]. He reigned three months and ten days.

It should be understood that once someone has enslaved himself to any one vice, he will be subject not to one master but to many. Thus Jehoiakim, whom Pharaoh had previously compelled to pay tribute to him, is now forced by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to serve him for three years. And whom shall we understand Nebuchadnezzar to be other than the same one whom we have said Pharaoh is—the prince of confusion and ruler of this darkness?

Therefore, when the ancient enemy persuades someone to pay him the tax of sin, he immediately urges him to bring everything under his dominion and render full service. What else, then, is it to be a servant of the king of Babylon than to be subjected, through persuasion, delight, and consent, to the ancient enemy, and, in thought, word, and deed, to be wholly devoted to vices, as though freely possessed by him?

The remaining deeds of Jehoiakim and his abominations, which he committed and which were found in him, are contained in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. The Books of Kings and Chronicles alike relate how wicked this Jehoiakim was. Jeremiah also bears the fullest witness in his book to the madness of this man. He not only provoked the Lord by his evil deeds and by his disposition—which was the greater offense—and despised the words of the prophets who were sent to him; he also took the book of Jeremiah, which Baruch had written from the mouth of the prophet himself. When it had been read aloud before him, he cut it with a knife and threw it into the fire that was over the brazier, until the entire scroll was consumed by the fire; yet they were not afraid and did not tear their garments.

Concerning the statement about the abominations he committed and what was found in him, the Hebrews relate that, among the other evils he perpetrated, he also did to his body the things that the Lord had forbidden when he said: “You shall not shave your head round, nor make marks upon your bodies for the dead” (Leviticus IX). After he died, these things were found upon his body.

His son Jehoiachin therefore reigned in his place. Jehoiachin was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did evil in the sight of the Lord.

It should certainly be understood that the name of this Jehoiachin, who is also called Jeconiah, is written at the end among the Hebrews with different letters from those used for his father Jehoiakim, who is also called Eliakim. They write the former—that is, the father—with *kappa* and *mu* at the end of the name, but the latter, that is, the son, with *chi* and *nu*. Therefore no one should think that the Jehoiakim at the beginning of Daniel is the same as the Jehoiachin written at the beginning of Ezekiel. The former has the final syllable *kim*, the latter *chin*. For this reason, in the Gospel according to Matthew, one generation appears to be missing: the second group of fourteen generations ends with Jeconiah, son of Josiah, while the third begins with Jehoiachin, son of Eliakim. Porphyry, ignorant of this, brought a charge against the Church and displayed his own lack of learning by attempting to accuse the Evangelist Matthew of falsehood.

When the year had come around, King Nebuchadnezzar sent messengers who brought him to Babylon, carrying away at the same time the most precious vessels of the house of the Lord. This is related more fully in the Book of Kings, where it is written:

“At that time the servants of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up against Jerusalem, and the city was surrounded with fortifications. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against the city with his servants to besiege it. Jehoiachin, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon—he, his mother, his servants, his princes, and his eunuchs—and the king of Babylon received him in the eighth year of his reign.

“He brought out from there all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the royal house. He cut up all the golden vessels that Solomon, king of Israel, had made in the temple of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord. He carried away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty men of the army, ten thousand, into captivity, together with every craftsman and smith. Nothing was left except the poor of the people of the land.

“He also carried Jehoiachin to Babylon, together with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his eunuchs, and the judges of the land. He led them from Jerusalem into captivity in Babylon, together with seven thousand strong men, craftsmen, and smiths—one thousand in all—every strong man and warrior. The king of Babylon led them captive to Babylon and appointed Mattaniah, his uncle, in his place, and changed his name to Zedekiah” (IV Kings XXIV).

In the mystical sense, this captivity of King Jehoiachin, by which he was led to Babylon, signifies the fall and ruin of the rulers of the Church. Deceived by the cunning of the true Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil—they are brought into the confusion of errors and vices. Those who, through the grace of the Lord and diligent good works, ought to have raised others to true religion through the word of teaching and through good examples are themselves slaughtered by various judgments and swallowed up by the death of sins.

This is what the name Jehoiachin signifies, for it is interpreted as “one who raises up” or “one who is rising.” Together with him, the Lord’s most precious vessels are carried into captivity, because those who excelled in intellectual acumen or shone with moral integrity, corrupted by the examples of evil superiors, have together with them become prey for the devil.

The prophet Jeremiah also seems to lament this in his Lamentations, where he says: “All her beauty has gone out from the daughter of Zion; her princes have become like rams finding no pasture, and they have gone away without strength before the face of their pursuer. The enemy has stretched out his hand toward all her desirable things, for he has seen the nations enter her sanctuary” (Lamentations I).

Hence the Psalmist, marveling at the sudden devastation of the Lord’s vineyard, says to the Lord himself: “Why have you torn down its hedge, so that all who pass along the road may pluck it? The boar from the forest has ravaged it” (Psalm LXXIX).

Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did what was evil in the sight of the Lord his God, and he was not ashamed before the face of the prophet Jeremiah, who spoke to him from the mouth of the Lord. He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had helped him by God’s agency, and hardened his neck and his heart so that he would not return to the Lord, the God of Israel.

Moreover, all the princes of the priests and the people transgressed wickedly, in accordance with all the abominations of the nations, and they defiled the house of the Lord, which he had sanctified for himself in Jerusalem. Yet the Lord, the God of their fathers, sent messengers to them, rising early and sending them, continually warning them, because he spared his people and his dwelling place. But they mocked the messengers of God, paid little regard to his words, and ridiculed the prophets, until the Lord’s fury rose against his people and there was no remedy.

For he brought against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of his sanctuary. He had no mercy on young man or maiden, old man or even the very aged; he delivered them all into his hands. He carried off to Babylon all the vessels of the house of the Lord, both the larger and the smaller, as well as the treasures of the temple, of the king, and of the princes.

What, then, is signified by Zedekiah, king of Judah, except those who undertake the governance of rule among God’s people? For, according to the interpretation of his name, Zedekiah means “the justice of the Lord.” They receive the law and the seat of justice when, in accordance with evangelical teaching, they receive honors and the dignity of office for carrying out works of righteousness—especially since, as sons of Josiah, that is, of “the salvation of the Lord,” they deserve to be so called through the grace of baptism and the anointing of sacred chrism.

But, degenerating from this dignity, they fall back into the filthiness of vices. They not only surrender themselves to impiety and shamelessness, but also make their subjects, whoever consent to them, participants in their crimes. They neither keep the faith they promised to God nor rightly preserve the covenants of peace with human beings.

Thus, divine law and the utterances of the prophets and apostles admonish such people daily to withdraw from sins and turn back to God through repentance [Col. 0533C]. But, once hardened, they despise the words of salvation and scorn to obey the Lord’s life-giving command. Therefore, in his anger, he sends against them the king of the Chaldeans—that is, the prince of darkness—with his attendants, namely, spiritual wickednesses, so that those who would not be corrected by a salutary instruction might be subjected to the torment of their enemies.

These enemies spare no age and show honor to no dignity. Whoever they capture, they transfer to Babylon—that is, into the snare of confusion—and they burn the house of the Lord when they compel the faithful, who seemed to have become the temple of the Lord through faith and catholic confession, to blaspheme.

They destroy the walls of Jerusalem when they cast down the guardianship of the shepherds. They overwhelm all the lands when they run beyond the ecclesiastical orders, which had held the summit of honor, through unlawful desires. They demolish whatever had been precious when, because of their impiety, they reduce to ruin and nothingness everything in which they had taken pride on account of their excellence in virtue and knowledge.

They serve the king of Babylon and his sons when, instigated by the devil, they are not ashamed to surrender themselves to various contaminations of vice and bind themselves to different passions of sin—until another kingdom arises, of which it was foretold in a prophetic proclamation, and the kingdom of sin falls under divine judgment. Hence it follows:

“He served the king and his sons until the king of Persia began to reign and the word of the Lord was fulfilled from the mouth of Jeremiah” [Col. 0534A], “and the land kept its sabbaths. For all the days of its desolation it kept sabbath, until the seventy years were completed.”

Solomon, then—to repeat what was said above—built the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem over seven years, but in the eighth year completed and dedicated it. This signifies that, during the age of this world, which revolves through seven days, the Lord builds the Church by gathering the faithful for the heavenly edifice. In the future life, when the glory of the resurrection appears, he completes it in its entirety and raises it into the joy of immortal life, in the vision of his eternal splendor.

Since he himself rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the week—the time of our resurrection is rightly expressed by the number eight. But the fact that, in the succeeding age, certain parts of the temple are built which begin to fall apart through excessive age, and that these same parts are soon restored through the zeal of the kings and priests who existed in those times and raised again to their former condition, signifies the daily and very slight faults of the faithful, of which Solomon says: “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again” (Prov. XXIV).

These faults are likewise corrected each day, through the Lord’s gift, by the diligence of the faithful, as it were through the work of God’s kings and priests—that is, through the examples and exhortations of those who came before them in righteousness. For all the perfect in the Church are rightly called kings and priests, since they are members of the supreme King and Priest, once they have learned to govern themselves well and to present their bodies to the Lord as a living sacrifice.

But when evils increased, the temple itself was profaned by the filth of idols, and finally destroyed and burned by the Chaldeans. This signifies the more serious falls of those who, although joined to the members of the holy Church through confession of the true faith and the sacrament of saving baptism, are again cast down from the state of faith by the deceit of evil spirits and consumed in the flame of vices.

When the temple had been destroyed and the city of Jerusalem likewise laid waste, its citizens migrated to Babylon. After seventy years, having repented of their evils, they were, through the Lord’s mercy, sent back to their homeland, and once again restored the same temple and holy city with great labor. Figuratively, this designates those who, deceived by the devil, lose not only the sincerity of faith and integrity of good works, but also, through the bitterness of their crimes, appear to be made like the nations and publicans, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a publican” (Matt. XVIII).

Nevertheless, some of these, recovering through the regard of divine grace, return to the Church. Struck with compunction through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, they begin again to hear and observe the precepts of divine law that they had abandoned. For there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet Isaiah enumerates with clear distinction (Isa. XI). The whole sum of divine law is contained in ten commandments, and seven multiplied by ten completes the number seventy.

Accordingly, with fitting symbolism, those who were taken captive into Babylon through perverse works are freed after seventy years and rebuild the house of God and the holy city. For through their sins they were never separated from the communion and fellowship of the holy Church, nor joined to the lot and number of unbelievers. Then, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, they diligently carry out acts of good works, and thereby are received into the fellowship of the faithful—the house, namely, and city of the Lord—from which they had been expelled.

In the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, to fulfill the word of the Lord which he had spoken through the mouth of Jeremiah (Jerem. XXV, XXIX), the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians. He commanded that a proclamation be made throughout his entire kingdom, even in writing, saying:

“Thus says Cyrus, king of the Persians: ‘The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judea. Who among you is of all his people? May the Lord his God be with him, and let him go up.’”

The end of the Book of Chronicles is similar to the beginning of the Book of Ezra the Priest. The Hebrews consider Malachi to be the last of the twelve prophets; in that book the edict of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and the return of the Jewish people to the land of Judah are described. Therefore this passage may be explained in a similar way, so that what the interpreters of that prophet said at the beginning of his book, we may place here at the end of this one.

Ancient histories relate—and the Scripture of the prophet Daniel agrees with them—that Cyrus, king of the Persians, joined to himself Darius, king of the Medes, and destroyed the empire of the Babylonians, after killing their last king, Belshazzar, and laying waste and destroying the city itself.

Cyrus, knowing that the kingdom had been handed over to him by the God of Israel, immediately after conquering that kingdom which had taken the people captive and oppressed them in slavery, granted that same people permission to return to their homeland and rebuild the house of their God, which had been burned there. He announced this decree of liberty not only verbally to those present, but also sent letters to those who were farther away throughout all the provinces of his kingdom. In a public declaration he confessed that the God of Israel is the true God and the Lord of heaven and the author of all kingdoms.

All these things the holy prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah clearly foretold. Jeremiah predicted both the number of years they would serve in Babylon and the time when they would be recalled to their homeland (Jerem. XXIX). Isaiah, moreover, without any obscurity in prophetic speech, even disclosed the name of the king by whom they would be freed from servitude, recalled to their homeland, and permitted to restore the temple.

Jeremiah says:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to every exile whom I carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: ‘Build houses and dwell in them.’ For thus says the Lord of hosts: ‘When the seventy years in Babylon begin to be completed, I will visit you and raise up over you my good word, and I will bring you back to this place.’”

Isaiah, however, says:

“Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer and your Maker from the womb: ‘I am the Lord, who makes all things.’” And shortly afterward:

“Who says to the deep: ‘Be desolate,’ and I will dry up your rivers; who says to Cyrus: ‘You are my shepherd, and you will fulfill all my will’; who says to Jerusalem: ‘You shall be built,’ and to the temple: ‘You shall be founded.’

“Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subject nations before his face and turn the backs of kings; to open doors before him, and the gates shall not be shut. I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious of the earth. I will shatter bronze doors and break iron bars, and I will give you hidden treasures and secret stores, so that you may know that I am the Lord who calls you by your name, the God of Israel, for the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel. I called you by your name; I have likened you, though you did not know me.

“I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no God. I girded you, though you did not know me” (Isa. XLV).

From this passage it should be believed above all that Cyrus, king of the Persians, loved the sons of Israel, removed them from captivity, sent them home, and ordered them to rebuild the temple because he had heard that their prophets, through the Spirit of God, had foretold the nature of his reign and the destruction of the Babylonians.

Indeed, those same prophets had specifically expressed the method by which he would purge Babylon. Isaiah says: “I who say to the deep: ‘Be desolate,’ and I will dry up your rivers” (Isa. XLIV). Jeremiah, moreover, says: “That broad wall of Babylon shall be utterly undermined, and its lofty gates shall be burned with fire” (Jer. LI).

For the histories relate that, after the Euphrates—which flowed through the middle of Babylon—had been divided and emptied into many channels, the enemy entered the city through its dried-up and desolated bed. We have said this much concerning the historical account.

But according to the mystical meanings, Cyrus the king designates the Lord and Savior both by his name and by his deeds. We learned this not from our own conjecture but from Isaiah’s most explicit words, in which he spoke in the person of the Lord: “I have likened you, though you did not know me” (Isa. XLV).

God likened him to his Son, although the Lord himself did not at all know that he was being likened to him. First, this was because God deigned to call him his Christ; then, because he ordained that he should be called Cyrus—which is interpreted as “heir”—long before he was born. This title rightly suits the one to whom God the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II).

The Apostle also speaks of him: “Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Hebr. V). And of him, when he appeared in the flesh, his enemies pursuing him said: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI).

Moreover, in that God the Father subjected nations before Cyrus’s face and turned the backs of kings, shattered bronze doors and broke iron bars—namely, those of Babylon and of the other cities he captured—and gave him hidden treasures and secret stores, that is, unknown resources of provinces, he likened him to our Lord and Savior.

When the apostles preached throughout the world, Christ subjected to himself the necks of all nations and also brought under his dominion the very rulers of earthly affairs and authors of secular wisdom. He destroyed the gates of hell, so that he might introduce his elect, whom he had rescued from there, into the liberty of their heavenly homeland. He crushed the errors of the nations and overthrew doctrines fortified by human reasoning through the mouths of the humble, so that, once corrected, he might open to them the light of his faith and truth, in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

Our same Lord possessed these treasures eternally from the Father in the nature of his divinity, but received them in time in the humanity he assumed.

Thus the Lord likened Cyrus to his only-begotten Son and our Lord Jesus Christ. For, just as, from the time he began to be human, Cyrus destroyed the empire of the Chaldeans, liberated God’s people and sent them back to their homeland, ordered the burned temple at Jerusalem to be rebuilt, and took care to make this same decree known in writing so that Jeremiah’s words might be fulfilled—for Jeremiah himself had foretold that this would happen—so the mediator between God and human beings, after destroying the devil’s kingdom throughout the world, gathers into his Church his elect, who had been scattered and recalled from the devil’s tyranny.

The Church, justified by faith in the present, has peace with God through him and hastens toward the vision of everlasting peace in the future. Jerusalem, indeed, is called “vision of peace.” He also restores the temple that had been burned when, bringing back to salvation those who had lost the faith through the snares of the ancient enemy, he makes them worthy of his indwelling.

He also sent the holy Scriptures throughout the whole world, through which he might proclaim faith in his name and the hope of salvation to all who belong to his kingdom—that is, to all the elect [Col. 0537C]. This was foretold not by Jeremiah alone, but by all the prophets with one accord, in accordance with what he himself said to his disciples: “For it is necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, king of the Persians, so that, having recognized the power and providence of the God of Israel, he might do what Scripture relates about him. In the Gospel the Lord says to the Jews: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing of myself, but speak these things just as the Father taught me” (John VIII).

But when Cyrus says in his decree: “The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth” (II Chron. XXXVI; I Ezra I), he rightly confessed the Lord, the God of Israel, as the Lord and God of heaven. He recognized that the Lord possesses all the kingdoms of the earth in his power and can give them to whomever he wishes. Yet what Cyrus says—that all the kingdoms of the earth had been handed over to him—seems to sound less true, unless perhaps it is understood that, at the time when he wrote these words, he had no opposing kingdom, or else that, after conquering and exhausting so powerful an empire—the ancient empire of the Chaldeans—he believed that no kingdom in the whole world could resist him.

In truth, however, this statement suits the majesty of the one who said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

The same decree of Cyrus continues:

“Who is among you from all his people? May his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judea, and build the house of the God of Israel. He is the God who is in Jerusalem” (I Ezra I).

Great faith appears in these words of the king, and great piety. His faith is shown by the fact that he understood the people of God to belong to God more than all other nations; his piety, by the fact that, without excluding anyone at all, he allowed all who wished to return freely to their homeland.

His faith is shown by the fact that he confessed the same Lord God to dwell in heaven, to be in Jerusalem, and to be able to ascend with each of those returning from Babylon to Jerusalem. Is it not clearer than daylight that he believed this God to be not corporeal or confined to a place, but spirit and present everywhere? He confessed him to dwell in Jerusalem and in the temple while not doubting that he simultaneously presides over the kingdom of heaven. He believed him to reign in heaven while nevertheless being with his faithful on earth and directing both their minds and their hands toward the accomplishment of what would be salutary.

Furthermore, all the words of this Scripture breathe a spiritual meaning. Since it is not readily apparent that only those with whom God is present can pass from confession of sins to works of virtue, as from slavery in Babylon to freedom in Jerusalem—for without him we can do nothing—who does not see that an ascent is rightly named in the same sentence?

For all who sin and serve the cares of this world are below; those who please God must raise their minds to higher things, sigh for heavenly realities, and transcend all the pageantry and allurements of the world through love of eternal things.

Jerusalem is also said to be in Judea—that is, in confession—so that we who through forgetfulness of God deserved to be taken captive by the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as “demons,” that is, to be enslaved to evil spirits, may through confession of divine mercy return to the vision of free peace and light.

There let us build a house for the Lord, the God of Israel—that is, in the unity of catholic peace, in confession either of our iniquity or of divine mercy and grace, let us prepare our hearts, in which the Lord himself may graciously deign to dwell and illuminate them by his presence. Let us also take care to kindle the hearts of our neighbors to praise their Creator and to works of piety.

For in both ways we build a house for the Lord: whether we exercise ourselves in works of righteousness, or urge those whom we wish to help along the path of righteousness by examples and words.

The rest of the same decree of King Cyrus follows:

“And let all the rest, in all the places wherever they dwell, help him—the men from their own place—with silver and gold, goods and livestock, besides what they freely offer for the temple of God, which is in Jerusalem” (I Ezra I).

The distinction of the words should be noted. The king granted all those who had been released from the injustice of captivity the power to go up, if they wished, under divine guidance, to build the temple for the Lord; but he did not order everyone to go up there.

He commanded that those of the same people of God who, more than others in whatever places, desired to enjoy the liberty granted to them should support those who went up, each from his own place, supplying them with money or livestock for the needs of so long a journey. He also wished them to give and entrust other gifts to them, which those who arrived there ought to bring to the temple of the Lord as a memorial of the senders.

All, therefore, were freed from Babylonian captivity; all devoted themselves to acts of piety. But the more perfect went up to build the temple for the Lord, while the rest helped those who had gone up. For although all who had been rescued from the power of darkness and brought into the liberty of the glory of the children of God belonged to that liberty, and although all rejoiced to be counted among the fellowship of the holy city—that is, the Church—not all, but only the perfect, labor in the building of that same Church by preaching to others.

Therefore such people are considered worthy of double honor above the other faithful by the Apostle, just as the angel says to Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars forever and ever” (Dan. XII).

These instructors of many, the more they teach their hearers to seek and love heavenly things, the less concern they themselves have for acquiring or possessing earthly things. Indeed, they very often abandon temporal possessions already acquired for the sake of hope in eternal things.

Their poverty, therefore, must be relieved by the generosity of the wealthy—who cannot preach—so that the preachers may continue their work and the wealthy themselves may also become partners in that preaching. In the person of such people John says to Gaius: “For they have gone out for the sake of his name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John).
