For this reason it is now said that those who went up to build the house of the Lord should be helped by the generosity of money from their friends wherever they lived—that is, whether in Chaldea or in other places to which they had fled through fear of the Chaldeans.

“Besides,” he says, “what they freely offer for the temple of God, which is in Jerusalem.” For those who abound in temporal wealth ought not merely to provide from it what is necessary for Christ’s poor; they should also willingly perform for themselves whatever good they can, so that through the merit of this voluntary offering they themselves may deserve to have a share in the temple of God, which is the Church.

The Fourth Book of the Commentaries of Rabanus Maurus on the Book of Chronicles ends.

When the book is finished, let praise and glory be to Christ;

Observe the final outcomes of all undertakings;

May almighty God preserve all who dwell here.

# EXPOSITION ON THE BOOK OF JUDITH

[Col. 0539]

## (IN THE YEAR 834.) EXPOSITION ON THE BOOK OF JUDITH BY THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

### DEDICATORY LETTER TO JUDITH AUGUSTA

(Mabillon, *Annals of the Holy Order of Saint Benedict.*)

[Col. 0539C] To the chosen Lady, rightly revered and loved by all for her great piety, Judith Augusta, Rabanus, servant of the servants of God, humbly wishes eternal salvation in Christ.

Since the exalted greatness of your majesty and the generosity of your kindness—which, instructed by the Lord’s own mouth, has learned to benefit not only friends but also enemies—make many devoted to you, we too, though only a very small part of the people entrusted to you by God and living under your protection, think that we ought to offer you devoted service.

Although we are not wealthy in resources of precious possessions, we are nevertheless not entirely lacking in the zeal of sacred prayers, which we unceasingly offer every day for you, and at the same time for your lord and your offspring. We pray that by his gift you may remain here in safety for a long time and in the future life always be happy and rejoicing.

Furthermore, because I have found that you excel in praiseworthy intelligence and imitate the virtues and devotion to good works of the holy women whom sacred Scripture commemorates, I have not thought it pointless to dedicate and send to your name the history of certain of them, translated by us into an allegorical meaning concerning the mystery of the holy Church—namely, Judith and Esther. You are the equal of one in name and of the other in dignity.

Because of their distinguished merit in virtue, they are worthy of imitation by men as well as women, since they conquered spiritual enemies by courage of spirit and bodily enemies by maturity of counsel.

So too, if your praiseworthy prudence, which has already overcome its enemies to no small extent, strives to persevere in the good work it has begun and to improve itself continually, it will happily overcome all its adversaries.

You still remain in the contest, and therefore it is necessary to implore divine help, so that he who conquered death by his own blood and took captive the author of death may produce for you a true victory in the contest of this world. Thus may he grant that, truly triumphing, you may reach the joys of eternal blessedness.

Receive, then, your namesake Judith, an example of chastity, and proclaim her in perpetual praises with triumphal acclaim. Above all, bless him who granted her such virtue that she conquered the unconquered among all human beings and overcame the insuperable.

Likewise, keep before the eyes of your heart Esther, queen beside a queen, worthy of imitation in every act of piety and holiness, so that, equaling the merit of her holiness, you may be able to ascend from an earthly kingdom to the summit of the heavenly kingdom. Through the grace, of course, of him who caused those holy women to triumph and who will make his entire Church—which they prefigured—triumphant in perpetual victory and, with them, a possessor of the heavenly homeland: namely, Jesus, our God and Lord, who may deign to guard you within and without, here and everywhere, now and always.

We wish you well, Lady Augusta, mindful of us.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0541]

Supreme Sower of all things, who created everything by your word,

And rightly prepared all your work by your hand,

Adorning heaven with lights and the fields with flowering branches,

And thus revealing the laws of your divinity

To the blessed, so that we may know you as the supreme Father;

And always believe Christ, born equal to you.

For this sacred breath remains equal to you

In clear divinity and lives with you forever.

You are God, ruler and Savior of humankind,

Who distributes rewards to the righteous and punishment to those who deserve it.

As Creator, you perceive sex, persons, and ages,

And, most just of all, give each one his proper reward.

I also beseech you not to allow anyone to harm

The queen beloved by your kindness through deceit.

May you, as a mighty Judge, cause her to reign peacefully here,

And thus prepare Judith herself to enter heaven.

May she be deemed worthy to be called there by Christ’s gift,

Whom she gladly remembers and appeases here; may you also be everywhere

With her, so that she may be able to sing hymns and speak of you even among the stars.

May she not now become liable through a vow, as she strives toward the lofty summit of Olympus,

And in her mind seeks the dwelling of the ordered and blessed,

And longs for the seat beyond the ether which you have granted her,

Almighty Judge, who alone reigns in the citadel.

Here, Christ, you preserve your kingdom through the ages,

And those whom you save there, here you correct beforehand with kindness,

A severe King, just, holy, gentle, and beloved.

Make us willing, I pray, to fulfill your commands properly

By deeds worthy of faith, while observing your laws well.

So may we, joyfully following you as King toward the heavenly seat,

Climb up and take possession of peaceful kingdoms,

Where there is perpetual light of life and true praise and glory,

Where the Father, the Son, and the gracious Spirit reign—

The living, true, and supreme God and Creator,

Who, just through the ages, heals the small and the great,

And is the maker and judge of all, equitable toward everyone.

## THE EXPOSITION ON THE BOOK OF JUDITH BEGINS

[Col. 0541]

### CHAPTER ONE [Col. 0541C]

#### Concerning Arphaxad, king of the Medes, who, after conquering many nations, built the city of Ecbatana, and how he was afterward overcome by Nebuchadnezzar

“Now Arphaxad, king of the Medes, had subjected many nations to his rule, and he himself built a most powerful city, which he called Ecbatana.”

Some consider it necessary to inquire at what time and under which kings the history of Judith was produced. This is especially because the kings themselves are named in the history—namely, Arphaxad and Nebuchadnezzar—but among those who wrote the histories of the Assyrians or Medes they are not found inserted in the succession of the kings of either kingdom.

For the first king among the Assyrians who was able to rise above the others was Ninus. He is said to have founded in the region of the Assyrians a city bearing his name, namely Nineveh, which the Hebrews call Niniveh.

After waging war against and conquering very many nations, his final war was against Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, who is said to have been the first to discover magical arts. After killing him, Ninus himself also died.

After him, his wife Semiramis, queen of all Asia, restored the city of Babylon and established it as the capital of the Assyrian kingdom. Thus the Assyrian kingdom stood for a long time with its power unshaken.

But when Arbatus—whom others call Arbaces—the prefect of the Medes, himself a Mede by nation, killed his king Sardanapalus in Babylonia, he transferred the name and supreme power of the kingdom to the Medes. Thus the kingdom of Babylon passed to the Medes in the same year in which, among the Latins, Procas, the father of Amulius and Numitor and the grandfather of Rhea Silvia, the mother of Romulus, began to reign.

When Arbatus departed to the Medes, the Chaldeans retained part of the kingdom for themselves, because they claimed Babylon for themselves against the Medes. Thus authority over Babylonia belonged to the Medes, while ownership belonged to the Chaldeans. Yet, because of the ancient dignity of the royal city, the Chaldeans did not wish to call it theirs, but wished to call themselves its people.

Hence it happened that Nebuchadnezzar and the other kings after him down to Cyrus, although powerful through the strength of the Chaldeans and renowned under the name of Babylonia, are not counted among the distinguished kings in the succession and order of kings.

Indeed, at the time when Azariah, also called Uzziah, reigned in Jerusalem over the two tribes, and Jeroboam, son of Joash, had reigned over the ten tribes of Israel in Samaria, the Assyrian kingdom was destroyed by Arbatus and transferred to the Medes. In the meantime, affairs were conducted without rulers, until Dejoces became king and founded the city of Ecbatana.

During the intervening period the Chaldeans were dominant in their own right; separate successions of their kings are reported, as stated above. Finally, the Assyrian kings Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, and Sennacherib are described as having devastated the land of the Israelites and led them into captivity during those same times, before Dejoces had begun to reign in Media.

Our Nebuchadnezzar, however, devastated Jerusalem.

Nevertheless, we find the names of certain kings of the Medes introduced between Arbatus and Dejoces in the Chronicles. It is reported there that, after Arbatus had reigned for twenty-eight years, Sosarmus the Second reigned among the Medes for thirty years. After him, a third Mede reigned for forty years; after him, a fourth, Carduceas, for thirteen years; then Dejoces for fifty-four years. After Dejoces, Phraates reigned over that people for twenty years.

After him Cyaxares, or Diocles, reigned for thirty-two years. The text is corrupt at this point: it says that, on dying, he deprived Astyages “ex filia” of the empire and kingdom, transferred the kingdom of the Medes to the Persians, devastated Babylonia, and utterly destroyed its kingdom, killing Belshazzar, the great-grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, with Darius—his kinsman, namely the son of Astyages, aged sixty-two—as his helper, as Josephus testifies.

We have set this out so that the diligent reader, finding in the work mentioned above some knowledge of the kings of the Assyrians and Medes briefly summarized by us, may be better prepared, once the successions of the kings are known, to investigate the truth of the history and determine which succession of the aforesaid kings best agrees with the narrative.

Eusebius, however, asserts in his *Chronicles* that Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, who reigned eight years in Persia after his father had reigned for thirty years, is called Nebuchadnezzar the Second by the Hebrews, and that the history of Judith was written under him.

But since the history itself says that Arphaxad was king of the Medes and Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians, reigning in Nineveh, and that Nebuchadnezzar overcame the king of the Medes and defeated him, I do not see how the kingdom of the Assyrians, after being destroyed and devastated by the Medes and Persians, could again prevail over those same Medes if Cambyses is understood to be Nebuchadnezzar.

Unless perhaps we say that Cambyses himself, since he is described as attacking neighboring nations and conquering Egypt, defeated and subjected to his rule some king named Arphaxad who resisted him in Media, at a time when the kingdoms of the Assyrians and Persians were united.

But we compel no one against his will to follow this opinion. Let each person choose what seems useful to him, provided only that his interpretation does not conflict with the truth.

[Col. 0544A] “And he himself built a most powerful city, which he called Ecbatana, from squared and cut stones. He made its walls seventy cubits high and thirty cubits wide, and he set its towers at a height of one hundred cubits.”

Ecbatana is the metropolis of the province of Media. We said above that it was founded by Dejoces, king of the Medes. But since the present history relates that a very powerful city was built by Arphaxad, with walls of extraordinary height and breadth and towers of great height, we may understand that it was first founded by Dejoces but enlarged by Arphaxad, just as Josephus also relates.

He says that the prophet Daniel, under King Darius, constructed in that same city of Media a very splendid and astonishingly magnificent mausoleum. This monument, as Josephus himself says, still remains to the present day; those who see it believe that it was built as a marvel, so that on the very day on which it is seen one might think it had just been constructed. Its beauty appears so new and solid, and it has not been worn away by the old age brought by so long a passage of time, although buildings undergo the same processes as human beings: they grow old, reach decay, lose their strength through the passage of time, and wither through the loss of their proper beauty.

To the present day the kings of the Medes, Persians, and Parthians are buried there alike. The person entrusted with its care is a Jewish priest, and this continues even to the present time.

The text continues:

*[The supplied source ends here, after “The text continues:”]*
“And he gloried as though he were powerful through the strength of his army and in the splendor of his chariots.”

In the twelfth year of his reign, therefore, King Nebuchadnezzar of the Assyrians, who ruled in the great city of Nineveh, fought against Arphaxad and defeated him in the great plain called Ragau, near the Euphrates and the Tigris, and at Jadason, in the plain of Erioch, king of the Elymaeans.

Through the names of the places, the location of the peoples is indicated. For geographers also report that, from the River Indus, which is in the East, to the River Tigris, which is in the West, these are the regions: Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Persia, and Media—lands mountainous and rough in their terrain. To the north they have Mount Caucasus; to the south, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. In their midst are the principal rivers, the Idapes and the Arbiminus. Within them are thirty-two peoples. Generally, however, the region is called Parthia, although Sacred Scripture often calls the whole area Media, from the River Tigris to the Euphrates. Mesopotamia begins in the north, between Mount Taurus and Caucasus; to the south of it lies Babylonia, then Chaldaea, and finally Arabia Eudaimon, which extends between the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Gulf in a narrow strip of land and toward the mountain. In these regions are twenty-eight peoples. Thus it happened that two very powerful kingdoms, clashing with one another, assembled armies from the many peoples within their borders; and in the end victory fell to the Chaldaeans, or Assyrians.

Mystically, Arphaxad may be understood as a type of the arrogant and proud. Their entire effort and labor, carried on through the swelling of presumption and the exaltation of the mind, easily falls into the portion of the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar—that is, the devil. For he is, as Scripture testifies, “the king over all the sons of pride.” Hence what follows:

“Then the kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar was exalted, and his heart was lifted up.”

For when the ancient enemy, by deceiving and overcoming the multitude of the rebellious, subjects them to his will, then his heart is lifted up, attributing this to his own strength rather than to the promise of divine judgment. And he burns all the more fiercely to destroy many because he sees that, through wicked suggestion, he prevails over some and has many as leaders in their own destruction. Concerning him it is next added:

“And he sent to all who dwelt in Cilicia and Damascus, and to the peoples who are in Carmel and [Col. 0545B] Kedar, and to those inhabiting Galilee in the great plain of Esdraelon, and to all who were in Samaria, and beyond the Jordan as far as Jerusalem, and throughout the whole land of Jesse, until one reaches the mountains of Ethiopia.”

Through various provinces the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar sends his messengers, when he disperses crowds of evil spirits to lead peoples astray. He spares no one, whatever dignity or honor may be permitted to belong to him, but wishes to drag everyone with himself to Gehenna and make them partners in his own destruction. He extends the wickedness of his activity even to the faithful, nor does he permit them to be secure and at rest; this is figuratively shown by the names Jordan and Jerusalem. Nor is it enough for him to take the Gentiles captive through error; rather, if possible, he also strives to overthrow the elect themselves. Concerning this it is written in Job:

“He swallows up a river and is not astonished; he has confidence that the Jordan will flow into his mouth.”

And again:

“His food,” he says, “is choice.”

But although he surpasses many, he is nevertheless despised by many and, as is just, is indignantly resisted and rejected with his wicked suggestions, as the following demonstrates, where it is said:

“All with one accord contradicted them and sent them away empty and dishonored.”

But although the malignant enemy is sometimes overcome by the devout, he nevertheless does not desist from the wickedness he has begun. Rather, persisting in his insolence, he rekindles wars again and pours out the whole tumult of his fury. Hence it is added:

“Then King Nebuchadnezzar became indignant and swore by his throne and his kingdom against the whole land that he would avenge himself upon all these regions.”

## CHAPTER II. Concerning Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, who, because his messengers had been rejected, sent Holofernes, commander of the army, with an army to subjugate the whole West to him

“In the thirteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar, on the twenty-second day of the first month, the word came to the house of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, that he should avenge himself. He summoned all the elders and all his commanders and warriors, and he held with them the secret of his counsel. He declared that his intention was to subjugate the whole land to his rule.” [Col. 0546A]

What does it mean that Nebuchadnezzar, filled with fury and lifted up by the arrogance of pride, promises to avenge himself upon those who resisted him and boasts that he wishes to subjugate the whole earth to his rule, except that the devil, stirred up by his own pride, promises himself dominion over the entire world and struggles with all his might to withdraw people from the worship of piety and make them partners in his impiety?

Once, boasting of the power of his kingdom, he spoke in his heart under the figure of the king of Babylon, according to the prophet’s declaration, saying:

“I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne. I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High.”

He also, leading our Redeemer onto an exceedingly high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said:

“All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.”

For arrogance knows no moderation, and its weakness has a sure fall, which will become clear at the end.

“King Nebuchadnezzar summoned Holofernes, commander of his army, and said to him: Go forth against every kingdom of the West, and especially against those who have despised my rule. Let your eye spare no kingdom, and you shall subjugate every fortified city to me.”

We may understand this Holofernes either as the ruler of the nations who persecuted the Church of Christ, or even as the head of all the wicked, the final son of perdition, who exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that, sitting in the temple of God, he displays himself as though he were God himself. Satan will enter wholly into him, so that he may do what his fathers did not do, nor the fathers of his fathers; he will not regard the God of his fathers, nor care for any god.

According to Daniel’s prophecy, he will rise up against all things and come in great multitude to crush and kill many. He will fix his tent broadly between the seas, upon the glorious and holy mountain, where he will also be crushed by divine power and fall.

According to the Apocalypse, the dragon also gave the beast his strength and power, and they worshiped the beast, saying:

“Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?”

And a mouth was given to it, speaking great things and blasphemy; and authority was given to it to act for forty-two months. It opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his dwelling, and those who dwell in heaven. It was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them. Authority was given to it over every tribe and people and language and nation. All who dwell on the earth will worship it, those whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world.

Through the deception of Antichrist and his false power, the devil promises himself dominion over the whole world. His eye will spare no kingdom, because he will arouse the greatest persecution throughout the entire world. For there will be, as the Gospel testifies, tribulations such as have not been from the beginning of creation, which God created, until now, nor will there be. And unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days.

Therefore, concerning the historical Holofernes, Scripture adds:

“And he went up against all their strongholds and seized every fortification.”

So that the ferocity and cruelty of the typological Holofernes may be expressed: he goes up against every stronghold and seizes every fortification, when he casts down and overthrows many of those who seemed to possess firmness of faith and excellence of virtue—partly by deceit, and partly also by open persecution—from the state of true religion.

“And he breaks down all their lofty cities,” because from among our shepherds, who have been set over the Lord’s flock, he breaks some by his cunning and plunders all their wealth. He takes captive the breadth of their knowledge, together with the other instruments by which they ought to have served God, through the allurements of pleasures, or compels them into open blasphemy and turns them to the use of his own service. Those who resist him he kills with the edge of the sword, because those whom he cannot bend to consent to his wickedness he strives to destroy by bodily death.

“He plundered all the sons of Tharsis and the sons of Ishmael, who were opposite the desert, and to the south of the land of Cellon; and he crossed the Euphrates and came into Mesopotamia.”

Through the various provinces and the names of the different places contained in the history, a distinction is signified among eighteen persons of great rank and dignity, from all of whom the devil strives to claim some portion for himself. He does not fear undertaking the difficulty of any struggle; rather, stirred by his own wickedness, he strives to bring about the grievous ruin of great power.

“After this he descended into the plains of Damascus during the days of harvest, burned all the crops, had all the trees and vineyards cut down, and his fear fell upon all who inhabited the land.”

What power of Gentile domination is expressed by Damascus—which is interpreted as “drinking of blood”—except that which eagerly thirsts to pour out the blood of the faithful, that is, of Christ’s martyrs, especially in that final persecution which will come near the end of the world, when the time of harvest, that is, the consummation of the age, approaches?

Then, through the most savage command of the second true Holofernes—that is, Antichrist—a very severe persecution will be stirred up throughout the breadth of the entire world against the universal Church. Whatever is green in the crops, whatever is flowering in the trees, or fruitful in the spiritual vineyards—for all this is found useful, delightful, and fruitful in holy men—he strives to lay waste entirely with the sword of persecution and burn with the flame of envy.

Hence what follows occurs:

“And his fear fell upon all who inhabited the land.”

For carnal hearts, bound by love of earthly things, tremble when they hear and see the savagery of this enemy. But those who, stripped of earthly cares and the enticements of carnal pleasures, can say with the Apostle:

“Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh, and our citizenship is in heaven. From there also we await our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who has transformed the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory,”

are not terrified by the temporal persecution of their enemies. Rather, lifting the eyes of their minds, they joyfully await the coming of their Judge and Redeemer, knowing that he is near.

## CHAPTER III. Where Holofernes, laying waste the provinces, received the envoys of various regions who had been sent to him and surrendered themselves and all they possessed to him; nevertheless, he destroyed their cities and gods

“Then the kings and princes of all the cities and provinces of Syria—that is, of Mesopotamia and Syria, Sobal and Libya and Cilicia—sent their envoys. Coming to Holofernes, they said: Let your indignation toward us cease. For it is better that, while alive, we serve the great King Nebuchadnezzar and be subject to you than that, dying, we should suffer the losses of our servitude together with our destruction.”

When Holofernes was laying waste the land of many peoples, kings and princes from various cities and places sent envoys to flatter and appease him—that is, from Syria, Mesopotamia, Libya, and Cilicia. For when the persecutor rages in the world, possessors of wealth, the powerful of the age, and lovers of earthly pleasures strive to reconcile the wicked ruler to themselves, so far as they can escape the danger of death and the loss of the things they desire.

Indeed, it is difficult—rather, impossible—for lovers of the world to become true lovers of the Lord, as Scripture says:

“Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God.”

And the Apostle John says:

“If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

Likewise, in the Gospel, the Lord spoke to his disciples concerning the rich man who possessed many properties and became sad at the word of God:

“Amen I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Elsewhere in the Gospel, in the parable of the sower, he says among other things:

“What was sown among thorns is the one who hears the word, but the anxiety of this age and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless.”

The names of the provinces mentioned above appropriately reveal the same meaning through their interpretation. For Syria is interpreted as “lofty,” or “thickets,” or “vain old age”; Mesopotamia as “elevated”; Libya as “of the one coming” or “of the one entering”; Cilicia as “assembly,” “mourning,” or “his vomit.”

Therefore, whoever slips downward in his heart through earthly desires and is lifted up by worldly pride, following the vanity of the old person, and entering the land by two roads, will undoubtedly be joined in hell to the assembly of mourners and of those who pay the penalty for their lust.

And according to the saying of the Book of Job:

“He passes from snow waters to excessive heat,”

where, according to the Gospel’s declaration:

“Their worm will not die, and the fire will not be quenched.”

“Then he descended from the mountains with horsemen in great strength and seized every city and every inhabitant of the land. From all the cities he took for himself strong and chosen men as auxiliaries for war. Such fear weighed upon those provinces that the inhabitants of all the cities—rulers and honored men together with the peoples—went out to meet the one who was coming, receiving him with crowns and lamps and leading dances with tambourines and flutes. Yet even by doing these things they could not mitigate the ferocity of his heart; for he also destroyed their cities and cut down their sacred groves.”

A savage multitude of persecutors descends from the mountains with horsemen, when it proceeds outward from the wicked counsel of a proud mind to perpetrate evil actions. He seizes the city and every inhabitant of the land when he turns carnal minds and their works to the use of his wickedness.

Strong and vigorous men from the cities serve as his auxiliaries in war, when he gathers from every side those whom he sees flourishing in cleverness of mind and bodily strength in order to exercise his malice, so that he may oppress the crowd of the innocent more forcefully the more he draws the companionship of many into agreement with his deception. And when he sees that he pleases the minds of some through earthly delights, he uses their efforts to overthrow the life of the simple completely.

Yet even Christians who carry out his will do not escape his ferocity by doing these things. Once he has fulfilled through them the contrivance of his deceit against others, he will consequently complete their destruction as well.

Hence it is added:

“He destroyed their cities and cut down their sacred groves.”

For not only does an evil end scatter their wicked deeds, but after the death of the body the fire of eternal punishment also torments their souls because of their pretense—the pretense by which they imagined that they could sin with impunity.

The author of this wickedness is in no way concealed; rather, he is revealed by the subsequent sentence, where it is said:

“For King Nebuchadnezzar had commanded him to exterminate all the gods of the land, so that he alone might be called God by those nations that could be subjugated by the power of Holofernes.”

For the devil himself, who is ruler and head of all the wicked, plots this through hidden snares and contrives it through open persecutions: that the entire thought and labor of earthly beings may be changed into his worship and that he himself may dominate all.

Nor is this surprising, since he attempts to do this among human beings when, through the deceit of his fraud, he dared to attack the Man who is God. Leading him onto a high mountain and showing him all the glory of the world, he tested him with this wicked speech:

“All these things I will give you if you will fall down and worship me.”

But, confounded, he departed from him, in whom he had achieved no result of his wickedness. Indeed, he lost the dominion of his power over us, because our victory is our Head, “who bound the strong man and plundered his goods,” and, destroying death itself by his death, rose triumphantly in glory,

“so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld, and every tongue should confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

## CHAPTER IV. Where the children of Israel, learning of Holofernes’ arrival, were greatly terrified and began to prepare fortifications and cry out to the Lord with the greatest urgency; and concerning the great priest Eliachim, who exhorted the children of Israel to trust in the Lord’s presence, so that they would not fear the attack of their enemies

“Then the children of Israel who dwelt in the land of Judah, hearing these things, were greatly afraid before him. Trembling and horror seized their minds, lest he should do to Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord what he had done to the other cities and their temples. And they sent throughout all Samaria round about as far as Jericho, and occupied all the summits of the mountains, surrounded their villages with walls, and gathered grain in preparation for battle.” [Col. 0550B]

While the persecutor raged, fear and trembling seized the Israelites, lest he should do to Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord what he had done to the other cities and their temples. So too the Church of Christ, compassionating the weakness of infirm souls entrusted to her care and fearing the fall of those who are inexperienced in the faith, strives to guard against the savagery and cunning of the ancient enemy, lest through his executioners—that is, pagans, Jews, and heretics—he deceive the hearts of the innocent and bring about a grave ruin among the people of the Lord.

For this reason it is said that the Israelites, sending forces all around, occupied all the summits of the mountains. The authority of the holy Church stirs the zeal of its superiors so that, with every intention, prayer, and exhortation, it may strengthen and preserve unharmed those who are upright and exalted in the pursuit of virtue. Thus, if the enemy should anywhere attempt to break into the camp of the Church through the injury of the simple, he may quickly be driven back by the strength and power of the faith of these men.

They surround their villages with walls when they strive to fortify those entrusted to them on every side with the shield of faith and the bulwark of virtues. They gather grain in preparation for battle when they store up the sayings of Sacred Scripture and the food of heavenly doctrine as nourishment for faithful souls, lest perhaps they despair through hunger for the divine word and become prey to spiritual enemies.

“The priest Eliachim also wrote to all who were opposite Esdraelon, which is opposite the great plain near Dothain, and to all through whom the roads could be traversed, instructing them to occupy the mountain passes by which there could be a road to Jerusalem and to guard the places where the way between the mountains could be narrow.”

The priest Eliachim, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord’s resurrection,” designates none more appropriately than our Redeemer, who says in the Gospel:

“I am the resurrection and the life.”

This priest therefore writes to all who were opposite the great plain near Dothain when, through the evangelical Scriptures, he warns all his faithful and devoted servants who fight against the pleasures of the world and carnal desires—which lead to the loss of life and eternal death—to guard the ascents of the mountains, that is, the subtlety of anyone’s understanding, lest heretical cunning find there a subtle path and through it introduce a destructive error into the camp of the Church.

For just as sharpness of understanding is of great benefit in those who, fearing God, humbly preserve the sincerity of the Catholic faith, so it is of great harm in those who, despising the fear of the Lord, do not hesitate in their pride to construct harmful sects against the faith.

But true Israelites, admonished by the writings of their priest and instructed in the sayings of the divine Testaments, obey the commandments through the way of their teacher. Hence what follows takes place:

“And all the people cried out to the Lord with great urgency, and they humbled their souls with fasting and prayers, both they and their wives. The priests put on sackcloth, and the children prostrated themselves before the temple of the Lord. They covered the altar of the Lord with sackcloth, and they cried out unanimously to the Lord God.”

They humble their souls with fasting, both they and their wives, who, through salutary continence, not only mortify the flesh but also discipline their minds by restraining them from unlawful desires. They prostrate the children before the temple, when they offer the prayers of the innocent humbly and tearfully before the sight of the Lord’s glory.

The priests put on sackcloth and cover the altar of the Lord with sackcloth when the teachers of the Gospel and leaders of God’s people assume, together with the people, both devotion and the practice of penitence, so that they may reconcile divine majesty to themselves and obtain his merciful compassion.

They themselves are the altar of the Lord who continually sacrifice an offering of praise upon the altar of their hearts. Sackcloth, woven from goats’ hair, represents sinners, for whom penitence is necessary, since without it sinners themselves do not find remedies for true salvation.

It should also be known that a great and especially important help in devout prayers is provided when meditation on the Lord’s Passion is applied. This Passion was completed upon the altar of the cross for our sins, because the blood of our Redeemer was poured out not only for our offenses but also as an expiation for all the sins of the whole world.

Concerning this John says:

“We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.”

“And they cried out,” he says, “unanimously to the Lord God of Israel, that their children might not be given over as prey, their wives as spoil, their cities to destruction, and their holy places to pollution.”

For the unanimity of the Church merits swift hearing before the Lord’s mercy, and the enemy’s wickedness cannot prevail against those for whom the labor of charity and unanimity strives.

Hence Paul teaches us to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace and to be unanimous in prayers. For, according to James:

“The prayer of a righteous person has great power.”

And Peter says:

“Charity covers a multitude of sins.”

“Then Eliachim, the great priest of the Lord, went around all Israel and spoke to them, saying: Know that the Lord has heard your prayers, if you remain steadfast in fasting and prayers before the Lord.”

For the spiritual Eliachim, our true priest, who has been made a high priest for us by God according to the order of Melchizedek, goes around the camp of the Church not only by himself in the time of his incarnation but also now in his apostles and teachers of the Gospel. He warns his faithful to guard against the snares of the ancient enemy and exhorts them to persevere steadfastly in the strength of faith and in constancy of prayer, which wins for them certain victory over all enemies.

Hence it is read in the Gospel that Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. Elsewhere he himself says to his disciples:

“Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man.”

For this reason Peter exhorts them, saying:

“Be sober and watch in prayers, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes around seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith.”

The examples of strong men also assist in waging this battle—men who displayed the excellence of right faith to all their enemies and constantly overcame them through the strength of their virtues.

Therefore Eliachim introduced the example of Moses, who fought against Amalek more by prayer than by weapons of war. Paul likewise, praising the strength of faith in the Letter to the Hebrews, summoned the abundant examples of the fathers as witnesses:

“Through faith they conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained promises.”

Concerning this James also says:

“Take, brothers, as an example of labor and patience the prophets who spoke in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“Therefore, in response to his exhortation, they continued praying to the Lord in his presence. Even those who offered holocausts to the Lord offered sacrifices to the Lord girded with sackcloth, and there was ashes upon their heads. And all prayed to God with their whole heart, that he might visit his people Israel.”

The faithful, strengthened by the exhortation of their preachers, remain in prayer, and all the more because they are stirred by the examples of good teachers, who say and do according to the Lord’s command.

The priests of the Church of Christ offer holocausts to the Lord girded with sackcloth when, crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires, they dedicate their whole life to God. They also offer sacrifices to the Lord when they offer an offering of praise with devoted mouth and heart.

Ashes are placed upon their heads when, mindful of their own frailty, with a contrite and humbled heart they pour out tears before the Lord for the salvation of the true Israel, so that, delivered from their enemies, they may reach the presence of their Redeemer.

## CHAPTER V. How Holofernes, hearing that the children of Israel had closed the mountain passes, was greatly angered and asked his princes where the children of Israel originated and what their strength was; Achior gave him a fuller answer concerning this. The princes of Holofernes became angry at his account

“It was reported to Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, that the children of Israel were preparing to resist and had closed the mountain passes. He burned with great fury and anger, summoned all the princes of Moab and the commanders of Ammon, and said to them: Tell me who this people is that occupies the mountains; what and of what kind and how great are their cities; what their strength is; what their numbers are; who is the king of their army; and why, above all who dwell in the East, these people have despised us and have not come out to meet us and receive us in peace.” [Col. 0553B]

It is announced typologically to Holofernes that the children of Israel are preparing to resist and closing the mountain passes, because this becomes known to all the persecutors of the holy Church who obey the devil’s will as members obey the head: that those who believe in Christ the Lord have decided with faithful courage to resist evil and detest all pride, through which the adversaries strive especially to break in and prevail.

The irritated enemy asks with wonder where they have such great steadfastness of mind, what fortress of faith they possess, who their king is, and what army has such strength that no power can resist it. They are rightly said to dwell in the East, because they always desire to be illumined by the light of faith and the radiance of knowledge, so that they may more easily conquer and drive back the forces of darkness.

“Then Achior, commander of all the children of Ammon, answered and said: If you deign to listen, my lord, I will speak the truth in your presence concerning this people who dwell in the mountains, and no false word will come from my mouth. This people is from the offspring of the Chaldaeans. They first dwelt in Mesopotamia, because they did not wish to follow the gods of their fathers, who were in the land of the Chaldaeans. Therefore, abandoning the ceremonies of their fathers, which consisted in a multitude of gods, they worshiped the one God of heaven, who also commanded them to depart from there and dwell in Choran.”

Through Achior, commander of the children of Ammon, who, although devoted to idolatry, nevertheless proclaimed certain truths concerning divine works and miracles, those may appropriately be understood who have not yet been reborn through the baptism of Christ and have not perfectly learned the Catholic faith, yet have heard certain notable teachings of the Gospel and do not fear to proclaim them to the knowledge of others because they agree with our faith.

Although such people do not refuse to fight against the unity of the Church together with the other persecutors of the Christian faith, nevertheless, overcome by the reason of truth, they cannot conceal the truth entirely; rather, they often bring it forth in clear statements.

Thus, in the Book of Job, Job’s friends, who had come to console him over the affliction that had befallen him, inflicted injury instead of consolation. Nevertheless, they stated some things truthfully, although they did not agree with the truth in every respect.

Heretics have this characteristic: they mix good things with evil so that they may easily deceive the understanding of the hearer. For if they said wicked things, they would quickly be recognized in their wickedness and would persuade no one of what they wished. Again, if they always thought rightly, they would certainly not have been heretics. But while, by the art of deception, they serve both sides, they infect good things with evil and conceal evil things within good things so that they may be received.

It is like one who offers a cup of poison touching the rim of the cup with the sweetness of honey. When what is sweet is tasted at the first touch, what is deadly is nevertheless unquestionably swallowed.

Thus heretics, although they mix what is right with what is perverse—so that by hearing good things they may attract listeners to themselves and, by presenting evil things, secretly corrupt them with a plague—are nevertheless sometimes saved from this perversity of their understanding by the preaching of the holy Church and by exhortation that corrects them.

So it was with Achior: seeing Judith’s victory, he abandoned his former error, joined himself to the Israelites through belief, circumcised the flesh of his foreskin, and was added to the people of God.

The friends of Job likewise offer the sacrifice of their reconciliation through the hands of the holy man and, whether condemned or recalled, are restored to the grace of the heavenly Judge. They are represented, however, by the healing of the ten lepers in the Gospel. For in leprosy one part of the skin is turned white while another part remains of healthy color.

Thus lepers represent heretics, who, while mixing what is perverse with what is right, sprinkle the healthy color with stains. Therefore, in order to be saved, they rightly cry out:

“Jesus, Teacher.”

For by signifying that they have erred in his words, they humbly call him their teacher and the one who can save them.

“When Achior had finished speaking these words, all the nobles of Holofernes became angry and considered killing him. They said to one another: Who is this man to say that the children of Israel can resist King Nebuchadnezzar and his armies—unarmed men, without strength and without knowledge of the art of war? Therefore, so that Achior may know that he has deceived us, let us go up into the mountains; and when their powerful men have been captured, then he too shall be pierced through with the sword together with them.”

The nobles of Holofernes become angry when they hear the testimony of the truth. So those who are proud in worldly arrogance are provoked by the Gospel’s testimony concerning the power of Christ. They threaten to kill his preachers together with the rest of the faithful, despising them outwardly as unarmed men incapable of battle, because inwardly they cannot perceive the strength of their spirit and the power of their faith, by which they fight invisibly against spiritual enemies.

As though they were a doomed crowd, they order the heralds of truth to be handed over, not realizing that they themselves have been deceived by the false hope of their own power.

Hence in the Gospel the Jews, who because of their faithlessness were typologically approaching the ranks of Holofernes, spoke to the man born blind after the Savior had illuminated him and they had expelled him from the synagogue, insulting and cursing him:

“You are his disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.”

They considered him lost because, separated from their fellowship, he had attached himself to the discipleship of the Redeemer; yet by then they had resolved to crucify him and hand him over to death.

Thus what happened to Achior rightly applies to such people, as Scripture records when it says:

## CHAPTER VI. Holofernes orders the priest Achior to be led to Bethulia and bound to a tree; the children of Israel released him from his bonds, brought him to Bethulia, and consoled him
“Then Holofernes ordered his servants to seize Achior, lead him to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites. So Holofernes’ servants seized Achior and set out with him across the plain. But when they had approached the mountains, slingers came out against them. They, however, turned aside along the flank of the mountain, bound Achior to a tree by his hands and feet, and thus left him tied with ropes; then they returned to their master.”

Holofernes’ servants lead the captured Achior across the plain when the persecutors of the Catholic faith desire to drag Christ’s confessors toward unlawful desires and onto the broad and spacious way of the world that leads to death. But when they approach the mountain, slingers come out against them and drive them away in terror with their missiles, because men of courage, who more frequently cling to heavenly contemplation, disturb the malicious with the arrows of their testimonies. But when they cannot bring their desire to fulfillment, they resolve to bind him hand and foot to a tree. Since they cannot lead Christ’s soldier astray by wicked persuasion, they strive to make him a participant in his cross and death. They return to their master because, not corrected but rather corrupted, they return to the service of their former master through the increase of their crimes.

“Then the Israelites came down from Bethulia to him; they released him and led him to Bethulia, setting him in the midst of the people. They asked him what had happened, and why the Assyrians had left him bound.”

What does it mean that the Israelites release Achior, who was tied to a tree, except that the teachers of the Church teach their catechumens not to fear the persecutors’ punishments—neither battle nor even death itself? To be released as though from being tied to a tree means that the fearful mind is strengthened by sound discourse against fear of the cross, and for suffering on behalf of Christ by evangelical teachings and the examples of the saints. This is rightly done if, following the example of those leaders—namely Ozias and Charmi, who comforted Achior and poured out devout prayers with all the people—the teachers of the Church strive, together with the rest of the faithful, to commend their hearers to the Lord in pious prayers, so that by his gift what human weakness cannot provide may be bestowed.  
[Col. 0555D]

“Then Ozias, when the council had ended, received him into his house, prepared a great feast for him, and, after all the presbyters had been summoned, they refreshed themselves together when the fast was completed. Afterwards the whole people were convened, and throughout the night they prayed inside the Church, asking help from the God of Israel.”

He prepares a great feast after the fast has ended who refreshes a languishing soul, long in need of the bread of God’s word, with evangelical teachings and the nourishment of virtues, adding all the presbyters to this banquet. For it is highly appropriate that presbyters and men of virtue be gathered for the instruction of neophytes, so that through their encouragement and examples the neophytes may be strengthened to perfect and preserve the faith they have received. Christ’s apostles did this when, to extend the preaching of the Gospel, they appointed men of holy order to assist them, so that the seed of the Gospel might be scattered far and wide throughout the whole expanse of the world by many preachers, and abundant fruit might be brought into Christ’s granary by many harvesters. The Truth himself also seems to have commanded this to those same disciples when he says in the Gospel: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for the harvest.” And again: “The harvest,” he says, “is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.”  
[Col. 0556A–B]

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Holofernes’ leading his army to Bethulia, ordering its water conduit to be cut, and keeping its people away from the springs; and concerning the citizens of Bethulia, pressed by lack of water, coming to Ozias and asking that the city be handed over to Holofernes, while he persuades them to wait five more days.

“On the following day Holofernes ordered his armies to go up against Bethulia. But when the Israelites saw their multitude, they threw themselves on the ground, putting ashes on their heads and praying unanimously that the God of Israel would show his mercy to his people. They took up their weapons of war and sat in the places that lead into the narrow passage between the mountains, keeping watch over them all day and all night.”  
[Col. 0556C]

The spiritual Holofernes, the most certain enemy of God’s people, urges his soldiers to go up against Bethulia—that is, against the Catholic Church, which is the house of God, built from living stones—so that they may remove from it and destroy by deceit as many as they can. But the Israelites cry out unanimously to the Lord, asking him to show his mercy to his people. They take up their weapons of war—that is, the practices of sacred virtues—and guard the narrow places of the road, namely, the inner chambers of their mind, lest the deceitful enemy find an open entrance anywhere through which he may introduce carnal delight by means of a harmful thought.  
[Col. 0556D]

“While Holofernes was making his circuit, he discovered that the spring which flowed into their water conduit was directed from the southern side outside the city, and he ordered their conduit to be cut. Yet there were springs not far from the walls, from which they seemed secretly to draw water, more for refreshment than for drinking. But the Ammonites and Moabites approached Holofernes and said: ‘The Israelites do not trust in spear or arrow; the mountains defend them, and they fortify the hills, being stationed on precipices. Therefore, so that you may overcome them without engaging in battle, place guards over the springs, so that they may not draw water from them; then you will kill them without a sword, or at least, exhausted, they will surrender their city.’”  
[Col. 0557A]

What does it mean that Holofernes orders the water conduit—which carried water from the spring into the city on its southern side—to be cut, except that the persecutors of the faithful forbid and threaten with death the removal of the Gospel teaching which holy teachers, illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, bring from the living spring into the city of the Church through the conduit of their mouths? They do this so that, deprived of vital drink, the faithful may first endure thirst in their souls, and so that afterward they may overthrow them completely by the punishments they inflict.

But there were springs from which they seemed secretly to draw water, both for refreshment and for drinking. At the prompting of the Ammonites and Moabites, the wicked plunderer likewise ordered these to be guarded, so that the Israelites might have no refreshment from them. What are these small springs from which the citizens of Bethulia secretly drank except the teachings of philosophers, which seem to offer the children of the Church some solace of knowledge and uprightness, both in philosophical and moral teaching and also in contemplative doctrine? But this harmful persecutor, likewise at the urging of the wicked, tries to take these away, so that, pressed on every side by the greatest deprivation, they may suddenly be left helpless.

Thus it is also read in the Book of Kings that the Philistines, having removed the ironworkers, took precautions lest they make a sword or spear for the Hebrews. Therefore all Israel descended to the Philistines so that each man might sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, and his hoe. This is what the devil strives with the greatest effort to accomplish: through his ministers to remove from the Church the rudiments of learning and the weapons of virtue, so that he may complete his wickedness in the destruction of God’s servants.  
[Col. 0557B–C]

It is also read in histories that the leaders of the nations, and especially Julian the Apostate, deprived Christians not only of divine philosophy but also of human philosophy by forbidding it. Yet God’s power—which, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, teaches his chosen not only through words but also through inward inspiration—does not abandon those who place their trust in him, but, according to the Psalmist: “He will redeem the souls of his servants, and none of those who hope in him will be condemned.”

“Then all the men and women, the young men and the children, gathered together to Ozias and said with one voice: ‘Let God judge between us and you, because you have done us harm by refusing to speak peaceably with the Assyrians; and for this reason God has sold us into their hands. Therefore there is no one to help us when we fall before their eyes in thirst and great destruction. Now gather together everyone who is in the city, so that we may all voluntarily surrender ourselves to Holofernes. For it is better that, as captives, we bless the Lord while alive than that we die and become a reproach to all flesh.’”  
[Col. 0557D]

This is the voice of the carnal, who remain in the Church by faith alone but are very far removed from it in their conduct. They resemble the parable in the Gospel in which the bad fish are said to be enclosed with the good in the Lord’s net until they are finally separated on the shore of the future judgment. These people, bearing heavily the troubles of the present life, believe it better to enjoy present pleasures than to suffer bodily punishments for Christ’s name and be rewarded for this with heavenly goods in the future. Such people frequently burden their teachers with unreasonable complaints and compel them to follow the luxury of the world. Hence he continues:  
[Col. 0558A]

“When they had grown weary from these cries and, exhausted by these tears, had fallen silent, Ozias arose, suffused with tears, and said: ‘Be of good courage, brothers, and let us wait these five days for mercy from the Lord. Perhaps he will turn away his indignation and give glory to his name. But if help does not come after the five days have passed, we will do what you have said.’”

These five days may be understood as the five bodily senses with which the present life is spent. For the sluggish teacher who indiscriminately promises his hearers bodily comfort to be given by the Lord in the present seems to ask for a respite of five days, as though the generosity of the supreme Giver were in his own hand, although the time and manner of giving lie more in the power of the giver than of the recipient. But if the supreme Judge refuses to grant them the benefit of the present life according to his promise, they immediately permit them to turn toward unlawful desire and, by yielding to their persecutors, to avoid bodily punishment. Our Judith—that is, the holy Church—rejects this agreement and despises it as harmful, as will be clearly shown in what follows.  
[Col. 0558B]

## CHAPTER VIII. Where Judith rebukes the presbyters Chabri and Charmi because the leader Ozias set a day of liberation for the Lord; and where, preparing herself to deliver the people, she does not wish anyone to inquire what she is about to do.  
[Col. 0558C]

“When Judith the widow heard these words—she was the daughter of Merari, son of Idox, son of Joseph, son of Ozias, son of Elai, son of Jamnor, son of Gedeon, son of Raphaim, son of Achitob, son of Melchias, son of Enan, son of Nathaniah, son of Salathiel, son of Simeon, son of Reuben—and her husband was Manasses, who died during the days of the barley harvest. For he was standing over those binding sheaves in the field, and the heat came upon his head, and he died in Bethulia, in his own city, and was buried there with his ancestors. Judith had been left a widow for three years and six months. In the upper part of her house she had made herself a private chamber, in which she remained shut in with her maidservants. She wore sackcloth around her loins and fasted all the days of her life, except on Sabbaths, new moons, and the festivals of the house of Israel. She was exceedingly beautiful in appearance. Her husband had left her great wealth, a large household, and estates filled with herds of oxen and flocks of sheep. She was most renowned among all people because she greatly feared the Lord, and no one could speak an evil word about her.

“When Judith heard that Ozias had promised that, after the fifth day had passed, he would surrender the city, she sent for the presbyters Chabri and Charmi. They came to her, and she said to them: ‘What is this word to which Ozias has consented—that he will surrender the city to the Assyrians if help does not come to you within five days? Who are you, that you tempt the Lord? This is not speech that calls forth mercy, but rather speech that arouses anger and kindles fury. You have set a time for the Lord’s mercy and appointed a day for him according to your own judgment. But because the Lord is patient, let us repent of this very thing and ask his indulgence with poured-out tears. For God will not threaten as a human being does, nor will he be inflamed to anger as a son of man is. Therefore let us humble our souls before him, and, remaining in a humbled spirit, let us serve him and say to the Lord with tears that he should show us his mercy according to his will.’”  
[Col. 0559A]

The tradition of the teachers demonstrates that Judith bears the type of the Church. Her name means “confessing” or “praising,” and she is the daughter of Merari—that is, of bitterness—because through the tribulation and bitterness of the present life the soul reaches future joys, where, even in mortal flesh, the holy soul will praise God forever.

The fact that this same Judith is found in Scripture as born in the fifteenth generation signifies that our Church was produced from the patriarchs and apostles through the sixfold and eightfold division of the Law and the Gospel, and destined to merit heavenly glory. For this number of steps is mystically placed in the Psalter and presents a type of the future ascent to heaven, to which the saints attain and can rightly say: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.”

She had Manasses as her husband; his name is interpreted as “forgotten” or “roused.” He stood during the barley harvest over those binding sheaves in the field, and when the heat came upon his head, he died. This signifies that whether joined and subject to the Decalogue of the Law or to the rite of paganism in ancient times, she was nevertheless associated with and bound to these things. But when Christ came and the sun of the Gospel shone forth, all that carnal observance ceased; and, like the gathering of an inferior harvest, it came swiftly to an end. She was therefore transferred through Christ to spiritual cultivation.

The apostle Paul demonstrates this in many passages. Writing to the Galatians, he says: “Before faith came, we were kept under the Law, shut up for the faith that was to be revealed. Thus the Law was our pedagogue to Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue. For you are all sons of God through faith, which is in Christ Jesus.”

And again: “I,” he says, “through the Law died to the Law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. Yet I live—not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live in faith in the Son of God.” And again: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.”

To the Romans he says: “My brothers, you have died to the Law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, who has risen from the dead.” And again: “The law of the Spirit of life has freed me from the law of sin and death; for Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.”

To the Ephesians he likewise says (Ephesians 2): “When you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air—the spirit who now works in the sons of unbelief—in whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved.”

And again: “Therefore remember that formerly you were Gentiles in the flesh, called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand; that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants, without hope of the promise and without God in this world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one and, by breaking down the middle wall of partition, the enmity in his flesh, abolished the Law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself. And coming, he preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near.”  
[Col. 0559B–560B]

The statement that Judith was left a widow for three years and six months after her husband’s death signifies that the Church, deprived of the allurements of the world, possesses faith in the Holy Trinity and perfection in good works. In the upper part of her house she made a private chamber in which she remained shut in with her maidservants, when she established a firm guard in the citadel of her mind, so that she might not flow away through various empty desires but, with pure thoughts, preserve herself undefiled in the sight of her Creator.

She wore sackcloth around her loins and fasted every day because, through self-control and the mortification of pleasures, she crucified earthly desires within herself and restrained the lusts of the flesh. She prepared herself entirely for the festivals of the future life and for the Sabbath of souls in the heavenly kingdom, where, in place of present tribulation, she will receive fullness of joy with the holy angels.

Her husband had left her great wealth, a numerous household, and estates full of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep. This signifies that, whether from the instruction of the Old Law or from the training of philosophical teaching together with moral disciplines, the Church, coming to Christ, preserved for herself manifold riches of knowledge. Hence the Teacher of the Gentiles also gloried that he had been trained at the feet of Gamaliel, who was an honored teacher of the Law. Moses too is read to have been educated in the wisdom and learning of the Egyptians.

If anyone dislikes the interpretation by which I said that Manasses, Judith’s husband, signifies either the Decalogue of the Law or the pagan rite, he may transfer it, in a more joyful mystery, to Christ, who is the true Bridegroom of the Church. He may rightly be called Manasses because he will make us forget our former calamity through the consolation of the future life.  
[Col. 0560C–561A]

Thus, during the days of the barley harvest—that is, at the conversion of the Jewish people—when he sent his apostles to preach the Gospel and gather believing sheaves from the land of the Israelites, heat came upon his head when they stirred up persecution against him on account of his divinity. The head of Christ is God. The Jews were especially scandalized because he said that his Father was God, saying to him: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because, although you are a man, you make yourself God.” And to Pilate they said: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

Thus the Lord Jesus suffered among his own people and was buried in the Jerusalem garden; on the third day he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, from there to come as judge of the living and the dead.

After her Bridegroom was taken from her, this bride therefore devoted herself to fasting and abstinence all the days of her life. Until the consummation of the age she preserves the chastity of faith and in no way consents to be polluted by the errors of heretics. Her husband had left her great wealth, clearly the wealth of spiritual wisdom and every virtue, and a numerous household, when he gathered to her an infinite multitude from all the nations. He also left estates consisting of herds of oxen and flocks of sheep, since he subjected to her not only those who could become useful in the Lord’s field but also those who would devote the innocence of their minds and their obedience through devoted action.  
[Col. 0561B]

She was most renowned among all because she greatly feared the Lord. Solomon explains her praises most fully near the end of his Proverbs, where, among other things, he says: “The woman who fears the Lord shall herself be praised; she is given the fruit of her hands, and her works praise her in the gates.” Hence Isaiah also says: “The fear of the Lord itself is his treasure.”

When Judith therefore heard that Ozias had promised to surrender the city after the fifth day, she rejected the decision, judging it unjust to set a time for the Lord’s mercy, since he alone above all knows both the time and the manner of his mercy. Therefore no one may presumptuously demand anything from the Lord, but should rather refer everything to his judgment, as it is read that one of the Fathers said only this in prayer: “Son of God, as you will and as you know, have mercy on me.”

Accordingly, in the Book of Daniel the three young men are read to have replied in this way to the most wicked king Nebuchadnezzar, who threatened to inflict punishments on them and blasphemed God’s power: “We have no need to answer you concerning this matter. For behold, our God whom we worship can rescue us from the furnace of fire and deliver us from your hands, O king. But if he does not wish to, let it be known to you, O king, that we do not worship your gods, nor do we adore the golden statue that you have erected.”

Therefore a Christian, to whom the glory of the heavenly kingdom has been promised, ought in no way to struggle excessively for the comforts of the present life or make disorderly demands of the Lord. The one who has given greater things will himself also provide the lesser. Concerning him the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek all these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”

Hence the Apostle also says: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all people the most pitiable.” Therefore let the present life be used by the faithful, but the future life be the fruit of salvation. Let temporal things be desired along the journey, eternal things upon arrival; let whatever is done in this world be viewed as though from the side, while the eyes of the mind look ahead, wholly intent on contemplating those things to which we shall attain.  
[Col. 0561C–562A]

“And now, brothers, since you are presbyters among God’s people and their souls depend on you, lift up their hearts by your speech, so that they may remember that our fathers were tested, to determine whether they truly worshiped their God. They ought to remember how our father Abraham was tested and, proven through many tribulations, became God’s friend. So Isaac, so Jacob, so Moses, and all who pleased God passed faithfully through many tribulations. But those who did not accept trials with fear of the Lord, and who brought their impatience and the reproach of their murmuring against the Lord, were destroyed by the destroyer and perished by serpents.”  
[Col. 0562B]

The courageous deeds of former leaders are salutary lessons for the present. Therefore Judith introduces the supreme patriarchs of the Israelite nation—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and their first leader, Moses, as examples of faith and patience. Conversely, she presents the wicked murmurers and complainers as testimony to their own cowardice and impatience, so that from the good we may take a useful example for imitation, and from the evil learn to avoid the wicked work of their perversity, lest we suffer the torment of their destruction. Hence she continues:

“Therefore let us not avenge ourselves for what we suffer; rather, considering these punishments themselves to be lesser than our sins, let us believe that the scourges of the Lord, by which we are corrected like servants, have come upon us not for our destruction.”  
[Col. 0562C]

This is the way of truth: in the Lord’s scourges we should humble our souls and strive to possess patience, considering that the things we rightly suffer for our sins—or rather, the vengeance that is even less than our merits—have been tempered for us by God’s goodness so that we may endure them. For he wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He has mercy on all and hates nothing that he has made; he overlooks human sins for the sake of repentance and spares them because of his great mercy, since he alone is our God.  
[Col. 0562D]

“Ozias and the presbyters said to her: ‘Everything you have said is true, and there is no fault in your words. Now pray for us, because you are a holy woman and fear God.’”

There is no fault in Judith’s words, but everything that is read is true. For everything that the Catholic Church proclaims in the confession of true faith or in the teaching of holy religion is highly praiseworthy and without any fault. Because of her merit and dignity, it must also be believed that each of the faithful is greatly aided before the Lord’s mercy. This is rightly accomplished if each person takes care that, just as he has recognized the truth of what the Church teaches, so he may imitate in his actions what she commends through honorable examples. Concerning this it continues:

“She said to them: ‘Just as you recognize that what I have been able to say is from God, so test whether what I have decided to do is from God, and pray that God may make my plan firm. You will stand at the gate tonight, and I will go out with my maidservant. Pray that, as you have said, the Lord may look upon his people Israel during these five days.’”

Judith entrusts the gate to the presbyters because the holy Church entrusts to Christ’s priests the careful guarding of God’s camps, so that with vigilant attention and diligent care they may fortify them by the weapons of prayer and preserve them unharmed against the enemy’s ambushes.  
[Col. 0563A–B]

## CHAPTER IX. Judith humbles herself and prays for the liberation of the people.

“When they had departed, Judith entered her oratory, clothed herself in sackcloth, put ashes on her head, and, prostrating herself before the Lord, cried out to the Lord and said: ‘Lord, God of my father Simeon, who gave him a sword for the defense of foreigners who proved violators in their defilement and exposed a virgin’s thigh in disgrace.’”  
[Col. 0563C]

Why, after the words she spoke to the presbyters, does Judith enter her oratory to seek the Lord, except that the concern of the saints, after completing the service of vigorous preaching, returns inward to the secret place of the heart, so that there, with a clean conscience, it may fulfill the duty of pure prayer, according to the Savior’s instruction in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

She clothes herself in sackcloth when she practices repentance for sins. She puts ashes on her head when she stores in her mind the memory of her own frailty. She cries out to the Lord while prostrating herself when, through an attitude of humility, she hopes to be heard by the Lord, for it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.”

In her prayer she rightly recalls the deed of the patriarch Simeon. Together with his brother Levi, he avenged with the sword of retribution the violation of his sister by foreigners, because it was destined that Holofernes, who wished to fulfill an act of lust against Judith, would be punished by the sword of divine judgment.  
[Col. 0563D–564A]

“Look now upon the camp of the Assyrians, as then you deigned to see the camp of the Egyptians, when they were running armed after your servants, trusting in their chariots, their cavalry, and the multitude of their warriors. But you looked upon their camp, and darkness wearied them. The abyss seized their feet, and the waters covered them. May these men also be dealt with in this way, Lord, who trust in their multitude, glory in their chariots, shields, arrows, and spears, and do not know that you yourself are our God.”

Just as above she compared the lustful with the luxurious, so now she compares the proud with the fearful. She likens the Assyrians, trusting in their weapons, to the Egyptians who formerly fought against the Israelites, in order to show that just as God’s power was manifested there in the overthrow of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, so it may also be revealed here in the overthrow of Holofernes and the Assyrians. For the Lord is the same, his power the same, and his justice the same then and now, and he remains so throughout all ages.  
[Col. 0564B]

“Lord, let his pride be cut off by his own sword; let him be caught in the snare of his own eyes through me, and strike him through the lips of my love. Give me firmness of mind, so that I may despise him and his power and overthrow him. For this will be a memorial of your name, when the hand of a woman has cast him down. For your strength, Lord, is not in multitude, nor is your will in the power of horses; nor have the proud ever been pleasing to you from the beginning. The prayer of the humble and meek has always pleased you.”

Some who understand these things less well seem to think that the prayers of the saints against the reprobate, which are sometimes recorded in Scripture, are curses. Yet these words in no way proceed from a desire for malice—which can never arise in the hearts of the saints—but from the spirit of prophecy. What the Holy Spirit foreknew would happen to the reprobate by a just judgment, he foretold through the mouths of the saints, as in the Psalms: “Let their table before them become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling block. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their backs.”
