Paul likewise wrote in his Epistle: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works.” In the Acts of the Apostles, when the high priest Ananias ordered him to be struck on the mouth, Paul said: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall” (Acts 23).

Thus Judith’s words—“Let him be caught in the snare of his own eyes through me, and strike him through the lips of my love”—are not to be understood as curses but as prophetic proclamations of future events. Through the mouth of the holy woman, the Holy Spirit wished to foretell what he knew the wicked ruler would deserve because of his depravity. He also wished to foreshadow mystically that every heretic, schismatic, Jew, or pagan who attempts to corrupt the Church through wicked doctrine or perverse example will have the head of his evil purpose cut off by the sword of his own pride, through the sentence of the just Judge, and will be subjected to the torments of hell, where he will eternally experience the punishments of suffering.  
[Col. 0564C–D]

## CHAPTER X. After her prayers, Judith, clothed in the ornaments of her beauty, went out through the city gates toward Holofernes. Received by the scouts, she was led to Holofernes, who asked Judith why she had come.  
[Col. 0565A]

“When she had ceased crying out to the Lord, she rose from the place where she had lain prostrate before the Lord. She called her maidservant, went down into her house, removed her sackcloth, took off her widow’s garments, washed her body, anointed herself with the finest myrrh, arranged the hair of her head, placed a turban on her head, and put on the garments of her beauty. She put sandals on her feet, took bracelets and lilies, earrings and rings, and adorned herself with all her ornaments. The Lord also gave her splendor, because all this adornment depended not on lust but on virtue; therefore the Lord increased her beauty in her.”

What does it mean that, after completing her prayer, Judith removes her mournful garments and puts on garments of delight, except that the holy Church, although at times she assumes an attitude of repentance for her sins, nevertheless greatly cheers her anxious heart with the hope of forgiveness and future reward?

She washes her body when she cleanses the actions of her body with tears of repentance. She anoints herself with the finest myrrh when, in the mortification of her own flesh, she fills herself with the fragrance of charity and the other virtues. She arranges the hair of her head when, with diligent discernment, she distinguishes each thought of her heart. She places a turban on her head when she surrounds her mind with the helmet of salvation. She puts sandals on her feet when she fortifies the steps of her works with evangelical teachings.

She takes bracelets and lilies, earrings and rings. In the bracelets, hope of future goods is expressed, which will be given to the saints at God’s right hand in the future. In the lilies, chastity; in the earrings, devoted obedience; and in the ring, the seal of faith are signified. The holy Church adorns herself with all these ornaments because she strives to illuminate herself with the beauty of every virtue.

The Lord also bestowed upon her the splendor of his grace, because all this adornment depended not on the lust of the present life but on the virtue of the future. Therefore the Lord increased this beauty in her, so that she might appear to all eyes with incomparable loveliness. For it is entirely just that the one who burns with love for God’s perfect charity should be considered worthy of honor by all.  
[Col. 0565B–D]

«And so she gave her maidservant a wineskin of wine, a vessel of oil, meal, cakes (*palathas*), loaves, and cheese, and she set out.»

What does it mean that Judith, about to proceed to the contest, placed upon her maidservant’s shoulder the things that would be necessary for her on the journey, except that holy Church, hastening to contend against the enemy in the arena of this world, makes use of certain carnal persons’ service against her enemies? If they faithfully perform that service, they will be able to attain true freedom, so as to become coheirs and partners in the possession to come, just as the aforementioned maidservant is remembered at the end of this book as having been released by her mistress Judith.

It often happens that those who are less perfect in knowledge and conduct, and who are in some way entangled by love of present things, participate in the Church’s sacraments, serve spiritual mysteries from their own resources, and render them bodily assistance; yet they are not capable of renouncing everything they possess and observing the standard of apostolic perfection. Thus the rich man in the Gospel answered our Redeemer that he had kept God’s commandments, but he was unwilling to strive toward perfection by selling all his possessions, giving them to the poor, and following him according to his admonitions.

This maidservant—namely, the crowd of carnal people—does indeed carry what holy Church entrusts to her: a wineskin, a vessel of oil, meal, and loaves, since she reverently preserves the divine sacraments, prepared from grain and wine—namely, the body and blood of the Lord—and the anointing of chrism. She also carries cakes (*palathas*) and cheese. Cheese is coagulated milk, and both of these can signify nourishment for souls in faith and love. Yet this maidservant is not permitted to turn all these things to her own pleasure or use them according to her own judgment; rather, she is ordered to preserve them for the use and administration of her mistress. For it is entirely just that one who does not yet know how to govern her own life should not suddenly become the ruler of another’s life, but should instead become subject to those who, by their life and teaching, uphold the rule of justice.

«Now it happened that, as she was descending the mountain around daybreak, Assyrian scouts met her and seized her, saying: Where do you come from, or where are you going? She answered: I am a daughter of the Hebrews, and therefore I fled from them, because I learned beforehand that they would be given over to you as plunder, since, despising you, they were unwilling to surrender themselves voluntarily in order to find mercy in your sight.»

Who are the Assyrian scouts except the philosophers of the gentiles and the curious investigators of human disciplines? Like Judith passing from the Jews to the gentiles, they attempted to seize our Judith when the preachers of the Gospel, abandoning the Jews on account of their faithlessness and hastening to preach to the gentiles, tried to conquer and overcome them by their doctrines. They led them to Holofernes’ tent when they handed them over to the rulers of the gentiles as though subject to them. But, having recognized the sincerity of their religion, they immediately released them from their bonds in the ruler’s house—that is, under secular authority—and allowed them to remain there freely.

Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles that Paul, staying at Athens, argued and debated about Jesus and the resurrection with the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. When they heard him announcing these things, they seized him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying: «Can we know what this new teaching is that you proclaim? For you bring certain strange things to our ears; therefore we wish to know what these things might mean.» When he had set forth the faith of God to them in the clearest speech, some of them mocked him, but others, joining themselves to him, believed. Among them were Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and several others with them. After this, leaving Athens, he came to Corinth. There he stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, worked at the craft of tentmaking, and testified about Jesus Christ to all who came to him.

Likewise, while remaining under free custody among the Romans, that same Apostle preached the word of God with complete confidence and received all who entered to him, with no one forbidding them. Hence ecclesiastical histories also report that the rulers of the gentiles, having observed the gentleness and moderation of the faithful, restrained the infliction of punishments and violence upon them.

Thus Tiberius Caesar had confirmed by edicts that no action should be undertaken against or contrary to Christ’s teaching, and he threatened the Christians’ accusers with death. Likewise the emperor Claudius, although he afflicted the Jews with various calamities, did not harm the Christians. Consequently, while he was reigning, the apostle Peter converted very many people to the faith of Christ by preaching in the city of Rome.

Likewise Trajan, although at first deceived by the name “Christian” and having persecuted those who confessed Christ, nevertheless, after being advised by the report of Pliny the Younger and instructed concerning the Christians’ moderation, tempered his edict with milder rescripts. Similarly, Aelius Hadrian, instructed and educated in the Christian religion by Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and by Aristides, an Athenian, ordered in a letter sent to Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that no one should be condemned as a Christian without an accusation of a crime or proof.

He was also called Father of his Country in the senate, beyond the custom of his ancestors, and his wife was called Augusta. Hadrian organized the state with just laws, waged war beyond the Sauromatae, and conquered the Jews, who had been thoroughly harassed by the disturbance of their crimes and were laying waste to the province of Palestine, once their own, and he subdued them by a final slaughter. He avenged the Christians whom they had immediately tortured under their leader Thebes because they would not join them against the Romans. He also ordered that no Jew should have permission to enter Jerusalem, while Christians were permitted to inhabit the city, which he restored to an excellent condition by constructing its walls and ordered to be called Aelia, from his own name.

«Then Judith saw Holofernes seated beneath a canopy woven of purple, gold, emeralds, and precious stones. When she fixed her gaze upon his face, she did him homage; and when she had prostrated herself upon the ground, Holofernes’ servants raised her at their master’s command.»

That Judith did homage to Holofernes was not a disturbance caused by fear, but the preservation of order. Whenever holy men offer honor to earthly authority, they do so not from the fault of flattery, but by right of the dignity of office. Therefore the chief of the apostles taught in his Epistle, saying:

«Therefore be subject to every human creature for the Lord’s sake, whether to the king as one who is preeminent, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. For this is God’s will: that by doing good you silence the ignorance of foolish people; as free men, and not as those who use freedom as a covering for evil, but as servants of God. Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear the Lord, honor the king.»

Paul likewise says:

«Be subject to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist will bring condemnation upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it; for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without cause. For it is God’s servant, an avenger in wrath against the one who does evil. Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes, since they are God’s ministers, serving precisely in this matter» (Romans 13).

And again: «Repay to everyone what is owed: tax to whom tax is due, revenue to whom revenue is due, fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due» (ibid.).

Therefore the prophet Elijah is said in the Book of Kings to have worshiped the most impious king Ahab—not, of course, with the piety of divine worship, but in the duty of honor.

The Apostle Paul mentioned above likewise, when pleading his case before King Agrippa and the governor Festus in the Acts of the Apostles, spoke gently and in a manner calculated to win his hearers, saying to Agrippa:

«Concerning all the things of which I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate that I am to defend myself before you today, especially since you know all the customs and questions that exist among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently» (Acts 26).

And when Festus rebuked him and said, «You are mad, Paul; your many writings are driving you mad,» he replied:

«I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking words of truth and sobriety. For the king knows about these matters, to whom I also speak boldly; for I do not believe that any of these things has escaped him, since none of them was done in a corner. Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you do» (ibid.), and so forth.

Similarly, the words that Judith speaks to Holofernes concerning her arrival and the future downfall of the Jews are not profane lies of flattery, but venerable mysteries of future prophecy. For she foretold the punishments that were to come upon murderers and transgressors of God’s law from the gentiles and Roman rulers, as well as the destruction that, on account of their sins, was impending over their entire land. Thus she says:

## CHAPTER XI. Holofernes, deceived by Judith, trusts that he can capture the children of Israel. Everyone also admired Judith’s beauty and wisdom.

«Nor is it hidden what Achior said, nor is it unknown what you ordered to happen to him. For it is clear that our God was so offended by sins that through his prophets he commanded the people that he would hand them over because of their sins. And because the children of Israel know that they have offended their God, your terror is upon them. Moreover, famine has overtaken them, and through lack of water they are already being counted among the dead. Finally, they are planning to slaughter their cattle and drink their blood; and the holy things of the Lord their God, which God commanded not to be touched—grain, wine, and oil—they have resolved to consume, and they wish to use up things that they ought not even to touch with their hands. Therefore, since they are doing these things, it is certain that they will be given over to destruction. Knowing this, I, your maidservant, fled from them, and the Lord sent me to announce these very things to you.»

For it is written in ecclesiastical history that, when the time of Jerusalem’s devastation was approaching, certain apostles, having first been driven out by them, went dispersed throughout every place in the power of Christ, who had commanded them:

«Go and baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.»

The Church that had been gathered in Jerusalem was ordered, after receiving a response from God, to emigrate and cross over to a certain town called Pella, beyond the Jordan. Thus, when the holy and righteous men had been removed from the city, a place was left for heavenly vengeance to be exacted both upon the sacrilegious city and upon the impious people through the destruction and overthrow of their homeland.

How great were the evils with which the entire nation was then punished, and how the land of Judea itself was devastated by war, famine, fire, and slaughter; how many thousands of people—fathers with wives and little children, without number or distinction—were slaughtered; what sieges of various cities took place; how great was the devastation of the magnificent and famous city of Jerusalem, and how great the ruin of its various mountains; what course the wars took in each of these events; how, according to what the prophets had foretold, the abomination of desolation was placed in the very temple once so famous as God’s temple; and how at last fire ravaged and flame consumed everything—if anyone wishes to know these matters more fully, let him consult the histories of Josephus.

We, however, shall take from them only those matters sufficient for the explanation of the work we have begun. Josephus reports that people from all Judea had gathered in Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, as though driven by some deadly force, and he says that there were thirty hundred thousand people—that is, three million—this time having been chosen by God’s just judgment for vengeance. For, since on the days of Passover they had violated the Savior and the saving Christ of the Lord with bloody hands and sacrilegious voices, the whole multitude, enclosed on those days as though in a single prison, received the destruction of the deadly punishment it deserved.

The historian reports in the fifth book of his Histories how great a famine and how great a calamity of Jewish sedition the nation endured before the city was captured, so that every hope of salvation was excluded from the wretched, and the growing harshness of famine ravaged houses, families, and the nation. For, while the corpses of women and children lay strewn in the innermost chambers, and the bodies of unhappy old men, consumed more by hunger than by age, lay throughout the streets, young men and every stronger age wandered about the roads and pathways like shadows, collapsing wherever starvation brought their steps to a halt.

Neither the number of the dead nor the weakness of their strength allowed them to bury the corpses of their relatives. Likewise, because each person was uncertain of his own life, some at last gave up their souls above those whom they were burying. Many, while following funeral processions, breathed their last before reaching the grave. Nor was the customary lament offered to the dead, nor mourning observed, because famine had claimed all of this for itself; nor had the dryness of starvation left anyone moisture for tears.

Deep silences had besieged the city, and a night full of death covered everything. Amid all these evils, only the more brutal plunderers flourished. They did not consider it unlawful even to break open tombs and strip corpses, seeking not so much plunder as an accumulation of crime through mockery and testing the edge of their swords by mutilating the dead.

«All these words pleased Holofernes and his servants, and they marveled at her wisdom. They said to one another: There is no woman like this upon the earth in appearance, beauty, and intelligence of speech. And Holofernes said to her: God has done well, who sent you ahead of your people, so that you might deliver them into our hands; and because your promise is good, if your God does this for me, he will also be my God.»

The first path of salvation for the gentiles was to receive the ministers of God’s word, or the preachers of the Gospel, gladly, to put faith in their words, and thus gradually to arrive through their teaching at knowledge of the truth. Therefore the Lord commanded his disciples in the Gospel:

«Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you leave. When you enter a house, greet it, saying: Peace to this house. And if the house is worthy, your peace will come upon it; but if it is not worthy, your peace will return to you.»

Our Judith, then, because she found access among the gentiles through devoted reception, attained the fulfillment of her purpose. Blessed, therefore, is the one who receives the ambassador of truth not with an evil intention but with sincere affection of heart. For whoever, with perverse intention, pretends with Holofernes and Herod to be seeking God will by no means rejoice to reach the sight of his glory in gladness, but will grieve at the end to pay the fitting penalties for his iniquity.

## CHAPTER XII. How Holofernes ordered Judith to remain where his treasures were stored; how, when summoned to his banquet, she abstained from his food; and how at evening she was brought into his chamber.

«Then he ordered her to enter where his treasures were stored, and commanded her to remain there. He also ordered that a portion of his banquet be given to her. Judith answered him and said: I cannot now eat of what you command to be given to me, lest offense come upon me. But I shall eat from what I brought with me. Holofernes said to her: If these things that you brought with you should fail, what shall we do for you? Judith said: As your soul lives, my lord, your maidservant shall not consume all these things until God accomplishes by my hand what I have planned.»

What does it mean that Holofernes ordered Judith to remain where his treasures were stored, except that the principality of this world often consents to the preachers of the Gospel having a place among those who possess an understanding mind receptive to sound faith? The intention of good will is therefore the most precious treasure of the heart. There the typical Judith remains, because holy Church remains steadfastly.

But Holofernes complains that the provisions Judith brought with her are failing, and he asks whether he might somehow make her a participant in his banquet. This signifies that among the rulers of the gentiles the practice of the Christian religion sometimes appears despised and worthless, and that its agents seek to draw people toward the uncleanness of idols or the allurements of carnal pleasures.

But the faithful promise themselves, with steadfast spirit and certain hope, that divine grace will swiftly come to their aid. They devote themselves to prayer throughout the night of this world, baptize themselves in a fountain of tears, and, with the psalmist, wash the bed of their hearts every night and water the couch of their thoughts with devout weeping. Thus, fulfilling the three days of catholic confession through faith, hope, and charity, on the fourth day at last—that is, when the light of the Gospel shines forth—they prepare victory for themselves over the enemy. They condemn the author of death and darkness, blinded by his own wickedness, as liable to eternal guilt.

And so Mother Church, with the help of God’s grace, frees the innocent from persecution and unjust oppression; returning to her own citizens, she brings back with her most gloriously the triumph over the wicked enemy.

«Then Vagao entered to Judith and said: Let the good young woman not fear to enter to my lord, so that she may be honored before him, eat with him, and drink wine joyfully. Judith answered him: Who am I to oppose my lord? Whatever is before his eyes, good and excellent, I shall do. Whatever pleases him will be best for me all the days of my life. Then she rose, adorned herself in her clothing, entered, and stood before him. Holofernes’ heart was shaken, for he was burning with desire for her.»

What Vagao persuades Judith to do pertains to illicit pleasures; what Judith replies displays the virtues of a good spirit. He invites her to the luxury of lust, while she declares herself ready to obey the command of heavenly authority. She adorns herself in her own garments because she displays the worship of true piety. She stands before the ruler because she urges him to flee the ruin of impiety.

But woe to the one who desires to use good things in the worst way, who, following Holofernes’ example, wishes to turn spiritual virtues toward carnal desires.

«But thanks be to God, who triumphs in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. To some we are the fragrance of death leading to death, but to others the fragrance of life leading to life.»

[Col. 0572A] «Holofernes said to her: Drink from this and recline in joy, because you have found favor before me. Judith said: I shall drink, my lord, because my soul has been exalted today above all my days. She took and ate, and drank before him all that her maidservant had prepared for her.»

Observe that Judith, while associating with Holofernes, was not defiled by the food or drink of the gentiles, but ate and drank what her maidservant had prepared for her. For the Church, dwelling among the gentiles, is in no way polluted by idolatry or gentile superstition, but makes use of what she judges suitable for her sustenance—what the devotion of the faithful prepares for her through obedience and the practice of good works.

Concerning this food, Truth itself says in the Gospel:

«Work for the food that does not perish, but endures unto eternal life.»

And elsewhere, when the disciples asked him to eat, he answered:

«I have food to eat of which you do not know; for my food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work.»

## CHAPTER XIII. How, while Holofernes lay drunken in his bed, Judith prayed and cut off his head, wrapped it in the canopy, and carried it to her fellow citizens; how, when a great crowd of people gathered at the city gates, Judith blessed the Lord and showed them Holofernes’ head, and all blessed Judith while praising the Lord; and how Achior, seeing Holofernes’ head, fell to the ground, overcome by fear.

«They were all exhausted from the wine, and Judith alone was in the chamber. Holofernes lay on the bed, overcome by excessive drunkenness.»

The wine of Holofernes and his attendants was that against which the Apostle restrained believers, saying:

«Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.»

And in the song of Deuteronomy it is written concerning such wine:

«Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their clusters are clusters of bitterness; their wine is the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps.»

Drunk with this wine, the enemy of the Church lay on the bed of wicked security, by which he trusted that he could sin with impunity, according to the saying:

«When the wicked comes into the depths of evil, he despises.»

But he was deceiving himself, because, unaware of what awaited him, he was advancing toward perpetual destruction.

«Judith told her maidservant to stand outside before the chamber and keep watch. Judith stood before the bed, praying with tears and, moving her lips in silence, saying: Strengthen me, Lord God of Israel, and look at the works of my hands at this hour, so that, just as you promised, you may raise up your city, and I may accomplish what, trusting that it could be done through you, I have planned. When she had said this, she approached the pillar that was at the head of his bed and released his dagger, which was tied there and hanging from it. When she had drawn it from its sheath, she seized the hair of his head and said: Strengthen me, God, God of Israel, at this hour. Then she struck his neck twice, cut off his head, removed his canopy from the pillars, and unrolled his mutilated body.»

The pillar that stood at the head of Holofernes’ bed signifies the hardness of an evil heart, which gives birth to the error of false security. The dagger tied and hanging from it is the wickedness of an evil intention. The hair of the head is the arrogance of a proud mind. The neck is the obstinacy of wicked action. The canopy—that is, the net for flies—signifies the snares of deceitful thought.

Our Judith therefore entrusts the guarding of the doors to her maidservant, because holy Church commands each of the faithful to observe the catholic faith. She herself prays with tears because she seeks heavenly help with the deepest devotion of heart. She approaches the pillar and releases the dagger by which she cuts off the head of the most wicked enemy when, exposing the wickedness of a hardened heart, she cuts away from the enemy the opportunity for insolent temptation.

She removes the canopy because she exposes the deceptions by which he strives to entangle the simple and unwary. Thus she unrolls the enemy’s mutilated body when she shows that the enemy himself is weak and feeble in every respect, so that Christ’s warriors may more confidently believe that they can conquer the most wicked enemy once they have fully learned that he is fragile and conquerable.

«A little later she went out and handed Holofernes’ head to her maidservant, ordering her to put it into her bag. The two went out according to their custom, as though going to prayer, passed through the camp, went around the valley, and came to the city gate. Judith called from a distance to the sentries on the walls: Open the gates, for God is with us, the God who has shown his power in Israel.»

What does it mean that Judith handed Holofernes’ head to her maidservant to put into her bag, except that the Church does not wish the memory of the completed battle to slip from the minds of her hearers, but wishes it to be carefully preserved in the memory of their hearts? We should rejoice in the triumph over the enemy, insofar as by divine grace we have overcome him in some measure, yet we should not doubt that he may again prepare battle against us.

For this reason the apostle Peter says:

«Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith.»

And Paul says:

«Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if somehow I may lay hold of that for which I have been laid hold of by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have laid hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. Let all of us who are perfect think in this way» (Philippians 3).

«And, going around the valley,» he says, «they came to the city gate.»

One goes around the valley on foot who preserves humility in every action. Such a person reaches the city gate because he attains the entrance to the heavenly kingdom. Therefore he who was made by God for us the supreme example of humility and obedience, through whom we have access to eternal life, says in the Gospel:

«I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will enter and go out, and will find pasture.»

Elsewhere he says:

«Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.»

«Judith called from a distance to the sentries on the walls: Open the gates, for God is with us, the God who has shown his power in Israel.»

The sentries on the walls—that is, the guardians of the Church’s camps—are the holy teachers, who by word, example, and constant prayer fortify the life of believers and prepare for them an entrance into eternal blessedness. Concerning them the prophet says:

«Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall never cease praising the name of the Lord.»

The angelic powers may also be understood as guardians of the spiritual walls, appointed for us so that by their assistance they may defend us against evil spirits.

Judith therefore calls from a distance to the sentries, asking that the gates be opened to her because God is with her. Likewise the Church, established in the pilgrimage of this world and on the road of the present life, cries out from the depths of her heart and asks that, through the intercessions of the saints, the entrance to the heavenly homeland may be opened to her, so that there she may fulfill the office of her name, saying with the prophet:

«Open to me the gates of righteousness; I shall enter through them and confess to the Lord. This is the Lord’s gate; the righteous shall enter through it.»

And she adds why she asks this, saying:

«Because he is with us, who has shown his power in Israel.»

For it is entirely just that one who recognizes himself as united with his head—of whom it is written, «The Lord will give strength to his people and will bless his people with peace»—should ascend with him to the summit of the heavenly kingdom, since without him he can in no way reach it. Therefore Truth itself says in the Gospel:

«No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.»

What Judith says to the sentries on the walls—«Open the gates»—may also be understood as the devotion of heart that she asks of her hearers: that is, that they prepare the intention of their hearts to receive what is said to them. Thus the Savior, teaching through parables, said in the Gospel:

«Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.»

And the apostle John repeatedly repeats the same sentence in his Apocalypse, saying:

«Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.»

Rightly, then, she who wishes to proclaim the mighty deeds of the Lord that he has performed seeks devoted hearers, because it is written:

«Blessed is the one who speaks his case into the ear of one who listens.»

«And when the men had heard her voice, they called the elders of the city. Everyone, from the least to the greatest, hurried to her, because they had hoped that she would no longer come; and, lighting lamps, they all gathered around her.»

At Judith’s voice the elders of the city gather with all the people, because at the teaching of holy Church everyone hastens forward—not only the lesser but also the greater—to hear her saving words and to receive them with pure intention for fulfillment.

This is what it means to light lamps: to offer the pious devotion of the heart for learning the truth and to drive away from oneself all the darkness of errors.

«She then ascended to a higher place and ordered silence. When everyone had become silent, Judith said: Praise the Lord our God, who has not abandoned those who hope in him, and through me, his maidservant, has fulfilled his mercy, which he promised to the house of Israel, and by my hand has killed the enemy of his people this night.»

What does Judith’s ascending to a higher place mean except that holy Church turns her discourse toward doctrines that are heavenly and above, so that she may lift our minds there and rouse those who are sluggish to praise God for all his benefits, which he truly and mercifully bestows upon Israel? His power killed the ancient enemy by the hand of that woman concerning whom, in the beginning, the Lord said to the crafty serpent:

«She shall crush his head.»

And Truth itself says in the Gospel:

«Behold, I give you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.»

«Then she drew Holofernes’ head from the bag and showed it to them, saying: Behold the head of Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army. And behold the canopy beneath which he lay in his drunkenness, where the Lord our God struck him by the hand of a woman. As the Lord himself lives, his angel guarded me as I went from here, remained there, and returned from there to this place. The Lord did not permit me, his maidservant, to be defiled, but brought me back to you without the pollution of sin, rejoicing in his victory, in my escape, and in your deliverance. Give thanks to him, all of you, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.»

Judith brings Holofernes’ head before the people and shows them his canopy beneath which he lay in his drunkenness. This signifies that holy Church, through clear speech, exposes to the faithful the proud mind of the ancient enemy and openly reveals to them his deception, in which he trusted though filled with wickedness. Thus they may know how perverse their enemy is and with what mercy the omnipotent God has overcome and subdued him under the dominion of faithful souls.

Divine protection has guarded those souls unharmed from every deception of the enemy and contamination of error, so that, having recognized all these things perfectly, they may render fitting thanks for them to their Creator and Redeemer and ceaselessly offer him devoted praises.

Hence the pastor of the Church admonished his hearers, saying:

«Be sober, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith» (1 Peter 5).

Paul likewise says:

«I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the truth that is in Christ Jesus our Lord» (1 Corinthians 11).

And again:

«Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, and put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the devil’s snares. For your struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places» (Ephesians 6).

«Then all worshiped the Lord and said to her: The Lord has blessed you by his strength, because through you he has reduced our enemies to nothing. Then Ozias, the ruler of the people, said to her: Blessed are you, daughter, by the Lord God Most High, above all women upon the earth. Blessed is the Lord who created heaven and earth, who directed you to the wound of the head of the ruler of our enemies. For today he has so magnified your name that your praise shall not depart from the mouth of human beings.»

The Church is blessed in the Lord’s strength because through her the Lord has crushed the devil’s power. She is blessed above all women upon the earth because the confession of her faith and the true religion of divine worship hold primacy throughout the whole world.

Her praise shall not depart from the mouths of those who remember her zeal and good works, because, through the love of God and neighbor in which she burns most fervently, she does not marvel at the greatness of present tribulations, but, full of faith and firm in hope, strives toward the height of heavenly rewards, where in the life to come she will share in the joy and blessedness of the holy angels.

«Moreover, Achior was summoned and came, and said to her: “The God of Israel, to whom you bore witness that he avenges himself upon his enemies, has himself this night cut off the head of all the unbelievers by my hand. And, to prove that this is so, behold the head of Holofernes, who, in contempt of his pride, despised the God of Israel and threatened you with destruction, saying: ‘When the people of Israel have been captured, I shall order your sides to be pierced with the sword.’” When Achior saw the head of Holofernes, he was overcome with fear, fell on his face upon the ground, and his soul was in anguish. But afterward, when he had revived after recovering his breath, he fell at her feet and worshiped her.»

By Achior, the leader of the Ammonites, as we said above, pagans or heretics are signified. When they see the holy Church, through the constancy of faith, overcome the ferocity of her enemies and persecutors, they are shaken by immense fear, fall from the obstinacy of their arrogance, and are compelled by overwhelming terror to venerate the holy Church. Thus, together with their followers, they hasten to abandon their error and to associate themselves with the number of the faithful through catholic confession and reception of baptism. Hence Isaiah says: «The bent sons of those who humbled you will come to you, and all who slandered you will worship the footsteps of your feet; they will call you the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel» (Isa. LX).

## CHAPTER XIV. Judith gives the people counsel that, going out beyond the gates, they should make a tumult with their weapons in order to strike fear into the Assyrians.

«Judith said to all the people: “Listen to me, brothers; hang this head upon our walls. And when the sun has risen, let each person take up his weapons, and go out with an assault—not so that you descend [Col. 0577A] downward, but as though making an attack. Then the scouts will have to flee to awaken their commander for battle. When their leaders have run to the tent of Holofernes and find him headless and rolling in his own blood, fear will fall upon them. When you know that they are fleeing, go after them without fear, for the Lord will crush them beneath your feet.”»

The Church teaches her children with maternal affection and authoritative instruction how they should pursue the spiritual enemy: namely, that when the sun has risen, they should hang the head of their enemy upon their walls. This means that, when the serenity of divine reconciliation and heavenly consolation has shone upon them, believers should immediately make known to everyone the crushed pride of the ancient enemy by the evangelical teaching with which they are fortified. Clothed in heavenly armor—that is, the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God—they should pursue the enemy’s ranks, not sluggishly but courageously.

Obedient in everything to the voice of their teacher, they do precisely as they have been instructed. Thus the terrified leaders of the opposing army are compelled to go and rouse their commander, when the foremost persecutors, seeing the unity and confidence of the holy Church raised against them, run to their idols and false deities so that they may be protected by their defense. But when they flee to them, they find them utterly defiled by their own wickedness and unable to offer them any consolation, since they themselves are deprived of every strength and power. Therefore, hoping to save themselves by the protection of flight, they abandon everything by which they had believed that they could temporarily excel others, and scatter through the roads of the plains and the paths of the hills. For there is neither strength, nor counsel, nor power among those who determine to rebel against the Lord, as it is written: «There is no prudence, there is no wisdom, there is no counsel against the Lord.» And Jeremiah says: «The swift shall not escape, nor shall the strong think that he can save himself. But the day of the Lord of hosts shall take vengeance upon his enemies; the sword shall devour and be satisfied, and shall become drunk with their blood» (Jer. XLVI).

## CHAPTER XV. The people put the Assyrians to flight and, after slaughtering very many of them, bring back great spoil. Joachim, the high priest, descends from Jerusalem to Bethulia to see Judith, whom he heaps with blessings; and the people give everything that had belonged to Holofernes to the victorious woman.

«When the children of Israel saw them fleeing, they followed them, descending while blowing the trumpets and raising cries behind them. And because the Assyrians, not united, were rushing headlong in flight, while the children of Israel pursued them in a single column, they weakened all whom they were able to find.»

The Israelites pursue their fleeing adversaries, blowing trumpets and raising cries, because the holy preachers drive away the army of their enemies not with carnal weapons but with the evangelical trumpet, and strive to gain victory over their foes. Hence, in the Book of Judges, when Gideon was about to fight against the Midianites, he took not a spear, shield, or sword, but trumpets and lamps, and through them gained his most famous victory over his enemies. This prefigured the future heralds of the Gospel, whose struggle was not against flesh and blood but against the rulers and powers of this age, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI): they would shine more by the voice of preaching and miracles than terrify and overcome all their enemies by the crashing of weapons.

And below it says that the Assyrians rushed headlong in flight, not united, while the children of Israel pursued them in a single column. This is because the errors of pagans, heretics, and all the ungodly are many, and the deviations of their iniquities are various; scattered among them, they can never unite upon the way of righteousness. But the people of God and the true confessors of Christ proceed along the path of truth in a single column—that is, with one consistent faith—and win a sure victory over their persecutors.

«Ozias sent messengers throughout all the cities and regions of Israel. Therefore every region and every city sent selected armed young men after them, and they pursued them with the edge of the sword until they reached the limits of their territory. But those who remained in Bethulia entered the camp of the Assyrians, took away the spoil that the fleeing Assyrians had left behind, and were heavily laden with it.»

Ozias, whose name means “the strength of the Lord,” sends messengers throughout all the cities and regions of Israel and urges them to come and pursue the enemies. In the same way, the zeal of the holy preachers, who have been strengthened by the faith of Christ, rouses everyone through the word of the Gospel against the enemies of the Christian religion, so that by right belief and good works they may strive to lay low the multitude of their enemies. Hence every city and the entire common region sent selected armed young men after them, because, at the preaching of the word of God, proven persons from the peoples and provinces, steadfast in spiritual strength, gather for the warfare of the Lord in order to crush his enemies. Isaiah, foreseeing them in the Spirit, says: «Behold, these shall come from afar; and behold, those from the north and the sea, and these from the southern land. Hear, O heavens, and rejoice, O earth; let the mountains resound with praise, because the Lord has comforted his people and will have mercy on his poor» (Isa. XLIX).

And rightly it is said that they pursued them with the edge of the sword to the limits of their territory, because a soldier of Christ ought not soon to be secure while the enemy remains within his homeland. Rather, he must labor with all his strength to expel him from the boundaries of his conduct—that is, from his thoughts, words, and actions—lest, if he grants him habitation anywhere, the enemy suddenly confound and crush him. When the battle has been completed, however, he can then return secure from the enemy and carry away the triumph.

«But those who returned victorious to Bethulia took away with them everything that belonged to them, so that there was no count of their sheep, cattle, and all their possessions, and everyone, from the least to the greatest, became rich from their plunder.»

We must observe that the text says that those who remained within the city carried away the Assyrians’ spoil, while those who returned victorious from the slaughter of the enemy brought away a multitude of sheep, cattle, and all their possessions. For although the labor of Christ’s soldiers is manifold, their intention and devotion ought nevertheless to be one and the same: that whatever they are able to snatch from the wicked possession of their enemies, they should convert to the adornment and riches of the holy Church. This means the gold of wisdom, the silver of eloquence, the gems of morality and virtues, and also people devoted to carnal understanding, who had been taken captive by idolatry and subjected to the servitude of vices. Thus all these things, which the proud Assyrian and the prince of this world unjustly possessed, may be brought back by Christ’s warriors to the dignity of divine worship.

[Col. 0579B] «Joachim, the high priest, came from Jerusalem to Bethulia with all his priests, to see Judith. When she came out to him, they all blessed her with one voice, saying: ‘You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the joy of Israel, you are the honor of our people, because you have acted manfully, and your heart has been strengthened because you loved chastity and did not know another man after your husband. Therefore the hand of the Lord also strengthened you, and therefore you shall be blessed forever.’ And all the people said: ‘Amen, amen.’»

What is signified by Joachim, the high priest from Jerusalem, except our Redeemer, who was made by God our priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek? Through him we have access to the Father and the hope of eternal life. The interpretation of his name also seems to express this: Joachim is interpreted as “the resurrection of the Lord.” Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: «I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me will not die forever» (John XI).

This high priest, therefore, comes from Jerusalem to Bethulia when he descends from heaven into the womb of the Virgin, taking flesh from her and becoming human for our sake. Hence he chose disciples, whom he himself called his brothers in the Gospel. They are rightly called priests because of the dignity of their office and the perfection of their wisdom, so that he might see Judith—that is, so that he might test the faith and confession of his Church.

«When she came out to him»—that is, when she displayed the devotion of her mind through good works—«they all blessed her with one voice, saying: ‘You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the joy of Israel, you are the honor of our people.’»

The Lord therefore blessed his Church when he filled her with the abundance of his gifts and showed her to be worthy of praise by all. For this reason, giving thanks to the Father in the Gospel, he says: «I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones» (Matt. XI). Hence Solomon also says: «Her children rose up and proclaimed her most blessed; her husband, and he praised her» (Prov. XXXI).

The holy Church is therefore the glory of Jerusalem, because she belongs to the heavenly city of God and to the fellowship and blessedness of the holy angels. She acted manfully by fighting against the principality of the world and despising the threats and persecutions of her enemies. She loved chastity because she preserved the purity of faith, through which the Apostle gloried in having betrothed the entire multitude of believers to the heavenly King, saying: «For I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ» (II Cor. XI). She guards herself undefiled for his marriage-bed and in no way consents to share in the error of heretics.

To the blessing of the high priest and the priests she responds: «Amen, amen»—that is, “Let it be, let it be”—because, from the greater to the lesser children of Mother Church, she alone shall be proclaimed throughout the whole world and shall everywhere and always be praised as worthy of her heavenly Bridegroom.

«For scarcely in thirty days were the spoils of the Assyrians collected by the people of Israel.»

These thirty days signify the whole period of the present life, because the people of God, by keeping the divine commandments through faith, hope, and charity, triumph over the enemy, gather his spoils, and despoil the spiritual Assyrian by laying waste his possessions. And rightly so, because by serving their king with confidence they stand strong and victorious everywhere in battle. Of him it is written: «The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle» (Ps. XXIII). In the Gospel parable Truth itself also says: «When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace; but when one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his armor in which he trusted and distribute his spoils» (Luke XI).

Hence Solomon also praises the strong woman, saying that «the heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will lack no spoils, because she girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm; strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day» (Prov. XXXI).

«Moreover, everything that had been proved to belong personally to Holofernes they gave to Judith: gold and silver, garments and jewels, and every possession. The people handed over everything to her.»

What does it mean that the people gave Judith everything that belonged personally to Holofernes, except that every one of the faithful who serve in Christ’s army dedicates collectively to the praise and service of holy Mother Church whatever they seize from the dominion or property of the enemy, and hastens to contribute it to her spiritual adornment? Thus she may shine in the gold of wisdom, gleam in the splendor of eloquence, radiate with the precious gems of virtues, and be clothed in the ornaments of various disciplines.

For whatever the unjust possessor had unjustly held from good things, she rightly draws to her own adornment. Hence, in Exodus, the people of God, departing from Egypt and heavily laden with the treasures of the Egyptians, carried them with them into the desert for the worship of God and the construction of his tabernacle. Likewise King David and the other righteous kings in the Old Testament consecrated to the service of God’s temple whatever they rescued from the hands of their enemies in various battles.

«And all the people rejoiced with the women, virgins, and young men, with instruments and lyres.»

All the people of God rejoice over the victory received, when all the members of Christ exult fully, at the end of the world, in the triumph over the ancient enemy. Then the praises of God resound on instruments and lyres, when they continually sing praises to the Almighty Lord both with a voice of rejoicing and with the harmonious melody of a perfected life. Then our Judith also sings a new song to the Lord, when she no longer fears anything from the corruption or injury of her enemies. Of this it is subsequently written.

## CHAPTER XVI. Judith’s marvelous song. How, after the victory had been accomplished, the people went to Jerusalem to pray to the Lord; and how Judith, having completed one hundred and five years, ended her life with a final end.

«Then Judith sang this song to the Lord, saying.»

Judith—that is, “confessing” and “praising”—sings a song to the Lord when the holy Church, the bride of the supreme King, after completing the battle of the present life, in which she fought against the devil and spiritual enemies for her triumph and deliverance, offers worthy thanks to the Lord and presents the ministry of her service to him fully and without impediment. Nothing of her ancestral name—that is, Merari, “remembrance”—will then hinder her, when no portion of former bitterness will remain, but every affliction of temporal sorrow will be transformed into the greatness of perfect joy.

Then, in accordance with the Apocalypse of John, «the tabernacle of God will be with human beings, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people; and God himself will be with them as their God. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more, neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any longer, because the former things have passed away» (Rev. XXI).

But let us see how Judith begins her song.

«Begin for the Lord with tambourines; sing to the Lord with cymbals; play for him a new psalm; exalt and invoke his name.»

Some say that the tambourine is a musical instrument, as though two bands met only at the ends, with dense leather stretched over them producing a resonant sound, which musicians strike in measured rhythm and modulate with a double resonance. Others say that the tambourine is a very small object because it can be carried in a woman’s hand, as it is written in Exodus: «Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand» (Exod. XV).

That it is made like a trumpet with a single pipe and a narrow opening through which one blows mystically signifies that the knowledge of the ancient law was once small in the hand of the synagogue of the Jews, but has now been expanded through Christ in the hands of the holy Church.

Cymbals, however, are very small bowls made from blended metals, with rounded cavities cast at their sides. When struck with artistic modulation, they produce a very sharp sound in pleasing harmony. They signify the movement of our lips, and have rightly been placed among musical instruments, because they bear a certain resemblance to cymbals and because human voices are demonstrably capable through them of producing the sweetest harmony.

Harmony is the joining together of diverse things brought into unity. This is also evident in the human voice, when the durations and syllables themselves are brought into a single concord of sound.

A psalm, as it has been handed down by our predecessors, is a musical instrument, like a lyre, a *pindarium*, and other instruments that respond to our voices with the sweetest melody. We have often said that this pertains to our most approved actions. We must therefore consider how our female singer commands us to sing praises to the Lord: first to begin for him with tambourines, then to sing with cymbals, and thus to play for him a psalm. She shows, namely, that if we wish our song to please God, we should strive to speak harmonious praises to him with heart, mouth, and good works.

The one who begins for the Lord with the tambourine is the person who continually meditates in the secrecy of his heart upon the commandments of the Lord’s law. The one who sings to him with the cymbal is the person who presents catholic confession with a fitting joy of the lips, together with spiritual songs. The one who plays for him a new psalm is the person who walks in newness of life and joins a good work, harmonious with the pious intention of his heart and the upright confession of his mouth.

Hence it is written in the Psalter: «Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise be pleasing to our God» (Ps. CXLVI).

Every human work demands that a reward be repaid to it, so that we may console ourselves with hope of the promised gift for what we accomplish laboriously. In praises of the Lord, however, the act itself possesses its reward, when what is now exercise will itself be the recompense. Since it is good to proclaim the Lord, each person is known to receive promised gifts from this very act. Indeed, he receives them when, in that angelic state, it becomes the singular privilege of the saints to undertake the Lord’s perpetual proclamation.

Let us therefore praise him with all the devotion we can, and here meditate upon those blessed gifts. What is happier than to practice now what you hope to be able to accomplish in future blessedness? For we have been saved in hope, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory. Hence what follows:

«The Lord who crushes wars—the Lord is his name—who has pitched his camp in the midst of his people.»

Our Redeemer, of whom it is written in the Psalm, «The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle» (Ps. XXIII), himself crushed the devil’s savagery through the blood of his cross and subjected the world to his authority. Rising from the dead, he said to his disciples: «All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age» (Matt. XXVIII).

He therefore pitched his camp in the midst of his people when he established his Church in the midst of the nations. Abiding in her always, he daily delivers his chosen from the hands of their enemies, but at the end of the world he will grant them complete deliverance, when what is mortal is swallowed up by life and death itself, the last enemy, is destroyed. Then the saints will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, and, seeing the destruction of all their enemies together with their head, they will laugh and say:

«Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity. But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in his mercy forever and ever, and I will confess to him» (Ps. LI).

Hence, now recalling the wickedness of his enemies in her song, she added:

«Assur came from the mountains of the north in the multitude of his strength; its multitude blocked the torrents, and its horses covered the valleys. It said that it would burn my borders, kill my young men with the sword, give my infants as plunder, and lead my virgins into captivity. But the Lord Almighty harmed him, handed him over to the hand of a woman, and she pierced him.»

Assur, whom Isaiah calls the rod of God’s fury and the staff of his indignation, mystically signifies the devil, who comes through his ministers—that is, unclean spirits, or pagan, Jewish, and even heretical people—from the mountains, meaning the paths of his pride. From the north—that is, from the coldness of unbelief—he prepared war against the people of God.

His army’s multitude blocked the torrents when he stirred up various persecutions against the faithful in temporal matters. His horses covered the valleys when the pride of his persecutors captured the humble in the bonds of their snares. His arrogance applauded itself for intending to devastate the boundaries of the Church and to kill her young men—that is, even those strong in faith and good works—with the sword of persecution. He intended to take the infants, of whom it is written, «From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise» (Matt. XXI), as plunder for seduction, and to carry off the virgins—that is, chaste and modest souls—into the prison of vices.

But although, in his blind folly, he applauded himself so greatly, the order of events did not yield to his desire. Rather, by the wonderful counsel of God, his pride was destroyed. He who elsewhere says, «I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High» (Isa. XIV), fell from heaven: Lucifer, who rose at dawn, fell to the earth, the one who wounded the nations.

The Lord Almighty therefore harmed him and handed him over to the hand of a woman, who is described long ago in Genesis as crushing the serpent’s head. She confounded him, binding him, namely, through her handmaids, who always offered devoted service to their Creator with humble hearts. Thus he who had promised himself the likeness of God through pride was dragged down to hell and plunged into the depths of the lake—that is, into the lowest hell, for the depth of the lake signifies this. For this reason, in the Gospel we read of «the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth» (Matt. VIII).

«For their mighty one did not fall by young men, nor did the sons of Titan strike him, nor did lofty giants oppose him; but Judith, the daughter of Merari, destroyed him by the appearance of her face.»

The enormity of the persecutors of the holy Church was not overcome by young men—that is, by the strength of the flesh. Nor could the ingenuity of human intelligence or the strength of earthly power inflict death upon them. Rather, divine power, through the humility and simplicity of the faithful, overcame, crushed, and scattered the hostile cohort. The appearance and splendor of all the virtues that shone in the speech of our Judith, and likewise in her actions, was the principal cause of the enemies’ ruin. For those who do not know how to love chastely the good found in others, but wickedly envy it, gain from the very source from which they might have found consolation an everlasting torment for themselves.

«For she stripped off the garment of her widowhood and put on the garment of joy in the exultation of the children of Israel. She anointed her face with perfume and bound her curls with a tiara; she took a new robe to deceive him. Her sandals seized his eyes, her beauty captivated his soul, and with a dagger she cut off his neck.»

The Church stripped off the garment of widowhood when she washed away in the water of baptism the deeds of the old person, for which she had deserved to be abandoned, and put on the conduct of the new person, who is renewed day by day according to the image of the one who created him, becoming a participant in heavenly joy. Hence Isaiah says of this exchange of spiritual garments, speaking of the typological Jerusalem: «You shall forget the shame of your youth, and you shall remember no more the reproach of your widowhood, because the one who made you shall rule over you; the Lord of hosts is his name» (Isa. LI).

She anointed her face with perfume when she received the anointing of sacred chrism upon her face, so that, according to the Psalmist, she might make her face radiant with oil. She arranged her curls with a tiara when she bound the wavering movements of her thoughts with divine fear and united them through firm hope; by this she most certainly deceived the efforts of the ancient enemy.

Her sandals seized his eyes because the coverings of her feet, with which she was shod for the preparation of the Gospel of peace, pierced the eyes of the enemy, and the beauty of her virtues made his soul powerless. Thus, having become superior, she struck down and condemned the neck of his obstinacy with the dagger of his own wickedness.

«The Persians were terrified by her steadfastness, and the Medes by her boldness.»

In the Persians, whose name is interpreted as “those who test,” and in the Medes, whose name echoes “those who fear,” the army of the devil may be understood: that is, the evil spirits who are always ready to test and deceive the servants of God. Hence in the Gospel we read that the tempter approached our Head in the desert, whom the same Scripture shortly afterward calls the devil. And the teacher of the nations, writing to the Corinthians, says: «Lest he who tempts tempt you» (I Cor. VII).

The spiritual Persians and Medes—that is, the devil’s phalanxes—are therefore terrified by the Church’s steadfastness and boldness, because they recognize that she has been given power by Christ to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. She has been founded upon the rock, and the gates of hell will not prevail against her. Hence Paul also admonished his hearers, saying: «Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.» For nothing is more proud and fierce than he when he is permitted to display the quality of his spirit, but nothing is weaker than he when divine power crushes him through the servants of Christ.

Note, reader, that he says that the Persians and Medes are terrified by her steadfastness, while the Assyrians howl. Consider whether the opinion we proposed above may perhaps be true concerning Cambyses, son of Cyrus, whom many believed to be the Nebuchadnezzar mentioned by history, who is shown to have ruled over the Persians, Medes, and Assyrians.

«Then the camps of the Assyrians howled, when my humble ones appeared, fainting with thirst.»

The camps of the Assyrians, whose name is interpreted as “the diligent,” howl when the persecutors of the Church, who were planning wars against the faithful, are conquered by the humility of those who, through abstinence, mortify the desires of the flesh within themselves and hunger and thirst for righteousness.

«The sons of maidens pierced them, and like fleeing children they killed them.»

The sons of maidens are the children of the Churches of Christ. They kill their enemies with the sword of the word as though they were fearful and unfit for battle, when they strip them of their boldness for fighting. Those, therefore, who have been commanded to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them do not desire to kill anyone with bodily weapons, but strive, with spiritual weapons—that is, sacred virtues—to overcome their enemies through divine aid. Thus reliable help is always granted to them, as our singer demonstrates in what follows.

«They perished in battle before the face of my Lord.»

For the Lord, the strong Lord, mighty in battle, himself gives strength and power to his people and is the protector of the salvation of his Christ—namely, the Christian people, who are members of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God blessed above all forever.

«Let us sing a hymn to the Lord; let us sing a new hymn to our God.»

The mystical Judith therefore rightly urges the new people redeemed by the Savior’s blood to sing a new hymn to the Lord—that is, to proclaim the mystery of the New Testament. It is called new because our age did not see the Lord’s incarnation with bodily eyes; otherwise nothing is new to God, since he knew all things beforehand before the foundation of the world.

Among the Greeks, a hymn (*hymnus*) is a form of speech—that is, praise composed according to the law of song. These were the hymns that the Gentiles also sang in honor of their idols. She added “to our God” so that we might clearly understand what kind of hymn she intended.

«Adonai, Lord, you are great and glorious in your strength, and no one can overcome you.»

Adonai is one of the ten names of God among the Hebrews, and it is interpreted as “Lord,” signifying that he rules over every creature. It should be noted that wherever the word “Lord” is placed second—as in the present passage, and in Ezekiel, where, according to the Septuagint edition, he speaks to the prince of Tyre, saying, «You shall die the death of the uncircumcised by the hands of strangers, because I have spoken, says Adonai the Lord» (Ezek. XXVIII)—the first name is the tetragrammaton, which properly belongs to the Lord and is called ineffable, in accordance with the common usage by which it is often found among human beings.

And rightly Adonai is called the co-begotten one of God, because he is God and human. The Lord, then, is Lord either because he rules over all or because he is feared by all. No one can overcome him in strength, but through humility and submission one can please him and incline him to mercy, for he is kind and merciful to all who flee to his goodness and clemency.

«Let every creature of yours serve you, because you spoke and they were made; you sent forth your Spirit, and they were created, and there is no one who can resist your voice.»

Observe that this female singer proclaims the Holy Trinity: the Lord the Father, who made all things by his command—that is, through his Word—and created all things through his Spirit. The Psalmist says something similar: «By the word of God the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power» (Ps. XXXII). No one can resist his voice—that is, his command—because all things have been placed within his will; what he wills, he accomplishes.

«The mountains shall be moved from their foundations with the waters.»

By the mountains is signified the pride of persecutors. They are moved from their foundations with the waters when they cease from wicked counsels and seditions—not willingly, however, but by necessity—for what the proud began, defeated by the power of God, they cannot bring to completion. Concerning this he added another comparison, saying:

«The rocks shall melt like wax before your face.»

That is, the hardness of the proud, which believed itself to be unconquerable, will weaken and fail in the presence of your coming. For just as wax gathered from honeycombs is a tender and soft substance, which is dissolved by the heat of fire until its entire mass is consumed, so sinners also perish before God’s judgment, just as wax is consumed by a nearby fire.

Yet he says that they will be dissolved before the face of God because they will never come to his grace and benefits. On the contrary, let us hear what will happen to those who fear God:

«Those who fear you,» he says, «shall be great before you in all things.»

Just as those who despise God are diminished and fail, so those who fear him shall be great before him in all things—that is, in the bestowal of virtues and in the increase of rewards.

After this the prophetess mentioned above returns again to explain the punishments of her enemies and says:

«Woe to the nation that rises up against my people, for the Lord Almighty will take vengeance upon them.»

By “her own people” she means the men who worship God, of whom it is written in the Psalm: «This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob» (Ps. XXIII). Opposed to this is that other generation, the wicked and perverse one, of which the Lord says in the Gospel:

«Behold, I send to you prophets and wise men and scribes. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues and pursue from city to city, so that upon you may come all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Truly I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation» (Matt. XXIII).

Woe, therefore, will be perpetual for this generation, because eternal torment without end remains for it, with the just Judge rightly repaying it for what it had previously wickedly done to its neighbors. Hence it follows:

«On the day of judgment he will visit them.»

He will indeed visit them—not to crown them with a heavenly reward together with the saints, but to torment them with the devil and his angels in everlasting punishments in hell.

“for he will give fire and worms to their flesh, [Col. 0587B] so that they may be burned and suffer forever.”

Hence, in a consoling voice, the Lord speaks through the prophet Isaiah to the righteous, saying:

“Do not fear the reproach of man, and do not dread their blasphemies. For just as a garment, so the worm will consume them; and just as wool, so the moth will devour them. But my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness throughout all generations” (Isa. LI).

For the torments of hell do not flow only into the sinners’ flesh, but also into their souls, because each substance will rightly be punished there if it neglected here to practice repentance for sins and to produce the fruit of good works. He therefore says that fire and worms are given to the flesh because the stench of worms ordinarily arises from the corruption of flesh and blood. Fresh meat is salted for this reason, so that, once its bloody moisture has been dried out, it cannot become worm-infested. Flesh and blood, therefore, produce worms. And because carnal pleasure—which the seasoning of continence resists—generates eternal punishment for the lustful, the Savior says in the Gospel: “Where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished” (Mark IX). He indicates the corruption of Gehenna by the worm, just as he indicates its burning by the fire; or by “worm” he means the tardy remorse for sins, which will never cease to gnaw the conscience of the afflicted amid their torments, so that the fire is punishment raging outwardly, while the worm is pain accusing inwardly.

“And it came to pass after these things that all the people, after the victory, came to Jerusalem to worship the Lord, and as soon as they had been purified, they all offered holocausts, vows, and their promises.”

“And it came to pass,” he says, “after these things”—that is, after the death of Holofernes, after the flight and destruction of the enemies, after the citizens had rejoiced with Judith over the divine aid granted to them, and over their deliverance and the praises they rendered to the Lord for it. All the people came to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and to present there holocausts, vows, and promises, because the temple of God, the altar, and the chief sanctuary were there.

Mystically, however, this signifies that each of the elect, after completing the battle of this world and winning a certain victory over his enemies, purified from every stain of sin, hastens to the heavenly city of God, where there is the true vision of peace, and where he may offer his Creator pure vows of the heart, an acceptable confession of the mouth, and pleasing holocausts of his entire manner of life. [Col. 0588A] Then what is written in the Apocalypse concerning the saints will be fulfilled: “God,” it says, “will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Apoc. VII). So great and exalted will be the splendor of that city, given by God, that no traces of antiquity will remain. Then heavenly incorruption will raise up the bodies, and the contemplation of the eternal King will nourish the minds. “And death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain; for the former things have passed away.” When the holy city has been glorified at the final judgment, pain, mourning, and mortality will remain only in Gehenna.

“Moreover, Judith offered as an anathema of oblivion all the weapons of Holofernes that the people had given her, and the canopy that she herself had taken from his bedchamber.” [Col. 0588B]

That Judith therefore consecrated to the Lord all the weapons of Holofernes given to her by the people signifies that holy Church, rescuing from the devil’s power those souls whom he had deceived by his wickedness and subjected to the use of his service—that is, to works of impiety—made them acceptable vessels to God through good endeavor, by water and the word, in accordance with that Gospel parable in which the Lord speaks to the Jews, saying:

“No one can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man; and then he will plunder his house” (Mark III).

When the Redeemer of the human race cast out the prince of this world and bound the strong man, the Church then received power over him, so that, plundering the enemy’s vessels, she might transform them into vessels of piety. Likewise, the zeal by which, in preaching, she exposed the frauds of the wicked seducer, she herself offers as an acceptable gift to her King and Creator.

Hence it follows: “And the canopy that she herself had taken, as an anathema of oblivion.” The canopy, which is said to be a net for catching flies, signifies the deceits by which the unwary are captured. Holy mother Church, however, anathematizes and condemns these, because she knows that they displease the Lord, whereas innocence pleases him, according to the Psalmist:

“He who has innocent hands and a pure heart, who has not received his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor—he shall receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior” (Ps. XXIII).

“And the people were joyful according to the appearance of the saints.”

Truly, the people of God will then be joyful when they have attained the contemplation of the face of their Creator; and even during this pilgrimage they are already, in hope of future goods, joyful and glad in a certain manner. Hence the Apostle says: “We have already been saved in hope” (Rom. VIII). And again: “Rejoicing in hope,” he says, “patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII). Hence Truth itself also says in the Gospel:

“When they persecute you and say every evil thing against you falsely for my name’s sake, rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. X).

“And for three months the joy of this victory was celebrated with Judith.”
