What does it mean for the joy of this victory to be celebrated with Judith for three months, [Col. 0589A] except that each of the saints, through faith, hope, and charity, rejoices with mother Church during his sojourn in this world and strives with all his strength so that, aided by divine grace, he may preserve his spirit, soul, and body blameless and whole for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ? Faith, as the Lord testifies, saves a person. Concerning hope the Psalmist says:

“He who hopes in the Lord will never be confounded” (Ps. XXX).

Hence the apostle John also said concerning charity: “He who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John IV).

For three months, therefore, every person who rightly desires to attain eternal blessedness celebrates such joy, and, leading a perfect life through a pious intention, upright speech, and good works, anxiously awaits the coming of his Judge. But when he has come and that person’s time of labor has passed, then what follows will take place:

“But after those days each one returned to his own home.”

For when the judgment has ended and the sentence has been received, the saints of God will depart from the pilgrimage of this world to possess the kingdom of the eternal Father, which was prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

“And Judith became great in Bethulia, and she was more renowned than all the land of Israel.”

For then the splendor and glory of holy Church, which had previously been hidden while she was involved in the troubles of this world, will appear. Then, according to the Gospel testimony, “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII). And the purity of faith—through which the Apostle gloried that he had betrothed all true believers as a chaste virgin to one man, Christ—will shine forth in the true Bethulia, that is, in perpetual virginity, when the most noble bride, truly joined to her heavenly Bridegroom, without stain, wrinkle, or any corruption, enters the heavenly Jerusalem.

Judith was therefore more renowned than all the land of Israel, because the Catholic Church alone stands out throughout the whole world, seeking heavenly riches, most worthy of the bedchamber of the heavenly King, and destined to possess an everlasting kingdom with him. Concerning her the Bridegroom himself says in the Song of Songs:

“There are sixty queens and eighty concubines; my dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the only one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her. The daughters saw her and called her most blessed; the queens and concubines praised her” (Song VI).

[Col. 0589D] “And chastity was also joined to her virtue, so that she did not know a man throughout all the days of her life from the time when Manasseh her husband died.”

The chastity of the Church is therefore admirable and greatly deserving of praise. After she had renounced the devil’s pomp and idolatry, and, according to the Apostle’s judgment, the world had been crucified to her and she to the world, she no longer allowed herself to fall back into the allurements of carnal pleasures and her former filth of sins. Washed and reborn in the laver of sacred regeneration, she lives for the remaining time in faith in the Son of God, to whom Paul says:

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.”

“And on feast days she went forth with great glory.” [Col. 0590A]

The feasts of the Christian religion—on which it recalls the time of the Lord’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, the coming of the Holy Spirit, and the births and triumphs of the holy martyrs and confessors—are occasions on which the Church goes forth with great glory, because through honorable conduct, upright morals, and praises she unceasingly commemorates the divine mysteries.

The prophet seems to command this to the new people, that is, to the Christian people, in the Psalter, where it is written:

“Appoint the solemn day in the gatherings, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII).

He says that what is to be released is to be consecrated by the honor given to the Lord and by the confession of the saints in the gatherings—that is, in the frequent professions of faith that the multitude of the people gathers together—and is rendered with the most celebrated festive devotion. But when he adds “even to the horn of the altar,” perhaps some are prohibited from doing what is customary for many: descending after hearing the Gospel reading. For those who are not filled for the sake of communion do not approach the horn of the altar. In my view, we suitably understand this of the visible altar, from which the body and blood of the Lord are given in solemn assembly. That other altar, however, is before the sight of the Lord, where, with purified souls, we are commanded to approach the holy things through contemplation, so that in this present solemnity we may always keep it in view.

“She remained in her husband’s house for one hundred and five years, and she released Abram, her freedwoman.” [Col. 0590C]

We may understand the house of her husband as the present world, in which the Church labors under the heat of tribulations, because after she renounced the error that she had previously served through pagan conduct, the burdens of persecutions immediately increased for her.

She remained there for one hundred and five years because, serving as a soldier under the law of God, she contended to attain eternal blessedness. The five books of the divine Law are therefore signified: in them the worship of the one God is commended, and service to all idols is utterly forbidden. The hundred, because it transfers the number from the left hand to the right, fittingly signifies eternal blessedness, as we have said.

And she released Abram, her freedwoman, when, by teaching, exhorting, and improving through good examples, she brings carnal conduct—which is always subject to fear—into the freedom of grace and the security of charity, so that what she had previously done in part through fear of punishments, in hope of rewards she may now strive to do through perfect love of the good itself. For, as John says:

“Fear, which has punishment, is not in charity; but perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John IV).

Hence the fearful are likened to the condition of slaves, and those full of love to that of free persons.

“And she died and was buried with her husband in Bethulia.”

He says that the Church died and was buried insofar as this applies to her members, who, from the beginning of the sin of our first parent until the end of the world, could not escape the law of bodily death. Concerning this the prophet says:

“Who is the man who lives and will not see death?”

According to the judgment of Ecclesiastes, the wise and the foolish will also die, and all hasten toward one end; the earth is likewise a common burial place for the good and the wicked.

Or, in a deeper sense, Judith died and was buried with her husband when the Church dies with Christ in baptism so that she may rise with him. Hence the Apostle says:

“For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

“And all the people mourned for her seven days.”

What does it mean that all the people mourned Judith’s death for seven days, except that God’s elect, throughout the whole period of the present life—which runs according to the number seven, the number of days—afflict themselves in sorrow and groaning because of the pilgrimage of the present Church, until the day dawns and the shadows decline? This mourning does not arise from despair, but rather from weariness with present things and from the longing for future things that the saints continually possess.

In their person the prophet speaks in the Psalms, saying:

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept when we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. XXXVI).

And again he says:

“My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. XLI).

Thus, as we have said, ecclesiastical lamentations are solemn rather than funereal. Hence it is read in the Gospel that “Rachel was weeping for her children and would not be consoled, because they are not” (Matt. II). Devout men cared for Stephen and made great lamentation over him. “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.” Conversely, “woe to those who laugh now, for they shall weep.”

The saints of God therefore weep now, “going and sowing their seed; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV).

“And throughout the whole span of her life there was no one who troubled Israel, nor for many years after her death.” [Col. 0592A]

How can it be said that during Judith’s lifetime no one troubled Israel, when the whole life of the human race is a time of testing upon the earth? Perhaps he is speaking of external devastation by enemies, saying that after the victory won through Judith they caused the Jewish people less trouble for a time.

The mystery, however, is clear: no one can utterly harm God’s elect in the present Church—that is, reach the destruction of their souls. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel:

“Everything that the Father has given me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.”

And again:

“Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.”

Hence the Apostle also says:

“Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. VIII).

Therefore, on all the days during which the Church journeys in the sojourn of this world, her elect children are protected unharmed beneath the shadow of God’s wings until the end. And if they are preserved without loss of salvation during this time, which is so full of pain and distress, how much more will they be guarded after the end of this life, without any distress, groaning, or danger, where there will no longer be any pain or groaning?

This is what is meant by “for many years after her death”: after the death of the present life, her years are the age of ages, during which she lives happily with Christ and reigns forever.

“The day of this victory’s festivity is counted by the Hebrews among the holy days, and it is observed by the Jews from that time to the present day.” [Col. 0592C]

Rightly, therefore, the festivity of this victory is counted by the Hebrews—that is, by those who are passing over—among the holy days and is observed by the Jews—that is, by confessors—from that time to the present day. For all who, placed on the road of this life, desire to pass over to the heavenly kingdom and confess to the Lord his mercy and his wonders toward the children of men, can in no way forget this solemnity. They count it among the holy days, celebrating it as the one occasion of joy among all their solemnities.

This applies from the time when they first escaped the enemy’s power through baptism until the present day—that is, until the present age comes to an end. But when the future life has come, then the festivity will be stable and perfect, when the God of gods is seen in Zion and his saints reign with him forever and ever.

[Col. 0599]

APPENDIX TO RABANUS MAURUS’S EXPOSITION ON THE BOOK OF JUDITH. JACOB PAMELIUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE SAME BOOK.

[Col. 0593]

PREFACE

[Col. 0593A] In this troubled age of ours, in which everyone, according to his own inclination, either rejects or approves whatever he wishes, certain particularly obstinate people remove from the sacred Scriptures not only many other books that the Church retains as sacred Scripture, but also this book, moved by the argument that the Hebrews do not receive it among the canonical Scriptures. They confirm this by the authority of Jerome in the Preface to the Books of Kings, where, after first listing the books accepted into the canon by the Hebrews, he concludes:

“Whatever, therefore, is outside Job is to be placed among the apocrypha; and consequently Wisdom, which is commonly entitled Solomon’s, and Jesus son of Sirach, the Book of Judith, and Tobit are not in the canon.”

Yet, to give a brief answer to this, it does not immediately follow that, if these books are not authoritative among the Hebrews, they are not to be received by the Christian Church, which, divinely instructed, holds and proclaims the whole of the New Testament—which the Jews reject—together with certain books published before the Gospel, as possessing canonical authority.

The sayings of God were indeed translated and handed down from the Hebrews to the Church of Christ, and the Scriptures of the Old Instrument remain common to Jews and Christians even to this day. But the Jews, now denying Christ, the end of all the prophets, have lost the true understanding of those same Scriptures; and they do not receive into the canon of their Scriptures many books that plainly proclaim Christ, though these were subsequently received by the Christian Church. Among these this book, which we have before us, is deservedly to be counted, since it is most certainly true and was produced by the divine Spirit, as has long been known to the Churches.

Jerome, however, says in the aforementioned prologue:

“To one who pays careful attention, it is clearer than it needs to be proved that I am enumerating the canon according to the opinion of the Hebrews, assigning the order and names of the books according to their custom. There will be a better opportunity below for citing its summary.”

It must now be demonstrated that, from the beginning—that is, from the primitive Church—this Scripture was regarded as canonical and was cited by the Fathers as such.

First, Origen, who flourished around the year [Col. 0593C] 196, although in the canon of the Scriptures that he lists in his Commentary on Psalm I, as cited by Eusebius in Book VI, chapter 8, of his Ecclesiastical History, he does not mention this Scripture—for he was reporting not the canon of the Church but that of the Hebrews, as is clear from the added phrase, “Thus the Hebrews relate”—nevertheless cites this history, just as he cites the other Scriptures cut off by them from the canon, in his final homily on the Books of Judges. A diligent reader may perhaps find more passages in him.

Chrysostom likewise draws the commendation of fasting especially from this history in many substantial passages of Homily 10 on Fasting.

Similarly, Ambrose treats this history as canonical: in On the Duties, Book III, chapter 3; in Book X of his Letters, Letter 83; in On Virgins, Book II; and in On the Instruction of a Virgin, chapter 2. He also develops this history at great length in his book On Widows, honoring it with an exposition that forms no small part of that work. [Col. 0594A]

Augustine, although in Book XVIII, chapter 26, of The City of God he says that the Book of Judith is not received into the canon by the Jews, nevertheless expounds this history at great length to the people in Sermons 229 and 230. He clearly implies that he held the same opinion concerning it as he did concerning the Books of the Maccabees in the same work, chapter 36—namely, that although the Jewish Church does not receive them, the Christian Church does receive them into the canon—in Book II of On Christian Doctrine, when, while reciting the canon of the Scriptures, he places this and the other Scriptures under dispute between us in the same order as the Books of Job, Esther, and Ezra.

“There is another order,” he says, “in which the histories are arranged as if in a different order, and which neither correspond with the preceding books nor with one another, such as Job, Tobit, Esther, Judith, the two Books of the Maccabees, and the two Books of Ezra.”

You have Augustine’s opinion. Let us now briefly examine what Jerome’s was.

First, in the prologue to this book Jerome says that the Nicene synod counted it among the sacred Scriptures. Moreover, it is evident that he himself regarded it as such from various passages in which he brings forward this history, like the other sacred histories, in confirmation of his statements.

Although in some places he adds a restriction—for example, in his letter to Furia, “if anyone nevertheless wishes to receive this book,” and in his commentary on Haggai, chapter 1, “if anyone nevertheless wishes to accept the book of the woman” (note this passage: perhaps he means “written by a woman,” namely Judith herself)—in other places, especially in his letter to Silvina on widowhood, he uses no restriction, but cites this history in the same manner as Esther and the Gospel passage concerning Anna, daughter of Phanuel.

But perhaps you will object that Jerome, in the aforementioned prologue, and likewise the Symbol—which some attribute to Cyprian and others to Rufinus—judge this book’s authority less suitable for strengthening matters that come into dispute.

This does not obstruct the argument, because there too he indicates that he is not speaking from his own judgment: he prefaces it with “among the Hebrews” and uses the verb “is judged.” One may also reply, lest anyone press the point, that the Symbol says:

“The Fathers wished all these books to be read in the Church, but not to use them to strengthen the authority of the faith.”

Although such books may not be suitable for confirming the faith against the Jews, who place them outside the canon, they are nevertheless held in the Christian Churches as books produced by the divine Spirit.

This can also be confirmed from the councils: first, from that Nicene council cited by Jerome, which, as Gregory reports, declares that it venerates this book as it does the four Gospels; and then from the Third Council of Carthage, at which Augustine himself was present. There, in canon 4, when they defined which books ought to be read and sung in the Church, Augustine also lists this book among the others.

The Fathers supplied what had been omitted in the final canon of the Council of Laodicea, following almost the same order as in the passage cited above. Innocent I preserves the same order in his decretal letter to Exuperius, chapter 7, as does Gelasius in the Roman council at its beginning; the Council of Constance and the Council of Trent later followed them.

Let this therefore now be clear: just as from the other books of Scripture, so from this book also, excellent interpreters—including men close to the successors of the Apostles—received testimonies as divine. Consequently, besides the three orders that Jerome lists, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, in the Prologue to the Books of Kings, there is among us a fourth order of books of the Old Testament. Although the Hebrews count these among the apocrypha, the Christian Church honors and proclaims them among the divine books.

It remains to consider at what time, under which king, and by what author this history was written. Here the variety among writers is so great that it is difficult to find even two who agree with one another. After citing several opinions, we shall, with God’s favor, demonstrate as briefly as possible which appears most probable. [Col. 0595B]

Two possibilities immediately present themselves which, as it seems, must be entirely rejected. The first is wrongly inferred from Augustine by the compiler who composed an index to all his works: namely, that the event occurred under Cyrus. How unlikely this is is too well known to require proof, since Cyrus was exceedingly favorable to the Jews until the very end of his life.

The second is the opinion followed by Eusebius in his Chronicles, by his followers Augustine in Book XVIII, chapter 26, of The City of God—for this can be inferred from that passage more readily than the opinion just mentioned—and Bede in On Times. One of the more recent writers, Ziegler, falsely attributes this opinion to Philo.

In my view, he is mistaken because he says that the king under whom the event occurred was Ahasuerus, and that the ancient Artaxerxes succeeded Cyrus. He believes that this king was Cambyses, whereas, as will be shown more fully below, the reference is to Darius Hystaspes.

The opinion is that the event occurred under the aforementioned Cambyses. But several considerations stand in the way. First, the length of his reign was too short, twelve years being assigned to it, whereas the consensus of all historians establishes that he did not reign for a full eight years. Nor does the explanation offered by some satisfy—that the twelve years refer only to the period during which he ruled after his father’s death, while he had previously reigned for six years when Cyrus had gone to war against the Scythians. For although this is certainly reported by Metasthenes, secular histories—if Sabellicus and Carion are to be trusted—say that he survived his father only a very short time, less than two years; the Greeks likewise assign only seven years and five months to his reign.

There is also a very serious obstacle in chapter 4 of this history, where mention is made of Eliakim and Joakim, the high priest—for according to Philo these names are synonymous among the Syrians and Egyptians. It is certain that this man held the high priesthood long after Cambyses, since Jesus son of Josedech, under whom the children of Israel were brought back from captivity, held the high priesthood first for thirty-six years and afterward for twenty years; he was eventually succeeded in the priesthood by his son Joakim. There are many other objections, which we omit for the sake of brevity. [Col. 0595D]

There are two other opinions that I would not dare wholly to reject, since they rest on fairly solid foundations, although I cannot approve them in every respect.

The first is the opinion of the aforementioned Ziegler and certain other recent writers, who think that the event occurred not after, as most believe, but before the capture of Jerusalem—under King Josiah, when he was still a minor, since we read in 2 Kings XXII that he began to reign in the eighth year of his age.

Accordingly, during his childhood they believe that responsibility for strengthening the province was entrusted to the high priest, first Hilkiah and then his son Eliakim, who is mentioned in 2 Kings XVIII and Isaiah XXII—not, perhaps, as high priest, but merely as a priest of the second order, elected by the priestly college because of his exceptional authority and proven piety, which he and his father had preserved inviolate under the impious kings Manasseh and Amon.

They understand the king who reigned in Nineveh as Nebuchadnezzar, called the Ancient, the first of that name, but the third king of the Chaldeans and the eighth of the Babylonians, the father of the great Nebuchadnezzar who devastated Jerusalem. Concerning the latter it is recorded in 2 Kings XXIV that he carried Jeconiah, who had voluntarily surrendered with his wife and children, into Assyria and appointed Zedekiah king.

They think that Arphaxad, against whom he waged war, was either Phraortes, king of the Medes, whom they say reigned among the Medes for twelve years under Nebuchadnezzar, or his father Deioces, who, according to Herodotus, founded Ecbatana with far greater magnificence than is described here. They favor the former opinion concerning Phraortes, because Deioces died around the twelfth year of Nebuchadnezzar.

This opinion would appear more plausible than the others if certain matters in the subsequent course of the book did not strongly oppose it. For since, according to Eusebius in his Chronicles, the Median king Cyaxares, who succeeded Phraortes and was the father of Astyages, completely destroyed Nineveh—or, as Eusebius calls it, Ninus—and since Jerome, citing Herodotus in the Prologue to his Commentary on the Prophet Jonah, testifies that this occurred in the time of Josiah, why may we not conjecture that, after Phraortes, king of the Medes, had been defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, his son Cyaxares—or, as Metasthenes calls him, Astybarus—together with his own son Axanda, whom we call Astyages, while they were ruling, took revenge upon Nebuchadnezzar? Having made war upon him, just as Nebuchadnezzar had conquered the royal city of the Medes, Ecbatana, they in turn conquered the royal city of the Assyrians, Nineveh, which had stood until that time. This opinion seems plausible to anyone.

Nevertheless, the first objection is that Joakim or Eliakim—for I do not press the variation in names—is called high priest in chapter 15. From Josephus it is clear that the Eliakim mentioned there was not the high priest: in Book VIII, chapter 10, of his Antiquities, when he lists the succession of high priests, Josephus substitutes not Eliakim but Seraiah, the son of Hilkiah. This difficulty might perhaps be removed if, because chapter XXII of Isaiah and Jerome’s Commentary seem to support the contrary opinion, we suppose that Seraiah was the same person and had been called by various names.

There is also the objection that, in the final chapter, Judith is said to have lived in her husband’s house for 115 years, and that during the whole span of her life and for many years after her death no one troubled Israel. Yet sacred history establishes that no more than about forty-two years after King Josiah Jerusalem was devastated.

Finally, even if someone could perhaps devise an escape from the preceding objections, I see no answer at all to what Achior says to Holofernes in chapter V. After saying that many of them had been led captive into a foreign land, he adds:

“But recently they returned to the Lord their God from the dispersion in which they had been scattered, and they were gathered together.”

From this it seems plainly proved that these events occurred after the return from captivity. Noticing this, as I think, Severus Sulpicius, in Book II of his Sacred History, inclines toward the second opinion. He therefore says that the event occurred after the captivity, rejecting Eusebius’s opinion concerning Cambyses because the years of his reign do not correspond. With a modest preface—“if it is permissible to form an opinion in history”—he thinks that the events occurred under King Ochus, who was second after Artaxerxes and under whom Esther flourished.

He reaches this conclusion partly because Ochus was by nature harsh and exceedingly thirsty for human blood and wars, if the accounts of pagan historians are to be trusted. Besides exercising great tyranny, he even killed his own brothers. He also invaded Egypt, which had defected from the Persian monarchy many years earlier, and at that time he is said to have mocked their sacred rites and Apis, whom they accepted as a god. Something similar is also reported of Cambyses, which seems to have influenced Eusebius and others. Later, the eunuch Bagoas, an Egyptian by nation, indignant at this, took vengeance by the king’s death.

This history mentions a certain Bagoas, when Judith is said to have been led by him to Holofernes’ bedchamber in chapter XII, and again in chapters XIII and XIV. Thus Sulpicius says that he was not without reason led to advance this as an argument for his opinion, namely, that King Nebuchadnezzar was Ochus, since the years also correspond, for Ochus reigned more than twenty-three years.

This opinion also seems to receive confirmation from the fact that, according to Orosius in Book III, chapter 7, of his History, Ochus led many Jews into exile and ordered them to live in Hyrcania beside the Caspian Sea. Orosius consistently reports that they were still there in his own time and would one day break out from that region.

I see no other objection to this opinion except that, apart from the fact that later writers would be placing this history, contrary to the common opinion of all, after the history of Esther, I do not see who this high priest Joakim or Eliakim was—for the Septuagint also reads “Joakim” in the earlier passage. For Philo establishes that the high priest Joakim, son of Jesus, lived only until the twelfth year of the great Artaxerxes; under Ochus, however, Joakim held the priesthood for twenty-three years, with two high priests intervening, until the end of Ochus’s life. Unless perhaps we say that both names belonged to the same person, with only the ending of the name changed. But even if we were to follow that opinion, which is less probable, I do not see whom we should make this Arphaxad. Leaving this for diligent students of history to investigate more deeply, I think we should hasten to the opinion of Philo, which appears safest of all—provided, of course, that the book does not falsely claim Philo as its author.

Philo, then, in his Brief Account of Times, reports that the event occurred under Ahasuerus the Ancient, Artaxerxes, who succeeded Cyrus. It is clear that he was not Cambyses, as Ziegler thought, but Darius Hystaspes, because Philo says that he was succeeded by his son Darius Artaxerxes Longimanus. Everyone knows that this Darius was not the son of Cambyses.

The fact that, following Metasthenes, Philo does not mention Cambyses or Xerxes when listing these kings appears to have arisen for two reasons. First, as stated above, Cambyses reigned only a very short time after his father’s death. Second, Xerxes, immediately at the beginning of his reign, went to Greece and left the administration of the Eastern kingdom to Artaxerxes. Since Xerxes did not remain in the East, he appears to have been unknown among the Hebrews. Thus the catalogue of these kings found among the Greek historians can be harmonized very well with that found in Metasthenes.

Philo adds that, when this king was preparing war against Arphaxad—for so he calls the supporter of the Tamarite faction, who had driven the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians into revolt—Jesus the high priest was sent to him to intercede for the Hebrews, because the leaders of Syria had written to the king against them. In the twelfth year of Ahasuerus, Jesus had left his son Joakim, also called Eliakim, in the high priesthood; but Jesus was not heard by the king, because he was occupied with the war.

Philo therefore says that this history occurred while Joakim was administering the high priesthood. Consequently, in the following year, when he heard of the slaughter of Holofernes, he issued a public decree forbidding the temple to be rebuilt, as we have it in the Book of Ezra. [Col. 0597D] This is his opinion.

We must now briefly answer the arguments that move others to think that this history occurred before the captivity, beginning with those that seem to derive their basis from the history itself.

The first of these is that in chapter 4, concerning the fear of the already terrified children of Israel, it is said: “Trembling and horror seized their senses,” lest he do to Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord what he had done to the other cities and temples. It is established, however, that in the time of this Darius Hystaspes only the foundations of the temple had been laid. Hence, they say, there should have been no fear that a temple would be profaned which did not yet exist, and much less that the city would be destroyed, since it too had not yet begun to be built.

It will be easy to answer this if we attend more carefully to what has been added in the Greek text—which most attribute to the translators of the Septuagint—as an explanation. Since they had recently come up from captivity and the whole people had lately been gathered from Judea, [Col. 0598A] and since the vessels, the altar, and the houses had been sanctified from profanation, it is clearly understood that by “temple” the already erected altar is meant. At it they were already offering the daily and nightly burnt offerings, as I Esdras 3 testifies: “They set the altar of God upon its foundations and offered upon it burnt offerings to the Lord morning and evening,” and so forth. By “Jerusalem” are meant the foundations already laid, together with the dwellings in which they lived. Hence in the Greek, as an explanation, “and their houses” is also read, as has been said.

Of less importance is what they bring forward secondly from chapter 6: since the children of Israel had returned from captivity only shortly before, so that their memory of it was still fresh, Holofernes could not have been ignorant of all these matters, yet he seriously inquires about them from the leaders of the Moabites and Ammonites. Those words may be understood as spoken out of amazement [Col. 0598B] and excessive rage, as though he were saying: “Who and what sort of people are these who dare to resist, and, I ask, with what assistance are they emboldened?” This interpretation is certainly not inappropriate.

Perhaps another escape may also be found by saying that Holofernes was neither an Assyrian nor a Persian, but came from the more distant regions of the world; because of his outstanding exploits he had been elevated to such dignity, and therefore these matters were unknown to him.

Finally, if one may drive out a nail with a nail, as the proverb says, I should like them to answer the following point. First, there is what we cited above from Achior in the passage that follows shortly: “But they had recently returned to the Lord their God from their dispersion,” and so forth. To this corresponds the reading of the Septuagint, who additionally preface these words: “And their cities had been devastated, and the temple had been desolated.”

What they bring forward concerning the destruction of Nineveh and the Medes’ monarchy, already occupied by the Persians, has the same degree of force. For if, as we must believe Jerome in the passage cited above, Nineveh was destroyed [Col. 0598C] under Josiah, and one hundred years elapsed between Josiah and this Darius, what is to prevent us from supposing that both Nineveh—where, after the Assyrians had defected, as I said shortly above from Philo, the Medes and Persians had ruled—and Ecbatana had been rebuilt?

For from the frequently cited interpretation of the Septuagint it is clear that it was not merely this Nebuchadnezzar—for that was a common name among the Assyrian kings, just as “Darius” and “Artaxerxes” were among the Persians—who overcame Arphaxat, but that he also captured the city of Ecbatana itself. Thus in chapter 1 they read, among many other details that are added beyond our common version:

“And he reached Ecbatana, and seized its towers, destroyed its streets, and gave its adornment over to disgrace.”

Yet it is established from I Esdras 6 that under this Darius’s successor, Longimanus—for Philo thinks that the temple was completed under him—Ecbatana was rebuilt. There it is said that the document in which Cyrus’s decree concerning the release of the Israelites from captivity had been recorded was found in Ecbatana. Josephus also testifies to this in book 18, saying that Daniel built at Ecbatana [Col. 0598D] a magnificent tower in which the kings of Persia continued, even to his own time, to be buried.

What they allege—that neither Nineveh nor the Medes had kings around this time—is worthless. If we examine the text more closely, Nebuchadnezzar is not called king of Nineveh, but is perhaps said to have ruled in it as its sole remaining possession, since he had also been expelled from Babylon, if Herodotus, Justin, and the other historians are to be believed; nevertheless, he later recovered Babylon through the efforts of a certain Zopyrus.

Similarly, where our text reads “Arphaxat, king of the Medes,” the Septuagint express the meaning better when they translate: “Arphaxat, who ruled the Medes in Ecbatana,” as though they were saying that he had seized the kingdom.

Severus Sulpicius likewise confirms his opinion on the basis of the mention of a certain Bagous in this book. In the same way this too may be confirmed, since Sabellicus openly mentions a prefect of this Darius, bearing the same name, through whom [Col. 0599A] he arranged the death of a certain Oliganus, who was plotting against his life.

So much for these matters. We shall now briefly add who the author of this book was.

As in the preceding discussion, so here Philo’s opinion appears to be the one that should be accepted. He makes Joachim, the high priest mentioned in this book, the author both of this book and of the Book of Esther. Joachim had administered the high priesthood: first, when his father was sent on an embassy, during which the events of this history took place, for eight years; at that time he composed this history and instituted an annual observance of the memory [Col. 0600A] of the deliverance. Later, after his father had returned and had in the meantime again exercised the priesthood, Joachim held it for forty-eight years—from the twentieth year of Longimanus to the twelfth year of the great Artaxerxes, or Ahasuerus, under whom Esther flourished.

Someone might perhaps infer from Jerome’s Commentary on Haggai, chapter 1, that Judith herself wrote the book, since he says: “If anyone nevertheless wishes to accept the book of a woman.” But we are often deceived by conjectures of this kind.

# JACOBUS PAMELIUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK OF JUDITH

[Col. 0599]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0599B] Nebuchadnezzar, having conquered Arphaxat, who had seized the kingdom of the Medes and thus his entire realm by force, strives to rule all kingdoms.

> “Arphaxat, therefore, king of the Medes, had subjected many nations to his authority.”

According to what we explained more fully in the preface, this Arphaxat, or Artaxat—as Philo calls him—was a supporter of the Thamarite faction, namely the faction through which Cyrus was defeated and conquered by Thamar, queen of the Scythians. Emboldened by that victory, the Scythians also became invaders of his empire. Among the foremost of them was the aforementioned Artaxat, who, according to Philo, compelled the Assyrians, Medes, and Persians to revolt. Moreover, it was through this faction that Darius Hystaspes, who here is called Nebuchadnezzar, was also deprived of Babylon, as the historians Herodotus and Justin testify.

This, then, is what is meant here by “Arphaxat, king of the Medes,” or—as the Greek text expresses it more clearly—“who ruled the Medes in Ecbatana”: he had subjected many nations to his authority and compelled them to revolt. He is called king of the Medes for no other reason than that he had seized their kingdom.

> “And he himself built a very powerful city, which he called Ecbatanis.”

Ecbatanis, or Ecbatana, as in I Esdras 6, is the metropolis of Greater Media. Because of its cold climate, kings customarily spend the summer there. According to Herodotus, book 1, it was founded by Deioces, king of the Medes, whose successor was Phraortes, the grandfather of Astyages, whom Cyrus expelled from the kingdom. If we are to believe Volaterranus, book 12, however, it was founded by Seleucus.

Hence our translator did not render the word correctly by “built”; it should rather be translated “enlarged,” or something similar. The Greek text also agrees with this, as we shall cite below.

> “He made its walls of squared and hewn stones, seventy cubits high and thirty cubits wide. He set its towers at a height of one hundred cubits; and on each side of their square, each face extended for a space of twenty feet. He set its gates at the height of the towers.”

The magnificence of the building of this city is described at greater length, both in respect of beauty and of strength, and the account is sufficiently clear. Nothing further need be said here, except that the Greek text differs somewhat. It reads as follows:

> “And he built in Ecbatana, all around, walls of hewn stones three cubits wide and six cubits long; and he made the wall seventy cubits high and fifty cubits wide. He set its towers above its gates, one hundred cubits high; and he made its gates, raised gates, seventy cubits high, and their width was forty cubits. And he gloried as a mighty man in the strength of his army and in the glory of his chariots.”

Nor is this anything other than the manner of warfare customary among the ancients, fighting from towers and chariots, as may be seen in the Books of Joshua, Judges, and Kings.

[Col. 0599D]

[Col. 0600B] 

> “In the twelfth year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians…”

Nebuchadnezzar is a common name for all the kings of the Assyrians, just as “Pharaoh” is among the Egyptians and “Caesar” and “Augustus” among the Roman emperors. We have discussed more fully in the preface which king is to be understood here, and we accepted as most probable the opinion found in Philo’s *Breviary of Times*: namely, that Darius Hystaspes is intended, whom Philo calls Ahasuerus and the ancient Artaxerxes, who succeeded Cambyses and Xerxes.

> “Who ruled in the great city of Nineveh.”

Nineveh was a city of the Assyrians, built by Asshur, as Genesis 10 relates. Others call it Ninus; Eusebius calls it Nisibis. It is called “great” almost everywhere it is mentioned. Hence the passage in Jonah 1: “I am going to Nineveh, the great city.” Its size is described in the same book:

[Col. 0600C]

> “Now Nineveh was a great city, requiring three days’ journey.”

The aforementioned Nebuchadnezzar appears to have ruled in Nineveh because he had been stripped both of nearly the whole empire and of Babylon, his royal city, by the aforementioned Thamarite faction, as we have shown above from Justin and Herodotus.

> “He fought against Arphaxat and defeated him in the great plain called Ragau.”

Here the Greek text differs greatly from ours. It presents only the preparation for the war, and later, at the end of the chapter, goes on to describe the victory. Here it first reads:

> “He made”—that is, he prepared—“war against Arphaxat in the great plain.”

This is the plain in the territory of Ragau. Thus, according to our text, it is the place of the battle; according to the Greek, it is the place where he assembled his forces.

> “Around the Euphrates and the Tigris, and Jadasan, in the plain of Erioch king of the Elymaeans.”

This appears to explain around which places the plain lay, and what territory belonged to the king of the Elymaeans, in which the battle took place.

[Col. 0600D]

Since, however, according to the cosmographers, these rivers—the Euphrates, the Tigris, and Jadasa, or Hystaspes, as the Greek text reads—are far removed from one another, so that the plain of Ragau or of the king of the Elymaeans could not reach all of them, the reading of the Greek exemplar appears much more explanatory. It reads:

> “And all the inhabitants of the mountains, and all the inhabitants of the Euphrates, the Tigris, and the Hystaspes, and the plain of Erioch king of the Elymaeans, came against him; and very many nations gathered for battle against the children of Gelod.”

The nations are therefore designated by the names of the places. For, as the cosmographers write, from the Indus River, which lies in the east, to the Tigris, which lies in the west, these regions are mountainous and rugged: Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Persia, and mountainous Media, which has Mount Caucasus to the north. To the south are the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf; between them flow the principal rivers, the Hystaspes and the Ardivus.

Within these regions are twenty-two nations. Yet Parthia is often also called Media, from Tyre as far as the Euphrates. The passage therefore signifies that all the nations subject to him gathered for battle.

[Col. 0601A]

> “Then the kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar was exalted, and his heart was lifted up. And he sent to all who dwelt in Cilicia, Damascus, and Lebanon, and to the peoples who are in Carmel and Kedar, and to those inhabiting Galilee in the great plain of Esdrelon, and to all who were in Samaria and beyond the river Jordan, as far as Jerusalem, and throughout the land of Jesse, until one reaches the mountains of Ethiopia. To all these Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, sent messengers.”

According to our version, Nebuchadnezzar sent to various peoples, demanding that they submit to him; according to the Greek text, he sent to them so that they might assist him in conquering Arphaxat.

These regions are too well known to require explanation, except that by the name “land of Jesse,” or Gesen, as it is read in Greek, Egypt is to be understood—specifically, the part of that country which the patriarch Jacob once inhabited with his household and which is called Gessen in Genesis 46. Jerome, in his *Hebrew Institutes*, considers it to have been the Thebaid.

[Col. 0601B]

The inhabitants of Samaria are to be understood as those who still remained from the captivity of the ten tribes in certain cities of Samaria—that is, in the kingdom of the ten tribes—for Scripture frequently uses the term in this sense.

The Greek text again lists these peoples somewhat differently, as follows:

> “And he sent to all the inhabitants of Persia, and to all the inhabitants as far as the west, and to the inhabitants of Cilicia and Damascus, and Lebanon and Antilebanon, and all the inhabitants opposite the coastland, and those among the peoples of Carmel and Gilead, and Upper Galilee, and the great plain of Esdrelon, and all who were in Samaria and its cities, and beyond the Jordan and Jerusalem, and Beth-shemesh, and Chellus and Kadesh, and the river of Egypt and Tahpanhes and Rameses, and the whole land of Goshen, until one reaches the rear of Tanis, and Memphis, and all the inhabitants of Egypt, until one reaches the borders of Ethiopia.”

[Col. 0601C]

> “All these with one mind refused, sent them away empty-handed, and rejected them without honor.”

That is, they were unwilling to submit to him, if we follow our text. The Greek, however, reads:

> “And they all treated the word of Nebuchadnezzar with contempt, and did not join him in war,” and so forth.

This passage should be noted against those who understand Cambyses here. The history of Nebuchadnezzar did not occur under the name of Cambyses. For it is established from book 2 of Herodotus that Cambyses found all the regions mentioned above prepared to receive him except Egypt, which he later invaded by arms and added to his empire.

[Col. 0601D]

> “Then Nebuchadnezzar the king became angry with all that land and swore by his throne and kingdom that he would defend himself against all these regions.”

That is, he would take vengeance upon them. For the Greek text translates the matter as follows:

> “And he swore by his throne and kingdom that he would avenge himself upon all the territories of Cilicia, Damascus, and Syria, and would kill by the sword all who inhabited the land of Moab and the children of Ammon, and all Judea, and all those in Egypt, until one reaches the borders of the two seas.”

The Greek text adds what our text does not contain:

> “And he drew up his battle line in his strength against Arphaxat the king in the seventeenth year. He prevailed in his war, together with all his chariots, and gained possession of his cities. He reached Ecbatana, seized its towers, destroyed its streets, and gave its adornment over to disgrace. He captured Arphaxat in the mountains of Ragau, pierced him with his spears, and destroyed him. Afterwards he returned to Nineveh, he and all his allied forces, a very great multitude of fighting men. There he became sluggish and held banquets, he and his army, for one hundred twenty days.”

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0602A] Holofernes is sent by Nebuchadnezzar to devastate all rebellious kingdoms and peoples.

> “In the thirteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar the king, on the twenty-second day of the first month, a word came forth in the house of Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, that he should defend himself.”

Lyranus’s opinion here is excessively free when he says that this thirteenth year was the second year of Cambyses’ reign after his father’s death. For history cannot establish that Cambyses ruled for more than six years while his father was alive. Moreover, both Sabellicus and Carion establish that he survived his father by no more than two years; and the Greeks assign him no more than seven years and five months for his entire reign.

This cannot be reconciled in any way if we admit that, according to the Greek text, he reigned ten years while his father was still alive. For the Greek reads:

[Col. 0602B]

> “In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar,” and so forth.

There it is again stated more explicitly than in our text that he would avenge himself upon the whole land. The first month among the Hebrews was March, toward the end of which the season was suitable for preparing for war.

> “He summoned all the elders, and all his leaders and warriors, and held a secret council with them. He declared that his intention was to subject the whole earth to his rule. When this proposal pleased everyone, Nebuchadnezzar the king summoned Holofernes, commander of the army.”

These matters are clearer than to require exposition. It should only be noted that the Greek exemplar adds “commander of his army,” meaning the one who stood second to him.

> “And he said to him: Go out against every kingdom of the West, and especially against those who have despised my rule. Let your eye spare no kingdom, and you shall subject every fortified city to me.”

He calls it the kingdom of the West because all these regions were western in relation to the Assyrians, who obeyed Nebuchadnezzar’s rule.

[Col. 0602C]

> “Then Holofernes summoned the commanders and officers of the Assyrian forces and counted one hundred twenty thousand fighting infantrymen and twelve thousand mounted archers for the expedition.”

It is more appropriately translated from the Greek:

> “And he counted chosen men for battle.”

Perhaps “for the expedition” should also be read here. The number of infantry was greater because, according to Vegetius’s *On Military Matters*, the strength of an army lies in its infantry. The text expressly mentions mounted archers because it was customary for cavalry to fight with bows, as was also the practice among the Moors.

> “He caused his entire expedition to come with a countless multitude of camels, together with supplies sufficient for the armies in abundance, and also herds of oxen and flocks of sheep, which were beyond number. He ordered grain from all Syria to be prepared along his route, and took an exceedingly large amount of gold and silver from the king’s treasury.”

The account describes at greater length the preparation for war, both the abundant supply train and the treasury of gold and silver for paying the soldiers’ wages.

[Col. 0602D]

> “He himself and his whole army set out with chariots and cavalry and archers, who covered the face of the earth like locusts.”

After describing the army’s equipment, the text describes its departure for war. This is a hyperbole expressing the great multitude of the people.

> “When he had crossed the borders of Assyria, he came to the great mountains of Auge, which are on the left of Cilicia, and he climbed all their strongholds and seized every fortress.”

The Greek text describes this departure somewhat more fully as follows:

> “And they went out from Nineveh, a journey of three days, across the face of the plain of Bectileth, and encamped at Bectileth near the mountain that is on the left [Col. 0603A] of Upper Cilicia,” and so forth.

Note that it says “the mountain,” not “the mountains.” The mountains called Auge here are Mount Taurus, which extends between Assyria and Armenia, directly toward the West.

> “He stormed the famous city of Melothi.”

He calls it famous because of the abundance of its merchandise. He invaded it both because of the strength of its location and because it provided a convenient base for traversing Cilicia by arms.

It should be supposed that this is the city Ptolemy calls Mallus, whose inhabitants are called Mallotae and whom II Maccabees 4 mentions: “The people of Tarsus and Mallus happened to revolt.”

The Greek text, meanwhile, reads quite differently, though more obscurely:

> “And he went from there into the mountains and attacked Phud and Jud.”

> “He plundered all the children of Tarshish and the children of Ishmael who were opposite the desert, and toward the south of the land of Chellon.”

Tarshish is understood in various ways in Scripture. Sometimes it means Carthage, as Jerome noted [Col. 0603B] in his *Interpretation of Hebrew Place Names*, because in Ezekiel, where according to the Septuagint we read “Carthage,” the Hebrew has *Tarshish*. Sometimes, according to certain interpreters, it means the Mediterranean Sea, as in the prophet Jonah and Psalm 71: “All the ships of Tarshish.” Others again think that India is meant, as in III Kings 10.

Here, however, without prejudice to the judgment of the learned, they plainly think that Tarshish is derived from Tarshish, the son of Javan, mentioned in Genesis 10. Indeed, it is likely that the same region is mentioned in the cited Book of Kings, in Psalm 71, in Isaiah 2, and in Ezekiel 10.

Hence the metropolis of that region, with theta changed into tau, acquired the name Tarsus; it was Paul’s native city, as stated in the Acts of the Apostles.

It should also be noted that the Greek text—unless this is an error—reads *Praeses* (“governor”) in place of Tarshish. It should likewise be noted that although, according to Lyranus, certain manuscripts had “Israel” instead of “Ishmael,” those manuscripts must be corrupt, since the Greek text also agrees with “Ishmael,” and the Hagarites, descendants of Ishmael, customarily lived in the deserts, unlike the children of Israel.

[Col. 0603C]

> “And he crossed the Euphrates and came into Mesopotamia, and destroyed all the lofty cities that were there, from the torrent of Mamre until one reaches the sea.”

Mesopotamia is a region of Greater Asia and part of Syria, lying between Babylonia and Arabia, on the left bank of the Tigris. More precisely, it lies between the two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, except for the Taurus to the north. Its Greek name itself shows that it lies between rivers: *mesos* means “middle,” and *potamos* means “river.”

I have not been able to discover which torrent of Mamre is meant; in Greek it is called Arbonai.

> “And he occupied its borders from Cilicia to the borders of Japheth, which are toward the south; he brought all the children of Midian and plundered all their wealth, and killed all who resisted him by the edge of the sword.”

As far as may be conjectured from the cosmographers, by the borders of Japheth he means Africa. [Col. 0603D] Berossus writes that Japheth, the son of Noah, possessed Africa, from whom the Gentiles descended. Pliny also writes in the Prologue to book 3 that Africa is the third part of the world, situated toward the south. This seems greatly to support the interpretation, since the text says “toward the south.”

The Greek text adds still more:

> “Toward the south and toward Arabia.”

It also reads “surrounded” instead of “brought.”

Midian is a city situated beyond Arabia, south of Judea, in the desert of the Saracens, east of the Red Sea. It was named after Midian, the son whom Abraham had by Keturah, as related in Genesis 25.

> “After this he descended into the plains of Damascus in the days of harvest, burned all their crops, caused all their trees to be cut down, and had all their vineyards cut up; and his fear fell upon all the inhabitants of the land.”

The Greek reads:

> “Upon all the inhabitants of the coastal region, who were in Sidon and Tyre, and the inhabitants of Sur and Ocina and Temnaan, and the inhabitants of Azotus and Ascalon.”

It immediately adds:

> “And they sent envoys to him with peaceful words, saying…” and so forth.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0604A] Holofernes spares neither the cities nor their gods, even when they voluntarily surrender.

> “Then the kings and rulers of all the cities and provinces sent their envoys to Holofernes—the rulers of Syria, namely of Mesopotamia, Syria Sobal, Libya, and Cilicia.”

Syria as a whole is a large region. To the north it is bounded by Cilicia and part of Cappadocia; to the west, by the Syrian Sea. The Hebrews call it Aram, after Aram, the son of Shem; hence the Syrians are called Aramaeans.

Syria Sobal, or Syria Soba, is mentioned in II Samuel 8, I Chronicles 18, and in the title of Psalm 60. It is the region called Palestine, extending to the Mediterranean Sea and situated west of Judea.

Thus Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 1, chapter 12.

Libya is a large part of Africa, though at that time it contained no provinces belonging to the allies, either of the Assyrians or of the Chaldeans.

[Col. 0604B]

> “When they came to Holofernes, they said: Let your anger cease against us. For it is better that we live and serve Nebuchadnezzar, the great king, and be subject to you, than that we should die and, together with our destruction, suffer the losses of our servitude. All our cities and every possession, all our mountains and hills and plains, herds of oxen, flocks of sheep and goats, horses and camels, all our resources, and our households are before you; let everything be subject to your law. We ourselves and our children are your servants. Come to us as a peaceful lord, and use our service as it pleases you.”

Nothing else is signified here except the greatest fear of all the regions mentioned and their submission: they preferred to surrender themselves to servitude rather than be delivered to death with their cities destroyed.

> “Then Holofernes descended from the mountains with the cavalry in great strength, and seized every fortified city and every inhabitant of the land. From all the cities he took for himself strong men and those chosen for war.”

The harsh rule of Holofernes is displayed here, since he did not spare even those who had submitted. It should also be noted that Scripture commonly uses “the whole land” for a particular land, as though it said “the whole land just mentioned.”

[Col. 0604C]

> “Such fear fell upon those provinces that the inhabitants of all the cities—their leaders and honored men together with the peoples—came out to meet him as he approached, receiving him with crowns and lamps, leading dances with tambourines and flutes. Yet even while doing these things they could not soften the savagery of his heart, for he destroyed their cities and cut down their sacred groves.”

For the sake of fuller explanation, the text again emphasizes Holofernes’ ferocity.

> “For Nebuchadnezzar the king had commanded him to exterminate all the gods of the land, so that he alone might be called God by those nations that could be subjected by Holofernes’ power.”

[Col. 0604D] The great impiety and arrogance of this king are described here: after extinguishing all the other gods, he wished to be worshiped as the sole God.

> “Passing through Syria Sobal, all Apamea, and all Mesopotamia, he came to the Idumeans in the land of Gabaa. He seized their cities and remained there for thirty days, during which time he ordered the whole army of his forces to assemble.”

The Idumeans are within the Jordan, and their metropolis is Jericho, beyond the mountains of the Arabian region. These mountains prevented Holofernes from entering Judea easily.

The Greek text, meanwhile, reads:

> “And he came opposite Esdrelon, near Dothaim, which is opposite the great land of Judea, and encamped between Gabaa and the city of the Scythians.”

These two cities are situated on the borders of the tribe of Judah.

## CHAPTER FOUR

[Col. 0605A] The children of Israel fortify themselves against Holofernes, encouraged to do so by the priest Eliachim.

> “Then the children of Israel who lived in the land of Judea, hearing these things, were very greatly afraid of him. Trembling and horror also seized their senses, lest he do to Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord what he had done to the other cities.”

After describing the persecution of the other nations, the text now turns to the persecution of the children of Israel, first recounting in this chapter their preparations for war.

This is one of the passages from which Ziegler attempts to prove that the history did not occur after the captivity, or in the time of Cambyses or Darius Hystaspes, as we maintain, but earlier. For, he says, it is established that in the time of this Darius Hystaspes only the foundations of the temple had been laid. Hence there should have been no fear that the temple would be profaned, since it did not yet exist, and much less that the city would be destroyed, since it had not yet begun to be built.

But, as we also noted above in the preface, by “temple” the already erected altar must be understood. At it, as I Esdras 3 testifies, the daily and nightly burnt offerings were already being offered. By “Jerusalem” are meant the foundations already laid, together with the dwellings in which they already lived.

This becomes completely clear from the Greek text, which mentions both their return from captivity and the altar recently sanctified. It reads as follows:

> “They were troubled on account of Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord their God, because they had recently come up from captivity, and the whole people had lately been gathered from Judea, and their vessels, altar, and houses had been sanctified from profanation.”

This, therefore, offers no obstacle to our opinion.

[Col. 0605B]

> “And they sent throughout all Samaria and its surrounding area as far as Jericho, and occupied all the mountaintops in advance. They surrounded their villages with walls and gathered grain in preparation for battle.”

This is a very suitable description of the preparations for war, both as regards the fortification of the towns and as regards provisions, the two things especially necessary.

As was also noted above in chapter 1, “Samaria” here does not refer only to that one city but to the whole kingdom of the ten tribes. The text therefore means all those who still remained from the captivity in those territories.

The Greek exemplar also sufficiently indicates this, reading:

> “And they sent to all the borders and villages of Samaria, and Bethoron and Belmen, and Jericho, and Choba and Esora, and the valley of Salem, and they occupied them,” and so forth.

Several cities situated among the ten tribes are thus enumerated.

Jericho was a very wealthy city in the tribe of Benjamin, one hundred fifty stadia from Jerusalem and sixty from the Jordan. It was famous for its palm trees and balsam gardens. Its beautiful description may be seen in Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 5, chapter 4.

> “The priest Eliachim also…”

[Col. 0605D] Some manuscripts read “for.” It should also be noted that the Greek exemplar consistently reads:

> “Joachim the high priest, who was in Jerusalem in those days.”

This is all the more significant because below, in chapter 15, this same Joachim is called by that name.

Philo therefore notes that among the Syrians and Egyptians these names are synonymous: Eliachim, Elich, and Joachim.

He reports that this man was Joachim, son of Jesus, son of Josedech, under whom the children of Israel returned from captivity. He further relates that this Jesus was sent to the Darius frequently mentioned above to intercede for the Hebrews, because the leaders of Syria had written to the king against them. Jesus left in the high priesthood, in the twelfth year of our Ahasuerus, or Nebuchadnezzar, his son Joachim, who was also called Eliachim.

Thus, while this man was administering the high priesthood, the events of this history took place.

This is above all the foundation of the opinion we follow, since, as we explained more fully in the preface, those who embrace another opinion cannot conveniently show who this Eliachim, or Joachim, the high priest, was.

Even Lyranus, who in the preceding passages firmly embraced the opinion that understands Cambyses here, was moved by this argument. After first offering the weak response that Jesus, the son of Jesedech, had had two names, he saw that the argument had not been answered and said: “Or it must be admitted that this history did not occur in the time of Cambyses, but after a long interval of time.”

For further discussion of this passage, I refer anyone who wishes to the preface itself, in which we refuted the opinions of the others more fully.

[Col. 0606A]

> “He wrote to all who were opposite Esdrelon, which is opposite the great plain near Dothaim, and to all through whose territory a road might pass, that they should occupy the mountain passes by which a road to Jerusalem might run, and guard the places where the route might be narrow between the mountains. And the children of Israel did according to what the priest of the Lord Eliachim had commanded them.”

The diligence of the high priest in making preparations for war is described here in considerable detail.

[Col. 0606B]

The city of Esdrelon, which has already been mentioned several times in the Greek exemplars, appears to have been situated not far from Samaria, since “near Dothaim” is added. Dothaim is known as the place where Joseph found his brothers tending the flocks, as related in Genesis 37. Jerome testifies that it still existed in his own time, twelve miles from Sebaste—which was once called Samaria—toward the north. It is also mentioned in II Kings 6.

The Greek text differs somewhat here as well and adds the following:

> “He wrote to those who lived in Bethulia and Bethsemesthan, which is opposite Esdrelon,” and so forth.

> “And all the people cried out to the Lord with great insistence, and humbled their souls with fasts and prayers, they and their wives.”

After fortifying themselves as far as human strength permitted, they knew that God inflicts calamities only because of sins, and that there is no evil in a city which the Lord has not caused. They therefore fled to prayers and fasts, offering an example to all of us: when we are placed in affliction, we should take especial and sole care that God be reconciled to us for our sins, and thus entrust our entire cause to God. There is no doubt that, as these people were heard, so shall we be heard.

“Then the priests clothed themselves in sackcloth, and the children prostrated themselves face down before the temple of the Lord, and the altar of the Lord was clothed in sackcloth.” This manner of doing penance was used in ancient times, as may be seen in Joel I and II, Jonah III, and very many other passages of Scripture. Here, however, a preposition seems to be missing for the completion of the sentence—namely, *se*—so that it should read: “And they prostrated themselves.” Thus the Greek text also reads: “They and their wives, their cattle, every resident alien, the hired laborer, and the slave put sackcloth around their loins; and every man, woman, and child fell face down before the temple.”

“And they cried out with one accord to the Lord God of Israel, that their children might not be given over as plunder, their wives for division, their cities [Col. 0606D] for destruction, their holy places for profanation, and that they might become a reproach among the nations.” After *with one accord*, the Greek text adds *constantly*, by which we are taught the condition of prayer required for it to be heard—or, rather, that prayer’s principal requirement is that it be constant and persevering. Hence below in this same chapter Eliachim promises victory to the Israelites, provided only that they persevere in fasting and prayer. Chrysostom treats this condition required for prayer most beautifully above, on Psalm IV, and again on Psalm VII, where, besides this, he sets out other conditions necessary for being heard.

“Then Eliachim, the great priest of the Lord, went around all Israel and addressed them, saying: Know that the Lord will hear your prayers if you remain steadfast in fasting and prayer before the Lord.” Here again the Greek copy reads *Joachim*. The expression “if you remain steadfast” is a Hebraism very common in Scripture, like “with desire I have desired,” and many similar expressions that may be found throughout. The meaning is as though he were saying: “If you persevere continually in fasting and prayer.” This is precisely what we have already said: the passage expresses the condition required for prayer. This passage should also be noted against the Lutherans, who strive to abolish all fasting; for here, as in countless other passages of Scripture, both the usefulness and the efficacy of fasting are demonstrated. It also shows that there is nothing surprising in the Church’s authorities establishing a manner of fasting today, since we find that this was practiced even in ancient times.

“Remember Moses, the servant of the Lord, who overthrew Amalek, confident in his strength, his army, his shields, and his cavalry, not by fighting with iron but by praying with holy prayers. So all your enemies will be, if you persevere in this work that you have begun.” He strengthens them through examples of the saints. Thus Paul too, commending faith in Hebrews II, brings forward a wealth of examples of the fathers, who through faith conquered kingdoms and practiced righteousness. The history touched upon here is found in Exodus XVII. Likewise John Chrysostom, elsewhere commending the power and efficacy of prayer, says: “Who, he asks, has not conquered an enemy by praying? Daniel’s visions are disclosed, flames are subdued, wild beasts are rendered harmless, enemies fall, adversaries are conquered. Therefore, the purer and more frequent the prayer, the swifter will be the vengeance upon the enemy.”

“Accordingly, in response to this exhortation of his, they continued entreating the Lord in the Lord’s presence, so that even those who offered burnt offerings to the Lord, girded with sackcloth, offered sacrifices to the Lord, and ashes were upon their heads. And with all their heart they all prayed to God that he would visit his people Israel.” He pursues at length their diligence and perseverance in prayer; how their prayers were heard will immediately be recounted below.

## CHAPTER V

Achior warns Holofernes not to attack the Jews rashly.

“And it was reported to Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, that the Israelites were preparing to resist and had closed the mountain passes; and he burned with excessive fury in great anger. And he summoned all the princes of Moab and the commanders of Ammon.”

After the particular occasion of the Israelites’ persecution has been described, the persecution itself is now described and begins to be set forth—first, Holofernes’ inquiry into the condition of the Jews among the Ammonites and Moabites, who knew them very well because of the neighboring territory. The Greek text differs somewhat here, especially in reading *for battle* instead of *to resist*. It then adds: “And they had fortified every summit of the high mountain and had placed obstacles in the plains.” Third, after mentioning the commanders of Ammon, it adds: “And all the satraps of the coastal region.” [Col. 0607D]

“And he said to them: Tell me who this people is that occupies the mountains; what and of what kind and how numerous are their cities; what their strength is; what their numbers are; who their military king is; and why, above all who dwell in the East, they have despised us and have not come out to meet us, to receive us in peace?”

He asks about various matters: first, what their origin is; then what they are like and how numerous they are, that they dare to resist, and what their strength and boldness may be; third, who their king is, and how prudent and wise; finally, if they possess nothing of this sort, why they resist more than all the other peoples whom he had already subdued. For this reason, Ziegler asks how he could have been ignorant of all these things when he inquired about them, since, if the Israelites had returned from captivity shortly before, he ought to have known them very well. He therefore declares that this is sufficient evidence that the history is older than the Babylonian captivity. [Col. 0608A]

But, as in the preface above, I chiefly oppose to him the answer of Achior, which we shall now present. Thus, “having returned from dispersion” may be understood; alternatively, these words may be spoken in astonishment, as though he were saying: “Who and what is this people, or under what king, or animated by what assistance, that it dares to resist?” This is not far removed from the text.

Finally, it is much more plainly probable that Holofernes was not an Assyrian or Persian, but originated in much more distant regions of the world, and that, as often happens, he rose to such dignity because of distinguished naval service rendered to the Assyrians. It is therefore not surprising if these matters were unknown to him. The final conjecture is strongly supported by the fact that, if we follow the Greek text, he calls all those princes to whom he speaks “sons of Canaan,” although it is established that the Ammonites and Moabites, along with many others, were distinct from the Canaanites. Further, whereas above, in chapter II, the regions of the West are called such by the king of the Assyrians, as being nearer to him, here the text says that the same regions dwell in the East. Lyranus, however, answers this final objection by saying that, although Judaea was westward in relation to the Assyrians, Judaea and the regions just mentioned were nevertheless nearer to the East than to the West in relation to the whole inhabited earth. But he may in turn be challenged that it is not plausible that a man who had devoted himself continually to military affairs was so exact a mathematician.

“Then Achior, commander of all the sons of Ammon, answered and said: If you will deign to listen, my lord, I shall tell the truth in your presence concerning this people who dwell in the mountains, and no false word shall come from my mouth.”

Here follows the answer to the questions of Achior, commander of the Ammonites. Since he himself had been born of the race of the Jews, from Lot, he recognized their nation as his own. First, however, he modestly prefaces his speech and seeks goodwill by appealing to his knowledge of the matter about which he had been questioned. Then, following the order of the questions, he begins his account of their origin in this way:

“This people is descended from the Chaldeans.” So it is stated in Genesis XI: “Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, and led them out of Ur of the Chaldeans.” That was the name of the city from which they originated. Achior, although an unbeliever, attempted something useful before Holofernes. “He did something useful,” says Jerome in his commentary on Matthew VII, “although he did not believe in the God of Israel, just as Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, gave Moses good counsel, though he certainly did not believe in the true God.”

“He first dwelt in Mesopotamia, because they did not wish to follow the gods of their fathers, who were in the land of the Chaldeans. Thus, abandoning the rites of their fathers, which consisted in the worship of many gods, they worshiped the one God of heaven.” The Greek text adds: “the God whom they had come to know,” and again adds: “And they dwelt there for many days,” namely, until the death of Terah, Abraham’s father. “And he commanded them to depart from there and dwell in Harran.”

This city is also called by that name in Acts VII. In the passage in Genesis just mentioned it is called *Haram*. It is a place in Mesopotamia where Terah remained with his household until his death. Since Genesis contains no specific command by which they are ordered to dwell in Harran, but only records that after the death of his father Terah Abraham received the command in Genesis XII to leave his dwelling and land and migrate into the land of Canaan, the Greek text seems much more correctly to read as follows: “that they should leave their dwelling and go into the land of Canaan; and they dwelt there, and were filled with gold and silver and exceedingly many cattle.” Only then does it add what appears in our text.

“When famine had covered the whole land, they went down into Egypt, and there they multiplied for four hundred years, so that their army could not be numbered.” In a few words he recounts both their descent into Egypt, described in Genesis XLVII, and the length of time they lived there, which is likewise stated in Genesis XV as four hundred years. Meanwhile, in order to have the complete number, these years must be reckoned from the fifth year [Note: [Col. 0609D] Something seems to be missing.] Isaac … Ishmael … the household of Abraham; if they are counted as in Acts VII, four hundred and ten years must be reckoned from Abraham’s seventy-fifth year. He did not sojourn in Egypt, which his descendants were to do.

“When the king of Egypt oppressed them and subjected them to mud and labor in the construction of his cities, they cried out to their God, and he struck the whole land of Egypt with various plagues.” Concerning this oppression and the promise regarding Egypt, you have an account of the many plagues in Exodus, immediately from the beginning through chapter XIII. The Greek text adds: “with various plagues in which there was no healing.”

“When the Egyptians had driven them away from themselves, and the plague had ceased among them, and they again wished to seize them and recall them to their service, as they fled, the God of heaven opened the sea for them, so that the waters were solidified like a wall on either side, and they crossed by walking on dry ground through the bed of the sea.” He briefly recounts what is described at length in Exodus XIII and XIV. There is therefore no need to linger here, since he merely reports the bare history, whose treatment belongs not here but there.

“When the innumerable army of the Egyptians pursued them at that place, it was covered by the waters in such a way that not even one remained to report the event to posterity.” The more delayed the vengeance upon sinners, the more just it is, after the likeness of Pharaoh, who, warned by severe plagues but not punished, persisted in hardness of heart and was finally overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea. So says Jerome in his commentary on Jeremiah XXXII.

“After they had crossed the Red Sea, the deserts of Mount Sinai confronted them, in which no human being could dwell, nor could any son of man find rest.” Some copies read this somewhat differently, though with the same meaning: “After they had gone out, etc., they also occupied the deserts.” According to Exodus XV, however, they first occupied the desert, and the desert of Sur first confronted them, along with certain other places; but they are said to have reached the desert of Sinai only in the third month after their departure, in Exodus XIX.

It should be noted here that the same order as in Exodus is not observed throughout, but that the history of the Israelites’ exodus is briefly repeated, with not all the places through which they passed being listed, but only the principal ones.
