This makes even more noteworthy what Jerome treats in his letter to Fabiola concerning the forty-two stations of the Israelites, when he discusses the eighth station. “It must be understood,” he says, “that all the wilderness as far as Mount Sinai is called the wilderness of Sin, and that from the entire province the place took the name of one station.” This, I say, should be noted, since otherwise it cannot conveniently be understood what the text means here by “the deserts of Sinai”—or *Sin*—where bitter springs were sweetened, as follows:

“There bitter springs were sweetened for them to drink, and for forty years they received food from heaven.” This alludes to Exodus XV: “They came to Marah, but they could not drink the waters of Marah, because they were bitter; therefore he gave the place the appropriate name Marah, that is, bitterness, etc.” It then refers to Exodus XVI, where first meat and then manna were given to them from heaven, which they used for forty years, during which they remained in the wilderness.

“Wherever they entered, without bow or arrow, and without sword or shield, their God fought for them.” Thus far he has set forth at length the origin and progress of the Israelites; now he consequently shows upon what strength they relied—namely, not their own, but God’s. Although they fought against Amalek and others while armed, they did not obtain victory through weapons but through divine power. Hence Amalek is said to have been defeated by Moses in the preceding chapter [citation uncertain], and in Joshua XVII; and in Joshua’s battle against the kings of Canaan, hailstones killed the adversaries and the sun stood still, as may be found in Joshua X. The remaining matters that follow are evident throughout Judges and 2 Kings.

“Finally, they struck down the king of the Canaanites, the Jebusites, the Chaereseans, the Hivites, the Hittites, and the Amorites, and all the powerful men in Heshbon; they themselves took possession of their lands and cities, and as long as they did not sin, good things were with them, etc.” The history touched upon here, drawn from the books of Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua, is preferable to any prolonged treatment here. All the kings briefly mentioned here are recounted more fully in Joshua XII, up to the number of thirty, etc. These peoples lived in the land that God had so often promised to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

“For even before these years, when they had departed from the land that God had given them so that they might walk in it, they were destroyed in battle by many nations, and many of them were led captive into a land not their own.” In particular, during the deportation of Jehoiakim and his captivity under Zedekiah, they were destroyed in battle by the kings of Assyria and Egypt, as is clear from 2 Kings; and many of them were led captive, first by Tiglath-pileser, in 2 Kings XV, and then by Shalmaneser, in 2 Kings XVII.

These words could be understood, as Ziegler does, as referring only to the destruction of the kingdom of Israel. But both the Greek reading and the words that follow make it entirely necessary to understand them also of the deportation of the kingdom of Judah to Babylon: first in the time of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, and second in the time of Jehoiachin, his son, in 2 Kings XXV. For the Greek adds: “And their cities were devastated, and the temple was deserted,” which plainly did not occur except in that final deportation of Judah to Babylon. The following words read as follows:

“But recently they returned to the Lord their God from the dispersion into which they had been scattered; they were gathered together, went up into these mountains, and again possessed Jerusalem, where are the ages of ages.”

This, I say, is a very serious obstacle to Ziegler’s interpretation, since nowhere do we read that the Israelites returned—those, namely, who had been subject to the kingdom of the ten tribes—unless perhaps they returned together with all the other Jews in the time of Cyrus, king of the Persians. Moreover, Jerusalem had not been lost before the time of Josiah, so that it could be said, “now they again possess Jerusalem.” For although we read in the Books of Kings that Jerusalem was plundered once and again, they nevertheless remained in possession of it until the devastation carried out by Nebuchadnezzar.

The text therefore plainly compels us to understand this as referring to the return from dispersion and captivity under Cyrus, who is mentioned immediately at the beginning of 1 Esdras I. Jerusalem, meanwhile, should appropriately be understood as the city of Jerusalem; thus nothing will stand in the way of what others object—that the rebuilding of the city had not yet been completed in the time of Nebuchadnezzar or Darius Hystaspes.

“Now therefore, my lord, inquire whether there is any iniquity among them in the sight of their God, and we shall go up against them, etc.” Having related the history of the Jews, he brings it to a close with the advice he gives Holofernes concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the matter at hand: namely, that he should recognize that he could not overcome the Israelites except through an offense against their God. Balaam once pursued a similar course, for, as Revelation II says, he taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites, so that they would eat and commit fornication—although Achior acted with a better intention than Balaam.

“And it happened that when Achior had finished speaking these words, all the nobles of Holofernes became angry and considered killing him, etc.” After Achior’s account, there follows the greatest indignation, both of the other Assyrians in this passage and of Holofernes himself in the next chapter, because Achior had said that they could not subjugate the Jewish nation by their own strength. In this indignation it followed that they threatened Achior himself once their enemies had been defeated—the very people whom he had praised so highly to the Israelites. Among other things they add:

“Let Achior therefore recognize that he has deceived us.” That is: “He has tried in every way to deceive us. Let us go up into the mountains”—that is, into Judaea, which was mountainous.

“And when their mighty men have been captured, he too shall be pierced through with the sword together with them, so that every nation may know that Nebuchadnezzar is the god of the earth,” etc. They do not say “the god of heaven,” but “of the earth.” They seem to have held the error of those who said that heavenly providence extended only to heavenly things, according to Job XXII: “He walks around the heavenly vault and does not consider our affairs.”

## CHAPTER VI

Achior is handed over by Holofernes to the Jews.

“When he had finished speaking, Holofernes was greatly angered and said to Achior: Because you have prophesied to us, saying, etc.” Here the indignation of Holofernes himself is also expressed. He repeats, first in very harsh words, what his commanders had previously conceived among themselves, and then carries it out in action. The words themselves require no explanation.

“Moreover, if you consider your prophecy true, do not let your face fall, etc.” It is not surprising that Achior was afraid, both because, standing among them, he could not resist if they attempted anything cruel against him, and because, although he firmly believed that God could protect and defend the Israelites, he did not know whether they themselves might already have offended God. He rightly calls it a prophecy. For prophecy is nothing other, says Chrysostom, in his homily on Isaiah’s words “I saw the Lord,” homily 2, than a faithful declaration of future events.

“Then Holofernes ordered his servants to seize Achior, lead him to Bethulia, and hand him over to the Israelites, etc.” Holofernes now carries out his words by command. Bethulia is a mountainous city in the region of Palestine, on the side where the mountains face west, situated opposite Scythopolis and three leagues from Tiberias; traces of Holofernes’ camp are still found there.

“But when they had approached the mountains, slingers came out against them. They, turning aside along the slope of the mountain, bound Achior to a tree by his hands and feet, etc.” He recounts how Achior came into the hands of the Israelites and into Bethulia—or *Bethulua*, as the Greek text gathers it. The Greek also adds: “To the mountains and to the springs that were below Bethulua.”

A sling is an instrument made of a cord, by which stones are slung—that is, thrown. It was first invented in the Balearic Islands. Hence those who used this instrument were called *funditores* and *fundibularii*, slingers. The interpretation of the name offered by Lyranus should not be followed here, any more than that of those who interpret *sacerdotium facinorum* [“the priesthood of crimes”].

“Then the Israelites, coming down from Bethulia, went to him, etc.” Here you see the Israelites’ compassion toward the prisoner: they released him from his bonds and led him into the city. Once they had entered it, they began, out of astonishment, to inquire why he had been bound in this way, and they placed him in the midst of all the people.

“In those days there were there the leaders Ozias, son of Micha, of the tribe of Simeon, and Charmi, who was also Gothoniel.” The Greek text lists three, saying: “Ozias, son of Micha, etc.; Chabris, son of Gothoniel; and Charmi, son of Melchiel.” It also seems clear that the Latin copies once had this reading, from the history called *Scholastica*, written by Comestor, which says that two leaders—a priest and the leader Ozias of the tribe of Simeon—were sent from Jerusalem to Bethulia.

These men are named because Achior was placed in their midst and in their presence. This is what follows:

“Thus, in the midst of the elders and in the presence of all, Achior related everything that he had said when questioned by Holofernes,” etc. Here the Greek text places before our version a passage belonging to the fuller explanation of the history: “And they summoned all the elders of the city, and all the elders of their city and the women gathered together at the assembly.” It then adds: “Thus, in the midst of them.”

“When Achior had explained all these things, all the people fell on their faces, worshiping the Lord, and with a common lament and weeping they unanimously poured out their prayers, saying,” etc. Now follows the consolation with which they consoled Achior, especially through the people’s devout and common prayer. The power of the Church’s common prayers is evident, along with many other passages of Scripture, from the single statement made elsewhere by Christ: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them.” If he is therefore in the midst of those who are gathered together, even if there are only two or three, what must we think is the power of those common prayers of the Church?

“Lord, God of heaven and earth, look upon their pride and regard our humility; and attend to the face of your saints,” etc. They knew the saying of the Wise Man: “The prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds.” Hence we should observe here their very humble yet brief prayer. This passage should also be noted against modern adversaries who reject all invocation of the saints. For you see how, not trusting in their own merits, they ask that their prayer be heard through their ancestors—namely, the saints Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other holy fathers who had long since died.

“When the weeping had ended and the prayer had continued throughout the whole day, they consoled Achior,” etc. At the end of the prayer, divinely strengthened, they turn to the consolation of Achior, presenting him with their confidence. They did not doubt that their prayers had been heard, and therefore they freely granted him perpetual permission to dwell among them, as may sufficiently be gathered from the text above.

“Then Ozias, when the council had ended, received him into his house and prepared a great banquet for him,” etc. He records with what humanity Achior was received by their leader Ozias: Ozias summoned all the priests and elders of the people to a richly prepared banquet in Achior’s honor. Their spirit had already been so divinely strengthened that they celebrated a feast in the midst of their enemies.

“Afterward, the whole people were summoned, and throughout the night they prayed inside the assembly, asking help from the God of Israel.” These people are an example to all who are in distress, showing that one must always flee to God. By “church” he means the particular synagogue in Bethulia, just as there was one in each of the other cities of Israel.

## CHAPTER VII

Holofernes torments the besieged in Bethulia with thirst by blocking their water supply, so that the people are almost driven into revolt.

“On the following day Holofernes ordered his armies to advance against Bethulia.” The Greek text adds: “and all his people who had come to assist.”

“There were one hundred and twenty thousand infantrymen and twenty-two thousand cavalry,” etc. He briefly records the forces of Holofernes, though the Greek copy differs somewhat in their number: it reads one hundred and seventy thousand infantrymen and only twelve thousand cavalry.

“And they came along the slope of the mountain up to the summit that looks over Dothaim, from the place called Belma to Gelmon, which is opposite Esdrelon.” [Col. 0613A] By “the slope of the mountain” we are instructed to understand its common or broad ascent. He describes the circuit of the city of Bethulia and the place where they encamped. The Greek copy explains this more clearly: “And they encamped,” it says, “in the valley near Bethulia, above the spring, and extended in breadth toward Dothaim as far as Belmaim, and in length from Bethulia as far as Giamon, which is opposite Esdrelon.”

“When the Israelites saw their multitude, they prostrated themselves upon the ground, etc. And taking up their weapons, they stationed themselves in the places that direct the narrow path between the mountains, and they guarded them all day and night.” Once again they first of all flee to humble prayers and to God, and then also make human preparations. Meanwhile, since it is not sufficiently plausible that they dared to maintain outposts outside the city in the presence of so vast and nearby an army, the reading of the Greek copy seems more suitable: “And each one took up his weapons of war, and they kindled a fire upon their towers, and remained on guard day and night.”

“Now Holofernes, as he went around the circuit, discovered that the spring which fed their aqueduct flowed from the southern side outside the city,” etc. That is, he found that the spring from which their watercourse began had its source to the south outside the city. Therefore, as is extremely common in warfare, he ordered the watercourse to be cut. Something similar is recorded in 1 Samuel XIII, where the Philistines had seen to it that there was no blacksmith in Israel, and thus the Israelites’ means of resisting them were taken away.

“But the sons of Ammon and Moab approached Holofernes, saying: The Israelites do not trust in lance or arrow, but the mountains defend them,” etc. In order to fulfill the hatred with which they pursued the Jews, and seeking to please Holofernes in this matter, they advise him to block even the small springs that remained. Their constant hatred of the Israelites is also clear from the Books of Judges and Kings. Their meaning is as though they were saying: “The Israelites have neither weapons nor military training, and therefore they do not come down against us into battle. If guards are stationed to prevent access to the springs, they will be compelled either to die of thirst or to surrender.”

“These words pleased Holofernes and all his attendants, and he stationed a hundred men around each spring.” Here he explains how the advice of the Ammonites and Moabites was put into effect. The Greek text develops this at greater length in the following manner:

“These words pleased Holofernes, and the camp of the sons of Ammon departed, together with five thousand of the sons of Assur. They encamped in the valley and seized the waters and springs of the Israelites. The sons of Esau and the sons of Ammon went up and encamped in the mountains opposite Dothaim; some of them were sent toward the south and the southeast, opposite Ecrebel, which is near Chusi and above the torrent Mochmir; and the remaining Assyrian army encamped in the plain and covered the face of the earth.”

Here, depicting the entire undertaking of the whole army at great length, the text says that those very men who had given the advice were sent to prevent the inhabitants of Bethulia from drawing water.

“When this guard had continued for twenty days, the cisterns failed,” etc. The *Scholastica* also agrees with this number of days, but the Greek copy reads thirty-four days. Here he explains the extreme scarcity of water, so that it had to be distributed to each person by measure.

“Then the men, women, young people, and children all gathered together before Ozias and said with one voice: Let the Lord judge between us and you,” etc. Here the people’s plaintive murmuring against Ozias, the city’s leader, is presented. The people, afflicted by thirst, wanted the city to be surrendered, but Ozias and the priests prevented this. Therefore the crowd calls its leader to God’s judgment, charging him with pride for maintaining such a defense. This is what follows:

“And for this reason God has sold us into their hands,” etc. That is: “Because of this rebellion of ours he has handed us over entirely into their hands, withdrawing all his assistance from us, since we are tormented by thirst.” Thus they draw a kind of conclusion:

“Now gather together all who are in the city, so that we may surrender ourselves voluntarily,” etc. They ask that the city be surrendered, and not without reason: it would be better, and a lesser evil, to serve Holofernes than to perish from thirst. Finally, when they see that none of their words is accomplishing anything, they add:

“Today we call heaven and earth to witness, and the God of our fathers, who punishes us according to our sins, that you should now surrender the city,” etc. [Col. 0614B] It is as though they were saying: “Today we summon heaven, earth, and the God of our fathers as witnesses against you and the priests, that you are treating us unjustly unless you surrender the city. For we see that God’s anger has already raged against us and that he wishes to avenge our sins.”

“When they had said these things, there was weeping and a great wailing in the assembly by everyone, and for many hours they cried out to God, saying: We have sinned with our fathers,” etc. Having been driven by a kind of despair to their preceding murmuring, they again search the depths of their minds and ask God for help, desiring above all that their sins be forgiven, since they knew that these were the cause of all their evils.

“Because you are merciful, have pity on us, or punish our iniquities with your scourge; and do not hand over those who trust in you to a people that does not know you, lest they say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’” This prayer is of marvelous efficacy and devotion, as though they were saying: “Scourge us as much as you please, but with your scourge; do not hand us over to the scourge of unbelieving men, into whose hands we beg you not to deliver us.” David’s prayer in 2 Samuel XXIV is very similar, although he preferred to be scourged by God rather than by human beings. It therefore seems that this prayer came from the lips of priests and righteous men, who feared the destruction of divine worship more than the loss of their own safety.

“When they had grown weary from these cries and tears and had fallen silent, Ozias rose, drenched in tears, and said: Take courage, brothers, and let us wait these five days for mercy from the Lord,” etc. Here one may see the indiscreet agreement of the leader with the citizens: he promised to surrender the city unless help arrived within five days. The fault did not lie in delaying the surrender of the city—for that was certainly permissible—but in prescribing a limit to divine mercy. For this reason Judith rebukes him in the following chapter, as will be seen there.

## CHAPTER VIII

Judith consoles and strengthens the wavering Jews who, out of fear, are considering surrender.

“And it came to pass, when Judith the widow had heard these words.” Thus far there have been only certain preliminary events leading to the present history. Now the account proceeds toward its very purpose: namely, the deliverance of the Israelite people through Judith the widow, whose origin and ancestry he briefly describes as follows:

“She was the daughter of Merari, son of Idex, son of Joseph, son of Ozias, son of Elaci, son of Jannor, son of Gideon, son of Raphaim, son of Achilob, son of Melchiah, son of Evan, son of Nathaniah, son of Salathiel, son of Simeon, son of Reuben.”

He traces her entire ancestry through her fathers, from Merari back to Simeon, the son of Jacob. Hence it is clear that she too belonged to the tribe of Simeon, since Simeon is placed last. I consider “son of Reuben” to be an error, because in the Greek copy “son of Israel” is placed last, and nowhere do we read that Reuben had a son of that name, although the sons of Reuben are listed in Genesis XLVI and 1 Chronicles V.

Accordingly, the final reading should be “son of Israel,” unless we prefer to follow Lyranus’ not implausible view. In the following chapter, where Judith calls her father “that Simeon who avenged the violation of his sister Dinah,” Lyranus believes that the list does not enumerate all her ancestors, even down to that patriarch Simeon. We shall present his view more fully there.

“And her husband was Manasseh, who died in the days of the barley harvest; for he was attending to those binding sheaves in the field, and the heat came upon his head, and he died in Bethulia, his own city, and was buried there with his ancestors.” He does not state from which tribe her husband came, since it was universally known that among the Jews marriages were contracted between those who belonged to the same tribe. Meanwhile, the Greek codex adds: “from his tribe and kindred.” At the same time, he recounts the origin of the illness by which Manasseh died: namely, that it was during the barley harvest, when he was urging the workers who were binding the sheaves to carry out their task more diligently, that the heat came upon his head; as the Greek text adds, he fell into bed and died. Some have thought that this “heat” was the same as what our physicians call catarrh; I do not know what grounds they have for this. It seems more probable to me that his head was afflicted by excessive heat, as we often see happen, and that some other illness was added to that severe headache, from which death followed. The Greek codex also adds the place where he was buried: “in the field that is between Dothaim and Balamo.”

“And his widow was left behind, already for three years and six months. And in the upper part of her house she made herself a private room, in which she remained shut up with her maidservants.” The Greek codex reads “four months”; Ambrose cites this passage in his book *On Widows*. “But so that you may learn,” he says, “the character of widowhood by nature, follow the sequence of Scripture itself. From the days of her husband, on which he died, she removed the garment of gladness and assumed one of mourning; throughout all the days she was devoted to fasting, and during the sacred festival seasons she did not indulge in refreshment but paid due regard to religion.” Her continence is here wonderfully commended: although she was still a young woman, when her husband left her a widow she did not wish to enter a second marriage. To carry this out more easily, and to avoid men’s glances and conversation, she built for herself a private room in which she lived alone with her maidservants.

“And wearing sackcloth over her loins, she fasted throughout all the days of her life, except on Sabbaths, new moons, and the festivals of the house of Israel.” The Greek codex inserts “except before the Sabbaths,” by which it seems to mean the vigils of the Sabbaths. She devoted herself to fasting to such an extent in order to restrain those impulses of desire. “For fasting,” Augustine says (*Sermon* 230, *On Time*), “purifies the mind, lifts the understanding, and subjects it to the spirit; fasting makes the heart contrite and humbled, which God does not despise; fasting disperses the clouds of desire, extinguishes the fires of lust, kindles the true light of chastity,” and so forth, as he continues there. She now carried out in practice the same teaching that Paul gives concerning the righteous in Galatians 5: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires”; and this truly is to crucify one’s flesh.

“And she was exceedingly beautiful in appearance,” and so forth. He recounts two great gifts of hers, which for many are the occasion of countless evils: wealth and beauty. Yet she not only did not abuse them; rather, she gained much from them for true piety. She received the highest commendation in Scripture because, although she could have transgressed, she did not transgress, and so forth.

“And she was the most renowned of all, because she greatly feared,” and so forth. Similar is the saying of the Wise Man: “A woman who fears God will be praised; let them praise her in the gates, and her works.”

“When she therefore heard that Ozias had promised,” and so forth, “she sent for the elders Chambri and Charmi.” The fact that she did not go to the priests herself was not due to pride, but to zeal for the chastity of widowhood, by which she considered it improper to run through the streets.

“What is this word by which Ozias has agreed,” and so forth? These are words of Judith, full of wisdom and continual devotion toward God. Although at first sight these words seem to indicate that Ozias was not yet present, but arrived while she was saying them, the Greek text makes it probable that he had been present from the beginning. It reads as follows in the preceding passage: “And she sent for Ozias, Chabris, and Charmin, and they came to her,” and so forth. Meanwhile, she directs her speech chiefly to the priests, as though they were more culpable, since they ought to have been more concerned than the rulers for the worship of God. Once this city had been captured, the way to Jerusalem would have been easy, and thus great danger threatened divine worship. It was therefore necessary to defend this city for as long as they could, even amid the greatest affliction.

“And who are you, that you tempt the Lord?” and so forth. She now explains in what way they had tempted the Lord, when she adds:

“You have appointed for yourselves a time for the Lord’s mercy,” and so forth. Ozias labored under the same error as the children of Israel once did during the forty years. He therefore also tempted God, despairing of God’s providence toward them if it did not arrive at once and according to his wish. Hence Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10: “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents.” When they said, “He brought us out of Egypt so that we might die in the wilderness,” they were tempting God; for whoever wishes to test divine goodness or power shows that he distrusts it. It is clear that this was likewise what had happened here.

“But because the Lord is patient, let us repent of this very thing,” and so forth. This is a notable example of patience and of confidence in God amid adversity. After showing them their sin, she urges them to repentance, and does so on the basis of God’s remarkable patience. Hence she adds:

“For God will not threaten as a human being does,” and so forth—as though she were saying: What a human being threatens, he immediately tries to fulfill insofar as he can; but God sometimes threatens what he does not intend to do, as is evident in the case of the Ninevites in Jonah 3, and of King Hezekiah in 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 38. Such threats are issued not according to the order of divine foreknowledge, but according to the existence of demerits, which is mutable, even though God’s presence is immutable.

“And therefore let us humble our souls before him, and, with a humbled spirit, serve him; let us weeping say to the Lord that he should deal with us according to his will,” and so forth. Since fasting and a contrite heart, without prayer, have little power, Judith therefore urges them to prayer. She trusted that all the people’s prayers would be heard by the Lord. For, as Augustine beautifully teaches in the sermon cited above (*Sermon* 230), just as there is no complete refreshment without drink, so fasting without prayer cannot perfectly nourish the soul. “What,” he asks, “is prayer except an ascent of the soul from earthly things to heavenly things, a seeking of what is above, a desire for invisible things?”

“For we have not followed the sins of our ancestors,” and so forth. She explains why she trusts and does not doubt that their prayers will be heard: namely, because they had not followed that manifold idolatry of their ancestors, which is treated at length in 2 Kings 2 and Chronicles 10. From the return from the Babylonian captivity onward, the people of Israel are not recorded as having worshiped idols up to this time. This passage must therefore also be noted against Ziegler’s opinion, since he thinks that this history occurred in the time of Josiah, whereas under Josiah, Manasseh, and Josiah’s other predecessors, idolatry flourished in the tribe of Judah more than ever, if at any other time. “Let us humbly await his consolation,” and so forth. A similar passage is found in the Psalm: “Wait for the Lord and act manfully, and the Lord will preserve you.” Hence also the Savior’s saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

“And now, brothers, you who are among the people of God, and upon whom their lives depend,” and so forth. She now addresses the priests, as the teachers of the people, reminding them of their duty and burden, since they must render an account of all their subjects, according to Ezekiel 3 (the printed citation is corrupt): “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘Wicked one, you shall surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, I shall require his blood at your hand,” and so forth. Nearly the same words may also be found in the same prophet, chapter 3.

“They ought to remember that your fathers were tested, so that it might be proved whether they truly worshiped God,” and so forth. In a few words she teaches the priests how they may raise the people’s hearts. There is a similar passage in Deuteronomy 13, where it says: “The Lord your God is testing you, so that it may become clear whether or not you love the Lord.” In both places the manner in which God is said to test a human being is shown: to test by God means nothing other than to prove in faith. Hence Augustine, alluding to James 1, says: “God is not a tempter of evil”—that is, he does not tempt anyone toward evil; for he himself tempts no one. In *On the Words of the Lord* he says: “There is a temptation that leads to sin, by which God tempts no one; and there is a temptation that proves faith, by which God deigns to test a human being.” Similar statements are found elsewhere in Augustine: *Letter* 136 to Constantius; *Book 3 on the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 4; and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 6. There he discusses the words, “Lead us not into temptation,” distinguishing a useful temptation according to the saying, “Test me, Lord, and try me,” Psalm 25, from a harmful one, by which, according to James, God tempts no one and which the Apostle signifies in 1 Thessalonians 3: “Lest the tempter have tempted you”—namely, the devil.

“They ought to remember how our father Abraham was tested,” and so forth. “And all who pleased God passed through many tribulations in faith,” and so forth. There is a similar passage in Timothy: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.” A similar passage occurs in Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews, chapters 11 and 12; and again, more explicitly, when he sharply rebukes them and says: “You have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons,” namely, Proverbs 3: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are rebuked by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives.”

He gives the examples of the testing of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses. Abraham was tested with respect to his son Isaac, in the matter of his sacrifice, Genesis 22; Jacob was tested in fleeing the persecution of his brother Esau, Genesis 27 and 28. The commentaries do not mention when Moses was tested. Perhaps, however, he may rightly be said to have been tested when God appeared to him in the bush and gave him three signs by which he was to move the people of Israel to believe, and yet he himself replied: “Lord, I am not eloquent, neither from today nor from the day before yesterday,” and so forth.

“But those who did not endure their trials with fear of the Lord,” and so forth. Just as she wishes to admonish the people by the example of the good, so she wishes to terrify them by the example of the wicked. She alludes to Numbers 11, where, because of the people’s murmuring while the meat was still between their teeth, the Lord’s anger was aroused against the people and he struck them with a very great plague; or to chapter 14, which concerns the sedition and murmuring that followed the return of the spies from the land of Canaan; or to chapter 17, which concerns the rebellion of Dathan and Abiram. Thus, both here and in 1 Corinthians 10, where it is likewise said, “They perished by the destroyer,” the name “destroyer” should be understood either as referring to the angel on whom God exercised vengeance, or to some destructive power and force of God that punished sins. As for the later punishment by serpents, the passage is Exodus 21, where the matter is treated at length.

“Therefore, let us not avenge ourselves for what we suffer,” and so forth—namely, by directing the punishments we endure back against God and murmuring against God. Unless perhaps we should say that some among them were so wicked that, as though out of a desire for vengeance born of impatience toward God, they refused to surrender the city of Bethulia, as if taking revenge against God because, once this city had been captured by the enemy, great danger would threaten the worship of God in Jerusalem.

“But considering these punishments themselves to be less than our sins.” This plainly alludes to the saying of the Wise Man cited above, Proverbs 3. There is also a very similar and beautiful exhortation by Saint Chrysostom in his homily to the people of Antioch: “Let us not collapse in tribulations,” he says, “but let us give thanks in all things, so that we may gain something great, so that we may be found approved before God, who permits tribulations.” Paul understood their gain; in the passage cited, Romans 8, he says: “Tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint.” At the end of her speech she also alludes to the saying: “God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

“And Ozias and the elders said to her, and so forth: ‘Now therefore pray to the Lord for us,’” and so forth. The gracious affection of Judith’s prayer is here shown: they entreat her to pray for them, for through both her life and her holy words they had conceived the belief that God’s grace was in her. Judith therefore replied:

“Just as you recognize that what I have been able to say is from God, so test whether what I have decided to do is from God, and pray,” and so forth. She does not mean that they should anxiously investigate what she will later do, since below she says, “I do not want you to scrutinize my action.” Rather, it is as though she were saying: Just as you recognize that what I have said is from God, so await the outcome, and when the people’s deliverance has taken place, you will see that what I have thought to do was from God. Judith’s humility must also be noted here: she did not rely on herself alone, nor solely on her own prayers and fasting, but requested that prayers be offered for her both by the priests and by the people. Hence she adds: “Let nothing else be done except prayer to the Lord for me,” and so forth. Thus the ruler, together with the priests, bade her farewell, saying: “Go in peace; may the Lord be with you,” and so forth—as though he were saying: As you have requested, we do not wish to scrutinize your action any further. Carry out whatever seems good to you and has been inspired by God.

## CHAPTER IX

Judith enters her place of prayer, clothed in sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes on her head, and prays prostrate on the ground for her people.

“When they had departed, Judith entered her place of prayer,” and so forth. “When that Holofernes,” Augustine says (*Sermon* 228, *On Time*), “the enemy of the sons of Israel and of his own destruction, claimed for himself authority over foreign nations and fought by siege, arms, and fire, and when he also turned the fields of many nations, laden with white harvests, into ashes as the flame consumed them, the most holy Judith, through whose prayers heaven was opened, raised up prayer before arms, by which she might do battle against adversity and by which a woman might avenge the men who were afraid. For the prayers of all the others who were in the city were not enough for her unless she also humbled herself as much as she could and joined them in the same work, knowing the saying of Ecclesiasticus 35: ‘The prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds.’”

She is said to have been clothed in sackcloth also outwardly, for, as was stated above in the preceding chapter, “wearing sackcloth over her loins, she fasted throughout all the days of her life.”

“Lord, God of my father Simeon.” She understands Simeon the patriarch. Hence, in the preceding chapter, we showed briefly that Judith belonged to the tribe of Simeon, not to that of Reuben. Nevertheless, since Reuben is placed last there, some, according to Lyranus, thought that on her father’s side she belonged to the tribe of Reuben, but on her mother’s side to the tribe of Simeon.

Yet it does not seem likely that so holy a woman had parents who did not observe the Law, since the Law commanded that everyone who departed from his tribe should declare it, Numbers 26. It therefore does not seem plausible. Accordingly, either one must say, as above, that there is an error in the preceding chapter and that “sons of Israel,” not “sons of Reuben,” should be read—a reading supported by the Greek codex, which places this expression last and makes no mention of Reuben, although there too “sons of Simeon,” which our text contains, seems to be lacking—or else, which is no less probable, Lyranus’s opinion must be followed: namely, that the preceding chapter did not trace all of Judith’s generations back to Simeon, but merely enumerated her immediate ancestors. The long span of years between the birth of Simeon and the age at which Judith became renowned makes this plausible: it amounts to 1,260 years or more, which constitutes more than thirty generations.

From the birth of Isaac to the exodus from Egypt, 400 years elapsed, as is clear from Genesis 15. If one subtracts 108 years—from the birth of Isaac to the births of Reuben and Simeon—there remain 300 years less eight [i.e. 292]. From the exodus from Egypt to the founding of the Temple by Solomon, 480 years elapsed, 1 Kings 6; from then until its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, according to the Hebrews, 410 years elapsed. This could be demonstrated from the reigns of the kings who ruled from Solomon’s time to the eleventh year of Zedekiah, with no disagreement. From then again to the fourth year of Cyrus, in which the Second Temple was founded, there were at least 70 years; and from then another eight years to Cambyses. Together these make 1,260 years. If one adds the eight years of Cambyses and the remaining years of Darius, under whom we say this history occurred, the total will be even greater.

That there were at least thirty generations during this span of years is evident both from the fact that everyone begot children at the age of forty, and from Christ’s genealogy in Matthew 1. From Abraham to the Babylonian deportation there are twenty-eight generations, yet three generations of the kings of Judah are omitted there, as Jerome testifies in his Commentary; and under the name of Boaz, three generations are again included as one. Moreover, from the Babylonian deportation to Darius, under whom this history occurred, approximately eighty-six years elapsed, which make at least two generations.

According to this view, then, this Reuben was some other member of the tribe of Simeon, at whom Judith’s genealogy ends because he was a man of great renown.

“You who gave him a sword for the defense of foreigners who had violated them in their defilement,” and so forth. As in chapter 1 above, so here “defense” must be understood as vengeance; hence the Greek codex reads “for vengeance.” This passage plainly shows that she is speaking of the patriarch Simeon, since it cannot be applied to any other history except the killing of the Shechemites for the violation of Jacob’s daughter Dinah, Genesis 34. This was carried out by Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers. It could also be understood, as Lyranus notes, that the sword was given to him for defense because the neighboring Gentiles did not dare to pursue Jacob and his sons, believing, as Genesis 35 relates, that they had been struck with fear by God because of Simeon and his brothers.

It is fitting that Judith recalls Simeon’s deed in her prayer: together with Levi he avenged the violation of his sister Dinah, and Holofernes, who wished to satisfy the impurity of his lust in Judith, was likewise destined to be struck by the sword of vengeance.

“Who were zealous with zeal for you,” and so forth. Although the manner of their vengeance was not commendable, because they broke the covenant they had made with the Shechemites, their zeal in avenging the violation was nevertheless lawful and just, since there was no judge to punish the crime: its author was the ruler of the city, and its people supported him. It is in this sense that Judith speaks here. According to the former view, however, Jacob in Genesis 49 speaks ill of them [the printed words are corrupt]: “Simeon and Levi are brothers, vessels of warring iniquity.” “Let my soul not enter into their counsel,” and so forth, unless we wish to say that this referred rather to the prophecy concerning Christ.

“For you made the former things and those things, and after them you devised,” and so forth. The Greek codex reads: “For you made their former things and those things, and the later things, and the present things, and the things that were to come, you devised.” The meaning is somewhat clearer: You made things that had never been made before those times—namely, from the creation of the world up to that time—and also those things, as well as the things that would never afterward exist; and you devised, ordered, and arranged the things that now exist and those that are to come. You disposed everything in order.

“Look now toward the camp of the Assyrians, just as then you deigned to look upon the camp of the Egyptians,” and so forth. Just as he compares the lustful Holofernes with the previously lustful Shechemites, so he compares the proud Assyrians with the proud Egyptians, as though he were saying: Just as divine power was displayed in the overthrow of those people, so it will also be manifested in the overthrow of these. She alludes to Exodus 14: “The Lord looked upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud and killed their army,” and to the Psalm: “The face of the Lord was upon the face of the sea.”

“And darkness wearied them,” and so forth. She alludes to the same chapter: “There was a dark cloud on the side of the Egyptians, but it illuminated the night on the side of the Hebrews, so that they could not approach one another throughout the entire night.”

“You who crush wars from the beginning,” and so forth—that is, from ancient times, as is evident in the case of Amalek when he fought against the Israelites, Exodus 17; of Og, king of Bashan, and Sihon, king of the Amorites, Numbers 21; of the kings who fought against Joshua, Joshua 10; and in many other passages.

“Let their strength fall in your anger, those who promise to profane your holy things,” and so forth. To move God more powerfully to mercy, she places before his eyes the destruction of divine worship that the Assyrians were planning and would have accomplished against Bethulia without great difficulty. They had promised this to King Nebuchadnezzar, so that he alone would rule in Cara and be called a god, as was stated above in Wisdom 3.

“Lord, make his pride be cut off by his own sword,” and so forth. She does not say this from delight in punishment but from love of justice. The prophets likewise, seeing in their wisdom what will come about by a just judgment, ask that it happen; such is the saying in Psalm 68: “Let their table before them become a snare,” and that in Acts 23: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall.” Here she appears to speak prophetically, since afterward what she requested occurred: Holofernes’s head was cut off with his own sword, as related below in chapter 13.

“Let him be caught by the snare of his eyes in me, and you will strike him through the snares of my affection,” and so forth. It is as though she were saying: Let him be so attracted by the sight of my eyes that I may become familiar to him, so that I may be able to accomplish what I have requested; and if I cannot accomplish this by my eyes alone, let it also be done through my words that pretend affection. Hence the Greek codex reads: “by the lips of my deception.” How Judith did this, and whether she asked God for it simply or in another way, we shall discuss in the following chapter, where we shall explain that her adornment arose not from lust but from virtue.

“Give me steadfastness of mind,” and so forth. Since what she requested was difficult, especially for a woman, whose nature is generally inconstant, she asks God to grant her steadfastness, so that she would neither fear the enemy nor be deterred by horror from carrying out the deed in Holofernes’s murder. She then adds the reason for her request:

“For this will be a memorial of your name,” and so forth. It is as though she were saying: Since this remarkable deed will have been accomplished through a woman, and a fragile sex will have dared to do so much, glory will be ascribed to you alone, God; for your power does not depend on a multitude, since by a single command you can overthrow them.

“And the proud have not pleased you from the beginning, but the prayer of the humble and meek has always pleased you,” and so forth. Again she proclaims the pride of the enemies and of her own people, as well as her own humility, knowing that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. The Greek codex contains several additional words expressing greater emotion: “But you are the Lord of the humble and the helper of the miserable, the defender of the powerless, the protector of those in despair, the savior of those without hope.””

Concluding her prayer, she says:

“Remember, Lord, your covenant,” and so forth. It is as though she were saying: If our merits or our humility do not deserve this mercy of yours, remember the promise made long ago; and if you do not spare us, at least spare the worship of your name, and prevent your name from being blasphemed among the nations.

## CHAPTER X

Judith adorns herself, leaves the city with her maidservant, is detained by the scouts, and is brought to Holofernes.

“When she had ceased crying out to the Lord, she rose from the place where she had lain prostrate before the Lord,” and so forth. After fortifying herself with the weapons of prayer, she begins to prepare herself to carry out what she had planned. She summoned her *abra*, that is, a young maidservant—for those familiar with the language say that this is what the Greek word means—and, descending from the upper room that she had built for herself after her husband’s death, first removed her sackcloth and widow’s garments.

“And she washed her body and anointed herself with the finest myrtle, parted the hair of her head, and placed a mitre upon her head,” and so forth. He explains more fully the adornment with which she adorned herself. In place of our reading “with the finest myrtle,” the Greek codex reads “with rich ointment.” Both readings, however, amount to the same sense, and the difference seems to have arisen from the similarity of the words. *Myron* is called “ointment” by Homer. If we read according to our text, it must be understood as an ointment prepared either from myrrh or from myrtle, since both are fragrant plants from which ointments are customarily made.

A mitre signifies a woman’s crown for adorning the head, such as young women commonly wear. From it hung little strips called *phylarae*, because they hung down like flowers. Isaiah, in chapter 3, also lists many ornaments of women, including several of those mentioned here.

“And she put sandals on her feet, took *dextrariola* and lilies, earrings, and rings,” and so forth. Lyranus says that sandals are a type of summer footwear not covered above with leather. Here too the Greek codex differs somewhat: it does not mention lilies or sandals, but reads: “And she put on ornaments for the arms, bracelets, and earrings,” and so forth. From this one might perhaps not unreasonably conclude that the first expression explains the second, so that *dextrariola* should be understood as ornaments for the arms.

What kind or sort of ornament this word signifies is highly uncertain. We do find the words *dextrale* and *dextrocherium* used by writers, but I do not know whether the word found here occurs anywhere else. It may therefore be understood either as a *dextrale*, an ornament worn on the right arm by both men and women, or as a *dextrocherium*, a woman’s ornament made of gold in the form of a broad ring woven with precious gems, commonly called a *bracolellen*. Julius Capitolinus uses the word when he writes that Maximian had a thumb so large that he used his wife’s *dextrocherium* as a ring.

The Greek word *ta psellia* supports the latter meaning; according to Ammonius, it signifies bracelets. Most people understand *armillae* as ornaments for the arms. It is no objection that military men formerly used to wear such ornaments, gifts from emperors, not on the right but on the left arm—ornaments that Cyprian calls *brachialia*—since women wore them on both arms, and especially on the right.

The “ribbons” seem to be those strips hanging from the mitre mentioned above, called *phylarae* because they hung down like flowers; or perhaps small golden knobs hanging at their ends in the form of threads. The little linen strips mentioned by Isaiah in the cited chapter, according to Jerome, seem to have been something of this kind.

“And she adorned herself with all her ornaments,” and so forth. The Greek codex adds: “with which she used to adorn herself in the days of her husband Manasseh’s life.” “Thus strengthened,” Ambrose says (*On Widows*), “by prolonged mourning and daily fasts, holy Judith, who did not seek the pleasures of the world, disregarding danger and made stronger by contempt for death, put on, not to contrive deceit in her mind, that garment of gladness in which she used to dress while her husband was alive, as though she would please a husband if she liberated her country. But she saw another husband whom she sought to please—namely, the one of whom it is said, ‘After me comes a man who was made before me.’”

Again, in *Book 2 on Virgins*, Ambrose says: “Judith adorned herself to please an adulterer. Yet because she did this from religious duty, not from love, no one judged her an adulteress. She rightly took this example: for if she who entrusted herself to religion preserved both modesty and favor, then by preserving religion we too shall preserve chastity. But if Judith had wished to prefer chastity to religion, she would have lost both chastity and her country.”

“And the Lord also bestowed splendor upon her, because all this adornment depended not on lust but on virtue,” and so forth. For understanding this and the preceding and following passages, it must be noted that there are two interpretations here. Some say that Judith’s intention to liberate the people was lawful and honorable, but that by pretending this affection she did and said certain unlawful things and requested that Holofernes be inflamed with lust; and that for this reason she adorned herself and presumed to make several statements to Holofernes and to her own people that involved lies. According to them, Scripture commends the former intention itself, and her prayers were heard and her beauty was divinely increased, just as in Exodus 1 the midwives are commended for the good intention they had in preserving the Hebrew children, but not for their lie.

Others, however, deny that she sinned in any respect here—not in the prayer mentioned above, nor in her adornment, nor even in the words that appear to be lies in what follows. They say that Judith intended one thing and foresaw another. She intended to become pleasing to Holofernes so that, by associating familiarly with him, she might reach the point of killing him; but she foresaw Holofernes’s unlawful love toward her. Nevertheless, this did not mean that she ought not to carry out her plan, just as God does not sin by punishing a sinner less because he foreknows that the sinner will thereby become worse. Or perhaps she sought Holofernes’s familiarity in such a way that she was willing to submit herself to severity [the reading is uncertain], and thus await an opportunity to carry out the killing.

Nor was such a stealthy killing a sin, since in a just war it is lawful to use stratagems, as is clear from Joshua 8. The war of the Israelites against Holofernes was entirely just, since it was fought on behalf of the worship of God. This interpretation is highly consistent with the passage and with Ambrose’s words, which would otherwise seem false. Whether her lie can likewise be excused in this manner, we shall discuss below.

“Then she placed a wineskin upon her *abra*.” I think that *ascoperam* should certainly be read, since it corresponds to the Greek text and its translators; the word denotes a leather wineskin or pouch, from *askos* (“wineskin”) and *pyra* (“bag”). Suetonius also uses the word in his *Nero*, saying that an *ascopera* was tied around another man’s neck. Thus *ascopera vini* means nothing other than a wineskin.

“And a vessel of oil, and parched grain, and *lapates*, and loaves, and cheese, and she departed.” The Greek codex reads somewhat differently: “And she filled a bag with flour, *palatha*, and pure loaves.” From this it appears that, in addition to the wineskin, there was also a pouch in which she could carry food. This reading seems more probable, since those items would be more convenient to carry than parched grain; and where our text reads *lapates*, it seems to be corrupt and should rather read *palathas*, since the former word is entirely unknown to writers.

According to Hesychius, *palaton* signifies a mass of raisins and figs; it is so called as though it had been compressed between shovels. The same word is found in 2 Samuel 16: “Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, appeared to meet David with two donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves, one hundred bunches of raisins, and seven masses of *palathae*.” The translator of the Greek codex reads “summer figs,” although, while the word properly signifies an entire mass of dried or pressed figs, in both places it seems to be used for the figs themselves and appears in the plural.

“Yet, without asking her anything, they let her pass,” and so forth. They obeyed the command imposed on them in the preceding chapter, that they should not scrutinize her actions. Ambrose, treating this passage in *Book 3 of Duties*, chapter 3, says: “How great the authority of virtue, that a woman should claim for herself counsel concerning the highest matters and entrust it to the leaders of the people! How great the authority of virtue, that she should presume upon God as her helper; how great the grace, that she should find him!”

“And when she was descending the mountain around sunrise,” and so forth. The narrative now explains how Judith fell into the hands of the enemy. She went out around sunrise so that she might appear to have slipped out secretly past the guards and thus deceive them more easily; for it is generally at that hour that sentries prepare themselves for sleep.

“That is why I fled from their presence, because I knew that what would happen was that they would be handed over to you as plunder,” and so forth. Whether these and the following words can be excused from lying, we shall discuss in the following chapter.

“Then they said to her: ‘You have preserved your life’; and they led her to the tent of Holofernes,” etc. The Greek codex relates this somewhat more fully: “And they selected one hundred men from among them, and harnessed a chariot for her, together with her maidservants, and led her,” etc. “She went forth,” says Augustine (Sermon 228, On Time), “content with the escort of a single maiden, and hastened into the camp with the assured step of the enemy. Within the walls she had been anxious; she became confident when she reached what was to be feared. In this woman the novelty of a deceptive beauty so greatly terrified the hostile army that they lost their strength in serving her, cast down their weapons, and bowed their necks. She was led to the commander’s quarters through ranks drawn up beneath her: the deception of Holofernes, and the victory of the grieving city.”

“When she had entered into his presence, Holofernes was immediately captivated by her appearance,” etc. That is, he was immediately inflamed with unrestrained desire for her. Whether he desired her only for fornication, or rather for marriage, is not clear from the text, for what follows appears at times to favor one interpretation and at times the other. For the present, Judith’s good intention, as stated above, is sufficient to show that she did not sin in adorning herself. Hence Augustine says at the passage cited: “When Holofernes saw her, he was released from his senses, about to lose his soul together with his head. He lay captive before the woman’s face. It was permitted to the woman to arm the young men and defeat the conquerors, to defend the anxious city, and overthrow the barbarian warrior. The sincere deceived the corrupted; the chaste outwitted the polluted. For she had so confounded those barbarous minds by the deception of her treacherous appearance that she made him defeated amid his armies and captive amid his weapons.”

“Then Judith saw Holofernes sitting beneath the canopy,” etc. Namely, on a chair above which, to magnify the seat, a canopy had been placed—a curtain, I mean, made like a pavilion in the form of a pyramid. This kind of covering was first devised to keep mosquitoes away from the bed; hence it is especially used by the Alexandrians, since mosquitoes swarm there from the Nile, and the Greeks call them *conopae* (“mosquitoes”). It may, however, be understood to have been so called from Conope, a town in Egypt; for elsewhere Lyranus also derives the term from *conus* (“cone”), at which point it would be absurd to pursue the matter more fully.

## CHAPTER XI. Judith, questioned by Holofernes about the reason for her flight, cleverly deceives him by the charm of her words.

“Then Holofernes said to her: ‘Be of good courage, and do not fear in your heart, for I have never harmed a man who wished to serve Nebuchadnezzar,’” etc. “Behold,” says Ambrose (*On the Duties*, book III, chapter 3), “Judith presents herself as a marvel. She approached Holofernes, the man feared by the nations, surrounded by the Assyrians’ triumphant multitude. At first glance she struck him by her grace and the beauty of her face; then she enclosed him within the elegance of her speech. Her first triumph was that she brought this modesty from the enemy’s tent; her second, that a woman carried away victory from a man. By her counsel she put the nations to flight, and the Persians shuddered at her boldness. But that he speaks so courteously with her because he was enticed by her beauty is evident, since what he says—that he had never known an impious man who wished to serve his master—is a lie, as he himself elsewhere makes clear; it must soon be refuted by a lie.”

[Col. 0624C] “And Judith said to him: ‘Accept the words of your maidservant, for if you follow the words of your maidservant, the Lord will accomplish a perfect deed with you.’” As though she were saying: “The Lord will bring you to the goal you have set.” Although some attempt here, as in the preceding chapter concerning the words she spoke to the guards, to excuse Judith from lying, and although her words may possess truth according to a certain mystical sense, nevertheless, since she does not appear excusable according to the literal sense—which must be established first of all, before the others—I think that the opinion should be embraced which calls these lies officious and therefore venial sins. It is not surprising if Judith is not excused from them, since even John the Evangelist and Apostle says of himself in the First Epistle, chapter 1: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” Nor does the praise accorded her in Scripture stand in the way; for certain things are praised in her not on account of perfect virtue, but on account of a certain disposition toward virtue—namely, because something praiseworthy appeared in them, from which they were moved to undertake unusual deeds. Thus the midwives in Exodus 1 are commended and receive remembrance because they feared God, not because they lied; so Judith too is praised not for the lie with which she deceived Holofernes, but for her desire to liberate the people, on account of which she exposed herself to danger.

“For Nebuchadnezzar the king of the earth lives, and the power that is in you lives,” etc.—so that she might deceive the deceiver and mock the mocker. First she magnificently exalts both his power and that of his lord. This should not be regarded as an oath, since otherwise it could not be excused from mortal sin, but merely as a simple assertion of what was false.

“Nor is it hidden from me what Achior said,” etc. In order to mock him further, she even approves Holofernes’ judgment concerning Achior, whom he had condemned to death after the Israelites were defeated. She confirms that this would indeed happen because of the people’s sins, on account of which God, as she says, had declared through his prophets that he was offended. This too must meanwhile be numbered among the lies; for if it had been so, she would herself have sinned by preventing the city from being delivered.

“Finally, they have determined to slaughter their cattle and drink their blood.” This too appears to have been false, since they had been most strictly forbidden to eat blood. How this can nevertheless be made true, even according to the literal sense, may be seen by anyone who wishes in Lyranus.

“And the holy things of the Lord their God, which God commanded not to be touched in connection with grain, wine, and oil, these they have planned to spend; thus they wish to consume what they ought not even to touch with their hands,” etc. At first sight the meaning appears to be that they had decided to spend the sacred vessels in purchasing grain, wine, and oil. But since no such vessels appear to have been in Jerusalem, “holy things” must here be understood as the firstfruits and tithes owed to the priests, as the Greek codex appropriately explains: “And the firstfruits of the grain and the tithes of the wine and oil, which the worshipers had set aside for the priests serving in Jerusalem before the presence of the Lord our God, they determined to consume—things which no one from the people ought to have touched with his hands.” There is also a lie in the final clause, since these things could be eaten in a time of necessity, as is clear from David in 1 Samuel 21, who ate the bread of the Presence with his companions, even with the high priest’s approval. The rest of her following words are of the same kind.

“And all these words pleased Holofernes,” etc. Holofernes and his leaders approved Judith’s words, so that, if everything turned out as she said, they seemed to promise her both marriage to him and the worship of his god. Whether they meant this sincerely or deceitfully is immaterial.

## CHAPTER XII. Judith is brought into the treasury, receives permission to eat food of her own, and to go out at night for prayer; then, brought before Holofernes for the banquet, she eats with him.

“Then he ordered her to enter where his treasures were kept,” etc. Judith’s reply, previously confirmed only in words, is now confirmed by action as well. Holofernes ordered her to be brought into the treasury as someone especially dear to him, and in whom he trusted no less than in his own wife—indeed, he also arranged for her daily food. Judith answered him and said:

“Now I cannot eat of these things that you provide for me,” etc. As though she were saying: “Excuse me for a short time, lest perhaps God, having been offended, fail to accomplish what I have already said.” Some of these foods appear to have been kinds of nourishment forbidden by the Law, since, as is clear from Galatians 2, the Jews considered it unlawful to eat with Gentiles. “But what,” says Ambrose (*On Widows*), “shall we say of her wisdom, which devised such a plan—that while she enticed the powerful man, intemperance drove the subordinates away, she prepared an opportunity for victory, and preserved the merit of self-restraint and the grace of chastity? For she was stained neither by food, as we read, nor by adultery; she carried away from the enemy a trophy of preserved chastity no less than one of her country’s liberation.” And again, in Epistle 82: “Judith imposed a banquet on the lustful Holofernes to no avail; under the mere title of sobriety she won a triumph with courageous spirit over one who was thought invincible, freed her country from siege, killed the commander of the army with her own hands, and taught Egypt that, just as luxury softened that terrifying warrior to the nations, so moderation in food made this woman equal to men. Here nature was not overcome in her sex, but in her food she overcame; by her fasts she brought down the proud king.”

“And Judith said, etc.: ‘Your maidservant will not consume all these things until God accomplishes by my hand what I have planned,’” etc. Here she speaks most truly and appears almost to prophesy, for Holofernes was first killed by her, and she herself had planned to do it, although Holofernes expected something else.

“And when she entered, she remained clean in the tent until she received her food in the evening,” etc. That is, she remained clean by avoiding association with the Gentiles. It says “until,” not because she did not remain clean afterward as well, but according to a manner of speaking used in Scripture, in which “until” and “unto” often signify an indefinite period, as in Matthew 1: “Until she had given birth to her firstborn son,” and Matthew 28: “I am with you until the end of the age.” Jerome offers a fine treatment of such passages in his work against Helvidius. It is meanwhile clear from these words that Judith fasted in Holofernes’ camp until evening, so that her prayer might be heard all the more. Hence Chrysostom, drawing from various passages in Matthew, says in Homily 10: “While joy covered Judith’s face, she carried away from the enemy the triumph of victory.”

[Col. 0626B] “And it came to pass on the fourth day that Holofernes made a banquet for his servants and said to Vagao, his eunuch,” etc. He now turns to the opportunity Judith used for the killing of Holofernes. He appears to have celebrated this banquet as a nuptial one, since he intended to marry her on the following night. Judith’s chastity was then in the greatest danger, unless God should help her. “Certainly,” says Ambrose (*On the Duties*, book III), “she did not fear the danger of death—but neither did she fear the danger to her modesty, which is more serious for good women. She feared neither the blow of a single executioner nor the weapons of the whole army. The woman stood among the ranks of warriors, among victorious arms, secure even in death. Judith therefore pursued honor, and while pursuing it, found usefulness. It was honorable to prevent the people from surrendering themselves to profane practices; to prevent them from betraying their ancestral rites and holy things; to prevent sacred virgins, widows, and grave, chaste matrons from being subjected to barbarian impurity; and to prevent the siege from being ended by surrender. It was honorable to prefer to face danger for everyone’s sake, so that she might rescue everyone from danger.”

[Col. 0626C] It should be noted here that the Greek codex reads somewhat differently: “And he said to Varoa the eunuch, who was in charge of all that belonged to him.” Thus it also appears that the name was formerly read as Barua or Baroa, not Varao, as our text reads. This is evident even from Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, where he especially confirms his opinion—that this history occurred long after the history of Esther, under King Ochus, who lived after Artaxerxes Longimanus—by the argument that Baquas, the eunuch of Ochus and an Egyptian by birth, avenged by the king’s death, after Egypt had been conquered, the injury that Ochus had done to the king of the Egyptians by mocking him. This history, however, mentions a certain Baquas both in this chapter and in the following one. Just as he confirms his opinion by such an argument, so it will likewise be possible to confirm ours, as we said in the preface, since the Hystaspes under whom we shall say this history occurred clearly had a certain prefect named Baquas, through whom, according to Sabellicus, he arranged the death of a certain Oliganus, who was plotting against his life.

“And Judith said to him: ‘Who am I, that I should contradict my lord?’” These words may be understood as spoken ironically, with ambiguous language by which she deceived the deceiver himself. Vagao or Baques, as the Greek codex has it, understood her to be speaking about Holofernes, whereas she appears to have been speaking about the Lord God.

“And she arose and adorned herself with her garments, and entered and stood before him,” etc. She adorned herself like a bride, already about to be joined to her bridegroom in marriage. The Greek codex expands somewhat more fully as follows: “She adorned herself with her garment and with every kind of feminine ornament. Her maidservant entered and spread out before Holofernes on the ground the skins which she had received from Bagoas for her daily use, so that she might recline and eat upon them; and Judith entered and reclined.” “But Holofernes’ heart was shaken,” etc. That is, it was stirred by an excessive ardor of lust. Even if this is understood to mean that he wished to know her as his wife, he would nevertheless do so from the heat of lust, not from hope of offspring.

“And Judith said: ‘I will drink, lord, because my soul has been exalted today,’” etc. For she saw that the hour of the people’s liberation was approaching. “A banquet,” says Augustine in Sermon 228, “is prepared for the king, and Judith is ordered to attend. She agrees in order to conquer; she approaches the banquet, intending to taste nothing of the enemy’s food or drink, since she wished to be content with her own provisions. Although that warrior, armed with weapons, watched the face of so chaste a woman in a diseased manner, she was thinking of the reason for which she had come—of his head, which, once removed, would enable her, strong in courage, to help her fellow citizens, and liberate, defend, and avenge many heads.”

“And Holofernes became cheerful toward her, and drank very much wine,” etc. Since, in the heat of lust, he had already lost the judgment necessary to guard himself against excess in wine. “By wine,” says Jerome in book III of his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, “a man’s senses are overturned; his feet, head, and mind totter; lust is kindled. Hence the Apostle says in Ephesians 5: ‘Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.’ Everyone has authority over his own judgment; I follow the Apostle in saying that there is debauchery in wine and drunkenness in wine, and that drunkenness is counted among the works of the flesh in debauchery. Nor can the person who is overcome by these passions deny it.” Augustine also has a very fine sermon on the same matter—namely, the avoidance of drunkenness—in Sermon 231, *On Time*.

## CHAPTER XIII. Judith cuts off the head of drunken Holofernes with his own sword and, carrying it to her fellow citizens, urges them to give thanks.

“When it became late, his servants hurried to their quarters, and Vagao shut the doors of the chamber and departed. Everyone was exhausted from the wine, and Judith alone was in the chamber,” etc. Having first described the circumstances leading to Holofernes’ killing, the account immediately adds his slaughter. One may here observe the high praise of sobriety and, conversely, the many evils that follow drunkenness. Hence Ambrose, in the work cited above, *On Widows*: “Temperance is the virtue of women, by which, when the men were drunk with wine and buried in sleep, the widow took away the sword, sharpened her hand, cut off the warrior’s head, and passed unharmed through the midst of the enemy. Consider, therefore, how harmful drunkenness can be to women, when wine so loosens men that they are conquered by women. For if Judith had drunk, she would have slept with the adulterer; but because she did not drink, the sobriety of one woman could both conquer and mock drunken armies.”

“And Judith told her maidservant to stand outside before the chamber,” etc. She undertook with great prudence the deed she had conceived. She had to leave the chamber in order to give her this instruction, since it had previously been said that she alone was in the chamber; then, having left the maidservant outside to watch lest anyone should arrive, she went back inside. Knowing that prayer is useful for every undertaking, she again had recourse to prayer, and said:

“Strengthen me, Lord God of Israel, and look at the works of my hands at this hour, so that, just as you have promised, you may raise up Jerusalem, your city,” etc. As though she were saying: “Since in deeds of this kind a woman’s mind is usually overcome by great fear, strengthen my mind and hands, so that I may complete in action what I have resolved; and let your promises attain their fulfillment—those promises which, through the prophets, you made that Jerusalem would be rebuilt after repentance, both because sins had to be removed and because of the promises themselves, through Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zechariah, Haggai, and others.”

“When she had drawn the dagger, she seized the hair of his head, struck his neck twice, and cut off his head,” etc. Augustine, in the often-mentioned Sermon 228, reads “three times” instead of “twice”: “When the banquet’s excess had reached its limit, and heavy sleep followed the cups, Judith saw the neck of the enemy’s body bent down by drunkenness. Rising, she seized his bloodstained neck and grasped the hair of the barbarian’s head in her hand. ‘Lord,’ she said, ‘strengthen my arm’; and she struck his neck a third time and cut off his head. She went outside, handed it to the maidservant, and put it into the bag. A little later she went outside as if for prayer, according to her custom. Behold chastity. Through the favor of prayer, chastity preserved her own modesty intact and undisturbed, while deceiving another’s. The corpse lies enclosed, and the head is already outside.”

“And she rolled his headless body,” etc. Lyranus interprets this as though she had rolled it from the bed onto the ground, so that no one inside would immediately notice that the killing had occurred. But since in the following chapter Vagao is said first to have clapped his hands before the curtain, it does not seem that this was done. Perhaps she should be understood to have rolled it from the canopy, which she took away with her.

[Col. 0628B] “And Judith said from a distance to the guards on the walls,” etc. Up to this point Holofernes’ killing has been described; now its disclosure is narrated—how Judith was first admitted by the guards, and then received honorably by the elders, the priests, and the whole people, because they hoped—that is, feared greatly, according to Virgil’s expression “to hope for great pain,” meaning “to fear”—that she would return. Having therefore been admitted and surrounded by the whole people:

“Ascending to a higher place, she ordered silence to be made,” etc. She sought every convenience and opportunity by which she might more easily be heard by the whole people and so encourage everyone to give thanks. Augustine, at the place often cited, beautifully supports the account of her return: “With palm-bearing chastity Judith hastens anxiously to her fellow citizens, and she is not prevented from returning, since she had been permitted to go forth earlier as if for prayer. Now the astonished city receives the triumphal palms of so great a victor; now grief is turned into joy; now the gates are opened in complete security; now the head hangs upon victorious walls. For when heaven has been repeatedly assailed by prayers, the power of arms is always trampled underfoot. Behold, prayer preserved the chastity of the glorious woman, while the multitude could not preserve the enemy; one woman was able to rescue the entire city, while so great an army could not guard its king.”

“When everyone had become silent, Judith said: ‘Praise the Lord our God, all of you,’” etc. Knowing that the entire triumph of that victory must be ascribed to God, she urges the people to give thanks. Having done so, she displays to them Holofernes’ own head and the canopy as confirmation of her words. Then:

“‘As God lives,’ she said, ‘his angel guarded me both when I went from here and when I remained there,’” etc. Lest any suspicion arise that she had suffered harm to her chastity from Holofernes or anyone else, she now confirms this by an oath before the whole people.
