She ends the prayer with which she had begun, concluding with praises of the Lord God and an exhortation to confess his praise and give thanks for so great, so sudden, and so extraordinary a victory.

“Then everyone worshiping the Lord said to her: ‘God has blessed you by his power,’” etc. The commendation and blessing of Judith now follow—first by the whole people, and then by the people’s ruler, who among other things says:

“‘He who directed you against the wounds of the head of our enemies’ leader,” etc. The Greek codex reads, apparently more appropriately, in the singular: “against the wound of the head,” and so forth. Nevertheless, since she struck his flesh twice, it is also plausible that she inflicted several wounds upon him.

“‘So that your praise may not depart from the mouths of human beings who will remember the Lord’s power,’” etc. The praise given by human beings to a just person, however great it may be, must not be the end of the good itself, says Augustine in his commentary on Psalm 118, “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity”; rather, such praise must itself be referred to the praise of God, on account of whom good men do good deeds.

“Now Achior, having been summoned, came,” etc. The Greek paraphrase does not contain this here, but in the following chapter, immediately after its beginning, where Achior is mentioned, it presents the matter in these words. That order certainly appears much more appropriate.

“When Achior saw the head of Holofernes, he was distressed from fear,” etc. He was not distressed from fear, since he had already been freed from the fear of death; rather, he was overwhelmed by excessive astonishment and wonder, as we often see happen when sudden events are reported that become causes of joy for us. It was indeed exceedingly astonishing that so great a deed had been accomplished by the hand of a woman. Hence he immediately suffered a kind of swoon, which is what is meant by the words:

“And his spirit was agitated,” although some manuscripts read “hesitated.” After he came back to himself, it was as though he had awakened from a kind of lethargic sleep.

“He worshiped her and said: ‘Blessed are you by your God in every tent of Jacob,’” etc. He worshiped her in the same way that Abraham is said in Genesis to have worshiped the people of the land—not with the worship of *latria*, says Augustine in Question-Sermon 61, but with that of *dulia*, as it is called.

## CHAPTER XIV. Holofernes’ head is hung upon the wall, and Achior is circumcised; the Jews attack the Assyrians, who, when they come to awaken Holofernes, find him dead.

“Then Judith said to all the people: ‘Hear me. Hang this head upon our walls, and when the sun rises, let each person take up his weapons,’” etc. After Holofernes’ death had been accomplished, Judith urges the people to destroy his army. To break the enemy’s spirit still further, she orders that his head be hung from the walls. “When Holofernes’ head had been hung up,” says Ambrose (*On Widows*), “what the counsel of men had been unable to devise, she raised the spirits of her own people, broke those of the enemy, arousing her own by shame and striking the enemy with shame, because they had been defeated and exhausted. Thus the temperance and sobriety of a single widow not only conquered her own nature but, what is more, made men stronger as well.”

“Then the scouts must flee to their commander,” etc. For they were not permitted to engage in battle without his authority. Among the Romans, says the author of the *History of the Jewish War*, not only to fight but even to conquer without a commander was regarded as disgraceful.

“Then Achior, seeing the power that God had shown to Israel,” etc. Here, as stated above, the matters concerning Achior that were discussed in the preceding chapter are first resumed, and these points are added. It is now described how, after seeing the miraculous works of God, Achior abandoned the Gentile religion, believed in God, and ordered himself to be circumcised, so that he and all his descendants were enrolled among the proselytes.

“Immediately, when day had dawned, they hung Holofernes’ head upon the walls,” etc. After Achior’s circumcision has been inserted, the fulfillment of Judith’s plan is explained: when the head had been hung upon the wall, the Israelite army rushed into the enemy camp in a body.

“When the scouts saw this, they ran to Holofernes’ tent,” etc. Holofernes’ death is now revealed, and the manner in which it occurred is described in precisely the order Judith had foretold.

“For no one dared to open the chamber of the Assyrians’ strength by knocking or entering,” etc. “The strength of the Assyrians” means their commander, in whom they believed the army’s strength resided, just as the body’s natural strength resides in the heart. Hence Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*: “Just as the heart is in the middle of the body, so the commander ought to be placed in the middle of the army.” When these men approaching saw the Jews—something they otherwise would not have dared to do—they attempted to carry it out. The commanders and military tribunes therefore assembled and attacked the chamber servants, since they were able to enter more familiarly.

“‘Enter and awaken him,’ they said, ‘for mice have come out of their holes and dared to challenge us to battle.’” As you see, they speak of the Jews with contempt and insult; but they are soon to pay the penalty for their insult.

“Then Vagao entered his chamber, etc.; and when he perceived no movement from the body by the sense of hearing, he approached close to the curtain, lifted it, and saw the corpse,” etc. He briefly explains how, at the command of the army’s leaders, Baques, or Vagao, as chief chamberlain, entered Holofernes’ tent and found Holofernes dead, his corpse headless, while Judith had already fled. Hence he cried out:

“‘A Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of Nebuchadnezzar,’” etc. As though he were saying: “It is exceedingly shameful for us to have been exposed in this way by a woman,” for this has always been regarded as a matter of the greatest disgrace. Thus in Judges 9, when Abimelech was wounded by a woman with a piece of a millstone, he ordered his armor-bearer to kill him, lest it be said that a woman had killed him.

“When the commanders of the Assyrians’ strength heard this, they all tore their garments,” etc. The confusion and dismay of Holofernes’ entire army are now described. This also caused them to prepare less effectively to resist the Israelites’ attack, for the disturbed make fewer provisions, as the Philosopher testifies. Tearing one’s garments is common in Scripture; it was done on account of excessive grief, indignation, or confusion, so that no further explanation is needed.

## CHAPTER XV. The Assyrians flee, the Jews pursuing them; the Jews gather the spoils and rejoice greatly, and Judith is blessed by the people and by Joachim, the high priest.

[Col. 0630C] “When the whole army heard that Holofernes had been beheaded, their courage and counsel departed from them,” etc. Once Holofernes’ beheading became known, his army was thrown into confusion and fled. They tried to outstrip one another so eagerly that they left behind all their equipment and all their treasures to be plundered by the enemy.

“When the Israelites saw them fleeing, they pursued them, descending while blowing trumpets and shouting after them,” etc. Once the Jews learned of the Assyrians’ flight, they pursued them with great haste to increase their terror, blowing trumpets as a sign of victory, just as Gideon once did when he fought against the Midianites in Judges 7 and, armed with trumpets and lamps, overcame them in their terror.

“And Ozias sent messengers throughout all the cities and regions of Israel,” etc. Not content with his own forces, Ozias sent messengers to every border of Israel, so that as few as possible of the enemy might escape in flight, and he urged them to pursue them. At his summons everyone, fully prepared, pursued them even to the remotest boundaries. The Greek paraphrase expands the account as follows:

“And Ozias sent [messengers] to Beromasthen, Bebe, Chobe, and Cota, and to every border of Israel, to announce what had happened and that all should spread out against the enemies for their destruction. When the Israelites heard this, they fell upon them with one accord as far as Chobe. Likewise those who had come from Jerusalem, from all the hill country, and from Gilead and Galilee, scattered them with a great slaughter until they had passed Damascus and its borders.”

“But those who remained in Bethulia entered the camp of the Assyrians,” etc. Those who had remained in Bethulia entered the enemy camp and were filled with their spoils and booty. So great was the treasure in the enemy camp, and so immense the quantity of ornaments of every kind, that there was enough even for all who inhabited Bethulia. Those who had pursued the enemy to the farthest borders also, when they returned, found more than enough, so that each of them reached his own country laden with booty. This is what follows:

“But those who returned victorious to Bethulia took with them everything that had belonged to them,” etc. That is, the booty which these returning men subsequently found could in no way be compared with what had already been taken; it was far greater, so that everyone grew rich from their plunder.

“Joachim the high priest came from Jerusalem to Bethulia with all his priests,” etc. That Joachim and Eliachim are the same name has been sufficiently demonstrated above, both in chapter IV and more fully in the preface. It should be noted here what honor Judith received: both the high priest and all the priests came to Bethulia merely to see her.

“When she had gone out to battle, they all blessed her,” etc. At first sight the text appears to say that, when the priest arrived there, he did not find her present, since she had gone to battle. My interpretation will therefore be more satisfactory if the reading is: “Because she had gone out to battle,” etc. Thus the reason for the blessing with which they blessed her is explained. The blessing itself is sufficiently clear; meanwhile, it should be noted that her chastity is credited with the fact that she was heard by God. Hence this passage should be noted as a commendation of chastity.

“Moreover, they gave Judith everything that had been proven to belong to Holofernes,” etc. After the priest and the whole people had blessed her by acclaiming “Amen,” or “So be it, so be it,” a spiritual blessing was followed by a temporal one, as Judith was given everything that had belonged to Holofernes. That there is also a certain temporal blessing is evident from Genesis 30, where Jacob says to Laban: “You have become rich, and the Lord has blessed you at my coming.”

“And all the people rejoiced with the women, virgins, and young men, with organs and lyres.” The word “organ” is common in Scripture. Hence Psalm 150: “Praise him with strings and the organ,” and Job 21: “The timbrel and lyre resound, and they rejoice at the sound of the organ,” along with many similar passages. At that time, “organs” primarily means, by extension, every kind of musical instrument, according to Augustine in his commentaries on Psalms 56 and 120. What the particular instrument was, however, is well known. It is clear from Jerome’s letter to Dardanus on the various kinds of musical instruments that it was somewhat different and more sonorous. Speaking of the organ, Jerome says that a hollow structure is joined from two elephant hides and is forced by the blowing of twelve bellows operated by smiths; through a kind of bronze lyre it produces an exceedingly loud sound, which it drives forth like thunder, so that it can certainly be heard perceptibly over a distance of a thousand paces and even farther. [Col. 0631D] Jerome says that this is confirmed among the Hebrews by the organs whose sound is heard from Jerusalem to Mount Olivet and beyond.

Most people say that there were meanwhile two kinds of organs: the first is the one just described; the other is the one mentioned in connection with the Israelites’ captivity among the Babylonians: “By the rivers of Babylon,” etc.

The lyre is also mentioned very frequently in Scripture, as in the passages already cited and again in Psalm 42: “I will praise you upon the lyre, O God, my God,” and many other places. Jerome writes in the preceding chapter that its use was customary among the Hebrews. It is the same instrument that is called a lyre; hence, where the Septuagint reads in Psalm 150, “Praise him on the psaltery and lyre,” Chrysostom notes that some translated it “with the *nablum* and lyre.” Jerome writes that it is shaped like the capital Greek letter delta and composed of twenty-four strings, which are made to sound through the fingers with various tones, ringing strikes, and different modes.

It resembles the psaltery, except that, as Jerome testifies in the same place, the psaltery is made only in the form of a shield with strings, according to Psalm 32: “I will sing to you on a ten-stringed psaltery.” Hence in the passages cited, and again frequently in Psalm 56, psalteries are mentioned; there too it says: “Awake, psaltery and lyre.” Jerome, Augustine, and Chrysostom also say that there is this difference between them—and therefore comment on Psalms 149 and 150, as well as Augustine on Psalms 32 and 36—that the lyre is struck from above, while the psaltery is struck upward; the lyre has its hollow part below, whereas the psaltery has it above. The hollow wooden part hangs down and resonates when touched, because the psaltery contains the air in its upper part, while the lyre has it in its lower part.

## CHAPTER XVI. Judith sings a song for the victory, urging the people to give thanks, and finally dies full of days.

“Then Judith sang this song to the Lord, saying: ‘Begin for the Lord with tambourines; sing to the Lord with cymbals; play for him a new psalm,’” etc. Rejoicing at the enemy’s overthrow and the faithful people’s deliverance, Judith, inspired by the divine Spirit, sings this song. From the beginning, it was customary among the faithful that, once victory had been won, they should immediately compose some song in which the event’s perpetual memory might be preserved. Such, above all, is Moses’ song: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc. (Exodus 15), which Miriam, Moses’ sister, is likewise said to have sung with a tambourine in her hand, in almost the same manner as Judith, to stir the other women to praise God. Tambourines and cymbals are instruments frequently used in Scripture. Tambourines are familiar to everyone: made of stretched and extended hide, flat on one side and hollow inside, they are struck with a stick and are generally carried in women’s hands, as Jerome testifies in the passage cited above. Cymbals too are well known. They were formerly much used in the sacred rites of Cybele, the mother of the gods; they are struck against one another with a small rod so as to produce a definite sound.

[Col. 0632B]

“‘The Lord will shatter wars,’” etc. Namely, those stirred up against his people, as became clear not only in the history under discussion, but also in the case of Pharaoh (Exodus 13), Amalek (Exodus 17), and the kings of Canaan (Joshua 10). Likewise in the case of Sennacherib and the eighty-five thousand who were killed in a single night in the time of Hezekiah—and very frequently elsewhere.

“‘He stationed a camp in the midst of his people, to rescue us from the hand of all our enemies.’” Hugh of Saint Victor interprets this passage as referring to the angels’ protection, on the basis of Genesis 32, where Jacob said of the angels who met him, “These are the camps of God.” Certainly, according to our text, I do not see what other sense can suitably be given to it. The Greek text points in a quite different and clearer direction, reading as follows:

“‘For in the camp in the midst of the people he rescued me from the hand of my pursuers.’” Here she first praises God for her own deliverance, and then proceeds to narrate the people’s deliverance, when it says:

[Col. 0632C]

“‘Assur came from the mountains of the north in the multitude of his strength,’” etc. She calls Holofernes the commander of the army and the Assyrian forces “Assur,” taking the name from that first Assur of Noah’s lineage who, according to Genesis 10, is said to have gone out from the land of Canaan and built Nineveh; from him the Assyrians were named. “‘He said that he would burn my borders,’” etc. After enumerating the power and size of his army, she now briefly pursues his threats. Although he threatened the Jews, none of these things achieved their intended effect; hence she also adds the adversative conjunction.

“‘But the almighty Lord warned him,’” etc. As in countless other passages, it is clear here too that the interpreter was not very concerned with grammatical rules—unless perhaps we should say that there is a textual error. He attributes nothing to himself, but the whole victory to the Lord, and does so in whatever manner he can. For, as Augustine says in the passage cited above, mortal eloquence is not sufficient to recount the distinguished prayers, triumphs, and noble virtues of all the righteous, which almighty God gave to those to whom he is accustomed to grant victory; he permitted men and women to flourish and cleansed the treacherous armies by striking off their heads. She recounts the whole history as briefly as she can, just as it happened; since it is clear from what precedes, we shall touch on it very briefly.

[Col. 0632D]

“‘The Persians were terrified by his steadfastness, and the Medes by his boldness,’” etc. This passage must also be noted against Ziegler. In his time, that Nebuchadnezzar who flourished in the time of Josiah did not have the Persians subject to him. Indeed, shortly afterward his sons were stripped of their power by Cyrus the Persian. Our Darius Hystaspes, however, ruled over the Persians, Medes, and Assyrians alike, and under him the Persian monarchy was already flourishing.

“‘Adonai, Lord, you are great, O God,’” etc. Here one may also see what Jerome says concerning the psalm’s words, “Lord our God”: when it is read in Hebrew, the name “God” is doubled, the first being the tetragrammaton and the second the common word for God. This may be demonstrated as follows: “Adonai, Lord”—for Jerome translated *Adonai* in Exodus 6 as the name of the tetragrammaton, that is, of the four letters, although elsewhere he generally interprets it as “Lord.” Thus, in his letter to Marcella, when listing this among the mystical names of the Lord, he translates it as “Lord.”

[Col. 0633A]

It should be noted that the four letters of this name—namely *he, vau, he, iod*—are not joined together so as to form an ordinary word from them; therefore the name is ineffable. Indeed, it appears to be called ineffable by the Hebrews because the mystery of the Trinity had not then been revealed to them, although it had been foreshadowed by the letters. Hence Exodus 6 says: “And I did not make my name, *he, vau, he, iod*, known to them.” If it were assembled into syllables and pronounced, it would signify being or essence, or generation.

Nor should it be overlooked that *iod, nun, daleth, aleph*—*Adonai*, “my Lords”—signifies a plural number when written with the same letters and vowel-points by which it is pronounced. In the Chaldean translation, however, the name of the tetragrammaton is always represented by three *iod*s, apparently to signify the mystery of the Trinity.

[Col. 0633B]

“‘The mountains will remain with the waters from their foundations,’” etc. This seems to allude to the final judgment, at whose approach, as Luke 21 says, “there will be distress among nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves,” and “the mountains and rocks will melt like wax in the fire of conflagration.”

“‘But those who fear you will be great in all things.’” The Greek Paraphrast reads this passage more fully in the following manner: “You will then be reconciled to those who fear you, because every sacrifice is small before you for a sweet-smelling aroma, and every little piece of fat is insufficient for your burnt offering; but whoever fears the Lord is always great.” Thus this is identical in meaning with the psalm: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,” and with what Samuel said to Saul: “Obedience is better than sacrifices,” etc.

“‘Woe to the nation that rises up against my people,’” etc. Now, as though moved by a prophetic spirit, she threatens all who persecute the faithful with the final judgment and eternal condemnation. Hence she adds:

“‘For he will give fire and worms to their flesh,’” etc. Scripture almost everywhere designates the punishments of hell in this way, and marks them by these names, as in the final chapter of Isaiah: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished.” This is what is added here: “So that they may be tormented and suffer forever.” How can this happen—that the bodies of the condemned should burn forever and yet never be consumed? Augustine treats this question in *The City of God*, book 21, chapters 1–3:

“This will then be in the bodies of the condemned which we now know to be in human souls: namely, that the soul can suffer pain but cannot die.”

[Col. 0633C]

As to whether that fire is bodily, he says in the same work, chapter 10:

“Why should we not say that, although in wondrous ways, nevertheless by true means even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire, since the spirits of human beings themselves are certainly incorporeal, and even now could be enclosed in bodily limbs, and then could be indissolubly bound by the bonds of their bodies?”

That Gehenna, therefore, which elsewhere is called a lake of fire or of sulfur, will be bodily fire and will torment the bodies of the condemned. But if someone asks where that fire is, and what sort of fire it is, Augustine replies in the same place, chapter 16:

“What the eternal fire will be like, and in what part of the world or of reality it will exist, I think no human being knows, unless perhaps the divine Spirit has shown it to someone.”

[Col. 0633D]

Once the song of Judith just mentioned has ended, the author returns in Book One to the continuation of the history.

“‘And it came to pass afterward that all the people, after the victory, came to Jerusalem to worship the Lord,’” etc. All the people went to Jerusalem to give thanks. When they arrived there, they purified themselves with the water of purification according to the rite described in Numbers 19. They offered holocausts and incense to the Lord, each according to his means.

“‘Moreover, Judith offered as a ban of oblivion all the war vessels of Holofernes that the people had given her, and the canopy that she had taken from his bed.’” Here Judith’s reverence toward God must be noted. She did not dare keep for herself the spoils rightfully given to her, but offered them to God and the priests in Jerusalem as a ban of oblivion—that is, on the condition that no one should ever use them, but that they should be preserved solely as a perpetual memorial of so great and wondrous a victory accomplished through a woman.

[Col. 0634A]

“‘The people were joyful according to the appearance of the saints,’” etc. This is added so that no one might think the people had become dissipated through excessive joy, but rather that they rejoiced devoutly and in the Lord, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Rejoice in the Lord always.” The phrase “according to the appearance of the saints” means the same as if he had said, “as befits the saints.”

“‘And Judith was more renowned than all the land of Israel.’” This appears to be an ellipsis, and one should supply “than all the women of the land,” or something similar.

“‘And chastity was joined to her virtue,’” etc. He now shows how, throughout the remainder of her life, she lived no less a holy and chaste life than she had previously lived from the beginning of her widowhood, and how her mind, exalted by victory, did not fall into the devil’s snares. Meanwhile, on feast days she enjoyed great honor—not from pride or empty glory, but as a perpetual remembrance of so great a benefit.

“‘She remained in her husband’s house for one hundred and five years,’” etc. In my judgment, this passage plainly confirms our position against Ziegler’s: how could Judith have remained in her husband’s house for one hundred and five years when, no more than forty-two years after the time of Josiah, the Temple had been destroyed and the whole people, both Judah and Israel, had been led captive to Babylon?

[Col. 0634B]

“‘And she died and was buried with her husband in Bethulia, and all the people mourned for her seven days.’” Scripture contains various passages in which the living mourned those who had died. Thus, in Genesis 23, Abraham mourned and wept for his wife Sarah. In Genesis 35, because of the mourning Israel made with his sons at the death of Rebekah’s nurse Deborah, that place was called “the oak of weeping.” Likewise, when Jacob died, Joseph and all the elders of Pharaoh’s household mourned with him; they came to the threshing floor of Atad, situated beyond the Jordan, where, as they conducted the funeral rites with great and intense lamentation, they filled seven days. Therefore the name of that place was called “the mourning of Egypt.” Genesis 50 also says at the beginning of the same chapter: “And Egypt mourned for him seven days.”

Similarly, Numbers 20 says: “When the whole congregation saw that Aaron had died, they wept for him thirty days, throughout all their families.” Likewise, Deuteronomy 34 says: “When Moses died, the Israelites wept for him in the plains of Moab thirty days.”

[Col. 0634C]

Thus, when Ambrose discusses the death of a brother in the first chapter of his work on whether the dead should be mourned, he says:

“Not every weeping is a matter of unbelief or weakness. One thing is the grief of nature, another the sadness of distrust; and there is a great difference between longing for what one has had and mourning what one has lost. The patriarchs also made great lamentation for their dead when they were buried. Tears, therefore, are signs of goodness, not of unlawful grief.”

Hence Chrysostom too says in his sixth homily on John:

“I do not forbid mourning, but mourning foolishly. I am not inhuman or cruel. I see that nature grieves and seeks its daily companionship. It is not permissible to be moved by no feeling or to shed no tears, but one must mourn gently and wisely, and with the fear of God.”

Many further remarks of this kind may also be found in the same author at the end of his thirty-second homily on Matthew.

[Col. 0634D]

Meanwhile, it must be noted here that Judith is said to have been buried in Bethulia, contrary to Ziegler’s repeatedly stated position. Regarding what we have just said about the destruction of Jerusalem and the period immediately following the time of Josiah, he seeks an escape by saying that she remained with her fellow tribesmen, just as many other remnants of the ten tribes remained. But again there is an obstacle: when Jerusalem was captured, Nebuchadnezzar transferred the entire people into captivity, except for a very few over whom Gedaliah, son of Ahikam, had been appointed governor. Not long afterward, fearing the Galileans, they migrated to Egypt.

Moreover, even if we suppose that some remnants of the ten tribes were spared, it does not in any way follow that Bethulia was spared, since the army of that same Nebuchadnezzar had suffered so great a disaster on its account. Yet here Judith is said to have been buried in Bethulia. Perhaps some escape from these difficulties could be devised, but what follows plainly proves his position false:

[Col. 0635A]

“‘Throughout the whole span of her life there was no one who disturbed Israel, nor for many years after her death.’” For how could Israel not be considered disturbed when it was transferred to Babylon amid such great affliction? This plainly occurred no more than forty-two years after the time of Josiah.

If, however, we follow our position concerning Darius Hystaspes, we do not find Israel disturbed until the time of the Maccabees under Antiochus. For although, according to Philo himself, our Artaxerxes, or Nebuchadnezzar, forbade the Temple to be completed after Holofernes’ death, this lasted only a few years—namely, only until the reign of Darius Longimanus. Therefore it could not properly be called a disturbance.

“‘The days of this victory are received by the Hebrews into the number of holy days,’” etc. This shows the great gratitude of the people of Israel for the marvelous victory granted by God; therefore they established an annual commemoration of it. Likewise, in Esther 9, it was instituted that the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar should be observed as feast days.

[Col. 0635]

*(A.D. 836.) Exposition of the Book of Esther by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz*

## Preface to Judith Augusta

[Col. 0635C]

The book of Esther, which the Hebrews number among the Hagiographa, contains in many ways, in mystery, the sacraments of Christ and the Church. For Esther herself, as a type of the Church, delivers the people from danger; and after Haman, whose name is interpreted as “iniquity,” has been killed, she sends a portion of the banquet and a celebrated day down to posterity.

The interpreter of sacred history asserts that he recovered this book from the archives of the Hebrews and translated it more exactly, word for word. Nevertheless, he did not entirely omit what he found in the Vulgate edition. Having rendered the material expressed in the Hebrew truth with complete fidelity, he added and appended at the end of the book the other things that he found externally.

[Col. 0635D]

We, however, have expounded allegorically what was brought forth from the Hebrew source. The remaining material, which was additionally added from the Greek language and writings and marked beforehand with an obelus, we have left unexplained. Yet the diligent reader, after carefully examining the earlier material, will be able to recognize its meaning sufficiently.

You, most noble queen, once you have properly understood the divine mysteries in the exposition, will rightly judge what ought to be thought concerning the rest. May almighty God, who raised up that queen’s mind to deliver the calamities of her people, deign to lead you, laboring with a similar zeal, to eternal joys.

[Col. 0636C]

## Chapter One. Concerning King Ahasuerus and His Famous Banquet

“‘In the days of Ahasuerus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, when he sat on the throne of his kingdom.’” The history of Esther is contained not only in the divine book but also in Josephus’ *Antiquities*, although they differ in certain details of historical narration.

The question is also raised: who was that Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces? The aforementioned Josephus reports that he was Cyrus, son of King Xerxes, who ruled in Persia after his uncle Darius.

He therefore says that this Cyrus was called Artaxerxes among the Greeks, surnamed Longimanus, and held the kingdom for forty years. But I do not think that Esther lived at that time. Ezra would never have been silent about her, since he writes that during this period Ezra and Menna returned from Babylon, together with the events that thereafter are reported as having been accomplished by them.

[Col. 0636D]

Eusebius, therefore, in his *Chronicle*, thought that this Ahasuerus was the one called Artaxerxes. He too reigned for forty years after his uncle Darius, surnamed Nothus.

“‘Susa was the beginning of his kingdom.’” Susa is the metropolis of Persia, which historians say was founded by Memnon’s brother. It was called Susa because it lies on the Susa River. There is the palace of Cyrus, built of white and variegated stone, with golden columns, coffered ceilings, and jeweled ornamentation. It also contains an image of the heavens marked with shining stars, along with other things unbelievable to human minds.

It is also reported that the present king held there an enormous banquet, with great magnificence and an abundance of riches, for the subject peoples. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0637B]

“‘Therefore, in the third year of his reign, he held a great banquet for his princes, the most powerful and renowned young men of the Persians and Medes, and the governors of the provinces in his presence, so that he might display the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the greatness and boastfulness of his power for a long time—namely, one hundred and eighty days.

“‘When the days of the banquet had been completed, he invited all the people found in Susa, from the greatest to the least. And for seven days he ordered a banquet to be prepared in the vestibule of the garden and grove, which had been planted and arranged with royal cultivation and workmanship.

“‘Tents of bronze-colored, linen-colored, and hyacinth-colored fabric hung on every side, supported by cords of fine linen and purple, which were inserted into ivory rings and upheld by marble columns. Golden and silver couches were also arranged upon a pavement laid with emerald and Parian stone, which was decorated with a painting of marvelous variety.

[Col. 0637C]

“‘Those who had been invited drank from golden cups, and food was served in various vessels, one after another. Wine too, abundant and choice, worthy of royal magnificence, was set before them. No one compelled those who were unwilling to drink, but, as the king had ordered, he appointed individual princes over the tables, so that each person might take whatever he wished.’”

Although this preparation for the most lavish banquet seems historically to display the pomp of riches and the luxury of a powerful king, in a more sacred mystery it signifies the greatness of the spiritual riches and the excellence of the resources of life that our most powerful King, namely the Lord Christ, generously distributes to each of his faithful according to the manner of his dispensation.

For that richest King, moved by the prayers of his most faithful wife, removed the impending destruction that the wicked were plotting against the Jews. This is appropriately applied in figure to our Redeemer, who, daily entreated by the prayers of the holy Church, his most beloved bride, delivers his elect from the hands of their enemies and subjects their enemies to deserved punishment.

[Col. 0637D]

That Esther represents the type of the Church is beyond doubt; nor can she in any way be called the bride of anyone other than Christ. Therefore no one should reject this interpretation because that historical king was faithless, as though for this reason he could in no way represent the type of a just king.

For we do not say that anyone’s faithlessness or sins—whether that person is faithful or even faithless—represent the actions of him “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2). “What fellowship is there between light and darkness? Or what agreement between Christ and Belial?” (2 Corinthians 7).

Rather, everyone’s good deeds and just judgments are more appropriately referred to him than to anyone else, since all goodness comes from him. Of him it is written: “He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in his truth” (Psalm 9).

[Col. 0638A]

For just as the errors and impious deeds of the Gentiles do not easily correspond by analogy to the truth, neither do the transgressions and sins of the faithful. We have said this because certain teachers transfer David’s deed against Uriah and his wife figurally to Christ and the Church.

What reason would there be for anyone to say that Moses’ doubt at the waters of contradiction, Aaron’s fabrication in the making of the calf, Solomon’s lust, Hezekiah’s arrogance, Peter’s denial, and Saul’s blasphemy figurally correspond to our Redeemer? Nevertheless, no one can rightly deny that their good deeds and sound teaching offered him abundant testimony.

Therefore no one should reproach us because we compare, by a certain analogy, the pious works and just judgments of a great king with the King and Judge of all ages. Whatever is good belongs to him, and all iniquity flees from him.

[Col. 0638B]

If what we say seems incongruous to anyone, let him read the prophet Isaiah, who compared Cyrus, king of the Persians, a Gentile, with our Redeemer. Speaking in the person of the Lord, he says:

“‘I will give you hidden treasures and secret things, so that you may know that I am the Lord, because I call you by your name, the God of Israel, for the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel. I have called you by your name; I have likened you, and you have not known me. I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no God. I girded you, and you did not know me’” (Isaiah 45).

Let him also read the short works of the Fathers, who said that the deeds or misfortunes of the reprobate kings Saul and Jeconiah figurally designated the most holy works of our Redeemer.

They interpreted Saul—anointed as king but killed on account of his crimes—in relation to the death of the innocent King Christ. They referred Jeconiah’s transfer from Judah to Babylon, which he suffered because of his sins, to the grace of that same Redeemer: he graciously migrated from the Jews, who had been abandoned because of their faithlessness, in order to save the nations throughout the world.

[Col. 0638C]

Those who handed down the teaching that the words and deeds of Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar should be understood typologically of the enemies of the Church give the following example:

Pharaoh ordered the male infants of God’s people to be killed in the river but the females to be preserved, because the devil desires to extinguish the strong works in us and nourish those that are weak and unstable.

Likewise, Nebuchadnezzar ordered all the peoples subject to him, when they heard the sound of musical instruments and singers, to prostrate themselves and worship his statue. The devil too strives, through the sweetness of earthly pomp, to bend the human race away from uprightness of mind and to pervert the hearts of the deceived toward the pursuit of desire, which is “the service of idols.”

[Col. 0638D]

If, then, certain deeds or just punishments of the reprobate preceded in figure not only evil things but also good things, why could not the good deeds or words of good people, which are contained in the prophetic book, prefigure the good deeds of those who would come later?

For, as someone has said, the power of sacred speech sometimes recounts events that have already occurred in such a way as to express things yet to come; it approves the maker in such a way as to contradict him in mystery; and it condemns deeds in such a way as to urge that they be performed mystically.

Let us also examine the short works of Saint Augustine, who said that the seven men who died childless, each having had the same wife, concerning whom the Sadducees—denying the resurrection—tested the Lord, possessed a clear figure of an ecclesiastical mystery.

[Col. 0639A]

He also taught that the woman, her barrenness, and her death, as well as the deaths of those men, were figures of memorable realities, even though neither the Lord himself nor any of the evangelists narrated this history in his own person. Rather, the evangelists inserted into their writings what the impious had uttered against the Lord with their wicked mouths, because of the Lord’s most sacred response.

Therefore, when the faithful reader finds these and similar examples in the sayings of the holy Fathers, let him not blame us if, following their example, we insert certain things of this kind into our own works.

“‘Therefore, in the third year of his reign, King Ahasuerus held a great banquet for all his princes and his most powerful young men of the Persians and Medes, so that he might display the riches of the glory of his kingdom.’”

When our Redeemer—whom Ahasuerus represents both by name and by rank, for his name is interpreted as “my door” or “my court”—with the Father and the Holy Spirit disclosed to the human race the mystery of his eternal dominion in the third period of this world, namely, in his incarnation, he opened for us the way of life and provided his faithful with spiritual banquets in the greatest abundance.

[Col. 0639B]

The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. In this third period he prepared for all nations the most lavish nourishment of evangelical preaching and of his body and blood.

The Lord himself commended the excellence of this banquet to us spiritually and mystically in the parable of the Gospel, when he spoke of a king who made a wedding feast for his son and of a great supper prepared by a man.

“‘For seven days the great king ordered a banquet to be prepared in the vestibule of the garden and grove, which had been arranged with royal cultivation and workmanship.’”

Our Redeemer, throughout the whole period of this life, which proceeds according to the number seven, satisfies his elect in the present Church with the nourishment of the divine word and the food of virtues. In this Church each of the faithful prepares himself through right faith and good works for entry into paradise and the heavenly kingdom.

He does this so that they may become fully capable of the delights and joy of the heavenly kingdom, where fruit-bearing trees have been planted—that is, holy men, distinguished by good merits, who by the gift of God display the beauty of holy conduct and sound teaching.

[Col. 0639C]

There, “‘tents of bronze-colored, linen-colored, and hyacinth-colored fabric hang on every side,’” because there the spiritual adornment of zeal and the radiance of heavenly wisdom shine, together with the splendor of virtues, for the instruction of those who worthily dwell there.

The linen-like color also, as some maintain, presents the appearance of gold and is rightly compared with the brightness of divine wisdom, which excels above all in the adornment and practice of piety.

“‘These tents were stretched out with cords of fine linen and purple and were supported by marble columns.’” Fine linen signifies the mortification of the flesh; purple, the blood of martyrdom; ivory, bodily chastity; and marble columns, the steadfastness of holy teachers.

It is therefore rightly said that tents of various colors were hung by cords of fine linen and purple, through ivory rings, upon marble columns. For the beauty of the holy Church—whether it consists in the contemplation of wisdom or in the advancement of virtues through bodily self-restraint and chastity, together with the dignity of martyrdom in the teachers of the holy Gospel—ought to shine forth and reach the knowledge of many both through their words and through their example.

[Col. 0639D]

Thus instructed, stirred, and strengthened by these things, many may rightly reach the court of the heavenly kingdom.

There too “‘golden and silver couches were arranged upon a pavement laid with emerald and Parian stone, which was decorated with a painting of marvelous variety,’” because the humility of the saints, adorned with various forms of diverse virtues, prepares for God’s elect the rest of inward contemplation in meditation upon the divine word and the investigation of true wisdom.

There the sweetness of the knowledge and love of God is poured out most generously by the gift of the Holy Spirit upon those who devoutly seek it.

Concerning this couch, the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Our couch is flowering” (Song of Songs 1). For whenever the saints enjoy tranquil times and are free from periods of tribulation, they devote themselves above all to sacred reading, fasts, prayers, and the other fruits of the Spirit. Then they raise themselves more deeply into contemplation of heavenly things, in order to behold the glory of the divine majesty, whenever they receive a time free from external occupations.

[Col. 0640A]

Emerald is a gemstone so called because of its intense greenness; Parian stone is a kind of extremely white marble. It is appropriately said that the pavement on which the couches were placed was decorated with these two stones, because the foundation of humility is well constructed through whiteness—that is, bodily chastity—and through the verdure of a good mind, which continually flourishes in the grace of God. Upon this foundation the reward of eternal rest is prepared for those who are worthy.

Hence it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). And: “Whoever humbles himself well will rightly be exalted” (Matthew 23).

For this reason the same Truth says elsewhere in the Gospel to the disciples: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

“‘Those who had been invited to the royal banquet drank from golden cups.’” Those drink from golden cups who draw divine wisdom from the precious sayings of the holy Gospel.

[Col. 0640B]

Food is served to them in various vessels when, in their reading of the Law, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Evangelists, they know how to receive the manifold dishes of spiritual teaching. These nourish souls that are being fed for eternal life.

Wine, too, abundant and choice, worthy of royal magnificence, is set before the banqueters when the gift of heavenly grace is most generously bestowed upon each of the faithful according to the dispensation of divine mercy and the distribution of the Holy Spirit.

Then, in accordance with Paul’s statement, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5), and:

“‘To one is given through the Spirit a message of wisdom; to another a message of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of speech’” (1 Corinthians 12).

[Col. 0640C]

The final statement—that no one compelled those who were unwilling to drink, but that, as the king had ordered, he appointed individual princes over the tables so that each person might take whatever he wished—signifies the freedom of grace. No one is compelled unwillingly to receive a spiritual gift; rather, the willing disposition of each person is sought, according to the Lord’s testimony: “Let whoever is able to receive it receive it” (Matthew 19).

And again: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (ibid.). And again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (ibid.).

For our King places his teachers at the table of sacred Scripture in the celebrated and holy banquet of the Church, so that they may distribute to each of the faithful an appropriate doctrine and adapt the quality of each person to the preaching of the word. Thus each person may take what he perceives to be possible and useful for himself.

[Col. 0640D]

The teacher’s voice must be regulated with such great skill that, although the vices of the hearers are different and a suitable remedy must be found for each, the voice itself is not inconsistent with itself.

It must pass between the passions in a single course, yet, like a two-edged sword, cut into the swellings of carnal thoughts from opposite directions. Thus humility must be preached to the proud without increasing fear in the timid; authority must be infused into the timid without increasing the lack of restraint of the proud.

Diligence in good works must be preached to the idle and sluggish without increasing the immoderate freedom of action among the restless; restraint must be imposed upon the restless without making secure sluggishness in the idle.

Anger must be extinguished in the impatient without increasing negligence in the gentle; the light-minded must be kindled to zeal without adding fuel to the fire of the irritable.

Generosity in giving must be infused into the grasping without preaching stinginess to the prodigal, and without increasing in the grasping the hoarding of possessions destined to perish.

[Col. 0641A]

Marriage must be praised to the incontinent without calling the continent back to luxury; bodily virginity must be praised to the continent without making the fruitfulness of the flesh contemptible among the married.

Good things must be preached in such a way that evils are not commanded incidentally along with them; supreme goods must be praised without despising lesser ones; lesser goods must be nourished so that, while they are believed sufficient, one does not fail to strive toward the highest.

Therefore the faithful and prudent servant, appointed by his master as steward, who gives his fellow servants their measure of grain at the proper time, is praised by the Lord’s voice and promised that he will be set over all his master’s goods.

[Col. 0641B]

Hence the one who serves the cups of the word must necessarily hold to the norm of discernment, so that from his ministry he may receive praise and reward rather than loss and punishment.

## Chapter Two. Concerning Queen Vashti, Who Refused to Come When Called by the King and Was Therefore Removed from Royal Dignity and Rejected by Her Husband

[Col. 0642B]

“‘Queen Vashti also held a banquet for the women in the palace where King Ahasuerus was accustomed to stay.’” What is expressed by Queen Vashti except the Jewish people, who seemed to reign like a queen when they were found to excel the other nations in the worship of the one God?

She therefore held a banquet for the women where the king was accustomed to stay—that is, in Jerusalem itself, where the Temple and the Holy of Holies had been. There she displayed observance of the Law in worship, or she did so in meditation upon the sacred Scriptures, in which, by granting knowledge of his divine power, he provides the nourishment of spiritual understanding to the souls of his people.

«And so, on the seventh day, when the king was in a more cheerful mood and [Col. 0642C] had grown heated from the excessive drinking of wine, he commanded Maumam, Bazatha, Harbona, Bagatha, Abgatha, Zethar, and Charchas—the seven eunuchs who ministered in his presence—to bring Queen Vashti before the king, with her diadem placed upon her head, so that he might display her beauty to all the peoples and nobles; for she was exceedingly beautiful. But she refused, and scorned coming at the king’s command.»

The seventh day of the banquet signifies the beauty of the times, in which the Lord, having become incarnate, manifested with more abundant grace all the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets, by which devout minds among religious people had until then been nourished. Concerning this fullness Paul, writing to the Galatians, says: «But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Gal. IV).»

And it is rightly said that he had grown heated from excessive drinking of wine, because through the coming of the Paraclete he poured abundant grace, the gift of the Holy Spirit, into his disciples. Concerning this wine we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when the Holy Spirit came upon the one hundred and twenty believers in the upper room of Zion, and the Jews supposed that they were filled with new wine, Peter answered, saying: «Men and brothers, these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: “And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your young men shall see visions, and your elders shall dream dreams. Indeed, upon my servants and my maidservants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy; and I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on the earth below” (Acts II).»

Tasting the sweetness of this wine at the mystical wedding of the Gospel, the master of the feast says to the bridegroom: «Every man first sets out the good wine, and when they have become drunk, then what is inferior. But you have kept the good wine until now.»

Therefore the king, in his gladness, commanded the seven eunuchs who ministered in his presence to bring Queen Vashti before the [Col. 0643B] king, with her diadem placed upon her head, so that he might display her beauty to all the peoples. This signifies that our Redeemer Christ, that is, the Lord, sent the order of the holy preachers, filled with the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, to summon the Jewish people to the spiritual banquet, so that the beauty and nobility it possessed by the prerogative of the Fathers and through knowledge of the Law and the Prophets, as well as through the worship of piety that it had before the Lord’s coming, might become renowned among the nations of the whole world. But she not only despised the messengers; she also scorned the supreme king’s command and refused to come.

The Lord himself made this known in the evangelical parables, when he declared that the merciful father, upon receiving the penitent prodigal son, had slaughtered a calf and prepared a banquet, while the elder son, although earnestly invited by his father, nevertheless scorned entering. Elsewhere, those who had been detained by ambition for other things are described as unwilling to come to the wedding that the king prepared for his son, and likewise to the great supper that a certain man prepared and to which he invited many. For this reason they are said to have been rejected in the just indignation of the supreme head of the household, while others were substituted in their place.

That elder son, therefore, and the ancient people of the Synagogue, represented in the person of Queen Vashti, refused to leave their dwelling—that is, to be detached from the letter of the Law. Content to live according to their own will, they labored amid earthly desires and became exiles, far from the homeland of the Holy Spirit and from the Father’s counsel, always [Col. 0643D] rigid and hard, filled with resentment and indignation. He is the one who says: «I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it; I ask you to consider me excused (Luke XIV).»

He is the one who buys five yokes of oxen and, weighed down by the burden of the Law, enjoys the pleasure of earthly senses. He is the one who, having taken a wife, cannot come to the wedding, and who, having become flesh, is utterly unable to be one with the spirit. In his person, too, the laborers of that parable find their counterpart: at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours—that is, through various callings—they are sent into the vineyard, and they are indignant that the laborers of the eleventh hour are made equal to them.

But let us hear what Scripture relates happened because of the obstinacy of the most foolish Queen Vashti:

[Col. 0644A] «Therefore the king, angry and inflamed with excessive fury, questioned the wise men who, according to royal custom, were always near him, and he did everything by their counsel, for they knew the laws and the rights of their ancestors. The first and nearest were Charsena, Sethar, Admatha, Tharsis, Mares, Marsana, and Mamuchan, the seven princes of the Persians and Medes, who saw his face and were accustomed to sit first after him. He asked what sentence should be imposed upon Queen Vashti, who had refused to carry out the command of King Ahasuerus, which he had delivered through the eunuchs.

«Mamuchan answered in the hearing of the king and the princes: “Vashti has wronged not only the king, but also all the princes and peoples who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For the word will go out to all women, so that they will despise their husbands and say: ‘King Ahasuerus commanded that Queen Vashti enter before him, and she refused.’ By this example all the wives of the princes of the Persians and Medes will regard their husbands’ commands as worthless; therefore the king’s indignation is justified. If it pleases you, let an edict go forth from your presence and be written according to the law of the Persians and Medes, which may not be violated: Vashti shall never again enter before King Ahasuerus, and her royal position shall be given to another who is better than she.”»

What does it mean that, when Vashti grew proud, King Ahasuerus sought the counsel of the seven wise men who, according to royal custom, were always beside him, and commanded that judgment be pronounced against her, except that our Savior, through his teachers filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit—who always strive to assist his presence with right faith and good works—pronounces sentence upon the insolence of the Jewish people, which is guilty of punishment and condemnation? It means that she should be expelled from the royal bed, that is, from fellowship with God, for which she had been appointed and chosen, and that her place should be received by another who is better than she: namely, the Church of the nations, with sincere faith and complete devotion.

That the Lord, promised through the Law and the Prophet for the summoning of the Jewish people and sent according to the counsel of the supreme Father, he himself shows in the Gospel, saying: «I was sent only to the sheep that had perished, of the house of Israel (Matt. XV).» And again: «It is not right, he says, to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs (ibid.).» But when the Gentile woman persisted in her petition, her great faith was deservedly praised by the Lord himself.

Elsewhere the faith of the centurion is preferred to the faith of the Jews, when he says: «Amen, I say to you, many will come from the east and the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of this kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. VIII).»

Again, elsewhere Truth itself says to Jerusalem: «Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you: how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling; behold, your house will be left to you desolate (Luke XIII).»

Concerning the calling of the nations, after his resurrection he commanded his disciples in this manner, saying: «Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age (Matt. XXVIII).»

Appropriately, too, Mamuchan, who is counted last in the order of the seven wise men, promulgated the sentence concerning Vashti; by him the person of the apostle Paul is represented, who was called to the apostolate last of all and through whom the Jews are rightly reproached for their unbelief. For he says of himself: «But I am the least of the apostles (1 Cor. XV).» And elsewhere: «To me, he says, the least of all the saints, this grace was given, that I should evangelize Christ among the nations (2 Cor. III).»

When he had preached the word of God in the synagogue of the Jews with Barnabas as his companion, and the Jews, filled with jealousy, contradicted what Paul said and blasphemed, he firmly declared to them: «It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations. For thus the Lord has commanded us: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth.” And when the nations heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who were ordained to eternal life believed (Acts XIII).»

## CHAPTER III. How, at the command of King Ahasuerus, virgin girls were gathered from various provinces, among whom was Esther, daughter of the brother of Mardochai the Jew, whom her uncle carefully raised

«When these things had taken place, after the indignation of King Ahasuerus had subsided, he remembered Vashti and what she had done and what she had suffered. The king’s young men and servants said: “Let virgin girls be sought for the king, and let them be brought to the city of Susa and placed in the women’s house under the care of Hegai the eunuch, who is in charge of and guards the royal women; and let them receive women’s ornaments and whatever else is necessary for their use. Whichever among them pleases the king’s eyes, let her reign in place of Vashti.”»

Thus, after the Jewish people had been rejected from royal fellowship, various nations and various persons from each nation, from different regions of the world, were brought by the holy preachers, who were ministers of the evangelical word, into fellowship with royal dignity. They were placed under the care of Hegai, whose name is interpreted as “hasty” or “solemn,” the overseer of the royal women—that is, under the care of the pastors and rulers of the Church, to whom the guardianship of faithful souls has been entrusted—so that they might provide them, by word and example, with whatever was necessary for the worship of piety. Thus every soul that pleased the inner eyes of the heart through right faith and a pure conscience might be brought, clean and holy, into the chamber of the eternal King in place of the rejected, insolent, and defiant Vashti.

«There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa named Mardochai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the stock of Jemini, who had been taken away from Jerusalem at the time when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, took away Jeconiah, king of Judah. He was the guardian of the daughter of his brother Edissa, who was also called Esther, and she had lost both parents. She was exceedingly beautiful and fair of face. After her father and mother died, Mardochai adopted her as his daughter.

«When the king’s command became widely known, and many beautiful virgins were brought to Susa according to his order and delivered to the eunuch Hegai, Esther too was delivered to him among the other girls, to be kept among the women. She pleased him and found favor in his sight. And he commanded the eunuch to hasten her women’s ornaments, to give her her portions, and to provide her with seven very beautiful girls from the king’s household; and he adorned and beautified both her and her attendants.»

What is signified by Esther, whose name is interpreted as “hidden,” and who was also called Edissa, that is, “mercy,” except the Church of the nations? Hidden in the chastity of her faith, she pleases God and finds mercy and grace before God’s eyes more than the Synagogue of the Jews, which on account of its impiety is rightly called “without mercy” through the prophet Hosea.

This spiritual Mardochai adopted her as his daughter, because she had lost both parents. And what is signified by Mardochai except the teachers of the nations? Most especially, blessed Paul the apostle, who also testifies that he is of the Jeminite stock, that is, of the tribe of Benjamin. When, by God’s calling, he had been converted from persecutor into apostle, the Church of the nations was entrusted to him. After her father and mother had died—that is, after pagan error and superstition—he in a certain sense made her his own, when through the grace of baptism and the word of the Gospel he regenerated her as a daughter for eternal salvation to the almighty Father.

Thus he himself said to them: «Although you may have many teachers, you do not have many fathers. For I begot you in Christ through the Gospel (1 Cor. IV).»

Once this Church had been led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, she had been transferred through the devil from the natural Law and the worship of the one God into the confusion of idolatry. But divine piety did not abandon her at all; rather, through its preachers it recalled her to the way of truth. They, taking the greatest care of her, had brought her up in all piety, righteousness, and truth.

To her Hegai the eunuch—that is, the most chaste order of pastors—provided women’s ornaments, namely, sound doctrine and examples of good works, and gave her her portions: surely, knowledge of the Scriptures and uprightness of morals. He also appointed seven beautiful girls as her attendants, because he placed under her most salutary discipline many faithful persons regenerated by the grace of the sevenfold Spirit and following her through good works, so that, adorned with the splendor of faith’s progress and every virtue, she might be found wholly fit for the bed of the eternal King.

«She did not reveal her people or her homeland, for Mardochai had commanded her to remain entirely silent about this matter.»

The Church of the nations, instructed by the commands of the holy teachers, did not wish to disclose the place of her homeland and people, because, cleansed through baptism from every stain of sins and the defilements of idolatry, she no longer endures the reproach of her former impiety. Concerning her the Lord also commanded through the Prophet, saying: «Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house; for the king has desired your beauty, because he is the Lord your God (Ps. XLIV).»

Therefore Scripture proceeds, revealing through the type of Mardochai the diligence of the teachers:

«He walked daily before the entrance of the house in which the chosen virgins were kept, caring for Esther’s welfare and wishing to know what happened to her.»

For the holy teachers keep watch daily with vigilant care over evangelical doctrine, to examine the faith and conduct of the people entrusted to them: whether they follow with attentive mind the rule of right faith, through which eternal salvation is attained; whether they are diligent in the worship of God and in the practice of good works, through which the reward of the heavenly kingdom is earned in the life to come. No hour of this concern can be empty for those in whose hearts the ardor of right faith and the fire of divine love burn without ceasing.

Thus the teacher of the nations, glorifying in truthful words the labors and persecutions he suffered for Christ, added: «Besides those things that are external, there is my daily burden, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire? (2 Cor. XI).»

And to the Romans: «God is my witness, he says, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I always remember you in my prayers (Rom. I).»

## CHAPTER IV. How Esther was brought to the king according to the order of her turn, was loved by him above all the women, and was made queen

«When the time came for the individual girls, in their order, to enter before the king, after everything pertaining to women’s adornment had been completed, the twelfth month was passing. They were to be anointed for six months with myrrh oil, and for the other six months to use certain perfumes and aromatics.»

What does it mean that the girls who were to be brought into the king’s chamber were prepared for twelve months with oil and aromatics, so that for six months they were anointed with myrrh oil, which is known to have a good fragrance, and for the other six months used various perfumes and aromatics, except that all souls invited to receive holy baptism and to enter the chamber of the true Bridegroom, namely Christ the King, are perfectly imbued with myrrh oil—that is, the light of faith and the richness of love—together with the aromatics of the virtues, so that they may deserve to become worthy of his fellowship?

For what else do the holy preachers do when they instruct their catechumens in the truth of faith, except teach them also to adorn that same faith with good works, so that through fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and the other [Col. 0648A] works of virtue they may hasten to wash away the former filth of the old person and put on the beauty of the new? Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the centurion Cornelius first pleased God through prayers and almsgiving, and then, when Peter arrived, received the cleansing of baptism and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore it follows:

«As they entered before the king, whatever they requested that pertained to adornment was given to them; and, adorned as they wished, they passed from the women’s dining hall to the king’s chamber.»

For every soul that strives to hasten to the chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom receives from its teachers adornment appropriate to this purpose, according to how devoted it shows itself to the knowledge of faith and the understanding of the virtues. Thus, from the number of those being instructed, through complete faith in the Holy Trinity and full confession, it approaches the reception of the one baptism and the anointing of the sacred chrism, where it is truly joined to the heavenly Bridegroom.

But what follows—

«She who entered in the evening went out in the morning, and from there was led into the second house,» and the rest—

mystically shows that after the sunset of vices the radiance of virtues must arise, and that this radiance shines rightly nowhere except in the unity of the holy Church. Whoever separates himself from it through some ugliness of error or vice is rightly said to be led into the second house, where the king’s concubines remained, because a fall from sound faith earns not advancement but restoration of honor. Such a person will no longer have the power to return to our King unless, visited by heavenly grace, he is restored by his calling to his former state of dignity.

«When the time had passed, the day came in its order on which Esther, daughter of Abihail, brother of Mardochai, whom he had adopted as his daughter, was to enter before the king. She did not seek women’s adornment, but whatever Hegai the eunuch, guardian of the virgins, wished, he gave her for adornment. For she was exceedingly beautiful, and because of her extraordinary beauty she appeared pleasing and lovable in the eyes of all.»

“When the time had passed,” he says—that is, when the five ages of the world had elapsed, during which the succession of the Fathers had gone before and the legal institution flourished among the Jews—the sixth age was at hand. In it the Redeemer came, and the multitude of the nations was to be summoned through the Gospel.

Then, mystically, Esther—that is, the Church—was brought from the nations to Christ the King through apostolic preaching, by belief in sound faith and the sacrament of baptism. She appeared beautiful, and because of the extraordinary beauty of her virtues she was pleasing and lovable in the eyes of all.

The apostle Paul recalls this time when he writes to the Galatians, saying: «After the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might recover the adoption of sons (Gal. IV).»

And to the Ephesians: «God, he says, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—for by grace you have been saved—and raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the abundant riches of his grace in goodness toward us in Christ Jesus (Eph. II).»

Therefore the precise moment when Esther was brought into the king’s chamber must also be considered:

«She was brought into the chamber of King Ahasuerus in the tenth month, which is called Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. And the king loved her more than all the women, and placed the royal diadem upon her head, and made her reign in place of Vashti.»

Tebeth, the month of the Hebrews, is the same month that among the Greeks is called Eudymos and among the Latins January. In this month the incarnate Lord was circumcised on the eighth day, and, already an infant, was worshiped by the Magi who had been led by the preceding star; he was honored with gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh as God, man, and king. In this month he was also preached and baptized by John.

In the seventh year of Ahasuerus, therefore, Esther entered the king’s chamber. So too the Church was brought to and joined with Christ the King, in whom the grace of the sevenfold Spirit remains unchangingly.

«The king loved her more than all the women,» and she found grace and mercy before him above all women—that is, above all the nations of the earth.

«He placed the royal diadem upon her head,» when he took her to himself as a partner in the kingdom; «and he made her reign in place of Vashti,» that is, in place of the Synagogue of the Jews, [Col. 0649C] which, by scorning and crucifying our King, lost the dignity of its honor.

Observing the excellence of this queen, the Prophet speaks to Christ the King, saying: «The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold, surrounded by variety (Ps. XLIV).»

And immediately, speaking to her, he adds: «Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house, for the king has desired your beauty. He himself is the Lord your God, and the daughters of Tyre will worship him; all the rich among the people will entreat your face with gifts (ibid.).»

«And he commanded a very magnificent banquet to be prepared for all his princes and servants for the union and marriage of Esther, and he granted rest to all the provinces and distributed gifts according to princely generosity.»

What does it mean that a very magnificent banquet was prepared for all the princes and servants for Esther’s marriage, except that for the spiritual union of Christ and the Church the greatest joy is celebrated throughout the whole world by all, great and small?

At this banquet, not bodily foods but the spiritual dishes of wisdom and the virtues are consumed by those who worthily participate. Here the faithful receive the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood as remedies for their salvation; in this the nourishment of eternal life is set before them.

Our King grants rest to all the provinces and distributes many gifts when he frees believers from the burden of sins and rewards them with spiritual gifts. [Col. 0650A] Therefore he himself says in the Gospel: «Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matt. XI).»

Concerning this the Prophet also says: «Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men (Eph. IV).»

To this the Apostle subsequently added, saying: «And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all reach the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (ibid.).»

[Col. 0650B] «When virgins were sought and gathered a second time, Mardochai remained at the king’s gate, and Esther had still not revealed her homeland and her people. According to Mardochai’s command, Esther observed everything he instructed; and she did everything just as she had been accustomed to do when she was being raised by him as a little girl.»

Virgins are sought and gathered for the king a second time because it is not enough for our Lord Jesus Christ to associate with himself the primitive Church from the Jews alone. Rather, through his preachers he acquires for himself a great multitude of the faithful from the nations, so that from both peoples there may be one catholic Church, namely his most noble bride, who has neither stain nor wrinkle.

Therefore he himself says in the Gospel: «I have other sheep that are not of this fold, and I must bring them also; they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd (John X).»

«Mardochai, he says, remained at the king’s gate,» because the holy teachers, remaining continually in evangelical doctrine, summon the nations to the entrance of faith and to the sacrament of baptism.

Nor has our Esther revealed her homeland and her people, according to the command of the typological Mardochai, because according to the teaching of faith the Church of the saints does nothing through arrogance, but in a pure conscience humbly observes everything commanded to her in the evangelical sayings. Concerning her it is said through the Prophet: «All the glory of the king’s daughter is within (Ps. XLIV).»

And the Apostle says: «Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience (2 Cor. I).»

## CHAPTER V. How the eunuchs who wished to kill the king were exposed by Mardochai and deservedly punished

«At that time, while Mardochai was staying at the king’s gate, Bagatha and Thares, two eunuchs of the king who were gatekeepers and presided at the first threshold of the palace, became angry and wished to rise up against the king and kill him. This did not escape Mardochai, and he immediately informed Queen Esther; and she told the king in the name of Mardochai, who had reported the matter to her.»

What is signified by these two eunuchs, who were gatekeepers of the royal house and presided at the first threshold of the palace, except the scribes and Pharisees of the Jews, concerning whom it was said that, possessing the key of knowledge, they neither entered themselves nor permitted others to enter?

They wished to rise up against the king and kill him because, always envying the Savior’s teaching and virtues, they plotted against him and, together with the servants of Roman authority, contrived how they might kill him.

Thus it is written in the Gospel that «the Pharisees went away and took counsel to trap him in his speech, and they sent their disciples to him with the Herodians, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you do not care about anyone, for you do not regard the person of men. Tell us, therefore, what do you think: is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. XXII).»

Elsewhere we read that «the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said: “What shall we do? For this man performs many signs. If we leave him alone, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI).»

A little later it adds: «From that day, therefore, they plotted to kill him (ibid.).»

The prophet Isaiah notes these two persons in the form of two houses, for whom the incarnate Savior became a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal, and a snare and a ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Many of them would stumble and fall, be shattered, entangled, and captured.
