For just as it would not be strange or absurd if God wished to forgive evil deeds previously committed by them because of later good deeds, so it is not strange that, at one time and in one matter, God—seeing both things—mercifully rewarded the deed that was good and, because of that good, forgave [Col. 0677B] the evil deed that had been done deceitfully.

“Do not court death through the error of your life, nor acquire destruction by the works of your hands. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living.” Above he enumerated the things harmful to human beings—namely, murmuring, detraction, and lying—from which he commanded them to guard themselves. Now he repeats the same instruction in other words, namely, that we should not do things subject to death, since our destruction is not pleasing to God, who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Through the prophet he says: “Why will you die, house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the dying, says the Lord [Col. 0677C] God” (Ezek. XVIII). “Turn back and live.” God is the author of salvation, not of our destruction; he saw everything that he had made, and it was very good. Yet, according to the Apostle, “the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. VI).

“For he created all things that they might exist; and he made the nations of the world curable; and there is no medicine of destruction in them, nor a kingdom of the underworld on earth.” By this statement, as also by the preceding one, it is made clear that the Lord is the author of good works, not of evil ones; therefore he is a just judge who punishes wicked acts and sins. We do not sin by necessity when we transgress, but by a perverse will arising from the quality of free choice. We know God to be the just and good creator of human substance and of its inner and outer senses [Col. 0677D], so that whatever belongs to nature is entirely from him, while whatever is contrary to nature is entirely not from him. Sin, however, is contrary to nature, and from it arise death and all that belongs to death. Human beings clothed themselves in these evils when the devil, finding humanity deprived of faith and obedience, led it away from God’s law into his own promises and, through the condition of the appointed stock, bound all the offspring of its posterity to himself. Concerning this it is further said:

“For justice is perpetual and immortal. But injustice is the acquisition of death. The ungodly summoned it by their hands and words; and, considering it a friend, they wasted away and made covenants with it, because [Col. 0678A] they are worthy of death who are of its party [reading uncertain: *ex parte illius*].” Justice is rightly said to be perpetual and immortal because it frees those who obey it from perpetual death. Injustice, however, is the acquisition of death, because the torments of hell are the certain recompense of sinners. The ungodly summoned injustice by their hands and words, because they follow it in speech and deed; deceived by error, they confidently suppose that they can sin with impunity and, consenting in no way to be separated from its companionship, do not strive to escape it, having already been condemned by God’s just judgment. Hence there is that saying of the Gospel: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God” (John III). And again: “Whoever believes,” he says, “in the Son of God has eternal life. But whoever is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon [Col. 0678B] him” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV. In which the ungodly, despairing of their salvation, assert that they will perish and live only in the present age

**(CHAPTER II.)** For the ungodly said, reasoning incorrectly among themselves: “Short and wearisome is the time of our life, and there is no refreshment at the end of a person, and no one is known to have returned from the underworld; for we were born from nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had not been, because smoke and breath are in our nostrils, and speech is a spark to stir our heart. For our body will be ashes extinguished, and our spirit will be dispersed like soft air; our life will pass like the trace of a cloud, and like a mist it will be dissolved, [Col. 0678C] which has been driven away by the rays of the sun and weighed down by its heat. Our name will be forgotten in time, and no one will remember our deeds. For our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return at the end of our life, because it has been sealed, and no one returns.

“Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use the creation as in youth, swiftly. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of time pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow that our luxury does not pass through. Let none of you be excluded from our luxury; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion and this our lot.”

This is the voice of the lost, who, like brute animals, look only at the present and do not think about the future, [Col. 0678D] nor have any hope of eternal rest after the end of this life. Of such people the Psalmist says: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII). The prophet Isaiah rebukes their voice, saying: “You have said: We have made a covenant with death, and with the underworld we have made an agreement. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope and have been protected by falsehood” (Isa. XXVIII). Therefore the Lord says this: “I will establish judgment as a weight and justice as a measure; and hail will overthrow the hope of falsehood and the protection of overwhelming waters, and your covenant with death will be erased, and your agreement with the underworld will [Col. 0679A] not stand. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will become its trampling; whenever it passes through, it will carry you away” (Isa. XXVIII). The prophet Amos uttered similar words, saying: “Woe to you who are wealthy, and who are set apart for the evil day, and who approach the seat of iniquity; who sleep on ivory beds and live wantonly on your couches; who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery, thinking that they have instruments of song like David; who drink wine from bowls and anoint themselves with the finest ointment, yet suffer nothing over the ruin of Joseph. Therefore they will now migrate at the head of those who migrate, and the company of the wanton will be taken away” (Amos VI). And again: “Because you plundered the poor and took choice prey from him, you will build houses of hewn stone [Col. 0679B], but you will not inhabit them; you will plant very lovely vineyards, but you will not drink their wine, because I know your many crimes and your mighty sins.” The pleasure-seekers and heretics continue and add the following to their earlier words.

## CHAPTER V. The counsel of the ungodly Jews against Christ, deliberating about his death and accusing him of reproaching them with the sins of the Law

“Let us oppress the poor righteous man and not spare the widow, nor respect the gray hairs of the aged. Let our strength be the law of justice, for what is weak is found to be useless.”

Although these words may generally apply to those who despise God and spare neither sex nor age, but wish to oppress everyone through injustice [Col. 0679C] and greed, they may nevertheless, in their deeper sense, be referred to the faithless persecutors of Christians and to heretics, who burden the poor people of the Church with their wickedness and persecutions. They think with the worst intention of crushing that widow of whom it is written: “Blessing I will bless his widow; I will satisfy his poor with bread”; and they strive to criticize the prophets and apostles, whom he here calls aged, in their statements. They endeavor not to keep the decrees of the divine Law, but to pursue the byways of their error; nor do they obey our Head himself, but presume to direct words of this kind of impiety against him.

“Let us surround the righteous man, because he is useless to us, opposes our works, reproaches [Col. 0679D] us with the sins of the Law, and denounces against us the sins of our discipline. He professes to have knowledge of God and calls himself a son of God. He has become a reproach to our thoughts. He is burdensome even to look upon, because his life is unlike that of others, and his ways are changed. We are regarded by him as triflers, and he keeps away from our ways as from defilements. He prefers the final destiny of the righteous and boasts that he has God as his father.”

The faithless Jews were then planning to surround the righteous man when, confronted by the Gospel’s words, they were admonished through Christ to abandon the former filth of their vices and follow the truth of God’s commandments. But, taking grave offense at the very one in whom they ought to have hoped for the cause of salvation, they planned to kill him as though he were a blasphemer [Col. 0680A]. Hence it is written in the Gospel: “The Jews picked up stones to stone him. Jesus answered them: I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me? The Jews answered: We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because, although you are a human being, you make yourself God,” and so forth (John X). Stirred by envy, they considered not what he himself was doing but what they themselves were unwilling to do, and so they became darkened amid the rays of light. Thus these words applied to them: “He is burdensome even to look upon, because his life is unlike that of others, and he keeps away from our ways as from defilements.” And because they did not think about the future life, they grieved that the final destiny of the righteous—that is, the hope [Col. 0680B] of future life—should be preferred to their own pleasure. Hence by wicked counsels they pursued his death, as the following words show.

“Let us see, therefore, whether his words are true, and let us test what will happen to him; we shall know what his end will be. For if he is truly the Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his enemies. Let us question him with insult and torment, so that we may know his gentleness and test his patience. Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for there will be regard for him because of his words.”

These things are fittingly described in the Gospel, where the chief priests and Pharisees took counsel about how they might hand Jesus over to death. When he had been placed on the cross, the chief priests, together with the scribes and elders, mocked him, saying: “He saved others; he [Col. 0680C] cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he wants him, for he said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (Luke XXIII). The phrase “a most shameful death” names the cross, since it was once the punishment of criminals even unto Christ’s passion, but is now the trophy of victory and the glory of believers. What it says—“there will be regard for him because of his words”—refers to his resurrection. The Jews, in their disbelief, wished to test whether he would be able to raise his flesh after death, because they remembered that he had said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II). And elsewhere: “Behold,” he says, “we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man will be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, [Col. 0680D] scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise” (Matt. XX). Hence during his passion they also said to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that this deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead’; and the final error will be worse than the first” (Matt. XXVII).

They thought these things, and they went astray. Their wickedness blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God; they neither hoped for the reward of justice nor judged the honor of holy souls. The envious and deceitful could not grasp the mystery of God’s counsel, [Col. 0681A] because “wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul” (Wis. I). Nor could they understand that Christ’s death is the honor and salvation of holy souls, since through it they hope for the reward of justice and receive entry into the heavenly kingdom.

“For God created the human being imperishable, and made him in the image of his likeness. But through the devil’s envy death entered the world; and those who belong to his party imitate him.”

By this statement the error of the Manichaeans is destroyed. They introduced two natures and substances, namely, a good one and an evil one; but our Creator is not the author of our ruin, and insofar as the truth of nature is concerned, we were created immortal by him. Through assent to the serpent’s suggestion, however, we were subjected to the sentence of death [Col. 0681B]. Nevertheless, the first robe of immortality—which the human race, created in God’s image from the beginning but deceived by the devil’s envy, lost in Adam—was received again through Christ’s death. Our death was destroyed in his death, and our life was restored in his resurrection. Yet this inheritance does not belong to those who choose to be imitators of the devil’s envy rather than of Christ’s humility and gentleness.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the holy martyrs: that their glory will be eternal through present tribulation

**(CHAPTER III.)** “But the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and the torment of death will not touch them.”

In the preceding chapter the sentence of the wicked was expressed, which they uttered with perverse understanding and wicked words against our Head [Col. 0681C]. Now their error is condemned: they thought that it would be realized in the destruction of his members when they slaughtered them with various punishments for confessing his name. The souls of the holy martyrs, therefore, are in God’s hand—that is, in his protection—and the torment of perpetual death can harm them in no way.

“They seemed, in the eyes of the foolish, to have died; and their departure was considered an affliction, and their going away from us an extermination, but they are in peace.”

They were truly foolish when they considered the martyrs’ crown to be affliction and destruction, since it became for them the cause of victory and perpetual rest. Hence it follows:

“Although in the sight of human beings they suffered torment, their [Col. 0681D] hope is full of immortality. Having been disciplined in a few things, they will be well established in many; for God tested them and found them worthy of himself. As gold in the furnace he proved them, and as a sacrificial offering he accepted them, and in due time there will be regard for them.”

Temporal death and the affliction of the present life produced for God’s saints the prosperity of perpetual recompense, because their unfailing hope and solid faith remained steadfast to the end. God disciplined them through various trials and, through the endurance of patience, proved them worthy of an eternal crown. The two examples he gives—gold tested in the furnace and holocausts consumed in fire—show their most thoroughly tested character and perfect purity [Col. 0682A]. For just as gold is not consumed by fire but is tested, so the holy substance of martyrdom is not brought to destruction but prepared for immortality and future glory. And just as a holocaust offered wholly through fire to God is a most acceptable sacrifice, so the passion of the martyrs, offered to the Lord through the heat of faith and the fervor of charity as a sweet fragrance, stands as a gift most pleasing and a most precious offering. Hence the Psalmist says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” What follows—“in due time there will be regard for them”—means that, contrary to the judgment of the reprobate, the death of the saints is not perpetual; rather, when Christ judges on the day of judgment, their recompense will be exceedingly abundant.

[Col. 0682B] “The righteous will shine, and like sparks they will run through the reeds.”

By introducing another example, he shows both the sudden recompense of the saints at the final judgment and the swift vengeance that will overtake the reprobate. When the elect are changed from corruption to incorruption, from mortality to immortality, and from dishonor to glory, then they will rise to judge their adversaries. And just as a spark of fire suddenly kindles a flame in reeds, so the sentence of righteous judgment will inflict upon the reprobate a powerful and swift vengeance of punishments. Hence it follows:

“They will judge nations, rule over peoples, and their Lord will reign forever.”

The saints will judge nations, but God judges through them, since he presides over their minds. They will rule over peoples because no adverse opposition can resist them. Their Lord will reign forever because Christ’s kingdom will endure without any end. Concerning this the angel said to Mary: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and there will be no end of his kingdom” (Luke I). Hence Isaiah also says: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace” (Isa. IX). The saints too will reign with their king—that is, the members with their Head—as the angel’s words to Daniel in a prophetic vision testify, saying: “The kingdom, power, and greatness of the kingdom under the whole heaven will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High, whose kingdom is an everlasting kingdom; and all kings will serve him and obey him” [Col. 0682D] (Dan. VII).

“Those who trust in him will understand truth, and the faithful will rest in love toward him, because grace and peace belong to his [Col. 0683A] elect.”

It is clear that whoever trusts perfectly in the Lord receives, in the present life, according to the distribution of the Holy Spirit and in the measure suited to him, an understanding of the truth. For now “we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face”; now “we know in part, but then we shall know even as we are known.” And now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; “but the greatest of these is charity.” When the others descend, it alone remains. Hence he says:

“The faithful will rest in love toward him,” because after the end of the world God’s elect, delighting in the good that they previously sought through faith and hope but then possess in reality, can in no way be separated from his fellowship; rewarded with the gift of eternal satisfaction, they will enjoy perpetual peace.

## CHAPTER VII. That the ungodly will receive punishments corresponding to what they have done, because they have departed from the Lord

“But the ungodly will receive correction according to what they have thought, because they neglected justice and departed from the Lord.”

When the universal judgment has been completed, the saints will enter with joy the kingdom of their heavenly homeland together with their king. Then the ungodly and sinners, who were careless about their salvation, will be plunged with the devil into the abyss of hell according to the wickedness of their hearts and deeds [Col. 0683B], where they will be tormented without end, because “their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.”

“For the unhappy person who rejects wisdom and discipline; their hope is empty, their labors fruitless, and their works uninhabitable.”

Now he shows what it means to have departed from the Lord, as he said above: it means to reject wisdom and discipline. Their hope is empty and their labors fruitless because they vainly hope that they can use temporal things forever, or that by committing sins they can escape punishment. Their labors are fruitless with respect to future reward, and their works are uninhabitable, because they cannot make their worker a participant in the heavenly dwelling. Concerning this the Psalmist, reproaching the head of all the wicked and predicting his crimes, says: “Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and pluck you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living” (Ps. LI).

Heretics may also appropriately be understood in this statement. Rejecting divine wisdom and the rule of right faith, they expend the labors of their teaching and the factions of their errors in vain and without the fruit of eternal life; their intention is foolish and their works most wicked. Hence it follows:

“Their women are senseless, and their children most wicked.”

By “women” he means either carnal lusts or interpretations expressing an impious sense. From these proceed most wicked children—that is, wicked deeds or perverse doctrines—which are liable not to the reward of the heavenly kingdom but to the torment of hell. Concerning this it is further said:

“[Col. 0683D] Cursed is their creation”—that is, their workmanship.

Divine wisdom does not impose the mark of a curse upon God’s creatures, whom their Creator created by blessing them in the beginning; rather, it shows that the activity of the reprobate is worthy of an eternal curse.

“For blessed is the barren woman, and the undefiled woman who has not known a marriage-bed in sin; she will have fruit when the holy souls are regarded.”

He praises the barren woman—that is, the chaste and continent soul—which has not been polluted by the filth of heretics or defiled by the uncleanness of idolatry. She will have fruit when the holy souls are regarded, namely, on the day of judgment, when the saints are snatched away to contemplate the [Col. 0684A] glory of God. Then she too will receive the reward of her labor in heavenly blessedness.

“And the eunuch who has not worked iniquity with his hands nor conceived the most wicked thought against God; for an elect gift of faith will be given to him, and a most acceptable portion in the temple of the Lord.”

According to the rule of allegorical interpretation, this blessed barren woman, or eunuch, may be understood as a virgin. Concerning him it is written in Isaiah: “Let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree,’ for thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: ‘Those who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast my covenant, I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that will not perish’” (Isa. LVI).

This barren woman is fruitful through virginity. This eunuch does violence to the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0684B] and seizes it violently. He is a guardian of the Sabbaths and will never perform the works of marriage. He chooses what the Lord desires, so that he offers more than is commanded; he considers not the concession of the Lord’s apostle but his will. He keeps the Lord’s everlasting covenant, so that he does not devote himself to prayer for a time and then return to it, but knows that he will receive an excellent place in the house of the Lord, which is his Church, for “there are many dwelling places with the Father.” Whoever is a eunuch and does everything that is written will have an excellent place within the Lord’s walls, so that he may become a tower of the Lord and stand in the priestly rank, having many spiritual children in place of children of the flesh.

Church [Col. 0684C] histories report that the evangelist John was such a eunuch, whom Jesus loved greatly: he reclined upon Jesus’ breast, and when Peter walked more slowly, John, lifted up on the wings of virginity, ran to the Lord. Let all Jewish mockery therefore cease; let them no longer make themselves objects of ridicule by waiting for half-men to receive the kingdoms of heaven through chastity—not through bodily weakness but through the will of the soul. Nor will idleness earn the reward of good, but rather devout striving. Hence it follows:

“For glorious is the fruit of good labors, and the root of wisdom does not wither.”

The fruit of good labors is truly glorious, because eternal joy and certain rest follow them. Nor do those shoots of teaching or action that have sprung from the root of true wisdom ever fall; rather, they bring forth the fruit of perpetual salvation. By contrast, the doctrines of heretics and their disciples and followers in wickedness will be destroyed. They will have no hope of salvation, but, condemned to bitter death, they will be handed over to perpetual oblivion. Concerning this it is also said:

## [Col. 0684D] CHAPTER VIII. That the children of adulterers—that is, of heretics—will perish at the consummation, while the offspring of the chaste will remain in perpetual brightness

“But the children of adulterers will come to an end, and offspring from an unlawful marriage-bed will be destroyed. Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing, and their final old age will be without honor. And if they die sooner, they will have no hope, nor consolation on the day of recognition. For the nations of the unrighteous are destined for terrible [Col. 0685A] destruction.”

The adulterers are heretics, who adulterate the word of God by attempting to transfer it into another meaning. Their children—that is, their disciples—will come to an end because they are heading toward eternal destruction. Nourished and raised from an unlawful, polluted marriage-bed, with the venom of conscience breaking forth, even if they live long upon the earth, this will profit them nothing when they are destined for the burning of eternal fire. Their final old age will be without honor because their memory will forever lack blessing. Nor on the day of recognition—namely, at the hour of the universal judgment, when the elect, recognized by their judge, are invited to possess the heavenly kingdom—will they be consoled by any hope of restoration; instead, they will be driven from the sight of the human King to be tormented forever.

**[Col. 0685B] (CHAPTER IV.)** “O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory! For its memory is immortal, since it is known both to God and to human beings. When it is present, they imitate it; and when it has departed, they desire it. Crowned forever, it triumphs, having conquered the prize of undefiled contests.”

Just as above he censured the founders of heresies and their schismatic followers, so now he praises Catholics and their disciples, whose faith is pure and whose teaching is simple and eternal. Their generation is worthy of remembrance because it has been approved by the Lord and honorably received among human beings. In the present life it produces the fruit of good works through holy examples, and, transferred to the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0685C], leaves a worthy memory of itself to posterity. Nor will there be any grief over the contest that has been completed, when the reward surpasses the magnitude of the persecutions.

“For the multitude of the ungodly, though of many kinds, will be of no use; and illegitimate offshoots will not take deep roots, nor establish a firm foundation.”

He speaks alternately about Catholics and heretics in order to show the praiseworthy wisdom of the former and demonstrate the blameworthy cunning of the latter. The varied and manifold doctrine of heretics will be of no use but will be harmful. Their excessive arguments, signified by “illegitimate offshoots,” have no root in truth; therefore they possess no firm foundation of strength. Struck by the wind of persecutions or by the examination of strict judgment [Col. 0685D], they quickly fall from their own stability. Hence it follows:

“Even if they put forth shoots in their branches in due season, being weakly planted they will be shaken by the wind and uprooted by the violence of the winds. For their imperfect branches will be broken, and their fruits will be useless, bitter to eat, and fit for nothing.”

He calls the statements of perverse Scriptures “branches,” and the meanings of those statements “fruits.” By “winds” he signifies either the troubles of persecutions or the examinations of judgment. For just as fragile branches are shaken by the wind, so their imperfect statements, struck by any adversity or examination, are easily broken. Their fruits are useless and bitter because the meanings of their words [Col. 0686A] are perverse and poisonous, and therefore suited to no useful purpose.

“For all the children born from the unrighteous are witnesses against their parents’ wickedness by their own examination.”

He calls the children of the unrighteous either their disciples or their works. Just as the disciples of heretics will, on the day of judgment, increase the grief of those who led them astray through wicked doctrines, so their evil works will, at the time of the final examination, provide evidence of their wickedness, and they will rightly be condemned.

## CHAPTER IX. That the souls of the righteous will be in refreshment after death, and that their departure should not be mourned

“But the righteous person, if overtaken by death, will be in refreshment.”

Having previously spoken about the destruction of the wicked, [Col. 0686B] he now goes on to describe the rest of the good. After the end of the present life, which is shared by the good and the wicked, the righteous will begin to live better precisely when they appear to perish utterly before the eyes of the wicked, because external rest will then be given to the righteous when perpetual punishment succeeds for the wicked.

“For honorable old age is not of long duration, nor counted by number of years. The gray hairs are the understanding of human beings, and the age of old age is an unblemished life.”

He shows what should be sought in old age, since it is not bodily age but maturity of mind and uprightness of conduct that are praised in it. Hence in the Book of Numbers the Lord commanded Moses to choose seventy elders whom he knew to be elders, so that he might appoint them teachers and judges of the people. And Paul, writing to Timothy [Col. 0686C], says: “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity.”

“Having become pleasing to God, he was loved, and while living among sinners he was taken away. He was snatched away lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit mislead his soul.”

God does not take from this world the person whom he loves because he is unable to preserve him from sin while he lives among sinners. He sent his disciples, like lambs among wolves, and commended them to the Father, saying: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you protect them from evil” (John XVII). Rather, he does so in order to observe the order of his judgment: those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, he calls, justifies, magnifies, and glorifies; but the rest [Col. 0686D] he condemns by a just judgment for their iniquity. Concerning this the Apostle Peter says: “God knows how to rescue the devout from trial, but to reserve the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment” (II Pet. II).

“For the fascination of frivolity obscures good things, and the inconstancy of desire perverts a mind without malice.”

Although this statement may generally indicate the wantonness of the reprobate, it more plainly rebukes the cunning of heretics, which turns the human mind away from the path of truth through perverse doctrines and harmful desire. For he fascinates—that is, burdens—the person whom he hinders by flattery or deceives by praise. We read in the Apostle: “You were running well; who fascinated you?” (Gal. III). And in Proverbs: “The gift of the envious torments the eyes.” [Col. 0687A] What is called “envious” among us is expressed more significantly among the Greeks as “one who fascinates”; from these examples we learn either that the envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, or that someone in whom there are good qualities is harmed when another fascinates or envies him.

For the envy of heretics, which usually offers mere trifles rather than a foundation of truth, often obscures the good in the simple. Hence the saying: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV). Therefore Wisdom forbids associating with such people, saying in Proverbs: “Do not eat with an envious person, and do not desire his foods, for he considers what he does not know to be like the work of a diviner and soothsayer. ‘Eat and drink,’ he will say to you, but his heart is not with you. You will vomit up the food you have eaten and lose your beautiful words” (Prov. XXIII).

[Col. 0687B] Completed in a short time, he fulfilled many years. For his soul was pleasing to God; therefore he hastened to lead him out from among iniquities. Just as in the preceding passage he stripped heretics of their faithlessness, so now in what follows he sets forth the glory of the martyrs. Although, in a short time amid the tortures of their persecutors, they spent a life worthy of praise, nevertheless that very death is reckoned to them as a full old age, because it brought forth for them eternal life. Their Creator, loving them, set them apart from the company of the wicked and led them out from the vexations of the present life, so that he might hide them in the secrecy of his countenance, in the heavenly kingdom, from the disturbance of men, and protect them in his tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues.

But the peoples saw and did not understand, nor did they take such things to heart: for grace and mercy are upon his saints. The persecutors of the martyrs were therefore utterly unable to recognize the glory that was to come and that followed upon them; instead, they thought that the martyrs would perish together with the punishments of their bodies and that they could not receive the blessedness of eternal life after death. But everything occurs differently for the two parties: just as life and victory will follow the good after death, so death and everlasting condemnation will follow the wicked after their temporal life.

But the righteous man, once dead, condemns the living impious, and youth brought swiftly to completion condemns the long life of the unjust. It is plainly evident that the martyrs of Christ will become judges of their persecutors after death, just as the divine voice reveals in the Apocalypse, in the condemnation of Babylon, saying: “Come out of her, my people, so that you may not be participants in her sins and may not receive any of her plagues, for her sins have reached as far as heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities. Repay her as she herself repaid you, and double the double according to her deeds. In the cup in which she mixed the drink, mix her a double portion. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much torment and mourning give her, because in her heart she says: ‘I sit as queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning.’ Therefore in one day her plagues will come: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be burned with fire” (Apoc. IV).

[Col. 0688A] For they will see the end of the wise man and will not understand what God had intended for him, nor why God had protected him; they will see and despise him. But afterward the Lord will mock them, and thereafter they will be dead without honor and in disgrace among the dead forever. For, as we have said, the persecutors of Christ’s Church regarded the end of the martyrs as destruction; therefore they despised the foundation of their faith. But the Lord will mock them when he shows them that what they hoped would benefit them had altogether harmed them, because, while they wished to defend the false deities of their gods against those who worship Christ, they were delivering themselves over to everlasting condemnation.

For he will shatter them, puffed up and without a word; he will shake them from their foundations, and they will be utterly desolated; they will be groaning, and their memory will perish. For the Lord will shatter those whom pride has puffed up, without [Col. 0688B] a word of excuse, so that at that time they will be entirely without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they became futile in their reasoning, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, reptiles, and four-footed animals. Therefore God handed them over to dishonorable passions and to a debased mind, so that they might do things that are improper, filled with every kind of injustice, wickedness, fornication, greed, and depravity; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and malice; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy. Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things deserve death (Rom. I). And he will shake them from their foundations, because he will utterly overturn the condition of their life; they will be desolated to the very end, because thereafter they will never be relieved by any consolation, but will groan amid punishments, and their memory will perish forever.

They will come, fearful, in remembrance of their sins, and their iniquities will confront them and convict them. The impious, therefore, will come to judgment fearful in their consciousness of sins, because their thoughts accuse them of the evils they previously committed; and no opportunity for defense is granted where there is no fruit of good works in the conscience.

## CHAPTER X

That at the Lord’s coming the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against their persecutors, and that those persecutors will at last repent too late in hell of their error and sins.

### (CHAP. V.)

Then the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labors. Seeing this, they will be shaken by dreadful fear and will be astonished at the sudden, unexpected nature of their salvation, saying within themselves, while repenting and groaning from anguish of spirit:

“These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We fools regarded their life as madness and their end as dishonorable. How, then, have they been counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints of God?”

Then indeed the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against their persecutors, who here afflicted them with undeserved punishments and condemned their labors as though they were foolish. Raised up by heavenly glory, they will be judges according to the truth of those who had previously condemned them unjustly. Therefore, when the persecutors suddenly see themselves brought from glory to disgrace, and, conversely, their adversaries transferred from temporal affliction to heavenly honor, they will then seek, in late and fruitless repentance, what earlier—while it was permitted—they could have profitably pursued if they had wished.

Therefore we have gone astray from the way of truth, the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us. The way of truth is the Gospel of Christ and the divine law, from which the impious went astray because they refused to believe and obey. For them neither did the light of justice shine nor did the sun of understanding rise, because Christ was not with them—the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I)—nor the sun of justice that rises for those who fear him. In his punishments also there is true healing, for in his protection is established the abundance of everlasting life. He did not shine for the faithless gentile philosophers, nor for the heretics, because, scorning the path of truth, they preferred to follow empty traditions and wicked sects. Therefore they continue:

“Weary, we have been, in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we have walked difficult roads, but we have not known the way of the Lord.”

The philosophers were weary in the way of iniquity and destruction because, while reasoning they sought to exalt the structure of the world with divine honor, and chose rather to serve the creature than the Creator, they failed in that very investigation and found not salvation but destruction. Likewise, the heretics, walking difficult roads in their pride, devised wicked sects and did not recognize the way of the Lord, which is truth and life. Therefore they handed themselves over to everlasting destruction, and the labor they devoted to the present life brought them no benefit, since after death punishment, not reward, followed them. Hence, grieving, they say:

“What did pride profit us? Or what did the boastfulness of riches bring us? All those things have passed away like a shadow, like a messenger running swiftly, and like a ship passing through storm-tossed water. When it has passed, no trace of it can be found, nor a path of its keel in the waves; or like a bird that flies through the air, of whose journey no sign is found, but only the sound of its wings beating the light wind and cleaving the air by the force of its passage. With beating wings it flew across, and afterward no sign of its journey is found; or like an arrow shot toward its appointed place: the divided air immediately closes again upon itself, so that its passage is unknown. So we too, once born, quickly ceased to exist, and we were unable to display any sign of virtue; but in our wickedness we were consumed.”

Through five kinds of comparisons, by which he declares that the fruitless repentance of the wicked laments their labors slipping away, the fleetingness of life and the transience of earthly things are shown to us. For just as a shadow has no firmness of standing, nor does a messenger running swiftly permit delay, and just as a bird in the sky, a ship on the sea, or an arrow in the uncertain air proceeds along an unstable course, so the course of transitory life is always unstable and uncertain. Nothing in it will remain fixed except what is expended in pious labor for the attainment of eternal life.

According to allegory, however, by the shadow we may understand either forgetfulness of mind or the death of the flesh, to which human life is subject. In the running messenger, the passions of the soul or illnesses of the body, which indicate and herald the decline of corruptible life. By the bird, the elevation of worldly boastfulness or heresy. By the ship, the fickleness of the human mind, which is driven across the bitter waves of this age by the blasts of unclean spirits. By the arrow, the deceits and ambushes of the wicked. All these things are caught up in the misery of the present life, but after its end has been completed they leave their possessors in hell with fruitless repentance; for them they will always groan and will be raised up by no consolation. Therefore Scripture continues, saying:

“Such things did those who sinned say in hell: ‘For the hope of the impious is like down carried away by the wind, like thin foam scattered by a storm, like smoke dispersed by the wind, and like the memory of a guest passing by after a single day.’”

He has introduced four further kinds of comparison to demonstrate the weakness of the hope of the wicked: they either thought that present things were stable and enduring, or believed that, while living in sins, they could escape unpunished. Down, which arises from the withering flower of grasses, expresses the frailty of the flesh, which is carried away by the wind of illnesses or bodily distress and is not permitted to remain for long, because “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and its flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL).

Foam, which rises from the waters and floats upon the waters, may be understood as the desire for human favor and popular boastfulness. It is scattered by the storm of temptations or by the disclosure of the future judgment, for by their experience it is shown how vain those things were. Smoke likewise demonstrates the vanity of passing life, because just as smoke is dispersed by the wind, so human life is dissolved by the changing of the times. Hence it is also compared to a passing guest, because we are all guests and sojourners here. Concerning this Ecclesiastes says: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever; therefore all is vanity” (Eccl. I).

For what is more vain than this vanity: that the earth, which was made for the sake of human beings, should remain, while the human being, lord of the earth, is suddenly dissolved into dust? Hence it follows: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place” (ibid.). For the sun itself, which was given to mortals as their light, daily indicates the destruction of the world by its rising and its setting—and all this in order to teach that human life wastes away and perishes amid the changes of the seasons and the rising and setting of the heavenly bodies, without knowing it.

Therefore the impious, placed in hell, rightly grieve because they placed their hope in that in which there is no stability, and turned their understanding away from him who remains the same before all things and after all things, now and forever.

## CHAPTER XI

Concerning the holy martyrs: that they live forever, and that the Lord avenges them upon their adversaries.

But the righteous will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and their concern is with the Most High. Therefore they will receive the kingdom of beauty and the crown of splendor from the hand of the Lord, because with his right hand he will cover them and with his holy arm defend them.

After describing the punishments of sinners and their late repentance in hell, he consequently narrated the glory and reward of the righteous with the Lord in heaven. Received into the heavenly kingdom, they enjoy blessed life in contemplation of God, because they placed all their hope and the intention of their mind in the goodness of their Creator, by whose hand they are also crowned and by whose right hand of power they are protected.

For the hand, right hand, and arm of God, because of their effective power, are names for the only-begotten Son of God: through him all things were made; in him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. The Father raised him from the dead and appointed him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age [Col. 0691C] but also in the one to come. He placed all things beneath his feet and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body and his fullness, who fills all things in every way.

He will take up zeal as armor and arm creation for the vengeance of enemies. He will put on justice as a breastplate and take sure judgment as a helmet. He will take equity as an unconquerable shield; he will sharpen his fierce wrath into a spear, and the world will fight with him against the senseless.

According to the historical sense, therefore, the Creator of all things, whose weapons are truth, justice, and judgment, rebukes and chastises the guilty through the creation subject to him. According to the allegorical sense, the same Lord arms creation for vengeance against his enemies when, through the preachers of the Gospel, he convicts the faithlessness of the Jews, the foolishness of the gentiles, and the deceit of the heretics concerning sin, justice, and judgment, and pierces their hearts with the weapons of words, so that, terrified by salutary fear, they may yield to the hand of almighty God and learn to be subject to him, whose admonition they ought in no way to resist, since they cannot in any way withstand his power.

When he says that the whole world will fight with him against the senseless, he shows that the whole Church of Christ, together with its king—that is, its members together with its head—fights against the errors and malice of the wicked with the weapons of truth and justice. It has been founded by the Lord’s authority upon the most solid rock and in no way fears collapse, because “the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI); rather, fixed and unshaken, it remains throughout all ages.

The emissions of lightning will go forth directly, and like arrows from a well-curved bow they will be hurled against the enemies and leap toward their appointed place. The emissions of lightning are the thunders of preaching or the flashes of miracles, which will go forth directly because, according to the dispensation of their author, they are made either for the benefit of the elect or for the condemnation of the reprobate. They will be hurled like arrows from a well-curved bow of clouds when, by the authority of divine Scripture and through the pious intention of the holy teachers, they are brought forth to terrify adversaries; and they will leap toward their appointed place because they will proceed by a straight course against those whom it is necessary to confront, nor can that be confused which divine wisdom has established as ordered [Col. 0692B].

And hailstones, full of stony wrath, will be hurled against them, because harsh rebukes are sent forth in proportion to their merits.

And the water of the sea will grow hoary over them, and the rivers will run together violently. By the waters of the sea he means the disturbances of the world, and by the rivers the upheavals of persecutions, because often the hearts of the wicked, which the lessons of preaching do not soften, are broken by the fear of the scourges of various corrections.

And against them will stand the spirit of power, and like a whirlwind it will divide them; and their iniquity will bring the whole earth to its end, and their malice will overthrow the seats of the powerful. The spirit of power is the vengeance of the final judgment. It will divide the impious and bring the whole earth of their iniquity to its end, when the just Judge, by his sentence, assigns both their earthly substance and their carnal works to the punishment of Gehenna and eternal desolation. For the malice of the reprobate will overthrow the seats of the powerful, because the wickedness of the reprobate is the cause of their condemnation.

### (CHAP. VI.)

Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man better than a strong one. Wherever wisdom dwells, therefore, it always governs the soul well. Bodily strength often drives the foolish into the precipice of sins. Hence the prudent is preferred to the strong, because prudence directs a person’s steps; but although bodily force sometimes appears to imitate strength when, through power, it overcomes someone, it will nevertheless be shown to be weak without the guidance of prudence, when it is brought to completion through foolish toil. Hence it is written in the Psalm:

“The Lord will not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor is he pleased with the legs of a man. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. CXLVI).

## CHAPTER XII

Wisdom rebukes the judges of the earth, who received authority from the Lord but did not keep the law of justice, foretelling the punishments they will suffer.

Hear, therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, O judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who hold the multitudes and take pride in the crowds of nations, because authority has been given to you by the Lord, and power by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor did you keep the law of justice, nor did you walk according to the will of God. Terribly and swiftly this will become evident to you, because a most severe judgment will be made upon those who rule.

He admonishes the rulers of the Church to keep the justice of God’s commandments and to hasten to learn and understand the truth of the divine testimonies. For just as they themselves have been appointed teachers and judges of their brethren, having received authority from the Lord, so that they might judge them according to the rule of equity and teach them to preserve the rule of faith with good works, so they too await the divine judgment, which neither deceives nor can be deceived. It judges not only their works but also their thoughts and intentions, and those who did not live according to God’s will and the law of his commandments, nor teach or judge others accordingly, it will judge with strict examination.

For mercy is granted to the lowly, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments. To those who, through ignorance, frailty, or even necessity, have committed some crimes, yet have not ceased to erase those sins through humility and repentance, the most merciful Judge grants the grace of forgiveness. But for those who, through obstinacy and contempt of God’s commandments, have committed many serious crimes and neglected to repent of them, he assigns more severe torments in hell. For as they were more powerful in committing impiety, so they endure stronger punishments in the fire of Gehenna.

For the Lord will not show partiality to anyone, nor will God fear anyone’s greatness, because he himself made both the small and the great, and he cares equally for all; but a stronger punishment awaits the powerful. “For God is not a respecter of persons,” as the apostle Peter testifies, “but in every nation whoever fears God and practices justice is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

But for those who are lying teachers, introduce sects of destruction, and deny the Lord who bought them, thereby bringing swift destruction upon themselves (II Pet. II), the gloom of darkness is reserved. For if God did not spare the angels who sinned, but dragged them down with chains into hell and committed them to Tartarus to be kept for judgment and punished; and if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, the eighth person, a herald of justice, when he brought the flood upon the world of the ungodly; and if he condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction by reducing them to ashes, making them an example of those who would act impiously; and if he rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the wicked conduct of the lawless—for that righteous man, by sight and hearing, was dwelling among those who day after day tormented his righteous soul with lawless deeds—so also now those who walk after the flesh in lust and impurity, bold and self-pleasing, who are not afraid to make sects and blaspheme, will perish in their corruption, receiving the reward of their injustice.

For God fears no one’s greatness, because he is above all, and there is no end to his greatness. He accepts no one’s person, because he will judge each according to his ways. He cares equally for all, because he himself is the Creator of all and provides fitting care for his work, granting it the help by which it can subsist.

After Wisdom had addressed the powerful and rebuked their hardness of heart with her words, she now turns a word of exhortation to the rulers themselves and wondrously unfolds the praise of Wisdom herself, saying:

Therefore, O kings, these are my words to you, so that you may learn wisdom and not transgress. For those who keep her justice will be justified justly, and those who have learned justice will find what they should answer.

He admonishes ecclesiastical rulers—or rather, all generally to whom the governance of their souls has been entrusted—to learn divine wisdom, so that they may not transgress by violating God’s commandments. Those who keep what is just will be justified justly; that is, those who follow justice will receive from the just Judge the reward of their justice. Those who have learned what is just—by believing rightly and acting well—will be granted what they should answer when each person is examined, because the merit of the present life seeks the blessed reward of everlasting glory.

## CHAPTER XIII

Wisdom urges the rulers of the Church to hear and desire her words, because she offers herself to them freely, granting at the same time integrity of body and chastity of soul.

Desire my words, therefore, and love them, and you will possess discipline. It is true that whoever loves wisdom and is assiduous in meditating upon her preserves discipline in his conduct; nor can a lover of wisdom be proved in any other way than by being a keeper of discipline. Hence Truth herself says: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XV). And again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV). Hence James also says: “Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves, because it is not the hearers of the law who will be justified before the Lord, but the doers of the law” (James XIV).

Wisdom is radiant and never withers; she is easily seen by those who love her and is found by those who seek her. The beauty of wisdom does not wither, and she is revealed only to those who love her in truth and diligently seek her. Those who seek her deceitfully, however, will in no way reach her, because, as was said above, “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit,” and wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul. Hence Wisdom says in Proverbs: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me” (Prov. VIII). And again: “Blessed is the person who hears me, who watches daily at my doors and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway. Whoever finds me finds life and will draw salvation from the Lord. But whoever sins against me harms his own soul. All who hate me love death” (Prov. III).

She anticipates those who desire her, so that she may first reveal herself to them. Whoever keeps watch for her at dawn will not labor; for he will find her sitting at his doors. [Col. 0695A] This Wisdom is Christ, the Son of God, concerning whom the Apostle says: “I speak of Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (I Cor. I).

He therefore anticipates by his grace all who yearn for his love, because he is the way, the truth, and the life: through him one goes, toward him one strives, and to him one arrives. Whoever, from the beginning of the faith dawning within him, keeps watch with a devout heart is not consumed by fruitless labor; rather, for his devotion to good works he is crowned by him. For he will find Wisdom sitting at his doors, because he will always have her help ready. Hence he himself says in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Apoc. III).

[Col. 0695B] To think upon her, therefore, is perfect understanding; and whoever keeps watch for her will soon be secure, because she herself goes about seeking those who are worthy of her, and she shows herself cheerfully to them in her ways, and in every providence she will meet them.

The thought of a pure mind is the desire for divine contemplation. How, then, will the person who is always intent upon the love of the highest good not possess perfect understanding? Blessed indeed will be the one who, with wakeful intention, seeks the highest Wisdom, whose true adoption is the reception of true sincerity. But no one suddenly becomes perfect; rather, ascent to the summit must be made through progress in the virtues.

In the present life, therefore, effort must be devoted to learning wisdom, and one must live according to the rule of her discipline. When she has instructed a person and has perfectly taken possession of him [Col. 0696A], she will make him a participant in eternal blessedness. Hence it also follows:

“For the beginning of her is the most genuine desire for discipline. Care for discipline is love; and love is the keeping of her laws; but the keeping of her laws is the consummation of incorruption; and incorruption makes one near to God. Thus desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom.”

The Apostle Peter sets forth the stages of progress toward this benefit in his Epistle, saying: “For this very reason, bringing all diligence to bear, supply virtue in your faith, in virtue knowledge, in knowledge self-control, in self-control endurance, in endurance godliness, in godliness brotherly love, and in brotherly love charity. For if all these things are present and abound in you, they will not make you idle or fruitless in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Pet. I).

For whoever lives in this world according to discipline because of love for wisdom, keeping God’s commandments, will through progress in the sacred virtues attain incorruptibility, immortality, and everlasting life, which consists in the knowledge of the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence he himself says to the Father in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). When he has truly known God, then he will enjoy everlasting blessedness in contemplation of him; and, reigning together with his King, he will remain in perpetual light.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0695]

## CHAPTER I

The wise man praises divine Wisdom, proclaiming her power.

Therefore, if you delight in thrones and dynasties, O kings of the peoples, love wisdom, so that you may reign forever. He necessarily admonishes the kings of the earth to love wisdom, because without wisdom it is impossible for anyone to reign properly. Hence comes that Platonic saying: “The commonwealth is then well governed when philosophers rule and rulers philosophize.” For wishing to hold a kingdom without wisdom is more a matter of tyrannical ferocity than of royal moderation.

Therefore, let the rulers of the Church consider how fitting it is that they should be constant in meditating upon the divine law. Whoever follows the rule of the sacred Scriptures in learning, teaching, and practice [Col. 0695D] will undoubtedly receive the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

But what wisdom is, and how she came to be, I shall relate; I shall not hide from you the mysteries of God, but shall investigate her from the beginning of her birth and bring her knowledge to light. I shall not pass over the truth, nor shall I travel with wasting envy, because envy will not be a participant in wisdom.

It is clear that the plague of envy is not a companion of wisdom, because through the envy of the devil death entered the whole world, while through the wisdom of God the human race was snatched from the snare of death. Hence it follows:

The multitude of the wise is the health of the world, and a wise king is the stability of his people.

The multitude of the wise is the assembly of holy preachers, whose teaching is the health of the world, because through it an innumerable crowd of diverse nations has been converted to the faith of Christ. The king of this crowd is the wise one—or rather, Wisdom herself and the power of God, Jesus Christ, our God and Lord—who becomes the stability of his elect, since, as the Psalmist testifies, “the Lord is the strength of his people and the protector of the salvation of his anointed” (Ps. XXVII). Concerning him the same Prophet says: “The Lord is my rock, my strength, and my savior; my strong God, I will hope in him” (II Sam. XXII).

## CHAPTER II

The same man explains the origin of human nature.

Therefore, receive discipline through my words, and it will benefit you. (CHAP. VII.) I too am a mortal human being, like everyone else, and descended from that earthly one who was made first. In my mother’s womb I was fashioned as flesh; for ten months I was coagulated in blood, from human seed and the pleasurable union appropriate to sleep. I too, once born, received the common air and fell upon the similarly formed earth, and I uttered my first cry, like everyone else, weeping. I was raised in swaddling clothes and amid great cares. For no king had any other beginning of birth. One entrance into life, therefore, belongs to all, and one similar departure.

Wisdom, therefore, intending to demonstrate her power through a vessel suited to her, first makes her own preacher humbly recount the origin of the human condition, so that each person may know what he has from the origin of flesh and what he has from the divine gift. When he says that he was coagulated in blood for ten months, from human seed and the pleasurable union appropriate to sleep, he indicates the distinction between the two sexes. For, as the physicians say, the seed of the man is white, while the seed of the woman is blood-tinged. Their mixture, at determined intervals of time, causes the infant’s body to be formed until, once endowed with life, it reaches the time of birth in the tenth month, although not all reach the tenth month, since some are born in the seventh, others in the eighth, and others in the ninth. But they assert that a birth occurring in the tenth month is more complete, more viable, and healthier than one occurring in the eighth or ninth month.

When he says that the beginning of birth is common to all human beings, both noble and lowly, and shows that everyone has one entrance into life and a similar departure, he demonstrates that every earthly human being, born from the seed of man and woman, receives the beginning of temporal life and passes from this world through death.

The heavenly Adam, however, who was born from a virgin mother without male seed, has a distinctive manner of birth; and by the sovereign power of his death he himself ordered his departure. Nevertheless, Christians celebrate his birth as occurring in the tenth month after the time of his conception. From the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when he is believed to have been conceived, to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, when he is reported to have been born, 276 days are counted. This number of days comprises nine months and six days. Thus that Gospel statement in which the same Savior foretold that the temple of his body, built by the Jews over forty-six years, would be destroyed reveals, through the multiplication of the number six, the perfection of his incarnation, because 276 contains forty-six sixes. Hence it is plainly evident that, just as Jesus Christ our Lord is perfect God, so also he is perfect man.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning his confession that he received the spirit of wisdom, in which he recounts many of her gifts.

Because of this I desired it, and understanding was given to me; I invoked, and the spirit of wisdom came into me. I preferred it to kingdoms and thrones, and I considered riches as nothing in comparison with it; nor did I compare any precious stone with it, because all gold, in comparison with it, is a little sand, and silver will be reckoned as clay in its presence.

The lover of wisdom said that he had desired, called upon, and sought wisdom, and that for this reason, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he attained it [Col. 0698A], since, as the apostle James says: “If anyone lacks this, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach” (James I). It is rightly preferred to kingdoms, thrones, and all riches, because all the precious things of the world become worthless in comparison with it. Hence wisdom herself says in Proverbs: “With me are riches and glory, exalted wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce than refined silver” (Prov. VIII).

For this reason Truth herself in the Gospel compares the kingdom of heaven to a merchant seeking good pearls. When he found one precious pearl, he went away, sold everything he possessed, and bought it (Matt. XIII). For whoever truly finds heavenly wisdom—that is, the word of God in the heights—despises all the gains of the present life, all human philosophy, and all the eloquence of orators [Col. 0698B], and rejoices to devote himself solely to divine contemplation. Hence it continues:

> I loved her above health and beauty, and I resolved to have her for my light, because her radiance is unquenchable. All good things came to me together with her, and innumerable riches through her hands.

The salvation of the soul, which consists in possessing divine wisdom together with works of righteousness, must be preferred altogether to every bodily health and every bodily beauty, because, as will be shown later, wisdom herself is more beautiful than the sun and, compared with light, is found to be purer than the whole array of the stars. Night and darkness succeed those lights, whereas her radiance is unquenchable.

That “all good things came to him together with her” was experienced by Solomon himself: when he asked God for wisdom alone, he obtained with it the greatness of the kingdom, riches, and glory. Mystically, whoever truly receives knowledge of Christ rejoices that he has received the grace of all the virtues together with it, and in the future will possess eternal life with him.

> And I rejoiced in all things, because this wisdom went before me, though I did not know that she was the mother of them all.

He rightly rejoices in all things whom wisdom governs, going before him in all his counsels and actions. But it is surprising that he says he did not know that she was the mother of all these things, when earlier he said that she anticipates those who desire her and shows herself prior to them. Perhaps, as his meditation progressed, he understood that he had advanced so far that, comparing his former knowledge with his later knowledge, he judged the former to be almost ignorance in comparison with the latter, when he saw the latter surpassing it [Col. 0698D].

This is like the saying in the Gospel concerning John the Baptist: although he proclaimed the Lord’s future coming and pointed him out as present with his finger, after baptizing him he said that previously he had not known him, but that he had been shown him when the Holy Spirit came upon him. Thus he says:

> “And I did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him like a dove, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John I).

So too, among the lights of the world, although the other stars are bright in themselves, they are nevertheless found to be not bright at all in comparison with the sun [Col. 0699A]. The sun itself is therefore so called because, alone among the other stars, it shines with the light of day.

> I learned her without deceit, and I share her without envy, and I do not hide her excellence.

Earlier he had said that the Holy Spirit, the giver of divine wisdom, flees deceitful instruction, and that wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul. Now the true possessor of wisdom says that he learned her without deceit, and therefore could truly attain knowledge of her, share her without envy, and not conceal her excellence. Envy can in no way coexist with true wisdom, which is known to be a lover of generosity and mercy.

“For what fellowship is there between light and darkness? Or what communion between Christ and Belial?” (2 Cor. VI). Hence the apostle James says:

> “Who is wise and disciplined among you? Let him show his works by a good manner of life, in the gentleness of wisdom. But if you have bitter jealousy and rivalry in your hearts, do not boast or lie against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, sensual, and demonic. For where jealousy and rivalry are, there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, agreeing with what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without hypocrisy” (James III).

Accordingly it is fittingly added:

> For she is an infinite treasure to human beings; those who have used her become participants in the friendship of God, commended because of the gifts of instruction.

He calls wisdom an infinite treasure because the more diligently someone learns it, the deeper he recognizes it to be; and the more he advances by meditating upon it, the more deeply he understands that it must be sought. Thus those who meditate upon it become participants in the friendship of God, because they become true knowers of God’s commandments and will. Concerning this, Truth himself says to the disciples in the Gospel:

> “I shall no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV).

> But God gave me the ability to speak with understanding and to form worthy judgments about the things given to me, because he himself is the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise. For in his hand are we, our words, all wisdom, and knowledge and discipline concerning works.

God is the guide of wisdom because the almighty Father is the author of the incarnation of his only-begotten Son, whom he sent into the world so that the human race might receive the illumination of truth. He gave him all authority in heaven and on earth, because “from him and through him and in him are all things”; and “he himself made us, and not we ourselves. We are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIX). Whatever we rightly think, whatever we rightly say, and whatever we accomplish in good works is his gift.

> For he himself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, so that I might know the arrangement of the world, the powers of the elements, the beginning, middle, and consummation of times, the changes of seasons and the alterations of temporal conditions, the course of the year and the ordering of the stars, the natures of animals and the ferocity of beasts, the force of winds and the thoughts of human beings, the differences among plants and the powers of roots. I learned whatever things are hidden and unforeseen, for wisdom, the craftsman of all things, taught me.

How greatly Solomon excelled in wisdom through the divine gift, Scripture shows when it says:

> “God also gave Solomon wisdom and very great prudence, and breadth of heart like the sand that is on the seashore. Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the East and of Egypt, and he was wiser than all human beings: wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. He was renowned among all the surrounding nations. Solomon also spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered one thousand and five. He discoursed on trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and he discussed beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. People came from all nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom” (1 Kings IV).

But our peacemaker, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, before whose eyes all things are naked and open, not only knows all things that are, that have been, and that will be; he also gives his own disciples—that is, unquestionably, his members—understanding of his mysteries. Thus they possess knowledge not only of visible but also of invisible things, and perfectly understand what history teaches, what allegory reveals, what tropology commends, and what anagogy indicates concerning heavenly things [Col. 0700C].

Hence the Gospel rightly says:

> “He is the light of the world, which illumines every human being coming into this world” (John I).

Whoever follows him does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.

> For in her is a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, sure, sweet, loving good action, one who forbids no one to do good, humane, kind, steadfast, certain, secure, possessing all power, observing all things, and capable of comprehending all intelligent, pure, and subtle spirits.

The prophet Isaiah, enumerating the divine gifts that he had foretold would rest through the sevenfold Spirit upon the flower of Jesse’s root, showed that the fullness of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit exists in the humanity of the Savior. In him “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden,” and “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” The Father does not give him the Spirit by measure; hence he confidently says:

> “All that the Father has is mine”; and “no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI).

When the author of this history wished to recount the power of wisdom herself, he said that in her is the Spirit of understanding, because through her the recognition of truth is granted.

She is “holy” because she sanctifies all things.

“Unique” because she creates unity and harmony among the elect.

“Manifold” because she grants variety of knowledge and virtues [Col. 0701A].

“Subtle” and “mobile” because “the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts” (Heb. IV).

“Eloquent” because she opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

“Undefiled” because no stain of sin clings to her.

“Sure” because she deceives no one and cannot be deceived.

“Sweet” because she is gentle and merciful toward all who call upon her.

“Loving good action” and forbidding no one to do good because she does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth.

“Humane” and “kind” because she is merciful, gentle, and devout; “steadfast, sure, secure,” she is the one who says in the Gospel:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

She is called “steadfast” because by her nature she contains all things. She is called “mobile” because everywhere she encounters even those who do not know it. Thus, while she holds all things steadfastly, she is called mobile because she presents herself as present to all [Col. 0701B].

A serious question arises in these words: why is this Spirit, who fills all things at once, called both mobile and steadfast? But if we return to ordinary human experience, we quickly understand the speaker’s meaning. A person who runs everywhere throughout the region in which he is located undoubtedly encounters people everywhere, and suddenly is found where he is not expected. Thus the almighty Spirit is described as mobile, possessing every virtue and observing all things, in order to signify that he is present everywhere. He gives strength to the weary and light to the blind, for he alone gives strength and might to his people.

He comprehends all intelligent, pure, and subtle spirits, because “in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and he beholds the heights of the mountains” (Ps. XCIV).
