In his name “every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II).

## CHAPTER IV. That Wisdom, who is the Son of God, reaches everywhere because she is always with the Father, and, remaining in herself, renews all things

> For wisdom is more mobile than anything mobile; she reaches everywhere because of her purity.

What could be more mobile and subtle than wisdom, which created all things, rules all things, orders all things, and governs all things? For “in her we live and move and are.” She reaches everywhere because of her purity, because she is light and there are no darknesses in her [Col. 0701D].

> For she is a vapor of the power of God and a pure emanation of the glory of the almighty God; therefore nothing defiled enters into her.

It is clear that the only-begotten Son of God, born from the substance of God the Father, is coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. Therefore nothing defiled is found in him, because nothing evil approaches the supreme good; rather, the simple good always remains the same.

> For she is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness.

The Apostle says of this same Son:

> “He is the radiance of glory and the exact representation of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power” (Heb. I).

For the Father calls Wisdom itself his Word—not in the manner of a spoken word sounding from the mouth, or a word thought before it is uttered. The former is completed through intervals of time, whereas the latter is eternal. By illuminating us, he tells us what must be said about himself and the Father; therefore he says:

> “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI).

The Father reveals through the Son, that is, through his Word. If this word that we utter is temporal and passing, and reveals both itself and the thing about which we speak, how much more does the Word of God, through whom all things were made, reveal the Father as he is—because the Word himself is also as the Father is, and is what the Father is according to wisdom and essence [Col. 0702B].

For according to the Word he is not the same as the Father, because the Word is not the Father; and “Word” is said relationally, just as “Son” is said, and the Son is certainly not the Father. Therefore Christ is the power and wisdom of God: because he is from the Father as power and wisdom, he himself is also power and wisdom. He is the light of God and light from the Father who is light, and the fountain of life with God the Father, who is himself the fountain of life:

> “For with you,” he says, “is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV).

For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son to have life in himself (John V).

> “And there was the true light that illumines every human being coming into this world; and this light was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

God is light, and there are no darknesses in him. This light is not bodily but spiritual—not spiritual in the sense that it was made by illumination, as was said to the apostles, “You are the light of the world,” but the light that illumines every human being: God himself, the highest and very wisdom of whom we are now speaking [Col. 0702C].

Thus the Son is Wisdom from the Father who is Wisdom, just as light is from light and God from God. Each individually—the Father—is light, and each individually—the Son—is light; each individually—the Father—is God, and each individually—the Son—is God. Therefore each individually—the Father—is Wisdom, and each individually—the Son—is Wisdom. Together they are one light and one God; together they are one Wisdom.

But the Son has become wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification for us from God, because we turn toward him temporally, from a certain point in time, so that we may remain with him eternally. And he himself, from a certain point in time, became the Word made flesh and dwelt among us [Col. 0702D].

> And although she is one, she can do all things; and remaining in herself, she renews all things. From generation to generation she passes into holy souls, making them friends of God and prophets.

Therefore, whenever Scripture pronounces or narrates something concerning wisdom—whether wisdom herself is speaking or something is said about her—the Son is chiefly indicated to us. By the example of his image, we too should not depart from God, because we also are the image of God—not equal, certainly, since we were made by the Father through the Son, not born from the Father as she was. We are illuminated by light, whereas she is the illuminating light; and therefore she is for us an example without precedent.

For she does not imitate anyone who preceded her to the Father, from whom she can never be separated, because she is precisely what he is, from whom she proceeds. We, however, imitate the one who remains, follow the one who stands, and, walking in him, advance toward him. He became for us a temporal way through humility, who is our eternal dwelling through divinity.

For to pure intellectual spirits who had not fallen through pride, he—the form of God and equal to God—provides an example. He also offered that same example of return to fallen humanity. Since human beings could not see God because of the uncleanness of sins and the punishment of mortality, he emptied himself—not by changing his divinity, but by assuming our mutability—and, taking the form of a servant, came to us in this world.

He was in this world, because the world was made through him, so that he might be an example above for those who see God, an example below for those who marvel at the human being, an example for the healthy to persevere, for the weak to recover, for the dying not to fear, and for the dead to rise again [Col. 0703B].

He holds the first place in all things. Since a human being ought to follow none other than God toward blessedness, but could not perceive God while following him, he was to follow God made human—both one whom he could perceive and one whom he ought to follow.

The almighty Father begot from himself almighty Wisdom, who, remaining in herself, renews all things. She is unchangeable and rules and orders all mutable things by her will; transferring herself into the souls of the elect by her grace, she makes them friends of God and establishes them as prophets.

> “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

Hence it is said:

> “You made all things in wisdom,”

because God made all things through his Son, that is, through his Word and Wisdom.

> For God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom.

If God loves no one except the one who dwells with wisdom, then certainly he hates all followers of folly. This sentence therefore makes clear that no one who hates instruction can be a participant in God’s grace, because “the Lord is far from the impious, and the one who hates reproof will die” (Prov. XV).

> The heart of the wise seeks instruction, and the mind of the righteous meditates on obedience. But whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool, and whoever walks wisely will be saved (Prov. XXVIII).

> For she is more beautiful than the sun and, compared with the whole array of the stars, is found to be purer than light.

According to the historical sense, he says that wisdom is more beautiful than the sun and all the brightness of the stars. Bodily light, which varies as night intervenes and appears at one time but is hidden at another, compared with the spiritual and everlasting light of wisdom seems scarcely to possess even the small brightness of a spark. Every transitory thing, when compared with what will remain, seems almost already not to exist, since it is consumed by eternity [Col. 0704A].

Mystically, likewise, the splendor of the wisdom of God, which is Christ, far surpasses the brilliance of whatever saints are here called by the names of sun and stars. They are mutable, whereas wisdom always remains the same.

The Psalmist, contemplating this, says to the Lord:

> “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and they will all grow old like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Ps. CX).

Concerning this it is further added:

> For night succeeds light, but wickedness does not overcome wisdom.

No one among the elect in this life is free from sin; but no wickedness approaches Christ. Of him it is written:

> “Blessed is the righteous man in the Lord, who was found without blemish” (Sir. XXXI).

And again:

> “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII).

When the ruler of this world came to him, he found nothing in him. Nevertheless, he himself bore our weaknesses and endured our sicknesses, because he bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness; “by his bruising we were healed” (1 Pet. II).

## CHAPTER V. That the same Wisdom reaches strongly from end to end and orders all things sweetly; that she teaches the four principal virtues—namely sobriety, wisdom, justice, and courage—and makes those who share in her glorious

> (CHAPTER VIII.) She therefore reaches strongly from end to end and orders all things sweetly.

The only-begotten Son of God is coeternal and entirely coequal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. “From end to end”—that is, from eternity to eternity—he reaches strongly because he is the power of God; and he orders all things sweetly because he is likewise the wisdom of God. In the Apocalypse of John he says:

> “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God” (Rev. XXI).

He is the beginning, whom no one precedes; and the end, whom no one succeeds in the kingdom. He is the one who is, who was, and who is to come, the almighty.

Elsewhere, through the prophet, he says:

> “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none” (Isa. XLIII).

In another sense, wisdom reaches strongly from end to end because, from the beginning of the world’s creation until the Lord’s coming, she strongly asserts through the Old Testament the wondrous works of God and the uncorrupted testimonies of the divine law; and from the incarnation of the Word until the end of the world, she sweetly expounds the delight of the divine commandments through the Gospel.

There is therefore one and the same creator of both Testaments: the mediator between God and human beings, who commended the fear of himself to his elect in the Law and the love of himself in the Gospel. Hence wisdom is elegantly said to reach strongly from end to end, because she is everywhere proclaimed to possess consummate and perfect virtue.

We frequently find “end” used in Scripture to mean perfection, as in the Apostle’s saying:

> “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. I).

And again:

> “The end of the law is Christ, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X).

For this reason Truth himself, when he wished to show that the two commandments of love are the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets, answered the lawyer in the Gospel:

> “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII),

that is, the whole teaching of the Law and the Prophets is fulfilled and completed in these [Col. 0705A].

> I loved her and sought her from my youth.

The lover of wisdom says that he sought wisdom from his youth—that is, from the cradle of human life—and therefore truly found her, because he was a diligent seeker of her, in accordance with the promise that she made elsewhere to her lovers:

> “Blessed is the person who hears me, who watches daily at my gates and keeps watch at the posts of my doors” (Prov. III).

> “Whoever finds me will find life and will obtain salvation from the Lord” (Prov. VIII).

And again:

> “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me” (ibid.).

> And I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty.

“I sought,” he says, “to take her as my bride”—that is, to bind her to myself by an everlasting covenant. I know that I can never be separated from her companionship, and I have chosen above all to desire her form. For the form of wisdom is truth, which all who are truly religious especially desire to know, because she alone is the one through whom all God’s elect hope to be blessed in eternal rest.

Hence Truth himself says to the Father in the Gospel:

> “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII).

Concerning this it is further said:

> She glorifies noble birth by having God as her companion.

The nobility and dignity of the only-begotten Son consist in having an eternal and almighty Father, with whom he remains coequal and coeternal from the beginning:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

> But the Lord of all also loved her.

The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand. For wisdom is the teacher of God’s instruction and the chooser of his works. John clearly confirms this in the Gospel, saying:

> “He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was before me. And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself made him known.”

[Col. 0705D]

> And if riches are desired in life, what is richer than wisdom, which produces all things?

The wisdom and power of God, the Lord Christ, through whom all things were made and who, together with the Father, arranges and rules all things by his own will, says in the Gospel:

> “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V).

He contains within himself the riches of all the virtues and distributes them to his lovers according to his will. This is declared equally in the New and Old Testaments.

Thus wisdom herself speaks in Proverbs:

> “With me are riches and glory, exalted wealth and righteousness. My fruit is better than gold and precious stone, and my produce than refined silver. I walk in the ways of righteousness, in the midst of the paths of judgment, to enrich those who love me and fill their treasuries” (Prov. VIII).

Likewise in the Gospel she cries out and says:

> “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII).

> “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI).

And elsewhere:

> “Everyone who has left house, brothers, sisters, father, mother, wife, children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

This sentence can also properly refer to those who meditate upon the divine law, meditating on it rightly day and night and remaining constantly in contemplation. Whoever seeks it with attentive heart and good will will be filled with the indescribable sweetness of its inner truth and will enjoy the abundance of all good things. Hence it continues:

> If understanding is at work, who among existing things is a greater craftsman than she?

If wisdom is the creator of sound understanding and profound intelligence, how could she not be the maker of all good works and sacred virtues, which offer steadfast salvation to her lovers?

> And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors possess great virtues.

No one can reach the palm of righteousness unless he follows the rule of wisdom, because she preserves the standard of equity and leads by the way of truth to eternal life. Her labors possess great virtues because there is nothing idle or contentious in her works. Rather, she does whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is holy, whatever is lovely, and whatever is of good repute; and she entrusts these things to her lovers to perform, so that by practicing the good they may obtain everlasting life. For the fruit of light consists in every goodness, righteousness, and truth.

> For she teaches sobriety and wisdom, justice and courage, things more useful than anything else in life to human beings.

Philosophers are not the only ones who hold that there are four principal virtues; our own teachers agree with them. Here they are called sobriety, wisdom, justice, and courage. Elsewhere, under different names, they are called prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

What these four virtues are, and what the works of each may be, we must briefly demonstrate, with the Lord illuminating us. Almost no one is unaware that the number four is consecrated to perfection. The whole world is found to be bounded by four regions or corners: east, west, north, and south. Adam himself, the father of the human race—or the general term “human being”—is expressed by four letters. The body too, constructed from four elements, contains within itself the mystery of the number four.

The ancients also subtly discovered that the soul itself has four affections, by which we use it either for good or for evil; later generations, approving their discoveries, accepted them. The four rivers flowing from the fountain of paradise, the four Gospels as the wheels of the divine course, and the four living creatures, with their four wings and four faces, abundantly commend the dignity of this number [Col. 0707A].

Therefore we must carefully consider how much holiness these virtues, which contain such perfection in their number, confer upon the Christian soul, and that nowhere is there any perfection that is not found in these virtues. For if temperance makes a person temperate, prudence prudent, justice just, and fortitude strong, then I do not know what could be more perfect than one who acts temperately, justly, prudently, and courageously.

It is difficult for us to identify the names of the virtues that arise from those four which we have called principal. But when we begin to disclose their properties and actions, the effects may perhaps reveal the virtues from which each derives.

Nevertheless, we must first know and retain that these four virtues, and all those that arise from them, are gifts of God. No one has had, has, or will have them except the one to whom God has granted them—God who is the essence and origin of every virtue. For at whatever time and among whatever people those who believed in God and lived by faith existed, they were able, through his gift, to become temperate and prudent, just and strong.

Those who lived without faith, whether ignorant of God or even blaspheming him, must be believed incapable of receiving or possessing any of those virtues from God.

> “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII).

Although they may have seemed to possess a certain appearance of piety, they completely failed to know its power, because they refused to submit to their Creator. Therefore, investigating various matters and pursuing different paths through inquiry and debate, they did not know the way of wisdom, nor did they find the way of instruction; and so they perished. Because they did not possess the wisdom of God, they perished through their own wisdom.

For God, our God, who is the fountain of life and the true light, the Word, power, and wisdom of God—before whom no other can be reckoned and to whom none is found to be like—discovered every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved.

> “Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III).

Therefore every usefulness of instruction, understanding, wisdom, and prudence must be referred to him, because:

> “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I).

Hence it continues:

> If anyone desires an abundance of knowledge, she knows things past and judges concerning things to come; she knows the subtleties of speech and the dissolution of arguments; she knows signs and wonders before they occur, and the events of times and ages.

It is clear that everything lies open to the eternal power and wisdom of God, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, and that all things are possible for him. Nothing is hidden from him, and nothing can resist his will. He does everything that he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.

He knows things past and judges concerning things to come. Through the prophet he says:

> “Before me no god was formed, and after me there shall be none” (Isa. XLIII).

And in Proverbs:

> “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning. From eternity I was established, and from ancient times, before he made the earth” (Prov. VIII).

And again:

> “When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he enclosed the abysses with a fixed law and a circle; when he made firm the heavens above and balanced the fountains of waters; when he set a boundary around the sea and established a law for the waters so that they would not pass beyond their limits; when he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering all things. I delighted day by day, playing before him” (ibid.).

He knows the subtleties of speech and the dissolution of arguments. In the Gospel he says to his disciples:

> “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke XXI).

He knows signs and wonders before they occur, and the events of times and ages. Instructing his elect about the future, he foretold the signs and marvels that would occur before the day of judgment and his final coming, saying:

> “There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves. People will faint from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. And then they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty,”

and so forth (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore I proposed to take her as my companion and live with her, knowing that she would share with me her good things, [Col. 0708C] and would be a consolation in my thoughts and weariness. The wise man, recounting many things about the virtues of Wisdom, finally added that he desired to be joined to her companionship, so that he might have consolation and relief from his weariness. Likewise, the people of the Church—who may truly be called king and genuinely wise, because they are members of the heavenly King and Lord—rejoice that they possess communion with divine Wisdom, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, as the apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (II Peter 2). They delight continually to remain in his embrace and spiritual banquet, knowing him to be most pious and kind, and the most generous dispenser of heavenly gifts. Thus he himself speaks in the Apocalypse of Saint John, saying: “Behold, I stand at [Col. 0708D] the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me. Whoever conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I also conquered and sat with my Father on his throne” (Apocalypse 3).

This passage can also be referred to the Virgin, Mother of God, who, possessing within herself the resolve of most chaste virginity, deserved to be made fruitful by the power of the divine Word; and by bearing the Son of God, she is venerated by all with the most renowned proclamation of praise for the salvation of the human race. Hence she herself says in the Gospel canticle: “Because he has looked upon the lowliness of his maidservant; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1). The words that follow in this passage also agree with this voice.

[Col. 0709A] “Because of her I shall have glory before the crowds, and honor among the elders, though a young man; I shall be found keen in judgment, and shall be admired in the presence of the powerful, and the faces of princes shall marvel at me. They will endure my silence; when I speak, they will look toward me; and when I speak at length, they will put their hands to their mouths.”

The Virgin’s childbirth has been wondrous to all ages. According to the word of blessed Simeon, he came for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign that would be opposed. Of him Isaiah also says: “The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples; kings will hold their mouths over him, and the nations will entreat him, and his tomb will be glorious” (Isaiah 11).

Alternatively, the assembly of holy teachers, instructed in the Savior’s teaching and enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, has glory before the crowds when, by preaching the Gospel and commending the word of God through miracles, it calls a multitude of the elect from all nations to faith in God. It has honor among the elders when it subjects the principalities and powers of this world to the Christian religion; or, according to the allegorical sense, it has honor among the elders when it is joined to the patriarchs and prophets in the heavenly kingdom. It is young and keen in judgment when it discerns and judges all things according to the decree of God’s law. It is admirable in the presence of the powerful when the kings of the earth and princes are astonished at the preaching of the Gospel; they look toward the speaker, and, marveling, show reverence, since they cannot resist the disputant. The book of the Acts of the Apostles and the sufferings of the holy martyrs under the New Testament testify that this happened very often.

[Col. 0709C] Thus we read in the aforementioned book that, when Peter was preaching, fear came upon every soul. “Many wonders and signs were also done through the apostles in Jerusalem, and great fear was upon them all” (Acts 1). Likewise, the same book relates that those who disputed with Stephen could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit by whom he spoke (Acts 6). Again, after Saul had received the faith of God in Damascus through the preaching of Ananias and had been baptized, he grew ever stronger and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus, affirming that “this is the Christ,” and acting boldly in the name of God (Acts 9). The same apostle, while preaching the word of God on the island of Cyprus, found there a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. When Paul discovered that this man was resisting him, he rebuked him and struck him with blindness. At once the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord (Acts 13).

Therefore through her I possess immortality, and I shall leave an eternal memory of myself to those who will exist after me. The saints possess immortality because, instructed in the truth of faith and rooted and founded in divine love, they already share in the hope of future immortality. Through the lessons of sound doctrine, the examples of good works, and the fruits of their virtues, they leave a blessed memory to generations that will come after them—and rightly so, because they will have a numerous crowd of faithful disciples from all nations who preserve their teaching. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0710A] “I shall arrange peoples, and nations shall be subject to me. Terrible kings will fear me when they hear me; among the multitude I shall appear good, and in war strong.”

Holy teachers arrange peoples and instruct nations subject to them to live according to discipline when, by explaining the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, they open them to understanding and make them obey the sacred sayings of the Gospel. They no longer allow them to depart, wavering among various sects, but compel them to preserve everywhere the truth of faith and the sincerity of doctrine. Even savage persecutors and terrible kings, conquered by these things, are forced to yield to their patience, because they are in no way able to resist the power of Christ, which works miracles through them. In the Gospel he says to his disciples: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16). And again: “Stronger is he who is in you than he who is in the world.” Therefore they themselves appear, among the multitude of believers, pious and kind; but in war they are faithful and most powerful against their adversaries. Now let us hear what Wisdom provides for them within, while they conduct these activities outwardly.

[Col. 0710B] “Entering my house, I shall rest with her, for her companionship has no bitterness, nor does her association bring weariness, but joy and gladness.”

After preaching the divine word and carrying out good works, by which holy men provide outward consolation to their hearers, they return to the dwellings of their own hearts and devote themselves to the contemplation of divine Wisdom. Thus, within, they find rest in heavenly sweetness amid the turbulent troubles of worldly affairs. For, he says, “her companionship has no bitterness, nor does her association bring weariness,” because bodily pleasures, when eagerly consumed, burden the body, whereas spiritual pleasures, the more they are received, the more they refresh the mind.

This is ordinarily the difference between the pleasures of the heart and those of the body: bodily pleasures, when they are not possessed, kindle within themselves a grievous desire; but when they are eagerly consumed, they immediately turn the one eating them toward disgust through satiety. Spiritual pleasures, by contrast, are distasteful when they are not possessed, but when possessed they are desired; and the more abundantly they are eaten by the hungry, the more they are hungered for by the one who eats them. In bodily pleasures, appetite is pleasing but experience displeasing; in spiritual pleasures, appetite is of little worth, while experience is more pleasing. In the former, appetite produces satiety, and satiety produces disgust; in the latter, appetite produces satiety, and satiety gives birth to appetite. Spiritual pleasures increase desire in the mind even as they satisfy it, for the more their flavor is perceived, the more one recognizes that they are to be loved with greater eagerness. For this reason, pleasures not possessed cannot be loved, since their flavor is unknown.

[Col. 0711A] “Considering and recalling these things within myself and in my heart: immortality is found in kinship with Wisdom, and in friendship with her there is good pleasure; in the works of her hands there is unfailing honor; in the contest of her speech there is wisdom, and in the sharing of her words there is splendor.”

Immortality is found in kinship with Wisdom because whatever is truly known about her nature is discovered to be wholly immortal and ever-living. In her friendship there is good pleasure; and the more someone advances in love of her, the more sweetly he burns with devotion to her. In the works of her hands there is unfailing honor, because she is the origin of all things, and through her all things were created—those in the heavens, those on earth, and those beneath the earth. Of this it is written: “You made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103). And in the Gospel he says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1).

In the contest of her speech there is wisdom, and in the sharing of her words there is splendor, because Wisdom opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent. Do not seek any of these things outside Christ. Everything that belongs to God is Christ: he is his Wisdom, his power, his justice, his holiness and redemption, and, to come to the present point, also his prudence. But because he is one in substance, he is called by different names according to the variety of meanings; “Wisdom” signifies one thing, and “justice” another. When he is called Wisdom, he establishes instruction in divine and human matters. When he is called Justice, the distributor and judge of merits is signified. When he is called Holiness, that virtue is described which makes those who believe in God holy.

[Col. 0711B] “I went about seeking her, so that I might take her for myself.”

This going about signifies the diligence of seeking and the zeal of meditation, through which the hearts of the elect strive to attain knowledge of Wisdom. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I will rise and go about the city, through the streets and squares, seeking him whom my soul loves. I sought him and did not find him; the watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves? A little while after I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 3).

[Col. 0711C] “I was an ingenious child, and I received a good soul.”

From the account in the Book of Kings we learn that, in his youth, Solomon asked the Lord for wisdom and a teachable heart, so that he might rightly judge the Lord’s people and discern between good and evil. He obtained this to such an extent that no king before him was like him, nor would one like him arise after him. In a certain sense, therefore, this statement can be fitted to him, since he received a good soul insofar as he possessed a wise and understanding heart. But we must see whether what follows can also pertain to him.

“When I was better, I came into a defiled body.”

Since Scripture reproves Solomon in many places because he loved foreign women, who turned his heart away, and because he offended the Lord by building idols for the sake of his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods, this seems to me more appropriately understood allegorically of the holy people. Regenerated by the washing of sacred baptism and instructed in faith in the Savior, that people received the childhood of a good disposition and a likeness to innocence; devoted to sacred studies, it strives to make progress and attain the summit of the virtues. Hence it follows.

## CHAPTER VI

That the Wisdom of God, which is the unchangeable good, came to the holy and undefiled Virgin, taking from her a defiled body; hence all generations call her blessed.—The lover of Wisdom asks God to give him wisdom, so that he may know what is acceptable before him at all times.

[Col. 0712A] “And when I was more good, I came into a defiled body.”

For it was written above that the keeping of God’s laws is the consummation of incorruption, and incorruption makes one near to God. But no one can attain such perfection unless divine grace raises him up. [Col. 0712B] From it, moreover, the gift of knowledge and the bestowal of virtues must be sought and hoped for, because, according to James’s statement, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). Perceiving this, the wise man consequently says:

“And when I understood that I could not otherwise be self-controlled unless God granted it—and that this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was—I approached the Lord, entreated him, and said with all my inmost heart:

## (CHAPTER IX)

‘God of my fathers and Lord of mercy, who made all things by your word and established humanity by your wisdom, so that it might rule the creature made by you; so that it might order the world in equity and justice, and judge judgment with uprightness of heart: give me the wisdom that sits beside your thrones, and do not reject me from among your children, for I am your servant and the son of your maidservant.’”

In the Gospel, after giving the example of the man who persistently asked his friend, shut inside a room, for three loaves, the Lord immediately turned his speech to the disciples, saying: “Ask and it will be given to you. Seek and you will find. Knock and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7). Likewise the apostle James exhorts his hearers to implore wisdom from God, saying: “If anyone among you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (James 1).

It is therefore clear that whoever asks rightly, and asks for the things that accord with God’s will, will not be deprived of the result of his petition. This cautious speaker therefore invokes God the Father, asking him to give him the Wisdom that assists beside his thrones—namely, the Wisdom that always remains and reigns with him and can never be separated from him. She is also his Word, through whom all things were made, and through whom rational humanity itself was created in the image of God, so that it might surpass all earthly creatures and, subject to God, govern the world placed beneath it.

In a higher sense, however, this can be referred to our Redeemer himself, who, sent by the Father into the world, deigned to be born human through a virgin, and who by his own will rules and governs the world of the Church. His judgment never fails, for, as the Prophet testifies: “Justice will be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his kidneys” (Isaiah 11). “He will judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth” (Psalm 95). He was not rejected but rather chosen by God; of him Isaiah says: “Behold my servant, I will receive him; my chosen one, in him my soul has been pleased” (Isaiah 42).

He also deigned to be called by the name of servant, and therefore the divine voice says to him through the aforementioned prophet: “It is too little that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to convert the refuse of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49). His mother likewise did not refuse to profess herself God’s maidservant. When the angel announced the divine birth to her, she replied in the Gospel: “Behold the maidservant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1).

[Col. 0713A] The saints are therefore his members. Through the Church their mother they have been reborn by water and the word, cleansed from the stain of sins by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and they humbly submit themselves to his service. The Son therefore prays to the Father, the head entreating on behalf of the body, that it may be enlightened by his grace and led along the way of justice. For he knows that whatever good he has in speech, will, and deed is his gift. Therefore he continues:

“A human being, weak and of short duration, and inferior in understanding of judgment and laws. For even if someone is perfect among human beings, if your wisdom departs from him, he will be counted as nothing.”

Of this it is also written in the Book of Job: “Is wisdom not found among the ancient, and understanding in length of days? With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding. If he destroys, no one can build; if he shuts a man in, no one can open” (Job 12).

It is plainly evident that, unless human weakness is sustained by divine help, it will fail amid countless falls and be reduced to nothing. We have been saved by the grace of God, and we possess every perfect gift from above. Understanding this, Paul says of himself: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7). And again he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; but I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (I Corinthians 15).

[Col. 0713B] “You chose me as king for your people, and as judge of your sons and daughters. You said that I should build a temple on your holy mountain and an altar in the city of your dwelling, the likeness of your holy tabernacle, which you prepared from the beginning; and with you was your Wisdom, which knows your works, which was also present when you made the world, and knew what was pleasing to your eyes and what was upright in your commandments. Send her from your holy heavens and from the seat of your greatness, so that she may be with me and labor with me, that I may know what is acceptable to you.”

The history in the Book of Kings relates that King David, wishing to build a temple, was forbidden by the Lord through a prophet, because his son, who would succeed him in the kingdom, was to build the temple for the Lord. Thus it happened that Solomon, who is considered the author of this book, built a magnificent temple for the Lord in Jerusalem. Therefore, the same king now recalls God’s benefits and asks that his Wisdom, through which he made the world, remain with him and direct his actions and heart according to God’s will.

But because that temple prefigured the Church of Christ—which the truly peaceful one, our King and Lord Jesus, builds daily through his workers, that is, holy preachers, for the praise, glory, and honor of his name—we may appropriately transfer these prayers, which Solomon offered for himself, to the persons of the teachers of the holy Church. They know that everything pertaining to the governance of God’s people comes not from their own ability but from a divine gift. Hence they ask daily that he who is the author of every good work may himself be the giver of supreme perfection.

[Col. 0714A] Whatever has been written about the Wisdom of God in the divine Scriptures, we must refer to no one other than the mediator between God and humanity. He is our peace, who made both one; he is called by the Apostle the power and Wisdom of God: “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him. He is before all things, and all things hold together in him. He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might hold first place in everything. For in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or those in the heavens” (Colossians 1).

Hence it follows:

[Col. 0714B] “For she knows and understands all things, and she will lead me prudently in my works and guard me by her power. My works will be acceptable, and I shall govern your people justly, and I shall be worthy of my father’s thrones.”

All things are naked and open before the eyes of God’s Wisdom, and no thought is hidden from her. Therefore she leads prudently along the path of the virtues the one whom she rules, and truly protects him from the injuries of adversaries. Making his works acceptable, she will render him worthy of the reward of the saints in the heavenly kingdom.

But since it belongs to God alone to know what he wills, and since he accomplishes all things by his own will, this praiser of God’s works suddenly fears and marvels at their greatness, and continues:

[Col. 0714C] “For who among human beings can know the counsel of God, or who can think what the Lord wills?”

Paul, astonished at God’s excellence, also says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory forever and ever” (Romans 2).

“For the thoughts of mortals are fearful, and our deliberations uncertain.”

The thoughts of mortals are fearful because they are fragile; human deliberations are uncertain because the soul is changeable and the flesh corruptible, as the following statement shows.

[Col. 0715A] “For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things. We scarcely judge the things that are on earth, and we discover with difficulty the things that are before us. But who will investigate the things that are in the heavens? Who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from the heights? And if the paths of those who are on earth have been made straight, and human beings have learned the things that please you?”

“The blessed person is always fearful” (Proverbs 28), and does not presume at any time to think, speak, or act. In contrast, the foolish people of the heretics are confident and ensnared, captured by their own words. Therefore Scripture says: “Whoever is hard of mind will fall into evil” (ibid.).

It is fitting for a servant of God to treat earthly things prudently and heavenly things cautiously, and to remember what is written: “Do not seek things higher than you; God created all good things in their time and handed the world over to their disputation, so that human beings might not discover the work that God has worked from beginning to end” (Ecclesiasticus 3). And elsewhere: “I applied my heart,” he says, “to know wisdom and to understand the order of affairs that takes place on earth; and I understood that no one can discover the reason for all the works of God, for the things that happen under the sun. The more he labored to seek, the less he would find. Even if the wise man says that he knows, he will not be able to discover it” (Ecclesiastes 8).

[Col. 0715B] Therefore it is rightly said here: “The things that are before us we discover with difficulty; but who has investigated the things that are in the heavens?” Yet, lest he leave us in despair concerning the investigation of divine things, he adds consolation from the grace of the Holy Spirit, saying:

[Col. 0715C] “But who has known your mind, unless you give him wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from the heights?”

It is evident that we can acquire knowledge of divine things only through the grace of the Holy Spirit, because no one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him. Likewise, no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. He himself enlightens the hearts of the saints and instructs them concerning invisible and heavenly things, so that they may perceive the understanding of the divine majesty according to their measure and be compelled always to love his goodness.

## CHAPTER VII

That through Wisdom, that is, Christ, all who pleased God are holy. That the Wisdom of God always remains with the Father before the ages, and through her all things were ordered under the Law, before the Law, and in the Gospel.

“For through wisdom all who pleased you, Lord, from the beginning were healed.”

He now begins to explain that through the Wisdom of God—that is, Christ—all who pleased God were healed.

[Col. 0715D] “She guarded the first-formed father of the world, when he was created alone, and brought him out of his transgression, and gave him strength to govern all things.”

By the goodness of the Creator, the first man was created and placed in paradise; by the ordering of his author he was set above all living creatures, so that Scripture relates that, after God had formed all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, he brought them to Adam to see what he would call them; and Adam called all the animals and all the birds of heaven by their names, as well as all the beasts of the earth (Genesis 2).

But when, because he transgressed the commandment, he was expelled from paradise and cast into the misery of this age, he was restored again through the divine Wisdom by which he had first been created—that is, through Christ. This is evidence of the great compassion of almighty God: he determined to restore the human being who had fallen into sin after being deceived by another’s persuasion, so that his work might not perish—the work which from the beginning he had made in his own image and likeness. “He made the nations of the world capable of healing” (Wisdom 1), and he who did not make evil acted so that his work would not become utterly ruined—that is, so that his work in humanity would not completely perish.

[Col. 0716A] “When the unjust man departed from her and went his own way, brotherhood perished through the anger of murder.”

This signifies Adam’s first offspring, Cain, who through the malice of envy departed from God and unjustly killed his brother Abel, bringing about his own destruction. When the punishment for that crime had been exacted in the Flood and Cain’s generation had been destroyed, divine Wisdom again preserved, through the construction of the ark, Noah, descended from the line of Seth, together with his sons, for the restoration of the world. The following statement demonstrates this:

[Col. 0716B] “Therefore, when water destroyed the earth, Wisdom again healed it, governing the just man through a contemptible piece of wood.”

In a deeper sense, Wisdom, governing the just man through a contemptible piece of wood, restored the human race when, through the Passion of Christ’s cross, it wiped away the sin of the whole world and led the lot of the elect to the entrance of the heavenly kingdom. But after the cleansing of the Flood, he next adds what Wisdom accomplished through a wondrous work:

[Col. 0716C] “When the nations had joined themselves in agreement with wickedness, she knew the just man and preserved him blameless before God, and she guarded a powerful mercy in his sons.”

After the devil, through pride in the construction of the tower, had deceived the human race, so that through this transgression the unity of the common language was lost, the Wisdom of God again united the offspring of Abraham in the truth of his faith. He gave them the Law and a worship by which they might prove themselves true worshipers of the one God. From his seed he also brought forth the redemption of the human race, blessing all the nations of the earth in him. Thus what the devil’s pride had confused, Christ’s humility, through his grace, united again in the knowledge and speech of all languages.

[Col. 0716D] “She rescued the just man from the wicked who were perishing, when he fled from the descending fire upon Pentapolis. As a testimony to their wickedness, its deserted land remains smoking, with trees bearing fruit at an uncertain time, and a figure of salt, standing as an incredible memorial of an unbelieving soul.”

Those who passed by Wisdom did not fall only into ignorance of good things; they also left to humanity a memorial of their folly, so that in the things in which they sinned they could not remain hidden. Wisdom, however, will free those who observe her from sufferings. Blessed Peter explained this statement in a certain way in his Epistle concerning God’s justice, writing: “He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes, setting them as an example for those who would act wickedly; and he rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the unjust conduct of the wicked. For by sight and hearing, while living among them, that righteous man tormented his righteous soul day after day with their lawless deeds. The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the wicked for punishment on the day of judgment,” and so forth.

The familiar account tells how God sent fire upon Pentapolis and, in just vengeance, condemned the sinful cities, reducing the most fertile land to a wilderness so that it would no longer produce a definite crop. This showed that condemned souls would burn forever in Gehenna without the fruit of repentance.

[Col. 0717A] When Lot fled from there and went toward the mountains, his wife looked back and, because she did not persevere in the journey she had begun, is said to have been changed into a pillar of salt. Mystically, this warns us that we who have been regenerated by God’s grace and called to eternal life must not look back toward the old person or, like fools, remain midway along the road. But the fact that the same wife looked back, remained behind, and was changed into salt provides an example for the seasoning of the faithful, so that others may be salted by them. Christ did not leave this unmentioned when he said: “Remember Lot’s wife”—that is, so that she might season us as with salt, so that we would not neglect things like fools but take prudent care; for this too she taught when she was changed into a pillar of salt. The Wisdom of God frees those who observe her from every suffering and preserves them perpetually in the repose of eternal peace.

[Col. 0717B] “She led the just man, fleeing from his brother’s anger, along straight paths, showed him the kingdom of God, and gave him the knowledge of the holy ones. She honored him in his labors and fulfilled his labors. She was present with him amid the deceit of those who surrounded him and made him honorable. She guarded him from enemies and protected him from seducers; she gave him a strong contest so that he might conquer and know that Wisdom is more powerful than all.”

Although this passage appears, according to the historical sense, to belong especially to the patriarch Jacob, who fled from his brother Esau and went to his uncle Laban in Mesopotamia, where on the journey he saw in a dream a ladder set up, with the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, and the Lord himself leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your offspring” (Genesis 28)—and who, on arriving in Mesopotamia, took Leah and Rachel, his uncle’s daughters, as wives, and for them fed his sheep for a very long time—nevertheless, although Laban tried by deceit to deprive him of his wages, Jacob was preserved unharmed through the Wisdom of God and brought back to his homeland enriched with great possessions.

[Col. 0717C] More generally, according to the allegorical sense, this pertains to the holy martyrs, whom divine Wisdom—namely Christ our Lord, through his mercy—freed from all the persecutions of their enemies and protected undefiled from their plots. He strengthened them by the grace of the Holy Spirit and by hope of the future reward, and finally, after all their enemies had been conquered, led them as most blessed victors to the eternal kingdom, so that there they might perpetually sing praises to him whose help they knew had preserved and saved them.

[Col. 0717D] “She did not abandon the just man who had been sold, but freed him from sinners. She descended with him into the pit and did not abandon him in his chains, until she brought him the scepter of the kingdom and power over those who oppressed him. She exposed as liars those who stained him, and gave him eternal glory.”

The historical account seems to refer to the accusations brought against the patriarch Joseph and afterward to his prosperity. Sold by his brothers, he was taken to Egypt; there, because of his mistress’s accusation, he was sent to prison. From there, through his interpretation of dreams, he was brought out at Pharaoh’s command and appointed ruler of Egypt.

[Col. 0718A] But just as the Wisdom of God freed Joseph from the hands of his enemies and made him ruler of the land, so also, in a particular way, it raises the holy martyrs from the punishments inflicted by persecutors and exalts them in the heavenly kingdom. There, enjoying eternal glory, they will come with Christ as judges of their enemies, assigning them eternal punishments for their crimes and lies.

## CHAPTER VIII

That he himself led the people of Israel out of Egypt, after whose type he freed the holy martyrs from the persecutions of the world.

[Col. 0718B] “She freed the just people and the blameless offspring from the nations that oppressed them. She entered the soul of the servant of God and stood against terrible kings with portents and signs. She repaid the just for the labors they had endured and led them along a wondrous road. She was a shelter for them by day and a light of stars by night. She brought them across the Red Sea and carried them through the mighty waters. But she submerged their enemies in the sea and brought them up from the depths of the underworld. Therefore the just carried off the spoils of the wicked, and they sang, Lord, your holy name, and together praised your victorious hand.”

He calls the Israelite people “the just people and the blameless offspring.” Descended from the seed of the patriarchs, they were worshipers of the one God, but they were oppressed by the Egyptians and other nations. They were freed from there under the leadership of Moses and Aaron and exalted by God’s miracles—namely, through the crossing of the Red Sea, the protection of the cloud by day, the brightness of the fire by night, and the other miracles that occurred among them in the wilderness in the greatest abundance.

Mystically, however, the Lord frees his elect from the hands of their persecutors and terrifies their adversaries through the radiance of miracles. He gives his servants wisdom, which all their adversaries cannot resist or contradict. Thus they stand fearlessly and boldly before the kings and powers of this world, speaking the word of God; and through the passion of the martyrs they attain the rewards of the heavenly kingdom, where [Col. 0719A] perpetually and without end they sing fitting praises to their King and Liberator.

“For Wisdom opened the mouth of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent.”

It is clear that without the Wisdom of God the human mind cannot think anything worthy, nor can the mouth utter it. Therefore sober understanding and the ability to speak soundly must be sought from him alone, because from him and through him and in him are all things.

## (CHAPTER XI)

He directed their works by the hands of a holy prophet. They journeyed through uninhabited deserts; in secluded places they pitched their tents. The earlier people, departing from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, traveled through the desert and pitched their tents in uninhabitable places, as the history of the Pentateuch relates. So also now the succeeding people—that is, the Christian people—journeys through the desert of this world under the guidance of prophecy, so that, with Christ reigning, it may reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom. The apostle Peter also makes this clear when he says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain; to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1).

They stood against their enemies and took vengeance on their foes; they thirsted and called upon you, and water was given them from the highest rock, and relief from thirst came from the hard stone. What that rock signified, from which the Israelites drank, Paul testifies when he says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). This rock, struck by the rod of the cross, which had been foretold in the hands—that is, in the writings—of the prophets, poured forth living water that fills all the elect and refreshes them with eternal satisfaction. Hence Truth himself says: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). And elsewhere he says: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give will have within him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4).

This rock, therefore, is called “highest” because it contains the most abundant grace of the Holy Spirit. It is called “hard stone” because it is firm and stable, upon which every wise person builds his house, so that it may not be shaken by any storm. Concerning this, Moses also says in the song of Deuteronomy: “They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the firm rock” (Deuteronomy 32). Nowhere is anything of this kind read in the historical account: if the whole sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed, nowhere did that people suck honey from a rock, and nowhere did it suck oil from a rock. But because, according to Paul’s word, the rock was Christ, those who saw the deeds and miracles of the same Redeemer of ours sucked honey from the rock. They sucked oil from the firm rock who, after his resurrection, deserved to be anointed by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Thus he gave honey from the firm rock when the Lord, still mortal, displayed to his disciples the sweetness of his miracles. But the firm rock poured forth oil because, after his resurrection, he had become impassible and, through the breathing forth of the Spirit, caused the gift of holy anointing to flow forth.

Of this oil it is said through the prophet: “The yoke decays before the oil” (Isaiah 10). For we were held beneath the yoke of demonic domination, but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit; and because the grace of freedom has anointed us, the yoke of demonic domination has decayed.

For by the very things through which their enemies suffered punishment—by the failure of their drink—they rejoiced when the children of Israel abounded. When these things were lacking to them, they were dealt with well. For in place of a spring of everlasting water, you gave human blood to the unjust. When their supply was diminished through the slaughter of the infants, you unexpectedly gave them abundant water, showing through the thirst that then occurred how you would exalt your own people and destroy their adversaries.

He recalls the benefits of God that were bestowed upon the earlier people through divine mercy, when, as they thirsted, he brought water from the rock and refreshed them with abundant drink. Conversely, he also recounts the punishments suffered by their enemies in the slaughter of their firstborn and in the various disasters that came upon them by God’s just judgment.

Mystically, however, he indicates that the people of God and the sheep of his pasture, whom the supreme Shepherd redeemed at the price of his blood, quench their thirst at the spring of living water, while their persecutors, failing through eternal poverty, will be handed over to everlasting death. Similar to this passage is what the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah against his adversaries: “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall praise because of the joy of their heart, but you shall cry out because of the sorrow of your heart, and because of the contrition of spirit you shall howl” (Isaiah 65).

That drink must here be understood as the drink that will arise from the springs of Israel. Whoever drinks it will have within himself a spring of water welling up to eternal life. The Savior also promises that he will drink it with the apostles in the kingdom of the Father—the drink that gladdens the human heart, so that those who drink may say: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5).

The mother of the Lord, filled with the Holy Spirit, also prophesied: “He has filled the hungry with good things”—those who previously did not possess the Lord’s food—“and he has sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1), namely, those who were given for his burial and rejected the prophet whom they had promised. Concerning them the Psalmist also sings elsewhere: “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Psalm 33), that is, the Jewish people. But those who seek the Lord—that is, the multitude of the Gentiles—shall lack no good thing.

When those who serve Christ and believe in him have rejoiced and praised the Lord with exultant hearts and gladness, then the others will be put to shame when they see that others have been received into their place. They will cry out from the sorrow of their heart, fulfilling what is written: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8), when the lambs of the Gentiles and of the righteous stand at the right hand, while the goats of the Jews and of the ungodly stand at the left—some receiving eternal rewards, others everlasting punishments.

The contrition of spirit caused by sorrow of heart is to be understood in the conscience of sinners, according to what is written: “Those who wander in spirit shall gain understanding” (Isaiah 29), and “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50). The spirit is crushed when it is lifted up, as is written of the wicked king of Israel: “The Lord hardened his spirit.” The same is written of the prince of the Babylonians, when his heart was lifted up and his spirit hardened, so that in his pride he said: “This is Babylon, and I have made it” (Daniel 4).

## CHAPTER IX. The text continues as above.

When they were tested, receiving discipline with mercy, they learned how the ungodly, when judged in anger, suffered punishments. Anyone who carefully examines the reading of the Old Testament easily recognizes how God often corrected the Israelites when they sinned, with fitting plagues, and again supported them, when they repented, with timely consolation. But the foreigners—that is, the Egyptians and Canaanites—he judged unworthy of his mercy and exterminated with harsh vengeance. Hence it follows:

“These people, as a father admonishing, you tested; but those people, as a stern king questioning, you condemned. For absent and present alike were tortured.”

When he says, “Absent and present alike were tortured,” this may signify, according to the historical sense, that not only those Egyptians who were present with Pharaoh before Moses and Aaron were struck by the ten plagues, but also all the others who lived throughout the land of Egypt were punished in the same way. Or it may refer to the time when not only those whom the Israelites killed in each city in their recent devastation suffered punishment, but all the peoples of the land of Canaan as well, who, hearing of the victory of God’s people and of the power of the signs performed at the Lord’s command during their deliverance, were greatly terrified by fear of them.

The words of Rahab the prostitute to Joshua’s spies also show this. “I know,” she says, “that the Lord has given you the land. For your terror has fallen upon us, and all the inhabitants of the land have fainted. We have heard how the Lord dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, Sihon and Og, whom you killed. When we heard these things, we were terrified, and our heart fainted; no spirit remained in us at your coming. For the Lord your God is himself God in heaven above and on earth below” (Joshua 2).

Although these things happened among the earlier people in the times of the Law, the reverse has nevertheless occurred: the Jews, who despised the incarnation of the Son of God and refused to receive his preaching, are tormented by various disasters, wandering and exiled not only within their homeland but throughout the entire world. But the nations that received the faith of God and turned from their idols to the true worship of the one God, whenever they sin, receive a father’s correction and are never deprived of God’s mercy. This is the changing of the right hand of the Most High: those who formerly were the head are now the tail, and those who formerly were the tail now become the head. “Lebanon has been turned into Carmel, and Carmel has been reckoned as a forest. The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Isaiah 29). Thus “the first shall be last, and the last first” (Matthew 19).

For double weariness and groaning had seized them, together with the memory of what had gone before. When they learned through their sufferings that they had been treated well, they remembered the Lord and, marveling, considered the outcome to the end. The one whom they had mocked when he was exposed in a wretched plight, they marveled at when thirsty, at the final outcome.

The ungodly have a double weariness when the memory of past evils is not diminished and the storm of present tribulations grows stronger. Hence they have no hope of relief in the future either. Although they may pretend to repent of their sins, they have no concern for their correction. Thus it is written of the Jews in Psalm 79: “When he slew them, then they sought him, and they returned early to him, and they remembered that God was their helper and that God Most High was their redeemer. They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him; but their heart was not right with him, nor were they faithful to his covenant.”

He did not deal with the righteous in the same way. Why does he not deal with them in the same way? Because they do not sin equally. “The righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked shall fall into evil” (Proverbs 24). For when the wicked person has entered into the depth of evils, he despises them. Hence it follows:

“For their senseless thoughts were the cause of their iniquities.” “According to their hardness and impenitent heart, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, for the hard heart shall fare ill” (Romans 2). “Judgments are prepared for mockers at the last, and evil shall pursue sinners, but good things shall be repaid to the righteous” (Proverbs 13).

## CHAPTER X. How he sent avenging beasts against the sinful people while they were sinning.

Because some of those who went astray worshiped many serpents and useless beasts, you sent upon them a multitude of many animals as punishment, so that they might know that by the very things through which one sins, by those same things one is also tormented. For your almighty hand was not unable—which created the world from invisible matter—to send upon them a multitude of bears, or bold lions, or unknown beasts of a new kind, full of wrath, or beasts breathing fiery vapors, or emitting the odor of smoke, or sending forth dreadful sparks from their eyes. Their attack alone could have destroyed them, but even their appearance could have killed them through fear.

Yet even without these, they could have been killed by a single breath, suffering persecution from the very things they had fashioned and being scattered by the breath of your power. It was fitting that those who worshiped a creature in place of the Creator should receive vengeance from the very source from which they sought help. For the whole world fights on his behalf against the senseless.

But because the kinds of unfamiliar beasts mentioned here are nowhere else found expressly in the history of the Old Testament, as though such monsters had bodily punished sinners, we shall transfer the passage more appropriately to the spiritual sense. We are to understand that all worshipers of idols, and heretics and schismatics who worship the sects of their errors in place of the truth, are deservedly punished by spiritual beasts—that is, by unclean spirits—from whom the Prophet prays that faithful souls may be delivered by divine grace: “Do not hand over,” he says, “the souls confessing you to the beasts” (Psalm 73).

Their appearance is terrifying, their cruelty excessive, and their fury immense, because their entire purpose is to pursue the human race with hatred and to reduce those whom they will torture with themselves to the torments of hell. But because God condemns no one unjustly and subjects no one improperly to punishment, it is therefore added:

“But you have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight.”

He does everything according to truth, judgment, and justice. Nothing in his works or deeds is disordered or inappropriate; rather, by moderating all his judgments on the scales of perfect equity, he governs and arranges them. This sentence may also be applied to the constitution of all creatures, because the almighty Creator created all his works, which he established from the beginning, with a definite number, measure, and weight.

Of this it is written: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name” (Psalm 146). Likewise, in Job, we read: “He looks to the ends of the earth and sees everything that is under heaven; he made weight for the winds and weighed the waters by measure, when he established a law for the rains and a way for the resounding storms” (Job 28).

Hence someone says: “All things whatsoever that were constructed from the primal nature of things appear to have been formed according to the reason of numbers; for this was the original pattern in the mind of the Creator.” From this came the varying multitude of the four elements, from this the alternation of the seasons, from this the motions of the stars and the revolution of the heavens. Since this is so, and since the state of all things is fashioned through the bond of numbers, that number too must necessarily remain always equal in its own substance.

Who, then, is sufficient to comprehend this measure, this number, and this weight of God, so as to be able to describe all his ordinances within these three definitions? In measure, I think, quality is established; in number, quantity; in weight, proportion. These are brought into equality in the judgment and mercy of God, because they are enclosed within these two holy limits, in which he established, governs, and will judge the world. Within these God, the just Judge, cannot be comprehended, nor can he be reproached.

Everything, therefore, that we have said above or shall say lies hidden from us for now within the enclosure of these three things. They will then be unlocked by the keys of God’s judgment and mercy, so that they may be known when, at the Lord’s coming, they are illuminated, and each person receives praise from God or punishment.

For great power has always belonged to you alone, and who can resist the strength of your arm? Nothing is impossible for the Almighty, and therefore no one can resist him. For everything rests upon the Lord’s will, and there is no one who can resist his will. “Whatever God wished, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses.”

The arm of the Lord means none other than the only-begotten Son of God, to whom Isaiah says: “Awake, awake; clothe yourself with strength, O arm of the Lord. Awake as in the ancient days, in the generations of the ages. Were you not the one who struck down the proud, who wounded the dragon?” and so forth (Isaiah 51). The prophet speaks in the person of the people to the arm of the Lord and entreats his coming, so that he who through many ages delivered his saints from dangers might, now coming in person, defend his elect from their enemies.

## CHAPTER XI. He praises the omnipotence of God, before whom visible and invisible things are all like a drop of dew and like a moment on the balance.

“For the whole world before you is like a moment on the balance, and like a drop of morning dew that descends upon the earth.”

A similar statement is read in Isaiah: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are reckoned like a moment on the balance” (Isaiah 40). A little later he says: “All the nations are before him as though they did not exist; they are reckoned by him as nothing and vanity.”

He wishes this to be understood of the mind, reason, and sense of the Lord through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made—the one of whom the Psalms sing: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32).

All the nations that did not know their Creator, or the whole mortal race, are, in comparison with God, like a drop from a bucket and like a moment on the balance, which is tipped to one side by a light weight. And just as a drop of morning dew is easily dried when the sun rises, or as a small drop falling from a bucket is disregarded by the person carrying it, so the whole multitude of the nations, compared with heavenly splendor, the ministries above, and the multitude of angels, is regarded as nothing.

Yet you have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of human beings so that they may repent. The power of God, therefore, always mingled with goodness, although it needs nothing, does not despise its work in human beings on account of their sins. Rather, by forgiving through repentance, it washes them from their sins and, with fatherly compassion, fosters and nourishes them so that they may return to him. Hence it follows:

“For you love all things that exist, and hate none of the things that you have made; for you would not have made anything if you hated it. How could anything endure if you had not willed it? Or how could anything be preserved that had not been called forth by you? Yet you spare all things, because they are yours, O Lord, lover of souls.”

A good craftsman loves, preserves, and governs his good work. Therefore, whenever human weakness turns aside from the way of truth by sinning, he bears with it in great patience, waiting for it to be converted to what is better through repentance. Hence he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5). But those who abuse God’s patience and do not turn to repentance are condemned by his just judgment, because “the Lord is just and loves justice; his face beholds equity” (Psalm 10).

## CHAPTER XII. Wisdom confesses that the Holy Spirit is gentle in all things and distributes God’s blessings throughout the whole world.

“O how good and gentle, O Lord, is your spirit in all things! Therefore you correct those who go astray little by little, and you admonish and address them concerning the things through which they sin, so that, abandoning their wickedness, they may believe in you, O Lord.”

The Spirit of God is gentle because he is himself the love of God and the giver of every good thing. He corrects human beings because he causes those whom he fills to correct sinners, just as Truth himself says to the disciples in the Gospel: “I tell you the truth: it is better for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I shall send him to you.
