And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment: concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer; concerning judgment, because the prince of this world has been judged” (John 16). Blessed is the person who hears the voice of this teacher and obeys his commands, for he will become an heir of the heavenly kingdom.

You willed to destroy through the hands of our ancestors the ancient inhabitants of your holy land, whom you detested because they performed hateful deeds against you through magical practices and unjust sacrifices—merciless murderers of their own children, eaters of human entrails, devourers of blood from the midst of your sacred rite, and authors and parents of helpless souls—so that the land, dearer to you than all others, might receive a worthy colony of the children of God.

Yet even with these people, as with human beings, you were merciful, and you sent wasps ahead as forerunners of your army, so that they might destroy them little by little. It was not because you were powerless to subject the ungodly to the just in battle, or to wild beasts, or to destroy them all at once by a harsh word. Rather, judging them step by step, you gave room for repentance, knowing that their nation was wicked, that their malice was ingrained, and that their way of thinking could not be changed permanently. Their seed had been accursed from the beginning, and you gave no pardon for their sins, since they feared none.

Historically, he recalls how the Lord expelled from their places the seven nations that had possessed the land of Canaan, because of the unbelief and injustices they had committed, and introduced the children of Israel—worshipers, that is, of his name—in their place.

Mystically, however, those seven most wicked nations signify the whole multitude of vices that, after the transgression of the first human being, began to possess the human race. But through the grace of Christ they have been expelled from the hearts of the faithful, and a multitude of sacred virtues has been introduced there, so that, once the impious possessors had been driven from the land of souls through the Gospel of Christ, the legitimate inhabitants—that is, the fruits of virtue—might, through the working of the Holy Spirit, bring forth living growth there.

If anyone thinks it necessary to ask how the Lord is said to have sent wasps, the forerunners of his army, among the most wicked nations so that they might destroy them gradually, when this is nowhere recorded as having happened bodily in the history of the Old Testament, let him know that many things could have occurred there as punishment for the wicked which the historian did not take care to express fully. Or, better, let him understand that “wasps” is here used figuratively for the terrors that the Israelites, while fighting the nations around them, inflicted upon them.

For the report of those wars, which were accomplished by the Lord’s power, pierced the hearts of the terrified with the sharpest stings of fear, so that it completely destroyed in them every strength to resist. This continued for as long as they faithfully offered worship to God. But after they sinned and neglected to serve God, they were handed over to the power of their enemies, so that those who had previously been subject to them later became superior to them.

For who can say to you, “What have you done?” Or who can stand against your judgment? Or who can come before you as the defender of unjust human beings? Or who can charge you if the nations that you made have perished? For there is no other God but you, who care for all, so that you may show that you do not judge unjustly. Neither king nor tyrant will inquire before you concerning those whom you have destroyed.

He clearly shows that in no way can the Creator be blamed for disposing of his creature according to his own will. Everything rests upon his will, and there is no one who can resist his will (Esther 13). Hence Paul says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me so?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9). “For from him and through him and in him are all things.” But “the Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works.” Hence it follows:

“Since you are just, you arrange all things justly; you consider it foreign to your power to condemn even one who ought not to be punished.”

Your power is the beginning of justice; and because you are Lord of all, you cause yourself to spare all. What does it mean that he condemns one who ought not to be punished, since condemnation itself is certainly punishment? Here, however, he has used “to punish” in the sense of “to correct,” as though he were saying: He who does not accept correction, you take up for correction; you justly condemn to eternal fire the one who is foreign to God’s power—that is, unworthy of divine compassion.

The power of God is the beginning of justice because God’s judgment, whether in the correction of the elect or in the condemnation of the reprobate, is the perfection of supreme equity. Therefore, through his goodness, he delays and suspends judgment for a long time, so that he may have more people to whom he can repay his beneficence. For when the proud creature rises up against its Creator and refuses to be subject to his dominion, he justly inflicts vengeance, lest the creature appear to prevail against its Maker.

This passage can also appropriately be transferred to the passion of our Redeemer, whom the Father handed over to death for us. Yet we must consider how he is just and disposes all things justly if he condemns one who ought not to be punished. Our Mediator ought not to have been punished for himself, because he committed no contagion of sin. But if he had not accepted an undeserved death, he would nowhere have freed us from the death we deserved. Therefore, since the Father is just, in punishing the Just One he disposes all things justly, because through this he justifies everything: he condemns the sinless one for sinners, so that all the elect might rise to the summit of righteousness precisely because the one who is above all endured the condemnation due to our injustice.

For you display your power, although you are not thought to have been perfected in power, and you expose the insolence of those who do not know you. The divinity displays its power in the correction of the guilty, lest the stubbornness of the proud presume upon its own strength. Yet he will receive this without any passion or disturbance, because God is impassible and never differs from himself by any change. Always remaining the same, he renews, disposes, and orders all things. The following sentence confirms this:

“But you, ruler of power, judge with tranquillity, and with great forbearance you dispose of us; for power is present with you whenever you will it.”

The omnipotent God judges all things with the tranquillity of his nature. But because God’s vengeance is patient, he appears to restrain his anger—although there is no such passion in him. Human affections, like bodily members, are attributed to God through figurative language, so that the divine utterances may conform to our manner and understanding.

Thus Scripture speaks of God’s eyes, ears, mouth, hands, and feet, of anger and fury, and of the other affections that are distinct in human beings. Yet the simple nature of God has no division, and true unity admits no separation. Rather, one and the same God always performs manifold and diverse works. Of him the Prophet says: “All things shall grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101).

The prophet Micah also writes: “The Lord will go forth from his place, and he will descend and tread upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains beneath him will melt, and the valleys will be split” (Micah 1). Likewise, in Isaiah: “The Lord of hosts will go forth, and he will crush the battle, and he will stir up the heavens, and he will cry out against his enemies with strength” (Isaiah 42).

God therefore goes forth from his place when he is compelled, for the correction of sinners, to break his quietness, gentleness, and clemency. Although by nature he is sweet, through our fault he becomes bitter—not to himself, but to those who endure the bitter torments.

Concerning his nature he also speaks through the prophet: “I am God, and I do not change” (Malachi 3). Hence James says: “With whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (James 1). Paul likewise says of Christ: “He is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1). And again: “To the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible God” (1 Timothy 1). It is also written in the Gospel: “No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him” (John 1).

## CHAPTER XIII. Wisdom praises God’s patience, because he gives sinners an opportunity for repentance and does not immediately take vengeance.

“But you have taught your people through such works that the righteous ought to be humane, and you have given your children good hope. For, when judging, you give room for repentance in sins.”

Through the wondrous works of almighty God, the faithful are instructed to beware of entangling themselves in the sins of the wicked. Rather, they should strive to keep themselves undefiled in their conduct and, while possessing faith and hope in the Lord, not neglect the time granted to them for repentance and good works. Indeed, with all their strength, through love, they should strive to serve their Creator.

“For if you punished the enemies of your servants, who deserved death, with such care, and then spared them, giving them time and opportunity by which they might turn from wickedness, with what care do you judge your children, whose fathers received oaths and covenants from you, together with promises of good things?”

The book of Exodus relates how the Lord, through Moses and Aaron, struck the Egyptians—that is, the enemies of God’s people—with ten plagues, and during the plagues sometimes allowed them relief, so that, once chastised, they might be corrected. But because they persisted in wickedness, they were cut down by divine vengeance.

The people of God, by contrast, to whom and to whose fathers the promise had been made, were corrected only moderately and were partly consoled, as long as they endured being instructed by discipline. But after they despised the Gospel of Christ and crucified the Son of God, they were transformed in a wondrous way from friends into enemies. Therefore they were expelled from their own land and scattered throughout the whole world, and at last, after being harshly chastised, they experienced what they previously had refused to understand when corrected by fatherly compassion.

We can understand this sentence in a similar way concerning the martyrs of Christ and their persecutors. When the persecutors tortured the confessors of Christ, they could, if they wished, have been instructed by their patience to abandon the worship of idols and submit themselves to the Christian religion. But just as the martyrs attained eternal glory through temporal punishments, so the persecutors, after the brief joys of this life, were plunged into everlasting punishments.

## CHAPTER XIV. How divine compassion commends its own goodness, which is just in all its judgments.

“Therefore, when you discipline us, you scourge our enemies in many ways, so that, when judging, we may consider your goodness, and when judgment is passed upon us, may hope for your mercy.”

This is what is written in the Psalm: “Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord” (Psalm 31). For there is a great difference between the judgment of the elect and that of the reprobate. The Lord corrects the elect in order to cleanse them from sins and restrain them from vices; but he corrects the reprobate so that they may suffer the penalties of their pride and unbelief and recognize that they cannot resist the ruler of all.

Blessed is the person who, in judging, always sets the compassion and goodness of his Judge before his eyes. Just as he wishes the Lord to have mercy upon him, so he should not refuse to have mercy upon others, because “judgment without mercy awaits the one who has shown no mercy.” “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5).

Hence, to those who in their lifetime lived senselessly and unjustly, through the things they worshiped you have given the greatest torments; for they wandered for a long time along the path of error, considering those things gods which are superfluous among living creatures, and living like senseless infants. Therefore, as though they were senseless children, you gave judgment over them as a mockery. Justly, those who in their lifetime lived unjustly and senselessly endured torments through the things they worshiped; and when they refused to know and duly honor their Creator, they were handed over, by divine judgment, to a depraved mind, to do what is not fitting, dishonoring their own bodies among themselves. In this they would have shame in the present and eternal torment in the future.

The Apostle Paul explains the truth of this matter in his Epistle to the Romans, saying:

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those human beings who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest in them. For God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things are clearly perceived and understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made: his eternal power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; rather, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible humanity, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents. Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonored their own bodies among themselves. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 1).

Thus their heart was so blinded that they changed the majesty of the invisible God—whom they had recognized from these created things—not into human beings themselves, but, what is worse and an inexcusable crime, into the likeness of human beings, so that God might be called by them the form of a corruptible human being—that is, an image of a human being. Those whom they would not dare to honor as living under the name of God, they received as images of the dead for the glory of God.

[Col. 0729D] What sickness, what folly, to call wise those who, to their own condemnation, regard the dead as more powerful than the living, and the dead as better than the living! For, having departed from the living God, they favor the dead. Among their number, as it is written: “A mortal fashions a dead thing with wicked hands” (Wisdom 15). Thus they diminished the majesty and glory of God, giving honor to the likeness of things that are least and insignificant.

The Babylonians were the first to call a figure the god Bel: a representation of a once-living man who is said to have ruled over them. They also worshiped the serpent-dragon whom Daniel, the man of God, killed, and whose likeness they possess. The Egyptians, however, worshiped a four-footed animal which they called Apis, in the likeness of a cow. Jeroboam imitated this wickedness, setting up cows in Samaria for the Jews to sacrifice to. They also worshiped birds, since pagans have sacred ravens.

The Egyptians nevertheless worshiped images of all the things I have mentioned, as well as others that it is unnecessary to mention now. These practices were devised by people who considered themselves wise in the world. Because they did not honor the invisible God by doing these things, they were unable to think rightly even about visible things.

Those who were not corrected by ridicule and reproaches experienced the judgment of God that they deserved. Indeed, those who were chastised by God’s scourges but were not corrected experienced the punishment appropriate to their condemnation. God chastises for the purpose of correction, unwilling that anyone should perish, since he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth. But whoever is ungrateful for God’s visitation and, through impatience, falls into murmuring is led from temporal scourging to everlasting torments. Therefore, concerning these same impious people it is added:

“For they were troubled by the things they suffered, and in their sufferings they were indignant. While they were being destroyed by the very things they had thought to be gods, they saw and recognized as the true God the one whom they had formerly denied knowing. Therefore the end of their condemnation will also come.”

Wretched paganism! For how long it served idols, deceived by this error, believing those to be gods by whose persuasions it was led astray, and for this reason was afflicted with various punishments. Hence many of them afterward recognized as omnipotent, in a just judgment, the true God whom previously they had refused to believe in through his benefits. He could not remain hidden who is evidently the ruler of all things: either here he shows mercy to those converted through repentance, [Col. 0730D] or in the future he assigns everlasting punishment to those who rebel through pride.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0729]

## CHAPTER ONE

On the error of idolatry: how idolaters themselves, in seeking the Creator among created things, could find him with his help if they wished.

**(CHAP. XIII.)** But all human beings are futile in whom the knowledge of God is not present. If every living human being is wholly vanity, how much more futile are those who do not acknowledge their Creator! All human beings are futile in whom the knowledge of God is not present—that is, the fear and reverence of God. Hence it is said through Job: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28). For the one who departs from the worship of idols departs from evil; the one who keeps God’s commandments fears God. “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Psalm 106).

And from the things that appear good they were unable to understand the one who is. From good works they could have recognized the good Artisan, who truly is: always unchanging, the only one who possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; who is always the same, whose years never fail; eternal and omnipotent, without beginning and without end, always abiding in himself, and by his will ruling and governing all things. Therefore the vanity of human beings is utterly vain when they venerate creatures instead of the Creator. Hence it follows:

“Neither did they pay attention to the works and recognize who their Artisan was. Instead, they considered either fire, or spirit, or swift air, or the circle of the stars, or mighty waters, or the sun and moon—the rulers of the world—to be gods.”

Some worshiped fire as a divine power, calling it Vulcan; others worshiped the ether or air, which they named Jupiter or Juno; others worshiped mighty water, calling it Neptune; others the circle of the stars, which they distributed into constellations and courses according to the various forms of animals; others revered the sun as a god, calling it Phoebus or Apollo; others the moon, which they were accustomed to call Diana.

Deceived by such an error, they attributed the power of the omnipotent God to their false inventions, so that one of the pagan poets concluded in three verses, saying:

> So many images of God, in forms so various,  
> He set upon the heavens, and scattered them through the dark shadows;  
> He commanded them to give bright lights to the ruined night.

But if it is impossible for the stars to be gods, then neither can the sun and moon be gods, since they differ from the lights of the stars not in nature but in size. If these are not gods, then neither is the heaven in which all these things are contained.

In the same way, if the earth that we tread, cultivate, and use for sustenance is not a god, then neither will the fields and mountains be gods. If these are not gods, then the whole earth cannot be regarded as God. Likewise, if water, which serves living creatures for drinking or washing, is not a god, then neither are the springs from which water flows. If springs are not gods, then neither are the rivers gathered from the springs. If rivers also are not gods, then the sea, which consists of the rivers, cannot be regarded as a god.

[Col. 0731D] And if neither heaven, nor earth, nor sea—the parts of the world—can be gods, then the whole world cannot be God either, although the Stoics themselves maintain that it is both animate and wise. For this reason they make God the world, although they were so inconsistent about him that nothing they said was left unoverturned by their own arguments.

If they considered these things gods because they were delighted by their appearance, let them know how much more beautiful their ruler is than they are; for the generator of beauty established all these things. Or if they admired their power and works, let them understand from those things themselves that the one who established them is stronger than they are. For from the greatness of their beauty and created nature, their Creator can be recognized.

It would have been right for the most beautiful and splendid Creator to be recognized through beautiful creatures. But they became futile in their thoughts and chose to serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. They are therefore refuted not only by the truth but also by their own words. Just as a house built for habitation perceives nothing by itself and is subject to the master who made or inhabits it, so the world, perceiving nothing by itself, is subject to God its Maker, who made it for his own use.

Thus the sinner is doubly at fault for his foolishness: first, because he prefers the elements—that is, the works of God—to God; and second, because he worships the forms of the elements themselves, conceived in human shape. They fashion images of the sun and moon in human form, and likewise of fire, earth, and sea, which they call Vulcan, Vesta, and Neptune.

[Col. 0732B] Such a desire for images possesses human beings that even things which are rarer are considered more valuable. They delight in gold, gems, and ivory; their beauty and brilliance dazzle the eyes, and they think there is no religion wherever these things do not shine. Thus, under the pretext of the gods, greed and desire are worshiped. They believe that the gods love whatever they themselves covet—whatever gives rise to thefts, murders, and robberies every day, and for which wars overthrow peoples and cities throughout the whole world.

Therefore they consecrate their spoils and plunder to the gods. These gods must certainly be weak and without the highest virtue if they are subject to desires. For why should we think them heavenly if they desire something from the earth? Or blessed, if they lack anything? Or incorruptible, if they take pleasure in things in which human desire is rightly condemned when it seeks them?

## CHAPTER TWO

The following continues as above.

But even here the complaint is still less serious. For these people perhaps err while seeking God and wishing to find him. Indeed, as they move among his works, they inquire, and they are convinced that the things they see are good. Yet even they should not be excused. If they were able to know enough to estimate the world, how did they fail to find its Lord more easily?

The Apostle Paul, writing to the Romans in his Epistle, expressed the likeness of this passage, as we have already shown above, saying:

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest in them, for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things are understood and clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, and his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Romans 1).

Knowledge of God is manifest from the structure of the world. For, so that God—who by nature is invisible—might also be known visibly, a work was made by him that would reveal its Maker through its own visibility, so that the uncertain might be known through the certain. Through what is impossible for all other things, people might believe that the one who made this work is God of all, “so that they are without excuse.”

No one doubts that the one whom they knew to exist and to work for their benefit had ordained the things produced for human use as the year unfolds. But although they knew him, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they became futile in their thoughts, saying that they were wise, and became fools (ibid.).

They consider themselves wise because they think they investigate physical explanations, examining the course of the stars and the qualities of the elements; but because they despise the Lord of these things, they are fools. If these things are worthy of praise, how much more their Creator?

Nevertheless, when overcome by shame at having neglected God, they commonly resort to this wretched excuse, saying that through these beings one can approach God, just as one reaches a king through his companions. Come now: is anyone so mad or forgetful of his salvation that he would claim the king’s honor for a companion? If anyone were found to make such a claim, would he not rightly be condemned for treason?

Yet these people do not consider themselves guilty when they place the honor of God’s name before the creature, and, abandoning the Lord, worship fellow servants—as though there were something greater that should be preserved for God! One approaches tribunes or companions through a king because the king is a human being and does not know to whom he ought to entrust the state. But there is no need of an intercessor to approach God, from whom nothing is hidden, for he knows the merits of all; a devoted mind is sufficient.

## CHAPTER THREE

He ridicules the error of idolatry in manufactured objects.

The hope of those who have called the works of human hands gods—gold and silver, the invention of craftsmanship, likenesses of animals, or useless stone, the work of an ancient hand—is miserable, and they place their hope among the dead.

They therefore come to the gods not so much for the sake of religion, which cannot exist in things badly fashioned and subject to decay, as to drink in gold with their eyes, to gaze upon the sheen of polished marble or ivory, and to handle with insatiable contemplation garments distinguished by precious stones and colors, or cups gleaming with inset gems. The more ornate the temples and the more beautiful the images, the more majesty they are thought to possess. Thus their religion is nothing other than what desire admires.

We have often said that silver and gold may be understood as speech and understanding. Since these were given by God to human beings so that they might speak or understand God and praise their Creator, they abuse this gift in fashioning idols, in accordance with what is written: “I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal out of my silver and gold” (Hosea 2).

When someone, terrified by fear of the Lord, first buries idols in the cave of his breast and hides them in the chasms of the earth, not daring to bring forth what he had wickedly fashioned, he then makes a second advance, casting away the images already carved and refusing to allow them to remain within himself, in accordance with Isaiah:

“On that day,” he says, “a person will cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and bats. And they will enter into the clefts of the rocks and the caves of the stones, away from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth” (Isaiah 2).

But let us see what is said further concerning images.

[Col. 0734A] “Or if some craftsman, a worker in wood, cuts a straight piece of timber from the forest, skillfully removes all its bark, and, using his craft, carefully fashions it into a useful vessel for the conduct of life, while using the remnants of his work for preparing food; and if, from what remains—serving no use—he carefully carves a crooked piece of wood full of knots, shaping it according to its natural hollowness and forming it through the knowledge of his craft, making it resemble the image of a human being or comparing it with some animal, coating it with red ocher, making its color red with pigment, and covering every blemish that is in it; and if he makes a dwelling suitable for it, places it on a wall, and secures it with iron lest it fall, watching over it, knowing that it cannot help itself—for it is an image, and the work itself is its support—then, making a vow concerning his possessions, his children, and his marriages, he inquires of it.

“He is not ashamed to speak with what has no soul. For health he begs from the sick; for life he asks the dead; he invokes the useless for help; for a journey he asks the one who cannot walk; and concerning acquisition, work, and the outcome of all things, he asks the one who is useless in everything.”

Wisdom has set forth these words to insult idols and idolaters, so that those who make and worship such things may understand how destructive and how close to eternal death it is to abandon the one omnipotent God, Creator of all, and to worship various inventions as divine powers, in contempt of God.

Hence, through the prophet, the Lord spoke long ago to his people concerning his own worship and the falsehood of idols:

“I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no other God. Who is like me? Let him call and announce it, and set forth for me the order of events from the time when I established the ancient people; and let him announce to them the things that are to come. Do not fear or be troubled. From that time I have made you hear and announced the future; you are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me, or a creator whom I do not know?

“All the makers of idols are nothing, and their most beloved works will not profit them. They are witnesses against themselves, because they neither see nor understand, so that they may be put to shame. Who has formed a god or cast a sculpted image that is useful for nothing? Behold, all who share in it will be confounded. For they are craftsmen, and they all assemble; they will all stand, tremble, and be confounded together.

“The ironsmith has worked with the file over coals; he has shaped it with hammers and worked with the strength of his arm. He will hunger and grow weak; he will not drink water and will languish. The woodworker has stretched out the measuring line and formed it with the plane; he made it with an angle tool and turned it with a compass. He made the image of a man, like a handsome human being dwelling in a house.

“He cuts down cedars, takes holm oak and oak that had stood among the trees of the forest; he plants a pine nourished by rain, and it becomes fuel for human beings. He takes some of it and warms himself; he kindles it and bakes bread. From what remains he makes a god and worships it; he makes a sculpted image and bows before it.

“He burns half of it in the fire; from half of it he eats meat; he cooks a stew, is satisfied, and warms himself, and says: ‘Ah! I am warm; I have seen the fire.’ But from what remains he makes a god and a sculpted image for himself; he bows before it, worships it, and begs it, saying: ‘Save me, for you are my god.’

“They do not know and do not understand, for their eyes are closed lest they see and their hearts lest they understand. They do not reflect in their minds, nor do they know or perceive enough to say: ‘I burned half of it in the fire and baked bread over its coals; I cooked meat and ate it; shall I make an idol from what remains? Shall I fall down before a mere piece of wood?’ Part of it is ashes. A foolish heart has worshiped it, and it has not delivered its soul; nor does he say: ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand’” (Isaiah 44).

The meaning of this prophetic narrative is as follows. When it says, “I am the first and the last,” it means the same as what is read elsewhere as spoken by the divine majesty: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 21).

It does not say that he is the only one in existence, but that outside his power and wisdom there is no other God. Condemning the opinion of many gods and their images, he says: “Who is like me? Let him call into existence things that do not exist, and let him set forth the order of my creation, by which I have brought all things forth in reason, from the time when I made the human being upon the earth. Nor do I merely wish to know the future; I also seek its knowledge.”

Therefore you, Israel, whose king and redeemer I am, must not fear the images that you learned on Mount Sinai are nothing. Or is there perhaps another creator whom I do not know, or besides this world another world that displays the power of an unknown god?

Not only will the things that are made be regarded as nothing, but so also will those who make them. When the time of vengeance comes, the works of their hands, which are blind and senseless, will in no way be able to rescue their craftsmen; rather, they will confound them.

For who could believe that a god is formed by his own file, drill, and hammer; that images are cast over coals; or that a measuring line, plane, angle tool, and compass suddenly produce gods? This is especially absurd when the craftsman’s poverty is shown by hunger and thirst. A wooden statue is made expressing human form, and the more beautiful it is, the more august a god it is thought to be. It is placed in a shrine and shut up in an eternal prison, although it grew over a long period in the forest and, according to the variety of trees, was a cedar, holm oak, oak, or pine.

In a wondrous fashion, its chips and shavings are thrown into the fire to warm the craftsman of the god and cook various stews, while the other part is fashioned into a god, so that when the work is complete its maker may worship it and beg help from his own work. Yet he neither understands nor reflects—or rather, he does not see with the eyes of either flesh or mind—that what has had one part consumed by fire cannot be a god, and that divine majesty cannot be made by human hands.

The prophetic discourse is developed more fully in ridicule of idols, but these matters are easy to understand and require no elaborate or excessive exposition. On this subject Flaccus also writes in his satire, ridiculing the images of the pagans:

> Once I was a fig-tree trunk, useless wood,  
> When the craftsman, uncertain whether to make a bench or Priapus,  
> Chose instead that I should be a god. From then on I, a god,  
> Became the greatest terror of thieves and birds.

[Col. 0736A] Whatever has been said about idols can also be applied to the leaders of heresies. They fashion and venerate images of their doctrines with an ingenious mind, knowing them to be fabrications of their own making. Their own error is not enough for them unless they have also deceived some simple people by their discourse; they think piety is a source of profit and devour widows’ houses. Abusing the ignorance of the common people, they fashion their god by dialectical skill, as though with a smooth axe, file, and plane; they hammer it out and gild it with the beauty of rhetorical speech. Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.

**(CHAP. XIV.)** Again, another person plans to sail and, beginning a journey across savage waves, invokes wood more fragile than the wood that carries him. Desire for acquisition devised the vessel, and craftsmanship fashioned it by its own skill. But your wisdom, Father, governs it.

This passage, like those preceding it, is placed as a reproach to idolaters. For it is the height of folly that a human being, created in the image of God and possessing from him a rational soul through which he was able to devise the art by which he might travel across the waves, constructing a ship according to his skill, should not grant honor to the one who gave him this knowledge, but instead invoke an idol which he himself fashioned by a similar art, though with greater vanity.

Since the human being is greater and better by nature and reason than the object he himself fashioned, insensible, into some image, he ought not to go astray so that the greater worships the lesser. The lesser should seek help from the greater, not the greater from the lesser.

From the divine gift one must ask not only for the preparation of a ship but also for a successful voyage, because the omnipotent Creator destroys whomever he abandons, while whoever is governed by him rejoices in complete prosperity. All heretics who construct various images of error in their doctrines are therefore engulfed in the waves of this world, because they have abandoned the ship of the Church and refused to have God as their helmsman.

“How you made a way in the sea and a most secure path among the waves, showing that you are powerful to save human beings, even if someone approaches the sea without a raft.”

According to the historical sense, the Lord’s power was demonstrated when he caused the Israelite people to cross the Red Sea on dry ground. Likewise, when they came out of the desert, he led the same people across the bed of the Jordan, dividing the waters on both sides, so as to strike terror into the nations of the Canaanites who were to be destroyed.

According to the allegorical sense, the Lord himself prepares for his faithful, amid the waves of the world and the torments of persecutors, a path of faith and steadfastness by which they may pass unharmed through every occasion of stumbling. There they will have no need of human comfort, where the power of the Most High displays the effects of his wondrous works.

“But so that the works of your wisdom might not be without purpose, human beings also entrust their lives to a small piece of wood. Crossing the sea, they were saved by a raft; but from the beginning, when the proud giants were perishing, the hope of the world, taking refuge in the raft, preserved for the world the seed of future generations, which was guided by your hand.”

The wondrous Creator gave his creature knowledge so that in the present world it might provide for its needs and serve the will of its Lord. Thus, in the beginning, when the human race began to serve idolatry and all evils were being committed on earth by the proud giants, the omnipotent Judge commanded his faithful worshiper Noah to make an ark, by which he and his descendants would be saved and the kinds of all living creatures preserved for the future restoration of the world.

The Apostle Peter explains the mystery of this event in his Epistle, saying:

“Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. In the spirit he also went and preached to those who were in prison, who formerly had been unbelieving when God’s patience was waiting, in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. And now baptism, corresponding to this figure, saves you as well” (1 Peter 3).

They say that the form of baptism is compared with the ark and the waters of the flood, and entirely rightly so, because the construction of the ark from smoothed timbers signifies the building of the Church, which is made from the gathering of faithful souls by the architects of the word.

And because, while the whole world perished, a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water, this signifies that, compared with the number of the perishing pagans, Jews, heretics, and false believers, the number of the elect is much smaller. Hence it is said concerning the narrow gate and constricted way that leads to life: “Few are those who find it” (Matthew 7). And again: “Do not fear, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12).

The fact that the water of the flood did not save those placed outside the ark but killed them undoubtedly prefigured that every heretic—even one possessing the sacrament of baptism—will be plunged into hell by those very waters, not into anything else, by which the ark is raised toward heaven.

The number eight itself, referring to the souls saved through water, signifies that the holy Church receives the bath of baptism as a sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection, so that, just as he rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we, cleansed from sins through the water of regeneration, may walk in newness of life.

“For the wood through which righteousness is accomplished is blessed. But the idol made by hands is accursed, as is the one who made it: for the latter made it, while the former, though fragile, was given the name of god.”

This is a comparison between two kinds of wood: one deserves blessing, the other a curse. The wood of the cross is blessed, for through Christ’s blood the world was restored upon it and the redemption of the human race was completed.

By contrast, the idol is accursed—that is, the image and worship of false gods—whose destruction is certain, while eternal torment remains for its maker. The devil will rightly be punished for persuading and consenting that divine honor be offered to him. Human beings who worshiped him as God will deservedly suffer torments for having attempted to venerate falsehood instead of truth and a created thing instead of its Creator.

But since we often find wood used in the sacred Scriptures in place of a human being, according to the rule of tropology, the person who speaks words of truth and does works of righteousness is blessed. The heretic, however, who venerates the inventions of his error is accursed and assigned to eternal destruction—both he himself and his work, that is, his doctrine, which he has presumptuously taught falsely in place of the truth. Concerning this it follows:

“Likewise, both the impious person and his impiety are hateful to God. For what was made will suffer torment together with the one who made it.”

Hence it is also said through Jeremiah:

“Every human being has become foolish through his knowledge; every maker is confounded by the sculpted image, because his cast image is a lie, and there is no spirit in them. For their works are vain and worthy of ridicule; at the time of their visitation they will perish” (Jeremiah 10).

Therefore there will be a visitation upon the idols of the nations, because they were made from God’s creation as objects of hatred and as a temptation to human souls and a snare for the feet of the foolish. The idols of the nations and their inhabitants—namely, the wicked spirits—are not worthy of pardon, because they were drawing human beings, created in the image and for the honor of God, away from their Creator and, by casting them into the trap of their error, were overthrowing them.

Likewise, if heretics persist in their wickedness, by which they lead human beings from truth into falsehood, and do not correct themselves or repent, they will not escape the judgment of eternal fire.

For the beginning of fornication is the search for idols, and the invention of them is the corruption of life; they did not exist from the beginning, nor will they endure forever. Although there are many kinds of fornication, the worst is that by which the soul fornicates, departing from God and worshiping idols.

Likewise pernicious is the abandonment of the truth of divine doctrine and the following of the falsehood of heretical opinion. The Apostle Paul also calls greed the service of idols (Ephesians 5). From this it may be inferred that every evil desire is rightly called fornication: when the soul, neglecting the higher law by which it is governed, is corrupted by prostituting itself, as though for payment, to the shameful will of lower natures.

But just as all these things were not created in the beginning, so they will not remain forever. For the Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and bring to ruin all who speak falsehood (Psalm 11). Hence it is also said through Jeremiah:

“May the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from the earth and from under the heavens. But the Lord God is true; he is the living God and the everlasting king” (Jeremiah 10).

The following statement shows from where idols first arose.

Human folly, then, devised these things throughout the world; and therefore their end was found to be brief. For a father, grieving in bitter mourning, quickly made an image for himself of the son snatched away from him; and he began to worship as a god the one who had then died as a human being, and established sacred rites and sacrifices for him among his servants. Then, as time passed and the wicked custom grew strong, this error was guarded as law, and images were worshiped by the command of tyrants. And those whom people could not openly honor because they were far away, for this reason had their likeness brought from a distance, and they made an evident image of the king whom they wished to honor, so that they might worship the absent one as though he were present through their devotion. The exceptional diligence of the craftsman also advanced the worship of such figures, including among those who were ignorant. For, wishing to please the one who had employed him, he worked by his art so as to represent the likeness as well as possible. The multitude of people, however, captivated by the appearance of the work, now considered a god the one who had previously been honored merely as a human being. And this was the deception of human life: because, serving either their affection or their kings, people bestowed upon stones and wood a name that cannot be shared with any creature.

Firmianus Lactantius, in the first book that he wrote on the false religion of the gods, brings forward similar material on this passage, saying:

> It is not obscure by what reasoning human beings began to be called gods. For, because of the depravity of human beings, who lived an uncivilized life without any ruler, there is no doubt that in those times they began to extol with the highest praises a human king and his entire people, so that they even called them gods. They did this either because, being still uncultured and simple, they truly thought this on account of the marvel of his excellence; or, as commonly happens, in flattery of the power present before them; or because of benefits by which they had been fashioned into civilized people. Then the kings themselves, when they had become dear to these people and had ordered their lives, left behind, once dead, a great longing for themselves. Therefore people set up their likenesses, so that they might have some consolation from contemplating the images; and, proceeding further through love, they began to honor the memory of the dead, both so that they might seem to repay gratitude to those who had deserved well of them and so that they might entice their successors to desire to rule well.

Cicero teaches the same in *On the Nature of the Gods*, saying:

> Common human custom, however, took up the practice of raising men distinguished by benefits to heaven through fame and popular approval. Hence Hercules, hence Castor, hence Pollux, hence Aesculapius, hence Liber.

And elsewhere:

> In most states it can be understood that, either to sharpen courage or because they would more willingly face danger for the sake of the republic, the memory of the best men and bravest heroes was consecrated in honor of the immortal gods.

By this reasoning, plainly, the Romans consecrated their Caesars, and the Moors their kings. Thus, little by little, religions began to exist, while those first people who had known them initiated their children and grandchildren, and then all their descendants, into this rite; and these supreme kings were nevertheless worshiped in every province because of the fame of their names. Privately, moreover, individual peoples honored with the highest veneration the founders of their nation or city, whether men distinguished for courage or women remarkable for chastity: thus the Egyptians honored Isis, the Carthaginians Urania, the Romans Quirinus, Samos Juno, Naxos Liber, the Moors Juba, the Latins Faunus; likewise Paphos Venus, Delos Apollo, the Macedonians Scabrius, the Athenians Minerva, Lemnos Vulcan. Thus various sacred rites were adopted among peoples and regions, while people desired to show gratitude to their rulers.

And why they should confer other honors upon those who are without life, I cannot discover. For this reason the piety of those who succeeded them contributed greatly to the error: so that they might appear to have been born from a divine stock, they bestowed divine honors upon them on behalf of their parents and ordered that such honors be bestowed. Therefore he says that they imposed a name that cannot be shared with any creature upon stones and wood: because they wickedly ascribed the incomprehensible name of the living and almighty God, who alone exists, to lifeless and fragile matter fashioned into images; and together with false religion they shamelessly destroyed themselves through every vice. Hence he says:

Nor was it enough for them to err concerning the knowledge of God; but also, while living amid the great war of ignorance, they call so many and such great evils peace. For either they sacrifice their children, or perform secret rites, or keep vigils full of madness; they no longer preserve either life or marriages undefiled, but one kills another through envy, or, committing adultery, causes grief. Everything is mixed together: blood, murder, theft and deceit, corruption and faithlessness, disorder and perjury, disturbance of what is good, forgetfulness of God, defilement of souls, alteration of birth, instability of marriages, disorder in adultery and shamelessness.

For they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents; and they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Although they called themselves wise, they became fools. For they were handed over to a disapproved mind, so that they might dishonor their own bodies [Col. 0740C]; and because they were unwilling to enter into a covenant with God through right faith and good works, they were placed under the worship of the devil and could in no way possess true peace with one another.

Therefore they sacrificed their children, as the gentiles themselves did in the rites of Saturn, sacrificing to that same Saturn out of hatred for Jupiter; and without any regard for compassion they extinguished tender and innocent souls, the age most beloved by parents. Others poured out human blood in sacrifice to the power whom they called Bellona; for the priests themselves sacrificed to her not with another’s blood but with their own, striking themselves with drawn swords. Concerning this Quintilian says very aptly: “If a god,” he says, “compels this, he is angry.”

Others, performing secret rites, kept vigils full of madness, as they were accustomed to do in the rites of Egyptian Isis and Eleusinian Ceres. For just as Osiris was sought there amid his mother’s lamentation, so here Proserpina, carried off into an incestuous marriage with her uncle, was sought. Since Ceres is said to have searched for her in Sicily with torches kindled from the summit of Mount Etna, her rites are therefore celebrated by the tossing about of burning torches. Likewise, in the rites of Father Liber, vigils full of madness were held; and also at the festivals of the Great Mother, where, in imitation of their gods—who, after being filled with banquets at her festival, passed the night in games—they spent the entire night in useless play.

The pagans themselves no longer preserved either life or marriages undefiled, because they thought that through lust and the impurities of life they pleased their gods. Everything was confused, where reason and true religion had no place; and the more wicked anyone was, the more he thought that he pleased his god.

For the worship of abominable idols is the cause, beginning, and end of every evil. No greater madness exists than to abandon the living God and serve dead idols. Therefore the worship of idols is the cause and beginning of every evil, because, after the human mind turns away from its Creator, it entangles itself in the errors of every crime. “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccl. X). Likewise, the end—that is, the completion or fullness—of every evil is the same idolatry. Nothing is lacking in any wickedness to the one who worships the devil in place of divine power; therefore everything is reckoned to him as evil and sin.

[Col. 0741B] For either, while they rejoice, they rave; or certainly they prophesy falsely; or they live unjustly; or they quickly swear falsely. For, while they trust in idols that are without a soul, they do not expect to suffer harm from swearing wickedly. Their whole life is established in errors. If they rejoice, whether at their festivals or their games, they rave, while either committing murders or polluting themselves obscenely with lust. When they prophesy, they deceive and lead their hearers astray. When they live unjustly, they are dead in soul. If they swear falsely, they are quickly led to hell. When they swear by idols, they pollute the name of God, who commands in the Law:

> “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. XX).

And again:

> “You shall not swear by the name of foreign gods, but in the name of the Lord your God” (Exod. XXIII).

But when they think that they can deceive God, they hurl themselves into eternal death. Allegorically, however, heretics who worship the images of their errors are themselves the cause of their own destruction: their doctrine is false, their life unjust, their joy insane, and their death abominable. Because, when they swear unjustly by an idol and do not trust in the true God, they despise justice and will receive the just vengeance due to their deeds. This he also indicates in what follows:

For the power does not belong to those who swear, but the punishment of sinners continually passes through the transgression of the unjust. Condemned by God’s just judgment, they repent too late and recognize what, while living, they had previously refused to believe. So also the Psalmist testifies, saying:

> “The Lord is known by executing judgments; the sinner is caught in the works of his hands. Sinners shall be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God” (Ps. IX).

## CHAPTER IV. He confesses to God that His wisdom governs all things.

**CHAP. XVI.** But You, our God, are kind and true, patient and ordering all things in mercy. For even if we sin, we are Yours, knowing Your greatness. And if we do not sin, we know that we are counted among those who are with You. Our God is kind, because His love is ineffable. He is true, because He deceives no one and is deceived by no one. He is patient and orders all things in mercy; for, patiently bearing with us because of His goodness, He awaits our conversion for the better, not wishing anyone to perish but everyone to be saved [Col. 0742A] and to arrive at the knowledge of the truth. Through the prophet He says:

> “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII).

If we sin, we cannot escape His hand, because we are His creature. But if we cease to sin and devote ourselves to good works, we shall receive a sure reward from Him, with whom the full number of all good deeds is preserved. For He knows everyone, and no secret is hidden from Him. What His knowledge confers upon us, the following statement makes clear.

For to know You is perfect righteousness, and to know Your righteousness and power is the root of immortality. Whoever truly desires to know God strives to abstain from every sin, as the apostle John confirms, saying:

> “Everyone who has this hope in Him sanctifies himself, just as He is holy” (1 John III).

And again:

> “Everyone who remains in Him does not sin, but everyone who sins has neither seen Him nor known Him” (ibid.).

To know God is perfect righteousness—that is, the highest perfection of blessedness—and to know His righteousness and power is the root of immortality. What, then, are the righteousness and power of God except the one of whom the Apostle says:

> “I speak of Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who has become for us from God wisdom and righteousness, holiness and redemption.”

To know God and His righteousness and power is the root of immortality (1 Cor. I); that is, it is the reception of incorruption and contemplation of truth in eternal life, just as Truth itself says to the Father in the Gospel:

> “This is eternal life: that they should know You, the one true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent. Him whom we now know in part through faith, we shall then know in truth, just as we have been known; for we shall see Him as He is. But now we see through a mirror and in an enigma; then face to face” (John XVII).

## CHAPTER V. On the various errors of idols, how they were introduced among the human race, and that the worship of idols is always the deceiver of human life.

For it was not the invention of human beings’ wicked art that led us into error, nor the shadow of painting, nor labor without fruit: a figure sculpted with various colors, whose appearance gives desire to the senseless person, who loves the likeness of a dead image without a soul.

He speaks in the person of the faithful, who, strengthened by God’s grace, in no way wish to mingle with the wickedness of the gentiles, nor do they deign to imitate their errors in idolatry and various crimes, because such labor is without the fruit of righteousness; rather, it deserves eternal death. Concerning this he adds:

Lovers of evil are worthy of death: those who place their hope in such things, those who make them, those who love them, and those who worship them. Therefore not only those who manufacture idols, but also those who love and worship them, placing their hope in them, are guilty and transgressors, because not only those who do evil but also those who consent to those doing it are worthy of death.

What sort of people those are who place their hope in their idols, the Psalmist shows:

> “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see. They have ears and do not hear; they have noses and do not smell. They have hands and do not touch; they have feet and do not walk; they do not cry out through their throat. For there is no breath in their mouth. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII).

A mortal fashions a dead thing with wicked hands, and a fool worships the most foolish thing. In the allegorical sense, however, the inventors and builders of perverse doctrines are the founders of heresies; their lovers and worshipers are their followers and disciples. All of them are guilty and liable to destruction:

> “All will tremble and stand, and together they will be put to shame” (Isa. XLIV).

> “The Lord will destroy this man who has done this, teacher and disciple” (Mal. II).

> “Woe to their souls, for evils have been repaid to them” (Isa. III).

But the potter also, pressing soft earth, laboriously fashions each vessel for our uses; from the same clay he fashions vessels for clean uses, and likewise those intended for the opposite purposes. The potter is the judge of the use of these vessels. And with vain labor the one who had shortly before been made from the earth fashions a god from the same clay, and after a little while returns himself to the place from which he was taken, repaying the debt owed by his soul.

Yet he is concerned—not because he will have to labor, nor because his life is brief—but because he competes with goldsmiths and silversmiths; he also imitates bronze-workers and displays his glory, because he fashions useless things. For his heart is ashes, his hope is worthless earth, and his life is cheaper than clay, because he did not recognize the one who fashioned him, who breathed into him the soul that works, and who breathed into him the life-giving spirit.

They also considered our life a game, and the conduct of life something arranged for profit, so that one ought to acquire gain from anywhere, even from evil.

Earlier he had spoken of those who fashioned idols from wood, stone, or various metals. Now he also speaks of those who followed the same vanity in the art of the potter, proving that they too were guilty through an equal error. For the gentiles fell into such great folly that they not only created idols from gold or silver, or even from precious stones, but also fashioned images in the same manner from cheap clay, calling him a god who had been formed from the muddy clay of the earth.

Therefore it was justly repaid to them that, although they had been made from the earth, they refused to follow the better part of themselves—that is, the rational soul created in the image of God—in worshiping the living God; and so they worshiped as god the baser part of themselves, imitating their earthly body in clay. In this way, afterward, without the fruit of good works, they themselves became senseless and useless to the lifeless earth from which they had been taken.

Mystically, however, all heretics and schismatics who suppress God’s truth in unrighteousness and worship falsehood instead of truth in the images of their doctrines are like this. Although they may sometimes possess an attractive manner of speaking or qualities that appear plausible, they will nevertheless prove to be altogether fragile, as though made of clay, because they fashion useless things. Therefore their heart is ashes—that is, their thought is foul—and their life is dirtier than every filth, because they do not know the one who fashioned them and gave them an intelligible mind.

But they vanish in their thoughts, despising the understanding of the holy Fathers, which those Fathers possessed in the divine Scriptures through the gift of the Holy Spirit. For human favor and earthly profit they shamelessly create new errors, as though they were empty games, wandering themselves and leading astray as many as they can, so that they may be without excuse on the day of judgment, when the Judge of all comes to judge the secrets of hearts and repay each person according to his works. Hence it follows:

This person knows that he is sinning above all others, who fashions fragile vessels and carved images from the material of the earth. For heretics have no excuse, because they sin knowingly: they refuse to follow the holy and catholic teachers in right faith and sound doctrine, but, according to their own perverse inventions, choose to mold an earthly and fragile understanding in their doctrines rather than a spiritual and heavenly one. For all foolish people are excessively proud in soul.

## CHAPTER VI. That all abominations were discovered by the gentiles because of idolatry, and that they suffered many torments on its account.

The enemies of Your people and those who ruled over them considered all the idols of the nations to be gods, although they had neither the use of eyes for seeing, nor noses for perceiving breath, nor ears for hearing, nor fingers of hands for touching; moreover, their feet were sluggish for walking.

For the proud enemies of God’s people and enemies of all righteousness, although they may appear for a time to rule on earth, are nevertheless exceedingly miserable, because they are foolish when they consider the senseless idols of the nations to be gods—idols that have neither sight, nor hearing, nor touch, nor any sense of life. They await the destruction of their souls in Gehenna, where there will be everlasting punishment and torment; for “their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished,” because they did not give honor to the living and true God but served the carved images that they themselves wickedly fashioned (Mark IX).

For a human being made them, and one who had borrowed breath fashioned them; no human being can fashion a god like himself. Since he is mortal, he fashions a dead thing with wicked hands. He himself is better than those whom he worships, because he lived, although mortal, whereas that idol never lived. A human being is better than idols according to the order of his creation, because he lives and understands, whereas they never do.

Nevertheless, because he followed the vanity of error more than the knowledge of truth, what the Psalmist says is fulfilled in him:

> “A human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

But they also worship the most wretched animals; for senseless things, compared with these, are worse than others. Nor can anyone, by looking at any of these animals, perceive anything good. Yet they fled from the praise of God and from His blessing.

The wretched gentile world not only worshiped as a divinity the human form fashioned in senseless objects, but also perversely adored the forms of other animals, and had no proper discernment in anything. According to the consideration of truth, living things are placed before the dead, things with sensation before those without sensation, and rational creatures before other living creatures. It was therefore fitting that those who did not know their Creator should also be unable to make a proper distinction among His creatures. For one who neglects to possess God’s praise and blessing within himself will prove himself to err also in the appearance and discernment of animals.

**(CHAP. XVI.)** Therefore, for things like these, they suffered torments that they deserved, and they were exterminated by a multitude of beasts.

If this is referred to the Egyptians, who, although they were idolaters and devoted to various errors, also unjustly persecuted God’s people, one can understand that in the ten plagues with which the Lord chastised them, because they refused to let His people go, they experienced the ferocity of beasts. For there, too, flies of various kinds and locusts are described as having devastated them; likewise frogs, beetles, and other animals of the earth. Concerning these it is written in the Psalm:

> “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; the frog, and it destroyed them; and He gave their fruits to the caterpillar, and their labors to the locust” (Ps. LXXVII).

In another sense, spiritual beasts—that is, evil spirits—tear apart, scatter, and destroy heretics, schismatics, and all wicked people. Because they consented to the will of these spirits, by God’s just judgment they were subjected to their power, so that the spirits might torment and destroy them.

For these torments You dealt well with Your people, to whom You gave the desire of their delight a new taste, preparing for them food, a quail, so that, while they desired the food on account of what had been shown and sent to them, they might also be turned away from their necessary desire. But these, after quickly becoming destitute, tasted a new food. For destruction ought to come upon those who exercised tyranny without excuse, while it was enough for the others merely to show them how their enemies were being destroyed.

It is read in the Book of Numbers that when the Israelite people desired the eating of meat in the desert, they received a multitude of quails when the Lord granted them; eating them, they were satisfied to the point of nausea. Yet the punishment of that very desire was not far from them, for the Lord’s anger was aroused against the people, and He struck them with a very great plague. That place was called “the grave of desire” (Num. XI).

Wisdom now recalls this, alternating its discussion between the destruction of the Egyptians and the correction of the Israelites: while the former, resisting God and exercising tyranny over His people, suddenly perished without excuse, the latter, corrected for a time and chastised in a disciplined manner, were nevertheless not entirely deprived of divine consolation. Hence it follows:

For when the fierce anger of beasts came upon them, they were destroyed by the bites of crooked serpents. But Your anger did not remain forever; they were troubled for a short time as a correction, having a sign of salvation as a reminder of the commandment of Your law. For the one who turned was not healed by what he saw, but by You, the Savior of all. In this also You showed our enemies that You are the one who delivers from every evil.

It is likewise read in the aforementioned Book of Numbers that when the children of Israel murmured at the thirty-fifth encampment, because they were weary of the journey and labor and because their food was meager, they stirred up the Lord’s anger against themselves. Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people. When many had been wounded and killed by their bites, they came to Moses and said:

> “We have sinned, because we spoke against the Lord and against you. Pray that He may take the serpents away from us.”

Moses prayed for the people, and the Lord spoke to him:

> “Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. Anyone who has been bitten and looks at it shall live.”

Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. When those who had been bitten looked at it, they were healed (Num. XXI).

But what is said here must be carefully considered: “The one who turned was not healed by what he saw, but by You, the Savior of all.” It was not the bronze serpent, which was placed figuratively as a sign, that saved them, but the sacrament of the mystery—that is, the death of Christ, who was represented in that serpent—which itself saved the human race. For “all these things happened to them in figure,” and “they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

But what does it signify that the wounds inflicted on people by the bites of savage serpents were healed when the bronze serpent was lifted up and looked upon, except that now, in the type of the Savior—who triumphed over the fierce and ancient serpent on the gallows of the cross—the poisons of the devil are overcome? Thus whoever truly and clearly looks upon the image of the Son of God and upon His Passion is preserved.

This is also signified by the words of the Lord Himself:

> “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III).

Rightly, therefore, the bronze serpent was the one who was hung on wood. Bronze is customarily more durable than the other metals, and plainly the bronze serpent was hung on wood, so that the Lord might be signified both as dead in the serpent and as eternal in the bronze: namely, so that it might be indicated that He was dead according to His humanity, yet was like bronze because of His divinity.

The bites of locusts and flies killed them, and no healing of their soul was found, because they deserved to be destroyed in this way. But the teeth of poisonous dragons did not overcome Your children.

The distinction must be noted. Just as correction sometimes tests and admonishes the elect, so that they may beware of sins, persist in works of righteousness, and carefully observe faith in God and the keeping of His commandments, so correction applied to the reprobate also casts them down and destroys them, because no worthy correction or amendment is found in them. Therefore, by God’s will, small creatures killed the idolaters; conversely, the power of poisonous serpents could not destroy the Israelites, worshipers of the true God, because “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment.” Hence it follows.

## CHAPTER VII. He confesses to God that He is kind and true, patient and merciful, saving the elect and judging the reprobate through His word.

For Your mercy, coming upon them, healed them; for they were tested in remembrance of Your words and were saved, lest, falling into deep forgetfulness, they should be unable to make use of Your help. For neither herb nor poultice healed them, but Your word, Lord, which heals all things. For You, Lord, have power over life and death; You lead down to the gates of death and bring back.

Note that he says those wounded by serpents were not healed by a poultice or by the work of physicians, but by the Word of the Lord—that is, by the Son through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. His power rules everywhere, and He does whatever He wishes in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses. He heals bodies; He also saves souls from spiritual beasts, that is, from evil spirits. No one can resist His will (Esther XIII).

A human being, however, kills his own soul through wickedness; and when the spirit has gone out, it does not return, nor can he recall the soul that has been taken away. But it is impossible to escape Your hand.

The human soul is killed through human wickedness—that is, through the evil of one’s own will and the outcome of a wicked deed. Hence someone says: No one can be harmed except by himself, because he is either himself the inventor of his own crime or the consenting supporter and ally of another’s wickedness. For if a person guards his mind and does not consent to an evil persuasion, he is free from every crime.

## CHAPTER VIII. He mocks the inventors of idolatry, showing how, when God judged, they were tortured by water, hail, and fire.

But the impious, who denied knowing You, were scourged by the strength of Your arm with strange waters; they suffered persecution through hail and rains and were consumed by fire. For, in the water that extinguishes everything, what was marvelous was that fire prevailed; for the world is the avenger of the righteous.

When Moses, by the word of the Lord, compelled Pharaoh to permit the children of Israel to leave Egypt so that they might sacrifice to the Lord in the desert, Pharaoh, hardened, replied in a profane voice:

> “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V).

Therefore he was chastised, together with his people, by various plagues. Among these he was struck by hail together with fire, as it is read in Exodus:

> “Hail and fire mingled together were carried along, and they struck everything that was in the fields, from human being to beast. The hail struck every plant of the field and shattered every tree of the region” (Exod. IX).

It is not surprising that two contrary elements—fire and hail—struck together, because all things obey the will of their Creator, and there is no opposition where divine majesty commands.

At one time fire was made gentle so that the animals sent by the impious would not be burned, but so that those who saw them might know that they were suffering persecution by God’s judgment. At another time, in the water, it burned with power greater than fire on every side, so as to destroy the wicked nation of the earth.

Thus, as it is read in the Book of Genesis that the Lord rained fire and sulfur from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord, in order to destroy the impious (Gen. XIX); and as in Exodus the mixture of hail and fire is said to have struck the impious (Exod. IX); so in the Book of Numbers fiery serpents are recalled as having destroyed the rebellious and murmuring, so that the insolent might recognize that every creature is ready to avenge the wicked when they are not afraid to rebel against the commands of their Creator (Num. XXI).

## CHAPTER IX. He proclaims that God gave the people of Israel, who feared Him, food of delight.

For these things You nourished Your people with the food of angels and supplied them with ready bread from heaven without labor, containing every delight and the sweetness of every taste. Your substance showed the sweetness that You have toward Your children; and, serving each person’s desire, it was changed into whatever each one wished.

But snow and ice endured the force of fire and did not melt, so that they might know that the fire burning in hail and flashing in rain destroyed the produce of the enemies. Here again, in order to nourish the righteous, it forgot even its own power.

Here Wisdom recalls that the Israelite people in the desert were given from heaven manna, exceedingly sweet and health-giving food, so that they might thereby return greater thanks to their Redeemer, who not only mercifully freed them when they were hemmed in by enemies, but also generously fed them when they were in need of food (Exod. IX).

If anyone thinks that he should ask what it means that snow and ice endured the force of fire and did not melt, let him understand either that it is there revealed how two contrary elements—fire and frozen water—struck the impious in harmony, or that some quality of the heavenly food given to God’s people as nourishment is expressed there: it endured the force of fire when necessary, yet, when necessary, melted in the heat of the sun.

It is also read in Exodus that in the wilderness there appeared upon the earth something white, small, and as though shorn like hair, in the likeness of frost. They experienced its taste as though it were fine flour mixed with honey, and it did not suffer deterioration from the force of fire. Hence it is written in the Book of Numbers:

> “The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance like bdellium. The people went around gathering it, and they crushed it with millstones or ground it in a mortar; they cooked it in a pot and made cakes from it, with a taste like a cake made with oil. When the sun rose, it melted” (Num. II).

Mystically, just as the harsh rebuke of Scripture is understood to torment sinners like the scourge of hail and fire, so the heavenly food signifies the consolation from above that daily refreshes the righteous and those devoted to God.

In another sense, manna signifies that bread of which the Gospel says:

> “I am the bread of life that came down from heaven, and I give life to the world. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.
