And again: The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world. And again: Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John VI).

Whoever, therefore, truly reaches participation in this bread will undoubtedly possess eternal life without end. The reprobate are tormented by spiritual hunger, while the elect are healthfully nourished by heavenly bread. The former are daily prepared by various labors for future punishment; the latter are daily nourished by divine help for eternal life.

The Prophet also testifies to this, saying:

> “Many are the scourges of sinners, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord” (Ps. XXXI).

## CHAPTER X. He relates that the Lord alone has power over death and life, governing all things by His command, punishing the impious with a scourge and refreshing the godly with heavenly bread.

For the creature, serving You, its Creator, flares up in torment against the unjust and becomes gentler in doing good for those who trust in life. This statement confounds all the impious and sinners: while the rest of creation serves its Creator, they alone are found to resist His will and commands.

But because no one can resist His will, they are deservedly scourged and chastised by the harmony of all creatures; and if they do not repent or correct themselves, they will be handed over to be tormented by everlasting punishments. True blessings are prepared only for the good, while unending torments are appointed for the wicked.

## CHAPTER XI. The following continues as above.

Therefore, at that time also, when everything was transformed, all creation served your grace, the nurse of all things, according to the will of those whom you desired, so that your children, whom you loved, O Lord, might know that it is not the fruits of birth that nourish human beings, but that your word preserves those who have believed in you.

Thus the people of God were cherished in the wilderness by divine mercy through manifold consolations. Manna rained down upon them from heaven; water in abundant measure was given them from the rock; they were fed with the flesh of birds; their garments were not worn out, nor their footwear consumed. By day the sun did not burn them, because he led them forth in the cloud of day, and throughout the night by the illumination of fire, so that they might become more devoted to their Creator, since he freely aided them in every necessity by providing for them. For this reason he cared for them temporally, so that they might love and understand him eternally, in accordance with the statement made in this passage: “It is not the fruits of birth that nourish human beings, but the word of God preserves those who believe in him.”

Moses also confirms this in Deuteronomy, saying:

> He afflicted you with want and gave you food, manna, which neither you nor your fathers knew, to show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Your garment, with which you were covered, did not fail through old age, and your foot was not worn down. Behold, it is the fortieth year, so that you may reflect in your heart that, as a man educates his son, so the Lord your God educated you, so that you might keep the commandments of your God, walk in his ways, and fear him. For the Lord your God will bring you into a good land (Deut. VIII).

But because they were always ungrateful and clung to the figures, unwilling to receive the very Truth who was coming to them, all these things were transferred to the fruits of the holy Church. For everything happened to them in figure. They were written for our correction, as Paul also plainly demonstrated when writing to the Corinthians:

> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ (I Cor. X).

Christ is the foundation of the whole Law and the truth of its figures. Whoever believes in him has fulfilled the whole Law; whoever does not believe will perish eternally as a transgressor of the Law.

Whatever could not be destroyed by fire immediately melted when warmed by a small ray of the sun, so that it might be known to all that one must anticipate the sun for your blessing, and that you must worship toward the rising of the light. We have already said above that the manna, although able to withstand the smell of fire, melted in the sun’s heat; but now, since he repeats the same mystery, we believe it sufficient to explain it.

That figurative food fed our fathers historically, but it melted at the rising of the true sun—that is, at Christ’s birth it was dissolved for spiritual use and transformed into a heavenly sacrament—so that we might anticipate the sun in blessings; that is, so that we might proclaim Christ’s divinity in eternal praises, saying with the evangelist John:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made, etc. (John I).

At the rising of the light—that is, at the Savior’s coming—let us say:

> The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

But let us see what follows concerning that carnal people.

The faith of the ungrateful melts and perishes like winter ice, like useless water. The hope that the ungrateful people—that is, the Jews—now place in the coming of their king, namely the Antichrist, melts like winter ice: that is, being cold in unbelief and without the fruit of righteousness, it withers; and it will perish like useless water, when their entire tradition of teaching is judged fit for no useful purpose. For our Savior says to us, speaking to the apostles:

> Leave them alone; they are blind guides of the blind. Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted (Matt. XV).

## CHAPTER XII

Wisdom praises God because his judgments are great and his words indescribable; he wondrously punished the adversaries.

**(CHAP. XVII.)** For great are your judgments, and your words are indescribable; therefore undisciplined souls have gone astray.

The judgments of almighty God are great, and indescribable are the words by which, through his wondrous command, he governs the whole of creation. For this reason the senseless souls of unbelievers went astray: they were unwilling to believe and understand their Creator, who made all things by his word, nor did they offer him the honor owed to him in the worship of devotion.

Nor is this statement contradicted by the fact that God’s words are said to be indescribable, whereas the Psalmist says:

> With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth (Ps. CXVIII).

The judgments that he wished to declare with his mouth—that is, to make known—are those that human weakness can understand and recount. But what God himself decreed should remain hidden, no one at all has been able to investigate.

While the wicked were convinced that they could dominate the holy nation, bound with the fetters of darkness and the chains of a long night, enclosed beneath roofs like fugitives, they lay there through your providence. While they thought they could hide in obscure sins, they were scattered beneath the dark veil of oblivion, terrified dreadfully and disturbed by overwhelming astonishment.

This recalls what the enemies of the people of God suffered in Egypt, in the darkness of night, which Scripture reports to have been so dense that it could be touched. In that darkness they endured excessive terror and were justly punished for the merit of their sins and their dark forgetfulness.

Mystically, however, all the persecutors of Christ’s Church—Jews, pagans, and heretics, as well as false Christians—suffer the enormous darkness of their crimes and error. They can nowhere be safe or secure; the rulers of these darknesses lead them according to their will and finally plunge them into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, to be punished with them forever.

That all evildoers are in darkness the Truth himself shows in the Gospel, saying:

> Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be reproved; but whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, because they have been done in God (John III).

And again:

> Whoever follows me, he says, does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John VIII).

Hence John also says:

> Whoever hates his brother is still in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes (I John II).

Concerning these people Peter likewise says to the believers:

> You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light—once not a people, but now the people of God; once without mercy, but now having obtained mercy (II Peter II).

Paul also says to the same people:

> You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light (Eph. V).

Nor did the cave that enclosed them guard them without fear. A sound descending upon them disturbed them, and grim faces appearing to them caused them terror. No power of fire could provide them with light, nor could the clear flames of the stars illuminate that dreadful night.

Horror always accompanies darkness; and the less a person can see and distinguish what is around him, the greater fear he has, suspecting danger on every side and dreading injury. The same happened to the Egyptians when they endured the greatest darkness for three days, which neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even the stars could illuminate. Wherever they hid, they trembled with overwhelming terror.

When it says that grim faces appearing to them caused terror, it may have happened that, through the machinations of evil spirits, certain phantoms appeared to them and inflicted excessive horror upon them, increasing their punishments.

Similarly, now also, darknesses of their sins surround on every side the persecutors of Christian faith and the enemies of truth, because they do not know the sun of righteousness, nor do the holy teachers illuminate them in any way with the radiance of their doctrines. The descending sound—that is, the heavenly preaching proclaiming the punishments that await them—disturbs them; and the grim faces—that is, the demons who will torture them—terrify them in anticipation.

Yet this does not produce fruitful repentance in them. Rather, after they have become worse, it prepares them without cessation for eternal destruction. For when they despair of themselves and are unwilling to correct themselves by abandoning their error and doing works of righteousness, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who renders to each according to his works.

## CHAPTER XIII

That savage presumption always troubles the conscience of the wicked, and that they are tormented after being terrified by various dreams and imaginings.

A sudden fire, full of fear, appeared to them; and, struck with terror at the unseen face, they judged the things that were seen to be worse. When that fire which scourged the wicked appeared, they were terrified and feared punishments on every side, because the more grievous the pains of punishment a person feels, the greater the horrors he fears will come upon him.

Their magical art was held up to derision, and the glory of their wisdom was reproved with disgrace. Those who promised to drive fears, terrors, and disturbances from the suffering soul themselves languished in fear amid derision. For although none of the apparitions disturbed them, they were shaken by the movement of animals and the hissing of serpents and perished trembling.

The Book of Exodus recalls how the magicians in Egypt resisted Moses, performing false wonders through magical incantations and deceiving the people. But when they saw themselves overcome by the power of the signs divinely performed through Moses and Aaron, they were forced to confess that this was the finger of God who accomplished these great deeds (Exod. VII). Those who shortly before proudly claimed to be physicians of every sickness were themselves afflicted by equal fear when serpents and other animals came upon them and tormented them.

So now also, in the times of grace, all who ridicule the Christian religion and boast of their own arts—that is, the diviners and haruspices of the pagans—as well as those who have withdrawn through apostasy from the unity of the Church, such as heretics and schismatics, are truly overcome by Christ’s power, although they pretend to be victorious. In the end they will suffer the ancient serpent, with his most savage followers, as their enemy.

And the air, from which no one could escape by any means, they denied that they saw. For they were often seized beforehand, when their very evil conscience rebuked them. Since wickedness is timid, it gives testimony that it has been condemned.

By saying that those wicked men denied seeing the air, whose presence every living and breathing creature cannot at some time avoid, the passage expresses the excess of fear that they suffered because of the oppression of impending punishments, while their evil conscience rebuked them. Since wickedness is always timid, its fear begins the punishments to which it has been condemned.

For a savage and disturbed conscience always presumes. Fear is nothing other than an aid to presumption, a betrayal of the mind’s imagined resources. When its expectation is less within, it considers the cause from which its torment increases to be greater.

A conscience that is always troubled and does not possess the serenity of tranquility raises itself presumptuously; but fear itself suppresses that presumption. Hence fear is said to be its aid—that is, its medicine. It also reveals the weakness of the mind that is puffed up, which deluded itself through thoughts of empty hopes of help, when it hoped that it could accomplish what it could complete by no means.

Thus, while its inner capacity was weaker than the things it suffered outwardly, it judged their power to be greater. The same often happens to the persecutors of the faithful. Because of the blindness of their hearts they consider themselves powerful when they torture the bodies of the saints with various punishments. But when, overcome by their endurance, they see that they cannot accomplish what they wished, they are crushed by the anguish of their own minds and finally recognize that they are not what they had previously imagined themselves to be. They perceive that the greater strength belongs to him who granted his soldiers the endurance to bear punishments and the power to overcome their enemies.

Those men, while sleeping a powerless night that came upon them from the lowest and highest regions of hell, were sometimes shaken by fear of apparitions, and sometimes their souls failed through terror. A sudden and unexpected fear had come upon them.

Then, if any one of them fell, he was guarded in prison, confined without iron. This refers to the fact that in Egypt the enemies of the people of God were surrounded by the horror of darkness and had no rest, whether awake or asleep. Either they were tormented in sleep by dreadful visions, or, while awake, they were afflicted by overwhelming terror. They were not given the freedom to withdraw anywhere, but were enclosed in a prison of darkness without fetter or iron chain.

Hence it is written:

> For three days no one saw his brother, nor did anyone move from the place where he was (Exod. X).

If any one of them was a countryman, a shepherd, or a laborer engaged in agricultural work, he was seized by an inescapable necessity. They were all bound by one chain of darkness.

Whether it was the whistling of a spirit, the sweet sound of birds among the dense branches of trees, the excessive force of running water, the loud noise of rocks hurled down, the unseen movement of playful animals, the powerful roar of bellowing beasts, or an echo resounding from the highest mountains—all these things caused them to faint with fear. The wretched were constrained by punishment on every side, because whatever they perceived with their ears as sound or sensed by any other faculty, they feared was directed toward their destruction.

The whole earth was illuminated by clear light, and its activities continued without hindrance. But only over them lay a heavy night, an image of the darkness that was to come upon them. They themselves were heavier than darkness.

Only the wicked were in darkness; the worshipers of God, however, abounded in the most generous light. Thus it is written:

> Wherever the children of Israel dwelt, there was light (Exod. X).

But we must also consider what he says: “Only over them lay a heavy night, an image of the darkness that was to come upon them, for they themselves were heavier than darkness.” This shows altogether that spiritual darkness, which the mind suffers, is heavier than bodily darkness, which the eye endures.

From these darknesses—that is, from unbelief, error, and crimes—a person is brought to the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. The darkness of the Egyptians had expressed this figuratively: just as their bodies there were held useless for every good work, so here both bodies and souls are enclosed in an eternal prison, incapable of every good work, since among the dead there is neither reason, place, nor time for doing works.

## CHAPTER XIV

Concerning the saints: in the darkness of Egypt, that is, the errors of the world, they were illuminated by divine light.

**(CHAP. XVIII.)** But your saints had the greatest light. Their voices they heard, but they did not see their form. And because they themselves had not suffered the same things, they magnified you; and those who had previously been harmed gave thanks because they were not being harmed. To establish a distinction, they asked for a gift.

Therefore you gave them a flaming pillar of fire as guide along an unknown way, and the sun without harm for their honorable hospitality.

The saints of God had the greatest light when they were illuminated both outwardly by bodily light and inwardly by spiritual light. The faith of God and purity of conscience illumined them within. Their enemies heard their voice but did not see their form, because darkness had blinded their eyes. And because they were not struck by the plague of temptation that had come upon the Egyptians, but were led by heavenly guidance—by the pillar of fire at night and the pillar of cloud by day—they rendered worthy thanks to their Creator.

Since those holy fathers who lived under the Old Testament prefigured the saints who serve Christ under the New Testament, the former labored under affliction in historical Egypt beneath Pharaoh, while the latter are wearied in the world by the pressures of the devil’s persecution. The greatest light shines upon those who diligently carry within the dwelling of their hearts the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world.

Their enemies hear the voice of their preaching, but do not recognize the form of the truth that is in them; therefore they do not believe them. The pillar of fire at night and the pillar of cloud by day lead them, because Christ’s incarnation always protects them in adversity and prosperity with the defense of his protection.

Those who guarded your sons in confinement were worthy to be deprived of light and to suffer the prison of darkness. They were plotting to kill the infants of the righteous; and when one child had been exposed and rescued, you took away a multitude of their children to their destruction, and destroyed them together in mighty water.

That night had been known beforehand by our fathers, so that, knowing truly in what oaths they had trusted, they might be more confident. The Egyptians deservedly endured the punishments of darkness. Blinded by the obscurity of envy, they wished to keep in their prison the people of God, through whom the incorruptible light of the Law was beginning to be given to the world. Since they also planned to kill their infants, one child—that is, Moses—was rescued by God’s judgment from death in the water, while through his ministry a multitude of the adversaries was drowned in mighty water.

So now also, when the spiritual enemies who seek to destroy the assembly of the faithful are defeated, God’s elect are freed from their enemies through the water of baptism, while those enemies alone, together with their king, the devil, are overwhelmed by Christ’s power in those same waters. The meaning of this mystery was prefigured long ago in the deeds of the ancients and has now been fulfilled through Christ’s coming.

## CHAPTER XV

Concerning the destroyer of Egypt, who did not dare to touch the Hebrew doorposts consecrated with the blood of the lamb.

Health for the righteous was received by your people, but destruction for the unjust. For just as you harmed the adversaries, so, by calling us forth, you magnified us.

For the righteous children of good people were secretly offering sacrifice and established the law of righteousness in concord, already chanting the praises of the fathers, while the righteous and the wicked were alike to receive good things and evil things.

At the time when the people of God were to be led out of Egypt by Moses and Aaron, that people, while still dwelling in Egypt, sacrificed the Passover victim at the Lord’s command. Therefore he says that they sacrificed secretly, because, terrified by fear of their enemies, they performed the rite covertly. They had also learned through Moses’ teaching how the law of Passover was thereafter to be observed. For a time they endured the trial imposed by the reprobate, but by divine help they were soon to be freed from the hands of their enemies.

In the same way now, in the times of grace, the servants of God, to whom the divine Law has been given in harmony with the two Testaments, may for a time be hindered outwardly by their persecutors from celebrating the worship of the Christian religion openly. Nevertheless, they can in no way be prevented from offering sacrifices worthy of the divine sight in the hidden places of their hearts, because it is written:

> A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise (Ps. L).

The same Prophet also says:

> In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay in praises to you (Ps. LV).

The vows of the righteous are pleasing to the Lord, but the sacrifices of the wicked are abominable.

The discordant voice of the enemies resounded, and the mourners’ lament for the infants was heard. Servant and master were afflicted by the same punishment, and subject and king suffered alike. Thus all, under one name of death, had countless dead.

The living were not sufficient even to bury them, for in a single moment their most distinguished nation was destroyed. Since they had not believed in any of this because of their magical practices, it was only then, for the first time, at the destruction of the firstborn, that they acknowledged the people of God.

This recalls what the Book of Exodus relates concerning the killing of the firstborn, when the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt in the middle of the night, from Pharaoh’s firstborn, who sat upon his throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, as well as every firstborn of the animals (Exod. XII). At that point they no longer pretended, as before, to agree to Israel’s departure, but openly urged the people of God to leave the land of Egypt quickly, saying:

> We shall all die.

When quiet silence held everything, and night had reached the midpoint of its course, your almighty Word leaped down from heaven, from the royal thrones, as a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction. Carrying your unfeigned command like a sharp sword, he stood and filled everything with death, and, standing upon the earth, reached even to heaven.

He says that in the middle of the night the almighty God’s Word leaped down from heaven, from the royal thrones, as a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction, and powerfully exercised the judgment of death upon the wicked.

For who is the Lord’s Word if not the Son of God? Concerning him John says:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word (John I).

Through him all things were made. Elsewhere he is called the arm of the Lord, as Isaiah says:

> And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? (Isa. LIII).

He is also called the right hand of the Lord because of the effective power of divine strength.

The Word himself must therefore be understood as exercising judgment through the evangelical ministry at that time upon the firstborn of the Egyptians. Later he would sanctify the firstborn of the Israelites for himself; and now, through the water of his baptism, he saves the multitude of believers, where he also destroyed the innumerable army of spiritual enemies.

He is said to have carried the Lord’s unfeigned command like a sharp sword, because the Word of the Lord is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword. In truth and without any deceit he judges and orders all things. Standing upon the earth, he reaches to the heavens, because although, having become incarnate, he lived among human beings on earth, in his majesty he nevertheless transcends all the heavenly realms.

Then the visions of evil dreams immediately disturbed them, and unexpected fears came upon them. One person, cast down in one place and half alive, showed why he was dying.

The visions that disturbed them foretold these things, so that they would not perish without knowing why they were suffering evil. It is rightly said that visions of evil dreams and unexpected fears disturbed the enemies of the people of God, so that no rest was granted to them, whether awake or asleep, since, because of their crimes, they were destined for eternal punishments.

That the plagues themselves warned the guilty so that they might recognize why they were suffering evil, lest they perish without understanding, is an expression of God’s goodness. He chastises sinners so that they may restrain themselves from sins and repent of past evils. But if they persist in evil and abuse God’s patience to increase their crimes, then, condemned by God’s just judgment, they will be punished in the future without excuse.

## CHAPTER XVI

Concerning Moses and Aaron: he relates that they led the people out of Egypt not by bodily strength but by faith and prayer.

At that time the trial of death also touched the righteous, and a disturbance of the multitude arose in the wilderness, but it did not long continue in your anger. A blameless man hastened to intercede for the peoples. Bringing forward the shield of his service and pleading his prayer with incense, he resisted the anger and put an end to the calamity, showing that he was your servant.

He overcame the crowds not by bodily strength or the power of weapons, but by the word he subdued the one who was afflicting them, recalling the oaths sworn to the fathers and the covenant.

Here he recalls the history related in the Book of Numbers: after the destruction of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying:

> You have killed the people of God.

When rebellion arose and the tumult increased, Moses and Aaron fled to the tent of the covenant. The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:

> Depart from the midst of this assembly, and I will destroy them at once.

They fell upon their faces. While they lay upon the ground, Moses said to Aaron:

> Take the censer, draw fire from the altar, and place incense upon it. Go quickly to the people and plead for them, for wrath has gone out from the Lord, and the plague has begun to rage.

When Aaron had done this and had run into the midst of the multitude that the fire was destroying, he offered incense and, standing between the dead and the living, interceded for the people; and the plague ceased. Those struck were fourteen thousand seven hundred, besides those who had perished in the rebellion of Korah (Num. XVI).

From this we must consider what happened in Sodom, where at least ten were required, through whom those dwelling in the Pentapolis of Sodom might perhaps scarcely have been saved; but now, if even two such people are found as Moses and Aaron, they can suffice for the salvation of the whole Israelite nation.

What, then, shall we say is present in these two—what such power, what merit—that six hundred thousand and more might be delivered from the destruction of the destroyer?

I think that Moses signifies the Law, which teaches human beings the knowledge and love of God. In Aaron resides the pattern of praying to God and entreating him.

If, therefore, God should at some time become angry with us or with the whole people, and a sentence of vengeance should proceed from God; but if the Law of God should return to our heart, admonishing and teaching us to turn to repentance, make satisfaction for our offenses, and plead for our faults, the anger will immediately cease and the indignation will be quieted. The Lord will be appeased, as though Moses and Aaron were interceding for us and pleading on behalf of the whole people.

But if God’s indignation should at some time arise and fierce correction should come because of our sins, while our hearts are hardened so that we do not turn to God or humble ourselves before him in order to calm his movement and anger through the confession of our prayers, and if instead we say:

> God does not care about the life of mortals, nor do these things concern God. He abandoned us long ago, and these matters do not come to his knowledge;

if we think such things in our hearts and they proceed from our mouths, it is certain that Moses and Aaron are not in us—that is, the knowledge of the Law and the fruits of repentance, through which we might escape the destruction of the impending ruin.

## CHAPTER XVII

He recalls how the children of Israel desired meat in the wilderness and quail was given to them.

When the dead had already fallen in heaps upon one another, he intervened, cut off the assault, and divided the path that led to the living.

On the robe of the high priest that he wore was the whole world, and the great deeds of the fathers were carved upon four rows of stones, while your majesty was engraved upon the diadem of his head.

When he says that the whole world was present on the robe of the high priest, that the great deeds of the fathers were carved upon four rows of stones, and that God’s majesty was engraved upon the diadem that the high priest wore upon his head, although these things express the sequence of all the virtues that God’s high priest ought to possess in teaching and conduct, we shall reserve their mystical meaning for discussion elsewhere, while setting down here the interpretation that the Hebrews have of the priestly garment.

The four colors therefore refer to the four elements from which the universe subsists. They assign linen to the earth, which is produced from the earth; purple to the sea, since it is dyed from its shells; hyacinth to the air, because of the similarity of its color; and scarlet to fire and to the ether, which in Hebrew is called *shani*. They also declare it fitting that the Creator’s high priest should pray not only for Israel but also for the whole world.

For this world consists of earth, water, air, and fire, and these are the elements of all things. Hence the first linen garment signifies the earth. The second, of hyacinthine color, indicates the air, because we are gradually raised from earthly things to things on high; and the hyacinthine garment, extending from the head to the ankles, indicates the air poured down from heaven to earth.

The pomegranates and bells placed below signify lightning and thunder, or earth and water, and the harmony among all the elements, all things being so intertwined with one another that everything is found in each individual element.

The fact that the aforesaid colors are woven with gold is understood to signify that the living color and the providence of divine understanding penetrate everything.

Concerning the shoulder-piece and the two stones, whether emeralds or onyx stones, placed above and covering both shoulders, they interpret them as the two hemispheres, one of which is above the earth and the other beneath the earth, or as the sun and moon that shine above.

The band by which the priest’s chest is tightened, together with the linen tunic—that is, the earth—which is bound by it, they interpret as the ocean.

They explain the breastpiece placed in the middle as the earth. Although, like a point, it contains everything within itself, it is nevertheless surrounded by all the elements.

They interpret the twelve stones either as the zodiacal circle or as the twelve months. A season is assigned to each of the individual rows, and three months are allotted to each.

It is beautifully called the *rationale* precisely because it is in the middle. Everything is full of reason, and earthly things cling to heavenly things. The mixture of earthly things, of the times of heat and cold, and the twofold temperance between them descend from the course and reason of heaven; hence the breastpiece is fastened more firmly together with the ephod.

Moreover, what is said to be in the breastpiece—the *analogian*, that is, manifestation, teaching, or truth—signifies that there is never falsehood in God’s reason, and that truth itself is shown to human beings through many signs and arguments and comes even to mortals.

Thus it has happened that we have come to know the courses of the sun and moon, the year, months, seasons, hours, and even changes in the weather, calm conditions, winds, and all things, receiving wisdom implanted by God, who himself, dwelling in and teaching us, demonstrates knowledge of his dwelling and workmanship.

Above all, the head-dress and the hyacinthine band show heaven; and the golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, upon which the name of God is written, shows that everything beneath is governed by God’s will.

The destroyer yielded before these things and feared them. For a single trial of anger was sufficient.

The destroyer therefore feared the spiritual, not merely figurative, form, because he recognized the greatness of the true High Priest.

Now ascend to the loftier traces of this word, and consider how the true High Priest, Jesus Christ, took up the staff of human flesh, placed upon it the fire of the altar—the soul, undoubtedly, that glorious soul with which he was born in the flesh—and added incense, which is the immaculate Spirit. Standing in the midst between the living and the dead, he prevented death from raging any further.

As the Apostle says:

> He destroyed him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, so that whoever believes in him might no longer die but live forever (Rom. IX).

This, then, was the mystery that the one who was later to ravage the people already feared at that time. He recognized the figure of the staff, the fire, and the incense, and foresaw what sacrifice was to be offered to God by him who stood in the midst of the dead and the living.

At that time the prefigured image saved them; for us, however, the truth of salvation itself has arrived. For that destroying angel would not have been frightened by the high priest’s garments woven of purple, wool, and fine linen.

### Chapter XIX

But upon the ungodly, your merciless punishment came at last. For you knew in advance what would happen to them: when they had allowed themselves to be led away, and after they had sent them on with great concern, repentance overtook them. For while they still had mourning in their hands and were lamenting at the tombs of the dead, they adopted another thought born of ignorance; and those whom they had driven away while pleading, they pursued as though they were fugitives. A fitting necessity was leading them to this end; and they lost the memory of what had happened, so that punishment might fill whatever was lacking in their torments. Your people, indeed, passed through wonderfully, but they found a new kind of death.

Therefore vengeance came upon the enemies of your people to the very end, because no worthy amendment was found in their conduct and life. Thus they pretended repentance by fabricated arguments, and therefore they did not receive complete pardon from the one who examines hearts. Hence it is read in Exodus that Pharaoh, whenever he and his people had been struck by some divinely inflicted plague, immediately promised that he would release God’s people if he escaped the present danger; but after recovering his breath for a little while, he returned again to his former cruelty, until at the end, when he pursued the departing people, he was submerged and perished in the waves of the Red Sea (Exod. XIV). Such is the obstinacy of unbelieving and proud enemies of Christ’s name: when they persist incorrigibly in wickedness, at last they experience how greatly the justice of almighty God prevails in judgment.

For every creature was reshaped according to its kind from the beginning, serving your commands so that your children might be kept unharmed. The cloud overshadowed their camp; and dry land appeared from the water that had previously covered it; and in the Red Sea there was a road without hindrance, and a field sprouting from the immense deep, through which the whole nation passed, covered by your hand.

Every creature is reshaped according to its kind from the beginning when it obeys the commands of its creator and serves his will in all things. For this is the purpose of creation: that it should become subject and obedient to its creator. How the cloud covered the camp of the Israelites, shining for them at night and shading them from the sun’s heat by day; and how the Red Sea was divided, preparing a road for God’s people and drowning their enemies when it flowed back upon itself—the history of Exodus makes sufficiently clear.

Nor is this any less evident: the cloud that provided guidance for God’s people signifies Christ’s incarnation, which illumines believers in this world with the light of the Gospel and protects and guards them by his grace from their persecutors. The Red Sea bears the sacrament of baptism, where the faithful are saved and hostile powers are drowned. But just as then the children of Israel, after being delivered, sang praises to the Lord, rejoicing with great gladness,

they saw wonders and marvels. For like horses they grazed on food, and like lambs they rejoiced, magnifying you, Lord, who had delivered them. They still remembered what had been done during their sojourn: how, in place of animals, the earth brought forth flies, and in place of fish, the river spewed forth a multitude of frogs.

So we too ought at all times to give thanks to our creator for our deliverance, rejoicing and saying with the Prophet: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards” (Ps. CII). The Apostle also seems to teach us this when he says: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you” (1 Thess. V).

### Chapter XVIII

He praises God for having magnified and honored his people, whom he led out of the land of Egypt.

Finally, they saw a new kind of bird when, driven by desire, they asked for food for their feast. In response to their longing, a quail-bird came up to them from the sea; and punishments came upon the sinners, not without the signs that had already been produced through the force of the rivers.

Note, prudent reader, that for God’s adversaries the earth produced flies and the river boiled forth frogs; but for God’s worshipers the earth gave fruit and the sea supplied food of flesh, because it is fitting that divine providence should provide nourishment for its faithful through its works. For its enemies, the justice of the Almighty prepares a punishment worthy of them through the creature subject to him.

For they suffered justly according to their wickedness. Indeed, they established a more detestable form of inhospitality: some did not receive strangers, while others reduced good guests to slavery. And not only this, but there was another consideration concerning them: they received foreigners unwillingly. Yet they afflicted with the fiercest pains those who had received with joy people enjoying the same rights [of hospitality].

They were struck with blindness, just as those men at the doors of the righteous man, when suddenly covered with darkness, each sought the way through the entrance. For if those who treated harshly and without mercy the ancient servants of God who came to them under an impious necessity received punishments worthy of them—so that, darkened in mind and hardened in feeling, they endured through their bodily senses the gloom of darkness and of various idols—how much more will those who dishonorably reject and despise Christ’s servants and preachers of the Gospel be tortured forever with immeasurable and indescribable punishments?

Hence Truth itself says to the disciples: “Whoever does not receive you or hear your words, when you go out from that house or city, shake the dust from your feet. Truly I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matt. X).

And it is rightly said that they were struck with blindness, just as those men were blinded by darkness who wandered at the doors of the righteous man—that is, Lot—seeking and failing to find a way through their entrance. For whoever inwardly suffers the darkness of error is hemmed in on every side by the gravest losses, since he does not know the way of life.

And that door of which the Gospel says, “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out and find pasture,” the wandering person will be unable to find (John X).

For the elements are changed into one another, just as in an organ the sound is altered according to the quality, while all preserve their proper sound. Thus, just as in an instrument the different sounds of an organ differ from one another, but musicians bring them into harmony with the melody through proper tuning, so the various elements, although differing from one another in quality, are nevertheless bent according to the will of their creator while preserving the law of nature. For our creator did not make his creation contrary to himself, but made it concordant with his will in all things.

This can also be judged from the sight itself with certainty. For things of the land were changed into things of the water, and whatever had been swimming passed over onto the land. Fire prevailed in water beyond its own power, and water forgot its extinguishing nature. Conversely, the flames did not afflict the flesh of mortal animals walking together, nor did they melt the good food that melted easily like ice.

Human beings and animals crossed the depths of the Red Sea with dry feet, while frogs came forth from the rivers and filled the houses of the Egyptians. Fire mixed with hail rained from heaven, and neither fire resisted water nor water fire; but, falling together, they struck the land of the Egyptians. But wherever the children of Israel were, they harmed no one, showing that all the elements of the world strive not merely according to their own nature, but, being subject to their creator, serve his will.

For in all these things, Lord, you magnified and honored your people, and you did not despise them, assisting them at every time and in every place. This conclusion of the book makes mention not only of the faithful of the earlier Fathers, but also of those of the present and future. For our almighty creator, the merciful and compassionate God, has never abandoned those who hope in him, nor will he abandon them; rather, by his gracious help he cherishes, protects, and governs them.

No one should object to us that the bodies of holy martyrs are handed over into the hands of their persecutors. This is permitted to happen not for their condemnation but for their testing, so that, just as gold is not consumed in the furnace of fire but is tested, so the souls of the elect, examined through the fire of tribulation, may be presented more numerous before the sight of their creator. For it is written: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them from them all. The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them shall be broken. He will redeem the souls of his servants, and he will not abandon all who hope in him” (Ps. XXIII).

[Col. 0763]

## (A.D. 840) Ten Books of Commentaries on Ecclesiasticus by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz

### Preface to Otgar, Archbishop of Mainz

To the most beloved lord in the Lord of lords, Otgar, archbishop, Rabanus, a sinner: greetings in Christ.

Knowing your benevolent intention and your most noble zeal in Christ’s service—you who adorn the Church of God with faith and worship in no undistinguished manner—I, the most unworthy servant of Christ’s servants, have undertaken to offer some consolation to your diligence, holy Father, by explaining the divine Scriptures, so that I might fulfill your desire and render the service owed to the Church of Christ.

For this reason I previously sent, to your veneration, the little exposition that I composed in three books on the book of Wisdom, commonly called Solomon’s. Now, with similar devotion, I offer the little work that I recently completed in ten books as an exposition of the book of Jesus son of Sirach, which is called Ecclesiasticus.

You are the high priest of Christ and the architect of the divine building. May you adorn, in accordance with the measure granted to you by God, the house of Wisdom, which she herself founded and raised upon seven pillars, with ecclesiastical writings, and increase the profit of God’s flock. I thought no other instrument more suitable for this purpose than the one that Wisdom herself dedicated in her own name and by her own art. It contains the power of knowledge and piety both on the surface and in its inner substance, as is made clear in the preface to the preceding book and in the beginning of the present one.

Blessed Jerome says in the prologue that he composed for Chromatius and Heliodorus, bishops, on the interpretation of Solomon’s books, that he found this book of Jesus son of Sirach among the Hebrews, not entitled Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but designated as Proverbs. Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs were joined to it, so that Solomon’s likeness might be matched not only in the number of books but also in the kind of subject matter. But the other book, namely Wisdom, he nowhere found among the Hebrews. Rather, it seemed to breathe Greek eloquence, and some even assert that it was by Philo.

It should further be noted that the book of Solomon called Ecclesiastes and this book of Jesus son of Sirach, called Ecclesiasticus, are extremely useful for the instruction of the Church of God—that is, the Christian people. We may call the former a preacher, but the latter a gatherer or collector.

Yet the Fathers established this distinction between Ecclesiastes and Ecclesiasticus: Ecclesiastes should be referred chiefly to Christ the Lord, whereas Ecclesiasticus can properly be applied to any righteous preacher who habitually gathers the Lord’s Church through his most holy exhortations. It is clear that the present book has done this. Because of the excellence of its virtues, it is called *panaretos*, that is, “possessing every virtue.” Its clarity and its Latinity are so great that the text itself serves as its own commentary. Would that what is grasped so quickly by the mind could be rendered with equal ease in conduct.

Therefore, holy Father, let the reading of this book be frequent for you, and let meditation on its testimonies be constant, so that the thought which continually accompanies you for the honor of your rank and the merit of your virtues may continually hear the word of God, understand the usefulness of instruction, and learn to preserve it. Thus may the man of God always be ready for every good work, and may Christian religion and the life of the faithful shine forth fully, while God is glorified through all things and in all people.

For the rest, I also warn the reader: if anywhere in this work our meaning displeases his prudence or our expression appears inelegant, let him not hastily condemn us with rash judgment, but rather grant pardon to our weakness and ignorance. Let him know that there are difficult passages here, very obscure because of various riddles; therefore he ought to forgive our labor. Or, if he is able to discover something better, let him know that we are ready to accept his judgment.

Provided that he understands that the pardon which we hope he will grant us, he too will at some time receive from others wherever he needs it. For it is written: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged.”

May the holy God, the Trinity, deign to preserve your blessedness everywhere and in all things, holy Father; remember us—

## Book One

### Chapter I

On the eternal Wisdom of God, that she has always been with the Father before the ages.

#### (Chapter I)

“Every wisdom is from the Lord God, and she has always been with him and is before the age.”

The beginning of this book therefore speaks of the eternal Wisdom of God, who is Christ, and says that she has always been with the Father before the ages. It agrees with the Gospel of John, which begins in this way: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.”

Therefore every wisdom is from the Lord God, because Christ, who is the fountain of life and “the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world,” was born from God the Father, and “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

But whoever lacks the light of this wisdom walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes. And whatever opposes this wisdom should be called folly rather than prudence. Hence Paul says: “The wisdom of this world is folly with God” (1 Cor. III). And again: “The prudence of the flesh is death, but the prudence of the spirit is life and peace” (Rom. VIII). For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be.

“Who has counted the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? Who has searched out the wisdom of God that precedes all things?”

He compares bodily things with spiritual things, so that what is wholly impossible may be estimated from things of the greatest difficulty. For if no one can count the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, or the days of the age, nor measure the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, or the depth of the abyss—although all these things were established by their creator with definite number, measure, and weight—how can anyone search out the wisdom of God, which exists without end or beginning and always remains ineffable and beyond estimation?

For the power and wisdom of God, which is Christ, was always with the Father; and just as the Father is without beginning, so also the Son is without beginning.

### Chapter II

On the wisdom of God, that is, the Son of the Father, who existed before every creature and through whom all things were made; and that the Word of God is God on high.

“Wisdom and the understanding of prudence were created before all others, from the age.”

The Fathers understand this statement, as well as the one in Proverbs where it is written, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII), as spoken of the Lord’s incarnation. For just as, according to his divinity, the Son was born from the Father before all the ages, so, before all times, he was predestined in the counsel of God the Father to become incarnate in time for the salvation of the human race.

The word “creation” pertains to the human nature, not to the divine. But because of the unity of the person, he is sometimes called begotten Son and sometimes created. He is therefore the beginning of the ways of God, as he himself says: “I am the way” (John XIV). Rising from the dead, he made a way for the Church to the kingdom of God and to eternal life.

“In his works,” he says: he was created from a virgin in order to redeem the Father’s works, assuming flesh so that he might free the Father’s works from the service of corruption. For Christ’s flesh existed for the sake of the works, but his divinity existed before the works. Hence it follows:

### Chapter III

The continuation as above.

“The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high, and his ways are eternal commandments.”

The origin of all wisdom first proceeded from the Word of God, who, God from God, always remains with the Father in heaven. But through the dispensation of the humanity he assumed, he entered the world and gave the commandments of eternal salvation.

Understanding this, the apostle Peter says to the Lord himself: “You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John VI). Concerning his origin and birth, the text continues:

### Chapter IV

On the prophecy concerning the wisdom of God: that the Son would be born from a Virgin through the Holy Spirit.

“To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed, and who has known her subtleties? To whom has the discipline of wisdom been revealed and made manifest? And who has understood the multiplication of her ways? There is one Most High, almighty creator, and a powerful and exceedingly fearful king, sitting upon his throne and ruling as God. He created her in the Holy Spirit, and saw, counted, and measured her. He poured her out upon all his works and upon all flesh according to his gift, and granted her to those who love him.”

When he asks to whom the root of wisdom has been revealed and made manifest, and who has understood the multiplication of her ways, he shows that no one can penetrate the depth of God’s counsel or comprehend the greatness of his goodness and mercy—through which, for the liberation and enlightenment of the human race, he himself deigned to become human.

Likewise the prophet Isaiah, astonished at the mystery of his birth, says: “Who will declare his generation?” (Ps. LIII). For God the almighty Father alone, through the Word co-eternal with him and together with the Holy Spirit, ordained and arranged the coming of his only-begotten Son: how he would proceed through a virgin’s childbirth for the salvation of the world, so that he might restore the creature he had made from the beginning, and bring human beings—whom he himself created upright but who made themselves perverse through disobedience—back again to knowledge and love of him, giving them the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that by his gift they might be saved and preserved forever.

“The fear of the Lord is glory and joy, and a crown of exultation.”

Finally, the fear of the Lord is the most certain salvation of the human being: it restrains him from sins and directs him in works of piety. Concerning this the Psalmist also says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly desires his commandments.” And shortly afterward: “Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. CXI).

For the glory of virtues and the glorying of right confession accompany him in the present life; in the future, the joy of perpetual life and the crown of eternal blessedness follow. Hence concerning this same fear it continues:

### Chapter V

On the fear of God, that it is itself the beginning of wisdom and the testing of the elect.

“The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and will give joy and gladness for a long succession of days.”

Two kinds of fear are read of in the divine books. One is the fear of which John says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment” (1 John IV). Those who have this fear are the ones who, because of fear of Gehenna, cease sinning and strive to improve their lives.

Another kind of fear is the one of which it is written in the psalm: “The holy fear of the Lord remains forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII).

There are two fears, as we have said. One is the fear by which people fear God lest they be sent into Gehenna. This is the fear that introduces love, but it comes in order to depart. For if you still fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one you fear in this way: you do not desire good things, but avoid evil ones. Yet by avoiding evil you correct yourself and begin to desire good things.

When you have begun to desire good things, holy fear will be in you—namely, fear lest you lose those very good things. This is not the fear by which you fear being sent into Gehenna, but fear lest the presence of the Lord whom you embrace depart from you, since you desire to enjoy him forever.

Of this fear it is said: “The fear of the Lord will delight the heart” (Ecclus. I), because it affects the mind it possesses with indescribable love. It grants inward sweetness, and in the future, eternal life. The following statement shows this, saying:

“The love of God is honorable wisdom. Those to whom it appears love it when they see it, and in the knowledge of its mighty works. The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.”

Therefore the love of God is truly wisdom. Through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us, it is poured into our hearts, filling us with the sweetness of love for God and with knowledge of his mighty works.

Writing about this in his Epistle, John says: “You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you know all things; you do not need anyone to teach you, but his anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John II). The spiritual anointing is the Holy Spirit himself; its sacrament is present in visible anointing. By his grace, the Spirit instructs his participant in all things, because unless that same Spirit is present in the heart of the hearer, the teacher’s speech is useless.

The love of God, which is the most certain gift of the Holy Spirit, very quickly kindles the heart it fills to understand and observe God’s commandments. It makes one begin to do good, it brings good to completion, and it will itself be our reward in the future life. Concerning this the Prophet says to the Lord: “You will fill us with joy by your presence; at your right hand are delights forevermore” (Ps. XV).

“It will be well with one who fears the Lord at the end, and he will be blessed on the day of his death; he was conceived with the faithful in the womb, he walks with elect women, and he is recognized among the righteous and faithful.”

Whoever, because of fear of God, preserves the rule of righteousness in belief, teaching, and action will receive, at the end—that is, after the death of the present life—the blessing of eternal blessedness.

Here he has been reborn and nourished with the faithful in the womb of Mother Church. He walks with elect women because he will be joined to holy souls; and he will be recognized among righteous believers when, on the last day, he is placed with the other saints at the Judge’s right hand and hears from the Lord himself: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV).

“The fear of the Lord is religious devotion to knowledge. Religious devotion will guard and justify the heart; it will give delight and joy.”

Anyone who promises himself religious devotion and knowledge while observing God’s commandments without the fear of God deceives himself. Hence the apostle James says: “If anyone thinks he is religious, but does not restrain his tongue” (James I), “but deceives his heart, his religion is worthless.”

He immediately shows what true religion ought to be, adding: “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself unstained by this world” (ibid.).

When he commands us to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, he indicates everything that we ought to do mercifully toward our neighbor. Its importance will be revealed at the time of judgment, when the Judge will say: “As long as you did it for one of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matt. XXV). Moreover, by commanding us to keep ourselves unstained by this world, he shows all the things in which we ought to preserve our chastity.

“The fullness of wisdom is to fear God, and its fullness comes from its fruits.”

The more anyone fears God, the wiser he appears; and the wiser he is, the fuller he is of the fruits of good works. For the fear of God is not an idle fear; it fills human life with the gifts of virtues and illumines the heart with the treasures of spiritual knowledge.

“The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling with peace and the fruit of salvation; and he saw and counted it.”

It is most certain that the fear of God bestows the crown of eternal life upon the person who walks wisely, because the one before whom all our works are present in number preserves for each person a fitting recompense. Good merits will never be forgotten before him; instead, he repays them with peace and the fruit of salvation. Hence Truth itself says to his disciples: “All the hairs of your head are numbered. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. X).

“Both are gifts of God”—namely, wisdom and the fear of God—“because every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I).

“Wisdom will distribute knowledge and understanding of prudence, and she exalts the glory of those who hold fast to her.”

He shows that through divine wisdom a person has knowledge of avoiding evil and understanding for doing good. She works both of these in her hearer and, at the end, exalts to eternal glory the one who properly holds fast to her. Elsewhere she speaks in this way: “Whoever hears me will not be confounded; those who work in me will not sin; those who make me shine forth will have eternal life” (Ecclus. XXIV).

“The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, for her branches are long-lived.”

For indeed: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; good understanding belongs to all who do it.” The branches of wisdom are therefore the sayings of the sacred Scriptures, which evangelical teaching has spread throughout the whole world for the benefit of human beings.

Hence in the Gospel, when the Lord puts forward the parable of the mustard seed, he says that the birds of heaven dwelt in its branches. The Lord demonstrates in the Gospel how the branches of wisdom are long-lived, saying: “Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. V).

“In the treasures of wisdom are understanding and religious devotion to knowledge.”

Both are revealed in meditation on the Lord’s law: how sins and errors are to be avoided, how spiritual wisdom is to be learned, and how good works are to be practiced. True religious devotion consists in these two things.

“But wisdom is an execration to sinners.”

For that teaching is hateful to the perverse which forbids sins and the pursuit of carnal desires, just as it is written in Proverbs: “The pestilent person does not love one who corrects him, nor does he go to the wise. The instruction of those who abandon the way of life is evil; whoever hates reproof will die” (Prov. XV).

“The fear of the Lord drives out sin, for whoever is without fear cannot be justified.”

It was written above that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, because it is the beginning of conversion to God and the path toward righteousness. Now he says that the fear of God drives out sin, because through repentance it cleanses a person from sins already committed, or restrains and prevents him from committing sins not yet committed. But whoever despises God can in no way attain the palm of righteousness.

“For the rage of his anger is his overthrow.”

Certainly, because the one who does not wish to restrain himself from vices through fear of God falls into the abyss of sin and is hurled into death.

“The patient person will endure until the appointed time, and afterward comes the recompense of joy.”

The truly patient person is the one who endures adversity with equanimity and gives good things in return for evil, not evil for evil, to the one who injures him. The apostle Peter bears witness to this concerning our Head, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges unjustly, and so forth” (1 Pet. II).

“Good sense will conceal his words for a time, and the lips of many will declare his understanding.”

Hence it is written in Proverbs: “The lips of the wise guard them” (Prov. XIV). And again: “The prudent person,” he says, “does everything with counsel, but the foolish person reveals folly” (Prov. XIII).

Therefore it belongs to a wise person to test his words and to do everything modestly. Nevertheless, many people proclaim and praise his self-control through their words and actions. What justice dictates cannot remain hidden; it must be made known.

### Chapter VI

Wisdom exhorts those who desire her to keep the commandments; thus the Lord teaches in the Gospel.

“My son, if you desire wisdom, preserve righteousness, and God will provide it for you.”

Wisdom herself shows us the path by which we can attain the perception of wisdom, because no one will reach the summit of wisdom without preserving righteousness. Hence the apostle James also teaches, saying: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” (James I). Again: “Who is wise and instructed among you?” he says; “Let him show his good conduct in the gentleness of wisdom” (ibid. III). Concerning this it follows:

“For wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord; and what is pleasing to him is faith and gentleness, and he will fill his treasures.”

It has already often been said that the fear of the Lord is the guardian of wisdom and discipline. Right faith and moderation of character are well suited to it, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI), and the whole life of good people is peaceful.

Hence Christ, the virtue and wisdom of God, taught his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). It is appropriately said that he will fill his treasures, because whoever truly fears God cannot be without faith and good works. These fill the person who fears God with sacred virtues and make him acceptable to God.

Hence it is written in Ecclesiastes: “To the good person in his sight God has given wisdom, knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he has given affliction and excessive care” (Eccl. II).

“Do not be unbelieving toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a divided heart.”

The one who approaches God must believe, as Paul testifies, “that he exists and becomes the rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. XI). And the one who “seeks God with a simple heart will find him” (ibid.).

Hence it is written: “The simplicity of the upright will guide them, but the treachery of the perverse will destroy them” (Prov. XI). For anyone who thinks he can find God with a divided mind, not with sincere faith and good intention, deceives himself.

Hence James says: “Whoever hesitates is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. A person divided in mind is unstable in all his ways” (James I). A person is divided in mind when he wishes to rejoice here with the world and there to reign with Christ. Likewise, a person is divided in mind when, in the good things he does, he seeks not an inner reward but outward approval.

“Do not be a hypocrite in the sight of people, and do not be a cause of scandal through your lips.”

Hypocrites are a most wicked kind of people: they do everything falsely, carrying one thing in their hearts and displaying another in their actions. The most wicked of all these are heretics, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII).

With wicked hearts they contrive evil and continually sow quarrels, so that they may overturn those who are walking on the way of truth. It is especially necessary to beware of them. Hence Solomon says:

“Counsel will guard you, and prudence will preserve you, so that you may be delivered from the evil way and from the person who speaks perverse things; from the one who abandons the straight path and walks along dark ways; so that you may be delivered from the foreign woman and from the stranger who softens her words, who abandons the guide of her youth and has forgotten the covenant of her God.

“For her house is inclined toward death, and her paths toward the underworld. All who enter into her will not return, nor will they take hold of the paths of life” (Prov. II).

“Take care in these matters lest perhaps you fall, bring dishonor upon your soul, and God reveal your secrets and strike you down in the midst of the assembly; for you have approached God deceitfully, and your heart is full of trickery and falsehood.”

It is clear that whoever follows heretics acquires condemnation for his soul, when the hidden things of hearts will be revealed in the divine judgment and the just Judge will repay each person according to his works; and he will destroy all who speak lies, [Col. 0771D] because the Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man. Therefore Truth himself admonishes his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy (Luke XII).” Elsewhere he testified concerning the ruin of the wicked servant who strikes his fellow servants, eats, and drinks with drunkards, saying: “The lord of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour of which he is unaware; he will cut him in two and assign him his portion with the hypocrites. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew XXIV).”

## CHAPTER VII. Wisdom admonishes those who approach the service of God to stand in justice and fear, and to prepare their souls for temptation, since, as the Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution.”

(CAP. II.) “My son, as you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.”

Having first taught what must be avoided, he now shows what must be done: namely, that whoever wishes properly to devote himself to divine service should remain in justice and preserve the fear of God, and thus prepare his soul for temptation, because it is impossible for one who attempts to abstain from the allurements of the world and to keep God’s commandments not to suffer the world’s adversities. [Col. 0772B] “For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ, according to Paul’s saying, suffer persecution (2 Timothy III).” The more someone strives to turn away from love of the world and hastens to unite himself to God’s service, the graver are the battles and temptations he endures from the enemy. For whoever hastens to gird himself for divine service is preparing himself for nothing other than combat against the ancient adversary, so that he may receive blows freely in battle, though previously he served in captivity under tyranny while at rest.

Yet in that very process by which the mind girds itself against the enemy, it abandons some vices while resisting others. Sometimes, however, it is permitted to retain some fault that does not cause very great harm. Often the mind, which overcomes many severe adversities, does not defeat one fault in itself—perhaps a very small one—even though it watches over it with great determination. This plainly occurs by divine dispensation, lest, shining with virtues on every side, it be lifted up in pride. When it sees something small that is blameworthy but nevertheless cannot subdue it, it attributes the victory not to itself but to its Creator in those matters that it is able to overcome courageously.

But because humility and patience are necessary to it, and because it must conform itself to the teachings of divine law in order to know how it ought to persevere in God’s service until the end of life, the text continues:

“Lower your heart and endure. Incline your ear and receive words of understanding, and do not hurry in the time of obscurity. Endure God’s supports. Join yourself to God and endure, so that your life may increase at the end.”

He commands the heart to be lowered, so that it may not swell with pride; he commands endurance, so that it may not fail in tribulations but rather become long-suffering. Yet because no one knows how to do these things perfectly except one who has learned them from the divine commandments, he sends him to meditate on God’s law. And because it is not enough to begin well unless one strives to persevere in it to the end, he commands that, not broken by faintheartedness, he should not desire a swift end to his labors; instead, by enduring equably according to the will of his Creator, he should await his judgment. Hence the text continues:

“Accept everything that is brought upon you, and endure in suffering, and have patience in your humiliation. For gold and silver are tested in fire, but acceptable people in the furnace of humiliation.” [Col. 0773A]

To make us long-suffering and strong in the time of our chastisement and testing, the Psalmist exhorts us, saying: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord (Psalm XXVI).” Concerning this it is also written in the Gospel: “The one who holds the word of God in a good and excellent heart will bear fruit in patience (Luke VIII).” Thus Truth himself says to the apostles: “By your patience you will possess your souls (ibid. XXI).” The possession of the soul is therefore placed in the virtue of patience, because patience is the root and guardian of all virtues.

It should be known that patience is usually exercised in three ways. Some things we endure from God, some from the ancient adversary, and some from our neighbor. From our neighbor we endure persecutions, losses, and insults; from the ancient adversary, temptations; and from God, scourges. But in all three forms the mind must watch itself with vigilant attention: lest, in response to the evils of its neighbor, it be dragged into repaying evil; lest, in response to the adversary’s temptations, it be seduced into the pleasure of or consent to sin; and lest, in response to the Creator’s scourges, it rush into excessive murmuring.

The adversary is perfectly conquered when our mind, amid his temptations, is guarded from pleasure and consent; amid our neighbor’s insults, from hatred; and amid God’s scourges, from murmuring. Nor, while doing these things, should we seek present goods as recompense. Rather, we should hope for good things in the life to come as the reward of patient labor, so that the reward for our labor may begin when all labor has already completely ceased. [Col. 0773C]

“Believe in God, and he will restore you; direct your way and hope in him.”

The one tested by pain and affliction must preserve faith in this God in all things, direct the steps of his actions before the Lord’s sight, and place his hope in God, because whoever trusts in him will not be put to shame. Concerning this the Prophet says: “Commit your way to the Lord, hope in him, and he will act (Psalm XXXVI).” Jeremiah likewise says: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence. He will be like a tree transplanted beside waters, sending its roots toward moisture; he will not fear when the heat comes, and his leaf will be green. In the time of drought he will not be anxious, nor will he ever cease to bear fruit (Jeremiah XVII).” [Col. 0773D]

“Preserve his fear, and grow old in him.”

That is: remain, because it will be well in the end for the one who fears the Lord. “The hope of Israel, its Savior in the time of tribulation.” Hence the text continues.

## CHAPTER VIII. Wisdom exhorts those who fear the Lord to hope in him, that is, to be secure in hope, lest their fear prove vain.

“You who fear God, wait for his mercy, and do not turn away from him, lest you fall.”

For the Lord is pleased with those who fear him and with those who hope in his mercy. Whoever truly fears the Lord patiently endures and awaits the bestowal of his compassion; but whoever turns away from him through faintheartedness and impatience will be near to ruin. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “All who abandon you will be put to shame; those who depart from you will be written in the earth, because they have abandoned the Lord, the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah XVII).”

“You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward will not be lost. You who fear the Lord, hope in him, and mercy will come to you for your delight. You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts will be enlightened.”

He rightly exhorts the one who fears the Lord to believe in him, so that he may attain a certain reward, because, according to the prophet’s saying, “The just person lives by faith (Habakkuk II).” In the Gospel the Lord also says: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you (Matthew IX).” And elsewhere: “Your faith has saved you (Luke VIII).” Likewise, mercy desired will come to the one who hopes in the Lord; and the one who loves him will, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, receive the light of wisdom more fully.

Note, reader, that he makes a threefold distinction concerning those who fear the Lord: first, he commands them to believe in God; second, to hope in him; third, to love him. For every faithful soul worships God by faith, hope, and charity. Through these modes it reaches contemplation of the Holy Trinity, which is its true reward in everlasting blessedness.
