“Look, children, upon the nations of human beings, and know that no one who hoped in the Lord was put to shame; no one who remained in his commandments was abandoned; and who has called upon him and he has despised that person? For God is gracious and merciful, and in the time of tribulation he will forgive the sins of all who seek him in truth.”

Here too, as in the preceding passage, he makes a threefold distinction, saying: that no one hopes in the Lord and is put to shame; that one remains in his commandments and is abandoned; or that one calls upon him and is despised. “For with the heart one believes unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation; and everyone who does the will of the heavenly Father will enter the kingdom of heaven (Romans X).”

He rightly says that the Lord forgives sins in the time of tribulation to all who seek him in truth, because “a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart he will not despise (Psalm L),” and, “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth; he will do the will of those who fear him, hear their prayers, and save them.” [Col. 0774D]

“Woe to the double-hearted, to criminal lips, to hands that do evil, and to the sinner who treads the earth by two paths.”

Above he warned that no one should approach the Lord with a double heart. Now he says that woe belongs to the double-hearted, to criminal lips, and to hands that do evil, because one who thinks wickedly, speaks perversely, and persists in evil deeds will suffer perpetual woe unless repentance intervenes. What follows is:

“Woe to the sinner who treads the earth by two paths.”

A sinner treads the earth by two paths when he does evil and hopes that good things may come to him, according to what is written: “Let us do evil so that good may come (Romans III).” Their condemnation is just. Or this occurs when he follows the works of the flesh in its desires and supposes that he can be perfected in the sanctification of the spirit through the fear of God; or when what he displays in action belongs to God, while what he seeks in thought belongs to the world. All such people, according to James’s saying, are unstable in all their ways, because they are very easily frightened by the world’s adversities and ensnared by its prosperity.

“Woe to those whose hearts are loosened, who do not believe God; therefore they will not be protected by him.”

He continues in the same line of reasoning, teaching us to avoid errors and love the truth. Whoever desires to be protected by God must preserve sincerity of faith and possess firmness of mind, because one who doubts in faith and wavers in hope will consequently fail to reach the crown. This crown is promised only to the faithful and to those who truly fear the Lord—that is, to those who produce the fruit of good works in patience.

But for those who depart from the faith through apostasy or heresy, persist in wicked works, abandon the path of truth, and fall into the gulf of vices, wrath, tribulation, and anguish will remain forever. Paul testifies to this, saying: “To those who by patience in good work seek glory, honor, and incorruption, eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, yet believe in iniquity, wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish upon every soul of a human being who works evil (Romans II).” Hence the text continues:

## CHAPTER IX. Wisdom threatens those who, after endurance, abandon the right ways and go along crooked paths.

“Woe to those who have lost endurance, who have abandoned the right ways and turned aside into crooked paths; and what will you do when God begins to inspect you?”

Although God is believed to inspect the good and the wicked at all times, and nothing can be hidden from him, Scripture very often uses “inspect” at the time when he is recognized either to approve or to disapprove something. What, then, will those do who have abandoned the right ways and entangled themselves in wicked works when the time of judgment has arrived and no opportunity for repentance is granted? When, according to Zephaniah, “The great day of the Lord will come, a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and battle cry. Against fortified cities and lofty battlements; people will be troubled and will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord. Their blood will be poured out like dust, and their bodies like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath. In the fire of his jealousy the whole earth will be devoured, because he will make a swift end of all the inhabitants of the earth (Zephaniah I).” In this life God awaits and accepts our conversion; in that life he will repay each person according to his works. [Col. 0776A]

“Those who fear the Lord will not be unbelieving toward his word, and those who love him will preserve his way. Those who fear the Lord will seek what is pleasing to him, and those who love him will be filled with his law.”

He speaks alternately of the fear and love of God, because “the fear of the Lord is holy and endures forever and ever,” and “everyone who loves is born of God and knows God.” Therefore the one who fears the Lord and loves him believes the holy Scriptures, keeps the Lord’s commandments by putting them into practice, and continually seeks through meditation what is pleasing to him; thus he will be filled with wisdom and the love of God. “For the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy I),” and whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

“Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts and sanctify their souls in his sight.”

O how blessed is the soul that daily cleanses its heart and thoughts so that it may receive God, its inhabitant, within itself! Whoever possesses him lacks no good, because he has within himself the author of all good. And because, in the cleansing of the heart, it is necessary to guard God’s commandments with patience in good works, by which one reaches perfect knowledge of divinity, the text continues:

“Those who fear the Lord keep his commandments and will have patience until his inspection, saying: If we do not repent, we will fall into the hands of God and not into the hands of human beings; for as his greatness is, so also is his mercy with him.”

It is indeed the custom of the saints to accuse themselves as sinners, so that they may receive the fitting reward of their humility, because just as a reward is assigned to humility, so punishment is assigned to pride. The apostle John plainly says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity (1 John I).”

Therefore he added: “For as his greatness is, so also is his mercy with him,” because, as the Prophet testifies, “As high as heaven is above the earth, so has the Lord established his mercy over those who fear him (Psalm CII).” And again: “The mercy of the Lord is from age to age and unto the age of ages upon those who fear him, and his justice upon children’s children who keep his covenant and remember his commandments in order to do them (ibid.).”

(CAP. III.) “The children of wisdom are the Church of the just, and their nation is obedience and love.”

He rightly says that the Church of the just is the children of wisdom, because whoever is truly wise is a true worshiper of justice, since true wisdom truly dictates the rule of justice. “Their nation,” he says, “is obedience and love.” How, then, does he call the obedience and love of the just a nation, when obedience and love are virtues possessed by the just? Only because, in a figurative expression, he designates the possessors of the virtues by the virtues themselves.

“Hear the judgment of the Father, children, and act accordingly so that you may be saved.”

God is naturally the Father of all, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, because from him, through him, and in him are all things; and he loves what he has made, so that they may remain what they were made to be. Whoever hears the judgment of this Father and carries out his commandments will undoubtedly be saved. His commandment is that reverent honor also be shown to an earthly father and mother, as in the statement: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land that the Lord your God will give you (Exodus XX).” Hence the text continues.

[Col. 0777B] “For God has honored the father in the children, and he will seek the judgment of the mother from the children.”

Since God has established honor for a parent in the parent’s offspring, it is not right for that parent to be dishonored by the children, because the Lord will inquire in his judgment how his commandment has been observed. Those who follow it are crowned, while those who despise it are punished.

“Whoever loves God will pray for sins, restrain himself from them, and in the prayer of his days he will be heard.”

The one “who loves God,” as he himself testifies in the Gospel, “keeps his commandments (John XIV),” and restrains himself from sins as far as human weakness permits. Nevertheless, he does not cease to pray daily for his transgressions, because he knows that God, the merciful Judge, hears his prayers at all times. And because, as Scripture testifies, the honor of parents is the first commandment with a promise (Exodus XX), the text continues:

“And whoever honors his mother is like one who stores up treasure.”

The one who honors his mother stores up treasure well, because, for keeping God’s commandments—he commanded that parents be honored—he will receive the rewards of eternal life.

## CHAPTER X. Children should honor their parents, so that the parents’ blessing may benefit their children.

“Whoever honors his father will rejoice in his children, and on the day of his prayer he will be heard.”

Here he calls children either offspring or disciples. One who previously inclined the ear of obedience to his teachers or parents will often rejoice in their upbringing. But because, according to history, this does not always happen—that those who honor their parents or teachers should have devoted children or disciples, since we often read that the offspring of holy men degenerated and departed from the path of their ancestors—I think the statement fits better according to its tropological meaning if we understand “children” as the fruit of good works. Therefore whoever honors his parents or teachers by obeying God’s commandments will rejoice at the end of his days in the multiplication of good deeds. And just as the prayer of one who turns away his ears so as not to hear the law will be accursed, so the prayer of one who obeys God’s commandments will be directed like incense in the sight of the Most High.

[Col. 0778A] “Whoever honors his father will live a longer life, and whoever obeys his father will refresh his mother.”

He will live a longer and happier life who, rewarded by the Lord, will enjoy eternal rest. He will refresh his mother who obeys his father, because he gladdens the mother Church who is obedient to the commandments of the eternal Father.

“Whoever fears God honors his parents, and like masters he will serve those who begot him, in deed and word, and with all patience.”

Note that he says that service must be diligently rendered to those who begot him—not from the womb of the body, but through deed, word, and patience—so that it may be shown that a spiritual father is especially worthy of honor. Remembering this, the Apostle wrote to the disciples whom he had begotten through the Gospel, saying: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you; hold them in especially abundant love because of their work. Be at peace with them (1 Thessalonians V).” And to Timothy: “Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine,” because “the laborer is worthy of his reward (1 Timothy V).”

“Honor your father, so that a blessing from God may come upon you, and his blessing may remain at the end.”

Honor of a father, whether spiritual or bodily, earns a blessing from the Lord. It is appropriately said that “his blessing may remain at the end,” because it is repaid with an eternal reward.

“The blessing of a father strengthens the houses of children, but the mother’s curse uproots their foundations.”

We find patriarchs who blessed certain of their sons, such as Noah, Shem, and Japheth (Genesis IX), but cursed the offspring of Ham (ibid. XXV). Abraham blessed his son Isaac, and Isaac blessed Jacob (ibid. XXVII), while Jacob gave individual blessings to the twelve patriarchs (ibid. XLIX). In all these blessings he was prefigured who descended bodily from the line of the patriarchs—namely, Christ our Savior, who is God blessed above all forever.

How the curse of parents harms their offspring is shown in the seed of Ham. His descendants were uprooted and destroyed from the promised land by the sons of Shem, that is, by the children of Israel.

“Do not glory in the dishonor of your father, for his disgrace is not your glory. A person’s glory comes from the honor of his father, and the father without honor is the son’s disgrace.”

That dishonoring a father or teacher displeases God is proved by many examples. Ham mocked his father after he had been exposed, and his descendants consequently endured perpetual servitude. Absalom drove David from the seat of his kingdom and violated his concubines, but paid a punishment worthy of his death. Likewise, the boys of Bethel mocked the baldness of the prophet Elisha, and two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys apart. The mystery of this event was fulfilled in Christ’s Passion: the childish folly of the Jews mocked him when he was crucified at the place of Calvary. But in the forty-second year after his ascension [Col. 0779A] into heaven, two bears—that is, Vespasian and Titus—came out of the forest of the nations and savagely tore apart the mockers.

## CHAPTER XI. A father’s old age is to be cared for by his children.

“My son, support your father’s old age and do not grieve him during his life; and if he should fail in understanding, grant him pardon, and do not despise him in your strength.”

It is fitting that children and disciples should cherish their parents and fosterers with honors and consolations, because the affection of charity is thereby increased. Hence Paul commanded widows to repay their parents in turn, because this is pleasing before the Lord.

The Lord himself also rebuked the scribes and [Col. 0779B] Pharisees in the Gospel because, through their traditions, they corrupted the purity of God’s law, saying to them: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment because of your tradition? For God said: Honor your father and mother, and whoever curses father or mother must die. But you say: Whoever says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,’ and does not honor his father or mother—you have made God’s commandment void because of your tradition (Matthew XV).”

In Scripture, honor is understood not so much in greetings and the rendering of services as in almsgiving and the bestowal of gifts. “Honor,” the Apostle says, “widows who are truly widows (1 Timothy V).” Here too honor means a gift. Likewise, the text next speaks of the generosity shown to parents:

“For the almsgiving of a father will not be forgotten; for the sin of a mother, good will be repaid to you, and in justice it will be built for you.”

The disposition toward mercy, together with works of devotion, will never be consigned to oblivion. Hence the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy (Matthew V).” And in Proverbs: “Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and he will repay him in return (Proverbs XIX).”

When it says, “For the sin of a mother, good will be repaid to you,” it calls almsgiving itself “sin” in a figurative expression, because almsgiving removes sins. Elsewhere too it calls the offering made for sin “sin,” as in the statement: “Let him place his hand upon the head of his sin and thus offer it to the Lord.” Therefore whoever practices works of mercy toward parents and other needy people will undoubtedly receive the reward of his justice, and, freed from sins, will possess the reward of eternal life. Hence it continues:

“In the day of tribulation you will be remembered, and like ice in fair weather your sins will melt.”

The prophet Daniel gave King Nebuchadnezzar advice of this kind, saying: “May my counsel please you, O king: redeem your sins with almsgiving, and your iniquities with mercies toward the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offenses (Daniel IV).” Truth himself also says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you (Luke XI).” At the future judgment he will likewise say to those who stand at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink, etc. (Matthew XXV).” As it is also written in Proverbs: “Whoever is inclined to mercy will be blessed.”

“How evil is the reputation of one who abandons his father; and cursed by God is the one who provokes his mother.”

The one who is irreligious toward his parents is held guilty of the crime of impiety, and especially the one who provokes a spiritual father or mother by wicked words and unjust deeds. Therefore it is necessary to observe the teaching of the following statement:

## CHAPTER XII. Wisdom teaches that works pertaining to the worship of God are to be undertaken in gentleness.

“My son, complete your works in gentleness, and you will be loved above all glory. The greater you are, humble yourself in everything, and you will find favor before God, for great is the power of God alone, and he is honored by the humble.”

Gentleness and humility produce the greatest grace and glory in those who possess them. By contrast, pride and anger drive those whom they possess toward the greatest ruin. For pride is the beginning of every sin: it made an angel into the devil, and anger casts those who obey it into death, because it destroys the path of charity.

Therefore, giving counsel against such plagues, the Lord offered himself as an example for imitation, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls (Matthew XI).” And again: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke XIV, XVIII).”

## CHAPTER XIII. Wisdom teaches that lofty things, that is, profound matters, are not to be sought.

“Do not seek things higher than you, and do not investigate matters stronger than you. But always consider what the Lord has commanded you, and do not be curious about many of his works. For it is not necessary for you to see with your eyes the things that are hidden.”

The teacher preserves the order of his instruction, namely that of humility. Just as he previously taught that gentleness should be maintained in conduct and humility in works, so now he teaches that purity of heart must be preserved, lest someone rashly presume to probe through careless argument what human reason cannot comprehend.

Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Do not speak rashly, nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven, and you are upon earth. Therefore let your words be few. Dreams follow upon many cares, and folly is found in many words (Ecclesiastes V).” In these words he seems to command that, whether speaking or thinking, we should not form a higher opinion of God than we are capable of holding. [Col. 0781A]

Let us recognize our weakness: as far as heaven is distant from earth, so far is our opinion separated from his nature. Therefore our words ought to be measured. For just as one who is occupied with many thoughts frequently dreams about the things he thinks about, so one who wishes to say too much about divinity falls into folly.

Paul likewise teaches: “Do not be wiser than you ought to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety and according to the measure of faith (Romans XII).” And elsewhere: “Do not be high-minded, but fear (Romans XI).” It is enough for a human being to consider with devout thought and fulfill in action what has been established and commanded by the Creator for him to observe. But one should not attempt to investigate the hidden and incomprehensible matters of God’s judgments. Rather, one should say with the Prophet: “The judgments of God are a great abyss (Psalm XXXV),” and, marveling with the Apostle, think in this way: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” And he will be repaid, because “from him, through him, and in him are all things. To him be honor and glory forever and ever (Romans XI).”

“Do not investigate superfluous words in a complicated manner, and do not be curious about many of his works. Very many things have been shown to you that exceed human understanding. Suspicion of them has also caused many to stumble and has held their understanding in vanity.”

To investigate superfluous matters is to wish to know rationally those things that reason teaches should not be investigated. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “What need has a human being to seek things greater than himself, when he does not know what is useful for him in his life, during the number of the days of his pilgrimage and the time that passes like a shadow? Or who can tell him what will happen after him under the sun? (Ecclesiastes VII).” And again: “Do not say, ‘What do you think is the reason that former times were better than these?’ For such an inquiry is foolish (ibid. VII).”

A sober understanding is best in all things: it refreshes the soul and does not burden the mind. Hence Wisdom teaches in Proverbs, saying: “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest perhaps, when you are filled, you vomit it up and swear falsely by the name of your God (Proverbs XXV).”

When it says that suspicion of those matters has caused many to stumble and has held their understanding in vanity, it shows that all heretics arise in two ways: either when they wish to investigate beyond measure matters concerning the Creator or the creation, and, thinking perversely, formulate erroneous doctrines; or because they refuse to yield to the teachings of truth. What follows shows what overtakes them:

“A hard heart will fare badly at the end, and whoever loves danger will perish in it.”

“According to his hardness and impenitent heart, he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works: eternal life to those who, by patience in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish to those who are contentious, who do not obey the truth but believe in iniquity (Romans II).”

“He who loves danger,” he says, “will perish in it.” One is said to love danger who neither cares nor strives to avoid it. Otherwise, who would wish to fall into danger, when everyone wishes to escape destruction? But in a certain sense the one loves danger who loves things that tend toward destruction, such as lust, greed, luxury, and other destructive desires, as well as heresies and presumptuous novelties, which are certain destructions of souls. Hence the text continues:

“A heart entering upon two paths will have no success, and a perverse heart will be scandalized in them. A wicked heart will be weighed down with sorrows, and the sinner will add to his sinning.”

The heart of heretics enters upon two paths when it mixes truth with falsehood and inserts falsehood into truth. They correctly understand and proclaim some statements of the holy Scriptures, but, according to their own madness, drag others into a perverse meaning and strive to commend them to their hearers. They “will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables (2 Timothy IV).”

Therefore they will be scandalized and will have no success, because their labors will come to nothing. Their inmost hearts are weighed down by the tricks of crafty deceit, and for this reason they are burdened with multiple loads of sin.

“The assembly of the proud will have no health, for the growth of sin will be uprooted among them, and it will not be understood.”

The assemblies of the proud are the gatherings of heretics. Their growth will be uprooted and will not be understood when their useless doctrine is condemned; nor is their fabrication approved by God. What reveals Catholics he shows by adding:

“The heart of the wise is understood in wisdom, and a good ear will hear wisdom with every desire.”

In the prudence of doctrine, the wise heart is understood according to the truth, and good hearers eagerly learn this doctrine, which commends virtues and attacks vices. This is shown in what follows:

“A wise and understanding heart will abstain from sins, and it will have success in works of justice.”

Therefore whoever rightly understands the tradition of God’s law restrains himself from sins and practices justice in his works. A noble part of these works is the giving of alms; for this reason the text continues.

“Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving resists sins; and God watches over the one who returns a kindness. He remembers him afterward, and at the time of his fall he will find support.” For just as the element of water, when poured out, extinguishes the fire’s heat, so almsgiving, expended out of charitable affection, will overwhelm the flame of sins. Therefore [Col. 0783A] the Lord teaches in the Gospel how almsgiving ought to be given, saying: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who is in secret, will repay you (Matt. 6).” Almsgiving must not be done for the sake of human praise or desire for present possessions, but out of love for God and desire for eternal blessedness. For then, if it has been expended in this way, it will have God as its rewarder, who at the time of one’s fall—that is, at the end of the present life—will repay the reward of eternal life.

## CHAPTER XIV. On almsgiving and the poor

[Col. 0783B] **(CHAP. IV.)** “My son, do not defraud the poor of alms, and do not turn your eyes away from the poor; do not despise the hungry soul, and do not embitter the poor in his distress.” How greatly almsgiving, given with a devout mind, avails before the Lord, he himself shows in the Gospel, saying: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you (Luke 11).” Elsewhere divine Scripture ascribes such importance to these acts that the Lord declares he will reckon only their fruit to those on his right, and only their barrenness to those on his left. To the former he will say: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom”; but to the latter: “Go into the eternal fire (Matt. 25).”

[Col. 0783C] Certainly, one must take care lest anyone suppose that those abominable crimes—such as are committed by people who will not possess the kingdom of God—may be perpetrated daily and redeemed daily by almsgiving. Life must rather be changed for the better, and through almsgiving God must be propitiated for past sins, not bought, as it were, so that it may always be permissible to commit them with impunity. For he has given no one license to sin, although in his mercy he wipes away sins already committed, provided suitable satisfaction is not neglected.

But there are many kinds of almsgiving. Thus, not only does the one who gives the hungry food, the thirsty drink, the naked clothing, the traveler lodging, the fugitive a hiding place, the sick or imprisoned a visit, the captive redemption, the weak assistance, the blind guidance, the sorrowful consolation, the unwell healing, the wanderer a way, the delirious counsel, and whatever is necessary to each person in need give alms; [Col. 0783D] the one who grants pardon to a sinner also gives alms. And “the one who corrects with a blow, when authority has been granted to him, or restrains someone by some discipline,” yet forgives from the heart the sin by which he has been harmed or offended, or prays that it may be forgiven him, gives alms—not only in forgiving and praying, but also in reproving and imposing some corrective punishment, because he shows mercy.

“Do not afflict the heart of the poor, and do not delay giving to one in distress. Do not reject the request of the afflicted, and do not turn your face away from the needy.” That the gift of almsgiving must not be delayed or postponed to another time when one has the means to give, Scripture shows by saying: “Do not say [Col. 0784A] to your friend, ‘Go and come back later,’ when you can give immediately (Prov. 3).” And elsewhere: “The one who despises his neighbor sins, but the one who has mercy on the poor will be blessed (Prov. 14).” The Apostle teaches how almsgiving should be given, saying: “Not from sorrow or compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 1).” Therefore the person who extends a little to the poor with a devout mind gives more to God than the one who expends much money with a sorrowful heart. Hence the Lord praised in the Gospel the offering of the poor widow who put two small copper coins into the treasury, saying: “She has put in more than all the others (Mark 12),” because the heavenly Judge weighs not the amount of the gift but the devotion of the heart.

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 0784B] On not turning one’s eyes away from the needy

“Do not turn your eyes away from the needy because of anger, and do not leave those who seek you an opportunity to curse you afterward. For when the one who curses you in the bitterness of his soul prays, his petition will be heard; and he will hear the one who made him.” In no way should the poor person be provoked because of anger; rather, he should be appeased by gentle speech, because the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God, and the one who hardens his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard. Let the person who possesses resources from which he can give provide for the one suffering need, because a hidden gift extinguishes anger, and a gift in one’s bosom, the greatest indignation. But the one who has no resources should at least extend a good word in reply, [Col. 0784C] because a good word is better than an excellent gift.

Otherwise, how does the person who despises his needy neighbor possess the affection of charity? For the Apostle John plainly says: “Whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, how does the love of God remain in him? (1 John 3).” James likewise shows that faith without works of mercy is dead, saying: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but has no works? Can faith save him? If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, keep warm and eat your fill,’ but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it? So faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself (James 2).” Therefore it is necessary that we believe and love not merely in word and speech, but in deed and truth.

“Make yourself approachable to the assembly of the poor, humble your soul before the presbyter, and humble your head before the great.” These statements commend gentleness and humility of heart to us, because gentleness despises no one, and humility places itself above no one but subjects itself to all. It is fitting for a Christian to be approachable and mild toward equals or inferiors, but submissive and humble toward elders, because every exaltation is a kind of pride. The Psalmist wonderfully distinguishes this, saying: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; [Col. 0785A] I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me, etc. (Ps. 131).”

“Bend your ear to the poor without sadness, repay your debt, and answer him peacefully and gently.” The poor person’s due is temporal consolation offered with gentleness; whoever neglects to give it does not render him his proper due.

“Rescue the one who suffers injury from the hand of the proud, and do not bear it grudgingly in your soul.” Thus, just as he previously showed that the expenditure of resources on the poor is almsgiving, so now he declares that liberating one who is unjustly oppressed by the proud is a work of mercy. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [Col. 0785B] “Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease delivering those who are being dragged to destruction. If you say, ‘We have no strength,’ the one who examines the heart understands; and nothing escapes the one who preserves your soul (Prov. 24).” Therefore here too it says, “Do not bear it grudgingly in your soul,” that is, wearisomely or unwillingly, because the person who does not strive to rescue his neighbor from an enemy shows that he lacks the fervor of charity toward him.

## CHAPTER XVI. On defending orphans and widows in judgment, showing mercy in place of a father

“Be merciful to orphans in judgment as a father, and be as a husband to their mother, and you will be like an obedient son of the Most High; and he will have more mercy on you than [Col. 0785C] a mother.” So that he might omit no form of almsgiving, he joins orphans and widows to parents and the poor, so that we may not disdain to care for them also but may bring them worthy assistance. For just as a father’s affection must be shown to an orphan, so the widow’s husband must be imitated by providing consolation. By doing these things, we will be shown to be sons of the Most High in obeying his commands, because in rewarding us he will have more mercy than a mother’s affection has ever shown in the work of nurturing.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the pursuit of wisdom: that those who love her should, with the Lord’s help, devote themselves to all the virtues of justice, as Truth herself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father”

[Col. 0785D] “Wisdom inspires life in her children, receives those who seek her, and goes before them on the way of justice; whoever loves her loves life, and those who keep watch for her will embrace her favor.” Divine Wisdom praises the little one who is suited to her—Wisdom herself, whom we understand to be none other than Christ, the Son of God. Of him the Apostle says: “I proclaim Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1).” For this Wisdom inspires life in her children when she grants her disciples and the other faithful the sacrament of her knowledge and reveals the mystery of the Gospel. She receives [Col. 0786A] those who seek her, because the Lord will receive the meek; and she goes before them on the way of justice, for he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness but will have the light of life (John 14).” Therefore whoever loves him loves life, because by keeping his commandments he will attain eternal life; and those who keep watch for her will embrace her favor. As she promises in Proverbs, saying: “Blessed is the person who hears me, who watches daily at my gates and keeps watch at the posts of my doorway (Prov. 8).” By her gates and the posts of her doorway she means the holy Scriptures and their teachers, without which we cannot enter the life she promises. For whoever watches at these gates—that is, perseveres in meditation with an attentive mind—perceives the sweetness of her greatness.

[Col. 0786B] “Those who hold fast to her will inherit life, and wherever she enters, God will bless.” The person truly holds wisdom who obeys Christ’s commandments, and wherever she enters, God’s blessing accompanies her there. Thus he will enrich with eternal blessing the one who seeks access to the heavenly kingdom through faith in and love of her. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will go in and out and find pasture (John 10).”

“Those who serve her will be obedient to the Holy One, and God loves those who love her.” For whoever truly serves Christ and places his hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy, because by doing justice he is just, just as he is just. Concerning this [Col. 0786C] the Lord commanded in the Law, saying: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy”; and God loves those who love her (Lev. 11, 19, and 20). For whoever loves the one who begot him loves the one born from him; the Father certainly loves him, and at the same time the Son loves him, as Truth herself shows in the Gospel, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him (John 14).” But since the proof of love is the manifestation of one’s deeds, it follows:

[Col. 0786D] “Whoever hears her will judge nations, and whoever looks upon her will remain confident. If he believes her, he will inherit her, and his offspring will be established, because in temptation she walks with him, and at the outset she chooses him.” For whoever loves Christ keeps his commandments, and he will judge nations, just as Truth herself promised in the Gospel, saying: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19).” And in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him and dine with him, and he with me. Whoever conquers, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne (Rev. 3).” Therefore the one who looks upon her—that is, places all the attention of his mind and the power of his faith in her—will remain confident. The temptation of the present life will not be able to overthrow him, but his works will be established, [Col. 0787A] and they will be preserved to be rewarded with the prizes of an eternal inheritance, for whose love he did everything. Thus, when he receives them, he will then say with the Prophet: “This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, because I have chosen her (Ps. 131).”

“She will bring fear, dread, and testing upon him; she will torment him with the discipline of her instruction until she tests him in his thoughts and trusts his soul. She will strengthen him, lead him by a straight path, uncover her hidden things to him, and store up for him knowledge and understanding of justice.” This statement confirms what came before, because when divine Wisdom enters and dwells in a person, it directs his works [Col. 0787B] and prepares him, by exercising and testing him through various temptations, to receive the joys of the future life. “She will bring fear, dread, and testing upon him,” because tribulation produces endurance; endurance, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint. “Because the love of God has been poured into the hearts of the elect through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to them.” Hence it says that she will strengthen him, lead him along a straight path, uncover her hidden things to him, and store up for him knowledge and understanding of justice, because wherever the grace of the Holy Spirit pours in the gift of charity, the hidden and obscure things of the mysteries will certainly be disclosed, and the treasure of knowledge and understanding will be revealed there.

“But if he goes astray, she will abandon him and hand him over [Col. 0787C] to the hands of his enemy.” The person who has gone astray from the way of truth is the one who has lost faith, hope, and charity. Wisdom abandons him because she has judged him unworthy of her dwelling. As the Lord himself says through the prophet: “My righteous one lives by my faith; but if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him, and he will hand him over to the hands of his enemy (Hab. 2),” when, after stripping him of his protection, he permits him by a just judgment to fall into the hands of his enemies.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 0787D] Wisdom urges us to stand firm for faith and justice in the time of tribulation, for the salvation of the soul

“Son, preserve the time, and avoid evil.” Earlier, in praising him, he commended the gift of wisdom; now he shows the effect of that wisdom, because whoever truly keeps the precepts of wisdom is cautious amid changing times and does not abandon the way of justice in a time of persecution and distress. Therefore Wisdom herself, exhorting her children, teaches them to preserve the time, because “there is a time for every matter under heaven; and there is a time for war and a time for peace.” For as long as we are in this world, it is a time of war: we must stand for faith and justice and fight for the salvation of the soul. Hence every evil—that is, every vice—must be avoided by us. But when we have departed from this world, the time of peace will come. For God’s dwelling is in peace, and our city, Jerusalem, has received its name from peace.

[Col. 0788A] “Do not be ashamed to speak the truth for the sake of your soul. For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace.” He exhorts Christ’s soldiers, when the time of persecution arrives, not to be afraid to lay down their lives for Christ’s name, nor to be ashamed to utter the confession of true faith with voice and mouth. For there is a shame that brings sin, concerning which Truth herself says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and the holy angels (Luke 19).” There is also another shame that brings glory and grace, when someone is pierced with remorse for his sins and practices repentance. Concerning this the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel to Jerusalem: “I will establish with you an everlasting covenant, [Col. 0788B] and you will remember your ways and be ashamed (Ezek. 16).” And shortly afterward: “You will know,” he says, “that I am the Lord, so that you may remember and be ashamed, and that you may no longer dare to open your mouth because of your shame, when I have been reconciled to you for all that you have done, says the Lord God (ibid.).”

“Do not show partiality against yourself, nor accept falsehood against your soul.” One must always fight and resist persecutors of the faith and heretics, and never yield or consent to their error. Hence it continues:

“Do not fear your neighbor in his fall, and do not withhold your word in the time of salvation.” Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “When you hear of wars [Col. 0788C] and uprisings, do not be terrified (Luke 21).” And again: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim upon the housetops. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matt. 10).”

“Do not hide your wisdom in its splendor. For wisdom is recognized by the tongue, and understanding, knowledge, and instruction by words of truth; and firmness by works of justice.” Wisdom must by no means be hidden from those who wish to receive and learn it with a devout mind, nor should the word of preaching be hidden from attentive hearers, because, as it is written in Proverbs: [Col. 0788D] “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples, but blessing will be upon the head of those who sell it (Prov. 11).” That is, the person who keeps within himself the words of holy preaching is cursed among the peoples, when he is condemned for the punishment of many whom he could have corrected, through the sole fault of his silence. He is the lazy and evil servant who, because he kept back the talent he had received, was sent into the outer darkness.

Those who sell grain are the ones who impart the word of life to their hearers; from them they receive the price of faith and confession, as the Lord says: “Trade until I come (Luke 19).” Blessing comes upon their heads when the Lord says to each of those returning from such commerce: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, [Col. 0789A] I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord.” And rightly wisdom is said to be recognized on the tongues of such people, as are understanding and knowledge; in their teaching are words of truth, and in their example the firmness of justice. For all these things they are crowned with eternal reward.

“Do not contradict the truth in any way, and be ashamed of the falsehood of your ignorance.” There are many who, when reproved by their superiors for wrongs they have committed, either deny what they have done unjustly or falsely deny what they know in their conscience to be true. Therefore he warns that no one should presume to contend against the truth or defend himself by making deceptive excuses, because the one who hides his crimes is not corrected, whereas the one who confesses them [Col. 0789B] and abandons them will certainly be healed. Hence the Psalmist asks the Lord to rescue him from such evil, saying: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips. Do not incline my heart toward an evil word, to make excuses for sins with those who practice iniquity (Ps. 104).”

“Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not subject yourself to every person because of sin.” Just as he urges confession of sin, so he forbids consent to a wicked deed. For what else is “do not subject yourself to a person because of sin” than not consenting to one who in some way entices you to sin? The teacher of truth and worker of justice always urges his hearer toward better and more perfect things. [Col. 0789C] By contrast, the defender of falsehood and perpetrator of iniquity drags those who consent to him into the pit of destruction.

“Do not resist the face of the powerful, and do not strive against the force of the river. Fight for justice for your soul; contend for justice even unto death, and God will conquer [Col. 0790A] your enemies for you.” Obedience must always be offered to superiors when their commands agree with the rule of truth and justice; both the Law and the Gospel teach this in the same way. But if human authority wishes to compel us to blaspheme or drag us into works of iniquity, we must in no way consent. Rather, for right faith and true religion—in which the salvation of the soul is certainly found—we must contend at all times. Hence [Col. 0789D] Truth herself says in the Gospel: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the Gehenna of fire. And if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter life maimed and lame than, having two hands or two feet, to be thrown into the eternal fire (Matt. 5 and 18).” Elsewhere, exhorting his disciples to the struggles of suffering, he says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me; for whoever wishes to save his life will lose it (Luke 9).”

When it says, “God will conquer your enemies for you,” it shows that adversaries are overcome not by human strength but by divine assistance. Hence Truth herself says to her confessors: “Therefore put it into your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you will answer. For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict (Luke 21).”

“Do not be quick with your tongue, nor useless and lax in your works.” To be quick with the tongue is extremely dangerous, because death and life are in the power of the tongue. “The one who guards his mouth guards his soul from distress, but the one who is heedless in speaking will experience evils.” For an unrestrained mouth produces ruin. Hence the Apostle James teaches, saying: “Let every person be quick to [Col. 0790B] hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger (James 1).” And again: “Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves (ibid.).” Hence elsewhere it is written: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. Whoever does the will of God remains forever (1 Cor. 4).”

To become useless and lax in one’s works is very disgraceful. Therefore it says in Proverbs: “The one who is soft and negligent in his work is a brother [the printed text reads *trater*, apparently an OCR or textual error for *frater*, ‘brother’] of the one who dissipates his works. The one who works his land will be satisfied with bread; the one who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty (Prov. 18).”

“Do not be like a lion in your house, overturning your household and oppressing your subjects.” Here he uses “lion” for a fierce person, because it is not fitting for Christ’s disciple [Col. 0790C] to be enraged or cruel. “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the earth (Matt. 5).” Heretics may also be indicated in this statement: in the house of the Church they seduce the hearts of the innocent through the volatility of their tongue and disturb the gentleness of the simple through the insolence of their behavior. According to the Apostle, they must also be rebuked so that they may learn not to blaspheme.

“Do not extend your hand to receive while keeping it closed for giving.” He certainly forbids greed and commends mercy, so that we may not greedily seize what belongs to others but may mercifully distribute what is ours. “For it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20).”

## CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 0790D] Do not place confidence in riches, according to the saying: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and whose will those things be that you have prepared?”

**(CHAP. V.)** “Do not set your attention on unjust possessions, and do not say, ‘My life is sufficient’; for it will profit nothing at the time of vengeance and destruction.” How foolish it is to long greedily for earthly possessions, and especially to turn one’s mind toward unjust profits, is shown by the mutability of things and the authority of the divine writings. For just as we brought nothing into this world, so undoubtedly we can take nothing away. The root of all evils is greed. Hence the Lord rebuked in the Gospel the rich man who was excessively planning future interest and profit over many years, [Col. 0791A] saying: “Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and whose will the things be that you have prepared? (Luke 12).” So it is with the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. Hence Paul also admonishes his disciple, saying: “Command the rich of this age not to be proud, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, and to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life (1 Tim. 6).”

“Do not follow the desire of your heart in your strength, and do not say, ‘How was I able?’ or ‘Who will subject me because of my deeds?’ For God will certainly take vengeance.” — “The Lord is just and loves [Col. 0791B] justice (Ps. 61); he repays each person according to his works (Prov. 24); he rains snares of fire and sulfur upon sinners, and a stormy wind is the portion of their cup (Ps. 10). The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt. 25).”

“Do not say, ‘I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?’ For the Most High is patient in repaying.” Nothing is more foolish than turning God’s kindness and patience into an opportunity for sin. He waits for those who offend so that they may turn to better things and repent of their sins. “For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful.” Through the prophet he says: “I do not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18).” But whoever is hard of heart and delays turning by neglecting the time of forgiveness [Col. 0791C] stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and revelation of God’s just judgment. Hence it continues:

“Do not be without fear, nor add sin upon sin, and do not say, ‘God’s mercy is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins.’ For mercy and wrath quickly draw near from him, and his wrath looks upon sinners.” The human spirit must never be without fear of God, because the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. He guards those who love him and destroys all sinners. Hence the blessed person is always fearful and never despairs of God’s mercy, because the Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies [Col. 0791D] are over all his works. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy.

For this reason it was commanded in the Law: “Do not take away the upper and lower millstone as a pledge (Deut. 24).” The upper and lower millstone are hope and fear. Hope carries one upward, while fear presses the heart downward. But the upper and lower millstones are necessarily joined to each other, so that one without the other is useless. In the breast of the sinner, hope and fear must continually be joined, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear justice; and he fears justice in vain if he does not also trust in mercy.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 0792A] Do not delay turning to the Lord, nor postpone from day to day, nor become arrogant in your thoughts

“Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not postpone from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” Hence the Lord admonishes us in the Gospel, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you (John 12).” And again: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near (Matt. 3, 4).” And once more: [Col. 0792B] “Therefore keep watch, for you do not know when the master of the house will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. What I say to you I say to all: Keep watch (Mark 13).” And again: “Therefore keep watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man (Luke 21).”

“Do not be anxious about unjust riches, for they will profit you nothing on the day of destruction and vengeance.” Unjust riches are those acquired unjustly and preserved greedily. The Christian, to whom the heavenly kingdom has been promised, ought not to yearn anxiously for them. The one who pursues greed troubles his own house, but the one who hates gifts will live. Hence the mere accumulation of riches cannot rescue their possessor from the hand of vengeance on the day of judgment, if they were not previously expended here in mercy on the needy. Therefore the Savior warned us beforehand, saying: “What does it profit [Col. 0792C] a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange can a person give for his soul? For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works (Matt. 16).”

“Do not toss yourself about in every wind, and do not go along every road; for thus the sinner is proved to have a double tongue.” He condemns instability, which is characteristic of fools, as it is written: “A fool changes like the moon, and a double-minded person is unstable in all his ways (Ecclus. 27).” The person tosses himself about in every wind and goes along every road who thinks he can both follow the luxury of the world and keep the fear of the Lord, and serve the world and Christ equally. [Col. 0792D] Whoever is deceived in this way, whether by speaking or acting, is clearly proved to be a sinner.

Alternatively, divine Wisdom warns us not to follow the vanity of heretics and the byways of their errors, because the doubleness of their teaching—in which they sometimes utter true things and sometimes false—proves them harmful. But the following statement shows what we must observe:

“Be firm in the way of God, and in the truth of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice follow you.” The person is firm in the way of God who, by believing rightly, keeps the rule of the Catholic faith and follows evangelical teaching by living rightly and doing good works. The word of peace and justice will follow him when [Col. 0793A] the reward of eternal glory is granted to him in return for his merits, as the Lord says: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord (Matt. 25).”

“Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand; and with wisdom give a true answer.” It is therefore always the custom of the good to hear and receive the word of truth with gentleness and to speak with moderation and prudence. Hence the Apostle James admonishes us, saying: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger (James 1).” And shortly afterward: “In gentleness receive the implanted word, which is able to save your souls (ibid.).” [Col. 0793B] By contrast, among the proud there are always quarrels, and pestilent people destroy a city. Therefore it is also written elsewhere in Proverbs: “Have you seen someone quick to speak? There is more hope for a fool than for his correction (Prov. 29).” Hence he continues, saying:

“If you have understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught in an undisciplined word and be put to shame.” Just as the person who possesses learning in doctrine but does not wish to benefit his neighbor by teaching sins, so the person who lacks knowledge of the Scriptures yet wishes to be a teacher of others commits no minor offense. Therefore he commands the person who is not capable of teaching others to guard his tongue and not utter an indiscreet word, [Col. 0793C] because whoever does not strive to avoid the snare of error falls into everlasting shame.

“For honor and glory belong to the sensible person in speech, but the tongue of the imprudent is his own downfall.” The honor of immortality and the glory of eternal blessedness follow the wise person; the Catholic teacher who is discerning in speech earns them. The downfall of eternal destruction will likewise follow the imprudent person, and the heretical babbler will not escape it.

[Col. 0793D] “Do not be called a whisperer in your life, and do not let your tongue catch and shame you.” He calls the slanderer a whisperer; his shame is genuine, because his condemnation is certain. Hence it is written in Ecclesiastes: “As a serpent bites in silence, so does the one who secretly slanders his brother (Eccles. 10).” And elsewhere: “The one who slanders any matter,” he says, “binds himself for the future (Prov. 13).”

Alternatively, we may understand heretics by “whisperers”: they secretly construct deceits and lay ambushes in order to deceive the unwary. But “the one who digs a pit will fall into it, and the wicked will be caught in their own snares.”

“For over a thief there are shame and repentance, and the worst disgrace is upon the double-tongued.” He calls heretics thieves because, in the likeness of a thief, they love the darkness of night and secretly lay snares of error, so that they may steal the spoils of virtue and right faith from the idle and negligent. Hence Truth herself says in the Gospel: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers; and the thief comes only to steal, and [Col. 0794A] kill, and destroy (John 10).” They are also called double-tongued because they speak in two ways—that is, sometimes truly and sometimes falsely. Their disgrace, however, is the worst, because it is everlasting shame.

“Hatred, enmity, and insult belong to the whisperer.” Hatred, enmity, and insult are rightly joined to whisperers, because their fraud and wickedness make them detestable to God and human beings. Hence Paul says: “Whisperers and slanderers are hateful to God” (Rom. I). And the Psalmist says: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. C). Of such a person Proverbs also reads: “The slanderer is an abomination to human beings” (Prov. XXIV). And again: “In the mouth of a fool is the rod of insult” (ibid. XIV).

[Col. 0794B] “Justify the small and the great alike.” He teaches equity in judgment, lest you become a respecter of persons and, through hatred of someone or through flattery, turn aside from the way of truth. Hence it is written in the Law: “Do not show partiality in judgment. You shall pursue what is just and only what is just” (Deut. I; Lev. XIX; Exod. XXIII).

## CHAPTER VI

“Do not become an enemy to your neighbor on account of a friend; for the wicked person will inherit reproach and insult, and every sinner is envious and double-tongued.” By this statement he shows us the law of true charity, because one who is truly a friend cannot turn back to enmity: “For charity does not act wrongly, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth.” Hence it is said below: “A faithful friend is a medicine of life and immortality.” [Col. 0794C] But heretics, who depart from the unity of faith and the fellowship of charity, do not remain in true friendship; rather, they are changed from friends into enemies. Hence John says of them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John II). But so that they may be recognized as not all being of us, these people leave reproach and insult to the followers of their corrupt teaching; and every sinner is envious and double-tongued, because every heretic hates the truth and sows falsehood.

“Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull, lest your strength be shattered through folly, your leaves be eaten, your fruits be destroyed, and you be left like a dry tree in the wilderness.” He forbids boasting and detests pride, because pride is the beginning of every sin, and every arrogance is an abomination before God. And lest we think it enough to avoid exaltation in our actions, he says: “Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull.” [Col. 0794D] God is the examiner of the heart, and he judges each person not according to outward appearance but according to truth. No one can deceive him through hypocrisy, because all things are naked and open before his eyes. If he sees within the soul a stiff-necked and swollen thought, he will not be pleased with it; rather, the strength of the proud person will be shattered through the folly of his exaltation. The leaves of his words are empty, the fruits of his deeds useless, and, like a dry tree lacking the greenness of love, he is counted among the barren deeds of the wicked. Hence it is written in the Psalm: “For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves; they are confounded, because God has despised them” (Ps. LII). The apostle Peter likewise says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. V). And Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 18).

“For a wicked soul will destroy its possessor; it gives him over to the joy of his enemies and leads him into the lot of the ungodly.” Just as the fruit of good works follows a good will, so nothing prosperous will come from a malicious mind. If love does not cling to the heart, a person pretends in vain that he is practicing virtue. [Col. 0796A] Hence it is written: “Whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James II). And elsewhere: “To everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. XIII). Thus the one who does not take care, through right belief and good works, to avoid entering the lot of the ungodly falls into the joy of his enemies—that is, of the malignant spirits. But since, in discussing conversion, he has fully shown what true conversion is—namely, the correction of conduct and speech—and has warned against repeating former folly, lest one fall into the joy of enemies and the condemnation of the ungodly, now that the first book has ended, let us disclose at the beginning of the other book what it teaches concerning true friendship and wise caution.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0795]

## CHAPTER I

On the grace of friends: that enmity does not creep in among pure and pleasant conversations.

“A sweet word multiplies friends and softens enemies; and a gracious tongue abounds in a good person.” Hence it is written in Proverbs: “The lips of the just instruct many, and wisdom is found on the lips of the wise” (Prov. X). And again: “A harsh word stirs up quarrels, but a gentle word calms those that have been stirred up” (ibid. XV). Thus the ecclesiastical man, in whom a gracious tongue—that is, one endowed with good favor—abounds, multiplies the multitude of the faithful by teaching; and by the evident reasoning of truth he often causes the fury of persecutors to grow calm.

“Let many be at peace with you, but let one out of a thousand be your counselor.” Therefore peace is to be maintained with all people, insofar as possibility allows; but counsel should not be sought from many. For it is written: “Many people are called merciful, but who will find a faithful man?” (Prov. XX). And elsewhere: “When an enemy has plotted deceit in his heart, and lowers his voice, do not believe him, for there are seven wicked things in his heart” (ibid. XXVI). Ecclesiastes says: “Among a thousand I found one man; among all women I did not find one” (Eccles. VII). There are some who possess devotion and good will but lack prudence of mind. Others are prudent in heart but perverse in will. Where devotion to faith and understanding are found together, useful counsel is sought at the appropriate time.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0795D] Wisdom marks out the friend who remains only for the banquets of the table and withdraws in time of need.

“If you acquire a friend, acquire him through testing, and do not readily entrust yourself to him; for there is a friend according to his appointed time, and he will not remain in the day of tribulation. There is a friend who turns to enmity, and there is a friend who will expose hatred, quarrels, and insults. There is also a friend who is a companion at table, and he will not remain in the day of need. If a friend remains steadfast, he will be to you like an equal, [Col. 0796B] and he will act confidently among your household.” By expressing the various kinds of false friends, he finally arrives at the description of the true friend, because many profess to be friends in prosperity but reveal themselves as enemies in adversity. Hence it follows:

“If he humbles himself before you, he will hide himself from your face.” He pretends outwardly to be devoted, but when necessity arises he will prove that he is alien in heart. Therefore it says, “he will hide himself”—that is, he pretends to be what he is not.

“You shall have a good friendship with one of one mind; separate yourself from your enemies, and be attentive concerning your friends.” Where there is unity of mind among friends, there the friendship is stable; but where there is pretense and not truth, there is no firmness of friendship at all. Hence he admonishes one to separate oneself completely from enemies, where enmity is evident, and to exercise caution in discerning friends. It should be noted, however, that this vigilance in discernment is especially necessary between Catholics and heretics, because heretics carry out all their schemes through hypocrisy, so that they may more easily deceive the unwary. Hence the Savior warns beforehand in the Gospel, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits,” and so forth (Matt. VII). The Apostle likewise writes to his disciple: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some have promised and, concerning the faith, have fallen away” (1 Tim. VI). And to the Romans: “I urge you, brothers, to watch those who cause dissensions and scandals contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly; and through sweet words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. XVI).

“A faithful friend is a strong protection; whoever finds him has found a treasure. Nothing compares with a faithful friend, and no weighing of gold or silver is worthy to be set against the goodness of his faith.” What, indeed, is a friend except a companion in love, to whom you join and attach your mind, mingling with him so that you wish two to become one? You entrust yourself to him as to another self, fearing nothing from him and asking nothing dishonorable from him for your own advantage. Friendship is not a matter of profit, but is full of honor and full of the grace of virtue. What is more precious than friendship? It is shared by angels and human beings. Hence the Lord says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke XVI). Our Lord himself made friends out of servants. As he says according to John: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John XV). He gave us the pattern of friendship that we should follow: we are to do what our friend wishes, reveal our secrets to our friend—whatever we hold in our heart—and remain ignorant of none of his mysteries. [Col. 0797B] Let us show him our breast, and let him open his to us. “For this reason,” he says, “I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.” A friend therefore conceals nothing if he is true, but pours out his soul, just as the Lord Jesus poured out the mysteries of the Father. Whoever preserves friendship is a friend of God and is honored by this name. But no one is more detestable than one who has violated friendship. Hence the Lord found in the betrayer the gravest kind of scandal, by which to condemn his treachery: he had not returned the favor of grace, but had mixed the poison of malice into the fellowship of friendship.

“A faithful friend is a medicine of life and immortality; and those who fear the Lord will find him.” [Col. 0797C] “A friend is so called as if he were the guardian of the soul. In a faithful friend there is indeed a medicine of life and immortality, because if he is faithful, he is certainly a friend according to God; and if he is a friend according to God, he always discusses with his friend those things that pertain to the medicine of eternal life and everlasting immortality. Hence there is that saying of Tullius Cicero: ‘Friendship cannot exist except among the good. For it is characteristic of a good man—whom one may also call wise—to observe these two things in friendship: first, that nothing be feigned or pretended.’ For it is plainly more honorable to hate openly than to conceal one’s judgment behind one’s face. Next, one should not merely repel accusations brought by someone against a friend, but should not even be suspicious, always supposing that something has been violated by the friend. [Col. 0797D] To this there ought to be added a certain pleasantness of speech and conduct, by no means a moderate seasoning of friendship. Sadness and severity in every matter certainly possess gravity, but friendship ought to be more relaxed, freer, sweeter, and more inclined toward every form of ease.”

“Whoever fears God will have a good friendship, because his friend will be according to God.” Thus the holy Fathers have taught that the full and perfect grace of friendship cannot endure except among perfect men who persevere in the same virtue. Hence they established certain steps by which one might reach its perfection and unbreakable stability. They said, therefore, that the first step of true friendship consists in contempt for worldly possessions and disdain for all the things we possess. The second is that each person cut back his own desires so thoroughly that, while judging himself wise and prudent, he prefers not his own decisions to those of his neighbor. The third is to know that everything, even what one considers useful and necessary, must be placed after the good of charity and peace. The fourth is to believe that one must never become completely angry, whether for just or unjust reasons. The fifth is to desire to care for a brother’s anger against oneself, even when it has arisen without reason, in the same way one would care for one’s own anger, knowing that another’s sadness is equally destructive to oneself, as though one had become angry against another—unless, so far as one can, one also removes it from the brother’s mind. The final step, which is undoubtedly the decisive destruction of all vices in general, is to believe that one will depart from this world every day. This conviction not only permits no sadness to remain in the heart, but also restrains all movements of desire and every sin. Whoever preserves these things, therefore, can neither endure nor inflict the bitterness of anger and discord.

## CHAPTER III

Wisdom exhorts the sons—that is, the Church of the faithful—to receive one doctrine, all in one and one in all, so that doctrine may be made clear through faith and works.

“My son, receive instruction from your youth, and until your gray hairs you will find wisdom.” Hence it is written in Proverbs: “My son, if wisdom enters your heart and knowledge pleases your soul, counsel will guard you and prudence will preserve you, so that you may be delivered from the evil way and from the man who speaks perverse things” (Prov. II). Whoever, therefore, in youth applies the ear of obedience to sound doctrine will reap the sweetest fruits of wisdom in old age.

“Approach it like one who plows and sows, and await its good fruits; for in its work you will labor only a little, and soon you will eat of its generations.” Whoever desires to eat the seed of the divine word and reap the sweetest fruits of sacred virtues must uproot the shoots of vices from his heart with the plowshare of the Gospel. When he says, “Await its good fruits,” he shows that patience is the testing of virtues. As Truth itself testifies in the Gospel: “The one who retains the word in a good and excellent heart will bear fruit in patience” (Luke VIII). “In its work,” he says, “you will labor only a little, and soon you will eat of its generations. For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). The tribulation of the present time will indeed work in us an immeasurable weight of glory in the future. For “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him.”

“How exceedingly harsh wisdom is to unlearned people! The senseless person will not remain in it. Its testing will be like the strength of a stone among them, and they will not delay in casting it away.” Meditation on wisdom is always hateful to the imprudent and foolish, and they detest those who rebuke them because they do not know the usefulness of discipline. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “A fool mocks his father’s discipline” (Prov. XV). And again: “Reprove a wise person, and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will hate you” (ibid. IX). And again: “The pestilent person does not love the one who corrects him, nor does he go to the wise” (ibid. XV). The ear that hears the reproofs of life will dwell among the wise; but whoever rejects discipline despises his own soul. They consider discipline harsh, and therefore they strive to cast it away from themselves. Although this statement applies generally to all foolish people, it especially marks out heretics, who through the hardness of their minds do not accept correction, do not endure being drawn away from their error, and do not allow themselves to be directed into the way of truth. Although they read the Scriptures constantly, they understand their force not at all. Hence it is written: “The scoffer seeks wisdom and will not find it” (ibid.). Among those who receive it, however, its testing will be like the strength of a stone—that is, the solidity of understanding—for no treasure of earthly wealth can be compared with it, since the state of true wisdom surpasses all things. The Psalmist, understanding this truthfully, says: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XVIII). Of this Proverbs also says: “Wisdom is better than all precious things, and no desirable thing can compare with it” (Prov. VIII).

“For wisdom is the teaching according to its name, and it is not manifest to many; but to those who know it, it remains until the presence of God.” The wisdom of teaching is the sincerity of the divine law. It is “according to its name”—that is, prudence, truth, and virtue—because “the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes,” and every word of God is a fiery shield. Hence Proverbs also reads: “Wisdom is prudence for a person, yet it is not manifest to many, because it joyfully shows itself on the way only to those who love it” (Prov. X). Those who despise it will be ignoble. But to those who recognize it—that is, who preserve it with right faith and good works—it leads them to the contemplation of God’s glory: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.”

“Listen, my son, and receive the counsel of understanding, and do not reject my counsel. Put your foot into its fetters and your neck into its chains; submit your shoulder and carry it, and do not grow weary of its bonds.” Wisdom teaches how one ought to submit to the divine law, because whoever consents to it will preserve himself forever. He puts his foot into its fetters who fortifies the course of his life with its commandments. He places his neck in its chain who regulates his speech according to its rule. He submits his shoulder to it for carrying who subjects his actions to its instruction and fulfills in practice what it commands. And lest anyone receive its teaching with weariness and difficulty, he adds:

[Col. 0800A] “Approach it with your whole soul, and preserve its ways with all your strength. Seek it, and it will be revealed to you; and once you have taken hold of it, do not abandon it. For in the end you will find rest in it, and it will be turned for you into delight.
