Its fetters will be for you a protection of strength, foundations of virtue, and its chains a robe of glory.” “One must approach wisdom more with the heart than with the body, because spiritual light is to be contemplated by the soul, not by the flesh; nevertheless, the senses of the body must be governed by the reason of the mind. Hence the Apostle teaches us, saying: ‘Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh,’ and so forth (Gal. V). Whoever meditates with a devoted soul and strives to know the wisdom of God, which is Christ, endeavors to keep his commandments and to restrain the indulgence of the body through continence, lest it dissolve into the pleasures of the present life, but rather lives under the rule of heavenly discipline. Such a person will certainly find rest at the end of life, when, released from the flesh, he receives the rewards of eternal glory for his present labor.” Hence it follows: “For adornment of life is in it, and its bonds are a salutary weaving. You will put on the robe of glory, and place upon yourself a crown of rejoicing.” Certain knowledge of wisdom makes a person close to God and an heir of perpetual life. No one can otherwise reach the robe of immortality and the crown of glory except through true knowledge of wisdom, since the sole blessedness of the saints in the heavenly kingdom is the contemplation of God’s face and the reception of truth. Hence Truth itself says to the Father in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). And again: “Father,” he says, “those whom you have given me,” and so forth, “because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV

Wisdom promises the rewards of eternity to those who love her.

“My son, if you attend to me, you will learn; and if you apply your soul, you will be wise; if you incline your ear, you will receive instruction; and if you love to listen, you will be wise.” Wisdom admonishes the ecclesiastical man—whom it calls “son”—to apply himself wholly to meditation on the divine law. First it urges him to learn; then to apply his soul to this; afterward to incline the ear of his heart; and finally to devote himself diligently to listening. Thus it promises that he will become wise, because whoever desires to receive perfect knowledge of true wisdom, which is Christ, must first humbly submit himself to the teachings of Catholic teachers and subject all the movements of his soul to their discipline. Then, turning the intention of his heart away from every evil desire, he must devote himself diligently to hearing the word of God. He must also take care that he devote his entire effort to meditation on God’s law not for ambition concerning earthly things or human praise, but solely out of desire for goodness itself. In this way he will truly receive the fruit of true wisdom. And lest anyone, trusting in his own intellect, attempt to investigate Holy Scripture without the tradition of teachers, he adds:

“Stand among a multitude of prudent presbyters, and join yourself to their wisdom from the heart, so that you may be able to hear every account of God, and that sayings of praise may not escape you. Even if you appear intelligent, remain vigilant toward him, and let your foot wear down the steps of his doors.” The many falls of heretics show how dangerous it is to rely on one’s own knowledge and despise the traditions of orthodox teachers. The arrogance of their pride brought them down above all, because they preferred their own sects to the teachings of the holy Fathers. Hence Wisdom reproves them in Proverbs, saying: “They abandon the straight path and walk along dark ways; they rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things. Their ways are crooked and their paths infamous” (Prov. II). Shortly afterward the same teacher of the faithful shows what must be done, saying: “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not rely on your own prudence. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will direct your steps. Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord and turn away from evil. Keep your thought on God’s commandments, and be especially constant in his precepts; and he will give you a heart, and the desire for wisdom will be given to you” (ibid. III). A pure understanding of the heart and the most salutary love of divine wisdom will rightly be given to the one who regulates his thoughts according to the commandments of the Most High and constantly meditates on those things that agree with the teaching of God’s law, striving in practice to fulfill what he knows to be entirely pleasing to his Creator.

## CHAPTER V

Wisdom speaks of the evils, however great, from which we must guard ourselves—not by our own strength but by her help.

## CHAPTER VII

“Do not do evil, and evils will not seize you. Depart from the wicked, and evils will depart from you.” This statement can be understood in two ways: first, as a general prohibition of every sinful act, for which perpetual punishment will be paid; and second, specifically, as a warning against the harmful association of heretics, which, as Scripture testifies, has abandoned the guide of its youth and forgotten the covenant of its God. For this reason its house is bent down toward death, and its path toward the underworld; and all who enter it do not return, [Col. 0801D] nor do they grasp the paths of life. Hence he now admonishes you to depart from the wicked, and evils will depart from you. No one who dwells with her can remain free from the filth of error. Therefore Paul teaches the disciple to avoid a heretical person after a second and third admonition (Titus III), because such a person is perverse. The following statement instructs us further, adding:

“Do not sow evil in the furrows of injustice, and do not reap it sevenfold.” He sows evil in the furrows of injustice who, laboring in perverse teaching, inserts examples of wickedness; he will reap their fruit sevenfold when, at the end of the present life, he receives complete vengeance in the fire of Gehenna. In Scripture the number seven sometimes signifies the fullness of something good and sometimes the fullness of something evil. Thus through Isaiah the fullness of divine gifts is described as resting in the flower of Jesse’s root through a sevenfold Spirit (Isa. XI). And in the Gospel the Lord himself says that the evil spirit brings with it into an empty house seven spirits more wicked than itself, so that the last state of that person becomes worse than the first (Luke XI). And lest anyone presumptuously seek ecclesiastical rank, judging himself worthy of the teaching office, he immediately adds:

“Do not seek leadership from a human being, nor a seat of honor from a king.” Ambition for preeminence in no way preserves the character of true humility; consequently, it cannot exercise the work of righteous governance, because it has neglected to possess the path of true piety. Hence Truth itself in the Gospel restrained by a salutary decree the carnal exaltation of his disciples, who were contending over primacy, saying: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you are not to be like that; rather, let the greater among you become like the younger, and the leader like the one who serves” (Luke XXII). Hence James also says: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you will receive a greater judgment” (James III). The shepherd of the Church likewise teaches concerning this, saying: “All of you, practice humility toward one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. V; James IV).

## CHAPTER VI

That a person ought not to justify himself before God or wish to appear wise.

“Do not justify yourself before the Lord; it is better to be humbled than exalted, because he himself is the knower of the heart. And before the king do not wish to appear wise.” No presumption is more harmful than for someone to trust in his own righteousness or knowledge, since Scripture says: “There is no one on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ps. XIII). And again: “The stars,” he says, “are not clean in God’s sight; how much less a human being, who is decay, and a son of man, who is a worm?” (Job XV, XXV). And in Proverbs: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. XX). And again: “Have you seen a person who appears wise to himself? A fool has more hope than he does” (ibid. XXVI). And in the Gospel the Lord says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, XVIII). Hence the Psalmist also says: “For God scatters the bones of those who please themselves; they are confounded because God has despised them” (Ps. LII). Therefore no one may judge himself wise before Christ the King, because every arrogance is an abomination before God. Hence Paul exhorts, saying: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. XI). And again: “I say, by the grace of God that has been given to me, to everyone among you: do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sober judgment, and according as God has allotted to each a measure of faith” (Rom. XII).

[Col. 0803A] “Do not seek to become a judge unless you are able, by your strength, to break through iniquities, lest you fear the face of the powerful and place a stumbling block in your justice.” Each person ought to weigh his own strength and, in proportion to his abilities, undertake responsibility for another’s affairs. Therefore anyone who is still occupied by earthly desires through weakness of soul must beware lest, by provoking the anger of the strict Judge more severely, he become an author of ruin to his subjects while delighting in the glory of his position. Each person must therefore measure himself carefully, lest he dare to assume a place of governance while some vice still reigns within him, lest one who is corrupted by his own crime desire to become a judge of the faults of others. The person who is to be drawn forward as an example of living must therefore be one who, having died to all the passions of the flesh, already lives spiritually; [Col. 0803B] who places the prosperity of the world after other things; who fears no adversity; who desires only inward things; whose intention is so well ordered that the body neither resists it altogether through weakness nor opposes it excessively through insolence; who is not led to desire what belongs to others but gives away what is his own; who, through the compassion of mercy, is quickly moved to forgive, but, in forgiving, never inclines away from the stronghold of righteousness more than is fitting; who commits no unlawful acts but mourns acts committed by others as though they were his own; who, from the affection of his heart, sympathizes with another’s weakness; who rejoices in the progress of his neighbor as in his own; who presents himself to others as worthy of imitation in all that he does, so that among them he has nothing, at least concerning his past, for which to blush; who strives to live in such a way that he can water even the parched hearts of his neighbors with the streams of teaching; who has already learned through the practice and experience of prayer that he can obtain from the Lord what he asks.

“Do not sin among the multitude of the city, nor mix yourself with the crowd.” He forbids the person who possesses reason and prevails by the power of free choice to be provoked to sin by the insolence of his subjects. Rather, that person must resist another’s wickedness with the strength of steadfastness and must not think that he sins with impunity when he has chosen to agree with the will of the majority. Hence it follows:

“Do not bind double sins together, for you will not be free from one.” He binds double sins together who not only fails to restrain himself from sins but also favors others by consenting to sin, although it would be enough for him to be guilty of one offense even if he did not involve himself in the other. [Col. 0803D] Therefore the Apostle rebukes transgressors of God’s law, saying: “Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. I).

“Do not be fainthearted in your soul; do not disdain to pray and to give alms.” Faintheartedness must be avoided because through it there often arises the sorrow of the world, which produces death. By contrast, those who are steadfast in spirit endure labor courageously through patience, because they despise every pain of the present life. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “Nothing that happens to the just will grieve him” (Prov. XII). Therefore the apostle James also urges those who are suffering sorrow to flee to the help of prayer, saying: “Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms” (James V). Likewise the shepherd of the Church commends equanimity and beneficence, writing in his Letter: “Beloved, do not be astonished at the fire that comes upon you as a trial, as though something strange were happening to you; but rejoice insofar as you share in Christ’s sufferings, so that you may also rejoice and exult at the revelation of his glory. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, you will be blessed, because the Spirit of the glory of God rests upon you. Let none of you suffer as a murderer, a thief, a slanderer, or a coveter of what belongs to others. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify God in that name, because it is time for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and the sinner appear? Therefore let those who suffer according to the will of God commend their souls to the faithful Creator in good works” (1 Pet. IV). But beneficence itself will then be acceptable to God if it does not abandon the way of humility or turn toward mental exaltation. Concerning this it follows:

“Do not say, ‘Because of the multitude of my gifts God will look upon me, and when I offer to God Most High he will receive my gifts.’” What a servant who does good ought to think about his deeds, the Lord himself shows in the Gospel through the parable of the servant who returned from the field and completed his master’s commands while serving in the house. He concludes the parable as follows: “Does he thank that servant because he did what he had commanded? I do not think so. So you also, when you have done everything that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke XVII). The more a person exalts his good deeds through boasting, the less merit they have before God. Therefore we must devote ourselves to good works. Yet above all we must preserve humility in our heart and be united with and compassionate toward our neighbors through charity. Concerning this it follows:

“Do not mock a person in the bitterness of his soul; for God, who sees all things, both humbles and exalts.” Hence it is written in Proverbs: “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice; and when he is ruined, let your heart not exult, lest the Lord see and it displease him, and he turn his anger away from him” (Prov. XXIV). By contrast, Paul beneficially teaches what ought to be done, saying: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, sharing the same mind with one another. Do not be high-minded, but associate with the humble” (Rom. XII).

## CHAPTER VII

On not uttering a lie against a friend.

“Do not love a lie against your brother, nor act similarly toward a friend.” If no lie is praiseworthy, and to cause anyone scandal is harmful, how much more blameworthy is it to plot something deceitfully against a friend? To impose a false accusation upon a brother is no small offense, since a lying witness will perish. Hence Wisdom says in Proverbs: “As one who throws spears and arrows toward death is harmful, so is the person who deceitfully injures his friend; and when he is caught, he says, ‘I was only playing’” (Prov. XXVI). And elsewhere: “Do not plot evil against your friend when he has confidence in you” (Prov. III).

«Do not be willing to tell any lie, for habitual lying is not good.» Every lie is harmful, because it is a sin. For the mouth that lies kills the soul; and the more often one uses it, the heavier a burden of sins one accumulates. Although there are different kinds of lies, nevertheless the first and capital lie, and one to be fled far away, is that which occurs in the teaching of religion. No one ought to be brought to this lie under any condition, because through it it is absolutely certain that a person is separated from God. Whoever thinks that some kind of lie is not a sin will shamefully deceive himself, while considering himself an honest deceiver of others.

«Do not be wordy in the assembly of presbyters, and do not repeat a word in your prayer.» Since above we said that a lie in the teaching of religion is capital, whoever observes this principle—that is, whoever chooses to listen more devoutly to the teaching of the elders than to put forward his own opinion impudently—will be far removed from this danger. For it is safer to listen than to speak. Hence James admonishes in his Epistle, saying: «Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger (Jas. I).»

[Col. 0805C] «Do not hate laborious work or agriculture, created by the Most High.» To devote oneself to useful labor and to flee idleness is praiseworthy, because idleness is the enemy of the soul. Hence Paul also wrote to the Thessalonians that they should work quietly and eat their own bread, adding that if anyone did not wish to work, neither should he eat. He set his own example before them, since he had not been troublesome among them, nor had he eaten bread from anyone without payment, but had worked in labor and weariness night and day, so as not to burden any of them (II Thess. II). By saying that agriculture was created by the Most High, he signifies that this sentence was given to sinful humanity: that it should seek its food by the labor of its hands. Thus it is written in Genesis: «In the sweat of your face, he said, you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen. III).»

[Col. 0805D] «Do not count yourself among the undisciplined; remember wrath, for it will not delay.» He calls undisciplined those who are restless and disobedient, who refuse to obey God’s commands. It is dangerous to associate with such people, because a sure punishment is reserved for them, which he calls “wrath,” unless they correct themselves and turn to a better life. Hence it is written in Proverbs: «Judgments are prepared for scoffers, and blows for striking the hearts of fools. Like the roaring of a lion is the terror of a king; whoever provokes him sins against his own life (Prov. XIX).»

[Col. 0806A] «Humble your spirit exceedingly, for the punishment of the flesh of the wicked is fire and the worm.» Just as pride is the beginning of every sin, so humility and fear of God are the beginning of wisdom. Blessed is the person who is always fearful, for «whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke XIV, XVIII).» The punishment of the flesh of the wicked is fire and worms, because the flesh of sinners, which abounded in lust in this world, is punished together with the soul in the future and tormented by the fire of Gehenna. The Lord himself recalls that there are both worm and fire in Gehenna, saying in the Gospel: «If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life maimed than, having two hands, to go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire, where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished (Mark IX).» By the worm he signifies the corruption of Gehenna, just as by the fire he signifies its burning; or by “worm” he means the tardy repentance for crimes which will never cease to gnaw at the conscience of the afflicted amid their torments, so that the fire is the punishment raging outwardly, while the worm is the pain accusing inwardly.

[Col. 0806B] «Do not betray a friend for money, nor despise your dearest brother for gold.» Many have perished because of greed, and, while possessing desire for earthly things, have neglected their neighbor—that is, the human being created in the image of God. Therefore he teaches that one should love one’s neighbor more than a treasure of money. «For the root of all evils is greed; by reaching after it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows (I Tim. VI).» And rightly so, because they have lost the love of God, which is the foundation of righteousness. Therefore John urges us, saying: «Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him (I John II).» And again: «If anyone has the world’s possessions and sees his brother in need but closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him? (I John III.) Whoever disregards loss for the sake of a friend is righteous, and whoever hates gifts will live (Prov. XII, XV).»

[Col. 0806C] «Do not leave the sensible and good woman whom you have received in the fear of God.» According to the historical sense, he teaches that the marriage covenant must be preserved and not easily broken, in accordance with the Gospel saying: «What God has joined, let no human being separate (Matt. XIX).» Or, more fully according to the allegorical sense, he forbids any believer to depart from the fellowship of the Church, because it is altogether necessary that he keep the covenant which he made with God in baptism, since a great reward will follow the person who faithfully fulfills the true religion. Hence what follows:

[Col. 0806D] «For the grace of her modesty is above gold.» — «What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II).» You may understand this woman as the wisdom of the sacred Scriptures, whom the Gospel calls a precious pearl, which the spiritual merchant, when he found it, went away and sold everything he had and bought it. Ecclesiastes also speaks of her: «Live life with the woman whom you have loved, all the days of your vain life which have been given to you under the sun (Eccles. IX).» Follow wisdom and knowledge of the Scriptures, and join this woman to yourself in marriage. The “days of vanity” signify the days of this age. The Apostle does not remain silent about them. What he says, «Live life with the woman,» is expressed ambiguously: either, “Live and contemplate life, both you yourself and your wife together.” For you cannot live safely or see life without such a wife. Beautifully, therefore, he commands that in the days of our vanity we seek true life together with wisdom as our wife; for she is our portion, and this is the fruit of our labor, if in this shadowy life we can find eternal life.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the good and faithful servant

[Col. 0807A] «Do not injure a servant who works faithfully, nor a hired worker who gives his life.» Wisdom admonishes us to preserve moderation and the rule of equity toward our subjects. For it is not fitting that a devoted and diligent servant should suffer abuse because of the insolence of his master, nor that a hired worker should be deprived of the wages due for his labor, since the legal and apostolic teaching clearly instructs us to treat every person equitably. For Paul, writing to Titus, commands servants to be subject to their masters, pleasing them in all things, not contradicting, not defrauding, but showing good faith in everything, so that they may adorn the teaching of God our Savior in all things (Titus II). Likewise, in his Epistle to the Colossians, after teaching servants to obey their earthly masters in all things—not serving merely for appearances, as people-pleasers, but in simplicity of heart, fearing God—he commands masters, saying: «Masters, provide your servants with what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven (Col. III).» Whoever does an injustice will receive what he has done unjustly, and there is no partiality with God. Concerning hired workers, the Lord commands in Deuteronomy: «You shall not withhold the wage of the needy and poor brother of yours, or of the resident alien who dwells with you in your land and within your gates; but on that same day you shall give him the payment for his labor before sunset, because he is poor and sustains his life by it, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it be counted as sin against you (Deut. XXIV).»

[Col. 0807B] «Let a sensible servant be dear to you as your own soul; do not deprive him of his freedom, nor abandon him in his need.» It is fitting that an intelligent and benevolent servant or disciple should not lack the affection of his master, nor be deprived of the appropriate power to work well, nor, oppressed by the violence of servitude, be reduced to poverty. Rather, he should be provided for in every way with suitable care and treated as a brother. For although by social condition he is inferior as a servant, nevertheless according to the nature shared by all he is equal. Paul also shows this, saying: «Whether slaves or free, we are one in Christ (I Cor. VII).» And again: «Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you; but if you are able to become free, make use of it. For the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman; likewise, the one who was called as a free person is Christ’s slave. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Let each one remain, brothers, in the condition in which he was called, with God.»

[Col. 0808A] «You have cattle? Attend to them; and if they are useful, let them remain with you.» He calls them “cattle” because of their simplicity of mind and humility. For just as an animal is entirely subject to the will of its master, so a good servant is always ready to serve the interests of his master. Therefore he does not deserve to be cast away shamefully, but should be preserved with every care.

«You have children? Educate them, and bend them from their childhood.» This statement clearly shows how the condition of servants should be nurtured. The affection due to children should therefore be fostered on account of the right of nature, but they should be disciplined with stronger correction because of the instability of the mind. Hence later in this book it is said: «Food, a rod, and a burden for the donkey; bread, discipline, and work for the servant. He works under discipline and seeks to rest; loosen your hand from him, and he seeks freedom (Eccles. XXXIII).»

[Col. 0808B] «You have daughters? Preserve their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face.» Just as above he taught that good servants should be treated in the place of children, so now he commands that maidservants should be treated in the place of daughters. Yet this must be done with discipline, just as children are to be treated. Hence it is written elsewhere: «Nurse your son, and he will make you fearful; play with him, and he will grieve you. Do not smile at him, lest you suffer grief and your teeth chatter at the end (Eccles. XXX).»

## CHAPTER IX. On children honoring their parents

[Col. 0808C] «Give your daughter in marriage, and you will have done a great work; give her to a sensible man.» He commands that a daughter be given and subjected to marriage, lest she become wanton in her parents’ house and fall into lust. Thus he calls the act accomplished a “great work,” that is, a useful one. For it is better that she remain protected and disciplined under the guardianship of a husband than that, when she is already fully grown, she should be corrupted through neglect in her parents’ house. But so that this may be accomplished more easily, he commands that she be given to a sensible—that is, prudent and energetic—man. For only in this way will she be preserved. As it is written in Proverbs: «Whoever walks wisely will be saved, but whoever supports prostitutes will lose his substance (Prov. XXVIII).»

[Col. 0808D] «If you have a wife according to your soul, do not cast her away; and do not entrust yourself with all your heart to one who is hateful.» Although this passage may seem to commend conjugal chastity, so that, while one lawful wife is retained, all the foulness of prostitutes and concubines may be rejected, nevertheless in a deeper sense it admonishes us to hold firmly to the catholic faith together with the true religion which we received immediately after baptism, and to reject utterly all the faithlessness of heretics. Concerning this Wisdom also urges us in Proverbs, saying: «My son, listen to me, and attend to the words of my mouth, lest your mind be drawn away in her ways, or you be deceived by her paths. For she has cast down many wounded, and the strongest have been slain by her. Her house is the way to the underworld, entering into the innermost places of death (Prov. VII).»

[Col. 0809A] «Honor your father, and do not forget your mother’s sighing; remember that you would not have been born except through them, and repay them as they repaid you.» He frequently commends the honor due to parents, because this is the first commandment with a promise. Hence Paul also teaches widows who have children and grandchildren to learn first to manage their own household and to repay their parents in kind, for this is acceptable before God. In another sense, we ought to honor God the Father by right faith and good works, and not forget the sighing of Mother Church, which labored greatly in giving birth to us. For if it had not been for them, we would not have been Christians and would not have been counted among the children of God. We ought to receive with thanksgiving all the good, just, and holy things which they have done for us, and return worthy praise to them. The following words also seem to support this interpretation.

## CHAPTER X. On the fear of God and the honor due to priests, and on offering first fruits to them

[Col. 0809B] «With your whole soul, he says, fear God, and sanctify his priests; love him who made you with all your strength, and do not abandon his ministers.» We ought therefore to demonstrate our fear and love of God by honoring his ministers, because he himself said in the Gospel: «Whoever honors you honors me; and whoever receives you receives me; but whoever despises you despises me (Matt. X).» But because honor sometimes signifies the provision of necessities and assistance through support, he adds:

«Honor God with your whole soul, honor the priests, and cleanse yourself with your arms.» Hence the Lord says to his disciples: «The worker is worthy of his food. Into whatever city or village you enter, inquire who in it is worthy, and remain there until you leave (Matt. X).» Hence the Apostle also says: «The farmer who labors ought to be the first to partake of the fruits (I Tim. II).» And again: «Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk? (I Cor. IX.)» And shortly afterward: «If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?» And again: «Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who serve at the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (ibid.).»

[Col. 0809C] The person who gives alms to the needy from the labor of his hands and does not delay in giving tithes and first fruits from his produce to the ministers of the Church cleanses himself with his arms. Concerning this it also follows:

«Give them a portion, as you have been commanded, of first fruits and purification, and cleanse yourself from your negligence with a little.» The offerings of first fruits, tithes, and various oblations which the Lord commanded to be offered in the Law belonged to the use of the priests and Levites. The Lord said to Aaron and his sons: «All the first fruits of the sanctuary which the children of Israel offer to the Lord I have given to you and to your sons and daughters as a perpetual right. It is an everlasting covenant of salt before the Lord for you and your sons. And the Lord said to Aaron: You shall possess nothing in their land, nor shall you have a portion among them. I am your portion and inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel. But to the sons of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession, in return for the ministry by which they serve me in the tabernacle of the covenant, so that the children of Israel may no longer approach the tabernacle and commit a deadly sin, while only the sons of Levi serve me in the tabernacle and bear the sins of the people. This shall be an everlasting statute throughout your generations. They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of the tithes which I have set apart for their use and necessities (Num. V).»

[Col. 0809D] To them was entrusted not only the gift of first fruits and tithes, but also the use of the offerings and sacrifices which were offered to the Lord. Hence he says that a portion of both first fruits and purification should be given to the ministers of God, because they bear the sins of the people and pray for them. What follows—

«And cleanse yourself from your negligence with a little»—

shows that an offering made to God from a humble mind and pure love, even if small in quantity, cleanses the negligence of many offenses. Concerning this it is written: «Love covers a multitude of sins (I Pet. IV).» And the Psalmist says: «A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps. L).» Hence in the Gospel the Lord himself did not reject the widow’s two small coins but gratefully accepted them (Mark XII).

[Col. 0810A] «You shall offer the gift of your arms and the sacrifice of sanctification to the Lord, and the first fruits of holy things; extend your hand to the poor, so that your propitiation and your blessing may be brought to completion—the grace of your gift before every living person.» Just as above he promised purification to those who offer gifts to the ministers of God, so now through the generosity of alms, which are given to the poor from just labor, he promises forgiveness of sins and the grace of blessing to the kind and merciful. For just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: «Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you (Luke XI).»

It must certainly be understood that those who live most wickedly, take no care to correct such a life and character, and nevertheless do not cease to give alms amid their crimes and disgraceful acts flatter themselves in vain. For the Lord says: «Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.» They do not understand how far this statement extends; but to understand it, let them consider to whom he said it. For thus it is written in the Gospel: «As he was speaking, a certain Pharisee asked him to dine with him. He entered and reclined at table. But the Pharisee began to consider within himself why he had not been washed before dinner. And the Lord said to him: Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish, but what is within you is full of plunder and wickedness. Fools! Did not he who made what is outside also make what is within? Nevertheless, give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you (Luke XI).»

[Col. 0810B] Are we therefore to understand this as meaning that everything was clean for the Pharisees, who did not possess faith in Christ—even if they did not believe in him and had not been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit—provided only that they gave alms, as they think alms should be given? Yet all whom the faith of Christ does not cleanse are unclean. Concerning this it is written: «Cleansing their hearts by faith (Acts XV).» And the Apostle says: «To the unclean and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled (Titus I).»

How, then, could everything have been clean for the Pharisees if they gave alms but were not believers? Or how could they have been believers if they were unwilling to believe in Christ and be reborn in his grace? Yet what they heard is true: «Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.» Whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly manner must begin with himself and first give alms to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy; and it has been said most truly: «Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God (Eccles. XXX).» For this reason we are reborn, so that we may please God, who rightly rejects what we contracted by being born.

[Col. 0810C] This is the first almsgiving which we gave ourselves, because through the mercy of the merciful God we sought ourselves in our misery, confessing his just judgment by which we became miserable. Concerning this the Apostle says: «The judgment from one offense resulted in condemnation (Rom. V).» And we give thanks for his great love, of which that same herald of grace says: «God demonstrates his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, at the appointed time Christ died for us (Rom. V).» Thus, judging the misery of our condition truthfully and loving God in the love which he himself gave, we may live piously and rightly.

The Pharisees, however, passed over this judgment and love of God, yet they tithed even the smallest portions of all their produce because of the alms they gave. They therefore did not give alms by beginning with themselves and first showing mercy to themselves. It was with reference to this order of love that it was said: «Love your neighbor as yourself (Mark XII).» When he rebuked them, they washed themselves outwardly, but inwardly they were full of plunder and wickedness. He was urging them first to give themselves a certain alms, which a person owes himself, and to cleanse what is within: «Nevertheless, he said, give alms from what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you.»

[Col. 0811A] Then, to show what he had urged and what they themselves did not care to do, and lest they think that he was unaware of their alms, he said: «Woe to you, Pharisees.» It was as if he said: “I have indeed urged you to give the alms through which everything is clean for you; but woe to you, who tithe mint, rue, and every herb. I know these alms of yours, so that you may not think that I am now admonishing you about them. Yet you pass over the judgment and love of God, by which you could be cleansed from every inner defilement through almsgiving, so that your bodies also, which you wash, might be clean—for this is what ‘everything’ means, both inner and outer.”

As it is read elsewhere: «Cleanse what is within, and what is outside will be clean.» But lest he seem to reject those alms which are made from the produce of the earth, he said: «These things you ought to have done—the judgment and love of God—and not to omit the others (Matt. XXIII and Luke XI),» that is, alms from earthly produce.

[Col. 0811B] Let those who imagine that through the very generous alms of their produce or of any money they can purchase impunity—while persisting in the freedom of their crimes and the wickedness of their disgraceful acts—not deceive themselves. For they not only do these things, but love them so much that they always wish to remain involved in them, provided only that they can do so with impunity: «Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul; and whoever hates his own soul is not merciful toward it, but cruel.» By loving it according to the world, he hates it according to God. If, therefore, he wished to give it the alms through which everything would be clean for him, he would hate it according to the world and love it according to God.

[Col. 0811C] No one gives alms of any kind unless he gives from what he has received from the one who has no need. Therefore it was said: «His mercy will go before me (Ps. LXXXV).»

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the dead, that comfort should be given to those who mourn

«And do not withhold kindness from the dead. Do not fail to comfort those who mourn, and walk with those who grieve.» That this refers to the giving of alms, inasmuch as burial is provided for the dead, the patriarch Tobias indicates by his actions. Scripture relates that, while he was in Assyrian captivity, he went through all his kinspeople, comforted them, and divided among each of them as much as he could from his resources. He fed the hungry, provided clothing for the naked, and diligently arranged burial for the dead and slain.

[Col. 0811D] But if it is an act of almsgiving to bury dead flesh, how much more is it an act of almsgiving to comfort a living person in distress and assist him with consolation. Hence Paul says: «Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Rom. XII).» He also testifies that he did this, saying: «Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?» «I became weak to win the weak; I became all things to all people, that I might save all (II Cor. XI).» Hence it also follows:

«Do not be reluctant to visit the sick; through these acts you will be strengthened in love.» The demonstration of love is also the performance of a deed. Concerning this John says: «If anyone has the world’s possessions and sees his brother in need but closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him? My little children, let us not love in word or speech, but in deed and truth.»

[Col. 0812A] But no one can perfectly avoid sin and devote himself to works of righteousness unless he hopes to depart from this world every day. Whoever considers what he will be like in death always becomes fearful in his actions; and since, in his own eyes, he is already almost not living, he desires nothing that passes away, contradicts all the desires of the present life, and considers himself almost dead, because he does not fail to recognize that he will die. For the perfect life is an imitation of death. While the righteous carefully practice it, they escape the snares of sins. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0812B] «In all your works remember your final things, and you will never sin.» Yet he does not say this concerning every sin, because «there is no human being on earth who does good and does not sin.» And John says: «If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (I John I).» But of what sin does he wish this to be understood? Certainly of the one that leads to death. Concerning this John says: «Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God (I John III).»

[Col. 0812C] When he says, «The one who is born of God does not sin,» he understands a certain sin which a person born of God cannot commit. Such is that sin that, if someone commits it, he confirms the others; but if someone does not commit it, he dissolves the others. The commandment of Christ is called love. Through this love sins are dissolved; if it is not held, it is both a grave sin and the root of all sins.

## CHAPTER XII. One must not quarrel with a powerful person

(CAP. VIII.) «Do not quarrel with a powerful person, lest perhaps you fall into his hands.» Perhaps here he wishes “powerful person” to be understood as “proud person,” against whom it is not useful to contend. Hence it is written in Proverbs: «Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him (Prov. XXVI).» For among the proud there are always quarrels. But a servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel; rather, he should be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, and correcting those who resist the truth with moderation.

[Col. 0812D] «Do not contend with a wealthy man, lest perhaps he bring a lawsuit against you; for gold and silver have ruined many and have reached even the hearts of kings and turned them.» It is dangerous, therefore, to litigate with one who is shown to be panting after earthly profits and the fever of greed, because from this arise envy, disputes, hatred, murder, and other crimes of this kind which plunge people into ruin and destruction. «For greed is the root of all evils; by reaching after it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows (I Tim. VI).»

[Col. 0813A] Such a pestilence often also pollutes and turns the hearts of kings toward the perversity of judgment, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the righteous. Therefore the Lord urges us to beware of every form of greed and teaches his disciples, saying: «You have heard that it was said: An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. But I say to you, do not resist evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. And to the one who wishes to go to court with you and take your tunic, give him your cloak as well; and whoever forces you to go one mile, go with him two more. Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you (Matt. V).»

«Do not quarrel with a talkative person, and do not heap wood upon his fire. Do not associate with an uneducated person, lest he speak evil of your family.» It is foolish to contend with someone indiscriminate in speech, where not reason but fury rules. Likewise, it is useless to argue with an imprudent person, because he is quick to utter insults. Although these two testimonies apply to all foolish and corrupt speakers, they nevertheless seem especially to designate heretics, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: «Under their tongue are trouble and sorrow, and the poison of asps is under their lips (Ps. XIII).»

[Col. 0813B] Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, and their feet are swift to shed blood. It is therefore dangerous to speak and associate with such people, because their mind and conscience are defiled, and their speech spreads like cancer: they are both wandering and leading others into error. Hence the Apostle commands that foolish and undisciplined questions be avoided, as well as profane and empty talk, which greatly advances ungodliness. He also wrote to Titus to avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted, sinful, and condemned by his own judgment (Titus III).

[Col. 0813C] This person speaks evil of our family when he blasphemes the Christian religion and the catholic faith. Yet his blasphemy harms only blasphemers, because «everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean.» They profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds, since they are detestable and unbelieving and rejected for every good work.

«Do not despise someone who turns away from sin, nor reproach him; remember that we are all under correction.» It is more fitting for a Christian to suffer with his neighbor than to reproach one who has fallen, because no one knows to what end his actions may lead, nor can anyone know what a day to come will bring forth for him. Hence Paul warns, saying: «Therefore let the one who thinks he stands beware lest he fall (I Cor. X).» And again: «But you, he says, why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ (Rom. XIV).» Thus each of us will give an account of himself to God.

[Col. 0813D] Hence it is recorded in the Gospel that the Lord received tax collectors and sinners and ate with them, and that he absolved a sinful woman who watered his feet with tears. When the Pharisees murmured, he answered them: «Go and learn what this means: I desire mercy and not sacrifice; for I have not come to call the righteous but sinners (Matt. IX).» And elsewhere he says: «There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance (Luke XV).»

«Do not despise a person in his old age, for we too grow old.» Considering this, Ecclesiastes says: «Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccles. I).» And again: «I saw, he says, the things that are done under the sun; and behold, all was vanity and affliction of spirit (ibid.).» And after some time: «All things, he says, have their time, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed periods.» Hence the blessed martyr Cyprian elegantly said in his book addressed to Demetrianus concerning mortality: «This sentence has been given to the world; this is God’s law: that all things which have arisen die, things that have grown grow old, the strong are weakened, and the great are diminished.» For while human life once extended in long duration beyond eight hundred and nine hundred years, it can scarcely now reach the hundredth number. We see gray hairs in children; hair fails before it grows; nor does age end in old age, but begins with old age: thus at its very birth life hastens to its end. Thus whatever is now born degenerates because of the old age of the world itself, so that no one should wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail when the whole world itself is already failing and at its end.

## CHAPTER XIII. One must not rejoice over a dead enemy, knowing that we all die

[Col. 0814A] «Do not rejoice over your dead enemy, knowing that we all die; and we do not wish to enter into joy.» “Of our enemies” is understood. For if, according to the Lord’s command, we love our enemies and do good to those who hate us, we can in no way rejoice at their downfall. Elsewhere Scripture also forbids us to do so, saying: «Do not rejoice at another’s misfortune (Prov. XVII).» Rather, grieving in their place, we lament their ruin as though it were our own. Death’s end is common to all; and therefore, just as we do not wish to fall into the joy of our enemies, so we ought not to rejoice at their destruction. Instead, we should always remember the sentence: «What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another (Tob. IV).» And likewise the Lord’s commandment, in which he says: «Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them (Matt. VII; Luke VI).»

[Col. 0814B] «Do not despise the account of wise presbyters; live among their proverbs. For from them you will learn wisdom and the teaching of understanding, and to serve the great without complaint.» He rightly admonishes the ecclesiastical people to be subject to holy teachers and to remain constant in their teaching, because from it they will attain understanding of wisdom and the moral character produced by discipline. Hence Paul commanded Timothy, saying: «Until I come, attend to the reading, exhortation, and teaching. Be occupied with these things, so that your progress may be evident to all. Attend to yourself and to the teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you (I Tim. IV).»

[Col. 0814C] Good teachers teach nothing other than what they themselves received from good instructors, and this in turn came to their knowledge from the supreme Teacher. As Ecclesiastes shows, saying: «The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply (Eccles. XII),» given through the counsel of teachers by one shepherd. Hence Wisdom itself continues to urge us, saying:

«Let the account of the elders not pass you by; for they learned from their fathers. For from them you will learn understanding and, in time of need, how to give an answer.» Thus also the apostle Peter admonishes, saying: «But sanctify the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0816B] in your hearts, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you» (I Pet. III). For it is fitting that a servant of God should diligently and carefully learn from teachers those things which he may afterward present prudently and beneficially to others, lest, if he is first sluggish and negligent in meditation, he should later prove useless to others in teaching.

«Do not kindle the coals of sinners by reproving them, lest you yourself be kindled by the flame of their sinful fire.» Whoever applies discipline to others must be cautious, lest excessive correction make the offender’s irritated spirit worse, or lest he himself, being injured, be burdened with another’s sins. Hence the Apostle admonishes the Galatians that those who are spiritual should restore anyone overtaken in some transgression in a spirit of gentleness, considering themselves, lest they too be tempted (Gal. VI). Hence also in Deuteronomy the Lord commands that, when someone has gone with his friend into the forest to cut wood, if the axe should slip from his hand and wound his neighbor, the one who struck his neighbor should flee to one of the cities appointed as places of refuge, and there be kept unharmed from the avenger of his neighbor’s blood (Deut. XIX). We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn with any neighbor to examine our faults; and we simply cut down wood when with pious intention we cut away the vices of offenders. But the axe slips from the hand when the rebuke draws itself into harshness beyond what is necessary; and the iron leaps from the handle when a harder word than correction warrants exceeds its proper bounds, [Col. 0816D] striking and killing the friend: he kills his hearer by uttering an insult and driving him from the spirit of love. For the mind of the one rebuked suddenly rushes into hatred if immoderate reproof subjects it more than it ought.

But the one who carelessly strikes the wood and destroys his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that, defended in one of them, he may live. For if, turning to the tears of repentance, he hides himself within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and charity, he is not held guilty of the homicide he committed; and the relative of the one killed, when he finds him, does not kill him. For when the strict Judge comes—the one who joined himself to us through participation in our nature—he certainly does not demand vengeance for the guilt from one whom hope, faith, [Col. 0817A] and charity have hidden under his pardon. Therefore guilt is more quickly forgiven when it has in no way been committed out of a desire for evil.

## CHAPTER XIV. On avoiding evil words, deeds, and thoughts through God’s help

«Do not stand before an abusive man, lest he lie in ambush for your mouth.» We may rightly understand the abusive man as the heretic, who is always seeking to twist our words and drag them toward the wickedness of his own understanding. His conversation is therefore harmful and must be entirely avoided, just as Wisdom exhorts in Proverbs, saying: «My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent» (Prov. I). And again: «My son, do not walk with them; restrain your foot from their paths. For their feet run toward evil, [Col. 0817B] and they hasten to shed blood» (ibid.).

«Do not lend at interest to one stronger than you; and if you have lent, regard it as lost.» Here he calls “stronger” not one powerful in bodily strength, but one swollen with arrogance, to whom he forbids us to give a loan at interest, because he does not approve of forming friendships with such a person. To associate with the proud—that is, with the heretic—is therefore more an increase of injury than a benefit of peace. For this reason his companionship must be avoided in every matter more carefully than any advantage or support of eloquence is to be sought through him. The one who lends to an ungrateful person loses his loan; and the one who shares with a perverse person diminishes his substance. Hence Solomon admonishes in Proverbs, saying: «Drink water from your own cistern, and have the streams of your own well for yourself alone; let strangers not share in them» (Prov. V).

[Col. 0817C] «Do not pledge beyond your ability; and if you have pledged, consider how you will repay.» It is good for everyone to consider the measure of his strength and thus moderate his promise, lest he incur the guilt of falsehood. Hence the Lord commanded through Moses, saying: «When you make a vow to the Lord your God, do not delay in fulfilling it, for the Lord your God will require it of you; and if you delay, he will count it as sin against you. If you refuse to make a promise, you will be without sin» (Deut. XXIII). «Whatever has gone forth from your lips you shall observe, and you shall do as you promised to the Lord your God, speaking from your own will and from your mouth.» Hence Ecclesiastes also says: «If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay in fulfilling it; for he dislikes an unfaithful and foolish promise. Whatever you vow, fulfill it; and it is much better [Col. 0817D] not to vow than, after vowing, not to fulfill your promises» (Eccl. V).

«Do not judge against a judge, for he judges according to what is right.» This saying teaches us morally to be subject to our superiors and judges, who judge us according to divine law. Allegorically, it forbids all adversaries of the truth—that is, Jews, pagans, and heretics—to oppose the Gospel of Christ, because he has been appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead: «He judges the world with equity and the peoples with his truth.»

«Do not go on the road with an insolent man, lest perhaps he burden you with his evils; for he walks according to his own will, and you will perish together with his folly.» Here we may understand the insolent as heretics, who establish sects according to their presumption. We must not walk in them at all, because they go according to their own will and not according to God’s will. Whoever walks in their perverse paths will perish together with their folly. Note that, just as above he forbade standing before an abusive man and lending to one stronger, so now he forbids walking on the road with an insolent man, because, according to the psalmist’s saying: «Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night» (Ps. I). Concerning this he further exhorts, [Col. 0818B] adding:

«Do not quarrel with an angry man, and do not go into the desert with an insolent man; for blood is as nothing before him, and where there is no help he will strike you down.» Although historically this admonishes us to avoid a vicious and furious person, mystically it teaches us to flee the company of blaspheming Jews and heretics, before whose eyes blood is nothing, because they either seek to slaughter flesh bodily or rather to kill souls spiritually through the depravity of error. Their feet are swift to shed blood, and ruin and misery are in their ways; they also lead people into the desert, because they strive to tear whomever they can from the soil of the Church and lead them into the trackless regions of their error. Concerning them it is further said:

«Do not take counsel with fools; for they cannot love anything except what pleases them.» All deserters from the truth are fools, because, abandoning the way of justice, they chose the way of iniquity and showed that they preferred to serve their own desires rather than follow the rule of their fathers. Hence it is written in Proverbs: «A fool does not receive words of prudence unless you say things that are in his heart» (Prov. XVIII). But they did not wish to guard against what Scripture elsewhere reveals, saying: «There are ways that seem right to human beings, but their end leads down to the depths of hell» (Prov. XIV). Hence disgrace, reproach, and everlasting destruction follow them.

«Do not take counsel in the presence of a stranger, for you do not know what he may bring forth.» A stranger to us is one who is alien to the Christian faith and religion. We must not enter into counsel with him—that is, debate the divine sacraments and more hidden mysteries—for we do not know the quality of his understanding, whether it will turn toward faith or blasphemy. Hence the Truth itself instructed us, saying: «Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine» (Matt. VII), lest they turn and tear you apart. Hence also the shepherd of the Church says: «Therefore, brothers, since you know these things beforehand, guard yourselves, lest, being led astray by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness» (II Pet. III). And John says: «Everyone who departs and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God; whoever remains [Col. 0819A] in the teaching has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, nor say “Hail” to him. For whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works» (II John I).

«Do not reveal your heart to everyone, lest perhaps he offer you false favor and reproach you.» What he stated above somewhat obscurely—that counsel should not be entered into with a stranger because one does not know what he may bring forth—he explains more clearly in this saying: namely, that we must beware of the hypocrisy of pretenders, lest, if we carelessly say or do something in their presence, we be caught by their snares. Hence earlier also he warned that many should be peaceful toward us, but that one counselor should be chosen from a thousand. Hence it is written in Proverbs: «When an enemy devises deceit in his heart, when he lowers his voice, do not believe him, for there are seven wickednesses in his heart» (Prov. XXVI).

(CAP. IX.) «Do not be jealous of the wife at your bosom, lest she display against you the malice of wicked teaching.» We find “woman” used in Scripture both in a good and in a bad sense. Woman in the good sense appears in Proverbs: «Who will find a strong woman? Her price is far away, from the ends of the earth» (Prov. XXXI). And in the Gospel: «A woman hid leaven in three measures of flour until it was all leavened» (Matt. XIII; Luke XIII). There the faith and devotion of the Church are proclaimed.

Conversely, woman is used in a bad sense in Proverbs, where we read: «Behold, a woman meets him, prepared with the adornment of a prostitute to capture souls, talkative and restless, unable to remain at home on her feet, now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait beside a corner. She seizes the young man and kisses him, and with an insolent face she flatters him, saying: “I vowed sacrifices for my well-being; today I have fulfilled my vows,” and so forth» (Prov. VII). Heretical depravity is signified by this figure, and it is described here under various forms. By “the woman at our bosom” we may understand false brothers, who live among us, feign peace outwardly, prepare deceit inwardly, and retain the malice of wicked teaching. The Truth itself taught his disciples to beware of them in the Gospel, saying: «Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves» (Matt. VII). Hence also the teacher of the nations frequently condemns pseudo-apostles in his Epistles and declares that he endured false brothers. Therefore caution is good in all things, lest pretense deceive the simple and malice overthrow the unwary.

## CHAPTER XV. Wisdom teaches a chaste man not to give a woman power over his soul, lest she destroy him through friendships, and not to associate with one who jokes

«Do not give a woman power over your soul, lest she enter into your strength and you be put to shame.» Historically, this saying teaches the modesty of chastity; allegorically, it teaches prudence against heresy. For whoever flees the pollution of lust does not give a woman power over his soul; and whoever strives to preserve the rule of true faith does not consent to heretical depravity.

«Do not look upon a woman who desires many things, lest perhaps you fall into her snares.» The woman who desires many things is the synagogue of heretics, because it does not seek to preserve the unity of catholic faith and the truth of evangelical teaching, but delights in proceeding through the byways of various errors. There it lays snares, constructing sects of perdition to deceive souls. We are forbidden to look toward it, because we are in no way permitted to mingle with its society.

«Do not be constantly with a dancing girl, nor listen to her, lest perhaps you become subject to her power.» We may better understand this dancing girl as the crowd of heretics, which, because of the instability of its mind, chooses now this thing and now that, and never knows how to remain in the state of truth. By the volatility of its tongue, turning as though in the rotation of a body, it plays for this purpose: to drag more quickly into assent to its depravity anyone whom it sees to be an admirer of its eloquence, as though he were inert. Solomon also shows this, saying: «She ensnared him with many words and drew him on with the flatteries of her lips. At once he follows her, like an ox led to the sacrifice, and like a lamb frolicking, unaware that the fool is being dragged to bonds, until an arrow pierces his liver; like a bird hastening to the snare, not knowing that his soul is at stake» (Prov. VII).

«Do not look upon a virgin, lest perhaps you be scandalized by her beauty.» Through careless looking, the inward movement of the soul is often disturbed. Therefore he forbids us to look upon a virgin, because he wants our mind to remain unharmed by lust. Hence elsewhere Wisdom also teaches, saying: «A woman captures a man’s precious soul. Let your heart not desire her beauty, nor be captured by her glances, for the price of a prostitute is scarcely one loaf of bread» (Prov. VI). Mystically, however, we must not love the beauty of the heretics’ eloquence, nor gaze upon the splendor of their pretended virtues, lest we be scandalized by their fabrications. Hence he adds:

«Do not give your soul in any way to prostitutes, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance.» We must have no communion with heretics and schismatics, lest, corrupted by their seductions, [Col. 0820D] we lose our souls and fail to attain the inheritance promised to us in our heavenly homeland.

«Do not look around in the streets of the city, nor wander in its squares.» Now he expresses under another image the same matter that he previously indicated by the woman. The streets of the city are nothing other than the assemblies of heretics, which have separated themselves from the camp of the Church and have not wished to persevere in the unity of the city of God, concerning which it is written: «Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God» (Ps. LXXXVI). We must not look around in these places, because we are not permitted to depart from the mind of the Church, lest we wander in its squares; for «broad and spacious is the way [Col. 0821A] that leads to death, but narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life» (Matt. VII).

«Turn your face away from a finely adorned woman, and do not look upon the appearance of a stranger; because many have perished because of a woman’s beauty, and from it desire blazes up like fire.» We understand this woman to be none other than the one whose society he previously forbade: adorned with the embellishment of words, she has become the cause of the destruction of many. Her appearance implants the fire of desire in the minds of the foolish; here she kindles in them the flames of illicit love, and in the future prepares for them the burning of Gehenna. Therefore we must entirely flee her communion and despise her appearance, because, as the following saying proves:

[Col. 0821B] «Every woman who is a prostitute will be trampled underfoot like dung in the road.» That is, every perverse teaching will be judged worthy of complete disgrace on the road of right faith. Hence the Lord himself, addressing his disciples in the Gospel, says: «You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt becomes tasteless, with what will it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled by people» (Matt. V). Thus, when tasteless salt has ceased to be useful for seasoning foods and preserving meats, it will be fit for no use. For, as another Evangelist testifies (Luke XIV), it is not useful for the earth, since when it is cast upon it, it prevents growth; nor will it benefit the agricultural dung heap, since, even when mixed with fertile clods, it naturally tends not to nourish the seeds of crops but to destroy them. So everyone [Col. 0821C] who, after acknowledging the truth, turns back is able neither to bear the fruit of good works himself nor to cultivate others. He must be cast outside—that is, separated from the unity of the Church—so that, according to another parable, his enemies may mock him, saying: «This man began to build and was unable to finish» (Luke XIV).

«Many have admired the appearance of a strange woman and have been made reprobate, for her conversation blazes like fire.» Thus many, admiring the eloquence of heretics, have been seduced by it into error, because their conversation kindles the flame of wickedness in the hearts of their hearers unless they quickly withdraw from their company. Therefore it is added:

«Do not sit at all with a strange woman, nor recline with her upon the couch, and do not quarrel with her [Col. 0821D] over wine, lest your heart incline toward her and you slip with your blood into destruction.» “Do not sit with her,” he says—that is, do not linger with her; nor recline upon the couch, namely, do not grow sluggish in good work; and do not quarrel with her over wine—that is, do not dispute with her in meditation upon God’s law. For wine signifies the grace of the Scriptures. Otherwise your heart may be enticed into loving her, and from there you may fall into the destruction of your own soul.

## CHAPTER XVI. An old friend must not be abandoned

«Do not abandon an old friend, for a new one will not be like him.» Since confidence based on things tested is greater than that based on things unknown, he therefore advises [Col. 0822A] that you not abandon a proven friend, nor imprudently entrust yourself to the faith of one unknown. Allegorically, he admonishes us not easily to depart from the authority of the holy catholic Fathers, who are faithful guardians of truth and justice. Nor should you quickly rush to inexperienced and newly appointed teachers, who, although they do not depart entirely from the truth, scarcely attain the summit of perfection. Hence the Savior also instructed us by his example in the Gospel, lest we rush immaturely into teaching: he himself, at twelve years of age, sat in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them (Luke II), and after his thirtieth year undertook the office of teaching (Luke III). What should be done in this matter the following saying indicates:

«New wine is a new friend; it will grow old, and you will drink it with pleasure.» An inexperienced teacher must strive first to receive fully the firmness of sound doctrine together with good works, and then prove useful and beneficial both to himself and to others. He is rightly called a friend who is a faithful executor of right faith and true wisdom. For, as the ancients wished, “friend” is so called as though he were a guardian of the soul. He guards his brother’s soul who discusses with him matters pertaining to eternal salvation.

«Do not be jealous of the glory and wealth of a sinner, for you do not know what his overthrow will be.» It is not useful to contend for earthly primacy and power, but rather to strive for advancement in the virtues. Hence the Savior admonished his disciples to strive to enter by the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, not by the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Luke [Col. 0822C] XIII); and to disdain the world’s wealth and riches so that they might have treasures in the heavenly kingdom. He said: «Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also» (Matt. VI). Hence the Psalmist, restraining the faithful from greed and wicked rivalry, says: «Do not be jealous of those who do evil, nor envy those who practice iniquity, for they will quickly wither like grass and soon fall like the green herb. Hope in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land and you will be nourished by its riches» (Ps. XXXVI).

[Col. 0822D] «Do not let the injury of the unjust please you, knowing that the impious will not please even as far as the underworld.» We must not rejoice in the slander of the good, but rather grieve over it, because the one who has been unjustly harmed will receive the reward of his patience; but the one who has unjustly harmed another will not escape the punishment due to his iniquity.

«Keep far away from a man who has the power to kill, and you will not suspect the fear of death.» What does this command to keep far away from a man who has the power to kill mean, unless it means that he wants us to be cautious in everything, lest through carelessness we fall into the danger of death? For the one who guards himself well against killing is the one who does not do things worthy of death. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0823A] «And if you approach him, do not commit anything, lest he take your life.» Paul also admonishes this, saying: «For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it; for it is God’s servant to you for good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for it does not bear the sword without cause. It is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil» (Rom. XIII).

It may be asked here: if they have been appointed by God for the purpose of inflicting vengeance upon the harmful and sinful, why are persecutors of Christians and heretics permitted to subject the innocent and religious to punishments? This is certainly permitted by God’s just judgment, so that the good may be crowned for their patience and the wicked condemned for their iniquity. In another sense, through wicked rulers, just as through good ones, God judges the guilty, so that those who punish crimes while committing the same crimes may afterward suffer punishments worthy of their own iniquities. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: «From the smoke of the pit locusts came forth upon the earth, and power was given them, as scorpions of the earth have power; and they were commanded not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, but only those people who do not have the sign of God on their foreheads» (Rev. IX). And after some further passage: «I saw horses in a vision,» he says, «and those sitting upon them had breastplates of fiery red, hyacinth-colored, and sulfurous; and the heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and from their mouths proceeded fire, smoke, and sulfur. By these three plagues a third of humankind was killed, by the fire, smoke, and sulfur that proceeded from their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; for their tails are like serpents with heads, and by these they inflict harm.»

Heretics inflict harm through fraud and prepare the killing of souls through deceit. For just as a scorpion advances by caressing but strikes with its tail, so the deceptive destruction of the wicked appears gentle and harmless in the face; but when they strike secretly, they bring death covertly. Again: «The power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails»—that is, in speech and office. For the prophet who teaches falsehood is himself the tail.

Those who do not fortify themselves with the sign of the living God on their foreheads, nor protect their hearts with vigilant care through catholic faith, are plainly destined for ruin. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0823D] «Know that there is a sharing in death, for you will walk in the midst of snares and tread upon the weapons of those who mourn. According to your ability, beware of your neighbor; and deliberate with the wise and prudent.» Therefore we must beware of the ambushes of the deceitful and discuss all our counsel with the wise and prudent—that is, with orthodox Fathers and brothers who fear God—and we must not abandon the way of justice and truth. Concerning this it is further said:

## CHAPTER XVII. On righteous banqueters, that is, companions of good reputation

«Let righteous men be your banqueters; let your glory be in the fear of God; let your thought be of God in your understanding; and let all your speech be about the commandments of the Most High.» This banquet pertains more to spiritual food than to bodily pleasures. Whoever therefore continually remains with righteous men in meditation upon the holy Scriptures and in the practice of sacred virtues, confessing the Lord at all times both in heart and with the mouth, will undoubtedly be filled with eternal satisfaction. «Blessed,» he says, «is the one who eats bread in the kingdom of God»—the bread, namely, of life; whoever eats it will not die forever, but will live and rejoice with the holy angels in the heavenly kingdom (Luke XIV). The Truth itself also promised this to his disciples in the Gospel, saying: «You are the ones who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one for me, so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel» (Luke XXII).

«In the hand of craftsmen works will be praised, and the leader of the people in the wisdom of his speech; but in the understanding of elders there is the word.» These craftsmen are the same as the leaders of the people, namely, the holy teachers. In their hand—that is, in their action—the work of the virtues and the observance of discipline will be praised. In their speech, too, the splendor of wisdom shines together with the eloquence of expression. In the understanding of elders there is the word—that is, the word of the Gospel. Concerning this Paul also says: «For the Lord has made the word concise over the whole earth» (Rom. IX). These are the elders concerning whom it is written in Deuteronomy: «Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you» (Deut. XXXII). They were also prefigured by those seventy elders whom Moses, at the Lord’s command, chose and set over the whole people. With these, the King of kings himself arranges his judgments according to truth. As Solomon shows, saying: «Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land» (Prov. XXXI).

On the other hand, what follows:

«A man of many words is terrifying in his city, and one rash in his speech is hateful,» signifies heretics. For they are always rash, loving quarrels, disputes, and conflicts. Hence they are hateful both to God and to human beings.
