They are terrifying in their city—that is, in the world—because, dragging into error as many as they can, they turn children of God into children of the devil and food for the eternal fire. Concerning them the Psalmist also says: «The man of many words will not be established upon the earth; evil will hunt the unjust man to destruction» (Ps. CXXXIX). Therefore Paul commanded, saying: «Avoid profane and empty talk and novelties of words. For they will advance greatly toward ungodliness, and their speech spreads like cancer» (I Tim. VI). And again: «There will be,» he says, «people who are lovers of themselves, greedy, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, harsh, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasure rather than of God; having the appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid such people» (II Tim. III).

Concerning them Jude also says in his Epistle: «For certain people have slipped in secretly, who long ago were designated for this condemnation as ungodly, turning the grace of our God into debauchery and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ» (Jude I). But since he has shown, toward the end of the present book, that those who are rash in speech are hateful, let us see at the beginning of the following book what he thinks about the righteous judge.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0825]

## CHAPTER ONE. Wisdom praises judges who judge their people

(CAP. X.) «A wise judge will judge his people, and the rule of a sensible man will be stable.» We can understand no one better as the wise judge than the Lord Christ, who protects his people against all enemies. Concerning him the prophet says: «The Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people» (Joel II). His rule will also be stable. For, as Isaiah testifies: «His rule is upon his shoulder, and his name will be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the coming age, Prince of Peace. His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and justice, from now and forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this» (Isa. IX).

The words of the angels in the Gospel to Mary also agree with this prophecy, testifying that Christ’s rule will endure: «The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end» (Luke I). His disciples certainly followed this rule, as the following saying proves, where it says:

«According to the judge of the people, so also are his ministers; and as is the ruler of the city, so are those who dwell in it.» The city of Christ is the holy Church, which follows his footsteps with devoted affection of heart and imitates him in the fruit of good works. In it, his ministers—that is, the rulers of the faithful and the holy preachers—will diligently obey his commands and earnestly instruct others to do likewise. Ecclesiastes praises the measure of this moderation, saying: «Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at the proper time, for refreshment and not for luxury» (Eccl. X). Conversely, concerning another king he says: «Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning» (ibid.).

Woe, therefore, to the land whose king is the devil, always greedy for novelties. He has as judges and princes those who love the pleasures of this age, who, before the day of death arrives, say: «Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.» In contrast, blessed is the land of the Church, whose king is Christ, the son of the freeborn, descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and also from the prophets and all the saints, over whom sin did not rule and who therefore were free. Its princes are the apostles and all the saints, who have as king the son of the freeborn and do not eat in the morning or hastily. For they do not seek pleasure in the present age, but will eat at the proper time, when the time of recompense arrives: «Blessed,» he says, «is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God» (Luke XIV).

«A foolish king will destroy his people.» That is the king of whom we spoke above, who is a child and whose princes eat in the morning; he will destroy his people—that is, he will hurl all who obey him with himself into the abyss of hell—

«And cities will be inhabited through the understanding of the powerful.» That is, the Churches of the Savior are strengthened through the teaching of holy preachers.

«For the power of the earth is in the hand of God.» This means that the Church’s stability flourishes under Christ’s governance. Concerning this land the Prophet says: «But God our King worked salvation in the midst of the earth from before the ages» (Ps. LXXIII). In it his will is fulfilled daily, and in it and with it he promised to remain until the consummation. Moreover, «all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him, and no one can resist his will.» For he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet. Concerning this it is added:

«And all the iniquity of the nations is accursed.» That is, it is condemned, because the just Judge in his judgment condemns all the sinners of the earth and destroys from his city all who practice iniquity. In another sense, all the iniquity of the nations is accursed because, through the preaching of the apostles, the unbelief and error of the gentiles were rejected. The Savior sent them into the world for this purpose: to rebuke the disobedient, teach the ignorant, and heal the weak. Hence it follows:

«And he raised up a useful ruler over it in due time; in the hand of God is human power, and upon the face of the scribe he will place his honor.» For the power of the holy teachers has been ordered by God’s dispensation, and he gave them the ministry of honor when he placed them over the human race in his own stead. They are the scribes concerning whom the Truth itself says in the Gospel: «He is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old» (Matt. XV). Concerning him the Psalmist also says: «My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe» (Ps. LXIV). This means one who briefly records divine mysteries under the veil of prophecy, because the Law and the Prophets lasted until John, and Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes: «For he is our peace, who made both one; and no other name has been given to human beings under heaven by which we must be saved.»

«Do not remember any injury done by your neighbor, and do nothing in the works of injury.» Similar to this saying is what is written in Leviticus: «Do not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens» (Lev. XIX). If we remember the Lord’s saying that commanded us to love our enemies, to do good to those who hate us, and to pray for those who persecute and slander us; and that, when someone takes our tunic, we should give him our cloak as well, and when he strikes one cheek, offer the other also—we truly fulfill this saying. For the one who does not remember his neighbor’s injury rightly is the one who offers love in place of hatred and blessing in place of slander to his neighbor.

“Pride is hateful before God and human beings, and every wickedness of the nations is accursed.” Hence it is written in Proverbs: “Every arrogant person is an abomination to the Lord, and the Lord will demolish the house of the proud (Prov. XVI).” Hence Peter also says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (I Pet. V).” Hence the Psalmist likewise says: “You will save the humble people, but you will humble the eyes of the proud (Ps. XVII).” And again: “You hate, O Lord, those who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak lies (Ps. V).”

“Kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices, wrongs, insults, and various deceits.” The histories of almost all nations attest the truth of this statement [Col. 0827C] and display the causes of the changes affecting different peoples. Nor can anyone remain ignorant of this who has read how the very powerful kingdoms of the Chaldeans, Persians, and Greeks were overthrown, and who sees the Roman Empire tottering, recognizing that nothing in this world is stable. Allegorically, this may signify that, because of the transgressions and blindness of the former people, the Gospel of Christ was transferred to the nations. Truth itself also intimated this to those same Jews in the Gospel, saying: “Therefore the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits (Matt. XXI).”

## CHAPTER II. On the evil of greed

[Col. 0827D] “Nothing is more wicked than the greedy person. Why does earth and ashes grow proud? Nothing is more unjust than loving money. Such a person even holds his own soul for sale, because in his lifetime he has cast away his inmost self.” After narrating the change of kingdoms, he appropriately adds a discussion of greed, because the force of righteous government is most seriously neglected on account of greed. For when someone, through covetousness, claims earthly possessions for himself beyond all measure, he is lifted up into pride and strives, out of envy, to drive another from his boundaries. “The love of money is the root of all evils; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows and various harmful desires that plunge people into destruction and perdition (I Tim. VI).” And because pride is always the companion of greed, together with envy [Col. 0828A] and the other vices, Paul therefore writes to Timothy: “Command the rich of this present age not to be high-minded or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, and to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life (ibid.).” Since greed is the service of idols, whoever pursues it is proved to be a despiser of God; and it is consequently shown that such a person cannot rightly become master even of earthly things, since he places the lowest before the highest and the cheapest before the most precious. He holds his soul for sale and, in acquiring profit, has cast away his inmost self during his lifetime. “For what, according to the testimony of Truth, will it profit a person [Col. 0828B] if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?”

“Every rule has a brief life.” “Today the grass of the field exists, and tomorrow it is thrown into the oven; for the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his works. The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

“Prolonged illness burdens the physician; a brief illness the physician cuts short.” He makes this comparison to show that, if the plague of greed possesses the mind for a long time, it will be difficult to cure; but if the mind’s reason resists it immediately at the outset, and access to it is barred by the fear of God and dread of punishments, so that it cannot enter through a harmful thought, its power is more easily extinguished [Col. 0828C]. It also greatly aids resistance to greed if the brevity of passing life, the future dissolution of the flesh, and the horror of Gehenna are recalled to the soul. Therefore he adds:

“So also the king is king today and will die tomorrow; for when a person dies, he will inherit serpents, beasts, and worms.” Worldly power and the riches of this age cannot grant a long life, because human frailty cannot pass beyond the limit of its course. A person will die, and dust will return to its earth; nor will the flesh that once flourished in youth escape the corruption of worms. All its delight will be consumed by stench. Mystically, however, the person who lived in sins, if he does not correct himself and restrain himself from offenses, is condemned to eternal death. There he will feel the ancient serpent and demonic beasts punishing him as most savage torturers; nor will he now have any hope of escape, since no rest is granted amid unending pain.

## CHAPTER III. On the evil of pride, which causes apostasy from God

“The beginning of human pride is to apostatize from God, because his heart has withdrawn from the one who made him.” No apostasy is greater than the creature’s turning away from its Creator. This is rightly attributed to pride, because pride consists in wishing to liken or equate a lesser good with the supreme Good. This was the beginning of the devil’s fall, and also the beginning of human transgression. Hence it is added:

“For pride is the beginning of every sin.” It may be asked why the apostle Paul says that the love of money is the root of all evils, while the wise man here says that pride is the beginning of sin. The Holy Spirit spoke the same thing through the prophet in the Old Testament and through the Apostle in the New, and cannot in any way contradict himself. We must therefore carefully consider why the former wished to call pride the beginning of every sin, while the latter called the love of money the root of all evils. Or perhaps the apostle Paul, as he often does, interpreted the prophetic statement? For whether one says “the beginning of every sin” or “the root of all evils,” one signifies the same thing [Col. 0829B]. Moreover, greed and pride are so completely one evil that neither can a proud person be found without greed, nor a greedy person without pride. The devil, in whom pride holds primacy, was desirous of his own power and of the destruction of humanity; and the human being, through desire for the forbidden tree and longing for likeness to God, showed himself afflicted with the disease of greed.

Many evils proceed from the plague of pride, bringing certain destruction upon those who possess them, as the following testimonies prove. Yet it benefits the reader if we set down some words from the writings of Saint Gregory—whose understanding we have often followed in this work—just as he uttered them. In Book XXXIII of the *Moralia*, after explaining the Lord’s statement concerning Leviathan, spoken to Job—“He is king over all the sons of pride (Job XLI)” [Col. 0829C]—he added this statement from Wisdom: “For it is written: ‘Pride is the beginning of every sin (Eccl. X).’” A little later, discussing pride at greater length, he says:

“By this he himself fell; by this he struck down the human being who followed him (ibid.).” For he attacked the salvation of our immortality with the weapon by which he extinguished the life of his own blessedness. But since the discussion of pride provides an opportunity, we ought to examine it more subtly and carefully, and show how great and of what kind it comes to human minds, and in what ways it creeps into them. Other vices attack only those virtues by which they themselves are destroyed: anger assails patience, gluttony abstinence, and lust chastity. Pride, however, which we have called the root of vices, is not content with the extinction of a single virtue; it rises against all the members of the soul and, like a general and deadly disease, corrupts the whole body, so that whatever is done while it invades—even if it appears to be virtue—is done not for God but solely for empty glory.

When pride breaks into the mind, it seizes an occupied city like a tyrant; and the richer the person it captures, the harsher its domination becomes. For the more extensively a virtuous action is performed without humility, the more widely pride dominates. Whoever receives its tyranny within himself with a captive mind first suffers this harm: with the eye of the heart closed, he loses the fairness of judgment [Col. 0830A]. All the things that others do well displease him; only what he himself has done badly pleases him. He always despises the works of others and always admires what he does, because whatever he has done, he believes he alone has done it. In what he displays, through his desire for glory, he favors himself in thought; and when he judges that he surpasses everyone in everything, he walks about with himself through the broad spaces of his thoughts and silently cries out his own praises.

Sometimes the mind is driven to such great exaltation that, in what makes it swell, it is also unrestrained in its display of speech. But the more shamelessly a person exalts himself before himself, the more readily collapse follows. Hence it is written: “The heart is exalted before ruin.” Hence Daniel says [Col. 0830B]: “He was walking in the court of Babylon. And the king answered and said: ‘Is this not Babylon the great, which I built as a royal residence by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendor (Dan. IV)?’” But he immediately added how swiftly this swelling was restrained by vengeance, saying: “While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: Your kingdom will pass from you; they will drive you away from human beings, and your dwelling will be with the beasts and wild animals. You will eat grass like an ox, and seven periods will pass over you.’”

Behold: because the swelling of his mind had extended into open words, the patience of the Judge immediately broke forth into sentence; and he struck him more sternly in proportion as his pride had risen more excessively. And because, by enumerating his advantages, he had said the things in which he delighted, he heard the evils enumerated by which he would be struck. It must be understood, however, that this very exaltation of which we are speaking possesses some people through secular matters and others through spiritual matters. One swells with gold, another with eloquence; one with lowly and earthly things, another with the highest and heavenly virtues. Yet the same one and identical pride is acted out before God, although, when it comes to human hearts, it is hidden from human view under different clothing.

For when someone who previously took pride in earthly glory later becomes exalted over holiness, exaltation has not at all left his heart. It has come to him in its customary way, but changed its garment so that it might not be recognized. It must also be understood that pride tempts those set over others differently from those subject to them. To a superior it suggests in his thoughts that he has grown above the rest through the sole merit of his life. If he has at some time done anything well, it insistently places this before his mind and suggests that by it he has been especially pleasing to God. To make the suggestion more readily persuasive, it calls upon the very reward of authority entrusted to him as testimony, saying: “If almighty God had not judged you better than all these people, he would not have placed them all under your rule.” It then immediately lifts up his mind and shows those subject to him as vile and useless, so that he no longer regards anyone as worthy of being addressed with equanimity. Thus the tranquility of his mind soon turns into anger.

For while he despises everyone and criticizes without moderation the understanding and life of all, he expands into anger all the more uncontrollably because he considers those entrusted to him unworthy of himself. Conversely, when pride stirs the hearts of subjects, it strives with all its strength to make them entirely neglect consideration of their own conduct and to become, in their silent thoughts, judges of their ruler. While they intently observe what they should criticize in him, they never see what they should correct in themselves. Hence they perish all the more terribly in proportion as they turn their eyes away from themselves.

They fall by stumbling along the road of this life while looking elsewhere. They assert that they are sinners, but not so greatly as to have been handed over to the authority of so harmful a person. While they despise his deeds and disregard his commands, they descend into such madness that they do not believe God takes care of human affairs, because they grieve that they have been entrusted to one who is, as they think, rightly criticized. Thus, while they grow proud against their ruler, they also swell against the judgments of their Creator. While they judge the life of their shepherd, they attack the wisdom that orders all things; and while they insolently oppose the words of their ruler, they call that same arrogance of speech freedom.

Thus exaltation puts itself forward as though on behalf of the uprightness of freedom, just as fear often presents itself in place of humility. For just as many remain silent out of fear while thinking that they are silent out of humility, so some speak through the impatience of pride while believing that they speak through the freedom of uprightness. Sometimes subjects do not reveal at all the insolent thoughts they harbor; and those whose loquacity can scarcely be restrained sometimes fall silent solely from the bitterness of inward resentment. By the pain of their mind they draw out words of insolence; accustomed to speaking badly, they are even worse when silent.

For when sinners hear something about correction, they angrily withhold even words of reply. When they are treated harshly, they often burst into complaints about that very harshness. But when their teachers gently anticipate them, they become even more indignant at the very humility with which they have been approached; and their minds are inflamed more strongly in proportion as they are said to have been more considerately weakened.

These people, because they do not know humility—which is the mother of virtues—lose the benefit of their labor. Even if there are good things that they appear to perform, the strong height of the building they raise is not secured, because it is not solidified by the strength of a foundation on rock. What they build therefore grows only toward ruin, because they do not first prepare the foundations of humility before raising the mass of the structure.

We can rightly reveal what lies within them if we display it briefly in outward behavior. In all who swell inwardly with pride there is shouting in speech, bitterness in silence, dissolution in cheerfulness, fury in sadness, shamelessness in action, dishonor in appearance, haughtiness in walking, and resentment in response. Their minds are always strong for inflicting insults but weak for enduring them; sluggish in obeying but eager to provoke others; lazy concerning what they ought to do and are capable of doing, but ready for what they neither ought nor are capable of doing. No exhortation bends them toward what they do not willingly desire; toward what they secretly desire, however, they seek to be compelled, because they fear becoming contemptible through their desire and wish to endure force against their own will.

Since, then, we have said that human minds are tempted differently by carnal matters and by spiritual matters, let the former hear: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass (Isa. XL).” Let the latter hear what is said to some after miracles: “I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity (Luke XIII).” Let the former hear: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them (Ps. LXI).” Let the latter hear that the foolish virgins, coming with empty vessels, are excluded from the inner wedding feast.

Again, since we have stated that those set over others are tempted differently from those subject to them, let the former hear what is said through a certain wise man [Col. 0832B]: “I have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them (Eccl. XXXII).” Let the latter hear: “Obey your superiors and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who must give an account for your souls (Heb. XIII).”

Let the former, when he boasts of the power he has received, hear what is said in Abraham’s voice to the rich man in torment: “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life (Luke XVI).” Let the latter, when he breaks into complaint against his rulers, hear what was answered through Moses and Aaron to the murmuring people: “Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord; for what are we (Exod. XVI)?” Let the former hear: “The fathers of orphans and judges of widows will be shaken before his presence (Ps. LXVII).” Let the latter hear what is said against the obstinacy of subjects [Col. 0832C]: “Whoever resists authority resists the ordinance of God (Rom. XIII).”

Let everyone hear together: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (Jas. IV).” Let everyone hear: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God (Job XV).” Let everyone hear: “Why does ash and earth grow proud (Eccl. X)?” Against the plague of this sickness, let us all hear what the teacher Truth teaches, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart (Matt. XI).”

For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our weakness; for this reason the Invisible appeared not only visible but also despised; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the reproach of derision, and the torments of suffering, so that humble God might teach human beings not to be proud. How great, therefore, is the virtue of humility, for the sake of teaching which alone the One who is immeasurably great was made small even unto suffering?

Because the pride of the devil offered the origin of our destruction, the humility of God was discovered as the instrument of our redemption. Our enemy, created among all things, wished in his exaltation to appear above all things. Our Redeemer, while remaining great above all things, deigned to become small among all things.

But we shall better expose the cause of exaltation and disclose the foundations of humility if we briefly touch upon what the author of death and the founder of life say. The former says: “I will ascend into heaven (Ps. LXXXVII).” The latter says through the Prophet: “My soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to the underworld (Isa. XIV).”

The former says: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven (Zach. II).” The latter says to the human race, expelled from the dwelling places of paradise: “Behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst (Exod. XXV, XXIX).”

The former says: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north (III Kings VI; IV Kings IV).” The latter says: “But I am a worm and not a human being, the reproach of humanity and the outcast of the people (Isa. XIV).”

The former says: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High (ibid.).” The latter says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II).” And through his members he speaks, saying: “Lord, who is like you (Ps. XXXIV)?”

The former speaks through his members, saying: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go (Exod. V).” The latter says through himself: “If I say that I do not know him, I will be like you, a liar; but I do know him, and I keep his word (John VII).”

The former says: “The rivers are mine, and I made them (Eccl. XXIV).” The latter says: “I can do nothing from myself (John V).” And again: “The Father who dwells in me himself does the works (John XIV).”

The former, showing all the kingdoms, says: “I will give you authority over all these things and their glory, because they have been handed over to me, and I give them to whomever I wish (Matt. IV).” The latter says: “You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or left is not mine to give, but belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father (Matt. XX).”

The former says: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil (Gen. III).” The latter says: “It is not yours to know the times or moments that the Father has placed in his own authority (Acts I).”

In order that the divine will might be despised and that he might persuade them to follow his own will, the former says: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise (Gen. III)?” And shortly afterward: “For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened (ibid.).” The latter says: “I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me (John V).”

The former speaks through his members, saying: “Let no meadow escape our indulgence; let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; everywhere let us leave signs of our joy (Wis. II).” The latter announces through his members: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice (John XVI).”

The former teaches the minds subject to him nothing except to seek the summit of exaltation, to surpass all things alike through swelling of mind, to rise above the fellowship of all human beings through lofty arrogance, and to raise themselves against the power of the Creator. As the Psalmist says of them: “They have gone beyond in the contrivance of their heart; they have devised and spoken wickedness (Ps. LXXII).” They have spoken iniquity on high.

The latter, coming to spitting, slapping, blows, a crown of thorns, the cross, the spear, and death, admonishes his members, saying: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me (John XII).”

Thus far Gregory. From here let us examine what follows in the history.

“He who holds fast to it,” he says, “will be filled with curses, and it will overthrow him in the end. Therefore the Lord dishonored the assembly of the wicked and destroyed them completely.” From pride arise heresies, schisms, detraction, envy, verbosity, boasting, disputes, hostility, ambition, exaltation, presumption, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind. But who would doubt that these also proceed from greed, since all who have been corrupted by all the diseases I have named are also considered greedy?

Likewise, since greed makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunken, grasping, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, defilers, incestuous, and disgraceful, how can such people become so without pride? Without pride, how can the commandments of God—which prohibit all the evils listed above—be despised? [Col. 0834B] Therefore, if we wish to complete the course of our struggle, let us above all beware of greed and pride—not two evils, but one—from which all evil acts take their beginning.

For without pride, what sins could even be begun, when it is said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin (Eccl. X)”? Or without greed, which is the root of all evils, what evils could be committed, since without a root all things are either judged nonexistent or dead? Moreover, if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to my own pleasure—which is characteristic of greed—and despise God’s commandments—which is the evil of pride—how could all evils not arise from greed, which is called the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin? On account of these evils [Col. 0834C] the Lord will dishonor the assembly of the wicked and destroy them completely.

“God destroyed the seats of proud rulers and made the meek sit in their place.” The mother of the Lord expressed the likeness of this statement in her Gospel song, saying: “He has brought down the powerful from their seat and exalted the humble (Luke I).” Although this may be understood generally of all proud and all humble people at the end of the world—for “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted”—it may nevertheless be transferred specifically to the teachers of the ancient Law, that is, the scribes and Pharisees, and to the preachers of the Gospel, that is, the apostles and evangelists.

God therefore destroyed the chairs and teaching authority of the scribes and Pharisees because they refused to receive the Son of God when he came in their presence; and he exalted the apostles—namely, exceedingly meek people and powerful imitators of their teacher—to the honor of their dignity, so that the nations of the world might be instructed by their teachings and examples. The Prophet also foretold this in the Psalms, saying: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over the whole earth. They will remember your name, Lord, throughout every generation and race (Ps. XLIV).”

But just as the teachers of the Jews were rejected because of their faithlessness, so the people themselves were scattered because of their unbelief, and the nations who believed in Christ and obeyed the Gospel succeeded to their place. Hence he adds:

“God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble from those same nations. The Lord overturned the lands of the nations and destroyed them to their foundations; he dried them up from among themselves and scattered them, and caused their memory to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and left the memory of the humble in understanding.”

The Lord dried up the roots of proud peoples when he expelled the Jewish nation with its ceremonies; and he planted the humble from among them when he chose apostles from that same people and established the primitive Church in Jerusalem. “The Lord overturned the lands of the nations and destroyed them to their foundations” when, through Roman commanders and a multitude of nations, he cast down the murderous city to its foundations. He also burned the temple in a fire and destroyed the transgressors themselves, some by slaughter, some by pestilence and famine, and some by captivity. Scattering their synagogue throughout every region of the world, he established the Church throughout the whole earth for the honor and worship of his name, so that the memory of the former might perish with a sound of ruin, while remembrance of the latter might remain forever before the eyes of God.

Nor can this passage inappropriately be applied to the persecutors of Christians and the martyrs of Christ. Who, then, does not recognize that the emperors, kings, and rulers of the world who once persecuted the Church of God out of hatred for Christ’s name and killed confessors of his name by savage deaths have now, together with their posterity, been wiped out, while the glory of the martyrs everywhere excels in the veneration of the faithful? Their memory will be handed over to perpetual oblivion [Col. 0835C], but the praise and victory of the martyrs will be proclaimed without cease in the Church of Christ. Therefore it remains for us to proclaim with prophetic exultation: “The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. The Lord guards all who love him and destroys all sinners. Blessed is the Lord forever. Amen, amen.”

“Pride was not created for human beings, nor anger for the race of women.” Vices, therefore, were not created in human beings, but were discovered in the perverse will of a rational mind. For all sins are contained in this one category: when someone turns away from divine and truly enduring things and turns toward mutable and uncertain things. Although these things are rightly placed in their own order and display a certain beauty of their own, it is nevertheless the act of a perverse and disordered mind to submit to things that ought rather, by divine order and right, to be subject to its command.

The good Creator, who made all the things he created very good, is not to be blamed for his works. Rather, the creature’s neglect, when it turns away from the supreme Good, is gravely blameworthy, since it places temporal things before eternal and passing things before enduring ones. The beginning of pride caused human beings to apostatize from God, because their heart withdrew from the one who made them. It is rightly said that anger was not created for the race of women, because the vice of anger arises through softness of spirit, which the female sex signifies; nevertheless, it is overcome and suppressed by the virtue of steadfastness.

[Col. 0836A] “The seed of human beings that fears the Lord will be honored, but that seed of human beings which disregards the Lord’s commandments will be dishonored.” He uses “seed” for “generation,” since we read in the Prophet: “The generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob (Ps. XXIII).” In the Gospel another generation is described, namely, a crooked and perverse one, and “broods of vipers (Luke III).” The generation of the upright, however, will be blessed; upon the perverse generation “will come all the righteous blood that has been shed from the beginning of the world,” that is, “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood” of the final saint who will come at the end of the world. “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

“In the midst of his brothers, their ruler will be held in honor, and those who fear God will be in his sight.” The ecclesiastical order is that teachers and preachers of the faithful should be held in honor among them, especially those who are shown to keep the fear of God before their eyes. Hence Paul commands that presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching; and in the Gospel the Lord says to the disciples: “Whoever honors you honors me, and whoever despises you despises me (I Tim. V).”

“The glory of honored wealthy people and of the poor is the fear of the Lord. Do not despise a poor righteous person, and do not magnify a rich sinful man.” The glory produced by the fear of the Lord is genuine, because it preserves justice and equity. It neither despises the righteous poor nor magnifies the rich sinner. It offers everyone the reverence appropriate to them and does not turn aside in either direction, abandoning the path of truth. Hence James admonishes in his Epistle, saying:

“My brothers, do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality. For if a man wearing a gold ring and splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in dirty clothing also enters, and you look upon the one wearing splendid clothing and say, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ while you say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool,’ are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts (Jas. II)?”

“Great is the judge, and powerful in honor; there is none greater than the one who fears God.” He asserts that although earthly power exalts itself in temporal honor, it cannot surpass the one who fears God, because, according to the Prophet’s statement, those who fear God lack nothing: “The rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing (Ps. XXXIII).”

“Free people will serve a prudent servant.” This often occurs according to the historical sense: someone who is of lowly birth but noble in faith and knowledge of Scripture is preferred to those who boast of the nobility of their lineage. Thus it is written in Proverbs: “A wise servant will rule over foolish sons and will divide the inheritance among brothers (Prov. XVII),” because, as Ecclesiastes says: “Wisdom will strengthen the wise person more than ten rulers who are in the city.” Wisdom can offer greater assistance to those afflicted by some tribulation than any very great power.

According to the allegorical sense, however, the ecclesiastical servant who preserves the Christian religion with a devoted mind is placed above the noble sons of the synagogue, according to what is written: “The elder will serve the younger (Gen. XXV),” and, “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau (Mal. I; Rom. IX).”

“A prudent and disciplined person will not murmur when corrected, and the ignorant person will not be honored.” Similar is what is read in Proverbs: “Reprove the wise person, and he will love you; rebuke a fool, and he will hate you (Prov. IX).” Whoever rejects discipline despises his own soul; but whoever accepts reproofs possesses a heart. And elsewhere: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored (I Cor. XIV),” that is, he will be despised and certainly will not be honored.

“Do not exalt yourself in doing your work, and do not hesitate in a time of distress.” He forbids anyone to boast of his good work, because all arrogance is an abomination before God; and he forbids anyone to cease from good work in adversity, because tribulation produces endurance, endurance testing, and testing hope; and hope does not disappoint.

Better is the one who works and abounds in all things “than the one who boasts and lacks bread.” It is better, certainly, for someone to strive throughout the days of his life to labor in good works, from which a sure reward remains for him, than to consume his days in vanity and become deprived of the bread that came down from heaven [Col. 0837C], the one who eats which will not die forever. Blessed is the one who eats bread in the kingdom of God.

“Son, preserve your soul in meekness, and give it honor according to its merit.” A person preserves his soul in meekness when he performs works of piety through humility; and he gives it honor according to its merit when he consoles himself through hope of the future reward for the pursuit of righteous labor, because, according to the Prophet, God will repay each according to his works (Ps. LXI). Let us hear, conversely, what is added concerning sinners:

“Who will justify the one who sins against his own soul? And who will honor the one who dishonors his own soul?” A person dishonors his soul when he pollutes it with sins; and who can assign the merit of righteousness to one who is plainly neglectful of his own salvation? “For we must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through his body, whether good or evil (II Cor. V).”

“A poor person glories in his discipline and fear, while there is someone who is honored because of his wealth.” Here you should understand “poor” as the humble person who places all his glory in the fear of the Lord and the observance of true religion. Paul says of him: “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends; he is approved.”

There is another person who boasts with proud intent in the abundance of his wealth. Concerning him the Apostle mentioned above writes to his disciple: “Command the rich of this age not to be proud in mind and not to hope in the uncertainty of riches (I Tim. VI).”

“But whoever glories in his poverty, how much more in his wealth?” Therefore the one who rejoices now in tribulations, necessities, and distress for Christ’s sake—how much more will he rejoice when he reaches the future recompense and the true riches kept for God’s elect in the heavenly kingdom?

«But let him who glories in wealth fear poverty.» This means that the man who places all his trust in the abundance of earthly possessions should fear future poverty and should always remember that evangelical parable about the rich man dressed in purple and poor [Col. 0838B] Lazarus: how the one was cast from temporal glory into eternal torments, while the other rose from the misery of the present life to everlasting joys. Of this it is also said through James: «Let the humble brother glory in his exaltation, but the rich man in his humiliation (James I),» because everyone who humbly suffers adversity for the Lord will receive from him the rewards of the kingdom in exalted fashion. But, conversely, let the rich man glory in his humiliation: this is said ironically, when he sees that the glory in which he was proud of his riches and despised—or even oppressed—the poor has been brought to an end by everlasting punishment.

## CHAPTER IV. The wise man is praised because he will be exalted and will sit among the great

[Col. 0838C] «(CHAP. XI.) The wisdom of the humble man will exalt his head and make him sit among the great.» The wisdom of the humble man is the faith of Christ, which works through love. It does not pursue human philosophy or the empty boasting of this world, but always imitates the gentleness and modesty of its Lord, who said: «Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart (Matthew XI).» Hence what follows will be fulfilled: «And you will find rest for your souls.» For wisdom will make those who possess it sit among the great when it grants them to share in the heavenly kingdom with the patriarchs and prophets, with the apostles and martyrs, and with the other saints.

«Do not praise a man for his appearance, nor despise a man for his looks. Small among flying creatures is the bee, [Col. 0838D] yet the fruit it produces has the beginning of sweetness.» He forbids anyone to judge the quality of the mind according to the appearance of the body, because just as the nature of soul and body is distinct, so too is their dignity different; nor does it follow that the measure of wisdom corresponds to bodily stature. Hence also in 1 Kings, when the Lord sent Samuel to anoint one of the sons of Jesse as king over Israel, and his firstborn Eliab had been brought before the prophet, the Lord said to him: «Do not look upon his face, nor upon the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I do not judge according to man’s appearance (1 Kings XVI).» A human being sees what appears, but the Lord looks upon the heart. And appropriately the image of the bee is taken from among the other flying creatures [Col. 0839A], since it both stings with its spur and produces honey through its work. Thus, too, within a small body there often dwells an ingenious soul, which is vigorous in sharpness and knows how to bring forth the sweetness of wisdom in its teaching.

«Never glory in clothing, nor exalt yourself on the day of your honor.» That the vanity of clothing should be avoided the Lord indicates in the Gospel, where he presents John the Baptist as praiseworthy for the roughness of his clothing, saying to the crowds: «What did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses (Luke 7).» John himself had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist; his food was locusts and wild honey. And the apostle Peter [Col. 0839B], in his Epistle, commands women not to adorn themselves with costly clothing, pearls, or gold ornaments, but rather with moral goodness and the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit (1 Peter III). Therefore, no one ought to exalt himself through worldly honors, but rather adorn himself with the dignity of virtues. Hence it follows:

«For the works of the Most High alone are marvelous, glorious, hidden, and beyond sight.» The works of God are marvelous and glorious because everything is done according to truth and equity; they are also hidden and beyond sight because no one can investigate their meaning completely. He alone brings them about according to his counsel and wisdom. Understanding this, the Apostle, astonished and filled with wonder, says: «O the depth [Col. 0839C] of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that recompense might be made to him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things (Romans XI).» He also does great and inscrutable things. Hence Ecclesiastes says: «I understood that no human being can discover the reason for all the works of God, for what is done under the sun (Ecclesiastes XVIII)»; and the more diligently he labors to seek it, the less he will find. Even if the wise man says that he knows, he will not be able to discover it. For the fact that God humbles one person and exalts another belongs to his power and judgment, as what follows demonstrates:

[Col. 0839D] «Many tyrants have sat upon a throne, and one who was unsuspected has worn a diadem; many powerful men have been violently oppressed, and glorious men have been delivered into the hands of others.» These words can also be understood according to history, because often, by God’s ordering, those rise to the summit of honor who previously possessed no dignity among human beings; and, conversely, those who were powerful are, by God’s judgment, brought down to poverty and contempt. Similarly, according to allegory, the former people, who boasted of the nobility of their ancestors and gloried in carnal power, were cast down from primacy by divine judgment because of their faithlessness. But the people of the nations, on account of faith in God, were appointed in the place of sons and, through Christ’s gift, received the blessing of the patriarchs as an everlasting inheritance [Col. 0840A] (Deuteronomy XVII, XIX; Matthew XVIII).

«Before you question anyone, do not reproach him; and when you have questioned him, correct him justly.» He forbids us to pass a rash judgment. Hence in the Law the Lord also commanded that no innocent person should be punished, nor should a matter be established by the testimony of one person against another, but that every word should stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Hebrews X). Likewise, the Apostle commands Timothy not to accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses; but he is to rebuke sinners in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear (1 Timothy V).

«Before you have heard, do not answer a word, and do not add your voice in the midst of speeches.» Concerning this [Col. 0840B] it is also written in Proverbs: «Whoever answers before he hears demonstrates that he is foolish and worthy of shame (Proverbs XVIII).» That is, whoever desires to be a teacher before learning does not avoid the guilt of folly. Whoever hastens disorderly to judge the deeds of his neighbors before fully understanding the case of both parties demonstrates that he is worthy of shame, because he proves himself stubborn rather than prudent.

«Do not contend about a matter that does not trouble you, and do not take your stand in the judgment of sinners.» He admonishes us not to be excessively curious about unnecessary matters and not to consent to the wickedness of sinners. The Apostle teaches: «Having food and clothing, let us be content with these (1 Timothy VI).» And elsewhere: «Not only [Col. 0840C] those who do evil, he says, but also those who consent to those who do it are worthy of death. For blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence (Psalm I).»

«My son, do not let your activities be many; and if you become rich, you will not be free from sin.» Wisdom teaches its children not to strive beyond measure to acquire earthly profits, because they do not avoid the plague of greed, envy, and similar vices. Hence it is written in Proverbs: «The man who hastens to become rich and envies others does not know that poverty will overtake him (Proverbs XXVIII).» And again: «He troubles his household, he says, who pursues greed (Proverbs XV).» Better is a little with the fear of the Lord than great and [Col. 0840D] unstable treasures. And in Ecclesiastes: «The greedy man, he says, is not filled with money, and he who loves riches will gain no fruit from them (Ecclesiastes V).»

According to the tropological sense, however, the care of government, once undertaken, often tears the heart in different directions; and each person is found unequal to individual tasks when his confused mind is divided among many concerns. Hence wisdom fittingly says here: «My son, do not let your activities be many,» because the mind is in no way gathered completely into the purpose of each work when it is divided among different things. And when it is drawn outward by excessive care, it is emptied of the firmness of inward fear. It becomes anxious about external affairs and ignorant of itself alone. It knows how to think about many things without knowing itself; for when it involves itself in external matters more than necessary, it forgets, as though occupied [Col. 0841A] on a journey, where it was heading. Thus, estranged from the pursuit of its own inquiry, it does not even consider the losses it suffers and remains unaware of how greatly it sins.

«For if you follow, you will not overtake; and you will not escape if you run ahead.» For it is not in the power of the one who receives, but of the one who gives. If, driven by the heat of greed, a person burns to accumulate riches, he will not seize true riches; but if he runs ahead in devotion to faith by practicing works of virtue, heavenly riches will pursue him in the future reward.

According to allegory, however, the activities of heretics are many because they refuse to preserve the unity of faith and the path of truth. Therefore all their labor is vain, which they expend in composing many books [Col. 0841B] filled with the abundance of rhetorical and dialectical art. Nor are they free from sin, because all their meditation is directed toward deceit. Hence Ecclesiastes admonishes us, saying: «My son, beware of making many books, for there is no end to them,» and what follows (Ecclesiastes XII).

It is the custom of the Scriptures to call several books one volume if they do not disagree among themselves and write about the same subject. Indeed, in Isaiah’s speech the whole Scripture of God is designated as one sealed scroll; and in one chapter the books of Ezekiel and John are joined together. The Savior, too, foretold in the words of all the saints who came before him, says: «In the beginning of the book it is written concerning me.»

According to this meaning, therefore, I think the command is now given that many books should not be made. Whatever you say, if it is referred to him who in the beginning was the Word, God with God, is one volume; and innumerable [Col. 0841C] books are one Law, one Gospel. But if you discuss diverse and contradictory matters and draw the mind here and there through excessive curiosity, then even in one book there are many books. Hence it is said: «You will not escape sin through much speaking (Proverbs X).» Such books, therefore, have no end. Every good thing and every truth is enclosed within a definite limit; wickedness and falsehood are without end, and the more they are sought, the greater their succession becomes.

«There is a man who labors, hastens, and grieves the ungodly, yet all the more does not abound; there is a man who is withered, in need of restoration, increasingly failing in strength, and abounding in poverty; and the eye of the Lord looked upon him for good, raised him from his lowliness [Col. 0841D], exalted his head, and many marveled at him and honored the Lord.»

This passage expresses especially the Christian age, in which those who pursue voluntary poverty abound more in every good thing than those who struggle daily to acquire earthly riches. The Psalmist also expressed this briefly in a single verse, saying: «The rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing (Psalm XXXIII).»

He distinguished the rich of the earth and the poor of Christ with magnificent contrast. For he says: «The rich have become poor and hungry.» When are the rich in need? When they do not possess right faith. When do they hunger? When they are not at all satisfied with the food of the Lord’s body. Such rich people are therefore in need; though their bellies are filled, they always hunger in spirit. [Col. 0842A] What do those who seek God possess? It follows: «But those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing,» because those who enjoy spiritual things lack no good; for when we love the Lord, we find everything in him. There is one whom we seek, but in whom all things are contained. O marvelous profit! O singular advantage! Why should we weary ourselves through many things? Let us therefore hasten with one accord to him, after whom we no longer seek all good things elsewhere but possess them, as the Apostle says: «We know that all things work together for good for those who love God (Romans VIII).»

«Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God.» In Isaiah the Lord is read to have said: «I am the Lord, and [Col. 0842B] there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil. I am the Lord, doing all these things (Isaiah XLV).»

Hence the question arises how good and evil, and life and death, can be from God, when Scripture says: «God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good (Genesis I).» And elsewhere: «God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living (Wisdom I).» But according to the context of what precedes, here we understand “good” as prosperity and “evil” as adversity; likewise, “life” signifies salvation and “death” the destruction of the flesh.

For God made nothing except good things; nevertheless, by his just judgment he permits adversity to befall sinners. God therefore himself makes things that are contrary to one another: light and darkness, that is, day and night; peace and evil, that is, leisure and war. Through these he signifies that he was angry with his people when they endured the darkness of captivity and the evils of servitude [Col. 0842C], and again that he had mercy when, having been released and restored to their homeland, they received peace and joy.

As darkness is contrary to light, so war is contrary to peace. Hence also the heresy that considers God the creator of evils is confuted, since here “evil” does not signify what is contrary to good, but affliction and war, according to what is written in the Gospel: «Sufficient for the day is its own evil (Matthew VI).» But since these things stand thus, let us see what follows.

«The gift of God, he says, remains with the righteous, and its [Col. 0842D] progress will have success forever.» Therefore the gift of everlasting light is preserved for the righteous alone—that is, for the faithful and those who fear God—and those who walk in the progress of virtues are rewarded forever with manifold recompense.

«There is one who grows rich by acting sparingly, and this is the portion of his reward in what he says: “I have found rest for myself; now I shall eat of my goods alone.” And he does not know that time passes, that death approaches, and that he will leave everything to others.»

The Savior narrated something similar in the Gospel parable about the rich man whose field produced abundant crops. He reasoned with himself and said: «I will tear down my barns and make them larger, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things stored up for many years; eat, drink, and rejoice (Luke XII).» While he was thinking such things, the Lord answered him: «Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things [Col. 0843A] you have prepared, whose will they be?»

Of him Ecclesiastes also speaks, saying: «There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the harm of their possessor; and those riches will perish in the most grievous misfortune, and a stranger will consume them (Ecclesiastes V).»

According to the plain sense, he describes the greedy rich man, who torments himself through utterly foolish frugality and preserves riches for others to devour. But, if we rise to a higher level, it seems to me that he is speaking of philosophers and heretics, who gather the riches of doctrines to their own harm. Neither can the discoverers derive any benefit from them, nor do they leave lasting fruit to their followers; instead, they and their disciples return to the earth and lose their riches.

But the ecclesiastical man, whose entire labor is devoted to the heavenly Scriptures [Col. 0843B], strives to turn everything he finds in the doctrines of wisdom toward the use of good works. Therefore he will possess heavenly life in the future reward. Hence what follows in sequence:

«Stand by your covenant, converse in it, and grow old in the work of your commandments. Do not remain in the works of sinners, but believe in God and remain in your place; for it is easy in the sight of God suddenly to honor the poor. The blessing of God hastens as the reward of the righteous, and its swift progress bears fruit in honor.»

He stands by his covenant and converses in it who faithfully remains in the commandment entrusted to him by God and constantly meditates upon it. He grows old in the work of God’s commandments who strives to persevere in good works to the end [Col. 0843C] and avoids all sins as far as possible. For whoever stands firm in faith and strives to live justly will be rewarded by God’s blessing with eternal blessedness and, filled with the fruit of virtues, will be placed in the heavenly citadel.

«Do not say: “What need have I, and what good will come to me from this?” Nor say: “I am sufficient for myself; what harm could come to me from this?”» This is the voice of the arrogant, who foolishly trust in earthly power and perishable riches and pleasures of the world. Such trust benefits them nothing, because their substance is unstable and passing away. Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER V. In good days, not to forget evil days; and in evil days, not to forget good days

«In the day of good things, do not forget evil days; and in the [Col. 0843D] day of evil things, do not forget good days, because it is easy before God, on the day of death, to repay each person according to his ways. The evil of the hour causes the forgetting of great luxury, and at the end of a man his works are laid bare.»

A person should always be apprehensive and concerned about the condition of his salvation and restrain the swelling of his mind through the fear of God, lest he be lifted up in prosperity; and he should relieve the anguish of his spirit through hope in God’s mercy, lest he fail in tribulation. For it is easy for God to exalt the humble and humble the proud.

At the end of a person it will be revealed with what state of mind he lived here and what his merit is, because «the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each according to his works (Matthew [Col. 0844A] XVI).»

When he says: «The evil of the hour causes the forgetting of great luxury,» he uses “evil” to mean adversity and tribulation. These, arriving suddenly, dissolve all the luxury of the past. Thus, for example, when a severe fever or great poverty seizes a person, it consigns to oblivion all the time he previously spent in health and pleasures; misery or sickness alone occupies him and no longer permits him to think of anything else. Or, if at some time, while he is being tortured, something of his former happiness comes to mind, it provides him no relief but increases his punishment.

«Before death, praise no one, because a man is recognized in his children.» It is utterly foolish to praise a soldier who is still standing in the struggle [Col. 0844B] as though he were already victorious, when it is uncertain whether he will conquer the enemy or be conquered by him. But when the battle has been completed, the victor receives the fitting palm.

So, too, when we see someone acting well and living justly, it is uncertain whether he will persevere in this to the end. But if he perseveres in right faith and good works until the end of life, then he is worthy of praise and should be proclaimed by all, because a man is recognized in his children—that is, his merit is proved by his good deeds.

«Do not bring every person into your house, for there are many snares of the deceitful.» Although this saying, in the tropological sense, warns us not to be careless and imprudent toward strangers and outsiders, because a feigned appearance often deceives the innocent, nevertheless, in a deeper sense it forbids association [Col. 0844C] with heretics. When they imitate something true and good in their words or actions, we should not quickly give them our assent; rather, according to the Apostle, who says: «Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John IV),» we should test everything and thus hold fast to what is good.

The Truth itself taught the disciples concerning this, saying: «Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits (Matthew VII).»

«For as the entrails of those who are full belch forth foulness, and as a partridge is led into a cage, and as a doe into a snare, so is the heart of the proud.» He used this comparison with animals more acute in sense and [Col. 0844D] keener in sight to show that those who consider themselves wise are often captured through the cunning of heretics.

For just as a full stomach foully belches out food that has been badly digested, so the hearts of heretics fraudulently bring forth the deceits that they construct within through malice, so that they may cast as many as they can into the cage of their error and the snare of their wickedness.

«And like one who watches for the fall of his neighbor. For he turns good things into evil and lies in wait, and he will place a stain upon the chosen.» The heretic watches for the fall of his neighbor and does not help him, because his entire intention is directed toward harming and subverting his hearer. He turns the good testimonies of the holy Scriptures [Col. 0845A] into evil doctrines according to the perversity of his understanding and is always ready to deceive. Hence he often casts the stain of his error upon those who seemed to be chosen through good works.

«From one spark the fire is increased, and from one deceitful man bloodshed is increased; but the sinful man lies in wait for blood.» Just as a great flame of conflagration is kindled from a small spark, so the malice of a single heretic becomes the cause of the destruction of many. The sinful man lies in wait for blood when the heretic attempts to inflict death upon human lives. Here “blood” is understood as human life. But let us see what wisdom advises us to do about this.

«Take heed of the pestilent man, he says, for he fabricates evils; lest perhaps he bring derision [Col. 0845B] upon you forever.» The heretic cooperates with the devil. Whoever he overturns through the machinations of deceit he shows to be deserving of eternal shame. Therefore we must take the greatest care and devote every effort to avoid being deceived by such people, whose doctrine and works are alien to the Church of Christ.

Hence in what follows he calls such a person an alien, because they are wholly strangers to the generation of those who seek the Lord and seek the face of the God of Jacob. They belong to that generation of which it is written: «A wicked and perverse generation, from which all the blood of the righteous will be required, blood shed from the beginning of the world, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, who was killed between the temple and the altar (Matthew XXIII).»

For they kill the innocent [Col. 0845C] and attempt to inflict death upon the ministers of Christ in the temple of God—that is, in the divine law. Hence it follows:

«Admit the alien to yourself, and he will overturn you in a whirlwind and estrange you from your own people.» Such an enemy must not be admitted to communion with the Church, because his society is dangerous. He will overturn his adherent in the confusion of error and make him alien from the members of Christ, after making him a participant in his perversity.

## CHAPTER VI. He praises works of almsgiving

(CAP. XII.) «If you do good, know to whom you do it, and there will be gratitude for your good deeds. Do much good to the righteous, and you will find a great reward; and if not from him, certainly from the [Col. 0845D] Lord.»

This is evangelical teaching and agrees with the Savior’s words. First, he urges you to give alms with a simple heart, because works of mercy are approved by God only when they are offered with a simple and pure intention: «Take heed, he says, not to practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them (Matthew VI).»

That is, beware of adopting this attitude: when you live justly or do some good work, do not place your good in being seen by people, pleasing them, and seeking to receive praise from them, thereby depriving yourself of the fruit of the true reward. Hence it is added: «Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven (ibid.).»

Again he says: «When you give alms, do not let your left hand [Col. 0846A] know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.»

«Do good, he says, to the righteous, and you will find a great reward.» He does good to the righteous who, for love of righteousness, extends assistance to the needy. His reward is great, because either he will receive here the return of brotherly love, or he will be rewarded by the Lord himself in the heavenly citadel in the future. «Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied (Matthew V).»

«It will not go well with him who is continually engaged in evil and does not give alms, because the Most High also hates sinners and has mercy on the penitent.» It is a very serious crime and must be counted as impiety when someone, after committing sin, does not [Col. 0846B] wish to repent or redeem his sins through almsgiving, but adds sin to sin and multiplies evil through many crimes. Despairing of himself, he in no way helps himself through the lament of repentance. Hence the Lord also says through the prophet: «For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back (Amos I).»

«Give to the merciful, and do not receive the sinner; and he will repay impious sinners with vengeance, preserving them for the day of vengeance.» Whoever gives alms to the needy and does not despise him because of some offense he has committed properly and rightly practices mercy, because in the distribution of alms one must consider nature, not the person. Hence he says: «Give to the merciful, and do not receive the sinner.»

But God will repay the harsh and merciless [Col. 0846C] with vengeance, reserving for them a fitting recompense on the day of vengeance, which the Apostle called the day of wrath: «For it is the day of wrath for sinners, on which they will be punished (Romans I).» It is wrath for them because they will experience punishment on the day when God’s righteous judgment is revealed. What is now denied as something still to come will then be revealed, that is, recognized; what is now reserved as though hidden will then be avenged as though manifest.

«Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner; do good to the humble, and do not give to the impious.» A similar passage is read in Tobit: «Place your bread and your wine upon the burial of the righteous, and do not eat or drink from it with sinners (Tobit IV).»

A person gives his bread and wine to sinners when he provides assistance to the wicked because they are [Col. 0846D] wicked. Hence certain rich men of this world, while Christ’s poor are tormented by hunger, nourish actors with lavish distributions. But whoever gives his bread to a needy sinner not because he is a sinner but because he is a human being clearly does not nourish a sinner but a righteous person, because in him he loves not guilt but nature.

Alternatively, if according to allegory you understand the sinner and the impious here as heretics, then one must not communicate with them as long as they persist in error. Hence the Truth itself says in the Gospel: «Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them under their feet, turn, and tear you apart (Matthew VII).»

We appropriately understand dogs as those who attack the truth and pigs as those who despise it [Col. 0847A]. Hence Paul also says: «After one or two admonitions, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a one is perverted and condemned by his own judgment (Titus III).» What follows can also be referred to the same meaning.

«Prohibit bread from being given to him, lest he become more powerful than you through it.» The bread filled with the heavenly mysteries of the word of God must not be given to such people, lest they break out into blasphemy and blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over us.

Hence Paul wrote to Timothy, saying: «Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words (2 Timothy IV).» Hence John also says: «If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine [Col. 0847B], do not receive him into your house, nor say “Greetings” to him. For whoever says “Greetings” to him shares in his evil works (2 John).»

The following sentence shows what heretical doctrine is like:

«For you will find double evils in all the good things that you do for him, because the Most High also hates sinners and will repay the impious with vengeance.» Every doctrine of heretics is double—that is, doubtful and deceitful. For in explaining the good statements of divine law they expend themselves, and therefore, while at times they unwillingly utter truths, at other times they willingly mix falsehoods with truths. Thus they corrupt and confuse everything, so that almost nothing among them is pure.

Hence the stain of their leprosy, possessing varied coloration, needs to be healed by the hand of the Lord. You will always find double [Col. 0847C] evils in all such people, because the double-minded person, according to James, is unstable in all his ways (James I). «Where there is jealousy and contention, there is instability and every evil work.» And elsewhere Scripture says: «Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways (Ecclesiasticus II).»

The sinner enters the land by two ways when the heretic hastens to defile the land of the Church, declaring some things truly but proclaiming other things falsely and in every way abominably. Therefore everlasting woe will remain for him, because the Most High hates sinners and will repay the impious with vengeance, when they go into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 00847D] Concerning good and evil friends, false and true

«A friend will not be recognized in good times, nor will an enemy remain hidden in evil times; an enemy is recognized in a man’s prosperity, and a friend in his sadness and misfortune.»

A friend and an enemy are tested much more readily and easily in adversity than in prosperity, because many friends of the table will not remain in the day of need. Whoever is truly someone’s friend grieves and suffers with him in his tribulation. But whoever is falsely a friend pretends to possess true friendship when prosperity smiles; he reveals himself to be a false friend when he does not grieve with the one in tribulation.

Did Paul not possess true friendship? He says: «Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, [Col. 0848A] and I am not on fire (2 Corinthians II)?» And again: «I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak (1 Corinthians IX).» And elsewhere: «Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep (Romans XII).»

But an enemy is proved to be such when he is saddened by the prosperity of his neighbor through envy and rejoices exultantly in his adversity. Prosperity does not reveal a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy. For the one is often covered by respect for our prosperity, while the other is disclosed by the confidence of adversity.

Therefore the righteous man, placed under blows, should say: «Whoever removes mercy from his friend abandons the fear of the Lord.» For whoever despises his neighbor because of adversity is plainly convicted of not having loved him in prosperity. And since almighty God sometimes strikes certain people in order both to instruct those who are struck [Col. 0848B] and to give those who are not struck an occasion for good works, whoever despises the one who has been struck rejects from himself an opportunity for virtue. He rises against the Creator all the more wickedly insofar as he recognizes him neither as compassionate in his own salvation nor as just in another’s wound.

«Do not trust your enemy forever; for his wickedness grows rusty like bronze. And if, being humbled, he goes bent over, direct your attention and guard yourself from him. Do not place him beside you, nor let him sit at your right hand, lest perhaps, when he turns, he stand in your place; lest perhaps, when he has turned toward your position, he seek your seat, and at the end you recognize my words and be goaded by my sayings.»

Although, according to history, the present chapter can be understood as referring to [Col. 0848C] false friends—that is, deceitful enemies—who are not at all firm in faith and affection and who should certainly not be readily trusted, but rather carefully avoided, nevertheless, in a deeper sense it designates the heretics whom he censured above.

They are true enemies, whose doctrine is full of the rust of error and wickedness. «Their word spreads like cancer,» and therefore one must not trust them forever, even if they pretend, by humbling themselves, to be faithful and catholic. We must agree with them in no respect, nor grant them power over us, which is signified by the right hand, lest they remove us from our place—that is, from the condition of right faith.

For they seek our seat, that is, they strive through their wickedness to overthrow our doctrine [Col. 0848D]. Whoever agrees with them will be tortured with eternal pain in the fire of Gehenna. Such people are also difficult to correct. Hence it follows:

“Who will pity a snake-charmer bitten by a serpent, or any who approach wild beasts? So it is with one who associates with an unrighteous man and is wrapped up in his sins.” For the spiritual snake-charmer is the heretic, since he performs the office of a teacher and believes himself to be a physician of souls; but once he has been bitten by the ancient serpent and has drunk in its poison of wickedness, he will be cured only with difficulty. Hence the Savior, teaching his disciples in the Gospel, says: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, with what will it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer except to be thrown outside and trampled by men” (Matt. V). Thus, when salt has become tasteless and has ceased to be useful for seasoning food and drying meat, it will no longer be fit for any use. Nor, as another evangelist testifies, is it useful for the earth, since when it is scattered upon it, it prevents it from sprouting (Luke XIV). Nor is it useful for the manure heap, since, even when mixed with fertile clods, it naturally destroys rather than nourishes the seeds of crops. So everyone who, after acknowledging the truth, turns back is able neither to bear the fruit of good works himself nor to cultivate others; he must instead be thrown outside—that is, separated from the unity of the Church. Whoever approaches wild beasts—that is, wicked spirits or heretics—and whoever associates with an unrighteous man, from whom the Psalmist prays to be delivered (Ps. XVII), and becomes entangled in his wickedness, is scarcely rescued from it. And therefore it is altogether necessary to avoid the company of such people. [Col. 0849A]
