“For one hour he will remain with you; but if you turn aside, he will not support you.” That is, for a time he pretends to be truthful and faithful; but if, by turning aside from the path of righteousness, you obey him, you will not be able to endure his wickedness.

“For the enemy is sweet upon his lips, but in his heart he lies in wait to overthrow you into a pit. The enemy weeps in his eyes, and if he finds an opportunity, he will not be satisfied with blood. If evils befall you, you will find him there first, and as though helping he will dig beneath your feet. He will shake his head and clap his hands, and, whispering many things, he will change his countenance.” In all these statements, therefore, he rightly suggests the deception of the wicked, who speak empty words to their neighbor. Their lips are deceitful in their heart, and they speak evil; they lie in wait to seize the poor, they lie in ambush in secret places to kill the innocent. When they have deceived someone, they shake their heads, clap their hands, and exultantly say: “Good, good—we have swallowed him up.” They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. II). But if they had remembered what Wisdom says about them in Proverbs, perhaps they would have repented. Concerning them it is written: “The apostate man, the worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, rubs his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a crooked heart, and sows quarrels at all times” (Prov. VI). His destruction will come upon him immediately, and he will suddenly be crushed, with no remedy remaining for him.

## CHAPTER VIII. He exhorts and admonishes us concerning association with the rich, from whom one must beware. [Col. 0849D]

(CAP. XIII.) “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it, and whoever associates with the proud will put on pride.” By the comparison with pitch he shows that fellowship with the proud is harmful: the proud man, polluted by the blackness of his vices, never ceases to stain the brightness of the humble. Hence it is written: “The companion of fools will become like them” (Prov. XIII). And again: “Do not be a friend to an angry man,” he says, “nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take a snare for your soul” (Prov. XXII). Although this statement can generally apply to all furious and angry people, it specifically signifies heretics, who are filled with every kind of wickedness. In general, however, we must say that just as perfect men ought not to flee from the wicked, because they often draw them toward righteousness and are themselves never drawn toward wickedness, so all who are weak ought to avoid the company of the perverse, lest they come to delight in and imitate the evils that they frequently see but are unable to correct.

“He takes a burden upon himself who associates with one more honorable than himself; and do not become a companion to one richer than you. What fellowship can a cooking pot have with a cauldron? For when they collide, they will be shattered. The rich man acts unjustly and rages, but the poor man, having been wronged, keeps silent. If you give generously, he will take you in; and if you have nothing, he will abandon you. If you have something, he will live with you and empty you, and he himself will not grieve over you. If you are necessary to him, he will trip you up, and, smiling, will give you hope, telling you good things. He says: ‘What need have you?’ And he will shame you at his table until he has emptied you twice and three times; and at the end he will mock you. Afterwards, when he sees you, he will abandon you and shake his head at you.” These words likewise instruct us, in accordance with the condition of mortal life, always to pursue humility and utterly flee what is proud. Hence the apostle James says: “My brothers, do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality toward persons. For if a man with a gold ring and splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also enters, and you pay attention to the one wearing the splendid clothing and say, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ while you say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit beneath my footstool,’ are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts? And so forth” (James II). Hence Peter also says: “All of you, practice humility toward one another, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V).

Mystically, however, he teaches that we must altogether avoid the rich Jew, who glories in the letter of the Law, and the heretic, who in proud intention despises the Catholic understanding and chooses things that he himself constructs through empty argument. For when they despise evangelical humility, they show that their perversity is harmful to all. These same people also empty us twice and three times when they corrupt the integrity of the two Testaments and do not cease, wherever they can, to remove the uprightness of faith in the Holy Trinity. At the end, too, they mock those whom they have deceived by their error, for they will show them to be worthy of eternal shame when they groan forever with the devil and his angels in the punishment of Gehenna. Therefore he says:

“Take care lest, deceived in folly, you be humbled.” That is, lest, corrupted by erroneous teaching, you be put to shame.

“Do not be humble in your wisdom, lest, having been humbled, you be led astray into folly.” He does not dissuade us from possessing the virtue of humility, which is praiseworthy in all things; rather, he teaches us to maintain firm authority against those who attack the truth. We must in no way yield to them, but resist them courageously. Hence Paul, writing to the Galatians, boasts that he courageously resisted such men and yielded not even for an hour (Gal. II). And to the Corinthians he says: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, demolishing arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every understanding captive into obedience to Christ, and being ready to punish every disobedience” (Tit. I).

Hence the same apostle instructed his disciple how he should rebuke certain people, saying: “Rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith and not attend to Jewish fables and the commandments of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, for both their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being detestable and disobedient and disqualified for every good work” (Titus I). Hence the apostle Jude also says: “In the last time there will be mockers, walking according to their own desires in ungodliness. These are the ones who separate themselves, worldly people, not having the Spirit. But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God; and rebuke these as already judged” (Jude XVIII).

“Withdraw from an advocate who is more powerful than you; for from this he will more readily bring a charge against you. Do not be shameless, lest you stumble; and do not stay far away, lest you pass into oblivion. Do not presume to speak with him on equal terms, and do not trust his many words; for by much speech he will test you, and smiling he will question you about your secrets. His spirit is ruthless, and he will preserve your words; he will not spare you from malice and bonds.” Wisdom teaches us to act with moderation toward the powers of this world, lest, if we walk with them carelessly, we offend. Their insolence and pride frequently mock the simplicity of the innocent and despise those whom they see abstaining from the affairs of the world. But since the order of mortal life is such that some excel in wealth and power while others are oppressed by poverty and want, the servant of Christ should so conduct himself with the powers of the world that he gives them the honor due to them according to the teaching of Scripture, yet in no way abandons the fear of the Lord or the keeping of his commandments. Peter also urges us to do this in his Epistle, saying: “Honor everyone as servants of God; love the brotherhood; fear God; honor the king” (I Pet. II). He wants us to be free from servitude to sins, so that we may remain good and faithful servants of our Creator; and he urges us to render appropriate honor to all, and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, “to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke XX). But whoever associates with such people carelessly and thoughtlessly, revealing himself to them more than is fitting, will later regret having been deceived by their cunning. Hence he adds:

“Beware of yourself and listen attentively, because you are walking with your overthrow; hearing those words as though in a dream, see and keep watch throughout your whole life.” Nothing is safe, nothing is firm, with the lover of the world, because as he eagerly clings to changing things, he is continually changed along with them. As it is written elsewhere: “The fool is changed like the moon” (Eccl. XXVII). You may also understand spiritually by these powerful people heretics and false Christians, to whom you must never give complete trust, because they are unstable in all their ways. If you do not guard yourself against them, when you have consumed your flesh and body, you will repent without end.

[Col. 0852B] “Love God and call upon him for your salvation.” Having rejected all other things that are changeable and fleeting, he commends this one thing, which is stable and enduring: that you love God, observe his commandments, and daily implore his help. For “the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him. He is near to all who fear him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him, he will hear their prayers, and he will save them” (Lam. III).

“Every animal loves its own kind; so every person loves his neighbor. Every flesh is joined to flesh like itself, and every person will associate with one like himself.” These words must be referred to what he said above: namely, that you should avoid the company of the rich and powerful of this world, who pride themselves on the abundance of their wealth, and join in friendship with one who is your equal and companion in zeal and religious devotion. For, as the holy Fathers have handed down, although there are many kinds of friendship that carnal and less intelligent people judge to belong to true love, only one kind of charity is indissoluble. It is joined neither by the favor of recommendation, nor by the greatness of office or gifts, nor by any agreement or calculation, nor by the necessity of nature, but solely by likeness of virtues. This is the kind that no circumstances can ever sever. Not only are intervals of place and time unable to separate or destroy it, but even death itself cannot tear it apart. This is true and unbroken love, which grows from the shared perfection and virtue of friends. Once its covenant has begun, no adversity can change it, nor can any variety of desires violate it. All other kinds of friendship, however, are frequently interrupted and divided by separation in place, temporal forgetfulness, and the involvement of words, causes, and business affairs. For just as they are ordinarily acquired through different associations for profit, lust, kinship, or various relationships, so they are dissolved whenever an occasion of separation intervenes. How unsuitable, therefore, is the association of those whom inequality of spirit and difference of character altogether separate. He proves this by what follows, using examples:

“If a wolf ever has fellowship with a lamb, so does a sinner with a righteous person. What fellowship has a holy man with a dog? Or what good share has the rich man with the poor? The lion’s prey is the wild ass in the desert; so the poor are the pasture of the rich. And as humility is an abomination to the proud, so the poor man is a curse to the rich.” For just as the wolf’s rapacity does not agree with the lamb’s innocence, so the fury of the greedy man in no way harmonizes with the modesty of the simple. What fellowship has a holy man with one who is unclean and polluted by the filth of sins? For “as a dog returns to its vomit, so one who repeats his folly.” Thus there is no equality between the pride of the rich and the humility of Christ’s poor. The former is always ready to seize; the latter abstains from all the attractions of the world. The former despises his neighbor through the arrogance of his mind; the latter endures his adversary through the humility of patience. But the former, becoming an imitator of the devil, falls from the heights into Tartarus; the latter, following Christ’s footsteps, ascends from earthly things to the heavenly kingdom.

“The rich man, when shaken, is strengthened by his friends; but the humble man, when he falls, is driven away even by his acquaintances. For a rich man who has been deceived there are many restorers: he has spoken proudly, and they have justified him. The humble man has been deceived, and is even rebuked; he has spoken sensibly, and no place has been given him. The rich man speaks, and everyone is silent, and they carry his word even to the clouds. The poor man speaks, and they say: ‘Who is this?’ And if he has offended, they overthrow him.” He continues the same argument that he began above concerning the rich and the poor, because many people, through flattery of the rich, exalt their words and deeds, while few rightly understand the teaching and virtue of the humble. The arrogant always find their own proclaimers; the humble, on the contrary, find their own despisers and critics. In accordance with what is written in Proverbs: “Riches add many friends, but even those whom the poor man had are taken away from him” (Prov. XIX). And again: “Many honor the person of the powerful, and everyone is a friend to one who gives gifts; the brothers of a poor man hate him, and even his friends withdraw far from him” (ibid.).

Ecclesiastes also saw this unjust judgment among human beings and reproved it, saying: “This wisdom also I saw under the sun, and it seemed very great to me: a small city with few men in it. A great king came against it, surrounded it, and built siegeworks around it; and the siege was completed. Then there was found in it a poor and wise man, and he delivered the city by his wisdom, yet no one afterwards remembered that poor man. And I said that wisdom is better than strength. How then is the poor man’s wisdom despised, and his words not heard?” while others say everything uncertainly, and the just man has no more than the unjust. I especially recognized the wisdom of God in this: contrary to everyone’s expectation, a poor and wise man delivered the city from such great danger. I marvel at the thankless forgetfulness of people who, after being rescued, remember no one—no one remembers that poor wise man, no one gives thanks for their safety. Instead, everyone honors the rich, who were able to provide no help in the danger. Although no one remembers that poor wise man when everything is joyful, and although everyone admires wealth and power, I nevertheless, following the teaching of the Fathers, honor all the more the despised wisdom and the words that no one considers worthy of hearing. [Col. 0854A]

“Good is the substance in which there is no sin in the conscience; and most wicked is poverty in the mouth of the impious.” Substance acquired through justice and gathered not through fraud or greed is good and useful, because the conscience of such a possessor is not shaken by the sin of deceit or wickedness. But the one who pursues greed troubles his own house, because it is an abomination before God. “A weight and a weight, and a deceitful balance, are not good.” This is the historical sense. Allegorically, however, the good substance is that of the holy Scriptures, which a faithful man accumulates in the bosom of his mind through meditation and good works; the sin of error does not pierce him because he has not abandoned the state of truth. Conversely, the doctrine of heretics, always poor in truth, is most wicked, because it has no wealth of charity. Therefore he says that most wicked poverty is in the mouth of the impious, because by wicked words he prepares eternal poverty for himself.

“The heart of a person changes his face, whether for good or for evil.” The movement of the mind, whether toward good or toward evil, is often detected from the expression of the face and the quality of one’s words. In accordance with what is read in Proverbs: “A rejoicing heart brightens the face, but in sorrow of spirit the spirit is cast down” (Prov. XV). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “The good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil from the evil treasure. For from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. XII).

“You will scarcely find, and only with difficulty, the trace of a good heart and a good face.” Because many live in hostility and speak deceitfully, he says that it is difficult to find a person in whom heart and face—that is, thought, conduct, and teaching—agree in goodness. Wherever you find such a person, give glory to God, because this is his gift, from whom also “every good gift and every perfect gift” comes (James I). All heretics and schismatics, however, are strangers to this gift, because they are far from right faith and good works: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, because their mind and conscience are polluted.”

## CHAPTER IX. He praises the man who has not stumbled with his mouth—that is, who does not utter a word by which he may be caught. [Col. 0854D]

(CAP. XIV.) “Blessed is the man who has not stumbled in speech from his mouth and has not been pierced by the sorrow of sin.” He calls blessed the one who exercises caution over his words, lest he say something of which he later repents; for “whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distresses.” The words of James agree with this statement: “If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James III). But the question arises how he can say that the person who does not offend in word is perfect, since the same apostle first says: “We all offend in many things” (James III). Solomon also says: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII). And the Psalmist says: “I said in the excess of my mind, ‘Every person is a liar’” (Ps. XXX). The evangelist John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I).

The answer may be that there are different kinds of offenses. The chosen offend in one way, and the reprobate in another, as Solomon testifies when he says: “The righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked will fall into evil” (Prov. XXIV). Even if the righteous person should offend through the weakness of the flesh or perhaps through ignorance, he nevertheless does not cease to be righteous, because just as such offense is daily and unavoidable, so there is also the daily remedy of prayers and good works. This quickly raises the righteous person who has fallen, preventing him from collapsing to the ground and staining the nuptial garment of charity and faith with the dust of vices. “Therefore, if anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man”—that is, in a word whose offense human frailty can avoid: a word of deceit, detraction, cursing, pride, boasting, excuse for sins, rivalry, dissension, heresy, lying, perjury, and also idle or excessive speech, even about things that appear necessary. Whoever guards himself without offense in such speech is a perfect man.

“Happy is the one who has not had sorrow in his mind and has not departed from his hope.” Happy is the one who is not saddened by the adversities of the present life, but commends his struggle to the Lord, hoping to receive from him the reward of his labor in the future life. Likewise, happy is the one who guards himself from sins. Rightly is anyone saddened who has entangled himself in them and who persists in good works, for which he ought to hope for the rewards of eternal life. Everyone who keeps God’s commandments and strives in the present life to preserve faith, hope, and charity will, if he perseveres to the end, possess eternal blessedness in heaven with Christ. The apostle John says: “Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight” (I John III). Our heart does not condemn us if we abstain from evil deeds and perform good works not for earthly praise but for heavenly glory. In accordance with the Lord’s command, we also forgive our debtors, just as we wish our own debts to be forgiven by him. Then we have confidence that we will receive whatever we ask from God, because we are ready to obey his will in all things. Great and desirable is this promise given to the faithful. But if anyone is so foolish and senseless that he takes no delight in heavenly promises, let him at least fear what Wisdom thunders terribly in contrast: “Whoever turns his ear away so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Prov. VIII).

[Col. 0856A] “For a greedy and grasping man wealth is senseless, and what use is gold to an envious man? He who gathers unjustly from his soul gathers for others, and another will squander his goods.” He describes the most wicked plague of greed, which torments the mind of its possessor and does not allow him to obtain the fruit of his labor. Instead, while living his life in poverty, he leaves to others for consumption everything he has gathered by fair means and foul. Concerning him it is written in Ecclesiastes: “If someone lives many years and has many days of life, but his soul does not use the good things of his substance, and he is deprived of burial, I declare that one who is stillborn is better than he. For he comes in vain and goes into darkness, and his name will be blotted out in oblivion” (Eccl. VI). He is clearly describing the greedy rich man who, tormenting himself with the most foolish thrift, preserves goods for others to devour, while his soul wastes away through desire and greed. He is in a far worse condition than that stillborn child who died immediately after being born. The latter saw neither good nor evil; the former, although he possessed good things, was always sad and tormented by his thoughts. Yet both will be carried away to an equal end.

“Whoever is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good? And he will not rejoice in his goods. Whoever envies himself, there is no one more wicked than he. And this is the return of his wickedness: if he does good, he does it unknowingly and without ability, and at the end he reveals his wickedness.” Although, historically, these words describe the will and life of the greedy and envious person, who labor in vain because they waste their work uselessly and will never have joy from their goods, in an allegorical sense they signify philosophers and heretics. Without the faith of Christ they gather the riches of doctrines to their own harm; they can derive no benefit from them themselves, nor leave any lasting fruit to their followers. Rather, both the inventors of evils and their followers deserve eternal punishment, and they lose the riches that they hoped would benefit them forever.

“Evil is the eye of the envious man, who turns away his face and despises his own soul.” Since he had said above that there is nothing more wicked than one who envies himself—that is, who does not lawfully use what has been granted to him—because through greed and thrift he neglects the good of generosity and mercy, he repeats the same point here, saying that the eye of the envious man is evil—that is, that his mind is wicked. Therefore he turns his face away so that he may not show mercy to the needy; nor does he care for his own soul, sowing earthly things in order to reap heavenly ones. He gathers riches to his own harm. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it, and his soul will not be filled with good things. Hence he adds:

“The insatiable eye of the greedy man is directed toward a portion of wickedness; it will not be satisfied until it consumes and dries up his soul.” For without the fruit of good works he consumes his life and hands over his barren soul to be tormented in the everlasting fires of Gehenna.

[Col. 0857A] “An evil eye is directed toward evil; it will not be satisfied with bread, but will be needy and sorrowful at its table.” Here he calls the intention of the mind an eye, by which the evil person always inclines toward evil, performing perverse deeds and committing grave sins. He will not be satisfied with the bread of life, but in the future reward he will suffer perpetual want. Mystically, however, the eye of heretics, because it is always intent on following errors, does not deserve heavenly bread—that is, the understanding of divine wisdom—but in the table of the holy Scriptures it is wasted away by everlasting deprivation.

## CHAPTER X. One must always do good, because death does not delay for a holy man, martyr, confessor, or righteous man: praise of Wisdom. [Col. 0857B]

“My son, if you have anything, do good to yourself, and offer offerings worthy of God. Remember that death does not delay, and the covenant of the underworld that has been shown to you. For the covenant of this world will die by death.” This is evangelical teaching, instructing us concerning the future and heavenly life, so that, having despised the luxury of the world, we may daily offer God the worthy offerings of good works. For the span of this life is short, and it is only during it that we are permitted to work. The end of all things is approaching, when it will no longer be time to work but to reward each person according to his merit. Hence Truth itself says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John XII). And again: “While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be children of light” (ibid.). And again: “Work while it is day; for night is coming, when no one can work” (John IX). Hence Paul also says: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, and especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. VI). Concerning this he also adds:

“Before your death, do good to your friend, and, extending your hand according to your strength, give to the poor. Do not be deprived of a good day, and let no portion of a good work pass you by. Will you not leave your labors and pains to others?” Here is the time for doing good; there, for receiving the reward. Here is the time of labor; there, of rest. Here is the hour of sowing; there, of reaping the fruit. Hence Paul says: “Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap”; and elsewhere: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows in blessings will reap from blessings eternal life. For God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX). Hence Wisdom admonishes us in Proverbs, saying: “How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you rise from your sleep? You will sleep a little, you will slumber a little, you will fold your hands a little to sleep, and poverty will come upon you like a traveler, and want like an armed man. But if you are diligent, your harvest will come like a fountain, and want will flee far from you” (Prov. VI). For the world and its desire pass away. But the righteous will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord.

[Col. 0858A] “In the distribution of the lot, give and receive, and justify your soul. Before your death, practice righteousness, because in the underworld there is no finding food.” He gives and receives in the distribution of the lot who here supplies his neighbors with the word of teaching and leaves them examples of good actions, so that in the future he may receive the reward of eternal life for this. He justifies his soul who cleanses his mind through confession and repentance; and he practices righteousness who carefully keeps God’s commandments, because in the underworld there is no finding food—that is, nourishment of life. “For there is no one,” he says, “in death who remembers you; and in the underworld who will confess to you?” (Ps. VI).

“Every flesh will grow old like grass, and like a leaf bearing fruit on a green tree. Some are born and others are cast down; so it is with the generation of flesh and blood: one ends and another is born.” He compares human nature, according to the condition of the flesh, with grass and a leaf, because just as grass on the earth or a leaf on a tree is born, grows, becomes green, dries up, and falls, so the nature of our flesh is born from the lineage of its parents, grows in infancy and childhood, blossoms in adolescence, matures in youth, dries up in old age, and falls in death. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “One generation goes, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. I). Isaiah also says: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of God breathed upon it. Truly the people are grass: the grass has dried up, the flower has fallen; but the word of our God remains forever” (Isa. XL).

Beginning with the general statement, “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass,” he proceeds to the particular, nevertheless saying of the people: “Truly the people are grass.” And indeed, if anyone considers the frailty of the flesh, and that we grow and diminish from moment to moment, never remaining in the same state, and that even what we speak, dictate, and write flies past from the portion of our life, he will not hesitate to call flesh grass and its glory like the flower of grass or the meadows of the fields. One who was just now an infant is suddenly a child; one who was a child is suddenly a young man; and through uncertain intervals he changes until old age, recognizing himself to be old before he wonders that he is no longer young. A beautiful woman who once drew behind her throngs of young men becomes furrowed in the forehead; what once inspired love later inspires disgust. The excellent orator among the Greeks also writes that the beauty of the body either fails through time or is consumed by sickness.

Therefore the flesh has dried up and beauty has fallen, because the spirit of God’s fury and judgment breathed upon it. To return from this general discussion to the order of Scripture: whoever bears the image of the earthly and serves vices and luxury has flesh that is grass and a passing flower. But whoever possesses and guards the image of the heavenly has flesh that beholds the salvation of the Lord. It is renewed daily in thought according to the image of the Creator; and, receiving an incorruptible and immortal body, it changes its glory, not its nature. “The word of our God,” and those who have been satisfied by the word, “remain forever.” Hence he adds:

“Every corruptible work will fail at the end; and whoever performs it will go with it; but every chosen work will be justified, and whoever performs it will be honored in it.” A corruptible work will fail at the end, when carnal desire, together with the fruitless works of the flesh, will fail at the end of the present life without receiving the reward of eternal life. Whoever performs it will go with it, when the soul, together with the flesh through which it sinned, goes into destruction for its sins. Every chosen work will be justified—that is, the result of good actions will merit the reward of righteousness—and the one who performs it will be honored in it, when he gains an eternal kingdom with the chosen angels and holy human beings. The apostle Paul also shows this in his Epistle, saying: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that he will also reap. For whoever sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. VI).

“Blessed is the man who will remain in his wisdom, who will meditate in his righteousness, and who will consider the discernment of God in his understanding.” He describes as blessed the person who remains in wisdom—that is, who is constant in meditation on the holy Scriptures—and who, according to what he reads there, performs works of righteousness by living rightly. In doing these things he seeks not human favor but divine praise, desiring to please only the one who examines the heart and whom no one can deceive.

“He who considers her ways in his heart and understands her hidden things, following after her like an investigator and remaining in her paths.” The ways of Wisdom are the divine commandments, and her hidden things are the heavenly mysteries. Whoever diligently learns these things and searches them out through devoted meditation, striving by this work to accomplish what he understands in sound faith, will undoubtedly be blessed, because he will truly please his Creator. The Psalmist likewise confirms this, saying: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII).

“Who looks through its windows and listens at its doors.” The windows are the testimonies of sacred Scripture; its doors likewise are the tongues of preachers. Whoever dwells among these through continual study, offering the eye of his mind and the ear of obedience, will undoubtedly perceive the radiance of the heavenly light.

“Who rests beside its house and fixes his tent-peg in its walls.” By the house of Wisdom we may understand sacred Scripture, where she herself lies hidden and is veiled beneath the covering of letters, but is salutarily found by those who seek her devoutly. Its walls, however, are the two Testaments. Whoever fixes his tent-peg in them—that is, applies himself to writing according to the rule of faith and with Catholic understanding—will not lose the reward of his recompense.

“He will set his chasuble beside her hands, and good things will rest in his chasuble forever.” And what is signified by the chasuble except the dignity of the priesthood? For he sets his chasuble beside the hands of Wisdom who, exercising the office of a teacher in the Church, joins works of justice to sound doctrine, so that he may instruct his hearers both through right teaching and through good example, and thus prove useful in the exercise of both duties.

“He will place his sons beneath her covering, and he will dwell beneath her branches. He will be protected beneath her covering from the heat, and he will rest in her glory.” [Col. 0860B] A good teacher will place his sons beneath the covering of Wisdom when he makes them subject to heavenly discipline; for they will also dwell beneath her branches when they conduct themselves blamelessly according to her tradition. He will be protected beneath her covering from the heat, because through her service he will be defended from the fury of his enemies. He will also rest in her glory, because through her guidance he will possess the hope of eternal life.

## CHAPTER XV

“He who fears God will do good, and he who is steadfast in justice will lay hold of her.” It is clear that no one can become an executor of wisdom except through the fear of God and a life of justice. For the more diligent someone is in keeping God’s commandments, and the more earnest in a just way of life, the more abundantly he rejoices in the perception of wisdom. [Col. 0860C]

“And she will meet him like an honored mother, and like a virgin bride she will receive him.” Wisdom is therefore rightly called a mother because of the grace of nourishment, and a virgin because of the beauty of her appearance and the holiness of her chastity, since there is nothing unclean or defiled in her. For she is the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness; through her all who pleased God from the beginning have been healed.

“She fed him with the bread of life and understanding.” There is said to be the bread of life, and there is also said to be the bread of deceit. But the bread of life is the body of Christ, or the teaching of divine Wisdom: “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV). The bread of deceit, however, is the teaching of heretics, which brings perpetual death upon those who consume it.

“And she gave him a drink of the saving water of wisdom.” Water is spoken of in a good sense, and also in a bad sense. Water in the good sense signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, or a draught of heavenly Wisdom, as in the Lord’s saying: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him,” he says, “will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV). Water in the bad sense is found in Proverbs: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant” (Prov. IX). This clearly signifies the sect and deception of heretics, which appears sweeter and more plausible to those who err because of the eloquence of their words. [Col. 0861A]

“And he will be strengthened in her, and he will not be shaken.” The strength of heavenly Wisdom will be established in holy men; it does not know how to yield in any way to heretics and to the enemies of the Catholic faith and true religion, but resists them courageously. This gift comes from God, who through the grace of his Spirit strengthens and fortifies the faithful against their adversaries. Hence it also follows:

“And she will hold him fast, and he will not be put to shame.” For whoever clings to the Lord will in no way suffer the shame of his enemies, but, with truth prevailing, will everywhere be sufficiently honored. Hence the prophet says to the Lord: “All who wait for you, O Lord, will not be put to shame; but the wicked who act vainly will be put to shame” (Isa. XLIX). And again: “Blessed is the man who fulfilled his desire among them; he will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies at the gate.”

“She will exalt him among his neighbors, and in the midst of the assembly she will open his mouth; she will fill him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and clothe him with a robe of glory. She will store up delight and exultation over him, and he will inherit her in an eternal name.” Elegantly he has expressed the form of the apostles and preachers of the holy Gospel, whom divine Wisdom—namely Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God—placed over the universal Church and set, above the other throngs of the faithful, in the citadel of dignity. This distinguished company of teachers divine power illumined inwardly through the grace of his Spirit, and outwardly supplied with abundance of eloquence, so that they might expound to others in fluent speech the good that they understood in their minds. And rightly, since the supreme Lord, who granted the dignity of the priesthood to his chosen disciples, would likewise grant them elegance in sound doctrine and eagerness for sacred virtues, so that for this they might inherit a good name and a great reward forever in the heavenly kingdom. [Col. 0861C]

“Foolish men will not lay hold of her, but sensible men will meet her.” Foolish men are the pagans, who worship empty idols instead of the true God. They are also the Jews, who crucified the Son of God and, rejecting his Gospel in the age of grace, wish to preserve the shadow of the Law. They are also heretics, who corrupt the sincerity of sacred Scripture with their errors and deceive people with false teachings. None of these will lay hold of wisdom, because the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul.

Sensible men, on the other hand—that is, Catholic and religious men—meet her, because in thought, word, and deed alike they determine and desire to obey the divine will. Earlier he had said that whoever was steadfast in justice would lay hold of wisdom and meet her like an honored mother. Now he says that a sensible person meets the same Wisdom, so that we may understand that divine mercy is always inclined toward compassion and willingly wishes to bestow its grace upon human beings, if it finds in them diligence worthy of receiving it. For Wisdom herself says elsewhere: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early will find me” (Prov. VIII).

But what follows—

“Foolish men will not see her, for she is far from pride and deceit”—

shows that the labor of heretics is vain and useless. They toil almost every day in teaching and writing, tossing about the sayings of the divine books, while they are far from understanding true wisdom. Their pride, by which they disdain to follow the rule of the holy Fathers, and their deceit, by which they strive to lead their hearers away from the path of justice, prevent them from attaining knowledge of her. For they are blind, and guides of the blind, and cast people into error; therefore they will fall together with their followers into the pit of perdition. [Col. 0862B]

“Lying men will not remember her, but truthful men will be found in her.” Who are the lying men except heretics and all corrupters of God’s Law? They do not remember God’s wisdom, because they are deserters of the truth and despisers of Christ’s commandments. If they had wished to be truthful, they would never have held or taught anything contrary to God’s Gospel. For Truth herself says: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” Truthful men, therefore, are found in her because through believing, meditating, and acting rightly they always dwell in her.

“And they will have advancement up to the sight of God.” These people will therefore have advancement—that is, progress in virtue—up to the contemplation of God’s face, until they are perpetually satisfied, with God’s angels, by the eternal splendor of the divine majesty, and in them is fulfilled what the Psalmist spoke concerning God’s elect under the figure of a good tree:

“He will be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season; its leaf will not fall, and everything that he does will prosper” (Ps. I).

For they will go from strength to strength; the God of gods will be seen in Zion. Let us see, on the contrary, what follows concerning the enemies of God’s Law.

“Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner, because he was not sent by the Lord.” The teaching of heretics is not pleasing to God, for it is full of fraud and wickedness and stained with falsehood. Nor are they sent by God—that is, directed by the Spirit of God—to preach. Rather, inflated by an evil spirit, they bring forth from their own hearts the things they perversely speak. Concerning them the Psalmist says:

“Deceitful lips are in the heart, and they have spoken evil from the heart. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue, who said: ‘We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own. Who is our lord?’” (Ps. II).

Hence it is also said through Jeremiah:

“The prophets prophesy falsely in my name: I did not send them, I did not command them, nor did I speak to them. They prophesy to you a false vision, divination, deceit, and the seduction of their own heart” (Jer. XIV).

[Col. 0863A] “For wisdom proceeds from God.” All wisdom, as the beginning of this book testifies, is from the Lord God, because Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, was born from God the Father. In the Gospel he says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI); and again: “I came as light into this world” (John XII). Wisdom proceeds from God because the teaching of truth came forth from the fountain of life; to it all praise, power, and glory rightly belong. Hence it follows:

“For the praise of God’s wisdom will stand, and it will abound in the faithful mouth, and the ruler will give it to him” (2 Tim. II).

The Lord gives his faithful lover understanding of wisdom and words of prudence, so that he may prove a true knower and capable teacher of his Law. Nor does he begrudge anyone the gift of his generosity, since he wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Therefore he next says:

“Do not say, ‘It is absent because of God’; for do not do what he hates.” We must beware of doing what we know he entirely dislikes, if we are truly to share in his wisdom. Hence it is written: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will provide it for you” (Ecclus. I). [Col. 0864A]

“Do not say, ‘He has led me astray’”—[the reading *implanavit* is uncertain in the supplied text]—“for impious people are not necessary to him.” The cause of our error and evil action must not be attributed to God, because our ruin is not necessary to him. Rather, he himself lifts up all who fall and raises up all who have been crushed. Concerning him the apostle James wrote in his Epistle:

“Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God; for God is not a tempter of evils” (James I);

“tempter” is understood here with reference to temptations. For he himself tempts no one with the temptation that deceives wretched people into sinning. “For the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lam. III).

[Col. 0864B] “God hates every abomination of error, and it will not be loved by those who fear him.” Just as God detests every error, so the person who fears God curses all the wickedness of error and hastens with every effort and discernment to attain knowledge of the truth.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0863]

## CHAPTER ONE

That when God established the human being from the beginning, he left him in the hand of his own counsel.

[Col. 0863C] “God established the human being from the beginning, and left him in the hand of his own counsel; he added his commandments and precepts.” When our Creator created heaven and earth and appointed in them the various kinds of plants and animals, he formed the human being in his own image and set him over the other living creatures. He gave him free will so that, bearing the image of God, he might be more glorious than the others and therefore more devoted in submission to his Creator.

But he abused this power that had been granted to him. Through the suggestion of the ancient serpent, he rose up in opposition to his Maker, wishing to use his own power and refusing to be subject to the dominion of his Creator. Thus it happened that, as a transgressor of God’s commandments, he came to have diminished throughout all the time of his pilgrimage what he had received more exalted than the other creatures. He could no longer be saved except through the grace of Jesus Christ, his Redeemer. Free will had blinded itself, and it could not illuminate itself.

Now, however, that same will has been turned, not overthrown. It has been granted to it to will differently, to understand differently, to act differently, and to place its safety not in itself but in the physician, because it does not yet enjoy health so perfect that the things which had harmed it can no longer harm it, or that it can now govern itself by its own healthy powers. Thus the human being who was evil in free will has become good in that same free will: evil through himself, but good through God, who restored him by a new beginning to that former honor, so that he not only forgave him the guilt of evil willing and acting, but also granted him the ability to will and do good and to persevere in it.

“For,” the apostle James says, “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James I).

He clearly shows what kind of free will is moved by the human spirit and what kind is governed by God, saying:

“But if you have bitter zeal and there are conflicts in your hearts, do not boast against the truth and be liars. This is not wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic; for where there is zeal and conflict, there are instability and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, persuadable, full of mercy and good fruits, not judging, without hypocrisy” (James II).

Therefore, whoever strives for and clings to these virtues has been illumined not by his own wisdom but by that from above, since “the Lord gives wisdom, and from his presence come knowledge and understanding” (Prov. II). This is their truest glory, if they glory not in themselves but in the Lord.

“If you wish to keep the commandments, they will preserve you, and you will keep faith pleasing to God forever.” Whoever chooses to guard God’s commandments and fulfill them in his works, and keeps right and Catholic faith to the end of life, will remain unharmed under the protection of almighty God from the snares of the ancient enemy. For Truth herself also shows this in the Gospel, where she says:

“If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death” (John VIII).

And again:

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

[Col. 0865A] “He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish.” In fire tribulation is expressed; in water, refreshment. Tribulation and prosperity have therefore been set before us. If we choose to carry out God’s commandments in action, we shall have the consolation of eternal life; but if we despise his commandments, the punishment of Gehenna’s fury will follow us. This is expressed still more clearly in the words that follow:

“Before a human being are life and death, good and evil; whichever pleases him will be given to him.” Sacred Scripture instructs us in many places how, through observance of God’s precepts, we may become heirs of the heavenly kingdom; and, conversely, how through negligence and contempt of his words we shall become fuel for eternal fire.

Hence it is written in Deuteronomy:

“If, hearing the judgments of the Lord, you keep and do them, the Lord your God will keep for you the covenant and mercy that he swore to your fathers; he will love you and multiply you” (Deut. VII).

And again:

“Know,” he says, “that the Lord your God is himself the strong and faithful God, keeping covenant and mercy with those who love him and those who keep his commandments for a thousand generations; and repaying immediately those who hate him, so that he destroys them and does not delay any longer, promptly rendering to them what they deserve” (ibid.).

Hence the Psalmist also says:

“The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners” (Ps. CXLIV).

Hence Solomon says:

“The life of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord; whoever follows justice is loved by him” (Prov. XV).

Hence Truth herself says in the Gospel:

“If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX).

And again:

“Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

And again:

“There is no good tree that bears bad fruit, nor a bad tree bearing good fruit; for every tree is known by its fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke VI).

“For God has much wisdom and is mighty in power, seeing everyone without interruption.” No one can escape God’s presence, nor can anyone think or do anything that is hidden from him. Hence it is written:

“All the ways of human beings are open to his eyes; the Lord is the weigher of spirits, because his majesty comprehends all things” (Prov. XVI).

The Psalmist, considering this, says:

“Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

Therefore it is necessary that a person be always cautious throughout his life and think, speak, and do what is worthy of the divine sight and capable of pleasing him.

“The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and he himself recognizes every work of a human being.” Although the eyes of the Lord always behold good and evil people and he knows everything, his eyes are properly said to look upon those who fear him because the gaze of his mercy is directed especially toward them. He is said to recognize those things which he is known to approve, and not to know those which he in no way wishes to approve.

Hence it is written:

“The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the wicked will perish” (Ps. I).

Here too we read in the Gospel that the Lord himself replied to the foolish virgins who knocked at the door and sought entry too late:

“Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV).

Therefore he next shows what we must do, saying:

“Watch, therefore, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

Blessed, therefore, is the one who always keeps watch and guards his garments—that is, his actions—so that he may not walk naked and appear at the Judge’s coming without good works. For “the anger of a man will not spare on the day of vengeance,” and “the king who sits upon the throne of judgment disperses every evil with his gaze.” The day of the Lord is near, and there the strong man will be troubled.

“He commanded no one to act wickedly, and he gave no one time for sinning.” Just as the Lord is not the author of our sins, so he has granted no period of time in which a person may sin with impunity. Rather, he always commands what is right and restrains the human being from offenses.

“For he does not desire a multitude of unfaithful and useless children.” Therefore only what is good pleases him; every perversity of the unfaithful and useless displeases him:

“For the Lord is just, and he has loved justice; his face has seen uprightness. He hates all who work iniquity, and he will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. X).

## CHAPTER II

That one should not rejoice in a multitude of evil children; their perverse works are recounted.

## CHAPTER XVI

“Do not rejoice in ungodly children if they become numerous; do not take pleasure in them if the fear of God is not in them; do not trust their life, and do not look upon their labors.” This statement applies against those who delight in a multitude of subjects and crowds of disciples, without caring whether they live according to the fear of God and devote themselves to works of justice, or whether they are entangled in various crimes. For true delight in subjects exists only where sound understanding and honorable conduct are commended.

Otherwise, it is better for someone to live a solitary life than to wastefully consume the span of his days among the undisciplined. Hence it follows:

“For one who fears God is better than a thousand ungodly children; it is useful to die without children rather than to leave ungodly children.” The Savior is also found to affirm this in the Gospel, where he taught his disciples to beware of every scandal, saying:

“If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than, having two eyes, to be thrown into the Gehenna of fire. And if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna” (Matt. IX).

“By one sensible person the homeland will be inhabited, and by three ungodly people it will be deserted.” That is, the land of the Church will be inhabited by the Catholic people who live in the unity of faith, and will be deserted by heretics who err concerning faith in the Holy Trinity. Concerning them the apostle John says:

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John II).

Alternatively, “one sensible person” may be understood as someone who, according to the rule of sacred Scripture, remains in the path of justice in faith and action. The three ungodly people who desert the homeland are those who in thought, speech, and deed sever themselves from the company of the good and no longer remain in the homeland, because through various crimes they cut themselves off from the fellowship of the faithful. [Col. 0867B]

“My eye has seen many such things, and my ear has heard things stronger than these.” The more ardently someone learns God’s Law, the more brightly he is illumined by the light of knowledge; and the more diligently he keeps God’s commandments, the more he rejoices that his heart is enlarged in the progress of virtue and charity. Hence Truth herself says:

“Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me; whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

“In the assembly of sinners fire will blaze, and among an unbelieving people wrath blazes.” The wrath of divine indignation and the fire of just vengeance rightly blaze among the multitude of sinners and among the assembly of the faithful, because their hardened mind did not fear the vengeance threatened by God, nor did it wish, out of reverence for his name, to restrain itself from sins and devote itself to works of justice. Hence it is said through the Prophet:

“He will rain snares upon sinners; fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. X).

“The ancient giants did not plead for their sins; they were destroyed because they trusted in their own strength. He did not spare the sojourn of Lot, and he cursed them because of the pride of their speech. He did not pity the people, destroying an entire nation that exalted itself in its sins.” He calls “giants” those who are ensnared by earthly desires and weighed down by the burdens of sins, who bear an untamed heart and refuse to bend it toward repentance. Therefore, unworthy of God’s mercy, they suffer the loss of their salvation and fall into eternal destruction.

Heretics may also be designated by this name. Trusting in the power of their knowledge and glorying in the riches of their rhetoric, they refuse to withdraw from the deviation of their error and turn to the way of truth. Therefore divine judgment will not spare their sojourn, by which they chose to become exiles from the Catholic faith. Rather, it will destroy their entire people, cursing them especially because of the pride of their wicked teaching and the arrogance by which they boast proudly in their sins, despising God’s judgment and casting themselves into the snare of eternal perdition. [Col. 0868A]

“And as with the six hundred thousand foot soldiers who gathered together in the hardness of their hearts.” He recalls the ancient history in which six hundred and three thousand Israelites who came out of Egypt were struck down in the wilderness because of the hardness of their hearts, and none of them entered the promised land except Joshua and Caleb, who remained steadfast in sincere faith and devoted service to God (Num. XIV).

“And if one had been stiff-necked, would it have been surprising if he had been spared?” The rigor of divine judgment preserves equity in all things. Therefore it will spare neither one nor many if they do not turn away from their sins. For, as God testifies in Scripture, no sin is left unpunished: either the person himself exacts the punishment of sin upon himself, or he will be punished by the examination of the strict Judge.

“With him are mercy and wrath; mighty is forgiveness, and he pours out wrath.” The mercy of the Lord overflows upon those who fear him, and wrath is prepared for those who despise him. With him pure and devoted prayer has great power, while his fury is poured out upon the unrepentant heart of the wicked person, upon whom the punishment of vengeance will rightly be poured.

“According to his mercy, so is his correction; he judges a person according to his works.” —“The Lord is therefore just in all his ways and holy in all his works. He will repay each person according to his works: eternal life to those who, through patient perseverance in good work, await his mercy and seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress to those who are contentious and do not obey the truth but believe iniquity” (Rom. II), so that they may be tortured perpetually by eternal punishment.

“A sinner will not escape through robbery, and the perseverance of the one who shows mercy will not be delayed.” The sinner will not escape through robbery, for he will pay the just penalty for his rapacity. The perseverance of the merciful person is not prolonged without reward, because the patience of the poor will not perish forever but will be repaid with a fitting recompense. Hence Truth herself says to the disciples in the Gospel:

“By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI).

“Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy.”

“Every act of mercy will make room for each person according to the merit of his works and according to the understanding of his pilgrimage.” Glory, honor, and peace will belong to everyone who does good, because whoever sows in blessing will reap eternal life from blessings.

When he says that mercy makes room for each person according to the understanding of his pilgrimage, he shows that whoever strives through good works to keep God’s commandments during the time of this pilgrimage, and labors devoutly with sighs and tears to cleanse his sins, will merit consolation in eternal rest. Hence it is written:

“Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they will be filled” (Matt. V).

Hence Wisdom says:

“Whoever follows justice and mercy will find life, justice, and glory” (Prov. XXI).

## CHAPTER III

Wisdom teaches that when someone sins—in the house, in the field, in the heart, or in bed—he should not say, “Let me hide from God, and who sees me?” For God sees and comprehends all things by his majesty.

“Do not say, ‘I will hide from God, and who from on high will remember me? I will not be recognized among a great people; for what is my soul in so immense a creation?’” He reproves those who say that God does not care about mortal affairs or examine human ways, plainly showing that this is an impious thought, since all sacred Scripture testifies that nothing is hidden from God and that everything lies open to his eyes.

Eliphaz the Temanite also rebukes this opinion of the erring in the Book of Job, saying:

“Do you not think that God is higher than heaven and exalted above the summits of the stars? And you say, ‘What does the Lord know? Does he judge as though through darkness? The clouds are his hiding place, and he does not consider our affairs; he walks around the hinges of heaven’” (Job XI).

So too the Psalmist, truly understanding God’s power, reproaches the wicked, saying:

“Understand now, you who are foolish among the people, and become wise at last, you fools. Does he who planted the ear not hear? Or does he who formed the eye not see? He who corrects the nations, will he not rebuke them? He who teaches human beings knowledge—the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Ps. XCIII).

And again: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. VII).

Hence it is also said through Solomon:

“All the ways of human beings are open to the eyes of God” (Prov. XVI).

Hence it is said through Paul:

“For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword; reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. IV).

“Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens, the abyss and the whole earth, and the things that are in them, will be shaken in his sight; the mountains together, and the hills and the foundations of the earth; and when God looks upon them, they will be shaken with trembling. Yet amid all these things the heart is senseless.” He enumerates the chief elements of God’s creatures and how he arranged and governs all things according to his will, so that it may be understood that, if his majesty comprehends greater things, smaller things likewise cannot be hidden from him.

No creature is invisible in his sight, because he is equally the Creator of great and small things. For all things are from him, through him, and in him; and all things fear and tremble at his command. Only the will of rational creation, when it is perverse, thinks contrary to him, but it will not prevail, because everything is placed within the will of the almighty Creator, and no one can resist his will. For he himself is Lord of all.

Mystically, however, by “heaven” he includes the heavenly host and the angelic powers, concerning which it is written:

“Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII).

By “earth” he signifies human beings and earthly creation; by “abyss,” the infernal places and the spirits who dwell there. All these will be shaken in the sight of the supreme Judge, because they are shaken by fear and terror of him and offer reverence to the power and wisdom of God, through whom all things were made, according to the Apostle’s saying:

“At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

By the mountains and hills, the persons of the powerful are signified; by the foundations of the earth, the counsels of human minds. These tremble at God’s gaze because they are entirely subjected to his dominion. In sacred Scripture the height of preachers is often signified by the name “mountains.” Concerning them the Psalmist says:

“Let the mountains receive peace for your people” (Ps. LXXI).

The chosen preachers of the eternal homeland are rightly called mountains, because through the elevation of their life they leave behind the low places of earth and draw near to heaven. Among those subject to the divine will, therefore, only the mind of the proud resists God’s elect. Yet in striving to oppose him, it breaks itself upon the sword of contradiction; it resists the inner order, but, conquered by its own efforts, it is bound by them.

Hence it is written in Job:

“Who has resisted him and had peace?”

For the perverse mind, from the very point at which it rises up against its Maker, is confounded within itself. It cannot have peace while resisting, because confusion follows pride; and what is foolishly performed through guilt is wonderfully ordered as the punishment of the one who acts.

“And every heart is understood by him, and who understands his ways, and the storm which no human eye will see?” Although the Creator’s wisdom knows all things and judges all things through knowing them, no one can penetrate the depth of his counsel and the power of his judgment, which is here signified by the name “storm.” For, as follows:

“For his works are very many and hidden, but who can declare the works of justice, or who can endure them?” No one can discern them completely:

“For his judgments are incomprehensible, and his ways are unsearchable.”

The creature’s understanding can therefore recognize only as much as the mercy of the Giver wishes to reveal to it. Hence it is said:

“Who can declare the works of justice, or who can endure them?”

For just as no one can declare the sublimity of God’s justice, so no one can endure the severity of his judgments, except the one to whom he himself grants this—and only to the extent that he grants it.

“The covenant is far from certain people, and the reckoning of all is at the consummation.” The covenant is far from pagans, who practice the falsehood of idolatry; it is also far from heretics, who, abandoning the truth of the faith, construct sects of error; and it is far from evil Catholics, who, although they hold the right faith, nevertheless do not possess works worthy of faith, and therefore are not truly participants in God’s covenant, “because it is not the hearers of the law who will be justified before God, but the doers of the law.” For they say that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him. Yet the reckoning of all these will come at the consummation, when on the day of judgment each will render an account to God for his own soul: “and then each person will receive according to what he has done in his body, whether good or evil.”

“He who is diminished in heart thinks of empty things, and the imprudent and erring man thinks foolish thoughts.” He is therefore diminished in heart who departs from the path of truth. Such a person thinks of empty things—that is, he meditates on establishing false doctrines in place of the truth—or, if he does not teach falsehood, nevertheless believes that he may safely carry out perverse deeds. Such a man is rightly called imprudent and erring, because this sort of judgment is foolish: “For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap”; for God is not mocked, but will repay each person according to his own merits.

## CHAPTER IV. Wisdom’s exhortation concerning how the way of discipline is to be maintained

“Hear me, my son, and learn the discipline of understanding; attend in your heart to my words, and I will speak of discipline in righteousness, and I will search out how to declare wisdom.” With fatherly concern the ecclesiastical man admonishes those whom he calls by the name of sons and wishes to have in that position, so that they may learn the discipline of understanding—that is, hear the truth of the faith—and attend in their hearts to his words, namely, that they may strive without ceasing to preserve those things that pertain to moral integrity, and thus truly become meditators on divine discipline and wisdom; for “he who retains the word of God in a good and excellent heart will bear fruit in patience.”

“And attend in your heart to my words, and I speak in the righteousness of the spirit of the virtues that God established in his works from the beginning; and in truth I declare his knowledge, and in God’s judgment, his works from the beginning.” Whoever desires to possess knowledge of the truth with an attentive heart hastens to acquire sober understanding, together with the practice of virtue, in the law of the Lord. In this way he will be able to attain the grace of God, so that he may know the order of God’s works from the beginning—works that he himself arranged according to his just judgment from the beginning and determined should remain in a state of righteousness.

But because part of creation fell through consenting to the devil’s persuasion, the power of its Creator raised it up again from its fall. For almighty God wonderfully established his creation from the beginning through his Word, and still more wonderfully restored it at the end of the ages through that same only-begotten Son, when he restored by his grace to its former condition the human being who had been created in the image of God but had fallen through freedom of choice, and taught him to live in an orderly and just manner, so that what its origin had failed to preserve, restoration might maintain. Although here he may in some way be weaving together an explanation of the history, he nevertheless clearly reveals, in a deeper sense, the condition of the holy Church.

“From the institution of them he distinguished their parts, and their beginnings among their nations.” Since God determined to extend the human race, he distinguished the origin of the individual nations among the separate regions of the world, so that each nation, named from the designation of its ancestor, might possess its own dwelling places in the several provinces.

Mystically, however, divine Wisdom, establishing his Church, extended her throughout all the regions of the world and placed her among the individual nations, so that she might claim special names for herself in different places. Hence it is that in the Apocalypse the word of God was addressed to the seven Churches that were in Asia, when John the evangelist, instructed by God’s command, wrote to the angel of the Church of Smyrna, the angel of the Church of Pergamum, the angel of the Church of Thyatira, and likewise to the others, announcing to each what required correction in them (Apoc. I, 2).

“He adorned their works forever; they neither hungered nor labored, and they did not cease from their works.” For God prepared the works of his Church and continually illumined her with the splendor of charity. Therefore they suffer no poverty of virtues, nor do they fail through the weariness of sloth; rather, intent upon good works, they are always devoted to them.

“Each person will not distress his neighbor, forever.” For “charity does not seek what belongs to itself (I Cor. XIII),” but what belongs to others. Hence the Apostle commanded, saying: “I speak as to sons: Be enlarged yourselves also, and do not bear the yoke with unbelievers.” The breadth of the commandment is charity, because where charity remains there is no narrowness. The Apostle was in this very breadth when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not narrowed within us (II Cor. VI).” Therefore it is also read elsewhere: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad (Ps. CXVIII),” namely, the broad commandment that was given: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another (John XIII).” Charity, therefore, is not narrowed. Do you wish not to be narrowed on earth? Live in spaciousness. Whatever a human being may do to you does not narrow you, because you love what does not harm you: you love the human being, you love God, you love the brotherhood, you love the law of God, you love the Church of God; there will be an everlasting reward. “You labor on earth, but you will reach the promised fruit: who can take from you what you love?”

“Do not be incredulous toward his word.” Earlier he had said how God, from the beginning, ordered his works in knowledge and judgment. Now, inserting a sentence into the middle of his exposition, he exhorts the hearer to observe his commandments, so that he does not presume to turn away from the state of righteousness by being incredulous toward his word. He then returns again to the interrupted narrative, showing how the Creator’s mercy restored the human race after its former fall, saying:

“After these things God looked upon the earth and filled it with his goods.” God therefore looked upon the earth of human nature when he determined to restore it through the regard of his mercy. He filled it with his goods, namely, with right faith together with works of virtue, distributing his Spirit in the hearts of believers, as it is written: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (I Cor. XII).”

And because every living soul exists in the presence of God, and the condition of the whole work looks toward the almighty Maker, the following sentence proves this when it adds:

“Every living soul has declared before his face, and their return is also to him.” A living soul declares before the face of the Lord when he sees its thoughts and the secret of its whole life lies open to him. Hence the Prophet says to the Lord: “You have understood my thoughts from afar (Ps. CXXXVIII)”; and again: “The thought of man will confess to you (Ps. LXXV)”; and once more: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings (Ps. XCIII).” Their return will also be to him, because God’s wisdom contains all things, and every creature is referred back to him, by whose power it was established according to the measure of its nature. And because human nature excels among the other creatures, since, being created in the image of God, it prevails through the power of reason, it immediately follows:

## CHAPTER V. That God created the human being from the earth, made him according to his image, and gave him knowledge

### (CHAP. XVII.)

“God created the human being from the earth and made him according to his own image.” The human being, therefore, formed from the clay of the earth, received from his Creator a rational soul, in which he expresses the image of his Creator.

The Apostle testifies in what respect the human being was made according to the image and likeness of God, when he carefully admonishes us to recover in ourselves, through the grace of that same Creator, the likeness that we lost in our first parent. “Be renewed,” he says, “in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth (Eph. IV).”

Adam, therefore, the new human being, was created from the earth according to God, so that he might be just, holy, and true—humbly subject and cleaving to the grace of his Creator, who eternally and perfectly exists as just, holy, and true. But because Adam corrupted by sin this most beautiful newness of the divine image within himself, and produced within himself a corrupted succession of the human race, the second Adam came—that is, the Lord himself and our Creator—born from a Virgin, created incorruptibly and unchangeably according to the image of God, that is, free from every sin and full of every grace and truth, so that he might restore his image and likeness in us through his examples and gifts.

He is truly the new human being created according to God, because he took from Adam the true substance of flesh, yet drew from him none of the stain of vice. To follow his examples according to our capacity, to cling to his gifts, and to obey his commandments is to recover in the new human being the image of God that we lost in the old.

The human being was therefore created according to the image of God not with respect to the body but with respect to the understanding of the mind. Yet even in the body there is a certain feature that indicates this: he was made upright in stature, so that by this very fact he might be admonished not to pursue earthly things, like the animals whose every pleasure is from the earth. Hence all other creatures are bent and prostrate toward the ground. In keeping with this, one of the poets said most beautifully and truly (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book I):

> While the other animals look down toward the earth,  
> He gave the human being an exalted face,  
> And commanded him to look upon heaven  
> And raise his upright countenance toward the stars.
