His body therefore also corresponds to his rational soul—not according to the outlines and forms of its members, but rather in that it is raised toward heaven, to contemplate the things above that are in the body of the world, just as the rational soul ought to be raised toward those things that now naturally excel in spiritual matters, so that it may set its mind on what is above, not on what is upon the earth.

This image must be considered more carefully from the nobility of the inner human being. First, just as God, being one, is always and wholly everywhere, giving life, moving, and governing all things—as the Apostle confirms when he says that “in him we live, and move, and are”—so the soul is wholly alive throughout its body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. It is not greater in the larger members of its body and lesser in the smaller, but wholly present in the smallest and wholly present in the greatest. This is the image of the unity of almighty God that the soul possesses within itself.

The soul also bears a certain image of the holy Trinity, first in this respect: just as God exists, lives, and knows, so does the soul. There is also another trinity in it, by which it was created according to the image of its Creator, the perfect and supreme Trinity, which exists in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Although the soul is of one nature, it nevertheless possesses three faculties within itself: understanding, will, and memory. This same reality, though expressed in other words, is indicated in the Gospel when it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind (Matt. XXII),” that is, with all your understanding, with all your will, and with all your memory.

For just as the Son is begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, so will is begotten from understanding, and from these two together memory proceeds—as anyone wise can easily understand. For the perfect soul cannot exist without these three, nor can any one of these three, insofar as its blessedness is concerned, be complete without the other two.

And just as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God possessing three persons, so also understanding, will, and memory are not three souls in one body, but one soul possessing three faculties. In these three, our inner human being will wonderfully bear the image of God in its own nature. From these, as from the soul’s more excellent faculties, we are commanded to love the Creator, so that, to the extent that he is understood and loved, he may always be held in memory. Understanding of him alone is not sufficient unless the will is formed in his love. Indeed, these two are not sufficient unless memory is added, by which God may always remain in the mind of the one who understands and loves him. Just as there can be no moment in which a human being does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy, so there ought to be no moment in which he does not have him present in memory.

Let this suffice concerning the image. Now understand something concerning the likeness, which is to be discerned in conduct. Just as God the Creator, who created the human being according to his likeness, is charity, is good and just and gentle, pure and merciful, and possesses the other marks of holy virtues that are read of him, so the human being was created to possess charity, to be good and just, patient and gentle, pure and merciful. The more each person possesses these virtues within himself, the nearer he is to his Creator and the greater likeness of his Creator he bears.

But if—God forbid—someone, through the byways of vices and the divisions of crimes, degenerates and wanders from this most noble likeness of his Maker, he does not preserve God’s likeness in himself.

When he had explained his judgment concerning the inner image of the soul, he immediately proceeded to the substance of the body, saying:

“And again he turned him into it.” That is, into the earth, in accordance with the Lord’s sentence by which he said to sinful humanity: “You are earth, and to earth you will go (Gen. III).”

“And he clothed him with strength like his own; he gave him a number of days and a period of time.” God therefore created the human being upright and endowed with sense and reason, so that by observing righteousness he might possess continuous life. But because he did not preserve the law of his Creator, through disobedience he lost the glory of long life, and received a number of days and a span of time in which to bring the present life to its close.

“And he gave him power over the things that are upon the earth; he placed his fear over all flesh, and he ruled over beasts and birds.” For it is chiefly in this that the human being was made according to the image of God: he surpasses irrational creatures because he was created capable of reason, through which he might rightly govern whatever had been created in the world and enjoy knowledge of the one who created all things. If, placed in this honor, he does not understand how to act well, he will be compared with those very senseless animals over which he was set, as the Psalmist also testifies, saying: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. XLVIII).”

“He created from him a helper like himself, counsel and tongue, and he gave them eyes, ears, and a heart for thinking, and filled them with the discipline of understanding.” The woman was made from the man’s side, and it should be believed that this happened in order to commend the power of that union. But the fact that she was made while he slept, and that flesh was supplied in place of the bone removed, was done for the sake of a deeper mystery.

It signified that from Christ’s side, when he was put to sleep in death upon the cross, the sacraments of salvation would proceed, namely blood and water, from which the Church, his bride, would be formed. For if there were no figure of so great a sacrament to be set forth beforehand in the creation of the woman, what need was there for Adam to sleep so that his rib might be taken, from which the woman would be made, when the same thing could have been done while he was awake and without pain? Why was it necessary that, when the bone taken from the man’s side was fashioned into the woman, not bone but flesh should be supplied in place of the bone? It was because it was being signified that Christ would become weak for the sake of the Church, while the Church would become strong through him.

Thus, just as he did for the man, God gave the woman bodily sensation and the power of understanding, because he gave each of them an individual soul and willed them to possess the power of knowledge. Hence it follows:

“He created for them the knowledge of the spirit, filled their hearts with understanding, and showed them good and evil. He placed his eye upon their hearts, to show them the greatness of his works, so that they might praise the name of his holiness; and to glory in his wonders, so that they might declare the greatness of his works.”

What does “he showed them good and evil” mean except that he granted them the power to distinguish good and evil? He “placed his eye upon their hearts” when he willed the faculty of understanding—by which they would differ from the other animals—to excel in their souls. In this way they were given the capacity to know the greatness of his works, to praise the name of his holiness, and to glorify his works.

“He added discipline to them, and the law of life; he bequeathed to them an everlasting covenant. He established justice with them and showed them his judgments; their eyes saw the great things of his honor, their ears heard the honor of his voice, and he said to them: ‘Guard yourselves from every injustice,’ and he commanded each one concerning his neighbor.”

By “discipline” and “law” here understand either the natural law, which God gave to every human being so that through it he might be subject to his Creator and preserve within himself the dignity of good works, living prudently, justly, modestly, and temperately throughout his life in this world; or understand the written law, which he determined should be recorded for the correction of morals and the restoration of the ancient law that had been abolished. Both the natural law and the written law convey this: that we should love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, and preserve his commandments in divine worship and love of our neighbor.

“Their ways are before him; they are never hidden from his eyes.” The ways of human beings are their wills and actions, which certainly do not escape God’s knowledge, since all things are naked and open before his eyes. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain (Ps. XCIII).” Yet he especially knows the ways of those whose actions he approves. Conversely, he is said not to know those whose works he rejects. Hence it is written: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.”

“In every nation he appointed a ruler, and the portion of God, Israel, was made manifest; and all their works were like the sun in the presence of God, and his eyes continually looked upon their ways.”

The rulers whom God appointed over each nation may be understood either as the angels whom he assigned to guard the individual nations, in accordance with the passage in Deuteronomy: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God”; and Daniel records a prince of the Greeks, a prince of the Persians, and also Michael as the prince of God’s people (Dan. X). Or they may be understood as the holy teachers whom divine election sent throughout the world to preach his word. Hence in the Apocalypse John is commanded to write to the angel of Ephesus, the angel of Smyrna, the angel of Pergamum, and the angels of the other Churches (Apoc. I, II).

The portion of God, Israel, was made manifest—that is, the approved congregation of the saints, whose doctrines shine like the sun in the presence of God and whose actions are pleasing to God. “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers, because their eyes are fixed upon the Lord and the love of their hearts yearns for him (Ps. XXXIII).” In their person the Prophet speaks, saying: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare (Ps. XXIV).”

But because the iniquity of those who resist the word of God and oppose the truth cannot suppress or destroy the Gospel of Christ, but rather, when it prevails, they themselves fail, it is therefore added:

“The covenants are not hidden by their iniquity, and all their iniquities are in the sight of God.” The word of the Lord is not bound, but those who hate it will be handed over to the eternal bonds of punishment, for they are already bound by the chains of their crimes. Each person is constrained by the cords of his sins, and therefore the Lord condemns such people by a just judgment, because he sees that their ways are perverse. “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.”

“For the almsgiving of a man is like a seal with him, and he preserved a person’s grace like the apple of the eye.” Works of mercy will restore in heaven to those who perform them the reward that has been recorded for them, and they will most certainly preserve the grace of virtues in those who have acted well, in accordance with the judgment of Truth himself, who says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy (Matt. V).” And elsewhere: “Give alms,” he says, “and behold, all things are clean for you.”

“And afterward he will rise and grant them their recompense, each according to what is upon his head, and he will turn them toward the innermost parts of the earth.” The Lord will rise in judgment—that is, he prepares himself for recompense—and will repay each person according to his merit and according to the intention of his heart, in accordance with which he regulates his judgments. Hence it says, “he will turn it into the innermost parts of the earth,” that is, he judges the secret of the inner will. For a good will prepares the rewards of eternal blessedness, just as an evil will, by contrast, earns everlasting torments.

“But to those who repent he gave the way of righteousness, and he strengthened those who were failing to endure, and appointed for them the portion of truth.” It is good that, after sins have been committed, a person should turn through confession and repentance toward works of righteousness. The Lord blots out the sins that have been committed, strengthens weak steps upon the path of virtue, and enables the person, after worthy labors, to receive heavenly rewards in the portion of the elect.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning turning to the Lord and abandoning sins

“Turn to God and abandon your sins; pray before the face of God and lessen your offenses; return to the Lord and turn away from your injustice; hate the abomination exceedingly; and know righteousness and the judgments of God; stand in the lot of the purpose and prayer of the Most High God.”

After Wisdom had narrated the creation of the human being—how he was created in the image of God from the beginning and, by God’s judgment, was placed in honor above the other earthly creatures—it now likewise exhorts him, after the fall into sin, to turn again to his Maker and abandon the error by which he deceived himself through self-delusion; to beseech the Lord continually for his offenses; to flee with the entire intention of his soul to divine mercy; to despise idolatry and the deceit of diabolical servitude; and to learn the perfectly straight rule of God’s commandments, so that he may remain in the portion of holiness to which he was predestined and persevere in the praises of the Most High.

“Go into the portions of the holy age, with those who live and give confession to God.” The holy age is the rest of eternal life, which elsewhere is called the eternal age, the age of the age, or the ages of ages. It is therefore necessary for each person, while he lives and has strength, to prepare for himself a place of eternal blessedness by right belief and good works, because after the end of this life there is no time for action, so that each person may receive according to what he did previously, whether good or evil.

Hence the Lord himself admonished his hearers in the Gospel, saying: “Walk while you have the light of life, lest the darkness overtake you (John XII).” And again: “Watch,” he says, “praying at all times, that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man (Luke XXI).” Hence Paul also says: “Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all (Gal. VI).” Ecclesiastes likewise says: “In the good day enjoy good things, and beware of the evil day (Eccl. VII).”

## CHAPTER VII. That one must not delay in the company of the wicked

“Do not linger in the error of the wicked; confess before death. Confession from the dead is as good as nothing. You shall confess while living; while alive and in good health you shall confess, and you shall praise God and glory in his mercies.”

To linger in the error of the wicked is certain destruction for human beings, because after the end of the present life all the pomp of human glory will be counted as nothing. But the person who spends the time of the present life in divine praise and, as long as he lives, persists in the work of righteousness will afterward be happily rewarded and rejoice in eternal blessedness.

Hence Ecclesiastes, instructing us in his customary manner, admonishes us not to waste the leisure of the time granted to us, but to turn it to our advantage, saying: “There is no one who always lives, and who has confidence in this. Whatever your hand is able to do, perform it diligently, because neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom will exist in the underworld, where you are hastening (Eccl. IX).”

“How great is the mercy of God and his propitiation toward those who turn to him.” Only those who turn to his mercy with their whole heart know the sweetness of God’s mercy. Hence it is said through Jeremiah: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him (Lam. III).” The Psalmist likewise says: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you; you have perfected it for those who hope in you in the sight of the children of men (Ps. XXX).”

“For not everything can exist in everyone, since the son of man is not immortal, and they have been pleased in the vanity of wickedness.” Everything cannot exist in everyone; rather, according to God’s dispensation, each person has his own gift from God, as Paul says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (I Cor. XII).”

When he says, “since the son of man is not immortal, and they have been pleased in the vanity of wickedness,” he shows what a human being possesses through corrupted nature and what he possesses through divine grace. For after humanity corrupted the good of its nature by sinning through free choice, it displayed many signs of its perverse will through evil examples. Hence it is written: “The inclination of the human heart is prone to evil at every time from its youth (Gen. VIII).”

And in Genesis it is read: “But when God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was directed toward evil at every time, he repented that he had made the human being on the earth (Gen. VI).” And again: “When God,” he says, “saw that the earth was corrupt—for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth—he said to Noah: ‘The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them together with the earth (Gen. VI).’”

But after the one who created humanity willed to become incarnate among human beings, “and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” the evangelist John says of him: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John I).” John, the forerunner of the Lord, also held a corresponding opinion concerning him, saying: “He who is to come after me was made before me, because he was before me (ibid.).” And from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace, because the law was given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

“What is brighter than the sun? Yet even it will fail; or what is worse than what flesh and blood has devised? Yet even this will be reproved.” He shows that the entire structure of the world is temporal and transitory, and that even the bodily light that illumines the earth will not remain forever the same. How much more unstable and utterly destined to fall are the vain thoughts expressed by human frailty?

“He himself beholds the power of the height of heaven, and all human beings are earth and ashes.” By “heaven” he designates the heavenly creature, and by “human being” the earthly creature. He wishes to show by this that the heavenly and earthly creature are equally his work.

Mystically, however, God beholds the power of the height of heaven when, by testing, he numbers the perfection of the saints. He likewise knows human fragility when, in rejecting the sinner, he despises his life. Their works are compared with dust and ashes because, under the examination of the coming judgment, they will be utterly scattered and reduced to nothing.

### (CHAP. XVIII.)

“He who lives forever created all things together.” The substance of things was indeed created together, but it was not formed together according to its species; and what existed together in the substance of matter did not appear together in the form of its species.

When heaven and earth are described as having been made together, the spiritual and bodily things together, whatever arises from heaven together, and whatever is produced from the earth together, this is what is indicated. Yet God made this creation of matter before every day of this age, when “in the beginning he created heaven and earth.” Although the earth was then formless and empty and darkness was over the abyss, within the nature of the earth and of the abyss—that is, of the waters—these things nevertheless lay hidden, as it were, together in substance through a seminal principle. They were afterward to be brought forth through the work of the Creator, though not all at once.

“God alone will be justified, and he remains the unconquered King forever.” What does it mean that God alone is said to be justified, when the Scriptures often speak of righteous human beings who, living justly, earned the praise of righteousness? It means that he alone is just by nature, just as he alone is good; all others are just by grace.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “No living person will be justified in your sight (Ps. CXLII).” And in Job: “Can a human being be justified in comparison with God, or can one born of a woman appear clean? Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight; how much less a human being, who is decay, and a son of man, who is a worm (Job IV, XXV)!”

When the goodness or justice of an angel or human being is compared with the goodness and justice of God, it no longer appears to be goodness or justice, because it is immeasurably surpassed by the majesty of eternal goodness and justice. Hence Truth himself said in the Gospel to the one who called him “Good Teacher”: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone (Mark X),” since every good must be referred to him. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James I).”

He remains the unconquered King forever, because his power conquers and surpasses all things. No one can resist him, but all things are established according to his will. Therefore this investigator and contemplator of God’s wonders, astonished, adds:

“Who is sufficient to declare his works? For who has investigated his greatness? Who will proclaim the power of his greatness? And who will add to the declaration of his mercy?”

By saying “who is sufficient,” “who has investigated,” or “who has proclaimed,” he shows that no one by himself is capable of penetrating the depth of God’s counsel, or of knowing or declaring in every respect the greatness of his power. Each person knows only as much as God wishes to reveal to him or grants him the ability to express with his tongue.

Hence Truth himself says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him (Luke X).” We must understand this statement in such a way that both the Father and the Son are revealed to us through the Son, because he is the light of our mind. For the Father declares himself through his Word; and the Word declares not only what is declared through the Word, but also declares himself.

Let Eunomius be ashamed of boasting that he possesses as much knowledge of the Father and the Son as they possess of one another. What if he argues from this and consoles his madness? For it follows: “and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” It is one thing to know by equality of nature what he knew; it is another to know through the condescension of the one who reveals.

“Do not diminish, nor add: nor is it possible to discover the mighty works of God.” In meditating upon and reading the Holy Scriptures, therefore, we must be cautious: we must neither add anything to what has been written nor take anything away from what the authors of the divine Scriptures have included in their books. Rather, we must hold with the utmost reverence whatever is found there and strive with all our strength to fulfill what is commanded there. For John plainly says in his Apocalypse, which is the concluding book of the entire divine canon: “I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God will take away his portion from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book (last chapter).” I have said this also because of falsifiers, not because of those who simply say what they think, without mutilating the prophecy in any way or corrupting its catholic meaning.

From this it is clear that it is sufficient for us to investigate the Holy Scriptures insofar as, by contemplating their elements, we may know and understand what has been made; but we should not inquire into the causes and reasons why each thing was made in this particular way, or why it ought to have been made otherwise than it was. For example, if someone wished to ask why God speaks thus to Moses—“Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?”—and said, “Why were the blind, deaf, and mute created in this way?” and raised other questions of the same sort, we should take as testimony in this matter the seventeenth Psalm, where it is said to the Lord: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the perverse you will overthrow”;” and we should say that God is holy with the one who is holy, and that he is perverted in relation to the one who, by his own will, was already perverse.

“When a man has finished, then he will begin; and when he has rested, he will work.” For when a man has completed the commandments of God through devout action, then he shows that he already knows the mysteries of hidden things. And when he has made himself free from all worldly cares in order to fulfill the truth of God and the justice of his will, then he will begin to perform the work of God—that is, to preserve the rule of sound faith. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life (John VI).” When the crowds replied and asked him how they could perform the works of God, he said: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent (ibid.).” For he believes rightly who properly keeps the commandments of God; but whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar. He professes that he knows God, but by his deeds he denies it.

“What is man, or what is his grace? And what is good, or what is his evil?” After this investigator of the mighty works of God turned from contemplating the divine majesty to considering human substance, everything he found in it seemed small to him, because he found nothing in it unchangeable or destined to remain the same for long, but rather everything mutable and soon falling away. Hence he adds:

“The number of a man’s days is, at most, a hundred years; they are reckoned as a drop of sea-water. And, like a grain of sand, so are his few years in the day of eternity.” The brevity of human life is rightly compared with a drop of sea-water and a tiny grain of sand, because, in comparison with perpetual happiness, it contains excessive shortness and the greatest misery. Hence it is written in Job: “Man born of woman lives for a short time and is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and he flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same condition (Job XIII).” And again: “Man,” he says, “is born to labor, and the bird to flight. The life of man upon earth is a warfare, and his days are like the days of a hired laborer (Job V, VII).”

“For this reason God is patient with them and pours out his mercy upon them. He saw the presumption of their hearts, because it was evil, and he recognized their overthrow, because it was wicked. Therefore he completed his propitiation in them and showed them the way of equity.” What tolerates our frailty except the goodness of our Creator, who cherishes the unworthy, feeds the ungrateful, bears with the contemptuous, recalls those who have turned away, mercifully receives those who have turned back in repentance, and grants the most generous forgiveness of all sins? What, then, can we repay that great goodness with? Or what can we render to “the Lord for all that he has rendered to us,” except what the psalmist says: “I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord (Psalm CXV)”? Let us also say with thanksgiving, together with the same prophet: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and of his greatness there is no end; the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and very merciful. The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works. My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and unto ages of ages (Psalms XLVII, XCV, CXLIV).”

“The mercy of man is toward his neighbor, but the mercy of God is over all flesh. Whoever has mercy teaches and instructs, like a shepherd his flock.” Rarely is one found who perfectly offers the aid of mercy to his neighbor; but the Lord’s goodness overflows throughout the whole world, for he “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust.” And rightly so, because he himself is the Creator of all and the Lord of the universe. For the Lord’s flock is the catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world; it has one shepherd, because from two peoples he built for himself one sheepfold, so that the Lord’s flock might become one flock and one shepherd.

“He has mercy on the one who receives the teaching of mercy, and on the one who hastens in his judgments.” He exhorts those who receive the evangelical teaching in which grace is proclaimed to extend mercy themselves to their neighbors and to hasten to forestall the day of judgment by works of mercy. They should always exalt mercy above judgment, because judgment without mercy awaits the one who has not shown mercy. “Blessed, therefore, are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy (Matthew V).”

“My son, do not give rise to complaint in good things, and with every gift do not give the sorrow of an evil word.” He rightly teaches that we should not mingle reproachful words with good works, nor stain a good gift with perverse speech, because “evil conversations corrupt good morals (I Corinthians XV),” and insulting words make a good gift unwelcome. The apostle James says of the Lord himself: “He gives abundantly to all and does not reproach (James I).” Therefore it is fitting that we commend a good gift with good words: “Blessed is the man who does not sin with his tongue (James III).” Whoever does not offend in word is a perfect man.

Yet there are some who, as soon as their needy brothers ask them for what is necessary, and before they bestow their gifts, hurl insulting words at those whom they are about to assist. In material things they fulfill the ministry of compassion, but in words they lose the grace of humility. Thus it often seems that, after the insults, they are making satisfaction for the injury already inflicted. Their giving is hardly a great work, since by the very act of giving they scarcely conceal the excess of speech in which they have indulged. To such people this passage rightly says: “With every gift do not give the sorrow of an evil word”; and shortly afterward: “Behold, a word is better than a good gift, and both are with a justified man”—that is, a gift should be presented through compassion, and a good word should be offered through humility.

“Will not dew cool heat? So also a word is better than a gift.” Just as dew, cooling the crops, protects them from the heat of the sun, so a good word, adding grace to the gift of the giver, protects him from the wickedness of an angry tongue. Hence it is written elsewhere: “A harsh word stirs up quarrels, and a gentle word calms those that have been stirred up (Proverbs XV).”

“Behold, a word is better than a good gift, and both are with a justified man.” Often a word precedes a welcome gift, because a gracious tongue offers the greatest favor to a man. Hence Solomon says: “Deep waters are the words from a man’s mouth, and an overflowing stream, a fountain of wisdom (Proverbs XVIII).” And again: “Whoever moderates his words,” he says, “is learned and wise, and the man instructed in a precious spirit (Proverbs XVII).” But he gives both—that is, a suitable word and a fitting gift—who walks in the way of justice, because he strives to offer both appropriately to his neighbor. On the contrary, the wicked man does the things that follow.

“A fool will reproach sharply, and the gift of the undisciplined makes the eyes waste away.”

“In the mouth of a fool,” as it is read elsewhere, “there is a rod of reproach”; and therefore his gift is ungrateful, because he exasperates the mind of the recipient with malicious words. In the mystical sense, however, this sentence denotes heretics, who pollute whatever they utter under the appearance of virtue by perverse speech, raising foolish questions, disputes, and battles over the Law. Therefore the Apostle commands us to avoid them, knowing that such people have been subverted: “Their word spreads like a cancer, and their whole teaching, which greatly advances impiety, is truly full of deceit and falsehood, and is reproachful (II Timothy II).” Hence it says: “The reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me (Psalm LXIV),” though their end is destruction and a storm of darkness, reserved for them forever. Therefore Wisdom admonishes her hearers to take thought for themselves in the future and to consider beforehand how they may escape the punishment of vengeance and find mercy before the eyes of God.

“Before judgment, prepare justice for yourself; and before you speak, learn; before illness, apply medicine; and before judgment, examine yourself, and in the sight of God you will find propitiation. Before illness, humble yourself, and in the time of weakness show your conduct.” All these things have been said for the caution of the faithful, so that they may always be prepared and never flatter themselves with a destructive security, but strive with every effort to labor in the service of God until the end of their lives—before the time of judgment and that day on which each person must render an account to God for himself.

He learns and prepares justice for himself who daily investigates what in his conduct and actions pleases God and what displeases him. He therefore strives through tears of remorse and bodily discipline to cleanse himself from sins, so that on the day of vengeance he will not need to undergo eternal torments again on account of the pollution of his sins. He calls that hour “illness” and that time “weakness,” when just recompense is paid to each person for his own deeds. No one is then permitted to work; rather, each person is allowed to receive the reward of his works.

The prophet Zephaniah shows what this day will be like, saying: “The great day of the Lord is near, very near and swift: the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the strong man will be troubled there. It is a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and alarm against fortified cities and high battlements. I will trouble men, and they shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord; their blood shall be poured out like earth, and their bodies like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath; in the fire of his zeal the whole earth shall be devoured, because he will make a complete end, and that swiftly, of all the inhabitants of the earth (Zephaniah I).”

## CHAPTER VIII. That we should not be hindered from praying to the Lord continually, according to the Apostle: “Pray without ceasing.”

“Do not be hindered from praying always, and do not fear being justified unto death, because God’s reward remains forever.” This is the apostolic exhortation, which says: “Pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning all of you (II Thessalonians II).” The same Apostle elsewhere discusses marriage: how the unmarried woman considers the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit, and how the married woman considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband. He then adds: “Moreover, I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what may enable you to entreat the Lord without impediment (I Corinthians VII).”

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Watch, therefore, praying at all times, that you may be worthy to escape all these things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man; for, he says, God’s reward remains forever (Luke XXI).” Wise reader, observe that he says that God’s reward remains forever. And know that heretics vainly suppose that the punishments of sinners are not eternal. According to the evangelical saying, therefore: “The wicked shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew XXV),” and the recompense of both orders remains perpetually.

“Before prayer, prepare your soul, and do not be like a man who tempts God.” Concerning this he warned his disciples beforehand in the Gospel, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins (Mark XI).” That man appears to tempt God who prays in the manner he has been taught, yet does not do what he was commanded. His prayer is fruitless, because only those are heard by him who raise their prayers to God with right faith and good works.

“Remember wrath on the day of consummation, and the time of recompense at the turning away of the face.” “Remember wrath,” he says—that is, the vengeance reserved for sinners on the day of universal judgment and at the resurrection of all, when immortal bodies rise again and each person receives such recompense as the just Judge restores to him. For the Lord is just and loves justice; his face has seen equity, and he will repay each person according to his works.

“Remember poverty in a time of abundance, and the necessity of poverty in the day of riches.” It is a most salutary teaching that, during the time of this life, when it is permitted to work, we should devote ourselves to almsgiving and deeds of mercy, and not waste the leisure granted to us, “because the time will come when it is no longer permitted to work.” This is the time he calls poverty and the day of necessity. Hence the Savior taught his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Walk while you have the light, lest perhaps the darkness overtake you (John XII).” And again: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

“From morning until evening the time will be changed, and all these things are swift in the eyes of the Lord.”

By “morning” he means the dawn of birth, and by “evening,” old age. “The time will be changed”—the age of man—because he is “filled with many miseries, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same condition (Job XIV).” Or alternatively: from morning, that is, from the beginning of the world’s creation, until the evening of the age, times will always change. Spring, summer, autumn, and winter, day and night, never cease; yet, compared with the state of eternity, all these things seem to pass swiftly, and nothing among corporeal things remains perpetual. Everything passes before the eyes of the Lord and is closed by a definite end. He alone always remains the same, and his years do not fail.

“A wise man fears in all things, and in the days of offenses he will guard against idleness.” “A wise man,” he says, “fears in all things,” because the blessed man is always fearful. For he is truly wise who always has the fear of God before the eyes of his heart, so that, insofar as possible, he avoids all sins, flees forgetfulness of God’s commandments, and strives to fulfill them in action, since the prophet testifies: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; there is good understanding for all who practice it (Proverbs IX).” For the thoughts of the strong man will always be in abundance, while every slothful person will always be in poverty.

“Every prudent man recognizes wisdom, and gives praise to the one who finds it.” The prudent man—that is, the diligent and attentive student of the law of God—recognizes that Christ is the wisdom of God. After he has found him and received knowledge of him with a believing heart, he will give him the confession of right preaching and the devotion of worthy action.

## [Col. 0887A]

“Those who are sensible in words have themselves acted wisely, and they have understood truth and justice, and have invoked proverbs and judgments.” Just as he previously said that the prudent recognize wisdom, so now he shows that those who are sensible in good words prove the wisdom of understanding by their actions. The sensible in words are the holy teachers, who not only understand the truth and justice of God’s commandments, but also produce sayings of instruction for the benefit of their hearers and never cease to set before them the example of good works for imitation.

## CHAPTER IX. On the restraint of the soul: that one should not follow the desires of the heart, that is, should not yield to vain thoughts, but should resist them with God’s help.

“Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your pleasure; if you grant your soul its desire, it will make you a cause of joy to your enemies.” Holy Scripture shows that every carnal desire is harmful. Hence it says in the Law: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him (Exodus XX).” And elsewhere it is written: “Desire turned away their hearts (Daniel XIII).” Concerning this Paul says: “For the love of money is the root of all evils; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains (I Timothy VI).”

Hence John also says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever (I John II).”

For whoever devotes himself to pleasures must fear that he may fall into the prophetic saying: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their desires (Psalm XIII).” And elsewhere: “Pleasure bears punishment, and necessity brings forth a crown.” For whoever grants his soul its desire will cause it to fall into the joy of wicked enemies—that is, evil spirits, who always desire our destruction. Hence the chief of the Apostles says: “The Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment (II Peter II),” especially those who walk after the flesh in the desire of impurity.

And because desire consists not only in lust and the pursuit of pleasures, but also in the ambition for precedence and the love of popular approval, where sin is difficult to avoid, it therefore continues:

“Do not delight in crowds, nor take pleasure in small matters; for their transgression is continual.” Whoever is not cautious in frequenting crowds and mingles with popular society is often compelled, whether in speech, laughter, or some vanity, to transgress the commandments of God. Yet while living among a crowd, he does not regard this as a serious fault, although Scripture says: “For every idle word that men have spoken, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment (Matthew XII).” And elsewhere: “Laughter,” he says, “will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning will seize the end of joy (Proverbs XIV).”

Hence our Lord, who came into this world to save sinners and to draw all things to himself (Matthew IX), is said to flee into a deserted place, to pray alone on the mountain, and to rest in a boat (Luke V), so that he might show us that solitude is sometimes beneficial for renewing the vigilance of our hearts. This was not because anyone could have harmed him or polluted him with any crime—for he is known to be free from all sin—but so that he might give us an example of how we can avoid the dangers of human life.

## CHAPTER X. That the drunkard will not become rich, and that by despising small things one gradually falls; and that women and wine cause men to apostatize from God.

“Do not be paltry in a dispute over a loan, when you have nothing at all in your purse; for you will be an enemy to your own soul.” This sentence urges us to works of mercy, so that we may not be sluggish in providing earthly benefits to our neighbors, since we will not thereby lack temporal support. Rather, if we neglect to do this, we will not realize that we are preparing future goods for our souls. Temporal almsgiving will be rewarded with an everlasting recompense.

**(Chapter XIX.)** “A drunken laborer will not become rich, and he who despises small things will gradually fall.” This sentence refers back to what was said above: “Do not delight in crowds, nor take pleasure in small matters, for their transgression is continual.” Thus, among the crowd, because of its most wicked customs, the vice of drunkenness is not thought to be a serious crime, although every disgraceful act is attached to its punishment, as will be demonstrated in what follows, where the evils that succeed drunkenness are clearly shown.

Although excessive drinking may seem a small crime to gluttonous people, they eventually discover that it is extremely harmful through the loss and destruction of good things and the multiplication of crimes—something they previously despised and regarded as insignificant. For it follows:

“Wine and women make wise men apostatize and bring the sensible to shame; whoever joins himself to prostitutes will be wickedness and corruption, worms will inherit him, he will be set up as a greater example, and his soul will be taken from the number.”

“Wine,” he says, “and women make wise men apostatize, and they rebuke the sensible.” It is as though he were saying that drunkenness and fornication make those who think themselves wise through acuteness of intellect and subtlety of understanding hostile and alien to true wisdom, and show them to be blameworthy, because, despite the outstanding gift of wisdom, they have fallen into the greatest folly.

Because they joined themselves to prostitutes, corruption and worms—the punishments to come—will follow them. By leaving an evil example to posterity, they will be taken away from the number of the saints and will not deserve to be counted among their fellowship. Solomon experienced this well: after receiving from God abundant wisdom, like a river, he forsook the God of his fathers and became attached to foreign women. Shamefully held by his love for them, he built profane shrines and various idols for them. Thus he lost the greatest glory of praise and deserved to be counted not among the elect but among apostates (III Kings XI).

This is said according to the historical sense. According to the allegorical sense, however, the wine is that of the heretics, concerning which it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Their grape is the grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness (Deuteronomy XXXII).” Their wine is the fury of dragons and the incurable venom of asps; their fornication is most wicked, by which, abandoning the truth of the faith, they have joined themselves to demons. They have turned to empty speech and, speaking in hypocrisy, utter falsehood. “Claiming to be wise, they became fools.” Their torment is like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a man, and “their worm does not die, nor is the fire extinguished (Proverbs I).” Thus, having become notorious and abominable to all, they are uprooted from the land of the Church and separated forever from the fellowship of the saints.

“Whoever believes quickly is light of heart and will be diminished, and whoever sins against his own soul will be held in contempt.” We must see to it that this sentence is not contrary to the apostolic saying concerning love: “It believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; love never fails (I Corinthians XIII).” There the perfection of good will is described, always ready for every good work; here, however, the lightness of spirit is described, which is always changeable and has no firm state.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “A fool changes like the moon.” Whoever, therefore, is easily overthrown and, having itching ears, turns his hearing away from the truth and turns instead to fables will be diminished in understanding and virtue; and, by sinning against his own soul, he will be counted among fools.

“Whoever rejoices in iniquity will be marked, and whoever hates correction will have his life diminished.” He rejoices in iniquity who does not possess that love of which it is written: “It does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth (ibid.).” He will also be marked, because through his wicked conduct he will be shown to be greatly blameworthy. Since he hates correction and does not wish to turn toward what is better, his life is diminished, because he will lack eternal rest.

“Whoever hates talkativeness extinguishes malice.” Talkativeness is a serious vice, as Scripture says: “In much speaking you will not escape sin, and the talkative man will not be directed upon the earth (Proverbs X).” Hence the apostle James also says: “The tongue is indeed a small member, yet it boasts great things. Behold, how great a fire, how great a forest it sets ablaze! And the tongue is a fire, the whole world of iniquity. The tongue is placed among our members; it defiles the whole body and sets on fire the wheel of our birth, being set on fire by Gehenna (James III).” Whoever restrains himself from much speaking extinguishes the malice of pride and iniquity.

“Whoever sins against his own soul will repent, and whoever takes pleasure in wickedness will be marked.” This sentence needs no exposition, because it is evident that whoever pollutes his soul with evil works will repent in the future, when every sin is punished by the just judgment of God. Whoever takes pleasure in wickedness will be marked, because those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst deeds will be condemned by the judgment of the most just Judge, who says to them: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, into the eternal fire, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Psalm VI).”

“Do not repeat an evil and harsh word, and you will not be diminished.” To repeat an evil word is to commit again, after weeping, what will once more require weeping. He repeats an evil word, and strives to defend it, who repeats by the worst deed what he conceived with a malicious mind and spoke wickedly. His diminution is certain, because after the perverse act no correction of him appears.

Thus Cain, after becoming angry against his brother and contemplating killing him, was rebuked by the voice of the Lord. But because he refused to correct himself and fulfilled by deed the malicious word he had conceived in thought, he received a just vengeance from the Lord, who repaid him according to the enormity of his crime (Genesis IV).

## CHAPTER XI. Wisdom advises that one should not hastily disclose a secret, whether to a friend or an enemy.

“Do not tell your thoughts to friend or enemy; and if you have a fault, do not uncover it. For he will hear you and watch you, and, as though defending the sin, will hate you; and so it will cling to you always.” He teaches us to exercise caution and discernment in everything, so that we do not disclose our secrets equally to friend and enemy, to catholic and heretic. For an enemy with a perverse design, although he may sometimes flatter us outwardly through hypocrisy, always prepares deceit and a snare for us in secret.

“You have heard a word against your neighbor? Let it die with you, trusting that it will not burst you apart. At the face of a word, the foolish man gives birth, like the groaning of a woman in labor.” The sensible and the foolish do not receive a spoken word in the same way. A harsh word will scarcely disturb the mind of the wise, but it completely unsettles the understanding of the fool, so that he expresses a groan of pain through a wicked act. Hence it is written: “Whatever happens, it does not disturb the just man; but he who is of a perverse heart will not find good (Proverbs XVII).”

Yet the one who trusts in the firmness of his heart must beware of retaining the memory of a harsh word in his heart for too long, because, once it has found an entrance, the serpent’s suggestion will not cease to pour in the venom of wickedness, and it quickly corrupts the mind it has invaded.

“An arrow fixed in the thigh of a dog [Vulgate: flesh], so is a word in the heart of a fool.” The dog sometimes has a positive meaning and sometimes a negative one. Its positive meaning appears in the Psalter: “They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city (Psalm LVIII).” This signifies teachers from among the Jews who, hungering for the justice of God’s law after the evening of Christ’s Passion, go around the city of the Church with diligent care and defend it by the barking of their preaching.

Hence we read in the Gospel that dogs licked the sores of Lazarus the beggar (Luke XVI). The dog has a negative meaning when it expresses the filth of sinners, as in the saying: “As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly (Proverbs XXVI).” An arrow is fixed in the thigh of a dog when evil desire, arising from diabolical suggestion, is fixed in the heart of a sinner. He is rightly called a fool, because he is dragged like an ox to the sacrifice and neither foresees nor guards against the ruin of eternal destruction.

“Correct your friend, lest perhaps he has not understood and says, ‘I did not do it’; or, if he did it, lest he do it again. Correct your neighbor, lest perhaps he has not spoken; and if he has spoken, lest perhaps he repeat it.” This is a very salutary and discerning teaching: that we should correct our erring friends with all patience, because sometimes one sins through ignorance, sometimes through negligence, and sometimes through contempt and disobedience. But if discipline is applied to such people with moderation, it generates shame and repentance in them concerning past evils, and it produces diligence and caution concerning the future.

Hence Paul admonishes his hearers, saying: “Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians VI).”

“Correct your friend, for an offense often occurs; and do not believe every word. There is one who slips in his speech, but not from the heart. For who is there who has not sinned with his tongue?” There is a great difference between one who sins through simplicity or ignorance and one who sins through malice. It can happen that someone gives offense by an evil word without suspecting that the word is evil—for example, through the ordinary and idle speech that proceeds not from deceit but from lightness of spirit. Such a word, although it is not free from fault, is nevertheless not equal in guilt to the word of one who is full of wickedness and deceit.

“For who is there who has not sinned with his tongue?” There is no person upon earth who does good and does not sin. But concerning those of whom it is written, “They acted deceitfully with their tongues; the venom of asps is under their lips, and their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness (Psalm XIII),” if they do not turn back and perform worthy repentance for their sins, the sentence of death will remain upon them. For destruction and misery are in their ways; they have not known the way of peace, nor have they had the fear of God before their eyes. Therefore, in the blindness of their hearts and in their iniquities, they will perish.

## CHAPTER XII. Wisdom advises that one should correct one’s neighbor before issuing a threat, according to the preaching of the Gospel.

“Correct your neighbor before you threaten him; and give place to the fear of the Most High, because all wisdom is the fear of God, and in wisdom there is fear of God.” This is what he already taught above: that patience and gentleness should have greater force in correcting the brothers than anger and harshness, because in this way room is given for fear of the Most High and for conversion from sins. For all wisdom is the fear of God, and in it a man learns nothing except to fear and honor God. Hence it continues:

“In all wisdom there is the ordering of the law; the discipline of wickedness is not wisdom, nor is the thought of sinners prudence.” The law of the Lord is divine wisdom, arranged and ordered; there is nothing wicked in it, nor any meditation upon sins, but it is wholly sincere and wholly filled with truth and justice. Hence it is written: “Your justice is justice forever, and your law is truth.” Apostolic teaching proclaims this, and the catholic Church throughout the world holds it. Concerning the teaching opposed to this—that is, the teaching of heretics—it is subsequently said:

“There is wickedness, and in it is execration.” The wickedness of heretics is execrable to all good and just people, and every Christian religion detests it. “For their word spreads like a cancer and greatly advances impiety.” Their fellowship is destructive, because, according to Solomon, “they have abandoned the guide of their youth and have forgotten the covenant of their God. For their house has been bent toward death, and their paths toward the underworld. All who enter to them will not return, nor will they grasp the paths of life (Proverbs II).”

“‘There is one who is foolish, being diminished in wisdom.’ This sentence seems to some to refer back to what precedes—namely, to the detestable wickedness of heretics, whose mind, in proportion as it has been taken captive by error, departs from the truth. But since the following passage seems to discuss not heretics but simple people who are less well instructed in knowledge of the Scriptures, it may not inappropriately be said of such people that ‘there is one who is diminished in wisdom’: that is, he lacks understanding of the mysteries of God insofar as doctrine is concerned. Nevertheless, he is not entirely removed from keeping God’s commandments. Therefore it continues:

“‘Better is the person who is diminished in wisdom and deficient in understanding, yet in the fear of God, than one who abounds in understanding and transgresses the law of the Most High.’” There is therefore a great difference between one who possesses knowledge of God’s law through learning but does not keep it in practice, and one who, although he does not possess profound understanding, nevertheless lives rightly in the fear of God, insofar as he knows and is able. Of the former it is said: “‘The servant who knows the will of his lord and does not do it will be beaten with many blows’ (Luke 12).” Of the latter, however: “‘The one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few blows’ (Wisdom 6).” Of the former it is written: “‘Those in positions of authority will suffer more severe punishments’ (ibid.).” Of the latter it is likewise said: “‘To the one of little understanding mercy will be granted.’” Of this matter the apostle James also says: “‘If anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he will be compared to a man who considers the appearance of his face in a mirror. For he considered himself and went away, and immediately forgot what he was like. But the one who has looked closely into the perfect law of freedom and has continued in it—not becoming a forgetful hearer but a doer of the work—this person will be blessed in his action’ (James 1).”

“‘There is a certain skill, and it is itself wicked; and there is one who utters a reliable word, declaring the truth.’” Here he begins to explain the difference between the faithful who walk according to the truth and hypocrites who do everything deceitfully, and to set forth the reason for it. “‘There is,’ he says, ‘a certain skill, and it is itself wicked’”—that is, the cunning of heretics, equipped with dialectical art, which acts deceitfully in everything, constantly schemes evil with a perverse heart, and at all times sows quarrels. “‘And there is one who utters a reliable word’”—that is, the vigor of holy teachers, who rightly preach the word of the Gospel and teach the truth of the faith. By teaching and acting, this vigor shows its followers the rule of justice; whereas the other never ceases, through the deceitfulness of its craft, to lead astray and deceive as many as it can. The one proceeds along the straight road; the other along the deviations of error. The one tends toward true life; the other toward eternal destruction.

“‘There is one who wickedly humbles himself, while his inward parts are full of deceit; and there is one who submits himself excessively through great humility.’” Concerning those who falsely humble themselves and are inwardly full of deceit, the Truth itself warned how they must be avoided, saying: “‘Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.’ Therefore, ‘you will know them by their fruits’ (Matthew 7).” Concerning those who truly wish to become humble, he commanded that they take an example from himself, saying: “‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matthew 11).” If, then, we wish to be disciples of the Truth, we must first draw the good of true humility from the root of the heart, and thus prepare outwardly, through it, examples of good works. What false humility accomplishes, however, the following sentence shows.

“‘There is one who lowers his face and pretends not to see what is unknown; and if he is prevented from sinning by weakness of strength, yet, if he finds an opportunity to do evil, he will do evil.’” Thus heretics, and thus all hypocrites, although they outwardly feign the appearance of virtues in dress and bearing, nevertheless, because they do not inwardly possess the virtue itself, cannot remain firmly in what they assume for a time. As soon as they find an opportunity to sin, they reveal openly what they had previously concealed under a veil by displaying it publicly. The following sentence also confirms this:

“‘A man is recognized by his appearance, and a sensible person is recognized by the encounter with his face. The clothing of the body, the laughter of the teeth, and a person’s manner of walking declare what he is.’” For the inner disposition of the mind is often detected through outward signs, and the quality of the will is shown through bodily gestures. Hence there is that Gospel saying: “‘There is no good tree that produces bad fruit, nor a bad tree producing good fruit. For each tree is known by its fruit’ (Luke 6).” And again: “‘The good person,’ he says, ‘brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’ (ibid.).” Thus the Apostle also expressed the signs of evil and good wills, saying: “‘Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control,’” and so forth. Thus the good fruits of good trees and the bad fruits of bad trees are revealed, because good works become manifest, and things that are otherwise cannot be hidden.

[Col. 0894B] “‘There is a false reprimand in the anger of an abusive person, and there is a judgment that is not proved to be good.’” Up to this point he maintains the line of thought he had previously followed, discussing the false humility of hypocrites and heretics: their reprimand is a deceitful teaching, and their judgment is false. For just as they err in faith and religion, so they stumble in the quality of their judgments; nor can a judgment be good when it is not carried out with a good disposition.

## CHAPTER XIII. That it is good to correct by speaking rather than, through anger, to harbor deceit in silence.

(CAP. XX.) “‘How good it is to correct rather than to become angry, and not to prevent one who confesses in prayer!’” It is therefore good to do everything with circumspection and patience, because the anger of a man does not accomplish the justice of God, and a person’s instruction is discerned through patience. Thus he also warned earlier: “‘Correct your neighbor before you threaten him, and give place to the fear of the Most High, lest through the agitation of anger he lose the fruit of correction in his neighbor’ (Ecclesiasticus 19),” and “‘do not prevent,’ he says, ‘one who confesses in prayer.’” One who confesses to God in his prayer and praises him with his mouth is not to be hindered, but instructed, so that he may bring into harmony right faith and good works, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, but “‘with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’” Therefore the Prophet says: “‘Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name’ (Psalm 110).” And elsewhere: “‘Let the lifting up of my hands,’ he says, ‘be an evening sacrifice’ (Psalm 140).”

“‘The desire of a eunuch deflowers a young girl; so does one who carries out an unjust judgment by force.’” He proves by an example what he had stated above in words: that it is good not to become angry. For just as the desire of a eunuch indeed defiles a virgin but does not produce offspring, so unjust violence indeed imitates a judgment but does not preserve the measure of equity.

“‘How good it is, when corrected, to manifest repentance; for thus you will escape voluntary sin.’” Just as previously he forbade anger to prevail in judgment, so now he praises the repentance of the disciple that follows the correction of the teacher. In this way sin is restrained by desire, and pardon for the offense is obtained. Hence in the Gospel the Savior instructed Peter, saying: “‘If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone; but if he repents, you have gained your brother,’” and so forth (Matthew 18). Hence Solomon also says in Proverbs: “‘Whoever rejects discipline despises his own soul; but whoever accepts reproof possesses a heart’ (Proverbs 15).”

“‘There is one who keeps silent and is found wise, and there is one who is hateful because he is forward in speaking.’” In this sentence the modesty of the good person is praised, and the rashness of the proud is censured; or, rather, the religious devotion and prudence of the good Catholic are commended, while the foolishness and forwardness of the heretic are condemned and detested. For just as the former displays his wisdom through excessive silence, so the latter reveals his foolishness through excessive talk. But since silence sometimes proceeds from good and sometimes from evil, it is added:

“‘There is also one who keeps silent because he lacks the sense to speak, and there is one who keeps silent because he knows the appropriate time.’” There are many who keep silent because they lack the ability and skill to speak. There are others who are silent not through ignorance but through knowledge, observing the proper hour for speaking, because “‘there is a time for keeping silent and a time for speaking,’” and not every time is equally suitable for everything. Hence it follows:

“‘A wise person will keep silent until the proper time.’” The tongue must therefore be restrained discreetly, not bound insolubly, so that, when it recognizes the opportune moment, it may set aside the discipline of silence and, by speaking what is fitting, devote itself to the service of usefulness.

“‘But the wanton and imprudent will not observe the proper time.’” It is always the practice of the prudent to moderate their speech and observe the suitable time; it is the practice of fools to observe neither place, time, nor measure, but shamelessly to pour out their whole spirit. Heretics and schismatics do this very often. Hence the Apostle teaches Timothy how to instruct his hearers, “‘so that they may not attend to myths and endless genealogies, which produce questions rather than the building up of God, which is in faith. But the goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith. Some, having wandered from these things, have turned aside to empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions’ (1 Timothy 1).” Wisdom still rebukes their foolishness, saying:

“‘The one who uses many words injures his own soul; and the one who unjustly assumes authority will be hated.’” Heretics use many words when, through human eloquence, they strive to conceal their wickedness. They unjustly usurp authority because, by holding opinions contrary to the truth, they improperly claim the dignity of teaching. Therefore they will be hateful, since they become shameful and detestable both before God and before human beings; their doctrine and their entire endeavor turn to their own detriment. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0896A] “‘There is success in evils for an undisciplined person, and there is an invention that results in harm.’” For labor and sorrow are under their tongue; they sit in secret places to kill the innocent. Therefore the whole contrivance of their deceitful invention will be reckoned to them as everlasting disgrace. Their table will indeed become a snare before them, and a retribution and a stumbling block.

“‘There is a gift that is not useful, and there is a gift whose recompense is double.’” A gift that is not useful is one given when a person spends alms for human favor. There is also a gift whose recompense is double, when a person gives alms for the love of God and from desire for eternal life. To such a person the honor of merits is granted here, and eternal glory will follow in the future reward. [Col. 0896B] Hence the Truth itself says in the Gospel: “‘There is no one who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or children, or fields for my sake and for the sake of the Gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now, in this present time, along with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life’ (Luke 18).” The meaning of this sentence is as follows: Whoever has abandoned earthly things for the sake of Christ’s Gospel will receive spiritual goods, which, in comparison and according to their worth, will be as though a hundredfold number were compared with a small one. For from brothers and companions in his chosen way, who are joined to him by a spiritual bond, he will receive much more gracious love even in this life, and in the future eternal rewards.

“‘There is one who is diminished for the sake of glory, and there is one who has lifted up his head through humility.’” This passage seems to be explained by the Gospel testimony where it is said: “‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted’ (Luke 14; 18).” A person is therefore diminished for the sake of glory when, because of the exaltation of his heart, the merit of virtue decreases in him; and he has lifted up his head through humility when, after the present abasement, his soul is raised to eternal glory.

“‘There is one who redeems many things at a small price, and restores them sevenfold.’” He redeems many things at a small price who, through a confession of humility, merits release from every offense; and “‘he restores them sevenfold’” when, in place of vices, he inserts an abundant number of virtues. For, as the Apostle says, “‘where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more, so that, just as sin reigned in death, so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans 5).”

“‘The wise person makes himself lovable in speech, but the favors of fools will be poured out.’” The wise person in speech is the Catholic teacher, who makes himself lovable in his teaching when he does not neglect to follow the truth in the divine Testaments. But the favors of fools—that is, the doctrines of heretics—will be poured out and will be suited to no good use. Concerning this it is further added:

“‘The gift of a foolish person will not be useful to you, for his eyes are sevenfold.’” The gift of a foolish person will not be useful because the doctrine of heretics is salutary to no one. His eyes are sevenfold because the intention of his will is stained by various wickednesses, being always ready to inflict harm. The number seven, which, because of the divine gifts that the prophet Isaiah enumerates as belonging to the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11), is consecrated to perfection, sometimes conversely signifies the fullness of wickedness. Thus in the Gospel the Savior spoke of an unclean spirit that had temporarily left a person: “‘When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it wanders through waterless places, seeking rest; and not finding it, it says, “I will return to my house from which I came.” And when it comes, it finds it swept clean; then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the final condition of that person is worse than the first’ (Luke 5).”

[Col. 0897B] “‘He will give little and reproach much, and the opening of his mouth is inflammation.’” The heretic will give little—that is, he rarely displays signs of truth throughout his doctrine—and he will reproach much, because in his excessive speech he pours forth many reproaches arising from error. The opening of his mouth is inflammation because his speech kindles the wickedness of error in his sinful hearers.

“‘Today someone lends at interest, and tomorrow he demands repayment; such a person is hateful.’” This sentence may signify the instability of heretics, who violently extort the assent of their hearers to their error. Hence they will be hateful both before God and before human beings. Or, in a deeper sense, it suggests that the person who gives alms to the poor and seeks repayment in the present life makes himself hateful in the sight of the divine majesty. The Truth itself clearly teaches in the Gospel why almsgiving should be performed, saying: “‘When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing’ (Luke 6).” And again: “‘Do not,’ he says, ‘store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither break in nor steal’ (Luke 14).” Elsewhere the same Lord said to a certain leader of the Pharisees: “‘When you prepare a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends, or brothers, or relatives, or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and repayment be made to you. But when you prepare a banquet, invite the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you (Luke 14)’”—but you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous.

“‘A fool will have no friend, and there will be no gratitude for his good deeds.’” A fool is both the person who seeks the reward of spiritual labor in this life rather than in the future, and the heretic who desires human praise and neglects to seek the glory that comes from God alone. Such people will therefore have no true friend, because their foolishness does not know how to have a true friend—one who is a friend according to God. Therefore their labor will receive no reward in the heavenly kingdom, because they sought above all the pleasures of transitory life.

“‘For those who eat his bread are tongues of falsehood.’” Those who share in the doctrine of heretics become liars in faith and knowledge. Therefore, through their error, they will be marked out before everyone, as the following sentence proves.

“‘How often and by how many will he be mocked? For he has not distributed what ought to be possessed with a straightforward understanding, nor likewise what ought not to be possessed.’” The assembly of heretics is therefore detestable because it does not interpret the divine canon, and the sacraments contained in it, with a straightforward understanding; nor does it present the exposition of its treatises—which is necessary to no one—with a Catholic understanding. For this reason both their preaching and their fellowship must altogether be avoided.

“‘The slip of a false tongue is like that of one falling on a pavement; so the fall of the wicked will come swiftly.’” Just as someone falls needlessly on a level pavement where there are no obstacles, so the understanding of heretics, blinded by its own wickedness, stumbles and falls for no reason on the path of truth, which is brighter than the sun. What brings about their ruin, the continuous discourse openly indicates.

“‘An ungrateful person is like *acharis*.’” Since the heretic is ungrateful, he has chosen, by the guile of the excellent intellect that he received as a divine gift, rather to devise his own error than to preserve the divine tradition in Sacred Scripture. Therefore, by straying without the grace of the Holy Spirit, he continually shows himself to his hearers to be bitter and harmful. *Acharis* means “bitter” or “without grace”; and rightly is he called bitter who has not deserved to be filled with divine grace.

[Col. 0898C] “‘An empty tale will continually be in the mouth of the undisciplined.’” The doctrine of heretics, which they chatter with their wicked mouths, is rightly called a tale because it follows vanity in every way.
