Hence the Apostle, rejecting such teaching, writes to Timothy: “‘As I urged you to remain in Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might charge certain people not to teach differently, nor to attend to myths and endless genealogies, which produce questions rather than the building up of God, which is in faith’ (1 Timothy 1).” And again: “‘Avoid,’ he says, ‘profane and old-womanish myths; train yourself in godliness. For bodily training is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for everything, possessing the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come’ (1 Timothy 4).” Since the speech of the perverse is reprehensible on every side, it is further added:

“‘From the mouth of a fool a proverb will be rejected, for he does not speak it at the proper time.’” The Jew is therefore a fool who teaches that the ceremonies of the law are necessary in the time of grace—circumcision, new moons, Sabbaths, and animal sacrifices—and who, interpreting these allegorically according to his own understanding, asserts that they must be retained, “‘since Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.’” The philosopher is also a fool who thinks he can comprehend everything by human reasoning, and who turns his teaching, through disputation, according to the elements of the world rather than according to the truth that is in Christ Jesus. The heretic too is a fool, who attempts by false arguments and sophistical expressions to destroy the teaching of the Gospel and the truth of the Catholic faith. The proverb of all such people will therefore be rejected—that is, their false argumentation, by which, while the truth shines everywhere through Christ, they wish to introduce into the Church the shadow of the old law and false fabrications.

“‘There is one who is prevented from sinning by poverty, and in his rest he will be goaded.’” Above he censured the falsity of heretical doctrine; now he similarly condemns the intention of the perverse will. There are people who, although at times they cannot carry out sin in deed because of some circumstance, nevertheless never wish to rest from an evil desire. They are little helped by being held captive outwardly through cunning and deceit.

[Col. 0899B] “‘There is one who loses his soul because of shame, and he will lose it because of an imprudent person; but through respect of persons he will destroy himself.’” He loses his soul because of shame who, fearing the transitory power of this world, does not dare to profess the truth of the Gospel. For the Lord himself plainly says: “‘Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his majesty.’” And again: “‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna’ (Luke 9).”

## CHAPTER XIV. He speaks of a common matter, because there are many who, out of shame, make promises to a friend and gratuitously make him an enemy by their lips.

“‘There is one who, out of shame, makes a promise to a friend, and has gained him as an enemy for nothing.’” There is a certain class of people who make a habit of promising others many things, but, because of their stinginess, customarily deliver few of them. Thus, by lying in their promises, they have gratuitously gained as enemies those whom they could have had as friends by making no promises.

“‘For a wicked reproach is falsehood in a person, and it will continually be in the mouth of the undisciplined.’” Falsehood is not a small vice but is numbered among the chief vices. Hence it is written in the Decalogue of the law: “‘You shall not bear false witness’ (Exodus 20).” And elsewhere: “‘The mouth that lies,’ he says, ‘kills the soul’ (Deuteronomy 5).” Its persistence is also exceedingly blameworthy and harmful. Hence it follows:

“‘A thief is better than the persistence of a lying person, but both will inherit destruction.’” He does not excuse the thief as though he were without sin, but by comparison with him he aggravates the persistence of lying. Thus in the prophet Ezekiel, when Jerusalem’s fornication is compared with Samaria’s fornication, Jerusalem is found to be more criminal (Ezekiel 16); nevertheless, both are worthy of death. In the Gospel too, the sin of Judas is declared by the Lord’s own mouth to be more serious when compared with the sin of Sodom; yet both are reserved for punishments corresponding to their deserts at the judgment (Matthew 10).

In a mystical sense, however, Jews may be understood as thieves, to whom Paul says: “‘You who preach against stealing, do you steal?’” (Romans 2). Heretics may be understood as liars, whose crime is more serious than that of the Jews because, after receiving the grace of baptism and the garment of Christ’s tunic with which they had been clothed, they returned to apostasy and insulted the Spirit of grace. Yet the guilt of both will encounter eternal destruction if they die without repentance.

“‘The ways of lying people are without honor, and their disgrace remains with them without interruption.’” The perverse ways of heretics are therefore not worthy of heavenly honor but of perpetual shame in hell, which remains with them without interruption in everlasting condemnation.

## CHAPTER XV. The word of parables.

[Col. 0900B] “‘The wise person will bring himself forth in words, and the prudent person will please the great.’” The wise person reveals himself in words when he demonstrates the prudence of his mind in good speech. The Truth itself shows this in the Gospel, saying: “‘The good person brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings forth evil from the evil treasure; for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks’ (Luke 6).” The prudent person will please the great because devotion pleases holy teachers in a disciple who obeys well, whose merits produce a reward for him in eternal life, as the following sentence indicates by explanation.

“‘The one who cultivates his land will raise up a heap of grain; and the one who practices righteousness will himself be exalted.’” He cultivates his land who, plowing his flesh with the Gospel’s plowshare, makes it produce the fruits of very many virtues and devote itself to works of righteousness. At the future examination the master of the household will praise his works and reward him suitably with heavenly honor, saying: “‘Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord’ (Luke 9).”

“‘But the one who pleases the great will escape iniquity.’” This is what he said above: “‘The prudent person will please the great.’” The devoted disciple pleases good teachers precisely by striving to flee every stain of iniquity. Hence through the Psalmist it is said: “‘Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord’ (Psalm 118).” And again: “‘Blessed is the person who fears the Lord and greatly delights in his commandments. His offspring will be powerful on earth; glory and riches will be in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever’ (Psalm 111).”

“‘Hospitality-gifts (*xenia*) and presents blind the eyes of judges; and, as though mute in the mouth, he turns away their corrections.’” Sacred Scripture commands in many places that gifts and money turn the judgments of judges from the path of equity onto the road of iniquity, saying: “‘You shall appoint judges and magistrates in all your gates which the Lord your God gives you throughout your tribes, so that they may judge the people with righteous judgment and not incline to either side. You shall not show partiality or accept gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the righteous. You shall pursue what is just and only what is just, so that you may live and possess the land which the Lord your God will give you’ (Deuteronomy 16).” The lover of money turns away corrections as though mute in his mouth, because on account of money he is silent about what ought to be said, or says what ought to have been kept silent. Both are useless in judgment, where truth must reign completely and justice prevail. The following sentence also proves this by an example.

“‘What use are hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure to either? Better is the one who conceals his foolishness than those who conceal their wisdom.’” Just as there is no usefulness in treasures buried in the earth, which remain hidden from human knowledge and sight, so wisdom indiscreetly concealed by its possessors brings no fruit, but rather the greatest harm. [Col. 0901B] Therefore, when the Lord praised in the Gospel the servant who multiplied his master’s money by trading, he restored to him a fitting reward; but he sharply rebuked the wicked servant who, binding the talent he had received in a cloth, hid it in the earth, assigning him a deserved punishment. Thus “‘it is better for people’” (as it is written here) “‘to conceal their foolishness,’” lest by bringing it forth they generate many sins, than to hide their wisdom, through which they could benefit others unto salvation by rightly preaching and living well, and prepare for themselves an everlasting reward in the heavenly kingdom—namely, on the day of judgment, when “‘each person will receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.’” Those who, although they can preach usefully, nevertheless shrink from doing so out of excessive humility must be admonished, so that from consideration of lesser matters they may understand how much they sin in greater ones. For if they were to hide from needy neighbors the money they possessed, they would plainly become agents of their misfortune. [Col. 0902B] Let them therefore consider by what guilt they are bound when, by withholding the word of preaching from brothers who are sinning, they conceal the remedies of life from minds that are dying.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0901]

## CHAPTER ONE.[Col. 0901B] Wisdom teaches that one person is in all and all in one; that sin must not be added to sin, but that God must be entreated to provide help.

(CAP. XXI.) “‘My child, have you sinned? Do not add again; [Col. 0901C] but also, concerning your former sins, beseech that they may be forgiven you.’” It gives a salutary counsel: since we have sinned—for there is no person on earth who does good and does not sin—we should not repeat our sins, but, doing worthy penance for our former sins, should beseech God to mercifully forgive what we have wickedly committed through our weakness.

“‘Flee sins as from the face of a serpent; and if you approach them, they will receive you.’” That ancient serpent, who always inhabits the shadows of sinners and reigns among the children of darkness, desires our destruction without ceasing and suggests criminal deeds to us. He must be fled from altogether, because if we approach him by consenting to his suggestions, he will receive us in order to lead us with him to the depths of hell, so that we may share in his torments and be companions in his condemnation. Therefore, continuing to speak of his ferocity, he adds: “‘His teeth are the teeth of a lion, killing the souls of human beings.’”

In Sacred Scripture the lion is sometimes understood in a good sense and sometimes in an evil one, because Christ is called a lion, while conversely the devil is called a lion. Christ is called a lion because of his strength, as in John: “‘Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered so as to open the book and break its seven seals’ (Revelation 5).” The devil is likewise called a lion because of his savagery. Concerning him Peter writes to believers: “‘Be sober and watchful in your prayers, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith’ (1 Peter 5).” [Col. 0902B] For he kills human souls because, once he has captured them in the snare of sin, he makes them liable to eternal death.

“Like a double-edged sword is every iniquity; there is no healing for its wound.”

[Col. 0902C] Human iniquity is a double-edged sword, because it brings death upon both aspects of his substance, namely the bodily and the spiritual: for the fire of Gehenna will torment both body and soul after the day of judgment. There is no healing for its wound, because once a person has departed this life without the remedy of repentance and has been condemned there by God’s just judgment, he will burn there without end. Hence, at the final examination, it is said to sinners themselves: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels; and the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25).

But since the opportunity of the passage has arisen for us to say something about the unforgivable sin, it has seemed fitting to set down some words of Saint Augustine, who, in a sermon to the people where he explained what blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is, says as follows:

“[Col. 0902D] First, therefore, for our receiving eternal life, which will be given at the end, the gift of God’s goodness comes to us from the beginning of faith: the forgiveness of sins. Through this benefit we are rescued from the power of darkness, and the prince of this world is cast out by our faith—he who works in the children of unbelief by no other force than through the fellowship and bondage of sin. In the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s people are gathered into one, the unclean spirit is cast out, the spirit who is divided against himself.

“Against this gratuitous gift, against this grace of God, the unrepentant heart speaks. Unrepentance itself, therefore, is blasphemy against the Spirit, which will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come. Against the Holy Spirit—for by him those are baptized whose sins are all forgiven, and whom the Church has received so that those whose sins she forgives may have them forgiven—[Col. 0903A] he speaks a very evil and exceedingly impious word, whether in his thought or even with his tongue. Although God’s patience leads him to repentance, he, according to the hardness of his heart and his unrepentant heart, stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each according to his works (Rom. 2).

“This unrepentance, then—for by some name we may in some fashion call blasphemy and the word against the Holy Spirit, which has no forgiveness forever—this unrepentance, I say, against which both the herald and the judge cried out, saying, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’ (Matt. 3); against which the Lord opened the mouth of evangelical preaching, and concerning which he foretold that the Gospel itself was to be preached [Col. 0903B] throughout the whole world—when he had risen from the dead, he said to his disciples: ‘It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem’ (Luke 24)—this unrepentance has no forgiveness at all, either in this age or in the age to come; for repentance obtains forgiveness in this age, and that forgiveness is effective in the age to come.

“But this unrepentance, or unrepentant heart, cannot be judged so long as a person lives in this flesh. No one is to be despaired of while God’s patience leads him to repentance and does not snatch the wicked from this life—he who ‘does not desire the death of the wicked, but rather that he should turn and live.’ [Col. 0903C] Today he is a pagan: how do you know whether tomorrow he will be a Christian? Today he is an unbelieving Jew: what if tomorrow he believes in Christ? Today he is a heretic: what if tomorrow he follows the catholic truth? Today he is a schismatic: what if tomorrow he embraces catholic peace? What if those whom you mark as belonging to any kind of error and condemn now as utterly hopeless repent before they finish this life and find true life?

“Whoever, throughout his entire life in this flesh, however long it may last, speaks any words, whether with his mouth or only in thought, with an unrepentant heart against the forgiveness of sins that takes place in the Church, speaks a word against the Holy Spirit. If, then, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit forgive sins, why is [Col. 0903D] that unrepentance which will never be forgiven said to pertain solely to blasphemy against the Spirit, as though the person bound by this sin of unrepentance were seen to resist the gift of the Holy Spirit, through which gift the forgiveness of sins takes place?

“Among other things, these matters are said in such a way that the inseparable operation of the Trinity is nevertheless understood. Thus, when the operation of the Father is mentioned, it is not to be understood that he operates without the Son and the Holy Spirit; when the operation of the Son is mentioned, not without the Father and the Holy Spirit; and when the operation of the Holy Spirit is mentioned, not without the Father and the Son. This is sufficiently familiar to those who believe rightly, or who understand it as far as they are able.

“And that saying about the Father—‘He himself performs the works’—was made because the origin even of the works is from him, from whom comes the existence [Col. 0904A] of the persons who cooperate; for the Son was born from him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from him, from whom the Son was born and with whom that same Spirit is shared. Hence the Lord Jesus cast out demons in the Holy Spirit. He was not unable to accomplish this by himself, nor did he take that Spirit as a helper, as though he were insufficient for the work; rather, it was fitting that a spirit divided against itself should be expelled by that Spirit whom the Father and the Son possess together, undivided against himself.

“So too, since sins are not forgiven outside the Church, they had to be forgiven in that Spirit through whom the Church is gathered into one. Finally, if someone outside the Church repents of his sins, yet possesses an unrepentant heart concerning this great sin, which is alien to the Church of God [Col. 0904B], what does that repentance profit him? By this one thing he speaks against the Holy Spirit, through whom he is a stranger to the Church, which received this gift so that forgiveness of sins might take place in the Holy Spirit. Although the Trinity grants this forgiveness, it is nevertheless properly understood to pertain to the Holy Spirit. For he is the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father,’ so that we may say to him, ‘Forgive us our debts.’

“Whoever, therefore, is guilty of unrepentance against the Spirit, in whom the unity and fellowship of communion are gathered into the Church, will never be forgiven, because he has closed himself off from the place where forgiveness is granted. He will justly be condemned with the spirit who is divided against himself, himself divided against the Spirit who is not divided against himself.

“Among other matters, [Col. 0904C] the reason this statement was made about blasphemy against the Spirit arose from the mention of the unclean spirit who is divided against himself. It had been said of the Lord that he cast out demons by the prince of demons. There the Lord himself says that he casts out demons in the Holy Spirit, so that the Spirit who is not divided against himself may conquer and expel the one who is divided against himself. But the person who refuses, through unrepentance, to pass into the peace of the one who is not divided against himself remains in that person’s destruction.

“For Mark narrates it in this way: ‘Amen, I say to you, all sins and blasphemies by which the sons of men may blaspheme will be forgiven them; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of an eternal sin’ (Mark 3).” [Col. 0904D] Having spoken these words of the Lord, he then joins his own words to them, saying: “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’” Thus he showed that the occasion for saying this arose from their having said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

“It was not because this itself was the blasphemy that will not be forgiven—for even this is forgiven if proper repentance follows—but because, as I said, it provided the occasion for the Lord to pronounce that sentence, when mention had been made of the unclean spirit, whom the Lord showed to be divided against himself, in contrast with the Holy Spirit, who is not only not divided against himself but also makes those whom he gathers undivided.

“For even if someone is so opposed to the truth that he resists God speaking not in the prophets but in the only [Col. 0905A] Son—for our sake he willed him to be a son of man, so that he might speak to us in him—he will be forgiven when, by repenting, he has turned to God’s goodness. Since God did not desire the death of the wicked but rather that he should turn and live, he gave his Church the Holy Spirit, so that whoever’s sins she forgave in him might have them forgiven.

“But whoever proves hostile to this gift, so that he does not seek it through repentance but contradicts it through unrepentance, makes the sin unforgivable—not any sin whatsoever, but forgiveness itself when despised or even attacked. Thus a word against the Holy Spirit is spoken when one never passes from dispersion into the gathering that received the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins.”

“Reproach and insults will destroy substance; [Col. 0905B] so the substance of the proud will be uprooted, and a house that is exceedingly rich will be destroyed by pride.”

In another edition it reads: “Reproach and insults will destroy substance.” According to the historical sense, the meaning is easy: wherever quarrels and insults increase, there substance will be diminished and decline, and the whole household, its possessions being destroyed, will lose the pride of those who quarrel. Among the proud there are always disputes; but wherever human disagreement prevails, the collapse of their possessions will immediately follow. Hence, when one of the wise was asked about the fall of a very powerful kingdom—why it had fallen so quickly—he replied: “By harmony small things grow; by discord great things are dissolved.”

According to the allegory, however, every structure of heretical wickedness and their manifold error, resting upon various arguments [Col. 0905C] and the conclusions of syllogisms, will therefore be destroyed and reduced to nothing, because they refused to follow the truth of the catholic faith and the unity of the peace of the holy Church.

“The supplication of the poor will reach from his mouth to his ears, and judgment will come to him swiftly.”

It is written in the Psalm: “The desire of the poor he has heard, O Lord” (Ps. 9); “your ear has heard the desires of their heart.” And in the Gospel, after the Lord had related the story of the widow who cried out to an unjust judge for her defense, he added: “Hear what the unjust judge says. And will not God avenge his elect who cry to him day and night, and will he have patience with them? I say to you, he will swiftly avenge them” [Col. 0905D] (Luke 18).

For a supplication from the mouth of the poor will come to the ears of the judge, because the anguish of the Church, which she endures amid various tribulations, will reach the ears of the most merciful judge; and he will rescue her from all her tribulations and subject all her enemies to punishments they deserve.

“Whoever hates correction is a footprint of the sinner; and whoever fears God will turn back to his own heart.”

Whoever does not wish to correct himself from sins and hates the admonition of the reprover gives evidence in himself of the wickedness of his seducer, because the evil one has hardened his mind so that he would neither believe nor obey the truth. But whoever possesses the fear of God within himself turns his heart toward hearing and fulfilling the commands of the divine law.

[Col. 0906A] “Known from afar is the powerful man of a bold tongue, and the sensible man knows that he slips away from him.”

Heretical presumption is therefore revealed in a rash tongue, by which he dares to speak wickedness against God; but the caution of the religious and faithful person guards itself so as not to fall into his error.

“Whoever builds his house with the possessions of others is like one who gathers his stones in winter.”

We can understand this saying in two ways. According to the allegory, it may signify the heretic who gathers together testimonies of the divine Scriptures that are entirely alien to their true meaning, in order to confirm his own error, and labors in vain, because the vengeance of just retribution will dissolve the hardness of his impious deed. Or, according to the tropological sense, it may signify the greedy plunderer who seeks to increase his profits from the possessions of others and, deprived of every good, will on the day of judgment suffer severe torments for his evil work.

## CHAPTER II

That the gathered stubble is the synagogue of sinners and the assemblies of heretics, just as the bundles of weeds are to be burned.

“The gathered stubble is the synagogue of sinners, and their end is a flame of fire.”

He compares the synagogue of sinners to a fragile thing, in order to show its worthlessness and exceedingly swift destruction; for just as a heap of stubble easily catches fire when fire is applied, so the assembly of sinners will perish without delay in the future retribution.

“The way of sinners is paved with stones, and at their end are hell, darkness, and punishments.”

He gives the reason why the destruction of the wicked is swift: their way—that is, their present life, by which they were advancing toward future recompense—was [Col. 0906C] full of hardships and hard works of sin. Hence, at their end, hell, darkness, and punishments follow upon them, by which they will deservedly be tormented forever. The righteous, by contrast, guards himself from all these things and prepares himself for heavenly repayment. Hence it follows:

“Whoever guards justice will preserve his understanding. The consummation of the fear of God is wisdom.”

Whoever, therefore, guards ‘justice’ will be preserved by it, and at the end eternal glory will follow him, because the fulfillment of his good will—which he possessed in the fear of God—will be rewarded by the knowledge and contemplation of his Creator.

“And his understanding will not be instructed who is not wise [Col. 0906D] in goodness. There is a foolishness that abounds in evil; and there is no understanding where bitterness abounds.”

By these sayings the error of heretics is confounded, because their understanding, which they apply to meditation on the sacred Scriptures, is not wholesome for those who examine it. Or rather, understanding should not be said to exist where wickedness and deceit abound, because the Lord created the human being upright, but they entangled themselves in endless questions.

“The knowledge of the wise will abound like a flood, and his counsel remains like a fountain of life.”

Whoever receives from God the gift of true wisdom will abound in the manifold fruits of learning and virtues, because in him that saying of the Lord will be fulfilled in which he says: [Col. 0907A] “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will have in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). And again: “Whoever thirsts,” he says, “let him come to me and drink; and from his belly will flow living waters” (John 7).

“The heart of the fool is like a broken vessel, and it will hold no wisdom.”

The mind of the foolish heretic is therefore like a broken vessel, because it has been pierced on every side by the goads of malice; nor is it now fit for the use of wisdom, because on account of its foulness it cannot contain the virtue of wisdom, which is sincere and pure. Hence he says: “It will hold no wisdom,” because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit”; “wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul.”

“Whatever wise word the ignorant hearer hears, he will praise [Col. 0907B] and add to himself; the pleasure-lover will hear it and dislike it, and will cast it behind his back.”

By *inscius* he means the humble hearer and attentive meditator on the word of God, who thirsts and longs with the prophet to reach the presence and knowledge of his Lord. According to the world he is foolish, but according to God he is eager to learn, “because the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their own generation.” Such a person, then, will praise and love whatever wise word he hears and will hasten to store it in his mind.

By contrast, the pleasure-lover and lover of worldly delights, when he hears the word of God, will dislike it and cast it behind his back—that is, he will render it ineffective and will not strive to fulfill it in practice.

[Col. 0907C] “The speech of a fool is like a burden on the road; but grace will be found on the lips of the sensible.”

The teaching of the heretic is therefore burdensome to all who are sound in understanding on the road of this age, because it is useful for nothing and contrary to every good. Grace will therefore be found on the lips of the sensible, because sound preaching and the grace of the Holy Spirit are found in the words of the catholic teacher.

“The mouth of the prudent is sought in the Church, and they will consider his words in their hearts.”

That is, the teaching of the catholic preacher is sought among the people of God, and devout hearers, reviewing his words, consider them in their hearts, so that by rightly understanding them and living well they may fulfill them in pious actions.

“Like a house [Col. 0907D] destroyed, so is wisdom to a fool, and the knowledge of the senseless consists of unspeakable words.”

A destroyed house can rightly be understood as the synagogue of heretics, where the wisdom of upright and catholic understanding is despised. Therefore their teachings are unspeakable words, because they are subject to manifold errors; for they do not teach what the truth possesses, but what their wickedness has falsely devised.

“Fetters on the feet of a fool are instruction, and like bands of the hands upon the right hand.”

The word of life, which liberates faithful souls from death, binds wandering souls with fetters, because it contradicts the steps by which they walk on the way of iniquity and places bonds upon their right hand—that is, upon their evil deeds—when it firmly reproves their actions by condemning them.

## CHAPTER III [Col. 0908A]

Wisdom shows that laughter is a fault, not joy, because joy is from God.

“A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh even quietly.”

Temperance in all things suits the prudent person well, whereas the fool is entirely unable to maintain it in word and conduct. According to another interpretation, the foolish company of heretics seeks the applause of its hearers through rhetorical skill and persuasive teaching; but the order of holy teachers so mingles the pleasantness of speech with its doctrines that it nevertheless does not deviate at all from the path of truth and the disciplines of the Gospel. Hence it follows:

“A golden ornament for prudent teaching, and like [Col. 0908B] a bracelet on the right arm.”

Since gold signifies the splendor of wisdom and the mystical meaning of the divine law, prudent teaching is like a golden ornament when its preaching is illuminated by divine wisdom; and it is like a bracelet on the right arm when discipline of the virtues surrounds all its works and its entire life. For he knows neither how to teach nor how to do anything other than what the norm of equity and the rule of justice prescribe.

“The fool’s foot is quick to enter the house of his neighbor; but the learned man is put to shame by the person of the powerful.”

The fool’s foot advances easily into his neighbor’s house when heretics strive to imitate the sect of their authors, lying hidden in the dwelling of their writings. But the learned man is put to shame by the person of the powerful when the catholic [Col. 0908C] teacher is ashamed to follow the error of a proud man.

“The fool will look into the house from the window; but the educated man will stand outside.”

This passage figuratively reveals the malicious cunning of heretics and the clear simplicity of catholics. The fool will look into the house from the window when the clever disputant searches in the house of the Scriptures for openings into a more hidden meaning, from which he may seize an assertion in support of his error. But the catholic teacher will stand outside, because he strives to make sacred Scripture plain and, through his preaching, to bring it to the knowledge of many. Truth does not love corners but walks along the path of light.

“It is the foolishness of a man to hear through the door; but the prudent man will be burdened with insult.”

[Col. 0908D] It is foolish for a person to wish to hear the word of preaching from the mouth of heretics, because from it he can receive a stumbling-block for his faith. The true preacher, therefore, is often subjected to the insults of the wicked, because he refuses in any way to depart from the rule of righteousness. This is the difference between the heretic and the catholic: the former seeks human praise, the latter divine glory; the former seeks worldly prosperity, the latter does not fear to suffer adversity for Christ; the former tends toward the gates of death, the latter toward the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

“The lips of the imprudent will recount foolish things; but the words of the prudent will be weighed on a balance.”

This indicates that the speeches of the foolish always bring forth the foolishness of a corrupt understanding, whereas the words of the faithful everywhere strive to preserve the rule of right [Col. 0909A] faith in their teaching.

“In the mouth of fools is their heart, and in the heart of the wise is their mouth.”

Their heart is in the mouth of fools when the foolish intention of heretics and schismatics seeks to embellish its words. But their mouth is in the heart of the wise when the speech of the elect strives faithfully to express the meaning of true wisdom.

“When the wicked curses the devil, he himself curses his own soul.”

The wicked person is not called wicked because he curses the evil devil, but because he does not cease, by perverse will and evil deeds, to follow as an enemy the one whom he knows to be evil. Hence the Lord says to the Jews in the Gospel: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father [Col. 0909B]” (John 8). They were not the devil’s children by the condition of their nature, but by their perverse imitation of his malice. The wicked person therefore curses himself in that, on account of his impiety, he chooses to imitate the devil, who has been condemned, rather than Christ, who was crucified for the salvation of the human race.

“A whisperer will defile his soul, and will be hated by all; and whoever remains with him will be hateful. The quiet and sensible man will be honored.”

No one can be understood better as a whisperer than the heretic, who secretly arranges ambushes and snares of error in his teaching in order to deceive the souls of the unwary. He will defile his soul with many crimes and will always be hateful in the eyes of the wise, both in word and in deed. Whoever, deceived by their sects, decides to remain in them [Col. 0909C] until the end of his life will likewise be hateful to all good people.

By contrast, the person who restrains his tongue and maintains measured silence in speech will, by the dignity of his good understanding and through Christ’s gift, possess heavenly honor.

## CHAPTER IV

This slothful man, who is stoned with a muddy stone and with ox dung, is the people of the Jews: with the muddy stone—that is, the people of the Gentiles who are ignorant of the law—it is reproached; and with the ox dung—that is, by Jews who have already come to faith.

(CAP. 22.) “The slothful man is stoned with a muddy stone, and all will speak of his disgrace.”

The slothful man is stoned with a muddy stone when the foulness of his crimes is reproached to the sinner through the hard [Col. 0909D] sayings of Scripture. “And all will speak of his disgrace,” because all good people detest and despise the filth of his deeds. And because such people are especially reproved through the offices of teachers, it is appropriately added:

“The slothful man is stoned with ox dung, and everyone who touches him will shake his hands.”

The slothful man is stoned with ox dung when the sloth of the wicked, who are sluggish in good works, is reproached by holy preachers through suitable discourse exposing their folly. Thus all who have in any way shared in their negligence may shake the hands of their works free from the squalor of their foulness and return, through useful activity, to observance of God’s commandments.

Alternatively, this slothful man, [Col. 0910A] who is stoned with a muddy stone or with ox dung, signifies the people of the Jews. They are reproached through the fragile and law-ignorant crowd of the Gentiles, represented by the muddy stone, because in the perversity of their understanding they openly refused to believe in Christ when he came among them, although he had been promised to them in the Law and the Prophets.

The same applies to the ox dung—that is, to believing Jews—who were born from the ancient oxen, namely the devout patriarchs who bore the yoke of the Law. They are mocked for the blindness of their heart, because they refused to receive with fitting faith the incarnation of the Savior, which had been given to them in their own time.

“The father is put to shame by an undisciplined son; but a foolish daughter will become a diminution.”

Any teacher is put to shame by the depraved conduct of an undisciplined [Col. 0910B] pupil, because he does not find in him a worthy fruit of his labor. Likewise, in an undisciplined daughter there is a diminution of his honor, because in the perversity of her conduct he has sadness rather than gladness of heart.

Was he not saddened by the wickedness of his disciples who wrote to certain people as follows: “I wish that I were with you now and could change my voice, because I am ashamed of you” (Gal. 4)? Elsewhere, rejoicing and exulting over the progress of his good children, he says: “I have great confidence in you; I have great boasting on your behalf; I am filled with consolation; I overflow with joy in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 7). And again: “In our consolation,” he says, “we rejoiced even more abundantly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you; and if I have boasted anything to him about you, I have not been put to shame [Col. 0910C]” (ibid.).

“A prudent daughter is an inheritance to her husband; but she who brings shame becomes a disgrace to her father.”

The soul, therefore, that prudently and devoutly performs the service of Christ will belong to his inheritance. But she who does things deserving of shame brings disgrace upon her spiritual father, who regenerated her in baptism through the grace of the Holy Spirit and adopted her as a daughter.

“An audacious woman brings shame upon her father and husband, and she will not be diminished by the impious; but by both she will be dishonored.”

The father of the Christian soul is God, and her husband is Christ. If, therefore, she falls into apostasy and shamelessly defends the error of heretics, she dishonors her spiritual father and husband. [Col. 0910D] Although she is not presently condemned by the impious and by those who share in her error, she will nevertheless be put to shame by both—that is, by the father and husband mentioned above—in the future judgment, and will be subjected to deserved condemnation and everlasting punishments.

“Music in mourning is an untimely tale; scourges and instruction are wisdom at every time.”

This is directed against those who seek, by their conduct, the applause and favor of the people in the Church and do not aim instead to arouse in their hearers the compunction of tears, since the Church’s bread is not the bread of those who laugh but of those who mourn.

Therefore he says that scourges and instruction are wisdom at every time, because at every time it is fitting for the people to be urged by their teachers to despise present things and [Col. 0911A] desire future ones, so that they may know that now is the time for mourning, but then the time for laughter; now the time of war, but then of peace. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted” (Matt. 5).

Elsewhere, by contrast, he threatens lovers of the world who seek the consolation of the present life, saying: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will weep.” Hence Solomon also says: “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools in the house of joy”—that is, in the house of such a man as reproves the delinquent and brings him to tears, “not in the house of joy,” where the teacher deceives and is deceived when he seeks not the conversion of his hearers but applause and praise. Here too, because he has been filled, he has therefore [Col. 0911B] received his consolation.

Finally, the verses that follow agree with this interpretation. For he says: “It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear a man listening to the song of fools; for as the crackling of burning thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool; and this too is vanity” (Eccl. 7). It is better to be reproved by a wise person than to be deceived by the flattery of those who praise. To this is similar the saying: “Better are the wounds of a friend than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27).

For just as the crackling of thorns burning beneath a pot produces an unpleasant noise, so the words of a flattering teacher are of no benefit to hearers when he urges them either toward the cares of the world, which are interpreted as thorns, or prepares them for the fire of the future.

## CHAPTER V [Col. 0911C]

That the person who speaks a word to one who does not pay attention is like someone who awakens a sleeper from a deep sleep.

“Whoever teaches a fool is like one who glues together an earthenware vessel.”

Just as an earthenware vessel, although fashioned with much labor by an artisan, nevertheless cannot be brought to the strength of a stone, but, made from fragile material, displays the fragile condition of its body, so the fool, even if nourished and instructed in every discipline through the diligent care of a teacher, can scarcely be brought to the perfection of a good pupil. But because he is brutish in understanding and undevout in spirit, he will likewise be far from perfect in knowledge and virtue. Hence it is added:

“[Col. 0911D] Whoever speaks a word to one who does not pay attention is like one who awakens a sleeper from a deep sleep.”

The comparison with a sleeper and one who does not pay attention is apt, because just as the former is weighed down by sleep, so the latter is oppressed by foolish understanding. Hence it follows:

“He speaks with a sleeper who recounts wisdom to a fool, and at the end says, ‘Who is this?’”

For he does not properly understand the word of instruction, nor does he gratefully receive the teacher’s effort. In such a loss there is more reason for sorrow than for joy, and one should pray with tears for the recovery of the sick person, because he himself does not know how to groan for his own salvation.

“Weep over the dead, for his light has failed; and weep over the fool, for his understanding has failed. Weep little over the dead, for he has found rest. For the life of a most wicked person is worse than the death of a fool. The mourning for the dead is seven days, but for the fool and the impious it is all the days of their life.”

[Col. 0912A] There are indeed two deaths: one of the body, which is common to all human beings; the other of the soul, which belongs especially to sinners. One ends in the present age; the other will never end, but will last forever. Therefore he says: “Weep little over the dead, for he has found rest.” For bodily death is the end of present labor and gives the saints rest from the pain of this life.

Likewise, the saying that “the mourning for the dead is seven days, but for the fool and the impious all the days of their life” signifies that bodily death takes place only within the span of the present life, which runs its course in the number of seven days. But the mourning for fools—that is, for sinners and the impious—continues throughout all the days of their life, that is, forever and ever, when their souls are tormented perpetually in hell without the interruption of death.

“Do not converse long with a fool, and do not walk with the senseless. Guard yourself from him, so that you do not suffer annoyance and are not defiled by his sin. Turn away from him and you will find rest, and you will not be wearied by his folly.”

In these sayings wisdom teaches us not to prolong conversation with foolish people, because we will find no benefit there, especially among heretics, whose folly is full of blasphemy. Such people [Col. 0912B] must be avoided, lest we be defiled by the filth of their sins and lose the quiet of peace and tranquility, since we will never find rest with them.

If they wish to turn back and abandon [Col. 0912C] their error, so as to recover from the snares of the devil, by which they were held captive to his will, they are then to be treated not as enemies but as brothers. But so long as they persist in their error, they must be entirely fled from and avoided, and must not be encouraged by any comfort of communion.

Hence the apostle John says: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Hail’ to him” (2 John 1); for whoever says “Hail” to him shares in his evil works. Paul likewise says: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second correction, knowing that such a person is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3).

And because the behavior and words of such people are difficult to bear, it is therefore added:

[Col. 0912D] “What is heavier than lead? And what other name does he have than fool? Sand, salt, and a mass of iron are easier to carry than an imprudent, foolish, and impious man.”

To this is similar what is written in Proverbs: “A stone is heavy, and sand is burdensome; but the anger of a fool is heavier than both” (Prov. 27). And again: “It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool confident in his folly” (Prov. 17).

Sand, as consisting of tiny particles, can signify the multitude of sins; salt, because it often stands for wisdom in the Scriptures, can here signify the philosophers of the Gentiles, who imitate the pursuit of wisdom; and the mass of iron can signify the hardness of pagan persecution.

And because [Col. 0913A] he compares all these things with an imprudent, foolish, and impious man—namely, the heretic, who is imprudent in knowledge, foolish in teaching, and impious in life—he signifies that the evil committed by one who has received sacred baptism, confessed the name of Christ, and recognized the truth, but has become an apostate, is more intolerable than what is committed either by the catholic person through a multitude of minor transgressions, or by the Gentile philosopher in writings of human wisdom, or by the pagan persecutor who has not yet come to faith and therefore, in ignorance, hates the truth and persecutes the Christian religion.

“For the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke 12).

[Col. 0913B] “A wooden framework fastened to the foundation of a building is not loosened; so also a heart confirmed in the deliberation of counsel.”

We therefore read that “wood” signifies righteous men, who will yield their fruit in its season, whose leaves do not fall, and everything they do prospers (Ps. 1). The foundation of the building signifies the apostles and prophets, whose preaching supports the building of the Church. For a wooden framework fastened to the foundation of a building is not loosened, because the faith in Christ’s Passion, joined in the hearts of believers to the apostles’ teaching, makes the Church an indestructible building, firmly bound together by the bond of true charity. It does not allow itself to be destroyed either by the threats and scourges of persecutors or by the plots of heretics. For “the foundation of the Lord stands firm,” [Col. 0913C] and the heart of a faithful man, confirmed in doctrines of this kind, cannot be weakened by any adversity; rather, strengthened by the hand of the supreme Craftsman, it remains unharmed forever. The following sentence also confirms this:

“A sensible man’s thought will not be corrupted at any time, even by fear.” For worldly adversity, the scourges of persecutors, the battles of heretics, or even the snares of evil spirits can in no way overthrow or corrupt the heart of a prudent man who, according to the counsel of the divine books, keeps God’s commandments and entrusts the whole counsel of his soul to almighty God with steadfast hope. By contrast, what happens to those timid in heart and lacking strength of mind is shown by the following comparison:

[Col. 0913D] “As straw in high places and cement laid without expense do not withstand the face of the wind, so a timid heart in a fool’s deliberation does not resist the onset of fear.”

Just as light straw placed in elevated places is carried away by the breath of the wind, and just as cement that has not been properly bonded by an admixture of lime cannot make a solid wall, but quickly makes it fall when a whirlwind arrives, so the timid heart of foolish heretics, when the Holy Spirit provides it with no support of right faith and no strengthening of true charity, cannot withstand the troubles brought by persecution, but lies especially exposed to ruin.

The Savior himself explained these two comparisons—that is, the firm heart of sensible people established on the foundation of the Catholic faith, and the timid heart of heretics wavering in the foolishness of their errors—[Col. 0914A] by a clear likeness in the Gospel, saying:

“Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock; and the rain came down, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them is like a foolish man who builds his house upon sand; and the rain came down, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it fell, and its ruin was great.”

The foundation that the apostle Paul, the architect, laid is one: our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon this foundation the Church of Christ is built—[Col. 0914B] stable and firm, founded in itself upon a solid mass. But upon sand, which is fluid and cannot be joined together or reduced to a single bond, every word of the heretics is built for the purpose of collapsing. What did he intend to be understood by the rain except the manifold temptations of the devil; by the rivers, open and unmistakable persecutions; and by the winds, evil spirits? For no one’s conscience that does not remain fixed in hope in God can stand either amid temptations, amid persecutions, or before evil spirits. And each person’s conscience is shaken more fiercely by evil spirits in proportion as the carnal mind is more separated from higher things in those matters that belong to the world, and more tightly bound to lower things.

[Col. 0914C] “As a sandy ornament on a polished wall, so is a trembling heart in the thought of a fool. It will not fear at any time; but whoever remains in God’s commandments, continually pricking his eyes, will draw forth tears; and whoever pricks the heart will bring forth understanding.”

He offers another example, in which he wishes to show that, just as a polished wall, because of its smoothness, does not receive the dust of sand, so the heart of a fool in its own thinking rejects remembrance of its crimes and does not wish to fear future punishments. But whoever remains steadfast in God’s commandments by good works pricks the eye of his heart with the goad of fear and draws from it tears of compunction, both from dread of the future judgment and from love of eternal life. Thus, keeping the fear of God always before the eyes of his heart, he strives [Col. 0914D] to understand Holy Scripture rightly and to preach it to others in truthful speech.

## CHAPTER VI. Wisdom speaks about quarrelling among friends: words of insult or secrets are not to be disclosed.

“Throwing a stone at birds will bring them down; so also whoever insults a friend will dissolve friendship.”

Wisdom teaches that when friends quarrel among themselves, they should not speak words of insult against one another, nor, in their fury, expose secrets that have long been concealed from each other. For just as a bird’s flight is brought down by the blow of a stone, so the strength of friendship is dissolved by an insulting word.

“If you draw a sword against a friend, do not despair: there is a return. If you open a sorrowful [Col. 0915A] mouth against a friend, do not fear: there is reconciliation—except in insult, reproach, pride, disclosure of a secret, or a treacherous wound; in all these things a friend will flee from you.”

He now explains what things can preserve a good friend and what can utterly drive him away and make him a stranger. If, out of affection for charity, you correct a friend by a word of reproof for some shameful deed, so that you wish to reform him, you should not despair of his friendship. Although he may for a time be distressed by the rebuke, later, once he recognizes the usefulness of the correction, he quickly returns to the right of his former friendship. He does not remain in his received sorrow because of the painful word, since he understands that everything done toward him was free from fraudulent plotting.

But if you wound him with insulting speech, [Col. 0915B] reproach, pride, disclosure of secrets, or the deceitfulness of wickedness, then in all these things a friend will flee; you may even despair of his return to his former friendship. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Do not trust a reconciled friend forever” (Ecclus. 12).

“Keep faith with your neighbor in his poverty, so that you may also rejoice in his prosperity. Remain faithful in the time of his tribulation, so that you may also be his fellow heir in his inheritance.”

A friend’s faith is tested more in adversity than in prosperity, because “many are table-companions, and they do not remain on the day of necessity.” Therefore he urges us to keep faith with our neighbor in poverty and tribulation, so that we may rejoice together with him in his prosperity. In the mystical sense, whoever in the present age shares his brother’s [Col. 0915C] and neighbor’s sorrow in the tribulation of this present life will share in his joy and glory in the inheritance of the future homeland.

“Before the fire of the furnace, vapor and smoke of fire rise up; so before bloodshed come curses, insults, and threats.”

Just as smoke precedes the burning of a fire, so the harshness of words precedes the evil of murder. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “A harsh word stirs up quarrels.” And again: “When the wood has failed, the fire will be extinguished, and when the whisperer is removed, quarrels cease. As coals to burning embers and wood to fire, so an angry man stirs up quarrels.”

For this reason the Savior also wished by his commandment to remove the cause of anger, lest the crime of murder be added, saying: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; whoever kills will be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment, and so forth.”

[Col. 0915D] “Let me not be ashamed to greet a friend; I will not hide myself from his face. And if evils befall me, I will endure them through him.”

It is impossible to recount how many good things there are in true friendship, and no one can express in words how many evils there are in hateful enmity. For just as friendship is a praiseworthy support of every good, so, conversely, enmity is a detestable sign of every evil. If good things happen to you, your friend will rejoice with you; but if evils occur, your friend will share your sorrow and strive to endure them with you.

“Everyone who hears will beware of him.”

[Col. 0916A] That is, everyone who understands how many good things there are in true friendship takes care not to lose it through negligence. He is careful not to embitter his friend by insult, reproach, or the other things listed above, and not to violate the rights of friendship.

“Who will give my mouth a guard, and a sure seal upon my lips, so that I may not fall by them and my tongue may destroy me?”

The wise man knows how many evils arise through the rashness of the tongue. Therefore he asks who will provide a guard for his speech, so that he may not turn toward an evil word, from which the surest harm to his soul might result. The extent of the danger to human life that lies in the power of the tongue is shown by the apostle James in his Epistle, saying:

“Behold, how great a fire sets ablaze how great a forest! And the tongue is fire; [Col. 0916B] the tongue is established among our members as the universe of iniquity. It defiles the whole body and inflames the wheel of our birth, being itself inflamed by Gehenna. For every nature of beasts and birds and serpents and the other creatures is tamed, and has been tamed, by human nature. But no human being can tame the tongue, an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who were made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth proceed blessing and cursing” (Jas. 3).

## CHAPTER VII. A prayer common to us all, in which we say: “Lord God, Father and ruler of my life, do not abandon me, and do not allow me to fall”—that is, restrain me, lest through presumption I bring ruin upon myself.

[Col. 0916C] (CHAP. 23.) “Lord, Father and ruler of my life, do not abandon me to their counsel, and do not allow me to fall among them.”

Earlier he had asked who would give a guard to his mouth and a sure seal upon his lips, because he found no one who could accomplish this perfectly. He therefore turns for help to the one who created him in the beginning, so that, just as it was by his work that he exists in nature, by his gift he may not fall into the abyss of vices.

“Who will place scourges upon my thoughts and the teaching of wisdom in my heart, so that they may not spare me for their ignorances, and their faults may not appear, and my ignorance may not increase, and my offenses be multiplied, and my sins abound, and I fall into the sight of my adversaries, and my enemy rejoice over me?”

Because the wise man understood that the crimes of vices were harmful and deadly to him, he therefore seeks to have the scourges of discipline in his thoughts and the teaching of prudence in his heart, lest, held fast by ignorance, he fail to recognize the dangers of his offenses, and the crimes of his wicked deeds increase, for which he might fall into the hands of adversaries and bring joy to his spiritual enemies.

“Lord, Father and God of my life, do not abandon me to their thoughts. Do not give me haughtiness of eyes, and turn every wicked desire away from me. Take away from me the cravings of the belly, and do not let the intercourse of lust seize [Col. 0917A] me, nor hand me over to an irreverent and unbridled soul.”

He asks God, the Father, maker, and ruler of all human life, not to abandon him or permit him to enter into the counsel of evil spirits. Rather, he asks him to remove from him mental arrogance and every wicked desire: the vice of gluttony—*gastrimargia*, that is, “belly-madness”—and the lust of fornication, and especially not to hand him over to a shameless and immodest soul, that is, not to let him be seized or bound by vices of this kind.

For God is said to hand a person over to some danger when, by a just judgment, he permits him to fall into it. Therefore we ask him in the Lord’s Prayer not to lead us into temptation—that is, not to permit us to be led into temptation. “For God tempts no one,” that is, he deceives no one, “because he himself is not tempted by evil temptations” [Col. 0917B] (Matt. 6).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the teaching that proceeds from the mouth and is to be heard.

“Hear the teaching of the mouth, children, and whoever guards it will not perish by his lips, nor will he stumble in the most wicked deeds.”

He calls the discipline of words “the teaching of the mouth.” He commands us to hear it—that is, to learn and preserve it diligently—because whoever guards it does not sin with his lips and does not stumble in the most wicked deeds, that is, in the practice of deceit and wickedness, falsehood, cursing, perjury, and detraction, which are the works of an undisciplined mouth. For whoever guards his mouth guards his soul from troubles.

[Col. 0917C] “In his vanity the sinner is caught, and the proud and the accursed will stumble in them.”

The sinner is caught in his vanity when he is taken captive by the desires and pleasures of this life. The proud and the one who curses will stumble in them when they do not hesitate to place it before the love of God and the desire for the future homeland. Therefore the apostle John admonishes us in his Epistle, saying:

“Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life; it is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (1 John 2).

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0917D] That an oath, whether good or bad, must be avoided.

“Do not let your mouth become accustomed to swearing, for there are many falls in it. Let the naming of God not be constant in your mouth, and do not involve yourself with the names of the saints, for you will not be free from them.”

He forbids oaths so that perjury may not occur, since whoever swears often eventually commits perjury. Hence the Lord prohibited oaths in the Gospel, because they are harmful and lead a person into perjury (Matt. 5). For just as one who does not speak cannot speak falsely, so one who does not swear cannot commit perjury.

Hence the apostle James also says: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by [Col. 0918A] any other oath. Let your oath be ‘yes, yes; no, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (Jas. 5). He wishes the deadly poison of the tongue to be drained completely from his hearers: he forbade them to slander one another, prohibited them from judging their neighbor, and forbade them to groan against one another in adversity—all of which are manifest sins. He adds even what seems light to some, in order also to remove the habit of swearing. For this too is clearly not to be considered insignificant by those who carefully consider the Lord’s saying: “Every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12).

Therefore, he says, I restrain you from the fault of swearing, lest, by frequently swearing to the truth, you [Col. 0918B] sometimes fall into perjury; but you will stand that much farther from the vice of perjury if you do not wish to swear even to what is true except in the greatest necessity. Yet the person who, although he never commits perjury, swears to the truth more frequently than necessary also falls under the guilt of judgment, because he sins through the very idleness of excessive speech and offends the Judge, who forbade both every useless word and every oath.

“For just as a servant who is constantly questioned is not diminished by resentment, so no one who continually swears and invokes the name will be completely cleansed from sin.”

By “a servant who is questioned” he means one chastised by corrections. Thus in the passions of the martyrs we find “questioning” used for scourges and torments. For just as a servant who is continually corrected is not withdrawn from the crime of resentment but [Col. 0918C] is instead provoked to hatred, so no one who continually swears and invokes the name of God and the names of his saints in his oath will thereby be cleansed from sins; rather, he is further polluted.

“A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and a scourge will not depart from his house. And if he deceives, his offense will be upon him; and if he pretends, he will sin twice. And if he swears in vain, he will not be justified.”

Therefore the man who has the habit of swearing more than is proper will be burdened with the offense of transgression, by which he transgresses God’s commandment that one should not swear at all. Hence the scourge of vengeance will not depart from the house of his body, because through the transgression of his tongue he will undergo punishment in Gehenna together with his soul.

[Col. 0918D] If, then, he commits fraud in swearing, his sin will be upon him. But if he conceals the truth by pretending to reveal it through an oath, he sins twice: first because he concealed the truth by pretence, and second because by falsehood he led others into error. Moreover, if he does not take care to swear often in vain and without any necessity, in idle speech, he will not be able to possess the merit of righteousness; rather, guilty of sin, he will suffer torments at the final judgment. Hence it follows:

“For his house will be filled with the worst retribution.”

There is no other retribution worse than the punishment of hell, where the gnawing worm does not die and the tormenting fire is not extinguished.

“There is also another kind of speech contrary to death; let it not be found [Col. 0919A] in the inheritance of Jacob. For all these things will be taken away from the merciful, and they will not wallow in sins.”

He seems to wish to signify another kind of speech contrary to God’s commandments and liable to death: blasphemy, which is even more harmful than the others he listed previously. Hence he desires that it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob—that is, among the ecclesiastical people, who are rightly called Jacob because they supplant vices and serve God in virtues. For all these things will be taken away from the merciful—that is, from God’s elect—because they flee from them and do not defile themselves in the filth of sins.

“Do not let your mouth become accustomed to undisciplined speech, for in it is the word of sin.”

He commands that we not entirely abandon discipline and that we not become accustomed to uttering our words with an undisciplined [Col. 0919B] mouth, because then the word of sin will cling to us completely—that is, the word of deceit, detraction, error, and blasphemy—from which the destruction of future death is prepared.

“Remember your father and your mother, for you stand in the midst of great ones; lest God perhaps forget you in their sight, and, made foolish by your constant association with them, you suffer reproach, and wish that you had not been born, and curse the day of your birth.”

Our Father is God, and our mother is the Church. The great ones and rulers of the people are the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, in whose midst we stand, because we are surrounded on every side by their teachings and good examples, and it is no longer permitted us to go beyond the boundaries of their faith and tradition.

Therefore it is fitting that at all times [Col. 0919C] we flee forgetfulness of God’s commandments and of the teaching by which Mother Church daily teaches and nourishes us. Rather, we should always strive to meditate attentively on the divine commandments and fulfill them in our deeds, saying with the Prophet: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I look upon all your commandments” (Ps. 118), lest God forget us because of our iniquities and cast us into Tartarus, where, because of eternal torment, we shall regret having been born and curse the day of our birth. The prophets Job and Jeremiah seem to have cursed it, detesting the time of mortality and the course of human transgression.

“A man accustomed to words of reproach will not be instructed throughout all his days.”

[Col. 0919D] A man accustomed to words of reproach is a heretic, whose blasphemous mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Throughout all the days in which he chooses to persist in his error, he will not be instructed by the doctrine of the Catholic faith. Rather, wandering and leading others into error, he hastens toward the pit of destruction and the snare of death.

“Two kinds abound in sins, and a third brings anger and destruction. A heated soul is like a burning fire; it will not be extinguished until it swallows something. And a wicked man in the mouth of his flesh will not cease until he kindles a fire. For a fornicator every loaf is sweet; he will not grow weary of transgressing to the end.”

In these three forms, three principal vices are indicated: avarice, pride, and fornication.

“A heated soul is like a burning fire” [Col. 0920A]: this is the mind of the avaricious person, which burns with desire for earthly things. The flame of this burning is not moderated until it is filled with earthly profit. But because the disease of avarice resembles the disease of dropsy—where the more someone suffering from it drinks, the more he thirsts—so the soul of the avaricious person, the more it acquires through the pursuit of money, the more fiercely it burns with ambition for it.

Therefore, when it is said, “it will not be extinguished until it swallows something,” the healing of the disease is not expressed in him, but the multiplication of his perverse habit is indicated: when he obtains the profit he desires, he is thereby made, as though already released, readier to desire other things.

But the wicked man in the mouth of his flesh does not cease until he kindles a fire, when each proud person, swelling with the exaltation of a carnal heart, barks words of [Col. 0920B] abuse against his neighbor until he kindles in him the fire of hatred and enmity.

For every fornicator, too, every loaf is sweet: that is, every act of adultery and every immodesty is perversely sweet through lust, and the transgressor does not cease until he completes the deadly sin of fornication in deed.

In the mystical sense, heretics and schismatics have a hot and burning soul while they seek human praise through ambition for approval. In the manner of a perverse mind, they kindle a fire of the flesh when they cast the heat of error into the hearts of their hearers through wicked teaching. They are the fornicators, because they have not kept the covenant they made with God when they received baptism; instead, abandoning their former husband and joining themselves adulterously to the idols of their errors, they have defiled themselves. They remain in this crime until, stripped of the enclosure of the flesh through [Col. 0920C] present death, they fall into everlasting death.

## CHAPTER X. Wisdom recounts the words of the unjust man who plans to sin, as in the saying: “The righteous man spoke so that he might sin against himself.”

“Every man who transgresses his marriage bed, despising his soul and saying, ‘Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, walls cover me, and no one looks around me; whom should I fear? The Most High will not remember my sins,’ does not understand that his eye sees everything, nor that the fear of such a man drives away the fear of God, while he fears the eyes of human beings. He does not know that the eyes of [Col. 0920D] the Lord are far brighter than the sun, surveying all the ways of human beings, the depth of the abyss, and the hearts of human beings, observing their hidden parts.”

For the man who loses the virtue of chastity and gives himself over to the vice of immodesty, since his mind itself is dark, supposes that he carries out the works of darkness without anyone else’s knowledge. Because he drives the fear of God away from himself, he is especially deceived in supposing that he can elude the creator of all hidden things. Yet, as we have learned from the testimony of the Prophet, “the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their remembrance from the earth” (Ps. 33). And: “The Lord questions the righteous and the wicked; but whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10).

[Col. 0921A] Before the sun of righteousness nothing can remain hidden, for all human ways are open to God’s eyes. “He himself holds the throne of the heavens and looks upon the abyss” (Prov. 16). “He measures heaven with a span and encloses the earth in his fist; he knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain, and he understands the thoughts of each one from afar. A human being sees the face, but God looks upon the heart” (Isa. 40).

## CHAPTER XI. Wisdom, seeing all things beforehand, speaks because all the ways of the one who acts, speaks, and thinks are known to God.

“For all things are known to the Lord God before they were created; so also after completion he regards all things.”

God’s work was known to him from the beginning, and nothing new can happen to him, because before all [Col. 0921B] times he foreknew the works he wished to make in time. After the work was completed, nothing was lacking or had passed away from him, because for him there is neither anything past nor anything future; all things are present before him. In almighty God, the times that are to come always exist as present. Neither do future things arrive for him, nor do past things depart; rather, all things stand together before his eyes. Eternity has no “having been” or “being about to be”; for him, past things do not pass away, nor do future things arrive—he sees all things as present.

“This man will be punished in the streets of the city and will be driven away like a colt; and where he did not expect it, he will be seized. And he will be a disgrace to all because he did not understand the fear of God.”

He is speaking of the adulterer and lustful man mentioned above, who, unbridled like a raging horse and mule, runs about in wantonness after lust and remains in the street—that is, [Col. 0921C] on the broad and spacious way that leads to death. Therefore, where he does not fear the trap, he will find the snare of destruction. And because he neglected to have the fear of God, polluted by the filth of vices, he will be disgraced and despised before the eyes of the saints at the future judgment.

[Col. 0921D] “So also every woman who abandons her husband and establishes an inheritance from another marriage: first, she was unbelieving toward the law of the Most High; second, she abandoned her husband; third, she committed fornication in adultery and established children for herself by another man. She will be brought into the assembly, and attention will be paid to her children. Her children will not put down roots, and her branches will not yield fruit. They will leave her memory under a curse, and her disgrace will not be erased.”

Divine judgment condemns adultery equally in man and woman, and the offspring of such a union is not beloved by the Lord. Nor can a work please him that is clearly produced from the contagion of sin.

In the mystical sense, the synagogue of the heretics—or every soul deceived by heretical perversity—will no longer be pleasing to God, because it has abandoned its former husband and the guide of its youth, who joined it to himself in the covenant of holy baptism and adorned it with ornaments of various virtues. Concerning this it is written at length in Ezekiel: “She joined herself to another husband”—the devil, clearly—“who stained her with various errors [Col. 0922A] and made her guilty in every respect.”

Therefore he says that she first sinned because she was unbelieving toward the law of the Most High, when she refused to follow the faith and tradition of the holy Fathers in the sacred Scriptures. Second, she abandoned her husband because she scorned to possess love of God and neighbor. Third, she committed fornication in adultery when, through error, she entered into a most shameful covenant with the devil. From him she received ignoble children when, at his wicked prompting, she generated corrupt doctrines and perverse works.

She will be brought into the Church, and attention will be paid to her children, when her perversity is exposed everywhere in the assembly of the faithful through the diligence of holy teachers and her doctrine is condemned everywhere. Since her sect has no foundation of truth, [Col. 0922B] it cannot produce a lasting fruit of good works; rather, leaving behind a disgraceful memory, it will be confounded with everlasting shame.

Thus all the faithful, recognizing her future condemnation, reject her association and choose to maintain the firmness of the Catholic faith in all things. For it follows:

“And those who have been abandoned will recognize that there is nothing better than the fear of God and nothing sweeter than to look upon the commandments of the Lord. Great glory is to follow God, for length of days will be received from him.”

Nothing benefits a person more toward attaining everlasting salvation than the fear of God, and nothing is sweeter than to look upon his commandments. Hence the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” [Col. 0922C] And again: “Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz” (Ps. 118).

Great glory is to follow God, because whoever walks in the light does not stumble. Hence Truth itself says: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.” Length of days is also given to him, because everlasting life in eternal blessedness is bestowed upon him, where, with the holy angels, he will praise and confess his Creator forever and ever.

## CHAPTER XII. Praise of Wisdom, through whom all things were made.

(CHAP. 24.) “Wisdom will praise her own soul, and she will be honored in God; she will glory in the midst of her people; she will open her mouth in the assemblies of the Most High, and she will glory in the sight of his power.”

[Col. 0922D] This Wisdom is none other than the one of whom the Apostle said: “I speak of Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). He “praised his own soul” because he showed everyone that his life was worthy of praise. “And she will be honored in God,” because together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit he is worshiped in heaven and on earth. “And she will glory in the midst of her people,” that is, he is proclaimed gloriously among the angelic assemblies and Christian peoples.
