Hence, at his birth, the angels sang, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” “She will open her mouth in the assemblies of the Most High,” because in the gathering of the faithful he proclaims his Gospel, concerning which it is written: “And opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in [Col. 0923A] spirit,” and so forth (Matt. 5). “And she will glory in the sight of his power,” because by displaying his miracles he moved the crowds of the peoples to praise God.

Concerning him it is written: “The multitude of the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits were healed.” And: “The whole crowd sought to touch him, because power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke 6). And elsewhere: “When all the people saw it, they gave praise to God” (Luke 18). And again: “Fear seized everyone, and they glorified God, saying, ‘A great prophet has arisen among us,’ and, ‘God has visited his people’” (Luke 17). And again: “When the crowds saw this, they were afraid and glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings” (Matt. 9).

[Col. 0923B] “He will be exalted in the midst of the people, admired in the holy fullness, praised in the multitude of the elect, and blessed among the blessed.”

“In the midst of the people,” he says, “he will be exalted,” that is, he will be raised to honor in the midst of the Christian people. Concerning him the Psalmist says: “Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of his feet, for it is holy” (Ps. 98).

“And he will be admired in the holy fullness,” because in our Redeemer it pleased the whole fullness to dwell. For he is before all things, and all things hold together in him; he is the head of the body, the Church, who is the beginning and firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place in all things.

Hence John says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, [Col. 0923C] glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1). And from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace.

“In the holy fullness,” he says, “he will be admired,” because God is wonderful in his saints. Hence also “he will have praise in the multitude of the elect, and among the blessed he will be blessed.” For he will give strength and power to his people, the blessed God. “For in the seed of Abraham, that is, in Christ, all the nations of the earth will be blessed.” All his works bless him, and he is also God, blessed above all, forever.

He proclaimed the following words about himself through the vessel suited to him, saying:

## CHAPTER XIII. [Col. 0923D] Praise of Wisdom, through whom all things were made. Wisdom speaks—that is, Christ, the Son of God, the power of God and the wisdom of God, through whom all creatures are ordered.

“‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.’ Wishing, therefore, that the Wisdom of God, who is Christ the Son of God, should show that, according to his divinity, he was not created from any existing things or even from nothing, but begotten from the substance of God the Father, he says: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclus. XXIV). To him the Father says elsewhere: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you’ (Ps. XIX), that is, from the secret place of my substance, from the very Godhead—wholly from the Whole, omnipotence from Omnipotence, light from Light, the Highest from the Highest—a mystery which no inquiry and no understanding can reach. For how can that be comprehended of which it is written: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isa. LIII). This is a marvelous brevity and a measure sufficient for our weakness, since we can grasp no more, and it is entirely enough to have believed this much. And because the Word of God—that is, the Son and Wisdom of God—is so called, he rightly says: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High,’ so that it may be understood that all things were created through the Word and Wisdom of God. ‘For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made’ (John I).

“But when he says that he is the firstborn before every creature, he shows that he was not created together with creation, or created before creation, but begotten from the Father in the beginning. For he is the source of all good, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, has always existed without beginning; through him the Father, whenever he willed and however he willed, made every creature. But because Paul elsewhere calls Christ ‘the firstborn from the dead’ (Col. I), while elsewhere he calls him ‘the firstborn of all creation,’ some ask how, since Christ God and man is one person in the Trinity, the humanity he assumed can be regarded as the firstborn of all creation, since it did not exist before every creature but was received in the last times in order to exist. They do not understand that ‘firstborn’ is said not only with reference to time, but also frequently as a term of honor, because the firstborn is truly so called in relation to those who were begotten after him.

“Scripture therefore often uses this name, ‘firstborn,’ by transference and for the sake of honor, as in the statement addressed to David: ‘I will make him firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth’ (Ps. LXXXVIII); and elsewhere it is written: ‘Israel is my firstborn son’ (Exod. IV), that is, he is honorable to me. For there were also others before Israel who had been considered worthy to be called sons of God. Of them Moses says: ‘The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful, and they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose’ (Gen. VI).

“So also in this passage, where the Apostle had said of Christ that he was ‘the firstborn of all creation,’ that is, honorable above every creature: if he had said simply ‘firstborn,’ he would have called him merely honorable. But because he added ‘of all creation,’ he designates the one who is honored by every creature. Yet Christ, insofar as he is according to the flesh, is also truly called the firstborn in time of the whole creation that was made in him. It is of this that blessed Paul appears to have spoken here.

“Hence, when interpreting what he had said—‘the firstborn of all creation’—he adds: ‘For in him all things were created.’ He did not say ‘through him,’ but ‘in him.’ Nor does he speak of the first creation, but of that division of creation which was made in him, according to which all things formerly divided were brought into one harmony. Thus elsewhere he says: ‘To recapitulate all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth.’ For, because of human wickedness, all creation, so to speak, seemed to be torn apart. The angels and all invisible powers were turning away from us because of our irreverence toward God; [Col. 0925A] moreover, we ourselves were dissolved by death, which brought with it the separation of the soul from the body. Indeed, every bond of creation was thereby being undone. From the beginning, the human being had been made like an animal joined by kinship to all things, since the body consisted generally of everything—that is, of the four elements—while the soul seemed to possess affinity with the invisible powers. A certain union of all things was therefore thought to have been established from that point onward, because of the iniquity that all things seemed to bear toward humanity, with everything converging toward one purpose, so that with one accord they might render due worship to God with watchful care.

“Thus the Wisdom of God himself made all things that are in heaven and on earth. Hence it follows:

“‘I caused the unfailing light to arise in the heavens, and like a cloud I covered all flesh.’ By ‘heaven’ he comprehends spiritual creation, and by ‘flesh,’ bodily creation. The Wisdom of God therefore caused spiritual creatures—that is, angels and human souls—to possess the light of rational understanding; while bodily creatures, according to the will and ordering of their Creator, possess the form proper to their making, so that everything in the nature of things that lives, senses, and understands has its origin from him, because ‘from him, through him, and in him are all things’ (Rom. XI). Notice that he said that she caused light to arise in the heavens and that a cloud covered all flesh, because just as light surpasses the darkness of the cloud by its brightness, so spiritual creation in a certain way surpasses bodily creation in the dignity of its nature. Thus, just as living things precede all things devoid of life, so the soul endowed with reason, by the nobility of its nature, precedes everything that lacks the power of discernment.

“‘I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud.’ Here the Wisdom of God, Christ, shows us both his natures, namely, the divine and the human: the divine in saying that he dwells in the highest places—that is, that together with the Father and the Holy Spirit he reigns as one God above every height of the heavenly kingdom; the human in saying that he has his throne in a pillar of cloud, because the body conceived from the Holy Spirit and brought forth by the virgin mother was not weighed down by any burden of sin, nor bound by the pleasures and desires of earthly things, but was raised up by heavenly power. The throne of royal dignity shone forth in him, and upon it the power of divinity mightily orders and dispenses all its judgments.

“That a cloud signifies the Savior’s flesh Isaiah demonstrates when he says: ‘Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it’ (Isa. XIX). This prophecy therefore refers to the time of the Savior, when he ascended upon a light cloud—that is, the human body which he had assumed from the virgin, not weighed down by any seed of human intercourse—or because he was carried by a light cloud, that is, by a virginal body; and at his entrance all the demons trembled. [Col. 0926A] And since the first overthrow of idols could not endure the presence of the Lord, the Savior’s incarnation is fittingly called a pillar, because of the uprightness of its teaching and the firmness of its action: for he raises his elect to seek everlasting salvation, and he himself carries and sustains the entire structure of his Church.

“‘Alone I traversed the circuit of heaven, penetrated the depths of the abyss, walked upon the waves of the sea, stood in every land, held primacy among every people and every nation, and by my power trod upon the hearts of all the lofty and the lowly.’ This saying expresses everywhere the dominion and strength of the Wisdom of God, because in a single continuous statement it encloses all creation under four names. By ‘heaven’ he comprehends all heavenly things; by ‘the depth of the abyss,’ the things beneath the earth; and by ‘the waves of the sea’ and ‘the earth,’ he indicates everything that consists in these two elements. It therefore signifies that there is nothing in the nature of things that does not lie under his sovereign power. David confirms the same point, when in the Psalms he briefly summons all creation to praise God by a threefold enumeration, saying: ‘Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and all that is in them’ (Ps. LXVIII).

“From this the Apostle, wishing to show that Christ, the Wisdom and Power of God, because of his humble obedience has primacy over every rational creature and by his own power rules over all authorities and kingdoms, elegantly says: ‘Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father’ (Phil. II).”

“‘And among all these I sought rest, and in his inheritance I shall dwell.’ The Wisdom seeks rest for herself among all nations, because from all nations the holy Church is gathered. She is his chosen inheritance, where he himself remains and reigns forever and ever. Concerning her he says through the Psalmist: ‘My inheritance is exceedingly beautiful to me’ (Ps. XV); and in Isaiah: ‘Blessed is my people Egypt, and Assyria, the work of my hands’ (Isa. XIX); but Israel is my inheritance.

“[Col. 0926D] ‘Then the Creator of all things, and he who created me, commanded and said to me: He rested in my tabernacle and said to me: Dwell in Jacob, and take Israel for your inheritance, and put down roots among my elect.’

“What does Wisdom mean when she says that the Creator of all things commanded her, except that the Son, according to his humanity, understands that the Father is greater than he? Hence it follows: ‘He who created me,’ she says, ‘rested in my tabernacle.’ For God’s creating means that he brought forth the humanity of the Only-Begotten Son, conceived in singular purity from the Holy Spirit and born from the virgin Mary. This humanity may rightly also be called a tabernacle, because, insofar as he is the head of the body of the Church, he is the tabernacle of God, in whom it pleased the entire fullness of divinity to dwell.

“It is therefore asked why in the sacred Scriptures almost nothing is said about Wisdom except to show that she was begotten or created by God: begotten, certainly, through whom all things were made; but created or made, as happens in human beings when they turn toward and are illumined by her who was not created or made, but begotten. For in them something comes to be that may be called their wisdom. Or this is foretold or narrated in the Scriptures: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’ In this way Christ became Wisdom, because he became human.

“Is that why Wisdom does not speak, or is anything said about her, in those books except what shows her to have been born or made by God, although the Father himself is also Wisdom? It is because in that Wisdom we were to be commended and instructed to imitate her, and by her imitation we are formed. The Father speaks her as his Word—not in the manner in which a spoken word is brought forth from the mouth or conceived before utterance. This takes place through intervals of time, whereas that is eternal; and by illuminating us he tells us what must be said about himself and about the Father.

“Therefore he says: ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him’ (Luke X), because the Father reveals through the Son, that is, through his Word. If this word that we utter is temporal and passing, and both displays itself and the subject about which we speak, how much more does the Word of God, through whom all things were made? He displays the Father as he is, because he himself is also as the Father is, and this is what the Father is, insofar as he is Wisdom and Essence.

“According to his being the Word, however, he is not the same as the Father, because the Word is not the Father; and ‘Word’ is a relative designation, just as ‘Son’ is, which certainly does not mean ‘Father.’ Thus Christ is the Power and Wisdom of God because, being from the Father who is Power and Wisdom, he himself is also Power and Wisdom, just as the light of God is from the Father who is Light, and the fountain of life is with God the Father, who is the fountain of life. ‘For with you,’ he says, ‘is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light’ (Ps. XXXV), because, ‘as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself.’

“But when he says, ‘Dwell in Jacob and take Israel for your inheritance,’ he either expresses the fact that, through the Savior’s incarnation, the Jewish people were granted the privilege of using his presence, just as he himself replied to the Canaanite woman: ‘I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel’ (Matt. XV); and to the disciples: ‘Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished of the house of Israel’ (Matt. X). Hence it was in Jerusalem that he first founded the primitive Church of God’s elect;

“or it signifies that God’s elect were to be called not only from the former people but also from the Gentiles. For Jacob is sometimes found in Scripture to stand for the ancient people of God, while Israel stands for the people that followed, namely, the Gentiles. Hence it is written in the Psalm: ‘Let Jacob rejoice and Israel exult’ (Ps. XIII, CXLIX). Thus God’s elect were called to the faith of Christ from both peoples, and the root of the Gospel’s teaching was firmly planted in them.

“CHAPTER XIV. [Col. 0928A] Wisdom speaks of her power and of the ordering of her works with the Father.

“‘From the beginning, before the age, I was created, and until the age to come I shall not cease, and in the holy dwelling I ministered before him.’ Christ, the eternal Wisdom of God, affirms that the mystery of his incarnation was foreknown and predestined before the ages. Its power remains without any diminution of itself throughout the age, and in the dwelling of the holy Church it orders and arranges every rite of true religion. Concerning this he adds:

“‘And thus I was established in Zion, and likewise I rested in the sanctified city, and my power was in Jerusalem. And I took root among an honored people, and in the portion of my God was his inheritance, and my lodging was in the fullness of the saints.’

“Zion and Jerusalem therefore signify none other than the city of God, namely, the holy Church, which is built from the first elect to the last. Concerning her the Psalmist says: ‘Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in unity’ (Ps. CXXI). And again: ‘Its foundations,’ he says, ‘are upon the holy mountains. The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God’ (Ps. LXXXVI).

“In this city, therefore, the Wisdom of God bears fruit daily, because there she gathers his elect into the unity of his faith; there she also rests, because she rejoices in the pious intention and good devotion of her saints. ‘Upon whom,’ he says, ‘shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?’ There also her power is manifested, because there her will is continually fulfilled. For although God’s power is absent nowhere, since he does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses, it shines forth most clearly where the observance of his commandments grows strongest.

“‘And I took root among an honored people, and in the portion of my God was his inheritance, and my lodging was in the fullness of the saints.’ By ‘an honored people’ he means the Christian people, which has deserved honor through the distinguished proclamation of his name. It is called his portion and inheritance because, among all the nations of the world, it alone belongs to his lot; and his lodging is in the fullness of the saints, because they are members of his body, and he is all things in all.

“No provision, therefore, could have been made more benevolently for the human race than when the Wisdom of God herself—that is, the only Son, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father—deigned to assume the whole human being: ‘And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’ In this way he demonstrated to carnal people, who cannot contemplate the truth with the mind and are devoted to bodily senses, how exalted a place human nature has among creatures—not merely by appearing visibly. For that could also have been done in some ethereal body adapted to endure the sight of our eyes; but he appeared to human beings in a true human being. The very nature that was to be liberated had to be assumed. And so that no one might perhaps think that either sex had been despised by its Creator, he assumed a man and was born from a woman. He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition, although he did drive the buyers and sellers from the temple with blows. But what of that, or how great is it? Even though he also expelled demons unwillingly from human beings—not by persuasive speech, but by the force of his power.

“For the old slavery had passed away, and the time of freedom had dawned. It was now fittingly urged upon humanity; and he who was to be subjected to suffering in the human being he bore won faith for God by miracles, showing how free in will humanity had been created.

“‘Like a cedar I was exalted in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion.’ The cedar and the cypress are trees of extraordinary height and exceptional fragrance. Lebanon is the highest mountain of the Phoenicians, remembered by the prophets; it is named from incense because incense is gathered there. [Col. 0929B] Zion is a hill rising above Jerusalem, and it is interpreted as ‘mirror.’

“These names of trees and mountains therefore suit the more eminent members of Christ, who can say with the Apostle: ‘We are the good fragrance of Christ to God’ (II Cor. II); ‘Our citizenship is in heaven’ (Phil. III); and ‘Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?’ (Rom. VIII). And so forth.

“But the fact that the fragrance of cedar is accustomed to kill and drive away serpents, in accordance with the poet’s words (Virgil, Georgics III):

> Learn also to kindle fragrant cedar in the stalls,  
> and drive away the heavy serpents with the scent of galbanum,

is fittingly applied to those same holy teachers, who by the power of the heavenly word are accustomed to repel the poisonous doctrines of heretics and drive them away from the seduction of the simple.

“Moreover, who does not see how fitting for those same holy preachers is the fact that its resin, called *cedria*, is so useful for preserving books that those coated with it neither suffer moth damage nor grow old with time? Through their spiritual understanding the holy Scripture has been composed; it can be corrupted by no heretical cunning and consumed by no passing age. Thus the Lord says: ‘Until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one stroke shall pass from the law until all things are accomplished.’ Since the Lord said this of the Law, how much more did he leave it to be understood of the Gospel?

“The cypress, too, in that it is suitable for healing bodily ailments and does not lay aside the beauty of its foliage under any force of the winds, expresses the constancy and activity of those who adorn the holy Church with the higher ornaments of virtue.

“‘Like a palm I was exalted in Kadesh.’ The palm is a tree with long-lasting leaves and sweet fruits. It is called *palma* because it is the adornment of a victorious hand, or because its branches are spread out in the form of a human palm. It is a tree distinguished by victory, with a tall and beautiful shoot, clothed in enduring foliage.

“The Greeks call it *phoenix*, because it lives for a long time, taking its name from that Arabian bird which is said to live for many years. This tall tree is therefore compared with the holy Church, which refuses to bend toward earthly desire and raises its entire self toward the attainment of heavenly things. Concerning her the Apostle admonishes: ‘Watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully’ (I Cor. XVI). Concerning her the Lord himself also says: ‘I am the Lord, who brought you out of the slavery by which the Egyptians oppressed you, so that you might walk upright’ (Exod. VI).

“The palm is the adornment of a victorious hand; moreover, among the ancients, whoever won in a contest was crowned with a golden palm. The stature of the bride is therefore likened to a palm when, standing upright in love of heavenly things, the entire intention of the faithful meditates upon them, while she remains in the battle line awaiting that prize with which she is to be rewarded as victor when the contest is ended.

“Furthermore, because the palm appears rough near the ground but displays beauty and sweet fruit at the top, its stature is rightly compared with that of the Church, or of every faithful soul, which bears harsh labors on earth for the Lord but hopes to receive from the Lord a most delightful reward in heaven. The palm is rough near the ground because the elect suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. It is beautiful and sweet at the top because they rejoice in afflictions and exult, knowing ‘that their reward is abundant in heaven.’

“Likewise, since the palm is clothed in enduring foliage and preserves its leaves without succession, who does not see that it represents the form of faith? Amid the changing condition of the passing age, faith always retains the same words of right confession, like leaves that never fall; and it preserves undefiled among its elect, until the end of the age, the same perfection of works that it received at the beginning, like the beauty of palm branches.

“Quite appropriately, Kadesh is assigned to the exaltation of the palm. We read in the Book of Numbers that, at the thirty-third encampment, the children of Israel pitched their tents in the wilderness of Sin, that is, Kadesh, where Miriam died and was buried; and because of the waters of contradiction Moses and Aaron offended the Lord and were forbidden to cross the Jordan (Num. XXXIII).

“It seems to me that in the dead Miriam a prophecy was made of the end imposed upon the Law and the priesthood of the Jews in Moses and Aaron: they themselves were unable to cross into the promised land, nor could they lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this world. There the state of the Church also began to be ordered through Christ, because he is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

“Kadesh is interpreted as ‘changed’ or ‘transferred.’ These names suit the holy Church well, for she was transferred from the worship of idols and changed from pagan error, and began to be the true worshiper of the one God.

“She is therefore exalted like a palm in Kadesh when holy and perfect men in the Church are raised up in faith and conduct to seek the homeland of the heavenly kingdom and to possess the everlasting joys of the life to come. After the exaltation of the palm tree, Scripture adds another comparison, saying:

“‘And like a plantation of roses in Jericho.’ The rose is named from the appearance of its flower, because it is red with a glowing color. It signifies the blood of martyrdom. Jericho was a city which Jesus destroyed after crossing the Jordan, killing its king. In its place Oza of Bethel, from the tribe of Ephraim, built another, which the Lord and Savior deigned to honor by his presence. But this city too, at the time when Jerusalem was being attacked by the Romans, was captured and destroyed because of the treachery of its citizens. In its place a third city was built, which still exists today, and the traces of both cities are shown to the present day.

“Jericho is interpreted as ‘its fragrance,’ or ‘moon.’ A ‘plantation of roses in Jericho,’ therefore, exists when the fragrance of virtues, together with the suffering of martyrdom, breathes forth in the merits of the saints. The moon, because of the increase and decrease of its light, figuratively expresses the Church’s pilgrimage amid the mortality of the present life, in which some are born daily and others depart from this life.

“‘Like a beautiful olive tree in the fields.’ In Greek the olive is called *oleon*, from which the word *oliva* was taken into Latin. The *olea* is the tree itself, the olive its fruit, and oil its juice. It is a tree notably associated with peace.

“What else is signified by the olive except the holy Church? Transplanted in the fields of the whole world, she illumines the entire world with her beauty and sanctifies believers through the grace of the Holy Spirit by the anointing of sacred chrism. For through the richness of oil, by which tired and weakened limbs are refreshed and the grace of light is supplied, the inner love of the mind and the work of mercy are often signified.

“Hence the Psalmist says: ‘But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of my God forever and ever’ (Ps. LI). It is as though he plainly said: Because I have offered the fruit of mercy to those in need, I too have hoped that the grace of mercy will be repaid to me by God forever.

“‘And like a plane tree I was exalted beside water in the streets.’ The plane tree is named from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and broad; for the Greeks call broad *platos*. Scripture has expressed both the name and the form of this tree when it says: ‘Like a plane tree I was spread out in the streets.’

“It has very tender and soft leaves and resembles the vine. Mystically, this tree signifies the Lord Christ, who is spread throughout the whole world in his members and everywhere displays to the faithful the saving examples of his gentleness and innocence.

“Concerning this tree it is written in the Psalms: ‘And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water’ (Ps. I). In my judgment, the Lord Christ is rightly compared with a fruitful tree because of the cross which he accepted for the salvation of humanity. It is deservedly called the tree of life, since upon it was suspended the Lord Christ, who is our life, and to the thief who confessed on that same cross it was said: ‘Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.’

“Indeed, even today everyone who believes in him receives the gifts of eternal life. Or, as the historical account relates, there truly was a tree of perpetual life in paradise, had detestable disobedience not intervened. For how would death have gained entrance if Adam had shown an attitude of devotion? From this the most holy Fathers poured forth their sweetest honey, saying: ‘He gave a commandment, so that he might discover free choice; he fixed a law, so that he might make humanity more cautious.’

“But when Adam imprudently followed the enemy and unhappily abandoned the author of life, then, deceived by a lamentable fate, he lost the perpetual life he was about to possess and fell into the death he had not possessed. But, to return to the terms of the comparison we began, when it says that it was planted—that is, that the wood of the cross was established by God so that it might always grow green and increase in faith—it continues, ‘beside streams of water,’ maintaining the force of the comparison.

“For just as flowing earthly water is the life of green trees, so spiritual water floods the sign of the cross, which is known to be the salvation of faithful souls. This is the water of which it is said in the Gospel: ‘If you knew who it is who asks you for water, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water, and so forth’ (John IV).

“It is also worthwhile to consider why he said ‘beside streams of water’: namely, so that neither excessive flooding would destroy the tree, nor irrigation located too far away would dry it out. Thus the cross of Christ’s passion was exalted beside water in the streets, because the wondrous mystery of our redemption became known to all the nations throughout the world through the preaching of the Gospel, so that everyone might recognize that the effect of their salvation rests in him and therefore understand that they ought rightly to offer their Redeemer a pure affection of love.

“‘Like cinnamon and balsam giving fragrance, I gave a sweet smell.’ Cinnamon and balsam are aromatic trees. Cinnamon is so called because its bark is round and slender like a reed. It grows in the regions of India and Ethiopia, on a short shrub only two cubits high, darkish or ash-colored, with very slender branches. What grows thick is despised; what grows more slender is excellent. When broken, it emits a visible breath resembling a cloud or dust.

“Pliny the Elder reports the following about balsam (Book XII, chapter 24): ‘In the same region aspalathus balsam grows, with a white thorn, the size of a small tree, and a rose-like flower; its root is sought for ointments. They say that in whatever shrub the rainbow bends its arch, that same aspalathus possesses a sweetness of fragrance, but in balsam an indescribable one. Some call it *erysisceptrum*, others *sceptre*. It is tested by its reddish or fiery color, its dense texture to the touch, and its beaver-like odor. It is exchanged at fifteen pounds.’

“These two little trees, because of their shortness, are classified by some among the fragrant herbs. They rightly signify those who are humble in spirit because of their very smallness, and theirs is the kingdom of heaven. They are, as it were, clothed in purple, always mindful of the Lord’s passion, always ready themselves to suffer for the Lord, like the one who says: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter’ (Ps. XLIII).

“This is also the virtue that is accustomed especially to chastise and remove among us the movements and lusts of the soul, as though they were pains of the entrails, when we reflect upon what God suffered for us and recognize that we suffer less than we deserve.

“Cinnamon and balsam are therefore rightly joined, because the state of our conduct ought to be conformed to the mystery of the Lord’s passion, so that, in accordance with John’s teaching, just as he laid down his life for us, so we too may learn to lay down our lives for our brothers (I John III).

“That cinnamon is said to be darkish or ash-colored suits the souls of the humble, who, conscious of their own frailty, know how to say to God in their daily prayers: ‘I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes’ (Gen. XVIII). And again: ‘I condemn myself, and I repent in dust and ashes’ (Job XLII).

“But the fact that balsam resembles a white thorn with a rose-colored flower signifies that we ought daily to imitate the pain of the Lord’s passion in the narrowness of our conduct, in accordance with the Gospel saying: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me’ (Luke IX). And that its root is sought for ointments signifies that Christ’s humility commends the fragrance of every virtue and overflows for God’s elect into the sweetness of eternal delight.

“‘Like choice myrrh I gave the sweetness of fragrance.’ What else is signified by choice myrrh except the praiseworthy continence of the saints? It breathes forth before the Lord with the sweetest fragrance because the sweetness of charity inflames it most abundantly.

“Myrrh and aloe express bodily continence, since it is the nature of these aromatics that bodies anointed with them do not readily decay, as the evidence of the Lord’s burial also testifies. Just as the corruption of dead flesh signifies the putrefaction of lust, so its preservation—when interpreted typologically in a positive sense—most aptly demonstrates the virtue of continence and chastity, which restrains our members from vices.

“Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, up to five cubits high, resembling the thorn which the Greeks call *acanthon*. Its sap is green and bitter, from which it also receives the name *myrrh*. All these features appropriately correspond to the mortification of the flesh, which is felt as bitter for a time but is most willingly accepted in hope of the ever-green homeland—that is, the homeland of which Peter says: ‘He regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, into an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance’ (I Pet. I), one that does not fade, kept in heaven for you.

“It is rightly compared with a thorn, because, in order to preserve the mind forever, it afflicts the body temporarily with the pricks of labors. Moreover, since its sap, flowing spontaneously, is more precious, while that extracted by wounding the bark is judged inferior, who does not see that greater virtue before God is shown when someone strives to chastise his healthy and vigorous body and subject it to servitude, even while worldly abundance smiles outwardly, than when, pressed by illness or other adversities of the world, he unwillingly restrains the flesh from lust and confines it to the remedy of abstinence?

“Nevertheless, this too must rightly be counted among the great virtues, when someone patiently, humbly, and gratefully receives the scourges of paternal correction and, chastened by them, arrives at the gifts of the promised inheritance.”

“‘And like storax and galbanum, and onycha, and gum.’ These spices are therefore regarded by physicians as exceedingly precious, and sacramentally signify the forms of the virtues which spiritual physicians apply to the healing of human beings. For storax is an Arabian tree resembling the Sidonian apple, whose little branches, around the rising of the Dog Star, let fall tears through openings. Its distillation, when it falls onto the ground, is not clean, but is preserved in a hollow of its own bark; that which clings to the branches and shoots is clean and whitish. Afterwards it becomes yellow because of the sun; and this storax, called “calamite,” is fat, resinous, of pleasant fragrance, moist, and emitting something like a honeyed liquid. It is called storax because it is the flowing and congealed drop of a tree. For the Greeks call it a drop of styrax. In Greek it is styrax; in Latin, storax.

“Galbanum, as Pliny reports (Book XII, chapter 25), is produced by Syria on Mount Amanus; it is the resin of a ferula of the same name, which they call *stagonitis*. They especially praise the cartilaginous, pure kind, resembling ammoniacum and as little woody as possible. Onycha is the same substance that is called *onycha* in Exodus (Exod. XXX); it was prescribed, together with the other aromatics, for making the Lord’s incense. What is called *onyx* in Greek is called *ungula* in Latin, because it is shaped like a human fingernail.

“Gum, which is also called ammoniacum, drips tears in its own sands. There are two varieties: *straton*, which resembles male frankincense and is especially prized; and another, fatty and sandy, which they call *pirama*. It is adulterated with sand seemingly seized while it was growing; nevertheless, it is judged by its clods, which should be as small and pure as possible. This gum, or ammoniacum, possesses the medicinal property of curing hardenings contracted from some necessity.

“These kinds of aromatic substances are fragrant because, at the Lord’s command, they were assigned for making incense. Wherever our books have ‘incense,’ the Hebrew reads *necotha*, which Aquila translated as ‘storax’; it signifies the incense of prayer together with the fragrance of holy virtues. We make incense compounded from aromatics when we give off fragrance on the altar of good works through the multiplicity of virtues. It becomes mixed and pure, because the more one virtue is joined to another, the more sincerely the incense of good works is offered.

“Therefore Exodus rightly says: ‘And when you have crushed all these things into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the tabernacle of testimony’ (Exod. XXX). We crush all the aromatics into the finest powder when we examine our good deeds, as it were, in the hidden scrutiny of the heart, and carefully reconsider whether they are truly good. To reduce aromatics to powder, then, is to wear down the virtues by recollection and to recall them for the subtle examination of what is hidden. It should also be noted that of this same powder it is said: ‘You shall place some of it before the tabernacle of testimony’ (ibid.), because our good deeds are truly pleasing in the sight of the Judge when the mind, by more subtle recollection, crushes them and, as it were, produces powder from the aromatics, so that what is done may not be coarse and hard; nor, if the tight hand of reconsideration fails to pulverize it, may it fail to spread its fragrance with greater subtlety.

“‘And like uncut frankincense I gave forth my fragrance throughout my dwelling.’ If we follow the Hebrew etymology, *Libanus* is interpreted as ‘whiteness’; if the Greek, ‘frankincense.’ Thus, in the Song of Songs, where we read, ‘to the hill of incense,’ some manuscripts have, ‘to the hill of Lebanon’ (Song IV). It is evident to everyone that both names signify the diligent practice of virtue.

“It is worthwhile to instruct the uninformed briefly about the nature of this aromatic. It is an Arabian tree, resembling, they say, the laurel in bark and leaf, emitting a sap like an almond, which is collected twice a year, in autumn and spring. In preparation for the autumn collection, the trees are cut in the bark during the fiercest heat of summer; a rich foam bursts forth, and when it congeals it thickens wherever the nature of the place requires, being caught in a covering of palm leaves. What remains clinging to the tree is scraped off with iron; for this reason the purest frankincense appears bark-covered. This is also the white frankincense.

“The second harvest is in spring. The same trees, when their bark has been cut in winter, produce this red substance, which is not comparable to the former. The frankincense of a young tree is believed to be whiter, but that of an old tree more fragrant. What hangs from it in a rounded drop we call ‘male.’ The frankincense-bearing region is called Sarvia. The Greeks say that this name signifies ‘mystery’; it is inaccessible on every side because of cliffs and, on the right, impassable to the sea because of crags. It is carried out by one narrow route. The forests are one hundred thousand paces long—or, as some report, eighty thousand—and half that in breadth. High hills rise up, and trees that have grown spontaneously run down into the plains. The soil is said to be clayey, with few springs, but springs rich in natron.

“These observations about the nature and location of frankincense, drawn briefly from the books of the ancients, have been stated because nearly all of them, if one pays careful attention, correspond figuratively to the virtues of the saints—especially the fact that the region in which it grows is called ‘mystery.’ For the fact that the trees grow spontaneously aptly applies to those whose highest virtue is wondrous not because they are compelled by legal decrees, but because of voluntary offering, as the Lord says: ‘If you would be perfect, go, sell …’ (Matt. XIX).

“That frankincense flows as a tear from trees that have been cut—what does it indicate but the compunction of the humble heart, from which pure prayer, sweetened by tears, is customarily born? The fact that the region has rare but natron-bearing springs suits those from whose belly flow, as Scripture says, rivers of living water (John VII)—that is, gifts of spiritual teaching which are also suitable for cleansing the minds of their neighbors. For natron is especially useful both for healing illnesses and for washing away impurities.

“The fact that the region is surrounded on every side by the protection of cliffs and crags corresponds to the merits of those of whom the Lord speaks in a parable: ‘There was a householder who planted a vineyard and surrounded it with a hedge’ (Matt. XXI). For the Lord planted the Church by establishing it in the commandments of life, and he surrounded it with a hedge, protecting it everywhere with the guardianship of his protection, so that it could not be destroyed by wicked spirits or human beings.

“‘And like unmixed balsam is my fragrance.’ The balsam tree was found in Judea within an area of only twenty *iugera*. After the Romans had taken possession of that region, it was propagated across very extensive hills. Its trunk resembles a vine; its leaves resemble those of rue, but are whiter and evergreen.

“The balsam tree itself is called *balsamum*; its wood is called *xylobalsamum*; its fruit or seed, *carpobalsamum*; and its sap, *opobalsamum*. The name is qualified in this way because, when the bark of the wood is struck with iron instruments, a drop of exceptional fragrance flows through openings. An opening is called *ope* in Greek; they adulterate the drop by mixing in cyprine oil or honey. Its purity is tested against honey if it coagulates when mixed with milk, and against oil if, when sprinkled into water or mixed with it, it is easily dispersed. It is also tested by whether woolen garments stained with it remain unmarked. Adulterated balsam does not coagulate with milk, floats upon water like oil, and stains clothing.

“If balsams are pure, they have such force that, when the sun grows hot, they cannot be held in the hand.

“This liquid, balsam, is mentioned mystically in the Song of Songs, where the bride speaks of the bridegroom: ‘While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he will lie between my breasts. My beloved is a cluster of henna to me, in the vineyards of Engaddi’ (Song I).

“According to the surface meaning of the words, the sense of this final verse is indeed as follows: just as the island of Cyprus is accustomed to produce clusters larger than those of other lands, and just as in the Judean city called Engaddi more excellent vineyards grow than elsewhere, since from them flows not wine but the liquid of balsam, so my beloved is special to me, joined to me by love above all others, so that no creature can tear me away from his affection.

“Typologically, however, just as myrrh, because of its bitterness—for it is as beneficial in healing illnesses as it is bitter to the taste—signifies the sorrow of the Lord’s Passion, when he himself received myrrhed wine from the soldiers to drink and, as we have said, was anointed with myrrh by the disciples for burial, so the cluster not incongruously announces the joy of the resurrection. Wine gladdens the human heart. The Lord, therefore, who had been a bundle of myrrh in his Passion, became a cluster of Cyprus in his resurrection.

“Rightly does he remain between the breasts of the bride, because the same one has been changed into a cluster of the vine. Therefore the holy Church never removes the memory of the Lord’s death from her heart, because he who died for her sins also rose from death for her justification, and he grants to her, as she follows his footsteps, an example of rising after the anguish of death.

“He is also rightly remembered as being in the vineyards of Engaddi. For, as we have said, balsam grows in the vineyards of Engaddi. It is customarily mixed into the olive oil in the preparation of chrism and consecrated by pontifical blessing, so that all the faithful may be marked by this anointing through the laying on of the priest’s hand, by which the Holy Spirit is received. By it also the Lord’s altar is dedicated, and the other things that ought to be sacred are anointed.

“Accordingly, the divine charisms are most rightly represented by the vineyards of Engaddi; and the bridegroom is in the vineyards of Engaddi because the Lord himself, appearing in the flesh, is full of the Holy Spirit, and he himself bestows the Spirit’s gifts upon believers.

“He calls the balsam trees vineyards because they rise in the manner of vineyards and sustain themselves without supports, being more like vines than myrtles. Distinguished by their perpetual foliage, they reach a height of no more than two cubits. Their seed resembles wine in taste and is reddish in color; their branch is thicker than that of the myrtle. At a certain season of the year they exude balsam. The farmers also cut their shoots with sharp stone or bone knives, since contact with iron harms them. Through these incisions a sap of exceptional fragrance flows forth. Caught in wool and dripping beautifully like tears, it is collected in small horns. Because it flows through an opening in the bark, it is more often called *opobalsamum*; for, as we said, an opening is called *ope* in Greek.

“The more abundant vein of each tree is struck three times during the heats: the tear has the highest value, the seed the second, the bark the third, and the wood the least. All these things, if carefully considered, suit our Redeemer most aptly. Humble in the flesh, yet appearing full of grace and virtue, he ‘was wounded for our iniquities’ and poured forth from his wounds the sacraments of life and salvation for us.

“Therefore he himself, who is the power and wisdom of God, says here in Ecclesiasticus: ‘And like unmixed balsam is my fragrance.’ Truly remarkable is the order of the words: first the bride says that, when the king was reclining, her nard gave forth its fragrance; then she compares him to a bundle of myrrh; third, she calls him a cluster of Cyprus; finally, she recalls him as being in the vineyards of Engaddi. For first, while the Lord was reclining at the supper, a devout woman poured nard over him. Then the disciples wrapped him, crucified and destined for burial, in linen after anointing him with myrrh. After this, when the joy of the resurrection immediately arrived, he distributed spiritual gifts to the faithful.

“Nor should it be passed over that Engaddi is interpreted as ‘the spring of the kid.’ By this name the bath of holy baptism is clearly indicated: into it we descend while still sinners and worthy of the left hand, but, cleansed from the foulness of sins, we ascend to be counted among the lambs.

“And rightly, when it signified the joy of the Lord’s resurrection by saying, ‘My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me,’ it immediately added, ‘in the vineyards of Engaddi,’ that is, ‘in the springs of the kid.’ This is plainly to say: in the spiritual gifts that are bestowed upon the faithful from the time of baptism.

“Up to this point the Church has received from her Redeemer the gifts that she testifies to be pledges of love. Divine Wisdom therefore rightly says, ‘Like unmixed balsam is my fragrance,’ because it has no contamination of error, admits no fellowship with the faithless, but its teaching is pure and sincere, free from every stain of heretics. It gives off the fragrance of sacred virtues and pours the grace of the Holy Spirit into the minds of the faithful.

“‘I spread out my branches like a terebinth.’ The terebinth is a tree with a Greek name, producing resin superior to every other resin. Pliny the Second reports the following about the terebinth:

“‘Syria has the terebinth. Of these, the male trees are without fruit; of the female trees there are two kinds. In one, the fruit is red, the size of a lentil; in the other, it is pale, ripening with the vine, not larger than a bean, more pleasant in smell, and winding in shape. Around Mount Ida in the Troad, and in Macedonia, it is a short tree and fruitful. In Damascus of Syria it is large in timber, very tough and shining; its flower is clustered like that of the olive, but red; its leaves are dense. It also produces pods that emit certain creatures resembling gnats, and a lighter resin that bursts from the bark.’

“What, then, is signified by the terebinth except the condition of the Church, which extends her branches throughout the whole world? Through the preaching of the Gospel she spreads the branches of faith among every people and enlarges the place of her dwelling. Through another likeness Isaiah says to her: ‘Enlarge the place of your tent, and do not spare to stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; lengthen your cords and strengthen your nails. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations and inhabit deserted cities’ (Isa. LIV).

“Her resin is most excellent because her medicine, by which she comes to the aid of the illnesses of souls, is perfect. This also corresponds to what we have already said about the varieties of this tree: the male trees are without fruit, while there are two kinds of female trees, one of which has red fruit and the other pale fruit, ripening with the vine.

“For those who, through arrogance of mind, attribute some vigor of their own virtue to themselves exist without the fruit of virtues. But those who, recognizing their weakness, place all their hope in the help and grace of their Creator seek either the fruit of martyrdom through endurance of suffering, or, through continence and purity of heart and body, possess a special reward in the heavenly kingdom with the Lamb. They will sing that song which, as Revelation records, the one hundred and forty-four thousand who stood with the Lamb upon Mount Zion sang: ‘No one could sing that song except the one hundred and forty-four thousand who were purchased from the earth, who were not defiled with women, and are without blemish before the throne of God’ (Rev. XIV).

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0937]

## CHAPTER ONE

Wisdom speaks with a mother’s affection, as in the passage: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wanted to gather your children, like a hen.”

“‘I bore fruit like a vine, the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are the fruit of honor and dignity.’ What is expressed by this vine except the one who says to his disciples in the Gospel: ‘I am the true vine, and you are the branches’ (John XV)? Its wine gladdens the human heart when, by drinking his blood, people joyfully praise the venerable sacrament of their redemption. This vine produces the sweetness of fragrance when the fame of evangelical preaching is spread throughout the whole world. Its flowers are the fruit of honor and uprightness, because the joy and beauty of all virtues daily blossom and shine through his gift among the crowds of believers.

“‘I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope.’ The Wisdom of God, therefore, which is Christ, is the mother of beautiful love and the source of all virtues, because through his grace the affection of true charity, salutary fear, understanding of spiritual knowledge, and hope of eternal life and future joy are generated in the hearts of the elect. Without him we have no good thing, since ‘every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights’; he himself is the fountain of life, and ‘in his light we shall see light’ (James I). Of him Paul also says: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’ (II Cor. XV). Hence it follows:

## CHAPTER TWO

Wisdom exhorts, saying: “You who desire me, be filled from my generations; and my Spirit is sweeter than honey”—that Spirit, namely, of whom he says: “The Father sends the Spirit of truth in my name”; and, “He will receive from what is mine and teach you all things,” and so forth.

“‘In me is every grace of life and truth; in me is every hope of life and virtue.’ Through him we have our present life, because ‘in him we live and move and are’; through him we shall have true and everlasting life in the future; through him we hope to receive immortality and the heavenly crown of glory. Therefore, by his gift, we strive according to our measure, walking along the path of virtues, to arrive at the rest of our heavenly homeland.

“‘Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled from my generations.’ With motherly affection Wisdom admonishes her children to hasten to her, to be enriched by her gift, and to be restored by her help. The testimony of the Gospel is similar, in which the Savior mercifully encourages those who labor to come to him: ‘Come,’ he says, ‘to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matt. XI). And again: ‘Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink; and from his belly will flow rivers of living water’ (John VII).

“‘For my Spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance is sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.’ This Spirit is none other than the Holy Spirit, who is common to the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the Father and proceeds from the Son; he is sent by the Father and sent by the Son, as Truth itself testifies in the Gospel, saying: ‘The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything I have said to you’ (John XIV). And again: ‘I will send,’ he says, ‘the promise of my Father upon you; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’ (Luke XXIV).

“This Spirit is sweeter than honey because the love of God, which is poured into the hearts of the elect through him, is sweetness beyond comparison. And the heavenly inheritance that will be given to the saints in the knowledge and love of God, when they see him face to face and delight in his right hand forever, cannot be expressed but is wholly beyond estimation, because it is written: ‘Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him’ (I Cor. II).

“‘My memory is for the generations of the ages.’ The memory of the Wisdom of God will endure through the generations of all ages, because the angels praise it, the archangels praise it together with them, the prophets proclaim it, the apostles preach it, and the whole army of heavenly virtues and the countless multitude of holy souls adore and glorify it forever.

“‘Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst.’ There is a great difference between bodily pleasures and spiritual ones. Bodily pleasures, when they are not possessed, kindle a grievous desire; but when they are eagerly consumed, they immediately turn the eater to disgust through satiety.

“Spiritual pleasures, by contrast, are distasteful when they are not possessed, but desirable when they are possessed. The more they are eaten by the one who eats, the more they are hungered for by the hungry. In bodily pleasures the appetite is pleasing but the experience displeasing; in spiritual pleasures the appetite is contemptible, while the experience is more pleasing. In the former, appetite produces satiety, and satiety produces disgust; in the latter, appetite produces satiety, and satiety produces appetite.

“Spiritual pleasures increase desire in the mind even as they satisfy it. The more their flavor is perceived, the more one understands what must be loved with greater eagerness. For this reason they cannot be loved when they are not possessed, because their flavor is unknown. Who can love what he does not know? Accordingly, the Psalmist admonishes us when he says: ‘Taste and see that the Lord is sweet’ (Ps. XXXIII). It is as though he were saying: You do not know his sweetness if you do not taste it at all; but touch the food of life with the palate of the heart, so that, having tested its sweetness, you may be able to love it.

“Human beings lost these pleasures when they sinned in paradise. Cast away from the food of eternal sweetness, they closed their mouths. We too, born amid the misery of this exile, come here already full of disgust; we do not know what we ought to desire. The disease of our disgust grows stronger the farther the soul is separated from eating that sweetness, and it no longer longs for inward pleasures because it has long and extensively grown unaccustomed to eating them.

“Thus we waste away in our disgust and are worn down by the long plague of hunger. Because we do not wish to taste inwardly the sweetness set before us, miserable as we are, we love our outward hunger. Yet heavenly mercy does not abandon even those who abandon it. It recalls those pleasures we have despised before the eyes of our memory and, by setting them before us as a promise, shakes off our torpor and invites us to repel our disgust.

“But what benefit the taste of spiritual pleasures possesses, the following sentence makes clear:

“‘Whoever hears me will not be confounded, and those who work in me will not sin.’ What is it to hear and love the Lord except to obey his commandments? As he himself says in the Gospel: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word’ (John XIV). Such a person will certainly not be confounded, because he will be crowned with an eternal reward for obedience to God’s commandments. Those who work in the wisdom and love of God will not sin, but will altogether flee the stain of sins. For it is written: ‘Charity,’ he says, ‘does not act wrongly, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth’ (I Cor. XIII). And the apostle John says: ‘Everyone who remains in him does not sin’ (I John III).

“‘Those who make me shine will have eternal life.’ What is it to make wisdom shine except to receive its full and perfect knowledge? Whoever possesses perfect knowledge of God will possess eternal life and the joys of the heavenly kingdom. Of this Truth itself says to the Father in the Gospel: ‘This is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent’ (John XVII).

“But because no one in this life can enjoy the vision of God perfectly, as he himself testifies, saying, ‘For no human being shall see me and live’ (Exod. XXXIII), this grace is reserved for the future life: ‘For now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face. Now we know in part, but then we shall know even as we are known.’

“‘All these things the book of life’—the phrase implies—contains. And it immediately adds what that book is:

“‘The testament of the Most High and the knowledge of truth.’ This book contains the New and Old Testaments, in which there is knowledge of the truth, because through it the faith and teaching of the Savior are revealed. The prophet Ezekiel mentions this book (Ezek. II), and the apostle John does not remain silent about it in his Apocalypse (Rev. X).

“‘Moses commanded the law in the precepts of righteousness, and an inheritance to the house of Jacob, and promises to Israel.’ It is clear that through Moses the Lord gave the law to the house of Jacob, that is, to the former people, in which there were commandments of righteousness: namely, that they should beware of sins and serve God through holy virtues. In this law God’s promises to Israel were found, because through the coming of the Savior the redemption of the human race was foretold in it, as in that Mosaic passage in Deuteronomy: ‘The Lord,’ he says, ‘will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him’ (Deut. XVIII).

“And this promise was made not only in the law but also in the prophets, as it is written: ‘The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: From the fruit of your womb I will place upon my throne’ (Ps. CXXXI). Hence it follows:

“‘He appointed David his servant to raise up from him a king, very strong, sitting upon a throne of honor forever.’ This statement does not refer to the historical Solomon, who lost the kingdom because of sin, but to the true peacemaker, namely our Lord, who, strong in battle, conquered the strong one, the devil; ‘whose power is eternal, and whose kingdom shall have no end.’ Born from David’s seed according to the flesh, he possesses perpetual kingship not only over Judea but also over the whole world—indeed, over heaven and earth.

“‘He fills, like the Pishon, with wisdom, and like the Tigris in the days of new growth; he fills, like the Euphrates, with understanding; he multiplies, like the Jordan, in the time of harvest; he sends discipline like light, and, standing forth like the Gihon, in the time of vintage.’

“Let us first speak of the natures of the rivers, as we have learned them from writers on natural matters, and then unfold their allegory accordingly.

“Pishon is a river that is also called the Ganges. It flows out from paradise and proceeds toward the regions of India. It is called Pishon, that is, ‘crowd,’ because, when ten great rivers are joined to it, it is filled and becomes one. It is called Ganges after Gangar, king of India. It is said to rise in the manner of the Nile and to burst forth over the lands of the East.

“The Tigris is a river of Mesopotamia that rises from paradise, runs toward the Assyrians, and, after many circuits, flows into the Dead Sea. It received this name because of its speed, running with extraordinary swiftness like the beast called the tiger.

“The Euphrates is a river of Mesopotamia rising from paradise, exceedingly rich in gems, which flows through the middle of Babylon. It received its name from crops or fertility, for in Hebrew *Euphrata* is interpreted as ‘fertility.’ In some places it irrigates Mesopotamia just as the Nile irrigates Alexandria. Sallust, a most reliable authority, asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from one spring in Armenia; then, traveling in different directions, they separate over a considerable distance, leaving many thousands of miles between them. The land enclosed by them is nevertheless called Mesopotamia.

“Jordan is a river of Judea named from two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan. When these, although far apart, are joined together in one channel, the river thereafter is called Jordan. It rises beneath Mount Lebanon, divides Judea and Arabia, and, after many circuits, flows near Jericho into the Dead Sea.

“The Gihon is a river flowing out from paradise and encircling the whole of Ethiopia. It is called by this name because, by the increase of its flooding, it waters the land of Egypt. For *ge* in Greek signifies ‘earth’ in Latin. Among the Egyptians it is called the Nile because of the silt it carries, which produces fertility. Hence the name Nile is said to be derived as though from *Niam ciaon*. Formerly, the Nile was called *Melo* in Latin.

“It appears in Lake Nilides, from which it turns southward and is received by Egypt. There, driven back by the northern winds, its waters struggling backward, it swells and produces the inundation of Egypt.

“The fact that Wisdom compares the four rivers of paradise, proceeding from one source, to the king who arose from David signifies that from our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and also the true Son of man—that is, David, because he was born from David’s seed according to the flesh—the four Gospels proceed. By their preaching they water the whole land of the nations and cause those who believe in Christ to bring forth manifold fruits of virtue.

“From him also the channel of the Jordan proceeds, because the sacrament of baptism came into the world through this dispensation to wash away the sins of the human race. He sends discipline like light because his commandments grant the light of eternal life to those who faithfully practice them. Therefore, after his resurrection, when he sent his disciples to teach and baptize the nations, he said to them in the Gospel: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matt. XVIII).

“‘He perfects the first knowledge of her, and the weaker person will not investigate her. For his thought has abounded from the sea, and his counsel from the great abyss.’ Truly our Lord is the author of spiritual knowledge and saving doctrine. He himself established the law first through Moses; he inspired the prophets; he taught the apostles; he appointed the evangelists and preachers of the New Testament. No one is a full and perfect investigator and knower of the wisdom of God except the one who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one God. Of him it is written: ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him’ (Matt. XI; Luke X).

“What is said—‘His thought has abounded from the sea, and his counsel from the great abyss’—shows that the depth of divine wisdom is beyond estimation and comprehension. No one can penetrate all its secrets except God alone, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who knows himself in all things and is the true knower of his own counsel. He grants his creature to know as much about him as he knows to be expedient for it, and according to the manner of his dispensation he grants his faithful understanding of his teaching.

“‘I, Wisdom, poured out rivers; I was like a channel of immense water from a river.’ Christ, therefore, the Wisdom of God, poured into the world the rivers of evangelical teaching, which most abundantly refresh and satisfy the eager minds of the elect. He is the channel of immense water from a river, because, just as God is from God and light from light, so he may figuratively be called immense water from the Father, the fountain or river, since the Father is the origin of divinity. For just as the Son is begotten from the Father, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. In the Gospel the Lord called him by the name of water, saying: ‘Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life’ (John IV). And again: ‘Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink, and from his belly will flow rivers of living water’ (John VII). Elsewhere it is written: ‘He gave him to drink of the water of saving wisdom’ (Ecclus. XV).

“‘I was like the river Dorix, and like a watercourse I went out from paradise.’ Some interpret this river historically as the Araxes, a river of Armenia, which rises from the same mountain as the Euphrates but in a different form. It is called this because it throws everything down by its violence. Thus, when Alexander wished to cross it by building a bridge, it flooded with such force that it destroyed the bridge. At short intervals from the source of the Euphrates it raises its head and is then said to flow into the Caspian Sea.

“The Greeks believe that it was called Doricus. There is a part of Greece called Doris, from which the third language of the Greeks was called Doric.

“Mystically, Wisdom compares herself to a very swift river and to water flowing out from paradise, because the Savior’s teaching, proceeding from the heavenly treasury, breaks and shatters all obstacles of error and persecution through its speed and strength, so that through the mouths of preachers it flows throughout the whole world, far and wide. Hence it is written: ‘Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’ (Ps. XVIII).

“‘I said: I will water my garden of plantings and drench the fruit of my meadow. And behold, my channel became abundant, and my river drew near to the sea, because I will illuminate doctrine for all like the dawn, and I will declare it to the distant. I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth, and I will look upon all who sleep and illuminate all who hope in God.’

“The garden of Wisdom’s plantings is the holy Church, which Truth itself continually waters and drenches with its teaching, so that daily it may produce the fruit of spiritual birth—namely, in catholic doctrine and holy virtues. This is fitting because she is enlightened by the true light, ‘which enlightens every person coming into this world’ (John I), by the Sun of justice and by him who himself rises, of whom it is written: ‘The Dawn from on high has visited us.’ And elsewhere: ‘Behold, the man whose name is Dawn’ (Zech. VI).

“He causes his teaching to be declared in the distant places, that is, to the ends of the world, so that all may recognize that truth has come for the salvation of the human race. He penetrates the lower parts of the earth because he searches out the hearts and thoughts of carnal people. He looks upon all who sleep, whether they slumber in the sleep of ignorance or in the torpor of negligence, and he illuminates those who hope in God with right faith and knowledge, because blessed is the one who hopes in God. ‘The Lord is pleased with those who fear him, and with those who hope in his mercy’ (Ps. CXLVI).”

“Again I will pour forth instruction as prophecy, [Col. 0944D] and leave it for those who seek wisdom, and I shall not cease for their generations unto the holy age.”

The writer of the history intimates by this statement that this mystical book seeks a spiritual understanding, and that it is very useful to read, because according to the historical sense it teaches morality, while according to the allegorical sense it imbues the reader with the sacrament of faith. “And I shall not cease,” he says, “for their generations unto the holy age,” because Sacred Scripture never ceases, from age to age, to teach the human race, so that it may understand from God’s commandments what it ought to avoid and what it ought to do. Thus no one can properly excuse himself by claiming that he did not know what was commanded in the divine law, since Wisdom openly demonstrates to all the way of truth and the rule of righteousness [Col. 0945A]. Concerning this it is further added:

“See that I have labored not only for myself, but for all who seek the truth.”

Therefore the ecclesiastical teacher, by writing and teaching the words of God, labors not only for himself but also for others: for himself, on account of eternal reward and rest; for others, on account of true salvation and everlasting repose. Hence it is written in Daniel: “Those who are learned shall shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. XII). Hence James also says: “Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James V). Concerning this Paul too, writing to Timothy, says: [Col. 0945B] “Pay attention to yourself and to sound doctrine; persist in these things. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (II Tim. IV). Hence Truth itself also says in the Gospel: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). And again: “You,” he says, “are the light of the world. Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

## CHAPTER III. Wisdom declares that three things are pleasing to its spirit: harmony among brothers, love of neighbors, and a man and woman who are well suited to one another.

[Col. 0945C] (CHAP. XXV.) “There are three things pleasing to my spirit, which are approved before God and human beings: harmony among brothers, love of neighbors, and a man and woman who are in good agreement with one another.”

Divine Wisdom is pleased by those things which are shown in God’s law to be commendable and acceptable, and beneficial to human beings—namely, harmony among brothers, concerning which the Apostle urges the Ephesians that, bearing with one another in love, they should be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Elsewhere he asks his hearers to be of the same mind and all to speak as one; and love of neighbors, of which the same Apostle wrote, saying: “Love of neighbor does no evil” (Phil. IV). Therefore love is the fullness of the law (Gal. V).

“And a man and woman who are well suited to one another”: [Col. 0945D] I can understand this both according to the historical sense and according to the allegorical sense. Historically, apostolic authority commands men to love their wives as Christ loved the Church, and likewise commands women to be subject to their husbands as to God, because the man is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church (Eph. V). Allegorically, however, we can understand the man as the spirit and the woman as the soul; if these agree in the fear and love of God, whatever they ask according to God’s will, they will obtain. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If two of you agree together about anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father” (Matt. XVIII).

“My soul hates three kinds of people, and I am greatly burdened by their souls: a proud poor man, a lying rich man, and a foolish and senseless old man.” [Col. 0946A]

Wisdom, then, which hates all vices, says that three kinds of people are hateful to it, and declares itself burdened by the souls of the wicked because they think things contrary to it: namely, it detests the proud poor man who, contrary to the condition of his poverty, is arrogant in his uplifted spirit; the lying rich man who, although granted possessions, does not enjoy them in truth according to God’s law but abuses them in falsehood; and the foolish and senseless old man who negligently wastes the leisure of his long life, since he has no zeal for learning wisdom.

Mystically, however, the truly poor man is one who becomes destitute of virtues and yet refuses to bend his proud spirit toward the practice of virtue. The lying rich man is the heretic, who abounds in understanding and speech but chooses to devote these gifts to error rather than to truth. The foolish and senseless old man is one who prefers the pleasures of the present life to the life to come, and loves what is perishable more than what is eternal. The Apostle John expressly forbids this, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world; for the world and its desire are passing away, but whoever does the will of the Lord remains forever” (I John II).

These three hateful kinds of people may also, by way of signification, be referred to the apostate angel, that is, the devil. He is poor and proud: after losing heavenly glory through his pride, he still does not cease to be proud. He is rich and lying, because, possessing earthly riches in greedy and covetous owners, he is wholly devoted to falsehood, as Truth itself testifies about him in the Gospel, saying: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (John VIII). “When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and the father of it.” The foolish and senseless old man is one who, although he was created in the beginning among the other angelic powers in heavenly glory through the wisdom of God, did not preserve the wisdom given to him because he refused to be subject to his Creator; and he persists in that very folly to this day, since he does not cease to rebel against his Creator.

Concerning this foolish old man Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: “Better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king who does not know how to foresee the future, when he comes forth from the house of prisoners into a kingdom” [Col. 0946D] (Eccles. IV). Origen and Victorinus interpreted this passage concerning Christ and the devil, intending the poor child to be understood as Christ, who was born in the kingdom of the old man, the devil, and therefore says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII). In the kingdom of that foolish old man, who showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, the excellent child was born, and he came forth from the house of prisoners. Concerning these Jeremiah speaks in the Lamentations, saying: “And humble all the prisoners of the earth beneath his feet” (Lam. III). He proceeded to the kingdom so that he might hold the heavenly and earthly things alike under his power. Hence after his resurrection he himself said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.”

[Col. 0947A] “What you did not gather in your youth, how will you find it in your old age?”

It is plainly evident that whoever had no zeal for learning wisdom in youth will have none of its fruit in old age. For it is written in Proverbs: “The soul of the laborer labors for himself.
