The slack hand produces poverty, but the hand of the strong prepares riches. Whoever gathers in harvest-time is a wise son, but whoever sleeps in summer is a son of confusion” (Prov. X). Wisdom likewise exhorts its children, saying: “Hear, my son, and be wise, and direct your mind in the way. Do not be among drinking companions, nor at their banquets” (Prov. XXII). Hence it is also read in the Psalm that whoever meditates on the law of the Lord day and night will yield fruit in its season, his leaf will not fall, and everything he does will have a prosperous outcome (Ps. I).

“How beautiful is the judgment of the gray-haired, and for presbyters to know counsel! How beautiful is wisdom in the aged, and glorious understanding and counsel! The crown of the old is abundant experience, and their glory is the fear of God.”

It is fitting that those whose heads are gray should possess prudence of understanding and that a long life should know the usefulness of counsel, so that, according to the fear of God, they may know and be able to render just judgment, and govern and judge their neighbors according to the equity of justice. For great glory grows for them from this, if they themselves live rightly according to the divine precepts of God’s law and teach others well both by words and by examples.

Let presbyters and the superiors of God’s churches therefore hear this: they are not permitted to be ignorant of knowledge of God’s law and the teaching of wisdom. Hence Paul commands Timothy to entrust the ministry of teaching to those who are capable of teaching others (II Tim. II). He also commands Titus to appoint as steward of God’s Church one who is not proud, not hot-tempered, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, and holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it (Tit. I).

The ignorance of shepherds is reproved by the voice of Truth when it is said through the prophet: “The shepherds themselves have no understanding” (Isa. LVI). Again the Lord detests them, saying: “Those who hold the law have not known me” (Jer. II). Truth therefore complains that it is not known by them, and declares that it does not know the leaders of the ignorant, because certainly those who do not know the things that belong to the Lord are not known by the Lord, as Paul attests when he says: “But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV).

This ignorance of shepherds often corresponds to the merits of their subjects. Although, through their own fault, these subjects do not possess the light of knowledge, strict judgment nevertheless decrees that, through the ignorance of those who lead them, even those who follow should stumble. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. XV). But when he says that the fear of God is the glory of the aged, he immediately adds:

[Col. 0948A] “I have magnified nine things beyond suspicion of the heart, and the tenth I will declare to people with my tongue: a man who rejoices in his children, living and seeing the overthrow of his enemies. Blessed is the one who dwells with a sensible woman, who has not stumbled with his tongue, and who has not served those unworthy of him. Blessed is the one who finds a true friend, and who declares righteousness into the ear of one who listens. How great is the one who has found wisdom and knowledge! Yet there is none above the one who fears God. The fear of the Lord has set itself above all things. Blessed is the one to whom it has been granted to possess the fear of God. Whoever holds fast to it—to whom will he be likened? The fear of God is the beginning of his love; the beginning of faith must be joined to it.”

What does it mean that he says he has magnified nine things beyond suspicion of the heart and declared the tenth with his tongue to people, except that “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation”? The nine, then, are things beyond suspicion—that is, certain and true gifts of the virtues, free from every suspicion of falsehood, which right faith produces in a person. These are: that a man may rejoice in his children, living, as it were, in the fruit of good works, and seeing the overthrow of his enemies—living for God and seeing the overthrow of demons and vices, as Paul says: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

And again: “Stand,” he says, “with your loins girded in truth, and put on the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace; in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI) [Col. 0948C].

Blessed is the person who dwells with a sensible woman—that is, with wisdom and prudence. Hence it is written: “Acquire wisdom, acquire prudence” (Prov. IV). “If wisdom enters your heart and knowledge pleases your soul, counsel will guard you and prudence will preserve you.”

Likewise blessed is the one who has not stumbled with his tongue, because whoever does not offend in speech is a perfect man. “Whoever guards his mouth guards his soul from distress.”

And blessed is the one who has not served those unworthy of him—that is, wicked spirits or sins. For whoever is overcome by something is made its servant.

Blessed is the one who finds a true friend: that friend, namely, who says to his disciples in the Gospel: “I have called you friends, because everything I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV).

And blessed is the one who declares righteousness into the ear of one who listens—that is, one who devoutly receives the word of God, understands it correctly, and acts well.

How great is the one who finds wisdom and knowledge! The integrity of this statement is divided into two parts, namely, wisdom and knowledge. For the ancients wished there to be this difference between wisdom and knowledge: that it belongs to wisdom to do good, and to knowledge to avoid evil. Hence it is written in Job: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to depart from evil—that is understanding” (Job XXVIII).

For this reason the fear of God is added to these nine kinds of virtue, because, just as the number nine is incomplete until it is supplemented by ten, so every work of virtue is imperfect without the perfection of the fear of God. “For the fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.” It is the foundation of faith; it is the origin of love. Through it good is done, and through it one reaches the reward.

But since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. I, IX; Sir. I), and in the Epistle of John we read, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment” (I John IV), and in the Psalm it is written, “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing” (Ps. XXXIII), the question arises how fear, if it is the beginning of wisdom and the beginning of love for God, is not in love; how all the saints love the Lord, while those who fear him lack nothing; and how it is true that the holy fear of God remains forever and ever.

This question is resolved as follows. The fear of the Lord by which a beginner in works of righteousness fears lest the strict Judge should come and, finding him insufficiently chastened, condemn him—that fear love casts out, since, on account of the merit of righteousness, love possesses confidence on the day of judgment. Perfect love also drives from the soul the fear of present adversities. This was the fear sought by the one who, entreating the Lord, said: “Deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy” (Ps. XXX); and it was the fear possessed by the one who said: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or nakedness, or hunger, or danger, or the sword?” and so forth (Rom. VIII).

Nor should it be thought contrary to the words of blessed John that the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII). For there are two kinds of fear. One is the fear by which people fear God lest they be sent into Gehenna. This is the fear that introduces love, but it comes in order to depart. For if, while still fearing God on account of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way, you do not desire good things but avoid evil ones. Yet because you avoid evil, you correct yourself and begin to desire good. When you have begun to desire good, there will be in you the holy fear—not the fear by which you dread being sent into Gehenna, but the fear that you may lose those very good things; not fear of punishment, but fear that the presence of the Lord whom you embrace, and with whom you desire to enjoy eternal life, may depart from you.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the wickedness of woman, in whose company he forbids a chaste man to remain if he wishes to be chaste.

“Every wound is sorrow of heart, and every wickedness is the wickedness of woman.”

Just as there is no greater grace than true love in the joy of a good mind, so there is no greater wound than the sorrow of a deceitful heart in idolatry or the error of heretical depravity. For all wickedness is in her wickedness. But because in the hardness of a soul led astray through error there is a wound of iniquity, while she herself does not perceive the ruin of her deception, it is therefore added:

“And she will see every wound and no wound of the heart; and every wickedness and no wickedness of woman; and every covering and no covering of those who hate; and every vengeance and no vengeance of enemies.”

She sees the wound of the heart when she understands the injustice of her depravity. Yet she will not see it, because she will not provide for her salvation through repentance and correction of her crime. She senses the wickedness of error, but nevertheless will not avoid the punishment of future torment. She does not fail to recognize the justice of the most equitable Judge, who by future vengeance erases the name of those who hate him and punishes his enemies with the fire of Gehenna; yet she prepares no escape for herself from those evils.

Thus what the Apostle wrote to the Romans concerning the despisers of God and the ungrateful is fulfilled in her: “Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them” (Rom. I). For they knew that these things displeased God, but they did not wish to take them to heart: “Those who do such things are worthy of death,” and not only those who do them but also those who approve of those who do them.

Approval is participation. There are some who do not consider themselves guilty if they do not themselves practice evil things, but they approve those who do them. To approve is, for example, to remain silent when one could offer correction, or to flatter someone while listening to his empty stories. Knowing that his impurity and wickedness are not unknown, and that he is not avoided but even honored, such a person boasts of being what he is. Nor can he be ashamed in these matters when he sees others favoring and accommodating him, even though they themselves are not like him. Thus those who provide fuel for the offenses of others are themselves worthy of being held guilty of the same crime.

There are others who not only do evil things but also approve those who do them—so that they both commit evil and approve those who commit it. Their wickedness is therefore double. Those who commit evil but oppose those who commit it are not so evil: although they know what is wicked, they do not sanction it. But those are exceedingly wicked who both do evil and approve those who do it, so that they neither fear God nor cease to desire the increase of evil. For this reason they do not punish such acts, in order to persuade others that they need not be avoided.

“There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no anger above the anger of a woman. It will be more pleasing to dwell with a lion and a dragon than to live with a wicked woman.”

The wickedness of heretics, therefore, compared with poisonous serpents and savage earthly creatures, is found to be more ferocious and more harmful: those creatures injure the body, but this destroys the soul; those bring temporal death, but this brings eternal death. Therefore her companionship is harmful to all and beneficial to no one. Hence it follows:

“The wickedness of woman changes her face, and she blinds her countenance like a bear and displays herself like a sack. In the midst of her neighbors her husband groaned, and, hearing, he sighed briefly.”

The perversity of the heretical faction changes her face when she speaks falsehood through hypocrisy and displays counterfeit appearances of virtue. She blinds her face like a bear when, through the hardness of her heart, she darkens the sight of her mind and does not foresee the judgment of her future condemnation. She displays herself like a sack in the midst of her neighbors when she brings forth before her hearers inept novelties of doctrine and conceals the shamefulness of her understanding beneath a foul covering of words.

Nor does she imitate the conduct of that most strong and wise woman of whom it is written in Proverbs: “She sought wool and flax and worked according to the counsel of her hands.” The strong woman seeks wool and flax and works according to the counsel of her hands when Holy Church diligently searches for the works of piety in which she may exercise herself and for the means by which she may cleanse herself from carnal allurements—and she does both with the most prudent counsel, namely, with regard solely to heavenly recompense.

Concerning her it is again written: “She made herself a variegated garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing” (Prov. XXXI) [Col. 0951B]. The variegated garment, which is customarily made exceedingly strong through its diverse weaving, signifies the Church’s powerful works and the various ornaments of her virtues. Concerning these the Prophet sang in praise of the supreme King, that is, of that man: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round about with variety” (Ps. XLIV).

Fine linen and purple are also her clothing: fine linen signifies chastity in conduct, and purple the shedding of precious blood. Fine linen is white in color, while purple is made from the blood of a living creature called the purple-fish and itself has the appearance of blood. Hence the Fathers beautifully said that Holy Church, flowering with the blossoms of the elect, possesses lilies in peace and roses in war.

What is added—“hearing, he sighed briefly”—signifies that although the perverse mind of heretics is rightly reproved by Catholic teachers, it is nevertheless difficult to bend it toward true repentance. And if it sometimes pretends to repent, because it does not correct its error it reveals that it persists in the wickedness it has begun.

“Every wickedness is brief compared with the wickedness of woman; the lot of sinners will fall upon her.”

This is what he said earlier: “There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no anger above the anger of a woman.” Every wickedness is small in comparison with idolatry and heretical depravity, because in these sins are not committed through the weakness of the flesh but through the pride of the mind. Everything done in them is done in contempt of God. Therefore it is called impiety, which we can also call by another name, denial of God. If it is not corrected, it has no pardon but eternal punishment.

For this reason, in the prophet Zechariah, a leaden mass is thrown upon the mouth of the woman sitting in the midst of the ephah, and she is carried away to Babylon (Zech. V). Impiety, which sat upon the sins of Israel and gloried in its crime, is later cast into the midst of Babylon and oppressed by the evil of captivity, so that it has a hardened mouth and can no longer boast of itself; or certainly it is crushed by the angels of God, so that what previously lay hidden in crime may fall silent in eternal silence.

“As a sandy ascent is on the feet of an old man, so is a woman of many words to a quiet man.”

He makes a beautiful comparison. Just as shifting and unstable sand is difficult to walk upon for the weak feet of an old man, so the excessive talkativeness of a heretic is burdensome to the hearing of a modest Catholic [Col. 0952A]. Therefore, showing her companionship to be harmful, he consequently forbids communion with her, saying:

“Do not look upon the appearance of woman, and do not desire a woman; in the appearance of woman are anger, irreverence, and great confusion.”

The appearance of this woman is the crafty doctrine of heretics, adorned with the cosmetics of words. If you love her deceitful eloquence, you will endure eternal punishment and confusion. Solomon shows in Proverbs what the appearance of this woman is, saying: “For the lips of a prostitute drip honeycomb, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. V).

When the sweetness of eloquence resounds from a heretic’s mouth not merely sufficiently but excessively, falsehood is regarded by fools as truth because it is seen to be skillfully expressed. Catholic faith is consecrated by the oil of the Holy Spirit, but heretics display their throats as smoother than oil when they prefer their own opinions to the faith of the Fathers.

The reference to a prostitute is clear, since she seeks both sweetness of speech and bodily beauty in order to capture the wretched. “Her end,” he says, “is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword.” A draught of wormwood becomes bitter within, in the entrails, while a sword strikes the limbs externally. Thus, to show that the wicked at the final vengeance will be filled inwardly and surrounded outwardly by everlasting punishments, he asserts that they will be tormented by the bitterness of wormwood and cut down by the sword. Why, however, is the sword called two-edged? The Lord makes this clear when he says: “But fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X).

“If a woman holds the chief place, she is contrary to her husband. A humble heart, a sorrowful face, and a wound of the heart is a wicked woman; weak hands and loosened knees belong to a woman who does not make her husband blessed. From a woman sin began, and through her we all die.”

According to the historical sense, these words show that a woman’s preeminence is more harmful than useful, because the weaker sex ought to be subject to the stronger sex, not placed above it. Hence, at the beginning, the Lord said to the woman who sinned and seduced the man: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions; in sorrow you shall bear children, and you shall be under the power of the man, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III).

Hence the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: “Let a woman learn in silence with all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but to remain in silence” (I Tim. II). He immediately gave the reason why he commanded this, saying: “For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and was in transgression” (I Tim. II).

Mystically, however, we can understand this woman as the synagogue of the heretics. Concerning it Proverbs says: “She has abandoned the guide of her youth and forgotten the covenant of her God” (Prov. II), because she abandoned the teacher from whom she had learned the faith of the Church and forgot the covenant of her God—that is, the ordinance of the Lord’s faith contained in the Creed, which she had promised to preserve on the day of her baptism.

If she holds the chief place, she will also be contrary to her husband, namely, the Catholic teacher, by thinking perversely and teaching wicked things. Her heart—that is, her thought—is vile and contemptible; and her face is sorrowful because she does not possess the joy of the Holy Spirit. She also brings upon her lovers the wound of eternal death.

Her work is weak and her step unstable, because she did not make her former husband blessed. With him she had first entered into a covenant that she would obey him and preserve his faith, but she committed adultery with a foreign husband. From her sin began, because the pride of her arrogance, by which she presumed to abandon the way of truth and turn aside into the byways of error, became the origin and cause of eternal destruction both for herself and for all who obeyed her.

[Col. 0953B] “Do not give your water an outlet, not even a small one, nor grant a wicked woman freedom to go out. If she does not walk at your hand, she will bring you to shame in the sight of your enemies. Cut her off from your flesh, lest she continually abuse you.”

Here water signifies the teaching of wisdom. He therefore teaches that you should not grant your instruction permission to go beyond the bounds of uprightness, nor consent to the soul deceived by heretical depravity through the devil’s art, nor give it freedom to teach. But if, by withdrawing from error, she refuses to submit to you and stirs up arguments and disputes against you before the foolish and ignorant, separate her from the communion of the Church, lest she continue to abuse you for the indulgence of her depravity.

Hence the Apostle also commands Titus to avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment (Tit. III). John likewise warns in his epistle that we should not even say “hail” to such people, nor receive them into our house.

The following passage from Proverbs is therefore not contrary to this one: “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well; let your springs flow out, and divide your waters in the streets. Possess them alone, so that strangers may not share them with you” (Prov. V).

He teaches that we must beware of heretics and attend to the guardianship and reading of the Scriptures. “Keep for yourself,” he says, “the knowledge with which you preach to others, and pour it forth through the irrigation of your speech. Let your springs flow out, and divide your waters in the streets.” When you have kept them for yourself, then preach to others also, [Col. 0953D] and in the great breadth of your audience distribute the divine words according to the capacity of each person.

“Possess them alone.” We divide the waters in the streets and nevertheless possess them alone when we pour preaching outwardly far and wide, yet do not seek human praise through it. “Let strangers not share them with you.” Unclean spirits become partners of the teacher if, while he preaches, they corrupt his mind either through the arrogance of pride, through heresy, or through any other vice. He alone possesses the waters when, faithfully joined to the members of the Church, he keeps himself free from the companionship of outsiders.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the good woman: that the good woman is the virgin Church, whom Christ made good with his own blood, cleansing her through the laver of regeneration.

(CAP. XXVI.) “Blessed is the husband of a good woman, for the number of her years is doubled.”

Just as earlier he opened his mouth in denunciation of the wicked woman, so now he turns his speech toward praise of the good woman. The good woman is either, in a particular sense, the soul of a just and good person, or, in a general sense, the entire Church of the elect. Her husband is described as blessed because Christ, who is her husband, is proclaimed throughout the whole world as blessedness and exaltation.

“For the number of her years is doubled,” because here the Church lives under the guardianship of God’s commandments with the integrity of the virtues, [Col. 0954B] while in the future she will truly rejoice in the reception of heavenly rewards.

“A strong woman delights her husband, and she will complete the years of his life in peace.”

The strength of the Church is the delight of Christ. She does not possess it from herself but from his gift, and he will complete her years in peace when, in the present, he enriches her with the gift of his peace and, after this life, perfects her in eternal rest by making her equal to the holy angels in perfect peace. This accords with what he himself said to his disciples in the Gospel: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV)—as though he were saying: Here I leave it; there I give it. I leave it to those who follow; I give it to those who arrive.

Concerning this strong woman it is also written in Proverbs: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the ends of the earth. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no need of spoils” (Prov. XXXI).

The Catholic Church is called a strong woman: a woman, because she is accustomed to beget spiritual children for God from water and the Holy Spirit; strong, because she despises all the adversities and prosperities of the world alike for the faith of her Creator. When he appeared in the flesh, he found her weak, but by his finding her—that is, by his loving visitation—he made her strong. Hence, after her redemption, as he returned to heaven, he joyfully said to the citizens above: “Rejoice with me, because I have found the sheep that was lost” (Luke XV).

Therefore, seeing the human race entangled in innumerable errors, and recognizing that no patriarch, no prophet, indeed no one among the elect except the sole Mediator between God and human beings [Col. 0954D], was sufficient for its salvation, Solomon said: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the ends of the earth.” It is as though, in wonder, he openly proclaimed the future grace of the Lord: Who possesses such virtue, who such merit, that from the many unbelieving and criminal nations of the world he might gather for himself one Church of the elect and make her strong and unconquerable against all adversaries?

When he says, therefore, “The heart of her husband trusts in her,” the expression is plainly drawn from human custom. Just as a man who has a strong, faithful, and chaste wife trusts her completely, because she can do nothing against his will and cannot even be touched by an adulterous thought, and would willingly endure all adversities for her love and desire to convert as many as she can to her friendship, so the Lord and our Redeemer trusts the Church. For he knows the spirit of grace that he has given her; he knows the strength of love that he has infused into her inmost heart. Therefore he does not doubt that she can in no way be corrupted from the integrity of her faith, and that she will persist in gathering many into the unity of that same faith.

This is what follows: “And she will have no need of spoils.” The Church strips the devil when, through her preachers, she recalls to the path of truth those whom he had deceived. It is rightly said, “She will have no need of spoils,” because the Church will never cease restoring to the faith of Christ the souls liberated from the devil’s fraud until, when the course of the world has been completed, the predetermined number of her members also has been fulfilled [Col. 0955B].

“A good portion is a good wife; in the portion of those who fear God she will be given to a man for good deeds.”

The good portion and the good wife are the Catholic Church, which is numbered among the lot of those who fear God, because she belongs to his inheritance. Concerning this it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy: “The Lord’s portion is his people, Jacob the lot of his inheritance, Israel (Deut. XXXII).” To her also, established at his right hand, he himself will say at the future judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt. XXV).” She was given to her husband Christ for good deeds, namely, for the redemption of the human race, as Isaiah testifies, saying: “If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand (Isa. LIII).” Hence also, appearing to his disciples after his resurrection, he himself said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII).” What benefit the faith of Christ and the sacrament of baptism confer upon the human race, the following sentence makes clear:

“But the heart of the rich and of the poor is good; at all times their faces are cheerful.” God is not a respecter of persons: whether rich or poor comes to Christ’s grace, if he perseveres in it with devoted mind, his face will rejoice, enjoying the perpetual contemplation of God. What becomes of those who are alien to this gift, he indicates by adding:

[Col. 0955D] “My heart feared three things, and at the fourth my face was afraid: the informer against the city, and the gathering of the people, and the lying accusation—all things more grievous than death; the anguish of the heart and mourning, a jealous woman.” By these kinds, therefore, those who are outside the Church and do not remain in the unity of true religion are represented—that is, Jews, pagans, heretics, and also false Christians. In the informers against the city, that is, traitors to the Church, we may understand false Christians, who confess that they know God but deny him by their deeds. Nor do they wish to possess charity, which provides the greatest protection to the assembly of the faithful; instead, they do everything deceitfully. In the gathering of the people, persecution by the Gentiles may appropriately be understood, and in the lying accusation, the blasphemy of the Jews. In the jealous woman, likewise, are represented heretics, who fight against the truth through zeal and envy and inflict the greatest anguish and mourning upon the Church their mother. All these things are more grievous than death, because it is more bearable to undergo temporal death than to suffer eternal burning in Gehenna for sins.

“In an unfaithful woman there is the scourge of the tongue, communicating with everyone.” This means that in a Gentile soul, or one deceived by heretical depravity, blasphemy and perverse speech resound. Whether it conceives evil in the heart or utters wicked words with the mouth, it is always ready to do harm, and therefore will be harmful to all who agree with it.

[Col. 0956B] “Like the yoke of oxen that is moved, so also is a wicked woman.” Here he uses the yoke of oxen as a figure for the folly of fools. For just as brute animals do not know how to distinguish between friend and enemy, between truthful and deceitful, between good and evil, so fools do not understand the difference between Catholic and heretical doctrine, between truth and falsehood, or between justice and iniquity; they are equally ready to obey false and true teachers. This is contrary to the Apostle’s command: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God (1 John IV).” Similar is what is written in Proverbs concerning the shamelessness of the prostitute, who entangled the young man with many words and drew him on with the flatteries of her lips: “Immediately he follows her like an ox to the slaughter, and like a lamb playing; [Col. 0956C] and he does not know that the fool is being led to the slaughter, until the arrow pierces his liver (Prov. VII).” For he does not know his danger until he falls into evident destruction.

“He who holds her is like one who grasps a scorpion.” He aptly compares heresy to a scorpion, because just as a scorpion injects its poison not by its mouth but by striking with its tail, so the cunning of heretics deceives the unwary not openly, but through deceitful wickedness.

“A drunken woman has great anger; and her disgrace and shame will not be concealed.” The drunken woman is the synagogue of the heretics, completely filled with deceit and wickedness. Great anger and disgrace follow her when severe punishment and everlasting condemnation succeed her iniquity, at which time the shame of her error [Col. 0956D] will be revealed in the final judgment.

“A woman’s fornication is seen in the lifting of her eyes, and recognized in her eyelids.” Although historically he describes the appearance of a prostitute, who displays the lust of the flesh through wanton bodily movements and the gestures of her eyes, mystically he nevertheless reveals the conduct of heretical depravity. It boasts of its fornication in the pride of its understanding and in the eloquence of its words, so that it may more easily draw the curious and lovers of novelty into its exaltation. Concerning such people it is written elsewhere that, “itching in their ears, they will turn away from hearing the truth and turn instead to fables (2 Tim. IV).”

“In a daughter who does not turn herself away, keep firm watch, lest, finding an opportunity, she abuse herself; beware of all disrespect in her eyes.” This advises that a teacher should take diligent care of the person entrusted to him. He must not neglect her, but carefully nourish her and teach her to live under discipline, lest, finding an opportunity through carnal desire, she rush into some crime. For the sense and thought of the human heart is directed toward evil at all times from its youth. Therefore he adds correspondingly:

“And do not be surprised if she has neglected you: as a thirsty traveler will open his mouth toward a spring, so she will drink from every nearby water, and she will sit opposite every stake, and open her quiver against every arrow, until she is exhausted.” By these three examples he indeed shows the curiosity of the human mind, which is fickle and always open to the allurements of the world. Hence the apostle John distinguished it in a threefold division, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world is passing away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever (1 John II).” By these names of vices he comprehended all kinds of vice.

The desire of the flesh is everything that pertains to bodily pleasure and luxury, among which food, drink, and sexual intercourse are the chief. Concerning these Solomon says: “The leech has two daughters saying, ‘Give, give’ (Prov. XXX).” The desire of the eyes is every form of curiosity: in learning wicked arts, in contemplating shameful or useless spectacles, in acquiring temporal possessions, and even in discerning and criticizing the vices of one’s neighbors. The pride of life is when someone boasts of honors and, through the exaltation of an empty mind, serves vainglory and arrogance.

Human desire is tempted through these three things alone. Adam was tempted and overcome through them: through the desire of the flesh, when the enemy showed him the food of the forbidden tree and persuaded him to eat; through the desire of the eyes, when he said, “You will know good and evil, and your eyes will be opened (Gen. III)”; and through the pride of life, when he said, “You will be like gods.” The Lord was tempted through these things and conquered: through the desire of the flesh, that is, food, when it was suggested, “Say that these stones become bread (Matt. IV)”; through the desire of the eyes, that is, curiosity, when he was taken to the pinnacle of the Temple and urged to throw himself down, to test whether he would be received by angels; and through the pride of life, that is, empty boasting, when all the kingdoms of this world were shown to him from the mountain and promised to him if he would worship.

“The grace of a diligent woman delights her husband, and she will make his bones fat.” The grace of good devotion and obedience, which every holy soul possesses—or, more generally, which the whole Church of the elect possesses—pleases the mind of a good teacher, or rather of Christ our Lord, who is the true bridegroom of the Church. Whoever obeys him with devoted humility, by keeping his commandments, shows that he possesses the richness of his charity in the marrow of his heart. Hence he will also obtain his love, as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him (John XIV).” But since no one loves him before his grace has provoked that person to love him, the following sentence declares:

“Her discipline is God’s gift.” Every good thing in the Church is indeed God’s gift, because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration. For he brought us forth willingly by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of first-fruits of his creation (James I).”

“A sensible and quiet woman; there is no change in an instructed soul.” The wisdom of God, which imbues the souls of the elect and grants them custody of the mouth and effectiveness in action, does not permit them to be changed away from him or to turn aside into the byways of error. John makes this clear in his Epistle, saying: “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God (1 John V).” Yet he does not say this concerning every sin, but concerning violation of right faith and charity. Whoever has within himself the seed of God—that is, the word of God by which he was reborn—cannot commit that violation.

“Grace upon grace, a holy and modest woman.” Therefore, above the grace of the Law and of the synagogue established under it, there is the grace of the Gospel and the beauty of the holy Church, which chastely and inviolate preserves the faith of her Savior and eagerly learns divine wisdom. In reading the Law and the Prophets she does not have the Mosaic veil over her heart, but with unveiled face contemplates the glory of the Lord and enters God’s sanctuary to understand the ordinances established from the beginning of the world.

“No wealth is worthy of a continent soul.” Clearly, all the riches of the world and the wealth of secular wisdom cannot equal her devotion, which she possesses in Christ’s service and in spiritual knowledge. She is that merchant who, in the Gospel, purchased the most precious pearl, rejecting temporal goods so that she might possess it forever (Matt. XIII). Hence what follows:

[Col. 0958D] “As the rising sun is for the world in the highest places of God, so is the good appearance of a woman for the adornment of her house.” The splendor of the Sun of Justice shines in the appearance of this woman, and adorns her entire house—which has been extended throughout the whole world—with the ornament of wisdom and virtues (Wis. III). For this she will also obtain the radiance of heavenly glory, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII).”

“A shining lamp upon a holy lampstand, and beauty of face upon a steadfast age.” The lamp of evangelical doctrine shines upon the Church’s lampstand, and the beauty of the virtues that gleams in her face—that is, in her works—will be established for perpetual ages [Col. 0959A] and rewarded with eternal recompense. Concerning this lamp the Lord himself instructed his disciples by a similitude, saying: “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house (Matt. V).”

The apostles are called the light of the world because through them the world was to be illumined by the light of faith and knowledge. The mountain signifies Christ, upon whom the city of the Church—that is, the Church founded upon his faith—is established. The lamp, as we have said, is evangelical doctrine. The lampstand is the soul of every faithful person. To put the lamp under a bushel, therefore, is to place bodily comforts above the preaching of truth, so that someone does not preach the truth because he fears suffering some hardship in bodily and temporal matters. Whoever obscures and conceals the light of good teaching with temporal advantages puts the lamp under a bushel. But he places it upon a lampstand who subjects his body to God’s service, so that the preaching of truth is above and bodily service below.

“Golden columns upon silver bases, and firm feet upon the soles of a steadfast woman.” The golden columns are holy teachers, illustrious with the light of wisdom. They are placed upon silver bases when they rest their preaching upon the utterances of the sacred Scriptures. The apostles and apostolic men are rightly compared to columns, because they press earthly vices down below and raise heavenly virtues up to the grace of the heavenly King. [Col. 0959C] Their feet are firmly established upon the soles of the steadfast woman, because the course of their preaching, by which they spread the word of God throughout the whole world—“Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII)”—stands firmly upon the stability of the Catholic faith. Concerning this it follows:

“Eternal foundations upon a solid rock, and the commandments of God in the heart of a holy woman.” For the whole preaching of the apostles and evangelists is founded upon the solid rock, that is, Christ. Therefore the commandments of God have been transplanted into the heart of the holy woman, that is, the Church. He is rightly called the foundation, since he so upholds his Church that no upheaval can make her totter, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Cor. III).” Rightly, therefore, the beginning of spiritual building is taken from him, since he is manifestly the beginning of all things.

[Col. 0959D] “My heart was grieved at two things, and at the third anger came upon me: a warrior failing through poverty, a sensible man despised, and one who passes from justice to sin; God has prepared him for the sword.” By these sentences Wisdom condemns the folly of human understanding when, through the weakness of the flesh, it loses the labor of virtue; or when, through derangement of heart, it does not know how to choose the better thing; or when, abandoning the path of truth, it turns aside into the byways of error.

A warrior fails through poverty [the text reads *mopiam*, evidently an OCR corruption of *inopiam*, “poverty”] when one who has endured many labors in the contest of this world for Christ is finally broken by some adversity and loses the labor through instability of mind. A sensible man is despised when a Catholic teacher and herald of truth is spurned by fools, and a human philosophical sect is preferred to his sound doctrine. He passes from justice to sin who, first instructed in the Catholic faith and having received Christ’s baptism, later abandons the rule of right faith through pride and arrogance and turns himself toward the apostasy of heretical depravity.

God therefore prepares him for the sword, because on account of his iniquity he reserves him for everlasting punishment, as the Lord himself testifies through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, according to all the abominations that the wicked is accustomed to practice, none of all his righteous deeds that he did will be remembered. In the transgression by which he transgressed and in the sin which he committed, in these he will die (Ezek. XVIII).”

[Col. 0960B] “Two kinds appeared difficult and dangerous to me: it is difficult for a merchant to strip himself of negligence, and an innkeeper will not be justified from the sins of his lips.” This passage, unless it is examined carefully, seems to contain some contradiction and to raise a question. For if every merchant or innkeeper is altogether to be condemned, and those who practice other trades do not escape this punishment, what else is commerce than wishing to sell at a higher price what can be obtained more cheaply?

Moreover, in the Lives of the Fathers we read that the most holy man Paphnutius was compared through a revelation to a merchant, and today we find in the Church people conducting commerce while possessing the highest integrity of faith. It is the wicked deed, not the honorable occupation, that is condemned. Likewise, we read that the rich man does not enter the kingdom of heaven, although Job, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob the patriarchs were exceedingly wealthy.

Those merchants, therefore, are considered detestable who, giving no consideration to the Lord’s justice, are polluted by immoderate greed for money, burdening their merchandise more with perjuries than with prices. Such men the Lord drove from the Temple, saying: “Do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce, and a den of thieves (Matt. XXI).” It is difficult, therefore, for the merchant whose mind burns with the desire for money to strip himself of negligence; and an innkeeper will not be justified from the sins of his lips when, through some fraud or fabricated words, he strives to undermine the justice of his neighbors.

## CHAPTER VI. Many sin because of poverty, but those in whom there is no charity of God; for no creature can separate us from the charity of God.

“(CHAP. XXVII.) Many have sinned because of poverty, and whoever seeks to become rich turns away his eye.” Many therefore sin because of poverty, but more because of poverty of heart than of body. For we read that many holy men were poor in the possessions of this world but rich in faith and virtues. They preserved that same faith in Christ and his justice amid the adversities of this age until the end of life, and thus attained the crown of eternal life; they sought the heavenly treasure more than the earthly.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” But he who seeks to become rich in this world turns his eye away from the fear of God and follows the desires of this world; therefore he will lack the blessing of the heavenly kingdom.

“As a stake is fixed in the middle of a structure of stones, so between the middle of selling and buying he will be constricted by sins.” By the fitting comparison of a stake fixed amid stones, he expresses the destruction and distress of the avaricious man in buying and selling, to whom what he has seems as lacking as what he does not have. For while he fears losing what he possesses and seeks to seize what belongs to others, he burns incessantly in his mind, and harmful anxiety continually torments him. Yet although he suffers such torment here, if he does not correct himself, it is certain that he will not escape the future punishment of Gehenna. There what follows will certainly occur:

“Sin will be crushed together with the sinner.” There the ambition for money will cease, when both the soul and body of the robber are punished at the final judgment. But since there is one means by which human nature can be saved, he immediately shows by adding how these many dangers may be avoided:

“If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overturned.” It is clear that the fear of the Lord guards a person’s life; if he abandons it, he will at once be exposed to the plots and seduction of his enemies. “It will always go well with one who fears the Lord,” because the fear of the Lord is the fountain of life, glory, joy, and a crown of exultation. Whoever holds fast to it increases here through the worthy merits of good works, and in the future will possess joy and gladness through length of days.

“As dust will remain in the shaking of a sieve, so is a man’s difficulty in his thought. The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation in tribulation tests righteous people.” By an apt example he shows that the fear of God purifies a person’s soul. For just as a sieve gathers impurities and separates grains from chaff, so the fear of God drives all dirty thoughts from the heart through the care and anguish of the soul. And just as the flame of a furnace tests the potter’s vessels, so the temptation of tribulation cleanses righteous people from sins.

*Aporia* is a Greek word, and it is interpreted as “flow,” or “derivation,” “spur,” or “trouble.” The temptation of Satan may also be understood under the image of the sieve. The Lord himself mentions this sieve in the Gospel, saying to Peter: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail (Luke XXII).”

Lest the eleven apostles boast or attribute to their own strength the fact that they alone, almost among so many thousands of Jews, were said to have remained with the Lord in temptations, he shows that they too, unless protected by the help of the Lord who assisted them, could have been crushed by the same storm as the others. But when Satan demands to test them and shake them as one who cleanses wheat by winnowing, he teaches that no one’s faith is tested by the devil except with God’s permission. For Satan’s desire to sift the good means that he pants with the heats of malice for their affliction. In proportion as he enviously seeks their temptation, he requests it as though seeking their testing.

But when the Savior, praying for Peter, asks not that he be tempted but that his faith not fail—that is, that after the fall of denial he might rise again through repentance to his former state—he intimates that it is useful for holy people to be examined by the flames of temptations. Thus either, having been tested, they may show that they are strong, or, having recognized their weakness through temptations, they may learn to become stronger; and when they have been proved, they too may receive the crown of life that God promised to those who love him.

[Col. 0962B] “As cultivation shows the fruit of a tree, so a person’s considered word shows his heart.” Truth itself explained the meaning of this sentence in the Gospel, where it says: “Each tree is known by its fruit; for they do not gather figs from thorns, nor grapes from a bramble. The good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil from the evil treasure; for from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt. VII; Luke VI).”

The cultivation of a tree therefore reveals its quality to the one who cultivates it through its fruit, because a good tree produces good fruit, while an evil tree bears evil fruit. The Apostle shows what fruit distinguishes a good or evil tree, saying: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousies, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, modesty, self-control (Gal. V).”

The treasure of the heart, then, is the same as the root of the tree, and what proceeds from the heart is the same as the tree’s fruit. Whoever therefore has in his heart the treasure of patience and perfect love, pouring forth excellent fruits, loves his enemy, does good to one who hates him, blesses the one who curses him, prays for the one who slanders him, does not resist the one who strikes or strips him, gives to everyone who asks, does not demand back what has been taken from him, does not desire to judge or condemn, corrects the one who errs patiently and lovingly, and does the other things that the Savior taught above. But whoever keeps an evil treasure in his heart hates his friend, curses the one who loves him, curses the one who blesses him, and does the other things that the Lord’s word condemns.

“Do not praise a man before his speech; for this is the testing of human beings.” If a man’s speech reveals his thought, it is fitting that no one praise another before he has proved him worthy of praise by clear indications. And because “speech” often stands in Scripture for deeds, “speech” here may be understood as action, so that we praise no one before testing his good actions. Hence it is written elsewhere: “Do not praise anyone before death,” because “whoever perseveres in goodness to the end will be saved (Ecclus. XI).” Praise that has not been tested is rightly called a testing of human beings, because it proceeds from levity of mind, not from the judgment of justice.

“If you follow justice, you will grasp it, and clothe yourself in it like a robe of honor; you will dwell with it, and it will protect you forever; and on the day of recognition you will find strength.” Whoever follows justice by teaching rightly and living well will grasp it when he is rewarded with eternal life on its account. He will clothe himself in it like a robe of honor and dwell with it. A *poderis* is a tunic reaching to the ankles. What, then, is an ankle-length tunic except a completed action? Just as an extended tunic covers the ankle of the body, so a good action covers us before God’s eyes all the way to the end of life.

Hence Moses also commands that the tail of the sacrificial victim be offered upon the altar, so that whatever good we begin we may complete with a persevering end. Whoever therefore perseveres in good action to the end of life, the Lord will protect forever. On the day of recognition—that is, on the day of judgment, when the Lord comes, illuminates the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the counsels of hearts—he will find strength, because then he will receive the true and firm reward of his justice.

“Flying creatures gather to those like themselves, and truth will return to those who practice it.” We may understand the flying creatures as the holy souls of the elect, who lift themselves from earthly and carnal association on the wings of virtues and desire to be associated with the holy angels in heavenly joy. They will also be joined to them in the future life, when Truth, Christ, returns on the day of judgment and gathers to himself those who have kept his commandments by practicing them well. What remains, on the contrary, for sinners, he demonstrates by what follows.

“A lion always lies in wait for its prey; so sins lie in wait for those who practice iniquity.” The lion is the devil, who always lies in wait for the human race in order to deceive it through perverse schemes. Whoever does not beware of his ambushes but favors them by consenting to his wicked suggestions will undoubtedly fall into the snare of everlasting death.

“A holy man remains in wisdom like the sun, but a fool changes like the moon.” The wisdom of a holy man is aptly compared to the unchanging splendor of the sun, which shines perpetually and never changes its radiance. But the fool changes like the moon, because he is inconsistent and changeable in everything. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “The heart of fools will be unlike itself (Prov. XV).” The heart of the wise is always like itself, because, while it yields to right counsels, it directs itself steadfastly toward good action. But the heart of fools will be unlike itself, because, displaying itself as varied through its mutability, it never remains what it was.

“In the midst of the senseless, keep your word according to the time; but in the midst of those who reflect, be constant.” This sentence teaches moderation and caution in our speech, so that we observe the proper time and measure in speaking. For it often happens that inconsiderate speech causes scandal to weak hearers and, through loquacity, destroys those whom it could have saved through moderation in teaching. It is indeed safer to listen than to speak.

Therefore he commands here that we keep our words according to the time and be constant in the midst of those who reflect—that is, those who diligently meditate upon and study the teaching of God’s Law in their hearts. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “The heart of the wise seeks instruction, and the mouth of fools feeds on ignorance (Prov. XV).” And again: “The instruction of fools is folly. The heart of the wise will instruct his mouth, and will add grace to his lips.” Hence James also says: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak (James I).”

But since now there are more preachers of the word than practitioners of it—as I must sadly say—he reveals by what follows what their teaching is like before God:

“The speech of sinners is hateful, and their laughter is in the pleasures of sin.” Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V).”

This may also be understood morally. One breaks God’s commandment who does not fulfill it, although he does not break the commandment in itself but in himself. For God’s commandment is firm, and Scripture cannot be broken. The Law is therefore, in a certain sense, a bond. Whoever transgresses God’s bonds breaks the commandments in himself, not in the commandments themselves. Such a person will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, because he is most despised in the Church of the saints. For here the kingdom of heaven also signifies the present Church, as elsewhere where it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea,” and, “The kingdom of God is within you (Matt. XIII).”

“But whoever does,” he says, “and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. V).” In doing the commandments of the Law, the one who teaches deserves the name of great, because not teachers or hearers, but doers of the Law will be justified before God. When he says, “Their laughter is in the pleasures of sin,” he shows that worldly luxury and love of pleasure—among which they rule—gather a great accumulation of sins over them.

[Col. 0964D] “Speech that swears greatly will set the hair of the head on end, and its irreverence is the hardening of the ears.” Frequent swearing therefore causes horror in the head—that is, in the human mind—and brings weariness to honorable ears. Hence the Lord himself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not perjure yourself, but you shall render your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no.’ Anything more than these is from evil (Matt. V).”

The Lord’s command is therefore understood as forbidding oaths, lest anyone seek an oath as though it were a good thing and, through the habit of continual swearing, slip into perjury. Consequently, the person who understands that an oath belongs not among good things but among necessities restrains himself as far as he can, so that he does not use it except from necessity, when he sees that people are slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe unless it is confirmed by an oath. Yet no one knows, except one who has experienced it, how difficult it is both to extinguish the habit of swearing and never rashly to do what necessity sometimes compels one to do.

“Bloodshed occurs in the quarrel of the proud, and their cursing is grievous to hear.” Among the proud there are always quarrels; and wherever quarrel and strife are frequent, there will also be bloodshed. Their cursing is grievous to hear, because just as their conduct is opposed to every good thing, so their speech is ready to curse and is always burdensome for good people to hear.

## CHAPTER VII. That whoever exposes, as he says, a friend’s secrets—that is, his hidden matters—loses faith.

“Whoever exposes a friend’s secrets loses faith, and will not find a friend after his own heart. Love your neighbor, and join faith to him. But if you expose his hidden things, do not pursue him afterward. For just as a man who loses a friend is, so is one who loses the friendship of his neighbor. And just as one who releases a bird from his hand is, so are you when you have let your neighbor go and cannot catch him; do not pursue him, for he is far away. He has escaped like a doe from a snare, because his soul has been wounded. You will no longer be able to bind him together with you, and concord belongs to the accursed. But to expose a friend’s secrets is despair for the soul of the wretched.”

In this chapter, therefore, Wisdom shows what most seriously damages friendship: the evil of betrayal and wickedness. Through it a person loses faith, does not preserve the equity of friendship, and therefore destroys all charity and causes his friend’s affection to flee from him. It adds a beautiful comparison: just as a bird escapes from a fowler’s trap and a doe from a snare and thereafter has no spontaneous return, so friendship wounded by faithlessness will never afterward be restored with the faithless person.

This was also made clear above, where the duty of preserving friendship was discussed: betrayal is the greatest evil, and its correction is difficult. It was likewise demonstrated in the example of Judas the betrayer, concerning whom the Prophet says in the psalm: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly magnified his treachery against me (Ps. XL).” Terrified by the consciousness of his sin, he despaired and ran rather to the noose than to the saving remedy of repentance. Hence it is written concerning him: “He loved cursing, and it will come to him; he did not desire blessing, and it will be far from him (Ps. CVIII).”

“By a nod of the eye he devises wickedness, and no one will cast him out; in the sight of your eyes he will trample upon his mouth, and he will marvel at your words. At last, however, he will pervert his mouth, and in your words he will give offense. I have hated many, but I have not equated him with them, and the Lord will hate him.”

Since above he had discussed the traitor, whose conversion would be difficult, he now reveals the instability of his character: he acts deceitfully and fraudulently in everything, and persists in evil above all because no one casts him out—that is, no one reproves or disciplines him. Wherever this occurs, it increases crime rather than producing the benefit of correction.

And because no one is more appropriately signified by the traitor than the heretic or schismatic, who abandons the faith and sells the truth through the crime of betrayal, this passage appropriately concerns the demonstration of their wickedness, [Col. 0966B] whose intemperance and dishonesty Solomon also shows in Proverbs, saying:

“An apostate man, a useless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, rubs with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a crooked heart, and at all times sows quarrels (Prov. VI).”

For above he had spoken about heresies and had established the teacher for the other kinds of vices; he had roused the sluggish person, but now he rebukes the schismatic as well. Here it should be noted that the one whom he wished to call a sower of quarrels he first named an apostate, because unless, in the manner of the proud angel, he had first fallen inwardly from the sight of the Creator through an aversion of mind, he would not afterward have come forth to sow quarrels.

He is rightly said to “wink with his eyes, rub with his foot, and speak with his finger.” For there is an interior guardianship that keeps the outward members ordered. Therefore, whoever has lost the stability of his mind flows outward into instability of movement, and by outward restlessness shows that he has no inward root by which he remains established.

And because it has already been said that no other evil can be made equal to this kind of plague in a corrupted person, since the Lord would hate him, the wise man mentioned above makes this clear, saying:

“There are six things that the Lord hates, and the seventh his soul detests: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that pour out innocent blood, a heart devising the worst thoughts, feet swift to run into evil, one who utters lies, and one who sows discord among brothers (Prov. VI).”

By saying that God’s soul detests the seventh, he indicates the same person whom he had described above more fully as hateful to God because he sows discord. When he speaks of the Lord’s soul, he does so in human fashion, to signify that he hates such people with full intention and not lightly. So too in Isaiah: “Your new moons and your festivals my soul has hated (Isa. I).”

“He says: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that pour out innocent blood, a heart devising the worst thoughts, feet swift to run into evil, one who utters lies, a false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers.”

He enumerates six capital crimes, yet by comparison with the sower of discord he sets them down as lesser, because surely that deed is greater by which the unity and brotherhood joined together through the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0967A] are destroyed.

Anyone may throw up his eyes arrogantly, lie with his tongue, be stained by homicide, devise evil against his neighbor, subject his members to other crimes, or bring false testimony against someone. But this should not be thought to be the same as what he names above, “a lying tongue.” For one can tell a lie without telling it against one’s neighbor. Indeed, blessed Augustine teaches in the book he composed on lying that there are eight kinds of lies.

I say that anyone who has been ruined may inflict such evils either upon himself or upon others while the peace of the Church remains intact. But what Donatus and Arius and their followers did was more serious: by sowing discord they tore apart the harmony of fraternal unity.

What retribution will follow these malicious men and fabricators of deceit, [Col. 0967B] Scripture indicates, saying:

“He who throws a stone upward will have it fall upon his own head, and the deceitful blow of the deceitful man will divide his wounds. He who digs a pit will fall into it; he who places a stone before his neighbor will stumble over it; and he who prepares a snare for another will perish in it.”

He throws a stone upward who, by blaspheming the divine majesty, brings accusation against it, speaks blasphemous words against his Creator, and provokes to anger by insulting speech the One whom no one can adequately praise. But the severity of its vengeance will come upon him and torment his mind with perpetual pain.

Likewise, the malicious blow of the deceitful man increases the wounds caused by sins; it does not heal the souls of those who sin. So too he who prepares a pit of destruction for another will fall into it; [Col. 0967C] he who constructs for his neighbor an occasion of offense will himself be guilty of eternal torment; and he who lays the snares of ambushes for another will himself, captured by the deceit of his own wickedness, perish forever in them.

“Upon the one who devises a most wicked plan it will roll back upon himself, and he will not recognize from where the mockery and the reproach of the proud have come to him. And vengeance will lie in wait for him like a lion.”

Whoever, therefore, devises a wicked plan against his neighbor with a perverse heart will roll himself into destruction through eternal punishment. But how is it said that he does not recognize from where the mockery and reproach of the proud come to him? It is because he does not consider from where he incurs the guilt for which he pays the penalty.

For the heretic [Col. 0967D] and every schismatic judge that his false election is better than the true preaching of the Catholic faith. Thus he mocks himself, since he does not follow the path of Catholic doctrine. He loves the transgression of God’s commandments and does not fear eternal destruction; he follows error and does not guard against the vengeance of future judgment.

The mockery arising from his own error and the seduction of the devil—who is rightly called a lion because of his ferocity—will make the wicked undergo perpetual vengeance in hell.

“Those who delight in the downfall of the righteous will perish by a snare. But pain will consume them before they die.”

The snare of eternal destruction captures the persecutors of Christians and all who delight in the downfall of the righteous, or who perish through the deception of their neighbors. Pain arising from envy and their own malice torments them inwardly before the end of their lives; after death, however, unending death will follow them without relief.

“Wrath and fury are both accursed, and the sinful man will be tenacious of them.”

He now begins to discuss those who burn with excessive fury and allow prolonged anger to rule in their breast. He says that wrath and fury are accursed in the sight of God, and that the sinful man clings to them. For the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God.

But because it is written, “Anger is better than laughter (Eccl. VII),” and the Prophet says, “Be angry and do not sin (Ps. IV),” the question arises [Col. 0768B] what kind of anger this is that wisdom so greatly condemns. We are permitted to become angry against vices, so that in zeal for God we may pursue them in ourselves and in our neighbors.

All human beings, since they are sharers in our nature, are to be loved; but in everything the best course is moderation and discernment, and nothing should be done without fear and love of God. Anger is pardonable when it does not reach the execution of its indignation. As it is written: “He who conquers anger is better than he who captures a city (Prov. XVI).”

Therefore a remedy is prescribed: if we have already become angry, we must not sin through unconsidered rashness. We cannot, because of human frailty, keep the ardent movement of the soul entirely under our control; yet, with the support of God’s grace, we restrain it by disciplined reason.

Therefore the blessed Prophet permitted what belongs to ordinary human practice, but prohibited what belongs to guilt. For if we become angry and are not restrained by consideration of the Lord, but are prevented from carrying out our intention by some obstacle of necessity, then it is clear that we still bear the guilt of the deed, even if we cannot accomplish what we wished. Or, as some prefer, we ought to become angry at past sins so that we may escape present wickedness. For we cannot avoid recent offenses unless we condemn the old ones with laudable detestation.

What else is repentance but becoming angry with oneself, so that one may dread what one has done and demand suffering from oneself, lest the angry Judge inflict it instead?

## CHAPTER VIII. On the remission of sin

[Col. 0768D] (Chapter XXVIII.) “He who wishes to take vengeance will find vengeance from God, and he will carefully preserve that man’s sins.”

In this chapter, therefore, the teaching agrees in every respect with the Gospel, where it teaches not retaliation according to the Law but patient forbearance according to grace. Hence Paul, writing to the Romans, says:

“Do not be wise in your own estimation; repay no one evil for evil; provide what is good not only before God but also before all people. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people. Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath; for it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord. But if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good (Rom. XII).”

“Forgive your neighbor when he wrongs you; then, when you pray, your sins will be forgiven.”

This is like the Gospel saying: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins (Matt. VI).”

“Does a man preserve anger against another man and seek healing from God? Does he show no mercy to a man like himself and plead for his own sins? Though he himself is flesh, he preserves anger and asks God for pardon?”

It is unworthy that one who wishes to have God favorable to him should show himself cruel and hostile toward his neighbors, especially since no one can obtain forgiveness of his own offenses from God if he refuses to grant pardon to one who has offended him. Hence it follows:

“Who will plead for his offenses?”

As though he said: No one. For it is useless for anyone to pray to God on behalf of the man who does not wish to have the charity toward his brother that God commands.

“Remember the last things and cease being hostile; for decay and death threaten in his commandments.”

Whoever keeps the final hour before the eyes of his heart must necessarily restrain himself from vices, as Scripture testifies, saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin (Eccl. VII).”

Decay and death threaten in the commandments, because in the commandments of God, where salvation exists for those who fear God and keep his precepts, vengeance is also prepared for the disobedient and for those who despise God.

Hence Truth itself says to the Jews in the Gospel: “Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope (John V).” And again: “He who rejects me and does not receive my words has one who judges him: the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day (John XII).”

“Remember the fear of God, and do not become angry with your neighbor. Remember the covenant of the Most High, and disregard your neighbor’s ignorance.”

Whoever fears God restrains anger and fury within himself, and does not forget the covenant of the Most High, who established an agreement between himself and human beings: whoever wishes to receive forgiveness of sins from him must not refuse graciously to forgive the offenses of his neighbors.

For Truth itself says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you (Luke VI).” In the Lord’s Prayer we also have the agreement of this covenant, when we say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matt. VI).”

“Refrain from strife, and you will lessen your sins; for an angry man kindles strife, and a sinful man will disturb friends and introduce hostility among those who are at peace.”

How great an evil strife is, and how disgraceful it is for a Christian to devote himself to quarrels and disputes, Paul shows, saying: “Let there be no jealousy and contention among you (I Cor. III).” And again: “See that, by biting one another, you are not consumed by one another (Gal. V).”

If we consider how great a good peace is, we will easily understand how great an evil discord is. If “blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God,” then without doubt contentious people are wicked and sons of the devil, since they sow discord among those who are at peace and generate hostility.

Heretics and schismatics are their chief representatives, because while they desire to defend useless sects, they do not fear creating contentions and scandals. Therefore the Apostle Paul commanded Timothy, saying: “Do not contend about words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear (II Tim. II).”

And again he says: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist the truth (II Tim. II).”

“For according to the wood of the forest, so the fire blazes; and according to a man’s strength, so will be his anger; and according to his resources, he will magnify his wrath.”

This is a beautiful comparison by which he likens the power of the furious man to a forest of wood. For just as wood provides fuel for fire, so the power of an angry man increases his crimes. The greater the power he has at his command, the stronger he is in the excesses of fury; and the more people he has under his domination, the more people he harms through his savagery.

“A hasty quarrel will kindle a fire, and a quarrel pursued in haste will pour out blood, and a tongue giving testimony will bring death.”

What is signified by a hasty quarrel except an indiscreet action? Whatever is done indiscreetly is easily turned into vice. Hence the command: Let nothing be done to excess.

Thus Ecclesiastes also teaches, saying: “Do not be excessively righteous, and do not be wiser than necessary, lest you become bewildered (Eccl. VII).” Concerning this he says again: “Do not speak rashly, and do not let your heart be quick to utter a word before God (Eccl. V).”

Again it is written: “An inheritance toward which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end (Prov. XX).” And elsewhere we read: “He who is hasty with his feet stumbles (Prov. XIX).”

Therefore immoderate discipline excites the heat of fury, and insolent speech produces the shedding of blood and leads into the snare of death. But because it is within our power whether we complete our anger or not, it follows:

“If you blow upon a spark, it will blaze like a fire; and if you spit upon it, it will be extinguished; both proceed from the mouth.”

Thus anger is aroused by inconsiderate speech; and if a word is spoken prudently and moderately, the anger that has been aroused will quickly be extinguished. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “A harsh word stirs up quarrels, but a gentle word calms those that have been stirred up (Prov. XV).”

And it is rightly said that both proceed from the mouth, because death and life are in the power of the tongue, as Truth itself testifies, saying: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned (Matt. XII).”

## CHAPTER IX. On the evil of the tongue committed by the whisperer and the double-tongued person

“For the whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed, for they will disturb many who are at peace.”

Whom can we more fittingly call a whisperer and a double-tongued person than the heretic, who secretly devises deceits in order to deceive the innocent? He is double-tongued because sometimes he puts forward truths in his doctrine, and at other times falsehoods; thus he mixes and confuses everything, so that it is useless to all who possess a sound and upright faith.
