He “will disturb many who are at peace,” because he makes those who stand in the unity of the faith and the peace of the Church depart from the rule of truth.

“A third tongue has stirred up many and scattered them from nation to nation. It destroyed the fortified cities of the wealthy and dug up the houses of the great. It cut down the strength of peoples and dissolved strong nations. A third tongue drove out strong women and deprived them of their labors.”

He calls the doctrine of the heretics itself a third tongue, because it agrees neither with the Old Testament nor with the New. It always disturbs the hearts of its hearers with superstition and, proceeding from nation to nation, arouses seditions.

“It destroys the fortified cities of the wealthy and digs up the houses of the great” when it casts down from the state of uprightness those whom others consider great, or who, through the pride of their minds, trust that they are great, and when by its deceitful contrivances it digs up and overturns the dwelling place of their cruelty.

By its wickedness it cuts down the strength of peoples and the zeal of learners, and dissolves strong nations in useful work, because, by not allowing them to possess a sound faith, it scatters all their labor. “Without faith it is impossible to please God (Hebr. XI).”

This also signifies what he says about the third tongue driving out strong women and depriving them of their labors: it defrauds human souls devoted to pious works through wicked counsels and destroys their labor.

“Whoever looks upon it has no rest, nor will he dwell with rest. The blow of a scourge produces a bruise, but the blow of the tongue crushes bones. Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as those who have perished through their tongue.”

Therefore whoever attends to the vanity of the heretics never has rest. The blow of their tongue inflicts upon him the bruise of a wound and crushes the strength of his vigor. No fall is more cruel than their ruin, because they pursue not the body but the soul; and whomever they are able to deceive, they deliver to everlasting fires.

“Blessed is he who is protected from an evil tongue, who has not passed into its anger, who has not drawn its yoke upon himself, and who has not been bound in its chains. For its yoke is an iron yoke, and its bond is a bronze bond. Its death is a most evil death, and hell is preferable to it.”

He attributes blessedness to the one who does not consent to the wickedness of the heretics and whose heart their eloquence cannot overturn. Since he is alien to their malice, he will likewise be free from the punishment of vengeance.

He did not consent to entangle himself under its yoke and bonds, because its yoke is exceedingly hard and its fetter long-lasting; these lead the person who consents to them into everlasting death. Hence he says that hell is preferable to it, because it is better to lose bodily life temporarily than to have perpetual fellowship with it in Gehenna.

Indeed, since it will not prevail against everyone but only against the sons of destruction, he appropriately continues:

“Its persistence will not endure, but it will obtain the ways of the unjust; and in its flame it will not burn the righteous. Those who abandon the Lord will fall into it; it will blaze against them and will not be extinguished, and it will be sent against them like a lion, and like a leopard it will injure them.”

Although it dares to test the hearts of the elect, it will not be able to overturn them or burn them in the flame of its malice. But it will seize the deeds of the unjust and capture the minds of those who sin against God.

“It will blaze against them and will not be extinguished,” because those who burn here in wickedness will be tortured in the perpetual flame of hell. There the most savage lion—that is, the devil, who may also be called a leopard because of his various crimes and the varied torments of punishments—will punish them without end.

“Fence your ears with thorns, do not listen to an evil tongue, and make doors and bolts for your mouth.”

After discussing the evil of the whisperer’s tongue, he turns to the instruction of the devout hearer, admonishing him to fence his ears with thorns—that is, to restrain his hearing with the goads of the fear of God, lest he hear wicked speech and a perverse tongue.

Let him set a guard over his mouth and a door of circumspection around his lips, so that his mouth may not turn toward an evil word, to make excuses for sins. Let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. For it is written: “The righteous man will detest a lying word (Prov. XIII).”

Where there are very many words, there is often poverty. And because it is necessary that a Catholic Christian possess both a pure understanding and upright speech, he immediately adds:

“Refine your gold and silver, make a balance for your words and straight reins for your mouth; and take care lest you slip with your tongue, fall in the sight of your enemies lying in wait for you, and your fall be incurable unto death.”

He refines his gold and silver who purifies the understanding and consideration of his heart and the speech of his mouth by testing them in the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that he may be entirely harmonious with the truth of the Catholic faith and the rule of the sacred Scriptures.

But whoever does not take care to guard his words will consequently fall in the sight of his enemies—that is, the evil spirits lying in wait for him. His fall into everlasting death is likewise incurable.

## CHAPTER X. On interest, and what should be done or avoided in it

[Col. 0973A] (Chapter XXIX.) “He who shows mercy lends to his neighbor, and he who prevails with his hand keeps the commandments.”

Wisdom urges its hearers toward the kindness of mercy and the generosity of beneficence, showing them that whoever is ready to show mercy and generous in providing alms keeps God’s commandment and prepares a good reward for himself in the future.

The Lord himself says: “Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from one who wishes to borrow from you (Matt. V)”; and again: “Give, and it will be given to you (Luke VI).”

But because it is just before God that equity be preserved in all things—that is, that a loan be granted to a needy neighbor and that the borrower in turn repay the lender his due—while many commit fraud in lending, he immediately adds, so that no fraud may occur in any transaction:

“Lend to your neighbor in his time of need, and repay your neighbor at the proper time. Confirm your word and deal faithfully with him; and at all times you will find what you need.”

For if faith and justice are preserved by both parties—that is, by the lender and by the one who receives the loan—and no fraud is permitted to dominate their transaction, they will always find what they need, because they will have the grace of God, which is the greatest profit of all things.

The Lord himself says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. VI).” But since many lose this through the wickedness of deceit, he describes their schemes and behavior in what follows.

“Many have regarded interest as a means of profit and have caused trouble for those who helped them. Until they receive the money, they kiss the hand of the giver, lower their voice in their promises, and at the time of repayment they ask for time, speak words of annoyance and complaint, and make excuses about the time. If he has been able to repay, he resists firmly; scarcely will he repay half, and he will reckon that as a gain. But if not, he will defraud him of his money, acquire him as an enemy without cause, and return insults and curses to him; instead of honor and benefit, he will repay him with abuse.”

No other thing cures this kind of disease of wickedness better than fear of the divine majesty. Whoever always has God present in his heart surely fears committing fraud against any person in any matter.

“Many have lent, not because of wickedness, but because they were afraid of being defrauded without cause.”

By this sentence he expresses the character of those who do not desire to harm anyone through deceitful wickedness. Yet they are blameworthy in this respect: because of fear for perishable possessions, they do not wish to benefit others.

Against this evil, therefore, the remedy of mercy and charity must be applied, together with remembrance of that saying of the Lord in which he says:

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither dig through nor steal (Matt. VI).”

Hence elsewhere we read concerning the wealth of this same charity: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.” The following testimony agrees with this:

“Nevertheless, be stronger than the humble in spirit, and do not drag him along on account of almsgiving.”

Mercy must therefore be bestowed upon every needy person with a devout spirit, and the love of one’s neighbor must not be lost for the sake of money. “For whoever sees his brother in need [Col. 0974C] and closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him?”

That the poor man must not be afflicted on account of alms or a loan that has been given, Scripture shows, saying:

“When you reclaim from your neighbor something he owes you, you shall not enter his house to take away his pledge; instead, you shall stand outside, and he will bring out to you whatever he has. But if he is poor, the pledge shall not spend the night with you; you shall immediately return it to him before sunset, so that, sleeping in his garment, he may bless you, and you may have justice before the Lord your God (Deut. XIV).”

The following passage declares this same point abundantly, but it must be begun with another introduction.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0973]

## CHAPTER ONE. On what is given to one’s neighbor—that is, he calls every human being one’s neighbor

“Because of the commandment, take in the poor man, and because of his poverty do not send him away empty.”

Wisdom urges us toward generosity in almsgiving, so that we may be able to win the grace of God, who commanded that poverty be supported by earthly assistance. For it is written: “He who closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard (Prov. XXI).”

In the Gospel we read that the rich man clothed in purple and abounding in luxury was buried in hell because of his stinginess, while the beggar Lazarus, on the contrary, was received after death into Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI). Therefore it is necessary that, according to the Savior’s command, we make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when we fail, they may receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke XVI).

“Lose your money for the sake of your brother and friend; do not hide it under a stone to your destruction.”

He loses his money temporarily who mercifully distributes it to the poor; but he will receive it a hundredfold when, after the judgment has been completed, he is happily invited by the King of all ages to receive the eternal kingdom.

But whoever hides his money under a stone—that is, under an unfeeling and hard heart—stores it up for his own destruction, because after the end of the present life, when the just Judge assigns it, he will receive the fitting reward of his stinginess: when “the wicked will go into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt. XXV).”

“Place your treasure in the commandments of the Most High, and it will benefit you more than gold.”

The commandment of the Most High is that we give alms to the needy. This will benefit us more than gold, because it will confer the reward of eternal life.

Hence Truth itself commanded his disciples in the Gospel, saying:

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves neither dig through nor steal. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart (Matt. VI).”

## CHAPTER II. On mercy toward the poor

“Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will plead for you against every evil.”

As we have often said, almsgiving consists not only in food and clothing, by which provision is made for the needy, but in every act by which mercy assists one suffering want, whether bodily or spiritual.

Whoever therefore instructs the ignorant, or encourages a lazy person to do the good that he knows, rightly performs almsgiving. Hence he expressly says, “Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor,” to show that inward assistance (interiorem opem) is almsgiving, since mercy may rightly be practiced in the soul just as in the body.

And this almsgiving will plead for its giver against every evil—that is, it cleanses him from every offense. For just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.

“A man’s almsgiving is like a purse with him; it will preserve human favor like the apple of the eye, and afterward it will rise up to repay them, repaying each one upon their own heads.”

That the almsgiving mercifully given here to the needy will be abundantly restored in the future life by the Rewarder of all is attested both by prophetic and apostolic speech.

The Psalmist says concerning this: “He distributed and gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever; his horn will be exalted in glory (Ps. III).”

Hence Paul also says: “He who sows in blessings will reap eternal life from blessings (II Cor. IX).” And again: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that you may abound in everything and be enriched (II Cor. IX).”

Hence Truth itself promises in the Gospel that on the day of judgment he will give the kingdom of his Father to those who will be at his right hand, because they sustained his least brothers in this world, so that they may become perpetual possessors of eternal blessedness.

The following sentence also makes clear that almsgiving grants protection against all enemies:

“Upon the shield of the mighty and upon the spear he will fight against your enemy.”

The prayer of almsgiving is more powerful against the flaming darts of the wicked one and against every power of the enemy than earthly weapons are against bodily enemies in the present life. For earthly weapons always lie under uncertain fortune, whereas the former will produce the most certain victory for its soldiers, so that death itself will be swallowed up in victory, and what is mortal will be consumed by life.

“A good man gives security for his neighbor, and he who has lost shame will leave grace for himself.”

The present sentence proves what we said above about spiritual almsgiving, because every teacher, for the love of God and compassion for those who share the common human nature, takes responsibility for his neighbors. He is not ashamed to serve the character of the weak or to cure their sickness by his words, possessing through God’s gift the means by which he can benefit his neighbor through instruction, according to the Prophet’s saying:

“The Lord,” he says, “has given me a learned tongue, so that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word (Isa. L).”

Without doubt he will receive a fitting reward for his labor, and he will never lose the grace of his teaching; rather, he will find eternal mercy from the Lord because of it.

“Do not forget the guarantor, for he gave his life for you.”

The Catholic teacher is a guarantor, [Col. 0976C] because he gave himself for the salvation of his neighbors when he assumed responsibility for them under his governance. The diligence of his disciples must not forget him, because the sanction of apostolic teaching commands this, as in the saying:

“Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him (Gal. VI).”

Hence Truth itself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever rejects you rejects me (Luke X).” And again:

“Into whatever house you enter, first say: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon it; but if not, it will return to you. Remain in that same house, eating and drinking what they have, for the laborer is worthy of his wages (Matt. X; Luke X).”

Hence Paul also says: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you; hold them in the highest love because of their work. Live at peace with them (II Thess. V).”

And again: “Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for God is pleased by such sacrifices. Obey your leaders and submit to them; for they keep watch as those who will give an account to the Lord for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for this would not be useful to you (Hebr. XIII).”

And because the hearer is sometimes ungrateful and despises his teacher, it follows:

“The sinner and the unclean flee from the guarantor.”

The criminal flees from the guarantor—that is, from his teacher, who promises him eternal life from the Lord on account of good works—not by changing his place, but by despising and abandoning the commandment. Therefore he will not obtain the heavenly reward, which is promised in the future only to those who do good and keep God’s commandments.

But because many hope to be saved by their own merit rather than by the divine gift, the following sentence rebukes them, saying:

“The sinner attributes to himself the good things of his guarantor, and, ungrateful in understanding, abandons the one who is saving him.”

This testimony strikes at Pelagius, who places free will before grace, although the elect are freed from every offense through the grace of Christ alone. Hence the Apostle says: “By grace we have been saved (Eph. II).” And again: “Who will free me,” he says, “from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. VII).”

And again: “By the grace of God I am what I am (ibid.).” And: “His grace toward me was not empty (I Cor. XV).”

And because heretics, despising this kind of teaching, construct wicked sects and seduce as many as they can through perverse doctrines, while through the shamelessness of their understanding they cause others to withdraw from them, therefore:

What follows is added:

A man gives surety for his neighbor, and when he has lost reverence, he will be abandoned by him.” He loses respect who does not observe the rule of the sacred Scriptures. For this reason he is abandoned by all prudent people, because the doctrine of truth is not found in him.

“An utterly wicked promise has destroyed many who were directing their steps, and it stirred them like the waves of the sea.” Thus the perverse tradition of heretics leads many who thought they were walking on the path of righteousness—because of their faintheartedness—from the true faith into the byways of error, and, as though torn away by a storm, drives them toward ruin, because it finds them placed not upon rock but upon sand. For whoever, according to the Savior’s saying, builds the house of his faith upon rock does not fear the tempest of storms, but will remain unharmed by every scandal (Matt. VII). Whoever, however, lays the foundations of his house upon sand will be shaken by the force of the winds, the violence of the rains, and the power of the waves, and will be exposed to the greatest ruin.

“He caused mighty men, turning them about, to migrate, and they wandered among foreign nations.” By “mighty men” he wishes proud and arrogant men to be understood. “Turning them about,” he made them migrate—that is, he uproots them from the state of right faith through varied error and mingles them with the crowd of those who wander. They are rightly called “a foreign nation,” because they are exiles from the unity of the Catholic Church. Of them the Psalmist says: “Sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood” (Ps. LVII).

“A sinner who transgresses the Lord’s commandments will fall under an evil promise; and whoever strives to do many things will fall under judgment.” The sinner who transgresses the Lord’s commandments will fall under an evil promise—namely, the one of which it is written in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the words of the Lord’s law and fulfill them in deed” (Deut. XXVII). For, according to Solomon’s saying, “Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his soul; but whoever neglects his ways will be put to death” (Prov. XIX). And because the conduct and activity of the perverse are always unstable, it is therefore added: “Whoever strives to do many things will fall under judgment.” He strives to do many things who does not care to preserve the unity of right faith and the sincerity of God’s law, but prefers to entangle himself in various errors and different crimes. He will fall under the judgment of the reprobate—that is, everlasting condemnation—when at the final judgment he is told, together with those who will stand at the judge’s left hand: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). Therefore Wisdom says: “My son, do not let your acts be many” (Eccl. XI); and Ecclesiastes says: “Many cares bring dreams, and in many words folly will be found” (Eccl. V). In the same book the same teacher gives this warning: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply; they were given through the counsel of teachers by one shepherd. Beyond these, my son, do not seek more. There is no end to the making of many books” (Eccl. XII).

It is customary in Scripture, even when there are several books which do not disagree with one another and which write about the same subject, to call them one volume. In Isaiah’s language, too, the whole Scripture of God is designated as one volume, and this is also recognized in a single chapter of the books of Ezekiel and John. The Savior, moreover, foretold in the words of all the saints of former times, saying: “In the beginning of the book it is written about me” (Ps. XXXIX). According to this interpretation, therefore, I think the command is now given that many books should not be made. Whatever you say, if it is referred to him who in the beginning was God the Word with God, is one volume, and innumerable books are one law, one Gospel. But if you discuss diverse and contradictory matters, and in excessive curiosity draw your mind here and there, even in one book there are many books. Hence it is said: “You will not escape sin through many words” (Prov. X).

“Recover your neighbor according to your strength, and take heed to yourself lest you fall.” This is a perfectly sound teaching and a most useful counsel: that you offer your neighbor consolation according to your strength, and take care of yourself lest you fall into the snare of sin or error. These too are the distinguishing marks of the Christian religion, the way of truth, and the rule of righteousness. Hence the apostle James also wrote in his Epistle, saying: “Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, and to keep oneself undefiled from this world” (Jas. I).

Because he had said that the doer of the work would be blessed in his deed, he now says what deeds especially please God: namely, mercy and innocence. For when he commanded that orphans and widows be visited in their tribulation, he indicated everything that we ought to do mercifully toward our neighbor, since the value of this will be revealed at the time of judgment, when the judge will say: “As long as you did it to one of these, my least brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. LII). Further, when he commanded us to keep ourselves undefiled from this world, he showed all the things in which it is fitting for us to preserve ourselves chaste. Among these are also the matters he had previously urged us to observe: that we be slow to speak and slow to anger.

## CHAPTER III. On honorable frugality, that is, continence, moderation, and hospitality

“The beginning of human life is water and bread and clothing, and a house protecting nakedness.” In this chapter Wisdom teaches frugality, propriety, and hospitality, so that we may have moderation in food and clothing, uprightness in conduct, and generosity in receiving the brethren. For when he says that the beginning of human life consists of water and bread, clothing, and a house protecting nakedness, he shows that in the beginning human beings did not have such luxury of food and drink as exists now, nor such ambition in the adornment of clothing and the construction of towers and palaces. Rather, it was enough for each person that the earth supplied through its simple produce and that the nature of the place provided in dwellings.

Thus we read that the ancients ate the fruits of trees and the shoots of vegetables, and that, because of Adam’s sin, the Lord made tunics of skin for him and his wife and clothed them. But now, the greater the attention devoted to providing a variety of foods and drinks and to the adornment of clothing and houses, the less diligence there is in observing good disciplines, and the greater the wickedness in transgressing the divine commandments. Therefore, rebuking the wickedness of Jerusalem, the Lord brought forward the sin of Sodom as an example, for Jerusalem had imitated it—indeed, surpassed it (Matt. X). As the prophet’s words testify: “Behold,” he says, “this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, abundance, and ease belonged to her and her daughters, and they did not extend a hand to the needy and poor. They were lifted up and committed abominations before me, and I removed them, as you saw. Samaria did not sin even half as much as your sins; you surpassed them in crimes, and justified your sisters in all the abominations that you committed” (Ezek. XVI).

“Better is the food of the poor beneath a roof of boards than splendid banquets abroad without a dwelling.” According to the historical sense, it is more comfortable for anyone to eat modest food safely beneath a mean hut than to seek splendid banquets here and there in uncertain places amid excessive weariness and needless anxiety. According to the allegory, however, better is the spiritual nourishment of understanding which is held beneath the humble covering of letters by the poor people of the Church in Catholic unity than the ambitious delights of philosophical doctrines, which are contained in the various books of rhetors by philosophers or heretics more falsely and speculatively than truthfully. There great labor, superfluous care, and little benefit are found. Of such people Paul says: “Always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth” (II Tim. III). For God has made foolish the wisdom of this world, and the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.

“Let a little please you as much as a great deal, and you will not hear the reproach of exile.” It is as though he plainly said: Let what you have be sufficient for you, and do not seek wealth excessively, which you cannot obtain. Hence one of the wise men says: It is better not to have what you can give than shamelessly to seek what you do not have. Concerning this it is also written in Proverbs: “Better is a little with the fear of God than great and unstable treasures. Whoever loves feasts will be in poverty; whoever loves wine and rich foods will not become rich” (Prov. XV). And again: “A good name is better than great riches; and good favor is above gold and silver.”

“A wicked life is to lodge from house to house; and wherever he lodges, he will not act confidently, nor will he open his mouth.” How good it is for anyone to remain stable in his position and way of life, and how disgraceful it is to wander through different places in the manner of the Circumcellions, the evangelical and apostolic teaching makes clear. Hence the Savior commanded his disciples, saying: “Do not go from house to house; and into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you, and heal the sick who are in it” (Luke X). For this reason Paul, writing to the Thessalonians, rebuked wanderers, saying: “We hear that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but acting as busybodies” (II Thess. III). To those who are such we announce and beseech in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they eat their own bread.

When he says, “Wherever he lodges, he will not act confidently, nor will he open his mouth,” he shows that it is difficult for him to find security among strangers—a security which Solomon placed above all delights, saying: “A secure mind is like a continual feast” (Prov. XV). For it is a great punishment to live diligently among people in whom one trusts neither in mind nor in words, but always suspects, in their faithless heart, a snare of capture and a stumbling block of offense.

“He will lodge, and feed, and give drink to the ungrateful, and for these things he will hear bitter words.” He will lodge, that is, received ungratefully in another’s house, where he eats and drinks while always fearing misfortune; and often, provoked by another’s tongue, he hears reproach.

“Pass on, guest, and adorn the table; and feed the others with what you have in your hand. Withdraw from before the honor of my friends; because of the need of my house, a brother has become my guest.” These are words of reproach, describing what the lodger hears bitterly from his host. Their context may have this meaning: You who always wish to use another’s hospitality, withdraw from us and return to your own people; there, from your own labor, feed yourself and others, and do not seek excessive nourishment for yourself from another’s house. For me, the reception and fellowship of neighbors and brothers are sufficient for sharing my house. You, however, ought to withdraw from the dwelling of my friends and among your own people do what, among strangers, you do not cease shamelessly to seek.

“These things are grievous to a sensible man: the rebuke of a household and the reproach of a moneylender.” For a man of modest understanding, it is grievous to receive such rebuke and reproach from the mouth of a moneylender. But an impudent man will be corrected neither by a word nor amended by reproof.

Mystically, however, this passage admonishes the ecclesiastical man to remain diligently in the house of the Church, where he can have the food of true wisdom and remain safe from the injury of perverse doctrines. If, by dangerously lodging among philosophers and heretics, he seeks the teaching of secular wisdom—where he will in no way be able to find the benefit of sound doctrine—then at the future examination he will be compelled to endure, for his insolence, the reproach of everlasting confusion. Let the Catholic man therefore say to his fellow the prophetic words:

“But you, a man of one mind, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food: let us walk in agreement in the house of God. Let death come upon our adversaries, and let them descend alive into hell; for wickedness is in their dwellings, in their midst, and so forth” (Ps. LIV).

## CHAPTER IV. On the discipline of children: with what affection they are to be loved or corrected

(CAP. XXX.) “Whoever loves his son applies the rod to him continually, so that he may rejoice in his final state and not knock at the doors of his neighbors.” This saying admonishes not only carnal fathers but also spiritual fathers—that is, teachers of the faithful—to care for those entrusted to them and to devote effort and diligence to the instruction and nourishment of their children, so that they may teach them to live in discipline and to flee every dishonesty. Let them live at home with upright conduct, lest by behaving wantonly they uselessly run about after other doctrines. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “Discipline your son, and do not despair; but do not set your soul on his death” (Prov. XIX).

“Whoever teaches his son will be praised in him, and will be glorified in the midst of his household.” Whoever instructs his disciple in sound doctrine and imbues him with the truth of faith will assuredly obtain perpetual praise and glory for such devotion in the fellowship of the saints. Scripture says that the just man who makes the discipline of his teaching known publicly and glories in the law of the Lord’s covenant will be praised by many for his wisdom, and his memory will not be erased forever. “His memory will not depart, and his name will be sought from generation to generation” (Eccles. XXXIX).

“His father has died, and it is as though he had not died, for he has left behind him one like himself during his lifetime.” The succession of holy sons, who after their fathers have departed this life imitate their good devotion in holy religion and upright conduct, presents their dead parents as though restored to life, since by preserving their teaching and discipline in all their own words and deeds they openly show this.

“He saw him and rejoiced in him; at his death he was not grieved, nor was he confounded before his enemies. For he left behind a defender of the house against enemies and one who renders gratitude to friends.” What else did the holy apostles and the first teachers of the Church do except leave behind them, from among those whom they had nurtured, shepherds and rulers of the peoples, so that these might, in a fatherly manner, resist adversaries with the shield of faith and truth and offer the grace of right doctrine and good examples to those subject to them?

For this was instituted by the Lord himself: that twelve loaves of the presence should continually remain on the table of the tabernacle, yet in such a way that every Sabbath the old loaves were removed and new loaves placed in their stead (Lev. XXIV). What does this signify except that each teacher of the holy Church, when the time of his holy labor is complete, is rewarded with eternal rest in heaven and leaves others after him to labor at the same work of preaching the word, under the same hope of reward? Observing this, the Psalmist proclaimed beforehand in prophetic spirit, saying: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them princes over all the earth. They will remember your name, Lord, throughout every generation and offspring” (Ps. LIV).

But because that assembly of holy teachers not only sympathizes with its children with intimate affection of heart, but is even ready to endure bodily torments and lay down its life for their salvation, it is added:

“For the souls of his children he will bind up his wounds, and at every cry his inward parts will be shaken.” Hence the teacher of the nations, rejecting every word of perverse doctrine and preserving evangelical truth, glories in the passions, necessities, tribulations, and distresses which he endured for Christ, saying:

“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us. In everything we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed; we are perplexed, but not despairing; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but do not perish, always carrying in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies” (II Cor. IV).

But let us hear what Wisdom thinks about undisciplined children:

“An untamed horse becomes obstinate, and an undisciplined son becomes headstrong. Fondle your son, and he will make you afraid; play with him, and he will grieve you. Do not laugh with him, lest you suffer grief and in the end your teeth become numb. Do not give him power in his youth, and do not despise his thoughts. Bend his neck in his youth, and strike his sides while he is a child, lest he become hardened, fail to trust you, and become a pain to your soul. Teach your son and work upon him, lest you stumble over his shame.”

For just as the pride of an untamed horse is prone to plunge into a precipice, so the wantonness of an undisciplined son is close to the ruin of sin. Therefore it teaches the leaders of the Church and spiritual fathers to nourish their children and disciples with discipline, to preserve them always with every caution, to correct them at the proper time, and never to loosen the reins of freedom for them without measure, lest they fall into the shame of vices and consequently suffer everlasting disgrace.

## CHAPTER V. On the good of health, because poverty and health are better than riches

“A poor man who is healthy and strong in his own powers is better than a rich man who is weak and scourged by wickedness.” Here, therefore, he praises not so much bodily health as that of the soul, because a man who is sound in mind is not harmed by being troubled in body. Hence Paul says of himself: “When I am weak, then I am strong; therefore I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (II Cor. XII).

It does not help anyone to abound in bodily health and worldly riches if he is weak in faith and tormented by the goad of wickedness, for better is the poor man who walks in his simplicity than the rich man who walks in crooked paths. Nothing is lacking to Christ’s poor who fear him. But the rich of the world will be needy and hungry, and every day they will fail in poverty of spiritual and true riches; those who seek the Lord, however, will lack no good thing. The following saying also proves this:

“The health of the soul in the holiness of righteousness is better than all gold and silver, and a strong body than immense wealth.” The true health of the soul is righteousness preserved according to God’s commandments, and immense weights of gold and silver cannot be compared with it, because these things fall away and quickly pass, whereas the former remains forever. Hence Truth itself says: “See and beware of every form of greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Luke XII).

Solomon likewise says: “Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but righteousness will deliver from death. The righteousness of the simple will direct his way, and the wicked man will fall in his wickedness. The righteousness of the upright will deliver them, and the wicked will be caught in their own snares” (Prov. XI).

When he says that a strong body is better than immense wealth, he shows that the body is truly healthy when it labors vigorously in the work of God. No great wealth can be equated with such health, because, according to Ecclesiastes: “Sweet is the sleep of one who works, whether he eats little or much; but the abundance of the rich does not allow him to sleep” (Eccles. V). Since sleep sometimes signifies natural rest and sometimes the common departure from this life, the future rest of the one who works in the present and lives according to his strength in good works will be better than the riches of those of whom it is written: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation” (Luke VI).

“There is no wealth above the health of the body, and there is no delight above the joy of the heart.” This is what he said above: that the health of the soul consists in the holiness of righteousness, and that in a strong body there is a dignity surpassing the treasure of gold and silver. For no earthly joy can be compared with the delight of true wisdom, which consists in true charity, or with contemplation of truth itself, which is the sure knowledge of God. Nor can any business of this world be equal to the works of virtue, to which the devotion of the faithful is always devoted, because they differ in dignity as much as they differ in duration.

“Better is death than a bitter life, and eternal rest than enduring sickness.” It is written in Ecclesiastes: “I praised the dead who are already dead more than the living who are still alive; and happier than both I judged the one who has not yet been born and has not seen the evils that are done under the sun” (Eccles. IV). There he shows that, in comparison with the miseries which press upon mortals in this world, the dead are happier than the living. Happier than both—the living and the dead—is the one who has not yet been born: one still suffers evils, while the other has escaped naked, as it were, from a shipwreck. The one who has not yet been born is happier because he has not yet experienced the evils of the world.

This saying, which declared death better than a bitter life and eternal rest better than enduring sickness, according to the simple understanding shows that the death of which it is written, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV), is better than the bitter life led by sinners occupied in wicked works. It also shows that the eternal rest which the righteous possess in the sight of the Lord is better than the enduring sickness by which those who remain in sins waste away daily. Their end is destruction, and their glory is turned into their own confusion, because they set their minds on earthly things.

“Good things hidden in a closed mouth are like dishes set around a tomb.” This testimony applies against those who neglect to preach to others the talent of God’s word which they themselves have received through understanding. Their knowledge is as useless to the living as dishes placed around the tombs of the dead, who neither eat nor drink nor obtain any fruit from them. Hence it follows:

“For what benefit is a libation to an idol? For it will neither eat nor smell. So is one who flees from the Lord and carries the wages of iniquity: seeing with his eyes and groaning, like a eunuch embracing a virgin and sighing.”

There is no reason for a rational human being to abandon God his creator, who created him for the honor and glory of his name, so that he might offer him the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord, and then present libations to vain idols which neither perceive nor understand anything and have no share in human nourishment. Hence Scripture says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths but will not speak; they have eyes but will not see. They have ears but will not hear; they have nostrils but will not smell. They have hands but will not touch; they have feet but will not walk; they will not cry out through their throat” (Ps. CXIII). For there is no spirit in their mouths.

What reward is repaid to their makers, the following verse shows by saying: “Those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.” The comparison of the eunuch with the virgin demonstrates the same thing under another image: just as a eunuch is incapable of embracing a virgin, so the worship of idols is unfitting for those who seek some assistance from them but find absolutely none.

“Do not give sorrow to your soul, and do not afflict yourself in your own counsel.” Sorrow is one of the eight principal vices: namely, worldly sorrow, which produces death and casts a person into despair. But the sorrow that is according to God produces abiding salvation and cleanses a person from all sins, since, according to the Psalmist’s saying, “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. L).

“Do not give sorrow to your soul,” he says, “and do not afflict yourself in your own counsel”—that is, in your own thought—because a sorrowful thought greatly afflicts the soul. Therefore it is necessary for a person always to turn his mind toward God and continually entrust his hope to him, from whom he will find certain salvation. Hence the prophet addresses his soul in consoling words, saying: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will confess to him, the salvation of my face and my God” (Ps. XLI).

“Joy of heart is the life of a man, and a treasure of holiness without failure.” True joy of heart exists nowhere except in true charity. There the life of a person remains, together with the treasure of the virtues, in unfailing holiness, because no virtue can endure without its help. This is the more excellent way which the Apostle placed above all languages, martyrdom, and almsgiving, and showed to surpass faith and hope, saying: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity, because when the others pass away, it alone remains” (I Cor. XIII).

“The exultation of a man is longevity.” In saying this he is not discussing the length of the present life but the happiness of the future one, because true exultation is found where true blessedness is also found. The present life, on the other hand, is entirely full of misery and is always unstable and changeable, as the noble poet also explains in verse:

> Each best day of life for wretched mortals  
> Flees first; diseases follow, and sad old age,  
> And toil and the mercilessness of dreadful death carry all away.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* III)

What grants us sure rest, the following saying makes clear:

“Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God, and exercise restraint; gather your heart in his holiness, and drive sorrow far from you. For sorrow has killed many, and there is no benefit in it.”

There are many kinds of mercy, as we have often already said, but the chief kind is that mentioned here: that through continence, holiness, and righteousness we strive to please God, and gather the whole affection of our spirit for this purpose, so that we may be acceptable to him and offer him the fruit of good works with humility and devout reverence. Let us drive sorrow far from us, because no gift offered with worldly sorrow will be acceptable before God. Hence, when the Apostle exhorts the Corinthians to generosity in almsgiving, saying: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows with blessings will reap from blessings eternal life” (II Cor. IX), he immediately adds: “Each one according to what he has determined in his heart, not from sorrow or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver” (ibid.).

“For sorrow has killed many, and there is no benefit in it.” How can there be any benefit where there is barrenness of good works and the peril and death of the whole life? The following saying proves this:

“Jealousy and anger shorten the days, and anxious thought brings on old age before its time.” It is clear according to the historical sense that jealousy and a perverse disposition weaken the body. We read in Genesis that, because of anger and envy, Cain’s countenance fell (Gen. IV). In the Book of Kings, Jonadab, the friend of Amnon son of David, detected through the thinness of his face the disturbance of spirit which he had because of his desire for his sister Tamar (II Kings XIII). Solomon expressed a similar thought in Proverbs, saying: “A joyful spirit makes the age flourish, but a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. XVII).

According to the allegory, however, jealousy and anger shorten a person’s days when they make him unworthy of eternal life. They bring on old age before its time, because “men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Ps. LIV)—that is, they cannot possess forever the prosperity without vengeance which they promise themselves.

“A bright heart is good at feasts, for its feasts are prepared diligently.” Certainly the good will of the elect rejoices in the feasts of the virtues, and those feasts possess unfailing riches of spiritual wealth.

## CHAPTER VI. Vigilance on account of the fear of God wastes away the flesh—that is, subdues it; for wakefulness for perpetrating evil is criminal

(CAP. XXXI.) “Vigilance in propriety will waste away the flesh, and its thought will take away sleep.” Vigilance in propriety is the mind’s careful watchfulness joined with devotion to the virtues. It wastes away the flesh because, in God’s elect, it puts carnal pleasures to death. Its thought takes away sleep because the attentive concern which they have daily in God’s service drives from them the weariness of sloth. Hence the prophet, who felt himself making progress in God’s service and growing in his love, says: “How I have loved your law, Lord; it is my meditation all day long. I will exercise myself in your commandments and consider your ways. Fasten my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII).

“Thought of foreknowledge turns away the senses, and severe infirmity makes the soul sober.” The thought which a person has in the fear of God—foreknowing that everything sacred Scripture foretells concerning the future reward of the good and the coming punishment of the wicked is true—turns the human mind away from every evil desire, so that it neither desires to possess nor seeks to fulfill in wicked longing what it knows displeases its creator. Likewise, severe bodily infirmity makes the soul sober with respect to sins.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “The bruise of a wound will wipe away evils, and blows in the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. XX). The bruise of a wound wipes away evils because the pain of scourging washes away sins either contemplated or committed. The “belly” is often understood as the mind, because just as the belly consumes food, so the mind digests anger by considering it. That the belly signifies the mind is taught by the saying: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a man, searching all the hidden places of the belly” (ibid.). It is as though he said: When the illuminating breath of divine inspiration enters a person’s mind, it illumines and reveals it to itself; before the arrival of the Holy Spirit, the mind could carry perverse thoughts but did not know how to weigh them.

“The bruise of a wound will therefore wipe away evils, and blows in the innermost parts of the belly,” because when we are struck outwardly, we are recalled silently and sorrowfully to the memory of our sins. We bring before our eyes everything that we have done badly, and through what we suffer outwardly we grieve more deeply over what we have done inwardly. Thus, amid the manifest wounds of the body, the hidden wound of the belly cleanses us more fully, because the hidden wound of sorrow heals the wickedness of evil deeds. Hence Paul also says: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” For when he endured outwardly the scourges of persecution, inwardly he grew through the gift of spiritual graces.

“The rich man has labored in the accumulation of wealth, and in his rest he will be filled with his goods; the poor man has labored in reducing his sustenance, and in the end he becomes destitute.” In many places of Scripture riches are praised, and in many they are censured. Where they are praised, spiritual riches are signified; where they are censured, bodily wealth and the worldly desires of the present age are condemned. Therefore in this chapter, discussing good and bad riches in turn according to the character of the persons involved, he first praises the rich man laboring in the accumulation of riches, by which he will be filled with good things in his rest. Then he censures the poor man because he has labored in reducing his sustenance and will attain poverty in the end, adding how many evils follow the greed for gold and money. Afterwards he again praises the rich man according to God, who is found without blemish.

The righteous rich man therefore labors in the accumulation of spiritual wealth: namely, in meditating on knowledge of the holy Scriptures and gathering the fruits of good virtues. For all these things, after the end of the present life, he will receive eternal rest and the recompense of heavenly rewards. By contrast, the poor man in knowledge and destitute of virtue labors daily in earthly desires. In the end he will possess not an abundance of heavenly joy but will suffer the punishments and pains of hell.

“Whoever loves gold will not be justified, and whoever pursues destruction will be filled with it.” We may understand gold as every kind of money and earthly treasure, which is gathered by its lovers only through greed and reserved through parsimony for their own harm. Whoever consumes the present life in this ambition will be filled with everlasting disgrace.

“Many have been given over to the downfall of gold, and their destruction has come through its appearance.” He is given over to the downfall of gold who is held captive by ambition for it. Its appearance generates his destruction, because he does not fear becoming excessively inflamed by love of it. For greed, as the Apostle says, is the service of idols (Col. III). And where will idol-worshipers and idol-servants be assigned except to the abyss of hell, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished” (Isa. LXVI)? Concerning this it is immediately added:

“Gold is a tree of offense for those who sacrifice. Woe to those who pursue it, and every imprudent person will perish in it.” In the sacred Scriptures, “offense” is called the desolation of idols, because true worship of God is destroyed in it, and God is especially offended by false worship. Gold is a tree of offense for those who sacrifice because, just as Adam, deceived by the serpent’s suggestion when he transgressed regarding the forbidden tree, greedily hoped that the exaltation of many gods would come to him, so lovers of gold, serving the images of various errors, sacrifice their souls to demons as though offering them in sacrifice, so that they may become possessors of abundant riches. But woe to those who pursue this plague, because in their imprudence they acquire eternal condemnation for themselves through it. According to the rule of allegory, this may also be understood of the gold sacrificed to idols—that is, the doctrine of heretics and philosophers—which shines with the splendor of eloquence and everywhere announces the ruin of the curious. Whoever, captivated by love of it, does not guard against the snares of its hidden wickedness will fall, bound by the traps of error and sins, into everlasting punishments.

But let us see what he subsequently says about the chosen people, who are rich in divine knowledge, right faith, and good works.

“Blessed is the rich man who was found without blemish, who did not go after gold, nor place his hope in treasures of money. Who is he, and we shall praise him? For he did marvelous things in his life. Whoever was tested by it and proved perfect will have eternal glory. Whoever could have transgressed and did not transgress, and could have done evil and did not do it. Therefore his good things have been established in God, and the Church of the saints will recount his almsgiving.” [Col. 0988D] That rich man is blessed whom no stain of error obscures and no ambition for worldly money pollutes. He did marvelous things in his life by devoting himself to the sacred virtues—or by shining through miracles and granting healing to the sick and weak—because he faithfully remained in the love of his Creator, advancing daily. Thus perpetual rest and the eternal glory of the heavenly kingdom remain for him. For, according to the freedom of will granted to him, he could have transgressed the commandment, but did not transgress; he could have done evil, but did not do it. I do not mean that he never sinned, but that through repentance, by the grace of his Creator, he washed away the stains of all his sins. Therefore the good things he accomplished in this present life are preserved, established for the rewards of future recompense, and the Church of the saints will proclaim and recount his works of mercy from generation to generation.

## CHAPTER VII. On Restraint in Food

“You have sat at a great table; do not open your throat over it first.” Although historically this saying seems to commend restraint to us, so that we may not be intemperate in eating and drinking through an appetite for gluttony, but sober and pure, nevertheless, in a higher sense it teaches us to be cautious and prudent in meditating on the law of God. The great table is the abundance of the divine Scriptures. Sitting at it, we must not be presumptuous, snatching something from it unworthily, without a teacher and without prior preparation; rather, following the well-trodden path of the holy teachers and instructed by their disciplines, we should hold to the rule of truth, lest, disturbed by some scruple, we suppose that anything there is doubtful or uncertain. Therefore he adds:

“Do not say, ‘There are many things upon it’; remember that the evil eye is wicked. What has been created is more wicked than the eye? Therefore it will weep from its whole face when it sees.” We must not believe that anything false is found there, but that all things are true and established with the highest reason, although the wicked tradition of heretics strives to stain them with perverse interpretation. Nothing is more wicked than their impious intention. Therefore, when what was previously hidden has been disclosed in the future judgment by the revelation of the just Judge, they will be tormented with perpetual weeping and unquenchable fire.

[Col. 0989C] “Do not stretch out your hand first, and, contaminated by envy, be ashamed.” This means: do not act presumptuously or with excessive insolence; before you have learned, do not put your hand to writing, lest, contaminated by the devil’s envy through error, you be ashamed at the future judgment, when the Judge says: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Ps. VI).

“Do not be constricted at a banquet by wine; understand your neighbor’s matter from yourself.” There is wine in which there is debauchery, and there is wine in which there is grace. We must therefore beware lest, contrary to the Apostle, we become drunk with wine in which there is every kind of debauchery. Wine in which there is the teaching of grace must be used prudently, lest by drinking it beyond measure we wish to be wiser than we ought to be; rather, let us strive to have sober judgment. [Col. 0989D] Hence he continues:

“Use, like a frugal person, what is set before you, so that, when you eat much, you may not be hated. Stop first for the sake of discipline, and do not be excessive, lest perhaps you offend. And if you have sat among many, do not stretch out your hand before them, nor ask first to drink.” It is most fitting and worthy of virtue that a Christian love sobriety and do everything temperately—nothing in excess—lest he offend; lest, if he exceed the measure of temperance, he fall into the scandal of perpetual shame. It is therefore fitting for a man trained in the disciplines of the Gospel to practice humility above all, to remain a cautious reader in meditation on the Scriptures, to hold right faith, and not neglect to maintain moderation in silence, knowing that the rule of charity must be observed in all things within it. Thus he will be pleasing before God and approved before human beings.

“How sufficient for a learned man is a little wine! You will not labor in your sleep because of it, and you will feel no pain.” It is clear that a frugal and light diet is useful both to body and soul. Conversely, excessive food or drink produces bodily illness and diminishes the soul’s understanding. Concerning this he adds:

“Wakefulness, bile, and torment are for a foolish man.” Therefore the Apostle instructed his disciple concerning the moderation of diet, saying: “Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. V). [Col. 0990B] So too, spiritual wine, if taken sparingly and in moderation, prepares a sure rest for the soul. But when its drinking exceeds measure and reason, it turns a person into madness and compels him to withdraw from God. Anxiety, great disturbance, and perpetual torment follow; nor will there be any remedy for one who, after recognizing the truth, chooses to follow the path of heretical perversity to the end.

“Sleep is health for a moderate person; he will sleep until morning, and his soul will delight with him.” Historically, sleep is healthier for one who uses a frugal diet than for one who stuffs his belly through excessive eating and drinking. As he said above: “Wakefulness, bile, and torment produce illness.” Mystically, however, the person who is a sober drinker of spiritual wine rests sweetly in contemplation of the truth until the morning of the resurrection. Then, at the coming of his Judge, invited to eternal rewards, he will forever enjoy the promised blessings in the heavenly kingdom. Toward this good the Prophet, aspiring with joyful mind to the Lord himself, says: “You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence; delights are at your right hand forever” (Ps. XV).

“And if you are compelled to eat much, rise in the midst of it and vomit, and it will refresh you, and you will not bring illness upon your body.” Physicians say that if a fasting person induces vomiting, he cleanses the stomach’s disorders and diminishes bile. Mystically, however, whoever exceeds the measure in the desires of the flesh and is weighed down by sins [Col. 0990D] must vomit out the filth through confession of sins, and thus, through fasting and bodily discipline, return to his former state of health.

“Listen to me, my son, and do not despise me, and at the end you will find my words. In all your works be quick, and no infirmity will come upon you.” Wisdom warns us not to waste the time granted to us, but to spend it all in the exercise of good works and the keeping of God’s commandments. Thus, in the future life, we shall find rest for our souls. This is what he says: “In all your works be quick, and no infirmity will come upon you”—that is, whatever our hand finds to do in this present [Col. 0991A] life, let us perform diligently, and let no weakness of weariness seize us. While we have time, let us do good to all, since there is neither time nor opportunity for working among the dead. After the end of this present life, when the just Judge renders recompense, each person will receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

A similar statement is written in Proverbs: “Have you seen a man quick in his work? He will stand before kings and will not be among the ignoble” (Prov. XXII). That is, whoever you see quick in his work—namely, in the good work that he ought to perform diligently and attentively—know that on the day of the final examination he will stand before the apostles, who will sit with Christ to judge the world, because he has kept their commands. He will not be placed among the ignoble teachers whose error he avoided, that is, on the Judge’s left.

“Lips of many will bless the one who is splendid in bread, and the testimony of his truth is faithful.” Historically, this saying seems to exhort us to generosity in almsgiving, since, according to the Apostle Paul, “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessings will reap eternal life from blessings; for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX). Spiritually, whoever faithfully expends the bread of God’s word upon his neighbors and does not conceal the testimony of truth before willing listeners will receive from many the praise of blessing, and from the Lord himself will draw the grace of eternal reward. Hence it is also written in Proverbs: “From the fruit of a man’s mouth his belly will be filled, and the produce of his lips will satisfy him” (Prov. XVIII).

Conversely, let us hear what follows from the perverse doctrine of heretics:

“In the most wicked bread the city will murmur, and its testimony of wickedness is true.” Thus, in the most wicked doctrine of heretics, who adulterate the word of God and feed not on the bread of life but on the bread of falsehood, whatever their poisonous speech produces is confirmed by the true testimony written about them: “A false witness will not go unpunished, and whoever speaks falsehood will perish.”

“Do not provoke those who delight in wine, for wine has destroyed many.” The Ecclesiastic teaches us not to associate with drunkards, because they are quick to anger. [Col. 0991D] “For wine has destroyed many”—that is, drunkenness has overthrown many. It diminishes understanding, arouses anger, inflames lust, and exposes the mind’s secrets through rage or desire. Hence he adds:

“Fire tests hard iron; so wine, when drunk in drunkenness, will expose the hearts of the proud.” That is, just as fire softens iron’s hardness by its heat and makes it glow according to its nature, so wine drunk in drunkenness inflames the hearts of the proud with its heat, suddenly provoking them to commit crime and granting greater boldness to their proud intention for the perpetration of evil.

“Wine is life for human beings when drunk in moderation; if you drink it moderately, you will be sober.” Wine drunk in moderation does not take life away from human beings; rather, it brings sobriety together with the other adornments of virtue. What evil drunkenness brings to its followers, the following saying makes clear:

“What kind of life belongs to one who is diminished by wine? What defrauds life? Death.” He calls wine—namely, drunkenness—the death that kills life, because the vitality of understanding is diminished by it and bodily illness arises from it. As though reproving death itself, he asks why it defrauds life, condemning excessive drinking as the deceiver of humanity.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Drunkenness

“Wine was created for joy and not for drunkenness from the beginning.” The Creator made earthly fruits for this purpose: so that human beings, appointed by their Maker as lords of the earth, might obtain from them nourishment for temporal life, not harm to their health. Concerning these fruits of the earth—namely, grain and wine—the Creator of all things and Redeemer of humanity made an appropriate mystery, converting them into the sacrament of his body and blood. Concerning this it is written in the Prophet: “Wine gladdens the heart of man,” and “bread strengthens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII), so that human nature might have nourishment for its salvation in both substances and might return more abundant thanks to its Author, recognizing that all things had been provided for it well and beneficially.

“Exultation of soul and heart is wine drunk moderately.” [Col. 0992C] He repeats the same things frequently so that he may impress their memory more firmly upon the minds of his hearers, commend the sequence and beauty of the virtues to them more strongly, and, as far as possible, utterly destroy the shamefulness and harmfulness of vices. Therefore he adds further:

“Wine drunk in excess causes irritation, anger, and many ruins. Wine drunk in excess is bitterness of soul; the boldness of drunkenness is the offense of the imprudent, diminishing virtue and causing wounds.” What could have been said more clearly than that irritation, anger, and many ruins arise from drunkenness; that bitterness of soul is generated by it; that the bold offense of the imprudent proceeds from it; that the sequence of virtues is diminished by being weakened; and that crimes multiply wounds? Therefore blessed is the person who guards himself from such a plague and establishes the hope of his salvation in the Lord’s will. For the Lord guards all who love him, and mercy will surround those who hope in him.

“In a banquet of wine do not rebuke your neighbor, and do not despise him in his enjoyment. Do not speak words of reproach to him, and do not press him by repeating them.” It frequently happens that a frail person exceeds the measure in drinking, yet does not pursue the vice of drunkenness in wicked practice. Therefore he forbids us to rebuke our neighbor at a banquet of wine, to despise him in his enjoyment, or to address him with reproachful insults. Rather, according to the Apostle, let us bear one another’s burdens, and thus we shall fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

We have an example of this in the sacred Scriptures. When Noah was drunk with wine and lay naked, and Ham, his middle son, mocked him, Ham earned an eternal curse. Conversely, his first and last sons, namely Shem and Japheth, possessed a perpetual blessing because they covered their father’s nakedness and did not wish to see his shame (Gen. IX). Similarly, in a higher sense, the Jews who mocked our Savior’s death on the cross lost both life and the kingdom. Conversely, the nations that reverently honored Christ’s Passion merited to be blessed by him in this age and in the future.

## CHAPTER IX. On Rulers, Bishops, and Judges

(CAP. XXXII.) “They have appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of them.” This is ecclesiastical and apostolic teaching: the person who presides over others by rank should offer many an example of humility and gentleness. Hence Truth itself taught the disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as the servant” (Matt. XX). Peter also, admonishing the pastors of the Church, says: “Therefore I appeal to the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, who also share in the glory that is to be revealed: shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples of the flock from the heart. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory” (1 Pet. V).

“Take care of them, and consider them in this way; and when all your care has been completed, recline, so that you may rejoice because of them, receive the crown as an ornament of grace, and obtain the honor of the assembly.” He therefore teaches perseverance in preaching, since a person should not quickly promise himself the security of rest after beginning his labor, but should persevere in it continually until the end of life, so that, having safely completed the contest of his struggle, he may say with the Apostle: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the just Judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his coming” (2 Tim. IV).

The Savior himself shows what the reward of holy preachers will be in the future life, saying: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so. Truly I say to you, he will appoint him over all that he possesses” (Luke XII).

“Speak, you who are older; for the first word befits you, with diligent knowledge, and do not interrupt the music.” It is fitting for a Catholic teacher to speak the word of God with all confidence, as an elder—not through bodily advancement in age, but through the understanding of a sober mind. He should always attend first to this: that his speech may benefit his hearers more toward instruction than it may win empty favor from admirers through eloquence. Thus Paul instructed Timothy, saying: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his coming and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. IV). What empty eloquence contributes to its lovers, he makes clear by adding: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and they will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn to fables.”

And because the teacher of the Gospel ought to exercise discernment in preaching, so that he may offer speech where he sees that he can produce improvement, he adds:

“Where there is no hearing, do not pour out your speech at an inopportune time, and do not presumptuously exalt yourself in your wisdom.” It is not useful to prolong speech by multiplying words where he observes that he finds no fruit among his hearers. Hence one of the poets says:

> Blessed is the one who speaks a matter into a prudent person’s ear.

Our Lord, who commanded his disciples, says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they turn and tear you apart” (Matt. VII). Solomon likewise says in Proverbs: “Whoever instructs a scoffer brings injury upon himself, and whoever reproves a wicked person generates harm for himself. Do not reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you. Give an opportunity to the wise, and wisdom will be added to him. Teach the just, and he will hasten to receive it” (Prov. IX).

“A carbuncle gem in gold ornament, and a comparison of music at a banquet of wine.” Among all fiery gems, the carbuncle holds primacy. It is called carbunculus because it is fiery like a coal; its brilliance is not overcome even by night, for it shines in darkness so brightly that it shoots flames into the eyes. He therefore compares the carbuncle to the splendor of gold, and musical melody to a banquet of wine, because, just as a precious gem joined to gold doubles the beauty of its radiance, so sweet melody added to a banquet of wine multiplies its pleasure.

Mystically, gold signifies divine wisdom, the carbuncle the glory of sacred virtues, wine spiritual grace, and music the preaching of the Gospel. For just as the radiance of virtues adorns divine wisdom, so true preaching of the word is fitting for spiritual grace. To this comparison he subsequently adds another likeness:

“As in the working of gold the emerald is its mark, so is the number of musicians in pleasant and moderate wine.” The emerald is a stone of extraordinary greenness, surpassing all green herbs, leaves, and gems. It tinges the air around it with reflected greenness, and it benefits from pure wine and green oil, although it is naturally endowed with this quality. There are many kinds, but the noblest are the Scythian; the Bactrian hold second place; the Egyptian, third.

It signifies souls ever green with faith. The more they are tested by the adversity of the world—which the figure of Scythia represents—the more they hope, by conceiving it in their minds, to preserve the unfading and eternal inheritance kept in heaven, and they strive to spread it among their neighbors by preaching. They also advance toward contempt of the world through the cup of the Lord’s Passion and the inward richness of charity, which is given through the Holy Spirit. For just as in the working of gold the emerald’s brilliance increases its beauty, so charity, which works through love, amplifies the learning of a man of faith, and they reverently honor the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion with a fitting sacrament.

“Listen in silence, and by reverence good grace will come to you.” After discussing the spiritual joy of music at the banquet of mystical wine, he added a word about modesty, lest anyone suppose that he wished to raise the shouting of his voice or the laughter of mockery at the banquet just mentioned. “Listen,” he says, “in silence, and by reverence good grace will come to you.”

Thus the lawgiver shows how good the reverence of silence is when he says to the former people: “Listen, Israel, and be silent.” Solomon likewise says: “My son, attend to my wisdom and incline your ear to my prudence, so that you may guard your thoughts and your lips may preserve discipline” (Prov. XXII).

Conversely, he speaks of the strange and alien woman who makes her words sweet: “She is prepared to capture souls; talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, and unable to stand firmly in her own house.” James, the brother of the Lord, also admonishes us in his Epistle, saying: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (Jas. I). And again: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you assume a greater judgment; for we all offend in many things.” But if anyone does not offend in speech, he is a perfect man. Therefore Wisdom instructs the disciple, saying:

“Young man, speak in your own cause only with difficulty, when it is necessary. If you have been questioned twice, let your answer have a head. In many things be as one who does not know, and listen silently while also asking questions. Among the great do not presume, and where there are elders do not speak much.”

The teacher ought therefore to speak and teach, while it is fitting for the disciple to be silent and listen. If it should ever happen that he speaks, let him offer few and reasonable words, lest he seem to speak more than is expedient. The Lord himself taught us to do this by his example when, at twelve years of age in Jerusalem, he sat in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. Concerning this Scripture immediately adds: “And all were astonished at his understanding and his answers” (Luke IV).

The teacher of angels did not wish to become the teacher of human beings on earth before the age of thirty, so that he might pour the force of the most salutary fear into those who rush ahead; although he himself could not fall, he preached the grace of perfect life only at a perfect age. It must therefore be considered with vigilant attention that, when Jesus is said to have been twelve years old and seated among the teachers, he is found not teaching but asking questions. By this example it is shown that no weak person should dare to teach, if that child wished to be taught by asking questions—he who, through the power of his divinity, supplied the word of knowledge to those very teachers. If divine Wisdom, assuming human nature, taught humanity by example to speak and listen, why does human presumption seek to chatter emptily with needless loquacity?

“Before hail comes lightning; and before shame comes grace, and by reverence good grace will come to you.” The flash of lightning precedes the weight of hail; so the brightness of grace precedes the grace of modesty and, through reverence, increases the gift of heavenly glory.

“And do not delay when it is time to rise. Go first ahead to your house, and there withdraw yourself, and there play, and exercise your thoughts—not in sins or arrogant speech. And above all these things bless God, who made you and filled you with all his goods.” He warns us not to be sad or sluggish in the discipline and meditation of wisdom, but to return to our own mind, withdraw into the house of our conscience, and there, through sober thoughts, winnow and ruminate upon the words of sacred Scripture. Let us carefully guard against allowing proud thought to creep upon us and make us guilty before God, imagining that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves as though by ourselves. Rather, let us recognize that our sufficiency is entirely from God, who by the gift of his Spirit has made us teachable and attentive for learning his wisdom.
