Let us always bless him who made us and filled us with his good things by his grace. To him be honor, glory, and power for ever and ever. Amen.

“Whoever fears God will receive his teaching, and whoever watches for him will find his blessing.” This is the sign of fear of God: that a person diligently meditates on his law, humbly receives his teaching, and remains watchful and energetic in keeping his commandments. Thus, without doubt, he will receive the blessing of his recompense.

“Whoever seeks the law will be filled by it, and whoever acts treacherously will stumble because of it.” There is a great difference between the benevolent searcher of God’s law and the treacherous trapper of right doctrine; between the Catholic follower of right faith and the heretical inventor of false dogma. The former rightly carries out what is just; the latter strives to turn truth into falsehood. The former is a devoted hearer of God’s word; the latter is a malicious interpreter of the Scriptures. The former, seeking good things, will be filled with good things; the latter, plotting scandals, will stumble because of them. Hence he adds:

“Those who fear the Lord will find just judgment, and they will kindle righteousness like a lamp. The sinful person will avoid correction and, according to his own will, will find a comparison.” Those who fear the Lord, kindling the righteousness of right doctrine and good works like a lamp for the instruction of their neighbors and causing it to shine before many, will find just judgment, because they will receive heavenly reward for their good deeds. Conversely, sinners who avoid and flee salutary correction will find in the fiery Gehenna, according to the choice of their perverse will, a fitting recompense for their sins.

“A man of counsel will not destroy understanding.” The more prudent a person is, the more he makes use of the counsel of his neighbors; thus understanding is added to him, and his knowledge is not diminished.

“An alien and proud man does not fear fear, even after he has acted without counsel; he will be reproved for his own attacks.” Whoever, therefore, through proud intention makes himself a stranger to the fellowship of good counselors does not fear God, whose fear and love belong to the faithful. After relying on his own decision and wickedly doing something without counsel, he will be found blameworthy and reproved for his own attacks.

This passage may be applied to the Catholic and the heretic. The Catholic, being good and fearing God, does everything according to the counsel of orthodox teachers and the instruction of the sacred Scriptures. The heretic, however, because he relies on his own thought and does not cease to cling to perverse inventions, will be restrained by divine judgments through holy preachers after his folly has been exposed.

## CHAPTER X. Everything Is to Be Done with Counsel, but Good Things with God’s Help

“My son, do nothing without counsel, and after doing it you will not repent.” Counsel is, as some wish to define it, deliberation of mind, or the reasoning of understanding, or judgment. He admonishes us to do nothing without discretion, reason, and judgment. By contrast, rash people, when they anticipate the proper time for good actions, corrupt their merit and often fall into evil because they do not discern good things. They do not examine what they should do or when they should do it; rather, they frequently recognize afterward that they acted wrongly. Hence Solomon says: “Let your eyelids precede your steps” (Prov. IV).

The eyelids precede the steps when right counsels precede our action. Whoever neglects to foresee through consideration what he is doing advances with closed eyes: he completes his journey by walking, but does not pay attention by foreseeing for himself. Therefore he falls more quickly, because he does not perceive through the eyelid of counsel where he ought to place the foot of action.

It should also be noted that a similar statement is written in Ecclesiastes: “Therefore it is better for two to be together than one, for they have the benefit of their companionship. If one falls, the other will support him. Woe to one who is alone, for when he falls he has no one to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they will be warmed together; how will one be warmed? And if someone prevails against one, two will resist him” (Eccl. IV).

It describes the benefit of companionship and the common comfort of friends: one person’s fall is lifted by the other’s help, and the one who has a faithful friend manages household cares and even the rest of the night better than the person who alone devotes himself to acquired wealth. And just as two joined by love differ from one, so it is clear that the fellowship of three is even stronger. True charity, violated by no envy, grows in strength as it increases in number.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that many enter into counsel but find no foundation of truth and peace. As we read in the Gospel, the scribes and Pharisees “went away and took counsel against Jesus, so that they might trap him in his speech” (Matt. XXII). Again: “The chief priests took counsel about how they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him” (Matt. XXVI). Hence the Psalter says that the blessed man is one who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence, but whose delight is in the law of the Lord and who meditates on his law day and night (Ps. I). Therefore the only salutary counsel is that which, from the gift of the Holy Spirit and according to the divine law, is offered through the instruction of faithful people who fear God.

“Do not go in the way of ruin, do not stumble against stones, and do not commit yourself to a difficult path, lest you place a scandal before your soul.” The way of ruin is heretical doctrine, in which one must not walk, because the offense of error and crimes is found there. When he says, “Do not commit yourself to a difficult path, lest you place a scandal before your soul,” he shows that we must not persist in countless and irrational questions, lest we fall into error if we wish to investigate hidden things beyond measure. Hence it is written: “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, having been filled, you vomit it up” (Prov. XXV). And again: “Whoever trusts in his own thoughts acts impiously, and whoever is a scrutinizer of majesty is overwhelmed by glory” (ibid.).

He teaches both things: that we should beware of alien errors and that we should not, by seeking and debating our own matters beyond measure, bring ourselves to ruin. He adds a third matter that we must observe, saying:

“Beware of your children, and pay attention to your household.” [Col. 0998D] We must also beware lest we be seduced into sin by the evil actions of Catholics and the perverse examples displayed in the Church by false brothers and by carnal people. Rather, let us pursue what he adds below:

“In all your work trust in the faith of your soul; for this is the preservation of the commandments. Whoever believes God will attend to his commandments, and whoever trusts in him will not be diminished.” Whatever we must do according to the rule of Catholic faith, we must regulate according to the keeping of God’s commandments, because whoever truly believes God keeps his commandments. But whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar (1 John II). Those, therefore, who trust in him will not be diminished and will not be scandalized by the evil one. Hence the Prophet says: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; whoever dwells in Jerusalem will not be moved forever” (Ps. CXXIV). And elsewhere: “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (John XIII).

## CHAPTER XI. Evil Will Not Overtake Those Who Fear the Lord, but the Rewards of Eternity Will Come According to Their Merits.

### (Chapter XXXIII)

“Evil will not overtake one who fears the Lord, but in temptation God will preserve him and deliver him from evil.” It is certain that future evils, which have been prepared for the wicked on account of their sins, will not overtake one who fears the Lord. But in temptation God will preserve him because, in the words of blessed Peter, “God knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to keep the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment” (2 Peter 2). For the Lord has delivered his chosen from evils, because he defends them from the wicked suggestions of malignant spirits and the perverse deeds of evil people: “For the Lord sends his angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33). “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” and he is their protector in time of tribulation.

“A wise man does not hate commandments and ordinances, and he will not be dashed to pieces as though in a storm at sea.” The wise man is one who does not hate but loves God’s commandments and keeps his ordinances. Placed in the ship of the Church, he will not be dashed to pieces by the storm of persecution and the whirlwind of temptations; rather, through Jesus—who by his command stills the storms and treads upon the waves of the raging sea—he will be delivered and brought to the harbor of salvation.

“A sensible man believes the law of God, and the law is faithful to him.” If the sensible and wise man is the one who believes the law of God, then the senseless and foolish man is altogether the one who neither believes nor obeys the divine law, because God’s law is faithful and there is no iniquity in it, but complete blessedness. For, according to the Psalmist, the law of the Lord is blameless, “converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Psalm 18).

“He who makes his question known will prepare his answer, and, having entreated, he will be heard; he will preserve discipline, and then he will answer.” He speaks of holy teachers, who, in order to respond suitably to questions put to them, prepare the word in their hearts and beseech the Lord to reveal to them the truth of the matter. They preserve through worthy action what he himself commanded them to keep; and thus, by meditating, praying, and acting, they offer a fitting answer to those who question them. For Paul taught his disciple in this way, saying: “Take careful heed to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed worker, rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2). Hence Peter also says: “Sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts, always prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope and faith that are in you” (1 Peter 3).

On the other hand, concerning foolish preachers, what follows:

“The innermost thoughts of a fool are like a wagon wheel, and like a turning axle is his thought.” Just as a wagon wheel and a turning axle, in unstable motion, shift from the highest points to the lowest and from the lowest to the highest, so the inner thoughts of fools and the perverse thinking of heretics are always unstable. At one time they think, do, and teach one thing, and at another time something else; nothing fixed or stable remains among them, but they are always changed in various ways. Hence it is written of them: “A fool is changed like the moon” (Sirach 27). And again: “The heart,” he says, “of fools will be unlike itself” (Proverbs 15).

“A stallion, like a mocking friend, neighs at everyone who sits upon him.” He makes an elegant comparison between an irrational animal and a foolish friend, because just as there is no reason in a brute animal, so there is no order of fairness in a false friend. For just as a wanton and arrogant horse does not distinguish by its neighing between its true master and a stranger, so a foolish and mocking person does not distinguish in his spirit between a hypocrite and a faithful friend; through the services of his mouth, he equally lays open to both the secrets of his mind.

“Why does one day surpass another day, and likewise one light another light, and one year another year, through the sun? They have been separated by the knowledge of the Lord, when the sun was made and the commandment was kept.” Since he previously censured the imprudence of the foolish person, because he recognized no distinction amid the diversity of things, he now wishes to show from the Creator of all that the most fitting order exists in every part of creation. Thus, “one day surpasses another day, and one light another light, and one year another year” because of the course of the rising and setting sun, which waters toward the south and turns toward the north, illuminating everything in its circuit. By its rays it grants brightness to the lesser lights, distinguishing seasons, days, and years, because in summer it makes the days longer and brighter than in winter, and it causes the year of the moon and those of the other stars to differ from one another in an orderly manner. For it was created, together with the other stars, so that they might serve as signs for seasons, days, and years, and might show definite times of festivals to human beings who were to receive the law of God. Hence it follows:

“And he changed their seasons and their feast days, and on them they celebrated festivals at the appointed time. From them God exalted and magnified them, and arranged them according to the number of days.” What else did the Lord command in the law concerning the observance of days, months, and years than what the sun and moon indicate by their courses? Hence the Sabbath, hence the new moons, hence Passover, hence Pentecost, hence the seventh month, hence also the seventh year and the fiftieth year are celebrated according to their proper rite, so that we may understand that everything has been established by God in an orderly fashion, and especially that what is done according to order and reason is pleasing to him.

“And all human beings are from the soil and from the earth, from which Adam was created. In the abundance of discipline the Lord separated them, and he changed their ways. From among them he blessed and exalted; from them he sanctified and drew to himself; and from among them he exalted and humbled, and turned them away from their separation.” After discussing the disposition of the stars and the order of the seasons, he added a discussion of the creation of human beings, so that we might understand that everything subsists through God’s ordering and that nothing in the universe is confused or without order. “And all human beings,” he says, “from the soil and from the earth”—we are to understand, he made them. For he formed our first parent from the clay of the earth, from whom the entire human race derives its origin.

But after human beings began to multiply, and some of them bound themselves by various errors and sins, he distinguished among them and separated those who persisted in their faith and righteousness from the others. Those who were worthy he blessed; but those who acted impiously he justly condemned as liable to eternal curse. Hence Holy Scripture counts Abel, Enos, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints who rightly devoted themselves to divine worship and served the one God with true religion. But those who abandoned the true God and served false idols, making themselves liable to many crimes, he partly destroyed and consumed through the Flood, partly through the devastation of pestilence, and partly through the sword and destruction inflicted by the true worshipers of God.

Therefore he says, “And he turned them away from their separation,” because by his judgment he distinguished them, so that he might give fitting rewards to some for their good deeds and repay others with just punishments for their evil deeds. Thus the supreme craftsman, with powerful hand, brought about an appropriate distinction in his work according to his will.

Hence it is added:

“Like clay in the hand of the potter, to mold it and arrange it. All his ways are according to his ordering; so is the human being in the hand of the one who made him, and he will repay him according to his judgment.” The almighty Creator, therefore, holding the mass of human nature in his power, fashions and forms each vessel according to his will; “and there is no one who can resist his will.” Yet no one should call him unjust, because he does everything justly and according to order.

Thus the Apostle, discussing God’s foreknowledge and power in his Letter to the Romans, takes Jacob and Esau as examples, showing how he chose one according to his foreknowledge and abandoned the other according to his judgment. So that no one might think this had been done unjustly, he says among other things: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means.” And shortly afterward: “Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9).

Great is the injustice and presumption of a human being who answers back to God in adversity, the unjust to the just, the evil to the good, the ignorant to the perfect, the weak to the strongest, the corruptible to the incorruptible, the mortal to the immortal, the wicked servant to the best Lord, and the creature to the Creator. For it is in the power of the author to create the creature as he wishes.

Thus God, although we all derive our substance from one source and from the same mass and are all sinners, has mercy on some and looks down upon others—but not without justice. In a human potter, the will exists only according to free choice; but in God, the Creator of all, the will is always just together with omnipotence. Hence it is written: “He has done whatever he has willed.” For he knows whom he ought to pity according to his foreknowledge and predestination, and whom to look down upon according to his justice and judgment. Supreme justice can neither will nor do anything except what is altogether just.

Hence it is said:

“All his ways are according to his ordering; so is the human being in the hand of the one who made him, and he will repay him according to his judgment.” Since God is the parent of all, he wishes evil upon no one. Because he made them, he wishes them to remain unharmed, and it is unfitting that he should be unjust. His benevolence is so great that he not only caused things that did not exist to exist, but also bestowed eternal life and glory upon those very things, so that his work might possess something resembling his majesty. Since he is so provident and good, there should be no doubt that he is just.

“Against evil there is good, and against death there is life; so also against the righteous man there is the sinner. And so consider all the works of the Most High: two and two, and one against one.” The diligent investigator of God’s works and the devout examiner of his ways discovers a distinction in the order of things and a certain opposition among them, yet one wonderfully arranged by God’s wisdom. Hence he says: “Against evil there is good, and against death there is life; so also against the righteous man there is the sinner.”

God, therefore, is not the creator of evil, concerning whom it is written: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1). Nor is he the author of death, concerning whom it is elsewhere written: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wisdom 1). Rather, he himself is the arranger of the universe, wondrous and ineffable.

For it is one thing to be nature and another to be vice; one thing to be essence and another to be defect; one thing to be form and another to be deprivation. I say that all things are good, and, to make the point clearer, I add: insofar as they exist. Everything, therefore, that exists, insofar as it exists—that is, insofar as it is nature, essence, or substance, or whatever other word more clearly expresses the same reality—we say is from God.

But the vices of essences, which are deprived of form and beauty, do not derive their existence from God. If you ask where they come from, consider carefully what they do. Just as every nature is compelled to be nothing other than existence, so vice—for it is contrary to nature—is driven in the opposite direction, that is, toward nonbeing, so that what exists may perish most miserably. Hence the most vicious thing is ruined and destroyed; although *nequissimum* is also the familiar name for the utterly wicked, since those already lost are called “lost,” and *nequitia* itself is said to have drawn its name from nothingness, and in truth it tends toward nothingness.

“I was the last to awaken, and like one who gathers grapes after the grape-gatherers. In God’s blessing I too have hoped, and like one who gathers grapes I have filled the winepress.” The guardian of humility did not wish to display himself arrogantly, yet he did not wish to conceal the truth about himself altogether. He did not wish in any way to place himself before the ancient writers of the sacred books, whom he calls gatherers of spiritual wine, but he did not deny that he was their fellow worker.

He says that he was the last to keep vigil and to hope in God’s blessing, and that for this reason he filled the winepress like a grape-gatherer, in order to show that divine grace was present with him, as with the other fathers, so that he might bring forth abundantly the fruit of knowledge.

The Apostle Paul likewise, thinking humbly of himself, did not wish to conceal the grace bestowed upon him. Relating in his Letter how Christ appeared to the disciples after the resurrection, he added concerning himself: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 1).

“Consider that I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek discipline.” A catholic teacher is useful not only to himself through his labor, as he acquires the light of wisdom by seeking and meditating, but also beneficial to others, when through his teachings he offers them correction of life and the burden of discipline.

“Listen to me, great ones, and all peoples; rulers of the Church, hear with your ears. Do not give authority over you in your lifetime to son or wife, brother or friend; and do not give your property to another, lest you afterward regret it and plead on their behalf.” He admonishes all alike—great and small, rulers and subjects, noble and ignoble—not to neglect the proper exercise of their authority, because otherwise they cannot possess peace and tranquility in their lives.

For whoever irrationally loses the authority of his primacy places himself in contempt and distress. But whoever preserves his position with right faith, sound doctrine, and good works guards himself and directs his children and disciples toward ordered discipline and progress in virtue. Hence it is added:

“While you still survive and breathe, no flesh will change you. For it is better that your children should ask you than that you should look to the hands of your children. In all your works be outstanding, lest you bring a stain upon your glory. On the day when the days of your life are completed, and at the time of your departure, distribute your inheritance.”

This whole teaching instructs fathers historically concerning how they should rightly govern their children and nurture them with discipline until they reach mature age, so that after their parents’ departure they may be worthy heirs. It also instructs rulers of the Church spiritually, so that they may retain the dignity of their office with reasonable authority and just moderation until the end, and thus leave behind disciples well nourished and useful heirs of their labor.

Yet amid these matters it must be recognized that the human mind is often lifted up even when it is supported by no power. How much more does it raise itself on high when power is also joined to it? That power is rightly administered by one who carefully knows both how to take from it what helps and to overcome what tempts; how to regard himself as equal to others in it, and yet to place himself before sinners through the zeal of correction.

The highest position is therefore well governed when the one who presides dominates vices rather than brothers. But when superiors correct delinquent subjects, they must carefully attend to this: by the obligation of discipline, let them strike at offenses with a certain authority, but through the guardianship of humility let them recognize themselves as equal to the brothers whom they correct.

They must carefully take care that, while the virtue of humility is guarded beyond measure, the rights of governance are not dissolved; and that, while a prelate humbles himself more than is fitting, he does not become unable to bind the lives of his subjects under the bond of discipline.

Let rulers retain outwardly what they undertake for the benefit of others, but inwardly preserve what they fear concerning their own estimation. Nevertheless, through certain becoming signs that break forth, even their subjects should perceive that they are humble within themselves, so that in their authority they may see what they fear, and in their humility recognize what they should imitate.

Let those who preside strive without ceasing to ensure that, the greater their power appears outwardly, the more deeply it is humbled within them: lest it overcome their thoughts, lest it carry their minds away into self-delight, lest their minds, now placed beneath it, become unable to govern it because they have submitted to it through the desire to rule.

For one is rightly counted among hypocrites who turns the ministry of governance, under the appearance of discipline, into the use of domination. Yet sometimes the offense is more serious if, among the perverse, equality is guarded more than discipline (2 Kings 2, 4). Because Heli, overcome by false compassion, was unwilling to strike his delinquent sons, he struck himself together with them by cruel condemnation before the strict Judge.

Therefore let the rulers and teachers of the Church rightly maintain their order, and let them govern and guard their subjects with discipline, so that, having ministered well, they may acquire for themselves a good standing and, through Christ’s gift, receive the eternal kingdom at the end of life.

### Chapter Twelve: Concerning the discipline of servants

“Food, a rod, and a burden for an ass; bread, discipline, and work for a servant. He works under discipline and seeks rest; loosen his hands, and he seeks freedom. Yoke and rein bend the stiff neck, and constant labors humble a servant. For an ill-disposed servant, torture and fetters: send him to work so that he may not be idle, for idleness has taught much wickedness. Set him to work, for this is fitting for him. But if he does not obey, bend him with fetters; and do not be excessive toward any flesh. Yet do nothing severe without judgment.”

Here he discusses the discipline of servants, who sometimes display degraded dispositions through perverse habits. Such persons must necessarily be restrained by the severity of their masters, and must not enjoy an unlawful freedom to sin. For it is not their natural condition that is to be despised, but the depravity of their habits that must be restrained, so that they may know that they ought to be subject and not insolently exalt themselves in a stubborn will.

Those are rightly called servants who subject themselves to the dominion of vices. But those who submit themselves to obedience to justice and equity, and rightly maintain the truth of the catholic faith, are in every respect to be enrolled in that freedom by which Christ set us free, who says in the Gospel: “If therefore the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8). For, as one of the poets says:

> No freedom or greater power is better
> 
> Than to serve God, whom love serves well.

Thus Wisdom describes what the maintenance of servants ought to be and how strict discipline should be exercised toward the ungovernable: they should have food and clothing, but should not be permitted the leisure of wandering about idly, since idleness is the enemy of the soul. But because all things ought to be done with moderation, it adds:

“If you have a faithful servant, let him be to you as your own soul; treat him as a brother, for you have acquired him at the price of your life. If you injure him unjustly, he will take to flight; and if he departs in pride, you do not know whom you should seek, or on what path you should seek him.”

Above he had laid down a rule for a good servant, saying: “Do not injure a servant who works in truth, nor a hired laborer who gives his life. Let an intelligent servant be beloved to you as your own soul; do not deprive him of freedom, nor leave him in need,” and so forth. This shows that, if they are well-disposed and obedient, they are of the same nature as ourselves and ought to be treated as brothers; but if they are hard and proud, they ought to be restrained by fitting punishment and discipline.

When he says that he should be treated as a brother because we have acquired him at the price of blood, he means that we ought to love the common nature in him and, if necessary, lay down our own life for them as for brothers. For we must not hate and persecute a human being; rather, we must resist utterly the vices that harm a person and, if they prevail, certainly draw him to destruction.

## BOOK EIGHT

### Chapter One: Concerning dreams that are not to be believed, nor their promises accepted, because Wisdom teaches that divinations and omens are the lies of error and that the dreams of evildoers are vanities

[Col. 1005]

### (Chapter XXXIV)

“Vain hope and falsehood belong to a senseless man, and dreams exalt the imprudent. Like one who grasps a shadow and pursues the wind is the one who attends to lying visions. Such as this is the vision of dreams: before a person’s face, the likeness of another person. Who can be cleansed by the unclean? And what truth will be spoken by a liar? Divination of error and lying omens, and the dreams of evildoers, are vanity. And as a woman in labor, your heart suffers fantasies, unless a visitation has been sent by the Most High. Do not give your heart to them, for dreams have caused many to err, and those who hoped in them have fallen.”

He indicates that dream visions often deceive people through the falsehood of wicked spirits and cast those who believe them into harmful errors, unless they take care to discern them prudently. Hence he warns, saying: “Who can be cleansed by the unclean? And what truth will be spoken by a liar? Divination of error and lying omens, and the dreams of evildoers, are vanity.”

Hence this was commanded in the law: “You shall not observe dreams, nor shall you follow divinations and omens” (Leviticus 19).

But since revelations sometimes occur through dreams, as we frequently find demonstrated in the divine books, I do not think it displeasing to the reader if we insert in this little work the words of blessed Gregory concerning the discernment of dreams. When his deacon Peter asked whether what is shown through nocturnal visions ought to be observed, he answered as follows:

“It must be known, Peter, that dream images touch the mind in six ways. Sometimes dreams are produced by fullness or emptiness of the stomach; sometimes by illusion; sometimes by thought together with illusion; sometimes by revelation; and sometimes by thought together with revelation. We all know by experience the two causes I mentioned first; the remaining ones, however, we find in the pages of Sacred Scripture.

“For unless dreams were usually produced by illusion from the hidden enemy, the wise man would never have said: ‘Dreams have caused many to err, and those who hoped in them have fallen,’ or certainly, ‘You shall not practice omens, nor observe dreams.’ By these words their detestable character is clearly shown, since they are joined with omens.

“Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with illusion, the wise man would not have said: ‘Dreams follow many cares.’ And unless dreams sometimes arose through the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen himself in dreams as destined to be preferred to his brothers (Genesis 37), nor would an angel have warned Mary’s husband in a dream to flee into Egypt after taking away the child (Matthew 2).

“Again, unless dreams sometimes proceeded from thought together with revelation, the prophet Daniel, explaining Nebuchadnezzar’s vision, would never have begun from the root of thought, saying: ‘You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen after these things, and he who reveals mysteries has shown you what is to come’ (Daniel 2). And shortly afterward: ‘You were looking, and behold, as it were one great statue; that great statue, and its stature was lofty, stood before you, etc.’ (ibid.).

“Thus, when Daniel reverently discloses both the dream that was to be fulfilled and the thought from which it arose, it is plainly shown that this kind of dream is often produced by thought together with revelation.

“But because dreams vary according to so many qualities of things, it ought to be more difficult to believe them, since it is also less easy to discern from what impulse they come. Holy men, however, distinguish between illusions and revelations themselves through a certain inward perception of the voices or images of visions, so that they know what they receive from a good spirit and what they suffer from illusion.

“For if the mind is not watchful concerning these matters, through the deceiving spirit it plunges itself into many vanities. That spirit sometimes foretells many true things so that at the end it may be able to ensnare the soul through some empty falsehood. It is certain that this recently happened to one of our own: while he paid very close attention to dreams, he was promised in a dream a long span of this life. After he had gathered much money as provision for a longer life, he suddenly died, leaving all of it untouched, and carried nothing of good work away with him.”

“Without falsehood the word of the law will be perfected, and wisdom will be planted in the mouth of the faithful.” Rejecting the inventions of dreams, the wise man urges that greater belief be given to the teaching of wisdom, which, planted in the mouth of a faithful man, brings the word to completion without falsehood, rather than to the empty deceit of the perverse.

What the divine law and the Gospel teach must be held and preserved in every respect. One must turn neither to the right nor to the left from it, because the things written there, through the distribution of the Holy Spirit, have been sent into the world for the salvation of the human race.

But because some people, deceived by spirits of error, follow vain dreams, while others follow the false doctrine of heretics, he therefore warns in what follows that the one who has learned the truth from the divine books and has experienced that the falsehood of the devil prevails among heretics and their followers should separate himself from them and follow in every respect the teaching of the divine books.

“He who has not been tested—what is he? A man experienced in many things has thought about much; and he who has learned much will declare understanding. He who has not been experienced recognizes little.”

Here “testing” signifies the experience of tribulation, which is presented to the elect for their proving, as it is written: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Sirach 27).

The more someone experiences the hardships of tribulation, if he perseveres in faith and preserves patience, the stronger he will become in the virtue of endurance against other hardships. And the one who has learned much—that is, who gathers many mysteries of the Sacred Scriptures into the bosom of his mind—will be able to declare rightly to others the word of sound understanding and spiritual consolation.

Hence Paul also says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we too may console those who are in every distress, through the encouragement with which we ourselves are encouraged by God” (2 Corinthians 1). “For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.”

The same apostle says elsewhere to the same Corinthians: “We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia, that in much testing through tribulation their abundant joy and their deepest poverty overflowed into the riches of their simplicity” (2 Corinthians 8). “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (2 Corinthians 8).

“Whoever, therefore, has no experience of tribulation cannot possess an abundance of virtues.” Therefore he says: “He who has not been experienced recognizes little.”

“But whoever has been involved in many things has multiplied his wickedness.” What does he wish to indicate by saying, “Whoever has been involved in many things has multiplied his wickedness,” except that the person who is changeable in mind and divided among many worldly cares and anxieties is unstable and often becomes liable to the crimes of many vices through his actions?

Or alternatively, the one who, having lost the unity of faith, follows in deception the many sects of heretics, entangled in the impieties of many crimes, has disastrously abandoned it and displays the great wickedness of a malicious mind.

“I have seen many things while wandering, and very many customary expressions.” This shows that whoever meditates upon Sacred Scripture with an attentive mind and humbly beseeches God to grant him understanding of it through the grace of his Spirit will, by God’s gift, receive an abundance of knowledge of things and words. It also shows that grace is often accompanied by the distress of persecution. Hence he adds:

“Several times I was in danger of death because of these things, and I was delivered by the grace of God.” For “power is made perfect in weakness.” Hence the Apostle Paul was given a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet him (2 Corinthians 12). And not only Paul but also the other preachers of the Gospel suffered many grievous insults from persecutors, so that, admonished by their affliction, they would not lose the good of humility and would preserve the grace of their virtues.

But the Lord delivers his elect from every distress and will not abandon all who hope in him. Hence it follows:

## Chapter Two: Concerning those who fear the Lord

“The spirit of those who fear God is sought, and they are blessed in his presence. For their hope is in the one who saves them, and the eyes of God are upon those who love him.” The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. He observes the spirit—that is, the wills—of those who fear him, and he hears their prayers, granting them heavenly blessing; and he will save them by bestowing eternal life upon them. He guards all who love him and will destroy all their enemies.

Therefore they console themselves and rejoice with certain hope concerning the future reward, saying with the aforementioned teacher of the nations: “Although our outward man is being corrupted, yet our inward man is being renewed day by day. For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4). “For we know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5).

“He who fears the Lord will fear nothing and will not be afraid, because he himself is his hope.” For how can the one who fears the Lord and places his hope in him dread the threats and persecutions of enemies? Hence the Apostle Peter also exhorts us, saying: “Do not fear their fear, and do not be troubled. But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts” (1 Peter 3).

“Blessed is the soul of one who fears God. To whom does it look, and who is its strength? The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him: a protector of power, a support of strength, a covering from heat and a shade at midday, a plea against offense and a help in falling, exalting the soul and humbling the eyes, giving health, life, and blessing.”

When he says that the soul of one who fears God is blessed, he seems, as though ignorant, to ask toward whom that soul looks and who its strength is; yet he immediately answers his own question. This figure is called in Greek *erotema*: when an appropriate answer is given to the one asking.

For he says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him,” that is, his merciful regard is upon those who believe in him. He is the protector of power, protecting them from every adversity; the support of strength, strengthening them. He is their covering against the heat of temptation and their shade against the fierce heat of persecution—for this is what “midday” signifies. He is the propitiation that wipes away the offense of sins. He provides help to his own, lest they fall into the greatest sins, exalting the souls of his faithful to the summit of perfection and enlightening the eyes of their minds, granting them the grace of inward contemplation.

He gives them the health of incorruption, the life of immortality, and the blessing of an eternal inheritance. “Come,” he says, “blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

## Chapter Three: Wisdom commands that nothing arising from unjust possessions is to be sacrificed—that is, offered—or that alms are to be given from the loss suffered by others

“An offering from an unjust thing is a defiled sacrifice, and the mockeries of the unjust are not pleasing. The Lord is with those who sustain him in the way of truth and justice.” About to discuss the quality of offerings, he first demonstrates that a sacrifice offered from unjust profit is despised and detestable in the sight of God. He also calls it a mockery of the righteous, because it is, as it were, an insult before God when someone supposes that what is evil is pleasing to God.

For the divine majesty accepts no other gift except what is offered to it from a just acquisition, according to the rule of truth, through true faith and love.

“**The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked, nor does he regard the offerings of the wicked; nor will he be propitiated for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices.**” It is certain that the one who commits iniquity [Col. 1010B] and takes no care to avoid sin cannot offer an acceptable oblation to God, nor merit forgiveness for his offense. But the one who flees vices and strives to erase his sins through worthy repentance and an outpouring of tears offers acceptable gifts to God, because “a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50).

Alternatively: In this passage the carnal offerings of the Jews are condemned; after Christ’s coming they were offered not to God but to demons. They did not fear shedding the blood of prophets and apostles, yet hoped that the multitude of their victims would please God, although long before, through Isaiah, the Lord had rejected their sacrifices, saying:

“Of what use to me is the multitude of your victims? says the Lord. I am full. I do not want the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you came before my sight, who asked these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not offer sacrifice any longer in vain: incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure the new moon, the sabbath, or other festivals; your assemblies are wicked. Your new moons and solemnities my soul has hated. They have become burdensome to me; I am weary of enduring them. When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply your prayers, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely, learn to do good, seek judgment, [Col. 1010D] assist the oppressed, judge the orphan, defend the widow. Then come and accuse me, says the Lord. Though your sins be like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red like the worm, they shall be white as wool. If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling and provoke me to anger, the sword shall devour you, because the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1).

What sacrifice pleases God, the Lord himself declares through the Psalmist, saying: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. LXI).

“**Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who slaughters a son in the sight of his father.**” What could be more intolerable than the death of a son before his father’s eyes? Thus it is shown with what anger this sacrifice is regarded: it is compared with the grief of a bereaved father. Yet such people often weigh how much they give, while they refuse to consider how much they seize; they count their payments but decline to reckon their sins. Let them therefore hear what is written: “He who gathered wages put them into a pierced purse” (Hag. 1). When money is put into a pierced purse, it is seen; but when it is lost, it is not seen. Those who look at how much they give but do not weigh how much they seize put their wages into a pierced purse: for they gather them by looking toward them as the hope of their confidence, but lose them because they do not look toward their loss.

“**The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; whoever defrauds him is a man of blood.**” The poor do not accumulate riches but procure what is necessary for sustenance. Whoever takes from him the means by which he ought to live kills him, as though shedding his blood. Hence it also follows:

“**Whoever takes away bread earned by sweat is like one who kills his neighbor.**” By the sweat of his face the poor man acquires bread for himself; but whoever violently takes it from him kills his neighbor with the sword of his rapacity. Therefore such an offering will not be pleasing to God, because it is acquired not through one’s own labor but through another’s loss: he violently extorts what he distributes as though mercifully. But it is one thing to show mercy for the sake of sins, and another to sin in order to show mercy. The latter can no longer be called mercy, because what is made bitter by men of a poisonous root does not produce sweet fruit.

For this reason the Lord also rejects such sacrifices through the prophet, saying: “I am the Lord, who love judgment and hate robbery for a burnt offering” (Isa. 61). Again he says: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, because they are offered from crime” (Prov. 21)—those who often take away from the needy what they give to God.

“**The one who sheds blood and the one who defrauds a hired worker are brothers.**” He calls them brothers not by generation but by imitation of crimes and resemblance in sins. For this reason he repeatedly compares the shedding of blood with robbery and fraud: so that, from the guilt of homicide—which everyone recognizes as the gravest crime—the other deeds, which seemed less harmful, may be recognized as monstrous and deserving of everlasting death.

“**One builds and another destroys; what benefit do they have except labor? One prays and another curses; whose voice will the Lord hear?**” This means what he said above: that a sacrifice is not acceptable to God when someone strives to offer him what has been taken by robbery. Whoever offers a gift from crime seems to himself to be preparing a building of virtues, but does not consider that this act of generosity is not generosity at all, but a crime of greed. One prays as though blessing God for his deed; the other raises his voice and brings before the Lord a complaint about his poverty. Therefore the prayer of these people does not ascend to the Lord with the fragrance of sweetness, because the harmony of love does not carry it to the ears of divine mercy.

“**Whoever is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what benefit does his washing bring? So also the person who fasts in his sins and again commits the same things: what benefit does his humbling bring? Who will hear his prayer?**” A person is baptized by a dead person when he is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead when, after weeping, he repeats his offense. What benefit does his washing bring when his cleansing does not endure? He fasts and weeps for his sins, yet does not wish to depart from them; therefore his prayer does not deserve to be heard by the Lord.

For what is it to weep over an offense except to show God the humility of one’s devotion? And what is it, after weeping, to do evil except to exercise proud [Col. 1012B] hostility against the one whom one had entreated? As James bears witness when he says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

The Lord therefore instructs us through Isaiah what we must do, saying: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely, learn to do good, and so forth” (Isa. 1). Whoever does not preserve the innocence of life after tears neglects to remain clean after washing. Thus those who do not cease to weep over their committed sins, but again commit sins for which they must weep, are washed yet are by no means clean.

By contrast, the one who washes himself from filth and remains clean washes away past sins with tears and strives not to commit them again; instead, he hastens to devote himself to good works as far as he is able. Thus he will rightly find the Lord’s grace on account of his good conduct. Concerning him it is also said:

## CHAPTER IV. The discipline of keeping the law, and attention to what sacrifice is salutary

**(CHAP. XXXV.) “Whoever keeps the law multiplies the offering. The salutary sacrifice is to attend to the commandments, to depart from every iniquity, and his supplication will find favor before the eyes of God.”** He prays well who keeps God’s commandments, and offers a salutary sacrifice who presents to God the gift of true faith working through love. Such a supplication will find favor before the eyes of God because, by doing good, he has preserved justice.

Hence Isaiah says: “Dissolve the bonds of wickedness, loosen the bundles that oppress, set free those who are broken, and break every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Then your light shall break forth like the morning, and your health shall rise quickly; your justice shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you. Then you shall call, and the Lord will hear; you shall cry out, and he will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58).

“**He repays favor who offers fine flour; and whoever shows mercy offers a sacrifice.**” Both gifts are acceptable to God: that which is rightly offered to God on the altar in the offering of bread and wine, in remembrance of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that which, through the affection of charity, is mercifully supplied to one’s neighbor in his needs. But these are worthily presented to God by the offerer only if he strives to keep himself free from sin. Therefore it follows:

“**It is pleasing to the Lord to depart from iniquity, and a supplication for sins is to depart from injustice.**” The person who departs from the fellowship of erring heretics is pleasing to the Lord; and his supplication has great power with God, because he is in no way joined to the company of those who do evil. Hence it is written: “To practice mercy and judgment is more pleasing to God than sacrifices” (Prov. 21).

“**You shall not appear before the sight of God empty. For all these things are done because of the commandment of the Lord.**” One appears empty before the Lord who carries nothing with him from the fruit of his labor. One person sweats to acquire honors, another burns with desire to multiply his possessions, another pants after winning praise. But because, when he dies, everyone leaves all these things here, he appears empty before God, since he has brought nothing with him before the Judge.

Thus the Law salutarily admonishes us, saying: “You shall not appear empty before the sight of the Lord” (Exod. 23; 34). Whoever has not provided, by doing good, the reward of life he is to earn appears empty in the sight of the Lord.

For this reason the Psalmist says of the righteous: “They shall come indeed with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125). They come to the examination of judgment carrying sheaves who display in themselves the good works by which they may merit life.

“**The offering of the righteous fattens the altar, and it is a fragrance of sweetness in the sight of the Most High. The sacrifice of the righteous is accepted, and the Lord will not forget his memory.**” The offering of the righteous fattens the altar because it is offered from the devotion of true charity; and it is a sweet fragrance in the sight of God because the ardor of mercy and truth burns within it. The sacrifice of the righteous is acceptable to God because the gift of his good works is most pleasing to God. Therefore the Lord will not forget his memory: “For the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil tidings.”

“**Glorify God with a good disposition, and do not diminish the firstfruits of your hands.**” No gift that is not given with a good disposition can in any way merit favor in the sight of God, because human beings look at the face, but God looks into the heart. Hence the Lord rejects the empty praises of the Jews through the prophet, saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). “In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men” (Mark 7).

“And do not diminish,” he says, “the firstfruits of your hands.” A person diminishes the firstfruits of his works when he does not offer with inward affection of good will what he outwardly performs through labor. For this reason he adds:

“**In every gift make your face cheerful, and sanctify your tithes with rejoicing.**” God loves a cheerful giver, as Paul bears witness (2 Cor. 9), and regards the good will of those who offer as most pleasing. Thus in the Gospel the Savior placed the two small coins of the poor widow above all the gifts that various people were bringing to the temple (Luke 21), and declared that a cup of cold water given among the people would not be without reward (Matt. 10).

The Lord therefore commanded the Israelites in Exodus to give firstfruits and tithes, but they are acceptable only when they are offered with a good disposition (Exod. 22; 23; 34). Mystically, the firstfruits of crops or of the firstborn signify the beginnings of good works, or good will itself, which precedes the work. The Pelagians offend by attributing this to themselves; but when God commands us to offer it to him, he indicates that it belongs to his grace.

In offering tithes to God, the number ten signifies perfection, because counting increases up to it. Therefore, just as in the firstfruits we are commanded to refer the beginnings of our intentions to the Lord, so in the tithes we are commanded to refer the completion of our works to him, from whom both the beginning of a good work and the effect of its perfection are given.

“**Give to the Most High according to his gift, and with a good eye make an offering from the work of your hands; for the Lord is one who repays, and he will repay you sevenfold.**” He gives to the Most High according to his gift who, mindful of God’s benefits, first offers himself to God by rightly believing and doing good, because he has from God what he is in substance, since “from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11). Then, whatever he possesses outside himself as a gift, let him spend entirely with good intention in God’s praise.

This is what he says: “With a good eye make an offering from the work of your hands; for, he says, the Lord will repay sevenfold”—that is, he will bestow a perfect recompense. The number seven is perfect because of the gifts of the Holy Spirit manifested in it; and because the same number embraces the inner and outer substance of the human being: the nature of the soul in the number three, and of the body in the number four.

Hence the Law commands the human being: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6). The body, moreover, consists of the four well-known elements: earth, water, air, and fire.

The renewal of the human being can be signified by the sevenfold recompense, when, through Christ’s gift, he is brought with an incorruptible body and immortal soul to possess the kingdom of the heavenly Father. Then the human being is repaid sevenfold what was given to him, when, on account of his good conduct, he himself is restored by the gift of the just Judge so that he may live and rejoice in eternal blessedness.

Since the number seven has been mentioned here, it is pleasing to set down some observations concerning its perfection from the sayings of the holy Fathers. The whole of time revolves through seven days. The eternal day that follows when the succession of seven days has been completed is the eighth. Therefore, when the Psalmist was considering the day of resurrection and was about to speak of the severity of the final judgment, he prefaced the psalm with the title: “For the end: a Psalm of David for the eighth.”

To show which eighth he meant, he followed with the beginning of that psalm, speaking of the day of dreadful terror: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury” (Ps. 6).

The perfection of eternity is indicated by the number seven: the seventh day is called sanctified for the Lord’s rest, and it is no longer said to contain an evening, because the rest of eternal blessedness is confined by no limit. For this reason also, once the Law had been given, the seventh day was commanded to be a day of rest (Exod. 13; 35), so that eternal rest might be signified, because the totality of the present life is represented by the number seven.

This is shown even more clearly when the number eight follows it. When another number follows seven, the meaning of seven itself is expressed: time is brought to an end and enclosed by eternity. It is written: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight.” Through the number seven, the present time—which is carried out in seven days—is expressed; through the number eight, perpetual life is signified. The Lord disclosed this life to us through his resurrection when he rose on the Lord’s day. Since that day follows the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, it is found to be the eighth from the beginning.

In the cycle of years, the number seven, multiplied seven times and with one unit added, reaches fifty, so that the most sacred rest of the Jubilee may be observed as the enjoyment of perpetual blessedness.

The number seven is considered perfect by the wise men of this world according to a certain rationale, because it is completed from the first even and the first odd numbers. The first odd number is three, and the first even number is four. Seven consists of these two, and, multiplied by its own parts, rises to twelve. For whether we multiply three by four or four by three, we arrive at twelve.

But because by heavenly gift we have received the principles of truth, we trample these matters beneath us as unworthy of the height of knowledge, holding this absolutely with unshaken faith: those whom the sevenfold Spirit of grace fills, he perfects, granting them not only knowledge of the Trinity but also the operation of the four virtues—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

## CHAPTER V. Wisdom warns that wicked gifts should not be offered—that is, not at an uncertain time—nor should prayers and supplications be disordered and fruitless, because prayer is good together with fasting and almsgiving

“**Do not offer wicked gifts, for he will not receive them; and do not look upon an unjust sacrifice, for the Lord is judge, and with him there is no regard for persons.**” Before the heavenly Judge, neither the size of the gift nor the status of the powerful is weighed, but the measure of devotion and the humility of the heart. Therefore he urges us not to offer gifts to God from unjust profit but from honest labor, because the Lord is a just Judge: he does not accept the person of the rich, nor despise the person of the poor. Hence it follows:

“**The Lord will show no partiality against the poor, and he will hear the supplication of the afflicted. He will not despise the prayers of the orphan, nor the widow when she pours out a speech of groaning. Do not the widow’s tears descend to her cheek, and her cry against the one who causes them? For from her cheek they ascend to heaven, and the Lord, who hears, will not take pleasure in them.**”

The Lord will show no partiality against the poor, and he will hear the supplication of the afflicted, because he judges no one according to the distinction of persons but according to the reason of the case. “For the Lord is just and loves justice; his face has seen equity. He neither rejects nor despises the prayers of the poor, the orphans, and the widows; but when they cry to him, he will hear them and save them, because they have hoped in him” (Ps. 10).

Mystically, these persons—the poor, the orphan, and the widow—can signify the Church and the Christian people. Of them it is written: “To you the poor man is left; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Ps. 9). “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “Blessing I will bless her widow; I will satisfy her poor with bread” (Ps. 131).

The tears of this widow therefore ascend from her cheek to heaven, because the sufferings of the persecutions she endures in the present age do not escape the sight of the Godhead. Hence the just Judge will restore to her the reward of her labor in the future, and will repay her enemies with the punishment they deserve in hell.

“**Whoever worships God in gladness will be received, and his supplication will draw near to the clouds. The prayer of one who humbles himself will pierce the clouds; and until it draws near, he will not be comforted, nor will he depart until the Most High looks upon him. And the Lord will not delay, but will judge the righteous and execute judgment; and the Most Strong will not have patience with them until he crushes their backs. He will repay the nations with vengeance until he removes the fullness of the proud; he will crush the scepters of the wicked until he repays people according to their deeds, according to the works of Adam, and according to his presumption, until he judges the judgment of his people and delights the righteous with his mercy.**”

This entire passage looks back to the preceding sense, because the Lord mercifully hears the prayer of his faithful, which in devout affection rises beyond the clouds and penetrates the heavens. They entreat him daily with persistence and perseverance, both for themselves and for all their people, and do not cease until they receive consolation from him.

Therefore the Lord himself will not withhold his help from them, but will judge the righteous and execute judgment for them. In his strict judgment he will pronounce vengeance upon their adversaries, not ceasing until he has fully punished their enemies, repaying them with fitting vengeance until he removes the entire multitude of their proud persecutors from the face of the earth. He will crush the scepters of the wicked tyrants who killed his confessors with various torments, repaying the perverse according to their deeds and according to the works of Adam—that is, according to the fall of the first human being, who presumptuously transgressed God’s commandments and thereby brought upon himself and his entire race the punishment of exile and death.

This will continue until, at the final examination, the Judge of the living and the dead executes judgment upon his people and delights the righteous with his mercy, transferring them to the kingdom of the Father, where they will live blessedly in the contemplation of his face and enjoy everlasting delight.

## CHAPTER VI. Supplication to God and praise of God’s mercy

“**The mercy of God is beautiful in a time of tribulation, like a rain cloud in a time of drought.**” Just as in a time of drought a cloud supplies the earth with timely rain, so God’s mercy necessarily comes to the aid of human weakness in a time of tribulation. For it belongs uniquely to God, through his manifold work, to bestow the help of his compassion. Of him it is written: “The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144).

## CHAPTER VII. The Prayer of Wisdom

**(CHAP. XXXVI.) “Have mercy on us, God of all, and look upon us; show us the light of your mercies. Send your fear upon the nations that have not sought you, and let them know that there is no God except you, so that they may declare your mighty works.”** In the person of the faithful, Wisdom directs a prayer to God, asking that he defend them with the right hand of his power and repay their enemies with the recompense of just vengeance, so that, being worthily chastened thereby, they may acknowledge the one true God and, abandoning false idols, offer worship of devout religion to the true God alone.

It should be noted, however, that when holy men appear in their words to pray against their adversaries, they either pray that those adversaries, instructed by such scourges, may abandon vanity and the filth of sins and turn to right faith and works of piety, or they foretell to them in the prophetic Spirit that what will certainly happen to them is a deserved vengeance.

The Church prays for her persecutors, that they may turn from their error and do penance for their sins. O supreme desire of a holy mind! Who could have asked more on his own behalf than she requested for her fiercest enemies? The Lord therefore has mercy on such people, who do not neglect the opportunities for mercy, as it is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

“**Raise your hand over foreign nations, so that they may see your power. For just as you were sanctified in us before their sight, so you will be magnified in them before our sight, so that they may know you as we too have known you, for there is no God besides you, Lord.**” Foreign nations are the pagans, who are alien to the Christian religion in faith and worship. The Lord raises his hand over them when he converts them to the faith through preaching and miracles, so that those who were previously enemies and persecutors [Col. 1018A] of God’s people may afterward become brothers and coheirs of the heavenly kingdom.

“**Renew signs and change wonders. Glorify your hand and your right arm. Stir up fury and pour out wrath. Remove the adversary and afflict the enemy. Hasten the time and remember the end, so that they may declare your wonders.**” This prayer asks that the divine majesty, through the hand and right arm—that is, the Lord Christ—renew in the time of grace the miracles that were performed in ancient times, so that he may be understood to be the one and the same God of the old and the new Law: namely, Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, alone performs wonders both then and now.

By asking that fury be stirred and wrath poured out, so that the adversary may be raised up [the reading is uncertain; perhaps “removed,” as in the quoted lemma] and the enemy afflicted, he means that at Christ’s coming the devil is necessarily removed from the hearts of unbelievers, lest he hold them captive any longer in error and idolatry. The Savior himself expressed this in the Gospel, saying: “When a strong armed man guards his courtyard, the things he possesses are at peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11).

He is the true enemy and adversary of God’s people, upon whom God’s wrath will be poured out until the end, and whose wound is not healable. When he says, “Hasten the time and remember the end,” this is what the Prophet says to God in the Psalms: “You will arise, Lord, and have mercy on Zion, because the time has come to have mercy on her” (Ps. 101).

He prays that, since it is the time of the final hour and the end of the world is approaching, the one who was promised may come and have mercy on the human race, because he is himself the expectation of the nations.

“**In the wrath of the flame let the one who is saved be devoured, and let those who mistreat your people find destruction.**” This foretells that those who love their own souls in the pleasure of this life, who are unwilling to lay them down for Christ, and who persecute the catholic people and deliver God’s faithful to slaughter, will be devoured in the flame of future wrath and will find eternal destruction in the fire of Gehenna.

“**Crush the head of the rulers of the enemies who say, ‘There is no other besides us.’**” The devil is the head of all the wicked and unbelieving. The Church asks that he be crushed, since he is the prince of this age and incites idolaters to persecute Christians, saying, “There is no other besides us,” because they imagine that they alone rule in the world and refuse to be subjected to God’s eternal power.

“**Gather all the tribes of Jacob, so that they may know that there is no God except you, so that they may declare your mighty works, and you will inherit them as from the beginning.**” After completing his prayer against sinners and their head, the devil, Wisdom prays for the state of the Church and the salvation of believers. For what are the tribes of Jacob except the Churches gathered from the nations? The younger son, who seized his brother’s blessing, prefigured them.

He asks that they be gathered—that is, made firm in the unity of catholic faith—so that, faithfully knowing God, they may proclaim his wonders in the preaching of the holy Gospel, and so that they may remain his inheritance forever, just as they have been possessed by him from the beginning of faith. Concerning this it continues:

“**Have mercy on your people, over whom your name has been invoked, and on Israel, whom you have made equal to your firstborn. Have mercy on the city of your sanctification, Jerusalem, the city of your rest.**” The people of God are the same as the city of God: namely, the catholic Church, spiritual Jerusalem, the vision of peace, and the dwelling place of the Most High. God’s name has been invoked over her because she is his people and the flock of his pasture. She is also called Israel, which is interpreted as “upright with God” or “a man seeing God,” because she walks along the straight path of faith and contemplates God with a pure mind.

He made her equal to his firstborn—that is, he made her coheir with his only-begotten Son, who is the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. Hence it follows:

“**Fill Zion with your unspeakable words, and fill your people with your glory.**” Zion is interpreted as “contemplation,” and rightly is the holy Church called contemplation, because from there the hearts of the faithful contemplate the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

The Lord fills her with his unspeakable words when he instructs her in the knowledge of the divine books, in which the indescribable power of God and the immeasurable glory of his majesty are proclaimed; and when he causes her to stand out among all nations through signs and miracles, so that she becomes both a terror and an honor to all the surrounding peoples.

Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when Paul was preaching and performing miracles, fear fell upon all in the city of Ephesus—that is, upon the Jews and Gentiles who lived there—and they magnified the name of the Lord Jesus. Many believers came, confessing and declaring their deeds. Many of those who had practiced curious arts brought their books together and burned them before everyone; and when their prices were calculated, they found them worth fifty thousand denarii. So powerfully did the word of the Lord grow and prevail (Acts 19). The statements that follow continuously agree with this interpretation:

“**Give testimony to those who have existed from the beginning of your creation, and raise up the proclamations spoken in your name by the earlier prophets.**” All the prophets bore witness to the incarnation of our Savior, that God would become human and build for himself a Church of the faithful, presenting her to himself as a glorious bride without stain or wrinkle.

Therefore he says: “Give testimony to those who have existed from the beginning of your creation.” The Church is God’s creation, which he acquired for himself through the grace of Christ and the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that, according to Paul’s statement, “through the same Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the eternal purpose that he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him” (Eph. 3).

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.” This is what Wisdom prays: that the promises which the earlier prophets spoke concerning the calling of the nations to faith in Christ may be fulfilled through Christ’s coming. Hence it continues:

“**Give a reward, Lord, to those who wait for you, so that your prophets may be found faithful, and hear the prayers of your servants. Abraham rejoiced that he would see Christ’s day; he saw it and was glad**” (John 8).

Isaiah says: “Lord, we have waited for you; your name and your remembrance are the desire of our soul” (Isa. 26). Many kings and righteous people desired to see what the apostles saw but did not see it, and to hear what they heard but did not hear it.

For this reason Simeon also received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. When he received him present in his arms, he said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared before the face of all peoples: a light for revelation to the nations and for the glory of your people Israel” (Luke 2).

A reward is given to those who wait for God when the future recompense of life is granted to the faithful who await the grace of Christ and hope in him. Thus the divine prophets are found both faithful and truthful, and the devout prayer of his servants is heard—those who pray daily “that the kingdom of God may come and that his will may be done [Col. 1020C] as in heaven, so on earth.”

“**According to the blessing of Aaron, give to your people, and direct us in the way of justice; and let all who inhabit the earth know that you are God, the observer of the ages.**” For what is the blessing of Aaron except the order and rite of the priesthood that the Lord gave to his people when he united them to Christ, his only-begotten Son?

He is the true priest who offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father for us and handed down to us the sacraments of his body and blood. Of him it is written: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). He made us a kingdom and priests for his God and Father.

Thus the apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light. Draw near to him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by human beings but chosen and honored by God; and you yourselves, as living stones, are built upon him as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 2).

The blessing of Aaron is therefore truly given to God’s people when they are directed in the way of justice, so that what Aaron prefigured in the bodily sacrifices of the Law, the people may fulfill in the spiritual sacrifices of the Gospel.

“Let all who inhabit the earth know,” he says, “that you are God, the observer of the ages.” That is, let all nations recognize, in the marvelous salvation of the Christian people, that you are God before all ages and remain the same after all ages—the one who ordered past times in such a way that, for the sake of Christ’s grace, you would cause future times to surpass them.

“**Every food the belly will eat, and one food is better than another. The jaws taste the food of the wild beast, and the discerning heart the words of deceit.**” After completing the prayer and the prophecy by which he foretold the future calling of the nations to faith in Christ, Wisdom teaches us to maintain discernment amid differing doctrines. He uses the example of the human belly and jaws: just as the throat, judging foods, separates sweet food from bitter, so the prudent mind, discerning differences among doctrines, should distinguish truthful teaching from deceitful teaching.

“An evil heart will cause sorrow, and a knowledgeable man resists it.” The evil heart of heretics meditates injustice all day long; their tongue has contrived deceit; and a knowledgeable man, grounded in Catholic doctrine, resists it with the shield of true faith and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

“A woman will receive every male, and one daughter is better than another daughter.” A woman receiving every male is understood of those who say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I to Cephas” (1 Cor. XII). The better daughter is understood of those who say, “I belong to Christ.” She is the one who is nearest to him in the Song of Songs, among the daughters: “Like a lily among thorns” (Song of Songs II). Alternatively, in the male we may understand the word of divine law, which makes the intelligent soul fruitful in the prudence of wisdom and in good works.
