Hence it is also said through Isaiah: “As the rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but drench the earth, water it, and make it germinate, giving seed to the sower and bread to the one who eats, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth: it shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and it shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. LV). By saying, “One daughter is better than another daughter,” he shows that there is a difference in progress in knowledge and in the practice of virtues, and that some works are good while others are perfect, as the Lord himself demonstrates in the Gospel, saying: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX). And again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor; and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me” (ibid.). Therefore Paul too, wishing it to be understood that there is a difference in the reward of the saints, says: “Star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead.”

“The appearance of a woman gladdens her husband’s face, and her desire surpasses every human desire.” We may understand this woman either specifically as the faithful soul or generally as the whole Church. For the appearance of this woman—that is, the beauty she possesses in right faith and good works—gladdens the face of her husband, namely her bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, who delights in her progress. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will lack no spoil. She will render him good, not evil, all the days of her life” (Prov. XXXI). And again: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day” (ibid.). No human desire can be compared with this longing, for it is written: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (ibid.). The woman who fears God—she shall be praised.

“If there is a tongue of healing, there is also one of mitigation and mercy.” Here he calls the grace of Christ “mercy”; through the preaching of the Gospel it heals the wounds of souls and mitigates the heat of carnal desire. This mercy, then, overflows in the Catholic Church. Hence he says that its longing is above every human desire, because in it the beauty of virtues and the loveliness of doctrine shine forth wondrously.

“Her husband is not according to the sons of men.” The husband of the Church is Christ, who is not according to the sons of men, because his dignity far surpasses human nature. Therefore it is written of him in the Prophet: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever” (Ps. XLIV). But since Isaiah says, “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; his facial appearance was without honor, rejected above all men” (Isa. LIII), one may ask how this husband is described as the most beautiful above the human race. This is not because his bodily form possessed the beauty of a milk-white complexion, or because he shone with blond hair, or because he surpassed others in distinguished stature; rather, he was truly more beautiful than the human race because he had no sins. For we rightly call that beautiful which is adorned with the grace of the purest holiness, although the father Augustine says that the appearance of his body was worthy of praise. But the example cited above from Isaiah refers to the time of his passion, when he is read to have been struck with blows, crowned with thorns, and covered with spittle.

The Church, however, which bears the image of the Lord and Savior, is read in the Song of Songs to have said: “I am dark and beautiful” (Song of Songs I)—that is, dark in carnal body, beautiful in heavenly merits. Why he called him beautiful is proved by this: when Christ spoke, the world was reconciled to God through grace. What, then, could there be in the human race so like him as to behold the very one who became incarnate, through whom the whole world receives the gift of redemption? For the aforesaid book of Solomon also declares of him: “Your lips and your speech are beautiful” (Song of Songs IV, V).

It follows: “Therefore God has blessed you forever.” “Therefore,” he says, because of his outstanding preaching and singular piety in every respect: he bestowed nothing on anyone according to merits, but granted everything rather through his own goodness. He is blessed forever, whose kingdom will have no end. It was rightly said by the form of a servant, “God has blessed you”: that form both endured the passion and reached the kingdoms of heaven.

“He who possesses a good woman begins a possession.” This sentence therefore shows that Christ’s inheritance is the holy Church, which he himself, the most glorious bridegroom, first founded through the gift of faith and the sacrament of baptism, and thus caused the nations of all peoples to hasten to her. Hence the paternal voice says to him in the psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

This is said with reference to the appearance and form of a servant, because he is the son of a virgin. Whatever Christ received in time, according to his humanity he acquires what he did not possess. Hence he is commanded to ask according to the lower nature and to possess what he receives. For according to the power of the Word, the Son possesses without distinction everything that the Father possesses, nor is it necessary for him to ask for what he is likewise acknowledged to possess.

The nations signify the peoples scattered throughout the whole world, whom the blood of Christ embraces as distinct and separate. For the very fact that he says, “your,” demonstrates the incarnation of the Word, so that nothing may be understood as divided when everything is possessed by one majesty, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Everything that the Father has is mine, and everything that is the Father’s is mine” (John XVII).

“And your possession,” he says, “to the ends of the earth.” Here it is made clear that all nations will believe in the name of Christ, through whom the world, its superstitions having been driven out, has been reconciled to God. For when he also says here, “your possession,” he accepted the nature of humanity, whereas he had always possessed the divine nature. Nothing that he already possessed could be given to his majesty. The ends of the earth are those which encircle and enclose the earth; or it signifies not only the dry land but also the surrounding substance of the entire air and the integrity of all creatures, as he himself briefly sums up in the Gospel, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). And the Apostle says: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

“Her help is according to him, and a pillar for rest.” The Church’s help is according to the dispensation of the Lord, her bridegroom; she seeks consolation nowhere else but from him, because in him she will find timely assistance for all her need. Hence he says in the psalm: “My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart” (Ps. VII). From him she also receives support in weakness and rest from labor. Therefore she is said to become a pillar for rest, because he who is now the support of her weakness will in the future become the fullness of her rest.

“Where there is no hedge, the possession will be plundered; and where there is no woman, the needy man groans.” This indicates that where there is no wall of Catholic faith, founded through the mouths of holy teachers, the possession of virtues is gathered in vain, because it will be entirely plundered by unclean spirits. “For it is impossible to please God without faith” (Heb. XI). Hence it may be inferred that all the labor of the pagan philosophers who debated ethics and imitated certain forms of virtue is empty and altogether useless to them, because whatever is done outside the holy Church produces perpetual groaning, not eternal joy.

“Who will believe one who has no nest, and who, wandering wherever darkness falls, leaps from city to city like a bandit with his garments girded up?” Here he calls the holy Church a nest, where the devout souls of the elect nourish children of good works. Hence it is written in the psalm: “The sparrow has found a home for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young” (Ps. LXXXIII). Where, then, can one who does not remain within the holy Church have rest and protection? For wherever he turns aside through the doctrines of heretics or the studies of philosophers, he will always be in error and will nowhere find the light of sincere truth. He also leaps like a bandit with his garments girded up from city to city, because, unstable in everything, he wanders and flees, falling from one error into another. It follows.

## CHAPTER VIII. That one must not be a friend in name only, but in deed, faith, and charity

(CAP. XXXVII.) “Every friend will say, ‘I too have formed a friendship’; but there is a friend who is a friend in name only.” Earlier, when he discussed friends, he explained more carefully what a true friend and a false friend are, because elsewhere it is said: “There is a friend according to his appointed time, and he will not remain on the day of tribulation; and there is a friend who turns from enmity. There is also a friend who shares the table, and he will not remain on the day of need” (Eccli. VI). By contrast, no comparison can be made with a faithful friend, because a faithful friend is a medicine of life and immortality.

Every friend—that is, true and false alike—professes himself to be a friend; but the one who remains steadfast is rightly adorned with the honor of this name. Since firm faith is not found in a false friend, he therefore adds:

“Is there not sorrow even unto death? But a companion and a friend will turn into an enemy.” It is the greatest evil, and something to be lamented with continual grief, that where fidelity is expected, malignity is found; and where charity has been made to resemble friendship, the perversity of enmity is discovered.

“O most wicked presumption, from where have you arisen, to cover dry barrenness with his malice and deceit?” The wise man therefore wonders at the origin of wickedness, although it is clear that it was brought forth from the creature’s evil will. He vehemently detests hypocrisy, because it is the worst vice for anyone to pretend to be what he entirely is not: when the evil person pretends to be good, the unjust person just, the wicked person fair-minded, and the enemy a friend. He covers deceit and arid deceit—where there is no richness of love and mercy—for he truly deceives himself when he thinks that he is an honorable deceiver of others.

“A companion rejoices with his friend in pleasure, but in a time of tribulation he will be an adversary. A companion grieves with his friend for the sake of his belly, and against the enemy he will take up a shield.” The historical writer therefore continues to rebuke false friends, because through the art of simulation they deceive the eyes of the simple and conceal poison beneath an appearance of beauty. They rejoice in the pleasure of delight, but in a time of adversity they withdraw. They raise weapons against the enemy for the sake of their belly, but they will not be faithful defenders of their friend, because they love not their neighbor but their pleasures.

Heretics may also, not inappropriately, be understood among these false friends, because they do everything deceitfully. They pretend to be guardians and counselors of human salvation, but, as becomes increasingly clear, they are deceivers and destroyers of souls. Therefore they must be altogether avoided and shunned, just as the Lord warned his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves. Therefore you will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII). And elsewhere: “Beware,” he says, “of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (Matt. VII).

“Do not forget your friend in your heart, and do not be unmindful of him in your deeds.” A true friend does not disagree in heart and deed; rather, just as he loves in his mind, so he will be beneficial to his brother in action. The apostle John also teaches this in his Epistle, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (Luke XII).

“Do not take counsel with one who lies in wait for you, and hide your counsel from those who are jealous of you.” In the father-in-law, who is joined to the kinship on the female side, he shows a womanly and changeable disposition, from which your trust can never be expected. Likewise, jealousy, which especially prevails in the female sex, signifies an instability of mind to which trust must never be granted. “For,” as someone has said, “just as a shore without a harbor is an untrustworthy anchorage for ships, so a mind without faith is dangerous in the company of friends.”

“Every counselor reveals counsel, but there is a counselor who is so in himself.” Counsel should not be taken with many, since few are perfect in faith and prudent in mind. Hence it is written: “Let your friends be many, but one your counselor out of a thousand” (Eccli. VI). Yet there is a counselor who is so in himself, because he has chosen to do what he knows will please his Creator in every respect. This is the one counsel, poured into the human heart through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Guard your soul from a counselor. First learn what his need is, or what he is considering in his mind, lest perhaps he drive a stake into the ground and say to you, ‘Your way is good,’ while he stands opposed and watches to see what will happen to you.” He repeats what he said above, so that we may not be careless in choosing friends and counselors, nor act rashly beyond measure in accepting friends and employing counselors. For many appear outwardly to preserve fidelity in friendship, but devise deceit in their minds and plot snares in their hearts.

Hence Jeremiah instructs us to beware of such evil, saying: “Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him not trust any brother, because every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will proceed deceitfully; and a man will mock his brother, and they will not speak the truth. They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IX). And again: “Their tongue,” he says, “is a wounding arrow; it has spoken deceit with its mouth. He speaks peace with his friend, but secretly lays snares for him. Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord, or shall my soul not take vengeance on such a nation?”

## CHAPTER IX. Wisdom teaches with whom one should deliberate—that is, with the religious and the just

“Deliberate about holiness with a religious man; do not take counsel about justice with an unjust man, or with a woman about what she envies. With a timid man, about war; with a merchant, about a crossing; with a buyer, about a sale; with an envious man, about giving thanks; with an impious man, about piety; with a dishonorable man, about honor; with a field laborer, about every kind of work; with an annual laborer, about the completion of the year; with a lazy servant, about much labor. Do not heed such people in any counsel.”

Here he enumerates various kinds of counselors, among whom he nevertheless identifies many persons whose will is at variance with the truth and who are therefore not useful in the giving of counsel. Hence, in accordance with the beginning of this chapter, Wisdom commands that counsel not be taken with such people, and similarly warns at the end that they are not to be heeded in every counsel, because when hearts and actions do not agree, counsel is undoubtedly endangered. Therefore anyone who wishes to take proper counsel with another must first weigh his counselor’s prudence, faith, will, and religious devotion, and then use his counsel. Of this the following passage also speaks.

## CHAPTER X. He urges that one should always associate with the just and those of good reputation

“Be especially constant with a holy man, whoever you know to observe the fear of God, whose soul is like your own, and who, when you stumble in darkness, will grieve with you. Establish within yourself the heart of good counsel; for you have nothing better than it.”

When you know someone to fear God, you may hope that he will be faithful and devoted to you. But whoever has abandoned the fear of God and walks in the darkness of vices will in no way be able to preserve complete faith with you or offer useful counsel. Above all, you must choose the heart of good counsel and hold it dearer than all else at every time.

## CHAPTER XI. Wisdom tells of the soul of the holy man, which, filled with the sevenfold number of virtues of the Holy Spirit, prophesies

“The soul of a holy man sometimes declares truths more surely than seven observers seated on high to keep watch.” After discussing above the diversity of counselors, he next adds how far the knowledge of the holy man surpasses human wisdom—a knowledge infused into his soul by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The seven observers are the teachers of the liberal arts, which they themselves comprise under the number seven. Yet it is clearer in all respects that the modest doctrine of the Catholic man, which rests upon the divine books, is truer than all the multifarious skill of philosophers in disputing and arguing. In the former, truth shines forth in every respect, irreproachable in a few and pure words; in the latter, a wandering opinion concerning obscure matters appears in garrulous loquacity—or rather, manifest falsehood appears.

But since all wisdom is from the Lord God, and no one can possess it without his gift, he therefore adds:

“And in all these things pray to the Most High, that he may direct your way in truth.” Tobias also admonished his son concerning this very matter, saying: “Bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your ways, and let all your counsels remain in him” (Tob. IV). Hence the Psalmist likewise prays to the Lord: “Direct me in your truth and teach me, for you are God, my Savior, and I have waited for you all day long” (Ps. XXXIV).

“Before all works, let a truthful word go before you, and before every action, steadfast counsel.” This word too is to be understood not as external but as internal—the word that proceeds from the mind’s thought, according to which external speech and actions are ordered. Hence it is written: “From the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. XII). For if a person’s thought orders his word and counsel in truth and good will according to the fear of God, all his actions take place in peace. Conversely, concerning another word he continues:

“An evil word will change the heart.” That is, an evil counsel disturbs the whole conscience of a person and confounds his will when it deals with things displeasing in the sight of God.

“From it four parts arise: good and evil, life and death; and their ruler is the continual tongue.” “From it,” he says—that is, from the word of the heart—four parts arise: good and evil, namely good or evil counsel, and their recompense, life or death, because “the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. VI). By saying that their ruler is the continual tongue, he shows that the secrets of the heart are disclosed through the tongue’s ministry. Death and life are in the power of the tongue; hence Truth himself says: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matt. XII).

“A knowledgeable man has instructed many, and he is pleasing to his own soul.” Since he had spoken beforehand about the works of the tongue, he now proceeds to explain the matter of good and evil teachers. One who is knowledgeable in Sacred Scripture and is proved truthful in speech and upright in conduct benefits and heals many through his instruction; and his own labor will bring sweetness to his soul for eternal life.

## CHAPTER XII. On crafty and sophistical speech—that is, philosophical display

“But one who speaks sophistically is hateful; in every matter he will be defrauded. For grace has not been given to him by the Lord; he has been deprived of all wisdom.”

In this sentence both crafty speech is censured and heretical wickedness condemned. The disciplines of disputation and number do not pertain, then, to the bodily senses but to the mind’s reason. In them the truth is piously sought and usefully found by those who fear God. The discipline of disputation is of great value for all kinds of questions that must be penetrated and resolved in the sacred writings. Only the desire to quarrel and a certain childish display aimed at deceiving an opponent must be avoided there.

For there are many things called sophisms—false conclusions of reasoning—which often imitate truth so closely that they deceive not only the slow-witted but even the intelligent when they are insufficiently attentive. Someone proposed the following to a man with whom he was speaking: “What I am, you are not.” The other agreed, for it was true in part—or because the first was crafty while the other was simple-minded. Then the first added: “But I am a human being.” When the other had accepted this as well, he concluded: “Therefore you are not a human being.”

Scripture, as I believe, detests this kind of deceptive conclusion in the present passage, where it says, “One who speaks sophistically is hateful.” Yet speech may also be sophistical when it is not deceptive but pursues verbal ornament more abundantly than dignity permits.

In this sophistical speech certain heretics are denoted: they construct everything craftily and maliciously in order to lead others astray. They are hateful both to God and to all good people; they have been deprived of every useful thing and of true doctrine, because the grace of the Holy Spirit has not been given to them by the Lord. For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. I). Hence they have also been deprived of heavenly wisdom: they do not understand the things that are God’s, but those that are human, wandering and leading others into error (Matt. XVI).

“There is a wise man who is wise for his own soul, and the fruit of his understanding is praiseworthy.” One who is truly wise perceives, teaches, and does what pertains to the salvation of his soul. Therefore the fruit of his understanding is praiseworthy, because he considers in his mind what pleases God, declares it with his tongue, and practices it through useful action.

“A wise man instructs his people, and the fruits of his understanding are trustworthy.” The ecclesiastical teacher instructs the people entrusted to him by his word and teaches by his example. The fruits of his understanding, which he has produced either by writing or by preaching, are trustworthy, because heresies and the perversities of schisms are not found in them. Thus what follows will come to pass.

“A wise man will be filled with blessings, and those who see him will praise him.” He will indeed be filled with blessing when he is rewarded with heavenly recompense. Those who see him will praise him when the good angels and the souls of the saints, contemplating his merit, rejoice with him in the bestowal of his reward. Nor is this surprising, since the master of the household himself will say in the future judgment to the servant who has rightly done good: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. XXV).

“The life of a man is limited to a number of days, but the days of Israel are innumerable.” What does he mean by saying that the life of a man is contained within a number of days and then adding that the days of Israel are innumerable, except that he shows the life of the saints in heavenly blessedness to be eternal and without end?

That the present life of human beings is established with a definite number in God’s foreknowledge and disposition, Job demonstrates when he says: “The days of man are short; the number of his months is with you. You have appointed his limits, which he cannot pass” (Job XIV). But the days of Israel—that is, of holy men who in the present life have continually worshiped the Lord with right faith and good works—after the end of their present labor, contemplate with pure mind the serene face of God perpetually in the heavenly kingdom. Just as there is no stain on this blessedness, so there is no end to its joy.

“A wise man will inherit honor among the people, and his name will live forever.” Here he speaks of the wise man concerning whom he also spoke above: the one who instructs his people according to the truth of the Catholic faith and whose understanding produces trustworthy fruits. He will be filled with heavenly blessing and will obtain eternal praise.

He will inherit among the people because, remaining glorious in the body of the Church, he joyfully awaits in hope the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. His name lives forever, because “the righteous will be in everlasting remembrance, and his name will be sought from generation to generation.” Concerning him Truth himself commanded his faithful in the Gospel to rejoice, since he knew that a great reward was prepared for them: “Rejoice,” he says, “and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

“My son, in your life test your soul, and if it is wicked, do not give it power. For not everything is suitable for everyone, and not every kind of thing pleases every soul.” Wisdom commands a person carefully to guard his life, lest through carelessness he dissipate himself among various desires and fall into the death of sin. Therefore he says that he should test his soul—that is, examine the inclination of his soul—and if it is perverse, he should not grant it the power to carry that inclination out, because not everything is suitable for everyone, and not every kind of desire or action is useful for every soul.

Accordingly, the apostle Paul, wishing to make us cautious, wrote: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John IV). And again: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good, and abstain from every appearance of evil” (1 Thess. V). And elsewhere: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything” (1 Cor. VI, X).

“Do not be greedy at every feast, and do not pour yourself out over every food. For in many foods there will be weakness; insatiety, greed, and gluttony draw near even to cholera. Because of gluttony many have died, but whoever is abstinent will add to his life.”

In these sentences, according to the literal sense, he praises moderation in nourishment and censures greed and an excess of food, because these lead the intemperate person to nausea and the illness of cholera. Mystically, however, he admonishes us to be temperate in spiritual foods and to avoid excess, lest, if we wish to exceed the measure of knowledge, we fall into error and, through excessive investigation of incomprehensible matters, come into the greatest folly, leaving certain death and destruction for ourselves.

Hence Solomon also says: “Have you found honey? Eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are filled, you vomit it up and perjure the name of your God” (Prov. XXV). Paul likewise teaches: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sober judgment, and according as God has allotted to each the measure of faith” (Rom. XII).

## CHAPTER XIII. On honoring the physician

(CAP. XXXVIII.) “Honor the physician because of necessity, for the Most High created him. For all healing is from the Lord, and from the king he will receive a gift.”

He wishes us to be discerning in everything and not to act rashly, because all the works of God are not only good but very good. Therefore we must not despise what we know our Creator has produced for our benefit and health; rather, we should receive it with thanksgiving and apply it to our uses.

There are bodily physicians and spiritual ones. But just as bodily physicians heal diseases of the body through medicines made from herbs, so spiritual physicians heal the infirmities of souls through the remedy of divine commandments. Both, therefore, are to be held in honor; but spiritual physicians are to be preferred with the greater reverence, inasmuch as their works are found to be more lasting and more salutary.

“The discipline of the physician will exalt his head, and in the sight of the great he will be highly praised.” The discipline of the spiritual physician will produce everlasting glory for his soul, and in the sight of the holy angels and holy souls he will receive the reward of eternal life.

“The Most High created medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not reject it.” From earthly things God provided remedies for human infirmities. Therefore what wise person would dare to despise and scorn medicine? For what the Creator of all things has mercifully brought forth for our weakness must not be despised.

“Was not bitter water sweetened by a piece of wood, so that its power might be known to human beings? And the Most High gave human beings knowledge, to be honored in his wonders; and in these, when he heals, he will mitigate pain” (Exod. XVII).

He recalls the history of old, in which the children of Israel, walking through the desert of Sur, did not find water for three days. At last, when they came to Marah, they could not drink the waters of Marah because they were bitter. But the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood; when he had cast it into the water, the waters were changed into sweetness.

Here, according to the literal sense, the power of the Lord is demonstrated: through medicinal art, the waters were made sweet by means of wood. The mystery of this event is readily apparent. The people murmur when they see the water and cannot endure drinking it. Moses casts the wood into the water, and it becomes sweet.

Understand the bitter waters as the deadening letter and the figure of the law. When the confession of the cross is cast into them and the mystery of the Lord’s passion is joined to them, then the bitter water becomes sweet, and the bitterness of the letter is changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding. Hence it is also written: “The Lord established a law and judgments for his people, and he tested them.”

In another sense, the fact that bitter waters become sweet when they receive wood within them indicated that the bitterness of the nations would one day be changed through the wood of Christ’s cross into an instrument of sweetness. For this reason the Most High gave human beings knowledge of things wondrously created by him, so that through their beneficially granted use they might be moved to honor and glorify their Maker.

“And the perfumer will make an ointment of sweetness, and will prepare an anointing for health, and his works will not be completed. For the peace of God is upon the face of the earth.”

Physicians employ their art in different ways against different illnesses: in foods, drinks, plasters, and ointments, adapting an appropriate medicine according to the nature of the diseases. Thus spiritual physicians, according to the skill of their art, customarily act beneficially for the salvation of souls. They provide fomentations of instruction, ointments of exhortation, and a poultice of continual prayer. They also prepare medicinal drinks and foods from the divine Scriptures. Where necessary, they apply the burning of excommunication or the cutting of disciplinary rods, so that by whatever means they can, they may lead a person from the sickness of vices to the health of good virtues.

By saying that his works will not be completed, he signifies that until the end of the world our true physician does not cease, through his ministers, to work healings daily in his Church, until at the final judgment, through his grace, everything mortal is swallowed up by life. Then what follows will take place: “The peace of the Lord is upon the face of the earth,” when, death having been swallowed up in victory, the dead will rise incorruptible and be transferred to possess the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

But because, until this occurs, we must always devote ourselves to prayer, continually entreat the Lord for the state of our life, turn away from sins, and labor with all our strength in good works, the following sentence shows this.

## CHAPTER XIV. On praying to God the Father in a time of weakness, temptation, and desire

“My son, in your weakness do not despise yourself, but pray to the Lord, and he himself will heal you. Turn away from sin and direct your hands, and cleanse your heart from every sin.”

He first commands that in weakness we must not despair of ourselves, because despair afflicts the soul and brings it certain death. Rather, we should pray to God and entrust the care of our salvation to him, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of believers (1 Tim. IV).

The apostle James instructs us concerning him, saying: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James V).

But this is done worthily if we turn the eyes of our mind away from every evil, direct our hands toward good action, and cleanse the thoughts of our heart from every deceit and wickedness. For thus we deserve to be heard by the Lord and to obtain his mercy. In addition, the offering of the saving sacrifice is added; it especially assists the infirmity of our souls if it is offered from a pure mind, as the following sentence proves.

“Give the savor and remembrance of fine flour, fatten the offering, and give place to the physician, for the Lord created him; and let him not depart from you, since his works are necessary.” Thus the sacrifice of bread and wine, offered in remembrance of the Lord’s passion, chiefly heals the wounds of souls when it is offered to God upon the altar through the ministry of the priest, together with sacred prayers. Hence, as blessed Gregory says in the books of the *Dialogues*: “If sins after death are not insoluble, the sacred offering of the saving victim is accustomed greatly to help souls even after death. So much so that sometimes the souls of the departed themselves seem to seek it; and this same sacrifice is believed to be of great benefit not only to the dead but also to the living, if it is offered worthily.” [Col. 1032C] This is why we have heard of a certain man who was held captive among enemies and bound in chains, for whom his wife was accustomed to offer sacrifice on appointed days. After a long time he returned to his wife and revealed on which days his chains had been loosed; his wife recognized that these had been the days on which she had offered sacrifice for him. This happened through the grace of almighty God, so that mortals might learn from visible things how greatly the spiritual victim, offered invisibly for the salvation of souls, can accomplish its work.

“There is indeed a time when you fall into their hands; [Col. 1032D] but they will entreat the Lord to direct their repose and their health because of their conversion. Whoever sins in the sight of him who made him will fall into the hands of the physician.” When he says that there is a time when a person falls into the hands of physicians, he indicates the time of illness and bodily suffering, when those who are unwell necessarily require treatment. Illness itself is imposed according to God’s providence for the testing or correction of the elect, and for the rebuke or condemnation of the reprobate. Hence he says: “Whoever sins in the sight of him who made him will fall into the hands of the physician.” It is just that one who, through pride, refused to obey God’s commandments should be humbled by being chastised through illness; [Col. 1033A] and that the one who, while unharmed, previously refused to understand his benefactor should, when scourged, seek his help. Mystically, however, holy teachers and spiritual physicians of souls are always seeking a suitable time when they may apply appropriate medicine to sick souls. Through sacred prayers and the works of the virtues they earnestly beseech the Lord to direct their labors and grant refreshment to those who have suffered from various illnesses of the vices.

## CHAPTER XV. On the rites for the dead and the moderation of grief

“Son, pour out tears for the dead, and, as though he had suffered dreadful things, begin to mourn; and, according to judgment, cover his body, and do not despise his burial.” After discussing the sickness of illnesses and the treatment provided by physicians, he next brings forward a discourse on the rites for the dead: for just as medicinal treatment is useful in illness, so the provision of burial is necessary in death. Yet because the misery of death compels a person to shed tears, and because we read of solemn lamentations being made at the funerals of deceased fathers, he teaches that there should be measure in the shedding of tears and in mourning, lest excessive grief weaken the bodies of those who sorrow and God be offended by the madness of those who despair. The sentence of death was indeed given to mortals because of sin, but through the grace of Christ the confidence of hope has been given to believers.

“Because of his departure, bear bitter mourning for him for one day, and console yourself because of the grief; and make mourning according to his merit for one or two days because of his departure. For from grief death hastens, and it will cover strength, and sorrow of heart bends the neck.” “Because of his departure,” he says—that is, because of the departure of your neighbor—grieve over his fall for a short time, and console yourself in the hope of resurrection, lest excessive grief cast you into destruction. “From grief death hastens”: the death of the despairing soul; grief obscures all the strength of its good action, softens the firmness of the heart, and causes it to grow weak.

“In abduction grief remains, and the substance of the needy according to his heart.” For where immoderate pain occupies the heart and the mind is carried away, so that it does not receive consolation, there grief remains: because it begins here through the affliction of pain and remains in future punishment, on account of distrust of heavenly consolation. Truly, the substance of the needy man is measured according to his heart, because as much as he lacks in faith and hope, so much does his sorrow increase in distress and pain.

“Do not give your heart to grief, but drive it away from you, and remember the last things. Do not forget, for there is no return, and you will profit him nothing, and you will make yourself worse.” Since the meaning of this passage is obscure because of the difficulty of its wording, let us say something that may explain it in clearer speech. Let not worldly grief, which produces the death of the soul, occupy your heart; cast it away from you, and remember the final times, because as you depart from here, so you will be presented before the Judge, to receive what belongs to your body according to what you have done, whether good or evil. Therefore never consign the departure of the final hour to oblivion, but always be ready, because after you have departed from here you will by no means return here again to have opportunity for good works. For this reason be cautious in everything, lest you grieve beyond measure at the death of your neighbor, since your weeping will profit him nothing if you harm yourself by afflicting yourself with immeasurable sorrows.

“Remember my judgment, for yours will be the same: yesterday for me, and today for you.” He calls his judgment his departure from this world, which is proper to everyone, both those of former times and those now living, because “there is no person on earth who lives and does not see death.” And he rightly says, “Yesterday for me, and today for you,” as though he were saying: What has already been completed in me is now approaching its fulfillment in you. This is the admonition of good fathers: they warn their sons so that they may learn from the deaths of those who came before them that their own condition in the present world is not lasting, and therefore prepare for themselves the provision of good works, by which they may live forever in the future life with the holy angels.

“In the repose of the dead, cause his memory to rest, and console him at the departure of his spirit.” He gives this admonition: at the passage of the dying person, do not consign his memory to oblivion, but continually preserve it in your mind for your own improvement; and strengthen by faith and comfort with hope the one who is beginning to depart from this world, so that in the distress of his final time he may not fail in faith but entrust his hope to God. For the one who promised the reward to those who fight well through the merit of faith is himself powerful to grant an everlasting kingdom to those who hope in him.

“Write wisdom in a time of leisure, and the one who is less occupied with work will acquire wisdom.” He therefore teaches that, while we have leisure and rest, we should learn divine wisdom and write it upon the tablets of our hearts, because the one who ceases to serve the desires of the flesh and the pleasures of the world will rejoice in the gift of heavenly contemplation by meditating attentively on Scripture. Yet, since those who devote themselves at the proper season to agriculture and possess skill in the various crafts at which people diligently labor in the present life are not entirely strangers to the gift of wisdom, he first enumerates their knowledge; then, by adding to it, he sets before them true wisdom, which consists in the recognition of God’s will and in the keeping of his commandments through love. Thus wisdom itself holds the citadel of dignity, since it alone possesses power for righteous government. We too, first briefly touching upon the history of the individual crafts, shall then proceed by explaining the allegory:

“What wisdom will fill the one who holds the plow and the one who boasts in the goad? He drives oxen with a prod, is occupied with their work, and his discourse concerns the offspring of bulls; he will give his heart to turning the furrows, and his vigilance will be devoted to fattening cows.” As regards the historical sense, he shows that, by the gift of wisdom, a person has this ability: to devote himself to useful labor by which he can benefit himself and his neighbors, to practice agriculture, and to care for the feeding of animals and beasts of burden, which were created for human use, so that he may prepare food and clothing both for himself and for his own people, by which the misery of human life is sustained in the present world and without which it cannot completely exist. Mystically, however, the one who holds the office of teacher and ought to cultivate human hearts with the evangelical plow boasts in the goad of divine testimonies. He sows the word of God with the prod of exhortation and urges the brutish, so that they may not live sluggishly but conduct themselves vigorously in good works. He chastises the proud with the word of preaching and tames them by evangelical discipline, so that they may not waste their time in idleness but, mortifying their flesh and putting to death their carnal desires within themselves, may hasten to uproot every vice from themselves and strive to plant spiritual virtues in their place. By saying that, through the stirring of oxen and bulls, the shepherd’s vigils are devoted to the fattening of cows, he shows that it is the duty of a good ruler to care for both sexes and, through the zeal of preaching, to feed, nourish, and sustain them.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the individual craftsmen

“Thus every smith and architect, who spends the night as though it were day, who carves engraved seals, and whose diligence varies the design: he will give his heart to the likeness of the picture, and his vigilance will complete the work.” What else are signified by this smith and architect, who diligently labors night and day at his work, carving seals and fashioning the image of a person by the art of gem-working, than holy preachers? At every moment, whether by teaching, exhorting, or displaying good examples, they instruct their hearers, so that they may draw out the virtue of the inner person and refashion the human soul according to the image of its Creator. Was not that man an energetic smith and architect in his art who wrote in his Letters, saying: “For we are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it” (II Cor. III). But let each one see how he builds upon it. And elsewhere: “My little children,” he says, “for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV). And in another place: “Be renewed,” he says, “in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV). And again: “Therefore be imitators of God, as dearly beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us” (Eph. IV). And again: “Do not grieve,” he says, “the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption, etc.” (Eph. IV). For as many kinds of virtues as there are, so many good works and examples the holy teachers strive to impress upon the minds and conduct of the elect, so that they may be holy in both body and spirit, saying with the Apostle: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. V).

“Thus the blacksmith sits beside the anvil and observes the work of the iron; the vapor of the fire burns his flesh, and he is engaged in the heat of the furnace. The sound of the hammer renews his ear, and his eye is fixed upon the likeness of the vessel; he will give his heart to completing the works, and his vigilance will adorn them to perfection.” By the blacksmith the same figure as by the architect is expressed: namely, the order of holy preachers. Sitting beside the anvil—that is, beside the hard labor of the present life—they forge spiritual weapons, namely divine teachings, by writing and teaching, so that they may instruct their own people to fight bravely against the temptations of the ancient enemy, to avoid the perverse sects of heretics and philosophers, and to despise the threats of persecutors. The flesh of this smith—that is, his body—is burned by the vapor of the fire and the heat of the furnace when the tribulation and persecution of the world do not cease to weary him. The sound of the hammer renews his ears when the edicts of rulers continually bring the terror of torments to his senses. Yet he gives his heart to completing the work of his office, and he devotes the vigils of his diligence to bringing the vessels of elect souls to perfection in knowledge and virtue.

Hence the Apostle Paul, the foremost maker of these weapons, writes to certain of his hearers as follows: “Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having perfected everything, to stand. Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth, and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI).

The same Apostle shows elsewhere how these weapons are to be used in the labor of the present life, saying: “In everything let us present ourselves as God’s ministers: in great patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful, as unknown and yet known, as dying—and behold, we live; as chastised and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet making many rich; as having nothing and possessing everything” (II Cor. VI).

“Thus the potter sits at his work and turns the wheel with his feet; he is always occupied with his work, and all his labor is innumerable. With his arm he will shape the clay, and before his face he will bend his strength; he will give his heart to completing the smoothing, and his vigilance will cleanse the furnace.” And whom else does this potter signify except those holy preachers of whom we have spoken above? They worthily carry out the ministry of their rank through various offices and temper their teaching according to the character of their hearers: the wise must be admonished in one way, the foolish in another; the strong in one way, the weak in another; the young in one way, the old in another; men in one way, and women in another. They cultivate the Lord’s field with the plow of the Gospel; they feed the Lord’s sheep and animals with the nourishment of the word; they carve the seals of the new person in human hearts; through the ministry of their tongues they forge weapons of virtue; and by words and examples they shape and strengthen the fragile and weak, so that they may make them honorable vessels and most suitable for God’s service.

This potter turns the wheel with his feet in his work when, through the footsteps of good works, he turns the changeable conduct of the present life into an example for his followers. He takes care of those entrusted to him, so that they may devote themselves to good works; by his deeds he strengthens the activity of the weak and offers them examples of humility and gentleness. He directs the whole will of his heart toward this: that whatever is harsh in the character of his subjects may be softened by the example of his gentleness. To this end he devotes all his vigilance: in the furnace of the heart, melting all the activity of his disciples in the fire of love, he consolidates it with the flame of affection. For the whole work suffers loss if the bond of love does not unite it.

“All of them have hoped in their hands, and each one is wise in his craft.” That is, all the holy teachers of God’s Church are zealous for good works, and each of them, according to the distribution of the Holy Spirit, possesses a useful gift of sound doctrine. For “to one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

“Without all these things the city is not built. And they will neither inhabit nor walk about, nor will they leap into the assembly; judges will not sit upon the judgment seat, and they will not understand the covenant of judgment, nor make discipline and judgment public, nor will they be found in parables. But they will strengthen the creature of the age, and their prayer will be in the work of their craft, applying their soul and searching the law of the Most High.” Without all these things—that is, without the spiritual gifts—the city of the Church is not built. The faithful will not dwell in it, nor will the saints walk from virtue to virtue, nor will the entrance into the heavenly court be opened to them. Without these gifts, preachers of the Gospel do not properly occupy the seat of honor; they cannot possess an understanding of God’s law, or worthily bring forth the word of teaching, or properly perform any good work. Therefore these holy teachers, recognizing that by divine charism they have been appointed to the work of the word, strengthen the human creature, created by God for a temporal existence, in faith and good works through the aforementioned forms of the heavenly gift. Their prayer, together with their good works of virtue, will be acceptable to God, because they have given their souls for their brothers according to the commandment of the law of the Most High, who says to his disciples in the Gospel: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his soul for his friends” (John XIII). How greatly divine wisdom excels human wisdom, the following discourse shows.

## CHAPTER XVII. The praise of Wisdom, that is, of the Son of God, because through her all wisdom and prophecy exist, since she is always everywhere with the Father and the Holy Spirit in work and power

**(CHAP. XXXIX.)** “The wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients, and he will devote himself to the prophets. He will preserve the account of renowned men, and will enter together into the subtleties of parables. He will seek out hidden proverbs, and will dwell among concealed meanings. He will serve in the midst of great men, and will appear in the presence of a ruler. He will pass through the land of foreign nations, for he will test good and evil among human beings.” The ecclesiastical man seeks and diligently learns the wisdom of the patriarchs and prophets, and devotes himself to meditating upon their writings. He preserves the account of renowned men—that is, of the apostles and evangelists—by believing rightly and acting well. He also diligently examines the evangelical parables, and, seeking the mystical meaning in the divine sayings, investigates the hidden allegory in the historical narrative, so that he may know what the clear discourse contains of usefulness according to morality and the rule of faith, and what it signifies as spiritually understood according to allegory and anagoge.

Thus he “will serve in the midst of great men” when he conducts himself in a disciplined manner among catholic teachers and diligently ministers in ecclesiastical offices. He does this not to seek human praise but to please in the sight of the inner Observer, who presides over heaven and earth and rules all creatures. When he has been well instructed in the divine language through the diligence of catholic teachers and sufficiently trained in ecclesiastical discipline, he receives the office of teacher. Passing through foreign nations—which had indeed been alien to the faith of true Israel and to its religion—he preaches the word of God, testing where he may introduce the truth of sound faith, where he may find a devoted hearer, and where an ungrateful and contemptuous one.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Wisdom reveals that the Holy Spirit gives understanding to those who pray and, like rain, pours forth utterances by giving, suggesting, and teaching, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The Spirit intercedes for us,” etc.

“He will devote his heart to keeping watch at dawn for the Lord who made him, and he will pray in the presence of the Most High. He will open his mouth in prayer and will pray for his sins.” Wisdom clearly explains the character and life of a good teacher, who, preserving the rule of the catholic faith, continually preaches the Lord’s commandments both in word and by example. He therefore “devotes his heart to keeping watch at dawn for the Lord” who drives bodily sluggishness away from himself and commends the beginning and completion of all his actions to the Lord, so that he himself may direct his intention, words, and entire conduct according to his will. In pure prayer he continually begs for this: that the most merciful Judge grant him pardon for his sins and bestow upon him the excellence of good works.

[Col. 1039B] “For if the Lord, who is great, wills it, he will fill him with the Spirit of understanding. And he himself will pour forth the words of his wisdom like showers, and in prayer he will confess to the Lord. He himself will direct his counsel and discipline, and he will deliberate in his hidden matters. He will make known the discipline of his teaching, and he will glory in the law of the Lord’s covenant. Many will praise his wisdom, and it will not be blotted out forever. His memory will not depart, and his name will be sought from generation to generation.” The Lord gives his faithful suppliant and diligent seeker of heavenly wisdom the Spirit of understanding, so that he may know when, where, and how he ought to utter the divine words. He directs the counsel of his good will and the discipline of his upright conduct, and through inward inspiration he consoles and strengthens him, so that he may confidently preach the precepts of the divine covenants amid the adversities of the world. Hence many praise the wisdom of his teaching and preserve the memory of his good works from generation to generation. The following sentence bears witness that this grace is given not to others but to the teachers of the Gospel and the more glorious members of the body of Christ, being ministered from the head itself through the office of the individual members.

“The nations will declare his wisdom, and the Church will proclaim his praise.” Thus the catholic Church, preaching among all nations—indeed, throughout all nations—proclaims the praise of Christ: that the same Son of God, who is the power and wisdom of the Father, is the author of all teaching, prophecy, and every good virtue, and the distributor of spiritual graces, one and the only God reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages.

“If his name endures, he will leave more than a thousand; and if he rests, it will benefit him.” He wishes to show that a good teacher, who is approved both in his conduct and in his teaching, will win many and become the cause of salvation for many if he lives a longer life; but if he dies, he will pass into eternal rest, where the fitting reward for his merits will be repaid by the just Judge. Hence the teacher of the nations, confidently hoping for a sure reward after the struggle of his contest, says: “I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course; I have kept the faith. As for the rest, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will give me on that day” (II Tim. IV). And elsewhere: “According to my expectation and hope, I shall be put to shame in nothing, but with all confidence, as always, Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me, living is Christ, and dying is gain. But if living in the flesh is for me the fruit of labor, I do not know what I should choose. I am hard-pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (Phil. I).

“Still I will deliberate so that I may declare it, for I am filled with fury in speech.” The holy man, understanding through the impulse of the Spirit that God’s wisdom wishes to add still more to the earlier discourse, says that he is inwardly eager and burning and deliberating with himself so that he may declare what still remains concerning God’s wonders: namely, how good things will come to the good and evil things to the wicked according to the merit of their works. He stirs up his hearers so that, as long as they live, they may not cease to produce the fruit of good works, saying:

“Obey me, divine fruits of the waters, and bear fruit like roses planted beside a stream of waters.” In sacred Scripture, water sometimes signifies the Holy Spirit, sometimes sacred knowledge, sometimes wicked knowledge, sometimes tribulation, sometimes flowing peoples, and sometimes the minds of those who follow the faith. Through water the infusion of the Holy Spirit is signified. As it is said in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII). The Evangelist then added: “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

Again, holy wisdom is signified by water, as it is said: “He gave them to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Eccli. XV). Water can also designate wicked knowledge, as in Solomon, where the woman who bears the type of heresy entices with crafty persuasions, saying: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX). Waters are sometimes understood as tribulations, as it is said through the Psalmist: “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. LXVIII). Peoples are designated by water, as John says: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. XVII). Water also signifies not only the flow of peoples who stream onward but the minds of good people who follow the teachings of faith, as the prophet says: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. XXXII). And through the Psalmist it is said: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” (Ps. XXVIII).

What, then, are the waters designated in this passage except the hearts of the elect, who have already received through understanding the hearing of the heavenly voice? “Obey me,” he says, “divine fruits of the waters, and bear fruit like roses planted beside a stream of waters”—as though he were saying: Attend to my teaching, you abundant minds of the elect regenerated through baptism, and do not fear to produce the fruit of martyrdom throughout the course of mortal life, because from this you offer the Lord a most fragrant odor and an acceptable sacrifice. Hence it follows:

“Have the fragrance of sweetness like Lebanon. Bloom, flowers, like the lily, and give forth fragrance; put forth leaves in grace, and sing the hymn of praise; and bless God in his works.” The Prophet, recognizing that the passion of martyrdom is most pleasing to the Lord, says in the Psalter: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV).

And since, just as the rose signifies martyrdom, so the lily signifies chastity, to show that both are acceptable to our Creator, he says: “Bloom, flowers, like the lily”—as though he were openly saying: Give forth most joyful flowers together with the chastity of heavenly virtues, whose fragrance and leaves may be scattered throughout the whole world as an example to the souls of the faithful. For this is to sing the hymn and bless the Lord in his works: that the whole person—heart, mouth, and deed together—may render thanks to his Creator for his good gifts.

“Give magnificence to his name, and confess him with the voice of your lips.” He gives magnificence to the Lord’s name who, living rightly, duly preaches his power, so that those who hear his sound preaching and observe his good deeds may in return offer praises and fitting thanksgiving to the Lord. In accordance with that dominical commandment: “Let your light shine,” he says, “before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). Hence also in the Lord’s Prayer we pray to the Lord, saying: “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI), so that we may proclaim his holiness with our voice and demonstrate it to others through good examples. But to those who dishonor God by a wicked way of life and depraved conduct, Scripture says: “For through you the name of God is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. II). Their end will indeed be destruction, and their glory will be turned into the confusion of those who set their minds on earthly things. But let us see what Wisdom still says to the faithful.

[Col. 1041D] “With songs of the lips and with lyres—and thus you shall say in confession: ‘All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good.’” This is what we said above: that we should preach the Lord with our lips and by our deeds. Therefore the Prophet, exhorting the righteous to praise God, says in the psalm: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise is fitting for the upright. Confess to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery” (Ps. XXXII).

The lyre is a wooden instrument with a hollow cavity situated at the bottom of its belly; it sends the strings upward and speaks through very sweet sounds when struck. It received this name because it is struck with rapid repetition. Works that are extended from earthly things toward heavenly grace are rightly compared to it: for example, when we feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and so forth. Although these acts may appear carnal, they are nevertheless performed out of love for divinity. We also play the lyre when, in our sufferings or losses, we say securely and joyfully: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it has pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I).

The ten-stringed psaltery has its belly above, in reverse order to that of the lyre, and from it the resonant strings descend toward the lower part. The commandments of the Decalogue are suitably applied to it, because according to the form of this instrument we receive the Lord’s commands, which come from above. Consider also that it is the only musical instrument which, because of its excellence, is called ten-stringed; for we do not remember that this has been read of the lyre or of other instruments of this kind.

The ten-stringed psaltery, as the ancients said, also indicates this mystery: that we should refer three commandments to God, because he is Trinity. The first is: “You shall have no other gods before me.” The second: “You shall not make for yourself a graven image.” The third: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX). In this enumeration he joins the commandment concerning the Sabbath. The seven that follow, they said, pertain to love of neighbor: “Honor your father and your mother. You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not speak false witness against your neighbor; you shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife,” and so forth. Thus the complete power of the ten-stringed psaltery is shown to us as perfect and honorable.

We also sing with ten strings when, through the five bodily senses and the five spiritual senses, we conduct ourselves in a manner worthy of approval. In truth, the things we are saying are not placed outside us, as in the discipline of music; the psaltery is within us. Indeed, we ourselves are the instruments when, through the grace of the Lord, we sing in the quality of our deeds according to their likeness. This is also made clear by that example where he says: “In me are your vows, O God, which I shall repay in praises to you” (Ps. LV).

When he commands us to say in confession, “All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good,” he may intend, according to the historical sense, to show that all the works of the Lord which he made from the beginning were created good by the good Creator, in accordance with what is written in Genesis: “The Lord saw all that he had made, and behold, it was exceedingly good” (Gen. I). Or, according to the allegory: all the works that God the Father accomplished through Christ in the restoration of the human race are exceedingly good, because, as Paul testifies, “in him it pleased God the Father, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things, those in heaven and those on earth” (Eph. I). In him we have also been called by lot, predestined according to his purpose, who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory. It is therefore right that we should always and without ceasing speak praise and glory to him.

“In his word the water stood like a heap, and in the speech of his mouth, like reservoirs of water, [Col. 1043A] because at his command appeasement takes place, and there is no lessening in his salvation.”

For God the Father made all his works through his Word, that is, through his only-begotten Son. Hence it is written: “For he spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. XXXII).” The water stood in his word like a heap when he gathered the waters into one place and the dry land appeared, and made the firmament in the midst of the waters, and divided the waters from the waters. They could not flow back beyond their appointed order, but remain placed according to their proper measure and preserve their appointed course.

Or otherwise: the water stood like a heap when, at the passage of the children of Israel out of Egypt, the waters of the Red Sea were divided. Scripture relates that the waters were for them like a wall on their right and on their left (Exod. XIV). In the mystical [Col. 1043B] sense, however, the waters of persecutions, from which the Prophet prays to be saved, saying, “Save me, O God, for the waters have entered even to my soul (Ps. LXVIII),” are restrained by the word of the Lord and cannot proceed beyond his dispensation. For the Creator of all grants the help of his mercy to his faithful, and the hand of the Almighty is not powerless to bestow deliverance and salvation upon his elect. Those who trouble and those who are troubled are before God, and nothing is hidden from him. Hence it follows:

“All flesh’s works are before him, and nothing is hidden from his eyes. From age to age he looks, and nothing is wonderful in his sight.”

God’s foreknowledge therefore precedes all things, [Col. 1043C] and whatever takes place temporally in the world was present before him before all times. Hence nothing is new or wonderful in his sight, because he comprehends all things that were, that are, and that will be in a single act of vision, and they always remain present to him.

Thus the Apostle also wrote concerning the only-begotten Son: “For in Christ Jesus there is not ‘yes’ and ‘no,’ but ‘yes’ is in him (II Cor. I).” And again: “Jesus Christ,” he says, “yesterday and today, the same also for ever and ever (Heb. XIII).”

“There is no saying, ‘What is this?’ or, ‘What is that?’ For everything will be sought in its own time.”

He forbids us to be inquisitive and foolish investigators of hidden matters, which it is not fitting for us to know and which are still concealed from our understanding. For everything will be revealed in its own time, namely, “when, according to Paul’s statement, the Lord comes and brings to light the things hidden in darkness and reveals the counsels of hearts (I Cor. IV).”

Something similar is written in Ecclesiastes: “Do not speak rashly, nor let your heart be quick to utter a word before God (Eccles. V).” And again: “God made everything good in its time, and he delivered the world to their disputation, so that man may not discover the work which God has done from beginning to end, since all things pass in their own time, and there is a time for destroying and for building, for acquiring, for being silent, and for speaking,” and so forth.

We uselessly try to extend these statements, which concern the opposition of times, and we regard the brief labors of this life as perpetual, nor are we content, according to the Gospel, with the evil of the day, but think of nothing for tomorrow. For everything God made is good, because each work is good in its turn according to God’s arrangement. God also gave the world to human beings for habitation, so that they might enjoy the variations of the seasons and not inquire into the causes of natural things—how everything was created, or why he caused this or that to grow, remain, or change from the beginning of the world to its consummation.

“His blessing overflowed like a river; and as the cataclysm drenched the dry land, so his anger will inherit the nations that did not seek him.”

The blessing of God, therefore, and the gift of his grace abound over those who fear him, like a river of living water. Concerning this same water the Truth himself says: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will have within him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John IV).” He waters them abundantly, so that what the same Lord says may be fulfilled in them: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly (John VII).”

Conversely, the waters of heavenly vengeance drown those who proved unbelieving toward his words and did not seek his law in order to keep his commandments. Thus, in the days of Noah, when God’s worshipers were saved through the ark, the impious and unbelieving—who possessed neither the verdure of right faith nor that of good works—perished in the flood of the cataclysm (Gen. VII).

“How he turns the waters, and the earth is dried up, and his ways are made straight with their ways: so are offenses to sinners in his anger.”

Just as, after the outpouring of the flood, the waters went back and forth so that the dry land might again appear and the earth bring forth its fruits, so after the destruction of the impious the elect of God were given the opportunity to bring forth the fruits of good works.

When he says that the Lord’s ways are made straight with their ways, he shows that his retributions are dispensed according to their merits: “For the ways of the Lord are his judgments; the way of human beings is their works.” Hence the Lord, “who is just in all his ways and holy in all his works, and renders to each according to his works (Rom. II), guards all who love him and destroys all sinners (Ps. XCVIII).” Hence it follows:

“Good things were created for the good from the beginning; so for the wicked, good and evil.”

The good things of eternal life were prepared for the good from the beginning. Hence at the judgment the Lord will say to those who are at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt. XXV).”

For the wicked there are both good and evil: good, if they turn from their sins and practice repentance; evil, if they persist in their error and transgressions and neglect to repent. To them the most just Judge will say with terror at the final examination: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. XXV).” Thus the impious will go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life.

## CHAPTER XIX

Wisdom describes the foundations of human life, revealing the instruments of necessary things. [Col. 1045A]

“The beginning of what is necessary in human life is water, fire, iron, and salt, milk and bread made of fine flour, honey and a cluster of grapes, oil and clothing. All these things are for good to the holy; so also for the impious and sinners they will be turned into evil.”

Wisdom describes the foundations of human life, revealing the instruments of necessary things, in order to restrain human minds from the luxury of the world and the desire for illicit things. For bodily life is nourished chiefly by the elements of water and fire, while the material of iron has been provided for the tools of various crafts. So also salt has been appointed by divine providence for seasoning foods and restraining corruption.

Likewise, before the flood human beings fed on the produce of the earth and natural food, since the eating of meat had not yet been granted to them. But because all these things themselves were created by the good Creator for human use, those who use them temperately and, living according to the commandments, strive to exercise discretion in all things, find these good things to be a means of attaining future goods.

For those, however, who serve the enticements of the world and make the worst use of good things, they become a preparation for future punishment, since by illicitly abusing present goods they neglected to seek future goods.

“There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they have established their torments.”

He speaks of the evil spirits, whom the good Creator created good in the beginning. But through their pride—for they were the first inventors of it—they fell from heavenly joy into the greatest misery. After the human being, created by God, was led astray through the devil’s suggestion, he was justly handed over to the devil’s power, because, transgressing the commandments of his Lord, he consented to the perverse persuasions of the wicked enemy.

Thus almighty God—who is supremely good, indeed the supreme Good, and the best governor of all things—subjected proud human beings to the dominion of proud angels, so that, being corrected by them, they might learn how great is the difference between service to the true and most merciful Lord and service to the most cruel tyrant.

The demons themselves, the most savage torturers of human beings, establish their torments in their fury. At the future judgment they will undergo eternal punishments for their own wickedness and for the seduction of the human race. But because they will be especially hostile to the human race at the end of time, and will then chiefly plot its destruction—when Satan will be released from his prison and go out to deceive the nations that are upon the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and gather them for battle, and when the man of sin, the son of perdition, has been revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God—a man devoted to God foretells this in prophetic fashion, saying:

“At the time of consummation they will pour forth their strength, and they will appease the fury of the one who made them.”

For then, according to the Gospel testimony, there will be tribulations such as have not been from the beginning of the creation that God made until now, nor shall there be again: “And unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he will shorten the days.”

And rightly it is said, “They will confound the fury of him who made them (Matt. XXIV),” because in their iniquities and in the hostility they bear toward the Church of Christ, they do not fear to provoke heavenly vengeance against themselves.

## BOOK NINE

[Col. 1045]

## CHAPTER ONE

Wisdom relates that vengeance proceeds because of human sins: famine, war, drought, barrenness, and mortality.
