“Fire, hail, famine, and death—all these were created for vengeance. The teeth of wild beasts, scorpions, serpents, and the sword that takes vengeance, for the destruction of the impious. They will feast at his commands, and in their need they will be prepared upon the earth, and in their appointed times they will not pass over the word.” [Col. 1045D]

When the human being, created by God, obeyed his Creator, he suffered no adversity; everything went well for him, and he held all the animals of the earth under his dominion. But when, in his pride, he transgressed the commandment of his Creator, he was expelled from the happiness of paradise and fell into this valley of tears, where he was harassed by various afflictions.

There, laboring, he had barren earth, which brought forth thorns and thistles instead of grain, and he was beaten by the elements themselves. Thus, suffering the necessity of famine and afflicted by diseases, he finally received the loss of death.

Likewise, the animals and reptiles of the earth, which had previously been gentle and tame under him, after the commission of sin were turned against him into opposition and harm, because the sword of heavenly vengeance was exercising divine judgment upon the impious.

When it says, “They will feast at his commands, and in their need they will be prepared,” it indicates that, according to the heavenly sentence, the vengeance sent forth lays waste to sinners at the appropriate time. Something similar is read in the Song of Deuteronomy, spoken in the person of God: “I will sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand will execute judgment; I will repay judgment to my enemies and render recompense to those who hate me. I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword will devour flesh, from the blood of the slain and from the captivity, from the head of the princes of the enemies (Deut. XXXII).”

“Therefore from the beginning I was established and took counsel, and I reflected and left things written.”

This statement refers back to what was said above, where it is written: “There is no saying, ‘What is this?’ or, ‘What is that?’ For everything will be sought in its own time (Ecclus. XXXIX).”

The wise man saw that God’s judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable. He did not dare to put forward rashly, whether by speaking or writing, anything concerning them. Rather, while discussing God’s magnificent works with moderation, he left their cause and mode manifest in the divine counsel and decree. Hence it follows:

“All the works of the Lord are good, and every work will supply what is needed in its hour. There is no saying, ‘This is worse than that’; for everything will be approved in its own time.”

This passage agrees with what is read in Ecclesiastes: “Do not say, ‘What do you think is the reason that former times were better than they are now?’ For such a question is foolish (Eccles. VII).”

Therefore the former age is not to be preferred to the present, since God is the one Creator of both. Virtues make the days of the good person good; vices make them evil. Do not say, then, that the days under Moses or under Christ were better than those of the present. For even at that time there were many unbelievers, and their days became evil; while now many believers are received, concerning whom the Savior says: “Blessed are those who have not seen me and have believed (John XX).”

All the works of God are good, and the whole universe remains under the administration of its Creator. Therefore it is more appropriate for a human being to remain silent concerning God’s wondrous judgments than to speak, since the order of the whole world proceeds under his governance.

“And now, with every heart and mouth, praise together and bless the name of the Lord.”

This is the one counsel given to us: when we see God’s wonders and his magnificent works, we should not rashly presume to scrutinize them. [Col. 1047C] Rather, let us praise, bless, and glorify the excellent Creator with heart, mouth, and deed, because he alone is the one whom we are commanded to love with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. We must keep his commandments and remain daily in his service, so that from the good Lord, as useful servants, we may be crowned at the fury of judgment for right faith and good works.

(CHAP. XL.) “Great occupation has been created for all human beings, and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial into the mother of all.”

This is what is written elsewhere: “Human beings are born for labor (Job V).” Great occupation, therefore, has been created for all human beings, because the first-formed ancestor of the human race was created by God in such a way that he might devote himself to useful work, yet without any affliction or labor.

Hence we read in Genesis: “Therefore the Lord God took the human being and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it (Gen. II).” But after he fell into the guilt of transgression, he was immediately expelled by God’s just judgment from the happiness of paradise and cast down into this valley of miseries. There he and his offspring, working daily with labor, could scarcely and with difficulty find the fruit of their labor.

And rightly so: he who did not wish to keep the commandment while enjoying happiness was to endure the punishment of disobedience together with labor. The Lord said to him: “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labors you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return (Gen. III).”

Hence it is rightly said that “a heavy yoke was placed upon the children of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial into the mother of all”—that is, from the beginning of human birth, when the mother brought him forth in pains and troubles, until the day of death, when the dead flesh will be buried in the earth, which is the mother of all mortals.

Something similar is found in Job: “The life of human beings is a warfare upon the earth (Job VII),” or, as another translation has it, “The life of human beings is a temptation upon the earth.”

A human being could have possessed the flesh in peace if he had wished to possess it as it had been rightly created by its Author. But when he strove to rise up against his Creator, he immediately found within himself the insult of the flesh. Since punishment is propagated together with guilt from the beginning, we are born with the uncertain defect of weakness, and we bring with us, as it were, an enemy whom we must overcome with labor.

Human life itself is therefore a temptation, since from itself arises that by which it is destroyed. Even if it continually cuts away through virtue what it generates through weakness, it nevertheless continually generates through weakness what virtue must cut away. Thus human life is a temptation: although the perpetration of iniquity may already be restrained, in the very good works themselves it is darkened now by the memory of evil, now by the darkness of deception, now by the interruption of its purpose.

“Their thoughts and fears of heart, the invention of expectation, and the day of decision.”

He now begins to enumerate the evils that mortals endure because of their sins: various anxieties of mind, fears of heart, and inventions of diverse activity, by which they are afflicted during the days of expectation—for they await death—and finally, on the day of decision, receive the definite sentence of the Judge according to their merits.

And because the just Judge does not accept the person of anyone, but judges all according to the equity of his judgment, the following sentence proves this:

“And those seated upon a glorious throne, down to the one humbled in earth and ashes; from the one who wears hyacinth and carries a crown, down to the one covered with raw linen: fury, jealousy, tumult, agitation, and fear of death, abiding anger, and contention.” [Col. 1048D]

God does not accept the person of a human being, because the Lord is a just judge. Glory of person has no standing before him, nor does he accept a person’s status in the case of the poor; rather, he renders to each according to his works.

Fury and jealousy are displayed in vengeance, when sinners are tortured for their offenses in punishment. There are tumult and agitation, because “there is no order there, but perpetual horror dwells there (Job X).” There there are fear of death, abiding anger, and contention.

Truly there is fear of death where the continual burning of Gehenna’s fire is present. Anger abides and contention persists, because there is no peace there and no mitigation of pain.

The prophet Isaiah foretold long beforehand concerning the rejected and those handed over to punishment: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished”; and they will be “unto the satiety of vision for all flesh (Isa. LXVI).”

What more horrible thing can be said or imagined than to receive the wounds of condemnation and never bring the pains of those wounds to an end? In the torments of this life, fear contains pain, but pain does not contain fear, because dread no longer torments the mind once it has begun to suffer what it feared.

Those handed over to the fires of hell feel pain in their punishments, and in their pains they are struck by anguish, while fear continually assails them, so that they endure what they fear and again continually fear what they endure. Here the flame that burns also gives light; there the fire that torments obscures. Here fear is lost once what was feared has begun to be endured; there pain tears apart and terror constricts.

“And at the time of refreshment, in the bed, the sleep of death changes his knowledge: for a little while, as though nothing, in repose.”

He calls the time of refreshment the time of recompense, when the body has been placed in the bed of the grave and the soul is assigned to places of punishment for its sins.

Then the sleep of death changes his knowledge, because he feels very differently then about his actions than he felt before in this life. For everything that was previously hidden will then be revealed, and the things that were neglected or consigned to oblivion here will be brought back to his memory by the evil spirits.

Then what the Savior had foretold to Jerusalem with tears concerning its destruction will be fulfilled: “Days will come upon you,” he said, “and your enemies will surround you with a rampart on every side, and they will hem you in on every side, and they will cast you and your children who are within you down to the ground (Luke XIX).”

The evil spirits constrict the soul on every side when they repeat to it not only the sins of its deeds, but also of its speech and even of its thoughts, so that the soul which previously spread itself widely through many crimes may at last be constricted by them all in retribution.

Then the soul is cast down to the ground through the thought of its guilt, when the flesh—which it believed to be its life—is forced to return to dust. Then its children fall in death when the unlawful thoughts that now proceed from it are destroyed in the final vengeance of life.

Then “a little while, as though nothing, is in repose,” because although the dead and insensible flesh may seem for a time to rest from pains in the earth, the living soul nevertheless feels pain before the day of judgment; and on the day of resurrection it will receive again the very body through which it sinned, now immortal, and live in everlasting punishments.

In a terrifying manner, therefore, the reprobate will then have pain together with dread, and flame together with darkness, if indeed the weight of supreme justice is to be felt in this way by the condemned.

Because while they lived they did not fear to depart from the will of the Creator, eventually, in their destruction, the torments themselves will conflict with their own qualities, so that the sufferings by which they attack one another may increase, and because they arise in different forms, they may be felt in many ways.

For the punishments of hell torment those who are submerged in them beyond their strength, while extinguishing within them every support of life they preserve them, so that the end of life may punish them in such a way that torment always lives without end. It hastens toward an end through suffering and yet endures, failing without end.

For sinners devoted to the punishments of hell, death without death, an end without end, and the dead without dying are produced. Death lives, the end is always beginning, failure never ceases to fail; death destroys but does not extinguish. Pain torments but in no way drives away terror; flame burns but in no way dispels darkness.

As far as can be gathered from the knowledge of the present life, the punishments have no order, because they do not retain their own quality in every respect. Although the fire there does not shine for consolation, nevertheless, to torment them more, it shines to some degree. The reprobate will also see their companions in evil with whom they share the torments, illuminated by the flame—those whose love caused them to sin—so that those whom they had carnally loved against the commandments of the Creator may afflict them by their own destruction as an increase of their condemnation.

We also gather this from the Gospel, in which, as the Truth announces, that rich man who descended into the torments of eternal fire is described as remembering his five brothers. He asks Abraham to send Lazarus to instruct them, lest they should later come there and be tormented by the same punishment (Luke XVI).

If, then, to increase his own pain he remembered absent relatives, there is no doubt that shortly afterward he could also see those who were present, thereby increasing his punishment. How such things come upon sinners is made clear when it adds:

“And from him, as in dreams, as though in the day, there was a look; he was troubled in the vision of his heart, like one who has escaped on the day of battle. In the time of his salvation he rose up, and, wondering at no fear, with all flesh, from human being to beast. And sevenfold upon sinners.”

The wicked will be tortured in the punishment of Gehenna because in the time granted to them they did not foresee the need to cease sinning and devote themselves to good works. Deceived, as though in a dream, by worldly prosperity, they thought that the time was one of peace and not a day of battle, although this span of temporal life is granted to human beings solely so that, through a good struggle, they may hasten to the reward of eternal life.

In the time of his salvation, of which Paul says, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” he rose up—not to perform good works, but in pride. Burning with desire for earthly things, he fought without any fear of God against every class of human beings: against noble and ignoble, weak and powerful, rich and poor, men and women, so that by fraud or violence he might take from them whatever he could and claim it for himself.

Therefore sevenfold vengeance—that is, full and perfect vengeance—will come upon sinners of this kind, so that those who did not cease sinning during the time of bodily life, which runs through the number of seven days, may be tortured in punishments without any end or rest. Hence it follows:

“Besides these, death, blood, contention and the sword, oppressions, famine, destruction, and scourges: all these things were created against the unrighteous, and because of them the cataclysm came to be.”

Because of the sin committed, the just Judge appointed manifold punishment for human beings as vengeance, so that, corrected by it, they might repent of the evils they had committed and thereafter beware lest they fall into a similar ruin. But the sinner did not strive to amend his guilt; rather, he increased it. Therefore, because of his many sins and unspeakable crimes, it came about that the just Arbiter poured out the flood upon the whole world and wiped from the face of the earth the human being whom he had created, except for the eight souls preserved in the ark for the renewal of the race.

Hence it is written: “The Lord saw that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth and that every inclination of the thought of their heart was directed toward evil at all times. The Lord regretted that he had made the human being upon the earth, and he was touched with grief in the depths of his heart. ‘I will destroy,’ he said, ‘the human being whom I created from the face of the earth, from human being to animals, from reptiles to the birds of the sky; for I regret that I made them (Gen. VI).’”

But in comparison with the future punishment, everything that a human being suffers in the present is small, because present torments have an end, whereas future ones will end with no limit.

“For everything that is from the earth will return to the earth, and all waters will return to the sea.”

Something similar is read in Ecclesiastes: “All the torrents go to the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the torrents flow, there they return, so that they may flow again (Eccles. I).”

The Hebrews understand human beings to be signified metaphorically by the name of torrents and sea: they return to the earth from which they were taken. They are called torrents, not rivers, because water is swiftly poured in, while the earth is nevertheless not filled by the multitude of the dead.

But if we rise to higher things, the waters rightly return to the sea from which they also arose. And, unless I am mistaken, apart from an added qualification, “torrent” is nowhere used in a good sense; while the sea is insatiable, like the daughters of the leech in Proverbs (Prov. XXX). Hence it is said, “The sea is not filled (Eccles. I).”

“Every gift and iniquity will be destroyed, but faith will stand forever.”

All monetary gain, gathered through avarice, will perish from the present life together with its possessor, and his rapacity will have an end; but the punishment of his crime will endure perpetually.

The faith of the saints, however, which works through love and keeps the obligations of mercy, establishes and confirms the life of its Savior in the reward of eternal blessedness and fixes it in everlasting light.

“The resources of the wicked will dry up like a river, and they will resound like great thunder in the rain. In opening his hands he will rejoice; so transgressors will waste away at the consummation.”

The treasure of the wicked, therefore, is gathered inopportunely and indiscriminately, and so it is scattered powerfully and swiftly. Like thunder, it creates a storm in the rush of avarice, but it quickly collapses amid the very tumult.

Hence it is written: “The swords of the enemies have failed to the end, and you have destroyed their cities; their memory has perished with a noise (Ps. IX).”

They rejoice for a time in worldly prosperity when they open their hands to seize what belongs to others. But because they transgressed God’s commandment, which says, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” they will waste away at the consummation, when, empty of good works, they are plunged into hell for their sins.

“The descendants of the impious will not multiply branches, and unclean roots resound upon the summit of a rock. Greenery is upon every water, and at the bank of the river they will be plucked up before every blade of grass.”

According to the historical sense, we often see that the offspring of the impious will soon come to an end and will not advance through a long succession, especially where children imitate the iniquity of their parents.

Spiritually, however, the descendants of the impious do not multiply branches when the works of sinners do not acquire the fruit of heavenly reward, but deserve the destruction of Gehenna’s punishments.

In the rocky place—that is, in the hardness of their heart—where they do not possess the abundant soil of good devotion and perseverance by which they might bear the acceptable fruit of good works, they begin, after a temporary compunction, to display some likeness of virtues. But they do not possess a firm root of perseverance, because “they believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away (Luke VIII).”

They begin to sprout as though planted beside water, but when the storm of temptation fluctuates and the heat of persecution arises, they suddenly wither, and they are torn up before every blade of grass: “They become like the grass on rooftops, which withers before it is pulled up (Ps. CXXVIII).”

Hence it is written concerning such people in Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He will be like a tamarisk in the desert and will not see when good comes, but will dwell in dryness in the desert, in a salt land and uninhabited (Jer. XVII).”

Conversely, let us hear what he says concerning good and holy men: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence. He will be like a tree transplanted beside waters, sending its roots toward moisture; he will not fear when the heat comes, his leaf will be green, and in the time of drought he will not be anxious, nor will he ever cease to bear fruit (Jer. XVII).” Hence it follows:

“Grace is like a paradise in blessings, and mercy endures forever.”

The grace of God, therefore, which abounds in the faithful and elect of God, bears various kinds of virtues like a paradise. Hence the mercy that they merit for right faith and holy conduct endures forever, because they will receive eternal life in the heavenly kingdom for their good merits. “Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy.”

“The life of the self-sufficient worker will be made sweet, and in it you will find treasure (Matt. V).”

The life of the capable worker is rightly said to be made sweet to him, because an eternal reward will be repaid to him for his good and useful labor, and he will find the treasure of heavenly recompense, where he will enjoy perpetual joy and sweetness.

Something similar is said in Proverbs: “Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he eats little or much (Eccles. V).” Conversely, it is written concerning the idle: “Desires kill the lazy, for his hands refused to do anything (Prov. XXI).” And again: “Every lazy person will always be in poverty.”

“My son, the building of a city will establish the name; and above these things an undefiled woman will be reckoned.”

The construction of good works establishes the Christian name, because the person truly proves himself to be a Christian who preserves Christ’s commandments by believing rightly and acting well. Above these things, an undefiled woman—that is, a pure, holy, and unpolluted soul—is reckoned.

Among the merits of those who build, virginity therefore possesses the chief and highest reward: it is joined to the angels in heaven and follows the Lamb wherever he goes.

“Wine and music gladden the heart, and above both is love of wisdom. The flute and the psaltery make sweet melody, and above both is a sweet tongue.”

Wine and the art of music, with their instruments, naturally soothe and move the human spirit through the resonance of sound; but love of wisdom and a tongue teaching sweetly strengthen the understanding of the heart far more. Alternatively: evangelical doctrine and spiritual understanding are much better than the austerity of the Law and the historical tradition of the Old Testament, which the Jews followed with carnal understanding. Hence the bride says of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest perfumes” (Song I). By “wine” [Col. 1053C] he means the fervor of legal knowledge, but by “breasts” the rudiments of evangelical faith. Of these Paul says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). And again: “For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

The breasts of the bridegroom, therefore, are better than wine, because the rudiments of the New Testament regenerate all who are born again of water and the Spirit, and immediately make them fit to enter heavenly life—something that prolonged observance of the Law could in no way accomplish, not even in those who, inflamed by a taste of heavenly sweetness, could truthfully say to God: “And how excellent is your intoxicating cup!” The Apostle confirms this when he says: “For the law brought nothing to perfection” (Ps. XXII).

But if Christ’s breasts—that is, the beginnings of the Lord’s faith—are better [Col. 1053D] than the wine of the Law, how much more does Christ’s wine—that is, the perfection of evangelical doctrine—surpass all legal ceremonies! (Heb. VII.) If the sacraments of his incarnation lead to life, how greatly does the knowledge of his divinity glorify, and how greatly does its vision glorify!

The finest perfumes are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, with which Christ’s breasts are fragrant, because holy teachers—namely, ministers of evangelical milk—advance through the anointing of the Spirit in the love of the virtues. The perfumes with which prophets and priests were visibly anointed under the Law were indeed good, but those with which the apostles and their successors were invisibly anointed are the finest perfumes. Of these Paul says: “It is God who anointed us, who also sealed us and gave the pledge [Col. 1054A] of the Spirit in our hearts” (II Cor. I). And the apostle John says: “Let the anointing which you received from him remain in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you.” But just as his anointing teaches you about everything, so they are fragrant with the finest perfumes when they spread the reputation of their good conduct or preaching far and wide. As they themselves say: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place” (II Cor. II). The statements that follow in the same chapter refer to this.

“Your eye will desire grace and beauty, and above this, green plantings. A friend and companion at a suitable time, and above both, a woman with her husband. Brothers are for help in time of tribulation, and above them mercy will deliver. Gold and silver establish the foot, and above both, pleasing counsel. Wealth and food exalt the heart, and above these, the fear of the Lord. There is no diminution in the fear of the Lord, and there is no need to seek help in it. The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing, and above every glory they have covered him.”

The preaching of the Gospel, sown throughout the whole world by the faith of the nations and the greenness of good works, surpasses [Col. 1054B] the grace and beauty of the former people: the temple’s adornment, the variety of ritual, and the observance of feasts that the earlier people possessed under the Law. It surpasses “a friend and companion at a suitable time,” because the fellowship [Col. 1054C] of Christ and the Church surpasses in many ways the companionship of the fathers of old. The mercy of deliverance surpasses the help of a brother in time of tribulation, since the mercy of our redemption, bestowed through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ—by which he provided for the human race through his Passion—is greater than all the consolations of parents who, seeing the human fall, could sympathize but were unable to help.

Gold, silver, and riches given by the Lord in the time of the Law strengthened the hearts of the ancients, who served the Lord for earthly goods; to them it was said in that very Law: “If you are willing and obey, you shall eat the good things of the land.” But above all wealth and delights excels the fear of the Lord, as does the voluntary poverty of the Church of Christ, which renounces the world [Col. 1054D] and its pleasures, contends daily for the heavenly kingdom, and serves God. “For blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

There is therefore no diminution of virtues in the fear of the Lord, nor is there any need in it to seek earthly help, because the fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing for those who fear God, and heavenly glory covers them above every earthly splendor. Hence the Prophet says: “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for those who fear him lack nothing. The rich have become poor and hungry, but those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing” (Ps. XXXIII). And in the Gospel Truth himself says to the disciples: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or with what you shall be clothed; for your [Col. 1055A] heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI).

## CHAPTER II. On the misery of want and on the remembrance of death

“Son, do not be in want during your lifetime, for it is better to die than to be in want.”

Wisdom admonishes us not to waste through idleness the time granted to us, but rather to labor by believing rightly, diligently meditating on God’s law, and doing good works, so that here we may possess the wealth of virtues and in the future eternal life. It is better to depart quickly from the present life than to live here uselessly for a long time, because prolonged idleness will have a greater punishment in torment. Similar to this saying is what is written in the Gospel [Col. 1055B]: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea” (Matt. XVIII). “It is better for him” is said because it is much more advantageous to end bodily life by an innocent, though extremely harsh, temporal punishment than to earn the perpetual death of the soul by injuring a brother.

“A man who looks toward another man’s table—his life is not concerned with the thought of food, for he nourishes his soul with another’s provisions.”

It is foolish for anyone to neglect exercising himself in good works and to seek a reward from another’s labor, since the just Judge will repay each according to his works. Hence in the Gospel the foolish virgins, who carried empty vessels and begged oil from the prudent, saying, “Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out,” [Col. 1055C] received this answer from them: “Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you; go rather to the sellers and buy some for yourselves.” But while they went to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready entered with him into the marriage feast, and the door was shut (Matt. XXV). No further opportunity to enter was given to those who were not found ready for the wedding with the others.

“But a disciplined and instructed man will guard himself.”

He will therefore guard himself from being idle at the proper time, when he is permitted to work, lest, while time passes, he be consumed by want; rather, he will become rich through a manifold reward for good deeds. Such was the evangelical servant who received five talents from his master and, by trading, [Col. 1055D] multiplied his money and received from him a generous reward. But the one who idly preserved the talent entrusted to him paid penalties to his master for his idleness at the time of reckoning (Matt. XXV). Hence it also follows:

“In the mouth of the shameless man want will become sweet, and in his belly fire will burn.”

For whoever now prefers to languish in the idleness of sloth rather than benefit his neighbors by the word of instruction will, in the future punishment, burn and be tormented without remedy by the pains of repentance in his seething spirit.

## CHAPTER XLI

“O death, how bitter is the remembrance of you to a man who has peace in his possessions, to a tranquil man whose ways are straight among men, and who is [Col. 1056A] still strong enough to receive food!”

For one who relies on the prosperity of this world and the pursuit of riches, the death of the flesh—which is the end of bodily life—seems bitter, because he does not know how to love the joys of the future life. But because the world and its desire pass away, all who love it will mourn at its downfall. Hence in the Apocalypse, after the overthrow of spiritual Babylon, it is written that all the kings of the earth who fornicated with her and lived in luxury mourned over her, saying: “Woe, woe, the great city, in which all who had ships at sea became rich through her wealth, for in one hour she has been made desolate” (Rev. XVIII). But let us hear what will follow for the poor of Christ and the heirs of the age to come.

[Col. 1056B] “O death, how good is your judgment to a needy man; to one whose strength is diminished, whose age has failed; to one who is concerned about everything; and to one who is incredulous and loses patience!”

It is therefore good for the worshipers of Christ to meditate on the judgment of the present death, since through it those who are poor and needy in earthly things pass into eternal life, having abandoned everything for Christ. Their strength is diminished because, thinking humbly, they rely not on their own strength but on the power of the Savior; their age has failed because they persevere in an upright way of life. Of one of them it is written in Genesis: “The days of Abraham’s life were one hundred and seventy-five years. Then he died, failing in old age, at a good age and advanced in years, and full of days [Col. 1056C]” (Gen. XXV).

“To whom everything is a concern,” he says: namely, the concern that they preserve all God’s commandments, or that they hasten, as far as they can, to benefit their neighbors. Of this Paul says: “My daily burden is my concern for all the churches.” They are “incredulous” because they do not consent to the error and faithlessness of heretics. They lose the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God, so that they may truly be wise, drawing from that wisdom “which is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” Concerning this the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “If anyone among you seems to be wise, let him become a fool so that he may be wise” (I Cor. I).

And because the death of the flesh is not to be feared by Christ’s faithful, but rather through it one must pass into the rest of life, he immediately adds:

[Col. 1056D] “Do not fear the judgment of death. Remember what came before you and what is to come upon you: this is the judgment from the Lord upon all flesh. And what will come upon you according to the good pleasure of the Most High? Whether the years are ten, one hundred, or one thousand. For there is no accusation of life in hell.”

The judgment of temporal death is not to be feared; rather, he is to be feared who has power over life and death, the key of the abyss and dominion over hell. Of him it is written: “The Lord puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back” (I Sam. II). Hence Truth himself says to his disciples: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body [Col. 1057A] in Gehenna” (Matt. X).

The death of the present life, which the condition of the flesh deserved on account of the sin of the first man, when the divine sentence said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III), is common to every human being, and no one can escape it, even if he lives one hundred or one thousand years, or longer. Hence it is written in Ecclesiastes: “No one lives forever, nor has anyone confidence in this matter” (Eccl. IX). Hence the Psalmist also says: “Who is the man who lives and will not see death, or who will save his soul from the hand of the underworld?” (Ps. VI).

But this death will one day have an end, when the dead rise incorruptible, and those who sleep in the dust of the earth awake—some to eternal life, others to disgrace, to see forever. For, according to the judgment of Truth, “the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs [Col. 1057B] will hear his voice; and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

When he says, “There is no accusation of life in hell,” he shows that in the place of punishments there is no confession of glory, but only the weeping of sorrowful souls. Hence the Prophet says to the Lord himself: “For there is no one in death who remembers you; but in the underworld, who will confess to you?” (Ps. XXXIII). The prison of the underworld, therefore, has been assigned to the wicked, so that they may groan there forever—not to the good, so that they may sing praises there, as is demonstrated in what follows.

“Sons of abominations become sons of sinners, and those who dwell beside the houses of the ungodly.”

The sons of sinners are therefore abominable [Col. 1057C] to the Lord—not because they were born of sinful parents, since many righteous men had wicked fathers, as Hezekiah had Ahaz and Josiah had Jotham, but because they imitated the disgraceful deeds of their wicked fathers. Hence he adds: “Those who dwell beside the houses of the ungodly,” that is, they followed the crimes of their reprobate parents, who lived criminally. Therefore they too will be deprived of the inheritance of the heavenly homeland and will remain in perpetual shame, as the following saying shows.

“The inheritance of sinful sons will perish, and with their offspring there will be continual disgrace.”

Hence also in Psalm Fifty-First, which the Prophet uttered against the head of all the wicked, namely the Antichrist, after enumerating his crimes, it immediately adds: [Col. 1057D] “Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from his dwelling, and your root from the land of the living, etc.” (Ps. LI).

“Children complain of an ungodly father, because on his account they are in disgrace.”

Whoever raises his children well and teaches them to live in a disciplined manner will not lose the reward of his upbringing. But whoever leads them astray by wicked teaching or perverse example will suffer the loss of their destruction. We can also understand spiritually by “the children of sinners” their works, which they wickedly produced from an evil will; for these works their author, examined in the inquiry of the just Judge, will be handed over to everlasting death. Hence it is written: “The Lord examines the just and the wicked, but whoever loves [Col. 1058A] iniquity hates his own soul. He will rain snares upon sinners; fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms will be the portion of their cup” (Ps. X).

“Woe to you, ungodly men, who have abandoned the law of the Most High Lord! If you are born, you will be born under a curse; and if you die, your portion will be under a curse.”

Every human being, born from the seed of a man and a woman, is born with sins; and unless he is reborn through Christ’s grace and freed from that curse, he will not be saved. Hence the Psalmist says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. L). And again: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (ibid.).

But the ungodly who do not deserve to be freed through Christ’s grace from the ancient curse in which they were born, [Col. 1058B] adding their own crimes, go after the end of this life into everlasting cursing. To them it will be said at the future judgment: “Go, you accursed, into the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

“All things that are from the earth will return to the earth. So the ungodly, from the curse, go into destruction.”

This saying agrees with what came before, where he discusses temporal death. Just as the human being, created according to the flesh from the earth, must on account of the sin of the first man again be reduced to the dust of the earth—although through Christ’s grace he will be restored to incorruption on the day of judgment—so the ungodly, cursed on account of their sins, will then go with body and soul into everlasting destruction, “where their worm does not die and the fire [Col. 1058C] is not extinguished,” because they did not deserve to find redemption with Christ among the elect.

“The mourning of men is in their bodies, but the name of the ungodly will be erased.”

Here he uses “men” for the wise, who make good use of reason in their souls and submit themselves obediently to the divine commandments. These have mourning only in the present life; afterward they will rejoice in everlasting joy. Hence it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V).

But the name of the ungodly will be erased, because, plunged into the underworld, they will be handed over to eternal forgetfulness. To them the Judge will say: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity. Truly I tell you, I never knew you” (Ps. VI).

“Take care of a good name, for this will [Col. 1058D] remain with you more than a thousand great and precious treasures.”

He will have a good name who lives holily and religiously. The acquisition of this name—that is, the acquisition of right faith and sacred virtues—is better than all earthly possessions and all the treasures of the present age. Similar to this is what is read in Proverbs: “A good name is better than great riches; good favor is above gold and silver” (Prov. XV).

He says “a good name,” not one bestowed by the speech of the ignorant crowd, but one praised by the testimony of the faithful, even if they are few. For he did not reject a good name, but sought to be praised only by the good, who said: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I).

A good name, therefore, is [Col. 1059A] the name of religion, which is rightly preferred to worldly riches. Even if someone were to gain the whole world, he would rightly despise it merely so that his name might be written in heaven and his memory be fixed forever among holy men. “Good favor is above silver and gold”: this signifies the favor received when someone is praised by the good for a good work; indeed, the Father who is in heaven is glorified for the gifts of merits bestowed upon him.

“The number of the days of a good life is good, but a good name will remain forever.”

The number of the days of a good life will be good because the fullness of eternal blessedness will crown it. Thus the Prophet, speaking in the person of the Lord about one who hopes in God, testifies in the Psalm: “I will deliver him and glorify him; I will fill him with length [Col. 1059B] of days and show him my salvation” (Ps. XC).

But a good name will remain forever because the reward of good merit will remain eternally with the saints in the contemplation of God. How this can happen he makes clear by adding:

“Preserve discipline in peace, children.”

He preserves discipline in peace who strives to live in holiness and righteousness according to the two commandments of charity. Of this Paul writes to the Hebrews: “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII).

And because it is not enough for anyone to live well by himself if he does not strive, as far as he can, to benefit his neighbors through sound teaching, it immediately follows:

“For what use are hidden wisdom and a concealed treasure [Col. 1059C] in either case?”

Those who, although they are able to preach usefully, nevertheless shrink from doing so through sloth or excessive humility must be admonished to infer from the lesser consideration how greatly they offend in greater matters. If they were to hide from needy neighbors the money they possessed, they would undoubtedly be responsible for their calamity. Let them therefore consider by what guilt they are bound when, by withholding the word of preaching from sinful brothers, they hide the remedies of life from dying minds.

If hunger were wearing down a population and they themselves stored away hidden grain, they would undoubtedly be authors of death. Let them therefore consider with what punishment they should be chastised when souls perish from hunger for the word and they do not distribute the bread of the grace they have received. Hence Solomon rightly says [Col. 1059D]: “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. XI).

To hide grain is to keep within oneself the words of holy preaching. Such a person will be cursed among the peoples because, through the guilt of silence alone, he is condemned for the punishment of many whom he could have corrected.

“For the man who hides his foolishness is better than the man who hides his wisdom.”

He hides his foolishness who avoids empty talk and refuses to open his mouth in perverse teaching, because, according to Solomon: “The man who speaks with flattering and deceitful words to his friend spreads a net for his steps” (Prov. XXIX). It is therefore better for such a person to remain silent than to deceive another with his glib tongue.

But the one who hides his wisdom [Col. 1060A] does great harm, because when he neglects to spend in good works for his neighbors the talent of intelligence entrusted to him by God for multiplication, he delivers himself into the snare of destruction. When he conceals the word of preaching within himself, let him hear the divine sentences against him with terror, so that fear may drive pride from his heart.

Let the learned and wise hear that the man who refused to distribute his talent lost it together with the sentence of condemnation. Let them hear that Paul believed himself clean from the blood of his neighbors precisely because he did not spare their vices when they needed correction, saying: “I testify to you this day that I am pure from the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts XXVI).

Let them hear that John is admonished by an angelic voice [Col. 1060B] when it is said: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. XXII). Thus, whoever hears the inward voice speaking to him should also draw others by crying out to the place toward which he himself is being carried, lest, although summoned, he find the doors closed if he approaches the one who calls while empty.

Let them hear that Isaiah, because he was silent concerning the ministry of the word, rebuked himself in a loud voice of repentance after being illumined by heavenly light, saying: “Woe is me, because I was silent” (Isa. XLII).

Let them hear that through Solomon an increase of the knowledge of preaching is promised to the one who is not held back by the fault of sluggishness in what he has already obtained. For he says: “The soul that blesses will be made rich, and whoever refreshes others will himself be refreshed” (Prov. XI). Whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives the richness of inward strengthening; and while he does not cease to intoxicate the minds [Col. 1060C] of his hearers with the wine of eloquence, he grows intoxicated and increases through the drink of an abundant gift.

“Nevertheless, return to the things that proceed from my mouth, for it is not good to observe every irreverence.”

Because he had first declared that a good life and a good name are useful to those who possess them, and afterward reproved those who, possessing knowledge of God’s law, are unwilling to devote the diligence of preaching to their neighbors, he now urges them, admonished by his words, to return to the work of teaching, because it is not good to be irreverent or disobedient toward one’s teachers.

Hence above the author of this work also beseeches the Lord in his reasoning not to hand him over to an irreverent and senseless soul. But because not everything that is said [Col. 1060D] pleases all minds that are established in the faith, he does not omit this point either, saying:

“And not everything pleases everyone rightly in faith.”

The same exhortation is not suitable to everyone, because not everyone is constrained by the same quality of character. Often what benefits one harms another: herbs that nourish some animals kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but excites puppies; a medicine that diminishes one person’s illness adds strength to another; and bread that strengthens the life of the robust kills the small.

The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that it may correspond to each person’s needs and yet never depart from the art of common edification. Since he first taught that every irreverence is not good, he now shows how all vices must be avoided through reverence.

[Col. 1061A]

## CHAPTER III. All vices must be avoided, but help must be sought from God, by whom human steps are directed so that iniquity may not rule over them

“Be ashamed before your father and mother because of fornication; before the ruler and the powerful because of lying; before the prince and the judge because of wrongdoing; before the synagogue and the people because of iniquity; before your companion and friend because of injustice; and, in the place where you dwell, because of theft; because of the truth of God and the covenant; because of reclining at banquets; and because of obscuring what is given and received; before those who greet you, because of silence; because of looking upon [Col. 1061B] a fornicating woman; and because of turning your face away from a kinsman.”

In the tropological sense these words instruct us to avoid vices and devote ourselves to virtues, because one who rejects better things and chooses worse is greatly deserving of shame, and everlasting shame will follow him on account of them.

In a deeper sense, before mother Church and God the Father the person is ashamed of fornication who follows the idolatry of the Gentiles or the folly of heretics. The soul that abandons fellowship with God and follows the error of the perverse commits spiritual fornication, and therefore will be condemned.

He is ashamed before the ruler and the powerful because of lying when he is convicted before the eyes of the divine majesty of having violated the pledge he made when he received baptism. Likewise, before Christ the Prince and Judge he will be confounded at the future [Col. 1061C] judgment if he has not taken care to observe or cleanse himself from sin.

He is also rebuked by the synagogue and the people for iniquity when, before the angels of God and the assembly of the saints, he is accused of committing various crimes. Similarly, he is reproved by his companion and friend for injustice when, at the future judgment, the angels sent forth will gather all scandals from God’s Church, place the good fish in their vessels, and throw the bad outside (Matt. XIII).

Then also he will be revealed who lived deceitfully against the truth and covenant of the Lord in the tabernacle of the present Church, committed theft by fraud, and paid no attention to the apostolic authority, which commanded: “Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may [Col. 1061D] have something to give to the one in need” (Eph. IV).

Nor will the one who disgracefully gave himself over to feasting and drunkenness then appear free from shame. Likewise, neither will the one who through greed seized from others what he ought not to have taken, nor the one who through stinginess failed to give to his neighbors what he had received from God to be possessed in common with all others. Nor will the one be free from guilt who wickedly hid the talent of the word and neglected to spend it for his neighbors, turned his face away from kinsmen and Catholic people, and mingled with polluted fornicators and utterly wicked heretics.

“Do not turn your face away from your neighbor, and do not take away your father and fail to restore.”

He turns his face away from his neighbor who disdainfully refuses to provide merciful [Col. 1062A] assistance for his needs. Hence Solomon says: “Whoever hardens his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard” (Prov. XXI). Therefore the elder Tobias instructed his son in works of mercy, saying: “Give alms from your possessions, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; for then it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you” (Tob. IV).

For whoever takes away part of another’s money and does not restore it to him sins in the same way, since God abhors all greed and deceit. Hence in the Law the Lord commanded: “You shall not commit injustice in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure” (Lev. XIX). And again: “You shall not steal; you shall not lie; nor shall anyone deceive his neighbor” (ibid.).

In Ezekiel [Col. 1062B] the prophet the Lord also praises the just man among his other virtues: that he did not grieve another, returned a pledge to its debtor, took nothing by force, gave his bread to the hungry, covered the naked with clothing, lent nothing at interest, and took nothing more than he had given (Ezek. XXII). “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts XX).

“Do not look upon another man’s wife, nor examine his maidservant, nor stand beside his bed.”

Another man’s wife is also the perverse doctrine of a heretic, who is alien in faith and religion from fellowship with God and the society of the faithful. Wisdom therefore forbids us to look upon her—that is, to love her eloquence. His maidservant is his carnal desire, which ought to have been subjected to the authority of the spirit, according to what the Lord said to Cain [Col. 1062C]: “Its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it” (Gen. IV); but in the conduct of the reprobate it itself, in reverse order, rules.

For this reason we are forbidden to examine this maidservant—that is, to submit to her suggestions—and to stand beside her bed, namely, to recline in her pleasures. Hence Wisdom in Proverbs rebukes this woman luxuriating in her bedchamber and enticing others to intercourse with her, and forbids us to rely on her ways, saying: “Now therefore, son, hear me and attend to the words of my mouth, lest your mind be drawn into her ways, nor be deceived by her paths. For she has cast down many wounded, and the strongest have been slain by her; her house is the way to the underworld, penetrating into the inner chambers of death” (Prov. VI).

“Before friends, refrain from reproachful speech.”

The omitted verb [Col. 1062D] is “refrain,” because it is not fitting to plot anything deceitful against a friend, since Scripture says: “Do not devise evil against your friend, when he trusts in you” (Prov. III).

“And when you have given, do not reproach.”

A gift is spoiled by the one who wounds his neighbor with reproach. It is therefore better to imitate that generous giver of whom the apostle James wrote: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (Jas. I). He deliberately says, “who gives generously to all,” so that no one conscious of his own frailty might doubt that he could approach as a petitioner to receive, but rather everyone might remember that the Lord hears the desire of the poor.

And as the same author says elsewhere [Col. 1063A]: “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small with the great” (Ps. CXIII). “And does not reproach,” because he despises no one and provokes no one; rather, mercifully cherishing all, he draws them to his love—he “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER IV. Reproachful speech must be removed from friendships
### Chapter XLII

“Do not utter a double speech upon hearing of a hidden utterance, and you will truly be without shame, and will find favor in the sight of all human beings.” By this sentence he forbids bringing forth from the secrecy of the heart both a good and an evil utterance at once, because it is written: “The words of a double-tongued person are as simple things, and they reach even to the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. XVIII). Hence the Apostle Paul admonishes us, saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but if there is any good speech for edification, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. IV). For this reason James says: “From the same mouth proceeds blessing and cursing. My brothers, this ought not to be so. Does a fountain pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (Jas. III). Just as sweet and bitter water cannot simultaneously boil forth from one spring’s channel, and even if they are mixed in a vessel or cistern, the sweet immediately becomes bitter through the bitter, while the bitter, by the admixture of the sweet, does not know how to be changed into sweetness, so blessing and cursing can in no way coexist in one mouth. Whoever is accustomed to bless God in prayer, or in preaching his word, yet does not refrain from cursing human beings, plainly consumes the sweetness of his blessing with the bitterness of his cursing. “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump, and praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (1 Cor. V).

Finally, if you make a tube with two mouths—one through which water enters and a single one through which it exits—and pour bitter water into one and sweet water into the other, then, without any doubt, when both reach the one outlet, the mixture will appear not sweet but bitter; for, clearly, when they are mixed, sweet is much more readily turned into bitter than bitter into sweet. From this example it is gathered that evil conversations, as the Apostle testifies, corrupt good habits (1 Cor. XV), and likewise corrupt good utterances.

Alternatively: “He doubles an utterance upon hearing of the revelation of a hidden utterance” who dares to stain the mystical words of the divine Law with the speech of a perverse doctrine, and by corrupting it turns the simple truth of the Catholic faith into varied error. Scripture makes clear how harmful this is, saying: “Evil thoughts are an abomination to the Lord, and pure speech, most beautiful, shall be established by him” (Prov. XV). The Lord therefore abhors the thoughts and words of heretics; indeed, he detests all sects opposed to piety. The pure speech of right faith will be established by him when, at the judgment, he will render fitting rewards not only for all deeds but also for all words.

He abhorred the evil thoughts of those who said: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” (Luke V). And he affirmed that the pure speech of the one who said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI), was most beautiful, when he replied: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). Therefore, the person who chooses above all else the rule of the Catholic faith in speech, and who persists firmly on the path of truth by teaching rightly and acting well, will be without shame and will have favor before every human being.

“Do not be put to shame because of all these things.” This testimony refers to those matters he had described above as to be avoided, and to those which he subsequently enumerated in this same chapter as likewise to be guarded against. Whoever carefully observes himself concerning these things will remain without shame both here and in the future.

“And do not show partiality so as to transgress against the law of the Most High and the covenant, or to justify the impious in judgment.” For it is written in the Law, when the Lord commands and says: “You shall appoint judges and magistrates in all your gates, which the Lord your God gives you throughout your tribes, so that they may judge the people with righteous judgment and not incline to either side. You shall not show partiality or accept gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and change the words of the righteous. You shall pursue with justice what is just” (Deut. XVI).

From this it is demonstrated how displeasing it is to the Lord, and how grave a sin it is, to show partiality in judgment, whether by condemning the righteous and justifying the impious because of fear or because of human favor. Hence Solomon says: “To recognize a person’s face in judgment is not good. Those who say to the wicked, ‘You are righteous,’ will be cursed by the peoples, and the tribes will detest them. Those who rebuke him will be praised, and blessing will come upon them” (Prov. XXIV).

Earlier he taught the king to fear, saying: “Fear the Lord, my son, and the king”; now he forbids recognizing a person’s face in judgment. From this it follows that subjects ought to offer their princes the temporal obedience that is owed to them in such a way that they never, out of regard for their reverence or fear, stray from the way of truth.

“Concerning the speech of companions and travelers, and concerning the giving of friends’ inheritance.” The implied instruction is: “Do not be put to shame.” Whoever takes care, before acquaintances and strangers, one’s own and others, not to speak false or foolish words, and not to contrive any evil deceitfully against a friend or any human being, will not suffer the punishment of the future judgment. Hence Paul teaches the ministers of Christ to give no one any occasion of offense, so that their ministry may not be reviled; rather, they should be sincere and without offense for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness to the glory and praise of God, doing good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith (2 Cor. VI).

“Concerning equality of the balance and weights, and concerning the acquisition of many things and of few things; concerning the corruption of buying and of merchants, and concerning the severe discipline of children.” To all these matters the answer is: “Do not be put to shame.” Every Christian and faithful servant of God must attend to this: in all things, let him follow the equity of truth and the rule of justice; let him preserve equality of balance and weights; and whatever he gains, whether much or little, let him do so not without justice; let him commit no fraud in buying or trading; and let him bring up those subject to him not with excessive but with measured discipline.

That hypocrisy and deceit are greatly displeasing to the Lord, Scripture makes clear, saying: “A deceitful balance is an abomination to the Lord, but an equal weight is his will.” A deceitful balance is held not only in the measuring of money but also in judicial discernment. Whoever hears the case of a poor person one way, that of a powerful person another way, that of a companion one way, and that of a stranger another way, plainly weighs with an unjust balance. Likewise, the person who judges his own good deeds better than those of his neighbors, and his own faults lighter than those of others, weighs with a deceitful scale. So too does the person who lays unbearable burdens on human shoulders but himself does not wish to touch them with even one finger; and likewise the person who does good publicly and evil secretly is abhorred by the Lord because of the iniquity of a deceitful scale. But the person who acts sincerely in all things, who distinguishes case from case with an equal balance, accords with the will and action of the just judge.

“To the worst slave, let his side bleed.” Above he described with what discipline slaves should be treated, when he commanded that torture and fetters be imposed on the malicious slave, but that the kindly slave be treated as a brother. Now also, when he advises that the sides of the worst slave should bleed, he implies that one who cannot be corrected by words should be restrained by blows.

In a deeper sense, however, this slave may be understood not according to the condition of his birth but according to the disposition of his mind, because “God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts X), and “whether slaves or free, we are one in Christ” (1 Cor. XII). Whoever serves vices and does not wish to be free from sins is deservedly chastised by harsh discipline. Of such a slave it is written: “A servant cannot be instructed by words” (Prov. XXIX). And in the Gospel the Truth himself says: “A slave does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains forever” (John VIII).

“Above a wicked woman, a good sign.” This is that woman whom he very often mentions in this book: the fornicating and adulterous woman, shameless and opposed to every good thing. Above her there is a good sign—namely, the sign of the Catholic faith, by which her perversity is crushed and her impiety overcome.

“Where there are many hands, close up; and whatever you hand over, count and weigh it. Describe everything given and received.” He does not teach by this that we should be sparing toward our needy neighbors in giving what is necessary. Rather, he instructs us mystically that where there are diverse intentions among those seeking spiritual gain, the administration of those who distribute should be cautious and prudent. Some seek a word from the teacher’s mouth with the desire to test, others with the desire to learn; but not everything is to be entrusted to everyone. For the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before pigs” (Matt. VII).

The distributor of sacred wealth must carefully attend to what he gives and to whom he gives it, and to how it is given and how it is received. “There is a time for everything under heaven: a time to be silent and a time to speak” (Eccl. III).

### Chapter V. On the discipline of the senseless and the foolish

“On the discipline of the senseless and the foolish, and on elders who are judged by adolescents. And you will be instructed in all things, and approved in the sight of all the living.” These words refer to what came before, where he commanded that whatever one handed over should be carefully counted and weighed, and that everything given and received should be recorded.

Whoever therefore rebukes offenders with suitable discipline, and, considering the quality of each person, applies to that person an appropriate manner of correction, gives a sure indication of his own instruction and shows himself to be an approved teacher in the sight of all men—that is, of holy and virtuous people. Nor should youthful age be despised in a teacher if he is found to possess soundness of mind and an exemplary life, because we read that Samuel and Daniel, while boys, judged elders (1 Kings VII; Dan. XIII).

Hence Paul also writes to Timothy: “Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity. Do not, he says, look to your age. Rather, apply yourself diligently so that you may say and do those things which ought to be said and done” (1 Tim. IV). Let them conduct themselves according to what is fitting, so that they may possess that charity which is directed toward all; so that they may be firm in faith; and so that they may devote themselves diligently to chastity. In this way you yourself should present yourself as a model to the faithful, for whom you rule your life, instructing them how it is fitting for them to conduct themselves, so that from your own deeds you may offer them testimony concerning your life.

“A daughter of a father is hidden; her vigilance and concern will take away his sleep, lest perhaps in her youth she become an adulteress, and, having lived with a husband, become hateful. Lest she be defiled in her virginity, and be found pregnant in her father’s house; lest perhaps, having lived with a husband, she transgress, or indeed become barren.”

Historically, he teaches parents to exercise proper care for their offspring, bringing them up with discipline, lest they become wanton and dissolute in tender age, pollute themselves with lust and the enticements of pleasures, and consequently become hateful to others. Concerning this he also argued carefully above and gave instructions to the one raising the child, saying: “Do not give power to your son in his youth, and do not disregard his thoughts. Bend his neck in his youth, and strike his sides while he is a child, lest you be put to shame because of his disgrace and suffer the greatest anguish of soul” (Eccli. XXX).

Spiritually, however, the father’s daughter is the faithful man’s soul, or the Church of the believing people, entrusted to an energetic teacher. Caring for her, he is ever watchful and shrewd in all things, lest, while she is still inexperienced in faith and knowledge, she become an adulteress through the craft of heretics, and thus become hateful to her lawful husband to whom she was betrothed, according to the Apostle’s words: “I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God. For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. XI).

He must also take care lest, placed under the nurture of her teacher, she be found pregnant with error, and, while dwelling in her husband’s house, transgress his law, thereby becoming barren in good works, so that she cannot deservedly say to him: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table. And may you see your children’s children, peace upon Israel” (Ps. CXXVII).

“Strengthen your watch over a wanton daughter, lest she cause you to come into reproach before enemies, into slander in the city and rejection by the people, and make you ashamed in the multitude of the people.” A wanton person therefore requires the teacher’s diligent supervision, because, if left to her own will, she brings shame upon her teacher. She makes him blush before the multitude of the people when she is found disgraceful and useless both at home and abroad, occupied with slander and mingling with the common crowd in shameful deeds.

Hence it is written: “A foolish son is born to his own disgrace; nor will the father rejoice in a fool. An angry father is a foolish son, and a sorrow to the mother who bore him.” By contrast, the father of the righteous rejoices with joy, having begotten a wise son, and will be glad in him.

“Do not fix your attention on every person’s appearance, and do not remain among women. For from clothing the moth proceeds, and from a woman comes a man’s iniquity.” Wisdom instructs us how we can preserve purity of heart and chastity of body: namely, by not gazing with a lustful mind upon the face of a shameless person, and by withdrawing our bodily presence from the company of women. Just as a moth, remaining for a long time in one place, eats away a garment, so prolonged thought in a lustful mind makes the human spirit grow weak from its strength.

Hence someone elegantly says: “The person whose face you frequently regard ministers danger to you.” For immodest eyes do not know how to contemplate the beauty of the soul, but only that of bodies.

“Better is a man’s iniquity than a woman doing good, and a woman bringing shame into disgrace.” In sacred speech, “woman” is used either for sex or for weakness. For sex, as it is written: “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. IV). For weakness, as it is read in Job: “A man born of woman, living for a short time” (Job IV).

Here too the wise man says: “Better is a man’s iniquity than a woman doing good.” For any strong and discerning person is called a man, whereas a woman signifies a weak or undiscerning mind. It often happens that even a discerning person suddenly falls into sin, while another who is undiscerning and weak performs a good deed. But the person who is undiscerning and weak is sometimes lifted up more by what he has done well, and falls more gravely into sin. The discerning person, however, even by recognizing that he has acted badly, brings himself back more strictly to the rule of discernment; and from the point at which he seemed for a time to have fallen away from righteousness, he advances more deeply into righteousness. Thus it is rightly said: “Better is a man’s iniquity than a woman doing good.” For sometimes even the fault of the strong becomes an occasion of virtue, while the virtue of the weak becomes an occasion of sin. This woman brings shame into disgrace because, doing things worthy of shame, she will suffer disgrace forever on account of them.

“Therefore I will remember the works of the Lord, and I will proclaim what I have seen: his works are in the words of the Lord.” Up to this point the writer of the history has discussed various matters and, describing the moral significance of each according as it seemed suitable to him, has expressed various kinds of virtues and vices. Now, however, he turns his discourse to the praise of the Creator and to the proclamation of his works. After this, recalling the fathers of former times, he describes their mighty deeds: “His works are in the words of the Lord,” he says, “because he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII).

“The sun, illuminating all things, has looked upon them, and the work of the Lord is full of his glory.” Here he calls the Lord Christ the sun, who is both the light of divine wisdom and the splendor of righteousness. Of him it is read elsewhere: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. IV). He is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I), and he sees all things, because “no creature is invisible in his sight” (Heb. IV). The work of the Lord is full of glory because his wisdom shines forth in his works. Hence the Prophet says: “How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. XC, CIII).

### Chapter VI. Wisdom narrates that holy men proclaim his wonders—that Wisdom through which all things were made

“Has not the Lord caused the holy ones to declare all his wonders, which the Lord established to be confirmed in his glory?” How do the holy ones declare all the wonders of God, when no one can penetrate the wisdom of God? “For his judgments are incomprehensible, and his ways are unsearchable” (Rom. XI). But all his wonders that are accessible to human knowledge have been revealed to us through his holy ones. The almighty God, stable in his glory and always remaining the same, formed and established them when he willed and in the manner he willed.

Similar is what the Prophet says in the Psalms: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). For “all the judgments” signifies those that have been written or spoken. But the totality cannot be declared, since no understanding is capable of grasping it, as it is said in another psalm: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV). Hence, when his passion was near, the Lord himself said to the apostles: “I have not told you everything” (John XVI). Therefore, figuratively, the whole is spoken of in place of the part, as is frequently found to be the case in the divine Scriptures.

“He searched out the abyss and the heart of human beings, and considered their cunning.” The Wisdom of God, therefore, who is Christ, knows the depth of God’s counsels, and he himself searches the various deliberations of the human heart, as it is written: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. VII). For: “As no one knows the Son except the Father, so no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI). Nor is the Holy Spirit excluded from this power. Of him it is written: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. II). For the holy Trinity alone, God almighty, knows himself in all things, and he himself comprehends all knowledge. Concerning this it follows:

“For the Lord knows all knowledge, and he has looked into the sign of the age, declaring what has passed and what is to come, revealing the traces of hidden things. No thought escapes him, and no word hides itself from him.” The Lord looks into the sign of the age because all the ages of the world, past, present, and future, are before him. With him nothing is past and nothing future, but he sees everything as present. He alone reveals mysteries, who knows the hearts of individuals; and no word can be hidden from him or any thought remain concealed, because all things are naked and open to his eyes.

“He adorned the great works of his wisdom—he who is before the age and unto the age. Nothing is added to it, nothing is diminished, and he does not need anyone’s counsel.” God adorned the great works of his wisdom when, through the Prophets and apostles, he revealed to his faithful the mystery of his counsel, which had been hidden from ages and generations. He himself is before all and after all; nothing can be added to his wisdom, nor can anything be diminished from it. He does not need anyone’s counsel, by whose counsel all things subsist. “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.”

### Chapter VII. The praise of the universe, which was made through Wisdom and created through the Word and power in the Son of the Father, God with God

“How desirable are all his works, and how like a spark they are to contemplate.” All the works of God are desirable because they are perfect. Concerning this it is written: “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment, and God saw everything that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. II). We contemplate them as a spark because we scarcely grasp any small portion of knowledge concerning them. Human weakness cannot penetrate the greatness and perfection of God’s works, nor know them in every respect, because this knowledge belongs only to the one who, according to the greatness of his wisdom, powerfully created all things.

“All these things live and remain forever, and in every necessity all things obey him.” All things live and remain forever for their Creator, because nothing perishes for him to whom all things were present before he created them. In every necessity all things obey him, because “all things are established in his will, and no one can resist his will.” Hence Solomon says: “I have learned that all the works which God has made endure forever” (Eccl. III).

We cannot add anything to or take anything away from what God has made, so that he may be feared. What has been made remains; what is to come has already been; and God restores what has passed away. Nothing in the world is new. The courses of the sun, the phases of the moon, and the barrenness or greenness of the earth and trees were born and created together with the world itself. Therefore God has governed all things according to a fixed order and commanded the elements to serve, so that human beings, seeing these things, may understand providence and fear before the face of God, recognizing the Creator from the character, course, order, and stability of created things.

“All things are twofold, one opposite another, and he has not made anything lacking; he has confirmed the good of each.” The Creator of the universe ordered and arranged all things in such a way that those which seemed to be different from one another should nevertheless fit together.
