Thus, although the four elements differ from one another in some respects, they are not wholly at odds but are most suitably joined together. Likewise, the four changes of the seasons, though differing from one another in their qualities, are most harmoniously united in the course of the year: what arises through the moisture of spring grows through the heat of summer, ripens through the dryness of autumn, and diminishes through the cold of winter, so that the earth may again be prepared to produce the fruits of the coming year.

For living and bodily creatures likewise agree in God’s work, so that the body bears the soul and the soul gives life to the body, lest this most noble union be dispersed by any discord. The best Creator therefore confirms the good of each thing and makes all things most useful for every delight. For this reason, the supremely wise man, astonished in admiration at God’s works, proceeds to speak of his indescribable glory and immeasurable sweetness, saying:

“And who will be satisfied when seeing his glory?” This satisfaction does not produce disgust but arouses desire; and the more someone receives refreshment from it, the more fiercely he burns with love for it. Hence Wisdom herself says earlier in this same book: “Those who eat me will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Eccli. XXIV). Blessed is the person who is filled by this satisfaction, for his soul will rejoice endlessly in eternal glory with the holy angels.

### Chapter XLIII

“The height of the firmament is its beauty; the appearance of the sky is seen in glory.” The craftsman of this work, in narrating historically, praises God’s creation; but according to the mystery, he more fittingly praises the divine aid in the Church of God. The beauty of the firmament, through the brilliance of the stars, displays the Creator’s power; but the manifold adornment of the Church in the virtues and miracles of the saints manifests more excellently the greatness of the Redeemer, because he alone, by his eternal splendor, illumines believers and, by the heat of his judgment, will punish sinners. Concerning this it follows:

“The sun, visible, proclaiming at its rising, is a marvelous vessel, the work of the Most High. At noon it will scorch the earth, and who will be able to withstand the sight of its heat? Guarding a furnace in works of burning: threefold is the sun, scorching the mountains, breathing forth fiery rays, and shining; by its rays it blinds the eyes.”

This sun, which rises for those who fear God, proclaimed the kingdom of God in sight—that is, in the presence of his incarnation. His birth is uniquely marvelous: not from the seed of a man but from the power of the almighty. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

“Who will be able to withstand the sight of his heat?” No one can endure the splendor of his divinity with bodily eyes. For he said to his servant Moses: “A human being shall not see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII). Therefore he clothed himself in human nature, so that human frailty might in some way endure the divine splendor. He assumed the veil of flesh, by which the human condition could more easily approach him.

He guards a furnace in works of burning because he prepares the punishments of the fire of Gehenna for sinners. He burns the mountains threefold when he torments the proud with eternal flame for evil thought, wicked speech, and iniquitous action. This sun, shining with its rays, blinds the eyes of the wicked when, through mystical words, it confounds the understanding of those who grow proud because of their wickedness.

Concerning this the Truth himself replied in the Gospel to the disciples when they asked about the parable of the seed: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Matt. XIII). Hence also it is said to Isaiah by the divine voice: “Go and say to this people: Hearing, hear, and do not understand; seeing, see, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted and I heal them” (Isa. VI).

But because these words chiefly refer to the time of the Lord’s incarnation, when the proud hearing and sight of the Jews were seized, so that they could neither understand the Savior’s words nor believe the miracles performed by him, let us say what follows:

“Great is the Lord who made him, and in his words he hastened his course.” Great, therefore, is the Lord, who so tempered and arranged the dispensation of the incarnation of the Mediator between God and human beings that the proud would be put to shame and the humble honored with the knowledge of God; so that the prudent and wise of this world would not grasp the divine wisdom, which has been revealed to the little and humble.

“Then in his words he hastened his course,” because in the preaching of the sacred Gospel the way of salvation was prepared and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom opened. Thus that fiery sword which, after the expulsion of the first human being from paradise, was appointed to guard the way to the tree of life, was removed through Christ’s blood, and the entrance to the everlasting way was opened for God’s elect.

“And the moon in all its seasons is a display of time and a sign of the age. From the moon comes the sign of the festival day; the luminary that diminishes at the completion of the month is, according to its name, a month, growing wondrously at its completion. A vessel of the armies on high, resplendent and glorious in the firmament of heaven.”

When he says that the moon is a display of time, a sign of the age, and of the festival day, he shows that by its monthly wanings and its course through the zodiac it demonstrates the sequence of years and the ages of the world. For the Hebrews measured all reckoning of time and the annual cycle according to the course of the moon. They honored as the first month the month in which they went out from Egypt, consecrating it to the solemnity of Passover, and they celebrated the new moons of each month.

Moreover, as Jerome testifies, they named their months from the moon, which they call *Jarem*. Hence it is said here: “The month is according to its name.” Similarly, the Latin word *mensis*—month—comes either from *mensura*, “measure,” or from the moon, which in Greek is called μήνη (*mēnē*). The ancients, as we have said, were accustomed to count their months not from the course of the sun but from that of the moon.

Thus whenever sacred Scripture, whether in the Law or before the Law, indicates on what day of the month something happened or was said, it signifies nothing other than the age of the moon. The Hebrews, to whom the oracles of God were entrusted, have never ceased, according to the ancient custom of their fathers, to observe the months. They call the first month of the new year, which has been consecrated to the rites of Passover, Nisan. Because of the moon’s wandering course, it now falls in the month of March, now in April, and sometimes occupies several days of May. Yet it is more correctly assigned to April, because it always either begins in that month, ends in it, or is wholly contained within it. In this way they reckon each month in order according to its proper calculation.

After discussing the sun, he consequently adds a discussion of the moon, because the Church follows Christ; and just as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Church is illuminated by Christ and established in his glory. Concerning this, in the psalm where the Prophet speaks mystically of the king and the king’s son, Scripture says: “He shall remain with the sun and before the moon forever and ever” (Ps. LXXI).

The sun is the Word of the Father, the Son of God, who remains Christ, one God and one man, from two and in two distinct and perfect natures. Christ remains before the moon—that is, before the sight of the Church, which continually beholds him with the eyes of the heart. The moon is rightly compared to the Church, which does not possess its own natural brilliance but receives light from the sun according to fixed phases, as astronomers carefully explain among other matters.

Thus the Church receives light in measured fashion from that true Creator. At one time she appears to diminish through persecutions, and again, after tranquility has been restored, she is filled with the joy of the most brilliant light. Hence it is said that she grows wondrously at her completion. She herself is the vessel of the armies on high, glorious and resplendent in the firmament of heaven, because she is the multitude of faithful souls that shines gloriously throughout the world in the firmament of truth and divine preaching.

“The appearance of the sky, the glory of the stars, illuminating the world on high—the Lord. And they shall stand in holy words for judgment, and they shall not burn hot in their watches.” The adornment of the Church is the beauty of the saints, whom the Most High Lord appointed to illuminate the whole world through the preaching of the Gospel and signs of virtue. Remaining in holy words—that is, in the teaching of true faith—they will await God’s judgment. They are not broken by the adversities of this age, nor stirred to anger; rather, enduring all things patiently, they persist in guarding the flock entrusted to them, always mindful of this saying of the Lord, turning it over diligently in their hearts:

“Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands, and be like people waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding” (Luke XII). “Be ready, because at an hour when you do not expect it, the Son of Man comes” (Matt. XXIV). “By your patience you will possess your souls.”

“Look upon the bow, and bless the one who made it; it is exceedingly beautiful in its splendor. It encircled the sky with its glory; the hands of the Most High opened it.” Almighty God placed the bow as a sign between himself and human beings, so that he would no longer destroy the world by a flood. Hence in that same bow the colors of water and fire are shown together: it is blue in one part and red in another, so that it may be a witness to both judgments—one that is to be carried out and the other that has been carried out; that is, because the world will be consumed by the fire of judgment, just as it was destroyed by the water of the flood.

We appropriately understand the bow as the Scripture of the New and Old Testament, which, as it were, embraces the necks of the devoted with two curved bends. Concerning it we read: “He bent his bow and prepared it” (Ps. VII). It displays a gentle yoke to the faithful, but declares terrifying weapons to the obstinate. The bow is exceedingly beautiful in its splendor because sacred Scripture is exceedingly glorious in its meaning and understanding.

“It encircled the sky with its glory,” because it sufficiently narrates things both heavenly and earthly. The hands of the Most High opened it when, through the power and wisdom of God—namely, the Lord Christ—the whole order of the Old and New Testament was established. Concerning this it is said: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isa. XXV).

“By his command he hastened the snow, and he hastens to send forth the flashes of his judgment.” In the snow we may understand the cold hearts of the wicked; in the flashes, the terrors of judgment or the miracles of virtues. But because the Lord often rebukes adversaries by threatening them through the sentences of sacred Scripture and terrifying them through the flashes of miracles, it happens that he brings the cold to the brightness of righteousness and makes them white through heavenly grace. For it is written: “You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (Ps. L).

By his own command the Lord also hastens the snow and the flashes when, through a rapid change of conduct, he transforms what previously displeased him and declares that the life of those who have been converted pleases him in good works. But because these things proceed from the hidden treasury of divine mercy, it is for this reason that he adds:

“Therefore the treasures were opened, and the clouds flew out like birds.” What is said here also accords with that which is spoken by the divine voice to blessed Job: “Have you entered the treasures of snow, or have you seen the treasures of hail, which I have prepared for the time of the enemy, for the day of battle and war?” It is as though he were plainly saying: Do not set yourself above anyone on account of your works, because you do not know how many of those whom you still see, through guilt, to be cold, I am going to make workers of righteousness and defenders of the true faith. Saul had been snow or hail through the insensibility of unbelief; but he became snow and hail against the breasts of adversaries, either through the whiteness of righteousness or through the correction of stern eloquence. O what a treasure he possessed in snow and hail, when the Lord, having secretly foreknown him as his chosen one, already knew him to be such while he was placed amid the life of the wicked! O against how many breasts of adversaries did he take up this hail in his hand, by which he struck down so many hearts resisting him? Let no one, therefore, be lifted up on account of his works; let no one despair of those whom he still sees to be cold, because he does not see God’s treasures in snow and hail. For who would have believed that, through the grace of the apostolate, the man who would surpass the stoned Stephen was the one who, at his death, guarded the garments of all those who were throwing stones? (Acts VII.) If, then, we turn our attention to these hidden gifts or judgments, we despair of no one at all, nor do we prefer ourselves in our hearts to those over whom we have for a time been set, because although we now see how far we have advanced, we do not know how far we shall be surpassed when they begin to run.

“In his greatness he set the clouds, and the hailstones were broken.” The clouds, therefore, are holy teachers, who carry the rain of heavenly doctrine and irrigate the soil of the human heart; they also bear within themselves the storm of reproof and pour it out wherever it is appropriate. Hence it is said that they break hailstones, when by strongly reproving the hardness of the wicked they soften them from persisting in persecution, lest they should any longer be able to strike the fruit of the life-giving shoot in Christ’s faithful.

[Col. 1074C] Of these clouds and hail together it is written elsewhere in the Psalm: “Before his brightness the clouds passed by; hail and coals of fire.” The clouds pass before his brightness because holy preachers traverse all the regions of the world with the splendor of miracles. They are also called hail and coals of fire because they strike through correction and set others aflame through the fire of charity. The free reproof of the saints is also suitably expressed in the nature of hail: hail, when it comes, strikes, and when liquefied, waters. Holy men likewise strike the hearts of their hearers by terrifying them, and pour themselves into them by gentle encouragement. The Prophet testifies to how they strike, saying: “They will speak of the power of your terrors, and they will tell of your greatness” (Psalm CXLIV); and he immediately added how they water by gentle encouragement: “They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will rejoice in your righteousness” (ibid.).

“In his presence the mountains will be moved, and at his will the south wind will blow.” Mountains signify proud and exalted people. The south wind, therefore, which is also called Auster, is a warm wind that dissolves waters bound by cold through the power of its vapor; figuratively, it represents the grace of the Holy Spirit, which loosens sins bound by the frost of death through the ardor of its heat. The south wind blows and the mountains are moved when the Holy Spirit sends forth the breath of sound doctrine through holy preachers. Thus the mountains are moved when the powerful of this world are stirred up to persecute Christians; yet it often happens that the same people are moved by the preaching of the divine word to correct their sin, and that the movement which had previously been condemnable becomes salutary for them. Of these mountains it is written in the Psalter: “The mountains melted like wax before the Lord; before the Lord the whole earth trembled” (Psalm XCVI). These mountains—that is, exalted people, who both seek the heights of this world and grow hard through senseless superstition—are wonderfully compared with melting wax, because they flow into repentance all the more readily the more they had believed themselves to be immovably hardened. We see this happening even today, when the powers of the world—whether pagans or heretics—are called, renounce their superstitious devotion, and choose instead to submit to divine service.

[Col. 1075B] “The voice of his thunder will strike the earth.” For what is signified by thunder except the preaching of heavenly terror? When human hearts perceive this terror, they are shaken. At times, however, the incarnate Lord himself is represented by thunder, because, in accordance with the fitting prophecy of the ancient fathers, he was brought to our knowledge as though from the collision of clouds; appearing visibly among us, he thundered out terribly the things that were above us. Hence the holy apostles themselves, begotten through his grace, were called *Boanerges*, that is, “sons of thunder” (Mark III). At other times, as has been said, thunder signifies his preaching itself, through which the terror of heavenly judgments is heard. The voice of thunder rebukes the earth when divine preaching makes its vices known by reproving carnal people—who are rightly designated by the name “earth”—so that, once these vices have been put aside, they may prepare themselves to hear the divine commandments.

Of this thunder it is also written: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel; your flashes have illumined the world; the earth was shaken and trembled.” This too is said comparatively, because the voice of thunder rolls as though it were heard coming from rumbling wheels. For when it is poured forth from on high, it passes through the regions of heaven with a rolling murmur, so that the sound itself seems whirling and winding; or rather, by “the wheel” we should understand the world, which is enclosed in the form of a wheel by its complete roundness. In the wheel, therefore—that is, in the world—the voice of his thunder went forth when Christ’s preachers filled the circle of the whole world with thunderous words. But the flashes that illumine the world follow those clouds and thunders. By the flashes he means the divine commandments, radiant with the light of truth, which dispelled human darkness throughout the world by a saving illumination. He says that these thunders and flashes brought about the shaking and trembling of the earth—that is, of our bodies. For he calls those shaken and terrified by so great a miracle who, faithfully hearing the word of God, attained, by Christ’s gift, the zeal for a changed way of life.

“The storm of the north and the gathering of the spirit; and like a bird settling down to sit, it scatters snow, and like a locust its descent plunges downward.” What is expressed by the north except the one who boasted that he would ascend into heaven above the stars of God and exalt his throne on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the north? His storm and the gathering of the spirit are various temptations which that ancient enemy strives to pour into human minds through evil spirits, so as to overturn them from the firm position of true faith and make them grow cold in the fervor of the love of God. Because of the exaltation of his heart, he is rightly compared to a bird that scatters snow for sitting, when, through the harshness of his malice, he prepares a dwelling for himself wherever he may perch. Like a locust, he plunges downward in his ascent, because whatever green or fruitful thing he finds he strives to gnaw away and uproot.

“His eye will admire the beauty of his color, and over his rain the heart trembles.” The eye will admire his beauty when he pretends to be a minister of light and an ambassador of peace; but over his rain the heart trembles when he raises open storms of persecution, so that those whom he could not seduce by flattering pretense he may overcome by the magnitude of torment. This contriver of deceit carries one thing within and displays another outwardly. He transforms himself into an angel of light and, by the cunning art of deception, often presents what is praiseworthy in order to lead people toward what is forbidden. He displays glorious things outwardly in appearance so as to conceal the shameful things he carries within his heart; but when he sees that he has been frustrated in this, he immediately bursts into open savagery, so as to accomplish through torments what he could not accomplish through flattery.

“He will pour frost like salt upon the earth, and when he has blown, it will become like the points of a thistle.” Frost represents the coldness of unbelief; salt, the barrenness of growth. For wherever salt is scattered upon the earth, it immediately turns it into sterility. Hence it is written: “A fruitful land into saltiness, because of the wickedness of its inhabitants”; and we read that certain cities were sown with salt by the anger of their conquerors, so that no growth might arise in them. The ancient enemy, therefore, will pour frost like salt over the earth when, through the coldness of unbelief, he renders the hearts of earthly people incapable of producing the fruits of good works; and when the storm of temptations blows, he makes them like the points of thistles—that is, exceedingly rough with the thorns of vices. Concerning this it is also added:

“The cold north wind blew, and the crystal froze from the water.” Crystal is ice hardened into many crystalline facets in the manner of glass, a liquid substance brought to a hardness like stone. Stubborn sinners are rightly compared with it, for, constrained by the rigor of faithlessness, they grow colder day by day. The devil’s incitement therefore makes people, naturally very pliable, into solid stones, because through the cold of faithlessness he makes them exceedingly hard. Of this it is written in Job: “From whose womb did the ice come forth, and who begot the frost from heaven? The waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone, and the surface of the deep is frozen” (Job XXXVIII). We have already said that ice and frost signify the devil’s faithlessness, and we have often taught that waters signify peoples. Satan, as it were, proceeded as ice from God’s womb, because he came forth as a teacher of iniquity, cold from the heat of God’s secrets through the numbness of his malice. He was begotten as frost from heaven because he was permitted to fall from the heights to the depths in order to constrict hearts. Though well established among heavenly beings, when he fell he bound the minds of his followers in the frost of guilt like frost itself; and, coming to earth, what he did among human beings is explained when it is added: “The waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone.” When he therefore came down to the depths, the waters were hardened into the likeness of stone, because human beings, imitating his malice, lost the tender inward parts of charity. Since his fraudulent counsels cannot be detected by those whom he has deceived, it is rightly added: “And the surface of the deep is frozen.” The surface of the deep is frozen because, while his persuasion is displayed as though it were good and solid ice, his hidden malice, which drags people down into the depths, is not seen.

“Upon every gathering of waters he rests, and like a breastplate he clothes himself with waters.” This passage either describes the time when unbelief prevailed most powerfully in the world before Christ’s incarnation and the multitude of the Gentiles devoted itself with all its strength to the worship of idols, or it describes the present time, when, although many believe in Christ, the same ancient enemy still has servants in every nation, in whom he somehow rests and against whom he arrays his warriors in opposition to God’s soldiers. The Apostle Paul instructs us how we ought to fight against them, saying: “Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil, because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having fulfilled everything, stand firm. Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth, and put on the breastplate of righteousness, and with your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians VI).

“He will devour the mountains, burn up the desert, and the green thing will be extinguished as by fire.” What are signified by mountains except proud and exalted people? And what is signified by desert except deserters of truth and righteousness? The devil therefore devours the mountains and burns up the desert when he reduces all proud and wicked people, stripped of every virtue, to serve as his food, and sets the desert ablaze with the fire of desire. If anything green with the growth of virtue and knowledge is found there, he immediately extinguishes it all through the fire of malice. In sacred Scripture, verdure sometimes signifies the glory of temporal prosperity, sometimes the devil’s nourishment, sometimes the support of preachers, sometimes good works, and sometimes the knowledge and teaching of eternal life.

Verdure signifies the glory of temporal prosperity, as the Prophet says: “In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flower and pass away” (Psalm LXXXIX). To flower and pass away in the morning like grass is for the fleeting beauty of temporal glory to wither rapidly amid the prosperity of this age. Grass signifies the devil’s nourishment, as the Lord says of him: “For him the mountains bear grass,” as though he were saying: When the proud and swollen lift themselves up through unlawful thoughts and actions, they feed him with their iniquities. But what resists the malice of this most wicked enemy is shown in what follows.

“Medicine for all in haste, clouds, and dew confronting the coming heat will make him humble with it.” What is signified by a cloud or mist except the incarnation of our Redeemer and his teaching? Through these divine mercy came to the aid of the human race, and, confronting the persecutions of the ancient enemy with the dew of heavenly grace, crushed him by the power of its strength and snatched the prey from his mouth. The prophet Isaiah also testified to this in the oracle concerning Egypt, saying: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt; the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it” (Isaiah XIX).

“The Lord will ascend upon a light cloud”: the body of the holy virgin Mary, not weighed down by the burden of human seed; or, certainly, his own body, conceived from the Holy Spirit. He entered Egypt, that is, this world, and immediately all the idols of Egypt were shaken, so that the divinations and the entire deceit of idolatry—which held the world captive—recognized that it had been broken. So completely was this the case that the Magi from the East, instructed by demons or understanding through the prophecy of Balaam that the Son of God had been born, came to Bethlehem and, when the star pointed the way, worshiped the child.

Concerning this dew the Lord also said to Job: “Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew?” (Job XXXVIII), as though he were saying: If not I, who freely sprinkles the dry earth of the human heart with drops of knowledge? Of this rain it is elsewhere said: “You will set apart a voluntary rain for your inheritance, O God” (Psalm LXVII). The Lord sets apart a voluntary rain for his inheritance because he grants it to us not according to our merits but as a gift of his kindness. For this reason he is called here the father of rain, because heavenly preaching is generated for us not from our merit but from his grace. The drops of dew are the holy preachers themselves, who, amid the evils of the present life, water the fields of our hearts—parched as though amid the darkness of a dry night—with the grace of heavenly generosity.

This dew made the devil humble—that is, despised—because it brought his hidden snares into the open through clear speech, so that the world, recognizing that it had long been deceived by the ancient enemy, might cease from idolatry and the storm of persecution. Hence it is also added:

“At his word the wind was silent; by his thought he calmed the deep, and the Lord planted islands in it.” At the word of the Gospel the world was calmed from the whirlwind of persecutions, because divine Wisdom, which created the world, calmed the deep that had been stirred by its own command. The deep is a very great multitude of waters, and it is often used both in a good and in an evil sense. Here it is rightly compared with superstitious people and persecutors. Notice that the Lord Jesus is said to have planted and calmed the deep, because he is the author of all things, “through whom all things were made, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

He showed how great his power was when, awakened from sleep by the disciples in a small boat, he rose and “commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm” (Matthew VIII). Here, according to the literal sense, it should be noted that all creatures perceive their Creator: those who are rebuked and commanded perceive the one commanding them—not through the error of heretics, who think that all things are animate, but through the majesty of the Creator, to whom the things that are insensible among us are sensible.

Mystically, however, the Lord rebuked the wind when he rose, because, through the resurrection that had been accomplished, he laid low the devil’s pride, destroying through death the one who held the power of death. Rising, he also caused the storm of the water to cease, because by rising from the tomb he shook the mad rage of the Jews, which, shaking its head, had cried: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew XVII).

“Those who sail the sea recount its danger; and hearing with our ears, we marvel: there are splendid and wondrous works, various kinds of beasts, every sort of cattle, and the creation of monsters.” Those who frequently travel upon it know how many dangers and obstacles the literal sea contains for navigation—reefs, Charybdis, and sandbanks. There too the wondrous works of God are displayed in various kinds of beasts and cattle and in the creation of monsters, as writers on natural matters reveal in their books, and as the Prophet recalls in the Psalter, saying: “This sea, great and broad, in it are creeping things without number, small animals and great; there ships will pass, this dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Psalm CIII).

Although at the beginning of this verse he seems to be speaking of a navigable sea, it is nevertheless suitably understood as this world, where the devil’s snares are seen to creep without number, and where the unstable will of souls is shaken as though by certain waves through the malice of demons. They themselves make the sea, as it were, when they compel people to suffer shipwreck, because there is no doubt that the one immersed in the whirlpool of sins suffers enormous waves. The sea is so called from *meare*, “to go,” because it continually goes and returns. Yet these innumerable spirits are known to God, who counts the sand of the sea and the drops of rain; and lest they be left wholly incomprehensible, he defined them by quantity, not by quality. Thus it is said of them: “Small animals and great,” because among them there are proved to be all kinds, both greater and lesser forms of wickedness.

“There,” he says, “ships will pass”—there, that is, in the world which he previously called the sea. By ships the Church is signified, for through the wood of the glorious cross she escapes the dangerous waves of the world, carrying the peoples who have believed through the sign of faith. The sailors and rowers are the holy preachers who govern the Church amid the waves of this age. In these ships Christ dwells; if he is awakened by believers, he tells the most violent storm to be still, and it is still.

It follows: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him.” Here he plainly signifies the devil, who is truly called a dragon because of the poison that he breathed into the first woman, Eve, through his deadly persuasions. He was created good, as it is read in Genesis: “The Lord made all things very good” (Genesis I). But after he sinned by his own will, he was formed by God in such a way that he might be mocked by angels, when, because of his detestable perversity, he was deprived of his native dignity. For, as the Lord says in the Book of Job: “Nothing has been made like him upon the earth, to be mocked by my angels.”

He is mocked by God’s angels either through the most just rebukes, so that the one created for the service of the Lord may be seen entangled in foul perversities, or rather he is mocked when, by heavenly authority, the souls of those who confess are taken away from his destructive power. He is also mocked by faithful people when, with detestation, they reject the incitements to his vices.

“Because of him the end of the journey was established, and in his word all things were ordered.” “Because of him,” he says—that is, because of the Son of God—the order of passing things was established, and the end of the world was fixed, because just as all things received their origin from the Word of God, so they come to an end in him. For he himself says in the Apocalypse: “I am α and ο, the beginning and the end.”

“We say many things and are in need of words, but he himself is the completion of speech.” Every utterance is small in comparison with his glory, and every tongue is poor in words; nor is it sufficient to proclaim his power, because what is immeasurable and ineffable cannot be measured or expressed by anyone. He himself is the completion of our words, just as he is the Creator of our nature.

“Glorying in all things, what will we be able to accomplish? For he himself is almighty above all his works.” What can corruptible creation accomplish by discussing the incomprehensible essence of God, whom no one has ever seen, and whom “no living human being on earth can see”? He is almighty above all his works, and all things remain under his power.

“The Lord is terrifying and exceedingly great, and his power is wondrous. Glorifying the Lord as much as you are able, his wondrous magnificence will still surpass your praise.” What is said here accords with the Psalmist’s calling all nations to praise God: “Clap your hands, all nations; shout to God with a voice of rejoicing, for God is most high and terrifying, a great king over all gods” (Psalm XLVI). And again: “Announce his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples, for the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, and terrifying above all gods” (Psalm XCV).

He gives the reasons why the Lord should be clapped for and hailed with rejoicing. First, because he is the Most High God; terrifying, because he himself will judge the world; a great king, because he is King of kings and Lord of lords. “Great” pertains to his power, because he is more powerful than all things; “praiseworthy” pertains to his mercy, because when we were captives he redeemed us with precious blood. “Exceedingly” applies to both, because it was impossible to explain either how great he is or how praiseworthy. But because the capacity of the one considering him failed, he beautifully added “exceedingly.” Thus, without explaining what he intended, he signified it most abundantly, and without comprehending what he wished, he made it known. For the same Prophet says elsewhere: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy, and of his greatness there is no end” (Psalms XLVII, XCV, CXLIV).

A wondrous combination, a true proclamation: to praise the Lord in such a way that you do not presume to explain how great he is. The understanding of all creation fails, and the effort to approach him continually expands. For just as he is confined by no place, so his praises cannot be brought to an end by any eloquence, however extensive: his power is inexpressible, his mercy incomprehensible, his wisdom ineffable. His true definition is that he has no end in the praises of the saints. And observe that, when it is said that there is no end to his greatness, you are never commanded to cease proclaiming him. Even in silence we give thanks when we conduct ourselves in a praiseworthy manner; although he cannot be comprehended by any praises, he is nevertheless indicated in each utterance when it is said: “Exceedingly great.” And again: “Of his greatness there is no end.”

“Blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you can, for he is greater than all praise.” Wisdom urges us to bless God, so that, insofar as it lies within us and insofar as he has granted us the ability, we may always praise him. Yet we must know in every way that we cannot praise him worthily, because we cannot attain the height of his greatness. Whatever we rightly express in his praises is his gift. Of him it is written: “The Lord will give strength to his people,” and “He will bless his people with peace” (Psalm XXVIII).

“Exalting him, be filled with strength, lest you grow weary. You will not have enough; for who sees him and will recount him, and who will magnify him as he was from the beginning?” We greatly need his help so that we may be filled with his strength for praising him. When he says, “Lest you grow weary; you will not have enough,” he shows that we ought not to investigate divine secrets, which exceed our capacity, because we cannot penetrate his hidden judgments at all. Hence it is written: “Do not seek riches to which you cannot attain” (Proverbs XXIII). And Ecclesiastes says: “I said, ‘I will become wise,’ but it withdrew farther from me. What exists is far beyond what has been, and deep is the depth; who will find it?” (Ecclesiastes VII.)

“Many things greater than these are hidden, for we have seen only a few of his works; but the Lord made all things and gave wisdom to those who act piously.” If we attend to the totality of God’s wonders, there are exceedingly few of which we have knowledge. Nevertheless, with sound and complete faith we believe and confess that the one almighty God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is the Creator of all visible and invisible things, and that he gives knowledge of himself to those who act piously, that is, to those who live religiously and seek humbly, insofar as he knows it will benefit them.

For the rest, we must restrain ourselves from searching into his majesty and say with the Apostle Paul: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor, or who first gave to him, and it will be repaid to him? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory forever and ever” (Romans XI).

But since earlier he had already discussed many matters morally, touching on allegory and anagoge in many places and explaining the mysteries of the divine sacrament, he now begins to speak of the holy Fathers and men of virtue.

# BOOK TEN

[Col. 1081]

## CHAPTER ONE. Praise of the Fathers—that is, of the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs—in whom the Spirit of the Lord spoke.

(CAP. XLIV.) “Let us praise glorious men and our fathers in their generation. The Lord has bestowed great glory through his magnificence from of old. Men ruling through their powers, great in strength and endowed with prudence, announcing in the prophets the dignity of the prophets, governing the present people, and through the power of their prudence giving the peoples most holy words. In their youth they sought musical modes and recounted the songs of the Scriptures. Men rich in strength, devoted to the pursuit of beauty, making peace in their households.”

Glorious men, therefore, existed in their own times and were in every respect worthy of praise: namely, the holy patriarchs, who deserved to enjoy both divine speech and divine vision; and the prophets, who, filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, foretold many future mysteries of Christ’s Church. They ruled through their powers because many of them were kings, rich in possessions; but they ruled themselves with greater power when they restrained themselves from unlawful desires. They governed peoples and instructed them through the power of their prudence. Some of them sought musical sounds, like David and the others who arranged psalmody with him. Others devoted themselves to the pursuit of beauty, like Moses and Solomon, who built the tabernacle and the temple for the Lord with various vessels and implements.

“All these attained glory in the generations of their people, and in their days they are held in praise. Those born from them left behind a name by which their praises might be recounted.” Holy men therefore possessed glory among the generations of their people because, on account of their prudence and virtues, they were rightly honored by those subject to them. Hence their descendants, who imitated their holy way of life, celebrated their praises both in word and in deed. Wicked people, however, and those perverse in character, did not deserve to attain this. Concerning them it is added:

“There are others whose memory does not exist; they perished as though they had never been. They were born as though they had not been born, and so were their children with them.” The ungodly and sinners, therefore, were not worthy of remembrance, because if anything is narrated about them in sacred Scripture, it pertains not to their praise but to their reproach. Of them it is written in the Psalm: “The enemies’ swords have failed utterly, and you have destroyed their cities. Their memory has perished with a roar.” For, at the consummation of the world, those who are known to belong to the devil’s city will fail amid his joy, and their memory will perish with the final cry when they are plunged into everlasting punishment. The example is drawn from what commonly happens when prosperous circumstances are brought to a close by a very grievous end: neither their power appears to remain nor their name to be seen. The statement that their children perish with them mystically signifies that the works of sinners perish together with them in eternal damnation.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the martyr, the confessor, and the priest

“But these were men of mercy, whose acts of piety did not fail, and their good works remain with their offspring; a holy inheritance for their descendants. Their offspring stood firm in the covenants, and their children, because of them, remain forever. Their offspring and their glory will not be abandoned. Their bodies were buried in peace, and their name will live from generation to generation. Let the peoples recount their wisdom, and let the Church proclaim their praise.”

Those men are indeed men of mercy who, through right faith and good works, obtained the Lord’s mercy. For “his mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him.” Their good actions did not fail in their reward but remained with their offspring—that is, with the worshipers of this God, who became their descendants and heirs—and the covenant of their religious way of life in the law of God stood firm. Their posterity remained for a long time because of their merits, and the glory of the holy Fathers will not be erased by any forgetfulness. Their bodies, resting in peace, await the day of resurrection so that they may receive the glory of incorruption; but their famous name continues among their descendants, who proclaim their wisdom everywhere and daily exalt their praiseworthy life with great praises in the Church of the saints.

According to the historical sense, these things appear to pertain to the patriarchs and prophets, whose offspring—that is, the Israelites—were often delivered from difficulties because of their merits and the promises made to them; and obtained forgiveness of sins not through their own righteousness but through the faith and good deeds of their ancestors. Thus, when Moses prayed for the same sinful people of Israel, he brought to mind Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom the promises had been given, so that the Lord, appeased by their merits, might grant forgiveness to their sinful children. In the same way, because of David’s merit, he helped his sons in many things, and, in remembrance of him, preserved the kingdom for his sons for a long time.

In a more sacred sense, however, men of mercy are the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ and the preachers of the New Testament, who daily beget children worthy of God through the word of the Gospel and holy baptism. Having become imitators of their parents, these children follow their examples in faith and conduct. Their bodies, after the end of the present life, sleep in the hope of resurrection, awaiting future glory, when the seed of their good works will be rewarded with a heavenly recompense by the Judge above.

## CHAPTER THREE. On Enoch

“Enoch pleased God and was transferred into paradise, to give repentance to the nations.” He therefore fittingly does not begin to enumerate the holy Fathers with Adam, who transgressed the divine command and, having been expelled, left paradise, but with Enoch, who walked with God and was transferred into paradise. For in this the election of the saints is made clear: they are transferred from the misery of this age to the rest of the heavenly kingdom. He is therefore believed to be destined to come with Elijah near the end of the world, in order to advise human beings to turn from sins to repentance, and thus, together with his companion, to discharge the debt of death during the persecution of Antichrist.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On Noah
## CHAPTER IV. On Noah

“**Noah was found perfect and just, and in the time of wrath he became reconciliation, so that he might give the nations repentance. Therefore the remnant of the earth was spared when the Flood took place; the covenants of the age were established with him, so that all flesh might not be destroyed by the Flood.**”

Noah, of whom Scripture relates that he was a just and perfect man in his generations, walking with God, is blessed. He became reconciliation in the time of wrath because, when the world was perishing in the Flood, he was preserved for this purpose: that he might proclaim repentance to the nations and demonstrate by his example that those who devotedly serve God would become exempt from eternal destruction. With him also the Lord established a pact and made a covenant, so as not again to destroy the earth by the waters of the Flood. This signifies the rulers of God’s people, who amid the waves of this age guide the ark of Christ’s Church, preach the baptism of repentance, and by prayers and sacred offerings render the divine majesty favorable to the human race.

## CHAPTER V. On Abraham

“**Abraham, great father of a multitude of nations. And no one was found like him in glory. He kept the law of the Most High and was in covenant with him; in his flesh he established the covenant, [Col. 1085A] and in testing he was found faithful. Therefore by an oath he gave him glory among his people, to make him grow like a mound of earth, and to exalt his offspring like the stars, and to give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth.**”

Abraham, according to the interpretation of his name, is the father of many—namely, of all the nations believing in Christ—for only the faithful are considered to be in the seed, since it is not those who are children according to the flesh, but those who are children according to faith, who are Abraham’s seed.

“**No one like him was found in glory**,” because in his own times he was outstanding and was found most faithful. He was in covenant with God when it was promised to him that all the families of the earth would be blessed in his seed. In his flesh God established the covenant of circumcision, so that our renewed nature might be signified through the baptism of Christ, after the stripping off of the old man and the putting on of the new, who was created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth.

This patriarch was found faithful in testing when, as a figure of the Lord’s Passion, he appeared to sacrifice his only-begotten son. Therefore the Lord, by an oath, gave him offspring among his people: that it would grow in his seed like the sand of the sea and like the stars of heaven, which cannot be counted because of their multitude.

Thus the promised seed is represented in two ways: in the likeness of the sand of the sea, in which sterile Jews are expressed; and in the likeness of the stars of heaven, in which all the nations believing in Christ are shown, who in the future will shine like the stars of heaven by the light of the resurrection. “**For star differs from star in glory; so also will be the resurrection of the dead.**”

Therefore his seed received an inheritance from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth, because Christ, born from Abraham’s seed, rules from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth; and his Church, that is, his body, occupies all the boundaries of the world.

It should be noted that Abraham bears a threefold figure in himself: first, of the Savior, when he left his kindred and came into this world; second, of the Father, when he sacrificed his only son; and third, in receiving three men and worshiping one, he bore the figure of the saints who joyfully received Christ’s coming in the flesh. [Col. 1085D] The mystery of this incarnation was accomplished by the whole holy Trinity, but only the Son assumed it: “**For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.**”

## CHAPTER VI. On Isaac

“**And in Isaac he acted in the same way; because of Abraham his father he gave him the blessing of all nations.**”

Therefore the Lord gave Isaac the blessing of all nations because of the oath that he swore to his father: “**In his seed**”—that is, in Christ—“**all the families of the earth would be blessed.**” To him the Father says in the Psalm: “**Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth.**”

## CHAPTER VII. On Jacob

“**And he confirmed the covenant over the head of Jacob; he acknowledged him in his blessings, gave him an inheritance, and allotted him a portion among the twelve tribes. And he preserved for him men of mercy who find favor in the eyes of all flesh.**”

For the covenant was confirmed over the head of Jacob—that is, over the gentile people, who came later to the grace of faith and the regeneration of baptism. Yet the fullness of the paternal blessing came to it: “**And he gave him an inheritance**,” namely, the heavenly homeland, “**and allotted him a portion among the twelve tribes**,” so that, instructed by the twelve apostles, it might possess the eternal kingdom of God together with them.

For this people the Lord preserved his mercy, so that it might find favor in the eyes of all flesh, because Christ’s Church is honored by all nations and, worthy of praise because of its worship of the true God, is proclaimed throughout the whole world.

To it also the Lord himself says through Isaiah: “**Behold, I lift my hand to the nations, and I raise my sign to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. Kings shall be your nurturers, and queens your nurses. With faces bowed to the earth they shall worship you, and they shall lick the dust of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, and those who await him shall not be put to shame**” (Isa. XLIX).

## CHAPTER VIII. On Moses

(CAP. XLV.) “**Moses, beloved by God and human beings, whose memory is in blessing. He made him like the saints in glory, magnified him in the fear of his enemies, and by his words appeased monsters. He glorified him in the sight of kings, commanded him before his people, and showed him his glory. In his faith and gentleness he made him holy, and chose him from all flesh. He made his voice heard by him and brought him into the cloud; he gave him commandments and the law of life, to teach Jacob discipline and the covenant, and his judgments to Israel.**”

Moses was beloved by God and by human beings because he was a gentle and exceedingly meek man, as Scripture relates (Num. XII). His memory is in blessing, since he was not inferior in glory to the other holy Fathers but is worthy of perpetual praise in every respect. He was magnified in the fear of his enemies when he performed many signs before Pharaoh and his servants and moderated those plagues whenever he wished; thus he attained glory in the sight of kings.

The Lord commanded him before his people and showed him his glory when he made him a participant in his secret counsel and a knower of his will. Of him it is written:

“**When he entered the tent of the covenant, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the entrance, and he spoke with Moses. All saw that the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the tent, and they stood and worshiped at the doors of their tents. The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend. In his faith and gentleness he made him holy and chose him from all flesh**” (Exod. XXXIII).

It is certain also that his faith and gentleness made him holy and acceptable to God. By divine providence he was chosen from the whole people to preside over them. On Mount Sinai the Lord gave him the law and established the commandments of life, speaking with him in the cloud while the children of Israel listened, so that through these things he might instruct his people and teach them to live in an orderly manner.

Although he has various figures in different passages, in this respect—namely, that he led God’s people out of Egypt through the waters of the Red Sea and educated them in the wilderness with the pillar of cloud preceding them and showing the way—he bears the type of the law. Through Christ’s leadership, that law liberated believers from spiritual Egypt and from the power of the true Pharaoh through the waters of baptism, so that, instructed and educated by divine commandments in the wilderness of this world, they might reach the promised land, namely the heavenly homeland, where they may possess an abundance of all good things and enjoy eternal life.

## CHAPTER IX. On Aaron

“**He exalted Aaron, his brother, and made him like himself, from the tribe of Levi. He established an eternal covenant with him, gave him the priesthood of the nation, blessed him in glory, and girded him with the belt of justice. He clothed him in a robe of glory and crowned him with vessels of strength in his bearing. He placed around his feet the undergarment, the trousers, and the shoulder-piece; and he surrounded him with many golden bells, to give a sound as he walked and to make a sound heard in the temple as a memorial to the sons of his people.

“**He made the holy robe of gold, hyacinth-blue, and purple, woven work, by the judgment of a wise man endowed with truth; twisted scarlet, the work of an artisan; precious gems set in a gold setting and engraved by the work of a stonecutter, as a memorial according to the number of the tribes of Israel; a golden crown impressed upon his turban with the sign of holiness and the glory of honor, a work of strength, adorned for the desires of the eyes. Such beauty had not existed before him from the beginning. No foreigner was clothed in it, but only his sons and his grandsons throughout all time.**”

He describes the rite of the priesthood of the Old Testament and the adornment of the high priest, which in every respect bore the figure of the New Testament and of the true priest, our Lord Jesus Christ, who “**entered once for all into the holy places, not by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption**” (Hebr. IX).

The high priest’s garments are nothing other than works of virtue and the teaching of wisdom, which truly adorn the Lord’s priest when he is found rightly to conduct himself in them. Hence it is also said here: “**He crowned him with vessels of strength.**”

The wise in heart, whom God filled with the spirit of prudence to make these same garments, are the prophets and apostles and the other teachers of truth. They show us most clearly how priests and ministers of the altar ought to live and how they ought to teach, whether by the example of their conduct or by the word of exhortation.

What these garments themselves are, which Moses made for his brother Aaron, that is, what sacred Scripture commends for the rulers of the law, Paul also shows when he says: “**For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward; not arrogant, not irascible, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonorable gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching**” (Tit. I).

The high priest therefore used to be clothed at the time of sacrifice in eight kinds of garments: the breastpiece, the shoulder-piece, the hyacinth-blue tunic, the close-fitting linen garment, the turban, the belt, the undergarment, and, above all—on the forehead—the golden plate on which the name of God was written.

The breastpiece was the covering of the chest, just as the shoulder-piece was that of the shoulders. The hyacinth-blue tunic, which had golden bells at its lower edge, was worn over the linen garment. The close-fitting linen garment, that is, the shirt, covered the whole body; the turban adorned the head. The belt fastened both the tunic and the shoulder-piece more tightly to the body.

Four of these were granted to priests of lesser rank: the linen undergarment, the tunic, the belt, and the turban. It was fitting that the greater the rank by which someone was distinguished, the more he should shine admirably through acts of virtue.

Everything was made of gold and precious colors, because nothing base or filthy ought to appear in a priest’s mouth or work. Rather, everything he does, everything he says, and everything he thinks ought to be distinguished before human beings and glorious in the sight of the internal judge.

Each kind of garment has a mystical meaning. In the breastpiece, the fullness of knowledge is expressed; in the shoulder-piece, the activity of good works; in the hyacinth-blue tunic, heavenly conduct; in the bells, the preaching of the sacred word; in the linen tunic—also called here the garment reaching to the feet, because it extended to the ankles—the completion of chastity; in the belt, self-control; in the turban, which covered the head, custody of all the senses; and in the undergarment, chastity of the body against lust.

The crown over the turban, on which the sign of holiness was inscribed, namely the name of almighty God, signifies the honor due to the divine majesty, which we ought to establish in the citadel of our state and above all else, so that in all our actions, words, and conduct God may be honored through Jesus Christ our Lord, who is the head of the body, the Church, and the Savior of all, especially of the faithful.

If anyone desires to know the spiritual meaning of these things more fully, let him read the various treatises of the holy Fathers on God’s tabernacle and the priestly garments. If he seeks a concise account of them, let him read our little work that we composed in four books on the book of Exodus; there, if I am not mistaken, he will find what satisfies his need.

“**His sacrifices were consumed daily by fire. Moses filled his hand and anointed him with holy oil. This became for him an eternal covenant, and for his seed, as the days of heaven: to exercise the priesthood, to receive praise, and to glorify his people in his name. He chose him from every living creature to offer sacrifice to God, incense, and a sweet fragrance, to make atonement in memory for his people. He gave him authority in his commandments, and in the covenants of his judgments, to teach Jacob his testimonies and to give Israel light in his law.

“**For strangers rose up against him, and through envy surrounded him: in the wilderness, the men who were with Dathan and Abiram; and the assembly of Korah in wrath. The Lord God saw it, and it did not please him, and they were consumed in the fury of his wrath. He performed signs against them and consumed them in the flame of fire, and he added glory to Aaron.

“**He gave him an inheritance and allotted him the first fruits of the land; he prepared bread for him first, in abundance. For they shall eat the sacrifices of the Lord that he gave to him and to his seed. Yet he did not give him an inheritance among the nations in the land, and he has no portion among the people. For he himself is his portion and inheritance.**”

How Moses consecrated his brother Aaron and his sons to the Lord with the oil of anointing, what victims he commanded to be offered for himself on the day of his anointing, the continual sacrifice that was to be offered every morning and evening, and his other duties are described at great length in the book of Leviticus. The book of Numbers also explains most clearly the revolt of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, which they raised against Moses and Aaron, and the vengeance brought upon them by the Lord because of it (Num. XVI).

These events mystically demonstrate that those who attempt to create heresies and schisms, deceive many by drawing them along with themselves, despise Christ’s priests, separate themselves from the fellowship of his clergy and people, and dare to establish churches and another altar, offering another prayer in unlawful words and profaning the truth of the Lord’s sacrifice through false sacrifices—when they strive against God’s ordinance, they too, because of their audacious presumption, will be swallowed up when the foundations of the earth are split open and a deep chasm appears.

Not only those who are leaders of these errors, but also those who, by consenting, become participants in them, will perish in the punishment prepared in the fire of eternal judgment. For Christ’s priesthood and the rite of sacrifices established by him remain forever and will not be changed by any alteration. To him the Father swore, saying: “**You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek**” (Ps. CIX).

## CHAPTER X. On Phinehas

“**Phinehas, son of Eleazar, is third in glory, imitating him in the fear of the Lord and standing in reverence among the people. In the goodness and eagerness of his soul he pleased the God of Israel. Therefore he established with him a covenant of peace, making him prince of the holy ones and of his people, so that the dignity of the priesthood might belong to him and to his seed forever.

“**And the covenant of King David, son of Jesse, from the tribe of Judah: an inheritance for him and his seed, so that he might give wisdom to our heart to judge his people in justice, lest their good things be destroyed; and he made their glory eternal among their people.**”

Phinehas, son of Eleazar, received a covenant of peace from the Lord, as the book of Numbers testifies, because, stirred by zeal for God, he killed at the same time an Israelite man fornicating with a Midianite woman. Concerning him the aforementioned book says that the Lord spoke to Moses:

“**Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned away my wrath from the children of Israel, because he was moved by my zeal against them, so that I myself would not destroy the children of Israel in my zeal. Therefore say to him: Behold, I give him the peace of my covenant, and it shall be a covenant of an everlasting priesthood both for him and for his seed, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the crime of the children of Israel**” (Num. XXV).

According to the mystical meaning also, the promise of an everlasting priesthood is rightly made to Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, because of the zeal he exercised against those committing fornication. For whoever, pierced by zeal for God, strives to restrain the impulses of his flesh, or rightly rebukes and restrains those subject to him so that through wantonness and lust they do not turn aside from the path of truth, will have in God’s Church the dignity of the everlasting priesthood that properly belongs to that priest. Of him it is written: “**You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek**” (Ps. CIX).

Together with him he will possess the everlasting kingdom perpetually in the heavenly light.

Phinehas is interpreted as “sparing with the mouth,” or “the mouth rested,” or “the oracle of the mouth”; Eleazar means “my God is a helper,” or “the help of God”; Aaron means “mountain of strength,” or “strong mountain.” These names appropriately express the same meaning that we have proposed. For the one who spares his mouth from speaking evil and rightly explains the heavenly mysteries by word to his hearers, fulfilling a pious labor through God’s help, will ascend by good works to the mountain of strength, concerning which the Prophet says: “**The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains and shall be exalted above the hills**” (Isa. II), and will happily arrive there.

When it is said that the covenant of David, king and son of Jesse, made an inheritance for Phinehas and his seed eternal through blessing and glory, it is shown that David, in distributing the ministers of the Lord—when he divided them into twenty-four courses so that they might minister in their turns before the Lord—did not diminish Phinehas’s glory but rather increased it.

Hence in Chronicles, where the Korahites are mentioned as being over the work of the ministry, guarding the entrances of the tabernacle, and their families guarding the entrance to the camps of the Lord in their appointed courses, the text adds: “**Phinehas, son of Eleazar, was their leader before the Lord**” (I Chron. IX). From this the Hebrews infer that Phinehas was still alive at that time and arranged the courses of those ministering in the tabernacle.

## CHAPTER XI. On Jesus son of Nave

(CAP. XLVI.) “**Strong in war was Jesus son of Nave, successor of Moses among the prophets. He was great according to his name, greatest for the salvation of God’s chosen, to overthrow rising enemies and obtain the inheritance of Israel. He acquired this glory by lifting up his hands and hurling swords against the cities.**”

Jesus son of Nave, both in name and in action, expresses a type of the Savior, to whom God the Father “**gave the name that is above every name. Therefore at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth**.” Since this name is above every name, it was not given as a surname to anyone throughout the many generations.

Moses wrote the book of Genesis, in which we read of Abraham and those born from him, among whom there were very many righteous men; yet none of them deserved to be called Jesus. Abel was not called Jesus, nor the one who began to call upon the name of the Lord God, nor the one who pleased God and was translated, whose death was never found; nor Noah, who alone in his generation was found righteous before God. Not even the one who received the promises of Abraham’s covenant was so called, nor Isaac who was born from him; nor Jacob the supplanter, nor any of his sons.

Moses was faithful in all God’s house, yet he too is not called Jesus. But I first find the name Jesus in Exodus, and I wish to observe when the name Jesus is first applied: “**Amalek came and fought against Israel, and Moses said to Jesus at Rephidim**” (Exod. XVII). This is the first use of the name Jesus: “**Choose for yourself powerful men from all the children of Israel, go out, and fight against Amalek tomorrow.**”

He is the one who afterward assumed command following Moses’ death; he is the one who leads the army and fights against Amalek. What is prefigured there on the mountain, with hands extended, he affixes to his cross, triumphing over principalities and powers in himself.

[Col. 1091C] “**Who before him thus withstood them? For the Lord himself struck down the enemies. Was not the sun stayed in his wrath, and did not one day become like two? He invoked the Most High, the Mighty One, while assailing enemies on every side; and the great and holy Lord heard him, with very mighty stones of hail. He made an assault upon the hostile nation and, in the descent, destroyed his adversaries, so that the nations might know his power, because it is not easy to fight against the Lord; and he pursued the mighty from behind.**”

The history of Jesus son of Nave explains how the sun was stayed at his command and one day became like two, when he fought with the children of Israel for the Gibeonites against the five kings of the Amorites. For it is written there: “**Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day when he delivered the Amorite into the sight of the children of Israel. And he said before them: Sun, do not move over against Gibeon; and moon, over against the valley of Aijalon; and the sun and moon stood still**” (Josh. X). Is this not written in the Book of the Just? “**So the sun stood in the midst of heaven and did not hasten to set for the space of one day; there was no day so long before or afterward, the Lord obeying the voice of a man and fighting for Israel.**” Then also “**the Lord sent great stones from heaven upon them**,” the Amorites, “**as far as Azekah, and they died; far more died from the stones of hail than the children of Israel had struck with the sword.**”

Mystically, the stones of hail are severe punishments sent from heaven upon the enemies of God’s people, or divine threats uttered in the sacred Scriptures against the wicked, where the fire of Gehenna and everlasting punishment are proclaimed to them. In this way Jesus, with his leaders and powers, is present to those who are assailed for his name by opposing powers. He not only gives help in battle, but also lengthens the time of day and, by extending the spaces of light, drives back the coming of night. The day is prolonged and sunset deferred; the sun never sets, but always rises, while the sun of righteousness pours the light of truth into the hearts of believers.

But when the measure of believers has been filled, and the last generation has arrived, an age already worse and more degraded; when, as iniquity increases, the charity of many grows cold, and very few remain in whom faith is found—then the days will be shortened. The same Lord, therefore, knows how to extend the day when it is a time of salvation, and to shorten it when it is a time of tribulation and destruction. Yet while we have the day and the space of light is prolonged for us, let us walk honorably as in the day and perform the works of light.

“**And in the days of Moses he showed mercy, he and Caleb son of Jephunneh, by standing against the enemy, preventing the people from sinning, and breaking the murmur of wickedness. They two were preserved from danger out of the number of six hundred thousand footmen, in order to bring them into the inheritance, into the land flowing with milk and honey. And the Lord gave Caleb strength, and his vigor remained with him even into old age, so that he might ascend to the high place of the land; and his seed obtained the inheritance, so that all the children of Israel might see that it is good to obey the holy God.**”

The book of Numbers likewise relates that Moses sent from the wilderness of Paran twelve spies, one from each tribe, to explore the promised land. When they returned and reported the fruits of that land, they drove all the people into despair except two—Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh—and made them murmur against the Lord. Because of this, a plague and a prohibition were sent upon them: none of those men who had come out of Egypt should enter the promised land, except the aforesaid Joshua and Caleb (Num. XIII).

The Lord gave Caleb a long life and unbroken prosperity, as he himself testifies in speaking to Joshua: “**I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the Lord sent me from Kadesh-barnea to examine the land, and I reported to him what seemed true to me. But my brothers who had gone up with me dissolved the heart of the people; nevertheless I followed the Lord my God. Moses swore on that day, saying: The land on which your foot has trodden shall be your possession, and that of your children forever, because you have followed the Lord my God. Therefore the Lord has granted me life, as he promised, down to this present day. Forty-five years have passed since the Lord spoke this word to Moses, when Israel walked through the wilderness. Today I am eighty-five years old, as strong as I was when I was sent to explore; the strength of that time remains in me to this day, both for fighting and for walking. Therefore give me this mountain, which the Lord promised while you too heard, in which are the Anakim and great fortified cities; perhaps the Lord will be with me, and I shall be able to destroy them as he promised me.**”

Spiritually, when the people under the Law, established under the ten commandments, went astray and could not enter the promised land, Jesus and Caleb—whose name is interpreted “as a heart”—enter it with the multitude of the new people, in order to possess it. Caleb’s statement, “**Today I am as strong as I was**,” signifies that every saint who understands in heart is equally strong in present things, past things, final things, old things, the Gospels, and the Law. This is what he means in saying that he is strong today under Jesus as he was then under Moses: a watchful heart is strong in the mysteries of both Testaments.

But let us also consider the request that this Caleb son of Jephunneh makes of Jesus: “**I ask you,**” he says, “**for this mountain, as the Lord said on that day.**” The saint seeks nothing low or base, nothing that lies in sunken valleys; rather, he seeks a lofty mountain, a mountain in which are great and fortified cities. He asked this because he knew how to wage war, as it is written: “**A wise man has taken fortified cities and will destroy the stronghold in which the ungodly trusted**” (Prov. XXI). Do you suppose that, in saying this, Solomon wished to teach us that a wise man would capture cities and destroy fortifications built of stones? Or does he rather indicate that cities and walls are the doctrines of the ungodly and the syllogisms of philosophers, by which they establish impious things contrary to the divine law, things observed among pagans or barbarians?

But those things must be reckoned as fortified cities and as set upon mountains which heretics place, as it were upon lofty mountains, in assertions from the Scriptures. Every wise person who preaches the word of truth therefore destroys these cities and overthrows lying cities with the battering ram of truth, as Paul also said: “**Destroying reasonings and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God**” (II Cor. X). Thus this most wise Caleb now also stands before Jesus, promises that he is strong for battle and ready for the contest, and therefore asks to be permitted, like a disputant, to engage with the dialecticians of the age, with those who establish falsehood in place of truth, in order to refute and overcome them and overthrow everything they have constructed by false assertions.

Therefore, seeing his eagerness, Jesus “**blessed him**,” that is, because he asked and dared such things. But if you too wish to devote yourself to study, meditate prudently upon the Law, and become a heart in the Law of God, you can overthrow those great and fortified cities—that is, the assertions of falsehood—so that you too may deserve to be blessed by Jesus and receive Hebron. Hebron is interpreted “union” or “marriage.” By it perhaps may be shown that Abraham the patriarch acquired there the double cave in which the marriages of the fathers and their remains lie: Abraham with Sarah, Isaac with Rebecca, and Jacob with Leah.

Caleb therefore deserved to receive the remains of the fathers as an inheritance, undoubtedly because, through the wisdom that was in him and flourished both under Moses and under Jesus, he understood the meaning of that union and perceived why Sarah alone lay with Abraham, and why neither Hagar nor Keturah deserved to be joined to him there; or why Leah alone appeared to lie with Jacob, while neither Rachel, who had been more dearly loved, nor any of the concubines had been joined to him in the tomb. Wise and prudent Caleb thus takes this inheritance in the memorials of the fathers. Jesus gives Hebron, the metropolis of the Anakite nations, to him, and it becomes his lot unto this present day.

[Col. 1094B] “**And the judges, each by his own name, whose heart was not corrupted, who did not turn away from the Lord, so that their memory might be in blessing and their bones might flourish from their place. Their name remains forever; the glory of holy men endures for their children.**”

After Jesus son of Nave, judges also governed God’s people, ruling them and defending them against their enemies. So too, after the passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of our Savior, the Apostles and apostolic men became rulers of God’s Church. They instructed it by holy admonitions and fortified it against spiritual wickedness and against all enemies by good merits together with holy prayers. It is fittingly said that their heart was not corrupted and that they did not turn away from the Lord, because they persevered in right faith and true religion to the end of life, so that their memory might be established in perpetual blessing and the strength of their good works rewarded with eternal recompense. Thus the memory of their name was handed down to their descendants with glory; for all peoples shall recount their wisdom, and the whole Church of the saints proclaims their praise.

## CHAPTER XII. On Samuel

“**Samuel, beloved of the Lord, prophet of the Lord, renewed the kingdom and anointed princes over his people. He judged the assembly according to the law of the Lord and beheld the God of Jacob.
