In his faith he was proved a prophet and was known faithful in his words, because he saw the God of light. He invoked the mighty God while assailing enemies surrounding him on every side, in the offering of an unblemished man. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and with a great sound made his voice heard; he crushed the princes of Tyre and all the leaders of the Philistines. Before the time of the end of his life and of the age, he gave testimony in the sight of the Lord and of his Christ: he took no money, even to footwear, from any flesh, and no man accused him. After this he slept, made himself known to the king, showed him the end of his life, and raised his voice from the earth in prophecy to destroy the impiety of the people.**”

The history is plain. It relates concerning Samuel that, while he slept in the temple in his childhood, the Lord appeared to him and instructed him about future things; that he renewed the kingdom when he himself anointed a king over Israel (I Sam. III)—first Saul and then David—and that, fighting against the enemies of God’s people, he offered a burnt offering to the Lord. It happened that, while he was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines began battle against Israel. “**And the Lord thundered with a great crash that day over the Philistines, terrified them, and they were struck down by the children of Israel.**” For he was found faithful in every respect and free from all avarice; he slept in peace and, appearing to Saul after his death, foretold the disaster that would befall him.

Mystically, the utterance of the holy prophets is found altogether true and faithful. It foretold that Christ’s kingdom was to come and announced beforehand that he would be anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. After the completion of the Old Testament and the end of the ancient Law, signified by the death of the prophet—for “**the Law and the prophets were until John**” (Matt. XI), and “**Christ is the end of the Law**” (Rom. X)—it now openly announces in its reading, in the times of grace, the punishment to come upon evil rulers and the consequent everlasting death.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Nathan.

(CAP. XLVII.) “After this, Nathan the prophet arose in the days of David, and, like fat, was separated from the flesh.” This Nathan flourished with distinction through the gift of prophecy among the Jewish people in the days of King David. He reproved David himself for his transgression, because he had transgressed in the adultery with Bathsheba and in the killing of her husband Uriah (II Samuel 12). He also foretold to him that he would not build a temple for the Lord; and he consecrated Solomon, David’s son, together with the priest Zadok, as ruler by sacred anointing (I Kings 1). But when it says that he was separated from the flesh like nourishing fat, it shows that, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, he was set apart and separated in character and life from the company of carnal and sinful people.

## CHAPTER XIV. On David

“Thus David played with lions, among the children of Israel, as with lambs of sheep, and did the same with bears, as with lambs of sheep. In his youth, did he not kill the giant and remove disgrace from the people? By raising his hand, with the stone of his sling he cast down the exultation of Goliath. For he called upon the Lord Almighty, and he gave him power in his right hand to overthrow a strong man in battle and to exalt the horn of his people. Thus, among ten thousand, he glorified him and praised him with the blessings of the Lord, offering him a crown of glory; he crushed enemies on every side and exterminated the Philistines, his adversaries, to this very day; he crushed their horn forever. In every work he gave thanks to the Holy One and to the Most High in words of glory. With all his heart he praised the Lord and loved God, who had made him, and gave him power against his enemies. He appointed singers before the altar, and through their music he made the psalms sweet. He gave dignity to the celebrations and adorned the sacred seasons until the completion of life, so that they might praise the holy name of the Lord and magnify the Lord’s holiness in the morning. Christ purified his sins. He exalted his horn forever and gave him the covenant of kings and the seat of glory in Israel.”

The writer of this book touches upon David’s history in passing, recalling his deeds. The books of Kings and Chronicles also relate them at greatest length. That King David himself mystically signifies our king Christ, mighty and desirable, is known to nearly all who read the Holy Scriptures: Christ crushed the lion, the devil, and the bear, the Antichrist; and he struck down the exceedingly proud giant—that is, Satan—with sling and stone. For, in the spiritual meaning of the Scriptures, through knowledge of God’s law he conquered and overthrew the power of the ancient enemy among idol-worshipers and defenders of perverse doctrines. Thus he freed the people of God from fear of their enemies, namely, the evil spirits. When he returned victorious from the slaughter of his enemies, women—that is, the souls of the faithful—sang him the praise of triumph and proclaimed him victor over ten thousand, because he completely overcame and overthrew all enemies, both spiritual and bodily. These numbers are perfected by tens and demonstrate Christ’s perfect victory everywhere.

Finally, our David, anointed as king with the oil of gladness above his companions, crushed and exterminated all the enemies of the Church. In himself, according to the type prefigured by the historical David, he orders the ecclesiastical ministry in the house of God, which is the holy Church, and arranges and administers the offices of each person according to his own judgment for the praise of God. Thus, in every place under his dominion, heavenly and earthly creation may bless the Lord at all times and continually sing his praise with its mouth.

Appropriately, it is said that Christ would purify David’s sins and exalt his horn forever, because, according to Peter’s declaration, “there is no other name on earth given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4). In this name, therefore, repentance is proclaimed, and forgiveness of sins to all nations. God the Father, because of his obedience to the cross, “exalted” him and “gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2).

## CHAPTER XV. On Solomon

“After him arose a sensible son, and because of him he cast down all the power of his enemies. Solomon ruled in days of peace; the Lord subjected all enemies to him, so that he might build a house in his name and prepare a sanctuary forever, as he had been instructed in his youth. He was filled, like a stream, with wisdom, and his soul covered the earth. You multiplied enigmas in comparisons; your name was spread as far as distant islands. You were loved in your peace, in songs, proverbs, comparisons, and interpretations, and the lands marveled. In the name of the Lord God, whose surname is the God of Israel, you gathered gold like bronze, and filled silver like lead; and you bent your thighs toward women. You had power over your body, and you brought a stain upon your glory; you profaned your offspring, bringing anger upon your children. In the rest of this, you displayed your folly, so that you made the kingdom twofold and caused a harsh kingdom to rule over Ephraim. But God will not abandon his mercy, nor will he corrupt or destroy his works, because he will not destroy the descendants of his chosen one, nor corrupt the offspring of the one who loves the Lord. He gave a remnant to Jacob and David from that same stock.”

The history that tells of Solomon, David’s son, is certainly not unknown. It relates how God, appearing to him in a vision, granted him permission to ask whatever he wished. When he requested an understanding heart, so that he might distinguish between good and evil and judge God’s people with just judgment (I Kings 3), his request pleased the Lord; and God gave him a wise and understanding heart, so greatly that no one before him had been like him, nor would anyone like him arise afterward. Moreover, he gave him riches and glory, so that no king in all former days would be like him, and he granted him peace on every side from his enemies.

Therefore his name was spread as far as distant islands, and he was loved in his peace, because he built a temple for the Lord with marvelous workmanship and appointed singers and arranged songs, so that he wisely uttered proverbs and composed comparisons and interpretations. Scripture relates of him:

“Solomon also spoke three thousand parables, and his songs numbered five thousand. He discussed trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; he discoursed about beasts, birds, reptiles, and fish. People came from all peoples to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and from all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom” (I Kings 4).

But afterward, when he was already old, his heart was corrupted by women, so that he followed foreign gods, and his heart was not perfect with the Lord his God as the heart of David his father had been. The angry Lord tore his kingdom apart and took authority from his sons, so that they would not rule over all Israel but only over two tribes, namely Judah and Benjamin.

Mystically, this same Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” signifies in his name and in many of his works our peaceful king, of whom the Prophet says: “In his days justice shall arise and abundance of peace, until the moon is lifted up” (Psalm 71). Another prophet says of him: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it in judgment and justice from now and forever” (Isaiah 9).

He built a temple for God—that is, the catholic Church, which is constructed from living stones. There his praise and glory remain now and always, throughout eternal ages. God gave him the riches of all nations, because he conferred upon him authority over heaven and earth and magnified him above all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. The whole earth desired to see Solomon’s face, in order to hear his wisdom, which God had given him in his heart; and each person brought him gifts, silver and golden vessels, clothing, and weapons of war. For he is exalted above the height of the saints who are truly called kings, and no one can be made equal to him, since “who among the clouds can be compared with the Lord, or who is like God among the sons of God?” “God, who is glorified in the council of the saints, is great and to be feared above all who surround him” (Psalm 146). And again: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no measure of his wisdom.” Hence John also says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1).

The whole earth desires to see the face of our king, because the entire Church of the saints desires only this: to reach the sight of his glory. To him the Prophet says: “My heart has said to you, ‘I have sought your face’; your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Psalm 26). And elsewhere: “As the deer,” he says, “longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 41). Each person brings him gifts, when each one, according to the strength available to him, strives to offer God service in word or deed.

But what shall I say now about the rest of Solomon’s works? Holy Scripture strongly rebukes and condemns him, and makes no mention at all of his repentance or of God’s indulgence toward him. In Solomon’s person there appears a marvelous excellence and a marvelous downfall. What therefore existed in him at different times—first good and afterward evil—is displayed in the Church in this present age simultaneously and at one time. For I think that by his good qualities the good in the Church are signified, and by his evil qualities the evil in the Church, as within the unity of a single threshing floor: just as in that one man we understand the good as grain and the wicked as chaff, or within the unity of one crop, the good as wheat and the wicked as weeds.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Rehoboam and Jeroboam

“Solomon came to his end with his fathers and left behind him, from his offspring, folly for the people. Rehoboam was diminished in prudence, and he turned the people away by his counsel.”

The history of Kings explains the meaning of this passage. It relates that Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, abandoned the useful counsel of the elders and took counsel with young men of his own age. Through the harsh reply he gave the people, saying, “My father placed a heavy yoke upon you, but I shall add to your yoke. My father scourged you with whips, but I shall scourge you with scorpions,” the people became angry, abandoned the house of David, and chose Jeroboam son of Nebat (I Kings 12).

Thus all Israel, except the two tribes, namely Judah and Benjamin, followed Jeroboam; ten tribes were under Jeroboam. Concerning him it continues:

“And Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin and gave Ephraim a path of sinning. Their sins overflowed greatly, for they turned them far away from their land, and he sought every wickedness until defense reached them. And he freed them from all their sins.”

“And Jeroboam son of Nebat,” it says—that is, he left behind him one who caused Israel to sin through the worship of idols. Fearing that the people of God, if they went up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord, would return to the house of David, he devised a plan, made two golden calves, and said to them: “You shall go up to Jerusalem no longer. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” He placed one at Bethel and the other at Dan. This became an occasion of sin, for the people went to worship the calf as far as Dan. He made shrines on the high places and priests from the lowest ranks of the people, who were not descendants of Levi. He established a solemn day in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, imitating the solemnity celebrated in Judah. He also set up an altar at Bethel, to sacrifice to the calves he had made. He appointed at Bethel priests for the high places that he had made, and he ascended the altar that he had constructed at Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, a day he had invented on his own, and he celebrated a feast for the children of Israel.

This wicked invention persisted among the people of the ten tribes until the Lord sent punishment upon them and caused them to be carried away to the Assyrians. When it says, “until defense reached them, and he freed them from all their sins,” I think this signifies no other defense and liberation than the coming of our Savior, who frees those who faithfully turn to him and are washed in his baptism from all sins, and defends them from every enemy. Thus it is written: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1).

Finally, Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, who abandoned the useful counsel of the elders and followed the counsel of the young, although he belonged to the house of David, did not walk in David’s way. For, as Scripture bears witness, Judah did evil before the Lord in his days, and they provoked him beyond everything their fathers had done in the sins they had committed. They too built altars, pillars, and sacred groves for themselves on every high hill and beneath every leafy tree. They also became effeminate in the land and committed all the abominations of the nations, which the Lord had destroyed before the children of Israel.

He therefore signifies wicked rulers in the Church who, devoted to earthly desires, neglect to care for their subjects. They delight in the multitude of those who obey them, yet do not show appropriate concern for those entrusted to them. Rehoboam is interpreted as “the breadth of the people.” Those may rightly be called “the breadth of the people” who, walking along the broad and spacious road by which many go to death, refuse to enter the narrow way, which belongs to the few and leads to eternal life. Abandoning the counsel of the holy fathers, whose words and examples strive toward the heights of perfection, they choose to obey the commands of the young—that is, of those enslaved to youthful desires, who burden them with wicked praise and flattery. In them is fulfilled what the prophet says: “As is the people, so is the priest” (Isaiah 24).

For all, from the least to the greatest, pursue greed; and, blind leaders of the blind, they fall together into the pit of destruction. Against them the wisdom of God threatens, saying: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiastes 10). Conversely, concerning the holy people and their king Christ, whom we must praise, it continues: “Blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose princes eat at the proper time, because everything they do will prosper” (ibid.).

Jeroboam, however, who separated the ten tribes from the house of David and from the temple of God and led them into idolatry, signifies heretics. They love dissension, divide the unity of the catholic faith through heresies, and, as though in obedience to the worship of evil spirits, hand themselves over to them. Jeroboam is interpreted as “judging the people.” Heretics also appear to judge the people when they make someone a follower of their error.

The words of the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh, who was sent to Jeroboam, aptly apply to this matter. He said: “Take for yourself ten torn pieces, for thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from Solomon and shall give you ten tribes. But one tribe shall remain for him because of my servant David and Jerusalem, the city that I chose from all the tribes of Israel’” (I Kings 11). Jeroboam received ten torn pieces when he corrupted the commandments of the law by violating them; and one tribe remained with David’s offspring, while the lot of the saints remained, according to apostolic teaching, within the rule of the catholic faith, because “there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism” (Ephesians 4).

## CHAPTER XVII. [Column 1100D] On Elijah

(CAP. XLVIII.) “And Elijah the prophet arose like fire, and his word burned like a torch. He brought famine upon them, and those who provoked him wasted away through envy. For they could not endure the commandments of God. By the word of the Lord he exalted heaven and brought down fire from heaven three times.”

Thus Elijah was magnified in his miracles. And who can glory like you in the same way? You raised the dead from the underworld, from the lot of death, by the word of the Lord God. You cast kings down to destruction and easily broke their power, and cast the glorious from their bed. You hear judgment on Sinai, and at Horeb judgments of defense.

“You anoint kings for repentance and make prophets successors after you. You were received in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot of fiery horses. You are written among the judgments of the ages to turn aside the anger of the Lord, to reconcile the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob. Blessed are those who saw you and were adorned by your friendship; for we live only in life, and after death our name will not be such.””

The history of Kings relates the marvelous deeds of Elijah the prophet: how he caused two captains of fifty, sent to him by King Ahaziah, to be consumed by fire sent from heaven; how he announced to the king himself, who was sick in bed, that he would not come down from his bed alive but would certainly die, because he had consulted Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, about his health and not the Lord God of Israel. It also relates how he shut up heaven for three years and six months, so that it did not rain upon the earth; how he ordered the priests of Baal to be killed; and how he foretold the death of the most wicked King Ahab. He spoke with God on Mount Horeb and saw visions.

He anointed two kings in punishment of the wicked: Hazael over Syria and Jehu son [reading uncertain] over Israel. He also appointed Elisha son of Shaphat after him as prophet for the Lord. After this, he was received into heaven in a fiery chariot. According to the prophecy of Malachi, he will come to earth before the day of judgment, to turn the hearts of fathers toward their sons and the hearts of their sons toward their fathers, lest the Lord come and strike the earth with a curse.

Mystically, in the fact that Elijah was fed by the widow of Zarephath during a time of drought, he signifies that, while the world—which lies in wickedness—remains dry and barren, the faithful who have been piously received and cared for in the catholic Church feed that most kindly mother with the gift of knowledge and wisdom. In her vessels the oil of grace and the flour of blessing now overflow, while famine remains among nearly all the nations. Their hunger for the word of God and their famine of faith in the Trinity were fittingly prefigured by that former famine of three years. In the fact that he raised the son of the mother of the household, stretching himself over the boy three times, he bears the type of the Savior, who, through faith in the Holy Trinity, comes to the aid of the world, raises it from the death of sin, and rescues it from the danger of future destruction.

As for the wicked king’s sending two captains of fifty with the soldiers subject to them to bring Elijah—and their being consumed by divine fire, while the third messenger was saved—this has the following mystery: the number fifty is a confession of repentance, by which the forgiveness of sins is declared. Therefore, the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge Christ as perfect God and as the prince of repentance, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and do you know Abraham?” (John 8). In the future, they will be extinguished in the burning of divine fire. But the third captain of fifty, because he turned to faith in the Trinity and recognized the sacraments of repentance, obtained pardon.

When God ordered Elijah to anoint kings and the prophet Elisha for the punishment of enemies, saying to him, “Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill,” and so forth (I Kings 19), this should not be understood to mean that God’s prophet Elisha would become a murderer and tyrant. It should rather be understood spiritually: divine justice, which repays each person according to his works, sometimes punishes sin by manifest vengeance and sometimes avenges it by hidden judgment through kings and commanders. It avenges it through prophets and priests when it causes some wrongdoers to be punished by the sword, while it pierces others with the sword of the tongue.

Thus David, Solomon, and the other kings exacted punishment from the guilty when they ordered them to be slaughtered. And elsewhere it is written concerning the punishment of the proud and disobedient: “I hewed them,” he says, “by the prophets; I killed them by the words of my mouth” (Hosea 6).

Elijah, being taken up, signifies the Lord’s ascension. Elijah postponed death but did not escape it; our Redeemer, however, did not postpone death but conquered it, destroyed it by rising again, and revealed the glory of his resurrection by ascending. It should also be noted that Elijah is read to have ascended in a chariot, so that it might clearly be shown that a mere human being needed assistance from another. For that aid was provided and displayed by angels, because he could not ascend even to the aerial heaven by himself, being weighed down by the weakness of his nature.

Our Redeemer, however, is read to have been lifted up neither by a chariot nor by angels, because he who had made all things was borne above all things by his own power. He returned there where he was, and went back from there where he remained: for while he ascended into heaven in his humanity, through his divinity he continued to contain both earth and heaven.

Just as Joseph, sold by his brothers, prefigured the selling of our Redeemer, so Enoch, translated, and Elijah, lifted up to the aerial heaven, signified the Lord’s ascension. The Lord had two forerunners and witnesses of his ascension: one before the law and the other under the law, so that he himself might eventually come, the one who could truly penetrate the heavens. The order in their two modes of being lifted up is also distinguished by stages of increase.

Enoch is said to have been translated, while Elijah was carried up to heaven, so that afterward he might come who, neither translated nor carried, would penetrate the ethereal heaven by his own power; and who would grant purity of flesh to us who believe in him, while under him the virtue of chastity would increase through the progress of the ages.

In their very translation—since they signified the Lord’s ascension as servants—and in the Lord himself, who ascended into heaven, this distinction is also displayed. Enoch had a wife and children, whereas Elijah is read to have had neither wife nor children. Consider, therefore, how purity of chastity increased through stages, as this is plainly shown both by the servants who were translated and by the person of the ascending Lord. Enoch was translated: he was begotten through intercourse and begot through intercourse. Elijah was taken up: he was begotten through intercourse, but did not himself beget through intercourse. The Lord, however, was taken up, neither begetting through intercourse nor begotten through intercourse.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Column 1103A] On Elisha

“Elijah was indeed covered in the whirlwind, and his spirit was completed in Elisha. In his days he did not fear a ruler, and no one overcame him in power. No word defeated him, and he prophesied even when dead. In his life he performed wonders, and in his death he worked marvels. In all these things the people did not repent and did not turn away from their sins, until they were expelled from their land and scattered throughout the whole earth. Only a very small people remained, and a prince in the house of David. Some of them did what pleased God, while others committed many sins.”

When Elijah was about to be lifted from earth to heaven by the will of God, Elisha, his disciple, asked that his spirit might be doubled in him; and, by God’s gift, he obtained this. Therefore, in power and might he was unconquerable by his enemies, and in his life and death he performed wonders of signs and marvelous works.

When it says that his dead body prophesied, it shows that the raising of the corpse was a mystical work. The corpse was thrown into Elisha’s tomb, as the history of Kings relates; but the people of Israel were not moved to repentance by such power of signs, nor did they turn away from their sins, until they were expelled from their land and led into captivity (II Kings 13).

When it says, “Only a very small people remained, and a prince in the house of David; some of them did what pleased God, while others committed many sins,” it shows that the descendants of the house of David and the tribes of Judah and Benjamin did not entirely abandon the worship of God and his temple, as did the ten tribes who were in Samaria. Some of them, however, were idolaters, such as Joram, Ahaz, Manasseh, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah; others clung to their God, as did Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah.

Their subjects likewise held differing opinions: some walked in the right way, while others limped through error. Consequently, when many had already departed from the truth, the punishment of captivity was finally sent, so that those who had worshiped images in their own land might also worship idols in a foreign land.

It may be asked how Elisha, when his teacher Elijah offered him the opportunity to make a request, could ask for a double spirit of Elijah, when the Lord says in the Gospel, “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matthew 10); yet everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher. If the mystery of this request is considered, it is judged not an inappropriate but a necessary petition.

Elijah therefore said to Elisha: “Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken from you.” And Elisha replied: “I beg that your spirit may be doubled in me.” He answered: “You have asked for a difficult thing. Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, it will be granted to you; but if you do not see me, it will not” (II Kings 2).

Whom does Elijah signify in this passage if not our head, namely the Lord and Redeemer? And whom does Elisha signify if not his body, which is the Church? Our Elijah gives the opportunity to ask when he says in the Gospel: “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew 7). And again: “Ask,” he says, “and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete” (John 16).

With this confidence received from the Lord, Elisha asks—that is, the Christian people ask—that the spirit of Christ may be double in them: namely, a double grace of the Holy Spirit, for the forgiveness of sins and for the bestowal of virtues. Our Redeemer, therefore, who had no sin, neither committed sin nor was deceit found in his mouth, had no need of the forgiveness of sins, since he had no sin. But he performed works of virtue in the Holy Spirit, as he himself says to the Jews in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has certainly come upon you” (Luke 11).

The works of the Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are therefore inseparable. The Truth bears witness, saying: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does” (John 5). And the Apostle says: “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Corinthians 9).

The Church rightly asks to receive the double spirit of Christ, because she needs both the forgiveness of sins, which Christ did not need, and the gift of virtues, which Christ grants from his fullness through the Holy Spirit. Ascending on high, he “led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Ephesians 4)—namely, to those who firmly place their hope in him.

Hence Elijah says to Elisha: “If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be granted to you; but if you do not see me, it will not” (II Kings 2). For unless someone fixes upon him the eyes of right faith and faithfully believes in his passion, resurrection, and ascension to the Father, he will not obtain the fruit of his request.

“Elisha died, therefore, and they buried him. In that same year, raiders from Moab came into the land. As some people were burying a man, they saw the raiders and threw the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came to life and stood upon his feet” (II Kings 13).

What does this raising of a dead corpse through contact with Elisha’s bones signify except the life of the faithful, which truly consists in the death of Christ? Whoever, therefore, touches Christ’s death with firm faith and truly places his hope in him will undoubtedly share in his resurrection. The Truth himself says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me will never die forever” (John 11). And elsewhere: “As Moses,” he says, “lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XIX. On Hezekiah
“Ezekias fortified his city, brought water into its midst, excavated a rock with iron, and built a reservoir beside the water. In his days Sennacherib came up, sent Rabshakeh, raised his hand against them, and lifted his hand against Zion; and he became proud because of his power. [Col. 1105A] Then their hearts and hands were shaken, and they suffered like women in labor, and they called upon the merciful Lord. Stretching out their hands, they raised them to heaven, and the holy Lord God quickly heard their voice. He did not remember their sins, nor did he give them over to their enemies, but cleansed them by the hand of Isaiah the holy prophet. The angel of the Lord overthrew the camp of the Assyrians and crushed them.”

The history of Ezekias is fully set forth in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, where it is related that he industriously repaired the entire wall that had been destroyed, built towers upon it, constructed another wall outside it, restored the Millo in the city of David, made weapons and shields of every kind, and appointed commanders [Col. 1105B] of the warriors. There too it is not passed over in silence that he brought water into the city, stopped up the springs and the stream that flowed through the middle of the land—that is, what is said here: “He excavated a rock with iron and built a reservoir beside the waters.” Mystically, however, this refers to the holy city, of which it is written: “The Savior is the city of our strength, which is situated upon a mountain and cannot be hidden” (Isa. XXVI). Concerning it another passage says: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God” (Ps. XLV). And again: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI).

He establishes and fortifies it. Concerning him the Father says, “He has built my city.” He restores and constructs the entire wall of sound faith and true religion, which had been partly dismantled by the wickedness of pagans or heretics, and he raises towers of virtues. [Col. 1105C] He also places outside it another wall, that is, an outer rampart, which in the construction of fortifications they commonly call *luricula*, when he teaches that the efficacy of good works must be maintained. For it is not enough to have the wall of faith unless faith itself is confirmed by good works. This wall and outer rampart are built from living stones, which, according to the Prophet, roll upon the earth.

The same king made weapons and shields of every kind when he composed various testimonies from the holy Scriptures and arranged evangelical teaching as a defense for his Church. He also appointed teachers to be commanders of the spiritual warriors, so that they might conduct the entire army rightly and rationally and defend the camp of the Church opportunely against all its enemies.

When Ezekias, while the Assyrians were harassing the land of the Jews by war and fighting against Jerusalem, ordered the springs and the stream flowing through the middle of the land to be stopped up, so that the invading kings of the Assyrians would not find an abundance of water, this signifies that diligence and caution must be employed against pagans and heretics who resist and blaspheme, and that the mysteries of the divine sacraments must be concealed from them. Nor should the word of God be shamelessly thrust upon blasphemers who do not know how to honor holy doctrine by upright conduct, but instead strive to tear it apart with their poisonous mouths.

As for the statement that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, sent a powerful force against Jerusalem through the blaspheming Rabshakeh in order to overthrow it, and that, when Ezekias and Isaiah prayed together with the rest of the people, the Lord delivered [Col. 1106A] both the city and its people by destroying their enemies, the Books of Chronicles show this, where we read:

“Therefore King Ezekias and Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, prayed against this blasphemy and cried out to heaven. And the Lord sent an angel who struck every strong man, warrior, and commander of the army of the king of Assyria; and he returned in disgrace to his own land” (II Chron. XXXII).

“The angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians.” They rose in the morning, and behold, all were the corpses of the dead. He departed and went away; “and Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, returned and dwelt in Nineveh.” And it happened that, “when he was worshiping in the temple of Nesroch, his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him with the sword, and they fled into the land of Ararat; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.”

One hundred and eighty-five thousand very powerful men were slain by a single angel in a single night. A savage death swept among them without wounds being inflicted on the slain, separating their souls from their bodies by the will of the Lord. The king alone was preserved at that time so that he might learn the power of God, restrain his blaspheming mouth, and become a witness to the majesty that he had shortly before despised. Pharaoh too was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he might perish last; and this man likewise was destined to suffer the same fate.

For when he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and worshiped in the temple of Nesroch, his god, as though he had returned victorious from his enemies, and proceeded triumphantly and joyfully into the shrine of his idol, he—the despiser of the true God—was slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity. Nor did he perish by the sword of an angel, which was a fate shared with many others, but by the murder committed by his own sons.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Prophet Isaiah

“For Ezekias did what was pleasing to God and walked valiantly in the way of his father David, which the great and faithful prophet Isaiah had commanded him in the sight of God. In his days the sun went backward and added life to the king. With great spirit he saw the final things, consoled those mourning in Zion forever, and revealed future and hidden things before they came to pass.”

How Ezekias pleased God through good works, how he was healed of his illness through the prophet Isaiah, and how, at his request for a sign, the course of the sun was altered for this purpose, so that it moved backward by ten lines, is sufficiently explained by the Books of Kings and Chronicles, as well as by the Book of Isaiah.

This Isaiah, therefore, with prophetic spirit, discussed at great length in his book the future and hidden mysteries concerning Christ’s advent, the redemption of the human race, the condition of the Church, and God’s future judgment. It would be superfluous to offer examples here, since almost the entire book, insofar as it concerns the spiritual meaning, is occupied with these matters.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Josiah

(CAP. XLIX.) “The memory of Josiah became like the work of a perfumer, composed of fragrant odors. In every mouth his memory will be sweetened like honey, and like music at a banquet of wine. He was divinely directed in the repentance of the nation and removed impiety from human beings. He guided his heart toward the Lord, and in the days of sinners he strengthened devotion.”

He rightly compares the memory of King Josiah to the fragrance of a perfumer’s work, to the sweetness of honey, and to a musical instrument, because the fame of his virtue, the sweetness of his moderation, and his zeal in restoring the worship of God surpass every fragrance of perfumes, every sweetness of honey, and every song of musical art. He could rightly say with David:

“How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth. Therefore I have loved your commandments above gold and topaz. Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. CXVIII).

Scripture relates concerning him that, while he was still a boy, he began to seek the Lord, the God of his father David. He cleansed Judah and Jerusalem from the high places, sacred groves, idols, and carved images; he destroyed the altars and idols, cut down the groves and carved images, and burned the bones of the priests upon the altars of the idols. He cleansed Judah and Jerusalem, and in the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, as far as Naphtali, he overturned everything.

According to the allegorical interpretation, this Josiah prefigures the Lord Savior, who is rightly called the salvation and strength of the Lord, because he is the one of whom Scripture says: “The Lord is strong, the Lord is mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII). And elsewhere: “He himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I).

He, in his zeal for God, cleanses the land of Judah and Jerusalem from every impurity and abomination; through the Prophet he said: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. LXVIII). John too says of him: “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will cleanse his threshing floor” (Matt. III).

Malachi also says of him:

“Behold, he comes, says the Lord of hosts; who will be able to consider the day of his coming, and who will stand to see him? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fuller’s herb. He will sit refining and cleansing silver; he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness. The sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem will please God as in the ancient days and as in former years. I will draw near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against sorcerers, adulterers, and perjurers; against those who oppress the wages of a hired laborer, who humble widows and orphans, and who crush the stranger, and who have not feared me, says the Lord of hosts” (Mal. III).

What is added afterward in the praises of Josiah is this:

“Apart from David, Ezekias, and Josiah, all committed sin; for the kings of Judah abandoned the law of the Most High.”

This indicates that these three kings were especially pleasing to God because of the devotion of heart and the worshipful piety that they displayed in God’s service. Although each of them was caught in some crime and found blameworthy, they erased what they had done wickedly through worthy repentance and therefore merited complete pardon.

There were also other kings in Judah whose works of piety are mentioned, but they were not as perfect as those of these three. Most of the kings of Judah, like the kings of Israel, had turned toward impious deeds and sinful crimes. Consequently, they received the punishment they deserved, as is shown below.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Jeremiah

“The kings of Judah failed and despised the fear of God. For they gave their kingdom to others and their glory to a foreign nation. They burned the chosen city of holiness and made its roads desolate by the hand of Jeremiah, for they treated badly the one who had been consecrated as a prophet from his mother’s womb: to overthrow and uproot, to destroy, and again to build and renew.”

What does it mean that he says the nations burned the chosen city of holiness and made its roads desolate “by the hand of Jeremiah,” except that in Jeremiah’s writings and words the future devastation of Jerusalem and her daughters was revealed? This prophet lived, as he himself testifies, during the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah, kings of Judah. He continually restrained the people from sins and urged them to conversion and good works; but they treated badly the one who had been consecrated as a prophet from his mother’s womb—to overthrow, uproot, destroy, and again build and renew (Jer. I).

For it is written in the same prophet, where the Lord says to him:

“Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and overthrow, to build and to plant” (ibid.).

It should be noted that four gloomy things are followed by two joyful ones. Good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor the best things planted unless the worst had been uprooted. “Every planting that the heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. XV). And a building that has no foundation upon rock but has been constructed on sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God. That building which Jesus will consume with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the advent of his presence—namely, “every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine”—he will destroy forever (II Thess. II).

Moreover, those things that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God and trust in their own wisdom, which is foolishness with God, he will disperse and bring down, so that humble things may be built in their place, and in place of what has been destroyed and uprooted there may be constructed and planted things that accord with ecclesiastical truth. Thus what the Apostle says may be fulfilled: “You are God’s building, God’s agriculture” (I Cor. III).

Many understand this passage as referring to the person of Christ. For Jeremiah is interpreted as “exalted of the Lord”; he destroyed the kingdoms of the devil, which the devil had shown him upon a high mountain. He defeated the opposing powers, erasing the record of errors on the cross. Concerning these, after the historical meaning, he speaks *tropically* (*tropikōs*, that is, figuratively) in the psalm:

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vain things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers gathered together” (Ps. II).

In place of those things uprooted, destroyed, ruined, and dragged down to the lower regions, the Church of God is built and planted.

## CHAPTER XXIII. [Col. 1109A] On Ezekiel

“Ezekiel, who saw the vision of glory that he showed him upon the chariot of the cherubim. For he was mindful of enemies in the rain and did good to those who showed the right paths.”

The prophet Ezekiel, therefore, in his first vision, in which he saw four living creatures of four kinds and four wheels beside them, saw the glory of the Lord in the likeness of the appearance of a man seated upon a throne. In another vision he saw the glory of the Lord above the cherubim, and the sound of the cherubim’s wings was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of almighty God speaking.

As for the statement that he was mindful of enemies in the rain and did good to those who showed the right paths, this signifies that he proclaimed that a rain of vengeance would come upon sinners and promised the consolation of mercy to those who walked in the way of God’s commandments. Concerning this way the Psalmist entreats the Lord, saying:

“Establish a law for me, O Lord, in your way, and direct me on a straight path because of my enemies” (Isa. XXVI).

Mystically, Ezekiel—whose name is interpreted as “strengthened by God”—dwelling in Babylon and foretelling the coming captivity to a sinful people, while promising forgiveness of sins to the converted and penitent, signifies the Lord Savior, who is the power and wisdom of God and is called by the Prophet the arm of the Lord. He visited us, placed as we are in the captivity of this age. There he foretold future punishments to sinners and promised eternal remedies to the penitent.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Twelve Prophets

“And the bones of the twelve prophets sprout from their place. For they strengthened Jacob and redeemed themselves by faith in power.”

Unless I am mistaken, he now names the twelve whom we call the Minor Prophets, whose short books exist together in writing. The first in their catalog is Hosea, and the last is Malachi, whom the Hebrews assert to have been Ezra the scribe and teacher of the Law.

Their bones therefore sprout from their place because they left their descendants a worthy remembrance of good examples. They strengthened Jacob by their preaching and redeemed themselves by faith in power when, by announcing the word of God to the people, they freed themselves from the guilt of harmful silence. This accords with the Lord’s statement to the prophet Ezekiel:

“Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Therefore, hearing the word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘Wicked one, you shall surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if, when you announce to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, he does not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but you will have saved your own soul” (Ezek. III).

## CHAPTER XXV. [Col. 1110A] On Zerubbabel and Jesus son of Jehozadak

“How shall we magnify Zerubbabel? For he too is like a signet ring in Israel’s right hand; and Jesus son of Jehozadak, who in their days built the house and exalted the holy temple for the Lord, prepared for everlasting glory.”

This Zerubbabel was the leader of the people of Israel. Returning from Babylon with Jesus the high priest, son of Jehozadak, and the rest of the Israelites, he restored the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem, as the present passage makes clear. How he is a signet ring in Israel’s right hand is shown by the prophet Haggai at the end of his book, where he says:

“On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant, says the Lord of hosts, and I will set you as a signet ring, because I have chosen you, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. II).

Finally, the prophet is commanded to speak only to Zerubbabel, because we have shown that, as a type of Christ, he preceded Christ on account of the assumption of a body from the seed of David. To him, therefore, the things that will occur at the end are spoken: that the form of this world will pass away, that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, that the Lord will shake heaven and earth, destroy every principality, power, and virtue, and overthrow the thrones of kings, after the destruction of the seats and strength of rulers, together with chariots, horses, and horsemen.

“On that day, says the Lord of hosts, I will take you, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, my servant.” He is called a servant on account of the human body, because then the Son himself will be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, and amid all things subjected, he too will be seen as subject. But when this has been fulfilled, God will set him as a signet ring in his hand.

For God the Father marks him, and he is the image of the invisible God, his form and substance, so that whoever believes in God may be sealed with him as with a ring.

As for the statement that Zerubbabel and Jesus built the destroyed house and exalted the holy temple for the Lord, this signifies that, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is our king and priest, after the captivity of demonic domination has been dissolved, those who recover from the devil’s snares—by which they had been held captive according to his will—had not only lost the sincerity and integrity of faith and good works, but through the bitterness of their crimes had also become like pagans and publicans, according to the Lord’s saying: “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a publican” (Matt. XVIII).

After seventy years—that is, after the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit through observance of the Decalogue—those whom he visited and consoled are set free, and they rebuild the house of God and the holy city. For sometimes those who, because of their sins, had been separated from communion and fellowship with the holy Church and joined to the society and number of unbelievers, again diligently practice good works through the gift of the Holy Spirit. By this means they regain fellowship with the faithful—the house and city of the Lord—from which they had been expelled.

It is rightly said that this holy temple is prepared for the Lord in everlasting glory, because it is not the material temple that Solomon built, but the temple that Christ constructed from living stones, which will remain in everlasting glory.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Nehemiah

“And Nehemiah, remembered for a long time, who raised up our fallen walls, made the gates and bars stand firm, and rebuilt our houses.”

Nehemiah, whose name is interpreted in Latin as “the Lord is a comforter,” was himself consoled by the Lord. He renewed the walls of Jerusalem and raised it, freed from the attacks of enemies, in observance of the divine Law. It is therefore clear that by his name, work, and person he appropriately signifies the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ. He indicated that he had been sent to console the poor in spirit when, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said to his disciples: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete—that is, a Comforter.” The Psalmist shows that through him the city of God, namely the holy Church, is to be built and the sorrowful consoled, when he says:

“The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel; he heals the brokenhearted, and so forth” (Ps. CXLVI).

The figure of Nehemiah also accords with the holy preachers, through whose ministry heavenly consolation is provided to us. When they promise the penitent hope of pardon and divine reconciliation because of the fall of sin, they restore, as it were, the walls and ramparts of Jerusalem that had been demolished by enemies.

The words of Nehemiah suit them well:

“I came to Jerusalem and remained there for three days. I rose during the night, I and a few men with me, and I told no one what God had put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. I had no animal with me except the beast on which I was riding. I went out by the Valley Gate at night,” and so forth, until he says: “I inspected the wall, then I returned and came to the Valley Gate, and I went back” (Neh. I).

He travels through the various ruined places of the city, examining each one carefully to determine how it ought to be repaired. So too it is the duty of spiritual teachers frequently to rise at night and, with diligent investigation, examine the state of the holy Church while the others are at rest, so that they may vigilantly inquire how they should correct and raise up through discipline whatever has been defiled or thrown down in it by the battles of vices.

The wall of Jerusalem lies dismantled when the conduct of the faithful is sullied by earthly and base affections. The gates have been consumed by fire when those who ought to have opened the entrance to life for others through teaching have abandoned the teaching of truth, grow sluggish with the rest through indolence, and serve temporal concerns.

And he said to them:

“You know the affliction in which we are, because Jerusalem is desolate and its gates have been consumed by fire. Come, let us build the wall of Jerusalem,” and so forth, until he says: “Their hands were strengthened for good” (Neh. II).

These words are plain and highly suited to the spiritual meaning, because holy teachers—or rather, all who burn with zeal for God—are in great affliction as long as they see Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace which the Lord left and entrusted to us, laid waste by the wars of dissension. They see the gates of the virtues, which according to Isaiah ought to have been occupied by praise, cast down and held in contempt because the gates of hell have prevailed.

Therefore they strive, gathering the ministers of the word into united action, to make the buildings of faith and good conduct that had seemed destroyed rise again more quickly.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Recapitulation concerning Enoch

“No one was born on earth like Enoch, for he too was taken from the earth.”

Why does he discuss Enoch above and now recapitulate concerning him again, except that by his translation he prefigured the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven? Christ was incarnate in the final age of the world, and all the patriarchs and prophets bore witness to him.

It is rightly said of him that no one was born on earth like Enoch—that is, “dedication”—for he dedicated his Church and consecrated it with his holy blood. He came into the world without sin and was received into heaven in glory.

Of him the Psalmist says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV); and again: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. LXVII).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Joseph

“And Joseph was born a man, prince of his brothers, support of the nation, ruler of his brothers, and stabilizing force of the people. His bones were visited, and after death they prophesied.”

Joseph, who in name and action prefigured the Lord Savior, is aptly called prince and ruler of his brothers, support of the nation, and stabilizing force of the people. His name Joseph is interpreted as “increased,” and our Lord is rightly said to be increased because he is completely filled with the grace of God. To him “the Father did not give the Spirit by measure,” but everything the Father has belongs to him, and in him “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” From his fullness we too have all received “grace upon grace.” In him also “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.”

He is the prince and ruler of his brothers—namely, those brothers of whom he himself says, “Go, announce it to my brothers” (Matt. XVIII)—and of whom the Prophet says: “I will announce your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. XXI).

He is likewise the support of the Jewish nation and the stabilizing force of the Christian people, because he himself “was sent as a light for revelation to the nations and for the glory of his people Israel” (Luke II).

As for the statement that Joseph’s bones were visited and prophesied after his death, historically it recalls that Joseph himself foretold to his brothers, before his death, their liberation from Egypt. He consoled them and said: “God will visit you; carry my bones with you from this place” (Gen. L). This was fulfilled, as the Book of Exodus records, when the children of Israel went out from Egypt. After they came into the promised land, they buried him in Shechem, in the city of his father, which is now called Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans (Josh. XXIV).

Spiritually, however, the fact that Joseph, like his father Jacob, desired the promised land with his whole mind and detested dwelling in Egypt instructs us that, as long as we are in this world, we should always desire to enter the land of the living and wish to rest there. This is rightly accomplished if we imitate the number of his years in our conduct.

He died after completing one hundred and ten years of life. Let us therefore strive, through observance of the Decalogue, to reach eternal blessedness, which the number one hundred signifies.

## CHAPTER XXIX. [Col. 1113B] On Seth and Shem

“Seth and Shem attained glory among human beings, and Adam was above every living being in the beginning.”

In an inverted order he first placed the prophets and afterward the most ancient patriarchs. But this is a very common practice of sacred Scripture, to alter places and times in its narrative.

Seth, therefore, the son of Adam, and Shem, Noah’s firstborn, attained glory among human beings because they surpassed the people of their age both in faith and in good conduct, when many were serving idolatry and God regretted that he had made humanity on the earth.

But if this interpretation displeases you, turn to the allegory and understand that in these two men he prefigured the one who is God and man, whom God the Father raised from the dead and established at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, and above every name that is named—not only in this age but also in the age to come—and placed all things beneath his feet.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Simon son of Onias the Priest, and on His Constancy in the Fear of God and His Wonderful Adornment of the Lord’s Temple

(CAP. L.) “Simon, son of Onias, the great priest, who during his life propped up the house and in his days strengthened the temple. The height of the temple was also founded by him: a double building, and the lofty walls of the temple.”

After the earlier fathers, the writer of the history comes to the people of his own time. This Simon was the son of Onias, who was born from Simon surnamed the Just [Col. 1113D] because of his careful devotion toward God and his ready clemency toward his fellow citizens.

According to Josephus, this Onias, being childish in mind and greedy for money, provoked King Ptolemy to anger by refusing to pay tribute. Josephus, however, a man distinguished among his people, was sent by the Jews as an envoy to Ptolemy. Because he had earned the king’s friendship through many services to him, he was appointed commander of Judea and the neighboring regions.

When the aforementioned Onias died, he left the high-priesthood to his son Simon. After Simon’s death, his son Onias succeeded him in office; King Darius of the Lacedaemonians sent an embassy and letters to him. This Simon was high priest of the Jews at the time when Ptolemy Euergetes ruled in Egypt, Seleucus in Syria and Asia, and Antigonus among the Macedonians.

It is quite clear that this Jesus expressed the modesty and zeal of this Simon plainly, since both lived at the same time among the Jewish people. For if he had not known his life and character, he would never have narrated so fully about him. Since we nowhere read elsewhere about this man’s deeds, however, we cannot explain what is unknown.

According to the mystical meaning, we can transfer the praiseworthy deeds and vigorous ministry of this Simon to the order and office of holy teachers. The name Simon aptly suits them, since by the word of preaching they summon the human race to repentance for sins and command them to obey God’s commandments.

Simon is interpreted as “put away sorrow” or “hear sorrow.” This spiritual Simon, during the present life, supports the house of the Church through the speech of teaching and strengthens the temple constructed from living stones. “The height of the temple was founded by him: a double building, the lofty walls of the temple.”

Hence Paul says:

“We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s agriculture, God’s building. According to the grace given to me, like a wise architect I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it” (I Cor. III).

The Apostle mentioned above makes clear what the foundation of this building is by adding:

“For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.”

Holy teachers therefore lay the foundation of the temple’s height when they place the incarnation, passion, and resurrection of Christ within the faith of believers, so that the summit of the entire building—that is, the form of good works—may rise from it.

Thus the double building makes the lofty walls of the temple when, by word and example, they raise many from Jews and Gentiles to the citadel of the virtues through teaching and exhortation. In the expositions of the Catholic Fathers we find that the two peoples are understood as the walls of God’s house—and rightly so, because the structure rising from them grows into a holy temple in the Lord.

“During his days wells of water flowed forth, and they were filled beyond measure, like a sea.”

We cannot better understand the wells of water than as the depth of knowledge of the holy Scriptures, which lay hidden in the divine books, enclosed as it were within figures, but through the mouths of holy preachers overflowed like a sea for the satisfaction of many. What had previously lain obscure in the depths of mystery was opened and brought forth through the labor of the orthodox preacher.

“He cared for his nation and delivered it from destruction.”

By the word of the Gospel, that is, and by the sacrament of baptism, he delivered his hearers from sins and from the dominion of Satan.

“He prevailed in enlarging the city,” when, through the grace of Christ, the labor of preachers advanced toward the salvation of many. The city of God is the holy Church. Concerning it the psalm says: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI).

The order of holy preachers therefore enlarges it when, through the word of preaching and the sacrament of baptism, it increases the number of believers. Through their conversion he too will be glorified when he receives his reward. Hence it follows:

“He attained glory in the conduct of the nation, and through entering the house and the court he was enlarged like the morning star in the midst of a cloud. Like the full moon in his days he shines, and like the radiant sun he gleamed in the temple of God.”

Through entering the house and the court, therefore, the most excellent order of holy preachers is enlarged, because the merit of teachers increases both among those who are still inexperienced in the faith, which the court signifies, and among the imperfect who enter the house of God by advancing in good works. Their merit overflows into heavenly reward.

When he compares them with the morning star, the light of the moon, and the brightness of the sun, he signifies the differences of learning and merit among the teachers themselves. They differ from one another because they possess different gifts, as Paul says:

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

Hence he says elsewhere:

“There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory. All indeed shine, but according to the gift given to each by God” (I Cor. XV).

“And like a radiant bow among clouds of glory.”

By the bow the knowledge of the holy Scriptures is signified, through which the arrows of divine testimonies are shot into the hearts of hearers. He rightly says that the bow shines among clouds of glory, because amid the obscurity of allegory the splendor of divine wisdom gleams.

“And like a rose blossom in the days of spring, and like lilies that are beside flowing water.”

What is expressed by rose blossoms in the days of spring except the blood of the martyrs in the greenness of the emerging Church? For at that time holy preachers were especially slaughtered for the doctrine of evangelical faith. And what is signified by lilies except the order of the chaste and virgins, who, amid the transience of the passing age, made themselves eunuchs for the love of God?

“Like fragrant incense in the days of summer, and like a fire shining, and incense burning in the fire.”

In incense, therefore, pure prayer is expressed. It is fragrant in the days of summer because its odor is spread in the brightness of faith, and it burns in the fire of love. Although incense naturally has a pleasant smell, when it is placed upon fire it gives off a stronger fragrance. So too pure prayer, although pleasing to God in itself, becomes more pleasing before God if, once the fire of trials has been applied, it perseveres in love.

“‘And like a solid golden vessel adorned with every precious stone.’ In the gold the splendor of wisdom is expressed; in the precious stones also the beauty of virtues is signified. When, therefore, sacred virtues are mingled with the radiance of wisdom, the soul possessing these things is shown to be most precious.

“‘Like an olive tree putting forth shoots, and like a cypress rising to the heights.’ In the olive tree one may rightly understand the light of faith and the affection of mercy; in the cypress, the height of perfection and the very sweet fragrance of good will possessed by the saints. But if anyone wishes to know more fully the meaning of the olive and the cypress, he can find it in what precedes.

“‘In receiving the robe of glory and clothing himself with the fullness of virtue. In ascending the holy altar he gave glory, the mantle of holiness. And in receiving portions from the hand of the priests.’ In receiving, therefore, the robe of glory and clothing himself with the fullness of virtues, the sacred order of preachers openly displays the judgment of its dignity with the adornment of right faith and the clothing of good works. Thus Moses commands that, in the priestly vestment, the ephod—that is, the shoulder-piece—be made first, because in a priest of Christ it is fitting that good works should shine forth first, and that he should proceed in this way to teach others. His works ought to be known first, so that, when what is outwardly evident to all has appeared irreproachable, the integrity of his heart and the sincerity of his faith may likewise be preserved in due course. For it is written of the very Prince of Shepherds: ‘Jesus began both to do and to teach’ (Acts I). Hence, ‘Whoever does the commandments of God and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever breaks one of the least of God’s commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. V). In ascending the altar he will give a mantle of holiness who rightly guards the rights of his priesthood, so that he may properly teach his subjects and daily pour out prayers to God for them. But he receives portions from the hand of the priests who demands from the ministers of good works an action that will be useful both to himself and to them. This is also rightly done if the teacher himself first displays the practice of good works before his disciples, so that they may have from him an example of virtue to follow. Hence it continues:

“‘And he himself stood beside the altar, and around him was a crown of brothers; and like a planting of cedars on Mount Lebanon, so they stood around him like branches of palm trees, and all the sons of Aaron in their glory; but the offering of the Lord was in their hands, before the whole assembly of Israel.’ It is good, therefore, that the one who is first in rank should be foremost in good works and in instruction. Then his brothers should surround him—that is, imitate him. For by ‘brothers’ here we can understand priests, deacons, and men of the other lesser orders, who follow the pious example of the good shepherd and, before the whole assembly of Israel—that is, the multitude of believers—worthily perform the duty of their order, so that all may thereby be moved to praise almighty God. For Truth itself thus commanded in the Gospel, saying: ‘Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. V).”

“‘And fulfilling his service at the altar, he magnifies the offering of the exalted King. He stretched out his hand over the libation and poured out some of the blood of the grape. He poured forth a divine fragrance at the foundation of the altar for the exalted Prince.’ The offering serves the exalted King in its fullness when Christ’s body is offered to God, the ruler of all, upon the holy altar. There too a libation is made from the blood of the grape when the Redeemer’s blood is presented in the chalice. This must be poured out at the foundation of the altar—that is, everything must be done in remembrance of our Redeemer. For he is the foundation that bears the entire structure of the Church. The fragrance of this offering is most sweet to the exalted Prince, because it is pleasing and exceedingly acceptable to God the almighty Father.

“‘Then the sons of Aaron cried out, and sounded the beaten trumpets, and made a great voice heard in remembrance before the Lord.’ The sons of Aaron are indeed the priests of Christ and ministers of the divine altar. They raise their voice on beaten trumpets—that is, they present the preaching of the doctrine perfected through suffering as a memorial before the Lord. They are fittingly called ‘beaten,’ because the faithful, struck by various sufferings, advance by the Lord’s generosity; and they grow all the more the more often they are struck by the blows of cruel hammers. For the hammer is the devil, of whom the prophet says: ‘The hammer of the whole earth has been shattered’ (Jer. L).

“‘Then all the people hurried together, and fell on their faces upon the earth to adore the Lord their God, and to offer prayers to the exalted almighty God, and they magnified, singing with their voices.’ When, therefore, the ecclesiastical office is worthily performed in remembrance of the Lord by the ministers of Christ’s altar, then the whole people of believers are also moved to praise and adore the Lord. They prostrate themselves on their faces—that is, they display before God the humility of their heart. They offer prayers and sing with a voice of rejoicing, because whatever they do in the fear and love of God is wholly prayer and an aroma of sweetness before God.

“‘And in the great house there was made a sound full of sweetness. And the people entreated the exalted Lord in prayer until the honor of the Lord was perfected, and they completed their offering.’ The great house, therefore, is the catholic Church, in which the greater and the lesser produce a sweet sound, because whatever is offered to God in the unity of right faith is presented rightly and in due order; but whatever is done outside the Church is wholly reckoned as impiety. A great sound is therefore made in the Church when, while the priests pray and bless, the whole people respond, ‘Amen.’ This sound pertains both to the cry of the voice and to the devotion of the heart, because a human being sees the face, but God looks upon the heart. The people therefore entreat the exalted Lord in prayer until the honor of the Lord is completed, because the whole Church of the faithful strives for this: it labors to persevere in prayer and in the praises of God until the consummation of the world, when the body of Christ will be honored in incorruption and the members will be joined to their head.

“‘Then, descending, he raised his hands over the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, to give glory to God with his lips and to glory in his name. And he repeated his prayer, wishing to show the power of God. And he prayed still more to the Lord of all, who has done great things throughout the whole earth, who has increased our days from our mother’s womb, and has dealt with us according to his mercy: may he grant us gladness of heart and make peace in our days in Israel for everlasting days; may Israel believe that the mercy of God is with us, so that it may deliver us in its days.’ Then the assembly of holy teachers, rejoicing, raises its hands over the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, when it gives thanks to God for the completion of its labor and for the salvation of the entire people. Then it multiplies its praises; then it repeats its prayer, because it never ceases from the praises of God, wishing to show the power of God—that is, to recount and proclaim the mercy of him who grants us gladness of heart and peace in everlasting times—so that all Israelites, that is, true worshipers of God and lovers of the eternal King, may acknowledge and proclaim the power and goodness of God in the deliverance of his people.

“‘My soul hates two nations; but the third is not a nation that I hate: those who dwell on Mount Seir, and the Philistines, and the foolish people who dwell in Shechem.’ He says that he hates two nations. One of them is the Jewish nation established under the letter of the Law, which is also designated by the name Seir, interpreted as ‘rough’ or ‘hairy.’ For Seir was the same as Esau, whose name is interpreted as ‘red,’ the elder son of Isaac and Rebekah; the younger was called Jacob. But why was he wholly red and hairy, unless because the earlier people were stained with the blood of the prophets and of Christ and were surrounded by the filth of sin and wickedness? The younger held his heel for this reason: mystically, the younger people were destined to overcome the elder people. For this is the crooked, perverse, and adulterous generation, according to the truthful word of the Gospel, which ‘killed the prophets and stoned those who were sent to it. Finally, it did not shrink from laying impious hands upon the heir himself and slaughtering the Son of God’ (Luke XIII). Wisdom therefore detests this nation because it persistently remains in hardness of heart and stupidity of understanding. It is said to sit upon a mountain—not, of course, upon the height of virtues, but upon the swelling of pride—because it was always rebellious against God with a stiff neck and an uncircumcised heart.

“The other nation is the Philistines, a name interpreted as ‘double ruin,’ signifying the nation of the Gentiles, which was simultaneously polluted by idolatry and wicked conduct, and therefore hateful because it wandered far from the way of truth. The third is the synagogue of heretics, whose foolish people dwell in Shechem—that is, upon shoulders or in labors—since, by writing perverse things and teaching what is wrong each day, it foolishly exhausts its labor. By saying that this is not a nation, he shows that heretics do not arise from one generation or from a single error, but that, originating in various places, they are subject to many errors and yet mutually opposed to one another. The Arians teach one way, the Sabellians another; the Novatians one way, the Donatists another. Likewise, the rest, divided from one another by false doctrines, differ in speech and are dissimilar, but equal in error.

“‘Jesus son of Sirach the Jerusalemite wrote the teaching of wisdom and discipline in this book, and renewed wisdom from his heart. Blessed is the one who occupies himself with these good things; whoever places them in his heart will always be wise. For if he does these things, he will be capable of all things, because the light of God is his guiding trace.’ The author of the book tells of his labor and of the usefulness of the work itself, showing how much grace it confers upon the one who does not refuse to meditate and work in it. The prologue of the book itself testifies that, when he came into Egypt in the time of Ptolemy Euergetes, the same Jesus produced the present book by interpreting it. Under the wording mentioned in the present chapter, it relates that he completed it solely for the benefit of those who read it attentively and faithfully obey its admonitions in their deeds. Hence he says, ‘Blessed is the one who occupies himself with these good things’—that is, by meditating on the divine commandments and fulfilling them in works. ‘For if he does these things,’ he says, ‘he will be capable of every good and useful thing,’ because the light of God—that is, divine wisdom—is his guiding trace and leader on the way of truth. Through it he will be able to reach the repose of the heavenly kingdom, if he perseveres in walking perfectly along its path.

“After this comes the prayer of the same Jesus, which we more suitably transfer generally to the whole Church than specifically to the person of any individual, because, since many kinds of tribulations and various consolations of assistance are described in it, they are better referred to the whole body than to some part of the body. For the Church prays to its Lord, Christ the King, and gives him thanks for the benefits he has abundantly bestowed upon it, beginning in this way.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Confession and Prayer, or Song, of the Same Son of Sirach
