(CAP. LI.) “I will confess to you, Lord King, and praise you greatly, God my Savior. I will confess to your name, because you have become my helper and protector, and you have delivered my body from destruction, from the snare of an evil tongue, and from the lips of those who practice falsehood.”

For Jesus Christ is Lord and King, God and Savior of the Church, and he is both its head and its bridegroom. Hence the Apostle, admonishing women to be subject to their husbands, wrote to the Ephesians, saying: “Let women be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church. He himself is the Savior of the body” (Eph. V). And again: “Husbands,” he says, “love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, so that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but so that she might be holy and immaculate” (I Cor. XI).

He therefore became the helper and protector of his bride when he gave himself for her, so that he might deliver her from the destruction into which she had fallen through the transgression of the first human being, and from the snare of an evil tongue—that is, from the blasphemy of idolatry, so that she might neither sacrifice to nor serve the creature rather than the Creator—and from the lips of those who practice falsehood, that is, from the false teachings of philosophers and heretics.

“‘And in the sight of those standing by you became my helper. And according to the abundance of the mercy of your name you delivered me from those roaring, prepared as prey.’” By this testimony he expresses the persecutors of the Church, who persecute the faithful out of hatred for the name of Christ and hand them over to various punishments and death, in order to turn them away from confessing the catholic faith and from worshiping the true and one God. He aptly compares them to savage beasts, which seek prey with a powerful roar and fierce open jaws. But the Lord delivers his chosen from them when he preserves their souls unharmed amid the heat of persecutions, on account of whose destruction the savage persecutors chiefly tear their bodies. Hence it follows:

“‘From the hands of those seeking my life, and from the gates of tribulations that surrounded me.’” What can we better understand as the gates of tribulations than the mouths of princes and tyrants? From them threats, deceitful persuasions, and proclamations of punishments proceed, so that, whether through feigned blandishments or through savage tortures, they may compel the servants of God to deny the faith of Christ. But “the Lord sends an angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them.”

“‘From the pressure of the flame that surrounded me, and in the midst of the fire I was not scorched.’” We often read that this happened historically in the sufferings of martyrs. Just as the three young men were preserved unharmed from the heat of the flame in the furnace of fire, so these too were preserved undefiled from the burning of the fire. But because this was not granted to all God’s martyrs, since many of them were physically consumed in the fire, while nevertheless their souls freely sought the secret places of heaven, we more properly understand here by fire and flame the intense heat of persecution. Although it could afflict God’s saints temporally, it could not reach as far as the destruction of their souls. Therefore it continues:

“‘From the depth of the belly of hell, and from a defiled tongue, and from a lying word, from an unrighteous king, and from an unjust tongue.’” We must understand, “He delivered me.” For the accursed power of the enemies could not prevail so far as to reach the destruction of souls—which he here calls the belly of hell—nor could a tongue defiled with blasphemies, nor lying words spoken by an unrighteous king and an unjust tongue, in any way violate the innermost hearts of the saints. Although they afflicted their bodies with various punishments and consigned them to temporal death, their souls nevertheless persevered in confessing the name of Christ until the end of life. Hence, more blessedly after death, they will rejoice without end in eternal life with God’s holy angels. Concerning this it is also said:

“‘My soul will praise the Lord until death, and my life was drawing near to hell below.’” He says that his life draws near to hell because the life of the flesh, daily failing, approaches death. Here “hell” is used for death, because the death of the flesh is the punishment for the first transgression, just as hell is the everlasting punishment of sinful souls. But no one escapes the death of the flesh. For who is the human being who lives and will not see death? Hence it is written elsewhere: “There is no one who lives forever and has confidence in this matter” (Eccl. IX). But holy people can escape the torment of hell through the grace of Christ, because, once released from the bond of the flesh, they will soon pass into heavenly joy.

“‘They surrounded me on every side, and there was no one to help. I looked for human assistance, and there was none. I remembered your mercy, Lord, and your cooperation, which is from eternity; for you deliver those who wait upon you, Lord, and free them from the hands of the nations.’” When the Church sees its members surrounded on every side by enemies and human consolation failing, it seeks help from the one from whom it knows the progress of every good thing to come. It therefore attributes its rescue and deliverance from enemies not to its own merits or to human deeds, but to God’s mercy. Indeed, it recognizes that it has not only been delivered but also already exalted by the honor of virtues and glorified by the splendor of miracles. Hence it says:

“‘You exalted my dwelling above the earth, and I prayed concerning the death that was ebbing away.’” For it sees that it shines in the world through the teaching of faith and signs of virtue, but it is not content with this gift alone, as though it wished to seek nothing further. Rather, it strives through worthy prayers to overcome the narrowness of the present life and thus happily reach the repose of the heavenly homeland.

“‘I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, that he might not abandon me in the day of my tribulation and in the time of the proud, without help. I will praise your name continually, and I will praise it greatly in confession.’” The day of tribulation and the time of the proud are the present life, in which the good are afflicted and the wicked are raised up in pride. The bride of Christ prays that God almighty, the Father of her Lord Jesus Christ, will not abandon her in the time of her need, when the pride of her enemies desires to afflict her with the torment of punishments. She promises that she will praise his name continually and praise it greatly in confession—that is, persevere in confessing his name until the end of life. And as though she were already secure in having obtained help, she continues:

“‘My prayer has been heard; for you delivered me from destruction and rescued me from the time of iniquity. Therefore I will confess, praise you, and bless the name of the Lord.’” This resembles what the Prophet says in the sixth psalm. After he entreated the Lord not to rebuke him in anger or chastise him in fury, asserting that he was troubled by anger and had grown old among all his enemies, he immediately cried out as though already secure in his escape from his enemies: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping; the Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer” (Ps. VI).

Here too the Church, declaring that its prayer has been heard, asserts that it has been rescued from its enemies and freed from the iniquity of the present life, in which confusion now prevails more greatly. It promises that it will perpetually sing praise and confession to its rescuer.

“‘While I was still young, before I wandered astray, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer. Before the time I asked for her, and until the end I will seek her.’” After the prayer that he offered in the person of the Church, the author of this work relates how, from his infancy, he sought wisdom and asked the Lord for it. By saying that, before he was young in age, he sought her and asked for her before the time, he shows that, before the errors of childhood and adolescence and before the season of youthful age, he desired her and earnestly asked the Lord to give her to him, promising that he would seek her until the end. Adolescence and youthful age are fraught with great danger, because the actions of the outward human being prevail especially in that age. As Solomon says in Proverbs: “I utterly failed to know the way of a young man in his adolescence” (Prov. XXX); and the Prophet entreats the Lord not to remember the sins of his youth and his ignorance (Ps. XXIV).

For this reason also the philosophers, adapting the letter Y to human life, assign its left-hand path to childhood and adolescence, but its right-hand summit to a stronger age, when a more vigorous understanding already rejects the folly of the earlier sense. Pythagoras first fashioned this letter as an image of human life in the following way: the thinner stroke at the bottom signified the uncertain condition of the earliest age, which is not yet devoted either to vices or to virtues. The fork that follows begins with adolescence; its right branch is steep but leads toward blessed life, while the left is easier but leads to ruin and destruction. Of this Persius says:

> And for you, to whom the Samian letter traced its branches,  
> It showed the rising path along the right-hand way.

“‘And she blossomed like an early grape; my heart rejoiced in her. My foot walked on the straight path; from my youth I sought her.’” He rightly compares the beauty of wisdom to an early grape, to show that joy is especially powerful in the one who readily offers his will to receive it. Early grapes are so called because they ripen quickly and are warmed by the sun before all others. The Greeks call them *lagos*, because they run swiftly toward maturity, like a hare. Hence he himself says: “Those who keep watch for me early will find me.” And who could find her better than the one who keeps the straight path of God’s commandments? Of him it is written: “If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and God will preserve her for you” (Eccl. I).

“‘I inclined my ear slightly and received her; I found much wisdom within myself, and I made great progress in her.’” To reach the perfection of wisdom is not a matter of human effort but of divine gift. Hence he considers his labor small in acquiring the great understanding that he received by God’s gift. Yet this must be understood: there is a great difference between one who seeks diligently and one who neglects indolently. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. But the indolent person loses through negligence the gain that he could have obtained through diligence.

“‘To the one who gives me wisdom I will give glory.’” He rightly gives glory to the giver of all good things for the gift of wisdom granted to him, because he acknowledges that he possesses the abundance of so great a gift not through his own diligence but through divine grace. But since it is right that, after receiving the gift of understanding, a person should exercise himself in good works, this lover of divine wisdom next sets forth his own example, so that the attentive hearer may imitate his zeal.

“‘For I resolved to practice her. I was zealous for the good, and I shall not be put to shame; my soul struggled with her, and in practicing her I was strengthened.’” Observe that he first says that he resolved to practice her; then that he burned with zeal for the good; afterward that his soul struggled with her; and finally that he was strengthened in practicing her. Understand that first one must form a resolution so that good may be distinguished from evil. Then the will must be turned toward loving what is good. Finally, zeal for good works must be applied, and one must remain in that effort not for a short time but continually and successfully. Thus, strengthened, he will attain the fruit of wisdom. Hence Wisdom herself says in Proverbs: “Counsel is mine, and equity; prudence is mine, and strength. I walk in the ways of justice, in the midst of the paths of judgment, so that I may enrich those who love me and fill their treasures” (Prov. VIII).

“‘I stretched out my hands on high, and my soul shone in her wisdom, and she enlightened my ignorance. I directed my soul toward her, and in knowledge I found her. From the beginning I possessed a heart with her; therefore I shall not be abandoned.’” He stretches out his hands on high who seeks heavenly help through devout prayers. His soul shines in her wisdom when he directs his heart toward meditating upon her with good will. Thus, in knowledge of her, he will find her. For to find wisdom is to receive her fully with an enlightened mind. Since this gift is granted to no others except those who prepare a pure heart for receiving it, he therefore says: “From the beginning I possessed a heart with her,” as though he were saying, “From the beginning I loved her with a pure heart; therefore I shall not be abandoned.” For it is impossible that the practitioner of true wisdom should be abandoned by her, since she herself says: “I love those who love me, and those who keep watch for me early will find me” (Prov. VIII). And elsewhere: “Those who work in me will not sin; those who make me shine will have eternal life” (Eccl. XXIV).

“‘My belly was troubled in seeking her; therefore I shall possess a good possession.’” By saying that his belly was troubled in seeking her, he either indicates that his mind was anxious in meditating upon her, since all discipline is bitter in the present life, or he intimates that through knowledge of her he was pierced with repentance for his sins. Hence it is written: “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.” For this reason John also relates in the Apocalypse that the angel gave him a book and said to him: “Take the book and devour it; it will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.” And he says: “I took the little book from the hand of the angel and devoured it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth. And when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter” (Rev. X). But he possesses a good possession in this, when through such conversion he reaches eternal rest. For “whoever turns back and groans will be saved” (Ezek. III); and, “Blessed are those who mourn now, for they will be comforted” (Matt. V).

“‘For the Lord gave me a tongue as my reward, and with it I will praise him.’” A well-instructed tongue, eloquent in goodness, is a good reward. Whoever possesses it as God’s gift can rightly praise God and properly instruct his neighbor. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “The Lord gave me an instructed tongue, so that I might know how to sustain the one who has fallen by a word.”

“‘Draw near to me, you who are unlearned, and gather yourselves into the house of discipline. Why do you still delay, and why do you say these things? Your souls thirst exceedingly.’” The wise man, with fatherly affection, urges the unlearned and undisciplined to hasten without delay or contradiction and gather themselves into the house of discipline, which is the Church, where true prudence is learned and moral uprightness is constantly maintained. He also reproves and criticizes them because, although they suffer thirst for the word of God, they do not wish to receive the refreshment of spiritual teaching. He immediately makes clear what they ought to do:

“‘I opened my mouth and spoke: Acquire wisdom for yourselves without silver, and submit your necks to her yoke, and let your soul receive discipline. For it is close at hand to find her.’” This is the finest kind of commerce, in which devotion can obtain what a great expenditure of money cannot secure. Whoever therefore learns attentively and lives in discipline will truly obtain the gift of heavenly wisdom. Isaiah expresses a similar thought when he says: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hurry, buy, and eat. Come, buy without silver and without any exchange, wine and milk. Why do you weigh silver for what is not bread, and your labor for what does not satisfy? Listen carefully to me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in abundance” (Isa. LV).

Having therefore rejected the silver and money with which we cannot buy the Lord’s waters, let us go to him who, holding the cup of the sacrament, spoke to his disciples: “Take and drink; this is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI). Wisdom mixed this wine in her bowl, calling all the fools of the age and world, who lack wisdom, to drink. Let us buy not only wine but also milk, which signifies the innocence of little ones. Paul spoke of this milk: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (I Cor. III). And Peter: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk” (I Pet. II).

Hence Moses too, understanding wine and milk mystically of Christ’s passion, testifies in figurative language: “His eyes are gracious from wine, and his teeth are white from milk” (Gen. XLIX). Therefore, the Lord does not promise the soul abundance and delicate foods, bodily fatness, pheasant birds, plump turtledoves, honeyed wine and unmixed wine, the beauty of wives, or swarms of children; rather, he promises those delights to which he mystically invites us, saying: “Delight yourself—or enjoy delights—in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Ps. XXXVI). And elsewhere: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CII). And in another psalm: “Bless the Lord, my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name” (Ps. XXVI), who fills your desire with good things. Finally he adds: “Listen to me, and your soul will live.” The promise of all good things is eternal life.

“‘See with your own eyes that I have labored little and found great rest for myself. Take discipline in great quantity of silver, and possess abundant gold in her.’” Good is the effort that, though expended moderately, will earn an eternal reward. Ecclesiastical discipline is therefore more precious than a great quantity of silver and an abundance of gold, because the former prepares eternal delights, while the latter fail entirely after a little while and in a short time; for the world is passing away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever.

“‘Let your soul rejoice in his mercy, and you will not be put to shame in his praise.’” He beautifully urges the soul to rejoice in God’s mercy, because the heart experiences great gladness when it remembers the mercy of the heavenly Judge: “The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. CXLVI). “‘And you will not be put to shame,’ he says, ‘in his praise.’” No one will be put to shame in praising the Lord except the one who, ungrateful for the gift, neglects to give thanks to God. For the Psalmist says: “All who wait for you, Lord, will not be put to shame” (Ps. XXIV). The wicked who do vain things will be put to shame.

Let us hear with what sort of conclusion this craftsman ends his work: “‘Perform your work before the time, and he will give you your reward at its proper time.’” The canon of the whole divine Law agrees with this saying; it resounds with it, teaches it, and urges us by it: while we have time, let us always devote ourselves to good work, so that at the appropriate time, when the most just Judge repays us, we may receive an eternal reward for it. Thus Ecclesiastes concludes his book, saying: “Let us all hear the conclusion of the discourse together. Fear God and observe all his commandments, for this is the whole human being; and God will bring everything that is done into judgment concerning every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil” (Eccles. ult.).

[Col. 1125]

(CIRCA THE YEAR 840.) COMMENTARIES OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE BOOKS OF THE MACCABEES.

## PROLOGUE. TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 1125]

[Col. 1125D] To the most excellent lord, and most zealous in the practice of the Christian religion, King LOUIS, RABANUS, the most worthless of the servants of God, wishes everlasting salvation in the Lord of lords.

Although I am ready in spirit to obey and serve your will, I think daily about what acceptable honor I might offer you, so that the memory of me may remain diligently with you and the devotion of my mind toward your service may be apparent. Hence a great anxiety of questioning troubles my mind as I consider what I might offer your Reverence above all, when others, according to what befits them, and with the resources supplied by their wealth, bring you manifold gifts. I, however, recognize that I cannot accomplish this by my own means; yet I shall not be wholly empty-handed, because, in proportion to the poverty of my abilities and the slenderness of my humble talent, I have resolved to offer what I have produced through meditation on the Holy Scriptures.

[Col. 1126D] Although these things may not be worthy of your prudence, I nevertheless believe that they are not everywhere to be despised. Last year I sent you a treatise on the prophet Daniel, which I composed not only from the sayings of the ancients but also from the insight of my own smallness. Now, since this is the time when the Roman Church has appointed that the books of the Maccabees be read in the Church, I bring to Your Excellence an exposition of those books, which several years ago, at the request of friends, I dictated in both a historical and an allegorical sense. Thus, if at some time you should take pleasure in recognizing the mystical sense through my work, you may have readily at hand a place where you can find it set forth—not, I say, with great eloquence or rhetorical speech, but in clear language and in the Catholic faith.

If, moreover, you find in the aforesaid work anything pleasing to you and properly expressed, attribute its grace to Him from whom every good thing comes. But if anything there seems to you to have been set down less correctly or inappropriately, attribute it rather to my inexperience than to malice. For as long as I live in this little body, I strive to labor in the service of Christ insofar as my ability permits. It belongs to His mercy that He who placed this desire in my heart may now bring me to completion in a good work. Of Him the Prophet says: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, and he does not abandon all who hope in him.”

May the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you here for a long time in safety, loving the truth of God’s law, for the salvation of many; and after the course of this life may it grant you to attain true and eternal blessedness.

## Another Prologue

[Col. 1127]

[Col. 1127B] To the most reverend and most worthy of every service of charity, GEROLD, archdeacon of the sacred palace, RABANUS, the unworthy servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in Christ.

I remember that, while I was stationed in the palace of the city of the Vangiones, I spoke with you about the excellence of the Holy Scriptures and about the difficulty of the divine histories. In some passages their meaning is obscure because of the variety of events and the situation of the provinces; moreover, their interpretation is concealed through the tropes of figures. Since at that same time I had recently delivered to the venerable abbot Hilduin commentaries on the books of Kings composed by us, you urged my smallness to compile commentaries on the books of the Παραλειπομένων—that is, the Chronicles—and of the Maccabees, following the footsteps of the ancients with equal devotion.

I did [Col. 1127C] what I could. I gave the exposition of the former book, prepared for King Louis, but I reserved the exposition of the latter to be delivered to Your Holiness, so that your request would not prove fruitless, nor could you reproach me for refusing, when you asked, to give you what I had freely given to others. Therefore, since you now possess the completed work, use it as befits a servant of Christ, in fellowship with many; and cause what you alone obtained to reach the benefit of the greatest number.

Furthermore, I wish Your Holiness to know that I wove this work partly from divine history, partly from the tradition of Josephus, the Jewish historian, and partly from the historians of other peoples. Since the book mentions not only the Jewish people and its princes but also other nations, I have compared many books so that the truth of sacred history might become evident and the meaning of its narrative clearer to the reader.

If you find anything pleasing and useful to you in the work mentioned, may the giver of all good things receive your thanks on my behalf. But if you perceive anything reprehensible in it, attribute it to our weakness and inexperience, and hasten through your holy prayers to obtain pardon for us from the merciful Judge. In this way you will give worthy honor to the bestower of all good things and timely consolation to a frail craftsman.

May the divine Majesty preserve your fraternity always mindful of us, endowed with prosperous success and made worthy of the joys of eternal blessedness.

# Book One

[Col. 1127]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1127C] Of Alexander, son of Philip; of Antiochus, the root of sin; of the city of Jerusalem burned; many from Israel consented to the king’s decree by sacrificing to idols; the law was burned, and many from Israel were slaughtered.

“And it happened after Alexander the Macedonian, son of Philip, who first ruled in Greece, had gone out from the land of Kittim and struck Darius the king of the Persians, that he waged many battles.”

The beginning of the book of the Maccabees resembles the beginning of the book of the prophet Ezekiel, where it is written: “And it happened in the thirtieth year, in the fourth month,” and so forth. Thus the first question that arises for us is why he who had not yet said anything began in this way, saying: “And it happened after Alexander struck,” and so forth. For “and” is a word of conjunction, and we know that what follows is not joined to anything unless it is joined to what precedes. Why, then, does he say “and it happened,” when there is no preceding discourse to which what he begins might be attached?

In this matter we must observe that, just as we behold bodily things, so the prophets and writers of the divine books behold spiritual things through their spiritual understanding. For them even those things are present which appear absent to our ignorance. Hence it comes about that, in the mind of the prophets, inner realities are so joined to outward realities that they see both together; and in them there takes place simultaneously, inwardly, the word they hear, and outwardly, the word they speak.

The reason is therefore clear why he who had said nothing began by saying: “And it happened.” Then he adds: “After Alexander the Macedonian, son of Philip, who first ruled in Greece, had gone out from the land of Kittim, he struck Darius, king of the Persians and Medes.” It is therefore evident to all that Alexander, son of Philip and Olympias, killed Darius, king of the Persians and Medes. Daniel also clearly expressed this in his vision, in which he describes the he-goat shattering with its horns the ram that was butting against it.

But it is asked how Alexander can be said to have been the first to rule in Greece, since many are found to have ruled there previously in different regions. Long before him, kings had ruled among the Argives, Athenians, Lacedaemonians, Corinthians, and Lydians. Nor is Alexander found to have been the first king in Macedonia, but the twenty-fourth. The first king of the Macedonians was Caranus, at the time when, among the Hebrews, Judah Azariah, also called Uzziah, was king (III Kings XII), and Jeroboam was king of Israel among the Hebrews (II Chronicles XXVI). Among the Latins there was also Procas Silvius; among the Lacedaemonians, Calcamenes; among the Corinthians, Alexander; and among the Athenians, Thespites.

Alexander is therefore said to have been the first to rule in Greece because, while other kings had previously ruled in their separate regions, he alone was the first to rule throughout the whole of Greece. After the overthrow of Thebes, he took up arms against the Persians, defeated the commanders of Darius in battle at the river Ganges, and finally struck down Darius himself, breaking his two horns, that is, the Medes and Persians. He placed him beneath his feet and subjected him on both sides to his own horn and authority.

When it is said that he went out from Kittim, this signifies that he came from Greece itself. Sethim was one of the descendants of Noah, namely the son of Javan, the son of Japheth, the son of Noah. He possessed the island of Sitamma [Ms., Cithiman], which is now called Cyprus, as Josephus testifies. In Hebrew, all the islands and maritime regions are called Kittim after that island.

Let us read the books of Varro’s *Antiquities*, those of Sisinnius Capito, the Greek Phlegon, and the other most learned men. We shall see that nearly all the islands, the shores of the entire world, and the lands near the sea were occupied by Greek settlers. From the Amanus [Ms., Damanus] and Taurus mountains they possessed all the maritime regions as far as the British Ocean.

“He waged many battles,” it says, “and seized all the strongholds, killed the kings of the earth, took the spoils of many nations, and the earth was silent before him.”

Therefore Alexander the Great, as the historians relate, after the death of Darius, subdued Hyrcania and the Macidans [Ms., Hyrcanians and Gyrodonians]. After this he undertook war against the Parthians, whom he destroyed after they had resisted for a long time, scarcely defeating them before he overcame them. From there he subdued the Thracians [Drangians], Evergetes, Parymas, Parxammenes, Hydaspes, and the other peoples who lived at the foot of the Caucasus, founding there the city of Alexandria beside the river Tanais.

Yet, insatiable for human blood—whether that of enemies or even of allies—he always thirsted for fresh gore. Thus, advancing into war with stubborn force, he compelled the Cherasini and Dracae [Ms., Choroasini and Aciati], an untamed people, to surrender. He killed the philosopher Callisthenes, who had been his fellow student under Aristotle, together with many other nobles, because, after the custom of salutation had been abandoned, Callisthenes would not adore him as lord.

After this he sought India, intending to bring his empire to the Ocean and the farthest East. He came to the city of Nisa, attacked the Daedalian mountains and the kingdom of Queen Cleophis [Ms., Deophylis], who, when she surrendered herself, redeemed her kingdom by a royal sexual union.

After Alexander had traversed and subdued India, he came to a rock of extraordinary ruggedness and height, to which many peoples had fled. He learned that Hercules had been prevented by an earthquake from attacking that same rock. Moved by rivalry, and wishing to surpass the achievements of Hercules, he seized the rock with the greatest labor and danger and compelled all the peoples of that region to surrender.

He waged a most bloody war against Porus, the bravest king of the Indians. Later, after capturing the eastern peoples of the various provinces through victories not won without bloodshed, he boarded ships and sailed along the shores of the Ocean. He reached a certain city ruled by a king named Ambiger [Ambira]. In the assault on the city he lost a large part of his army to arrows smeared with poison. Then, after a plant revealed to him in a dream had been given as a drink to the wounded, aid was brought to the survivors, and he assaulted and captured the city.

After he had gone around [after the turning-point had been passed] and entered the Ocean and the river Indus, he returned swiftly to Babylon. There ambassadors were awaiting him from the terrified provinces of the entire world: from Carthage and all the cities of Africa, from Spain, Gaul, Sicily, and Sardinia, and from many regions of Italy besides. Such fear had invaded the peoples of the farthest West of the commander established in the distant East that one might see a foreign embassy coming from across the whole world, from places which one would scarcely believe the report had reached. Hence it is well written: “The earth was silent before him,” because no one dared to rebel against him.

“And he gathered a very great force and a powerful army.”

After Alexander had everywhere conquered the nations, he carried off their treasures and wealth from every direction. Consequently, after his death, his attendants and soldiers disagreed among themselves because of the vast wealth he had accumulated and because of the power of the kingdom, as Pompey Trogus and his epitomator Justin show in their books of histories. They write that, after Alexander’s death, fifty thousand talents of gold were found in his treasuries, and thirty thousand in annual tribute.

Finally, Alexander, preserved by God’s will amid the dangers of war, was killed by a plot of the Medes while staying in the city of Babylon. The plot was chiefly the work of his commander Antipater, who destroyed him with poison through his son Cassander, as the aforesaid Pompey Trogus relates. He says that when Alexander had returned to Babylon [returning], after spending many days in idleness, he carefully established a banquet that had long been interrupted. Giving himself wholly to festivity and joining the night to the day in wakefulness, Alexander was already withdrawing from the banquet when the physician Thessalus, having renewed the revelry, invited him and his companions. After Alexander had taken the cup, halfway through the drink he suddenly groaned as though pierced by a weapon. Carried away from the banquet half dead, he was so tortured that he called for a sword as a remedy, and every touch by human beings became painful to him as though it were a wound.

In truth, however, it was a plot. For the aforementioned Antipater, seeing his dearest friends killed by Alexander and recognizing that, despite his great achievements in Greece, he was not so much loved by the king as hated, and that Alexander’s mother Olympias was harassing him with various accusations, sent his son Cassander to seize the king by administering poison. Cassander used to serve the king together with his brothers Philip and Iollas.

The force of this poison was so great that it could be contained neither in bronze, iron, nor earthenware [a potsherd], and it could be carried only in a horse’s hoof. Antipater had warned his son to trust no one except Thessalus and his brothers. For this reason the banquet was prepared and renewed at Thessalus’s house. Philip and Iollas, who were accustomed to taste and temper the king’s drink, put the poison into cold water; after tasting it, they added it to the drink.

On the fourth day, feeling certain death, Alexander said that he recognized the fate of his ancestral house, since most of the descendants of Aeacus had died before reaching thirty years. Then, when the soldiers were in turmoil and suspected that the king was perishing through a plot, he himself calmed them. After he had been carried to the highest place in the city, he admitted them all to his presence and extended his right hand for them to kiss as they wept.

While everyone was crying, he himself was not merely in tears, but showed no sign whatever of a more sorrowful state of mind, so that he consoled some who were grieving too impatiently and gave them messages for their parents. He was so invincible in spirit both against his enemy and in the face of death.

When his friends saw that he was failing, they asked whom he would make heir to the empire. He replied: “The worthiest.” So great was his nobility of spirit that, although he was leaving behind his son Hercules, his brother Arrhidaeus, and his pregnant wife Roxana, he forgot family ties and named the worthiest as heir—as though it were sacrilege for a brave man to be succeeded by anyone other than a brave man, or for the resources of so great a kingdom to be left to anyone other than the proven.

At this word, as though a war trumpet had sounded among his friends or he had cast among them the apple of discord, they all rose into rivalry and ambition, seeking the favor of the people through secret speech and the support of the soldiers.

On the sixth day, his voice having failed, he removed a ring from his finger and handed it to Perdiccas. This act quieted the growing dissension among his friends. For although he did not name an heir by voice, he seemed nevertheless to have chosen one by judgment.

Alexander died in the first month, at the age of thirty-three. Since Alexander’s reign is mentioned in the history of the Maccabees, I have inserted these matters from the books of the Gentiles so that the reader might understand that Alexander’s valor is not narrated without purpose, but that he was pre-eminent in greatness of spirit and action.

When it is said that Alexander divided his kingdom while he was still alive among his servants, who had been reared with him from youth, he did not so much divide it himself as leave it for them to divide. Thus Alexander oppressed the trembling world beneath him for twelve years. His commanders ruled for fourteen years; like greedy whelps tearing apart rich prey cast down by a great lion, they tore the kingdom apart, and, stirred against one another by rivalry for the spoil, they destroyed themselves in quarrels.

Ptolemy therefore received Egypt first, together with part of Arabia and Africa, by lot. Laomedon of Mytilene received Syria, adjoining that territory and constituting a province; Philotas with his son received Cilicia, and the Illyrians were assigned [Cilicia to Philotas, Illyria to Philo]. Acropatus was placed over Greater Media, and Alcetas, the brother of Perdiccas [the father-in-law of Perdiccas], over Lesser Media.

The Susian people were assigned to Sino; Greater Phrygia to Antigonus, son of Philip; Lycia and Pamphylia to Nearchus; Caria to Cassander; and Lydia to Menander. Leonantius received Lesser Phrygia.

Thrace and the regions of the Pontic Sea went to Lysimachus; Cappadocia with Paphlagonia to Eumenes; supreme command of the army fell to Seleucus, son of Antiochus; and Cassander, son of Antipater, was placed over the king’s bodyguard and attendants.

In Further Bactria and the regions of India, the former prefects who had begun to serve under Alexander remained in place. Taxilles held the Seres, situated between the two rivers, the Hydaspes and the Indus. Phyton, son of Agenor, was sent to the colonies founded in India.

Apiarches received the borders of the Caucasus Mountains. Aracusia and Gedrosia were assigned to Fibnutes [Sibyrtius]. Stantanes received the Drangae and Raneans; Auriota [Amyntas] received the Bactrians; the Sechodians, and so forth [the Sogdians were assigned to Scythaeus]; Nicanor received the Parthians; Philip the Hyrcanians; Phratafernes the Armenians; Neoptolemus the Persians; Pencestes the Babylonians; Arthous the Pelasgians; and Archesilaus obtained Mesopotamia.

Among all these kingdoms, however, only four stood out: Egypt, held by Ptolemy, son of Lagus; the kingdom of the Macedonians, possessed by Philip, also called Arrhidaeus, the brother of Alexander; Syria and Babylon, which Seleucus Nicanor claimed for himself; and Asia, held by Antigonus. This had been foretold in Daniel’s vision: when the one great horn on the head of that notable he-goat was broken, four smaller horns arose in its place and remained fixed.

Hence it follows:

“And the boys obtained the kingdom, each in his own place.”

After Alexander the Great died, his servants tyrannically plundered the entire body of the Macedonian kingdom, which he had gathered together with no small labor, and tore it apart through many severe wars, as is written at great length in the histories of the nations.

Passing over the many events that occurred among them, the writer of the present history comes to Antiochus Epiphanes, who committed many evils against the Jews, polluted the holy place, and profaned the law. Concerning him it follows:

After Alexander the Great, the first to rule Syria was Seleucus, surnamed Nicanor, for thirty-two years. The second was Antiochus, called Soter, for nineteen years. The third was Antiochus, called Theos, who ruled for fifteen years. The fourth was Seleucus, surnamed Gallerius [Callinicus], son of Antiochus, for twenty years. The fifth was Seleucus Ceraunus, son of Seleucus Gallerius [Callinicus], for three years. The sixth was Antiochus the Great, whom Scripture here calls the father of the illustrious Antiochus. He was the brother of Seleucus Ceraunus and son of Seleucus Callinicus, and he ruled for thirty-six years. The seventh was Seleucus, also surnamed Philopator, for twelve years.

After him came Antiochus Epiphanes, also called illustrious or noble, brother of Seleucus Philopator and son of Antiochus the Great. He ruled for eleven years. Scripture now says of him that from them there came forth “the sinful root,” the illustrious Antiochus, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome.

He is rightly called a sinful root, since he was an unprofitable offspring inclined to sins and exceedingly ready for impiety. Under him the persecution of God’s law and the wars of the Maccabees are narrated.

The entire period of the Greek kingdom, from the first year of Seleucus Nicanor to the beginning of the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes, amounts to one hundred and thirty-seven years.

“In those days there went forth from Israel wicked sons, and they persuaded many, saying: ‘Let us go and establish a covenant with the nations.’”

Greek and Roman history relates that Antiochus Epiphanes plotted against Ptolemy Philopator [Philometor], the son of his sister Cleopatra, whose uncle he was, and deprived him of the kingdom of Egypt. After Cleopatra’s death, when Alanicus, the eunuch and tutor of Philometor, and Leneus governed Egypt and demanded Syria, which Antiochus had occupied by fraud, war arose between the uncle and the boy Ptolemy.

When they engaged in battle between Pelusium and Mount Cassius, Ptolemy’s commanders were defeated. Antiochus, however, sparing the boy and pretending friendship, went up to Memphis. There, receiving the kingship of Egypt according to Egyptian custom and claiming that he would provide for the boy’s affairs, he subdued the whole of Egypt with a small force. He entered its wealthy and most fertile cities and did what his fathers and his fathers’ fathers had not done, as it is written of him in Daniel.

No one in the kingdom of Syria had devastated Egypt in this way or scattered all its wealth. He was so cunning that by his fraud he overturned the prudent plans of those who were the boy’s commanders.

“And Antiochus turned back after he had struck Egypt in the one hundred and forty-third year, and went up to Jerusalem with a great multitude.”

Accordingly, the aforementioned histories relate of the same king that, after he had been expelled by the Egyptians, he came into Judaea—that is, against the holy covenant—plundered the Temple, and carried away a very large quantity of gold. After placing a garrison of Macedonians in the citadel, he returned to his own land. Two years later he again gathered an army against Ptolemy in the south.

When the two Ptolemies, brothers and sons of Cleopatra, whose uncle Antiochus was, were being besieged in Alexandria, Roman envoys arrived. One of them, Marcus Publius Letias, found Antiochus standing on the shore and handed him a decree of the senate, by which he was ordered to withdraw from the friends of the Roman people and be content with his own authority.

When Antiochus said that he would take the answer to a council of his friends, Marcus is said to have drawn a circle in the sand with the staff he held in his hand, surrounded the king with it, and said: “The Senate and the Roman people order you to answer here what course you intend to take.”

Terrified by these words, Antiochus said: “If this pleases the Senate and the Roman people, we must withdraw from here.” And he immediately moved his army.

Josephus records a similar account: that King Antiochus, returning from Egypt because of fear of the Romans, led his army to Jerusalem. He arrived there in the one hundred and forty-third year after the reign of the first Seleucus, in the one hundred and fifty-third Olympiad, on the twenty-fourth day of the month Casleu, which the Macedonians call Apellaeus. He captured the city without anyone resisting, because those who consented to his will opened its gates for him.

After entering the city of Jerusalem, he killed many who opposed him in thought, and also killed those who, by opening the gates, had delivered the city of God to him. He took away much money from the Temple and returned to Antioch.

After he had plundered the Temple, carrying away the vessels of God, the golden lamps, the golden altar, the table, and the altar-shrine, he did not even spare the veils, which were made of linen and scarlet. He drained away the gold and the treasures, leaving absolutely nothing behind, and brought the Jews into the greatest mourning on account of these things.

He also prohibited the daily sacrifices that they offered to God according to the law. Destroying the whole city, he killed some and led others captive with their sons and wives, so that the number of captives appeared to reach ten thousand.

Mystically, however, this Antiochus, who entered the holy land in pride, devastated the Temple, and polluted the holy place with pagan superstition, represents the type of Antichrist. He wages a cruel war against the Church of Christ and strives by his error to pollute the souls of believers, which are truly the Temple of God.

Concerning him, under the figure of this Antiochus, it is written in the prophecy of Daniel (chapter XI):

“His heart shall be against the holy covenant, and he shall act and return to his land. At the appointed time he shall return and come into the south, and he shall become angry against the covenant of the sanctuary; and he shall act, and return, and devise plans against those who have abandoned the covenant of the sanctuary. And forces from him shall arise, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and they shall remove the continual sacrifice, and they shall set up the abomination of desolation. And the ungodly shall dissemble deceitfully against the covenant, but the people who know their God shall prevail and act,” and so forth.

There is no doubt that the things foreshadowed in the person of Antiochus Epiphanes—that is, the persecution of God’s people by a most wicked king—prefigure the savagery of Antichrist. He will persecute the Christian people, become angry against God’s covenant, and devise plans against those whom he wishes to abandon God’s law. He will pollute God’s sanctuary by corrupting human beings, who were created in the image of God, with various vices.

He will remove the continual sacrifice when he prohibits the offering of the sacrifice of praise to Christ the Son of God in the Church. He will set up the abomination of desolation in the holy place when he extorts divine worship from Christians for himself, so that, sitting in the Temple of God, he may show himself as though he were God.

For this reason many of our people think that, because of the magnitude of his cruelty and depravity, Domitian or Nero will be Antichrist. But although they were themselves antichrists insofar as they belong to his body and are his members, he himself is the one who will come at the end of the world as the head of all, when, according to the saying of Truth, there will be a tribulation such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be afterward (Matthew XII).

Yet, according to John’s statement, there are already many antichrists (I John II). Through these members of his, that same wicked enemy already works the mystery of iniquity, namely through heretics, schismatics, and pagans. He deceives many; and then, if it is possible, he also scandalizes the elect, because Satan will be released from his prison and will pour out upon Christ’s worshipers all his fury, insofar as he is permitted.

Antiochus therefore takes away the golden altar from Jerusalem when, through malignant persuasion, he tears out of the Church those who appear to be more perfect and who pray to the Lord with no ordinary devotion for the condition of the people.

He also takes away the lampstand of light and all its vessels when he drives from their order, whether through fear or through earthly desire, those who performed the ministry of preaching and were bound to shine among God’s people like lamps through the various forms of doctrine.

He takes away the table of the bread of the Presence [the table of proposition] and its vessels when, through heretics, he strives to confuse the Holy Scriptures with wicked interpretation and seeks by the cunning of his evil to corrupt and lead into error those who seemed to remain in meditation on God’s law like the vessels of God’s table and the loaves of the Presence.

The same ancient enemy also takes away the veil, the crowns, and the golden ornament that was on the front of the Temple, and he shatters everything. He does this when he turns the letter of God’s law—in which divine wisdom and heavenly mysteries lie hidden, and where the crown of eternal reward is promised in the heavenly kingdom and perpetual glory both to those who labor well and to those who keep God’s commandments—toward a foreign interpretation by breaking apart its judgments and perverting its meaning. In this way he deceives the souls that obey him.

By the gold, silver, and hidden treasures I understand nothing other than the beauty of speech, the purity of meanings, and the treasure of virtues stored in hidden hearts among the faithful. The devil strives to remove all these things from the kingdom of Christ when he attempts to drag their possessors, stripped of these goods, with him into the abyss of his destruction.

From this arises daily lamentation and groaning in the Church, when the assembly of the faithful is deeply saddened through compassion at the downfall of its members. Hence it follows:

“And he committed a great slaughter of human beings, and spoke in great pride, and great lamentation arose in Israel.”

Every rank, every age, and every sex grieves when the persecutor rages, because no person is immune from persecution. Each one groans both over the loss of tranquility and over the harm caused by those who fall from the faith. For, as Paul says (I Corinthians XII): “The members in Christ’s body are concerned for one another; and if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.”

The same Apostle, writing against those who loved empty glory, listed the labors that he himself endured bodily and then added (II Corinthians XI): “Besides those things which are internal [external], my daily burden is the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that belong to my weakness.”

And elsewhere: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep; having the same attitude toward one another—not aspiring to high things, but consenting to the humble.”

“And after two years of days the king sent the chief collector of tribute into the cities of Judaea.”

We said above that Antiochus represented the type of Antichrist. Likewise, in this passage the chief collector of tribute may be understood as the son of persecution [perdition], whom the prince of this world and ruler of this darkness, the devil, incites to demand tribute from the cities of Judah—that is, from the Churches of Christ—and to require them to pay him the tribute of sins.

He does not, however, demand this everywhere by the force of persecution, but sometimes through tortures, sometimes through flatteries, sometimes through threats and open savagery, and sometimes through fraud and deceit. Hence it is written: “He spoke peaceful words to them deceitfully.”

But whoever believes him prepares persecution for himself. For this most wicked enemy does the same thing through malignant persuasion, by means of lying signs and wonders, so that people may believe him to be a god and offer him divine worship. Those who believe him he spiritually kills in soul; those who resist he afflicts with bodily torture.

Hence it comes about—something that must be read with great anguish of mind—that he destroys many from Israel when he converts very many from the Christian religion to apostasy. He takes away the spoils of the city when he removes the ornaments of the Church. He burns it with fire when he devastates it through persecution. He destroys its houses and the walls around it when he scatters the congregations of believers and kills their defenders, namely their teachers.

He takes captive the women, the children, and the cattle because those who have softened hearts, who are children in understanding and serve carnal desires, live like irrational animals and are especially exposed to the captivity and snare of the ancient enemy.

After the Churches of Christ have been devastated and their ministers scattered by persecution, the evil enemy strives to erect in their place the craft of impiety and to substitute blasphemous worshipers, so that, if possible, through wicked people the Christian name—which alone has prevailed throughout the world—may be utterly destroyed and the devil’s will fulfilled in the pollution of idols and the multiplication of sins.

Hence it follows:

“And they poured out innocent blood around the sanctuary and defiled the sanctuary,” and so forth.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem flee when, as persecution rages, some flee bodily so that they may not be scandalized; others flee in mind and suffer grave scandal in their souls; while others persevere in confessing Christ even unto death and, freed from the hands of their persecutors, flee into heaven to receive their reward.

The holy land becomes the habitation of foreigners when, throughout the world, the number of persecutors multiplies against the members of Christ who are destined to be crowned through martyrdom. Its feast days are turned into mourning when the most solemn rites of the Christian religion are not permitted to possess the adornment of their splendor. Its Sabbaths become a reproach, and the hope they have in the future rest of souls is destroyed or mocked by the enemy of the faithful.

“According to her glory, her disgrace has been multiplied.”

For the glory of the Church of the faithful is defiled by disgrace when, while the enemy rules, the glory of the heavenly sacraments and the dignity of the divine offices endure the greatest reproach from impious blasphemers.

And King Antiochus wrote to his entire kingdom that all the people should be one, and that each person should abandon his own law.

What is written, and Antiochus’s spiritual letter, are the Gentile heretics and the Christian schismatics who seek to overturn the truth of Christ’s law and the ordinance of the catholic faith, for whom divine worship and the Christian religion are a source of pain. But the more eagerly they strive through error to unite people to themselves, the more they make them discordant with one another, because they themselves do not agree among themselves, but disagree and differ through various sects; and therefore they are less able to make their followers obedient and associate them in unity. [Col. 1137C] For, as Scripture bears witness, “Among the proud there are always quarrels,” and, according to the judgment of Truth, “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house.”

Antiochus’s books and letters command Jerusalem and the cities of Judaea to follow the laws of the nations, and therefore to cease offering holocausts, sacrifices, and acts of appeasement in the temple of God. For the greatest concern and effort of heretics and pagans is that in the Church of Christ they should either confuse divine worship or extinguish it altogether, so that the sincerity of right faith, which works through love, may not offer an acceptable holocaust to God on the altar of the believer’s heart; nor may the mystical sacrifices of the Lord’s body and blood, together with the sacred prayer and appeasement of the faithful through good works, be worthily presented in the true temple of God, the creator of all and [Col. 1137D] the giver of every good thing. Let the sabbath be forbidden to be celebrated, because they deny that there will be a future rest for the souls of the saints in the heavenly kingdom. They order altars, temples, and idols to be built, because they desire to make the minds of the faithful vessels of evil spirits. They order swine’s flesh and ordinary animals to be sacrificed—that is, to lead an unclean life and, after the manner of brute animals, to conduct oneself in luxury and the desires of the flesh. They order their sons to remain uncircumcised—that is, to restrain thoughts, words, and deeds by no vigilance, continence, or discernment, so that they forget the divine law and alter God’s ordinances into the practice of various crimes. And they compel all these things to be done not only by persuasion in words, [Col. 1138A] but also through the torment of various punishments. Hence it follows:

“And whoever would not act according to the king’s word would be put to death, in accordance with all these words.”

Cruelty grows hot when impiety burns; savagery rages when desire seethes. Throughout the kingdom Antiochus, by written orders, inflicts torments and death upon the worshipers of the God of the earth. So also Antichrist, through his most wicked ministers, seeks out various kinds of punishment in order to tear Christ’s worshipers away from the state of their most holy religion, crush them, and destroy them.

“On the fifteenth day of the month Casleu, in the one hundred and forty-fifth year, King Antiochus built the abomination of desolation, the idol.”

The month Casleu is the same among the Greeks as the month called [Col. 1138B] December among the Latins. On the tenth day of this month, in the one hundred and forty-fifth year of the reign of the Greeks—which they begin counting from the first year of Seleucus—Antiochus Epiphanes set up in the temple of God the abominable idol of desolation, that is, the image of Jupiter Olympius. It was in the eighth year of his own rule, in which year he also built on the summit of Mount Garizim in Samaria a shrine of Jupiter the Stranger, or Hospitable One, at the request of the Samaritans themselves, who asked by letter that he do the same, as Josephus testifies.

But we read in the Gospel according to Matthew that, when the disciples asked the Savior about the sign of his coming and the consummation of the age, he answered among other things: “Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, which was spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place—let the one who [Col. 1138C] reads understand” (Matt. XXIV). When we are summoned to understanding, this shows that what has been said is mystical. It is written in Daniel in this way: “And in the middle of the week my sacrifice and libations will be taken away, and in the temple there will be the abomination of desolation, and desolation will endure until the consummation of time and the end.”

The Apostle speaks of this (II Thess. II), saying that the man of iniquity, the adversary, will be exalted against everything that is called God and worshiped, so that he will dare to stand in the temple of God and show that he himself is the Lord. His coming, according to the working of Satan, will destroy those who have received him and reduce them to desolation. This may be understood simply either of Antichrist, or of the image of Caesar which Pilate placed [Col. 1138D] in the temple, or of Hadrian’s equestrian statue, which stood in that very place of the Holy of Holies until the present day.

According to the truth of Scripture, an abomination is also called an idol; and therefore “desolation” is added, because the idol was placed in a temple that had been desolated and deserted. Once the idol of jealousy had been set up in the temple of God throughout all the cities, the king’s most wicked ministers built altars all around, and before the doors of houses and in the streets they burned incense and sacrificed. For when the unclean Antichrist reigns in the house, his supporters and accomplices, and all the wicked, having rejected the worship of the one true God and despised God’s house, which is the holy Church, confused in mind and disorderly in conduct, offer in various places sacrifices polluted by demons of various errors and manifold crimes. [Col. 1139A] And it is rightly said that they built altars all around, because, abandoning the simplicity of truth, they follow erroneous sects of impiety. For, as the Psalmist testifies, “All the impious walk around” (Ps. XI). And they burn incense and sacrifice before the doors of little shrines and in the streets because they are not worthy to enter the altar of God and there offer to God the incense of pure prayer; rather, on the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matt. VII), they offer their deeds and words to the evil enemy.

“And they burned the books of the law of God with fire, tearing them apart.”

They tear apart and burn with fire the books of God who, through the fire of desire, seek by heretical perversity to rend the integrity of God’s law from its state of rectitude, [Col. 1139B] and who eagerly desire to slaughter with the sword of their malice the holy preachers to whom the treasure of God’s Testaments has been entrusted.

What else is indicated by the number twenty-five except those who, entangled in the five bodily senses and carnal desires, act and think contrary to the law of God, which consists in the two Testaments and in the two commandments—namely, love of God and love of neighbor?

Twenty-five, therefore, is produced by multiplying the number five by itself, and this number is rightly compared with deserters from the law, who through each bodily sense—that is, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—oppose the divine commandments written in the Pentateuch. [Col. 1139C] And therefore it is said that they sacrificed upon the altar that stood opposite the altar, because upon the altar of impiety, which pride had raised against the altar of catholic faith, all the wicked offer to the devil the ill-omened sacrifices of their deeds and words.

“And the women who circumcised their sons were put to death, according to the command of King Antiochus.”

The meaning of the history is clear: it explains the torments that wicked persecutors inflicted—and then in the Old Testament, and now likewise in the New—upon the worshipers of God. It is not easy for anyone to enumerate all the kinds of punishment that the most wicked torturers inflicted upon Christ’s martyrs.

But according to the allegorical meaning, what are signified by the women who circumcised their sons except honorable persons among the faithful, [Col. 1139D] who, examining their deeds, words, and thoughts with the greatest discernment, hasten to cut away with the sword of the Spirit whatever they find excessive in them? The spiritual Antiochus desires to slaughter these people, because he strives either to strike them bodily through torments or to kill them spiritually in their souls through denial.

Antiochus is interpreted as “silence of poverty,” and he is rightly designated by this name: deprived of spiritual knowledge and lacking sacred virtues, he persecutes out of envy in others what he himself entirely lacks. Hence it rightly follows:

“And they hanged the boys by their necks throughout their houses.”

For they do not delay in killing those who are little and humble in spirit, not in understanding but in malice, on account of their confession of [Col. 1140A] faith. Likewise, they slaughtered those who had circumcised them, because they harass with the greatest persecution the holy preachers who restrain and correct their subjects with the knife of devotion and the word of evangelical teaching.

“And many of the people of Israel resolved within themselves not to eat unclean things.”

No persecution or tribulation has ever been able to tear away from faith in Christ the saints of God who were predestined and called according to the foreknowledge of God the Father. Rather, persisting in the truth, they neither ate food sacrificed to idols nor consented to be defiled by the uncleanness of sins; nor did they allow the holy law of God to be violated and corrupted by heretical perversity. Instead, they chose to die for the name of Christ rather than consent to [Col. 1140B] impiety.

Therefore one of them, relying upon this confidence, wrote to the disciples and bore witness in these words: “For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angel nor principality, neither things present nor things to come, neither power nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VIII). But let us see what consolation was sent to the servants of God who were laboring.

## CHAPTER II. Matthias and his five sons mourn for the people, the temple, and the desolation of the law. Matthias is compelled to sacrifice to idols, but refuses; he kills the king’s minister who was sacrificing. Those fleeing into the desert are killed on the sabbath; Matthias decrees that they should fight on the sabbath; he and his sons kill the sinners and overthrow the altars of the idols. As Matthias is dying, he admonishes his sons to defend Israel, etc.

“In those days Matthias, son of John, son of Simeon, a priest, arose, etc.”

In the Book of Daniel, where mention of this passage is made under an enigma, it is written as follows:

“And the impious will pretend deceitfully to honor the covenant; but the people who know their God will prevail and act. And the learned among the people will teach many, and they will fall by the sword, by flame, by captivity, and by plunder for days. When they fall, they will be raised up by a little help, and many will join themselves to them deceitfully. And some of the learned will fall, so that they may be refined, chosen, and made white, until the appointed time, because there will still be another time.”

How much the Jews suffered from Antiochus, the present history of the Maccabees reports, and their triumphs bear witness: for the preservation of God’s law they endured flames and swords, slavery and plunder, and the most extreme punishments. No one doubts that these things will occur in the future under Antichrist, with many resisting his power and fleeing in different directions. The Hebrews interpret these words as referring to the final destruction of the temple, which occurred under Vespasian and Titus; they say that at that time there were many among the people who knew their God and were killed for the preservation of the law.

“When they fall,” he says, “they will be raised up by a little help, and many will join themselves to them deceitfully. And some of the learned will fall, so that they may be refined, chosen, and made white until the appointed time, because there will still be another time.”

Historically, the little help signifies Matthias from the village of Modin, who rebelled against the commanders of Antiochus and attempted to preserve the worship of the true God. It calls this “little help” because he lived scarcely any length of time after beginning the defense: after one year had passed, he died; afterward his son Judas, who was called Maccabaeus, fell in battle, and his other brothers were deceived by the trickery of their adversaries.

[Col. 1141A] Mystically, however, Matthias signifies the Lord Savior, who is prince of God’s people and defender of his elect; his sons fight for the house of Israel and defend God’s sanctuary and divine law. Matthias is interpreted as “gift of God,” and the mystery of this name disclosed to us the sacrament of his incarnation. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: [Col. 1141B] “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III).

For the one who was given by God is the perfect gift of God. But these things have been said only about his incarnation. As for his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, we must believe that he carried out this dispensation together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, too, is read of as the gift of God, yet together with the Father and the Son he is believed and worshiped as one God. Hence in the Gospel he is read of both as sent and as having come willingly, as in the Lord’s saying: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John XIV); and again: “When the Paraclete has come,” he says, “whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit [Col. 1141C] of truth” (John XV). To Nicodemus he says: “The Spirit blows where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John III).

Thus Matthias is said to be the son of John, son of Simeon, a priest from the sons of Joarib. John is interpreted as “grace of God,” Simeon as “hearing,” and Joarib as “the Lord exalting.” These interpretations rightly suit this mystery, because the mediator of God and human beings may be called “the grace of God,” as in the Apostle’s statement: “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Heb. II); “hearing,” because he himself says in the Gospel: “What I have heard from the Father, these things I speak in the world” (John XV); and “the Lord exalting,” of whom the Prophet says: “Be exalted, Lord, in your strength” (Ps. XX). He is rightly called a priest, of whom it is written: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: [Col. 1141D] You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

All the saints are the sons of this Matthias, for they are called members of his body. But how they can be designated by the number five is reasonably asked. Historically, Matthias is read to have had five sons: John, who was surnamed Gaddis; Simeon, who was surnamed Tharsi; Judas, who was surnamed Maccabaeus; Eleazar, who was surnamed Abaron; and Jonathan, who was surnamed Alphus. Let us therefore see whether this number is found anywhere in the New Testament to express the same reality. We also read the Apostle Paul speaking of Christ to the Ephesians in this way: “He who [Col. 1142A] descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things; and he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (Eph. IV).

Here five classes are indicated in those persons whom divine calling appointed for teaching in the Church. Let us consider, then, how the sons of Matthias, with the interpretations of their names, can be fitted to these classes.

The first of his sons was called John, who was surnamed Gaddis. John is also said to mean “his grace,” while Gaddis means “kid” or “my temptation.” These names rightly suit, if I am not mistaken, [Col. 1142B] the order of the apostles, who were chosen through the Lord’s grace for this summit of honor, yet suffered many temptations and injuries from sinners and persecutors. The Savior appears to have foretold this to them when he says in the Gospel: “I chose you from the world, so that you should go and bear much fruit, and your fruit should remain” (John XV); and again: “Behold, I am sending you like sheep among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves, etc.” (Matt. X). Behold, those who are filled with the Lord’s grace are shown to have been afflicted by the insults of every kind of evil, and not lightly.

The second son of Matthias was Simeon, who was surnamed Tharsi and is called Simon in many subsequent passages. Simon, or Simeon, [Col. 1142C] is interpreted as “hearing,” or “he heard sadness”; Tharsi as “the exploration of joy.” These meanings also suitably fit the order of the prophets, who, enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, both foresee the future punishments of the wicked and, by inwardly tasting the consolation of the saints’ future rewards, know them beforehand; and they persuade others to guard against future evils and desire future goods.

The third son in order was Judas Maccabaeus. Judas is interpreted as “confessing” or “glorifying,” and Maccabaeus as “warrior.” This designation very appropriately suits the evangelists, who preach throughout the world the Gospel of the peace and glory of Christ and conquer the wicked errors of pagans and heretics.

The fourth son was Eleazar, who was surnamed Abaron. The former name signifies “the help of God,” [Col. 1142D] while the latter means “lofty generation.” He is not inappropriately compared figuratively with pastors, who, strengthened sufficiently by God’s help and exalted in faith and virtues, are appointed over the Church so that by rightly feeding God’s sheep with sound faith and good examples they may lead them to the green pastures of the heavenly homeland.

The last of these sons was called Jonathan, surnamed Alphus, and he most aptly suits the holy teachers according to the interpretations of his names. Jonathan is interpreted as “gift of the dove,” or “the Lord’s willing one.” Alphus means “fugitive” or “thousand.” These names rightly express Christ’s teachers, who, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, willingly submit themselves to the Lord even unto death; and, having fulfilled [Col. 1143A] the embassy of his life, preach God’s law in the world and teach people to flee earthly desires and seek everlasting joys, so that there, according to the significance of the number one thousand, God rewarding them, they may receive the fullness of their recompense and possess true blessedness with Christ and his angels without end.

What follows here is:

“These men saw the evils that were being done among the people of Judaea and Jerusalem, etc.”

For these men, recognizing with compassion the various scandals that the wicked continually [ingeruntur, “bring upon”] in the Church of God, desire to avenge them with the spiritual sword; they do not fear to offer themselves as a sacrifice and hand themselves over to death for the salvation of their own people. Hence it follows:

“And Matthias tore his garments, and his sons, etc.”

What is it to tear one’s garments except to hand over one’s [Col. 1143B] body to punishments? And what is it to be covered with sackcloth except to punish the righteous as though they were sinners, [Note: [Col. 1143D] Something is missing.] or to punish them with torment? Sackcloth is also made from goats and is rough and bristling, signifying torment. For goats rightly refer to sins, since at the Lord’s judgment they are placed among the sinners (Ps. XXXIV).

Therefore, because the Lord assumed the flesh of sin, he is said to have clothed himself in sackcloth; for if we take the matter historically, we nowhere read that he used sackcloth. Thus, while the Jews harassed him with insults and plots, he concealed his divinity from darkened minds beneath the veil of flesh, because they did not deserve to recognize the one whom, in such impiety, they were treating and attempting to kill.

Because of the sins of the peoples, the Redeemer of the human race handed over his flesh to death and sympathized with our weakness. Concerning him the [Col. 1143C] Lord himself says through Isaiah: “Because of the transgression of my people I struck him” (Isa. LI), and: “He himself will bear their iniquities. Therefore I will distribute to him many, and he will divide the spoils of the strong, because he handed over his soul to death and was reckoned among the transgressors; he himself bore the sins of many and pleaded for transgressors” (Isa. LIII).

Likewise his sons—that is, his apostles and martyrs, instructed by his example—did not hesitate to die temporally for the laws of God and the salvation of their brothers, so that by this means they might merit the joys of the heavenly kingdom with the holy angels. Hence the Apostle John says: “By this we know love: that he laid down his soul for us, and we ought to lay down our souls for our brothers” (I John III).

“And those who had been sent came there, etc.”

For the spiritual Antiochus [Col. 1143D] sends agents to the city of Modin, which is interpreted as “judgment”—that is, to the holy Church, where God’s judgments are most diligently kept—in order to compel those who had fled there seeking a remedy for their souls to depart from the law and pay to the devil the sacrifice of sinners and the worship of impiety.

But we cannot read what follows without groaning, when we see many from the people of Israel consenting and approaching them, compelled by torments to apostatize from the religion of devotion; others lured by desire for this world falling back; others deceived by the cunning of heretics; and still others returning through their own luxury and lust to the former filth of their vices. [Col. 1144A] Nevertheless, what follows brings great joy: Matthias and his sons stood firm. Without doubt, those who persist in truth and justice are the ones who have deserved to be sons of the true Matthias—that is, Jesus Christ—and who, preserving his faith and commandments, strive [contendunt; the printed text has compescunt] with steadfast heart, through his grace, to obtain the rewards of eternal life.

“And those who had been sent by Antiochus answered and said to Matthias: ‘You are a prince,’ etc.”

Whether by deceit or by force, the ancient enemy is always plotting how to overthrow the worship of devotion in the Church of Christ. He is the one who approached our Redeemer in the desert to tempt him, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves” (Matt. VII); and after placing him on the pinnacle of the temple in the holy city, [Col. 1144B] he said: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (ibid.). For it is written: “He has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will lift you up in their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone” (Ps. XC). Then transferring him to a high mountain, he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said to him: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. VII).
