Every day he deceitfully suggests the same things in his members through his ministers, so that, for the sake of worldly ambition, they may abandon the way of justice and carry out the command of the most wicked king who reigns over all the sons of pride (Job XLI), etc.

“And Matthias answered and said in a loud voice, etc.”

The steadfastness of Matthias strengthened the courage of his sons; likewise, the patience and long-suffering of our Lord Jesus Christ strengthens [Col. 1144C] the faith of all believers. Hence he says to his disciples: “Do not be surprised if the world hates you; know that it hated me before you” (John XV). “And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X). “In your patience you will possess your souls, and your reward will be great in heaven” (Luke XII). “But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

“And when he had ceased speaking these words, etc.”

The Jew who sacrificed to idols before the eyes of everyone signifies wicked Catholics who, through depraved works and the notoriety of their sins, scandalize their neighbors. They are shown to sacrifice to idols because they are evidently held captive by chief vices.

[Col. 1144D] Hence the Apostle Paul calls avarice the service of idols (Gal. V). But the sword of Matthias slaughters these people upon the altar, because the vengeance of the most just judge exercises a just punishment against such persons.

Likewise, he killed at that very time the man whom Antiochus had sent to compel the sacrifice, because on the final day of judgment not only sinful human beings but also the instigators of sins—namely, evil spirits—will receive the punishment deserved by eternal damnation. At the same time the altar of impiety will be destroyed, because after the judgment has been completed no further opportunity for sinning will be granted to the wicked.

What follows—“He was zealous for the law, as Phinehas was zealous against Zimri son of Salomi” (Num. XXV)—shows [Col. 1145A] [Col. 1145A] that the mighty deeds of the holy fathers foreshadowed the most renowned act of our Redeemer in the final times.

“And Matthias cried out in a loud voice in the city, saying, etc.”

These words of Matthias foreshadowed the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, who daily exhorts us to abandon the vanity of this world and seek the heavenly joys of the kingdom. For he says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not renounce everything [all: omnibus] that he possesses cannot be my disciple. Whoever loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and whoever does not carry his cross every day and follow me is not worthy of me. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it” (Luke XIV); “but whoever loses his soul for my sake [Col. 1145B] will find it” (Matt. X). “For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul, or what exchange will a person give for his soul?” (Luke IX). “For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and he will repay each person according to his works” (Matt. XVI).

Our Redeemer and his innocent sons fled and left behind whatever they possessed in the city, because under the leadership of Truth we desire to climb the heights of the virtues; and, regarding as superfluous the things that belong to worldly luxury, we reject and cast them away.

For this reason we read in the Gospel (Matt. V) that the same Lord led his disciples onto a mountain, sat there, and taught them there; there he prayed and there he fed the crowds, so that by his examples he might always summon us onward—to higher and more [Col. 1145C] perfect things, etc.

“Then many descended, seeking judgment and justice, into the desert, and they and their sons sat there.”

Whom can we better understand allegorically as those who did not ascend the mountains with Matthias and his sons but descended into the desert, so that, sitting there, they might seek judgment and justice, than the Jews who, after receiving the grace of Christ’s baptism, thought that circumcision and the old law should still be observed?

They are rightly said to have gone into the desert because, while the truth of the Gospel was dawning, they regarded the deserted shadow of the law as still necessary for themselves and preached that the legal sabbath ought to be observed, although all these things had preceded in the times of the law as signs and were to be observed spiritually in the New Testament. [Col. 1145D]

Against them the Apostle argues at great length in his Epistles, asserting that “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. XX). These people, therefore, are rightly struck by the sword of spiritual enemies, because they do not consider the grace of Christ sufficient for salvation.

According to the tropological meaning, the lovers of the desert may also be understood as all the idle and sluggish, who, having received the grace of the Christian religion, think it sufficient for them that they have received divine gifts and the cleansing of baptism. They do not wish, after the cleansing of their filth, to practice works of virtue, nor do they remember that evangelical parable in which the Savior spoke in the Gospel about an unclean spirit, saying that the unclean spirit had gone out from a person [Col. 1146A] and wandered through waterless places, seeking rest and not finding it.

Again, when it found its former house empty, swept clean, and adorned, it returned with seven spirits more wicked than itself. Such people are easily overwhelmed by spiritual enemies, because they did not take care to arm themselves with the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the breastplate of justice, and the sword of the Spirit (Eph. VI), with which they ought to have resisted those enemies.

Hence it is added that Matthias and his companions mourned over their destruction, because the Church is afflicted with great sorrow when it recognizes that some of its own number have fallen through the snares and persecution of evil enemies into the precipice of sins.

“And one man said to his neighbor: ‘If we all do as our brothers have done, etc.’”

The good, therefore, greatly detest idleness, which is the enemy of the soul. Rather, they choose each day to fight against spiritual enemies with virtues than to grow sluggish in the idleness of evil, especially since they presume to have the hope of victory not from themselves but from divine assistance. They promise themselves security not in the present but in the future, when, after all adversities have been destroyed, death itself—the last enemy—will also be destroyed (I Cor. XV); and there will no longer be mourning, crying, or pain, because the former things have passed away (Apoc. XII). Then the saints will rejoice in the joy of God’s face and enjoy salutary delight at his right hand forever (Ps. XX).

“Then the assembly of the Jews [the Assidaeans], strong in might, from Israel, was gathered to them, etc.”

[Col. 1146B]

The account of Scripture makes it clear that, when the Savior and his apostles [Col. 1146C] preached the Gospel, many from the Jewish people came to faith, believing the law and the prophets who bore witness to Christ’s coming. Many proselytes and newcomers also, abandoning their idols and the superstition of paganism, flocked from everywhere to hear the word of God and were added to the number of believers:

“And they struck down sinners in their anger and wicked men in their indignation.”

Stirred by zeal for the faith, they expelled evil spirits from people possessed through error and exposed the poisons of their deceit. The Jews too, compelled, fled to the nations, in accordance with the Gospel passage in which, after people had been healed, demons were permitted by the Savior to go into swine (Mark V), so that unclean possessors might possess vessels of uncleanness.

“And they recovered the law from the hands of kings.”

The soldiers of Christ recovered the law from the hands of kings when, [Col. 1146D] persisting in the truth of the Gospel, they yielded to no error; rather, through prayer and preaching they subjected their opponents to the truth. Hence it happened that many of those who, previously lifted up by worldly arrogance, had been persecutors of the Christian religion, later converted and became the firmest defenders of the truth. They did not give a horn to the sinner, because they did not consent to iniquity, in accordance with Esther’s prayer: “Do not hand over your scepter, Lord, to those who are not” (Esth. XIV).

“And the days of Matthias drew near for him to die, etc.”

[Col. 1147A] This exhortation of Matthias, in which he urged his sons to be imitators of God’s law and give their souls for the covenant of the fathers, aptly accords with evangelical teaching. For Truth itself instructed his disciples by words and examples how they should resist all the errors of Jews, pagans, and heretics, and convert the world to faith through their preaching. He also affirmed his teaching from the testimony of the law and the prophets, showing that the author of the New Testament is the same as the author of the Old.

“You, therefore, my sons, take courage and act manfully in the law.”

We read in the Gospel of John that the Savior, hastening toward his passion, on the very night on which he was handed over, after the mystical supper and the washing of the feet [Col. 1147B] that he performed for his disciples, girded with a linen cloth, gave them many examples of exhortation. Among other things, he foretold the passion that was to come upon them in the world and promised the glory of the future kingdom and the joy of the heavenly homeland (John XIII).

But because the death of Matthias prefigures the passion of the Redeemer, let us hear how he established the Church’s teaching for the whole period of the present life.

“And behold, Simeon your brother—I know that he is a man of counsel. Always listen to him, and he will be your father.”

Above we said that Simeon is interpreted as “hearing.” He rightly said that Simeon was a man of counsel, because those who, taught by the grace of the Holy Spirit, are instructed through inward hearing are in every respect useful and capable in counsel. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks [Col. 1147C] within me, for he will speak peace to his people, etc.” (Ps. LXXXIV). And in the Apocalypse: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Apoc. XXII).

The heavenly Teacher exhorts us to listen to those whom he himself, teaching them inwardly, has made salutary teachers for us.

“And Judas,” he says, “Maccabaeus, strong in might, shall be your commander in the army; he will wage the war of the people.”

What is signified by Judas Maccabaeus except the first preachers of the Gospel, who, instructed by the Savior himself, were made capable of waging war for the Christian people?

But because Judas is interpreted as “confession,” and in many passages bears the type of the Savior himself, let us understand that our warfare is rightly conducted when he deigns to direct both our counsel and our action. Hence Truth himself says to the disciples: “Remain in me, and I in [Col. 1147D] you. Just as a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me, because without me you can do nothing” (John XV). And: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

And he blessed them, and was gathered to his fathers, etc. It is written in the Gospel how the Savior, after he had finished the supper that he had with his disciples before his passion, and had completed his final instruction to the disciples on that night, finally concluded with a prayer directed to the Father, commending his disciples to him for safekeeping, saying: “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one as we also are” (John 17). And shortly afterward: “Sanctify us,” he says, “in the truth. Your word is truth; just as you sent me into the world, so I also sent them into the world; and for them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in the truth,” etc. (ibid.). By such words our Matthias instructed and blessed his disciples. And so he was gathered to his fathers, because in every respect, by his passion, resurrection, and ascension, he confirmed by fulfillment the words of the holy fathers, just as it had been written concerning him.

And he died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year, and was buried by his sons in the tombs of his fathers at Modin. It was said above that Matthias rose up in the one hundred and forty-sixth year, when the nations were profaning the temple of God, and that his sons were zealous for the law of God and avenged the holy things. Now Scripture likewise reports that this same Matthias died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year. From this it appears that he lived with his sons for no more than one year after beginning the vengeance, and thus died. This number of years aptly accords with the mystery of the Lord’s passion, because, after the fullness of time in which God had determined to send the Son, according to the testimony of the Law and the Gospel, in the sixth age of the world the Savior perfectly redeemed and restored the human being—created on the sixth day and suffering on the sixth day—by the price of his blood. But the statement that he was buried by his sons in the tomb of his fathers at Modin signifies that the memory of his passion is fittingly venerated daily by the faithful in the holy Church, where the place of judgment and equity is, and that a salutary mourning is celebrated there, because holy men, inflamed by the desire for eternal life, strive to be pierced by life-giving tears in the chambers of their hearts.

## CHAPTER III

Judas Maccabaeus rose up in defense of Israel; he killed Apollonius and took away his sword. He also killed Seron, commander of the army of Syria. Antiochus ordered Lysias to destroy Israel and wipe it completely from the earth.

And Judas, who was called Maccabaeus, his son, rose up in his place. When Matthias departed, his son Judas Maccabaeus succeeded him; all his brothers and all who had joined themselves to his father assisted him. What, then, is indicated to us by this event except that our Redeemer, after completing his passion and resurrection and ascending into heaven, first appointed the apostles as his successors in evangelical preaching, sending the Holy Spirit from heaven? They are rightly designated by the name Judas, that is, “confessors,” because Luke says of them in the Gospel: “They were continually in the temple, praising and blessing the Lord” (Luke 24). All his brothers and all who had joined themselves to his father assisted him, therefore, because men of lesser rank, and all believers who came together in faith through the teaching of Christ, worked with the apostolic choir, each according to his strength, in bearing witness to the Gospel.

And they fought Israel’s battle with joy, and he enlarged the glory of his people. For that apostolic company, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, preached the word of God everywhere with persistent zeal, rejoicing in tribulations, distresses, and necessities, and everywhere increasing and multiplying the number of those who believed in the Lord.

He clothed himself with a breastplate like a giant. For he fortified himself on every side with the strength of faith.

He girded himself with weapons of war. In accordance with the saying of the apostle Paul, who taught: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; in all things take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the Evil One; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6). Thus he fought against the enemies and protected the camp of the Church.

And he became like a lion in his deeds, and like a lion’s cub roaring in the hunt. He was like that lion of whom it is written: “The lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5); and of whom the patriarch Jacob said figuratively in the mystical blessing of his sons, among other things: “Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son. You have lain down and rested like a lion, and like a lioness; who will rouse him?” (Genesis 49). That hunt was spiritual, when spiritual hunters captured human beings for the faith in the nets of the Gospel. Thus Judas mystically persecuted the wicked and set ablaze those who disturbed his people, because, whether persecuting human persecutors or evil spirits with such zeal and action, they inflicted only a slight disturbance, kindling the flames of envy.

And the enemies were driven back because of their fear of him. And he angered many kings—namely, those who strove to resist the Gospel of Christ.

And he gladdened Jacob by his deeds—when he strengthened the people of believers by word and example.

And his memory is forever in blessing. In accordance with the saying of the wise man: “They will declare the wisdom of the saints among all peoples, and the assembly of the saints will proclaim their praise” (Ecclesiasticus 44, 39).

And he went through the cities of Judah and destroyed the impious among them. For, examining the faith of the Churches, he struck down with anathema the heretics who held opinions contrary to the right faith.

And his name was known to the ends of the earth. For “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

And Apollonius gathered the nations. What is expressed by Apollonius except the savagery of the Jews, who had gathered great strength from Samaria against Israel? For by observance of the letter of the Law they strove to overcome the faith of Christ as though it were contrary to the commandments of God.

But Judas went out to meet Apollonius, struck him, and killed him. For Christ, through his apostles, overcame and crushed the error of the Jews by the testimony of the Law itself and of the prophets, showing that the shadows prefigured by the Law and the prophets pointed toward the truth of the Gospel.

And many of them fell wounded. For many of the Jews, wounded by envy, fell. But the rest fled. That is, they sought salvation from ecclesiastical teaching. Judas took their spoils, when the disciples of Christ converted all the ceremonies of the Law, which those people had held carnally, to spiritual use.

And Judas took away Apollonius’s sword, and he was fighting with it every day. We understand Apollonius’s sword to be nothing other than the discourse of the Law and the prophets. The holy preachers take it up and fight with it every day, when, taking from the carnal people the history of divine Law interpreted according to spiritual understanding and apostolic tradition, they overcome the errors of all nations. Throughout all the days of this age, the power of joy produces for the holy Church a most glorious victory.

And Seron, commander of the army of Syria, heard that Judas had gathered an assembly and a congregation of the faithful with him, and he said: “I will make myself a name, and I will be glorified in the kingdom,” etc. Through Seron, commander of the army of Syria, the power of this world is signified, and it is rightly designated by the name Syria: for Syria is interpreted as “lofty” or “moistening,” because this world is cultivated by pride and boasts in luxury. Seron therefore prepares to overcome Judas and those who are with him, when worldly arrogance plots against holy teachers and the people of the faithful, gathering the camps of the impious for this purpose, so that, relying on the support of many guilty men, it may oppress the innocent, trusting more in the power of the kingdom than in the strength of God.

But the outcome was contrary to his expectation, because “the stone cut from the mountain without hands” (Daniel 2) will crush the statue of pride, shatter the gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and “the kingdom will be given to the people of the saints.” “The lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Revelation 5), he to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (Matthew 28).

And they came as far as Beth-horon, and Judas went out to meet them with few men. It is rightly said that the army of Syria approached, because it brings forth all its activity with tumult. Beth-horon, however, is interpreted as “house of anger.” Judas met it with few men, because the choir of the saints answers its enemies not with anger but with patience and humility. The Lord commanded it, saying: “Be reconciled quickly with your adversary while you are on the way with him. But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also; and to the one who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, give him your cloak as well” (Matthew 5).

But when they saw the army coming to meet them, these words express the weakness of fear in certain subjects, who, considering their own frailty more than the danger, are afraid, rather than possessing confidence in the Lord through the strength of faith. Yet the skill of the teachers restrains that fear with pious exhortations and grants them certain hope of God’s future assistance, for he is the protector of all who faithfully hope in him.

And Seron and his army were crushed in his presence. For the humility of the holy fathers often mitigates the fury of persecutors, and the gentleness of the humble casts down the boldness of the proud. Hence Paul teaches, saying: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12).

And eight hundred men fell from them. The total of those who fell is fittingly and salutarily concluded by the number eight, because those who voluntarily yield to the truth, spiritually cutting away all pleasures from themselves by spiritual circumcision, strive to gather within themselves the virtues of the eight beatitudes.

But the rest who fled came into the land of the Philistines. For some persecutors, although they cannot resist the truth in any way, nevertheless choose rather to flee to the hiding places of their errors than to yield and obey the useful counsel of spiritual teachers. And it is rightly said that they fled into the land of the Philistines. Philistines is interpreted as “twofold ruin”; a person has a twofold ruin who first falls into sin and then, despairing of himself, persists in evil.

And the fear of Judas and his brothers fell upon all the nations around them, etc. The fear of Judas and his brothers fell upon all the nations when the power of Christ shone forth through virtues and miracles in his members.

And his name reached the king. This means that his evangelical preaching became known to the power of this world; and all the nations recounted the battles of Judas when the peoples of the entire world proclaimed the victory of our Redeemer over death and the author of death.

But when King Antiochus heard this, etc. The historical passions of this Antiochus, by which he burned with immoderate force—that is, anger, greed, and pride—aptly express the spiritual character of Antiochus, through which he now violently attacks the whole world through his members, but at the end of the world through himself, when there will be a tribulation such as has never been before and will never be again (Matthew 24).

He grows angry when he hears of the glory and the strength and steadfastness of the saints. He gathers an army and gives it pay for a year, when through the advantages of the present life and ambitious honors he incites various people to persecute the faithful. By the wickedness, worldly arrogance, and greed of life he chooses his nobles to administer the affairs of the kingdom, when he appoints his ministers and followers for the purpose of suggesting the allurements of present things and, by provoking them to earthly pleasures, dragging those who agree with him along with them.

Those who are imitators of Christ are designated by the name “sons.” He nourishes them through his nobles when, by corrupting them with various vices through the most wicked men, he makes them fuel for the eternal fire. Above all, he orders his magistrates to uproot the virtues of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem and to establish foreigners in their place, because the devil has no invention or endeavor greater than to overthrow the Church of Christ, weaken the strength of faith in the elect, and introduce vices in place of virtues.

And he chose Lysias, Ptolemy son of Doriminus, and Nicanor and Gorgias, powerful men from the king’s friends. What is signified by Lysias except worldly arrogance, which through three men—that is, three ranks of persecutors—brings war upon the Church of Christ: through pagans, heretics, and false Christians? Forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen are assigned to them so that they may destroy Judas according to the king’s word.

What is signified by the number forty except the whole span of time in which the Church endures persecution in the world? For there are four principal parts of the world—East, West, North, and South—in which the Church, spread abroad, remains established. To gather it, the Son of God descended into the world. Before his passion he fasted forty days and forty nights, showing the temptation of our flesh in his own flesh, which he graciously accepted from our mortality, wishing to share in it. Hence, from the hour of his death until the dawn of his resurrection, there are forty hours, if the ninth hour itself is counted. After the resurrection he likewise willed to remain on this earth with his disciples for no more than forty days, mingling with their life in human fellowship and receiving mortal nourishment with them, although he was no longer destined to die. By those forty days he signified that he would fulfill by his hidden presence what he had permitted, when he said: “Behold, I am with you all the days until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

The number seven, however, by which the thousands of horsemen are described, signifies nothing other than the fullness of persecutions. For just as the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is shown by the number seven, so, conversely, we read in the Gospel that an unclean spirit brought with it seven spirits more wicked than itself into a person (Matthew 7), and elsewhere we read that the Lord cast seven demons out of a sinful woman (Luke 8). Thus all persecutors are rightly gathered together, at the instigation of the devil, for the destruction of the Church of Christ and to compel the confessors of almighty God to blaspheme; and they accomplish this not sluggishly but with all their strength.

And they set out to go with all their force, etc. What is signified by Emmaus except lovers of this world, who through worldly greed neglect to have friendship with God? Hence it is written: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (James 4); and John says: “If anyone loves the world, the love of God is not in him” (1 John 2). Such people are rightly called by this name. For Emmaus is interpreted as “rejected people”; those are worthy of rejection who, through love of the present age, prefer it to the love of God. Hence the Truth himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10). Nor is it inappropriate that Emmaus is said to lie in a level land, because “broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it” (Matthew 7).

And the merchants of the regions heard their name. I think that these merchants, who seek the service of the Hebrews, signify no one better than evil spirits. They desire the destruction of the faithful and strive to deprive us of heavenly glory through earthly greed and to turn the freedom we have in the grace of Christ into the worship and slavery of the devil. Hence it is read in the Gospel that the devil himself, leading our head—the mediator of God and human beings—onto a high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and, tempting him, said: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4).

And it is rightly said that the armies of Syria and of foreign lands were added to them, because all the luxurious and those alien to the true worship of God join themselves to our enemies and, contriving our destruction, cooperate with the unclean spirits.

And Judas and his brothers saw that evils had multiplied and that armies were approaching their borders; and they understood the words of the king, which he had commanded the people to carry out for destruction and annihilation. While the persecutors burned with zeal and prepared battle against the faithful, the latter, following the example of Judas and his brothers, were rather stirred to increase in faith and progress in virtue, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “When the impious man exalts himself, the poor man is set ablaze” (Psalm 9).

The intention of God’s servants, therefore, must be such that they fight for the people and for his saints. For the state of the faith of the Christian religion and the salvation of their brothers require them to fight earnestly against spiritual wickedness and evil people and to implore assistance by continual prayer. For he is the one of whom it is written: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation; to you alone the poor man is left, and you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm 9). In fatherly compassion he considers the labor and sorrow of his own; “he will crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (ibid.); he judges the orphan and the humble, “so that human beings may no longer continue to exalt themselves upon the earth” (ibid.).

And they gathered together and came to Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem, because Mizpah had previously been a place of prayer in Israel, etc. Those who had gathered to fight against the enemies came to Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem. What, then, is signified by Mizpah, which is interpreted as “judgment,” except the Old Testament? Mizpah was a place of prayer, and it always looks toward the New Testament and offers testimony to the Gospel of Christ. Spiritual soldiers of God must therefore turn the intention of their hearts there, so that from divine reading they may be instructed how they ought to fight against spiritual enemies.

For Mizpah was a place of prayer—not, however, in Israel, because the divine oracles first became known to us through the books of the Law and the prophets, and afterward through the Gospel.

They fasted on that day. For they devoted themselves to abstinence.

They clothed themselves in sackcloth and put ashes on their heads. For, doing penance for their sins, which they had contracted through the frailty of the flesh, they served God worthily.

And they tore their garments. When they chastise the body and mortify within themselves carnal desires.

The statement that follows—“They opened the books of the Law, in which the nations searched for the likeness of their idols”—shows that those who are proved worthy to serve as soldiers demonstrate the memory of the divine commandments through good works. For “the law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls” (Psalm 18); it condemns the evil deeds of the faithless, detests the worship of idols, and rejects every impious act.

They raise up the priestly ornaments—those who worthily perform the duties of the ecclesiastical priesthood. They offer first fruits and tithes—those who devote to God the beginning and perfection of a good work. They raise up the Nazirites who have completed their days—those who strive, through purity of chastity, to offer God a pleasing life at all times. And “he cried out with a loud voice to heaven”—those who summon the Divinity to mercy by pious prayers and good works. For just as the cry of the impious, which they utter through blasphemy and wicked deeds, provokes God, so the confession and faith of the saints, working through love, appease the divine majesty at all times.

And after this Judas appointed leaders of the people, tribunes, and centurions. He calls those who commanded a thousand soldiers tribunes—whom the Greeks call χιλίαρχοι, “commanders of a thousand”—he calls centurions those who commanded a hundred soldiers, and decurions those who commanded ten. The holy preachers organize their subjects so that nothing disordered may be found among them, but that they may carry out the service of Christ rationally. Hence Paul says to his hearers: “Let all your things be done honorably and according to order” (1 Corinthians 14); and again: “No one,” he says, “will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2).

And he said to those who were building houses, betrothing wives, and planting vineyards, etc. It is therefore written in Deuteronomy (chapter 20): “Let the fearful man and the fainthearted not go out to battle; let him go and return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers fearful, as he himself is terrified by fear.” These words teach that no one who still fears being stripped of earthly works can undertake the army of religious profession and contemplation or of spiritual warfare, lest he return again through weakness of mind to his former filth, draw others away from evangelical perfection by his example, and weaken the strength of the faithful.

Such men are therefore ordered, leaving the battle, to return to their houses, because they cannot fight the Lord’s wars with a divided heart. “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” Such people ought not even to undertake the beginning of renewal. It is better for them to remain in the active life than, pursuing contemplation lukewarmly, to involve themselves in greater danger. It is better not to make a vow than to make one and not fulfill it.

Similarly, a man who has taken a wife or planted a vineyard, etc., is suspended from such warfare. A servant of a wife cannot serve in the divine army, nor can one who is still fixed in the pleasure of the flesh attain the pursuit of contemplation. “No one,” says the Apostle, “who serves as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2).

And they moved the camp and stationed it south of Emmaus. It is rightly said that Judas’s army stationed its camp south of Emmaus, because, when Christ’s soldiers plan to fight against their enemies, they choose to animate themselves more by the warmth of faith than to grow numb through the cold and torpor of unbelief.

And Judas said: “Gird yourselves and be mighty sons; be ready in the morning, so that you may fight against these nations that have gathered to destroy us.” Such must be the teaching and exhortation of the holy preachers: they must stir the minds of their hearers, strengthen their hearts to resist the devil and his army, and entrust the hope of victory to God alone.

## CHAPTER IV

After defeating Gorgias and Lysias, Judas purified the temple; concerning the dedication of the altar and the adornment of the temple.

And Gorgias took five thousand men and chosen horsemen. Gorgias took five thousand men into his army when the devil strives to unite to himself those devoted to the five bodily senses through the allurements of pleasure. He takes a thousand horsemen with him when he plans to conduct his entire warfare in pride and contempt for God’s commandments, so that he may overcome the ranks of the opposing side by persuading them to transgress God’s commands. For “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclesiasticus 10), in which the author of death finds ruin both for himself and for those who follow him.

And it is rightly said that he advanced his camp by night, because he desires to exercise all his wickedness in his subjects through blindness of mind, so that they may in no way foresee what ruin threatens them from consenting to sin.

And the sons of those who were from the citadel were those commanders. The citadel here signifies not the height of virtues but the eminence of empty glory. Those who dare to raise themselves up in pride provide leadership to sinners. The evil spirits may also be understood in these commanders, for they belong to the party of him who said: “I will ascend into heaven and set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14). These commanders of iniquity never cease dragging those who consent to them into the pit and abyss of crimes.

And Judas heard this, and he and his mighty men rose up. Note, reader, that the opposing side allied with Gorgias arranged all its warfare by night, whereas Judas and his followers did so by day. For those who work crimes and carry out errors are always defiled as rulers of darkness, hating the light of the divine commandments and loving the darkness of worldly pleasures. Hence Paul says: “Those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night. But we, who belong to the day, are not children of night or of darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Judas, however—that is, the confessor of God—arranges all the equipment of war in the light of faith and meditation upon God’s Law. Thus he appears in the field with only three thousand men, namely, with those who act confidently not in worldly power but in faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and who strive to lead an honorable life in this world with simplicity of mind.

And the foreigners lifted up their eyes. As the enemies came from the opposite side to battle, Judas’s companions sounded the trumpet, and the nations were crushed, because the sound of the trumpet expresses the voice of preaching. Judas’s soldiers sound the trumpet when Christ’s preachers announce the Gospel throughout the world. Hence the enemies are crushed, because the nations are subjected to the faith of Christ; and spiritual enemies too are crushed by Christ’s power and, slain by the sword of the Holy Spirit, plunged into the depths of the abyss.

And they pursued them as far as Gezeron, and to the plains of Idumaea, Azotus, and Jamnia. The names of the places to which Judas pursued his enemies demonstrate the effectiveness of his power. Gezeron is interpreted as “beside my light”; Idumaea as “red” or “earthly”; Azotus as “kindred fire”; Jamnia as “sea” or “his right hand.”

What, then, is signified by Gezeron except the light of faith? What by Idumaea except the Gentiles? What by “kindred fire” except the ardor of charity? And what by Jamnia except the depth of knowledge and the accomplishment of good work?

The choir of holy teachers therefore pursues the Gentile people until it leads them from the error of paganism to the light of faith, kindles in them the fire of charity, and urges them to meditation on divine Law and the pursuit of good work. This persecution is salutary, and this slaughter is beneficial. Hence it follows:

And three thousand men fell from them. Just as there were three thousand companions of Judas who pursued them, so three thousand fell on the side of the enemies. They fell not so that they might perish utterly, but so that, raised up after their fall, they might stand more firmly, because, instructed in faith in the Holy Trinity, they strove to reach the fellowship of those whom they recognized they had pursued with pious intent.

And Judas and his army, which followed him, returned, etc. Christ’s soldiers should by no means be quickly confident of victory when battle threatens; rather, they ought to fight until they are certain that their spiritual enemies have been cut down. When, by pursuing sinful or unbelieving people, they have converted them to repentance for sins and to faith in Christ—which works good deeds through love—then they ought to gather their spoils, that is, make use of their knowledge and share in the industry of their pious labor.

By gold we may understand knowledge; by silver, eloquence; by hyacinth, heavenly conduct; by purple, the shedding of blood in martyrdom. We gather these riches fruitfully when we find them acceptable in the right faith, provided that we transfer this victory to the spiritual enemies. We may be confident when, after the end of the present life, it is no longer necessary to fear the ambushes of enemies. We gather spoils beneficially when we receive from Christ worthy rewards for our labor.

Hence it is rightly said that Judas exhorted his companions not to desire spoils while the savage wars of the enemies were still threatening. When the enemies had been completely overcome, he returned with his men to gather the spoils of the camp. For every preacher must admonish his hearers to guard against the arrows of their enemies while it is still the time of war.

But when the time of peace has arrived—the peace, namely, which the Savior promised his disciples, saying, “My peace I give you” (John 14)—then rulers and subjects alike will possess eternal joy in the reward they have received. They will no longer fear the future pain of labors and tears, because then it will be time to sing praises to God their helper. Hence it is written:

And they turned and sang a hymn and blessed God toward heaven, because he is good, because his mercy is forever. There is great salvation in Israel when the number of believing peoples is multiplied in the Lord—those who acknowledge the Savior by faith, confess him with their mouth, and glorify him in one manner of life. Or, alternatively, there will then be great salvation in Israel when there is no adversity in the Church of Christ.

And it is significantly added, “on that day”—on the day, certainly, of the resurrection, when the most noble bride will be joined to her bridegroom in the heavenly kingdom above, when all the saints in the presence of God will rejoice not only in the rest of their souls but also in the immortality of their bodies. Hence it is written:

But whoever escaped from the foreigners came and reported to Lysias everything that had happened. Finally, the foreigners who escaped announce Judas’s victory to Lysias, because some who are not yet captured as a salutary prey through the ministry of Christ’s teachers announce the glory of Christ to the teachers by whom they are nourished for death, even unwillingly, because compelled by the truth.

Lysias, for his part, is interpreted as “generating” and signifies the powerful of this world, who, although they have been begotten, have not yet merited to be reborn through Christ’s baptism. When these soldiers hear of Christ’s victory, therefore, they are dismayed and lose heart, because things did not happen in Israel as they wished or as the king had commanded. Their desire was that the preaching of the Gospel through the holy teachers should not prevail and that the multitude of believers in the Lord should not increase. They knew that such things also pleased their rulers—that is, the unclean spirits—for through profane images of idols, worshiped by human beings with divine honor, those spirits persuaded people not to receive the faith of Christ. But they did not prevail, because the Father reveals the glory of his Son throughout all nations, far and wide.

And in the following year he gathered sixty thousand chosen men. Lysias chose sixty thousand men and five thousand horsemen to wage war against Israel. Throughout the entire period of this world, which is divided into six ages, the prince of this age, through the five bodily senses, and with the rulers of these darknesses inciting him, strives to overcome Christ’s soldiers by loosening them into various vices, and through evil people plots the death of the good.

But Judas met them with ten thousand men. The army of our king is stronger than the others in this respect: it strives in every way to obey the divine commandments, and, sending continual prayers to the Lord, it is strengthened by his hand, in whose power it places its chief confidence. It persists in battle until its enemies and their hostile spiritual weapons have been utterly slaughtered by the sword.

Hence Judas’s prayer continues:

Strike them down with the sword of those who love you. There are five books of the Law of God, and, as we have said, five senses of the body. Whoever, according to the teaching of the Law, restrains the desire of the flesh—turning his eyes away so that they do not see vanity, stopping his ears so that they do not hear the slanderous tongue (Psalm 118) or obscene songs directed against worldly people, by frequent hearing of which the inner person is defiled; restraining his sense of smell and his taste so that he does not indulge the allurements of pleasure; restraining his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; turning away from evil and doing good, seeking peace and pursuing it (Psalm 36)—will overcome his enemies, gain a most salutary victory, and rejoice in an abundant triumph.

But although the spiritual Lysias, once, twice, and three times crushed, has taken flight, he nevertheless does not abandon the wickedness he has undertaken; rather, he revives his battles again and again. Hence it is written:

But when Lysias saw the flight of his men, etc. And Judas said, etc. It is rightly said that Judas, after crushing the enemies and quieting the wars for a time, exhorted his men to cleanse and renew the holy places, because the holy teachers have great concern that, wherever the Church entrusted to them has been injured by enemies, it should again be restored to the former state of holy conduct.

According to the tropological sense, each believer must cleanse his own mountain—by which we can appropriately understand Mount Zion, since Zion is interpreted as “mirror,” and “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see the Lord” (Matthew 5)—with attentive sight, if anything in it has been polluted through the enemy’s deceit, until it is completely renewed.

There we can understand the abandoned sanctuary, the profaned altar, and the burned gates, because there the sacrifice of praise was offered to God upon the altar of faith, and the entrance into heavenly life was contemplated. In the courts, however, shrubs grow when a multitude of superfluous thoughts arises in human hearts.

The storerooms, he says, they saw demolished. In Greek, *pastophoria* means chambers or rooms in which the Levites kept watch in the courts of the Lord’s house; mention is made of them in the final vision of the prophet Ezekiel. The storerooms are therefore demolished when the secret places of the mind are torn apart by illicit desires. But all these things must be most earnestly purified through repentance for sins, amendment of conduct, and devout prayers to the Lord. Hence it is rightly written concerning Judas’s army that, when they saw the sanctuary deserted, they tore their garments and mourned with great lamentation.

Then Judas appointed men to fight against those who were in the citadel until they had cleansed the holy places, etc. It is aptly said that Judas appointed men to fight against those who were in the citadel until they cleansed the holy places, because our Redeemer ordains this through his preachers: that his soldiers should diligently fight against those who inhabited the citadel of pride—that is, men lifted up by a spirit of arrogance, or evil spirits swollen with pride—until the hearts of the elect are cleansed from every stain of iniquity. And they chose priests without blemish, having a will directed toward the law of God, and they cleansed the holy places. For after those who bore upon themselves the leprosy of error or the stain of crimes had been expelled from ecclesiastical office, they chose as ministers of the word men willing and upright in conduct, so that the gatherings of the holy Church might be made free from every contagion of error. Indeed, it is added that he removed the stones of defilement to a clean place, because he publicly showed that the heretics who refused, through the conduct of right faith and sound doctrine, to become precious stones were reprobate, having been struck with anathema and expelled, etc.

And he considered what he should do with the altar of burnt offerings, which had been profaned, etc. The altar of burnt offerings is the pure faith, pure doctrine, and [pure] conduct of Christ’s ministers. But because this altar had been profaned by heretical perversity or the enormity of crimes, it was already to be destroyed—that is, removed from the dignity of the priesthood—lest it should be a reproach to the holy Church that it had depraved and criminal teachers who had been seduced by diabolical cunning. Hence the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by men” (Matthew 5). Concerning this Paul also writes to Titus: “Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.” Hence also he says to certain sinners: “Through you the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles.”

Therefore, after that mystical altar has been removed [restored], those mystical stones must be set back upon the mountain of the house, in a suitable place, until the prophet comes and responds [teaches] that sinners must be brought under penance, until, through the holy teachers, a sanctification appropriate to the crime committed has been carried out and judged. In their place, sound stones according to the law must be substituted, so that a new altar may be made according to what existed before. For men sound in Catholic faith, instructed in knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and devout in good conduct must be appointed in the place of those who fell from the office of governance as transgressors [transgressing], according to the authorities of divine law, so that in the holy Church—which Christ acquired for himself as a bride at the price of his blood, “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5)—a ministry may be presented to God without reproach, in newness of life and according to the rule of righteousness.

And they built the holy places and the structures that were inside, next to the house; they sanctified the temple and the courts, etc. Holy preachers build the holy places within the house and the temple when they adorn the people entrusted to them inwardly with sound knowledge of the faith and outwardly with honorable conduct. They sanctify the courts when, by instructing those newly coming to the faith in the divine sacraments, they dedicate them. They make new holy vessels when they render human hearts capable of receiving the word of God. They bring the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table into the temple when they awaken in the Church of God the light of spiritual doctrine, the purity of holy prayer, and meditation upon the holy Scriptures. In the lampstand, therefore, in which lamps ought to shine, we may rightly perceive the word of evangelical doctrine, in which holy teachers, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, ought to shine so that those who enter may see the light.

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matthew 5). By the altar of incense we can understand nothing better than the perfected life of the saints, from which the fragrance of virtues and of holy prayer daily rises before the sight of the Most High. The Lord’s table, therefore, we understand to be none other than the holy Scripture, in which the perfection of souls consists.

As for the statement that they hung the curtains and completed all the works they had undertaken, the hanging of the curtains expresses the concealment of the mysteries. For the mysteries of divine law are not to be disclosed to everyone in their entirety, but according to each person’s intellectual capacity and progress in knowledge and virtues. Hence the Lord commanded the apostles, saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7). And Paul says to inexperienced disciples: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, and indeed you are still not able” (1 Corinthians 3). Concerning the knowledge of the perfect he says elsewhere: “And we, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord, being transformed into the same image, as by the Spirit of the Lord,” etc.

They therefore complete all the works that must be done in the house of God when, in faith, word, and deed, they strive to fulfill all the Lord’s commandments according to their order. Nothing is lacking in perfection where the human will obeys the divine will in all things.

And before dawn they rose on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, etc. Concerning this renewal Josephus narrates as follows (Antiquities 12.10):

> “On the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, which the Macedonians call Apelleon, they lit lamps upon the lampstand and burned the burnt offerings that they had offered upon the new altar.”

These things took place after three years, on the same day on which their religion had been changed into the profane observance of their idols. [Note: [Column 1159D] The passage is corrupt.] For the temple, destroyed by Antiochus, remained thus for three years: for the work in the temple was done in the one hundred and forty-fifth year, on the twenty-fifth day of the month Apelleon; in the one hundred and forty-ninth year, in the one hundred and fifty-fourth Olympiad. The desolation of the temple occurred according to Daniel’s prophecy, which he had foretold eighteen years earlier, signifying that the Macedonians would destroy it.

Judas celebrated sacrifices with his fellow citizens for the renewal of the temple for eight days, omitting no kind of delight and feeding them with the most precious foods. They glorified God with praises and psalms and delighted one another with songs. For the renewal of the solemn rites, after religion had been restored following a long interval, those who received the law decreed that their descendants should celebrate this renewal of the temple for eight days. Hence from that time until now we have celebrated this festival, calling it “Lights,” because, contrary to hope, this splendid light of the worship of religion appeared for us. Mystically, however, the renewal of the temple is the conversion to repentance of people who had been defiled by various errors and crimes. Then every believer must sing, rejoice, be glad, exult, and give praise, when they see their neighbors restore within themselves, through correction of their ways and meditation upon God’s law, what they had previously destroyed through negligence.

Hence the sacred Gospel also tells that the Savior said (Luke 15) that joy arises in heaven over one sinner who repents. If there is joy over one, how much greater will be the exultation over many converted to the true worship of God? For, as it is written, “In the multitude of the people is the dignity of the prince” (Proverbs 14)—namely, of that Prince “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2).

And Judas and his brothers and the entire assembly of Israel established that the day of the altar’s dedication should be observed at its appointed times. The Savior himself is read to have honored this solemnity in the Gospel through his preaching, where it is written: “The Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter; and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico,” etc. (John 10).

It should therefore be understood that this Dedication, which we know from the Gospel reading to have taken place, does not belong to the first dedication of the temple but to the last; this is easily inferred from the fact that it is said to have occurred in winter. The first dedication took place under Solomon in autumn; the middle one, under Zerubbabel and Joshua the priest, in spring; and the last, under Judas Maccabeus, in winter. At that time it is specifically recorded that the same dedication was established to be recalled every year through solemn observances, as we learn from the aforesaid Gospel passage that it continued to be observed until the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

This was the reason for the second and third dedications. Solomon completed the temple that he founded for the Lord in seven years, but in the eighth year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, which we call October, he dedicated it with great glory. Four hundred and thirty years later the Chaldeans came against this temple; after destroying the city of Jerusalem, they led the people of Israel captive to Babylon. After seventy years, under the rule of the Persians, the people were sent back to their homeland, and the temple was rebuilt over forty-six years. On the third day of the twelfth month, which we call March, the work was brought to completion.

At that time the work was directed by the most vigorous leaders of the people, as we have said: Zerubbabel, of royal lineage, and Joshua, the high priest. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah also assisted them and strengthened the heart of the people against the plots of those who hindered the work. Then, after approximately three hundred and fifty-six years, the most wicked king of the Greeks, Antiochus, having seized Jerusalem by treachery, profaned the same temple with the filth of idols. He removed and smashed the golden altar of the Lord, the table of the bread of the Presence, the lampstand of the light, and the other objects mentioned above.

But Judas Maccabeus, being of priestly descent, gathered an army of righteous men, took up arms against the commanders of Antiochus, expelled them from Judea, and brought an end to the fiercest persecution. He cleansed the temple of the images of idols, made new altars and the other vessels and ornaments, replaced them in the temple, and dedicated them together with the temple. He purified and renewed it on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, which we call December; and it is beyond doubt that this belongs to winter.

He also established the decree, as we have said, that every year the day of the Dedication—that is, of the renewal and dedication of the temple—should be celebrated with festive devotion, as this passage now bears witness.

All these things, as the Apostle teaches (1 Corinthians 10), were done as figures of us and were certainly written for our sake; indeed, they must be examined by us with more careful spiritual understanding. King Solomon, whose name means “peaceful,” typologically signifies our Redeemer, concerning whom Isaiah says: “His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace.” The temple that he built is his Catholic Church, which he gathers from believers throughout the world, as from living stones, into one structure of faith and charity.

The fact that the temple was built over seven years signifies that throughout the entire duration of this age, which unfolds in seven days, the holy structure of the Church never ceases to grow. Its dedication in the eighth year, and that most renowned and greatest solemnity which King Solomon offered to all the children of Israel at the completion of the dedication, mystically indicates that, when the number of the elect has been perfected at the end of the world, there will be the secure festival of the immortality long desired. Once the miracle of the universal resurrection has been accomplished, all who belong to the kingdom of the peaceful true King—namely, Solomon—will immediately enter with him the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland.

Because our Lord wished to be raised from the dead on the eighth day—that is, after the seventh day of the week—the number eight rightly signifies the future festival of our resurrection as well. The fact that the temple, burned by enemies, is rebuilt through the Lord’s mercy, and that, after being defiled by idolaters, it is cleansed again through the aid of heavenly compassion, signifies the various events of the holy Church. Now it is oppressed by the persecution of unbelievers; now, when it has been made freer from persecutors, it serves more peacefully, with the Lord’s aid. At one time the Church is endangered in some of her members by the snares of the ancient enemy; at another, through the vigilance of faithful teachers, she receives back those whom the enemy seemed for a time to have destroyed, once they have been chastened through repentance.

The fact that the temple was built in forty-six years spiritually refers to the meaning of the Lord’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin. Concerning this he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2), since, after his body had been destroyed by suffering, he himself raised it to life on the third day.

Physicians report that the human body is formed in the differentiation of its members on the forty-sixth day after the beginning of conception. This did not happen by chance but was divinely arranged, so that the temple would be built over the number of years corresponding to the number of days in which the Lord’s body, signified by the temple, had to be perfected in the Virgin’s womb.

The decree that the Dedication should be celebrated every year surely admonishes us always to retain in our minds the memory of the Lord’s resurrection, which we believe has already taken place, and to live in such hope of our own future resurrection that we may deserve to rise not for judgment but, as the Lord promised those who have done good, for life.

And at that time they built Mount Zion, with high walls all around and strong towers, etc. Holy teachers build Mount Zion when, through word and example, they urge the holy Church toward progress in virtue. They construct high walls around it when they fortify it on every side with the height of Catholic faith and the work of prayers. They raise strong towers when they command that all hope be placed in God’s goodness, lest the nations trample it as they did the former mountain, and lest the wickedness of evil spirits or the malice of corrupt people prevail any longer against them.

“And he stationed an army there to guard it,” he says, etc. An army is stationed in Zion to guard it when a multitude of ministers devoted to preserving God’s law is assigned to administer the rite of the heavenly sacraments in the Church. They fortify it to guard Beth-zur when, through strong exhortations, they urge ecclesiastical persons to preserve divine worship according to rule—for Beth-zur is interpreted as “house of the strong.” This is so that the people may have a defense against the face of Edom: that is, so that they may preserve the steadfastness of faith against enemies and against the obstinacy of the raging world.

## Chapter 5. Judas defeats the nations seeking to destroy Israel. Concerning Timothy, commander of the Ammonites. Simon, sent by his brother, attacks the nations. Concerning Judas’s wars against Timothy, etc.

And it happened that the nations around heard that the altar and sanctuary had been built as before, and they were exceedingly angry, etc. The nations are provoked when they see the worship of God renewed, because visible or invisible enemies, who burn with envy against the progress of faith and virtues, grow angry, suffer, and persecute the servants of God, wishing to reduce them to nothing, when they see them intending to observe good works upon the altar of right faith.

Hence it is said that they planned to destroy the race of Jacob who were among them, and began to kill them. For when the Gospel of Christ shone forth in the world and everyone received the faith of God, the persecutors were tormented and sought to turn them away by slaughtering them with punishments. In the same way, spiritual enemies, when they see some people wishing to restore themselves from indolence and negligence to the worship of piety, contrive to kill them with the sword of impiety and to butcher them as though for the death of sinners.

But Judas, resisting the enemies bravely with the shield of faith, defeats the sons of Esau in Idumea. For the chorus of holy teachers, destroying with the sword of the Spirit the idolaters who are exceedingly harsh through the thorns of vices and most foul through deadly sacrifices and worldly luxury, makes those who were opposed subject to the truth and turns enemies into friends.

And those who were in Acrabathane, because they surrounded the Israelites, etc. Those who lived in the places mentioned—namely Acrabathane and Bean—and who, surrounding the children of Israel, lay in wait for them as a snare and a stumbling block, signify Jews and heretics, who continually arrange scandals and plots against the Church of God.

Such people, however, are shut up by Judas and his companions in their towers when, through the diligence of teachers, they are captured within the contrivances of their pride and their errors are condemned by anathema. Their towers are burned with fire, together with all who are in them, when the authors of crimes and inventors of errors are now consumed by the heat of the divine word on account of their sins and, at the future judgment, unless they have previously performed worthy repentance, will be burned with the fire of everlasting vengeance.

And he proceeded against the sons of Ammon and found a strong force and a numerous people, etc. What is expressed by the sons of Ammon, whose name is interpreted as “son of my people,” except schismatics and heretics? Once they seemed to be sons of the holy Church, but after departing and casting themselves into error, they became sons of the devil. Hence the Apostle John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2).

They have Timothy as their commander—that is, heresiarchs—who, according to the interpretation of their name, are praised among them but, according to the truth of understanding, are by no means found to be so among us. *Timothy* is interpreted as “with benefits”; but this is the opinion held concerning heresiarchs by those whom they have deceived. Among us, however, they are called poisoners, because by their sorceries they mix the poison of error for their hearers.

Against them Judas rises, gains the victory as the superior, destroys their errors in Judea—that is, in the confession of praise to God—and returns in triumph from the enemy.

And the nations in Gilead assembled against the Israelites who were within their borders, to destroy them, etc. The nations in Gilead assemble against the Israelites to destroy them when a multitude of heretics and schismatics gathers for the purpose of attacking the Catholic faith, which endures forever, by twisting the testimonies of Scripture according to their own sense. For Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” and the name aptly suits those who devote themselves to meditation upon the Scriptures.

But the Israelites flee to a stronghold when each of the faithful takes refuge in the truth of the faith and asks Judas and his brothers to bring aid, because through the ministries of holy preachers they desire to be defended against the spiritual Timothy, of whom we spoke above, and his companions.

The Israelites’ complaint over the killing of their men and their captivity shows that the grief among the faithful peoples is not small when they see some of their own depart from the truth and fall into the error of the wicked, etc.

And behold, other messengers came from Galilee, with their tunics torn, announcing these words, etc. Those who gathered from various foreign places to consume the people of God plainly signify the peoples of the nations who, while still in unbelief, continue to stir up wars and persecutions against Christians.

But when the speeches were heard that the various embassies had brought to Judas and his companions, the great assembly of the Church came together to consider what they should do for their brothers who were in tribulation and being attacked by enemies. For the greatest concern and care of the entire holy Church is how she may defend her children against various enemies—Jews, pagans, heretics, and schismatics. Here too, with prudent counsel and every effort, she acts together with those who appear more learned and stronger in faith and in the work of virtue, considering how she may resist the enemies and defend her own at the proper time.

And Judas said to his brother Simon, etc. Just as the Church’s attacks from enemies are various, so the battles of the spiritual warriors must also be distinct. Simon therefore goes into Galilee—that is, the wheel—with three thousand men, as what follows shows, to free his brothers; Judas and Jonathan, however, go into Gilead with eight thousand.

What is signified by Simon, who is sent into Galilee, that is, “the wheel,” except preachers sent among the nations? Going with three thousand—that is, with faith in the Holy Trinity—they prepare to advance against their adversaries, striving through evangelical preaching to cast down the enemies and free believers.

Judas and Jonathan, however, signify those teachers who, preaching the word of God in Judea, strive through the testimonies of Scripture to overcome both Jews and heretics who abuse those testimonies, by the truth of sound understanding.

Note that Simon alone with his men is sent against the Gentiles, whereas two go against the Jews and heretics with a larger force. Among the Gentiles, only idolatry together with pagan error had to be defeated; among Jews and heretics, partly an ancient practice and partly a new superstition had to be corrected through the spiritual knowledge of the two Testaments. Eight thousand men are taken because there they teach that either the circumcision of the law must be observed spiritually or the resurrection of Christ must be believed truly.

And Simon went into Galilee and fought many battles with the nations, etc. Simon fights many battles with the nations when holy preachers throughout the world strive to defeat idolatry and the confused errors of the nations. The nations are crushed before them when they lay aside their obstinacy in resisting the Gospel of God.

He pursues them to the gate of Ptolemais when, in the inventions by which they contrived through vain studies to oppose the word of God, they are themselves overcome and captured by the truth and subjected to the confession of right faith. Hence it is aptly added:

And nearly three thousand men fell from the nations. Those who fall from their most wicked state of pride into repentance for sins deserve, through rising again by right faith, to be raised up into the state of good works. Simon receives their spoils when the Catholic teacher strives to convert to the service of God whatever they have achieved through literary knowledge or investigation of the truth.

Hence many of them who had been trained in the liberal arts under pagan conduct [Note: [Column 1166D] Something is missing.] [lacuna] Those who had been in Galilee, together with their wives and children and everything that was with them, he brought into Judea with great joy, when he rescues various Catholics entangled in the affairs of the world through the doctrine of the Gospel and teaches them to pursue the things of God with complete care and effort.

And Judas Maccabeus and Jonathan his brother crossed the Jordan, etc. Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan, sent with their companions against those who held captive the Jews in Gilead, crossed the Jordan and traveled for three days through the desert.

Thus holy preachers, sent into the world to summon people to the faith of Christ and to overcome Jewish and schismatic errors, first cross the Jordan—that is, they teach that one must first pass through the sacrament of baptism from the darkness of unbelief into the grace of Christ. Truth itself bears witness that unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

Then they travel for three days through the desert, because they affirm that the faith of the Holy Trinity, which every believer professes in baptism, must be observed throughout the entire time of this world’s pilgrimage together with good works.

The fact that the Nabataeans met them peacefully and recounted what had happened to their brothers in Gilead signifies that the words of the holy prophets bring timely comfort to holy teachers, when by their testimony they make manifest all the torments that believers in Christ will suffer. For Nabataeans is interpreted as “those who prophesy,” and they foretell by true prophecy the errors that the sons of perdition contrive to set against the truth of the Gospel of Christ.

Hence Hosea pursues the cows of Beth-aven and the inhabitants of Samaria (Hosea 4), and Amos condemns those who sacrifice from fermented dough as an offering, as well as those who turn judgment and justice into wormwood, accept a bribe, and oppress the poor at the gate (Amos 4).

The fact that the Nabataeans indicate that certain Jews had been seized in Barasa and Bosor aptly expresses the outcome of the matter through the interpretation of their names. For Barasa and Bosor are interpreted as “tribulations” and “anguish,” because, in accordance with Paul’s saying, all who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution; nor will anyone who strives to preserve the doctrine of sound faith escape the abuse of heretics.

The Apostle John describes such people in his Apocalypse as inflicting torment like the torment of scorpions when they strike a person. For just as scorpions carry their poison in their tails, so heretics conceal malice at the completion of their fraud, so that they may harm the unwary not with an open front but through hidden snares.

And Judas and his army turned back, etc. Above he relates that the cities of Gilead in which the Jews had been seized were fortified and large, and that Judas resolved to capture and destroy them in a single day. This is because holy preachers resolve through unity to destroy all the fortifications of false doctrines that heretics establish in order to deceive innocent souls and hold them captive in their errors.

Now, however, he says that Judas occupied the city of Bosor in the desert of Bosor, killed every male with the edge of the sword, took their spoils, and burned it with fire. For holy teachers strive with great dedication, once they have seized the fortification of the heretics, to destroy with the sword of the Holy Spirit—which is the word of God (Ephesians 6)—all the strength of the wicked sects that they establish through the philosophy of the world and empty deceit. In this way, what those people fabricated through their boastfulness as something preeminent, these teachers show to be nonsense and worthless.

They take their spoils when they seize from them, as from unjust possessors, the testimonies of the holy Scriptures that they have abused, and burn their very confession with perpetual anathema. The statement that follows, that they rose during the night, shows that they had been left in the darkness of their error.

And it happened at dawn, when they raised their eyes, etc. What is expressed by the ladders and engines of the nations except the exultation and defiance of the proud, by which they desire to attack and overthrow the Church of Christ?

But our Judas, who arranges the entire apparatus of war in the light, fights against them in three ranks: either through faith in the Holy Trinity, or through the twofold doctrine—that is, historical, allegorical, and tropological [the source appears to enumerate three modes despite saying “twofold”]. He cries out with trumpets toward heaven because, through strong preaching, he raises his voice in exultation and, with the innermost cry of his heart, calls upon God as his helper in prayer.

And the camp of Timothy recognized that he was Maccabeus, and they fled from before him. The camp of Timothy fled from before Maccabeus when it recognized him, because heretics, having recognized the power and truth of our Lord Jesus Christ, flee in terror. They are struck with a great blow because, through the holy teachers, the vengeance of anathema is justly exercised against them.

Nearly eight thousand men of them fall when the whole mass of those whom they were attempting to gather against the true understanding of spiritual circumcision, or against faith in the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and of his members, is destroyed by the conquering Truth itself.

Hence the Savior, abolishing the typological Sabbath in the Gospel, revealed to us the mystery of his resurrection on the first day of the week, which is also the eighth day after the seventh. Hence the Apostle Paul also teaches (Colossians 2) that circumcision not made by hand is to be carried out not in the stripping off of the body of flesh but by the Spirit of the living God in the hearts of believers. Thus the old law also taught that the foreskin of the heart must be circumcised.

After these events Timothy gathered another army and pitched camp against Raphon, etc. After Timothy had been defeated once and again, he did not cease increasing his wickedness but multiplied his malice. He renews his army against Judas and his companions, because it is not enough for heretics to engage once or twice in disputes on a small scale; they continually stir up new wars against the Church and pour forth the many poisons of their treachery.

They pitch camp against Raphon beyond the torrent because with the utmost effort of their pride they arouse fury and stir up the storm of wars. They also lead the Arabs, whose name is interpreted as “those of the open country,” as auxiliaries, because they take voluptuous people who pursue the luxury of this age into the service of their error.

Hence all these people constructed against the Church no small wickedness of their error. But Judas sends an army to reconnoiter them when holy teachers lead their hearers to guard against the tumult of the wicked, lest the act of their fraud should bring simple souls to destruction.

Timothy, as though gathering an army, says to the commanders of his army: “When Judas and his army draw near to the torrent of water, if he crosses over to us first, we shall not be able to withstand him, because he will be strong enough against us. But if he is afraid to cross and pitches camp beyond the river, we shall cross over to them, and we shall be able to oppose him.”

This shows that all heretics fear the confidence and steadfastness of a people who believe rightly, and recognize themselves to be weaker in proportion as they see that people stronger in the unity of faith. But if they see that some of the Catholics have become slower in the contemplation of God’s law and in the practice of good works, they promise themselves a triumph over these people and their captivity, rejoicing together.
