When Judas drew near to the torrent of water, etc. Judas crosses the torrent of water and appoints the scribes of the people to exhort the multitude behind him to go into battle. This occurs when our Redeemer, approaching the passion of the cross, appointed apostles who would teach those who believed in him to despise the torment of bodily death and to trust in the power of heavenly truth.

Hence comes the saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10). And again: “In your patience you will possess your souls,” and “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Luke 12). Elsewhere he says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

Hence it is rightly added:

He crossed over to them first, and all the people followed him, because it was necessary that the Mediator between God and human beings should first complete the mystery of his passion, and that thus the faithful from all nations, strengthened by his example, should learn to despise death by suffering for him.

And all the nations were crushed before them, when the errors of various peoples are crushed by the power of God’s virtue.

They threw down their weapons and fled to the sanctuary that is in Carnaim. When the obstacles of contention have been abandoned, the persecutors of truth, no longer daring to resist, hide themselves in the shrines of their gods; but from the place where they seek protection, from that very place they meet their ruin. Carnaim, moreover, is interpreted as “horns”; and horns can aptly be understood as kingdom and defense. But their expectation did not help them; rather, it deceived them, because Judas seized the city itself and burned the sanctuary with all who were in it. For our Savior not only destroys every contrivance of the error of heretics and persecutors [Col. 1169C], but also burns with the fire of just retribution all who trust in it. Hence the Lord commanded in Deuteronomy, saying:

“If you hear in one of your cities, which the Lord your God will give you to inhabit, that some are saying, ‘The sons of Belial have gone out from among you and have led away the inhabitants of their city, saying, “Let us go and serve foreign gods whom you do not know,”’ inquire carefully and diligently. When the truth of the matter has been investigated, if you find that what is said is certain and that this abomination has been committed in fact, you shall immediately strike the inhabitants of that city with the edge of the sword and destroy it, together with everything in it, even the livestock. Whatever household goods are found there, you shall gather in the midst of its streets and burn them together with the city itself, so that you may consume everything for the Lord your God; [Col. 1169D] and it shall be an everlasting mound” (Deut. XIII).

And Judas gathered all the Israelites who were in Gilead, etc. Judas gathers the Israelites from Gilead when our Redeemer, through his teachers, calls back to the catholic faith those who have been taken captive by heretics through the word of the Gospel. For this is what it means to come into the land of Judah: to praise the Lord with right faith and good works.

And they came as far as Ephron, and this was a great city, etc. All the battles of the nations signify the varied wars of vices and errors. We have said that those nations who were in the land of Gilead and attempted to take the Israelites captive signified heretics and Jews. But now, after those who were in [Col. 1170A] Carnaim have been overcome, the people who were in Ephron again attempt to resist Judas and his companions. For when various heretics have been crushed, those who follow the letter of the Old Testament still refuse to open the entrances to spiritual understanding.

For what does Ephron mean—interpreted as “dust of mourning,” or “dust and uselessness”—except the superfluous observance of the law insinuated into the time of grace? In this observance the Jews, while confessing themselves, enclose and shut themselves in, blocking the doors with stones. Devoted to the shadow, they set the historical tradition—which is written on the stones of the law—against the preachers of the Gospel; they refuse in any way to be separated from it, nor do they allow us to follow a more correct understanding. Hence: “Woe to you lawyers, who have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered” (Luke XI).

But Judas sends to them [Col. 1170B] with peaceful words, saying: “We will pass through your land to go into our own land, and no one will harm us.” For the holy preachers, in accordance with the command of our Lord, first offer peace to the opposing party, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not,” he says, “it will return to you” (Luke X).

“We will pass through your land to go into our own land,” they say—as if they were saying: “Let us read the history of your books, so that there we may find, in an allegorical sense, the homeland promised to us in heaven. And no one will harm you, because our passage will do you no injury; we shall pass only on foot, when by the walk of good works we desire to approach the kingdom above.” They did not wish to open, because in the law handed down [Col. 1170C] to them they did not wish to share fellowship with the preachers of the Gospel.

And Judas commanded that proclamation be made in the camp, etc. What does it mean that Judas commanded proclamation in the camp, so that each person should approach the city at the place where he was, except that the holy teachers grant their hearers free understanding in the sacred Scriptures? Thus, whatever each person seeks to have opened to him in divine reading—whether through allegory, tropology, or anagoge—according to the desire of his longing, he receives, with heavenly grace consenting, the opportunity to enter.

And note that the men of valor are said there to approach and to attack the city all day and all night. For unless someone is a man of valor, desiring to put into practice what he has learned from the teaching of his masters, and unless he diligently [Col. 1170D] meditates on the law of God all day and all night—that is, at every time—he will not be victorious over the aforementioned city.

Hence the Psalmist calls blessed the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, who does not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, stand in the way of sinners, or sit in the seat of pestilence (Psalm I).

But when it says that they killed every male with the edge of the sword and uprooted the city, and thus took its spoils as he passed through the whole city over the slain, and afterward crossed the Jordan, it shows us that, if we wish to possess the law of the Lord and receive its spoils—that is, its various meanings—according to right faith, we must first strive to crush the surface of the letter and condemn all the errors of heretics [Col. 1171A]. Thus purified through baptism from our burden, let us cross over into the broad field—that is, pass into the liberty of glory—where the sun of righteousness shines upon us, in whose wings there is true healing; he illuminates the darkness, the things hidden in darkness, and reveals the secrets of mysteries to those who seek him not with feigned pretense but with the truth of faith.

Hence Wisdom admonishes us, saying: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who have faith in him. For perverse thoughts separate from God, and proven virtue rebukes the foolish. Since wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body enslaved to sins. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, [Col. 1171B] and withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding” (Wisdom I).

And Judas was gathering the stragglers and exhorting the people along the whole road, etc. The fact that Judas, returning with his army into the land of Judah, gathered the stragglers and exhorted the people along the whole road until they came into the land of Judah instructs the teachers of the holy Church by his example what concern and diligence they ought to show toward those entrusted to them. Along the road of the present life they should not neglect to offer them the word of exhortation, but by teaching, admonishing, rebuking, and consoling should always strive to benefit them. As far as lies within them, they should permit none to fall away from their company and perish; rather, they should hasten, preserving the number of those entrusted to their care, to return joyfully to the land of Judah [Col. 1171C], in accordance with Paul’s statement (Hebrews XII): to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem; to the gathering of many thousands of angels; and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven; and to the God who is judge of all. Then they may render worthy thanks and praises to him, by whose gift they were able to reach the seat of rest and peace.

And in the days when Judas and Jonathan were in the land of Gilead, etc. What is signified by those two leaders, Joseph and Azariah, who, stirred by rivalry with Judas in virtue, sought through boastfulness to acquire a name for themselves in battle, except the person of hypocrites? They do not desire to imitate the virtues of the saints with a simple intention, but in the arrogance of pride. But just as matters did not turn out well for those who acted without good purpose, [Col. 1171D] so for these their attempt is followed not by true glory but by everlasting disgrace. For they will not deserve to rejoice in their own victory; rather, they will mourn their own perpetual condemnation and that of their followers. Hence it is rightly added:

And there was a great flight among the people, etc. Rightly, therefore, he suffers the downfall of a great blow who does not heed the saving counsel of the spiritual Judah. And because they were not among the elect—those who, stirred by the Spirit of God, perform works of virtue—they will, through their shameless daring, be disgracefully confounded and found at the end among sinners.

And the men of Judah were greatly exalted in the sight of Israel, etc. It is rightly said that the men of Judah were greatly exalted in the sight of all the nations, because those who [Col. 1172A] hold the true confession of right faith in such a way that they fulfill in deed what they preach with their mouth are deservedly praised by the voice of all nations. People come to them, acclaiming blessings; that is, blessing them through the keeping of his commandments, they offer praises of Judah to the heavenly King, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying. Considering the good things of the Church, he says: “They called the people blessed who have these things; blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Psalm CXLV). Hence also our Savior commanded his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V).

And Judas and his brothers went out and fought the sons of Esau in the land toward the south, etc. What is understood by Esau, who, through his desire for food, sold his [Col. 1172B] birthright to his younger brother Jacob, except the former people? Because of their desire for earthly things, they showed themselves unworthy of the honor of the firstborn, and for this reason the entire dignity was transferred to the people of the nations.

And it is fitting that the sons of Esau are said to dwell in the land toward the south, because the Jewish people, on account of the law they received and the writings of the prophets handed down among them, seemed to draw near to the light of the eternal Sun. But because they were blinded in mind and, though placed near the light—namely, the light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John I)—refused to receive it when it was set before them, they are therefore openly remembered as having been defeated by Judas and his brothers.

For the holy teachers, reproaching them for their error, justly rejected and condemned them for their disobedience and turned to the preaching of the nations [Col. 1172C]. Striking the error of the faithless with the sword of God’s word, both in the synagogue itself and in individual persons, they burned with the fire of deserved condemnation the towers of pride that those people, in their exaltation of mind, had erected against the Gospel of Christ.

And he moved the camp to go into the land of the foreigners, etc. Note, reader, that he now briefly touches upon and recapitulates all those kinds of adversaries whom he had mentioned earlier: Jews, gentiles, and heretics. For shortly before, after recounting that the sons of Esau had been defeated, he immediately added that the camp of the foreigners, together with their altars and the spoils of their gods, had been burned; then he described the march through Samaria. He now mentions Samaria because not only Jewish superstition but also the error of the gentiles and heretical perversity are overcome, confounded, destroyed, and reduced to nothing through the Gospel of Christ preached by the apostles [Col. 1172D].

Above all, however, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, conquered (Revelation V); and who will resist him? “Judgment was shot from heaven; the earth trembled and was still, when God arose for judgment and saved all the quiet of the earth” (Psalm LXXV).

But what is said among other things—that priests fell in battle when they went out to fight without counsel—is a most fearful warning.

## CHAPTER VI

On the death of Antiochus and the succession of his son, who sent an army to fight Judas and was defeated; how he deceitfully grants peace and quickly breaks it; here elephants are said to have been used in battle. [Col. 1173A]

And King Antiochus traveled through the upper regions, etc. After the many impious deeds that Antiochus had committed in the holy place and among the people of God, he was justly put to death by divine judgment, as he himself testifies in what follows, saying that he had recognized that these evils had overtaken him because of those deeds, and that he was perishing in sorrow in a foreign land.

Although Polybius of Megalopolis—[the reading “Anegalopolita” is evidently corrupt]—the historian, as Josephus records, writes that he perished solely because he wished to devastate the temple of Diana in Persia, this opinion is in no way accepted by the faithful, who [Col. 1173B] know that all the gods are demons and that the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands (Psalm CXIII).

Because he swelled with pride against the almighty Lord, he received a fitting retribution. So also do all the impious; and likewise, at the end, the new son of perdition, who exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped (II Thessalonians II)—of whom this Antiochus was a type—will perish, because of the impious deeds he will commit, under the judgment of the One who visits from above. The Lord Jesus, in accordance with Paul’s word, will kill him with the breath of his mouth (ibid.) and destroy him by the brightness of his coming. Hence this Antiochus represents the persecutors of Christ and the Church.

And King Antiochus died there in the one hundred forty-ninth year, etc. It is not surprising that a savage son was begotten from a cruel [Col. 1173C] father, since he imitated the wicked deeds of his most wicked father. Concerning him the Lord says in the Gospel to the Jewish elders and proud men: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires; for he was a murderer from the beginning” (John VIII). And rightly the son of a murderer plots murder—not only bodily murder but also spiritual murder, that is, the destruction of souls that die in sin and impiety.

And those who were in the citadel had confined Israel around their holy places [the supplied text reads *suorum*, “their own”; “sanctorum,” “holy,” is editorial], etc. Who are those who, from the citadel, confined Israel around their own [holy places] and were always seeking evil for them, as a support for the nations, except those who raise themselves up in the citadel of pride and persecute true religion, so that they may suffocate the word of God [Col. 1173D] and restore error and idolatry?

Against them Judas prepares to fight, because the whole intention of the holy teachers is directed above all toward this: that errors be defeated and overcome by the eminence of truth. But stirred by this effort, some among the gentiles, such as philosophers, and some from impious Israel, who are heretics, provoke the ruler of this world to hatred against the servants of God, so that, aided by this support, they may more easily exalt their impiety. Hence we read that, coming to the king, they said to him:

“How long will you refrain from judging and avenging the brothers of the city? We decided to serve your father, to walk according to his commands, and to obey his words. But for this reason the sons of our [Col. 1174A] people were alienated from us, and whoever was found among us was killed, and our inheritances were plundered. Nor did they extend their hand only against us, but against all our borders.”

And the king was angry when he heard this, and summoned all his friends and the commanders of his army, etc. The Antiochus who signifies the type gathers an army not only from his own people but also from foreigners, because the savagery of persecutors, not content with internal sedition, also raises monstrous wars from outside against the servants of Christ. They organize infantry, arrange cavalry, and prepare elephants, so that nothing may be lacking from their cruelty; whatever impiety can imagine, atrocity prepares in its entirety.

Figuratively, just as infantry and cavalry can signify executioners and torturers, so elephants, because of the enormous size of their bodies and the cruelty of their minds [Col. 1174B], can signify the arrogance of rulers. To this corresponds the fact that they displayed before the beasts the blood of grapes and mulberries to intensify their rage, because the savagery of persecutors was aroused by the shedding of the martyrs’ blood.

And it is rightly said that a thousand men stood beside each elephant, wearing coats of mail joined together, with bronze helmets on their heads, and that five hundred horsemen were assigned to each beast. For many people support rulers by flattery; their coats of mail are joined together—that is, they are entangled with one another in the deceptions of wicked counsels. They have bronze helmets on their heads when they surround their minds with the hardness of iniquity. And horsemen are arranged there, because the elevation of pride will not be absent wherever the equality of the common human nature is not considered through mercy [Col. 1174C], but the vanity of worldly favor is sought.

The wooden towers, moreover, which were placed upon the beasts and contained thirty men each, express the frailty of the power by which persecutors always imagine that they will prevail over the martyrs. And it is rightly said: “Inside was the master of the beast, with the remaining horsemen on either side,” because the cruelty of their minds, which devised every evil, burned within the hearts of the persecutors—an act of pride—and was outwardly defiled in the torture of the innocent.

With these arrangements made, Judas resolved to encourage his army, because the holy preachers, when engaged in the wars of persecution, do not cease by their words to strengthen the hearts of their hearers. And although earthly glory may shine in worldly pomp, or various kinds of torment may blaze in the instruments of torture, nevertheless the martyrs of Christ remain undaunted. Clinging to the side of their judge—namely, the spiritual Judas—they conquer and overthrow the audacity of the impious [Col. 1174D].

And Eleazar son of Saura saw one of the beasts armored with the king’s armor, etc. It should be noted that Josephus affirms Eleazar to have been Judas’s brother; above, he was said to have been one of the five sons of Mattathias, called by this name. But one may ask how he is said to have been the son of Saura if he was the son of Mattathias, unless perhaps Mattathias himself was called Saura by another name.

What is signified by Eleazar, who killed the elephant and died, except the person of the arrogant? When they wish to accomplish something bravely, but not with a simple spirit, rather with an uplifted one, they are defeated and fall in their [Col. 1175A] endeavors. This matter can also, not inappropriately, be transferred to the meaning of hypocrites. For when hypocrites struggle through abstinence against lust, gluttony, or bodily sins, subduing the flesh through fasting, vigils, and other works of abstinence, they do not properly guard themselves against spiritual wickedness. Thus they either fail to beware of pride, envy, or greed; and at some point, while conquering, they are conquered. For while they overcome certain things, they are incautiously crushed by others in the very victory.

And the king’s army approached Judea and Mount Zion, and he made peace with those who were in Beth-zur, etc. The mystical Antiochus advances toward Judea and Mount Zion because he directs the entire preparation of war toward the overthrow [Col. 1175B] of the Church of Christ. He makes peace with those who were in Beth-zur when he offers not true peace but a false one to those whom he wishes to deceive and mislead through pretense.

But only those come out of the city to him who, being shut in, had no provisions. For only those are seduced away from the protection of the Church who lack the nourishment of knowledge and charity by which their minds are fed. They also keep Sabbath wrongly when they love not the pursuit of virtue but the idleness of sloth. And they return under the dominion of the enemy who captures them because they refuse to guard against his snares.

When it is said that the king turned his army toward the holy place for many days, this signifies that persecutors do not easily cease from the cruelty of persecution but inflict wars throughout all the days until the consummation [Col. 1175C] of the age—against some believers for their testing, and against others for their deception. For while the mystical woman, expressed figuratively through Eve, crushes the serpent’s head, that poisonous snake will never cease to lie in wait for her heel.

What follows—“And only a few men remained in the holy places, because famine had overcome them, and each was scattered to his own place”—signifies that, while the persecution of unbelievers burns fiercely, many of those who remained in the Church outwardly rather than with the steadfastness of faith are scattered because of fear of punishments. This accords with what the Lord foretold in the Gospel would happen in the last times: “For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. And they will fall by the edge of the sword and will be led captive into all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Luke XXI).

And Lysias heard that Philip, whom King Antiochus had appointed while he was still alive, etc. It does not seem unworthy to insert here what Josephus reports about this; nor should it seem burdensome to the reader if the accounts of different histories are compared with one another, since they appear mutually to assist in explaining the truth of the matter by reconstructing it historically. Josephus narrates it in this way (Book XII of the *Antiquities*, chapter 14):

“Lysias, the commander, and King Antiochus, when it was announced to them that Philip, coming from Persia, had [Col. 1176A] presumed to assume the authority entrusted to him and wished to take over the government of Antiochus, decided to abandon the siege and march against Philip. They did not wish to disclose this plan to the other commanders. Instead, the king ordered Lysias to tell the commanders that a prolonged siege could accomplish nothing for them, since the enemy’s position was clearly fortified and the lack of provisions was pressing upon them, and that it would be advantageous to make peace with the Jews and allow them to use their ancestral rites, from which, having been prohibited by us until then, they appeared to have become alienated.

“Having said this, he decided that Philip’s tyranny should be kept secret, lest the uncertain hearts of his army learn of it. When Lysias had spoken thus, the army and the commanders approved the proposal. Then the king sent to Judas and promised peace to those under siege, assuring them that they might live according to their ancestral laws [Col. 1176B]. They accepted his words, and after the oaths and pledges had been confirmed, they came out of the temple.

“But when Antiochus entered and saw the fortified position, he shamelessly violated his oaths and ordered the whole army standing around it to demolish the walls down to their foundations. After doing this, he returned to Antioch, taking with him Onias, the high priest, who was also called Menelaus.

“For Lysias persuaded the king to kill Menelaus if he wished the Jews to be at peace, saying that he had been the beginning of the evils, since he had induced his father to compel the Jews to abandon their ancestral religion. Therefore the king sent Menelaus to Beroea, a city of Syria, and killed him after the tenth year of his high-priesthood. And, in order to obtain the high-priesthood himself, he had urged the Jews to transgress the laws.

“After Menelaus’s death, Alcimus, who was also called Joachim, was appointed high priest. But King Antiochus, finding Philip in control of affairs, fought against him and, having brought him under his power, killed him.

“The son of Onias the high priest, whom we mentioned earlier, was still a small boy when his father died. Seeing that the king had killed his uncle Menelaus and given the high-priesthood to Alcimus, who was not of the priestly family—the king having been persuaded by Lysias to transfer the honor from that family to another house—he fled to Ptolemy, king of Egypt. He received honor from him and from his wife Cleopatra and requested a place in the region of Heliopolis, where he built a temple like that of Jerusalem.”

Thus far Josephus.

But the fact that Antiochus made a treaty with the Israelites [Col. 1176D], and that he and his commanders swore an oath, yet did not keep the oath but broke his pledge and violated the pact, signifies that no firm treaty of alliance can exist in any way with heretics and unbelievers, because observance of an oath is not fixed among them. Hence one must never make a covenant with vices or with the author of vices, even if they promise peace and feign prosperity. Rather, at all times one must fight against them diligently with the shield of faith and the weapons of righteousness. The battle will cease only when the enemy Antiochus is no longer silent in the world but, submerged, is confined in hell.

## CHAPTER VII

Demetrius, after killing Antiochus and Lysias, obtained the kingdom. Concerning Alcimus and Bacchides and their wickedness; concerning the bloodshed around Jerusalem. Demetrius sent Nicanor against Israel: Judas prayed and conquered. [Col. 1177A]

In the one hundred fifty-first year Demetrius, son of Seleucus, went out from the city of Rome, etc. Pompey Trogus relates the following about this Demetrius in his *History*:

“When Antiochus withdrew [read: died], leaving behind a very young son, for whom guardians had been appointed by the people, his uncle Demetrius, who was a hostage at Rome, learned of the death of his brother Antiochus and approached the Senate. He said that he had come as a hostage while his brother was alive, and that, since his brother was dead, he did not know whose hostage he was. It was therefore just that he should be released to seek the kingdom, which by the law of nations had passed to the elder [Col. 1177B] brother and now belonged to him, who was older than the ward.

“When he realized that the Senate would not release him, judging by a silent decision that the kingdom would be safer under the ward than under him, he left the city under the pretext of hunting and, secretly at Ostia, boarded a ship with companions in his flight. He was carried to Syria and received there with the favorable support of all; after the ward was killed, the guardians handed the kingdom over to him.”

And wicked and impious men from Israel came to him, with Alcimus as their leader, etc. What is signified by King Demetrius except the rulers of the nations who stir up persecution against the Church of Christ? The interpretation of his name aptly explains this, for it means “one who binds tightly” or “one who persecutes excessively.”

To this ruler, then, come wicked and impious [Col. 1177C] men from Israel, with Alcimus as their leader, when those who, after receiving the faith of Christ, have returned to apostasy blaspheme the Christian religion and disparage ecclesiastical worship. Their leaders are heretics, who through ambition for high status wish to appear great to everyone.

After receiving such a betrayal, Demetrius sends, figuratively, Bacchides, who ruled beyond the River in the kingdom, to establish the impious Alcimus as priest and to take vengeance on the children of Israel. This occurs when various pagans who are powerful in the world—who have not yet deserved to be washed in Christ’s baptism and counted among the faithful—lend support to the arrogance of heretics and inflict the [Col. 1177D] torment of suffering upon Christ’s true confessors. But although such persons speak deceitfully to Judas and his brothers with peaceful words, they nevertheless do not accept their words, because they in no way trust their faithlessness.

And Judas saw all the evils that Alcimus and those who were with him had done, etc. What does it mean that Judas takes vengeance on the transgressors except that our Redeemer avenges his elect and permits none of his own to perish in vain? He exercises vengeance upon those who deserve it in two ways. Some he summons from the fountain of his great mercy to repentance for their error, causing them to rise up against themselves so that by lamentation they may punish what they had previously done. Others, however, after they have committed their crimes, he leaves by a just judgment to persist uncorrected in their hardness, so that afterward he may inflict upon them the punishments they have deserved by their wicked deeds [Col. 1178A].

And the king sent Nicanor, one of his more noble commanders, who was hostile toward Israel, etc. Through this Nicanor, whom we read elsewhere to have been appointed over the elephants, we may understand false apostles or false prophets who, coming from the Jews and advancing in the exercise of their pride, went to the Church of the gentiles [the wording *functioni* is uncertain]. While pretending to be peaceful, they attempted to introduce error into the Church of Christ; but, as will appear at the end, they were most savage enemies.

Concerning them the apostle John writes in his Apocalypse (chapter II): “Those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan.” The teacher of the nations [Col. 1178B] calls them false apostles in his Epistle (II Corinthians XI), deceitful workers who disguise themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, since Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works.

These men, like Nicanor, putting forth [*exerentes*; read *extendentes*, “stretching out”] their hand against the temple of the Lord, blaspheme, because they disparage the power of Christ, who is in the Church, as though it were weak. They say to the brothers: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (for they are recorded as having taught this in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter XV). But once victory has been won through our Judas and his companions, the blasphemous head of this error, together with Nicanor and the right hand of its wicked action, is cut off, so that no further injury of such blasphemy may be inflicted upon the divine majesty [Col. 1178C].

For the apostle Paul says to us (Ephesians II): “By his grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.”

## CHAPTER VIII

Concerning the renown and power of the Romans. Judas sends envoys to Rome for the sake of peace: the Roman reply to the Jews.

And Judas heard of the name of the Romans, that they were powerful in strength, etc. Judas sends envoys to the Romans to establish friendship and alliance with them [*mittit*; variant *mittens*, “sending”] [Col. 1178D]. This signifies that our Redeemer, through his preachers, offers the Gospel of peace to the nations and summons them to his faith.

They wrote their reply on bronze tablets as they had been asked, and sent them to Jerusalem so that a memorial of peace and alliance might be there among them. For the nations converted to belief in Christ establish a covenant of firm faith, signifying that it will endure for a long time, and they hand over a monument of true confession in the catholic Church, so that there may be there an everlasting memorial of their fellowship.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “Behold, the Lord has caused it to be heard and has sent messengers to the nations” (Jeremiah XLIX). Again: “And the angel of his presence will save them, in his love and in his mercy; he himself redeemed them” (Isaiah LXIII). And again: “It is a small thing,” he says, “for you to be my [Col. 1179A] servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to convert the refuse of Israel” (Isaiah XLIX); “I have given you as a light to the nations, so that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isaiah XLII). And again: “I have given you as a covenant of the people, to raise up the land and possess the scattered inheritances” (Isaiah XLIX).

What does it mean that Judas sent two envoys to the Romans for the sake of establishing peace except that our Redeemer, to summon the nations to faith and the fellowship of peace, sent the two Testaments into the world? Or, in another sense, he sends two messengers because of the sacrament of charity, since there are two commandments of charity, and charity cannot exist properly with fewer than two. No one is properly said to have charity toward himself; rather, by love he extends himself toward another, so that charity may exist.

In the Gospel the Lord sends his disciples to preach two by two [Col. 1179B], silently indicating to us that one who has no charity toward another must in no way undertake the office of preaching. It is rightly said that he sent them before his face into every city and place where he himself was about to come (Luke X). For the Lord follows his preachers: preaching goes before, and then the Lord comes to dwell in the habitation of our mind, when words of exhortation precede and through them truth is received in the mind.

## CHAPTER IX

Demetrius sends an army against the Jews. Concerning the death of Judas Maccabaeus. Concerning wicked men and the wickedness of Bacchides. Concerning weddings turned into mourning. Jonathan obtains the leadership; Alcimus, wishing to destroy the temple, became mute, etc. [Col. 1179C]

Meanwhile, when Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, etc. Demetrius again renews the war against Judas through Bacchides and Alcimus, because through pagans and heretics who have fallen away from the faith of Christ, the ruler of the world renews his ancient snares against the Church every day by new devices. With them he also sent the right wing, when he entrusted a strong force of auxiliaries to carry out such a wicked deed.

Against them Judas goes with three thousand men, because the entire assembly of teachers, together with the faithful, prepares to fight against all the enemies of the faith, so that through faith in the holy Trinity it may overthrow the host of enemies that, in its proud presumption, dares to rise against its creator. But let us see what is written next [Col. 1179D]:

And they saw the multitude of the army, because it was large, and they were greatly afraid, etc. Although many may appear to remain in the confession of the catholic faith, when persecution burns fiercely it will become clear who were fixed in faith and who merely appeared outwardly to be in it. Hence it is written in the Gospel parable (Matthew XIII) that when the sun rose, the crops that had been in rocky ground and had not had much earth withered, because those who do not hold firm roots of belief in their hearts, believing for a time, withdraw in the time of temptation.

Of the three thousand, therefore, only eight hundred men remained with Judas [Col. 1180A], because when the reprobate fall away from the communities of the Church, only the elect—those predestined to receive eternal blessedness—will remain steadfast in sound faith, etc.

And the army moved out from the camp, and they stood opposite them, and the cavalry was divided into two parts. What does it mean that, when the army had advanced from the camp, the cavalry is said to have been divided into two parts, except that among the proud and arrogant unity and firm harmony can never be preserved? Scripture bears witness, saying: “Among the proud there are always quarrels” (Proverbs XIII).

“And slingers,” he says, “and archers went before the army.” What are meant by the slingers and archers except those who, in order to entice human minds toward idolatry or apostasy, seek either to pervert the faithful by flattering them with empty promises of prosperity, as though by the whirling motion of a sling, or strive to deceive them by terrifying them with threats of tortures, as though with the blows of arrows? They are appropriately described as going before the army, because it was always the practice of persecutors to precede the infliction of tortures with such efforts.

“And the earth was shaken by the voice of the armies,” etc. “And the earth was shaken,” he says, “by the voice of the armies”—that is, the hearts of carnal people were shaken by fear of persecutions.

“And battle was joined from morning until evening.” From the dawn of the light of faith until the end of the world, the camps of the devil do not cease to fight against the Church of God, nor do they ever cease trying to move the good by the adversity of tribulations. For, according to Paul’s statement: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (I Tim. III).

[Col. 1180C] Judas saw that the stronger part of Bacchides’ army was on the right, and, having gathered together with him all who were steadfast in heart, he crushed it: when the appropriate supports of the faithful have been joined together, the holy teachers strive to repel the assault of the pagans by the word of faith and bring them to the tranquility of faith. That part of them seemed stronger because they were inflamed on the side of pagan error against the Church by the enormity of their tortures, whereas they deceitfully laid snares for their brothers through feigned friendships. But Judas pursues Bacchides’ army as far as Azotus, when the preachers of the Gospel strive to lead the fury of the pagans toward the fire of holy love. For Azotus is interpreted as “kindred fire.” That love which burned in the hearts of the patriarchs may be said to be the love which the zeal of the teachers desires to form [Col. 1180D] in the minds of their children, so that what is written concerning Elijah may be fulfilled: “To turn the hearts of the fathers toward the children and the disobedient toward the wisdom of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke I).

“And those who were on the left wing saw that the right wing had been crushed,” etc. When the right wing, which had been stronger, fell, the left wing pursued Judas from behind; because, when the severe persecution of the pagans has in a certain manner been quieted, heretics, with a sinister intention, do not cease to persecute the holy Church by deceitfully laying snares and secretly wounding it, as though from behind. Hence it follows:

“And the battle grew fierce, and many wounded fell [Col. 1181A] from among them,” etc. The battle grows fierce when pagans attack the Church of Christ through open persecution and heretics through deceptive seduction. Many wounded fall from both groups when the wicked, envying the good, fall in great numbers, pierced by the arrows of their own wickedness; compelled by the tortures of evil men, they are forced to blaspheme. This happens especially where the peoples are deprived of the help of their teachers. Hence it is added: “And Judas fell, and the others fled.” For when the shepherds have been slaughtered, the flocks are forced to flee in different directions, as it is written prophetically in Zechariah, in anticipation of Christ’s passion: “Strike the shepherd,” he says, “and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII). The evangelist introduced this as a testimony in the Lord’s passion, when, after he himself had been seized by the crowds, all the disciples left him and fled; because what went before in the Head must necessarily follow in the body.

“And Jonathan and Simon took up Judas their brother and buried him in the tomb of his fathers in the city of Modin,” etc. The downfall of good teachers through the passing of temporal death cannot occur without the sorrow of their disciples. Hence it is said that all the people of Israel mourned Judas with great mourning. A similar event is also recorded in the passion of Stephen: “Devout men cared for Stephen and made great mourning over him” (Acts VIII). Yet although the departure of their own touches the minds of the faithful through compassion, they are not without the consolation which they possess through the sure hope of the future rest of souls. The saints are saddened in some measure by the pain of their body, but rejoice only a little in spirit at the reward assured to them in the heavenly kingdom. Hence the Savior, preaching to his disciples in the Gospel about the greatness of suffering and the certain reward of his triumph, says: “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and falsely say every evil thing against you because of my name. Rejoice on that day and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V).

“And the remaining words concerning the wars of Judas and the deeds of valor which he performed,” etc. There are many wars and deeds of valor which the saints perform—or rather, which the Lord performs in them—and no one can grasp knowledge of them all; they remain known only in the recognition of their author. Hence the Lord says of them in the Gospel [Col. 1181D]: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, know them” (John X); and again: “Rejoice and exult,” he says, “because your names are written in heaven; for,” he says, “all the hairs of your head are numbered, and not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke X). Concerning this it is also written elsewhere: “The Lord knows those who are his” (Matt. X); and again: “He alone knows the hearts of all the children of Adam” (Luke XXI). Hence the Prophet says in the psalm: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name” (Ps. CXLVI); and again: “Wonderful,” he says, “is the Lord among his saints; he will give strength and power to his people” (Ps. LXVII). Therefore it is necessary that each one and all should say: “Blessed is the Lord, who alone has done great wonders, and blessed is the name of his majesty forever and ever” (Ps. XV).

“And after Judas’s death, the wicked arose in all the borders of Israel,” etc. Earlier, where the death of Mattathias was recalled, it is found written that he died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year. In his place Judas his son arose, and he fought the battle of Israel. Likewise, in what follows, it is found written that Jonathan assumed the leadership after his brother Judas. After him, in the one hundred and fifty-third year, Alcimus ordered the walls of the holy house and the works of the prophets to be destroyed; he died at that time. Josephus, however, relates that after Alcimus—who was also Joachim—had held the leadership of the priesthood for four years, he entered upon the priesthood, and that the people of Judah opposed him; he says that after he had exercised the leadership of the priesthood for three years, he died. In all these matters it is understood that after the death of his father Mattathias, Judas exercised leadership over the people for seven years. During these years, after expelling the commanders of Antiochus from Judaea through four years of fighting and cleansing the temple of the images of idols, he restored the ancestral laws to his fellow citizens, in the one hundred and fourth [first] Olympiad, and thus assumed the leadership of the priesthood and completed three years in it. Hence it is also found in the Chronicles that Jonathan assumed leadership of the Jews in the sixth year of Demetrius Soter, and held it for nineteen years—that is, ten years after the death of his father Mattathias, in the one hundred and fifty-fifth Olympiad.

That infestation by wicked people which disturbed the children of Israel after Judas’s death mystically signifies that, when good teachers have been removed, the faithful hearers suffer no small loss, since, when an opportunity has been perceived, not only pagans but also heretics wear out the Church of God through severe persecutions. For this reason Paul, about to proceed to Jerusalem, summoned the elders of Ephesus and said among other things: “Now, behold, I know that you will all see my face no more, among whom I passed preaching the kingdom of God. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am pure from the blood of all. For I have not shrunk from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood. I know that after my departure ravenous wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, in order to draw the disciples after them. Therefore keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears. And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build up and give an inheritance among the sanctified” (Acts XX).

“In those days there was a very great famine,” etc. When famine arose, the whole region surrendered itself to Bacchides: because, when preachers were lacking through a famine of the word of God—the food by which souls ought to be nourished—for, according to the statement of the Truth, “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV), some, compelled by tortures, and others, enticed by empty persuasions, surrender themselves from among the ecclesiastical number to the pagans. They search for the friends of the true Judas, whom, as Scripture testifies, all his brothers praise; and when they find them, they mock them and exact vengeance upon them.

Everyone who reads ecclesiastical history recognizes that this interpretation came to pass in the earliest times among the worshipers of Christ. But the spiritual forces of wickedness, which serve the will of the ancient enemy, when they see that human souls lack the bread of the word of God, strive to lead them into error and drag them toward vices, so that they may make prey for Satan out of the friends of Judas and turn the vessels of God into food for eternal fire.

“And there was great tribulation in Israel, such as there had not been,” etc. After no prophet was seen in Israel, there was great tribulation, because, when teaching ceased among the people, the plague of sins was stirred up; and from this there proceeded against them the vengeance of God. Therefore it is necessary that the teachers of the Church be diligent in teaching their subjects, and that the hearers be attentive to hearing the word of God. Hence Solomon also says: “Good instruction gives grace” (Prov. XIII). “The lips of the wise guard them. Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty; but where there are abundant crops, there is evident strength” (Prov. XIV). “For the good there will be abundance in every good work. Mercy and truth prepare good things” (ibid.).

“And all the friends of Judas gathered together, and they said [Col. 1183C] to Jonathan,” etc. What does it mean that after Judas’s death Jonathan is read to have been chosen by the people for the priesthood, so that he might fill his brother’s place, except that when the first teachers of the Church have departed through martyrdom, their successors, through the administration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, are substituted in their place? The effectiveness of this administration is demonstrated by the interpretation of Jonathan’s name. For it is interpreted as “their dove,” as was shown above: he brings forward the preachers of the word so that they may worthily carry out the office of their leadership among the people of God and provide suitable defense against their enemies for those subject to them. Yet, as with the earlier teachers, so also against the later teachers of the people of God, savage weapons are launched by infidels and heretics, and the cruel hostility of enemies opposes them. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1183D] “And Jonathan assumed the leadership at that time,” etc. Jonathan fled into the wilderness of Thecua when war threatened, because, when the persecution of enemies blazes up, holy teachers with their followers penetrate by prayers into the secret place of the heavenly court, so that there, by invoking almighty God, they may find help; with their whole-hearted purpose they ask him to come to their aid. For Thecua is interpreted as “trumpet” or “blare.” What is added—“And they settled beside the water of the pool of Asphar”—signifies devoting oneself to tears of compunction, by which they strive more easily to obtain the consolation of almighty God, since they seek refuge not elsewhere but solely in his mercy. Hence Asphar is interpreted as “he sat” or “earth,” because when the heart is healed of vices and moved to compunction, the moisture of tears is poured more abundantly from the eyes outward, to call forth the mercy of God.

“And Bacchides learned of it, and on the Sabbath day he came, himself and all his army, across the Jordan,” etc. What does it mean that Bacchides came across the Jordan with his army on the Sabbath day against the Jews, except that the persecutors of Christians, envious of the peace and quiet of the Church, strive, by bursting in with tumult, to disturb the sacrament of baptism and overturn the state of faith? For this they call upon their friends, the Nabataeans, for assistance, because they associate heretics and malicious people with themselves for the crushing of the faithful. The Nabataeans, as some assert, are interpreted as “profane,” according to the wickedness of their heart; and heretics can appropriately be called “profane” in this passage, for they do not commend the truth by teaching sound faith, but, according to the wickedness of their heart, bring forth the falsehood of error. Hence in the Law the prophets who dreamed empty dreams and prophesied lies were judged [adjudged] worthy of death according to the Lord’s sentence. This most certainly happens to heretics, who separate themselves from God through schisms and useless sects, and through error and blasphemy unite themselves to the devil.

“And the sons of Jambri went out from Madaba, and they seized John and everything that he had,” etc. Who are represented by the sons of Jambri except the pleasure-seekers of this world? They are said to go out from Madaba—that is, from the nativity of the Lord—when they seek to pursue carnal desire, which they originally contracted on the side of the flesh, without alteration [or: “without transformation”]. These, then, seize John and everything that he had and depart carrying it, when they drag away to themselves through unlawful desires someone from the sons of the Church who has been washed in the water of baptism and reborn by the grace of God; and, perverting the good pursuits in which he served God, they turn him toward the enticements of pleasures.

But Jonathan and Simon, desiring to avenge these things, overthrow and kill the bridegroom who had married the daughter of one of the great princes of Canaan with great pomp, together with all his equipment and his friends. This happens when holy teachers rescue from a wicked purpose some whom they see with all their strength to be longing for the pleasures of the world and inclined toward lust—those whom the prince of this age, in order to deceive them, presents as burning with carnal desire and draws into his fellowship—and when, with the sword of the divine word, they kill in them that which was harmful and opposed to the divine commandments. Such a victory rightly befits those who have learned from the heavenly Teacher to love their enemies and do good to those who hate them; to pray for those who persecute and slander them; to bless those who curse them and not return curses. They take their spoils when they convert all their efforts [or: “uses,” variant] to ecclesiastical use. Hence it is appropriately added:

“And the wedding was turned into mourning, and the voice of their musicians into lamentation.” For the holy preachers teach those whom they seize as a saving spoil, and whom they wholly kill with respect to carnal life and the deeds of the old person, to change the world’s empty joy into the mourning of repentance, and empty amusements and useless songs into divine psalmody accompanied by tears of compunction. Thus they return to the bank of the Jordan when they lead them to the state of Christian religion and to the reception of holy baptism, so that there the evangelical rite may be fulfilled, for the sake of which all the labor was undertaken.

“And Bacchides heard and came on the Sabbath day as far as the bank of the Jordan with great force,” etc. When the persecutors of the faithful, on the spiritual Sabbath—during which the worshipers of Christ abstain from earthly desires in order to hear the word of God and sing praise to the Lord—are stirred by envy and strive to disturb them, attempting through secular power to defile the sacrament of baptism, the mystical Jonathan urges his own people to spiritual battle: that is, to fight against their enemies by patience of mind and strength of faith. This does not mean that they should harm them by fighting or striking them, but that they should overcome them more effectively by enduring them with patience and gentleness and repaying them with benefits, according to the Savior’s statement to his disciples: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’; but I say to you, do not resist evil. If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also; and to anyone who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, give up your cloak as well” (Matt. V). And again: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI). Hence Paul also says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. XII). By such sacrifices God is won over; he gives victory to his servants and lays their enemies low beneath their feet. Hence it is written later that Jonathan made peace with Bacchides, and that Bacchides swore that he would do him no harm throughout all the days of his life; and he restored to him the captives whom he had previously taken from the land of Judah.

“And in the one hundred and fifty-third year, in the second month, Alcimus ordered the walls of the house to be destroyed.” We said above that Alcimus, the defiler of the Law and betrayer of his homeland, signified heretics, who do not fear to profane God’s Testament with wicked sects and disturb God’s Church. Here he is now recalled as destroying the walls of the inner holy house and demolishing the works of the prophets. This can fittingly be applied to heretics themselves, who strive not only to corrupt the utterances of the prophets with empty traditions, but also, by whatever means they can, to violate and dispute the bulwark of faith—which is guarded with attentive mind in the hearts of believers for the observance of God’s mystical law.

But let us see what follows in common:

“At that time Alcimus was struck down, and his works were destroyed,” etc. Although heretics may boast in empty arrogance, and although they may seem for a time to prevail over the faithful through the support of the powerful of this world, nevertheless, by the judgment of almighty God, they will be overthrown at the end [Col. 1186A], and the strength of their wicked will shall be dissolved, when they cannot bring to completion what they desire. Nor will it be possible for them to be established in their own house—that is, in the conduct that follows from them—when the sentence of the heavenly Judge is already imminent. Rather, what the Psalmist says will come to pass: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. They said: ‘With our tongue we shall prevail; our lips are our own; who is our lord?’” (Ps. XI).

“And Alcimus died at that time in great torment.” Because heretics persist in their wickedness until the end of this present life, a second death follows, and, according to the sentence of the Apocalypse of John (ch. XIV), they will be sent into the lake of eternal fire. They will be tormented with fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and in the presence of the Lamb; and the smoke of their torments will rise forever and ever. They will have no rest day or night, those who worshiped the beast and his image; they gnaw their tongues in pain and blaspheme the Lord of heaven because of the pains of their wounds, and they do not perform fruitful repentance for their deeds, because they were unwilling to cleanse themselves from their errors while it was permitted.

“And Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead, and he returned to the king; and the land was quiet for two years.” For a time the Church enjoyed peace from the persecution of infidels and the attacks of heretics, according to what is read in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. IX): “The Church throughout all Judaea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace, and it was built up, walking in the fear of the Lord; and it was filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit.” But because peace and security will not be lasting and permanent in the present life, the following statement makes this clear, where it is written:

“And all the wicked conspired, saying,” etc. All the enemies envy the peace and quiet of the Church of God. Therefore, when they see that the prosperity of the good is arising through fortunate success, they seek the assistance of the wicked in order to cause harm. This is signified by Bacchides’ letter, secretly sent to his associates who were in Judaea, so that they might seize Jonathan and those who were with him in Judaea. For when savage persecutors from outside cannot overthrow the confessors of Christ by tortures, they construct snares within through false brothers who appear to remain in the Church, so that those whom the former could not overcome by the sword, the latter may deceive by guile. Hence the Apostle Paul often complains in his Epistles (Gal. II) of the fraud of false brothers who secretly entered and perverted the truth of the Gospel, but could not prevail because their design became known. For it is the diligence of a good teacher to know how to provide for the people subject to him and to beware of the craftiness of the wicked.

“And he seized,” he says, “men of the region who were commanders of the army, and they were killed by Bacchides.” What else can these signify except those who, content with the surface of the legal letter, wish to observe the Pentateuch of the Law not spiritually but carnally, in circumcision and verbal observances? The teacher of the Gentiles rebukes them when writing to the Galatians, where he says: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? How are you turning again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew? You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear that perhaps I have labored among you in vain. You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. I have confidence in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise; but whoever troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.”

After such people have been destroyed by the faithlessness of the ancient enemy in the death of their soul, let us see what follows:

“And Jonathan withdrew, and Simon, and those who were with him,” etc. What does it mean that, while Bacchides was causing turmoil, Jonathan withdrew with his men into Bethbessen, which is in the wilderness, and rebuilt it after its destruction, strengthening it, except that the holy preachers, when they see the hand of their persecutors prevailing so that they cannot proceed publicly with the word of preaching, withdraw for a time into secluded places, in order there to devote themselves to fasting and prayers? Whatever, through negligence, had slipped away from the certainty of their life while living among the people, they renew again in its entirety by the persistence of good discipline in separation.

For Bethbessen is interpreted as “house of the flowering mouth.” The mouth flowers when it resounds in concert with prayers, psalmody, and hymns of God [sic]. This also seems to be commanded by the Lord in the Gospel to his disciples, when he says: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” [Col. 1187C] (Matt. XX). Hence the Truth himself, when the Jews were planning to kill him, “no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and there he remained with his disciples” (John XI). And elsewhere it is read that he went out onto a mountain to pray, where he spent the night in the prayer of God (Luke VI).

Likewise Paul and Barnabas, when they were preaching the word of God in Iconium (Acts XIV), and an attack by Gentiles and Jews with their rulers arose so that they might insult and stone them, understanding the danger, fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and the whole surrounding region, and there they evangelized. But the wickedness of the ancient enemy permits no place in the world to become safe from snares. Hence Bacchides also leads an army against Bethbessen to attack it and does not permit the worshipers of God to live in peace.

“And Jonathan left his brother Simon in the city and went out into the region,” etc. What does it mean that Jonathan left his brother Simon in the city while he himself went out into the region to pursue the adversaries, except that the holy teachers labor inwardly in virtues and yet do not cease outwardly to fight against enemies with the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit? The enemies of the Church, however, are not uniform; rather, they are diverse and manifold according to the various kinds of persecutions, since Jews, pagans, heretics, and schismatics, as well as false Christians, devise calamities in order to harm the good, as was shown above.

The names themselves also expound this not inappropriately through their interpretations. [Note: Col. 1187D: The passage is corrupt.] For Odaren is interpreted as “his generation,” and Phaseron as “confusion.” Therefore Odaren and his brothers may denote those who, through the unity of the catholic confession, pretend to the good and simple that they belong to the same generations, but show by their wicked deeds that they are separate from their fellowship. The Apostle speaks of such people: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him.” By Phaseron, however, the others are signified—those who differ from the unity of the Church not only in religion but also in their profession of faith. Such people never cease to prepare schisms, quarrels, and calamities for true Christians (Tit. I); but the spiritual leaders turn their devices and deceits back upon them and do not permit them, through their frauds, to harm Christ’s soldiers.

“And he turned away and went into his own land and did not come again into their borders,” etc. When the storms of war had ceased, Jonathan went out into Michmash, and, dwelling there, judged the people and exterminated the wicked from Israel. For when the wars of the wicked have been quieted, the holy preachers strive to restore what had previously been proclaimed concerning the morality of their subjects but had been interrupted by the impending storms of battle; and in every way they strive to pay to their Creator the debt of proper service through good conduct.

Historically, Michmash is a large village which is still shown in the territory of Aelia, retaining its ancient name; it is nine miles from there, near the village of Rama. Michmash is interpreted as “village of the tribes” or “decree.” By this the holy Church is signified, where God is served diligently every day, where, according to the decrees of God’s Law, just judgments are carefully exercised by learned teachers of the faithful, and where the wickedness of the wicked is driven far from true Israel.

## CHAPTER X

Alexander kills Demetrius and takes the daughter of King Ptolemy as his wife. Concerning Jonathan’s glory: how he defeats Apollonius, and how Alexander sends him a golden clasp.

“And in the one hundred and sixtieth year Alexander, son of Antiochus, who was called the Noble, went up and seized Ptolemais,” etc. He calls Antiochus the Noble the man whom the Greeks call Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus [Col. 1188D] the Great, concerning whom more is related above.

“And King Demetrius heard and gathered a very large army,” etc. It does not seem irrelevant to consider what Pompey Trogus and his abridger Justin report concerning this war between Demetrius and Alexander. For thus it is written in the thirty-fifth book of the Epitome of Pompey Trogus:

“Demetrius, having occupied the kingdom of Syria, judged that leisure was dangerous for his newly acquired position and decided to enlarge the strength of his kingdom and increase its wealth through wars against his neighbors. Therefore, hostile to Ariarectes, king of Cappadocia, because of the rejection of his sister’s marriage, he received his brother Holofernes, who had been unjustly expelled from the kingdom, as a suppliant. Rejoicing that an honorable pretext for war had been given to him, he decided to restore Holofernes to his kingdom. But Holofernes, with an ungrateful spirit, entered into an agreement with the Antiochenes, who were at that time offended by Demetrius, and began to plan to expel from the kingdom the man through whom he was being restored. When Demetrius learned this, he spared Ariarectes, lest the fear of a neighboring war deprive him of life, but ordered Holofernes, after he had been captured, to be kept under guard at Seleucia. Nor did the Antiochenes, terrified by this judgment, desist from their revolt. Accordingly, with the assistance both of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, and of Attalus, king of Syria, he sought by arms to recover the kingdom as though it were hereditary; and, so that no insult might be lacking, the name of Alexander was given to him, and he was said to have been born from King Antiochus. Such hatred of Demetrius existed among all that, by general agreement, not only royal power but also nobility of descent was attributed to his rival. Therefore Alexander, by an astonishing reversal of circumstances, forgetting his former lowliness and girded with nearly all the forces of the East, made war upon Demetrius, and, after defeating him, stripped him alike of life and kingdom.

“Yet Demetrius was not lacking in courage in repelling the war. For at first he put the enemy to flight, and when the kings renewed the war, many thousands fell in Mysia. At last, however, still unconquered in spirit, he fell while fighting most bravely among the bravest.

“At the beginning of the war, Demetrius had entrusted two sons to a certain host of his, together with a great weight of gold, so that they might be removed from the dangers of war and, if fortune so required, preserved for vengeance upon their father’s behalf. Of these, the younger Demetrius, having passed beyond the age of puberty, heard of Alexander’s luxury. Unexpected wealth and the ornaments of another’s prosperity held Alexander, as though captivated, idle in the palace among a crowd of prostitutes. With the help of the Cretans, the younger Demetrius attacked him while he was secure and feared no hostile action. The Antiochenes also, wishing to correct their former offense against his father by new services, surrendered themselves to him. The paternal soldiers too, inflamed by affection for the young man and preferring the sanctity of their former oath to the arrogance of the new king, transferred their standards to Demetrius. Thus Alexander, destroyed by fortune with no less force than that by which he had been raised, was defeated in the first battle and killed. He paid the penalty to Demetrius, whom he had killed, and to Antiochus, whose lineage he had falsely claimed.”

“And Jonathan came to Jerusalem,” etc. While Demetrius offered peace by letters, Jonathan, dwelling in Jerusalem, began to renew the city. For although persecutors sometimes terrify the faithful with threats and at other times support them with flatteries, the holy teachers nevertheless persist continually in spiritual construction and renew the city of the Church, so that its enemies may be unable either to break into it by force or to encircle it by deceit.

Hence Jonathan ordered Mount Zion to be fortified on every side by those doing the work with squared stones, because the preachers of the Gospel take special care to surround the camp of the Church with holy and strong men, whom the squared stones signify, so that an enemy seeking to invade the holy city may not easily find an opening. For everything square customarily stands firm, however it is turned. The hearts of the elect are fittingly likened to this figure: they have learned to stand so firmly in the faith that no adversity of circumstances, not even death itself, can cause them to incline from the uprightness of their state.

Beth-zur, which is interpreted as “house of the strong,” signifies the Church, and at times Holy Scripture, in which the strong—that is, the holy teachers and apostolic men—appear to dwell. But just as in the present Church good and evil remain until the Lord’s net, gathering good and bad fish, brings them to the shore (Matt. XIII), that is, to the end of the world and to the judgment of final separation, so Holy Scripture has devout readers who search it out in a catholic sense, and wicked readers who try to draw it toward their own perverse meaning and thereby corrupt it. Hence the Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, says: “Every Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for reproving and correcting, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (II Tim. III). But evil people and deceivers advance toward worse, wandering and leading others into error. Hence the chief of the apostles says that the unlearned and unstable distort the sacred Scriptures to their own destruction (II Pet. III).

Therefore, when the persecutions of the pagans from outside have ceased, heretics and schismatics strive to wage war within against the good Catholics, because they have abandoned the Law of the Lord and refused to observe the way of truth. For this reason Beth-zur is said to become a refuge for them, because whatever they devise with a wicked understanding or utter through perverse speech, they strive to confirm entirely by testimonies of Holy Scripture that have not been rightly understood.

“And King Alexander heard the promises which Demetrius had promised to Jonathan,” etc. That the kings of Syria and Egypt, contending over the kingdom, each sought Jonathan’s help and friendship signifies, I believe, nothing other than that all the carnal, proud, avaricious, and pleasure-seeking, although they always disagree among themselves and can never firmly preserve peace and a treaty, nevertheless sometimes, when they see the immunity and harmony of Holy Scripture or of the holy Church, pay it honor. For some venerate in it the gift which they do not see themselves to possess, because they desire its friendship or wish to be assisted by its timely support, so that through prayer and the practice of virtues they too may be improved.

“In the one hundred and sixty-fifth year Demetrius, son of Demetrius, came from Crete into the land of his fathers.” What else is signified by Apollonius, prefect of Coelesyria, whom Demetrius sent with an army into Judaea, except the lictors and ministers of earthly power? Their masters entrusted them with the task of attacking the faith of Christ and compelling his confessors to blaspheme. Relying wickedly on the number of their own people—exalting themselves, that is, in the support of the proud—they taunt Jonathan because he exercises authority in the mountains with the holy teachers. They mock the hope they have in heavenly assistance and challenge them to the plain—that is, to earthly desires and the pleasures of the world—so that they may more easily overwhelm them while they are dwelling in the depths. For broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it (Matt. VII).

[Col. 1191A] But Jonathan and Simon engage Apollonius and his army with ten thousand men and, overcoming him, strike him down. This signifies that the holy preachers of Christ, joined by a number of the faithful who rightly observe the commandments of the Decalogue, steadfastly fight against the persecutors of the faith and, with divine aid, conquer and overcome all their enemies who devise evil against them.

For Joppa, which is interpreted as “beauty,” appropriately signifies the world, whose appearance seems beautiful to the carnal-minded, because they desire to satisfy the desires of their flesh. There Jonathan attacks Apollonius’s garrison, when the company of teachers, by overthrowing vain worldly philosophy and its followers through the truth of the Gospel, tramples them down. This same gathering of holy preachers also fights against Azotus, which is interpreted as “kindred fire,” when it seeks to extinguish in human beings the desire for earthly things.

But Apollonius’s armies flee to Azotus, to Dagon, their idol, in order to save themselves, when unbelievers seek protection from the demons whom they worship through superstition. For Dagon is interpreted as “fish of sorrow,” signifying the devil, who lurks in the sea of this age and strives to deceive those whom he can. But Jonathan sets Azotus and the temple of Dagon on fire and kills with the sword those who have fled into it, because the holy teachers, after destroying the idols by the fire of anathema, likewise condemn the devil together with worldly desire forever, and kill idolaters with the sword of the divine word, since they preach the punishment that will follow them into Gehenna.

And those who fell by the sword, together with those who were burned, were eight thousand men, etc. By the number eight, as we have often said, both spiritual circumcision and the day of resurrection are signified; there all who are not circumcised here by the sword of the divine Spirit are handed over to punishment.

And from there Jonathan moved the camp, etc. Jonathan advanced the camp and came to Ascalon, when the holy preachers arrange the equipment of a pious struggle in order to defeat the errors of the nations and convert the nations themselves to the faith of Christ. These nations receive them with devotion when they gladly offer obedience to them in the Gospel. Hence the text rightly adds, in common:

And Jonathan returned to Jerusalem, etc. When the Gentiles, while the teachers of the New Testament are preaching, behold through the faith of believers the happiness that comes from the word of God, they immediately return to the Church of Christ to offer thanks to God, so that they may render worthy praises to him by whose grace they have received this gift, in which they rejoice with great exultation.

And it happened that when Alexander heard these reports, etc. What does it mean that Alexander, hearing of Jonathan’s deeds, increased his honors by giving him royal attire, except that the rulers of the nations, recognizing the greatness of spirit and strength of the Church, grant her the honor of royal dignity, because they truly recognize her as the bride of the heavenly King? They grant her cities as possessions, handing over to her the habitation of their territories.

## CHAPTER XI

[Col. 1192A] Ptolemy rises against Alexander, and Alexander is killed. The covenant with Jonathan is confirmed. Trypho raises Antiochus, Alexander’s son, against Demetrius, who is saved by Jonathan’s aid, etc.

Now King Ptolemy obtained control of the cities as far as Seleucia on the coast, etc. Ptolemy Euergetes, who ruled in Alexandria after Ptolemy Philometor, as the books of the chroniclers testify, gave his daughter in marriage to Alexander son of Balas, king of Syria. Later, when hostility arose between him and his son-in-law, he took her away and gave her in marriage to Demetrius son of Demetrius, together with the kingdom that he had taken from Alexander. Scripture now appears to recall this event.

[Col. 1192B] In those days Jonathan gathered those who were in Judea in order to attack the citadel that is in Jerusalem, etc. What does it mean that Jonathan attacks those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem through those who are in Judea, except that the holy teachers pursue the obstinacy of those who, relying on exaltation of heart and pride, dare to resist the divine commandments? Against them he makes many siege engines, because they strive to attack them by varied discipline and diverse teaching from the Scriptures and to summon them to humility.
