But just as at that time certain wicked men among those who hated their own nation approached the king and accused Jonathan, so now those who refuse to accept ecclesiastical discipline detest those who try to remove their wickedness from them, accusing them before the powers of the world so that they may turn them against those men and provoke persecution against them. But they do not prevail, because God is their helper and protector, and he has delivered them from all their tribulations.

And Jonathan asked the king to make Judea exempt from tribute, etc. He calls “toparchies”—that is, the governance of villages or towns—those places that Demetrius added to Judea from the kingdom of Samaria. He speaks of them below, namely Lydda and Ramah. Lydda is a city of Palestine situated on the shore of the Great Sea, while Ramah is a city of Samaria, about which the Book of Kings gives an account (I Kings 1).

Therefore, by right of friendship, King Demetrius granted Jonathan immunity and added the aforementioned cities to Judea, remitting the census of tithes and tributes, as well as the salt works, in which the production of salt was owed to the commonwealth. He also forgave all the other dues that were rendered to him with the customary pomp of that region, according to the agreement made with Jonathan.

Now Trypho had previously belonged to Alexander’s faction, etc. Pompeius Trogus shows how Demetrius came to be hated by his army, saying:

“After recovering his ancestral kingdom, Demetrius himself, corrupted by the success of his affairs, slipped through the vices of youth into indolence, and incurred as much contempt among all as his father had possessed hatred because of his arrogance. Therefore, when cities everywhere began to revolt from his rule, he decided to wage war against the Parthians in order to erase the stain of indolence. The peoples of the East did not view his arrival unwillingly, because of the cruelty of Arsaces, king of the Parthians, and because the newly subjected peoples, accustomed to the ancient Macedonian rule, bore the arrogance of the new regime with indignation. Thus, aided by the Persians and other neighboring peoples, he routed the Parthians after devastating them in many battles. Finally, deceived by a pretended peace, he was captured, led through the cities before the peoples who had deserted him, and displayed as an object of derision in place of the favor he had enjoyed. He was then sent to Hyrcania and treated kindly, in accordance with his former rank.”

And Jonathan sent to Demetrius that he should expel those who were in the citadel, etc. What does it mean that Jonathan asks King Demetrius to expel those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem and in the garrisons, who were also attacking Israel, while Demetrius, in turn, asks him for aid against his enemies, except that the holy teachers seek from the rulers of the nations the defeat of error and pride, while those rulers likewise ask the holy teachers for the support of instruction and prayer in overcoming spiritual enemies?

Neither order can properly complete the work of its ministry without the assistance of the other. The holy teachers cannot gain the reward of winning souls without the conversion and obedience of their subjects, nor can the subjects obtain salvation without the teaching and instruction of their masters. Each order, as has been said, is supported by the other and is made divine by the other [sic].

Thus Paul says to the Thessalonians (chapter III): “For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord, because we rejoice on your account before our God.” And to the Corinthians he says: “You are our glory, just as we also are yours on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Cor. I).

And the inhabitants of the city saw that the Jews had gained the city as they wished, etc. The fact that the Jews gained victory over their enemies and compelled them to ask for peace and to have hands given to them signifies that the strength of the holy Church surpasses all her enemies. Whether she causes them to yield beneficially through their way of life, or justly punishes those who despise her and persist in their stubbornness, she has received from her Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Luke X). Concerning this, elsewhere in the Gospel, speaking to his apostle Peter, he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

And they were named, he says, as Jews in the kingdom. The confessors of Christ appear glorious throughout the world, but holy men do not ascribe this glory to themselves; they ascribe it to their King, namely God, the giver of all good things. Hence it is also added:

They returned to Jerusalem bearing much spoil. The Psalmist testifies that he offers such thanks to God, saying: “I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I will not restrain my lips” (Ps. XXXIX). Thus, in the Church, all the faithful return bearing the spoils of virtue, so that they may praise God, attributing the victory they have gained not to their own strength but to divine grace, saying with the Prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, because of your mercy and your truth” (Ps. CXIII).

And King Demetrius sat upon the seat of his kingdom, etc. The fact that Demetrius repaid Jonathan’s benefactions with evil signifies carnal fools who, when counsel is given to them for their salvation, do not repay their benefactors according to the benefits owed, but according to the wicked counsels of their hardened hearts. Whatever is done for their advantage, they regard entirely as harmful, and, driven by the spur of envy, they choose to serve their most evil will.

And Jonathan went out and traversed the cities beyond the river, etc. By Jonathan’s crossing beyond the river we may understand the preaching of the word to those who have not yet been washed by the baptism of Christ, because the holy preachers sometimes summon Gentiles to sacred baptism and sometimes stir the faithful to advance in virtue.

When Jonathan therefore returns across the river, the Syrian army comes to him in support, because when the apostles moved from the Jews to preach to the nations, immediately many from the Gentiles gathered to the faith and baptism of Christ. They became helpers to the holy preachers in the Gospel of God, so that they might bring the pagans to belief.

He proceeded to Ascalon, which is interpreted as “hung up” or “infamous fire,” and the people of the city met him honorably. So too, when those who served the ambition of the world heard the word of God from the holy preachers, they immediately abandoned worldly desire and hastened to obey the Gospel.

And he went to Gaza and besieged it, and those who were in Gaza shut themselves in. By Gaza, which is interpreted as “fortitude,” the obstinacy of unbelievers is expressed, in which the deceived minds of the wicked are enclosed because they refuse to yield and consent to the truth.

Jonathan besieged it and set fire to the surrounding cities when the teachers of Christ hem in the faithless on every side with testimonies from the holy Scriptures and, by overthrowing the contrivances of their errors, lay them waste.

Therefore the Gazans asked Jonathan to give them the right hand of peace, and he took their sons as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. When their wickedness has been conquered and the proud can no longer resist the truth for long, they ask the teachers of the Church to grant them treaties of peace and hand over their sons as hostages—that is, they promise in the Church pledges of their renunciation of error and submission to obedience—so that a certain hope of their conversion may be established.

When Jonathan heard that the princes of Demetrius had rebelled at Kadesh, which is in Galilee, with a large army, wishing to remove him, etc. The princes of Demetrius who rebelled at Kadesh of Galilee may appropriately be understood as the secular powers. Although they are counted among the faithful because of their Catholic confession—for Kadesh is interpreted as “holy” or “changed,” and Galilee as “transmigration,” that is, “a migration made”—these things nevertheless figurally express the fact that such men often plot fraud and deny the grace of the heavenly kingdom.

Jonathan confronts them, because the skill of the holy teachers must meet such men lest they carry out in deed the fraud they have devised in their minds. Nevertheless, he left his brother Simon between the provinces to protect it inwardly against the insolence of the impudent. So also the holy preachers, although they sometimes go out to regulate worldly affairs and restrain the attacks of the undisciplined, never cease in any way to order the ministry of their own vine within the Church. Rather, they always have someone there who preserves regular discipline in everything, so that they may be found useful in external matters and salutary everywhere.

[Col. 1195B] And Simon came to Beth-zur and attacked it, etc. What is signified by Beth-zur except the reading of the holy Scriptures? For Beth-zur is interpreted as “house of the strong,” and Sacred Scripture may rightly be called the house of the strong, because in it all the brave and strongest continually dwell by speaking and doing good. With the Psalmist they meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. CXVIII).

At times heretics appear falsely to dwell in this house, when they are shown to read the Scriptures but not to understand them at all. Hence it is said that Simon attacked Beth-zur for many days, captured the city, and expelled its wicked inhabitants, placing a garrison there. This means that the holy teachers devote themselves above all to this effort: they strive with all their strength to overcome the heretics, destroying their false opinion and rescuing the Scripture of God’s law from their hands.

“Placing a garrison there”—that is, pious investigators and meditators upon divine wisdom who strive to understand and proclaim the divine word correctly.

And Jonathan and his army came to the water of Genesar, etc. What does it mean that Jonathan brought his army to the water of Genesar except that the company of holy preachers, inflamed by the Spirit of God, prepares to confront the worldly waves amid the persecutions of the faithful?

They say that the lake of Gennesareth is the same as the Sea of Galilee. The Sea of Tiberias was named from the neighboring city, which was formerly called Gennesareth but was restored by Herod the Tetrarch and named Tiberias in honor of Tiberius Caesar.

Genesar, on the other hand, is so called from the nature of the lake itself: because its rippling waters are said to raise a breeze from within themselves, it is called by a Greek term meaning, as it were, “generating a breeze for itself.” For the water does not lie spread out like that of a pond, but is stirred by frequent currents of air; its water is sweet to drink and suitable for drinking.

But according to the custom of the Hebrew language, every gathering of waters, whether fresh or salt, is called “sea.” This lake, through which the Jordan flows, extends for one hundred and sixty stadia in length and sixty in breadth.

Since, therefore, the pond or sea signifies the present age, our Jonathan, together with his companions, hastens to resist worldly turmoil and strives to keep watch before dawn in the plain of Hazor—that is, he carefully watches against the devil’s ambushes with vigilant attention.

For Hazor is interpreted as “arrow of light,” and the Apostle, writing about that same apostate angel, says: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (II Cor. XI). Hence it is not surprising if his ministers also transform themselves as ministers of righteousness.

There the foreigners, meeting them, lay ambushes in the mountains, because either evil spirits or wicked men strive to seduce whomever they can through the luxury or pride of the present life, or through worldly desires. The soldiers of Christ must run against them and fight them courageously, lest they consent to their persuasions and be weakened by their pleasures and enticements.

But when the battle had begun, all those who had been on Jonathan’s side fled, and none remained except Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Calphi, commander of the army.

[Col. 1196B] For, alas, many of the clergy are overthrown by ambition and the pleasure of this world. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel parable (Luke VIII) that thorns choked the crop—that is, riches and a life of pleasure choked the crop, so that it bore no fruit.

Nevertheless, Mattathias, whose name is interpreted as “gift of God,” and Judas, that is, “confessing,” remain with Jonathan. Those who have been enlightened and strengthened by the gift of God and who, by rightly believing and doing good, are truly confessors of God, persevere in the camp of the Church. They press the enemy vigorously until they crush him and restore to their former camp those of their own who had fled by yielding to the enemy.

But let us see what Jonathan did when his soldiers turned to flight.

And Jonathan tore his garments and put earth upon his head, etc. Thus the leaders and teachers of the Church ought to act when they see their own hiding in battle and turning their backs to the enemy: they should tear their garments—that is, afflict their bodies with fasts and tears—and put earth upon their heads—that is, turn the frailty of the body over in their minds—and pray to the Lord for their own sins or those of the people, so that he, who is almighty, may work salvation for the weak and restore them to their former health.

In this way each person must be exhorted to repent of the snares of the devil, by whose will he had been held captive, and to return to the Lord, who will have mercy on him, and to our Lord, for he is abundant in forgiveness (Isa. LV).

And three thousand men of the foreigners fell on that day, etc. Note that the foreigners are struck down by the number three, because through faith in the Holy Trinity all the enemies of the Church are crushed, overcome, and cast down. The company of believers returns with its leader to the mystical Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, so that there it may offer thanks and praises to our God forever and ever.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 1197A] Jonathan sends envoys and letters to the Romans and Spartans; he routs the princes of Demetrius and their army and strikes the Arabs. Trypho, wishing to take the kingdom of Antiochus, acted deceitfully toward Jonathan and killed him and his army.

And Jonathan saw that the time favored him, and he chose men and sent them to Rome, etc. The fact that Jonathan sends letters to the Romans, the Spartans, and other places so that they might renew the treaty and friendship that his brother Judas had previously entered into with them of his own accord demonstrates that the holy preachers ought to show great concern to renew and preserve everywhere, with complete devotion, the peace that Christ offered to the world.

For the Son of God himself came to earth to reconcile heavenly and earthly things in his flesh (Col. I). At the beginning of his birth he wished the angels to sing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II). Once he had become human, that same mediator of God and humanity commended this peace to his disciples, saying: “Have peace among yourselves” (Matt. IX); and: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV).

For the whole body of Christ is united, governed, and established by peace and concord. Whoever does not wish to have peace with his neighbors has no fellowship in the body of Christ and can no longer attain eternal rest, from which he has separated himself through contention.

And this was written, etc. How the Spartans were descended from Abraham is not easily established. It could nevertheless have happened that Abraham had more sons, apart from Isaac, whom Sarah bore to him, namely by Hagar and Keturah, as Scripture makes clear, and that the origin of the Spartans proceeded from one of them.

But Josephus, when mentioning this passage, does not seem to intend to assert a true kinship between the Spartans and the Jews, but rather to express some form of association. He reports the letter of the Lacedaemonians as follows:

“King Onias of the Lacedaemonians to Jonathan the high priest, greetings. In reading the Scriptures, we have sometimes found that the Jews and Lacedaemonians came from one [kindred], and that they had a friendly relationship with Abraham. Therefore, since you are our brothers, it is right for us to write to you and ask for whatever you consider necessary. We shall do the same, and we regard your possessions as our own and ours as common to us both. Demotites, the bearer of the letter, is bringing you the letters written in a rectangular form, bearing a seal with an eagle carrying a dragon in its claws.”

The letter, therefore, sent by the king of the Lacedaemonians contained the following text.

And Jonathan heard that the princes of Demetrius had gone out with a large army, larger than before, to fight against him, etc. What does it signify that Jonathan went out from Jerusalem to fight against the princes of Demetrius who had gone out against him, and met them in the region of Hamath, except that the sacred order of teachers is always prepared to fight against the persecutors of the Church—that is, Jews, pagans, and heretics—and to resist their faithlessness?

Going out from Jerusalem, he meets them in the region of Hamath because, although through inward contemplation and the eye of the mind they behold the greatness of the Creator and the majesty of heavenly rewards, they nevertheless come forth for a time to fight against their enemies. Yet they do not in any way depart from the uprightness of the truth, for Hamath is interpreted as “my truth.”

Whether they contend against their errors in the conflict of disputation, or patiently endure their scourges and killings, they do not in any way abandon the truth of righteousness. Nor do they grant them the opportunity to enter the territory of the Church by fraud. They strive with the utmost effort to crush their wicked deceit at the very beginning and preserve the camp of the Church unharmed.

[Col. 1198B] And he sent scouts into their camp, etc. Jonathan investigates the enemy’s camp by sending scouts, when the holy preachers investigate the deceit of their enemies through capable men, so that, once their wicked plans have been discovered, they may more easily guard against their trickery.

The scouts announced that the enemy intended to come against them that very night. Those who prepare to come by night are the ones who, with blind hearts, meditate on performing works of darkness.

Jonathan, on the other hand, commands his men to keep watch and remain armed and ready for battle throughout the night, because it is characteristic of chosen teachers to instruct their subjects to be constantly vigilant and cautious throughout the whole period of this life, in which they live amid uncertainty while striving toward a certain end.

When the adversaries heard that Jonathan and his men were ready for battle, they were greatly afraid, lit fires in their camp, and planned their flight. Jonathan pursued them but did not catch them, because he found them already beyond the river.

The adversaries fear when the members of the Church prepare themselves for spiritual battle. By lighting fires in their camps—that is, they pretend to display the strength of war in their bands—they feign courage. But at the dawn of dawning faith, the spiritual Jonathan pursues his enemies, whom he nevertheless does not catch, meaning that he does not bring them to belief, because, seeing them burning in their love for the unstable world, he judged them to be beyond recall.

And Jonathan returned and summoned the elders of the people, etc. The fact that Jonathan, on returning, arranged to build the walls of Jerusalem and, after taking counsel with the elders of the people, built fortifications and a great height between the citadel and the city in order to separate it from the city signifies that the holy teachers, after being occupied for a time with external wars, confer inwardly with spiritual men concerning the fortification of the Church, lest she be harmed by internal enemies.

Those, therefore, who belonged to the city of Marche [sic] and lay in wait for the inhabitants of Jerusalem signify heretics. Placed in the citadel of their pride, they never cease plotting against the Church.

Mystically, Jonathan shuts them off with a spiritual defense, so that they may remain apart and neither buy nor sell: expelled from the unity of the Church by the strongest excommunication, their sect is not received, nor is ecclesiastical teaching entrusted to them, like the most filthy and foul-smelling swine, for them in any way to pollute it. The Lord and Savior himself contradicts and forbids this in the Gospel, saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart” (Matt. IX).

The mute man, therefore, who fell beside the torrent at sunrise and whom Jonathan restored signifies those who seemed in the Church to exercise some guardianship over the flock entrusted to them. But relying on transitory things and serving worldly ambition, they fell into the pleasures of this life and fell from their proper state. The skill of the saints must strive to restore such men and endeavor to lead them back to their former firmness by strengthening them with ecclesiastical doctrine.

[Col. 1199B] And when Trypho had considered reigning over Asia and taking the diadem, etc. This Trypho represents hypocrites and heretics, who act one way and speak another, while plotting something else in their intention.

Jonathan meets him with forty thousand men, because evangelical doctrine and observance of God’s commandments are necessary against such men. Whoever observes the precepts of the law according to the teaching of the Gospel will safely penetrate the ranks of his enemies.

But the fact that Trypho deceitfully persuaded Jonathan to dismiss his army and receive him peacefully with him [Note: [Col. 1199D] Thus in the manuscript. Perhaps “come”], and then, after deceiving him, captured him and killed those who accompanied him, signifies the ruin of those who do not keep watch lawfully and do not exercise vigilance in the scrutiny of their hearts and the conduct of their bodies.

[Col. 1199C] They did not heed the teaching of the Gospel in which the Savior commanded his disciples: “Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation” (Matt. II); and again: “Beware,” he says, “of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII). Therefore their army is rightly overcome and destroyed, because the teaching of heavenly authority is not properly observed by them.

In Jonathan’s place, his brother Simon exercises the priesthood and leads the people. So, in the present Church, when some depart, others are appointed in their place to hold the position of governance and diligently train the soldiers of Christ in the spiritual camps, so that they may be able to resist all their enemies appropriately in warfare.

But Trypho, in the same figurative manner, attempts to deceive such men by fabrications of words, just as he had deceived his brother, because the ancient enemy never ceases, through himself and his ministers, to arrange ambushes for the worshipers of Christ. But whoever worthily performs the office of Simon—that is, of one who obeys and rightly submits to the divine commandments—can, aided by heavenly assistance, avoid the scandal of all his enemies.

Trypho also killed Jonathan’s sons together with him, although he had promised to preserve them along with their father, because the ancient enemy drives all whom he seduces into the death of sin. Their sons—that is, their works—which he had previously concealed beneath a pretense of peace, he will at the end reveal as deserving eternal torment.

Jonathan may also represent the simple-minded who are in the Church. The cunning of the clever seems for a time to take them captive when it afflicts them with bodily sufferings, but their souls, remaining steadfast in the truth of the faith, will escape into perpetual light after the death of the flesh.

Hence many of them, after the end of the present life, have deserved to have signs of victory near their tombs, just as Simon is later read to have built a memorial for his father, mother, and brothers at their tombs.

The saints, moreover, whom the Savior strengthens as they remain in the simplicity of their innocence, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do to you; rather, fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. X); and again: “Blessed are you,” he says, “when people curse you and persecute you and falsely say every evil thing against you because of me. Rejoice on that day and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V); and again: “Rejoice and exult,” he says, “because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

Concerning them the Psalmist says: “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil report” (Ps. CXI). These saints are believed to be stronger after death and to live more happily, since their King and Lord himself, Jesus Christ, is known to proclaim their triumphs throughout the whole world by shining signs and miracles.

Thus, near the memory of their relics, sight is granted to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, and speech to the mute; healing remedies are provided for hidden illnesses through their prayers. Conversely, in the same places the wicked and malicious are attacked by “Demetriuses” [read: demons], the depraved and unbelieving are punished, and the demons themselves are tormented with powerful tortures, in accordance with what they are forced openly to confess while roaring.

## CHAPTER XIII

Simon is appointed leader in place of his brother; he sends money and Jonathan’s two sons to Trypho. Concerning the death of Jonathan and his sons. Concerning the construction of the tomb. Trypho deceitfully kills the young Antiochus and places the diadem of Asia upon himself. Demetrius establishes peace with Simon, etc.

And Simon heard that Trypho had gathered a large army in order to come into the land of Judah, etc. And Simon built over the tomb of his father, etc.

Simon constructs a memorial of polished stone over the tombs of his father, mother, and brothers, when the holy preachers, by recalling the deeds of the fathers who preceded them and their glorious end as an example for the present, display them with great authority.

For placing a polished stone in front and behind signifies that they carefully make clear to their hearers, through faithful narration, how those earlier men lived before the end of their lives for doctrine and holy conduct, and what example of their patience and endurance they left to posterity after their death.

The fact that holy men are called father, mother, and brothers is shown by the Savior in the Gospel, when he says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. XII).

Hence the Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says (I Cor. IV): “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel.” And concerning Timothy he says to the Philippians: “You know his proven character, how, like a son serving his father, he served with me in the Gospel.”

Simon also set up seven pyramids, one opposite another, for his father and mother and his four brothers, when every teacher demonstrates how the light of wisdom of each of the former fathers [perhaps “fathers”] was bestowed upon each person through the sevenfold Spirit granted to the faithful.

And he surrounded them with columns [and upon the columns] weapons for an eternal memorial, when he indicates their strength and uprightness in faith and how, in that same faith, they fought against their enemies with spiritual weapons.

And beside the weapons, carved ships, which all who sailed the sea could see. In this way they confirm by teaching, for the sake of the hope of consolation, how the righteous who preceded them crossed the sea of the present life by the ship of Christ’s cross amid the troubled waves of this world. They show that, just as that ship safely brought them to the shore of rest, so faith in Christ’s passion and in our redemption through it will bring them to the harbor of eternal salvation, if they are willing to possess works worthy of that faith.

Trypho, however, while traveling with the youthful King Antiochus, killed him by deceit, etc. Pompeius reports this as follows:

“While these things were taking place in the regions of Syria, Trypho, who had striven to be appointed by the people as guardian of Antiochus, Demetrius’s stepson, invaded the government of Syria after killing his ward. He held it for a long time, but finally, when the favor of his recent rule began to fade, he was defeated in war by Antiochus, a very young boy and brother of Demetrius, who had been raised in Asia. Once again the kingdom of Syria returned to the descendants of Demetrius.”

And Simon chose men and sent them to King Demetrius, etc. The fact that Simon sent men to King Demetrius so that he might grant remission to the region signifies, unless I am mistaken, that the holy Church sends her preachers to the rulers of this world so that she may reconcile them to herself through the word of faith, annul the deeds of the figurative Trypho—that is, of heretics and schismatics—and crush, through the severity of external powers, their pride, because they refused to yield to ecclesiastical gentleness.

The envoys also bring them a golden crown and peace [Vulgate: *bahem*], which they say is an ornament made entirely of golden rings according to the custom of the province. In return for their good struggle, they promise them the crown of eternal life, and for the timely consolation by which they assist the churches through their decrees and defenses, heavenly rewards. Thus in common.

In those days Simon approached Gaza and besieged it with an army, etc. What does Simon’s undertaking to attack Gaza signify, unless that preachers strive to overcome errors destined for condemnation? Gaza, which is interpreted as “his strength,” signifies the obstinacy and hardness of the nations [Col. 1202A]. Simon therefore constructs many siege engines against Gaza, when holy teachers bring various spiritual forces of doctrine against the strongholds of the nations, so that they may reduce them as a saving spoil for the Lord their king, namely Jesus Christ. In this he struck and captured one tower, when he cast down the pride of the gentiles and led their hearts into obedience to the Gospel.

But who were those who, with their wives and children, climbed upon the wall with torn garments and asked Simon to give them his right hand, unless those who, entangled in the concerns and desires of this world and its riches, were afterward converted and, by repentance, tore not their garments but their hearts, seeking to receive from the ecclesiastical [Col. 1202B] authorities the right hands of reconciliation and fellowship? In mercy, Simon the spiritual assents to their request: he does not strike them with the sword of anathema, but leads them out of the superstition of gentile belief and removes their errors by cutting them away, so that he may prepare for the Lord Christ a fitting dwelling in those who were sinners. “They had burst through the siege engine into the city.” For although the insolence of the barbarians sought, as it were, to escape the Gospel, it has nevertheless been bound and restrained by the truthful testimonies of God’s law.

“And there was a great commotion in the city.” When the whole world was shaken by the preaching of the Gospel, a great commotion arose in the city, when the ferocity of the nations was stirred up to persecute Christ’s confessors, so that those who were faithful defenders of Christ’s faith and doctrine might become true martyrs.

[Col. 1202C] “Then he entered it with hymns, blessing the Lord,” etc. Then also, when the errors of the gentiles have been cast out, holy teachers will enter the assemblies of the nations with praises of God. Then too they appoint men who observe the law there, because through pious preaching they make true worshipers of Christ present in those places.

“And he fortified it and made a dwelling for himself there.” When through the Gospel they strengthen the Church everywhere with the fortification of faith, those very teachers, dwelling in its habitation, await from the Judge of the living and the dead the eternal rewards to be repaid to them at the end for the pious labor which they expended for their own confession.

“Those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem were forbidden to go out,” etc. Those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem and harassed the Jews signify heretics and schismatics, who establish themselves in the citadel of their pride and stir up disputes and wars against Catholics. Simon forbids them to go out or enter the region, or to buy or sell, because holy teachers, together with Catholics, forbid such people any communion of fellowship; and for this reason many of them perished from hunger, because many of them, having been separated from communion with the Church under anathema, perish from hunger for the word of God and from spiritual starvation.

But because, compelled by extreme necessity, they asked the Church to give them such right hands of communion, this agreement is imposed upon them by the Church: that they abandon their errors, anathematize the wicked sects to which they had previously adhered, and cleanse their conscience from every wickedness of the heretics. Thus they are restored to communion with the Church. Accordingly, it is fittingly added:

“And they entered it on the twenty-third day of the second month, in the one hundred and seventy-first year, with praise,” etc. These numbers—the one hundred seventy-first and the twenty-third—are full of sacred mysteries. The hundredth, in which Abraham fathered Isaac, the son of promise, signifies the perfection of life; the seventieth, in which the captivity of the Jerusalemites was released, signifies the remission of sins. But because this exists only in the truth of the Church, a unit has therefore been added to the number seventy.

Moreover, the number twenty-three [Col. 1203B] signifies faith in the Holy Trinity together with the two commandments of charity, in which the whole fullness of the law consists. The second month, in which it appeared that those who were pure in soul were celebrating Passover, points to the time of grace and the calling of the nations.

Therefore, when according to this arrangement and significance of the mystical numbers victory is won by the faithful—that is, when they preserve whole, according to evangelical teaching, faith in the Holy Trinity together with the two commandments of charity, and, possessing the perfection of life in proportion to their capacity, reach the fullness of remission by remaining in understanding and faith within the unity of the Church—then they will rightly enter the heavenly Jerusalem with song and palm branches, that is, with true praise and certain victory. They will continually offer manifold [Col. 1203C] thanks and praises to their Creator for the salvation and security they have attained, because the great enemy has been crushed out of Israel, and death itself, having died together with its author, has been condemned forever.

Nor does this conflict with the sense of the following exposition, where it is written that Simon decreed that the joy of this day should be celebrated every year, and that he fortified the temple mount, which was beside the citadel, and that he himself and those with him dwelt there. For throughout the whole time of this life the memory of that day must be retained in hope, on which, triumphing over death through the grace of our Redeemer, we shall be restored to eternal life.

Indeed, when every year we celebrate the solemnities of the Lord’s resurrection, we signify that through his resurrection we hope for victory over death, and that the resurrection of our bodies will take place at the end of the world, together with everlasting life in the heavenly kingdom. For this reason we must fortify the temple mount, which is beside the citadel—that is, we must hold firmly in our hearts by faith the incarnation of Christ, which by its perfection transcends every height of the perfection of the saints. Throughout the whole time of our life, both through ourselves and through those entrusted to us or joined to us in fellowship, we must labor piously in this way, so that, joined and united to his body, we may likewise become heirs with him, the head, of the heavenly kingdom.

The blessed apostle Peter commends the joy and memory of this day to us in his Epistle, saying:

“Let this one thing not escape you, beloved: that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promise [or: ‘his promised word’], but deals patiently for your sake, not wishing anyone to perish, but all to return to repentance. But the day of the Lord will come like a thief; on that day the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by heat. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought we to be in holy conduct and piety, awaiting and hastening the day of the Lord, by which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire? But we await new heavens, a new earth, and his promises, in which righteousness dwells. Therefore, beloved, while awaiting these things, strive to be found spotless and at peace, and regard the patience of our Lord Jesus Christ as salvation” (II Peter III [Col. 1204B]).

“And Simon saw that his son Joachim [Vulgate: John] was a strong man,” etc. When Simon entrusted his son Joachim with the command of all the virtues after seeing that he was a man, he showed that no teacher ought to entrust his son or disciple with the authority and office of ecclesiastical governance unless he has first seen that he is a man—that is, approved in understanding and diligent in works of virtue.

But since we said above that Simon represents the figure of the holy teachers, this passage can express the meaning of the chief Shepherd, who gave the Catholic people the ministry of sacred governance and the knowledge and practice of every virtue. To him the following statement also most suitably applies:

## CHAPTER XIV

On the sublimity and power of Simon, king of the Jews, and on the abundance of peace in those times. Friendship is renewed between the Romans and the Jews, etc.

“And the land of Judah was at rest throughout all the days of Simon,” etc. The prophet Isaiah wrote of the Lord the Savior himself:

“His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of peace. He will sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to confirm and strengthen it with judgment and righteousness, from this time forth and forever” (Isa. IX).

His principality and dominion will be over the throne and kingdom of David, which had been destroyed after the Babylonian captivity, so that he might confirm and strengthen it and show it to be everlasting, lest God’s promise be judged empty. The Prophet says in the Psalm:

“In his days righteousness will arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away” (Ps. LXXI).

For this promise applies to no one else but the mediator of God and human beings, Christ Jesus, who, having been incarnate for us through obedience to the cross, became possessor of heaven and earth. To him the Father says in the Psalter through the Prophet:

“Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

“All the land of Judah was at rest throughout all the days of Simon,” because the land of the Church, from the time of Christ’s incarnation to eternity, although it endures persecutions from enemies outwardly, nevertheless enjoys true peace within. The same Savior says to it in the Gospel: [Col. 1205A] “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John XIV)—he who builds up good things for his people.

“And his power pleased them, and his glory pleased them throughout all the days.” Clearly, all good things were bestowed by him upon the Church for the remission of sins and the mastery of virtues. Therefore, his power and his glory please it, because it has chosen to serve him alone at all times.

“He took Joppa as a harbor and made an entrance into the islands of the sea.” When he founded for himself a Church as the entrance of faith from the people of the nations, he opened through the Gospel an entrance into the faith for the nations of the whole world.

Joppa is interpreted as “beauty.” And what is more beautiful than the holy Church, to which the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful you are, my beloved; how beautiful you are! Your eyes are like those of doves, apart from what lies hidden within” (Song I [Col. 1205B])? Thus he enlarged the boundaries of his nation, that is, of the Church, and gained possession of the region of the whole world.

“And he gathered a great captivity.” Concerning this it was written above: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Ezek. VI).

“And he ruled over Gazara, Bethsura, and the citadel.” [Note: The passage is corrupt, as are many other passages.]

Because, having cleansed the work through the Gospel, he subdued it and brought it back under the Lord’s possession, removing the uncleanness of sin and of the vices and cleansing it through the bath of regeneration.

“And there was no one who resisted him.” Concerning this it is written: “All things are placed in your will, O Lord, and there is no one who can resist your will. For you made heaven and earth and all that is contained within the circuit of heaven; you are Lord of all” (Esther XIII).

[Col. 1205C] “And each person cultivated his land in peace.” That is, exercising his own body in virtues, or cultivating the land of the Church through good works. Each of the saints cultivates it according to his strength.

“And the land gave its fruit.” That is, our flesh likewise produces the fruit of good works.

“And the trees of the fields.” This means that human beings, always flourishing in the verdure of faith, bring forth the shoots of virtues.

“All the elders sat in the streets, discussing the good things of the land, and the young men clothed themselves in glory and garments of war.” By the elders we can understand the prophets, apostles, and teachers of the holy Church, who assist their hearers with counsel and strengthen them with their words. The young men are the assemblies of the faithful, who, relying on the glory of their confession of Christ, clothe themselves in the arms of virtues [Col. 1205D], so that they may more easily crush the army of their enemies.

“He supplied the cities with provisions.” This means that they supplied the Churches with sermons and teachings.

“Which he appointed to be vessels of fortification.” That is, so that they might preserve the treasure of spiritual wisdom in a pure conscience and unfeigned faith (I Tim.). He did this until the name of his glory was proclaimed to the ends of the earth, because the sound of the apostles’ preaching went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII). Hence it is said through the prophet Isaiah: “The Lord will make the glory of your voice heard, and will show the terror of his arm” (Isa. XXX).

[Col. 1206A] “He made peace throughout the land.” For he is our peace, who made both one (Eph. II).

“And Israel rejoiced with great joy.” For “the righteous will rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart will be praised” (Ps. LXIII).

“And each person sat beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, and there was no one to terrify them.” This is according to what is said in Machaea: “Each person will rest beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, and there will be no one to frighten him” (III Kings IV).

This is the vine that spoke in the Gospel: “I am the vine and you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer. Everyone who does not bear good fruit will be cut off and cast into the fire” (John XV; Matt. VII; Luke III). Its fruits are drunk and eaten and gladden the human heart; they intoxicate the bride’s friends [Col. 1206B], and in the kingdom of God they are drunk continually.

The person who enjoys the sweetness of the Holy Spirit and is filled with its fruits—charity, joy, peace, self-control, and patience—rests beneath the fig tree and fears no ambush. Of such a person it is said by the planter who plants a fig tree and eats its fruit (Deut. XX). Such are those who built houses and planted vineyards, concerning whom the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III). “He will eat the labors of his hands, and the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (I Cor. III), and he will not be overthrown by the deceits of the devil and his minions.

“And he strengthened all the humble of his people and sought out the law” (Gal. VI). The humble of the people are the saints whom the Gospel calls “poor in spirit” (Matt. V) [Col. 1206C]. The works of God’s people will not grow old, but will be renewed and brought to completion, or strengthened, every day, so that they do not walk in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit (Rom. VII). This is the law our Simon sought, and he removed every unjust and evil person, when now, through the holy teachers, he excommunicates heretics and schismatics and, at the end of the world, sends all the pious, and they gather all scandals out of his kingdom (Matt. XIII).

“He sanctified and multiplied the vessels of the saints,” when he taught the religion of the New Testament to be observed orderly and properly in his Church.

“And it was heard in Rome that Jonathan had died, and as far as the Spartans; and they were greatly saddened,” etc. When Simon received the priesthood, various nations sent ambassadors to him, asking for what pertains to peace. This signifies that, after Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, when the apostles and teachers of the New Testament were preaching the Gospel throughout the world, a multitude of nations flocked to the faith and earnestly requested that they might have peace with the Church.

“Sending letters.” This means that they disclosed the secrets of their hearts to them through confession, so that, receiving the words of truth, they might learn from them the rule of righteousness.

“Bronze tablets, an everlasting memorial.” For it is written: “The righteous will be in everlasting remembrance; he will not fear hearing evil” (Ps. CXI). Bronze is a metal that endures for a long time and resounds; so the friendship and fellowship of the saints possess an exceedingly firm and renowned state of dwelling.

“After this Simon sent Numenius to Rome,” etc. Simon’s sending to the Romans a golden shield weighing one thousand minas, in order to establish fellowship with them, signifies that holy teachers, in preaching the Gospel to the nations, promise the heavenly kingdom and eternal blessedness to those who are willing to receive the faith of Christ and preserve evangelical teaching to the end of life. The roundness of the shield, the splendor of gold, and also the perfection of the number one thousand signify, figuratively, the crown of eternal rest, etc.

“And they granted them freedom and recorded it on bronze tablets” [Col. 1207B], etc. Ebul [Vulgate: Elul] is the eighth month among the Hebrews, called Γορπιαῖος among the Greeks and September among the Latins. But the sequence of the numbers is scattered because different peoples begin their years at different points.

The Hebrews, who place the first month, Nisan—that is, April—in the first position, have the aforementioned Ebul in the sixth position. The Greeks, however, who begin their year with their first month, called Ἀπρίλλος—that is, from the Kalends of December—count Γορπιαῖος as the tenth month. The Latins, on the other hand, who in ancient times began their year from the Kalends of March, counted September as the seventh month.

“And Simon accepted it, and it pleased him to exercise the high priesthood and to be commander,” etc. In Greek, περίβολος means the wall of the court of the house of the Lord, which enclosed the entire temple in a square circuit, as the blessed Jerome shows in the thirteenth book of his Exposition of the Prophet Ezekiel. In a prominent place in the inner court of the house, therefore, bronze tablets were set up, on which Simon’s priesthood and that of his sons had been confirmed in writing.

Mystically, however, the priesthood of Christ and of his sons—that is, of the Christian people—is confirmed in the court of the house of the Lord, that is, in the present Church, with Scripture bearing witness; and it is declared to be stable and everlasting among all nations.

Hence the statement written in the Psalm: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). And again:

“Once I have sworn by my holiness: If I lie to David, his seed will remain forever, and his throne will be like the sun in my sight, and like the full moon forever, and a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

[Col. 1207D] “It is the custom [Note: An addition by heretics, or something similar.] frequently to swear so that someone may believe them. God, however, swears once, because he is not changed by any variation of time. We have said that his swearing means his promising future things, for he binds himself by his own religious obligation, since he has no one greater. He says ‘by your holiness,’ in Christ, who said, ‘Guard my soul’ (Ps. XXIV), because ‘I am holy.’ ‘If I lie to David’ is expressed negatively, as common usage also has it.

The seed of Christ consists of all who have believed in him with faithful minds, because the kingdom that is to come has been sown in them, as the future harvest shows. Thus he himself says in the twenty-first Psalm: ‘My seed will serve him.’ The saints, therefore, will remain forever, those who dwell in an excellent and blessed way of life. We do not properly say that those who are rejected from the Lord’s kingdom remain.

The throne of God is to be understood here as the faithful soul, in which he truly sits when he has filled it with the illumination of his majesty. Thus it is written: ‘The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.’ He added: ‘like the sun in my sight.’ For that soul of the righteous was radiant; we have called it the seat of the Savior. By saying ‘like the sun,’ he makes a comparison with visible things. For if it is a great thing to shine from the creature, it is much better to shine from the Creator.

The full moon signifies the transformation of the body from corruption into [incorruption—text as supplied reads ‘corruption’]. Then the nature of our bodies will be perfect, when mortality or corruption no longer exists. That the moon itself, which waxes and wanes, signifies the mutability of human flesh can be demonstrated in many passages of Scripture.

We have placed these testimonies from the Psalms in order to show that the priesthood of the true Simon is most firm and everlasting.”

## CHAPTER XV

Antiochus, son of Demetrius, receives his father’s kingdom and writes letters to the Jews. He persecutes Tryphon. Simon sent aid to Antiochus, but he refused to accept it, etc.

“And King Antiochus, son of Demetrius, sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon the priest,” etc. This Antiochus, who was surnamed Εὐεργέτης, “Benefactor,” or “faithful,” was the son of Demetrius Soter and the younger brother of Demetrius. After Alexander Philopator [Philopolus] had been king in Syria, he ruled there.

Demetrius Soter, after Antiochus Eupator, son of Antiochus Epiphanes, reigned for twelve years, as the Chronicon of Eusebius and Jerome attests. After him Alexander Philopolus reigned for eleven years. After him Demetrius, son of Demetrius, reigned for three years. When he was captured by the Parthians, he was confined in Hyrcania by King Arsacides. After him his brother Antiochus Assidetes [Sidetes] held the kingdom for fourteen years. After his death, Demetrius was restored to the kingdom, which he held for four years.

How the succession to the kingdom came to the brothers Demetrius and Antiochus should not seem burdensome to the reader if something from the History of Pompeius Trogus is introduced here. In Book XXX he reports it thus:

“Accordingly, Antiochus, remembering that his father had been hated because of his arrogance and his brother despised because of his inactivity, lest he fall into the same faults, married Cleopatra, his brother’s wife, and pursued with the utmost diligence the cities that had revolted at the beginning of his brother’s reign. Having subdued them, he added them again to the boundaries of his kingdom. He also subjugated the Jews, who under Demetrius his father, during the Macedonian rule, had won their freedom by force of arms. Their strength was so great that afterward they tolerated no Macedonian king, and, governed by their own domestic rulers, they harassed Syria with great wars.”

Again, in Book XXXVIII, in the thirty-eighth year, he adds the following to his earlier account:

“For Demetrius, as was said above, when he had made war upon the Parthians and had been victorious in many engagements, was suddenly surrounded by an ambush and captured after losing his army. Arsacides [Note: This could not be read in the manuscript.]—the manuscript here has the incoherent words “Hircania non cultum flumen regnum”; the supplied correction reads: “Arsacides, king of the Parthians, with great and royal generosity, having sent him to Hyrcania, provided not merely a royal establishment”—also gave him his daughter in marriage. He promised that he would restore the kingdom of Syria, which Tryphon had occupied during Demetrius’ absence.

“After Arsacides’ death, when his return was despaired of, Demetrius, unable to endure captivity and wearied of a private, though wealthy, life, secretly planned his flight to the kingdom. His adviser and companion was his friend Gallimander, who, after Demetrius’ capture, had traveled from Syria through the deserts of Arabia, reached Babylon in Parthian dress, and obtained guides with money.

“But Phrahates, who had succeeded Arsacides, intercepted Demetrius as he fled by the speed of his cavalry and led him back by shorter routes. When he was brought before the king, Gallimander was given not merely pardon but also a reward for his loyalty. Demetrius, however, after severe punishment, was sent back to his wife in Hyrcania and ordered to be kept under stricter guard.

“After some time, when his wife and the freedman whom he had received inspired confidence in him, he attempted flight again, accompanied by the same friend. But with equal misfortune he was discovered near the borders of his kingdom and, brought back to the king once more, was removed from his sight as a hated man. On that occasion too he was given to his wife and children in Hyrcania and sent back to his punitive city. He was also presented with golden [shackles?—the supplied text is corrupt], as a reproach for childish fickleness.

“But this exceptionally mild clemency of the Parthians toward Demetrius was caused neither by the custom of the nation nor by regard for kinship, but because they were seeking the kingdom of Syria and intended to use Demetrius against his brother Antiochus, according as the time or fortune of the war required.

“When he heard these things, Antiochus judged that he must undertake the war. He led against the Parthians an army hardened by many wars with neighboring peoples. But luxury produced an equipment no smaller than the military force: [Note: Observe here a manuscript error.] many thousands of armed men were followed by three hundred thousand camp-followers, among whom the cooks [the supplied correction reads: ‘eighty thousand armed men were followed by three hundred thousand camp-followers, among whom cooks, etc.’] and bakers were more numerous.

“There was certainly so much silver and gold that common soldiers fastened gold onto their boots and trampled underfoot the material for which peoples [the printed reading says “abandon” (dimittunt); the correction reads “fight” (dimicant)] with iron. The utensils of the kitchens were also made of silver, and it was altogether as though they were going to a feast, not to war.

“Many eastern kings came to meet Antiochus as he approached, surrendering themselves and their kingdoms while cursing Parthian arrogance. There was no delay before the engagement. Antiochus, victorious in three battles, began to be regarded as a great man after he occupied Babylonia. Thus, as all peoples flocked to him, nothing remained for the Parthians except their ancestral boundaries.

“Then Phrahates sent Demetrius into Syria with a Parthian escort to seize the kingdom, so that Antiochus would thereby be called back to Parthia to defend his own territory. Meanwhile, since he could not attack him by force, he harassed Antiochus everywhere with ambushes.

“Because of the army’s great size, Antiochus’ forces were divided among the cities for the winter, and this became the cause of their destruction. For when the cities saw themselves burdened by the advance levy of supplies and by the injuries inflicted by the soldiers, they defected to the Parthians. On the appointed day they attacked the army, which had been divided among them, each city attacking the troops stationed there by ambush, so that they could not aid one another.

“When this was reported to Antiochus, he went forward with the force that was wintering with him in order to bring aid to the nearest troops. On the way he encountered the king of the Parthians, against whom he fought more bravely than his army. At last, however, although the enemy were being overcome by his valor, he was abandoned through fear by his own men and was killed. Phrahates gave him a royal funeral and, having fallen in love with the maiden, married Demetrius’ daughter, whom Antiochus had brought with him.

“Afterward he began to regret having released Demetrius. He sent cavalry squadrons in haste to bring him back, but the men he sent found Demetrius, who already feared precisely this, in his kingdom. Having attempted everything in vain, they returned to their king.

“After Antiochus and his army had been destroyed in Parthia, his brother Demetrius, freed from the Parthian siege and restored [to the kingdom], found all Syria in mourning because of the lost army. As though the Parthian [the printed reading is the corrupt patriarcha] wars of both father and brother—one of whom had been captured and the other killed—had been successfully waged, he decided to make war upon Egypt.

“Cleopatra, his mother-in-law, promised him the kingdom of Egypt as the price of assistance against her brother. But while he sought what belonged to another, as commonly happens, he lost what was his own through the defection of Syria.

“For the people of Antioch were the first, under the leadership of Tryphon, to curse the king’s arrogance, which had been made intolerable by his association with Parthian cruelty. Soon the people of Apamea and the other cities followed their example and, during the king’s absence, revolted from Demetrius.

“Ptolemy, king of Egypt, who had been attacked by the same man in war, learned that his sister Cleopatra had placed the wealth of Egypt aboard ships and fled to her son and her son-in-law Demetrius in Syria. He sent a certain Egyptian youth, the son of the merchant Protharsis, to seek the kingdom of Syria by arms. A fabricated story was devised, as though the youth had been received into the royal family by adoption by King Antiochus. Since the Syrians were unwilling to endure Demetrius’ arrogance and rejected just anyone as king, the youth was given the name Alexander, and great forces were sent from Egypt.

“Meanwhile, the body of Antiochus, who had been killed by the king of the Parthians, was sent back to Syria for burial in a silver coffin and arrived there. The cities and King Alexander received it with great enthusiasm, in order to strengthen the credibility of the fiction. This won great popular favor, since everyone thought that the tears shed for him were genuine.

“Demetrius, however, defeated by Alexander and oppressed by troubles pressing in upon him from every side, was finally abandoned even by his wife and children. Left with a few servants, he sought Tyre, intending to defend himself by the sanctity of the temple. But as he was leaving, he was killed at the command of the governor.”

For the reasons stated above, when Antiochus demands back from Simon the cities he had acquired through warfare, this signifies that the ancient enemy always envies the virtues of the saints and wishes to subject them to himself in unjust servitude. But Simon the spiritual, by claiming them for himself, declared them to belong to him and to be the inheritance of his fathers, and said that the enemy had no fellowship there, because possession of the virtues belongs properly to the elect, not to the rejected.

Thus the lands of the Canaanites into which the children of Israel were introduced had once been allotted to the sons of Shem in the division of the world. Later, their descendants possessed them through force and power and by the wickedness of persuasion. In this the most righteous judgment of God is also confirmed: he expelled those men from foreign places that they had wrongfully occupied, and restored these lands to the saints as the possession of their fathers, since they had been assigned to their lineage in the division of the world. The same is recognized with absolute certainty in us.

For the Lord’s will naturally assigned possession of our hearts not to vices but to virtues. After Adam’s transgression, when vices grew insolent—like the peoples of Canaan expelled from their own region—once those virtues have been restored to them above through God’s grace, our diligence, and our labor, we must not think that they have occupied foreign lands, but that they have recovered their own.

“And the king appointed Cendebaeus commander of the coastal region and an army of cavalry,” etc. What is signified by Cendebaeus, the coastal commander whom Antiochus sends to fight the Jews, except the powers of this world and the persecutors of the Christian religion? Antiochus, the mystical Antichrist, sends them with an army of executioners and torturers for the destruction of the Christian people, so that they may trample upon the true Judea—that is, the Church—and either take the faithful captive through error or kill them through blasphemy.

Cendebaeus is also ordered to build Cedron. Cedron is a torrent or valley beside Jerusalem, on the eastern side, which the evangelist John also mentions in the Lord’s Passion (John XVIII). He was ordered to build Cedron so that the city gates might be blocked and the people confined.

Cedron is interpreted as “sadness,” “mourning,” or “sorrow,” and fittingly the man to whom it was entrusted to inflict the sorrow of punishments upon Christ’s confessors was sent to build Cedron.

## CHAPTER XVI

Simon sent his two sons to fight against Cendebaeus the commander. Judas, Simon’s son, was wounded. Simon was killed with his sons at a banquet. His son John succeeded his brother in the high priesthood.

“And John went up from Gazara and reported to his father Simon,” etc. We said above that Simon represents the chief priest, namely the one who through obedience to the cross offered himself to the Father for us, in whose house the two sons are the peoples of believers from the Jews and the nations. The Father entrusts to these the strength of war against all the enemies and adversaries of truth—that is, against Jews, pagans, and heretics, and also against evil [Col. 1212A] spirits—so that they may defend the Christian faith and protect God’s true confessors.

“Take my place,” he said, “and that of my brothers, and go out and fight for our people; and may help from heaven be with you.” Who are these brothers except those of whom Truth itself, rising from the dead, said in the Gospel to the women visiting his tomb: “Go, tell my brothers to go into Galilee; there they will see me” (Matt. XXVIII)?

The saints therefore occupy the place of Christ and his apostles. By doing the will of the heavenly Father, they seek the victory of truth and the salvation of souls. Their help comes from heaven, from the one of whom it is written in the Psalm: “The Lord is wonderful in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give strength and power to his people” (Ps. LXVII).

“They chose twenty thousand fighting men,” because they regard as suited to spiritual warfare only those who become executors and doers of God’s commandments in the two commandments of charity.

“And he and his people brought their camps face to face with them,” etc. When the commander saw the people trembling at crossing the torrent and crossed first, this shows that those who serve in the place of the sick [perhaps: “teachers”] and in the office of doctors in the Church ought to strengthen the timidity of their subjects by the example of their faith and steadfastness, and sharpen them for battle against their enemies with sacred trumpets—that is, with divine doctrines.

Thus the spiritual Cendebaeus and his camp are put to flight, and many of them fall wounded, because, shaken by fear, they at last feel the power of the divine majesty [Col. 1212C].

“Then Judas, the brother of John, was wounded,” etc. The fact that Judas was wounded in battle and John pursued the enemies signifies, unless I am mistaken, what Paul says: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the nations should enter, and then all Israel would be saved” (Rom. XI).

For while the Jewish people delay in the faith of Christ, the Church of the nations presses the enemies vigorously, until by a saving struggle it converts them to repentance, or, if they persist in wickedness, punishes them by proclaiming their future punishment. But when the times of the nations have been fulfilled and their fullness has entered into the faith, then all Israel—that is, the whole Church, from both peoples—will be saved by a saving confession through faith, hope, and charity, by the gift of Christ [Col. 1212D].

And Ptolemy son of Abubus had been appointed commander in the district of Jericho, etc. What is signified by Ptolemy except hypocritical and crafty men? These people, therefore, attaching themselves to good teachers under a pretended discipline and feigning piety, whose power they entirely fail to understand, very often attain ecclesiastical honor and dignity because those very teachers promote them. For this is what it means to be the son-in-law of the high priest: those persons whom good teachers have regenerated by water and the word are received into the authority of their government. But when, having obtained rank, they begin to belong to themselves, each serving his own desires, they strive by deceit and falsehood to supplant and overthrow the very authors of their honor [Col. 1213A]; and they kill their sons and their children alike, since they spare no person living with them, but secular powers [lacuna] money and flattery for themselves; they harass the Church through secret plots or open persecutions. [Note: [Col. 1213D] Something is missing.]

Nor is it surprising that such wickedness can sometimes prevail in the Church, since we read that the Church suffered the deceit of Judas the traitor. Simon Magus was baptized by Philip, but was not cleansed of the wickedness of his mind. Julian the Apostate, raised up from the position of lector in the Church, persevered to the end of his life as a savage enemy in the evil he had begun. Our own age, too, has some such men, who, although they do not kill their teachers with the sword, nevertheless do not cease to persecute them with envy and hatred.

And a certain man, running ahead, announced to John in Gazara [Col. 1213B] that his father had perished, etc. John, indeed, after his father had been killed by treachery, carefully guards himself against the enemy and kills the men who had come to destroy him. For anyone from the number of the faithful who has been saved by God’s grace, and who is prudent and concerned to preserve his salvation, when he hears of the deception practiced by other enemies, strives to avoid their ambushes and crush their wicked schemes. For simplicity alone is not sufficient for preserving anyone’s salvation; together with simplicity there must likewise be prudence. Hence the Savior says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. 10). And the Apostle says: “Do not become children in your thinking, but in malice be infants” (1 Cor. 14). We must therefore possess simplicity, so that we harm no one; and we must also possess prudence, so that we are not despised [Col. 1213C] by others. There is not much difference between being able to deceive someone and being able to be deceived by another.

And the rest of John’s speeches and battles, etc. This John, commander and at the same time high priest of the Jews, was a man of virtue and accomplished many remarkable deeds. He also took the name Hyrcanus, and, seeking the right of friendship from the Romans, was enrolled among their friends by decree of the senate. Since Josephus relates what happened concerning this same Hyrcanus, it does not seem inappropriate to insert his account here, in order to make clear what was briefly stated at the end of the Book of Maccabees. After he had recalled some events concerning Simon’s victory, he reports his end as follows (Book 13 of the *Antiquities*, chapters 13–17): [Note: [Col. 1214D] What follows, translated from Josephus, is everywhere disfigured by foul and incurable corruption.]

Simon, therefore, having held the chief authority of the Jewish priesthood for eight years, died at a banquet, having been caught in the ambush of Ptolemy, his son-in-law. Ptolemy, after shutting Simon’s wife and two of his sons in custody, sent trusted friends to kill John, the third son, whose name was Hyrcanus. When he learned of the attack that was being prepared, the young man hastened toward the city, relying on the support of a large crowd, both because of the memory of his father’s enduring virtue and because Ptolemy’s wickedness was hated by everyone. Ptolemy also wished to enter the city by another gate, but was rejected by the people, who had already received Hyrcanus earlier. He immediately withdrew from there to a certain fortress beyond Jericho called Dagon.

Hyrcanus, having obtained his father’s honor of high priest, [Col. 1214A] after offering sacrifices to God, quickly sought Ptolemy, intending to assist both his mother and his brothers. When he attacked the fortress, he was superior in other respects, but yielded to just grief. For whenever Ptolemy was hard pressed, he brought Hyrcanus’s mother and brothers onto the wall, where they could be plainly seen, beat them, and threatened to throw them down. Thus Hyrcanus was moved more by fear than by anger. His mother, however, terrified neither by the blows nor by the threatened death, held out her hands and begged her son not to spare them. She regarded the death that Ptolemy had prepared for her as preferable to remaining alive, provided that he imposed punishment for what Ptolemy had perpetrated against her household.

John, meanwhile, now thinking of his mother’s determination and listening to her pleas, was driven to fight; but whenever he saw her being beaten and mutilated, he became utterly weakened and was filled with grief. Because of this, while the siege was prolonged, the sabbatical year arrived, during which it is customary among the Jews to desist from labor every seventh year, following the example of the seven days. Ptolemy, therefore, having obtained a respite from the siege, killed John’s brothers together with their mother and fled to Zeno, who was surnamed Cotilas [Cotilas], the tyrant of Philadelphia. Antiochus, angered by what he had suffered at Simon’s hands, led an army into Judaea and, encamping there at Jerusalem, besieged Hyrcanus. Hyrcanus, however, having opened the tomb of David, who had been the richest of kings, and having removed from it more than three thousand talents of money, persuaded Antiochus, by giving him three hundred [Col. 1214C] talents, to withdraw from the siege. He was the first of the Jews to begin nourishing foreign auxiliaries with the resources of his own wickedness.

Afterward, when Hyrcanus learned of Antiochus’s death, he immediately prepared an expedition against the cities of Syria, judging that they were without defenders, as indeed they were. For he captured Medaba, Samoga, Shechem, and Gerizim with the neighboring territories, as well as the proud race of the Cuthaeans, who inhabited the areas around a sanctuary built after the model of the one at Jerusalem. He also captured not a few other cities of Idumaea, and in addition Adoreon [Aoracum] and Marasan [Marisam]. Advancing into Samaria, to the place where the city of Sebaste now stands, founded by King Herod, he surrounded it on every side and appointed his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus [Col. 1214D] to conduct the siege. Those within the city, compelled by hunger, came to such desperation that they were forced to eat unfamiliar flesh.

Accordingly, they summon Antiochus, surnamed “Spirit of the Lord,” to their aid. When he had complied with their eager request, he was defeated by Aristobulus and Antigonus, and fled as far as Scythopolis, pursued by the brothers just mentioned.

The brothers, however, returned to Samaria, drove the multitude inside the walls once more, captured the city, demolished it, and led away its inhabitants as captives. Although they had achieved success and were withdrawing, they did not allow their eagerness to cool. Advancing with the army as far as Scythopolis, they attacked that city as well and divided among themselves all the fields between it and Carmel. Envy of John’s success and that of his sons stirred up a revolt among the nations, and many who had gathered against them did not cease until they were defeated in open war. John, meanwhile, lived in the greatest prosperity and administered affairs most successfully for thirty-three years. He died leaving five children.

He was plainly a most blessed man, one who had given no occasion for anyone to complain to Fortune about him. In the end, he alone possessed three especially notable distinctions: he was leader of his nation and high priest, and in addition he was a prophet with whom God conversed, so that he was entirely ignorant of nothing concerning the future. For he foresaw and foretold that two of his sons would not remain rulers of the nation [Col. 1215B].

According to the testimony of the chronicles, after his father’s death he held the high priesthood for twenty-six years. His father Simon had been high priest before him for eight years; before Simon, his brother Jonathan had held it for eighteen years. Judas, the brother of Jonathan and Simon, held the high priesthood for only three years, although before that he had fought many wars against the commanders of the kings of Syria. After John, his son Aristobulus received the high priesthood among the Jews. Wishing also to become king, he assumed the insignia of the diadem.

After four hundred and eighty-four years of the city of Babylon, this man killed his brother Antigonus by treachery and, after completing one year in the kingship, ended his life by a miserable death as a fratricide [Col. 1215C]. His brother Amiectus [Jannaeus], also called Alexander, succeeded him in the kingdom. He held it for twenty-seven years, with such cruelty that, when the people had been provoked and he asked them what he might do to reconcile their feelings to himself, they replied: “If he were to die; perhaps only with the dead would those who had endured such grievous things be reconciled, so that they might lay aside their hatred of the deceased.”

Stirred by this reply and accustomed to warfare, he killed many of them and forced the rest into a city called Belselel. Its capture brought upon them a plague more bitter than usual, and he advanced in such a savage course of cruelty that he crucified [or: impaled] eight hundred of them in the middle of the city. In their sight he ordered their wives and children to be slaughtered. He watched this while reclining among his concubines, joyful amid wine and cups, but intoxicated more by blood than by wine [Col. 1215D].

By this one act he terrified the people more than by war, so that on the following night eight thousand Jews fled beyond Judaea; their flight ended in Alexander’s death. After his death, his wife Alexandra, also called Salome, reigned in Jerusalem for nine years.

Then, while Alexander’s two sons, the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, were fighting over the kingdom, the Romans found an opportunity to invade Judaea. Thus Pompey, invited by Hyrcanus, came to Jerusalem, captured the city, and, after plundering the Temple, entered as far as the Holy of Holies. He took the younger brother Aristobulus with him, but confirmed Hyrcanus in the high priesthood and made Antipater, son of Herod the Ascalonite, governor of Palestine. In this way Hyrcanus, a man of sluggish spirit, with the assistance of the aforementioned governor Antipater, held the high priesthood for thirty-four years.

After Antipater was killed by poison at a banquet, his son Herod succeeded to the kingdom, and he also killed Hyrcanus. Hence Herod, son of the aforementioned Antipater the Ascalonite and of his Arabian mother Cypris [or: Cypridis], received from the Romans the leadership of the Jews. In his time, with the birth of Christ [near], the kingdom and priesthood of Judaea, which previously had been maintained through hereditary succession, were destroyed. The prophecy was fulfilled which speaks through Moses:

“From Judah the ruler shall not fail,
nor the leader from his thighs,
until he comes for whom it has been reserved;
and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49).

At this point the Christ also received his end, whom the Scripture of Daniel foretells (Dan. 9). For until Herod, the priests of Christ [that is, the anointed ones] were kings of the Jews. They began to rule from the sixty-fifth Olympiad and the restoration of the Temple under Darius, until Hyrcanus and the one hundred and eighty-sixth Olympiad, with four hundred and thirty-three intervening years. Daniel also signifies this when he says:
