“And you shall know and understand: from the beginning of the word concerning the restoration and building of Jerusalem until the rule of Christ, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.”

These sixty-nine weeks amount to four hundred and eighty-three years. During them the Christs—that is, the priests—consecrated through anointing [Col. 1216C], ruled until Hyrcanus. When the last of them had been captured by the Parthians, Herod, son of Antipater, received from Augustus and the senate a Judaea that had no connection with him. His sons ruled after him until the final captivity of Jerusalem. No high priests of priestly descent were appointed, nor did men serve God with the continuity of life required by the law of Moses. Instead, men of no distinction—one at one time, another at another—and some for a single year or a little longer, purchased the priesthood from the Romans.

Daniel the prophet also foretold all these things, saying:

“And after the seven weeks and the sixty-two weeks, the anointing shall perish, and judgment shall not be in it; and the holy Temple the people shall corrupt. With a leader coming, they shall be cut down in the catastrophe of war.”

And afterward:

“And upon the Temple,” he says, “shall be the abomination of desolations; and until the consummation of time, a consummation shall be decreed upon the desolation.”

Herod summoned a certain Ananel [Ananellus] from Babylon and appointed him high priest of the Jews. After a short time he appointed Aristobulus, his wife’s brother and Hyrcanus’s grandson, as Ananel’s successor. When Aristobulus was killed after a year [or: after the year had passed], he restored the priesthood to Ananel. From then on there was no longer a lawful succession in the priesthood. As the end of the law and the priesthood approached, everything had become confused.

This Herod was energetic in warfare, in the administration of the kingdom, and in restoring buildings, but most unfortunate and utterly savage in character. At Jerusalem he built many large churches [Col. 1217A]. He raised Samaria, which had long lain among the ashes, from its foundations and, in honor of Augustus, called it Sebaste. In Paneas he built what is called Panion. He founded Caesarea in Caesar’s name; previously it had been called Straton’s Tower. He also founded Anthedon, Antipatris, and Herodium, naming them in honor of his father Antipater and himself. In each of the cities he governed he built countless works with great skill.

But he killed Hyrcanus, who had once been high priest of the Jews and had returned from Parthian captivity, as well as Hyrcanus’s son, who had succeeded his father in the priesthood. He also most cruelly killed his sister—his own wife—together with his own two sons, now young men, and the mother of his slain wife, his mother-in-law. Herod himself, lest he perhaps be exposed as a foreigner of low birth and not of Jewish descent, burned all the books in which the nobility of the Jewish nation had been recorded and preserved in the Temple, so that, when the evidence had disappeared, he too might be thought to belong to that lineage; moreover, he wished to mingle his own offspring with their royal family.

After he had taken as his wife an indolent Jerusalem woman whom he had married while still a private citizen, and after his son Antipater had been born, he joined himself to Mariamne, daughter of Alexander and granddaughter of Aristobulus, the brother of Hyrcanus, who had previously been king of the Jewish people. She bore him five sons. Of these, he himself killed two, Alexander and Aristobulus, in Samaria. Not long afterward he murdered their mother as well, whom he had loved above all things, in a similar crime. Aristobulus had fathered Herod from Berenice, and this Herod is the one whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles was struck by an angel (Acts 12).

In addition to the acts of cruelty mentioned above, he added this: he killed the husband of his sister Salome, and, after giving her to another man in marriage, he killed that man as well. He also murdered the scribes and interpreters of the divine law in a similar crime.

When he learned from the report of the teachers that Christ our Lord had been born in Bethlehem in the thirty-second year of his reign, he ordered all the infants to be killed. But after he had completed the thirty-seventh year of his reign, or [perhaps] when he was suffering from dropsy and his entire body was swarming with worms, he died a miserable and fitting death.

It does not seem inappropriate to insert into this work what Josephus relates about Herod’s end; he reports it as follows (*Antiquities*, Book 17, chapter 9) [Col. 1217D]:

He had a fever, and not a moderate one; moreover, he suffered from intolerable itching over the entire surface of his body. His neck was tormented by continual pains, and his feet had swollen as though from the disease of dropsy. His abdominal distension and the putrefaction of his testicles generated worms. In addition, frequent breathlessness, broken sighs, and the contraction of all his limbs tormented him, so that those who attributed these things to divine judgment said that they were punishments inflicted by the sophists [reading uncertain].

Although he struggled under the tortures of so many ailments, he nevertheless desired life and hoped for recovery through devised remedies. Finally, he crossed the Jordan and used the hot waters at Callirhoe [Callirhoen]. These waters flowed into a lake rich in bitumen, called Asphaltitis, and were drinkable because of their sweetness. There his body, which the physicians had decided should be fomented with hotter oil, was immersed in a tub filled with oil and became so relaxed that even his eyes, as though he were dead, turned painfully in their sockets.

Then, when those caring for him were thrown into confusion, he appeared to look toward them when they cried out. But, having lost hope of recovery, he ordered that fifty drachmas and a large amount of money be distributed among his commanders and friends. When he returned and reached Jericho, he was seized by black bile and was almost driven to death. Then he devised a dreadful act: he ordered the most distinguished men from every village throughout Judaea to be gathered and confined in a place called the Hippodrome.

Afterward, when his sister Salome and her husband Alexander had been summoned to him [Col. 1218B], he said: “I know that the Jews will celebrate my death with festive rejoicing. Yet through others I can be mourned and can obtain the highest honors at my burial. Therefore, if you do what I command: when I have breathed my last, immediately surround these men whom you hold in custody with soldiers and kill them, so that the whole of Judaea, and every household in it, may weep—something hateful to me.”

At the same time, letters arrived from the ambassadors he had sent to Rome. They reported that, by Caesar’s command, Archelaus was “intemperate” (sic), while Antipater had been condemned to death; the letter stated that Caesar had allowed Herod to decide whether his son should instead be sent into exile.

Herod, somewhat revived by this news but again overcome by pain, was weakened by the combined violence of fasting and disease. Thus, attempting to anticipate his fate [Col. 1218C], he took an apple and asked for a knife, since he was accustomed to eat it cut up. Then, looking around to see whether anyone was watching and might prevent him, he raised his right hand as though to strike himself.

But when his cousin Aciabus came running and held back his hand, a great wailing immediately arose in the palace, as though the king were dead. Antipater heard of it and, encouraged, became joyful. He asked the guards to release and set him free, even offering them money. Their commander not only prevented this from happening but quickly reported it to the king.

Herod then cried out more loudly than the strength of a sick man seemed capable of, sent attendants, and killed Antipater. He ordered him to be buried at Hyrcanium without any honor. Then he revised his will once more, naming Archelaus, the eldest brother of Antipater, as his successor [Col. 1218D], and Antipas as tetrarch.

After his son’s death, six days had passed when Herod himself died. He had possessed the kingdom for thirty-four years from the time he killed Antigonus, and for thirty-seven years from the time the Romans had declared him king. He therefore died in the forty-seventh year of the reign of Augustus. In his place his son Archelaus, appointed by Augustus, reigned for nine years—that is, until the end of Augustus himself. Then, because the people could bear Archelaus no longer and brought accusations against him before Augustus, Augustus, seeing his ferocity, banished him to Vienna, a city of Gaul. To diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom and tame its insolence, four of his brothers were appointed tetrarchs in his place: Herod, Antipater, [Col. 1219A] Lysias, and Philip, and afterward Archelaus [the text is corrupt].

After Archelaus, Herod the tetrarch held authority over the Jewish people for twenty-four years. The emperor Tiberius had granted him this power. In Tiberius’s twelfth year, Pilate was sent by him as governor of Judaea, and remained there continuously for ten years, almost until the very end of Tiberius’s reign.

In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar (Luke 2), and likewise in the fifteenth year of Herod’s reign, as the histories report, John, son of Zechariah, preached in the desert beside the Jordan River and bore witness that Christ the Son of God was present among them. The aforementioned Herod, at the urging of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, ordered John to be beheaded at a banquet in response to the request of a dancing girl, as the sacred Gospel plainly shows [Col. 1219B] (Matt. 14).

The Lord Jesus Christ himself then announced to the peoples the saving way through signs and miracles, proving the truth of what he said. Likewise, in the eighteenth year of both rulers, Jesus Christ, in accordance with the prophets who had foretold him, came to his passion. There, having been presented to this Herod by Pilate’s messengers, he was not received in faith but rejected through worldly pride. Clothed in a white garment, he was sent back to Pilate, by whom, through the agency of soldiers, he was crucified; on the third day he rose from the dead.

The divine Scripture reports that the beginning of the evangelical preaching took place in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, and that Jesus completed the entire period of his teaching under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. He began to teach at the beginning of the period of their priesthood and continued until the beginning of Caiaphas’s tenure. Within this span scarcely the full course of four years is contained.

By that time the legal ordinances had also ceased, together with ambition for them. No one was being restored to the dignity of the high priesthood on account of Judah or of hereditary merit. Instead, through Roman power, the highest priesthood was granted now to one man and then to another, so that the office changed with annual interruptions.

Finally, Josephus himself (*Antiquities*, Book 18, chapter 4) reports that, after Annas, four men in succession performed the duties of the high priesthood until Caiaphas. He writes in these words:

Valerius Gratus, after removing Annas from the priesthood, appointed Ishmael son of Bassi. But not long afterward he also deposed him and substituted Eleazar, the son of Annas the high priest, in the high priesthood. He removed this man from office after the first year and entrusted the office of high priest to a certain Simon, son of Camithus. After Simon too had held it for no more than a single year, he received Joseph as his successor, whose name was also Caiaphas.

Thus, throughout the entire period in which our Lord and Savior is described as having taught on earth, within the span of four years in which these four successions of high priests mentioned by Josephus occurred, scarcely did any one of them administer the office for a full year.

Josephus also reports how Herod the tetrarch lost his kingdom, saying:

When Herod the tetrarch had been accused, Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, whom his father Herod had killed, came to Tiberius. Since Tiberius did not accept the accusation, Agrippa remained in Rome, seeking acquaintance with certain powerful men. He showed the greatest attentions to Gaius, the son of Germanicus, while Gaius was still a private citizen.

One day, during a lavish banquet at which they were dining, Agrippa finally stretched out his hands and openly began to pray that, with Tiberius quickly dead, the imperial power might be given to Gaius. When this was reported to Tiberius, he immediately ordered Agrippa to be confined. Agrippa was held in prison under great distress for six months, until Tiberius died.

After Tiberius died, having reigned ten years and three days, Gaius Caesar succeeded him in the empire, released Agrippa from his chains, and gave him the tetrarchy of Philip, who had already died; he also called him king. When Agrippa had come into power, he stirred up the desires of Herod the tetrarch through envy. Herod’s wife especially incited him by the appearance of the kingdom, reproaching him for their harmony and saying that, because he had been unwilling to sail to Caesar, he was deprived of greater authority. For if Gaius had made Agrippa a king from a private citizen, why would he hesitate to honor Herod with the same dignity after he had been a tetrarch?

Moved by these considerations, Herod went to Gaius. But after being severely reproached for his greed, he fled to Spain. The accuser Agrippa had followed him, and Gaius added Herod’s tetrarchy to Agrippa’s possessions. Thus, while Herod was living in exile in Spain, his wife Herodias also died there with him.

Pontius Pilate, who was governor in the same year in which the Savior suffered, secretly set images of Caesar in the Temple at night, as Josephus relates. This became the evident cause of the first sedition and disturbances. Later, by spending on an aqueduct at Jerusalem the sacred treasury, which the Jews call the *corban*, he provided the seeds of a second sedition [Col. 1220C].

When the same Pilate reported to Tiberius about Christian doctrine and mentioned something concerning the deeds, passion, and resurrection of the Redeemer, Tiberius referred the matter to the senate, so that Christ might be received among the other sacred beings. But when, following the senate’s decision, it was resolved that Christians should be expelled from the city, Tiberius threatened the accusers of Christians with death by an edict, as Tertullian writes in the *Apologeticus*. Many senators and Roman knights were also killed by him.

Thus divine vengeance condemned the Jews for the crime they had committed. Pilate himself, who had acted as an unjust judge against the Savior, was likewise tormented at that time by such great and terrible calamities that he is reported to have pierced himself with his own hand and violently ended his wicked life. For the servant of so great a crime could not escape unpunished, as we find in the histories of the Greeks—specifically those who record the Olympiads and compose annual books of events for the memory of posterity.

Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, who was a son of Herod, who, after killing James the son of Zebedee, sent the apostle Peter to prison (Acts 12) and stirred up persecution against those who believed in Christ, did not escape unpunished. Luke makes this clear in the Acts of the Apostles, and Josephus records it in Book 18 of the *Antiquities*. He relates the following about him (Book 19 of the *Antiquities*, chapter 8):

He had completed the third year of his rule over the whole of Judaea when he happened to arrive at Caesarea, previously called Straton’s Tower. There he set up spectacles for the citizens in honor of Caesar, on what appeared to be the ceremonial day of Caesar’s safety. Since men of distinction from the entire province, possessing both honor and wealth, had gathered there, on the second day of the spectacles he came forth at daybreak wearing a gleaming garment wonderfully woven of gold and silver.

He proceeded to the theater. When the first rays of the sun had fallen upon the folds of the silver garment, the reflected brilliance cast upon the spectators a doubled light from the flashing radiance of the metal, so that it dazzled their eyes and, through this, his contriving arrogance falsely claimed for him something more than human nature. Immediately the voices of the flattering crowd resounded, proclaiming his honor and comparing him with the rising sun. From every side the flatterers shouted that he was a god and simply prayed that he might be propitious. The people said: “Until now we feared you as a man, but from this moment we confess that you are above human nature.”

The king did not suppress this acclamation, made contrary to divine law, nor did he recoil from the impiety of the unlawful flattery. Then, looking up shortly afterward, he saw an owl sitting above his head on a rope. He recognized it as the instrument of his imminent death, although previously he had known it as the presager of honors.

And suddenly a torment seized him, through an exceedingly severe pain in his belly and a swelling. Looking toward his courtiers, he said: “Behold, I, your god, am immediately compelled to exchange life. Some divine power has just exposed as false the voices that were recently bestowed upon me. You called me immortal a moment ago, and now I am being carried away to death. Yet the judgment that God has appointed must be accepted.

“For we have lived not contemptibly, and we have completed the longevity that was considered blessed.” Having said this, he was driven by the violence of the pain with increasing force and was quickly carried back to the palace. When it became known that he would soon die, a vast crowd of every age and sex gathered. Following ancestral custom, they lay on sackcloth and entreated almighty God for the king’s safety.

The entire royal household resounded with lamentations and groans. Meanwhile the king himself, reclining in an upper chamber and looking down, saw all the people prostrate and lying face downward in tears; he too could not restrain his own tears. After being tormented by abdominal pains for five continuous days, he violently ended his life at the age of fifty-four. He had reigned seven years: four years under Gaius Caesar, three years holding the tetrarchy of Philip, and in the fourth year also acquiring that of Herod, while the remaining three years were completed under Claudius Caesar.

After Agrippa the father had held the kingdom of Judaea for six years, his son Agrippa was appointed king in his place by Claudius. He held the kingdom for twenty-six years—that is, until the second year of Vespasian, when the destruction of the city took place.

We have judged it appropriate to set down here what Josephus relates about him (*Antiquities*, Book 20, chapter 13). He says:

Claudius appointed Agrippa, the son of Agrippa, king of the Jews. He sent Fadus [Cuspium Fadum] as governor of the entire province, including Samaria, Galilee, and the region called Transjordan.

A little later he added the following:

A most bitter sedition was also inflamed by the high priests against the priests and the leading men of the Jerusalem populace. Each of them, by complaining, drew after him crowds of wicked young men who delighted in new laws, and each appeared to be their leader. They brought themselves into conflicts, disparaged one another, and stoned one another; there was no one to restrain them. Everything was done as though the city had no governor.

The high priests consequently fell into such poverty that, sending their slaves to the threshing floors, they seized the tithes owed to the priests. It happened that some of the poorer priests, whose food supplies had been plundered, perished from hunger. Thus the violence of the seditions had confused right and justice.

A little later he adds this:

Sometimes, even in the middle of the city, they rushed upon one another and killed one another. This happened especially on festival days. Assassins, mingling with the crowds and concealing daggers, wandered about. Whenever a designated victim approached them, they killed him at close quarters. Then, by a wicked artifice, when the man whom they had struck down with a hidden wound had fallen, the assassins themselves pretended indignation against those who had committed such a deed in the middle of the city. In this way their secret crimes continued, and Jonathan the high priest was the first of all to be killed by them. After him very many others were slaughtered, so that fear of death itself became heavier than the deaths, since everyone, as though always stationed for battle, expected at every moment to be killed [Col. 1222C].

When Claudius had completed fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days in power, he died. Nero received the empire and held it for fourteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. In his second year Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judaea; by whom Paul was sent to Rome in chains, where he remained for two years in unrestricted custody (Acts 25). After this he was released for preaching, while Nero had not yet burst into the enormities that history recounts concerning him. James, the brother of the Lord, after governing the Church of Jerusalem for thirty years (Acts 12), was killed by the Jews in Nero’s seventh year, who exacted from him the vengeance they had been unable to exact by killing Paul.

Festus was succeeded in the administration of Judaea by Albinus, and Albinus by Florus. The Jews could no longer endure Florus’s luxury, greed, and other crimes, and rebelled against the Romans. Vespasian, commander of the army, was sent against them and captured many cities of Judaea. Nero, first among all in his crimes, also persecuted the Christians; from their number he killed Peter at Rome by crucifixion and Paul by the sword. Having ventured nothing at all in military affairs, he nearly lost Britain. For two very distinguished towns there were captured and destroyed under him.

Finally, when the Senate was seeking his punishment, he fled from the palace and killed himself at the fourth milestone from the City, on his freedman’s suburban estate between the Salarian and Nomentan roads. He was thirty-two years old, and with him the entire family of Augustus was extinguished.

[Col. 1223A]

After Nero, Galba in Iberia, Vitellius in Germany, and Otho at Rome seized the empire. Galba was beheaded in the seventh month of his reign in the middle of the Roman Forum. Vespasian, having defeated the Jews in two battles, forced them to their deaths. Otho, in the third month of his reign, died by his own hand while hunting [at Bedriacum]. Vitellius was thrown into the Tiber by Vespasian’s generals.

Vespasian, the seventh of the Romans, reigned eight years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. Having been proclaimed emperor by the army in Judaea, he soon entrusted the war to his son and departed for Rome by way of Alexandria. In his second year Titus, after Judaea had been captured and Jerusalem overthrown, killed six hundred thousand men. Josephus, however, explicitly states that six hundred [eleven hundred] thousand men perished by the sword and famine, and that another one hundred thousand captives were publicly sold.

[Col. 1223B]

He reports that the reason such a multitude was found in Jerusalem was the Feast of Unleavened Bread: Jews from every nation had flocked to the Temple and were shut up in the city as though in a prison. For they had to be killed during those same days of Passover on which they had crucified the Savior.

The entire period, from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar and the beginning of the evangelical preaching to the second year of Vespasian and the final destruction of Jerusalem, amounts to forty-two years. From the captivity that they suffered under Antiochus there were two hundred thirty-eight [nine] years. From the second year of Darius, under whom the Temple was rebuilt, there were five hundred ninety years. From the first construction of the Temple under Solomon to its final destruction under Vespasian there were five hundred ninety-two years [“eleven hundred and two years”].

[Col. 1224B]

## INTO THE SECOND BOOK

The Second Book of Maccabees, although shorter than the first book of the same work in its historical narrative, nevertheless in some measure repeats earlier periods, except that the first book briefly mentions Alexander the Great of Macedon at its beginning. This book also recalls the benefits that King Seleucus, surnamed Nicanor, conferred upon the Jews. The History of Josephus’s *Antiquities* and the chronicle of Eusebius attest that Seleucus treated the Jews honorably in their commonwealth and assigned them equal status with the Macedonian and Greek inhabitants. Likewise, Antiochus the Great, as the authorities mentioned above attest, praises them in frequent letters and presents them with many gifts.

The same book has, in a certain sense, a narrative different from that of the first; nevertheless, it does not destroy the truth of the history. Although it contains many accounts also found in the first book, it inserts several matters that are not found there. It appears to have been written by people who lived in the land of Judah for those who had fled into foreign regions. Thus it begins as follows.

## CHAPTER ONE

*The Jews in Jerusalem send greetings to the Jews in Egypt. Antiochus was killed in the temple of Nanea. Concerning the sacrificial fire hidden in a well. Nehemiah’s prayer was such that the miracle of the transformation of fire into water, and conversely, was made known to the king of the Persians.*

“The brothers, the Jews who are in Jerusalem and in the land of Judaea, send greetings to the Jewish brothers who are throughout Egypt, and so forth.”

This Demetrius, under whom the Jerusalemites are said to have prayed, was established in Egypt. He ruled Asia and Syria after Antiochus Eupator, and he too was surnamed Soter, that is, “Savior.” The number of years here is calculated with reference to him: namely, the one hundred sixty-ninth year.

For Antiochus Epiphanes, who began to reign after the one hundred thirty-seventh year of the Greek kingdom, reigned eleven years. Antiochus Eupator reigned two years, and Demetrius Soter twelve years. These are the years from the beginning of the reign of Seleucus Nicanor, king of Syria, from whom the years of the Greek kingdom are reckoned, up to the end of Demetrius: one hundred sixty-two years. To these must be added the seven years of the reign of Alexander, who is described by Pompeius Trogus as obscure, vicious, and unworthy of royal dignity; but since he is described as having held the kingdom for ten [seven] years, the total becomes one hundred sixty-nine.

Let us give another calculation. The first to rule Asia after Alexander was Antigonus, for nineteen years. After him Demetrius, also called Poliorcetes, ruled for seventeen years. In the seventeenth year of his reign this Demetrius surrendered himself to Seleucus, and Asia was joined to the kingdom of Syria in the twenty-eighth year of Seleucus Nicanor.

If, therefore, we now begin to reckon the sequence of years from the first year of Antigonus’s reign—he ruled in Asia for seven years before Seleucus began to reign in Syria—and place those same seven years before the reign of Seleucus, then carry the reckoning of the years of the Syrian kingdom forward in this manner to the last year of Demetrius Soter, the entire total of the earlier number is found there.

But it is surprising that later Judas is said to have sent greetings in the one hundred eighty-eighth year to Aristobulus, a member of the council and tutor of King Ptolemy, and to have sent instructions concerning the purification of the Temple, which they themselves were to perform on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, when in the first book mentioned above Judas is read to have died much earlier, while Demetrius was still alive. Indeed, according to the testimony of the chronicles, he is found to have been killed in the sixth year of Demetrius.

But because the authors of the books themselves are uncertain, they seem not unreasonably to differ in their reckoning of the periods, especially since in the legal books the edition of the Seventy Interpreters differs greatly from the Hebrew text in its calculation of years.

[Col. 1225A]

“We Jews have written to you in the tribulation and distress that came upon us in these years,” and so forth.

Jason is the brother of the high priest Onias. The succeeding portions of this book relate that, out of ambition for the high priesthood, he went over to Antiochus Epiphanes—that is, “the Noble”—and persuaded him to establish a Gentile rite at Jerusalem.

“The people who are in Jerusalem and Judaea, and the council,” and so forth.

This Aristobulus was Jewish by nation, but is recognized as a Peripatetic philosopher. As the chroniclers report, he wrote commentaries on Moses for Ptolemy Philometor, at the time when Antiochus Epiphanes was ruling Syria and Asia.

[Col. 1225B]

“We give magnificent thanks to God for having delivered us from great dangers,” and so forth.

The first book of this history records how Antiochus Epiphanes—who inflicted more evils upon the Jews than all the kings who had ruled Syria before him—lost his kingdom and ended his life. Josephus also bears witness to this in the twelfth book of his *History of Jewish Antiquities*, saying:

“King Antiochus, traveling through the upper province, heard of a city of the Persians distinguished for its wealth, called Elymais. He had heard that it possessed an exceedingly precious temple of Diana, filled with ornaments of every kind; moreover, that Alexander, the king of the Macedonians and son of Philip, had left arms and breastplates there. He therefore set out against Elymais and besieged it. But the inhabitants were not at all frightened by his assault or siege; they resisted stubbornly, and he withdrew, deceived in his hope. For they came out of the city, drove him away, and pursued him as far as Babylonia. When he arrived there after losing many of his soldiers, one of the Jews reported to him the destruction of the commanders whom he had left to fight against the Jews, and that the strength of the Jews had increased.

“As this evil grew under his earlier administration, he fell into an illness. When it lasted a long time and his sufferings increased, he understood that he was dying. Calling his friends together, he told them that his illness was dreadful. He confessed that he was suffering these things because, while afflicting the Jewish nation, he had plundered the Temple and despised God. Having said this, he immediately expired.”

[Col. 1225C]

Thus I wonder at Polybius of Megalopolis, who, although he was a good man, says that Antiochus perished because he wished to devastate the temple of Diana in Persia. For one who did not actually commit the sin but merely conceived the thought was held guilty of no offense. If Polybius thinks that Antiochus ended his life for that reason, it seems far more plausible that the sacrilegious destruction of the Temple at Jerusalem caused the king to perish.

## CHAPTER TWO

*The narrative continues as above.*

“Since we intend to purify the Temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, we considered it necessary to inform you,” and so forth.

These matters—which the Jewish Jerusalemites, writing to the Jews throughout Egypt, relate concerning fire found in a well and changed into something resembling thick water—we have been unable to find anywhere in the writings or statements of Ezra or Nehemiah. Nor can we find in the book of Jeremiah itself what they later assert concerning the hiding of the ark and the tabernacle by Jeremiah.

It is therefore clear that they either learned these things through the tradition of their ancestors or found them written in their apocryphal books. We shall therefore not investigate curiously what is uncertain, but turn our pen to those matters that are manifestly established by the testimony of the canonical books.

## CHAPTER THREE

*Simon betrays the treasures of God’s Temple. Heliodorus is sent to seize them. The priest and the people beseech the Lord that the deposited treasures may be preserved. Heliodorus, wishing to plunder the Temple, is struck down and delivered from the blow through the sacrifice that is offered.*

“Now when the holy city was inhabited in complete peace,” and so forth.

Because there were high priests under different kings, we considered it necessary, following the account of the historians, to recite the names of those who held the high priesthood during the reigns of the kings, as well as the names of those who belonged to the Jewish nation after the Babylonian captivity, so that the truth of the history might appear more clearly.

The first high priest was Zadok of the Temple that Solomon built. After him his son Ahimaaz succeeded to the honor. After him came Joram, and after Joram Anxidranius. Then Judas; after Judas, Sudeus. After him Hylus; Hylus was succeeded by Joatham. Then came Uriah, and Uriah was succeeded by Neriah. After Neriah came Odeas. After him came Sella, and then Elchias. After him Zara, and after Zara Josedech, who was taken captive to Babylon.

These men succeeded their fathers in the high priesthood in order. After Josedech, his son Joannes received the priesthood; under him the Temple was rebuilt. After him came his son Joachim. When Joachim also had died, his son Joannes assumed the honor. When Joannes ended his life, his son Jaddus succeeded to the primacy of the priests; under him Alexander of Macedon came to Jerusalem.

After him his son Onias is regarded as distinguished. After him came his son Simon, who was surnamed Justus because of his diligent devotion to the worship of the Lord and his ready clemency toward his fellow citizens. Then Eleazar, the high priest of the Jews and Simon’s brother, undertook the Temple ministry, with Simon’s son Onias left still a very small child. At the request of Ptolemy Philadelphus, this Eleazar sent the Seventy Interpreters to translate the divine Law.

After Eleazar, his uncle Manasseh received the priesthood. After Manasseh, Onias, son of Simon the Just, is recognized as a distinguished high priest of the Jews. Because he failed to pay the customary tribute to King Ptolemy, he provoked him to anger. Josephus, however, a man noble among his own people, was sent by the Jews as an envoy to Ptolemy. Having earned the king’s friendship through many services to him, Josephus was appointed commander of Judaea and the neighboring regions.

After Onias, Simon, the son of Onias, is recognized as a distinguished high priest of the Jews.

[Col. 1227A]

Under him, Joannes, son of Sirach, composed the Book of Wisdom, which he called *Pahareton*, that is, “possessing every virtue,” and in it he mentioned Simon.

After Simon, his son Onias is regarded as distinguished. To him Arius, king of the Lacedaemonians, sent envoys. He held office while Antiochus the Great and his son Seleucus Philopator ruled Syria and Asia, continuing until Antiochus Epiphanes. Under this high priest Onias, the events narrated concerning Simon, the Temple superintendent, took place, while Seleucus Philopator was reigning in Syria and Asia and Antiochus Epiphanes succeeded him in the kingdom.

Simon, the superintendent of the Temple at Jerusalem, took refuge with Apollonius, the commander of Phoenicia. After promising him many gifts, Simon began to claim the priesthood for himself. When Seleucus heard this, he sent Heliodorus to investigate the matter. When Heliodorus reached Judaea, he judged unjustly and carried out many prosperous undertakings, but was terrified by divine signs directed against him and returned to Seleucus.

“Onias the priest had arranged for Simon to become a fugitive,” and so forth.

Finally, according to the rule of allegorical interpretation, this history intimates that all who, stirred by pride, have presumed to defile the sanctification of the Lord and handle it unworthily with polluted hands must be punished by heavenly judgment. For, as the Truth bears witness, “the house of prayer” is for all nations (Matt. 21; Isa. LI), and no one may turn it into a den of thieves.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “Holiness befits your house, O Lord, for length of days” (Ps. 92). Nor is it permissible to conduct or store anything there except to devote oneself to the praises and prayers of God alone.

For this reason the Lord himself in the Gospel (John 2) drove from the Temple those who were selling and buying in it, poured out the money-changers’ coins, and overturned the seats of those selling doves. After these things had been done, he taught daily in the Temple.

According to the allegory, Onias, the great priest of God and the symbolic guardian of the Temple, signifies the Lord Savior, who, made high priest by God the Father forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109), is the guardian and inhabitant of the true Temple, which is the Church. The name Onias seems sufficiently to express this, for Onias is interpreted as “the Lord’s sorrow” or “the Lord of sorrow.” And who can more truly be called the sorrowing Lord than our Redeemer, of whom Isaiah says:

“We saw him, and there was no appearance in him, and we desired him despised and last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity. Surely he himself bore our weaknesses and carried our sorrows.”

Heliodorus, the invader and plunderer of the Lord’s treasury, signifies pagans, Jews, and heretics, who wish without reverence for God to abuse God’s gifts and turn them to an impious purpose.

The pagans invade the treasury of God’s Temple when they attempt to destroy the faith and merit of Christ. The Jews invade it when they wish to confuse the Christian religion with the ceremonies of the old Law. The heretics invade it when they strive to corrupt the truth of the Gospel and the purity of God’s Law with false doctrines.

[Col. 1228A]

But while Onias was praying, a terrifying horseman descended, wearing golden armor—the very one of whom John wrote in his Apocalypse, saying (Rev. 19):

“I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and with justice he judges. His eyes were like a flame of fire; upon his head were many diadems; he had a name written that no one knows except himself. He was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name is called the Word of God.”

When the members of Christ pray, he himself comes to their aid, he who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), both to defeat enemies and to terrify the presumptions of the wicked.

His horse was incorrupt, and his garment bloodstained, because the death of his flesh was innocent; and he was terrifying because he is exceedingly wondrous and is the most just judge. He was adorned with the finest coverings because he is the brightest splendor in the beauty of every virtue. All his weapons were golden because his works are marvelous. For by his gift the Church possesses the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. With these weapons he himself fights daily in his members against his enemies.

This horseman struck Heliodorus first with a violent blow from his hooves, because the mystery of the Incarnation prostrates all enemies—that is, Jews, pagans, and heretics—so that, confounded by the enormity of their crimes, they may at last cease.

The two young men who appeared with the horseman—beautiful in virtue, excellent in glory, and splendid in their clothing—who stood on either side of Onias and scourged Heliodorus without ceasing, beating him with many blows, signify the teachers of both Testaments.

Standing around Christ’s incarnation, beautiful in the virtue of faith and good works, excellent in the glory of miracles, and splendid in the garment of holy knowledge and wisdom, they exist in various ages and by their preaching beat down the insensibility of the wicked and force them to fall to the ground.

Thus the proud man who attacked the Temple will appear, through the correction of discipline, to be powerless. For “there is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21), because “he has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths,” and no one can resist his will; “the Lord of all” himself (Ps. 134).

But the fact that Onias, offering a saving sacrifice for the man’s salvation, rescued Heliodorus when he was surrounded by great darkness signifies that the mercy of our Redeemer often grants the benefit of conversion to the ungrateful and undeserving. Through the grace of him who offered himself as a saving sacrifice for the sins of the world, they may strip away their errors, be delivered from the power of Satan—whose captives they once were, subject to his will—give thanks to their Redeemer, and proclaim his praise throughout the whole earth.

[Col. 1228D]

## CHAPTER FOUR

*The plots of Simon the traitor against Onias. Jason corrupts King Antiochus with gifts. The priests hasten to the athletic school, neglecting the sacred rites. Menelaus excludes Jason from the priesthood, and Lysimachus succeeds him, and so forth.*

“But after Seleucus had died, when Antiochus, who was called the Noble, had assumed the kingdom,” and so forth.

Josephus narrates the matter as follows (*Antiquities*, book 12, chapter 6):

“At that time, when Onias, the chief of the priests, had died, the king entrusted the high priesthood to his brother Antiochus, for the son whom Onias had left behind was still an infant. We shall demonstrate individually, in their proper place, the matters that seemed to concern the boy.

“But the king, angered against Jesus—for this was Onias’s brother—took the high priesthood away from him and gave it to their younger brother, whose name was Onias. Simon had three sons: to these, as we have said, the high priesthood came. Jesus called himself Jason, while Onias was named Menelaus.

“First, therefore, Jesus, the high priest, stirred up a revolt against Menelaus. When the multitude of the people was divided between them, the sons of Tobias stood on Menelaus’s side, while the greater part of the people supported Jason.

“Thus Menelaus and the sons of Tobias, being hard pressed, departed for Antiochus. They informed him that they wished to abandon their ancestral laws and observe the way of life and customs of the Greeks. They therefore asked him to permit them to build a gymnasium at Jerusalem. When he granted permission, they concealed their circumcision so that, when naked, they would not appear different from the Greeks. Abandoning everything else that their ancestral custom required of them, they followed the practices and rites of other nations.”

This is Josephus’s account.

But I wonder how Josephus himself can say that, after Onias’s death, Antiochus gave the priesthood to Jason’s brother, when this history does not agree with that account, as will be shown in what follows.

Eventually Antiochus Epiphanes, having withdrawn by order of the Senate from the region of the Ptolemies, which he had suddenly invaded, came into Judaea. There he entrusted the high priesthood to Jesus, who was also Onias’s brother. After expelling him, he gave it to Onias, surnamed Menelaus, as his successor. Thus, when a dispute arose among the leaders over the dignity of the priesthood, the seeds of immense misery began to sprout.

These deeds of the proud and transgressors of God’s Law do not offer us some useful allegory for edification. Rather—alas!—many imitators of their crime are found in our own time: those who are placed over the people of God in the Church, redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son, abandon the teaching of the Gospel and true religion, and turn away from the worship of the one God commended and proclaimed there toward a secret idolatry through wicked conduct.

By ambition for money and wealth in the present life, they lead luxurious and detestable lives before God. Attending to the favor of flatterers, they draw many along with themselves to destruction.

These people, in the words of the Apostle, “profess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1). They are not content with moderate food and clothing, but, desiring to become rich, fall into temptation, the devil’s snare, and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition.

For “the root of all evils is avarice”; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows (1 Tim. 6).

[Col. 1230A]

“When the five-year contest was being celebrated at Tyre and the king was present,” and so forth.

When Uzziah, also called Azariah, the leprous king, was reigning in Judaea, Pekah in Israel, Aeschylus among the Athenians, and no one among the Latins, in the second year of Aeschylus, the Athenian judge, the first Olympiad was held, in which Coroebus of Elis became the victor.

The Eleans celebrate a five-year contest, with four complete years intervening during which four annual rulers are appointed. This Olympiad was first instituted by Iphitus, son of Praxonidas or Aemon. From this time the Greek history of chronological periods is believed to be reliable; before this, they put forward differing opinions, each according to his own judgment.

Antiochus is described as having celebrated this five-year contest at Tyre at that time. The events subsequently mentioned concerning Jason and Menelaus occurred afterward.

Jason, who had imprisoned his own brother—namely, the elder Onias, son of Simon—was accused before the king by Menelaus, that is, by the younger Onias, who had two names. Deceived by the king, Jason fled and was expelled into the region of the Ammonites.

Menelaus obtained the high priesthood, but did nothing about the money he had promised the king for the priesthood. For this reason he too was removed, and Lysimachus succeeded him.

While Menelaus was still in possession of the priesthood and Antiochus was absent, he thought that, because of the favorable circumstances involving the Tarsians and Mallotians, he had found a suitable opportunity. He stole certain golden vessels from the Temple and gave them to Andronicus, whom the king had left to govern the region.

The elder Onias, brother of the man whom Jason had imprisoned, was therefore angered. He accused Menelaus of the impiety he had committed, while remaining in a secure place at Antioch, near Daphne.

Menelaus then approached Andronicus and asked him to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias and, after giving him his right hand with an oath—although Onias suspected him—and persuading him to come out of the sanctuary, immediately killed him. He did not fear justice, although not only the Jews but also the other nations were indignant and deeply grieved at the death of so great and unjustly murdered a man.

[Col. 1230D]

The Jews and Greeks therefore together approached the king when he returned from the regions of Cilicia and reported what had happened. Antiochus was so moved that he shed tears. Remembering the dead man’s sobriety and modesty, and inflamed with anger, he ordered Andronicus, stripped of his purple robe, to be led through the entire city and, in the very place where he had committed his impiety against Onias, to be deprived of his life as a sacrilegious man. Thus the Lord repaid him with a punishment worthy of his crime.

After Lysimachus had committed many sacrileges in the Temple at Menelaus’s advice and the report had spread, a crowd gathered against Lysimachus. Some seized stones, others strong sticks, and some threw ashes at Lysimachus. Many were wounded, some were struck down, and all were put to flight. They killed Lysimachus himself, the sacrilegious man, near the treasury.

Judicial proceedings against Menelaus then began. When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the elders brought the case before him. As Menelaus was being defeated, he promised Ptolemy a large sum of money to persuade the king.

Ptolemy therefore approached the king, who was seated in a certain courtyard as though to take refreshment, and diverted him from his judgment. He acquitted Menelaus of all the charges. But the wretched Jews, although they had pleaded their case before the governors and had been judged innocent, he condemned to death.

When a false report arose that Antiochus had died, Jason, taking no fewer than a thousand men, suddenly attacked the city. The citizens rushed to the wall, but at last, when the city had been captured, Menelaus fled to the citadel.

Jason did not spare the slaughter of his fellow citizens, nor did he consider that prosperity against one’s kindred is the greatest evil. He thought he would carry off trophies from enemies, not citizens.

He did not, however, obtain the high priesthood. The outcome of his plots instead began with his own disgrace, and he fled again to the region of the Ammonites.

Finally, trapped for destruction by Aretas, the Arab tyrant, and fleeing from city to city, hated by all as a deserter from the laws and an accursed man, as an enemy of his homeland and fellow citizens, he was expelled into Egypt. He who had expelled many from their homeland died in exile after going to Lacedaemon.

[Col. 1231C]

Menelaus, meanwhile, was plotting similar deceits against Antiochus Eupator. The King of kings stirred up Antiochus’s anger against the sinner; when Lysias suggested that Menelaus was the cause of all the evils, Antiochus ordered him to be seized and killed in the customary manner.

At that very place there was a tower fifty cubits high, piled all around with ashes, overlooking a steep drop. He therefore ordered the sacrilegious man to be thrown into the ashes, while everyone pushed him toward his destruction. Thus the transgressor of the Law happened to die by such a law. Menelaus was not given to the earth, because he had committed many offenses against the altar of God, whose fire and ashes were holy; he was condemned to die in the ashes.

Josephus reports, as we showed in the preceding book, that the son of the high priest Onias was left still a very young boy when his father died. Seeing that the king had killed his uncle Menelaus and had given the high priesthood to Alcimus, who was not of priestly descent, and that Lysias had persuaded the king to transfer the office from that family to another household, he fled to Ptolemy, king of Egypt.

Ptolemy and his wife Cleopatra granted him an honor, and he asked for a place in the region of Cleopatris. There he founded a city bearing his own name and built a temple modeled on his father’s Temple.

Alcimus, however, who was hostile to Judas Maccabaeus, died soon afterward, struck down by the anger of God. Thus, with the approval of all the Jews, the priesthood was awarded to Judas Maccabaeus.

All these matters seem to build up a moral rather than an allegorical understanding. They clearly demonstrate that the most just judge and fairest retributor restores to each person a fitting reward, according to what his deserts require: eternal rewards to the devout and God-fearing; punishment by everlasting fire to the impious, sinners, and blasphemers.

No one should flatter himself because of earthly happiness or the prosperity of the present life if he wishes to live impurely in sins. Nor should the person who acts rightly despair of future salvation when he is constricted in the present life by severe sufferings or various tribulations, if he perseveres in the path of righteousness. For it is written:

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from them all” (Ps. VII);

and:

“Many are the scourges of sinners, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord. Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. 31).

## CHAPTER FIVE

*Concerning the heavenly signs that occurred in Jerusalem. Concerning the death of Jason, the persecutor of his fellow citizens. Antiochus, pursuing Judas, killed the people and plundered the Temple under the leadership of Menelaus. The Lord chose the place on account of the people, not the people on account of the place, and so forth.*

“At the same time Antiochus prepared a second expedition into Egypt,” and so forth.

Portents sometimes foretell favorable events, but sometimes prefigure disasters; they always do so according to what the supreme arbiter judges appropriate to individual circumstances and times.

It is therefore not surprising that in the time of the Maccabees horsemen wearing golden robes and armed cohorts were seen rushing through the air, and that the shining brilliance of golden weapons foretold the adversity that was to come and the disaster awaiting the Jews. For before the destruction of Jerusalem, as Josephus testifies (*The Jewish War*, book 7, chapter 12), we learn that a brilliant star resembling a sword hung over the entire deserted city, and that a comet appeared to burn throughout the whole year with flames portending destruction.

But before the time of the ruin and the war, when the people had assembled for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, on the eighth day of the month of Antiochus, which is April, at the ninth hour of the night, such a great brilliance of light surrounded the altar and the Temple that everyone thought broad daylight had appeared. It lasted for half an hour. To the inexperienced and ignorant this seemed a good omen, but the learned in the Law and all honorable teachers recognized that it was a fatal portent.

During the same festival, a heifer brought to the sacrifices and standing among the hands of the ministers gave birth to water. Moreover, the door of the inner sanctuary, which faced east, although covered with solid bronze of immense weight and able to be closed only when twenty men pushed it with all their strength, and although secured with iron bars and bolts and held shut by bars lowered from above, suddenly appeared, at the sixth hour of the night, to have opened of its own accord.

[Col. 1232D]

After the festival had ended, and several days had passed, on the twenty-first day of the month Artemisius, which we call May, a prodigious and almost unbelievable vision appeared. It would truly have been judged false had not the ensuing calamity confirmed the truth of the hidden [perhaps: eyewitness] evils.

For near sunset chariots and four-horse carriages were seen being carried through the air over the entire region, and cohorts of armed men traversing the clouds and surrounding the cities.

On another festival day, called Pentecost, the priests entered the temple at night to complete the customary rites. At first they sensed certain movements and noises. Then they heard subdued voices saying, “Let us depart from here.” Something still more terrifying was added. For a certain Jesus son of Ananias, a common and rustic man, four years before the war, while the city continued in peace and prosperity, suddenly began to cry out on the day of the Feast of Tabernacles:

“A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem, and a voice against the temple, against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against all this people.”

He shouted this continually, day and night, walking around all the streets, until certain leading men of the people, moved to indignation as though by an ill-omened prophecy, seized the man and inflicted many blows upon him. But he said nothing at all on his own behalf, nor did he entreat even those who stood around him; instead, with equal stubbornness and shouting, he repeated those same words. Then the magistrates, understanding that the matter was as it truly appeared, judged the man’s impulse to be more divine and brought him before the Roman governor. There, after being torn by scourges down to the bones, he shed neither prayers nor tears; rather, emitting the same voice miserably and with a kind of wailing, he uttered it almost word by word, adding this also: “Woe, woe to Jerusalem.”

Thus the wretched city deservedly endured all these portents, because it had always, according to the testimony of the giver of the Law, rebelled against the Lord; and, ungrateful for his benefits, it treated with mockery and killed the servants of the supreme master of the household who had been sent to it by him. Finally, after killing the heir himself, they cast him outside the camp. Hence the Lord himself, rebuking the unbelieving city, says in the Gospel:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling. Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23).

This had indeed been foretold in ancient times; and afterward the most savage murderers received a fitting recompense for their guilt, so that some were killed by famine, some perished by pestilence, and some, slain and taken captive, were led by their enemies into every region of the world. Thus was fulfilled that saying of Jeremiah, which he prophesied concerning the same people and city:

“Judah migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude; she dwelt among the nations and found no rest. All her persecutors seized her amid her distresses. The roads of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn feast. All her gates are destroyed, her priests groaning, her virgins defiled, and she herself oppressed by bitterness” (Lamentations 1).

After these events the king suspected that the Jews would abandon their alliance, etc. After the historian had recounted the death of the impious and sacrilegious Lysimachus and Jason, and had further recalled the vision of signs and portents in the air, he returned to the sequence of his narrative—that is, to the departure of Antiochus Epiphanes from Egypt. Angered because, by order of the senate, he had been commanded to withdraw from the territory of the Ptolemies, which he had invaded, he came to Judaea with a savage spirit, as was shown above; he captured Jerusalem by force of arms, punished the people, plundered the temple, and committed many wicked acts there.

That Antiochus prefigures Antichrist himself is made perfectly clear first of all by the tradition of the saints. For just as the Savior sent Solomon and the other saints beforehand as types of his coming, so Antichrist is rightly believed to have had as his type the most wicked king Antiochus, who persecuted the saints and violated the temple.

When he had been appointed against the Jews, he sent the hateful commander Apollonius with an army of twenty-two thousand, ordering him to kill all persons of full age and to sell the women, young men, and virgins, etc. The previous book also recalls this passage, where it relates together the killing of the Jews during the Sabbath rest, the wickedness of Apollonius, and his death in Judaea.

That Antiochus ordered Apollonius to kill all males of full age and to sell the women and young people signifies that Antiochus, their enemy, especially plots the death of those whom he sees to be perfect in Christian religion. But those who are soft and unstable—of whom it is written, “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclesiasticus 27)—he separates from the soil of the Church by scattering them, entangled in various errors, through diverse vices, and casts them far away into the depths of wickedness.

Judas Maccabaeus, who had been the tenth, withdrew into the wilderness, etc. I do not find how he can say that Judas Maccabaeus was the tenth, unless perhaps this history, by counting the high priests who existed among the Jewish people during the period of the Greek kingdom, has reckoned the years. The first high priest was Onias, son of Jaddi; the second, Simeon, son of Onias; the third, Eleazar, Simeon’s brother; the fourth, Manasses, Eleazar’s uncle; the fifth, Onias, son of Simeon the Just; the sixth, Simon, son of Onias; the seventh, Onias, son of Simon; the eighth, another Onias, who was called Jason, brother of the earlier Onias; the ninth, Menelaus, Jason’s brother; the tenth, Judas. When Alcimus attempted to seize the Jewish high priesthood and was destroyed by divine judgment, Judas received the dignity of the chief priesthood by the marvelous agreement of all.

Spiritually, however, Judas is rightly called the tenth, because he is found to have kept the precepts of the Decalogue in perfect faith and devotion, and, out of zeal for the Law, to have been the first after his father to defend it by arms against the hands of its enemies. He is truly said to have lived with his companions among wild beasts in the mountains and to have eaten grass, because, following the examples of the saints—for they are the mountains of God—he despised the bestial behavior of his persecutors, chose a life pleasing to God, and considered it best to feed always on the ever-green pasture of the virtues, so that, nourished by unfailing food for the soul, he would not feel perpetual hunger.

The reading of Judas’s deeds benefits us only if we wish to imitate his virtues of steadfastness and sobriety, and if we do not place the pleasures of the world and the pomp of this age above the justice and truth of God, always remembering that saying of the Lord:

“For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16).

And again:

“He who loves his life will lose it, and he who hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life” (John 12).

## CHAPTER VI

The king sent orders that the Jews should be compelled to abandon the law of God and to defile the temple. The Jews are compelled to sacrifice to idols. Concerning the suffering of two women with their children, and of Eleazar.

But not long afterward the king sent a certain old man from Antioch, who was to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their ancestors and from the laws of God, etc. The same events are related in the preceding book: Antiochus, through his envoys, defiled the temple by building in it the abomination of desolation over the altar of God. We have set forth the allegory of that passage there.

No one, however, simply confessed that he was a Jew. They were led by bitter necessity, on the king’s birthday, to sacrifice, etc. The pagans called Liber Pater the lord of wine, whose rites Antiochus ordered to be celebrated especially on his birthday, because he believed that Liber favored him on the day of his birth.

They wish Liber to be named from *libera mens*, “a free mind,” because men, as though males, are freed through his benefit when their seed is discharged in intercourse. For this reason Liber is depicted with a womanly and delicate body. They say that women and wine were attributed to him for the arousal of lust. Hence his forehead is encircled with a vine shoot; but he has a vine crown and a horn—the corrupt reading is *facto* [perhaps *capite*, “with the head”]—because when wine is drunk in Greek fashion [*parce*, perhaps “sparingly”] and moderately, it produces joy, but when drunk beyond measure, it provokes quarrels and as it were gives horns.

He is also called Lyaeus, from the drinking of *Lyaeus*, because the limbs are loosened by much wine. In Greek he is called Dionysius, from Mount Nysa, where he is said to have been nurtured. There is also a city called Nysa in which this same Liber is worshiped; hence he is called Nysaeus.

Orpheus first introduced the rites of Liber Pater among the Greeks and first celebrated them on Mount Boeotica and at Thebes, where Liber was born. Because he frequently resounded with the music of the lyre, he was called Cithaeron. These rites are now called Orphic rites, in which he himself was torn apart and afterward also captured, at approximately the same time as Faunus. But who preceded the other in age may be doubtful, since Latinus and Priam reigned during those same years. Their fathers likewise were Picus and Laempdon, under whose reign Orpheus came with the Argonauts to the shore of Athens.

Thus Eleazar, one of the chief scribes, an advanced old man, etc. This Eleazar, whom the impiety of the most savage king Antiochus compelled in his old age to eat pork, signifies the Christian people, whom the cruelty of Antichrist will strive, before the end of the world, to convert to idolatry and the uncleanness of life.

His name, Eleazar, is interpreted as “My God is my helper,” and this name most fittingly suits the people of the faithful, who know how to say to the Lord with the Psalmist:

“You are my helper; do not abandon me” (Psalm 32);

and again:

“My deliverer, my God; I will hope in him” (Psalm 17).

But just as the savagery of the most wicked king could not compel Eleazar to eat pork, so the cruelty of Antichrist will in no way be able to contaminate the assembly of the elect with any uncleanness.

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning the suffering of the seven brothers and their mother.

It happened that seven brothers with their mother were seized and compelled by the king to eat pork contrary to the Law; they were tortured with scourges and leather whips, etc. What is signified by this mother of seven sons except the fruitfulness of Mother Church, who through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit gives birth to adoptive sons for God the Father?

Although the cruelty of the Antiochus who is a type—namely, Antichrist—may tear them, together with their mother, with various tortures, both through his ministers and by himself [Note: The reading should be, “Although he tears them through his ministers and by himself,” etc.], it nevertheless cannot drag them into blasphemy.

What reward awaits this woman and her sons for the labor they endured in the present life, Isaiah shows when he says:

“Praise, O barren woman who does not bear; sing praise and cry aloud [*hinni*], O you who did not give birth, because the children of the forsaken woman are many [source reading: *nulli*; variant: *multi*, ‘many’], more than those of her who has a husband, says the Lord. Enlarge the place of your tent and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. You will break forth to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations. Do not fear, for you will not be put to shame, and you will not blush. For you will not be ashamed, because you will forget the shame of your youth and will remember the disgrace of your widowhood no more. For he who made you will rule over you; the Lord of hosts is his name, and your redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, will be called the God of all the earth. For the Lord has called you as a woman abandoned and grieving in spirit, and as a wife rejected from her youth, says your God. For a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while, but with everlasting mercy I have had pity on you, says the Lord, your redeemer.

“Poor little one, shaken by the storm, without any consolation: behold, I will lay your stones in order and establish you on sapphires. I will make your battlements of jasper, your gates of carved stones, and all your boundaries of precious stones. All your children will be taught by the Lord, and great will be the peace of your children. You will be founded in righteousness. Withdraw far from calumny” (Isaiah 54).

That the mother too was consumed after her sons demonstrates that, after the triumphs of each of the Church’s sons, by which they conquered their enemies, they will enter eternal rest as liberated souls. Finally, at the end of the world, that mother of all the faithful will herself be brought to completion, and, taking the trophy of glory from all her enemies, will possess an everlasting kingdom.

We have judged it appropriate to insert here how the most blessed martyr and most delightful teacher Cyprian, writing to Fortunatus about these same seven brothers, discoursed in the eloquent style of rhetoricians. Among other things he says:

“What else do the seven brothers in the Maccabees signify—similar both in their birth and in the lot of their virtues—except the number seven fulfilled in the sacrament of perfect completion? For the seven brothers united in martyrdom correspond to the seven days of the divine ordering, which first contained seven thousand years; to the seven spirits and the seven angels who stand and move before the face of the Lord; to the sevenfold lamp in the tabernacle of martyrdom; to the seven golden lampstands in the Apocalypse (Revelation 1); and to the seven columns upon which Wisdom built her house in Solomon (Proverbs 9).

“So also here, the number of the seven brothers, by its quantity, embraces the number of the seven Churches, according to what we read in the First Book of Kingdoms (chapter 2), that the barren woman bore seven. And in Isaiah seven women take hold of one man, asking that his name be called over them (Isaiah 4). The apostle Paul, who remembers this legitimate and established number, writes to seven Churches. And in the Apocalypse (Revelation 1) the Lord directs his divine commands and heavenly precepts to seven Churches and to their angels. Thus this number is found here in the brothers, so that legitimate completion may be fulfilled.

“The mother is plainly joined to the seven children as their origin and root: she herself afterward gave birth to the seven Churches, being the first and one Church founded upon the rock by the voice of the Lord. Nor is it without significance that in the account of the sufferings the mother alone is with her children. For the martyrs, who testify in their suffering that they are sons of God, are now reckoned as having no father except God the Father, just as the Lord teaches in the Gospel, saying: ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven’ (Matthew 23).

“What proclamations of confession they uttered, how splendid and great were the proofs of faith they provided! The hostile king Antiochus—or rather, Antichrist represented in Antiochus—sought to defile the glorious mouths of the martyrs, joined [variant: *invicta*, “unconquered”] by the spirit of confession, with the contamination of swine’s flesh. After he had beaten them severely with scourges and had been unable to accomplish anything, he ordered frying pans to be heated. When they had been heated and kindled, he ordered the one who had spoken first, and who had provoked the king’s anger most strongly by the steadfastness of his courage and faith, to be brought forward and fried. First, however, his tongue, which had confessed God, was drawn out and removed [variant: *exsecta*, “cut off”]. This happened to the martyr as a greater glory; for the tongue that had confessed the name of God ought itself to go to God first.

“Then, for the second, he devised harsher punishments. Before torturing the other members, he stripped off the skin of his head together with his hair, plainly out of deliberate hatred. For since Christ is the head of the man, and God is the head of Christ, he who tore the head on the martyr was persecuting God and Christ in the head.

“But he, confident in his martyrdom and promising himself the reward of resurrection from God’s recompense, cried out and said: ‘You, indeed, powerless man, destroy us from this present life; but the King of the world will raise us who have died for his laws to the resurrection of eternal life.’

“When the third was asked for his tongue, he promptly thrust it out, for he had already learned from his brother to despise the punishment of having his tongue cut out. He also steadily extended his hands to be amputated, greatly blessed by this kind of punishment, since it was granted to him, with his hands extended for suffering, to imitate the Passion of the Lord.

“The fourth likewise despised the tortures with equal courage and, answering the king with a heavenly voice to blunt his attack, cried out and said: ‘It is better to await the hope from God of being restored by him to life again, when we have been put to death by men; for you will have no resurrection to life.’

“The fifth, in addition to trampling by the strength of his faith upon the king’s execution and his harsh and varied tortures, was also inspired by the spirit of divinity with foreknowledge and knowledge of future things. He prophesied to the king the indignation of God and the vengeance that would swiftly follow:

“‘Although you have power among men and are mortal, you do what you wish. But do not suppose that our race has been abandoned by God. Wait and see his great power, how he will torture you and your offspring.’

“What relief for the martyr, how great and immense a consolation amid his torments, not to think of his own sufferings but to proclaim the punishments of his torturer!

“In the sixth, not only courage but also humility must be praised. He claimed nothing for himself and did not parade the honor of his confession with proud words; rather, he attributed to his sins the fact that he suffered persecution from the king, while assigning to God the vengeance that would afterward be exacted. He taught martyrs to be modest, to trust in vengeance, and to boast of nothing in their suffering:

“‘Do not wander aimlessly in error. We suffer these things because of ourselves, since we have sinned against our God; but you, do not think that you will remain unpunished, since you have undertaken to fight against God.’

“The mother too was admirable. Neither broken by the weakness of her sex nor shaken by the loss of so many children, she willingly watched her sons die. She counted not the punishments of her children but their glories, offering to God so great a martyrdom through the strength of her eyes as her sons had offered through the torments and suffering of their limbs.”

When six had been killed and punished, one of the brothers remained. The king promised him riches, power, and many other things, so that his cruelty and savagery might be encouraged by the consolation of having subdued at least one. He asked that the mother join him in entreating the son to yield. She did entreat her son—but as befitted the mother of martyrs, as befitted a woman mindful of the Law and of God, as befitted one who loved her sons not tenderly but bravely.

She entreated him to confess the Lord; she entreated him so that her son would not be separated from his brothers in the fellowship of praise and glory. She then counted herself the mother of seven sons if it should be granted her to have borne seven sons for God, not for the world. Thus arming and strengthening him, and at that moment giving birth to her son through a more blessed labor, she said:

“My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, nursed you for three years, fed you, and brought you to this age. I beg you, my son, look upon heaven and earth, and, seeing all that is in them, understand that God made them and the human race from nothing. Therefore, my son, do not fear this executioner; but, having shown yourself worthy of your brothers, accept death, so that in that mercy I may receive you with your brothers.”

Great was the mother’s praise in exhorting him to courage, but greater still in the fear of God and the truth of faith. She promised neither herself nor her son anything from the honor of the six martyrs, nor did she believe that the prayer of the brothers would benefit the salvation of one who denied the faith. Rather, she persuaded him to become a participant in their suffering, so that on the day of judgment he might be found with his brothers.

After this the mother also died together with her children. Nothing else was fitting, since she had borne and made martyrs: she should be joined to them in the fellowship of glory and follow those whom she had sent ahead to God.

## CHAPTER VIII

Concerning Judas Maccabaeus. The impious Nicanor is sent into Judaea; Judas exhorts his men to steadfastness, etc.

Judas Maccabaeus and those who were with him entered the fortresses secretly, etc. The historian of the present book, pursuing brevity and omitting what the earlier book relates about Mattathias, the father of Maccabaeus and of his brothers, turned to narrating the deeds and battles of Judas, recounting some things about them but omitting very many in his customary manner.

But since we have already explained most of his allegory above, we do not think it necessary to repeat what has once been said. If anyone asks what is signified by the six thousand men who joined Judas at the beginning, let him recognize that, through the perfection of the number six and of the number thousand, the perfect sincerity of the soldiers of Christ in faith and devotion is signified.

Hence it is written in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the Jews of the primitive Church:

“The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that any of the things he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all” (Acts 4).

When Philip saw the man gradually advancing toward improvement, etc. In the earlier book it is written that Antiochus, when he was setting out for Persia, left Lysias within the kingdom—a nobleman of royal descent—in charge of royal affairs and to raise Antiochus his son. Lysias himself chose Ptolemy son of Dorymenus, Nicanor, and Gorgias, powerful men among the king’s friends, and sent them with forty thousand men to destroy the Jews according to the king’s command.

Now, however, it is reported that Philip wrote to Ptolemy the commander to bring assistance for the king’s affairs, and that Ptolemy sent Nicanor for this purpose, giving him twenty thousand armed men and joining Gorgias, a military man, to him.

For the aforementioned king Antiochus, returning from Persia toward Babylon, had placed this Philip over his entire kingdom and had given him a diadem, a robe, and a ring, so that he might educate and raise his son Antiochus and reign in his place. When the aforesaid Lysias returned to Antioch with the younger Antiochus and found Philip ruling the city, he attacked him.

Hence the question arises: how can Philip be said to have arranged Ptolemy’s dispatch of Nicanor and Gorgias into Judaea, when the earlier history relates that, while the elder Antiochus remained in Persia, the same Nicanor and Gorgias as commanders, together with Lysias as their organizer, were defeated and put to flight by the Jews, and that Antiochus learned of this on his return and consequently fell ill from grief because what he had planned concerning the Jews had not been accomplished?
