This, unless I am mistaken, can be resolved in no other way than by supposing that Philip, after the government had been entrusted to him, wrote back to the commanders of Syria that the same measure should be undertaken which Lysias had previously been attempting to undertake—but which he had not completed, nor been able, through his own mission, to accomplish against the Jews as he had planned, as the following history demonstrates.

Nicanor set two thousand talents as tribute for the king to pay to the Romans, etc. This was briefly mentioned in the preceding book: namely, that merchants assembled with gold and silver in order to purchase the children of Israel as slaves. Here, however, it is narrated more clearly that the merchants themselves were invited by Nicanor to purchase Jewish slaves, since he had promised the king that he would supply the tribute owed to the Romans from the sale of Jewish captives.

When Judas learned of this, he informed the Jews who were with him of Nicanor’s arrival, etc. The earlier book does not explicitly speak of this arrival of Nicanor in Judaea under Antiochus. Nevertheless, in relating that Lysias selected him together with Ptolemy and Gorgias, powerful men, and with a great crowd of companions, to invade and destroy Judaea, it also asserts that under Demetrius he was sent there and wished to seize and invade Judaea by treachery, but was unable to prevail.

That Nicanor himself represents the type of hypocrites, who do everything deceitfully, has already been stated above. But Judas fights against Nicanor and his allies with seven thousand men and conquers them, because through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit the people of the Church, with its rulers, conquers all its enemies. No Jew, pagan, heretic, schismatic, hypocrite, or wicked person will ever gain victory over it; rather, together with its conquering king, it will possess the trophy of glory forever.

When they were celebrating the victory festival at Jerusalem, they burned the man who had set fire to the sacred gates—namely Callisthenes—after he had taken refuge in a certain dwelling, etc. In another edition I read, “days of victory,” instead of “victory celebrations.” Thus, after overcoming the enemies, Judas celebrates a festival, because when anyone among the saints triumphs over the ancient enemy through the grace of Christ, he should, filled with spiritual joy, offer fitting praises and return abundant thanks to his author. It is not fitting for one to be ungrateful who remembers that he has been helped by a divine work.

## CHAPTER IX

Antiochus was defeated at Persepolis. The Lord struck Antiochus with a plague; he repented amid his sufferings and died.

At that time Antiochus was returning dishonorably from Persia, etc. What was briefly noted in the earlier book concerning the end of Antiochus is explained more fully in this one.

Mystically, it shows that the persecutors of Christians will in the future receive from the Lord a just recompense of punishments for their evil deeds and works of injustice, and that he who here did not fear to trouble the hearts of the faithful will, in the final vengeance, be tormented by inward pains and belated repentance.

Concerning him it is written in the Book of Wisdom:

“Then the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labors. Seeing them, they will be troubled with terrible fear and will be astonished at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation. Groaning in anguish of spirit, they will say within themselves as they repent:

“‘These are the ones whom we once held in derision and made an object of reproach. We fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. Behold, how they have been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth; the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun of understanding did not rise upon us. We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we have traveled difficult paths, but we did not know the way of the Lord. What did our pride profit us, or what did the boasting of our riches bring us? All those things passed away like a shadow,’ etc. (Wisdom 5).

## CHAPTER X

Judas Maccabaeus recovered the temple and Jerusalem. The festival was celebrated. The son of Antiochus obtained his father’s kingdom. Ptolemy ended his life with poison. Gorgias and others were defeated.

On the day when the temple had been defiled by foreigners, etc. This festival, which is read as having been celebrated on the twenty-fifth day of the month Casleu, called December by the Latins, is likewise mentioned in the earlier book.

But when it relates that they had previously kept the Feast of Tabernacles in the mountains and caves, and for that reason carried thyrsi, green branches, and palms before the one who had prospered the cleansing of his own place, it shows that in the present life, where there is a place of tribulation and sorrow, we ought to recognize ourselves as pilgrims. There we should strive to offer God, for the attainment of eternal life and as the heavenly King’s reward, the flowers of virtues and the ever-green branches of good works.

For a *thyrsus* is, generally speaking, a central shrub among grasses or vegetables, so called because it rises upward from the earth. Likewise, from our earthly substance a useful shoot ought to rise, so that we may always render acceptable fruit to the cultivator of our heart, who cultivates us through the gift of his Spirit.

And the death of Antiochus, who was called the Noble, took place as follows, etc. The history of the earlier book relates that Antiochus the Noble, when setting out for Persia, appointed Lysias over the royal affairs from the Euphrates River to the river of Egypt, and instructed him to raise Antiochus his son until he returned.

Now, however, it is related that Antiochus himself, the son of Antiochus the Noble—that is, Eupator—appointed the same Lysias over the royal affairs. But since he says that he has abbreviated many events that occurred in the wars, he shows that he passed over in the historical sequence the battles that the younger Antiochus himself fought against the Jews, when he came there with elephants and a great multitude gathered both from his own people and from other nations; and when Eleazar son of Saura killed the largest of the elephants, believing that the king was upon it.

When Gorgias was commander of the region, he took foreign troops and frequently fought against the Jews, etc. As we have already shown above, the earlier book relates that Lysias, together with Ptolemy and Nicanor, acted to attack Judaea. The nature of that attack is reported in both the earlier and present books, but it is made clear that victory remained with the Jews.

That Gorgias himself represents a type of the devil, because he incited various nations to fight against the Jews, has already been stated above. He incites unbelievers against the Church of Christ and stirs up war against his faithful. But since it is written there that Gorgias chose seven thousand men for battle, while here, according to the fivefold number multiplied within itself, twenty-seven thousand are reported to have been slaughtered, this signifies that all who serve the devil through carnal desires with the seven senses of the body are punished with a fitting death.

Some, however, had fled into two very strongly fortified towers, etc. When the spiritual Maccabaeus fights, the enemies are compelled to flee into two towers. Those who sought to attack Christ’s army, although entirely unable to resist the truth of the Gospel, nevertheless, in their ignorance and without salutary belief, and without fearing the future judgment of the Lord, choose rather to flee into the towers of pride and idolatry than, pierced by the pains of repentance, to abandon their errors.

Against them Judas sends soldiers with Simon and Joseph. But some of them, deceived by love of money, neglected to carry through the battle that had been undertaken. For it often happens that those to whom priestly dignity and the warfare of spiritual struggle have been entrusted, deceived by earthly greed, prefer to satisfy their avarice rather than, despising earthly advantages, exalt the will of Christ by fighting lawfully.

Such men, however, will not escape their deserved punishments. Rather, when the true teachers, strengthened by the Spirit of God, have destroyed the enemies by fighting and overcoming them, these men themselves will justly be punished by them with the vengeance of anathema.

But Timotheus, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, having summoned an army of foreign troops, etc. This Timotheus represents the type of heretics, as we demonstrated in the earlier book. Whether by themselves or with the assistance and support of others, they always strive to destroy the faith of Christ and the truth of the Gospel. But against their wickedness the holy teachers ask help from the Lord, and, trusting with certain hope in heavenly assistance, they fight bravely against their enemies.

The five horsemen who appeared on horses with beautiful golden bridles and provided leadership for the Jews signify the five books of the Law. When these are brought to spiritual understanding and drawn back from the typical veil of the letter to the spiritual understanding of the Gospel, they provide timely consolation to those who carry them out. Guarding the true confessors of Christ on the right and left by the two commandments of charity, they hurl fiery arrows of judgment against their adversaries, and the adversaries, confused by blindness of mind and filled with disturbance of understanding, fall.

Of these, twenty thousand five hundred are struck down, signifying that all who think contrary to catholic doctrine—which is contained in the two Testaments—and to the grace of the Holy Spirit are overcome and cast down when truth prevails. Likewise, six hundred horsemen are crushed, signifying that the pride of their minds, by which they often hoped to prevail over Catholics, is completely destroyed by a heavenly command.

But Timotheus fled to Gazara, a fortified stronghold over which Chaereas presided. Maccabaeus and those who were with him, rejoicing, besieged the stronghold for four days, etc. What else is signified by Timotheus, defeated by Judas and fleeing with his followers into the fortified stronghold of Gazara, from which he hurled curses at the people, trusting in the strength of the place, except that heretics, divided from the unity of the true faith and overcome, entrust themselves to the hiding places of their errors and, relying on the protection of their cunning, hurl words of cursing against Catholics?

Timotheus is interpreted as “beneficent,” or rather “sorcerous,” and Gazara as “division” or “battle.” But Judas, besieging the stronghold with his companions for four days, finally broke into the fortification through twenty young men who had been inflamed in spirit because of the blasphemy. They set fire to the towers and gates and burned the blasphemers alive.

This signifies that the holy teachers, shutting in the enemies on every side with the four books of the Gospel, destroy their devices through those who observe the commandments of the Law by means of the two commandments of charity, and burn the enemies themselves alive with the fire of grief and repentance. Thus, with the aid of the two Testaments, they devastate the stronghold of every error over two days, and with the sword of God’s word they kill the true Timotheus—that is, the devil, the head of every error and author of all evil—who wishes to lurk in his own wickedness.

When these things had been done, they blessed the Lord with hymns and confessions, who had done great things in Israel and had given them victory [Col. 1243D], etc. In the earlier book of this history it is written that Lysias, having been entrusted by Antiochus—who was surnamed Epiphanes, or “Noble”—with the administration of the kingdom, fought against the Jews. In that battle five thousand men of Lysias’s army were killed. When Lysias saw the flight of his men and the boldness of the Jews, he went to Antioch to gather the army’s forces again and return once more to Judaea. Now, however, since it is reported that he came again to Judaea under Antiochus Eupator and, after an unsuccessfully conducted battle, disgracefully escaped in flight, it is evident that the same Lysias fought against the Jews under both kings named Antiochus—that is, father and son—and that in both battles he was defeated by the Jews. But [Col. 1244A] at last, compelled by his own humiliation and terrified by Philip’s invasion of the kingdom, as has been shown elsewhere, he persuaded the king to make peace with the Hebrews, although he did not keep it.

## CHAPTER XI

Lysias Attempts to Conquer the Jews and Sell the Priesthood. A Bishop in a White Garment Is Sent by God to the Jews for Their Aid, etc.

And approaching Beth-zur, which was in a narrow place five stadia from Jerusalem, he was attacking that stronghold. Beth-zur was a city in the tribe of Judah or Benjamin, and even today Beth-zur is visible to us as we travel from Aelia to Hebron, at the twentieth milestone. Near it there is a spring that bubbles up at the foot of the mountain and is swallowed by the same earth from which it rises. The Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1244B] also report that the eunuch of Queen Candace was baptized there by Philip (Acts 8).

But when Maccabaeus and those who were with him learned that the strongholds were being attacked, they pleaded with the Lord amid weeping and tears, etc. It has already been said that Lysias, the fiercest enemy of the Jews, who holds the leadership of the pagans, signifies those who harass the Church of God with the gravest persecutions. When he persecutes the teachers and confessors of Christ with the most serious scandals, relying on the arrogance of his pride and exalting himself in the empty favor of those who follow him, he plots in his heart to profane the sanctuary and trample upon God’s law. But in his actions he does not prosper according to the fraud he has devised; rather, he is driven away and overthrown by the soldiers of Christ, who seek heavenly aid through the humblest prayers [Col. 1244C].

A mounted commander in a white garment and with golden weapons is sent to them for their aid, because the most pure incarnation of God and humanity is granted to them to crush the insolence of all enemies. His golden weapons—that is, his words and examples—are most bright and splendid; and there is no power in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth that can resist him.

But just as it was prefigured in Daniel’s prophetic vision (Dan. 2), a precious stone cut from the mountain [perhaps “without hands”] crushed the gold, silver, bronze, and iron. It became a great mountain that filled the whole earth; its kingdom would never be destroyed, nor would its kingdom be handed over to another people. Christ will crush and consume all kingdoms [Col. 1244D] and will stand forever. The saints of the Most High God, moreover, will receive the kingdom and possess it forever, even forever and ever.

In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the twenty-fourth day of the month Dioscorus. The king’s letter contained the following: “King Antiochus to Lysias, his brother, greetings. Since our father has been translated among the gods, and since we wish those who are in our kingdom to live without disturbance and to attend diligently to their affairs, we have heard that the Jews did not agree with my father,” etc. That month which among the Greeks is called Dioscorus is the same as that which among the Latins is called June. The constellation of the Twins is therefore assigned to this month. For the Twins—that is, Castor and Pollux—are called Dioscuri in Greek. A city called Collorum [Col. 1245A] is a witness to this matter—[the text reads] “Collorum”—which, after being shattered by Amphion and Circius, the charioteers of the Twins, was named Dioscuri after them. For Dioscuri are interpreted by many as “charioteers”; but the Twins, as we have said, are Castor and Pollux.

That Lysias, compelled by fear of the Jews, persuaded Antiochus to enter into a pact with the Jews demonstrates that the enemies of the Church are often defeated by divine power and, although not willingly, yield to necessity when they cannot bring to completion what they desire.

In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, on the seventh day of the month Pandicus, the Romans also sent a letter, etc. The month Pandicus among the Athenians is the same as the month called April among us and Nisan among the Hebrews. Among the Hebrews, according to the commandment of the law, this is the first month [Col. 1245B] of the year. They also celebrate Passover in it.

## CHAPTER XII

The Joppeans Treacherously Kill Two Hundred Jews, and Judas Avenges Them. Timothy Is Defeated and Overcome by Judas after the Defeat of the Arabians. Concerning Sacrifices for the Dead, etc.

The Joppeans committed the following outrage. They invited the Jews with whom they lived to board boats that they had prepared, together with their wives and children, as though there were no enmity between them. Thus, according to the common decree of the city, and with the Jews consenting and suspecting nothing, supposedly for the sake of peace, when they had gone out to sea they drowned no fewer than two hundred of them, etc.

These Joppeans of whom Scripture speaks were inhabitants of a town in Palestine called [Col. 1245C] Joppe, situated on the coast in the tribe of Dan. And, to touch briefly upon the tales of the pagans, even today there are shown there lofty rocks situated on the seashore, on which Andromeda is said once to have been bound and liberated by Perseus.

According to the mystical sense, these same Joppeans, who lived beside the sea and caused scandal to the Jews, signify heretics living near the turbulent waves of the present age. They are always plotting against the Jews—that is, against the true confessors of Christ—and strive to drag as many as they can from their number into the pit of their error.

The Joppeans therefore construct boats in which they drown the Jews, drawn away from the shore, in the deep, when heretics formulate wicked doctrines and adorn them with attractive speech. This is aptly signified by the name [Col. 1245D] “Joppe,” for it is interpreted as “beauty.” In this way they more easily deceive simple people by the fluency of their speech; and when they have drawn them away from the stability of the true faith and gathered them to themselves, they recklessly hurl them into the abyss of perdition.

But the typological Judas does not allow this to continue for long. Rather, when he finds the murderers hiding in the darkness of their error, he torments them with the vengeance of just retribution. By exposing the frauds owed to eternal fire, he rightly strikes both the authors of the transgression and their followers with the sword of anathema, and does not permit the venom of their wickedness to remain hidden any longer.

But when he learned that those who were in Jamnia [Col. 1246A] likewise intended to act against the Jews living among them, he burned Jamnia and the harbor with the ships, etc. Jamnia, which is interpreted as “sea,” may signify the assembly of schismatics, who are always in a storm. Schism, therefore, as some maintain, is called a “cutting apart” of morals. For in all other respects it believes with the same worship and the same rite, but it takes pleasure in the division of the congregation alone. Schism arises when they say, “We all sanctify the unclean,” and similar things.

Judas recognizes that the Jamnites are acting in the same way as the Joppeans, plotting treachery against the Jews living among them, when the holy teachers, discovering that the fraud of the schismatics resembles the deception of the heretics, fear that the faithful may be deceived by them. They wage war against them; and when they find them in the darkness of superstition, they burn them, together with their engines, by the fire of excommunication, so that their conflagration is seen in Jerusalem [Col. 1246B]—that is, so that the condemnation of their error is made manifest to all worshipers of the true religion.

Therefore Paul, writing to Timothy and exposing the errors of the foolish, says (2 Tim. 3):

“But know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power. Avoid such people. For among them are those who enter houses and take captive little women weighed down with sins and led by various desires, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth. Just as Jannes and Jambres [Col. 1246C] resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: people corrupted in mind and rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not advance further, for their folly will become evident to all, just as theirs also did.”

Likewise the foremost of the apostles, warning the faithful to guard against the deceit of wicked men, says to them (2 Pet. 3):

“Therefore, brothers, since you know these things beforehand, guard yourselves, lest you be led astray by the error of the foolish and fall from your own steadfastness. Rather, grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord. To him be glory both now and on the day of eternity. Amen.”

When they had already gone nine stadia and were traveling toward Timothy, etc., the Arabians—whose name is interpreted as “humble” or “western”—can signify those who love worldly and secular wisdom [Col. 1246D]. It is rightly called humble and western because it does not know how to imitate true wisdom, which comes from heavenly things.

Thus, intent upon Judas and his companions, they engage them with five thousand men and five hundred horsemen. For those entangled in the senses and pursuits of the flesh regard everything that the holy teachers present to them from the spiritual sense as contrary and profane. Hence they strive to rebel against them. But, defeated as the truth hardens against them and overcome by the steadfastness of the holy preachers, they ask that their right hands be given to them, so that, abandoning their errors, they may seek the strength of the catholic faith and desire to join themselves to the confessors of Christ.

The spiritual Judas, judging that they could in many ways become useful to the Jews, promises them peace, gives them his right hand, and allows them to depart unharmed [Col. 1247A]. For such people, formerly imbued with worldly philosophy, often become more suitable and capable of destroying the folly and error of the pagans when they are converted to the faith of Christ. Once the word of faith has been fully preached to them, equipped with both kinds of armor, they fight more vigorously against unbelief.

For this reason Solomon asked Hiram, king of Tyre, for assistance in building the temple, to cut timber from Lebanon, because Hiram’s servants were more skilled in this craft than his own servants. Yet they did not labor at the work by themselves alone; rather, joined with Solomon’s servants, they completed it solemnly and appropriately. The reason is clear: the apostles knew more surely the word of God [Note: [Col. 1247D] Something is missing.] of the Gospel, which they had learned to hear from the Lord; but the Gentiles, converted from error and transformed by those same apostles [Col. 1247B] to the truth of the Gospel, knew the errors of the nations better. And the more certainly they knew them, the more skillfully they learned to conquer and abolish them.

He also attacked a certain fortified city, surrounded by bridges and walls, inhabited by crowds of mixed peoples, whose name was Casphin. Those who were inside, trusting in the strength of their walls and in their stores of provisions, acted carelessly, assailing Judas with curses, blaspheming, and speaking things that were not lawful.

I think that this city, under whose fortification great crowds of different peoples gathered and lived, signifies nothing more aptly than the power of this world. Under its domination different nations approached, so that under its protection [Col. 1247C] they might preserve the body and indulge the desires of their flesh. Such an assembly, trusting in the strength of its walls, assailed Judas with curses and spoke blasphemous things, when various people, favoring the flattery of rulers and rejoicing in their benefactions, acted against the holy preachers and, worshiping idols, hurled words of blasphemy against Divinity itself.

Judas therefore, having invoked the ruler of the world, captured the city through his assistance. For the holy teachers fought against their adversaries partly by prayers and partly by doctrines, until, through the Lord’s will, they captured the rulers themselves by the word of God. Thus they carried out indescribable slaughter among human beings—not so that they might perish utterly in eternal death, but so that, dying to the world [Col. 1247D], they might live more happily for Christ.

Peter too was commanded to carry out such a slaughter in the Acts of the Apostles (chap. 10), when in an ecstasy he saw that mystical vessel, lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners, containing all four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth, and birds of the air. A voice said to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

The animals signified all the nations, unclean through their errors but destined to be cleansed in the sacred baptism of the Holy Trinity. Having abandoned the image of a human being, they had taken on the forms of beasts and serpents through imitation. That heavenly voice commands Peter to kill and eat them, because it commanded him to kill in the nations what they had been and to make them what he himself was.

One who eats food placed outside draws it into his body [Col. 1248A]. He therefore commanded that the nations, placed outside the doors through unbelief, should have their former life killed and be joined to the fellowship of the Church, which Peter signifies. In accordance with this, the apostle Paul says of himself: “For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God, for Christ” (Gal. 2); and again: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (ibid.).

Nor is it without a mystery that the nearby pool appeared to flow with the blood of the slaughtered people. For the shedding of blood signifies the loss of a bloody life, as though blood were seen to flow after becoming water, when in the sacrament of baptism—where the faithful die to sin—the bloody works and filth of the fleshly [Col. 1248B] life are washed away. Then the old person is stripped off with his deeds and the new person is put on, who was created according to the Lord in the justice and holiness of truth (Eph. 4).

And they came to Charax, to the Jews who are called Tubianaeans. They did not capture Timothy in those regions, however, and, having accomplished nothing, he returned, leaving a very strong garrison in a certain place, etc. I once heard a Hebrew explaining that those Jews who came to Judas’s aid after summoning foreigners were called Tubianaeans, as though they had been hired with foreign trumpets.

Dositheus and Sosipater, who were commanders with Maccabaeus, killed ten thousand men whom Timothy had left in the garrison. These two commanders—Dositheus [Col. 1248C] and Sosipater—signify the holy preachers who, by the disposition of Maccabaeus, that is, of the most powerful warrior—for it is written in the Psalm, “The Lord is strong and mighty in battle” (Ps. 23)—are appointed to wage war against all the errors of the faithless.

They are appropriately indicated by the number two, because, sufficiently instructed in the spiritual knowledge of the two Testaments, they are known to carry out the Lord’s battle properly. Thus they kill the ten thousand men whom Timothy had left in the garrison, when by the authority and severity of the same law they justly slay with the spiritual sword the associates of the heresiarchs, appointed by them to defend their wickedness and thinking contrary to God’s law.

Judas, however, pressed on vigorously, punishing the profane [Col. 1248D], and struck down thirty thousand of them, etc. It is asked how Timothy is here said to have been released alive by the Jewish commanders because of the humility of his prayers, since he had many parents and brothers among the Jews, who would have suffered through his death if he had been killed, while a little earlier he is said to have been in the garrison at Gazara, where he was killed by the soldiers. For if he had been killed there at that time, he could in no way now have been released alive.

This, unless I am mistaken, can be resolved in no other way than by saying either that he is said to have been killed there by anticipation, or that one Timothy is to be understood as having been killed in the garrison at Gazara, while this is another Timothy who is read to have been released by Dositheus and Sosipater [Col. 1249A].

That Judas’s commanders spared Timothy when they considered the benefit of their brothers and the redemption of their own people shows that sometimes one must deal more gently with those who are in error—not, I mean, by consenting to their wickedness, but by providing, with paternal compassion, for their weakness. This is especially appropriate in places where some fruit may be hoped for from the conversion of those in error, so that through ecclesiastical gentleness they may be encouraged to escape the snares of the devil and come together into catholic liberty.

For this reason it was decreed in the African council concerning the Donatist heretics that they should be treated more leniently. It is written there as follows:

“Having examined and considered everything that seemed conducive to the benefit of the Church, with the Spirit of God consenting and admonishing us, we decree that we should deal gently and peacefully with the men mentioned above, although they hold an unsettled dissension [Col. 1249B] concerning the unity of the Lord’s body. Thus, as far as lies in us, it may become thoroughly known throughout all the provinces of Africa to all who are heretics in their communion and fellowship by what miserable error they have been overcome. Perhaps, as the Apostle says, while we correct those who think differently with gentleness, God may grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Tim. 2).

Judas then went out from Carnion, after twenty-five thousand had been killed. After their flight and death, he led the army against Ephron, a fortified city in which a multitude of different peoples lived. Strong young men stood by the walls and fought bravely [Col. 1249C], etc.

We said in the exposition of the earlier book, where Timothy was discussed, that his army signified the crowd of heretics. Likewise, concerning the inhabitants of the city of Ephron, we said that figuratively they represented those who weakened the rite of Judaism in the age of grace—such as the Jews themselves and the heretics who wanted to preserve the ceremonies of the law together with the Gospel.

Because these people, thinking in a fleshly manner, wanted to learn spiritual knowledge, they could not understand that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10), to the Jew namely as well as to the Gentile.

Five thousand are read to have been struck down in the battle at Ephron, just as in the battle that was concluded at Carnion, because “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” and “the wisdom of the flesh is death” (1 Cor. 3). For “the letter [Col. 1249D] kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3). Hence Paul also says: “God made the wisdom of this world foolish” (1 Cor. 1). And again: “The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them because they are examined spiritually” (1 Cor. 2).

For this reason the apostle James, writing to the dispersed, says (chap. 3):

“If you have bitter zeal and there are contentions in your hearts, do not boast and be liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, from the highest Father, but earthly, natural, and demonic.”

The foremost of the apostles [Col. 1250A] calls the followers of this sect springs or waters and clouds driven about by whirlwinds, for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved. They speak vanities, enticing in the desires of the flesh and sensuality those who have barely escaped and who live in error, promising them freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption (2 Pet. 2).

Judas, with his companions, struck down the enemy crowds everywhere and achieved victory, because the holy teachers, defenders of the truth and conquerors of every error, aided by divine power, everywhere win trophies of victory over their enemies.

Hence, with Paul, they can say: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place” (2 Cor. 2).

To be commonly common. (?)

From there they went to the city of the Scythians, which was six hundred stadia from Jerusalem, etc. The people of Scythopolis, who treated the Jews kindly and earned grace and praise from Judas for their benefactions [Col. 1250B], signify those who receive [the text has *rapiunt*, “carry off”; editorially *excipiunt*, “receive”] the holy teachers and confessors of the true faith and, according to their means, assist them with bodily support. Their reward will not perish in vain, especially since the Lord says of such people to the apostles in the Gospel:

“Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward; and whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, amen, I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matt. 10).

Therefore John, writing to Gaius in his epistle, says:

“Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, and especially for strangers, who have borne witness to your love before the Church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God, for they have gone forth for his name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to receive such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 5).

Paul likewise praised this when writing to the Corinthians:

“I urge you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they are the firstfruits of Achaia and have appointed themselves for the service of the saints. You also should submit to such people and to everyone who cooperates and labors. I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking in you. For they refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore recognize such people” (1 Cor. 16).

After Pentecost they went against Gorgias, the governor of Idumaea [Col. 1250D]. He went out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry. When they engaged, a few of the Jews fell.

Gorgias, governor of Idumaea, can aptly represent the devil, who has always delighted in a red and bloodstained way of life, though at times he pretends to display the appearance of virtues, even while he assiduously fights against the virtues through vices. Thus, by cunningly deceiving simple people from the number of the faithful, he kills them. Yet he does not win victory for the day, because, through the leadership of Judas, when his soldiers invoke the Lord as their helper and persist in prayers and hymns, the opposing side, confused by fear, is put to flight, and the honor of triumph is granted to the true worshipers of God.

Therefore Peter, writing to believers in his Epistle, says (chap. 5):

“Therefore humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation, casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you. Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith” [Col. 1251A].

James likewise says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4).

But the fact that Dositheus wanted to capture Gorgias alive, yet could not do so because, after his shoulder had been cut off, his enemy escaped, figuratively demonstrates that the ancient enemy is conquered not by human strength but by divine aid. For whoever, trusting in his own strength with the Pelagians [OCR: Peligranistis], hopes to obtain victory over the devil certainly does not conquer the enemy, nor does he preserve the state of his own will unharmed.

[Col. 1251B] On the following day Judas came with his men to take up the bodies of those who had fallen and place them with their relatives in the ancestral tombs. They found under the tunics of the slain objects dedicated to idols that had been at Jamnia, things from which the law forbids Jews, etc.

Those who were struck down by the enemy because of hidden idolatry are best understood as those who secretly defile themselves in their hearts through desire and greed. They carry under their tunic objects dedicated to idols when, for the sake of earthly desire or the ambition of human praise, they perform works of virtue outwardly but conceal within themselves, beneath a covering of piety, the deceit of wickedness.

Such people are rightly struck down by their enemies, because the venom of deceit, which escaped the sight of human beings, did not deceive the gaze of the internal Judge.

That desire and greed are idolatry is shown by Paul [Col. 1251C], who says (1 Tim. 6): “The root of all evils is desire; by pursuing it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.” And again (Eph. 5): “Know and understand this: no fornicator, or unclean person, or greedy person—which is the service of idols—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience [Vulgate: unbelief].”

Against this vice, wishing to heal human minds, the Savior teaches in the Gospel, saying: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 6). And again he says: “See and beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses” (Luke 12) [Col. 1251D].

The mystical Judas, observing that this fall had come upon his soldiers because of their dissimulation, does not abandon them but provides for them with paternal compassion. He intervenes for their sins through prayers and corrects their error through the word of preaching and exhortation, so that, restored again to the worship of piety, they may thereafter guard themselves more carefully and not fall again into something worse through a similar collapse, according to the Gospel saying: “Behold, you have been made well; do not sin again, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5).

But the most valiant Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves without sin, seeing with their own eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who had fallen. After a collection had been made, he sent [Col. 1252A] twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to offer a sacrifice for the sins of the dead, etc.

That prayer should be offered for the sins of the faithful after their departure from this present life, and that the work of almsgiving should be performed so that those for whose relief the matter is undertaken may be released from sins, is shown both by the present passage and by the Lord in the Gospel. Speaking of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, he identifies that sin as unforgivable when he says: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

When he identified that one sin as unforgivable, he showed that other sins can be forgiven both in the present life and in the future. How one should act for the salvation of the dead is shown by the holy Fathers in their writings.

Therefore it seemed good to insert one of Saint Augustine’s short works into this work, instructing the reader to seek similar passages in the sayings of the other Fathers. For the aforementioned Father reports in the work he wrote to Laurence, On Faith, Hope, and Charity, as follows:

“The time that lies between a person’s death and the final resurrection [Col. 1252B] holds souls in hidden receptacles, each according as it deserves either rest or affliction, according to what it acquired in the flesh while it lived.

Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their survivors when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or almsgiving is performed in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while they lived, earned the benefit of their later assistance. For there is a way of living that is not so good [Col. 1252C] that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death.

There is, however, a person so good that he does not require them, and again there is one so evil that after life has passed he cannot be helped by them. Therefore, all merit by which someone may be relieved or burdened after this life is acquired here.

Let no one think that what he neglected here he can merit from the Lord after he has died. Thus, the things that the Church regularly performs for commendation of the dead are not contrary to that apostolic sentence which says: ‘We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil’ (Rom. 14). For each person acquired this merit for himself while living in the body, so that these things might be of benefit to him.

They do not benefit everyone [Col. 1252D]. And why do they not benefit everyone, except because of the merits of the life each person lived in the body? Therefore, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any kind of almsgiving—are offered for baptized dead persons, for the very good they are thanksgivings; for those who are not very evil they are acts of propitiation; and for the very evil, even if they provide no assistance to the dead, they are, whatever their character, consolations for the living.

For those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that forgiveness may be made complete or so that condemnation may become more tolerable.”

## CHAPTER XIII [Col. 1253A]

Antiochus Comes against Judaea. Judas Kills Four Thousand in Antiochus’s Camp and the Largest of the Elephants, and Takes Ptolemais, etc.

But the king, unrestrained in mind, was coming to show himself more wicked toward the Jews than his father. When Judas learned this, he commanded the people to invoke the Lord day and night, since, as always, so now also, he should help them—especially because they feared being deprived of the law, their homeland, and the holy temple—and not allow the people, who had only recently drawn a little breath, to be subjected again to the blasphemies of the nations, etc.

The history that recounts the war of Antiochus Eupator and his governor Lysias against the Jews was recalled and explained allegorically in the earlier book. But what is subsequently narrated is that four thousand were killed by the Jews in the king’s camp during the night [Col. 1253B], together with the largest of the elephants. This is expressed more clearly in the earlier account, where it is reported that Eleazar son of Saura, a Jew, saw one of the armored beasts rising above the other animals and, thinking that the king was in it, rushed into the legion, ran beneath the elephant’s feet, and killed it. When it fell, it crushed him beneath its own weight, and he died.

Its spiritual significance was explained there, when the boasting of the proud is shown to be crushed by its own effort, as Scripture says: “Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to God” (Prov. 16); and again: “Before destruction the heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (ibid.); and elsewhere: “God resists the proud, but gives grace [Col. 1253C] to the humble” (Jas. 4). In the Gospel also the Lord said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 23).

After this, the history explains how Demetrius, son of Seleucus, came to Judaea, obtained the kingdom, and was incited by Alcimus against Judas and his companions. It is written as follows:

## CHAPTER XIV

Demetrius Is Incited against the Jews and Sends Nicanor, Who Fights with Simon; but Judas Escapes from His Hands. Concerning Razias and His Constancy.

A certain Alcimus [Col. 1253D], who had been high priest but had willingly defiled himself during the time of the mixture, realizing that he had no hope of salvation or access to the altar, came to King Demetrius, etc.

That Alcimus offered the king sprigs (*talos* [*thallos*]), together with a golden crown and a palm branch, shows that he promised him the dignity of kingship and victory over his enemies, together with the worship of the temple, as tokens of his gifts. Such objects are said to be offering vessels, made in the form of towers, with which they made offerings on the principal festivals; their likenesses are still preserved in certain places.

The Assideans are said to have been those Jews who always devoted themselves to divine worship. They were called Assideans from assiduity, as though they were “assiduous”; Judas [Col. 1254A] and his helpers were such in the worship of God and the observance of his law. Others assert that the Assideans were called from purity, as though “pure Jews,” because they guarded themselves from idolatry and the rite of the Gentiles.

When Demetrius heard the report of Alcimus and the others who were enemies of Judas and favored him in the accusation, he immediately sent Nicanor, the governor and commander of the elephants, into Judaea. He gave orders that Nicanor should capture Judas himself, disperse those who were with him, and appoint Alcimus high priest of the great temple.

When Nicanor came into Judaea, he first pretended that he wished to make a peace treaty with the Jews. Later, once his hostility had been revealed, he showed himself to be a most wicked man rather than a faithful friend. But, overthrown by divine power, he paid the penalty for the blasphemy uttered against God and for his obstinacy.

All these matters are contained in the history of the earlier book, although some things omitted there because of the narrator’s haste are inserted in the present account [Col. 1254B]. The allegorical meaning of the same matter was explained there according to the measure of my small intellect, and it does not seem worthwhile to repeat it.

But Razias, one of the elders from Jerusalem, a man who loved his city, was reported to Nicanor, and so forth. Some readers, however, finding it written there that Razias, inflicting death upon himself with his own hand, had chosen to die nobly rather than be subject to sinners and to have his ancestral dignity treated with unworthy insults, might perhaps, being of simpler understanding, believe that when necessity presses one ought rather to inflict death upon oneself by some act of one’s own than to fall alive into the hands of sinners. I therefore judged it useful to insert into this work of ours some passages from the sayings of the venerable Father Augustine, so that the sober reader might understand what ought to be done in such matters. The aforementioned Father, in the first book of his *City of God*, where he discussed at length whether anyone may kill himself, reports the following:

“Many have killed themselves so as not to fall into the hands of their enemies. We are not merely asking whether this was done, but whether it ought to have been done. Sound reason must indeed be preferred to examples; and examples agree with reason only when they are more worthy of imitation in proportion to their excellence in piety. The patriarchs did not do this, nor the prophets, nor the apostles, because the Lord Christ himself, when he warned them that, if they suffered persecution, they should flee from one city to another, could have warned them to lay hands upon themselves so as not to fall into the hands of their persecutors. But if he neither commanded nor advised this—that his own should depart from this life in such a manner, for whom, when they departed, he promised to prepare eternal dwellings—then, whatever examples nations ignorant of God may put forward, it is clear that this is not permitted to those who worship the one true God.

“It remains that we understand the saying, ‘You shall not kill,’ as referring to a human being: therefore neither another nor yourself, for whoever kills himself kills nothing other than a human being. That same divine authority, however, established certain exceptions to the rule that a human being may not be killed. Apart from those whom God commands to be killed—whether by a law given generally or by an explicit command addressed to a person for a particular time—the one who kills is not himself the killer, but performs a ministry for the one who commands, just as a sword is an instrument for the person who uses it. Thus those who, by God’s authority, waged wars, or who, exercising public power in accordance with his laws—that is, by the command of the most just reason—punished criminals with death, in no way acted against the commandment that says, ‘You shall not kill.’

“Abraham was not only not accused of the crime of cruelty; he was even praised under the name of piety because he wished to kill his son not criminally but obediently. And it is rightly asked whether what Jephthah did should be regarded as having been commanded by God: he killed his daughter, who came out to meet her father, after he had vowed that he would sacrifice to God whatever first met him when he returned victorious from battle (Jud. II). Nor is Samson excused in any other way, when he brought down the house upon himself and his enemies, except that the Spirit who worked miracles through him had secretly commanded this.

“Therefore, with the exception of those whom either a just law in general or God himself, the source of justice, specifically commands to be killed, whoever kills a human being—whether himself or anyone else—is bound by the charge of homicide. Those who have perpetrated this deed upon themselves may perhaps be admired for greatness of spirit, but they are not to be praised for sound wisdom. Indeed, if one consults reason more carefully, even greatness of spirit is not rightly named where someone kills himself because he is unable to endure either hardships of any kind or the sins of others. Rather, the mind is shown to be weak when it cannot bear either the harsh servitude of its own body or the foolish opinion of the crowd. The greater spirit is that which can endure a troubled life rather than flee from it, and which can disdain human judgment—especially that of the common people, usually enveloped in the darkness of error—in comparison with the light and purity of conscience.”

## CHAPTER XV

Onias and Jeremiah appear, and the golden sword sent by God is handed over to Judas. The Jews fought with their hands and prayed with their hearts. Nicanor’s head is cut off, and so forth.

“His appearance was as follows: Onias, who had been high priest, a good and kindly man, modest in appearance, restrained in conduct, and dignified in speech,” and so forth.

If anyone asks whether this vision can be referred to some ministry, I think its meaning may be understood from the following: Onias the priest signifies the priestly order; and Jeremiah the prophet—whose name is interpreted as “exalted of the Lord”—expresses the Lord himself, the head of the prophets. Of him Moses says: “The Lord will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers; you shall listen to him as to me” (Deut. XVIII). And Isaiah says: “Cease,” he says, “from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is regarded as exalted” (Isa. II).

Thus the priestly order, through the men who under the Old Testament duly performed the divine service in God’s temple, not only interceded for the sins of the people, but also demonstrated the future incarnation of our mediator, through whose aid the world was to be saved. Concerning him the apostle John says in his Epistle: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for our sins only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John II).

He therefore gave Judas a golden sword, when he granted teachers the divine Scripture, radiant with spiritual meaning, as a defense and protection for the whole Church and his people, so that they might use it as armor against all their enemies and overthrow the multitude of their foes, and so forth.

Accordingly, they were greatly encouraged by Judas’s good words, by which their courage might be lifted up, and so forth. The Book of Esther relates that, at Haman’s urging, King Ahasuerus ordered all the Jews in his kingdom to be killed. For carrying out this slaughter, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, called Adar, had been appointed, and their possessions were to be plundered. But by the Lord’s will that sentence was turned against their assailants, so that the aforementioned king, through the intervention of the Jew Mordecai, after the earlier writings had been followed by new letters, ordered that on the very day when slaughter had been prepared for them by their enemies, the Jews should kill their enemies and persecutors.

And this they did on the thirteenth and fourteenth days of the month. Concerning this the same history says: “The thirteenth day of the month Adar was, for all, a day of slaughter; and on the fourteenth day they ceased killing, which they established as a solemn day, so that thereafter, at all times, they might devote themselves on it to feasts, joy, and banquets.”

Hence it is now written that, after Nicanor had been killed and God’s aid had been manifestly displayed, all the Jews, by common agreement, decreed that the thirteenth day of the month Adar—which in the Syriac language is called the day before Mordecai’s day—should always be observed as a solemn day. Thus these two solemnities corresponded to one another: the one recorded in the history of the Maccabees and the one read in the history of Esther, so that those celebrated on the thirteenth and fourteenth days of the month Adar might be joined together.
