## ORDER OF THE CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ.

# Commentaries on the Four Books of Kings

[Col. 9] Preface. 9

## On the First Book

11

[Col. 1256D] **Chapter I.**—Elkanah and his two wives, namely Hannah and Peninnah. 11

**Chapter II.**—Hannah’s song, which she sang after Samuel’s birth. 16

**Chapter III.**—Samuel’s ministry in the temple and the misconduct of Eli the priest’s sons. Eli was rebuked by a man of God [Col. 1257] for the crime of his sons, whom their father did not properly correct. 25

**Chapter IV.**—The change from the priesthood of the old law. The battle of the Philistines against Israel, in which the ark of God was captured, Eli’s two sons were killed, the Israelite people were put to flight, and Eli died. 26

**Chapter V.**—The Philistines placed the ark of God beside the image of Dagon; because of this the Lord struck all the Philistines in their buttocks, as punishment for their insult. 27

**Chapter VI.**—The Philistines made a new cart drawn by nursing cows and sent the ark back to Beth-shemesh; and the mystical meaning of this event. 28

**Chapter VII.**—Samuel addressed Israel, telling them to abandon the Baals and Astartes and serve the Lord. While he was praying, the Israelites were delivered from the Philistines, and in Samuel’s days they no longer prevailed against them. 32

**Chapter VIII.**—Samuel appointed his two sons as judges over Israel, but they acted wrongly. Therefore the people asked for a king. Saul, seeking his father’s she-asses, came to the prophet, by whom he was anointed king. 35

**Chapter IX.**—The narrative continues as above. 36

**Chapter X.**—The narrative continues as above. 37

**Chapter XI.**—The war of Nahash the Ammonite against Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul, fighting with the Israelites, defeated. 38

**Chapter XII.**—The narrative continues as above. 39

**Chapter XIII.**—Saul, after being appointed king, organized his army; Saul himself offended the Lord when he offered the burnt offering; and the Philistines prevented weapons from being manufactured throughout the land of Israel. 40

**Chapter XIV.**—Saul, preparing to fight the Philistines, imposed a fast upon the whole army. Jonathan, unaware of it, broke the fast by tasting honey and was scarcely saved from death by the people’s prayers. 42

**Chapter XV.**—The war that Saul waged against Amalek at the Lord’s command. There he offended the Lord through disobedience, because, out of greed, he did not destroy all Amalek together with all its possessions. Therefore the Lord reproached him and rebuked him through the prophet. 44

**Chapter XVI.**—After Saul was rejected, David was chosen and anointed king by Samuel. David himself played the lyre before the enraged Saul. 49

**Chapter XVII.**—David’s battle against Goliath the Philistine, whom he killed by throwing a stone. 51

**Chapter XVIII.**—Jonathan’s covenant with David and the betrothal of Michal, Saul’s daughter. 54

**Chapter XIX.**—Saul wished to pierce David, who was playing the lyre, with a spear. Saul’s deception: how he was deceived by means of a statue placed in the bed and a hairy goatskin when he was seeking to kill David. 55

**Chapter XX.**—Saul sent messengers to seek David. When they came to the company of prophets, they themselves prophesied; and Saul also, coming there afterward, prophesied naked all day. Jonathan’s words to David and the sign of the arrow that he gave to David. 57

**Chapter XXI.**—David fled to Abimelech the priest, by whom he was fed; because of this Saul killed that priest and the company of priests with him. David’s flight to Achish, king of Gath. 58

**Chapter XXII.**—David fled to the cave of Adullam, where his brothers and his entire father’s household visited him, and many others gathered to him. 60

**Chapter XXIII.**—David hid in the wilderness of Ziph, in the forest; the Ziphites betrayed him to Saul. 61

**Chapter XXIV.**—David, hiding in a cave in the wilderness of En-gedi, secretly cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak. Saul had entered the same cave to relieve himself. 62

**Chapter XXV.**—Samuel’s death and the story of Nabal and his wife Abigail, and how they dealt with David. 63

**Chapter XXVI.**—David, fleeing from Saul, found him sleeping but did not kill him; he took only his spear and the cup of water. 66

**Chapter XXVII.**—The narrative continues concerning David’s deeds. 66

**Chapter XXVIII.**—Again, concerning Samuel’s death. 66

**Chapter XXIX.**—The pythoness who, at Saul’s request, raised Samuel, who announced his imminent death to him. 66

**Chapter XXX.**—David defeated the Amalekites and recovered the plunder that they had taken at Ziklag. 69

**Chapter XXXI.**—The battle of the Philistines against Jerusalem, and the death of Saul and his sons. 70

## On the Second Book

71

**Chapter I.**—David ordered the Amalekite messenger who reported the crime to be struck down before him because of Saul’s death. David’s mourning, in which he lamented Saul and Jonathan after their death; and he ordered the sons of Judah to be taught the bow. 71

**Chapter II.**—David was anointed king over the house of Judah. Through messengers he thanked the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul and his sons [Col. 1258]. Abner, son of Ner, made Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, king over Israel, while David reigned in Hebron over the tribe of Judah alone. Abner and the men of Ish-bosheth fought against Joab and David’s men at Gibeon, and Asahel, Abner’s brother, was killed. 74

**Chapter III.**—The prolonged conflict between the house of David and the house of Saul, and the names of David’s six sons who were born to him in Hebron. Abner urged the people to abandon Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, and transfer their allegiance to David. Joab treacherously killed Abner, and therefore David struck him with a sentence of curse through prophecy. 77

**Chapter IV.**—Rechab and Baanah killed Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son. 79

**Chapter V.**—All the tribes of Israel and the elders of Israel came to David at Hebron. He began to reign at thirty years of age and completed forty years of rule. David fought against the Jebusite and captured the citadel of the city, which he called the City of David. David’s wives, concubines, sons, and daughters whom he had in Jerusalem. David’s battle against the Philistines. 80

**Chapter VI.**—David brought up the ark, but because of an adverse event—namely, the striking down of Uzzah the Levite—he turned it aside to the house of Obed-edom, and from there transferred it to his own house. After completing the offerings of burnt offerings and sacrifices of well-being, he distributed food to the entire multitude of Israel. David danced before the ark of the Lord and was mocked by Michal, Saul’s daughter. 83

**Chapter VII.**—David wished to build a house for God, but was forbidden by the prophet Nathan in the Lord’s word, because, by God’s providential arrangement, his son would complete it. 88

**Chapter VIII.**—David’s battle against the Philistines; after striking down the Moabites, he measured them with a cord, making them level with the ground. He also struck the Syrians in the Valley of Salt. Concerning David’s sons who were priests. 93

**Chapter IX.**—How much kindness David showed to the lame Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s son. 95

**Chapter X.**—David’s battle against the king of Ammon, son of Ammon, because he had dishonored the messengers David sent to him. 96

**Chapter XI.**—David’s sin, which he committed with Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite. 98

**Chapter XII.**—The counsel of Joab, the commander, who said to David: “Be present at the victory of the war, lest afterward the victory be attributed to me, but rather to you.” David carried this out, crushed the Ammonites, and drove iron chariots around them. 101

**Chapter XIII.**—Amnon’s incest with his sister Tamar, for which his brother Absalom killed him. 103

**Chapter XIV.**—Joab tried, through a woman of Tekoa, to reconcile the king with Absalom. 104

**Chapter XV.**—Absalom’s conspiracy against David. 105

**Chapter XVI.**—The narrative continues concerning Absalom’s conspiracy. 106

**Chapter XVII.**—The narrative continues as above. 106

**Chapter XVIII.**—The battle of David’s servants against Israel and the death of Absalom, whom David mourned after his death. 109

**Chapter XIX.**—Mephibosheth’s arrival to meet the king; the return of all Israel to David; and the conspiracy of Sheba, son of Bichri, against David. 110

**Chapter XX.**—Joab treacherously killed Amasa. 112

**Chapter XXI.**—The three-year famine that had occurred in Israel because of the killing of the Gibeonites, whom Saul had killed as though out of zeal. In recompense for this, his descendants were destroyed. The four battles of David against the Philistines, in which tall men were found, one of whom had six fingers on his hands—or on his feet. 112

**Chapter XXII.**—David’s song, which he sang to the Lord on the day when He delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul. 114

**Chapter XXIII.**—The catalogue of David’s mighty men and their distinguished deeds. 115

**Chapter XXIV.**—David’s offense against the Lord when he numbered Israel, and the plague sent against Israel on account of it. David appeased the Lord by offering burnt offerings on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. 120

## On the Third Book

123

**Chapter I.**—David’s old age and chilliness; Abishag the Shunammite kept him warm. 123

**Chapter II.**—Adonijah, who desired to reign in place of his father David and also wanted Abishag the Shunammite as his wife. David’s instructions to Solomon concerning his adversaries. 125

**Chapter III.**—Solomon’s judgment concerning the women who disputed over the infants. 126

[Col. 1259] **Chapter IV.**—Solomon’s power, by which he ruled over all, and his wisdom, riches, pleasures, and the peace he enjoyed in his kingdom. Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered five thousand. He also discoursed about animals, birds, reptiles, and fish. The building of the house of God, and how the construction of the tabernacle signifies the one and same Church of Christ. 130

**Chapter V.**—How Hiram, king of Tyre, helped Solomon in the temple’s construction; how many workmen Solomon had for the temple; and what kind of stone the temple was made from. 134

**Chapter VI.**—When and where the temple was built; its dimensions; and how many years were spent building it. 140

**Chapter VII.**—The bronze columns and other matters: the vessels of the house of the Lord were made in the Jordan region; and the hinges of the doors were made at the completion of the work on the house of the Lord. 166

**Chapter VIII.**—When the ark of the Lord was brought into the inner sanctuary of the temple, the Holy of Holies, its poles no longer appeared externally as they had previously been accustomed to appear. A cloud filled the house of the Lord, and the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud. The dedication of the temple by Solomon and the people of Israel. 184

**Chapter IX.**—After building the temple and the royal house, Solomon built many cities and fortified with walls the villages belonging to him. Three times each year he offered burnt offerings, and he established a fleet to bring gold from Ophir. 190

**Chapter X.**—The queen of Sheba came to hear Solomon’s wisdom. Solomon made supports for the house of the Lord from thyine wood, and other things. He was enriched above all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom. 192

**Chapter XI.**—The foreign women whom Solomon loved. 198

**Chapter XII.**—The division of the ten tribes from the house of David because of Solomon’s sin, and how Rehoboam abandoned the counsel of the elders and obeyed the persuasion of the young men. 199

**Chapter XIII.**—The prophet who rebuked Jeroboam was deceived by a false prophet, ate contrary to the Lord’s command, and was consequently killed by a lion on the road. 200

**Chapter XIV.**—Shishak, king of Egypt, plundered Jerusalem because of Rehoboam’s sins. He removed the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king, including the golden shields that Solomon had made. In their place King Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the shield-bearers. There was continual war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and between Asa, king of Judah, and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout all their days. 201

**Chapter XV.**—The word of the Lord came to Jehu, son of Hanani, against Baasha, king of Israel, foretelling the punishments that would come upon him because he had caused Israel to sin. Concerning Omri, king of Israel, and how he bought the mountain of Samaria. Concerning the time of Ahab, and how Hiel of Bethel built Jericho, laying its foundation in Abiram, his firstborn, and setting up its gates in Segub, his youngest. 203

**Chapter XVI.**—Elijah the Tishbite: how ravens fed him while he was hidden by the brook Cherith, bringing him bread and meat in the morning and likewise bread and meat in the evening. 205

**Chapter XVII.**—The widow of Zarephath who fed the prophet; because of this the Lord blessed her flour and oil. Also concerning the son of the woman, the head of the household, whom Elijah raised. 206

**Chapter XVIII.**—Elijah’s dispute with Ahab’s prophets, and how, by offering sacrifice, he showed that the Lord was the true God of Israel, while the idols worshiped by Ahab were false gods. Also concerning the rain that Elijah obtained. 208

**Chapter XIX.**—Elijah’s flight from Jezebel, and how, sitting beneath a juniper tree, he asked that his soul might die. The angel of the Lord fed him there with a cake baked on hot stones and water. How Elijah, hiding in a cave on Mount Horeb, was comforted there by the Lord’s manifold speech. The Lord also ordered him to anoint kings and Elisha as prophet in his place, and gave them power to strike with the sword. 210

**Chapter XX.**—The war of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, against Ahab, king of Israel. A prophet appeared, encouraging Ahab, and victory was given to him through the young men of the provincial governors. After Ben-hadad, king of Syria, had once been defeated, he renewed the battle against Israel, but was similarly overcome. Taking refuge in the mercy of the king of Israel, he made a treaty with him without the Lord’s command; therefore Ahab was rebuked by a prophet sent by the Lord. 214

**Chapter XXI.**—Ahab, king of Israel, coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite. After Naboth was killed through Jezebel’s scheme, Ahab seized the vineyard for himself; therefore he was rebuked through the prophet Elijah. 217

[Col. 1260] **Chapter XXII.**—The vision of the prophet Micaiah, who foretold the death of Ahab, king of Israel. 219

## On the Fourth Book

221

**Chapter I.**—King Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his house. Because of this illness he sent to consult the idol of Ekron, whereupon the angry Lord gave him an appropriate answer through the prophet. 221

**Chapter II.**—Elijah’s being carried up into heaven by a whirlwind, and Elisha’s request that a double portion of Elijah’s spirit be made his. Elisha’s miracle at Jericho, where he called upon the Lord and changed the waters into sweetness. The boys who mocked Elisha and were torn apart by two bears because of it. 222

**Chapter III.**—The war of three kings—of Judah, Israel, and Edom—against the king of Moab, and the victory granted them by the Lord. 223

**Chapter IV.**—Elisha delivered a woman by the blessing of oil and from her creditor. Also concerning the Shunammite woman whose son Elisha raised; the bitter stew that Elisha sweetened by adding flour; and the offering of a man who came to Elisha. 228

**Chapter V.**—Naaman the Syrian, whose leprosy Elisha cured in the name of the Lord. 231

**Chapter VI.**—The sons of the prophets complained about the narrowness of their dwelling, and Elisha recovered an iron tool from the water. 233

**Chapter VII.**—The king of Syria plotted against Elisha. 235

**Chapter VIII.**—The famine in Samaria caused by the siege of Ben-hadad, king of Syria, and the miraculous deliverance of the Israelites through the Lord’s grace. 236

**Chapter IX.**—Jehu’s anointing as king. 238

**Chapter X.**—The tyranny of Athaliah, mother of King Ahaziah. 238

**Chapter XI.**—Jehoiada the high priest, and how he made Joash, son of Ahaziah, king. 239

**Chapter XII.**—The zeal of Jehoiada the high priest in restoring the temple. 241

**Chapter XIII.**—Elisha’s illness, during which, at the Lord’s command, he foretold to King Joash that the Syrian nation would be struck down. The death of Elisha, the man of God; when his funeral bier touched a certain dead body, it immediately came back to life. 243

**Chapter XIV.**—Amaziah, king of Judah, who struck Edom in the Valley of Salt. 245

**Chapter XV.**—Azariah, king of Judah, also called Uzziah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel. 246

**Chapter XVI.**—Ahaz, king of Judah. Because of his sins, Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight. 247

**Chapter XVII.**—The transfer of the ten tribes that reigned in Samaria to the Assyrians under Shalmaneser, king of Assyria. In their places the king brought other settlers, who worshiped there the gods they had worshiped in their own land, and nevertheless also worshiped the God of Israel. 250

**Chapter XVIII.**—King Hezekiah, in whose time Sennacherib, king of Assyria, sent messengers to Jerusalem with a powerful force to blaspheme the living God. 251

**Chapter XIX.**—Hezekiah’s prayer in the temple of the Lord against the words of the king of Assyria. The angel of the Lord struck down eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib, king of Assyria, perished. 255

**Chapter XX.**—Hezekiah’s illness and the Lord’s word delivered to him through the prophet Isaiah. The sign Hezekiah requested concerning the reversal of the sun’s course. The messengers of Berodach, king of Babylon, sent to Hezekiah, and the Lord’s word that Isaiah reported to Hezekiah concerning those messengers. 259

**Chapter XXI.**—Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, and how, after his sin, he repented and thereby deserved to be freed from prison. 266

**Chapter XXII.**—King Josiah, who cleansed the whole land of Judah from the pollution of idols. 266

**Chapter XXIII.**—Josiah defiled Topheth, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom; removed the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the Sun at the entrance of the temple of the Lord; polluted the high places; and dug up and burned the tombs of the dead. Josiah celebrated the most solemn Passover to the Lord in the eighteenth year of his reign. Josiah’s death and the succession of his son Jehoahaz to the throne of Judah; after him Jehoiakim reigned in place of his brother, who had been taken captive. Concerning King Jehoiakim, who is also called Jeconiah. 268

**Chapter XXIV.**—Nebuchadnezzar transported King Jehoiakim to Babylon, together with his mother, wives, eunuchs, the rest of the people, and part of the vessels of God. King Zedekiah, because of the enormity of his crimes, was handed over along with his sons and the entire people. 271

**Chapter XXV.**—Nebuzaradan, commander of the king of Babylon’s army [Col. 1261], devastated the land of the Jews, destroyed the cities, burned the temple, consumed the royal houses with fire, and carried all the plunder with him to Babylon. 274

# Commentaries on the Two Books of Chronicles

279

## Rabanus’s Prologue to Emperor Louis

279

## Book One

281

**Chapter I.**—A catalogue of the generations from Adam to Abraham, and again from Abraham to Israel. 281

**Chapter II.**—The generation of the twelve patriarchs from their father Israel. The genealogy of the patriarch Judah, extended through his various sons. 288

**Chapter III.**—King David and his descendants through the succession of kings, up to and beyond the Babylonian exile. 296

**Chapter IV.**—Again, an enumeration of Judah’s sons and those born from his sons; and concerning Jabez, who was renowned above his brothers. Caleb and his sons Machir and the men of Rechah. The sons of Kenaz and those born from him. Shelah, son of Judah, and the kinship of the household of those who worked in fine linen; and the potters who lived in plantations and royal settlements. The sons of Simeon and what was accomplished through them; and the sons of Gad. 302

**Chapter V.**—The sons of Reuben and their deeds. 309

**Chapter VI.**—The sons of Levi and the singers whom David appointed to sing before the ark of the Lord. Aaron and his sons. 311

**Chapter VII.**—The Benjamites. 313

**Chapter VIII.**—Again concerning the Benjamites; and the lineage of King Saul, who arose from that tribe. 314

**Chapter IX.**—Those of the sons of Israel who first lived in Jerusalem, and the offices of the priests and Levites. The genealogies of Saul and his sons are also repeated. 315

**Chapter X.**—The battle of the Philistines against Israel, and the death of King Saul and his sons. 320

**Chapter XI.**—David’s conquest of the Jebusites, who lived in Jebus, that is, Jerusalem. 326

**Chapter XII.**—The arrival of the sons of Israel to David in Hebron to establish him as king over Israel. A catalogue of David’s mighty men, who helped him become king over all Israel. The arrival of the sons of Gad and of Benjamin and Judah to David. Those who defected to him from Manasseh while David was at Ziklag; Jehoiada, leader of the lineage of Aaron; and the sons of Issachar, who provided David with support. 332

**Chapter XIII.**—David took counsel with the tribunes, centurions, and all the leaders so that, after gathering a multitude of priests and Levites, they might bring the ark of the Lord to him from the house of Abinadab. Uzzah the Levite was driving the cart and stretched out his hand to support the ark lest it should fall; because of the presumption of touching it, he was struck down by the Lord. When David saw this, he was astonished and turned the ark aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained for three months. 337

**Chapter XIV.**—After David’s kingdom over Israel had been confirmed, he took other wives in Jerusalem, who bore sons and daughters. David struck the Philistines at Baal-perazim, and in another victory struck them at Gibeon as far as Gezer. 342

**Chapter XV.**—David appointed singers who sang with musical instruments before the ark of the Lord: Heman, Asaph, Ethan, and the others who were with them. 344

## Book Two

349

**Chapter XVI.**—When David had brought the ark of the Lord with rejoicing into the tabernacle that he had pitched for it, the priests offered burnt offerings and sacrifices of well-being before the Lord. David blessed the people in the Lord’s name and distributed to everyone, man and woman alike, a round loaf of bread, a portion of roasted beef, and a cake fried in oil. The Levites whom David appointed to minister before the ark of the Lord, and Asaph and his brothers. The song that David composed to praise the Lord. David returned to bless his household. 349

**Chapter XVII.**—The words David spoke to Nathan the prophet concerning the building of the temple, and the Lord’s response to David through the same prophet. The confession in which David praised the Lord for all the benefits He had bestowed upon him. 363

**Chapter XVIII.**—David struck and humbled the Philistines, the Moabites, King Hadadezer of Zobah, and the Aramean of Damascus. From them King David transferred vessels of gold, silver, and bronze and consecrated them to the Lord. Abishai struck Edom in the Valley of Salt and established a garrison in Edom so that Idumea might serve David. David’s kingdom over Israel [Col. 1262] and the leaders whom he appointed over the people. 367

**Chapter XIX.**—Hanun, son of Nahash, king of the Ammonites, disgraced the messengers David had sent to him; consequently war was made against him. 371

**Chapter XX.**—Joab struck Rabbah and destroyed it; he attributed the triumph to David’s name. David’s various wars against the Philistines, in which he also killed certain giants. 372

**Chapter XXI.**—David ordered the Israelites to be counted and thereby offended the Lord; consequently a very severe plague of mortality was sent upon Israel. When David saw the angel of the Lord who was killing the people, he made an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, offered burnt offerings and sacrifices of well-being there, and called upon the Lord, who heard him. 375

**Chapter XXII.**—David resolved to build a temple to the Lord there; this was carried out by his son Solomon, to whom David gave very great funds and supplies. David instructed Solomon concerning the construction of the Lord’s temple and assigned to him various instruments of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, together with wood and stones that he himself had gathered for this purpose, as well as many craftsmen and masons for the temple’s work. 380

**Chapter XXIII.**—David appointed his son Solomon king over Israel and gathered all the leaders of Israel, the priests, and the Levites. He arranged their offices according to each ministry. 387

**Chapter XXIV.**—The twenty-four divisions by which David distinguished the sons of Eleazar and the sons of Ithamar for serving God in the Lord’s temple by their appointed turns. 391

**Chapter XXV.**—David and the commanders of the army set apart for the Lord’s ministry the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, to sing with lyres, harps, and cymbals before the ark of the Lord. 395

**Chapter XXVI.**—The doorkeepers and leaders of the Lord’s guard. All these mighty men, divided according to their turns, fulfilled their ministries and provided for the treasures of the house of the Lord. 396

**Chapter XXVII.**—The various leaders who were over the Israelites according to David’s arrangement. Those who supervised David’s property—that is, the cities, villages, fields, vineyards, olive groves, and livestock. David’s counselors and those who were with the king’s sons. 402

**Chapter XXVIII.**—David’s final words, in which he admonished his son Solomon and all Israel concerning the building of the temple and the worship of God. 407

**Chapter XXIX.**—David’s blessing, in which he blessed the Lord with all Israel, sacrificing victims to the Lord and offering burnt offerings. There they anointed Solomon, David’s son, a second time as the Lord’s leader, and Zadok as high priest. Solomon sat upon David’s throne, and all Israel obeyed him. God gave him the glory of the kingdom, such as no king in Israel had possessed before him. 412

## Book Three

413

**Chapter I.**—The beginning of Solomon’s reign: he offered a thousand victims at the high place of Gibeon, where the tabernacle of the Lord’s covenant then stood. Solomon gathered chariots, horsemen, and teams of horses from various provinces. 413

**Chapter II.**—Solomon selected the workmen for the house of God and sent to Hiram, king of Tyre, asking his assistance; Hiram willingly granted what he requested. The number of proselytes assigned to the work of the house of God. 417

**Chapter III.**—The building of the house of God, its length, width, and height. Solomon roofed the larger house with wooden boards, adorned it above with sheets of gold, and decorated it with various designs. The floor of the house of God, which he paved with the most precious marble. The Holy of Holies and the making of the cherubim in it. The veil spread before the ark of the Lord, separating the Holy of Holies from the sanctuary. The two columns that Solomon cast and placed in the vestibule of the temple. 423

**Chapter IV.**—The altar of burnt offering; the bronze sea and the oxen upon which it rested; the ten basins in which the victims were to be washed; the ten golden lampstands and ten tables; the courts of the house of the Lord and their divisions; and the various vessels that Hiram cast for Solomon in the Jordan region, pouring them in clay ground. The golden altar, that is, the altar of incense; the table of the showbread; the lampstand with its lamps; and the other vessels used in the ministry. The inner and outer sacrifices of the temple. 438

**Chapter V.**—Solomon brought into the temple of the Lord everything that David his father had vowed: gold and silver, all the vessels, the ark of the Lord, and the equipment of the tabernacle. When the priests placed the ark in the Holy of Holies, the Levites sang praises to God with cymbals, harps, and lyres, and a cloud filled the house of the Lord. 458

[Col. 1263] **Chapter VI.**—The bronze platform on which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple of the Lord. The solemnity of the temple’s dedication in the festive month, and the greatest celebration of that festival. 463

**Chapter VII.**—After twenty years had been completed, Solomon first built the house of the Lord, his own house, and many cities; he subdued foreigners and made them tributary. 463

**Chapter VIII.**—Solomon’s army commanders, and the Levites and priests whom he appointed for the Lord’s ministry. Solomon sent ships to Ophir to bring gold from there, and concerning the queen of Sheba. Hiram’s servants, together with Solomon’s servants, brought gold from Ophir, thyine wood, and very precious gems. 467

**Chapter IX.**—The two hundred spears, the three hundred golden shields, and the ivory throne that Solomon had made with marvelous workmanship. Solomon’s magnificence, wealth, power, and death. 472

## Book Four

483

**Chapter X.**—The reigns of Rehoboam and Jeroboam. 483

**Chapter XII.**—How Rehoboam, when Shishak king of Egypt came to Jerusalem, was oppressed by him, who carried away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal house. 484

**Chapter XIII.**—The reign of Abijah, son of Rehoboam. 486

**Chapter XIV.**—Asa, king of Jerusalem. 487

**Chapter XVI.**—The narrative continues concerning Asa. 487

**Chapter XVII.**—Jehoshaphat, king of Judah; his good deeds and the administration of his kingdom. 488

**Chapter XVIII.**—The narrative continues concerning Jehoshaphat. 489

**Chapter XX.**—The narrative continues concerning Jehoshaphat. 492

**Chapter XXI.**—Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, and his very evil end. 494

**Chapter XXII.**—Ahaziah, son of Joram, and his unspeakable deeds. Joash, king of Judah and Jerusalem, whom Jehoiada the high priest preserved. The killing carried out by Athaliah, who established herself as queen over the two tribes. 497

**Chapter XXIII.**—The narrative continues from the preceding account. 498

**Chapter XXIV.**—Joash ordered the priests to repair the damaged parts of the house of the Lord and renewed the worship of the temple. The end of Jehoiada the high priest, and the killing of his son Zechariah, whom King Joash ordered to be killed between the temple and the altar. The death of Joash. 500

**Chapter XXV.**—The reign of Amaziah, son of Joash, in Jerusalem. 506

**Chapter XXVI.**—King Uzziah and his presumption, by which he wished to offer sacrifice in the temple. As punishment, leprosy was sent upon him. 509

**Chapter XXVII.**—King Jotham and his good deeds. 513

**Chapter XXVIII.**—King Ahaz and his detestable deeds. 514

**Chapter XXX.**—Hezekiah, king of Judah, and his good works, by which he most splendidly upheld divine worship. 517

**Chapter XXXI.**—The narrative continues concerning Hezekiah. 518

**Chapter XXXII.**—King Sennacherib and the threats he made against Jerusalem and the temple of the Lord, against whom punishment was brought by the Lord. Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. The embassy of the Assyrians to Hezekiah concerning the portent that had occurred, and Hezekiah’s death. 518

**Chapter XXXIII.**—Manasseh, his son, and Ammon, his descendant. 525

**Chapter XXXV.**—King Josiah and his good deeds; King Necho of Egypt killed him in battle. 527

**Chapter XXXVI.**—Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim, sons of Josiah, and their deaths. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, led Jehoiachin the king into captivity, together with his mother and servants. King Zedekiah and the destruction of the city of Jerusalem. 530

# Exposition of the Book of Judith

539

## Dedication Letter to Judith Augusta

539

## Preface

541

**Chapter I.**—Arphaxad, king of the Medes, conquered many nations and built the city of Ecbatana; afterward he was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar. 541

**Chapter II.**—Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians, sent Holofernes, commander of the army, with an army to subjugate the entire West because his messengers had been rejected. 545

**Chapter III.**—Holofernes devastated the provinces and received the envoys of various regions who had been sent to him and surrendered themselves and all their possessions to him; nevertheless, he destroyed their cities and gods. 548

**Chapter IV.**—When the sons of Israel learned of Holofernes’ arrival, they were terrified and began to prepare fortifications and cry out to the Lord with the utmost urgency. The high priest Eliakim [Col. 1264] urged the sons of Israel to trust in the Lord’s presence, so that they would not fear the attack. 550

**Chapter V.**—When Holofernes heard that the sons of Israel had blocked the mountain passes, he became extremely angry and asked his leaders where the sons of Israel came from and what their strength was. Achior gave him a full answer concerning this matter. The leaders of Holofernes were angered by his report. 553

**Chapter VI.**—Holofernes ordered the priest Achior to be led to Bethulia and tied to a tree. The sons of Israel released him from his bonds, brought him to Bethulia, and comforted him. 536

**Chapter VII.**—Holofernes led his army to Bethulia and ordered its water channel to be cut off, barring the inhabitants from the springs. The citizens of Bethulia, pressed by lack of water, came to Uzziah and begged that the city be handed over to Holofernes. Uzziah persuaded them to wait five more days. 556

**Chapter VIII.**—Judith rebuked the elders Chabri and Charmi because Uzziah, the leader, had set a day of deliverance for the Lord. Preparing herself to deliver the people, she did not wish anyone to inquire what she was going to do. 558

**Chapter IX.**—Judith humbled herself and prayed for the deliverance of the people. 563

**Chapter X.**—After praying, Judith put on the ornaments of her beauty and went out through the city gates toward Holofernes. She was received by the scouts and led to Holofernes. Holofernes asked Judith why she had come. 563

**Chapter XI.**—Deceived by Judith, Holofernes became confident that he could capture the sons of Israel. Everyone also admired Judith’s beauty and wisdom. 568

**Chapter XII.**—Holofernes ordered Judith to stay in the place where his treasures were kept. When she was invited to his banquet, she abstained from his food; at evening she was brought into his bedchamber. 570

**Chapter XIII.**—While Holofernes, drunk, lay upon his bed, Judith prayed, cut off his head, wrapped it in her mosquito net, and carried it to her fellow citizens. When a great crowd of people had gathered at the city gates, Judith blessed the Lord and showed them Holofernes’ head. Everyone praised the Lord and blessed Judith. When Achior saw the head of Holofernes, he was overwhelmed with fear and fell to the ground. 572

**Chapter XIV.**—Judith advised the people to go outside the gates and make a clamor with their weapons, so as to instill fear in the Assyrians. 576

**Chapter XV.**—The people put the Assyrians to flight and, after killing very many, carried away great plunder. Joakim, the high priest, came down from Jerusalem to Bethulia to see Judith and heaped blessings upon her. The people gave everything that had belonged to Holofernes to the victorious woman. 577

**Chapter XVI.**—Judith’s magnificent song. Concerning what was accomplished…

The victorious people went to Jerusalem to pray to the Lord; Judith too, having completed 105 years, ended her life in extreme old age.

581 **APPENDIX TO RABANUS MAURUS’S EXPOSITION OF THE BOOK OF JUDITH.—JACOBUS PAMELIUS’S COMMENTARY ON THE SAME BOOK.**

593 **Preface.**

593 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Nabuchodonosor, having defeated Arphaxat, who had seized the kingdom of the Medes—and thus his entire realm—by force, strives to rule over all kingdoms.

599 **CHAPTER II.—**Holophernes is sent by Nabuchodonosor to lay waste all rebellious kingdoms and peoples.

602 **CHAPTER III.—**Holophernes spares neither those who voluntarily surrender nor their cities or gods.

604 **CHAPTER IV.—**The children of Israel fortify themselves against Holophernes, being encouraged to do so by Eliachim the priest.

605 **CHAPTER V.—**Achior warns Holophernes not to fight rashly against the Jews.

607 **CHAPTER VI.—**Achior is handed over by Holophernes into the hands of the Jews.

611 **CHAPTER VII.—**Holophernes torments the besieged inhabitants of Bethulia with thirst, having blocked their water supply, so that the people are almost driven to revolt.

612 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Judith consoles and strengthens the wavering Jews who, out of fear, are considering surrender.

614 **CHAPTER IX.—**Judith enters the place of prayer, clothed in sackcloth and with her head sprinkled with ashes, and, prostrated on the ground, prays to God for her people.

618 **CHAPTER X.—**Judith, adorned with ornaments, leaves the city with her maidservant. She is detained by the scouts and brought to Holophernes.

621 **CHAPTER XI.—**When Judith is questioned by Holophernes about the reason for her flight, she cleverly deceives him by the alluring character of her words.

624 **CHAPTER XII.—**Judith is brought into the treasury-house and obtains permission to eat her own food and to go out at night for prayer; when she is brought before Holophernes for a banquet, however, she eats with him as though participating in the feast.

625 **CHAPTER XIII.—**When Holophernes is drunk, Judith cuts off his head with his own sword and, carrying it to her fellow citizens, urges them to give thanks.

627 **CHAPTER XIV.—**With the head of Holophernes hung upon the wall, and Achior circumcised, the Jews rush upon the Assyrians. When the Assyrians try to awaken Holophernes, they find him dead.

629 **CHAPTER XV.—**The Assyrians flee while the Jews pursue them; the Jews then gather the spoils and rejoice greatly. Judith is blessed by the people and by Joachim the high priest.

630 **CHAPTER XVI.—**Judith sings a song on account of the victory, by which she urges the people also to give thanks; finally, full of days, she dies.

**EXPOSITION OF THE BOOK OF ESTHER.**

635 **Preface to Judith Augusta.**

635 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Concerning King Ahasuerus and his very famous banquet.

636 **CHAPTER II.—**Concerning Queen Vashti, who, when summoned, refused to come to the king; for this reason she was removed from her royal dignity and rejected by her husband.

642 **CHAPTER III.—**That, at the command of King Ahasuerus, virgin girls were gathered from various provinces. Among them was Esther, the daughter of the brother of the Jew Mordecai, whom her uncle carefully brought up.

645 **CHAPTER IV.—**That Esther was brought to the king according to the order of her turn, was loved by him above all the women, and was established as queen.

647 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning the two eunuchs who, wishing to kill the king, were exposed by Mordecai and deservedly punished.

650 **CHAPTER VI.—**Because Mordecai refused to worship him, Haman, hating the Jewish race, accused them before the king; and the king ordered all of them to be killed on a single day.

652 **CHAPTER VII.—**When Mordecai learned this, he clothed himself in sackcloth and sent word to Esther so that she might plead with the king for the Jews against the slaughter.

654 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Esther entered the king’s presence and invited both him and Haman to a banquet.

655 **CHAPTER IX.—**Because King Ahasuerus, after passing a sleepless night, ordered the histories and annals of former times to be brought to him, and, while they were being read before him, they came to the passage where Mordecai had exposed the eunuchs who were plotting against him, the king summoned Haman and ordered Mordecai to be adorned with a royal robe and diadem, mounted upon the royal horse, and proclaimed by Haman himself as the king’s friend. Therefore Haman returned home sorrowful.

657 **CHAPTER X.—**On the second day of the banquet, while the queen pleaded for her people, Haman was hanged on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai.

658 **CHAPTER XI.—**Mordecai is appointed in Haman’s place, and, at the queen’s suggestion, letters are sent for the safety of the Jews.

660 **CHAPTER XII.—**Concerning the glory of Mordecai and how the Jews took vengeance on their enemies; the ten sons of Haman were hanged on the gallows.

664 **CHAPTER XIII.—**That the days on which the Jews took vengeance were counted among the solemn feast days.

667 **CHAPTER XIV.—**King Ahasuerus made all the islands tributary. Here the history of Esther among the Hebrews comes to an end.

**THREE BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM.**

670 **Prologue to Otgar, Archbishop of Mainz.**

671 **BOOK ONE**

673 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Wisdom, who is Christ, commands the inhabitants of the earth to love justice, making known to them that perverse thoughts separate people from God and that wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul.

673 **CHAPTER II.—**Wisdom indicates that the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and that he himself fills the whole world, so that nothing can remain hidden from him.

674 **CHAPTER III.—**Wisdom commands her hearers to guard themselves from murmuring, slander, and lying, because justice is immortal and the ungodly will not seize it.

676 **CHAPTER IV.—**Where the ungodly, despairing of their salvation, declare that they will perish and that they will live only in the present age.

678 **CHAPTER V.—**The counsel of the ungodly Jews against Christ, deliberating about his death and accusing him because he reproached them for the sins of the Law.

679 **CHAPTER VI.—**Concerning the holy martyrs: their glory will be eternal through present tribulation.

681 **CHAPTER VII.—**The ungodly will receive punishments corresponding to what they have done, because they have departed from the Lord.

683 [Col. 1266] **CHAPTER VIII.—**The children of adulterers—that is, of heretics—will be incomplete, while the offspring of the chaste will remain in perpetual brightness.

684 **CHAPTER IX.—**The souls of the righteous will be in refreshment after death, and their passing should not be mourned.

686 **CHAPTER X.—**At the Lord’s coming the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against their persecutors; and the persecutors themselves will at last undergo late repentance in hell for their error and sins.

688 **CHAPTER XI.—**Concerning the holy martyrs: they live forever, and the Lord avenges them against their adversaries.

691 **CHAPTER XII.—**Wisdom rebukes the judges of the earth who have received authority from the Lord because they did not keep the law of justice, foretelling the punishments they were to suffer.

692 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Wisdom exhorts the rulers of the Church to hear and desire her words, because she freely offers herself to them, granting at the same time integrity of body and purity of soul.

694 **BOOK TWO**

695 **CHAPTER ONE.—**The wise man praises divine Wisdom, proclaiming her power.

695 **CHAPTER II.—**The same man explains the origin of human nature.

696 **CHAPTER III.—**He confesses that he has received the spirit of wisdom, in which he recounts many of its gifts.

697 **CHAPTER IV.—**Wisdom, who is the Son of God, reaches everywhere because she is always with the Father; while remaining in herself, she renews all things.

701 **CHAPTER V.—**The same Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things gently. She teaches the four principal virtues—sobriety, wisdom, justice, and courage—and makes those who share in her glorious.

704 **CHAPTER VI.—**The Wisdom of God, who is the immutable good, came to the holy and undefiled Virgin, taking from her an undefiled body; therefore all generations call her blessed. The lover of wisdom asks God to give him wisdom, so that he may know what is acceptable before him at all times.

712 **CHAPTER VII.—**Through Wisdom, that is, Christ, all who pleased the Lord were healed. The Wisdom of God remains eternally with the Father; through her all things were ordered under the Law, before the Law, and in the Gospel.

715 **CHAPTER VIII.—**He himself led the people of Israel out of Egypt; following their typological pattern, he delivered the holy martyrs from the persecutions of the world.

718 **CHAPTER IX.—**The exposition continues as above.

721 **CHAPTER X.—**When the sinful people sinned, he sent against them avenging beasts.

722 **CHAPTER XI.—**He praises the omnipotence of God: before him all visible and invisible things are like a drop of dew and like a moment on the balance.

724 **CHAPTER XII.—**Wisdom confesses that the Holy Spirit is gentle in all things and distributes God’s good gifts throughout the whole world.

725 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Wisdom praises God’s patience, because he gives sinners an opportunity for repentance and does not immediately take vengeance.

728 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Divine piety commends its own goodness, which is just in all its judgments.

728 **BOOK THREE**

729 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Concerning the error of idolatry.

729 **CHAPTER II.—**The exposition continues as above.

732 **CHAPTER III.—**He mocks the error of idolatry fashioned by human hands.

733 **CHAPTER IV.—**He confesses to God that his Wisdom governs all things.

741 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning the various errors of idols: how they were introduced among the human race, and how the worship of idols is always a deceiver of human life.

742 **CHAPTER VI.—**All abominations were discovered by the gentiles because of idolatry, and on account of it they suffered many torments.

744 **CHAPTER VII.—**He confesses to God that he is gentle and true, patient and merciful, saving the elect by his word and judging the reprobate.

747 **CHAPTER VIII.—**He mocks the inventors of idolatry, showing how, when God judged them, they were tormented by water, hail, and fire.

747 **CHAPTER IX.—**He proclaims that God gave the people of Israel, who feared him, food for delight.

748 **CHAPTER X.—**He relates that the Lord alone has power over death and life, governing all things by his will, punishing the ungodly with a scourge and refreshing the godly with heavenly bread.

749 [Col. 1267] **CHAPTER XI.—**The exposition continues as above.

749 **CHAPTER XII.—**Wisdom praises God because his judgments are great and his words ineffable; he wondrously punished his adversaries.

751 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Savage presumption continually troubles the conscience of the ungodly, and they are terrified and tormented by various dreams and imaginings.

752 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Concerning the saints: in the darkness of Egypt—that is, the errors of the world—they were illuminated by divine light.

754 **CHAPTER XV.—**Concerning the destroyer of Egypt, who did not dare to touch the Hebrew doorposts consecrated by the blood of the lamb.

755 **CHAPTER XVI.—**He relates concerning Moses and Aaron that they led the people out of Egypt not by bodily strength but by faith and prayer.

757 **CHAPTER XVII.—**He recalls how the children of Israel desired meat in the wilderness, and *artygometra* was given to them [the reading is uncertain].

758 **CHAPTER XVIII.—**He praises God for magnifying and honoring his people, whom he led out of the land of Egypt.

**TEN BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON ECCLESIASTICUS.**

763 **Preface to Otgar, Archbishop of Mainz.**

763 **BOOK ONE**

765 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Concerning the eternal Wisdom of God, who is always with the Father before the ages.

765 **CHAPTER II.—**Concerning the Wisdom of God, that is, the Son of the Father: he existed before every creature, and all things were made through him. The Word of God is also God in the heights.

766 **CHAPTER III.—**The exposition continues as above.

766 **CHAPTER IV.—**It was prophesied concerning the Wisdom of God that the Son would be born from a Virgin through the Holy Spirit.

766 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning the fear of God: it is the beginning of wisdom and the testing of the elect.

767 **CHAPTER VI.—**Wisdom exhorts those who desire her to keep the commandments. Thus the Lord teaches in the Gospel.

770 **CHAPTER VII.—**Wisdom warns those who approach the service of God to stand in justice and fear, and to prepare their soul for temptation, because, as the Apostle says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution.”

772 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Wisdom exhorts those who fear the Lord to hope in him—that is, to be secure in hope, so that their fear may not be vain.

773 **CHAPTER IX.—**Wisdom threatens those who, after endurance, abandon the right ways and go along crooked paths.

775 **CHAPTER X.—**Children must honor their parents, so that the parents’ blessing may benefit their children.

777 **CHAPTER XI.—**A father’s old age is to be cared for by his children.

779 **CHAPTER XII.—**Wisdom teaches that works pertaining to the worship of God should be commanded in gentleness.

780 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Wisdom teaches that lofty things—that is, deep things—are not to be sought.

780 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Concerning almsgiving and the poor.

783 **CHAPTER XV.—**One must not turn one’s eyes away from the poor.

784 **CHAPTER XVI.—**Orphans and widows are to be defended mercifully in judgment, as though on behalf of a father.

785 **CHAPTER XVII.—**Concerning devotion to wisdom: those who love her should, with the Lord’s help, devote themselves to all the virtues of justice. Truth herself says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father.”

785 **CHAPTER XVIII.—**Wisdom urges that, in a time of tribulation, one must stand for faith and justice for the salvation of the soul.

787 **CHAPTER XIX.—**One must not trust in riches, according to the saying: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you, and whose will the things be that you have prepared?”

790 **CHAPTER XX.—**One must not delay turning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day, nor become arrogant in one’s thoughts.

795 **BOOK TWO**

795 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Concerning the grace of friends: enmity does not creep in through pure and gracious conversations.

795 **CHAPTER II.—**Wisdom points out the friend who remains only for the sake of the table’s banquets and withdraws in time of need.

798 **CHAPTER III.—**Wisdom exhorts her children—that is, the whole Church of the faithful, all united as one and one in all—to receive instruction, so that doctrine may be clear through faith and works.

800 **CHAPTER IV.—**Wisdom promises the rewards of eternity to those who love her.

801 **CHAPTER V.—**Wisdom declares from what and how many evils we must guard ourselves, not by our own strength but by her help.

802 **CHAPTER VI.—**A person ought not to justify himself before God or wish to appear wise.

804 [Col. 1268] **CHAPTER VII.—**Concerning not uttering a lie against a friend.

807 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning the good and faithful servant.

808 **CHAPTER IX.—**Concerning children honoring their parents.

809 **CHAPTER X.—**Concerning the fear of God and the honoring of priests, and the offering of firstfruits to them.

809 **CHAPTER XI.—**For the dead: consolation is to be offered to those who mourn.

812 **CHAPTER XII.—**One must not quarrel with a powerful person.

813 **CHAPTER XIII.—**One must not rejoice over a dead enemy, knowing that we all die.

815 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Concerning the avoidance of evil words, deeds, and thoughts through God’s help.

817 **CHAPTER XV.—**Wisdom teaches the chaste man not to give a woman power over his soul, lest she destroy him through friendships; nor should he associate with a woman who makes sport.

819 **CHAPTER XVI.—**One must not abandon an old friend.

821 **CHAPTER XVII.—**Concerning upright banqueters, that is, companions of good reputation.

825 **BOOK THREE**

825 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Wisdom praises judges who judge their people.

827 **CHAPTER II.—**Concerning the evil of greed.

828 **CHAPTER III.—**Concerning the evil of pride, which itself causes apostasy from God.

838 **CHAPTER IV.—**The wise man is praised, because he will be exalted and will sit among the great.

843 **CHAPTER V.—**In good days, do not forget the days of evil; and in evil days, do not forget the good.

845 **CHAPTER VI.—**He praises works of almsgiving.

847 **CHAPTER VII.—**Concerning good and evil friends, false and true.

849 **CHAPTER VIII.—**He exhorts and warns concerning association with the rich, from whom one must beware.

849 **CHAPTER IX.—**He praises the man who has not stumbled in his speech—that is, who does not utter a word by which he may be caught.

854 **CHAPTER X.—**One must always do good, because death does not delay. Praise of wisdom concerning the holy man, martyr, confessor, or righteous man.

857 **BOOK FOUR**

863 **CHAPTER ONE.—**When God established the human being from the beginning, he left counsel in the human being’s own hand.

863 **CHAPTER II.—**One must not rejoice in a multitude of wicked children; their perverse deeds are recalled.

866 **CHAPTER III.—**Wisdom teaches that, when someone sins at home, in the field, in the heart, or in bed, he must not say, “I shall hide from God, and who sees me?” For God sees and comprehends all things by his majesty.

869 **CHAPTER IV.—**Wisdom’s exhortation concerning how the way of discipline is to be maintained.

871 **CHAPTER V.—**God created the human being from the earth, made him according to his image, and gave him knowledge.

873 **CHAPTER VI.—**Concerning turning to the Lord and abandoning sins.

878 **CHAPTER VII.—**One must not linger in the company of the ungodly.

878 **CHAPTER VIII.—**So that we may not be prevented from praying to the Lord always, as the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing.”

885 **CHAPTER IX.—**Concerning restraint of the soul: one must not follow the desires of the heart—that is, one must not consent to vain thoughts, but resist them with God’s help.

887 **CHAPTER X.—**A drunkard will not become rich; by despising small things one gradually falls away; and women and wine cause people to apostatize from God.

888 **CHAPTER XI.—**Wisdom warns one not quickly to reveal a secret to either friend or enemy.

890 **CHAPTER XII.—**Wisdom warns that one should first rebuke one’s neighbor before threatening him, according to the teaching of the Gospel.

891 **CHAPTER XIII.—**It is better to correct by speaking than, through anger, to conceal deceit in silence.

894 **CHAPTER XIV.—**He speaks of a common occurrence: many, out of embarrassment, make promises to a friend and, without cost, acquire an enemy through their lips.

899 **CHAPTER XV.—**The word of parables.

901 **BOOK FIVE**

901 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Wisdom teaches that there is one human being in all things and all in one; sin must not be added to sin, but God must be asked to provide help.

901 **CHAPTER II.—**The collected straw is the synagogue of sinners, and the gatherings of heretics are likewise bundles of weeds to be burned.

906 **CHAPTER III.—**Wisdom shows that laughter is a fault, not joy, because joy comes from God.

908 [Col. 1269] **CHAPTER IV.—**This lazy person who is stoned with muddy stone and ox dung is the Jewish people: with muddy stone—that is, with the people of the gentiles, who were ignorant of the King—it is reproached, and with ox dung—that is, by the Jews who now believe.

909 **CHAPTER V.—**One who speaks a word to someone who does not pay attention is like one who rouses a sleeping person from deep sleep.

911 **CHAPTER VI.—**Wisdom says that, in a quarrel among friends, words of insult or secrets must not be brought forth.

914 **CHAPTER VII.—**A common prayer for all of us, in which we say: “Lord God, Father and ruler of my life, do not abandon me, and do not allow me to fall”—that is, restrain me, lest by presuming upon myself I bring about my own ruin.

916 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning instruction to be heard from the mouth.

917 **CHAPTER IX.—**One must beware of an oath, whether good or bad.

917 **CHAPTER X.—**Wisdom recounts the words of the unjust person who resolves to sin, as in the saying: “The unjust man said that he should sin against himself.”

920 **CHAPTER XI.—**Wisdom, seeing all things in advance, declares that all the ways of the one who acts, speaks, or thinks are known to God.

921 **CHAPTER XII.—**Praise of Wisdom, through whom all things were made.

922 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Praise of Wisdom, through whom all things were made. Wisdom speaks—that is, Christ, the Son of God, the power of God and the Wisdom of God—through whom all creatures are ordered.

923 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Wisdom speaks of her power and of the ordering of her works with the Father.

937 **BOOK SIX**

937 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Wisdom speaks with a mother’s affection, as in the saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your chicks, like a hen.”

937 **CHAPTER II.—**Wisdom exhorts, saying: “You who desire me, be filled from my generations; and my spirit is sweeter than honey”—that is, the Spirit of whom he says: “The Father sends the Spirit of truth in my name”; and, “He will take from what is mine and teach you all things,” and so forth.

939 **CHAPTER III.—**Wisdom says that three things are pleasing to her spirit: harmony among brothers, love of neighbors, and a man with a woman who is well suited to him.

945 **CHAPTER IV.—**Concerning the wickedness of a woman, in whose company he forbids the chaste man to remain if he wishes to be chaste.

949 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning the good woman: the good woman is the virgin Church, whom Christ made good with his blood, cleansing her through the washing of regeneration.

954 **CHAPTER VI.—**Many sin because of poverty, but this occurs in those who do not possess the love of God; for no creature can separate us from the love of God.

960 **CHAPTER VII.—**“Whoever,” he says, “reveals the secrets of a friend”—that is, hidden matters—“loses trust.”

965 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning the remission of sin.

968 **CHAPTER IX.—**Concerning the evil of the tongue committed by the whisperer and the double-tongued person.

971 **CHAPTER X.—**Concerning interest-taking, and what should be done or avoided in it.

973 **BOOK SEVEN**

973 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Concerning lending to one’s neighbor; by “neighbor” he means every human being.

973 **CHAPTER II.—**Concerning mercy toward the poor.

975 **CHAPTER III.—**Concerning honorable frugality—that is, restraint, moderation, and hospitality.

979 **CHAPTER IV.—**Concerning the discipline of children: with what affection they are to be loved or corrected.

981 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning the good of health, because poverty and health are better than riches.

983 **CHAPTER VI.—**Vigilance on account of the fear of God wastes the flesh—that is, subdues it; for vigilance directed toward perpetrating evils is criminal.

986 **CHAPTER VII.—**Concerning restraint in food.

989 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning drunkenness.

992 **CHAPTER IX.—**Concerning rulers, bishops, or judges.

993 **CHAPTER X.—**Everything should be done with counsel, but good things with God’s help.

997 **CHAPTER XI.—**Evil will not overtake the person who fears the Lord, but, according to his merits, he will receive the rewards of eternity.

999 **CHAPTER XII.—**Concerning the discipline of servants.

1004 **BOOK EIGHT**

1005 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Dreams are not to be believed, nor are people to rely upon their hopes, because Wisdom teaches that divinations and auspices are falsehoods of error.

1005 **CHAPTER II.—**Concerning those who fear the Lord.

1008 **CHAPTER III.—**Wisdom commands that sacrifices—that is, offerings—must not be made from unjust gains, nor alms be given from the loss of others.

1009 [Col. 1270] **CHAPTER IV.—**The discipline of keeping the Law, and the fact that observing the commandments is a saving sacrifice.

1012 **CHAPTER V.—**Wisdom warns that wicked offerings must not be presented—that is, offerings made at an uncertain time, nor disordered and fruitless prayers and supplications; for prayer is good together with fasting and almsgiving.

1015 **CHAPTER VI.—**Supplication to God and praise of God’s mercy.

1017 **CHAPTER VII.—**The prayer of wisdom.

1017 **CHAPTER VIII.—**One must not be a friend in name only, but in deed, faith, and love.

1024 **CHAPTER IX.—**Wisdom teaches with whom one should deliberate—that is, with a religious and righteous person.

1026 **CHAPTER X.—**She urges that one always associate with the righteous and those of good reputation.

1026 **CHAPTER XI.—**Wisdom relates that the soul of a holy man, filled with the sevenfold number of virtues of the Holy Spirit, prophesies.

1026 **CHAPTER XII.—**Concerning crafty and sophistical speech, that is, philosophical display.

1028 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Concerning honoring the physician.

1030 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Concerning praying to God the Father in a time of sickness, temptation, and desire.

1031 **CHAPTER XV.—**Concerning the funeral rites of the dead and the moderation of grief.

1033 **CHAPTER XVI.—**Concerning individual craftsmen.

1035 **CHAPTER XVII.—**Praise of Wisdom, or of the Son of God: through her there is all wisdom and prophecy, because she is always with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, everywhere in work and power.

1038 **CHAPTER XVIII.—**Wisdom discloses that the Holy Spirit gives understanding to those who pray and, like rain, pours forth utterances by giving, suggesting, and teaching, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The Spirit pleads for us,” and so forth.

1038 **CHAPTER XIX.—**Wisdom relates the inner matters of human life, including the instruments necessary for it.

1044 **BOOK NINE**

1045 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Wisdom relates that, because of human sins, vengeance proceeds—that is, famine, war, drought, barrenness, and mortality.

1045 **CHAPTER II.—**Concerning the misery of want and remembrance of death.

1055 **CHAPTER III.—**One must turn away from all vices but seek help from God, by whom human steps are directed, so that iniquity may not rule over them.

1061 **CHAPTER IV.—**Words of reproach must be removed from one’s friends.

1063 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning the discipline of the senseless and foolish person.

1066 **CHAPTER VI.—**Wisdom, through whom all things were made, relates that holy men proclaim her wonders.

1068 **CHAPTER VII.—**Praise of the universe, which was made through Wisdom and created through the Word and power in the Son of the Father, God with God.

1069 **BOOK TEN**

1125 **Prologue to Louis, King of France.**

1125 **Second Prologue.**

1127 **ON THE FIRST BOOK**

1127 **CHAPTER ONE.—**Concerning Alexander son of Philip; concerning Antiochus, the root of sin; concerning the city of Jerusalem burned; many of Israel consented to the king’s edict by sacrificing to idols; the Law was burned; many of Israel were slaughtered.

1140 **CHAPTER II.—**Mattathias and his five sons mourn the people, the temple, and the desolation of the Law. Mattathias is compelled to sacrifice to idols, but refuses; he kills the minister of King Antiochus who was sacrificing. Those who fled into the desert were killed on the Sabbath. Mattathias resolved to fight on the Sabbath; he and his sons killed sinners and overturned the altars of idols. As Mattathias was dying, he admonished his sons to defend Israel, and so forth.

1148 **CHAPTER III.—**Judas Maccabaeus arose in defense of Israel; he killed Apollonius and took his sword. He also killed Seron, commander of the army of Syria. Antiochus ordered Lysias to destroy Israel and wipe it completely from the land.

1155 **CHAPTER IV.—**After defeating Gorgias and Lysias, Judas purified the temple; concerning the dedication of the altar and the adornment of the temple.

1155 **CHAPTER V.—**Judas fights against the nations wishing to destroy Israel. Concerning Timotheus, commander of Ammon. Simon, sent by his brother, attacks the nations. Concerning Judas’s battles against Timotheus, and so forth.

1173 **CHAPTER VI.—**Concerning the death of Antiochus and the succession of his son, who sent an army to fight Judas and was defeated. He pretended to grant peace, but soon broke it; he is said to have used elephants in battle.

1177 **CHAPTER VII.—**Demetrius, after Antiochus and Lysias were killed, obtained the kingdom. Concerning Alcimus and Bacchides and their wickedness; concerning bloodshed around Jerusalem. Demetrius sent Nicanor against Israel; Judas prayed and conquered.

1178 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning the fame and power of the Romans. Judas sends envoys to Rome for the sake of peace; the Romans’ written reply to the Jews.

1179 **CHAPTER IX.—**Demetrius sends an army against the Jews. Concerning the death of Judas Maccabaeus. Concerning wicked men and the wickedness of Bacchides. Concerning weddings turned into mourning. Jonathan obtains the leadership; Alcimus, wishing to destroy the temple, became speechless, and so forth.

1188 **CHAPTER X.—**Alexander kills Demetrius and takes the daughter of King Ptolemy as his wife. Concerning the glory of Jonathan, who defeats Apollonius and to whom Alexander sends a golden clasp.

1192 **CHAPTER XI.—**Ptolemy rises against Alexander, and Alexander is killed. The treaty with Jonathan is confirmed. Trypho raises up Antiochus, Alexander’s son, against Demetrius, who is saved with Jonathan’s help, and so forth.

1197 **CHAPTER XII.—**Jonathan sends envoys and letters to the Romans and Spartans; he puts Demetrius’s commanders to flight and strikes the Arabs. Trypho, wishing to assume Antiochus’s kingdom, dealt treacherously with Jonathan and killed him and his army.

1200 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Simon is appointed commander in place of his brother. He sends silver and Jonathan’s two sons to Trypho. Concerning the death of Jonathan and his sons. Concerning the construction of the tomb. Trypho treacherously kills the young Antiochus and places the diadem of Asia upon himself. Demetrius establishes peace with Simon, and so forth.

1201 [Col. 1272] **CHAPTER XIV.—**Concerning the greatness and power of Simon, king of the Jews, and the abundance of peace in those times. Friendship between the Romans and Jews is renewed, and so forth.

1208 **CHAPTER XV.—**Antiochus, son of Demetrius, receives his father’s kingdom and writes letters to the Jews. He pursues Trypho. Simon sent assistance to Antiochus, but Antiochus refused to accept it, and so forth.

1211 **CHAPTER XVI.—**Simon sent his two sons to fight Cendebaeus the commander. Judas, Simon’s son, was wounded. Simon was killed with his sons at a banquet. His son John succeeded his brother in the high-priestly leadership.

1223 **ON THE SECOND BOOK**

1223 **CHAPTER ONE.—**The Jews in Jerusalem send greetings to the Jews in Egypt. Antiochus was killed in the temple of Nanea. Concerning the sacrificial fire hidden in a well. Nehemiah’s prayer was as follows: the king of the Persians was informed of the miracle of the transformation of fire and water, and of water into fire.

1225 **CHAPTER II.—**The exposition continues as above.

1226 **CHAPTER III.—**Simon betrayed the gifts of God’s temple; Heliodorus was sent to take them away. The priest and the people implored the Lord that the deposited treasures might be preserved. Heliodorus, wishing to plunder the temple, was seized; he was freed from the affliction through the sacrifice that was offered.

1229 **CHAPTER IV.—**Concerning the plots of Simon the traitor against Onias. Jason corrupts King Antiochus with gifts. The priests hasten to the gymnasium, neglecting the sacred rites. Menelaus excludes Jason from the priesthood, and Lysimachus succeeds him, and so forth.

1232 **CHAPTER V.—**Concerning heavenly signs that occurred in Jerusalem. Concerning the death of Jason, the persecutor of the citizens. Antiochus, persecuting Judea, killed the people and plundered the temple under the leadership of Menelaus. The Lord chose the place not on account of the people, but the people on account of the place, and so forth.

1235 **CHAPTER VI.—**The king sent orders that the Jews be compelled to abandon the Law of God and to defile the temple. The Jews were compelled to offer sacrifices to idols. Concerning the suffering of the two women with their infants, and of Eleazar.

1236 **CHAPTER VII.—**Concerning the suffering of the seven brothers and their mother.

1239 **CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning Judas Maccabaeus. The wicked Nicanor is sent into Judea; Judas exhorts the people to steadfastness, and so forth.

1241 **CHAPTER IX.—**Antiochus was defeated near Persepolis. The Lord struck Antiochus with an affliction; amid his punishments he repented, and he died.

1241 **CHAPTER X.—**Judas Maccabaeus recovered the temple and Jerusalem. Concerning the solemn festival that was celebrated. Antiochus’s son obtained his father’s kingdom. Ptolemy ended his life by poison. Gorgias and others were defeated.

1244 **CHAPTER XI.—**Lysias attempts to conquer the Jews and to sell the priesthood. God sends the Jews a bishop in a white garment to help them, and so forth.

1245 **CHAPTER XII.—**The people of Joppa treacherously killed two hundred Jews, and Judas avenged them. Concerning the Arab men who were defeated. Timotheus is conquered by Judas. Concerning sacrifices for the dead, and so forth.

1253 **CHAPTER XIII.—**Antiochus comes against Judea. Judas killed four thousand men in Antiochus’s camp, including the largest of the elephants, and captured Ptolemais, and so forth.

1253 **CHAPTER XIV.—**Demetrius is stirred up against the Jews and sends Nicanor, who contends with Simon; but Judas escaped from his hands. Concerning Razis and his steadfastness.

1255 **CHAPTER XV.—**Onias and Jeremiah appear, and Jeremiah gives Judas a golden sword sent by God. The Jews fought with their hands but prayed with their hearts. Nicanor’s head is cut off.

**End of the One Hundred Ninth Volume.**
